Most likely it appears inside a larger sentence where 'a hacer' (to do/make) is followed by 'es' as the start of a clause (for example: 'Lo que voy a hacer es...' = 'What I'm going to do is...'). In such cases the meaningful unit is 'a hacer' together with the surrounding grammar, and 'es' belongs to the copular construction that follows.
additional_notes: Treat 'a hacer es' as a sequence occurring across a grammatical boundary, not as an idiomatic multi-word term. Commonly appears in constructions like 'Lo que voy a hacer es ...' or 'Lo que tenemos que hacer es ...'. Do not use 'a hacer es' standalone; it must be part of a larger clause. Translation depends on the full sentence: often corresponds to 'what ... is' or 'the thing to do is...'.
target_language_example: Lo que voy a hacer es hablar con ella.
native_language_example: What I'm going to do is talk to her.

meaning: to do it / to do what (is needed); part of constructions meaning 'to do' + object or clause.
additional_notes: This sequence appears when the verb 'hacer' (to do/make) is used with an infinitive or with 'lo' / 'lo que' to refer to something previously mentioned or implied. Often contracted into phrases like 'hacer lo necesario' (do what is necessary), 'hacer lo tuyo' (do your thing), or 'hacer lo que...' (do what...). 'A' before an infinitive can mark intention or near-future action (e.g., 'va a hacer' = 'is going to do').
target_language_example: Ella va a hacer lo que prometió.
native_language_example: She is going to do what she promised.

meaning: 'to do nothing' or 'not to do anything' (used after verbs like 'va/vas/voy a' or in negative constructions).
additional_notes: Common in negative sentences: 'no (voy/va/vamos) a hacer nada' = 'I'm not going to do anything.' Can also appear in phrases like 'no voy a hacer nada al respecto' (I won't do anything about it). In sentence 4 ('no te voy a hacer nada') it means 'I won't do anything to you' (reassuring, not a threat). Word order matters: the no typically precedes the verb phrase.
target_language_example: No voy a hacer nada hasta mañana.
native_language_example: I'm not going to do anything until tomorrow.

meaning: to do one's (something) — introduces doing a task that belongs to someone (e.g., 'to do his/her homework').
additional_notes: This is a sequence of words often found in verbs with the preposition 'a' + infinitive + possessive adjective + noun: empezar a hacer su tarea, ayudar a hacer su trabajo. 'Su' must agree with the possessor (his/her/their/your formal). English usually uses 'do' + possessive (do his homework). The phrase itself is compositional and literal; it's not an idiom. Common verbs that take 'a + infinitive' include empezar a, comenzar a, ponerse a, ayudar a, seguir a (context-dependent).
target_language_example: Ella va a ayudar a Juan a hacer su proyecto.
native_language_example: She is going to help Juan do his project.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase in Spanish; a combination of the preposition 'a' followed by the noun phrase 'hombre' appears only in certain contexts (usually preceded by an article or pronoun). On its own it usually signals a mistake—common intended forms are 'a un hombre' (to a man / I saw a man with personal 'a' + article) or 'al hombre' (to the man).
additional_notes: The sequence 'a hombre' without an article ('un', 'el', etc.) is ungrammatical or extremely rare in standard Spanish. Possible intended corrections: 1) 'un hombre' = 'a man' (indefinite article). 2) 'al hombre' = contraction of 'a + el hombre' meaning 'to the man'. 3) when using the personal 'a' before a specific person, use 'a + (article/pronoun/name)': e.g., 'Vi a un hombre' or 'Vi al hombre'. Use 'a hombre' only in nonstandard or poetic ellipsis contexts.
target_language_example: Dijo: «No le gusta a hombre», (esta frase es incorrecta en español estándar).
native_language_example: He said: "He doesn't like any man", (this sentence is incorrect in standard Spanish).

meaning: secretly; stealthily; on tiptoe or without being noticed.
additional_notes: Used to describe entering, leaving, or doing something quietly to avoid being seen or noticed. Often implies sneaking in/out or behaving furtively. Common with verbs like entrar, salir, colarse, or moverse.
target_language_example: Entró a hurtadillas para no despertar a nadie.
native_language_example: He sneaked in so as not to wake anyone.

meaning: to report (to someone) / to go report or inform
additional_notes: Used to indicate the action of informing or reporting, often followed by the person or authority being informed (e.g., a sus superiores, al Rey). Can mean 'to go and inform' when used with verbs of motion (e.g., 'fue a informar'). In administrative contexts it can also mean 'to notify' (e.g., informar un cambio de dirección).
target_language_example: Voy a informar al gerente sobre el problema.
native_language_example: I'm going to inform the manager about the problem.

meaning: to go look for or to go pick up (someone or something).
additional_notes: Common Spanish structure: ir a + buscar = 'to go to look for' or 'to go pick up'. In many sentences you see it as 'va a ir a buscar' (he/she/it is going to go pick up) — note the repetition when using future periphrasis (iba a ir a buscar = was going to go pick up). Use with direct objects or people (e.g., 'buscar trabajo', 'ir a buscar a usted').
target_language_example: Mañana voy a ir a buscar a mi hermana al aeropuerto.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I'm going to go pick up my sister at the airport.

meaning: to be going to (a place) — indicates movement toward a feminine noun (la + place).
additional_notes: This is the preposition + infinitive pattern 'ir a' (to go to) followed by 'la' (the feminine singular article). It's used before feminine places or nouns: e.g., 'Voy a ir a la playa' (I'm going to go to the beach). In spoken Spanish you often drop the second 'ir' and say 'voy a la playa' (I'm going to the beach). Use 'al' (a + el) for masculine nouns: 'ir al cine'.
target_language_example: Mañana voy a ir a la biblioteca.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I'm going to go to the library.

meaning: This is not a correct or natural Spanish multi-word expression. It appears to be a mistaken split or ordering of elements (for example mixing the preposition 'a' + infinitive and the verb+preposition combination 'ir con'). The correct expressions are 'ir con' (to go with) or 'ir a' (to go to).
additional_notes: 'A ir con' should be avoided. If you mean 'to go with', use 'ir con' (e.g., 'ir con alguien'). If you mean 'to go to [a place]', use 'ir a' (e.g., 'ir a la playa'). The sequence 'a ir' can appear in some constructions (e.g., subordinate clauses) but not followed by 'con' as a fixed chunk. The provided target-language example below is ungrammatical and shown only to illustrate the exact sequence requested; learners should not use it in practice.
target_language_example: No deberías escribir a ir con en una frase; 'a ir con' no es correcto.
native_language_example: You shouldn't write 'a ir con' in a sentence; 'a ir con' is not correct.

meaning: Not a correct Spanish phrase; likely a mistaken combination. Possibly intended: 'a ir' (to go to) or 'ir de' (to go (to/from) / to be about doing something).
additional_notes:
There is no valid Spanish construction 'a ir de' as a fixed multiword phrase. Two related, correct pieces are:
- 'ir de' + noun: used to say going somewhere for an activity or describing how someone is dressed (e.g., 'ir de compras' = to go shopping; 'ir de negro' = to wear black). 
- 'a ir' can appear when 'a' (to) precedes the infinitive 'ir' in some contexts (e.g., 'voy a ir' = I'm going to go). If you meant 'ir a' (to be going to), correct order is 'ir a' or 'voy a ir'.
For beginner learners, learn 'ir' (to go), 'ir a + infinitive' (to be going to do something), and 'ir de + noun' (to go for an activity).
target_language_example: Voy a ir de compras esta tarde.
native_language_example: I'm going to go shopping this afternoon.

meaning: to go to get/collect something; to go for (the purpose of obtaining something).
additional_notes: Used to express going somewhere with the purpose of fetching, picking up, or obtaining something. Common structure: 'ir a por + [thing/person]'. More common in Spain; some Spanish speakers (esp. in Latin America) prefer 'ir por' or 'ir a buscar'. The phrase focuses on purpose (to fetch) rather than just direction.
target_language_example: Voy a ir por el pan antes de que cierre la tienda.
native_language_example: I'm going to go get the bread before the store closes.

meaning: to leave (me)
additional_notes: This is the infinitive verb ir preceded by the preposition a plus the clitic pronoun me attached (a + ir + me → a irme). It expresses the idea of 'to leave' or 'to go (away)' from the speaker's perspective (i.e., 'for me to leave' or 'that I leave'). Commonly appears after verbs that require an infinitive: e.g., 'voy a irme' (I'm going to leave). In everyday speech the pronoun often attaches directly to the infinitive: 'irme'.
target_language_example: Creo que es mejor a irme ahora.
native_language_example: I think it's better for me to leave now.

meaning: matching; coordinated (used to describe things that go well together in color, style, or design).
additional_notes: Used before or after a noun/adjective to indicate that two or more items match or are coordinated (colors, patterns, outfits, accessories, furniture). Common in contexts like fashion, home decor, and product descriptions. Can be used with estar/venir/poner (e.g., "está a juego", "viene a juego").
target_language_example: Los cojines son a juego con la cortina.
native_language_example: The pillows match the curtain.

meaning: based on / judging by
additional_notes: Used in phrases like 'a juzgar por...' or 'a juzgar de...' to introduce a conclusion drawn from evidence or appearance (English: 'judging by' or 'based on'). Commonly followed by 'por' + noun or clause: 'A juzgar por su cara, está preocupado.'
target_language_example: A juzgar por el ruido, hay muchas personas en la fiesta.
native_language_example: Judging by the noise, there are many people at the party.

meaning: based on / judging by (used to draw a conclusion from evidence or appearance).
additional_notes: Common phrase to introduce a conclusion inferred from something you observe or have heard (a fact, appearance, a photo, a statement, etc.). Often followed by a noun or clause: 'a juzgar por + (noun/phrase)'. Can be used in formal and informal contexts.
target_language_example: A juzgar por su cara, no ha dormido bien.
native_language_example: Judging by his face, he hasn't slept well.

meaning: to the
additional_notes: Combination of the preposition a and the feminine singular article la. It is used before feminine singular nouns, and its exact meaning depends on context: direction or destination (a la playa), reference or topic (introducción a la jardinería), or set expressions (a la ida, a la casualidad). Unlike a + el, it does not contract.
target_language_example: Vamos a la playa este fin de semana.
native_language_example: We're going to the beach this weekend.

meaning: at the height/level of; up to (a standard or expectation).
additional_notes: Used in two main ways: 1) literal—refers to physical height or level (e.g., 'a la altura de la cintura' = at waist height); 2) figurative—to say someone/something meets (or doesn't meet) a standard or expectation (e.g., 'está a la altura de tus expectativas' = is up to your expectations). Can appear with 'de' to indicate what it's aligned with ('a la altura de...') or alone as an idiomatic comment ('A la altura' meaning 'Up to the task' or simply 'On level').
target_language_example: No creo que él esté a la altura del trabajo.
native_language_example: I don't think he's up to the job.

meaning: in the old-fashioned way; old-style
additional_notes: Used to say something is done in a traditional or old-fashioned manner. Can describe style (clothing, methods, customs) or preference for older ways. Context can be neutral or slightly nostalgic; sometimes implies not using modern methods. Not usually literal 'to the ancient'.
target_language_example: Prefiero cocinar a la antigua, con ingredientes frescos y sin procesados.
native_language_example: I prefer to cook the old-fashioned way, with fresh ingredients and no processed foods.

meaning: in front; leading; at the head (literally: 'at the head').
additional_notes: Used both literally (e.g., shot in the head: 'le dispararon a la cabeza') and figuratively to mean 'leading' or 'in charge' (e.g., 'a la cabeza del equipo' = at the head/leader of the team). Context determines whether it's physical (head) or leadership/position (head of group). Can appear in set phrases like 'poner/estar a la cabeza' (to put/be in charge) or exclamations like '¡manos a la cabeza!' (hands to your head).
target_language_example: Ella está a la cabeza del proyecto.
native_language_example: She is at the head of the project.

meaning: at the head of; leading; in front of (literally or figuratively).
additional_notes: Used both literally (physically in front) and figuratively (leader, top of a list, ahead in a competition, in charge of an organization). Common in phrases like 'estar a la cabeza de' (to lead) or 'poner/estar a la cabeza de la lista' (to be at the top of the list).
target_language_example: Ella está a la cabeza de ese proyecto.
native_language_example: She is leading that project.

meaning: to (go) to bed; a colloquial/fragmentary sequence where 'a la cama' is followed by an extra 'a' often before an infinitive (e.g., 'a la cama a dormir')
additional_notes: The canonical phrase is 'a la cama' meaning 'to bed' or 'to go to bed'. The extra trailing 'a' is nonstandard in neutral Spanish and typically appears when speakers append an infinitive immediately after ('a la cama a dormir'). For learners, use 'vamos a la cama' or 'me voy a la cama'. The sequence 'a la cama a' should usually be followed by a verb (infinitive) and is informal/colloquial in many dialects.
target_language_example: Voy a la cama a dormir, pero primero leo un rato.
native_language_example: I'm going to bed to sleep, but first I'll read for a while.

meaning: used to say someone goes to bed at a specific time (literally: 'to bed at [time]').
additional_notes: This phrase combines 'a la cama' (to bed) with a time expression introduced by 'a las' (at [hour], feminine plural for hours). Use 'a las' before clock times like 'a las diez' (at ten). For 1 o'clock use 'a la una'. Common in sentences like 'Se fue a la cama a las diez.'
target_language_example: Me acuesto a la cama a las diez.
native_language_example: I go to bed at ten.

meaning: to bed earlier (than usual or than a specified time).
additional_notes: Used with verbs like ir/se (ir a la cama, acostarse) to say someone goes to bed earlier than normal or before a specific time (e.g., antes de medianoche). Commonly followed by a time or comparison (antes de + time / antes de lo normal).
target_language_example: Me siento cansado, voy a la cama antes esta noche.
native_language_example: I feel tired; I'm going to bed earlier tonight.

meaning: to (go) to bed afterwards / later
additional_notes: Commonly used to say that someone will go to bed after something else happens (e.g., after dinner, after studying). The phrase is built from 'a la cama' (to bed) + 'después' (after/later). You can place 'después' before or after the clause depending on emphasis: «Después, voy a la cama» or «Voy a la cama después».
target_language_example: Termino la película y voy a la cama después.
native_language_example: I finish the movie and I go to bed afterwards.

meaning: made or ordered from a menu; chosen individually (not a set or fixed menu).
additional_notes: Common in restaurants: 'a la carta' (often written á la carta or à la carte) means ordering separate dishes instead of a fixed-price menu (menú del día). Also used more broadly to mean selecting items individually or à la carte in services or packages.
target_language_example: Prefiero pedir a la carta en lugar del menú del día.
native_language_example: I prefer to order à la carte instead of the set menu.

meaning: to the conclusion / to the end (of something)
additional_notes: Used to indicate reaching the final part or outcome of an event, argument, report, meeting, etc. Often appears in phrases like "llegar a la conclusión" (to reach the conclusion). Can also mean "upon concluding" depending on context.
target_language_example: Al revisar los datos, llegué a la conclusión de que necesitamos más tiempo.
native_language_example: After reviewing the data, I came to the conclusion that we need more time.

meaning: to the conclusion that / to conclude that
additional_notes: Used with llegar (llegar a la conclusión de...) to say you have formed an opinion or decision after thinking or examining evidence. Common pattern: 'llegar a la conclusión de que + (clause)'. Equivalent to 'to conclude that' or 'to come to the conclusion that'.
target_language_example: He llegado a la conclusión de que debemos cambiar el plan.
native_language_example: I have come to the conclusion that we must change the plan.

meaning: charged to the bill / put on the tab (to be added to someone's account).
additional_notes: Used when asking that something (a dish, drink, or charge) be added to your bill or account, often in restaurants, bars, or shared household/business accounts. Can refer to placing an expense on someone's tab or accounting record. Commonly used in contexts like 'poner a la cuenta' or 'cargar a la cuenta'.
target_language_example: ¿Puedes poner la botella a la cuenta, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you put the bottle on the bill, please?

meaning: turn/right to the right at (a place).
additional_notes: Used in directions to tell someone to turn right at a specific point (street, intersection, traffic light, landmark). Commonly follows a verb like 'girar' or 'gire' (formal) or 'gira' (informal). Can also appear as 'a la derecha' alone to mean 'to the right.'
target_language_example: Gira a la derecha en la segunda calle.
native_language_example: Turn right at the second street.

meaning: 'adrift' or 'drifting' — without control, direction, or support.
additional_notes: Used literally for boats/ice that are floating without control, and figuratively for people, projects, or plans that lack direction or guidance. Common in both physical and metaphorical contexts.
target_language_example: Después de perder el trabajo, me sentí a la deriva durante meses.
native_language_example: After losing my job, I felt adrift for months.

meaning: to the scene (of an event, e.g. crime, accident, location).
additional_notes: Used to indicate going to or arriving at the location where something happened. Commonly appears with 'del crimen' (of the crime) or a place (la cocina). Can be used literally (physical location) or figuratively (revisiting a situation). Often preceded by verbs like ir, llegar, volver.
target_language_example: El detective llegó a la escena del accidente.
native_language_example: The detective arrived at the scene of the accident.

meaning: by force; forcibly; against someone's will.
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something is done using physical force or coercion, or that it was necessary even if unwilling. Common in everyday and formal contexts. Can appear alone (A la fuerza.) meaning 'by force' or in phrases like 'tomar/quitAr a la fuerza' or 'llevar a la fuerza'.
target_language_example: Se lo quitaron a la fuerza.
native_language_example: They took it from him by force.

meaning: when (doing) / at the time of / when it comes to
additional_notes: Used to introduce the moment or situation in which something happens or should be considered. Commonly followed by an action (infinitive) or a noun (e.g., 'la muerte', 'la cena'). Can mean 'when it's time to' (specific time) or 'when it comes to' (consideration).
target_language_example: A la hora de viajar, siempre reviso el pasaporte.
native_language_example: When it's time to travel, I always check my passport.

meaning: to the church on (certain days) / to the church, the ... (depends on continuation).
additional_notes: This fragment looks like the beginning of a phrase that needs more words to be complete. 'A la iglesia' means 'to the church'. Adding 'los' usually introduces a plural noun or a day of the week used with plural article (e.g., 'los domingos' = 'on Sundays'). Common complete phrases: 'a la iglesia los domingos' ('to church on Sundays') or 'a la iglesia los viernes' ('to church on Fridays'). Alone, 'a la iglesia los' is incomplete and should be followed by a plural noun (often a day).
target_language_example: Vamos a la iglesia los domingos.
native_language_example: We go to church on Sundays.

meaning: to church every (plural noun) / to the church every (day/week/...)
additional_notes: This is a fragment commonly used before a plural time word (e.g., 'días', 'fines de semana') or a plural group (e.g., 'años') to mean 'to church every...'. It needs a final noun to be complete: for example 'a la iglesia todos los domingos' = 'to church every Sunday'. 'Iglesia' can mean the building or church as an activity/place of worship. Use 'a la iglesia' for going to church (feminine: la iglesia).
target_language_example: Vamos a la iglesia todos los domingos.
native_language_example: We go to church every Sunday.

meaning: in light of; considering; because of.
additional_notes: Used to introduce a reason, context, or perspective based on evidence, facts, or circumstances. Common in both formal and informal contexts. Can be followed by nouns or noun phrases (e.g., 'estos hechos'). Also used literally when referring to actual light (e.g., 'a la luz de una vela' = by candlelight), so context determines figurative vs. literal meaning.
target_language_example: A la luz de nueva información, cambiamos el plan.
native_language_example: In light of new information, we changed the plan.

meaning: nearby; within reach; readily available.
additional_notes: Used to say something is close at hand or easy to use when needed. Common in everyday speech to refer to objects, cash, information, or help that you can access quickly. Can be used literally (physically within reach) or more loosely (available/handy).
target_language_example: Tengo el cargador a la mano si lo necesitas.
native_language_example: I have the charger handy if you need it.

meaning: around the block (lit. 'around the apple').
additional_notes: Commonly used in Spain and Latin America to mean 'around the block' or 'a short walk/drive around the neighborhood.' Often appears in commands or plans (dar la vuelta a la manzana = to go/turn around the block). Literal words ('manzana' = city block or apple) — here it means 'block'.
target_language_example: Voy a dar una vuelta a la manzana y vuelvo en cinco minutos.
native_language_example: I'm going to walk around the block and I'll be back in five minutes.

meaning: 'maybe' or 'perhaps' (colloquial, used to give a possibility).
additional_notes: Informal expression used in some Spanish-speaking regions (especially in Latin America). It introduces a possible outcome or suggestion, similar to 'tal vez' or 'quizás'. Often placed at the start or middle of a sentence: 'A la mejor voy' = 'Maybe I'll go.' Not standard in formal writing.
target_language_example: A la mejor llego tarde si hay mucho tráfico.
native_language_example: Maybe I'll arrive late if there's a lot of traffic.

meaning: to hell with it / screw it; go to hell (rude)
additional_notes: Very informal and vulgar. Used to express strong dismissal, anger, or to tell someone off. Can be directed at a thing ("to hell with X") or at a person ("go to hell"). Avoid in polite contexts.
target_language_example: ¡A la mierda este plan, busquemos otra opción!
native_language_example: Screw this plan, let's find another option!

meaning: fashionable; in style.
additional_notes: Used to describe clothes, people, or things that follow current fashion. Can be used with estar (estar a la moda) to say someone/something is fashionable. Opposite: 'pasado de moda' or 'no estar a la moda.'
target_language_example: Ella siempre se viste a la moda y sigue las últimas tendencias.
native_language_example: She always dresses fashionably and follows the latest trends.

meaning: to the part / to the area (often 'to the back' when followed by 'de atrás' or 'trasera').
additional_notes: Literally 'to the part'. Often used in phrases like 'a la parte de atrás' or 'a la parte trasera' to mean 'to the back' or 'to the rear.' Common in commands or directions (ve/ven/vea a la parte de atrás). If used alone, it sounds incomplete; usually followed by a clarifier (e.g., 'de atrás').
target_language_example: Ve a la parte de atrás del coche.
native_language_example: Go to the back of the car.

meaning: perfectly; to perfection
additional_notes: Used to say something is done very well or flawlessly. Common in everyday and formal contexts. Can modify verbs (hacer, llevar, marchar, dibujar) and means with complete accuracy or excellence.
target_language_example: Ella resolvió el problema a la perfección.
native_language_example: She solved the problem perfectly.

meaning: in the shade; out of direct sunlight; also 'in the shadow (of)' meaning under the influence or living under someone/something.
additional_notes: Commonly used to describe a physical location sheltered from the sun (e.g., under a tree or next to a building). Can also be figurative: 'vivir a la sombra de' means to live in someone's shadow or under their influence/overshadowed by them. Use 'en la sombra' less often for physical shade; 'a la sombra' is standard.
target_language_example: Nos sentamos a la sombra para escapar del calor.
native_language_example: We sat in the shade to escape the heat.

meaning: at the same time; simultaneously; one at a time (depending on context).
additional_notes: Most often means 'at the same time' or 'simultaneously' (e.g., things happening together). In instructions or requests it can mean 'one at a time' or 'one by one' (saying to do only one question/item at a time). Context determines whether it's simultaneous or sequential ('a la vez' in 'Una pregunta a la vez' asks for one question at a time).
target_language_example: No puedes contestar dos correos a la vez; concéntrate en uno.
native_language_example: You can't answer two emails at the same time; focus on one.

meaning: about/to the life of; used to refer to someone's life (biography) or events involving a person's life
additional_notes: Commonly appears in titles or descriptions (e.g., 'la película a la vida de...' or 'un libro a la vida de...') meaning 'about the life of' a person. It can also be used in phrases like 'volver a la vida de alguien' meaning 'return to someone's life'. Not a fixed idiom by itself—its exact sense depends on context and the verb around it.
target_language_example: Es un libro a la vida de Frida Kahlo.
native_language_example: It's a book about the life of Frida Kahlo.

meaning: used to introduce a way of living or attitude — 'in (one's) life as', 'to life in/on/at' (depends on context).
additional_notes: This sequence is not a fixed set phrase by itself; it appears as part of larger expressions like 'a la vida en pareja' (life as a couple) or 'a la vida en la ciudad' (life in the city). 'A la vida' often means 'to life' or 'in life', and the preposition following (en, de, etc.) completes the idea. Check the full phrase in context to understand the intended meaning.
target_language_example: A la vida en el campo le falta el ajetreo de la ciudad.
native_language_example: Life in the countryside lacks the hustle of the city.

meaning: in sight; visible; within view.
additional_notes: Used to say that something can be seen or is visible/obvious. Common in literal senses ('within sight') and figurative contexts ('noticed', 'available to view'). Often follows the noun: 'X a la vista.'
target_language_example: La montaña ya está a la vista.
native_language_example: The mountain is already in sight.

meaning: in (plain) view of; visible to; in front of (someone).
additional_notes: Used to say something is visible or done where others can see — often followed by a noun or pronoun (e.g., 'todos', 'uno', 'cualquiera'). Can imply lack of privacy or exposure. Equivalent to 'within sight of' or 'in front of'.
target_language_example: Dejaron el paquete a la vista de todos.
native_language_example: They left the package in plain view of everyone.

meaning: just around (the) corner from; very close to (in space or time).
additional_notes: Used to say something is nearby (physically) or imminent (time). Commonly followed by a noun indicating place or time. Equivalent to 'around the corner from' or 'right after' depending on context. Can be used with distances (e.g., 'a la vuelta de la esquina') or with events ('a la vuelta de la semana').
target_language_example: La panadería está a la vuelta de la esquina.
native_language_example: The bakery is just around the corner.

meaning: just around the corner from / very close to (location)
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something is very near in distance or nearby in time (e.g., an event or place). Commonly followed by a noun indicating place or time: a la vuelta de la esquina (around the corner), a la vuelta de la tienda (right past the shop). Can be used literally (distance) or figuratively (soon).
target_language_example: La panadería está a la vuelta de la farmacia.
native_language_example: The bakery is just around the corner from the pharmacy.

a la vuelta de la esquina

target_language_multi_word_term: a la vuelta de la esquina
meaning: around the corner; very near (physically) — can also mean 'about to happen' (figurative).
additional_notes: Common phrase for something located very close by (e.g., a shop or house). Used literally: 'I live/it's around the corner.' Used figuratively to say something is imminent (e.g., 'danger/death is around the corner'). Can be preceded by qualifiers like 'justo' (right) for emphasis.
target_language_example: La panadería está a la vuelta de la esquina.
native_language_example: The bakery is around the corner.

meaning: up-to-date; the latest (fashion, trend) / at the last (as in 'the last one') depending on context.
additional_notes: Most commonly used to mean 'fashionable' or 'in the latest style' (a la última moda). In other contexts (like sessions, pages, etc.) it can mean 'the last' or 'to the last' (hasta la última). Context decides meaning; when followed by 'moda' it means fashionable. Not formal slang, but colloquial.
target_language_example: Llegó siempre a la última moda de la ciudad.
native_language_example: She always arrived in the city's latest fashion.

meaning: 'like' or 'similar to' (used to compare), and also used in counting phrases like 'on the count of...'
additional_notes: Two main uses: 1) Comparison: 'a la de + noun/pronoun' means 'like the one of...' or 'similar to...'. Example: 'parecida a la de una naranja' = 'similar to that of an orange'. 2) Counting/commands: in casual speech you may hear 'a la de uno/dos/tres' or simply 'a la de tres' as a way to say 'on the count of one/two/three' or to cue people to start together. Context tells which meaning applies.
target_language_example: Hazlo a la de ella para que quede igual.
native_language_example: Do it like hers so it looks the same.

meaning: next to; beside; at the side of
additional_notes: Used to indicate physical location (something is beside something else). The standard and more common form in Spanish is 'al lado' (the contraction of a + el). 'a lado' without the contraction is uncommon in standard Spanish and may be heard in some dialects, in colloquial speech, or as a truncation in fast speech; when specifying 'next to the', the normal phrase is 'al lado de' + noun (e.g., 'al lado del parque').
target_language_example: El perro se acostó a lado de la puerta.
native_language_example: The dog lay down next to the door.

meaning: for a long (time) / at length; used before a noun (often tiempo) to mean 'long' or in expressions like 'a largo plazo' ('in the long term').
additional_notes: By itself 'a largo' is incomplete and usually appears in set phrases: 'a largo plazo' (in the long term), 'a lo largo de' (along, throughout). When followed by a noun like 'tiempo' it means 'for a long time' (e.g., 'a largo tiempo'). Not commonly used alone without context.
target_language_example: A largo plazo, ahorrar te beneficiará.
native_language_example: In the long term, saving will benefit you.

meaning: in the long term; long-term.
additional_notes: Used to talk about effects, plans, or situations that extend far into the future. Can modify verbs or nouns (e.g., pensar a largo plazo, plan a largo plazo). Often contrasted with 'a corto plazo' (short-term).
target_language_example: Debemos invertir pensando a largo plazo.
native_language_example: We must invest thinking in the long term.

meaning: at five (o'clock).
additional_notes: Used to tell time when something happens at 5:00. Spanish uses 'a la(s) + hour' for times: 'a la una' (at one), 'a las dos' (at two) — use 'a la' for 1 and 'a las' for 2–12. Can refer to AM or PM depending on context or with 'de la mañana/tarde/noche'.
target_language_example: La reunión empieza a las cinco de la tarde.
native_language_example: The meeting starts at five in the afternoon.

meaning: at five o'clock (used with a time expression: 'a las cinco de la tarde' = at five in the afternoon).
additional_notes: This is the start of a time expression. In Spanish, 'a las' + [hour] is used for most hours (except 1:00 which uses 'a la una'). You usually complete it with 'la mañana', 'la tarde' or 'la noche' to specify morning/afternoon/night (e.g., 'a las cinco de la mañana'). It can also be followed by a day or date ('a las cinco de mañana' is less common than 'a las cinco mañana' — better: 'mañana a las cinco').
target_language_example: Nos vemos a las cinco de la tarde.
native_language_example: We'll meet at five in the afternoon.

meaning: start dealing with things; tackle matters (often followed by other words, e.g. 'a las cosas por su nombre' — call things by their name).
additional_notes: This fragment usually appears as part of longer expressions (e.g., 'a las cosas por su nombre' = 'to call a spade a spade') or followed by a noun/phrase that specifies how to treat or name things. It implies approaching matters directly, honestly, or in the correct way. Not typically used alone without the rest of the phrase.
target_language_example: Vamos a decir las cosas a las cosas por su nombre y decidir ya.
native_language_example: Let's call things by their name and decide now.

meaning: to call things by their proper name; to be frank or direct about something
additional_notes: This phrase is a shortened form of 'poner a las cosas por su nombre' or 'llamar a las cosas por su nombre' and is used to say someone is being blunt, honest, or naming things as they are. Often used before a direct statement. Common in spoken Spanish. Tone can be neutral or slightly confrontational depending on context.
target_language_example: Voy a llamar a las cosas por su: eso no fue un error, fue negligencia.
native_language_example: I'm going to call things by their proper name: that wasn't a mistake, it was negligence.

meaning: at ten o'clock (10:00).
additional_notes: Used to state a specific time of day. 'A las' + number is the standard way to say 'at [hour]' for most hours (except singular 'a la una' for 1:00). Can refer to morning or night depending on context (e.g., 'a las diez de la mañana' or 'a las diez de la noche'), but often context alone is enough.
target_language_example: La película empieza a las diez.
native_language_example: The movie starts at ten o'clock.

meaning: at nine o'clock of (used to specify 9:00 in combination with a time period like 'la mañana', 'la noche', or a date).
additional_notes: This phrase begins a time expression meaning 'at nine (o'clock) of ...'. It's usually completed with a period of day (e.g., 'la mañana', 'la noche') or with 'la noche' omitted when context is clear: 'a las nueve' = 'at nine o'clock'. Use 'a la una' for 1:00 (singular).
target_language_example: La reunión es a las nueve de la mañana.
native_language_example: The meeting is at nine in the morning.

meaning: at eight o'clock (used with a time of day, e.g. 'a las ocho de la mañana' = at eight in the morning).
additional_notes: This phrase combines the preposition 'a' (at) + the definite article 'las' for plural hours + the hour 'ocho' and 'de' which links the time to a period of the day (la mañana, la tarde, la noche). For other hours change 'ocho' (e.g. 'a las nueve de la noche'). Use 'a la una' for 1:00 (singular).
target_language_example: Nos vemos a las ocho de la noche en la entrada del cine.
native_language_example: We'll meet at eight o'clock at night at the cinema entrance.

meaning: at the first (moments/attempts); from the very beginning
additional_notes: Often appears as part of longer expressions like "a las primeras de cambio" meaning 'at the first opportunity' or 'right away/on first try'. By itself, "a las primeras" suggests 'at the first ones' or 'at first moments' and usually needs context (e.g., "a las primeras de cambio" or "a las primeras horas"). Commonly used in conversational Spanish to indicate something happening immediately or on the first try.
target_language_example: A las primeras de cambio, dijo que sí.
native_language_example: Right away, he said yes.

meaning: at six (o'clock) in the [time period]; used as the start of a time expression (e.g., 'a las seis de la mañana').
additional_notes: This phrase is not complete by itself: it needs a time-of-day word (la mañana, la tarde, la noche) or context to finish the expression. Use 'a las' for plural hour numbers (2–12). For 1 o'clock use 'a la una de'. Example structure: 'a las seis de la tarde' = 'at six in the afternoon.'
target_language_example: La reunión es a las seis de la tarde.
native_language_example: The meeting is at six in the afternoon.

meaning: at six in (the) — used to give a time and then specify a place or context (e.g., 'at six in the morning', 'at six in the kitchen').
additional_notes: This is a combination of the time expression 'a las seis' (at six o'clock) followed by a preposition 'en' to introduce a location or context. A complete phrase needs a following noun (e.g., 'a las seis en la mañana' is less common than 'a las seis de la mañana'; for time of day use 'de' instead of 'en'). Use 'en' when specifying a place: 'a las seis en la oficina'.
target_language_example: Quedamos a las seis en la cafetería.
native_language_example: We meet at six in the café.

meaning: at three o'clock (used with parts of the day or time expressions)
additional_notes: This phrase begins a time expression. Complete it with the rest of the phrase indicating what follows 'de': for time of day you usually say 'a las tres' or 'a las tres de la tarde/noche/mañana' (at three in the afternoon/night/morning). When mentioning minutes use 'a las tres y cuarto' (3:15) or 'a las tres y media' (3:30). With 'de' it's often followed by 'la mañana', 'la tarde' or 'la noche' to specify AM/PM.
target_language_example: La reunión es a las tres de la tarde.
native_language_example: The meeting is at three in the afternoon.

meaning: at (the) [time]
additional_notes: Used to indicate a specific clock time: a las + [hour]. For example, "a las ocho" = "at eight o'clock." It contracts with la/las for feminine plural nouns only in contexts like "a las ocho" (lit. 'at the eights' grammatically reflecting 'las ocho'). Not used for durations (use 'a' + infinitive for actions) and not to be confused with 'a la(s)' before singular/plural feminine nouns. When giving time in the 24-hour clock you can also say 'a las 14:00' or 'a las dos de la tarde.'
target_language_example: La reunión empieza a las tres.
native_language_example: The meeting starts at three (o'clock).

meaning: 'to hurt' or 'to injure' (someone).
additional_notes: Used with a person as the indirect object (often introduced by 'a') or reflexively (lastimarse) to indicate someone will be hurt or will hurt themselves. Common constructions: 'no voy a lastimar a nadie' (I won't hurt anyone), 'te vas a lastimar' (you are going to hurt yourself). Can be physical or emotional (hurt someone emotionally). The sequence 'a lastimar' often appears when combined with auxiliary verbs or periphrasis (e.g., 'iba a lastimar', 'voy a lastimar').
target_language_example: No iba a lastimar a nadie.
native_language_example: I wasn't going to hurt anyone.

meaning: 'to wash the' (used with plural body parts or objects) — marks purpose/infinitive after verbs like ir/ayudar/venir.
additional_notes: Common structure: [verb] + a + lavar + los + [noun]. The a + infinitive expresses purpose or what someone is going to/should help do (e.g., ayudar a lavar = help to wash). 'Los' is the plural definite article and agrees with the noun (los platos, los dientes). For singular use you'd see 'a lavar el...' or for feminine 'a lavar la...'.
target_language_example: Voy a ayudar a lavar los platos después de cenar.
native_language_example: I'm going to help wash the dishes after dinner.

meaning: to call (someone or something) — used with a feminine noun (e.g., la policía, la abuela).
additional_notes: This is the infinitive verb llamar preceded by a preposition a, often used after verbs of motion or intention (fueron a llamar, voy a llamar) or to indicate future intention (voy/va a llamar). 'La' is the feminine definite article and agrees with the noun that follows (la policía, la abuela). For masculine nouns use 'a llamar al' (a + el = al).
target_language_example: Voy a llamar a la abuela esta tarde.
native_language_example: I'm going to call grandma this afternoon.

meaning: to reach; to come to (a point, amount, or state); used to indicate arriving at something or coming to do something (often in the construction 'llegar a + infinitive').
additional_notes: This sequence appears when the verb 'llegar' is followed by the preposition 'a' and then a noun, number, or an infinitive. 'Llegar a + infinitive' often means 'to end up / manage to / come to (do something)'. With nouns or numbers it indicates reaching a place or amount ('llegar a + [lugar/cantidad]'). The entry shows the two-word sequence 'a llegar a' as it might appear in contexts where the preposition 'a' precedes an infinitive phrase starting with 'llegar a' (e.g., 'antes de llegar a...').
target_language_example: Antes de a llegar a la conclusión, debemos revisar los datos.
native_language_example: Before coming to the conclusion, we must review the data.

meaning: to take you (somewhere) / to carry you (away) — depending on context, often used to indicate someone will take you somewhere or figuratively sweep you off your feet
additional_notes: This is a phrase formed from the preposition a + the verb llevar in the infinitive + the pronoun te (you). It requires context: it can be literal (I'll take you to the station: te voy a llevar / voy a llevarte a la estación) or figurative (esa canción te va a llevar — it will carry you away). Word order can change (llevarte a, voy a llevarte). In commands or expressions it may appear as part of longer verbs (me va a llevar a…) or colloquial sayings.
target_language_example: ¿Quieres que te lleve a casa? Puedo a llevarte ahora mismo.
native_language_example: Do you want me to take you home? I can take you right now.

meaning: to lead you to / to bring you to (a place or result).
additional_notes: Commonly part of a larger phrase. Can refer to physically bringing someone to a location (llevar a alguien a un lugar) or to causing/leading someone toward a result, conclusion, or feeling (llevar a alguien a hacer algo / llevarte a pensar). Tone is neutral. The pronoun 'te' indicates 'you' (informal singular); change to 'me/lo/la/nos/los/las' for other persons.
target_language_example: Esta conversación podría llevarte a cambiar de opinión.
native_language_example: This conversation could lead you to change your mind.

meaning: in the style of
additional_notes: Used before a noun or name to mean 'in the style/manner of' that thing or person (e.g., a lo Picasso = in Picasso's style). Often appears in set phrases: 'a lo mejor' (perhaps/best), 'a lo largo de' (along), 'a lo que' (according to/that which). Context determines exact meaning. Not a complete phrase by itself — normally followed by a noun, name, or fixed expression.
target_language_example: Hicimos la cena a lo mexicano.
native_language_example: We made dinner in the Mexican style.

meaning: to (someone's place) / at (someone's place) — used to say you're going to or are at someone's home or business
additional_notes: Common in spoken Spanish (especially Argentina, Uruguay and some other regions). Use with a person's name or a place: 'a lo de Juan' = 'to Juan's (place)'. Can indicate visiting someone's house or going to their workplace. Often followed by verbs like ir, venir, estar, pasar.
target_language_example: Voy a lo de Ana esta tarde.
native_language_example: I'm going to Ana's (place) this afternoon.

meaning: in a big / lavish way; on a grand scale; living large.
additional_notes: Used to describe doing something extravagantly, luxuriously, or on a large scale (spending, living, traveling, etc.). Common in informal speech. Can imply showiness or excess.
target_language_example: Siempre sale de fiesta y vive a lo grande.
native_language_example: He always goes out partying and lives large.

meaning: along, throughout, or over the length of (space or time).
additional_notes: Used to indicate extension in space (along a river, road, coastline, sky) or in time (throughout a period). Often followed by 'de' + noun for spatial phrases (e.g., 'a lo largo del río') or by 'del' / 'del tiempo' for temporal uses ('a lo largo del tiempo').
target_language_example: Caminamos a lo largo de la playa al atardecer.
native_language_example: We walked along the beach at sunset.

meaning: throughout; along; over the course of.
additional_notes: Used to indicate duration or position along something. Can mean 'throughout' when referring to time (a lo largo de la vida = throughout life) or 'along' when referring to physical location (a lo largo de la calle = along the street). Followed by a noun phrase (de + noun).
target_language_example: Leí muchos libros a lo largo del verano.
native_language_example: I read many books throughout the summer.

meaning: in the distance; far away (visually).
additional_notes: Used to describe something seen from afar or at a distance. Commonly used with verbs of seeing (ver, mirar) and with places or objects (casa, torre, barco). Can indicate physical distance rather than emotional or figurative distance.
target_language_example: A lo lejos se veía una luz en la colina.
native_language_example: In the distance a light could be seen on the hill.

meaning: maybe; perhaps; it might be the case.
additional_notes: Used to express possibility or a guess. Common in spoken and informal written Spanish. Often appears at the start of a sentence but can also be mid-sentence. Less definite than 'seguro' and similar to 'quizás' or 'tal vez'.
target_language_example: A lo mejor mañana llueve, así que lleva paraguas.
native_language_example: Maybe it will rain tomorrow, so take an umbrella.

meaning: part of a longer phrase meaning 'to what I...' or 'to what I mean' (used to refer to something just mentioned)
additional_notes: This is an incomplete chunk that usually appears inside phrases like 'a lo que me refiero' (to what I mean) or 'a lo que me refería' (to what I was referring). It points back to an idea or thing just mentioned. Don't use it alone — it needs the rest of the expression (e.g. 'refiero', 'digo', 'refería').
target_language_example: A lo que me refiero es que debemos llegar temprano.
native_language_example: What I mean is that we should arrive early.

meaning: 'at most' or 'tops' (indicates the maximum/upper limit).
additional_notes: Used to give a maximum estimate or limit. Similar to 'como máximo' and often appears before a number, time, or short phrase. Neutral register and common in spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: Llegaré en media hora, a lo sumo.
native_language_example: I'll arrive in half an hour, at most.

meaning: to succeed in achieving (something); to manage to do (something).
additional_notes: Used with a verb phrase meaning 'to achieve' or 'to manage to' something. Often appears after a verb construction with ir/estar/andar + a + infinitive (e.g., 'va a lograr' = 'is going to succeed'). Common in affirmative and negative sentences: 'lo va a lograr' (he/she is going to succeed at it) vs 'no va a lograr nada' (he won't achieve anything).
target_language_example: Si trabajas duro, vas a lograr tus metas.
native_language_example: If you work hard, you are going to achieve your goals.

meaning: gave birth to a (female) child.
additional_notes: Part of the verb phrase 'dar a luz' = 'to give birth'. When followed by 'una' or 'una niña/hija' it specifies a girl/daughter. Use 'dio a luz' for 'she gave birth' (past). For a boy use 'a un' (dio a luz a un niño) — though more common is simply 'dio a luz a un niño' or 'tuvo un hijo'.
target_language_example: Ella dio a luz a una niña sana esta mañana.
native_language_example: She gave birth to a healthy baby girl this morning.

meaning: to send; to order or command (depending on context).
additional_notes: This phrase combines the preposition 'a' with the infinitive 'mandar'. It can mean 'to send' (e.g., send a letter, send someone somewhere) or 'to order/command' (give orders). Context determines meaning: with objects like 'una carta' it's 'to send'; with people or duties it can mean 'to send' someone or 'to put in charge', and with authority contexts it can mean 'to command'. Commonly used with verbs of motion (e.g., 'ir a mandar') or as part of infinitive constructions.
target_language_example: Voy a mandar el paquete mañana.
native_language_example: I'm going to send the package tomorrow.

meaning: 'to send (someone) to' or 'to order (someone) to go to' (followed by a place or person).
additional_notes: Commonly used with 'mandar a [lugar/persona]' to indicate sending someone somewhere (physically or as an assignment) or ordering them to do something by going to a person/place. Context determines whether it's literal (send to work, send to university) or colloquial/threatening (send to the streets). Often appears with a direct object (te voy a mandar a...) and a destination or recipient.
target_language_example: Voy a mandar a mi hermana a la tienda.
native_language_example: I'm going to send my sister to the store.

meaning: as a way of; in the manner of; by way of
additional_notes: Used to introduce the manner, method, or role of something — similar to 'como' or 'a modo de'. Commonly followed by a noun or noun phrase (e.g., 'a manera de ejemplo', 'a manera de homenaje'). Formal or neutral register.
target_language_example: Leí el artículo a manera de preparación para la clase.
native_language_example: I read the article as a way of preparing for class.

meaning: 1) even with someone / squared up (no debt or owed favors); 2) by hand / handmade.
additional_notes: Two common uses: (a) idiomatic: 'estar a mano' means to be even/equal with someone (e.g., you owe them nothing or you've repaid a favor). (b) literal: 'hecho a mano' means crafted by hand (not machine-made). Context tells which meaning applies.
target_language_example: Después de pagarle, ahora estamos a mano.
native_language_example: After paying him, now we're even.

meaning: to kill; used after verbs of motion or shooting to indicate purpose or intent to kill ("to kill" / "to go kill").
additional_notes: Often follows verbs like "disparar a" (shoot at) or "ir a" (go to) to express the aim or purpose of killing. Can be literal (to kill a person/animal) or used idiomatically for 'to finish off.' Context determines whether it's directional (shoot to kill) or purposeful (went to kill).
target_language_example: Se fue a matar al líder del grupo.
native_language_example: He went to kill the group's leader.

meaning: half-done; incomplete; partially.
additional_notes: Used to describe something done only partway or not fully (e.g., a task, effort, or measure). Can mean 'halfway' or 'half-finished.' Often implies dissatisfaction and that something needs to be completed or done properly.
target_language_example: No dejes el proyecto a medias; termínalo esta semana.
native_language_example: Don't leave the project half-done; finish it this week.

meaning: as ... (progresses) / tailored / custom-made (depends on context).
additional_notes: Two main uses: 1) adverbial: 'a medida que' means 'as' or 'while' when describing change over time (e.g., 'a medida que nos hacemos más viejos' = 'as we get older'). 2) adjectival phrase 'a medida' describes something made to measure or customized (e.g., 'traje a medida' = 'custom suit', 'se la hacemos a medida' = 'we make it to measure/for you'). Context determines whether it's temporal ('as') or means 'tailored/custom'.
target_language_example: A medida que practiques, mejorarás.
native_language_example: As you practice, you will improve.

meaning: as; while; as (something) happens or changes over time
additional_notes: Used to express that one action or change occurs simultaneously with or in proportion to another. Common translations: 'as', 'as... happens', 'as... progresses', or 'while'. Can indicate gradual change ('as we move forward', 'as time goes by').
target_language_example: A medida que practiques más, mejorarás.
native_language_example: As you practice more, you'll improve.

meaning: in the middle of; halfway through (an action, state, or amount).
additional_notes: Used before nouns or gerunds to indicate being partway through or at a half level. Common in phrases like 'a medio camino' (halfway), 'a medio cocinar' (half-cooked), or 'a medio terminar' (half-finished). Can describe time (halfway through the meeting), condition (partly done), or degree (moderately).
target_language_example: La casa quedó a medio pintar cuando empezó a llover.
native_language_example: The house was left half-painted when it started to rain.

meaning: unless; except if.
additional_notes: Used to introduce a condition that would prevent something from happening. Often followed by 'que' when introducing a clause (a menos que = unless). Without 'que' it can be followed by a noun or phrase: 'a menos de' + noun/number means 'unless' or 'unless there is/are'. Common in everyday and formal speech.
target_language_example: No voy a la playa a menos que deje de llover.
native_language_example: I'm not going to the beach unless it stops raining.

meaning: unless; except if
additional_notes: A subordinating conjunction used to introduce a condition that must NOT happen for the main clause to occur. It is followed by a verb in the subjunctive when the condition is hypothetical or doubtful (e.g., "a menos que tengas"). In everyday speech it commonly expresses exception or a negative condition.
target_language_example: No iremos a la playa a menos que pare de llover.
native_language_example: We won't go to the beach unless it stops raining.

meaning: often
additional_notes: A common adverbial phrase used to talk about things that happen regularly. It can appear at the beginning, middle, or end of a sentence.
target_language_example: Voy a menudo al mercado.
native_language_example: I often go to the market.

meaning: at the mercy of; powerless against; subject to the control or influence of someone/something.
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is vulnerable, helpless, or dependent on an external force (natural elements, people, circumstances). Common with storms, waves, currents, cruelty, or situations where control is lost. Followed by a noun (la corriente, la tormenta, su crueldad).
target_language_example: Estábamos a merced del temporal y no podíamos movernos.
native_language_example: We were at the mercy of the storm and couldn't move.

meaning: in my way / my way (doing things my own way).
additional_notes: Used to say you will do something according to your own style, preferences, or rules. Common in contexts about decisions, actions, or relationships. Tone can be firm or personal; not necessarily rude. Literal translation is 'in my way.'
target_language_example: Voy a decorar el apartamento a mi manera.
native_language_example: I'm going to decorate the apartment my way.

meaning: to my best (literally); used to say 'as best I can' or 'to the best of my ability' (informal/colloquial).
additional_notes: Literal translation is 'to my best.' In Spanish this exact phrase is not a fixed, formal expression but can appear in colloquial speech to mean doing something as well as one can (similar to 'a lo mejor mío' or 'lo mejor que puedo'). More common alternatives: 'lo mejor que puedo', 'lo intento con lo mejor que tengo'. Context and word order vary; native speakers may prefer other expressions.
target_language_example: Haré esto a mi mejor, aunque no soy experto.
native_language_example: I'll do this to the best of my ability, even though I'm not an expert.

meaning: in the middle of; halfway through; at half (of something).
additional_notes: Used to indicate being partway through an action, process, time period, or physical distance. Often appears as 'a mitad de' + noun (a mitad de la película, a mitad del camino) or 'a mitad' by itself to mean 'halfway' in informal contexts. Can also imply interruption (we stopped halfway).
target_language_example: Paramos a mitad del camino para comer.
native_language_example: We stopped halfway down the road to eat.

meaning: as a kind of / in the manner of / by way of
additional_notes: Used to introduce a comparison, an example, or to indicate that something is done in the style or form of something else. Commonly followed by a noun or phrase (a modo de ejemplo, a modo de explicación). Formality: neutral; useful in written and spoken Spanish.
target_language_example: Le preparó la carta a modo de disculpa.
native_language_example: He prepared the letter as a kind of apology.

meaning: 'to ride' (used with animals or vehicles) or 'to get on / learn to ride'.
additional_notes: This is the infinitive 'montar' preceded by the preposition 'a' used after verbs of motion or teaching (ir a montar, enseñar a montar). Common collocations: montar a caballo (ride a horse), montar en bicicleta / montar en (vehicle). When used with 'enseñar' it means 'teach (someone) to ride'.
target_language_example: Ella enseñó a su hermana a montar a caballo.
native_language_example: She taught her sister to ride a horse.

meaning: to be very (something); extremely — used before a noun or verb phrase to intensify (literally 'to die of').
additional_notes: Informal/emphatic expression used to exaggerate intensity. Often appears with emotions, feelings or sensations: e.g., 'a morir de risa' (extremely funny, 'to die laughing'), 'a morir de frío' (freezing). It follows 'a' + verb/noun phrase and conveys 'so much that you'd die (of)...' — not literal. Tone is colloquial and vivid.
target_language_example: La película era a morir de risa.
native_language_example: The movie was hilarious (literally: to die laughing).

meaning: 'to show' (infinitive with the preposition 'a' used after verbs that govern an infinitive)
additional_notes: Common structure: a + infinitive (e.g., 'voy a mostrar') expresses intention or start of an action ('going to show' / 'will show'). Also appears after verbs indicating beginning (e.g., 'empezó a mostrar' = 'began to show'). Not used alone; it needs a conjugated verb before it or a subject context.
target_language_example: Te voy a mostrar cómo funciona.
native_language_example: I'm going to show you how it works.

meaning: to/for many (feminine singular noun following 'mucha'); used with feminine nouns meaning 'to a lot of' or 'to many'.
additional_notes: This is the preposition 'a' + the adjective 'mucha' (feminine singular of 'mucho'). It commonly appears before a feminine noun (gente is feminine in Spanish) to mean 'to many people' or 'to a lot of ...'. 'A' marks the indirect object or the personal 'a' with people. For masculine or mixed groups you'd use 'a mucho' only in rare cases; more common is 'a mucha gente' or 'a mucha gente' vs. 'a mucha gente' is standard. For plural adjectives use 'a muchos'/'a muchas' as needed.
target_language_example: Les contó la noticia a mucha gente.
native_language_example: He told the news to many people.

meaning: 'to death' — indicates death as the outcome or goal (e.g., sentenced to death; fight to the death).
additional_notes: Used after verbs or nouns to indicate that death is the result or the intended end point. Common in legal contexts (ser condenado a muerte / sentenced to death) and in expressions like 'pelea a muerte' (fight to the death). Not informal. Can appear with or without the article (e.g., 'sentenciado a muerte' or 'condenado a muerte').
target_language_example: La banda luchó a muerte por el control del territorio.
native_language_example: The gang fought to the death for control of the territory.

meaning: used to add information meaning 'besides', 'in addition', or 'moreover'.
additional_notes: Commonly appears in expressions like 'a más de' (meaning 'in addition to' or 'besides') or informally as a short connector ('a más' = 'furthermore'). Alone it is less frequent; learners will often see 'a más de + noun' or 'a más' followed by a clause to add extra information. Use to introduce another point or emphasize an additional fact.
target_language_example: A más de eso, no tenemos tiempo.
native_language_example: Besides that, we don't have time.

meaning: as much as possible
additional_notes: An idiomatic expression used to intensify an action or state to the maximum degree. It often appears after verbs or adjectives, like reír a más no poder or cansado a más no poder.
target_language_example: Después del examen, estaba cansado a más no poder.
native_language_example: After the exam, I was extremely tired.

meaning: at the latest; no later than (deadline/time limit).
additional_notes: Used to set a latest possible time or deadline. Often follows a time expression (e.g., 'a las diez a más tardar') or is placed after the action. Common in both formal and informal speech.
target_language_example: Envíame el informe a más tardar el viernes.
native_language_example: Send me the report by Friday at the latest.

meaning: Part of a Spanish indirect-object construction meaning 'to/for me (and others) we/ us' — used with a prepositional phrase like 'a [name] y a mí' followed by a verb that agrees with 'nos'.
additional_notes: This appears after a phrase that names people (e.g. 'a Juan y a mí') and introduces the indirect-object or experiencer 'to/for us' or the subject 'we' in colloquial ordering. In standard grammar you'd usually see the full phrase 'A [name] y a mí nos...' or more simply 'A nosotros nos...' The verb that follows agrees with 'nos' (first person plural). Common in spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: A Marta y a mí nos invitaron a la fiesta.
native_language_example: Marta and I were invited to the party.

meaning: to nothing / anything (used after verbs to mean 'to' or 'at' nothing; often in negative or emphatic expressions).
additional_notes: Commonly appears after verbs with preposition 'a'. In negative sentences it means 'to nothing' or 'anything' (e.g., 'no le temo a nada' = 'I'm not afraid of anything'). In comparisons of affection it means 'more than anything' when used with 'querer' (e.g., 'Te quiero más que a nada'). Can be part of set phrases like 'no tomar a nada en serio' (not take anything seriously).
target_language_example: No le hablo a nada cuando estoy nervioso.
native_language_example: I don't speak to anything when I'm nervous.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase by itself; usually part of nonstandard or mistaken constructions. In correct Spanish, 'nada' combines with prepositions differently (e.g., 'no sirve de nada', 'no hay nada en').
additional_notes: The sequence 'a nada en' is uncommon and generally incorrect as a standalone phrase. It might appear in speech or writing due to errors or as part of larger, nonstandard regional usages. Prefer standard alternatives: 'no sirve de nada en...' (it's useless in...), 'no hay nada en...' (there is nothing in...), or 'de nada' (you're welcome).
target_language_example: No le prestes atención: eso no conduce a nada en la práctica.
native_language_example: Don't pay attention: that leads to nothing in practice.

meaning: Not a standard Spanish phrase; likely a typo or incorrect word order. Appears to be a mistaken repetition of the preposition 'a' after the phrase 'a nadie' or an extra 'a' before a subsequent word.
additional_notes:
Common correct forms:
- 'a nadie' = 'to nobody' / 'to no one'. Used after verbs or expressions to indicate that no person is affected: No le dije a nadie. (I didn't tell anyone.)
- If you encounter 'a nadie a' in written Spanish, it's usually an error. It might result from copying a segment that separates 'a' from the next word (e.g., 'a nadie a quien...' should be 'a nadie a quien' is possible but rare; more correctly 'a nadie a quien contárselo' should be 'a nadie a quien contárselo' only when the structure requires both 'a' for the indirect object and 'a' starting a relative clause, but normally one 'a' suffices). Check for a missing or extra word, misplaced punctuation, or dialectal mistakes.
If the intended meaning is 'to nobody' followed immediately by another 'a' introducing a clause, rewrite the sentence to remove the extra preposition or rephrase: 'No le dije a nadie' or 'No se lo conté a nadie' or 'No dije a nadie que...' (better: 'No le dije a nadie que...').
target_language_example: No le dije a nadie a quien pudiera importarle, porque no era asunto suyo.
native_language_example: I didn't tell anyone who might care, because it wasn't their business.

meaning: literally 'to nobody with' — not a standalone fixed phrase; appears as part of larger constructions meaning 'with nobody' or 'to nobody' (e.g., 'no hables a nadie con...').
additional_notes: This sequence by itself is uncommon and incomplete in Spanish; it typically appears inside longer sentences where 'a nadie' (to nobody) combines with a following 'con' (with) to introduce a companion or instrument. More natural full phrases include 'a nadie con quien...' (with whom nobody...) or 'con nadie' (with nobody). Beginners should learn the common alternatives: 'a nadie' = 'to nobody', 'con nadie' = 'with nobody', and 'a nadie con quien' = 'with whom nobody'.
target_language_example: No tengo a nadie con quien hablar sobre eso.
native_language_example: I don't have anyone to talk to about that.

meaning: by swimming; swimming (as a means of travel)
additional_notes: Used to say that someone or something moves through water by swimming. Common in contexts like crossing a river, reaching shore, or describing how a person or animal traveled. Often appears with verbs like 'ir', 'llegar', 'cruzar' or 'venir'.
target_language_example: Llegamos a nado hasta la playa.
native_language_example: We reached the beach by swimming.

meaning: to/at none; not to any (feminine).
additional_notes: Used with verbs of motion or direction (e.g., ir a) or with direct objects when negated to mean 'not to any' or 'to none.' 'Ninguna' is feminine singular; form changes with gender/number (ninguno/ninguna/ningunos/ningunas) and often appears after a or de (e.g., a ninguna parte = to nowhere). Common in negative sentences.
target_language_example: No mandé la carta a ninguna dirección.
native_language_example: I didn't send the letter to any address.

meaning: to/for children (plural); directed at or intended for children
additional_notes: Commonly appears after verbs or prepositions: e.g. 'dar algo a niños' (give something to children), 'película a niños' (a film for children). 'Niños' is masculine plural; use 'a niñas' for girls or 'a niños y niñas' / 'a l@s niñ@s' for inclusive phrasing. Context determines whether it's 'to' (indirect object) or 'for' (intended audience).
target_language_example: Leí un cuento a niños en la biblioteca.
native_language_example: I read a story to children at the library.

meaning: used to introduce a correction, disagreement, or stronger statement; like 'on the contrary' or 'no—actually'.
additional_notes: Often appears at the start of a sentence or clause to contradict what was just said or to add emphasis. Tone can be mild correction or stronger disagreement depending on context and intonation. Common in spoken Spanish. Not a fixed idiom with a single translation—choose English equivalent based on context (e.g., 'actually', 'no, rather', 'on the contrary').
target_language_example: A no, eso no es correcto; hubo un error en la cuenta.
native_language_example: No—actually, that's not correct; there was a mistake in the bill.

meaning: 'unless' or 'except (that)'.
additional_notes: Used to introduce an exception or condition that prevents something from happening. Often appears as 'a no ser que' + subjunctive when stating a hypothetical exception (e.g., 'No iremos a no ser que...'). Can also be used in negative constructions similar to 'except if' or 'unless'. Formal to neutral register.
target_language_example: Iremos al parque, a no ser que llueva.
native_language_example: We'll go to the park, unless it rains.

meaning: 'unless' or 'except if'.
additional_notes: Used to introduce a condition that makes the main statement not true. Equivalent to 'a menos que' or English 'unless'. Often followed by a verb in subjunctive when expressing a hypothetical or uncertain condition.
target_language_example: No iremos a la playa, a no ser que haga sol.
native_language_example: We won't go to the beach, unless it's sunny.

meaning: in the name of; registered to (someone).
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something (an account, bill, reservation, document, property, etc.) is registered, issued, or belongs under a particular person's name. Often followed by a person's name or a pronoun (e.g., 'a nombre de Juan', 'a mi nombre'). Common in administrative, legal, and commercial contexts.
target_language_example: La factura está a nombre de María.
native_language_example: The invoice is in María's name.

meaning: to nine / at nine (depending on context) — often part of constructions meaning 'to the number nine' or 'into nine (things)'.
additional_notes: Literal sense: 'a' + 'nueve' can mean direction toward the number nine, conversion into nine parts, or a target number (e.g., 'convertir a nueve idiomas' = 'into nine languages'). Spanish preposition 'a' has many uses; context decides translation. In short, 'a nueve' is not a fixed idiom—translate based on the verb: e.g., 'llevar a nueve mundos' = 'bring to nine worlds', 'criar a nueve niños' = 'raise nine children', 'traducir a nueve idiomas' = 'translate into nine languages', and 'a las nueve' (note the article) means 'at nine o'clock' (different phrase).
target_language_example: Ella tradujo el manual a nueve idiomas para la empresa.
native_language_example: She translated the manual into nine languages for the company.

meaning: at eight (o'clock) or to eight (depending on context)
additional_notes: Usually means 'at eight' when giving a time (e.g., 'a las ocho' is the full form). In some contexts, especially before a noun or number, 'a ocho' can indicate a rate, price, or measurement (e.g., 'a ocho euros' = 'at eight euros' or 'for eight euros'). Alone without 'las' it's less common for clock time but still understood in casual speech or abbreviated contexts (timetable labels, announcements).
target_language_example: ¿Nos vemos a ocho en punto?
native_language_example: Shall we meet at eight o'clock?

meaning: by estimation; roughly; by eye (without exact measurement).
additional_notes: Used when giving an approximate amount, measurement, or guess made without instruments — relying on sight, experience, or intuition. Common in everyday speech. Can be used with numbers (e.g., 'a ojo, unos cinco kilos') or to indicate rough timing or distance.
target_language_example: No tengo una regla, pero diría a ojo que son unos tres metros.
native_language_example: I don't have a ruler, but I'd say by eye it's about three meters.

meaning: to pay for; (often) to suffer the consequences for (something wrong).
additional_notes: Literally 'to pay for.' Commonly used both literally (to pay money for) and idiomatically to mean 'to be punished' or 'to face consequences' for an action. In the idiomatic sense it's often used in threats: 'Vas a pagar por eso' = 'You'll pay for that' (you'll be punished). Context (money vs. consequences) determines meaning.
target_language_example: Vas a pagar por lo que hiciste.
native_language_example: You're going to pay for what you did.

meaning: to participate / to take part (infinitive with preposition 'a' used after verbs that require 'a' + infinitive).
additional_notes: Commonly appears after verbs that are followed by another action, for example: 'empezar a participar' (to begin to take part) or 'invitar a participar' (to invite to participate). The 'a' is a preposition linking the first verb to the infinitive 'participar'. Use with appropriate conjugation: 'Voy a participar' = 'I am going to participate.'
target_language_example: Me invitaron a participar en el proyecto.
native_language_example: They invited me to participate in the project.

meaning: starting from; from (a certain time or source).
additional_notes: Used to indicate the point in time or source where something begins or is derived. Commonly used with time expressions (a partir de ahora, a partir de mañana) and with sources/materials (a partir de leche = made from milk). Can mean 'as of' or 'from' depending on context.
target_language_example: A partir de mañana estudiaré todos los días.
native_language_example: Starting from tomorrow I will study every day.

meaning: to go on to (do something); to proceed to (a next action or stage).
additional_notes: Used before an infinitive or noun to indicate moving on to the next action, stage, or topic. Common in instructions, narratives, or transitions: e.g., 'vamos a pasar a explicar' = 'we will now go on to explain'. Often followed by an infinitive (a pasar a + [infinitive]) or 'a pasar a' + noun/phrase.
target_language_example: Después de la introducción, vamos a pasar a explicar los resultados.
native_language_example: After the introduction, we will go on to explain the results.

meaning: used to indicate going to spend (time) — e.g. 'to spend the [time period]'.
additional_notes: Commonly appears with periods of time (el verano, el fin de semana) or with 'número' in a different sense ('pasar' = to give/send). Context decides meaning: 'pasar el' + time = 'to spend the [time period]'; 'te voy a pasar el número' = 'I'll give/pass you the number'. After 'a' it often follows verbs of motion (Voy a pasar el fin de semana = I'm going to spend the weekend).
target_language_example: Voy a pasar el fin de semana con mis amigos.
native_language_example: I'm going to spend the weekend with my friends.

meaning: nothing will happen; nothing bad will happen (reassurance)
additional_notes: This phrase appears in negative reassuring sentences like "No te va a pasar nada" or "No va a pasar nada." It's used to calm someone, telling them there will be no harm, danger, or problem. The standalone fragment "a pasar nada" without the preceding "no" is not correct — the full common forms include the negative: "no va a pasar nada" or "no te va a pasar nada."
target_language_example: Tranquila, no te va a pasar nada.
native_language_example: Relax, nothing's going to happen to you / nothing bad will happen.

meaning: at a pace / while walking / per step (depends on context)
additional_notes: Used to describe speed or manner of movement. Common uses: 'a paso lento/rápido' = at a slow/fast pace; 'a paso de' can indicate cadence (e.g., 'a paso de guerra' = at a marching pace). Can also mean 'per step' in technical contexts. Often followed by an adjective or noun describing the pace.
target_language_example: Caminábamos a paso tranquilo por el parque.
native_language_example: We walked at a relaxed pace through the park.

meaning: by kicking out; forcefully expelled (idiom meaning 'kicked out' or 'driven out')
additional_notes: Idiomatic expression used when someone is forced out or thrown out of a place, often abruptly and with force. Can be literal (physically kicked) or figurative (strongly expelled). Common in commands or recounting expulsions. Often used with verbs like echar, sacar, or echarse (echar a patadas / sacar a patadas).
target_language_example: Si no empiezas a comportarte, te voy a sacar a patadas.
native_language_example: If you don't start behaving, I'm going to kick you out.

meaning: used to introduce a request or wish, equivalent to 'to ask that' or 'to request that'.
additional_notes: Often appears in formal or written contexts when reporting requests, orders, or petitions. It typically precedes a subordinate clause with the subjunctive (e.g., 'a pedir que + subjunctive'). Can be part of longer expressions like 'salir a pedir' in some regional uses, but most commonly used in constructions meaning 'to ask that...'.
target_language_example: Fueron a pedir que se reconsidere la decisión.
native_language_example: They went to ask that the decision be reconsidered.

meaning: to go peel (something) / to go get peeling done (colloquial: to leave or go away - regional slang).
additional_notes: Literal: from the verb pelar (to peel). As a phrase with a (a + infinitive) it can mean 'to go do X' (e.g., 'a pelar papas' = 'to go peel potatoes'). In some regional/slang uses, 'a pelar' or simply 'pelar' can be used informally to tell someone to go away or to dismiss (similar to 'get lost'), but this is informal and may be rude. Check context and region before using the slang sense.
target_language_example: Voy a pelar las papas antes de cocinar.
native_language_example: I'm going to peel the potatoes before cooking.

meaning: colloquial: (someone) is going to be beaten/attacked; also used jokingly to mean someone will be scolded or reprimanded
additional_notes: Very informal, regional in some Spanish-speaking areas. Literally comes from 'pelar' (to skin/peel), but in slang can mean to beat, scold, or take someone down. Often appears in contexts like 'se va a pelar las' or 'le van a pelar las' followed by a body part or just plural article, implying trouble for the person. Tone can be threatening or playful depending on context.
target_language_example: Si sigue así, le van a pelar las.
native_language_example: If he keeps going like that, they're going to beat/scold him.

meaning: to lose (something) / to miss out on (it)
additional_notes: This is part of a verb phrase where 'perder' means 'to lose' and the direct object (la = feminine thing) follows. In different contexts it can mean 'lose' (a race, opportunity, battle, harvest) or 'miss' (an event/opportunity). The pronoun/article (la) agrees with the feminine noun being lost (la oportunidad, la batalla, la guerra, la cosecha). Often appears with verbs like 'vas a', 'vamos a', or 'echar a perder' (to ruin/spoil).
