In many cases Spanish prefers 'no ... con ningún...' or 'ni con ningún...' for emphasis or to continue a negative list.
target_language_example: No quiero ir con ningún amigo esta vez.
native_language_example: I don't want to go with any friend this time.

meaning: with our (feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: A simple combination of the preposition con (with) + the possessive adjective nuestra (our, feminine singular). Use when the noun that follows is feminine and singular: e.g. 'con nuestra casa', 'con nuestra madre'. If the noun is masculine use 'con nuestro'; for plural use 'con nuestras' or 'con nuestros'.
target_language_example: Voy al concierto con nuestra amiga.
native_language_example: I'm going to the concert with our friend.

meaning: with or — used to present an alternative that includes 'with' (often in lists or choices).
additional_notes: 'Con' means 'with' and 'o' means 'or'. Together they appear when offering alternatives that start with 'with', for example in phrases like 'con o sin' (with or without). On its own 'con o' is incomplete and usually followed by another word or phrase.
target_language_example: ¿Quieres café con o sin azúcar?
native_language_example: Do you want coffee with or without sugar?

meaning: with someone/something else; with another person.
additional_notes: Used to say that an action or relationship involves a different person or thing than the one expected. Can refer to people (e.g., a partner) or objects (e.g., confusing one item with another). Context determines whether 'otro' means 'another (one)' or 'someone else.'
target_language_example: No quiero salir con otro si no te interesa.
native_language_example: I don't want to go out with someone else if you're not interested.

meaning: with others; together with other people or things
additional_notes: Used to indicate interaction or being together with other people or items. Often appears as part of phrases like "unos con otros" (with one another) to emphasize mutual actions (e.g., "pelearon unos con otros" = they fought each other). Can refer to people or non-human things (e.g., "árboles").
target_language_example: Debo hablar con otros para aprender nuevas ideas.
native_language_example: I must talk with others to learn new ideas.

meaning: with (dad) / staying with dad
additional_notes: Literally 'with dad'. Used to indicate being together with, going with, or staying with one's father. Context determines exact sense: a short phrase like 'Con papá.' can answer 'Where are you?' ('With dad.') or 'Who are you with?' It can also express accompaniment ('Come with Dad') or that someone stayed with Dad (possibly against their will). Informal, everyday family language.
target_language_example: Voy al parque con papá.
native_language_example: I'm going to the park with Dad.

meaning: 'excuse me' / 'may I' — polite way to get past someone, interrupt, or ask permission.
additional_notes: Used to politely attract attention, ask to pass by someone, or request permission to speak or act. Formal and informal contexts; can be followed by a title or name (e.g., "con permiso, señora") or used alone. Tone is respectful; similar uses: "perdón" (sorry) and "disculpe" (excuse me, more formal).
target_language_example: Con permiso, ¿puedo pasar?
native_language_example: Excuse me, may I pass?

meaning: with dogs; indicating accompaniment or association with dogs.
additional_notes: Literal prepositional phrase meaning 'with dogs.' Commonly appears in proverbs about consequences of associating with bad company (e.g., 'El que con perros se acuesta, con pulgas se despierta' = 'He who lies down with dogs wakes up with fleas'). Can be used neutrally to say someone is physically with dogs (e.g., playing with dogs) or more figuratively to indicate association. Tone depends on context; one example sentence below contains explicit/graphic content unrelated to the phrase itself.
target_language_example: Paseo con perros por el parque todas las mañanas.
native_language_example: I walk with dogs in the park every morning.

meaning: with which / so that / therefore (depends on context).
additional_notes: This short phrase can have several uses: 1) 'con que' + clause can introduce a conclusion or reaction, similar to 'so' or 'so that's what/so that's why' (e.g., Con que te vas = So you're leaving). 2) It can mean 'with which' when connecting to a noun (less common in spoken Spanish). 3) In formal writing it may appear as 'con que' = 'with which' or 'having which'. Pay attention to tone and context; often used to express surprise, realization, or a consequence. Do not confuse with 'conque' (one word), which is an informal conjunction meaning 'so'/'therefore'—in many dialects 'con que' and 'conque' are interchangeable, but written Spanish often prefers 'conque' as the conjunction.
target_language_example: ¿Con que vas a mudarte el mes que viene?
native_language_example: So you're going to move next month?

meaning: 'with what' or 'using what' (asks about the tool, instrument, material, or reason).
additional_notes: Used in questions to ask which thing, tool, material, or means is used. Often appears at the start or inside a question: ¿Con qué...? It can be followed by a verb (¿Con qué cortaste esto?) or a noun (¿Con qué plato comes?). In casual speech it may contract with pronouns (¿Con qué lo hiciste?).
target_language_example: ¿Con qué abriste la puerta?
native_language_example: With what did you open the door? / What did you use to open the door?

meaning: with reason; no wonder; rightly/justifiably.
additional_notes: Used to say something is understandable or justified (no wonder) or that someone has a valid reason. Can stand alone as an exclamation meaning “no wonder.” Context determines if it means “with good reason” (justifiably) or “no wonder.”
target_language_example: Con razón llegaste tarde; había mucho tráfico.
native_language_example: No wonder you were late; there was a lot of traffic.

meaning: regarding; with respect to; concerning.
additional_notes: Used to introduce the topic or thing being referred to. Formal to neutral register; common in spoken and written Spanish. Often followed by a noun, pronoun, or clause. Similar to 'regarding' or 'about' in English.
target_language_example: Con respecto a tu pregunta, te llamaré mañana.
native_language_example: Regarding your question, I'll call you tomorrow.

meaning: with being; (rare/poetic) 'to be with' or 'having been'
additional_notes: This combination is not a common fixed phrase in everyday Spanish. 'Con' means 'with' and 'ser' is the verb 'to be'. You may encounter 'con ser' in literary, poetic, or archaic contexts (e.g., constructions like 'con ser así...' meaning 'even if it is so' or 'even being so'). In most cases, other constructions are used instead (e.g., 'siendo' or 'aunque sea').
target_language_example: Con ser difícil, lo intentaremos de todos modos.
native_language_example: Even though it is difficult, we will try anyway.

meaning: with his/her/their fist (or handwriting: 'with his/her hand' — literally 'with his/her fist')
additional_notes: Literally means 'with his/her fist'. Often used to say someone did something physically with a fist (e.g., hit, break) or, in some contexts, to emphasize that something was written or signed by the person's own hand (puño y letra). Context determines whether it refers to a literal punch or to handwriting/signature. Use possessive (su) to match the person.
target_language_example: El documento fue firmado con su puño y letra.
native_language_example: The document was signed by his/her own hand.

meaning: with his/her/its/their own (used before a noun to indicate possession or means)
additional_notes: Commonly followed by a noun (e.g., 'con sus propios ojos', 'con sus propios recursos'). 'Sus' agrees with the possessed item (his, her, its, their). Context determines whether it refers to one person or multiple people. Used to emphasize that something is done using one's own things, means, or abilities.
target_language_example: Ella resolvió el problema con sus propios recursos.
native_language_example: She solved the problem with her own resources.

meaning: with only / with just
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is done or achieved using a single thing, a small amount, or a short amount of time. Often followed by a noun, number, infinitive, or time expression (e.g., con sólo dos euros, con sólo escuchar, con sólo una hora). Accent on sólo is optional in modern Spanish; many style guides prefer no accent unless to avoid ambiguity with 'solo' (alone).
target_language_example: Con sólo cinco minutos, terminé la tarea.
native_language_example: With only five minutes, I finished the homework.

meaning: 'with such' or 'with so' (used before adjectives or expressions of degree, often in the structure 'con tan de/que' to introduce consequence or emphasis).
additional_notes: Usually appears in expressions like 'con tan de' (rare) or more commonly 'con tan...' + que (e.g., 'con tan poca' / 'con tan poco') to emphasize degree and introduce a result or surprise. More frequent alternatives are 'tan' alone or 'con tanta/ con tanto' when agreeing in gender/number with a noun. 'Con tan' is somewhat formal/literary and not extremely common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: No sabía que vinieras con tan poco equipaje.
native_language_example: I didn't know you would come with so little luggage.

meaning: in plenty of time / with enough time / early (enough).
additional_notes: Used to say you have or need enough time before an event or deadline. Commonly appears with verbs like llegar (llegar con tiempo = arrive with time/early), preparar, organizar, or with expressions like 'con tiempo suficiente'. Not a direct reflexive phrase; context determines whether it means 'early' or 'with enough time'.
target_language_example: Llegué al aeropuerto con tiempo y pasé por seguridad sin prisas.
native_language_example: I arrived at the airport with plenty of time and went through security without rushing.

meaning: with all due respect; politely disagreeing or introducing a potentially critical comment.
additional_notes: A polite formula used before saying something that may contradict, criticize, or correct someone. Tone can still be firm; context and intonation determine how polite or confrontational it sounds. Common in formal and informal speech. Can stand alone as an interjection.
target_language_example: Con todo respeto, no creo que esa sea la mejor idea.
native_language_example: With all due respect, I don't think that's the best idea.

meaning: despite
additional_notes:
Has multiple uses depending on context:
- As a short form of 'con todo y...' it means 'despite' or 'even with' (example 1).
- Literally 'with everything' when describing compatibility or inclusion (example 2: 'goes with everything').
- Can also be used more generally to mean 'with everything' in a blanket sense (example 3: 'meticulous about everything').
Choose the meaning from context. Not formal slang.
target_language_example: Aunque llovió, con todo, salimos a caminar.
native_language_example: Even though it rained, despite that, we went for a walk.

meaning: with all the / despite all the (depends on context)
additional_notes: Used before a noun or noun phrase to emphasize inclusion ('with all the...') or in fixed expressions like 'con todo lo que' meaning 'even though' or 'despite the fact that'. It's often followed by a subordinating clause ('que' + verb) or a noun. Context determines whether it expresses accompaniment/inclusion or concession.
target_language_example: Con todo lo que ha pasado, sigo adelante.
native_language_example: Despite everything that has happened, I keep going.

meaning: with difficulty; barely/only with effort
additional_notes: Used to say that something is achieved but only with effort or just barely. Often appears before a verb or phrase: e.g. 'con trabajo llegué a tiempo' = 'I barely arrived on time.' Not the same as 'con trabajo' meaning 'with work' in literal contexts — context determines sense.
target_language_example: Con trabajo terminé el informe antes de la reunión.
native_language_example: I barely finished the report before the meeting.

meaning: with three (something).
additional_notes: A simple prepositional phrase: 'con' = with, 'tres' = three. It must be followed by a noun or number context (e.g., 'con tres amigos', 'con tres casas'). Use to indicate accompaniment, quantity, or features involving the number three.
target_language_example: Voy al cine con tres amigos.
native_language_example: I'm going to the movies with three friends.

meaning: with an old man / with an old (male) one
additional_notes: Literal phrase meaning 'with an old man.' 'Viejo' can be affectionate (e.g., 'my old man' = my father or husband) or neutral/descriptive (an elderly man). Without context it simply indicates accompaniment with an older male person. Gender matters: 'un viejo' = male. In some regions 'viejo' used alone can be familiar/slang for 'guy' or 'my partner'—tone and context determine nuance.
target_language_example: Fui al parque con un viejo que conocí en la cafetería.
native_language_example: I went to the park with an old man I met at the café.

meaning: with one sentence / in one sentence
additional_notes: Used to ask for or indicate a brief summary or a short answer — literally 'with a sentence'. Common in contexts like 'explica con una frase' (explain in one sentence) or 'resúmelo con una frase' (summarize it in one sentence).
target_language_example: Explícame con una frase de qué trata la película.
native_language_example: Explain to me in one sentence what the movie is about.

meaning: with a phrase of / using a phrase of (often introduces an example phrase or specifies the wording to use).
additional_notes: Commonly used when giving or referring to a specific short expression, slogan, title, or wording. Often followed by a phrase in quotes or by specifying what the phrase should contain (e.g., 'con una frase de agradecimiento', 'con una frase de tres palabras'). Can be literal (with a phrase of) or idiomatic when asking for a phrase that fits certain conditions.
target_language_example: Escribe la tarjeta con una frase de agradecimiento.
native_language_example: Write the card with a thank-you phrase.

meaning: with a quince-phrase; used to refer to a set phrase or line of about fifteen words (or a line for a quinceañera).
additional_notes: This phrase is not very common on its own and its meaning depends on context. It could refer literally to 'with a phrase of fifteen (words)' — e.g., asking someone to respond using a sentence of roughly fifteen words — or to a short ceremonial line/phrase related to a quinceañera (a girl's 15th‑birthday celebration). If you encounter it, look at the surrounding context to decide whether it's about word count or the quinceañera tradition.
target_language_example: Por favor, responde con una frase de quince palabras para la actividad.
native_language_example: Please answer with a fifteen-word sentence for the activity.

meaning: with a girl / with a young woman.
additional_notes: Used to say someone is with, dating, or married to a young woman. Muchacha generally means 'girl' or 'young woman' (age context depends on sentence). 'Con' = 'with'. Can describe dating (salir con) or marriage (casarse con). Tone is neutral; 'muchacha' is informal/colloquial compared with 'mujer' or 'joven'.
target_language_example: Él está saliendo con una muchacha de su universidad.
native_language_example: He is dating a girl from his university.

meaning: with a cup (of ...).
additional_notes: Common phrase used to say you have or are doing something while holding/with a cup of a beverage (tea, coffee, etc.). Often followed by 'de' + drink: 'con una taza de té/café'. Used to describe accompaniment or routine.
target_language_example: Leo el periódico por la mañana con una taza de café.
native_language_example: I read the newspaper in the morning with a cup of coffee.

meaning: with one (feminine) / with her (colloquial referring to a woman or feminine thing)
additional_notes: A combination of the preposition con (with) + the feminine indefinite pronoun una (one/a) or the feminine pronoun 'one' as a substitute for a woman or feminine noun. Context determines whether it means 'with one (a woman/item)' or refers to 'with her' in casual speech. Common in everyday conversation when mentioning 'one (woman)' without naming her or when referring to a feminine noun previously mentioned.
target_language_example: Me acosté con una que conocí en la fiesta.
native_language_example: I slept with one (a woman) I met at the party.

meaning: with some / with a (feminine plural) — used before feminine plural nouns to mean 'with' + an unspecified small number or a particular set.
additional_notes: ‘Unas’ is the feminine plural of the indefinite article (like 'some' or 'a few') and is used before feminine plural nouns: con unas tijeras (with some scissors / with a pair of scissors), con unas amigas (with some friends / with a few girlfriends). Context decides whether it means 'some', 'a few', or 'a particular set'. It can also be used when referring to a specific but unspecified item(s) encountered earlier.
target_language_example: Voy al parque con unas amigas esta tarde.
native_language_example: I'm going to the park with some friends this afternoon.

meaning: with one
additional_notes: A compositional phrase: con + uno. It usually refers back to a masculine noun understood from context, often a person or thing. It is very commonly followed by de + plural noun: con uno de mis amigos = 'with one of my friends'. For a feminine noun, use con una.
target_language_example: Fui al cine con uno de mis amigos.
native_language_example: I went to the movies with one of my friends.

meaning: with some / with a few (people or things); used to indicate accompaniment or a few unspecified items/people.
additional_notes: Commonly used before plural nouns. When referring to people, it means 'with some friends/people' (unspecified). Can also mean 'with a few' for objects or abstract things (e.g., memories, cases). Tone is neutral and frequent in everyday speech. If you want to specify exact number or identity, replace 'unos' with a number or a determiner (mis, estos, etc.).
target_language_example: Salí anoche con unos compañeros de la universidad.
native_language_example: I went out last night with some university classmates.

meaning: 'alive' or 'alive and well' (literally 'with life').
additional_notes: Used after a person or animal to say they are alive or brought back alive. Common in contexts of rescue, danger, or returning from captivity. Literal translation is natural in English: 'bring/find someone back alive' = 'traer/encuentrar con vida'.
target_language_example: Queremos que los rehenes regresen con vida.
native_language_example: We want the hostages to return alive.

meaning: 'with a view' (followed by a noun or preposition: con vista al/ a la/ a)
additional_notes: Used to describe that a place (house, room, window, apartment) has a view of something. Commonly appears as 'con vista al mar', 'con vista a la ciudad', or 'con vista al río'. When the thing viewed is masculine singular use 'al' (a + el), and for feminine singular use 'a la'.
target_language_example: Buscamos un apartamento con vista a la montaña.
native_language_example: We're looking for an apartment with a view of the mountain.

meaning: with a view of / overlooking; also 'with the aim of' (formal).
additional_notes: Most commonly used to describe a location that has a view of something (e.g., a room with a sea view: "con vistas al mar"). In more formal or bureaucratic contexts it can mean 'with the aim of' or 'with a view to' (e.g., "con vistas a mejorar el servicio"). Use the preposition and article as needed: con vistas al (a + el), a la, a los, a las, or con vistas a + infinitive for 'with the aim of.'
target_language_example: Reservé una habitación con vistas al mar.
native_language_example: I booked a room with a view of the sea.

meaning: with him now
additional_notes: A short phrase combining the preposition 'con' (with), the pronoun 'él' (him), and 'ahora' (now). Used to say that someone is currently with a male person or to ask/say that something should be done together with him right now. Remember the accent on 'él' distinguishes the pronoun from the article 'el'. Word order can vary (e.g., 'ahora con él' is also possible).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes venir con él ahora?
native_language_example: Can you come with him now?

meaning: with him (sequence: preposition 'con' + pronoun 'él' followed immediately by 'de' to introduce a role, reason, or relation)
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom; it's a compositional sequence where 'con él' is followed by 'de' to link to a noun or descriptor (e.g., 'con él de conductor'). Often more natural alternatives exist (e.g., 'con él como...' or 'él, como...') depending on context. Spelling and punctuation matter: keep the space between 'con' and 'él' and between 'él' and 'de'.
target_language_example: Llegó con él de copiloto en el coche.
native_language_example: He arrived with him as the co-pilot in the car.

meaning: 'with him is' or 'with him it is' (literal) — often part of a larger sentence meaning 'with him it's ...' or 'it's with him that ...'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself; it's the words 'con' (with) + 'él' (him) + 'es' (is). You'll usually see it inside a full sentence (e.g., describing who has something, who is responsible, or giving an opinion: 'Con él es más fácil' = 'With him it's easier'). Remember the accent on 'él' distinguishes the pronoun 'him' from the article 'el'.
target_language_example: Con él es más sencillo resolver el problema.
native_language_example: With him it's easier to solve the problem.

meaning: a clear conscience; not feeling guilty.
additional_notes: Used to say someone feels no guilt or remorse about their actions. Often used in expressions about sleep or peace (e.g., 'no hay almohada más cómoda que una conciencia limpia' = 'there's no better pillow than a clear conscience'). Common in everyday and formal speech.
target_language_example: Puedo dormir tranquilo porque tengo la conciencia limpia.
native_language_example: I can sleep peacefully because I have a clear conscience.

meaning: 'clear conscience' or 'peace of mind' (feeling free from guilt or worry).
additional_notes: Used to say someone feels no guilt or moral worry about something they've done. Common in expressions like 'tener la conciencia tranquila' (to have a clear conscience) or 'irse con la conciencia tranquila' (to go/leave with peace of mind).
target_language_example: Después de ayudar, me quedé con la conciencia tranquila.
native_language_example: After helping, I was left with a clear conscience.

meaning: used to indicate an event (concert) of a particular type or by a particular artist ("concert of / by / featuring").
additional_notes: Literally 'concert of'. Commonly followed by an artist, genre, or occasion: concierto de rock, concierto de Shakira, concierto de música clásica. Can also appear in phrases like 'entradas para el concierto de...' (tickets for the concert of...).
target_language_example: Compré entradas para el concierto de la banda mañana.
native_language_example: I bought tickets for the band's concert tomorrow.

meaning: the concert was...
additional_notes: Concierto = concert; 'fue' is the preterite of 'ser' (to be). Together they start a past description: 'The concert was [adjective/noun phrase].' Use to describe how a specific past concert went (successful, wonderful, etc.). You can replace 'fue' with other tense/forms (es, fue, ha sido) to change time/nuance. Common structure: 'El/ Su concierto fue + adjective' or 'fue un gran éxito.'
target_language_example: El concierto fue inolvidable.
native_language_example: The concert was unforgettable.

meaning: conclusion of; the end or result of (something).
additional_notes: Used to indicate the ending, result, or summary of something (a text, event, argument, investigation, etc.). Often appears before a noun: conclusión de la reunión, conclusión del estudio. 'de' contracts with 'el' to form 'del'.
target_language_example: La conclusión de la investigación fue sorprendente.
native_language_example: The conclusion of the investigation was surprising.

meaning: the conclusion that / the inference that
additional_notes: Used to introduce what someone concludes or infers from evidence or reasoning. Often follows verbs or nouns related to thinking, analyzing, or observing (e.g., 'llegar a la conclusión de que', 'sacar la conclusión de que'). Common in written and formal spoken Spanish.
target_language_example: Llegué a la conclusión de que necesitábamos más tiempo.
native_language_example: I came to the conclusion that we needed more time.

meaning: provided that; on the condition that
additional_notes: Used to introduce a requirement or condition for something to happen. Often followed by a verb in the subjunctive when expressing a hypothetical or future condition (e.g., 'siempre y cuando' / 'con la condición de que'). It is more formal than simply 'si'.
target_language_example: Aceptaré la oferta con la condición de que haya flexibilidad en el horario.
native_language_example: I will accept the offer provided that there is flexibility in the schedule.

meaning: conference of / lecture on (phrase used to link 'conferencia' with its topic or organizer).
additional_notes: Used before a noun to specify the subject, organizer, or type of a conference or lecture. Common patterns: 'conferencia de X' = a talk about X (tema) or a conference organized by X (persona/entidad). If you mean 'give a lecture' you'd use 'dar una conferencia'.
target_language_example: Mañana asisto a una conferencia de historia del arte.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I attend a conference on art history.

meaning: press conference; a public media briefing by an official or spokesperson.
additional_notes: Used when officials, politicians, companies or organizations speak to journalists and answer questions. Common verbs: dar (dar una conferencia de prensa = hold/give a press conference) and ofrecer/convocar. Can refer to the event itself or to statements made there.
target_language_example: El alcalde dará una conferencia de prensa sobre la nueva política mañana.
native_language_example: The mayor will hold a press conference about the new policy tomorrow.

meaning: trust/confidence in his/her/one's (ability, leader, talent, etc.).
additional_notes: Used to say someone has trust or confidence in a person, their own ability, or a quality. 'Su' is a possessive that can mean his, her, your (formal), their, or one's — context determines which. To emphasize 'one's own', speakers may say 'su propia' or 'en sí mismo(a)'. Common collocations: 'confianza en su líder', 'confianza en su capacidad', 'confianza en su talento'.
target_language_example: Ella tiene confianza en su experiencia.
native_language_example: She has confidence in her experience.

meaning: (phrase form of confiar) to entrust something (el + masculine singular noun) to someone; to trust someone with something
additional_notes: This entry shows the phrase fragment 'confiar el' which is incomplete on its own. In Spanish, confiar is used either with 'en' (confiar en alguien = to trust someone) or as 'confiar + direct object + a + persona' (confiar algo a alguien = to entrust something to someone). 'Confiar el' typically appears when the direct object is a masculine singular noun that follows (e.g., 'confiar el paquete a...'). The full useful structure is: confiar el + [masculine singular noun] + a + alguien. Pronouns or clitic placement may vary (le/les).
target_language_example: Voy a confiar el paquete a mi amigo; confíar el paquete es fácil con la dirección correcta.
native_language_example: I am going to entrust the package to my friend; entrusting the package is easy with the correct address.

meaning: to trust each other (part of the phrase 'confiar el uno en el otro').
additional_notes: This is not a complete standalone phrase; it's usually part of reciprocal expressions like 'confiar el uno en el otro' or 'confiar el uno al otro' meaning 'to trust one another.' Spanish normally uses the reflexive/reciprocal construction 'el uno al otro' or 'el uno en el otro' after the verb confiar. Use 'confiar en' + person for 'to trust someone.'
target_language_example: Debemos confiar el uno en el otro para que el equipo funcione.
native_language_example: We must trust one another for the team to work.

meaning: to trust one another / trust each other
additional_notes: Used reflexively between people: literal structure is 'confiar el uno en el otro' (masc.) or 'confiar la una en la otra' (fem.) to mean 'to trust each other'. Often appears as 'confiar el uno en el otro' or 'confiarse el uno al otro' in variants. Verb usar: confiar (followed by 'en' + person). Subject agreement and gender affect 'uno/otra'.
target_language_example: En una relación sana, hay que confiar el uno en el otro.
native_language_example: In a healthy relationship, you must trust each other.

meaning: with me (followed by a verb or place) — literally 'with me to'.
additional_notes: Conmigo means 'with me'. The preposition a may follow when indicating movement toward a place or inviting someone to come with you to do something (e.g., 'ven conmigo a la tienda' — 'come with me to the store'). Native speakers more often say 'ven conmigo' (come with me) or 'ven conmigo a + place/infinitive'. 'Conmigo a' by itself is not a fixed phrase; it's the combination of 'conmigo' + 'a' used before a destination or an infinitive.
target_language_example: ¿Quieres venir conmigo a la playa este fin de semana?
native_language_example: Do you want to come with me to the beach this weekend?

meaning: with me in / on (used when specifying a place, situation, or device where someone is with the speaker)
additional_notes: This is the preposition 'conmigo' (with me) followed by 'en' to introduce a location, situation, or medium: e.g. 'conmigo en la foto' (with me in the photo) or 'conmigo en el coche' (with me in the car). It's a bit redundant in some contexts (often you'd say 'conmigo' alone or 'en...' alone), but it's common when you want to specify where the person is together with you.
target_language_example: ¿Quieres venir conmigo en el coche?
native_language_example: Do you want to come with me in the car?

meaning: 'with myself' — used to refer to oneself (often for emphasis: being honest, angry, or at peace with oneself).
additional_notes: Conmigo combines con + mí (with me). Mismo adds emphasis or reflexivity ('myself'). Common in expressions about feelings, conscience, or being able to live with one's actions (e.g., 'no podría vivir conmigo mismo' = 'I couldn't live with myself'). Use conmigo mismo for males; female speakers often say conmigo misma, though conmigo (without mismo/a) is also possible in some contexts.
target_language_example: Después de lo que hice, necesito estar en paz conmigo mismo.
native_language_example: After what I did, I need to be at peace with myself.

meaning: with me for; (used to indicate someone/something intended for or accompanying me)
additional_notes: This is a combination of 'conmigo' (with me) + 'para' (for/to). It often appears when saying someone or something is accompanying you or is meant for you: e.g., 'Viene conmigo para la reunión' (He/She is coming with me for the meeting) or 'Trajo un regalo conmigo para ti' (He/She brought a gift with me for you) — note that word order and prepositions can vary; sometimes speakers say 'viene conmigo a la reunión' instead. For beginners: focus on 'conmigo' = 'with me' and 'para' = 'for/to' and combine meanings.
target_language_example: Él viene conmigo para la fiesta.
native_language_example: He is coming with me for the party.

meaning: 'with me for' (literal sequence: conmigo + por); often part of larger phrases meaning 'with me because of', 'with me for the reason of', or 'with me on (a topic)'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but a sequence that appears when 'conmigo' (with me) is followed by the preposition 'por' introducing a reason, motive, duration, or cause. You will usually see it inside longer sentences, for example: 'ven conmigo por diez minutos' (come with me for ten minutes) or 'no estés conmigo por eso' (don't be with me because of that). Word order and context determine the exact meaning.
target_language_example: Ven conmigo por unos minutos.
native_language_example: Come with me for a few minutes.

meaning: "with me" + "if" (used in conditional sentences meaning 'with me if...')
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase itself; it's the combination of conmigo (with me) and si (if). You will see it in sentences giving a conditional offer, invitation, or stating that someone would come/act with the speaker under certain conditions. Word order in Spanish is flexible: 'ven conmigo si quieres' = 'come with me if you want.'
target_language_example: Él vendrá conmigo si le preguntas.
native_language_example: He will come with me if you ask him.

meaning: 'with me' followed by 'and' — literally 'with me and'.
additional_notes: Conmigo means 'with me'. When followed by y ('and') it links 'with me' to something or someone else (e.g., 'with me and [someone/thing]'). In spoken Spanish you may hear the two words together, but they are simply the prepositional phrase + conjunction. Use the normal word order: 'conmigo y [persona/actividad]'.
target_language_example: Ven conmigo y María al mercado.
native_language_example: Come with me and María to the market.

meaning: he/she/you (formal) knows the (feminine plural noun) / Tom knows the (feminine plural).
additional_notes: Conoce is the third-person singular (él/ella/usted) form of conocer — 'to know' (people, places, facts, or be familiar with). 'Las' is the feminine plural definite article ('the') and agrees with a following feminine plural noun (e.g., reglas, noticias, consecuencias). Together they appear in sentences like 'Ella conoce las noticias' or 'Tom conoce las reglas.' If the subject is 'yo' you'd say 'conozco las'; for 'tú' it's 'conoces las'; for plural third person it's 'conocen las'.
target_language_example: Ella conoce las reglas del juego.
native_language_example: She knows the rules of the game.

meaning: 'knows very' (third-person singular or formal 'you' form of conocer + adverb 'muy')
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but a combination: conoce (he/she/you formal knows or is familiar with) + muy (very). You will usually see it followed by an adjective, adverb, or past participle (e.g., 'conoce muy bien' = 'knows very well'). On its own 'conoce muy' is incomplete and needs more words to finish the idea.
target_language_example: Él conoce muy bien la ciudad.
native_language_example: He knows the city very well.

meaning: we know (someone).
additional_notes: Used with a direct object person introduced by 'a' (personal 'a') to say you know someone. 'Conocemos' = first-person plural of 'conocer' (to know/meet). Use 'conocemos a [persona]'. In contexts it can mean 'we know' (are acquainted with) or 'we have met'.
target_language_example: Conocemos a los vecinos desde hace tres años.
native_language_example: We have known/are acquainted with the neighbors for three years.

meaning: we have known (someone/something) since (a time or event).
additional_notes: Plural first-person form of conocer (conocemos) followed by desde to indicate the starting point in time or situation. Use with a date, duration, event, or phrase (e.g., 'desde 2010', 'desde la escuela', 'desde que éramos niños'). Can refer to people, places, or facts. Structure: 'Conocemos desde + (date/event)' or 'Conocemos a + [person] desde + (time)'.
target_language_example: Conocemos desde 2010, cuando empezamos a trabajar juntos.
native_language_example: We have known each other since 2010, when we started working together.

meaning: they know the
additional_notes: conocen is the third-person plural (ellos/ustedes) of conocer, meaning "to know" or "to be familiar with." When followed by "el" + noun, it means "they know the [noun]" or "they are familiar with the [noun]." Depending on context, conocer can mean knowing a person/place/fact or being acquainted with something. Watch for gender/number: "conocen la" for feminine nouns, "conocen los/las" for plural. "Conocer" differs from "saber" — use conocer for familiarity/acquaintance (people, places, things) and saber for facts/ability.
target_language_example: No conocen el barrio como nosotros.
native_language_example: They don't know the neighborhood like we do.

meaning: to meet/know you through (someone or something); to get to know you because of
additional_notes: Used to indicate the person, place, event, or reason through which someone became acquainted with another. Common with verbs like 'conocer' (conocerte) plus 'por' to mark cause or source: e.g. 'Te conocí por Juan.' Works in various tenses and constructions (conocerte, te conocí por, te conoceré por).
target_language_example: Fue lindo conocerte por casualidad en la feria; nunca lo olvidaré.
native_language_example: It was nice to meet you by chance at the fair; I'll never forget it.

meaning: known by everyone; well-known to all.
additional_notes: Used to say a person (or sometimes a thing) is widely known in a community or group. Often followed by a location (en la ciudad, en el pueblo) but can stand alone. 'Conocido' functions as an adjective meaning 'known' and 'por todos' = 'by everyone'.
target_language_example: Él es conocido por todos en el pueblo.
native_language_example: He is known by everyone in the village.

meaning: they met at / met (each other) in/at (a place or event).
additional_notes: Conocieron is the third-person plural preterite of conocerse (to meet/get to know one another). Use 'se conocieron en...' to say where or at what event two or more people first met. Commonly followed by a place, event, or time (en la secundaria, en una fiesta, en Caimán Brac).
target_language_example: Se conocieron en la universidad el año pasado.
native_language_example: They met at university last year.

meaning: 'met (someone) in/at'.
additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of conocer + preposition en. Used to say where or when someone first met another person. Subject can be yo/él/ella/usted/etc. For meeting places use 'en' + place/time (e.g., en Boston, en la universidad, en una conferencia).
target_language_example: Lo conoció en la fiesta del colegio.
native_language_example: She met him at the school party.

meaning: I met (him/her) at the… / I met (someone) in the…
additional_notes: Conocí is the first-person singular preterite of conocer (to meet/know). 'Conocí en la...' is used to say where you met someone (follow with a place: la estación, la biblioteca, la mezquita). If the direct object is masculine use 'lo' or 'le' before 'conocí' (Lo conocí / Le conocí); for feminine use 'la' (La conocí). Word order can vary: 'Lo conocí en la estación' or 'Conocí a Aitor en la estación.'
target_language_example: Lo conocí en la cafetería.
native_language_example: I met him at the café.

meaning: 'I met a' or 'I got to know a' (female noun follows).
additional_notes: Conocí is the first-person preterite of conocer (to meet/know). Use 'conocí una' when saying you met a woman or a feminine noun (e.g., conocí una amiga — I met a (female) friend). If the thing met is masculine, use 'conocí un'. Can also mean 'I learned about' or 'I became familiar with' depending on context.
target_language_example: Conocí una amiga nueva en la fiesta.
native_language_example: I met a new (female) friend at the party.

meaning: meet
additional_notes: From conocer a alguien, used before a person. In these examples it means meeting someone or becoming acquainted with them, not knowing a fact. Conozcas is the present subjunctive form of conocer, so it often appears after phrases like quiero que.... The a is the personal a used before people.
target_language_example: Espero que conozcas a mi hermano este fin de semana.
native_language_example: I hope you meet my brother this weekend.

meaning: that you meet/get to know me (subjunctive phrase; note: 'a mí' should have an accent and word order is unusual)
additional_notes: This phrase appears to be an attempt to use the verb conocer in the subjunctive with the direct object 'a mí'. Correct spelling and more natural forms: 'a mí' (accent on mí) and usually 'me conozcas' instead of 'conozcas a mí'. The raw sequence 'conozcas a mi' is unidiomatic in standard Spanish but may appear in nonstandard speech or as a literal translation from English. Use after verbs/expressions that trigger the subjunctive (e.g., 'Espero que...').
target_language_example: Espero que conozcas a mí algún día.
native_language_example: I hope you meet/get to know me someday.

meaning: I know (someone) from / I know about (a topic) from (a source).
additional_notes: Depends on context. With a person, 'conozco de' can mean 'I know (someone) from (a place or event)' (e.g., 'conozco a María de la universidad' → 'I know María from university'). With things or topics, it can mean 'I know about something from (a source)' (e.g., 'conozco eso de oídas' → 'I know that by hearsay'). Note: most commonly Spanish uses 'conozco a' for knowing a person and 'conozco' + noun/direct object without 'de' for knowing a topic; 'de' is used to specify origin, source, or context.
target_language_example: Conozco de esa película por las críticas que leí.
native_language_example: I know about that movie from the reviews I read.

meaning: I have known (someone) since / for (a period of time).
additional_notes: Used to say how long you have known a person. Often appears as 'conozco desde siempre' (since forever), 'conozco desde hace años' (for years), or with a specific time: 'conozco a María desde 2010'. The verb 'conocer' is conjugated to the speaker (conozco = I know). If speaking about others, change the conjugation: 'la conozco', 'los conozco', 'lo conozco'.
target_language_example: La conozco desde hace cinco años.
native_language_example: I have known her for five years.

meaning: I have known (someone/something) since (a time or event).
additional_notes: Used to state how long you've known a person or been familiar with something; it combines the verb conocer in the present (conozco) with 'desde que' + clause (since + point in time or event). The clause after 'desde que' can be a date, a year, an event, or another clause (e.g., 'desde que éramos niños', 'desde que llegaste'). For other subjects or tenses, change 'conocer' accordingly (e.g., 'conocemos desde que...', 'conocía desde que...').
target_language_example: Conozco desde que éramos niños y seguimos siendo amigos.
native_language_example: I've known (them) since we were children and we're still friends.

meaning: 'to get (hold of) someone' or 'to reach/contact someone' (or 'to obtain/arrange someone' in some contexts).
additional_notes: Used with a person as direct object introduced by the preposition a. Common meanings: to reach someone by phone, to find/obtain someone to do a task (e.g., cover a shift), or informally to 'get' someone (as in attract or succeed with them). Context determines sense—phone/reach vs. hire/find vs. pursue. Often followed by a name or pronoun (conseguir a Tom, conseguir a alguien).
target_language_example: No pude conseguir a María por teléfono, así que le dejé un mensaje.
native_language_example: I couldn't get María on the phone, so I left her a message.

meaning: to get, obtain, or manage to have something; 'something' = algo.
additional_notes: Conseguir = to obtain, get, or achieve. With 'algo' it means to get some/anything/a bit of something (depends on context). Used for tangible things (food, money) and abstract results (success). Verb can change meaning with tense (e.g., 'conseguí' = I got; 'estabas cerca de conseguir' = you were close to getting).
target_language_example: Voy a la tienda a conseguir algo de beber.
native_language_example: I'm going to the store to get something to drink.

meaning: 'to get/obtain the' (feminine singular object follows)
additional_notes: Conseguir means 'to get', 'to obtain', or 'to manage to' (when followed by an infinitive). When you see 'conseguir la', the direct object is feminine singular (la = 'her' or 'it' for feminine nouns). It can be followed by a noun (conseguir la entrada = get the ticket) or a past participle/verb phrase in contexts like 'conseguirla' (pronoun attached). In spoken/written Spanish the pronoun is often attached: 'conseguirla'.
target_language_example: Quiero conseguir la entrada para el concierto.
native_language_example: I want to get the ticket for the concert.

meaning: to get/obtain it (or him) — 'conseguir' + direct object pronoun 'lo' (masculine/neutral).
additional_notes: Conseguir means 'to get,' 'to obtain,' or 'to manage to (do)' something. When written as two words (conseguir lo) the pronoun is separated for emphasis, clarity, or in contexts like subordinate clauses or when using certain syntactic constructions; more commonly in standard writing the pronoun attaches (conseguirlo). 'Lo' refers back to a masculine or neutral thing/idea or to a male person. Placement and spelling change with mood/tense: it attaches to infinitives and affirmative imperatives (consíguelo) but is separate after conjugated verbs in some structures (creo que puedo conseguir lo — though most writers prefer "creo que puedo conseguirlo"). Informal speech often contracts or attaches the pronoun.
target_language_example: Si insistes, podré conseguir lo que quieres.
native_language_example: If you insist, I will be able to get what you want.

meaning: I got/obtained the (feminine noun).
additional_notes: Conseguí is the first-person preterite of conseguir (to get/obtain). 'La' is the feminine singular direct article (the) used before a feminine noun: e.g. la entrada, la llave, la pintura. Use 'conseguí el' for masculine nouns. Can also mean 'I managed to get' in contexts where obtaining required effort.
target_language_example: Conseguí la receta que pediste.
native_language_example: I got the recipe you asked for.

meaning: advice to his/her/your/formal (singular) [someone].
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but a short sequence: consejo (advice) + a (to) + su (his/her/your formal/their). It typically appears before a noun or pronoun (e.g., "consejo a su hijo" = "advice to his son") or before a verb phrase when referring to giving advice to someone. Pay attention to whose advice it is by the possessor su (can mean his, her, your formal, or their) and to number/formality context. For beginner use, treat it as 'advice to [someone]'.
target_language_example: Le di un consejo a su hermana sobre estudiar más.
native_language_example: I gave a piece of advice to his sister about studying more.

meaning: advice or tip from/about (followed by a person, source, or topic).
additional_notes: Use 'consejo de' to indicate the origin or topic of advice. Common structures: 'un consejo de [persona]' (advice from someone) or 'consejo de [tema]' (tip about a topic). To say 'a piece of advice,' use 'un consejo'. For advice directed at someone, use 'consejo para [persona]'.
target_language_example: Recibí un consejo de mi profesor sobre cómo estudiar mejor.
native_language_example: I received advice from my teacher about how to study better.

meaning: thoughtful/kind of (someone).
additional_notes: Used with a possessive phrase (su parte, tu parte) to say that an action or comment was thoughtful or considerate coming from that person. Common formulas: "Es muy considerado de tu parte" or shorter "Muy considerado de su parte." Not followed directly by a person (you say "de tu parte", not "de tú").
target_language_example: Es muy considerado de tu parte ayudarme con la mudanza.
native_language_example: It's very considerate of you to help me with the move.

meaning: construction of; building of; the act/process of constructing (something).
additional_notes: Used to talk about the building or creation of physical structures (roads, towers, buildings) or abstract processes (nation-building). Follows with the thing being built: 'construcción de + [noun]'. Can refer to a specific project ('la construcción de la Torre Eiffel') or a general activity ('la construcción de carreteras').
target_language_example: La construcción de la autopista terminará el próximo año.
native_language_example: The construction of the highway will finish next year.

meaning: the construction of (the)
additional_notes: A common phrase used to talk about building or erection of something. 'Construcción' = construction; 'del' = contraction of 'de + el' meaning 'of the'. Use before a masculine singular noun (el muro, el edificio, el hospital). If the noun is feminine use 'de la' (construcción de la casa) or plural 'de los/las'.
target_language_example: La construcción del puente terminará en diciembre.
native_language_example: The construction of the bridge will finish in December.

meaning: contact you / get in touch with you.
additional_notes: Common formal phrase used when someone (I/we/they) will contact or try to contact the person addressed (usted = formal you). Often appears in business or polite contexts. Verbs commonly used with it: ponerse en contacto (to get in touch), intentar/try, ponerse/te pondré/nos pondremos, etc.
target_language_example: Me pondré en contacto con usted mañana por la tarde.
native_language_example: I will get in touch with you tomorrow afternoon.

meaning: eye contact
additional_notes: Used to describe looking directly into someone’s eyes. Common in phrases about making, avoiding, or maintaining eye contact. Can be used with verbs like hacer (hacer contacto visual), tener (tener contacto visual), evitar, mantener.
target_language_example: No te preocupes, mantén contacto visual durante la presentación.
native_language_example: Don't worry, maintain eye contact during the presentation.

meaning: in cash; literally and emphatically 'cash' (immediate, physical money)
additional_notes: Used to emphasize payment in actual cash (not credit, check, or promise). Also used figuratively to stress that something is exactly or plainly what it is (often in rude or strong expressions). Common in Spain and some Latin American countries. Formality: neutral when about money, potentially coarse when used in insults.
target_language_example: Quiero el pago contante y sonante, no un cheque.
native_language_example: I want payment in cash, not a check.

meaning: to tell (something) to someone; to count/consider (someone) among (a group) — depends on context.
additional_notes: Primary use: contar a + person = to tell or relate information to someone (e.g., contar a alguien). Also appears in contexts meaning 'to include' or 'to count' when followed by a group or phrase (often introduced with 'sin contar a' = 'not counting'). Verb is transitive; direct object is the thing told, and the recipient is introduced with 'a'.
target_language_example: No le quiero contar a María lo que pasó ayer.
native_language_example: I don't want to tell María what happened yesterday.

meaning: to count on / to rely on someone or something; to have available (resources).
additional_notes: Commonly used to express trust or dependence (count on someone) or that something is available to you (you have something to rely on). Use with people or things. Conjugates like regular -ar verb in pronominal construction: 'puedes contar con él' = you can count on him. Can also mean 'to have' in contexts like 'contar con dinero/ayuda'.
target_language_example: Siempre puedes contar con mí para ayudar.
native_language_example: You can always count on me to help.

meaning: to be about / to tell (a story) about (something or someone)
additional_notes: Used when saying what a story, book, film, article, or conversation concerns. Often appears as 'contar (algo) del/de la/los/las (tema/persona)'. In many contexts Spanish speakers prefer 'tratar de' or 'hablar de' as alternatives; some varieties may favor 'contar sobre' or simply 'contar' without 'de'. Register is neutral; context determines whether it implies narration or subject matter. Example: 'El libro cuenta del viaje' is understandable but many speakers prefer 'El libro trata del viaje' or 'El libro cuenta el viaje'.
target_language_example: La escritora contó del miedo que sintió durante la expedición.
native_language_example: The writer told about the fear she felt during the expedition.

meaning: to count from one (to a given number).
additional_notes: Used to talk about counting starting at one up to some number (often spoken as 'contar del uno al diez', 'al cien', etc.). Common in questions asking if someone knows how to count in a language. The phrase is literal and compositional.
target_language_example: ¿Puedes contar del uno al veinte en español?
native_language_example: Can you count from one to twenty in Spanish?

meaning: 'to count the' or 'to tell the' depending on context (contar = to count / to tell).
additional_notes: Contar is a versatile verb: it can mean 'to count' (numbers, money, items) or 'to tell'/'to relate' (a story, a secret, someone's day). The article 'el' simply specifies a masculine noun that follows (el resto, el dinero, el secreto, el día). Word order and context determine whether it's 'count' or 'tell'. 'Sin contar' means 'not counting' or 'excluding'.
target_language_example: Voy a contar el dinero ahora.
native_language_example: I'm going to count the money now.

meaning: to tell to; to reveal to (imperfect subjunctive form of contar + the preposition a, indicating to whom something is told).
additional_notes: This is the imperfect subjunctive form (contara) of the verb contar combined with the preposition a to mark the indirect object (to whom). Common in subordinate clauses after verbs expressing desire, requests, fear, doubt, or commands (e.g., querer que, pedir que, rogar que, temer que). English equivalents often use phrases like 'that [someone] tell to [someone]' or 'that [someone] would tell [someone]'. Pronouns or noun phrases follow a. Example contexts: pedir que no se lo contara a nadie, querer que se lo contara a todos. Agreement and clitic placement follow Spanish subjunctive rules (e.g., se lo contara a todos).
target_language_example: La persiguieron para que no se lo contara a nadie.
native_language_example: They pursued her so that she wouldn't tell it to anyone.

meaning: 'I will tell a (story/joke/thing)'.
additional_notes: From the verb contar (to tell) in future first-person singular (contaré) plus the indefinite article una. Usually followed by a noun like 'historia' (story) or 'broma' (joke): e.g. 'Contaré una historia' = 'I'll tell a story.' Can be used to introduce something you will tell someone. Tone neutral; context decides what follows.
target_language_example: Contaré una historia sobre mis viajes.
native_language_example: I'll tell a story about my travels.

meaning: the contents of / the content of
additional_notes: Used to refer to what is inside or what is contained in something (a letter, bag, envelope, body, pockets, etc.). Followed by the container or thing being described: contenido de + [sustantivo]. Can refer to physical items or abstract content (ideas, information).
target_language_example: Revisa el contenido de la mochila antes de ir.
native_language_example: Check the contents of the backpack before leaving.

meaning: happy/pleased to (feminine speaker).
additional_notes: Used by a female speaker (contento for male) to say they are happy or pleased about something or to do something. Often followed by an infinitive (de + verb) or a subordinate clause introduced by que. Translate as ‘happy to’ or ‘glad that’.
target_language_example: Estoy contenta de conocerte.
native_language_example: I'm happy to meet you.

meaning: 'happy/content' that (followed by a subjunctive clause).
additional_notes: Used to express that someone is pleased about something that may be uncertain or dependent on another action; typically followed by a verb in the subjunctive (e.g., 'esté', 'haya', 'venga'). Agree 'contenta' with a female speaker (male would say 'contento de que'). Can also be used with plural forms (contentos/as de que).
target_language_example: Estoy contenta de que vengas mañana.
native_language_example: I'm happy that you're coming tomorrow.

meaning: 'happy/pleased that' (used with a clause).
additional_notes: Used to express that someone (female speaker or about a female) is happy or pleased about something. Often followed by a subordinate clause introduced by que + verb. Male speakers would say contento que. In casual speech, the indicative is common; the subjunctive may appear depending on nuance (e.g., deseo or emotion with uncertainty).
target_language_example: Estoy contenta que hayas venido hoy.
native_language_example: I'm glad that you came today.

meaning: happy/pleased that; glad to (followed by a clause or infinitive).
additional_notes: Used to express being pleased about something. Often followed by 'que' + subjunctive for feelings about events or people (e.g., 'estamos contentos de que vengas/estés'). Can also be followed by an infinitive or noun phrase to indicate being pleased to have or do something (e.g., 'contentos de tener'). Agreement: 'contentos' changes for gender/number ('contenta(s)/contento(s)').
target_language_example: Estamos contentos de que vengas.
native_language_example: We're happy that you can come.

meaning: he/she/it answered/replied (the...) — third person past of contestar + masculine singular article
additional_notes: This is the past (preterite) third-person form of contestar (to answer) followed by the masculine singular definite article el. It usually introduces the thing being answered (e.g., 'contestó el profesor' = 'the teacher answered') or begins a clause 'contestó el...' followed by a noun or clause. Gender and number must agree with the noun that follows (e.g., 'contestó la' for feminine).
target_language_example: Contestó el director que habría una reunión mañana.
native_language_example: The director answered that there would be a meeting tomorrow.

meaning: with you (followed by a verb or phrase that starts with 'a'), e.g. 'with you to...'
additional_notes: Contigo means 'with you' (familiar singular). It's normally used alone (contigo). 'Contigo a' appears when the preposition 'a' follows immediately — for example, in constructions like '¿Vas contigo a la fiesta?' (less common) or more naturally 'ir contigo a...' ('to go with you to...'). In many cases you will see 'contigo' + verb or 'contigo a' + noun/place. Use 'contigo' for informal you (tú).
target_language_example: Quiero ir contigo a la playa.
native_language_example: I want to go with you to the beach.

meaning: with you now / right now with you (often refers to being together or available to talk at this moment).
additional_notes: Combines 'contigo' (with you) and 'ahora' (now). Used to say you are currently with someone, available to speak now, or to emphasize timing (e.g., not ready to marry/leave someone right now). Context determines whether it means physically together or emotionally/temporally available.
target_language_example: No puedo hablar por teléfono, pero puedo estar contigo ahora.
native_language_example: I can't talk on the phone, but I can be with you now.

meaning: 'with you to' or 'with you at' (a fragment used before a verb or place)
additional_notes: This is not a complete fixed phrase by itself; it's the preposition 'contigo' (with you) followed by the contraction 'al' (a + el) meaning 'to the' or 'at the'. You will see it where a speaker says they are going somewhere or doing something together: e.g. "contigo al cine" (with you to the cinema) or before verbs in colloquial speech when 'a' introduces an infinitive (less common). Make sure the noun after 'al' is masculine singular because 'al' = 'a' + 'el'.
target_language_example: Voy contigo al mercado.
native_language_example: I'm going with you to the market.

meaning: with you (followed by a noun or phrase) — 'contigo' = with you; 'de' often links to what follows (e.g., 'contigo de viaje').
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself; 'contigo' means 'with you' (informal singular tú). The preposition 'de' after 'contigo' may be used when describing a relationship, role, or purpose (e.g., 'contigo de guía' — 'with you as a guide' or more naturally 'contigo como guía'), or in casual speech when followed by a noun phrase. More common constructions are 'contigo' alone (with you) or 'contigo como...' (with you as...). 'Contigo' is informal (uses tú).
target_language_example: ¿Vienes conmigo? — No, prefiero ir contigo de acompañante.
native_language_example: Are you coming with me? — No, I'd rather go with you as a companion.

meaning: 'with you' + a time or situation marker (e.g. 'with you in a minute', 'with you on a cold day').
additional_notes: Contigo = 'with you'. When followed by a time expression (en un minuto, en un segundo) it means you'll be with the person at that time. When followed by a situation (en todo, en un día frío) it links 'with you' to agreement or imagining someone in that situation. The two-word sequence is compositional and very common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Estaré contigo en cinco minutos.
native_language_example: I'll be with you in five minutes.

meaning: Literal components: 'contigo' = with you, 'esta' intended as 'está' (he/she/it is) but missing the written accent. As written ('contigo esta') is an unaccented form; in standard Spanish the correct form is 'contigo está' meaning 'is with you' (used to say someone/something is accompanying or present with you).
additional_notes: The written form should include the acute accent on 'está'. Without the accent, 'esta' can be confusing because 'esta' (without accent) is the demonstrative pronoun/adjective 'this' in some nonstandard writings, but standard Spanish requires 'está' for the verb. Typical word order is 'está contigo' rather than 'contigo está', though both are grammatically possible. Use when indicating presence or accompaniment: e.g. 'Él está contigo.'
target_language_example: Mi mochila contigo esta (debería escribirse 'contigo está').
native_language_example: My backpack is with you (should be written 'contigo está').

meaning: 'with yourself' — used to refer to being at peace, honest, or comfortable in your own company or with your own feelings/actions.
additional_notes: Commonly used after verbs/adjectives (estar, sentirse, vivir, sé) to talk about being comfortable, honest, or at peace internally. Can contract to 'contigo' when 'mismo' is unnecessary, but 'mismo' adds emphasis ('with yourself, really'). Used for both positive (estar en paz contigo mismo) and reflective commands (sé honesto contigo mismo).
target_language_example: Antes de criticar a otros, está en paz contigo mismo.
native_language_example: Before criticizing others, be at peace with yourself.

meaning: ‘with you if’ — used to say you'll go or do something with someone, conditional on their wish or a condition.
additional_notes: This is the phrase 'contigo' (with you) followed by 'si' (if). It appears in informal spoken Spanish to offer or agree to do something with someone, often shortened speech: e.g., 'I can go with you if you want.' Word order may vary ('si quieres, voy contigo') and punctuation often includes a comma: 'contigo, si...'.
target_language_example: Puedo ir contigo si quieres.
native_language_example: I can go with you if you want.

meaning: with you about / to talk to you about (something).
additional_notes: Used when addressing someone directly to introduce a topic you want to discuss with them. More natural word order in Spanish is 'hablar contigo sobre…' or 'hablar contigo de…'. 'Sobre' = 'about' (can also mean 'on' or 'on top of'). Often followed by the topic (esto, algo importante, Tom, mi horario).
target_language_example: Quería hablar contigo sobre el viaje de verano.
native_language_example: I wanted to talk to you about the summer trip.

meaning: with you a… (literally).
additional_notes: This looks like part of a phrase rather than a complete fixed expression. 'Contigo' means 'with you' (informal singular tú). 'Un' is the indefinite article 'a' or 'one' and must agree in gender/number with the noun that follows (e.g., 'contigo un rato' = 'with you for a while', though more natural is 'contigo, un rato'). Alone 'contigo un' is incomplete — you need a noun or phrase after 'un'.
target_language_example: ¿Vienes conmigo? — Sí, contigo un rato.
native_language_example: Are you coming with me? — Yes, with you for a while.

meaning: with you and (used to link 'with you' to something that follows).
additional_notes: Contigo means 'with you'. When followed by y ('and'), it connects 'with you' to another element: e.g. 'contigo y con otros' ('with you and with others') or in colloquial speech it can start a phrase like 'contigo y sin ti...' depending on context. Not a fixed idiom by itself — its exact sense depends on the words that follow.
target_language_example: Voy contigo y con María al cine.
native_language_example: I'll go with you and with María to the cinema.

meaning: 'against' or 'in opposition to' (used before a noun or pronoun).
additional_notes: Spanish normally uses just 'contra' to mean 'against' (e.g., 'contra la pared', 'contra el equipo'). 'Contra de' is less common and often considered nonstandard or regional; standard Spanish prefers 'contra' alone. 'Contra de' may appear in colloquial speech or certain dialects, especially before pronouns, but it's safer to use 'contra' in formal writing.
target_language_example: Estoy contra de eso, pero podemos discutirlo.
native_language_example: I'm against that, but we can discuss it.

meaning: against the (feminine singular noun) — a combination of prepositions sometimes used to indicate opposition or contact, though it's uncommon and can sound redundant.
additional_notes: 'Contra' alone or 'en contra de' are more typical for expressing opposition. 'Contra la' is usual for physical contact (e.g., 'contra la pared'). 'Contra de la' appears in some dialects or colloquial speech but is generally nonstandard; prefer 'contra la' or 'en contra de la' depending on context. When encountered, it functions compositionally as 'contra' + 'de' + feminine singular article 'la'.
target_language_example: Ella habló en contra de la propuesta y dijo 'votar contra de la propuesta sería un error'.
native_language_example: She spoke against the proposal and said, 'voting against the proposal would be a mistake.'

meaning: against me; opposed to me
additional_notes: This phrase is a nonstandard/colloquial sequence in Spanish. The more common and grammatically recommended forms are "en contra de mí", "en mi contra" or simply "contra mí". Use the accented pronoun "mí" after a preposition. "Contra de mi" (without accent and with both "contra" and "de") may be heard regionally or informally but is generally considered incorrect in prescriptive grammar.
target_language_example: Siento que todo está contra de mi en este momento.
native_language_example: I feel like everything is against me right now.

meaning: against his/her/their (something) — used to express opposition or contact with possession
additional_notes: This is a nonstandard or regional combination. Standard Spanish usually uses just contra + noun (e.g., contra su opinión) or en contra de + su. 'Contra de su' may appear in colloquial speech in some areas but is generally redundant. Use 'contra su' or 'en contra de su' for clarity. The possessive su matches the possessed noun in person (his/her/your/its/their).
target_language_example: Ella estaba en contra de su decisión, pero no dijo nada.
native_language_example: She was against his/her decision, but said nothing.

meaning: colloquial/nonstandard variant of 'contra el' meaning 'against the (masculine singular noun)'
additional_notes: Standard Spanish contracts the preposition 'contra' with the masculine definite article as 'contra el', not 'contra del'; 'contra del' is considered nonstandard or regional in some dialects and may be heard in informal speech. Avoid in formal writing. Use 'contra la/los/las' with feminine/plural nouns as appropriate; only 'el' is involved in this nonstandard form. Grammatically, 'contra del' results from analogical use of the preposition 'contra' with the contracted form 'del' (de + el).
target_language_example: El camión chocó contra del muro en la curva.
native_language_example: The truck crashed against the wall on the curve.

meaning: against me / against my (something) — indicates physical contact against the speaker or opposition to the speaker/will.
additional_notes: Used in two common senses: 1) physical contact: an animal or object rubbing or pressing 'against me' (often followed by a noun: contra mi pierna), and 2) opposition or lack of consent: acting 'against me' or 'against my will' (contra mi voluntad). 'Mi' is the unstressed possessive 'my' (no accent).
target_language_example: El perro se apoyó contra mi pierna para dormir.
native_language_example: The dog leaned against my leg to sleep.

meaning: against a (feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Contra is a preposition meaning 'against' or 'versus'. When followed by the indefinite article una it becomes 'against a' for feminine singular nouns (e.g., una enfermedad, una roca). Used for physical contact (golpeó su cabeza contra una roca), opposition or competition (carrera contra una tortuga), or contrast (contra una camisa blanca — meaning 'against a white shirt' in visual/contextual descriptions).
target_language_example: Se apoyó contra una pared mientras esperaba.
native_language_example: He leaned against a wall while he waited.

meaning: control of / the control of (used before a masculine noun).
additional_notes: A common phrase combining the noun 'control' with the preposition 'de' plus the definite article 'el' (contracted as 'del') to indicate possession or authority over something. Used with masculine singular nouns (el volumen, el Atlántico, el programa). In English often translated as "control of" or "the control of/over."
target_language_example: Ella tiene el control del proyecto.
native_language_example: She has control of the project.

meaning: remote control (device used to operate something from a distance).
additional_notes: Commonly refers to the handheld device for TVs, stereos, etc., but can also mean remote control in a broader sense (the concept or ability to control from afar). Used in everyday speech. Stress: con-TROL re-MO-to.
target_language_example: Pásame el control remoto, por favor.
native_language_example: Pass me the remote control, please.

meaning: to control the / to have control over the (masculine noun that follows).
additional_notes: This is the verb controlar ('to control') followed by the masculine definite article el. It requires a masculine noun after 'el' (e.g., el espacio, el avión, el día). Use it when saying you can or cannot control something. For feminine nouns use 'controlar la'.
target_language_example: No puedo controlar el tráfico hoy.
native_language_example: I can't control the traffic today.

meaning: 'I told (to)'. (Preterite of contar + indirect object marker 'a' to introduce the person told.)
additional_notes: Used to say you told someone something in the past. Spanish uses 'contar' (to tell) and places the person told after 'a' (Le conté a María...). With direct/indirect object pronouns you may see 'se lo conté' (I told it to him/her/them — note 'le/les' becomes 'se' before 'lo/la/los/las').
target_language_example: Ayer le conté a Ana la verdad.
native_language_example: Yesterday I told Ana the truth.

meaning: conversation in (a language or context).
additional_notes: Used to indicate the language or setting in which a conversation takes place (e.g., conversación en inglés = conversation in English) or the context/topic (conversación en la mesa = conversation at the table). Commonly appears before a language, place, or context. Followed by a noun or noun phrase. Not a fixed idiom—literal meaning.
target_language_example: La conversación en español fue muy útil para practicar.
native_language_example: The conversation in Spanish was very helpful for practicing.

meaning: conversion to (a change or transformation into something).
additional_notes: Commonly used before a noun to indicate transformation or change of state, form, use, or units (e.g., conversión al formato PDF, conversión al cristianismo, conversión al sistema métrico). 'Al' = 'a' + 'el' so the following noun is typically masculine. Use 'conversión a' when no definite article is required.
target_language_example: La conversión al formato digital facilitó el acceso a los documentos.
native_language_example: The conversion to digital format made the documents easier to access.

meaning: you will become (into).
additional_notes: Second-person singular future of 'convertir(se) en'. Used to say someone will change into or become something/someone. Often followed by a noun or noun phrase. When reflexive (convertirse en) it emphasizes a change of state or identity. English translations can be 'you will become' or 'you will turn into.'
target_language_example: Si sigues practicando, te convertirás en un buen pianista.
native_language_example: If you keep practicing, you will become a good pianist.

meaning: they/you (formal plural) become or turn into (someone/something).
additional_notes: From the verb convertir(se) + preposition en. Used to say that people or things change state or transform into something else (literal or figurative). Subject determines English pronoun: 'se convierten en' = 'they become/turn into' (or 'you become' in formal plural contexts). Often followed by a noun or phrase indicating the new state/identity.
target_language_example: Con el tiempo, se convierten en buenos amigos.
native_language_example: Over time, they become good friends.

meaning: became
additional_notes: Past tense (ellos/ustedes) of 'convertir(se) en' — indicates change of state or role: 'to become' or 'to turn into'. Often used with reflexive 'se convirtieron en' for people/things changing into something else (became friends, became a family, became hits). Can be translated as 'became' in most contexts. Not formal/informal by itself; register depends on context.
target_language_example: Con el tiempo, se convirtieron en muy buenos amigos.
native_language_example: Over time, they became very good friends.

meaning: became the / turned into the (masculine singular noun that follows)
additional_notes: From convertir(se) en + noun: 'convert/turn into'. 'Convirtió en el' is past (él/ella/usted or third-person) and is followed by a masculine singular noun or phrase (el + noun). Common in narratives: 'X convirtió en el Y' = 'X turned into the Y' or 'X made/turned into the Y'. If the subject is reflexive (change by itself) use 'se convirtió en el'.
target_language_example: La rana se convirtió en el príncipe después del hechizo.
native_language_example: The frog became the prince after the spell.

meaning: became a (feminine singular).
additional_notes: From the verb convertirse (to become, to turn into). Used with 'se' for reflexive construction: 'se convirtió en una ...' means someone or something changed into or became something else. 'Una' marks a feminine singular noun (use 'un' for masculine). Common for life changes, transformations, or becoming a role/identity.
target_language_example: Después de años de estudio, ella se convirtió en una doctora respetada.
native_language_example: After years of study, she became a respected doctor.

meaning: a cup/glass of; 'copa' can mean a stemmed glass, cup, or trophy; 'de' introduces what it contains or belongs to.
additional_notes: Used to say a serving or container plus its contents (una copa de vino = a glass of wine) or to indicate possession/association (la copa de tu madre = your mother's cup/trophy). 'Copa' often refers to a stemmed glass (wine, champagne) or a decorative cup/trophy; for coffee people more commonly say 'taza de' but 'una copa de café' is possible. Use 'de' to link to the content or owner.
target_language_example: Por favor, tráeme una copa de vino tinto.
native_language_example: Please bring me a glass of red wine.

meaning: Likely a fragment: 'copa' = cup, glass (for wine); 'y' = and. Together 'copa y' by itself is incomplete—usually part of a list (e.g., 'copa y plato' = 'glass and plate').
additional_notes: This looks like two separate words: copa (a drinking glass, goblet, or trophy) and y (and). By itself 'copa y' is not a fixed phrase; it's simply 'cup/glass and …' and must be followed by another item. Use 'copa' for a wine glass (la copa de vino), a drinking glass in formal settings, or a trophy (ganar la copa). 'Y' is the coordinating conjunction 'and'.
target_language_example: Una copa y un plato, por favor.
native_language_example: A glass and a plate, please.

meaning: the courage to / the bravery to (do something)
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive or noun to say someone has the courage/bravery to do something or to face something. Common synonyms: 'valor', 'tener coraje de' or 'tener el coraje de'. Often appears as 'tener coraje de + infinitive' or 'el coraje de + infinitive'.
target_language_example: Tuvo el coraje de empezar de nuevo.
native_language_example: He had the courage to start again.

meaning: the heart of (the) — used to say the central or most important part of something
additional_notes: Corazón means 'heart' (literal and figurative). When followed by del (de + el), it introduces what something is the center/core of: corazón del país, corazón del asunto. Use with masculine singular nouns (del). For feminine nouns use 'corazón de la'. Can be literal (anatomy) or figurative (core, center).
target_language_example: El corazón del pueblo está en su plaza.
native_language_example: The heart of the town is in its square.

meaning: Not a fixed phrase; likely a word sequence meaning 'heart is' (corazón = heart, es = is).
additional_notes: This is not a common fixed expression in Spanish. It is simply the noun corazón ('heart') followed by the verb ser in third person singular (es = is). Use depends on context, for example to describe the heart or speak metaphorically: 'El corazón es fuerte' (The heart is strong). If you saw this in poetry or song, the verb may introduce a characteristic or definition of 'the heart.'
target_language_example: El corazón es valiente cuando ama de verdad.
native_language_example: The heart is brave when it truly loves.

meaning: 'the heart is' (literal); commonly appears as part of sentences describing physical or emotional state of the heart.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase on its own; it's the verb phrase formed by the noun corazón (heart) + the verb estar ('to be'). Expect it in contexts like describing physical symptoms (e.g., "mi corazón está acelerado" — my heart is racing) or emotional states (e.g., "mi corazón está contento" — my heart is happy). Use estar (está) for temporary conditions; for more permanent characteristics Spanish uses ser (e.g., "mi corazón es valiente").
target_language_example: Mi corazón está acelerado después de correr.
native_language_example: My heart is racing after running.
