meaning: of extinction; used in the phrase 'en peligro de extinción' = endangered.
additional_notes: Usually appears in the fixed expression 'en peligro de extinción' (endangered). It describes species or things at risk of disappearing. 'De extinción' by itself often needs 'en peligro' before it in natural speech.
target_language_example: El lince ibérico está en peligro de extinción.
native_language_example: The Iberian lynx is endangered.

meaning: 'trustworthy' or 'reliable' (used after a noun or pronoun).
additional_notes: Common adjective phrase meaning someone or something you can trust. Often appears after nouns/pronouns (e.g., 'es de fiar', 'no soy de fiar'). Can describe people, groups, or things (e.g., 'mi gente es de fiar').
target_language_example: Ella es de fiar; puedes contarle el secreto.
native_language_example: She is trustworthy; you can tell her the secret.

meaning: of/end (part of compound expressions meaning 'end' or 'final').
additional_notes: Alone, 'de fin' is not a complete phrase in Spanish; it appears inside compound expressions like 'de fin de semana' (weekend) or 'de fin' as part of longer nouns/adjectives (e.g., 'ropa de fin de año'). It typically links a noun to a word meaning 'end' or 'final' and is followed by another noun (semana, año, temporada). Not used by itself to mean 'end'.
target_language_example: Voy a hacer una escapada de fin de semana.
native_language_example: I'm going on a weekend trip.

meaning: by the end of (a period: month, year, etc.).
additional_notes: Used with a time period (mes, año) to mean 'by the end of [period]' or 'before the end of [period]'. Common in phrases like 'antes de fin de mes' or 'fiesta de fin de año'. Often appears without an article: 'antes de fin de mes' (not 'antes del fin de mes').
target_language_example: Necesito entregar el informe antes de fin de mes.
native_language_example: I need to hand in the report by the end of the month.

meaning: 'in depth' / 'background' / 'long-distance' depending on context.
additional_notes: This phrase is multi-use. Common senses: 1) 'de fondo' = 'in depth' or 'underlying' (Hay algo más de fondo = there's something deeper/underlying). 2) 'trabajo de fondo' = background work / groundwork. 3) in sports, 'corredor de fondo' or 'esquí de fondo' = long-distance (endurance) runner/skier. Context determines whether it refers to depth/underlying matters, background tasks, or long-distance/endurance activities.
target_language_example: Hay que investigar más de fondo antes de decidir.
native_language_example: We need to investigate more in depth before deciding.

meaning: 'in a ... way' / 'in a ... manner' — used to describe how something is done.
additional_notes: Followed by an adjective or adverb (e.g., de forma ordenada, de forma segura) to say that something happens or is done in that manner. Common alternative: 'de manera' or simply using an adverb (ordenadamente → less common). Use to modify verbs or actions.
target_language_example: Habla de forma clara para que todos entiendan.
native_language_example: Speak in a clear way so everyone understands.

meaning: of photos / photo(s) (showing possession, content, or type)
additional_notes: A short prepositional phrase using 'de' + noun. It can indicate that something is made of, about, containing, or related to photos: e.g. 'muestra de fotos' = a photo exhibition/showcase; 'toneladas de fotos' = tons of photos. Word order: Spanish uses 'de' to link nouns or describe content/possession.
target_language_example: Hicimos un álbum de fotos del viaje.
native_language_example: We made a photo album of the trip.

meaning: of/from phrases; (used to indicate a quantity or relation involving phrases)
additional_notes: A simple prepositional phrase: 'de' (of/from) + 'frases' (phrases). Commonly appears after words indicating quantity (un montón de frases = a lot of phrases), possession or description (colección de frases = collection of phrases). Word order and agreement: 'frases' is plural, so use plural determiners or verbs as needed.
target_language_example: Encontré una colección de frases útiles para estudiar.
native_language_example: I found a collection of useful phrases to study.

meaning: 'face to face' / 'directly' / 'head-on'.
additional_notes: Used to describe something done directly, openly, or from the front (physically or figuratively). Common contexts: physical direction (facing someone/coming straight at you), speaking plainly/honestly ('te lo digo de frente' = I tell you directly), or confronting a problem head-on. Can be short (just 'De frente.') to indicate direction.
target_language_example: Si tienes algo que decir, dímelo de frente.
native_language_example: If you have something to say, tell me directly (face to face).

meaning: of force; relating to strength or use of force.
additional_notes: Used after a noun to indicate something is about force or strength (e.g., 'demostración de fuerza' = show of force) or to describe amount/intensity (e.g., 'más de fuerza' = more force/strength). Can refer to physical strength, legal/police use of force, or figurative strength. Commonly appears in fixed phrases like 'uso de fuerza' (use of force) or 'chalecos de fuerza' (literally 'force vests'—context: restraints/protective gear).
target_language_example: Necesitamos una demostración de fuerza para calmar la protesta.
native_language_example: We need a show of force to calm the protest.

meaning: to quit smoking (with a time reference: '... ago').
additional_notes: Dejar de fumar = to quit smoking. When followed by hace + time period, it indicates how long ago the action happened (e.g., 'dejé de fumar hace dos años' = 'I quit smoking two years ago'). Commonly conjugate 'dejar' to match subject (dejé, debí haber dejado, etc.). 'Hace' introduces the elapsed time.
target_language_example: Mi padre dejó de fumar hace cinco años.
native_language_example: My father quit smoking five years ago.

meaning: used to list actions stopped or avoided (literally: 'to smoke and to...'); here part of 'dejar de' meaning 'to stop (doing something)'.
additional_notes: Appears after verbs like dejar (dejar de), parar (parar de), or verbs of advice/command to indicate the actions that are being stopped. In examples it links two actions: 'dejar de fumar y de beber' = 'stop smoking and stop drinking'. The second 'de' before the next verb can be omitted in casual speech ('dejar de fumar y beber'), but including it is clear and common.
target_language_example: Decidí dejar de fumar y de comer comida rápida.
native_language_example: I decided to stop smoking and (to stop) eating fast food.

meaning: easy (to ...); of easy [something].
additional_notes: Used before a noun to describe that something is easy. Often part of phrases like "de fácil acceso" (easy to access) or "de fácil uso" (easy to use). Requires a complement (e.g., accesso, aprendizaje) or an infinitive with "de" + adjective construction in descriptions.
target_language_example: Es un programa de fácil uso para principiantes.
native_language_example: It's a program that's easy to use for beginners.

meaning: This is not a fixed phrase by itself; it's the combination of "de fútbol" (of/for soccer/football) plus a reflexive/passive-marker "se" used with verbs (e.g., "se jugará", "se pospuso", "se cubrió").
additional_notes: Break into two parts: "de fútbol" = "(related) to football/soccer" (used to describe matches, team, etc.). The word "se" here is a grammatical particle used with verbs to form impersonal or passive constructions (e.g., "se jugará" = "will be played"), reflexive actions (e.g., "se cubrió de gloria" = "covered itself in glory"), or middle/impersonal voice. Beginners should treat "de fútbol" as a noun phrase and learn that "se" changes the verb meaning/voice depending on context.
target_language_example: El torneo de fútbol se jugará mañana.
native_language_example: The football tournament will be played tomorrow.

meaning: formal; for special/ceremonial occasions (dress, event, uniform).
additional_notes: Used after a noun to indicate something is for a ceremonial or very formal occasion: vestido de gala (formal gown), uniforme de gala (dress uniform), cena de gala (gala dinner). Often implies dressy, elegant, or ceremonial. Not slang.
target_language_example: Fuimos a una cena de gala y llevé mi vestido de gala.
native_language_example: We went to a gala dinner and I wore my formal gown.

meaning: of winning the (masculine singular noun that follows).
additional_notes: This is a common sequence where 'de' links a noun or expression to an infinitive verb (ganar) and a specific masculine singular object introduced by 'el' (e.g., 'el premio', 'el partido', 'el juego'). It often expresses purpose, chance, expectation, or certainty about winning. Word order and gender matter: 'el' matches a masculine singular noun; for feminine nouns use 'de ganar la'.
target_language_example: Tengo muchas ganas de ganar el torneo este año.
native_language_example: I really want to win the tournament this year.

meaning: relating to the throat; used to describe pain, irritation, voice quality or a throat condition
additional_notes: Often appears after a noun to specify that something affects the throat (e.g., 'dolor de garganta' = 'sore throat') or after verbs/adjectives to indicate origin in the throat (e.g., 'voz de garganta' = 'throaty voice'). Common collocations: dolor de garganta, picor de garganta, infección de garganta, ronquera de garganta. Not used alone; normally follows a noun.
target_language_example: Tengo dolor de garganta desde ayer.
native_language_example: I've had a sore throat since yesterday.

meaning: of government / government (as an adjective, e.g., government official, government work)
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something belongs to, is run by, or relates to the government. Often follows nouns (trabajo de gobierno = government job; forma de gobierno = form of government) or combines with nouns to describe officials or agencies (oficiales de gobierno).
target_language_example: Aceptó un puesto de gobierno en la ciudad.
native_language_example: He accepted a government position in the city.

meaning: suddenly; all at once; with a sudden movement or action.
additional_notes: Used to describe something that happens abruptly or with a quick, often forceful action. Common with verbs of movement or change (abrir, entrar, terminar, pararse). Can imply surprise or violence depending on context. Equivalent to 'all of a sudden' or 'suddenly' in English.
target_language_example: La luz se apagó de golpe y todos se asustaron.
native_language_example: The light went out suddenly and everyone got scared.

meaning: as an adult; when (someone) is grown up
additional_notes: Used to talk about what someone will do, want, or be when they are an adult. Often follows verbs or phrases like 'ser', 'querer', 'cuando sea', or appears in constructions such as 'de grande quiero...' to express future aspirations. Not the same as 'grande' alone meaning 'big'.
target_language_example: De grande quiero ser médico.
native_language_example: When I grow up I want to be a doctor.

meaning: literally 'of gloves' — appears as part of expressions referring to gloves or figuratively about cautious/delicate behavior (usually within a larger phrase).
additional_notes: On its own 'de guantes' is incomplete and uncommon; it typically appears inside phrases like 'con guantes' or 'de guantes de seda' (often reordered in speech as 'guantes de seda' or 'con guantes de seda'). Figuratively, Spanish uses constructions with 'guantes' to mean handling someone/something gently or carefully. Context and surrounding words determine exact meaning.
target_language_example: Actuó de guantes con el recién llegado para evitar conflictos.
native_language_example: He acted with kid gloves toward the newcomer to avoid conflict.

meaning: on duty; serving a shift (usually for work related to safety, medical, security, police, etc.)
additional_notes: Used to indicate someone is currently assigned to a duty shift or is the person responsible at that time. Common with professions like doctors, nurses, police, security guards, and other roles that rotate shifts. Can be used as 'estar de guardia' (to be on duty) or in plural 'turnos de guardia' (duty shifts). In sentence 6 'disfrazado de guardia' uses 'guardia' as a noun meaning 'guard' (security officer); there it is not the fixed phrase 'de guardia'.
target_language_example: Esta noche yo estoy de guardia en el hospital.
native_language_example: Tonight I'm on duty at the hospital.

meaning: of/from the guitar; (used to describe something related to the guitar).
additional_notes: A short prepositional phrase. Commonly appears after a noun to indicate the instrument (e.g., 'clase de guitarra' = guitar class), the sound or style (e.g., 'música de guitarra'), or origin/material related to a guitar. Use 'de' + instrument to say someone plays the instrument: 'tocar la guitarra' is more common than 'de guitarra' alone for 'to play guitar', but you will see 'clase de guitarra', 'lección de guitarra', 'músico de guitarra'.
target_language_example: Tomé una clase de guitarra el sábado.
native_language_example: I took a guitar class on Saturday.

meaning: literally 'of having her/it' — used after certain verbs/adjectives to introduce a past infinitive with a direct object pronoun (her/it).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but a combination: de + haber + la (feminine direct object pronoun). It appears after verbs or adjectives that require 'de' before an infinitive (e.g., 'estar feliz de', 'seguro de') or in constructions expressing possibility with 'de' + haber + past participle (e.g., 'deben de haberla levantado' = 'they must have lifted her/it'). 'La' refers to a feminine singular direct object previously mentioned (a person or feminine noun). Swap 'la' for other pronouns as needed (lo, los, las, me, te, nos).
target_language_example: Estoy contento de haberla conocido.
native_language_example: I'm happy to have met her.

meaning: to have (myself) ...
additional_notes: This is a combination of the periphrastic modal 'de' (used with deber/ deber de, etc.) plus the infinitive haber and the reflexive pronoun me. It appears in perfect infinitive constructions like 'de haberme desmayado' or 'de haberme sentado' and translates as part of English perfect infinitives ('to have [done something]' or 'of having [done something]'). With verbs like 'deber de' it can express probability ('I must have...'). Word order: Spanish places the reflexive pronoun before haber (me haber) or attached to the infinitive (haberme); both are used, but 'de haberme' matches the examples.
target_language_example: Pudo de haberme llamado antes de salir.
native_language_example: He could have called me before leaving.

meaning: of rooms; indicates information about rooms associated with a noun (e.g., number or type of rooms).
additional_notes: Commonly appears after a noun to describe its rooms: noun + 'de' + number/type (e.g., 'casa de 3 habitaciones'). Can describe bedrooms or general rooms depending on context. Not typically standalone; part of a larger noun phrase.
target_language_example: Vendieron la casa de habitaciones contiguas.
native_language_example: They sold the house of adjoining rooms.

meaning: a fragment used in commands or descriptions meaning 'to stop/start doing X and (then) ...' when combined with phrases like 'dejar/dejar de' or in lists like 'hablar y ...'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase on its own but appears in verbs constructions: 'dejar de hablar y...' (to stop talking and...) or in lists 'hablar y escribir' (to speak and write). In imperatives you often see 'Deja de hablar y escucha' = 'Stop talking and listen.' When used with 'empezar a/ empezar a...' it can show sequence: 'dejó de hablar y empezó a comer' = 'he stopped talking and began to eat.' The fragment 'de hablar y' combines the preposition 'de' (part of 'dejar de' meaning 'to stop') plus the verb 'hablar' and the conjunction 'y' (and).
target_language_example: Deja de hablar y presta atención.
native_language_example: Stop talking and pay attention.

meaning: part of a phrase meaning 'of doing the [feminine noun]' or 'to do the [feminine noun]'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but rather a sequence you'll see when a verb or noun phrase requires the preposition 'de' plus the infinitive 'hacer' and then a feminine noun (la + noun). Often appears in constructions like 'la idea de hacer la cena' (the idea of making dinner) or commands/phrases like 'de hacer la tarea' (about doing the homework). The exact meaning depends on the surrounding words; translate literally as 'of/to do the ...'.
target_language_example: La decisión de hacer la cena fue rápida.
native_language_example: The decision to make dinner was quick.

meaning: used to refer back to doing something already mentioned ("about doing it" / "to do it").
additional_notes: This is a fragment often seen in longer phrases (e.g., hablar de hacer lo, pensar de hacer lo) where 'de' links a verb or noun to the idea of performing an action ('hacer lo' = 'to do it'). In natural Spanish you'd more commonly see full constructions like 'hablar de hacerlo', 'pensar en hacerlo', or 'la idea de hacer lo que...'. When combined, 'hacerlo' (one word) is more natural than 'hacer lo'.
target_language_example: Estoy pensando en la idea de hacer lo mañana.
native_language_example: I'm thinking about the idea of doing it tomorrow.

meaning: a prepositional + verb-pronoun sequence where 'de' connects a preceding noun/phrase to the verb phrase 'hacerle' (hacer + le = to do/make for/to him/her/you formal/them). Often translated as 'to [verb] to/for him/her/them' or as part of fixed expressions like 'el placer de hacerle llegar' = 'the pleasure of sending/bringing to you'.
additional_notes: 'De' is not part of a single fixed verb here but commonly links a noun or abstract phrase to the verb phrase 'hacerle'. 'Hacerle' is 'hacer' (to do/make/send/pay) plus the indirect object pronoun 'le' (to/for him/her/you formal/them). Translation depends on the full expression: e.g., 'el placer de hacerle llegar' = 'the pleasure of sending/bringing to you'; 'hora de hacerle una visita' = 'time to pay him/her a visit'; 'capacidad de hacerle frente' = 'ability to confront/face it'. Use changes with context and register; 'le' may refer to people or sometimes to things (neutral/impersonal use).
target_language_example: Correos tiene el placer de hacerle llegar la carta que le fue enviada.
native_language_example: The postal service has the pleasure of sending/bringing you the letter that was sent to you.

meaning: of/for doing something to you; 'to make/ do (something) to you' (used with verbs that follow).
additional_notes: This is the preposition 'de' + the infinitive 'hacer' + the clitic pronoun 'te' (you). It appears before another verb or as part of infinitive constructions: e.g. 'acabo de hacerte...' (I just made you...), 'tratar de hacerte...' (to try to make you...). Meaning depends on the main verb and context: can mean 'to make you (feel/think/etc.)', 'to do something to you', or 'to cause you to (do/feel)'. 'Te' is the object pronoun referring to 'you' (informal singular).
target_language_example: No quiero de hacerte responsable de algo que no hiciste.
native_language_example: I don't want to make you responsible for something you didn't do.

meaning: fairy- (as in 'fairy-tale' or 'magical; perfect').
additional_notes: Used as an adjective phrase after a noun to describe something like it's from a fairy tale (magical, ideal, enchanting). Commonly appears in expressions such as 'una boda de hadas' (a fairy-tale wedding) or 'un vestido de hadas'.
target_language_example: Tuvieron una boda de hadas en la playa.
native_language_example: They had a fairy-tale wedding on the beach.

meaning: in fact
additional_notes: Used to introduce a clarification, correction, emphasis, or confirmation of what was just said. Can appear at the start of a sentence (De hecho, ...) or within it (..., de hecho, ...). Registers as neutral — common in both spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: De hecho, ya había terminado cuando llamaste.
native_language_example: Actually, I had already finished when you called.

meaning: made of iron; (figurative) very strict or strong (ironclad).
additional_notes: Used literally to describe objects made from iron (e.g., 'una puerta de hierro'). Figuratively, it describes a strict, strong, or unyielding quality (e.g., 'mano de hierro' = 'iron hand' meaning strict rule). Common in set phrases like 'mano de hierro' or 'puño de hierro.'
target_language_example: Tiene una puerta de hierro en el patio.
native_language_example: He has an iron door in the yard.

meaning: of children / about children (possessive or descriptive phrase)
additional_notes: This is not a standalone fixed phrase; it's a fragment often used after a noun to indicate relationship or category (e.g., 'familia de hijos' — family of children, or 'libro de hijos' — book about children). Context determines exact meaning: can indicate possession ('la foto de hijos' = the photo of (my) children) or a topic/category ('actividades de hijos' = activities for/about children). You will commonly see it combined with articles or possessives: 'los hijos', 'mis hijos', 'de mis hijos'.
target_language_example: Tengo fotos de hijos en mi teléfono.
native_language_example: I have photos of children on my phone.

meaning: of/for a man; masculine (descriptive), or made for men
additional_notes: Used after a noun to indicate that something belongs to, is intended for, or is characteristic of a man. Common in phrases like 'ropa de hombre' (men's clothing), 'voz de hombre' (man's voice), or 'olor de hombre' (smell of a man). Word order: noun + 'de hombre'. Not idiomatic on its own; needs a noun before it.
target_language_example: Compré una chaqueta de hombre.
native_language_example: I bought a men's jacket.

meaning: from man to / from a man to (used to indicate movement, change, or comparison involving 'man')
additional_notes: This phrase is not a fixed idiom by itself; it's the preposition de + noun + a, here with 'hombre'. It appears in contexts like 'de hombre a hombre' (man to man), 'de hombre a mujer' (from man to woman), or 'de hombre a ___' to express direction, transformation, comparison, or a relationship between people. You will usually see it as part of a longer phrase or sentence; the exact meaning depends on surrounding words.
target_language_example: Hablaremos de hombre a hombre sobre el problema.
native_language_example: We'll talk man to man about the problem.

meaning: face-to-face between men; man-to-man; frankly, one adult to another.
additional_notes: Used to indicate a direct, candid conversation or confrontation between (typically) men — often implying honesty, seriousness, or a private one-on-one talk. Can describe discussion (Hablemos de hombre a hombre) or physical contest (pelea de hombre a hombre). Tone can be neutral or slightly informal; context determines whether it's literal (two men) or figurative (an honest, direct talk).
target_language_example: Quiero hablar contigo de hombre a hombre sobre lo que pasó.
native_language_example: I want to speak with you man-to-man about what happened.

meaning: part of phrases meaning 'the kind/type of man who...'.
additional_notes: This sequence appears in descriptions like 'el tipo de hombre que...' or 'la clase de hombre que...' and introduces a relative clause describing what kind of man someone is (e.g., brave, helpful, etc.). In English: 'the kind/type of man who...'. You will usually see an article before 'tipo' or 'clase' (el tipo de hombre que...).
target_language_example: Él es el tipo de hombre que siempre llama a su madre.
native_language_example: He is the kind of man who always calls his mother.

meaning: relating to shoulders; used in the fixed expression 'encogerse de hombros' = 'to shrug (one's shoulders)'.
additional_notes: Alone, 'de hombros' means 'of/relating to shoulders' (e.g., 'ancho de hombros' = 'broad-shouldered'). Most commonly appears in the phrase 'encogerse de hombros' meaning to shrug (express indifference, uncertainty, or resignation). Use 'se encogió de hombros' for 'he/she shrugged'.
target_language_example: Ella se encogió de hombros cuando no supo la respuesta.
native_language_example: She shrugged when she didn't know the answer.

meaning: for (each) hour; by the hour
additional_notes: Used to indicate a rate, duration, or measurement per hour (e.g., pago de hora, salario de hora). Often appears in phrases like 'pago/de pago de hora' or 'trabajo de hora' but may require a noun (hora) to be clear. In some regions you might see 'por hora' more commonly for 'per hour.'
target_language_example: Cobran de hora por el servicio.
native_language_example: They charge by the hour for the service.

meaning: made of bone; bone-colored (depending on context).
additional_notes: Literally 'of bone'. Used to describe something composed from bone (e.g., a button, a handle) or, in some contexts, something the color of bone/ivory. Context determines whether it refers to material or color.
target_language_example: Llevaba un collar de hueso muy antiguo.
native_language_example: She wore a very old bone necklace.

meaning: made of bones; of bones (describes something composed of or characterized by bones)
additional_notes: Used to describe objects, structures, or people figuratively or literally as being made of bones or extremely thin/skin-and-bones. Context determines whether literal (e.g., a building made of bones) or figurative (e.g., 'bolsa de huesos' = 'bag of bones' meaning very skinny). Often follows a noun (palacio de huesos = palace of bones).
target_language_example: Encontraron una figura hecha de huesos en la cueva.
native_language_example: They found a figure made of bones in the cave.

meaning: round-trip; there and back.
additional_notes: Used to describe travel (tickets, journeys) that go from one place to another and then return to the origin. Commonly used with transporte/tickets: billete de ida y vuelta, vuelo de ida y vuelta. Can also be used figuratively for back-and-forth actions.
target_language_example: Compré un billete de ida y vuelta a Madrid.
native_language_example: I bought a round-trip ticket to Madrid.

meaning: relating to languages; 'of languages' or 'language (as a subject)'.
additional_notes: Used after a noun to specify that it concerns languages (e.g., estudio de idiomas = language study, curso de idiomas = language course). Common in phrases about learning, teaching, or tools for languages. 'De' indicates relationship/subject. Not standalone; usually follows words like 'estudio', 'curso', 'aprendizaje', 'profesor', 'ayuda'.
target_language_example: Estoy buscando un curso de idiomas para mejorar mi inglés.
native_language_example: I'm looking for a language course to improve my English.

meaning: relating to fire or a fire (e.g., fire alarm, fire extinguisher, fire department).
additional_notes: Used as a modifier after a noun to indicate something is for, caused by, or related to fire. Common in phrases like 'alarma de incendio' (fire alarm), 'puerta de incendio' (fire door), 'equipo de lucha contra incendios' (firefighting equipment). Not a complete phrase by itself; it typically follows another noun.
target_language_example: La alarma de incendio sonó a las tres de la mañana.
native_language_example: The fire alarm went off at three in the morning.

meaning: immediately
additional_notes: Used to ask or state that something should happen without delay. Can be used in formal and informal contexts. Often interchangeable with 'ahora mismo' and 'enseguida'.
target_language_example: Por favor, ven a mi oficina de inmediato.
native_language_example: Please come to my office immediately.

meaning: to go
additional_notes: The sequence 'de ir' combines the preposition 'de' with the infinitive 'ir' (to go). It appears in several common patterns: 'antes de ir' (before going), 'tener opción/ganas/intención de ir' (to have the option/want/intention to go), 'impedir/dejar de' and similar verbs can take 'de ir' after them. In some contexts (e.g. 'hablar de ir') it means 'talking about going'. Also note regional/grammatical variation: after certain verbs like 'impedir' Spanish usually uses the infinitive without 'de' (e.g. 'me impidió ir'), but some speakers include 'de' (less prescriptive).
target_language_example: Tengo intención de ir a la fiesta mañana.
native_language_example: I intend to go to the party tomorrow.

meaning: part of a phrase meaning 'about/to go to the (feminine place)'; literally 'of/to go to the'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but a sequence that appears when combining a noun or expression ending in 'de' with the verb phrase 'ir a la' (ir a + feminine article 'la'). Example contexts: 'se trata de ir a la playa' (it's about going to the beach) or 'la idea de ir a la tienda' (the idea of going to the store). Use depends on surrounding words; 'ir a la' is used before feminine singular places (la casa, la playa).
target_language_example: La idea de ir a la playa me entusiasma.
native_language_example: The idea of going to the beach excites me.

meaning: before I go to bed / before going to bed
additional_notes: Common phrase used to talk about actions that happen immediately before going to sleep. The structure includes 'irme' (to leave/go, reflexive with 'me') + 'a la cama' (to bed). In other subjects replace 'me' with the appropriate reflexive pronoun (irte, irse, irnos, iros). Often follows verbs like 'olvidar', 'siempre', or expressions of routine.
target_language_example: Apagaré las luces de irme a la cama.
native_language_example: I'll turn off the lights before I go to bed.

meaning: about/to (the act) of leaving to go somewhere (e.g., home, to sleep).
additional_notes: Common in phrases that mean 'it's time for us to leave' or 'before we leave to...'. Often appears as 'es hora de irnos a...' or simply 'hora de irnos a...'. 'Irnos' is the reflexive plural form (we leave). Use 'a' + destination or activity (a casa, a dormir).
target_language_example: Es hora de irnos a casa.
native_language_example: It's time for us to go home.

meaning: used to introduce a time or condition for someone leaving; roughly 'about leaving when' or 'for leaving when'.
additional_notes: This phrase is not a fixed idiom on its own; it typically appears inside a larger sentence such as 'se trata de irse cuando...' or 'es mejor de irse cuando...'. It links the action of leaving (irse) with a specific time, condition, or circumstance. Word-for-word translation is possible, but pay attention to the surrounding grammar (verbs, subjects, or impersonal expressions often appear before it).
target_language_example: Es importante decidir de irse cuando la fiesta se vuelva aburrida.
native_language_example: It's important to decide to leave when the party becomes boring.

meaning: of play / for playing; related to games or play
additional_notes: Used after a noun to describe something meant for play or related to games (e.g., 'arma de juego' — toy gun, 'pieza de juego' — play piece). Context matters: 'de juego' can describe toys, components in a game, or figurative playful uses. Not a complete phrase on its own; usually part of a noun phrase.
target_language_example: Compré una espada de juego para el disfraz.
native_language_example: I bought a toy/play sword for the costume.

meaning: 'to play' (used after nouns or expressions to indicate purpose, topic, origin, or part of a verbal phrase with jugar).
additional_notes: De + infinitive can appear in several structures. 'de jugar' can follow words like 'ganas de jugar' (desire to play), 'tiempo de jugar' (time to play), or be part of a phrase indicating origin/subject ('la oportunidad de jugar'). It is not a standalone verb form — context shows whether it expresses purpose, possession of a desire/ability, or part of a noun phrase. 'Jugar' means 'to play'.
target_language_example: Tengo ganas de jugar al fútbol.
native_language_example: I feel like playing soccer.

meaning: of juice / juice (as the ingredient or type, e.g. 'orange juice').
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something is made of or contains juice (de + noun). Common in phrases like 'vaso de jugo' (glass of juice) or 'jugo de naranja' (orange juice). 'De' links quantity/container to the content (dos botellas de jugo = two bottles of juice).
target_language_example: Quiero un vaso de jugo de naranja, por favor.
native_language_example: I want a glass of orange juice, please.

meaning: of June / in June (used to give dates or refer to the month of June).
additional_notes: Used after a day to state a date (e.g., 'el once de junio' = June 11). Also used to refer to the month generally ('antes de junio' = before June; 'fines de junio' = end of June). 'de' links the day to the month in Spanish date expressions.
target_language_example: La reunión es el tres de junio.
native_language_example: The meeting is on June 3.

meaning: of the
additional_notes: Combination of de + la, used before feminine singular nouns. It often shows possession, origin, source, or relation. Unlike de + el, which becomes del, de + la stays separate.
target_language_example: Vengo de la estación.
native_language_example: I'm coming from the station.

meaning: of the house
additional_notes: A literal prepositional phrase meaning ownership, origin, or location related to a house. Commonly used for 'of the house' (part of the house), 'from the house' (coming from the house), or 'in the house' when context implies location. Use depends on surrounding verbs and context.
target_language_example: Salimos de la casa a las ocho.
native_language_example: We left the house at eight.

meaning: of/from someone’s house; indicating possession or location related to a house.
additional_notes: Used to show that something belongs to, is located at, or is near a person's house. Followed by a name, noun, or pronoun (e.g., de la casa de María, de la casa de ellos). In casual speech, possessive can also be expressed with 'su' (la casa de él = su casa), but 'de la casa de' is clear and explicit.
target_language_example: Había música viniendo de la casa de Ana.
native_language_example: There was music coming from Ana's house.

meaning: of the bill / of the account (literally); often part of phrases meaning 'on the bill' or 'from the account'.
additional_notes: This phrase appears in contexts about money, bills, or accounts. It is usually combined with verbs or nouns (e.g., 'cobrar de la cuenta', 'salir de la cuenta', 'apuntar en la cuenta') to mean something is charged to, taken from, or recorded on an account or bill. Without more context it can be ambiguous: 'cuenta' can mean bill (restaurant), bank account, or an itemized account/record.
target_language_example: Pagué la cena de la cuenta del restaurante.
native_language_example: I paid the dinner from the restaurant bill.

meaning: from the shelf; off the shelf.
additional_notes: Used to indicate something taken from or falling off a shelf (estantería = shelf/bookcase). Common in contexts with books or objects stored on shelves. Can be used with verbs like tomar, sacar, caer, quitar.
target_language_example: Ella sacó el jarrón de la estantería.
native_language_example: She took the vase off the shelf.

meaning: out of the room without (doing something)
additional_notes: This phrase combines 'salir de la habitación' (to leave the room) with 'sin' (without) to indicate leaving while not doing or saying something. Often followed by an infinitive (e.g., 'sin decir') or a subordinate clause with 'que' + imperfect/subjunctive ('sin que nadie se diera cuenta'). Common in everyday and written Spanish.
target_language_example: Ella salió de la habitación sin decir nada.
native_language_example: She left the room without saying anything.

meaning: of the electricity / relating to electricity or light (depends on context).
additional_notes: Commonly appears in phrases about the electricity bill (la cuenta de la luz). Literally 'of the light' — can refer to electric power, physical light, or be part of idiomatic expressions (e.g., 'la gente de la luz' = people associated with light, 'sacarlo de la luz' context-dependent). Pay attention to context to know whether it means electrical power, illumination, or a figurative use.
target_language_example: Pagamos la factura de la luz ayer.
native_language_example: We paid the electricity bill yesterday.

meaning: from the hand; (2) holding hands; (3) figuratively: caused by or connected with
additional_notes: Common literal uses: something taken 'from the hand' or body part (e.g., snatched off the hand). Used to describe people 'de la mano' meaning 'holding hands' (often with agarrados de la mano or simplemente 'de la mano'). In some contexts it can imply cause or connection (e.g., 'de la mano de' = 'by/with the help of' or 'under the direction of'). Context determines whether it's literal (physical hand) or idiomatic (relationship/causal).
target_language_example: Caminaban de la mano por el parque.
native_language_example: They walked hand in hand through the park.

meaning: in the same way; likewise; similarly.
additional_notes: Used to compare actions, feelings, or manners: 'in the same way as...' or to agree/echo someone ('me too' or 'likewise'). Can be followed by 'que' + clause to show comparison (de la misma manera que...).
target_language_example: Ella explicó el problema de la misma manera que yo.
native_language_example: She explained the problem in the same way as I did.

meaning: suddenly; out of nowhere; unexpectedly.
additional_notes: Used to say that something happens without warning or appears with no clear cause. Common in spoken and written Spanish. Can introduce an action (e.g., alguien aparece de la nada) or describe a change (e.g., todo empezó de la nada).
target_language_example: El gato apareció de la nada en la ventana.
native_language_example: The cat appeared out of nowhere at the window.

meaning: of/from the snow; (made) from snow
additional_notes: Literal phrase combining the preposition de + definite article la + noun nieve. Used to indicate origin, material, or possession related to snow (e.g., "capa de la nieve" = the layer of the snow, or "hecho de la nieve" = made of snow). Context determines whether it means 'of the snow', 'from the snow', or 'made of snow.'
target_language_example: Los huellas venían de la nieve.
native_language_example: The footprints came from the snow.

meaning: 'from the night of' or 'from (time) in the evening/night to...'.
additional_notes: Used to indicate a time span that starts in the evening/night and continues to another time (often omitted here; usually appears as part of a larger time expression, e.g. "de la noche a la madrugada" or "de la noche a la mañana"). Commonly follows a clock time: "a las 8 de la noche a las 11" (from 8 PM to 11).
target_language_example: La fiesta será de la noche a la madrugada.
native_language_example: The party will be from the evening into the early morning.

meaning: from the night to the... (incomplete phrase, usually part of 'de la noche a la mañana' meaning 'overnight' or 'from one night to the next')
additional_notes: This fragment by itself is incomplete. It's commonly seen in the full expression 'de la noche a la mañana' meaning 'overnight' or 'suddenly' (literally 'from the night to the morning'). You may also see 'de la noche a la mañana' shortened in speech to mean a fast or unexpected change. Do not use 'de la noche a la' alone without the final word; it will sound unfinished.
target_language_example: Su vida cambió de la noche a la mañana.
native_language_example: His life changed overnight.

de la noche a la mañana

target_language_multi_word_term: de la noche a la mañana
meaning: overnight; suddenly, in a very short time
additional_notes: Used to describe a rapid or unexpected change that seems to happen from one day to the next. Can be literal (overnight) but is most often figurative: 'became rich overnight' = suddenly became rich. Common in both formal and informal contexts.
target_language_example: No se hizo famoso de la noche a la mañana; trabajó años para eso.
native_language_example: He didn't become famous overnight; he worked for years for that.

meaning: of/from the earth; of/from (this) land or country; (idiom) 'of the earth' meaning humble or native.
additional_notes: Literal meaning: 'of the earth' or 'from the land'. Used in several senses: 1) geographic origin (una chica de la tierra de Kansas = a girl from the land of Kansas / from Kansas), 2) to describe all people or the whole world (el más solo de la tierra = the most lonely in the world), 3) idiomatic/figurative uses like 'la sal de la tierra' (the salt of the earth = humble, good people), or poetic/religious phrases (raza divina de la tierra). Context determines whether it refers to the physical earth/world, a country/region, or a figurative quality.
target_language_example: Él es el mejor músico de la tierra de nuestra región.
native_language_example: He is the best musician from the land of our region.

meaning: literally 'of the old woman' or 'of the old (female)'; commonly a fragment used within expressions to indicate something belonging to or done in the 'old' way, or referring to an older woman depending on context
additional_notes: 'De la vieja' by itself is a fragment, not a standalone idiom. It appears in longer phrases or sentences (e.g., describing something 'of/from the old woman' or 'of the old way'). Context determines meaning: it can be literal (possessions or relations of an older woman) or idiomatic when part of expressions about traditional methods. More common in informal speech and regional usages; not typically used alone in formal writing.
target_language_example: La receta de la vieja siempre ha sido la mejor de la familia.
native_language_example: The old woman's recipe has always been the best in the family.

meaning: of the rain / from the rain (shows possession or source: 'the sound of the rain').
additional_notes: Commonly used after a noun to indicate that something belongs to, comes from, or is caused by rain. Very literal and compositional: 'de' = of/from, 'la lluvia' = the rain. Can appear in phrases like 'el sonido de la lluvia' (the sound of the rain) or 'las gotas de la lluvia' (the raindrops).
target_language_example: Me gusta el olor de la lluvia después de la tormenta.
native_language_example: I like the smell of the rain after the storm.

meaning: of the
additional_notes: Combination of de + la, used before feminine singular nouns. It often shows possession or description ('of the') or origin/source/location ('from the'), depending on context. Compare with de + el, which usually contracts to del.
target_language_example: Vengo de la biblioteca.
native_language_example: I'm coming from the library.

meaning: 'to the side' / 'aside' / 'sideways' (depending on context).
additional_notes: Used both literally and figuratively. Literally: describe position or direction (e.g., move something to the side, place sideways). Figuratively: mean 'aside' or 'set aside' (put aside a topic, feeling, or habit). In phrases like 'mirar de lado' it means to look sideways or give a sidelong glance. Common in combinations: 'dejar de lado' = 'to leave aside / set aside / give up'.
target_language_example: Vamos a dejar ese problema de lado por ahora.
native_language_example: Let's put that problem aside for now.

meaning: 'of thieves' or 'belonging to thieves' — used to describe something related to or characteristic of thieves, or to label people as thieves.
additional_notes: Literal combination of de + ladrones. Commonly appears after nouns to indicate a group or characteristic (e.g., una banda de ladrones = a band of thieves). Can also be used in expressions accusing someone (acusó de ladrones = accused them of being thieves). Context determines whether it describes membership (part of a group) or an attribution (someone is called/accused a thief).
target_language_example: Encontramos pruebas en la bolsa de ladrones.
native_language_example: We found evidence in the thieves' bag.

meaning: of long / long (used before a feminine noun phrase like 'de larga duración')
additional_notes: This is a prepositional + adjective fragment meaning 'of long' or 'long' and is not a complete phrase by itself. It usually appears before a feminine noun (e.g., 'de larga duración' = 'of long duration', 'de larga distancia' = 'long-distance'). When paired with masculine nouns you'd see 'de largo' in some set phrases, but many common collocations use 'de larga' + feminine noun. Use it to describe length (time, distance, size) in compound expressions.
target_language_example: Tienen una relación de larga duración.
native_language_example: They have a long-term relationship.

meaning: part of a comparative phrase meaning 'of the most/one of the ...est cities' (e.g. 'one of the most ... cities').
additional_notes: This fragment appears inside comparative constructions: typically follows a noun or appears after a superlative adjective phrase. Common pattern: 'una de las ciudades más + adjective' = 'one of the most + adjective + cities' (e.g. 'una de las ciudades más bonitas' = 'one of the most beautiful cities'). Can also appear as 'de las ciudades más' + verb phrase when describing a group. Not a standalone phrase; you need an article/quantifier (una/una de) or context to complete the meaning.
target_language_example: Barcelona es una de las ciudades más interesantes de España.
native_language_example: Barcelona is one of the most interesting cities in Spain.

meaning: of the largest cities / from the biggest cities
additional_notes: A descriptive phrase used after a noun to indicate that something belongs to, comes from, or is about the biggest cities. Commonly follows prepositions or verbs (e.g., 'una de las ciudades más grandes' = 'one of the largest cities'). 'Más grandes' means 'bigger/largest' depending on context — with 'más' it usually means 'most' (superlative) when compared within a group.
target_language_example: Madrid es una de las ciudades más grandes de España.
native_language_example: Madrid is one of the largest cities in Spain.

meaning: one of the times; of the times (often part of expressions meaning 'sometimes' or referring to frequency)
additional_notes: This fragment usually appears inside larger phrases about frequency, e.g. 'una de las veces' (one of the times) or 'de las veces que' (of the times that / when). By itself it's not a complete sentence. Use to refer to a particular instance among several or to introduce a relative clause about occasions.
target_language_example: Una de las veces que fui al mercado, conocí a mi vecino.
native_language_example: One of the times I went to the market, I met my neighbor.

meaning: of washing / to wash (part of verb phrases like 'terminar de lavar' or 'máquina de lavar' — depends on context).
additional_notes: Not a standalone phrase—'de' combines with verbs or nouns. Common uses: 'terminar de lavar' (to finish washing), 'acabar de lavar' (to have just washed), and 'máquina de lavar' (washing machine). Context determines whether it expresses the action 'to wash' (with an infinitive) or indicates possession/type ('washing' as an adjective for a machine).
target_language_example: Acabo de lavar la ropa.
native_language_example: I have just washed the clothes.

meaning: of the lesson / lesson's (used to link something to a lesson)
additional_notes: This phrase is a simple prepositional phrase made of de + lección. It indicates possession, origin, topic, or relation to a lesson (e.g., material, vocabulary, exercises of the lesson). It is compositional and literal. You will most often see it inside longer phrases like "vocabulario de la lección" (vocabulary of the lesson) — note that in most contexts Spanish uses the article: "de la lección." Alone, "de lección" is uncommon without an article and may appear in clipped contexts (e.g., headings, labels) or fixed expressions.
target_language_example: Materiales de lección: ejercicios y lecturas.
native_language_example: Lesson materials: exercises and readings.

meaning: Not a complete standalone phrase in Spanish; typically part of a larger expression where 'de leche' (of milk / made with milk) is followed by 'en' to introduce additional information (e.g., 'de leche en polvo').
additional_notes: On its own 'de leche en' is incomplete and uncommon. You'll usually encounter it as part of compounds or descriptions such as 'de leche en polvo' (powdered milk), 'de leche en lata' (milk in a can), or within a clause like 'tarta de leche en la nevera'. If you find 'de leche en' in text, read the surrounding words to determine the full phrase; it is not a fixed idiom.
target_language_example: La fórmula de leche en polvo se etiqueta como "de leche en polvo" para indicar su origen.
native_language_example: The powdered milk formula is labeled as "de leche en polvo" to indicate its origin.

meaning: of/from reading this; used to refer to something that comes from or is related to reading this (text).
additional_notes: This is a short sequence of words rather than a fixed idiomatic phrase. It appears when someone talks about consequences, impressions, or information 'from reading this' (e.g., 'la conclusión de leer este artículo' = 'the conclusion from reading this article'). Depending on context, Spanish more naturally uses forms like 'al leer esto', 'de leer esto', or 'por leer esto'. Choose the form that fits the sentence structure.
target_language_example: La idea que saco de leer este libro es que nunca es tarde para cambiar.
native_language_example: The idea I get from reading this book is that it's never too late to change.

meaning: likely a fragment meaning 'to read it/her' or part of a larger phrase involving leer (to read); not a standalone phrase.
additional_notes: This looks like a sequence of words rather than a fixed multiword expression. 'De' can be a preposition ('of', 'from', 'about'), 'leer' is the infinitive 'to read', and 'la' is a direct object pronoun ('it' feminine or 'her') or a definite article. Without more context, 'de leer la' is not a common fixed phrase in Spanish. It could appear inside sentences like 'la costumbre de leer la prensa' (the habit of reading the press) where 'de leer la' links a noun + infinitive + article, or as part of a verbal construction with a preposition, but you should not treat it as a single phrase to memorize.
target_language_example: Tengo el hábito de leer la prensa todas las mañanas.
native_language_example: I have the habit of reading the press every morning.

meaning: part of a phrase meaning 'to read a(n)' (literally 'of/to read a').
additional_notes: This sequence by itself is not a complete phrase — it's the preposition/article + verb + indefinite article that appear inside longer sentences (e.g., 'la tarea de leer un capítulo' or 'me gusta de leer un libro' — note: the second example is ungrammatical; correct Spanish would be 'me gusta leer un libro'). In natural Spanish the verb 'leer' usually appears without the preposition 'de' unless it's part of a larger construction (e.g., 'la obligación de leer un informe', 'tengo ganas de leer un libro'). Pay attention to whether 'de' is required: some verbs and nouns call for 'de' before an infinitive, others do not.
target_language_example: Tengo ganas de leer un libro esta noche.
native_language_example: I feel like reading a book tonight.

meaning: 'to read it' or 'from reading it' depending on context
additional_notes: This is the preposition de + infinitive phrase leer + direct object pronoun lo. It can mean 'to read it' when used after verbs that take an infinitive (e.g., 'tratar de leerlo' = 'to try to read it') or indicate cause/source as 'from reading it' (e.g., 'me enteré de leerlo' — less common). Word order can change: 'leerlo' often stands alone; 'de leerlo' appears after nouns or verbs that require de. The pronoun lo refers to a masculine/neuter object (a text, message, book).
target_language_example: Intento de leerlo antes de la reunión.
native_language_example: I try to read it before the meeting.

meaning: 'by far' / 'from afar' (depends on context).
additional_notes: Has two common uses: 1) spatial: 'from a distance' or 'from afar' (e.g., looking at something from far away). 2) emphatic: 'by far' to indicate a clear difference or superlative (e.g., 'by far the best'). Context determines meaning.
target_language_example: De lejos, se veía la montaña más alta.
native_language_example: From afar, the tallest mountain could be seen.

meaning: of languages / related to languages (often part of phrases like 'enseñanza de lenguas' = language teaching).
additional_notes: Commonly appears after a noun to indicate the noun's relation to 'languages' (e.g., aprendizaje de lenguas = language learning; lenguas extranjeras = foreign languages). Usually combined with adjectives (de lenguas extranjeras) or other nouns (enseñanza de lenguas).
target_language_example: Trabajo en un departamento de lenguas en la universidad.
native_language_example: I work in a languages department at the university.

meaning: of getting up / about getting up (refers to the action of rising from bed).
additional_notes: This is the infinitive reflexive verb 'levantarse' ('to get up') preceded by the preposition 'de' as part of phrases like 'hora de levantarse' (time to get up) or 'hábito de levantarse' (habit of getting up). Used to talk about the act of rising from bed or starting the day. Infinitive + 'de' construction often links nouns (hora, hábito) or expressions to the action.
target_language_example: Mi horario de trabajo cambia el mes que viene, así que el momento de levantarse será distinto.
native_language_example: My work schedule changes next month, so the time to get up will be different.

meaning: 'legal' or 'by law'; also 'genuine' / 'official' depending on context.
additional_notes: Primary meaning: something that is permitted, required, or established by law (e.g., documento de ley = legal document). Informally, in some countries 'de ley' can mean genuine, authentic, or proper (similar to 'the real thing' or 'official'). Context determines whether it refers to legal status or authenticity. Commonly used after a noun.
target_language_example: Necesitamos un contrato de ley para este acuerdo.
native_language_example: We need a legal contract for this agreement.

meaning: textbook; typical, classic or perfect example of something
additional_notes: Used after a noun to say that something is the ideal or textbook example (e.g., comportamiento de libro = textbook behavior). Can also describe something literal from a book, but most common use is figurative: 'like in a book' / 'classic'. Often used colloquially in spoken Spanish.
target_language_example: Fue una ruptura de libro: sin dramas, todo claro y civilizado.
native_language_example: It was a textbook breakup: no drama, everything clear and civil.

meaning: of literature / about literature; used to indicate a subject or field (literature).
additional_notes: Commonly follows nouns like profesor, clase, estudiante to show specialization or the topic being discussed (e.g., profesor de literatura = literature professor; clase de literatura = literature class). Can specify types (literatura medieval, literatura francesa).
target_language_example: Ella es estudiante de literatura contemporánea.
native_language_example: She is a contemporary literature student.

meaning: 'to call you' when used after verbs or expressions that take 'de' + infinitive (indicates intention, attempt, or being about to do something)
additional_notes: Appears after verbs or phrases like 'tratar', 'estar a punto', 'tener intención', forming constructions such as 'traté de llamarte' (I tried to call you) or 'estuve a punto de llamarte' (I was about to call you). 'Llamarte' = 'llamar' (to call) + clitic 'te' (you). The 'de' is part of the governing expression, not part of 'llamar'.
target_language_example: Anoche traté de llamarte a tu celular.
native_language_example: Last night I tried to call you on your cell phone.

meaning: of keys / key (something) — describes possession, purpose or type related to keys
additional_notes: Used after a noun to indicate that the noun is related to keys (e.g., 'anillo de llaves' = key ring) or to show possession/purpose (e.g., 'caja de llaves' = box for keys). Common in compound nouns and phrases. The exact translation depends on context: 'de' can mean 'of', 'for', or indicate material/type.
target_language_example: Tengo una caja de llaves en la entrada.
native_language_example: I have a key box in the entryway.

meaning: of/from arriving here; used to refer to something related to the moment or act of arriving at this place (often part of larger constructions)
additional_notes: This is a fragment rather than a standalone idiom and usually appears after other words (e.g., prepositions or verbs) to indicate relation to the act or moment of arriving here. Context determines whether it expresses time ('from the time of arriving here'), cause ('because of arriving here') or reference ('about arriving here'). Not commonly used in isolation.
target_language_example: Hablamos mucho de llegar aquí y de lo que nos esperaba.
native_language_example: We talked a lot about arriving here and about what awaited us.

meaning: a preposition + infinitive fragment used when talking about carrying/taking something; often appears in compounds like 'comida de llevar' (takeaway food) or as part of phrases indicating suitability for carrying or taking away.
additional_notes: By itself 'de llevar' is a fragment (de + llevar) and usually depends on surrounding words to form a full meaning. Common uses: 'comida de llevar' (takeaway food), 'cosas de llevar' (things to take), or in regional/colloquial expressions. Context determines whether it's literal (to carry/take) or idiomatic; check the full phrase for precise translation.
target_language_example: Prefiero pedir comida de llevar esta noche.
native_language_example: I prefer to order takeaway food tonight.

meaning: of what
additional_notes: Not usually a complete expression on its own. de often means 'of', 'from', or 'about', and lo is a neuter form that refers to an idea, situation, or quality rather than a specific noun. You'll often see it in patterns like de lo que ('about/of what') or de lo + adjective, as in de lo importante ('about what is important').
target_language_example: No entiendo nada de lo que pasó.
native_language_example: I don't understand anything about what happened.

meaning: 'otherwise' or 'if not'.
additional_notes: Used to present the negative consequence or alternative that will happen if the previous condition or instruction is not met. Common in both formal and informal contexts; often appears at the start of a sentence or clause.
target_language_example: Termina la tarea ahora; de lo contrario, no podrás salir.
native_language_example: Finish the homework now; otherwise, you won't be able to go out.

meaning: about / regarding (something previously mentioned); 'about the thing of...'
additional_notes: Informal conversational connector used to refer back to a topic, event, or person already known in the conversation. Often followed by a noun or name (real or implied) or used alone: '¿Qué piensas de lo de [evento/tema]?' It can imply 'the matter of' or 'that thing about'. Common in spoken Spanish.
target_language_example: Hablamos mañana de lo de la fiesta.
native_language_example: We'll talk tomorrow about the thing regarding the party.

meaning: one of the best; really excellent; top quality
additional_notes: Used to praise people, performances, things, or efforts. Often follows a verb or noun (e.g., 'estar de lo mejor', 'lo has hecho de lo mejor', 'lo mejor de lo mejor'). Tone is positive and idiomatic — common in spoken Spanish. Can be used alone as a short compliment: '¡De lo mejor!'.
target_language_example: Ese restaurante es de lo mejor de la ciudad.
native_language_example: That restaurant is one of the best in the city.

meaning: very; extremely; highly (adds emphasis to an adjective or noun).
additional_notes: Used to intensify a descriptor: 'de lo más' + adjective or noun phrase = 'very/quite + adjective'. Often placed before adjectives or nouns (e.g., 'de lo más pequeño', 'una escena de lo más normal'). Tone is neutral; common in spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: La película fue de lo más entretenida.
native_language_example: The movie was very entertaining.

meaning: than
additional_notes: often appears after comparatives like más, menos, or adjectives/adverbs to mean "than": más fácil de lo que parecía. It can also mean "of/about what" after verbs or expressions that use de, as in hablar de lo que sabes. In sentences like De esto es de lo que hablo, it helps emphasize the thing being talked about.
target_language_example: Gasté menos de lo que pensaba.
native_language_example: I spent less than I thought.

meaning: of what/is (referring to the nature or quality of something).
additional_notes: Used to talk about the nature, quality, or identity of something in relation to what it actually is. Often appears in comparative or descriptive contexts like 'más de lo que es' (more than it is) or 'peor de lo que es' (worse than it is). It requires a preceding phrase (e.g., 'más', 'menos', 'mejor') or a clause to complete the thought.
target_language_example: Es mejor de lo que es en realidad.
native_language_example: It's better than it really is.

meaning: part of the phrase 'de lo que estaba hablando' — 'about what I/he/she was (was) talking', i.e. 'about what (was)'.
additional_notes: Used to refer back to something just mentioned or indicated: 'de lo que estaba hablando' = 'what I/he/she was talking about'. Often appears with demonstratives: eso/esto/eso es de lo que estaba hablando. In other contexts 'de lo que' can introduce a clause meaning 'than' (e.g., 'más de lo que...'), but in these examples it points to the topic being discussed or what is happening. Common pattern: [Eso/Esto] es de lo que estaba hablando.
target_language_example: Eso es exactamente de lo que estaba hablando.
native_language_example: That's exactly what I was talking about.

meaning: of/about what you have (done/said/accomplished).
additional_notes: A fragment used to refer back to something the person has done, said, or achieved. Often followed by a past participle (logrado, conseguido) to praise accomplishments, or by a clause to react to something said (e.g., luego de lo que has dicho). Common in expressions: 'estar orgulloso de lo que has logrado' (be proud of what you've achieved) and 'luego de lo que has dicho' (after what you said / given what you said).
target_language_example: Estoy sorprendido de lo que has conseguido este año.
native_language_example: I'm surprised by what you've achieved this year.

meaning: than I can / more than I can (do/endure/afford/etc.).
additional_notes: Used in comparisons to say that something exceeds the speaker's ability, capacity, permission or willingness. Commonly follows expressions like 'más' (more) or verbs/phrases indicating limitation (soportar, permitir, caminar, dar, expresar). Translate depending on context: 'more than I can', 'than I can handle', 'than I can afford', etc.
target_language_example: Eso es más de lo que puedo soportar.
native_language_example: That's more than I can bear.

meaning: about/what I want; literally 'of what I want' — used to refer to something the speaker wants or wants to talk about.
additional_notes: Commonly appears after words like 'algo' (something) or 'se trata' (it's about). It's a relative phrase introducing the thing being referred to: 'algo de lo que quiero hablarte' = 'something I want to talk to you about.' Word order in Spanish often places the relative clause after the noun ('algo de lo que...').
target_language_example: Hay algo de lo que quiero contarte antes de irme.
native_language_example: There is something I want to tell you before I leave.

meaning: a relative phrase used to compare or refer to something previously mentioned (literally 'than/of what one/it is'), often in comparisons like 'more than what is...'.
additional_notes: Commonly appears in comparative constructions (más/menos + de lo que se + verb/adjective) to mean 'more/less than is/was expected/said/needed.' It can also introduce reported content or a clause referring back to something already mentioned (e.g., 'de lo que se trataba' = 'about what it was/were about'). 'Se' is an impersonal or passive reflexive here and may contract with different verbs depending on context: 'de lo que se puede ver', 'de lo que se supone', 'de lo que se dice'.
target_language_example: Hay más en la historia de lo que se cuenta.
native_language_example: There is more in the story than is told.

meaning: crazy; unbelievable; insane (colloquial intensifier).
additional_notes: Used informally to describe situations, events, or places as chaotic, extreme, or hard to believe. Often follows nouns (e.g., 'una fiesta de locos') or appears in expressions like 'cosa de locos' meaning 'it's crazy.' Tone is colloquial; avoid in very formal contexts.
target_language_example: La fiesta fue de locos, no paró en toda la noche.
native_language_example: The party was crazy; it didn't stop all night.

meaning: one of the most / among the most (superlative grouping)
additional_notes: Used to compare someone or something as belonging to the top (or bottom) of a group for a quality: 'uno de los más + adjective' = 'one of the most + adjective'. Can be used with plural nouns ('los más buscados' = 'the most wanted ones'). Common in formal and everyday speech.
target_language_example: Es uno de los más rápidos del equipo.
native_language_example: He is one of the fastest on the team.

de los pies a la cabeza

target_language_multi_word_term: de los pies a la cabeza
meaning: from head to toe; completely, entirely (covering the whole body or whole person).
additional_notes: Used literally to describe something that affects the whole body (e.g., soaked from head to toe) and figuratively to describe a person's qualities or appearance as complete or thorough (e.g., thoroughly American, a good guy through and through). Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Estaba empapado de los pies a la cabeza después de la lluvia.
native_language_example: He was soaked from head to toe after the rain.

meaning: of the seven / from the seven
additional_notes: Literal phrase combining 'de' (of/from) + definite article 'los' (the, plural masculine) + numeral 'siete' (seven). Commonly used to indicate something belonging to or coming from a group of seven items or people (e.g., uno de los siete = one of the seven). Context determines whether it means 'of the seven' (possession/partitive) or 'from the seven' (origin).
target_language_example: Es uno de los siete libros que compré.
native_language_example: It's one of the seven books I bought.

meaning: a contraction meaning 'of the' or part of comparative/relative phrases like 'of those' or 'than the' in English
additional_notes: Commonly appears as part of longer phrases: (1) literal 'de' + definite article 'los' = 'of the' (e.g., 'es de los nuestros' = 'he is one of ours'); (2) in relative/comparative constructions 'de los que' = 'of those who' or 'than those who' (e.g., 'más de los que' = 'more than we can...'); (3) used before groups (los) or to link to a previously mentioned noun. Word order and meaning depend on the full phrase, so always check surrounding words ('de los que', 'uno de los', 'de los nuestros').
target_language_example: Es uno de los mejores estudiantes de la clase.
native_language_example: He is one of the best students in the class.

meaning: A colloquial shorthand meaning “those of (the ones)” or “the ones from/of [a previously understood group]”; it refers back to a previously mentioned group, type, or category without repeating the noun.
additional_notes: Used to avoid repeating a noun already understood from context. Common in spoken and informal written Spanish. Can refer to people or things. Often appears after comparatives, possessives, or expressions that contrast groups (e.g., “diferente de los de nuestra escuela”, “más altos que los de mi clase”). Not strictly grammatical in very formal registers; in formal writing you would typically repeat the noun or rephrase. Literal translation: “of the of the” (doesn't make literal sense in English but maps to “those of the …”).
target_language_example: Los uniformes son diferentes de los de nuestra escuela.
native_language_example: The uniforms are different from those of our school.

meaning: out of place; inappropriate; (also) standing/placed (in some contexts)
additional_notes: Commonly used as part of expressions meaning 'out of place' or 'inappropriate' (e.g., 'sentirse de lugar' is not typical — more common: 'fuera de lugar' meaning 'out of place'). Alone, 'de lugar' can describe something's location or placement ('poner algo de lugar' is uncommon) — learners should prefer 'fuera de lugar' for 'out of place' and 'en su lugar' for 'in its place'. 'De lugar' may appear in fixed phrases (e.g., 'por lugar' in older/legal texts) but is not a standalone neutral phrase in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Ese comentario sonó fuera de lugar en la reunión.
native_language_example: That comment sounded out of place at the meeting.

meaning: 'of places' / 'places' (used after nouns or verbs to indicate relation to places)
additional_notes: A simple prepositional phrase: de = of/from/about; lugares = places. Often appears after nouns (clase de lugares = kind of places) or verbs with 'cambiar de lugares' (to change places/seats). In many contexts it simply refers to locations or spots. Literal translation usually works.
target_language_example: Hay muchos mapas de lugares interesantes en la guía.
native_language_example: There are many maps of interesting places in the guide.

meaning: 'luxury' or 'luxurious'; used to describe something high-end, elegant, or very good.
additional_notes: Common phrase placed after a noun (e.g., 'hotel de lujo') or used alone in contrast ('Regular o de lujo?'). Generally positive, describing expensive, high-quality, or upscale items, places, or experiences. Can also be used colloquially to mean 'great' or 'excellent' in some contexts.
target_language_example: Compramos unas vacaciones de lujo este verano.
native_language_example: We bought a luxury vacation this summer.

meaning: relating to the moon; moonlit or moon-related (literal), or describing a pattern with moons (on fabric).
additional_notes: Used after a noun to indicate a connection with the moon (e.g., 'noche de luna' = moonlit night) or as part of descriptions like 'vestido de luna' meaning a dress with moon motifs. Not a fixed idiom; meaning depends on context. If you see 'de lunares' it's different—'lunar' can mean 'moon-related' or 'spotty' (from 'luna' = moon), so watch for similar forms.
target_language_example: Tuvimos una noche de luna preciosa.
native_language_example: We had a beautiful moonlit night.

meaning: of (the) moon of / relating to the moon of ... (used in names or poetic phrases)
additional_notes: This sequence is unusual by itself; it typically appears inside longer phrases or names (for example, 'de luna de miel' would be a mistaken split of 'luna de miel' = 'honeymoon'). Alone, 'de luna de' expects more words after it (possessive or descriptive), e.g. 'anillo de luna de plata' (rare/poetic) meaning 'ring of moon of silver' but such constructions are uncommon in everyday Spanish. Learners should check the full phrase before using it.
target_language_example: La leyenda habla de la luz de luna de la bahía.
native_language_example: The legend speaks of the moonlight of the bay.

meaning: starting on Monday / from Monday (used in time ranges like 'from Monday to ...').
additional_notes: Commonly appears in phrases that show a range of days: 'de lunes a viernes' = 'from Monday to Friday'. Alone, 'de lunes' usually needs a follow-up (e.g., 'de lunes a sábado') or context (e.g., 'trabajo de lunes' meaning 'I work from Monday...'). It can also appear in expressions like 'las mañanas de lunes' meaning 'Monday mornings'.
target_language_example: La tienda abre de lunes a sábado.
native_language_example: The store is open from Monday to Saturday.

meaning: in mourning; grieving for someone's death.
additional_notes: Used to describe people or groups who are grieving or observing a period of mourning. Can be used for individuals (Estoy de luto) or larger groups/official occasions (Estamos de luto; un día de luto). Often follows the verb estar. Not idiomatic/slang.
target_language_example: Después del funeral, toda la familia estuvo de luto durante semanas.
native_language_example: After the funeral, the whole family was in mourning for weeks.

meaning: 'in the early morning' or 'at dawn' (hours before/around sunrise, often very early, e.g., 1–6 AM).
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something happens in the very early hours of the day (late night / pre-dawn). Common in news and everyday speech. Can describe arrivals, crimes, work shifts, or the time of death. Not the same as 'de la mañana' which covers the whole morning; 'de madrugada' emphasizes very early, often when most people sleep.
target_language_example: Llegaron de madrugada y se fueron a dormir.
native_language_example: They arrived in the early morning and went to sleep.

meaning: badly, poorly, in a bad way (used after nouns/adjectives to indicate poor condition or feeling)
additional_notes: Short expression often used in phrases like 'estar de mal humor' (to be in a bad mood) or 'de mal en peor' (from bad to worse). It usually follows a noun or adjective and modifies the state; on its own it is uncommon. Not the same as 'de mala'/'de malos' which agree in gender/number when required.
target_language_example: Está de mal humor desde ayer.
native_language_example: He's been in a bad mood since yesterday.

meaning: used in expressions meaning 'getting worse' or 'more and more [badly]'; appears in phrases like 'de mal en peor' (worse and worse).
additional_notes: This fragment is not usually used alone; it's part of fixed expressions (most commonly 'de mal en peor' = 'from bad to worse' / 'worse and worse'). It indicates a change or progression in a negative direction. Followed by a comparative word (e.g., peor).
target_language_example: La situación va de mal en peor.
native_language_example: The situation is going from bad to worse.

meaning: getting worse and worse; going from bad to worse.
additional_notes: Used to describe a situation that continues to deteriorate. Common fixed expression; often follows verbs like ir, ponerse, andar, or haber (e.g., va de mal en peor, ha ido de mal en peor).
target_language_example: Después de la crisis, la empresa fue de mal en peor.
native_language_example: After the crisis, the company went from bad to worse.

meaning: used to form phrases meaning 'of bad/poor (something)' — e.g. bad taste, bad character, bad weather.
additional_notes: Commonly combines with nouns to describe a negative quality: 'de mal gusto' (bad taste), 'de mal carácter' (bad-tempered), 'de mal tiempo' (bad weather). Often preceded by an article or modifier (un/una, buen/ mal) and followed by a noun. Not a standalone phrase; it needs the noun that indicates what is 'bad'.
target_language_example: Es una película de mal gusto.
native_language_example: It's a movie in poor taste.

meaning: rude; ill-mannered.
additional_notes: Used to describe people or behavior that is impolite, disrespectful, or shows poor manners. Often placed after a noun (persona de mala educación) or used predicatively (es de mala educación). Tone is critical/negative. Can describe actions (un comentario de mala educación) as well.
target_language_example: Fue de mala educación interrumpir así durante la reunión.
native_language_example: It was rude to interrupt like that during the meeting.

meaning: reluctantly; unwillingly; with bad will
additional_notes: Used to say someone does something without wanting to, reluctantly or unenthusiastically. Common with verbs of doing, going, accepting, etc. Equivalent to 'reluctantly' in English. Tone is neutral — not slang.
target_language_example: Ella aceptó la invitación de mala gana.
native_language_example: She accepted the invitation reluctantly.

meaning: unlucky; in a bad mood; indicating something negative (depends on context).
additional_notes: Informal phrase. Can mean 'unlucky' or 'having bad luck' (e.g., 'estar de malas' = to be in a bad mood or unlucky). In some contexts it appears before a noun to describe something as bad/negative (e.g., 'malas costumbres' = bad habits, 'malas notas' = bad grades). In the example sentences, 'Eso me pone de malas' means 'that puts me in a bad mood.' Watch for gender/number agreement on the adjective that follows (malas, malos).
target_language_example: Hoy estoy de malas porque no dormí bien.
native_language_example: I'm in a bad mood today because I didn't sleep well.

meaning: 'wrong' or 'bad' (used in expressions meaning 'something wrong/bad with...').
additional_notes: Commonly appears in phrases like 'no hay nada de malo (en/con) ...' meaning 'there's nothing wrong with ...'. Use 'en' or 'con' after depending on the verb/noun that follows. It expresses that an action, situation, or thing is not harmful, improper, or objectionable.
target_language_example: No hay nada de malo en intentarlo una vez más.
native_language_example: There's nothing wrong with trying one more time.

meaning: of/for mom; belonging to or related to (mom).
additional_notes: A simple possessive phrase using 'de' + 'mamá' to indicate possession, relationship, or association with one's mother. Common in everyday speech: 'el libro de mamá' (mom's book), 'el cumpleaños de mamá' (mom's birthday). Can also be used colloquially to refer to behaviors tied to being breastfed (as in 'la leche de mamá'). Context shows whether it means ownership, a celebration for mom, remembering mom's name, or literal milk from mom.
target_language_example: Encontré la receta de mamá y la voy a preparar esta noche.
native_language_example: I found mom's recipe and I'm going to make it tonight.

meaning: of/to keep, maintain (used after verbs or nouns as part of a phrase).
additional_notes: This is not a standalone phrase but the preposition de plus the infinitive mantener or the preposition linking to a noun phrase (e.g., 'la posibilidad de mantener'). It appears in constructions like 'tratar de mantener' (to try to keep), 'tener fama de mantener' (to have a reputation for keeping), or 'la posibilidad de mantener' (the possibility of maintaining). In many sentences the useful chunk for learners is the verb phrase 'mantener' (to keep/maintain/support) and common patterns: 'tratar de mantener' (try to keep), 'ser capaz de mantener' (be able to keep), 'mantener a' (support financially), 'mantener el perfil bajo' (keep a low profile).
target_language_example: Trato de mantener la calma cuando hablo en público.
native_language_example: I try to keep calm when I speak in public.

meaning: of butter / made with butter (or 'butter' as a component, often part of 'mantequilla de ...' or '... de mantequilla').
