native_language_example: — You say you don't have time; and yet you still arrived late?

meaning: they say that
additional_notes: A common phrase used to report what others say. 'Dicen' is the third-person plural of 'decir' and can mean 'they say' or the impersonal 'people say.' 'Eso' = 'that' (refers to a statement or idea just mentioned or understood from context). Used for general statements (Everyone says that / That's what people say).
target_language_example: Siempre dicen eso cuando hablamos de política.
native_language_example: They always say that when we talk about politics.

meaning: the thing (that) was said / said what (followed by clause).
additional_notes: Used after a form of decir to refer to the content that was spoken. Often appears in phrases like 'he dicho lo que sé' (I've said what I know) or 'has dicho lo que querías decir' (you've said what you wanted to say). It's a neutral, common structure for referring back to words or information previously mentioned.
target_language_example: Ya te he dicho lo que tenía que decirte.
native_language_example: I've already told you what I had to tell you.

meaning: said that it/he/she/this/that is
additional_notes: Phrase combines the past participle 'dicho' (said/told) with a reported clause starting with 'que' + 'es' (is). Used to report what someone has said. English translation depends on context and the subject referred by 'es' (it/he/she/this/that). Often appears in contexts like 'me han dicho que es...' (they've told me that it is...).
target_language_example: Me han dicho que es caro, así que ahorraré.
native_language_example: They've told me that it is expensive, so I'll save up.

meaning: said that I'm
additional_notes: Combines decir (to say/tell) in a past participle construction with a following clause starting with estoy (+ adjective/state). Common in responses to insistence or to report what you've already told someone (e.g., 'I already said that I'm fine'). Can appear with different auxiliary verbs (he dicho, te dije, le hubieras dicho). The English equivalent often uses 'said' or 'told' + 'that I'm'.
target_language_example: Ya te he dicho que estoy cansado.
native_language_example: I've already told you that I'm tired.

meaning: said that it
additional_notes: This is a fragment combining pasado participle 'dicho' (said) with a subordinate connector 'que' and the direct object pronoun 'lo' (it / him). It appears in larger sentences like 'Ha sido dicho que lo...' or 'Te lo he dicho que lo...'; by itself it's incomplete and you'll usually see it followed by a clause or verb. 'Lo' can refer to a neuter idea ('it'), a masculine noun ('him'/'it'), or an abstract concept. Word order and meaning depend on surrounding words.
target_language_example: Me lo han dicho que lo arreglarán mañana.
native_language_example: They've told me that they will fix it tomorrow.

meaning: a phrase used when reporting what someone said with 'that' + 'not it/that' (part of longer reported statements like 'dicho que no lo hice' = 'said that I didn't do it').
additional_notes: This fragment appears in reported-speech constructions with verbs like decir (he dicho, me dijo, etc.) followed by 'que' and a negative clause containing an object pronoun (lo). In English you usually translate the full sentence (e.g. 'he dicho que no lo sé' → 'I've said that I don't know it' or more naturally 'I told you I don't know'). Alone it is incomplete—expect different verbs and pronouns to complete the idea (hacerlo, tenerlo, saberlo, conocerlo).
target_language_example: Ya te he dicho que no lo tengo.
native_language_example: I've already told you I don't have it.

meaning: a construction used to report what someone has said that someone (third person) does or should do; literally 'said that he/she/they...'.
additional_notes: This phrase combines the past participle 'dicho' (said) with a subordinate clause introduced by 'que' and the reflexive/impersonal pronoun 'se' used with a third-person verb. It appears in reported speech: 'He dicho que se vaya' = 'I have said that he/she should leave' or 'I've told them to leave.' Context and verb form after 'se' determine exact meaning (command, habitual action, plan). 'Se' can be singular or plural depending on context and sometimes refers to people in general.
target_language_example: Ya he dicho que se quede tranquilo.
native_language_example: I've already said that he/she should stay calm.

meaning: '(I/they) have said that you...' — introduces reported speech with a command or instruction directed at 'you'.
additional_notes: This phrase combines the past participle 'dicho' (said) plus a subordinate clause starting with 'que' and a reflexive/object pronoun 'te'. It commonly appears in reported speech to relay orders, requests or statements about what someone told 'you' to do (e.g., told you to leave, told you to stay, told you to take off your clothes). The tense and mood in the clause after 'que' vary (indicative or subjunctive) depending on context and whether the speaker reports a past command, a wish, or a factual statement.
target_language_example: Me han dicho que te vayas ahora mismo.
native_language_example: They've told me to make you leave right now.

meaning: 'told (you) everything' or 'said everything'.
additional_notes: Literal past participle phrase: dicho (said/told) + todo (everything). Used to indicate someone has revealed all relevant information. Common in contexts about confessions, explanations, or sharing complete details. Often appears with an indirect object pronoun (me, te, le) or a subject: 'me lo ha dicho todo' = 'he/she has told me everything.'
target_language_example: Ella me lo ha dicho todo sobre el viaje.
native_language_example: She has told me everything about the trip.

meaning: 'teeth with' — literal phrase used to indicate that something has teeth or a toothed/serrated feature; typically appears as part of a larger noun phrase (e.g., describing tools, edges, or anatomical features).
additional_notes: Compositional literal combination: dientes = teeth, con = with. Not a fixed idiom; usually appears within longer phrases (e.g., "borde con dientes", "herramienta con dientes"). Rarely used alone as a complete utterance.
target_language_example: La caja contiene una sierra con dientes con forma curva.
native_language_example: The box contains a saw with teeth with a curved shape.

meaning: literally 'teeth after' — not a standard fixed phrase in Spanish; likely two words used separately (dientes = teeth; después = after/later).
additional_notes: This is not a common multiword expression in Spanish. Treat it as the noun 'dientes' (teeth) and the adverb 'después' (after/later) appearing next to each other in a sentence. Examples: 'los dientes después de la comida' (the teeth after the meal) or 'me cepillo los dientes después' (I brush my teeth afterwards). For beginner learners, focus on the separate meanings and typical collocations: 'cepillarse los dientes' (to brush one's teeth) and 'después (de)' (after, afterwards).
target_language_example: Me cepillo los dientes después de comer.
native_language_example: I brush my teeth after eating.

meaning: 'teeth after' — literal sequence of words used to indicate teeth that come or are located after something (e.g., after other teeth or after a certain age/event).
additional_notes: Not an established idiom; it's a compositional, literal phrase. In natural Spanish you often see it inside longer phrases (e.g., "los dientes después de los molares" or "dientes después de los seis meses"). To talk about teeth emerging, verbs like "salir" or constructions like "los dientes que salen después de..." are common. For positional descriptions, prefer "dientes posteriores" or specify exact teeth (incisivos, caninos, molares).
target_language_example: Los dientes después de los incisivos suelen ser los caninos.
native_language_example: The teeth after the incisors are usually the canines.

meaning: teeth after eating (used to talk about brushing your teeth after meals)
additional_notes: This phrase appears in instructions or routines about oral hygiene. In Spanish you'd usually say 'cepillarse los dientes después de comer' (to brush one's teeth after eating). The literal words are transparent, but the full idea commonly implies brushing. Use with reflexive verb 'cepillarse' and possessive articles (los/mis/tus) as appropriate.
target_language_example: Siempre me cepillo los dientes después de comer.
native_language_example: I always brush my teeth after eating.

meaning: they gave (to) — past tense of dar, indicating someone gave something to someone.
additional_notes: ‘Dieron’ is the third-person plural preterite of dar (to give). When followed by 'a' plus a person, it marks the indirect object (to someone). Spanish often uses indirect object pronouns (le, les) or full prepositional phrases (a + name/pronoun) for clarity or emphasis: e.g., 'Le dieron a Grace' or 'Le dieron a él'. Context determines the direct object (what was given) and whether a pronoun is used.
target_language_example: Dieron a María las llaves después de la reunión.
native_language_example: They gave María the keys after the meeting.

meaning: they realized / they noticed.
additional_notes: From the pronominal verb 'darse cuenta (de/que)' meaning 'to realize' or 'to notice'. 'Dieron cuenta' is the third person plural preterite (they realized/noticed). Use 'de' + noun (darse cuenta de un ruido) or 'de que' + clause (darse cuenta de que... ). Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Al final, se dieron cuenta de la verdad.
native_language_example: In the end, they realized the truth.

meaning: they gave (her/him/it/the) — past tense, third person plural of 'dar' plus a feminine singular direct object article 'la'.
additional_notes: Used to say that 'they' gave or caused something to someone in the past. 'La' is the feminine singular definite article replacing a specific noun (e.g., la carta, la noticia, la oportunidad, la idea). The exact English translation depends on the noun: 'they gave her the news' / 'they gave the idea to me' (note word order differs). Context can also mean 'they caused her to have' (e.g., 'le cambiaron la cara' = 'it changed her face/expressions when they gave her the news').
target_language_example: Me dieron la noticia ayer.
native_language_example: They gave me the news yesterday.

meaning: they considered/declared (something) to be (a certain way); they assumed or pronounced (someone) as (something, e.g., dead, certain).
additional_notes: Common construction: dar por + past participle (dar por + adj/past participle) meaning 'to consider/assume/declare something as...'. Often used to express an assumption (dieron por sentado = they took for granted) or an official/accepted conclusion (lo dieron por muerto = they declared him dead). Subject is who does the considering; the thing/person considered follows 'por'.
target_language_example: Lo dieron por desaparecido después de la tormenta.
native_language_example: They considered him missing after the storm.

meaning: 'ten of' — used to say 'ten' followed by a noun (count or partitive) or to indicate a time (ten minutes past).
additional_notes: Most often 'diez' is followed directly by a noun (diez libros = ten books). 'diez de' appears when specifying a fractional/partitive expression (diez de las manzanas = ten of the apples) or in time expressions with minutes (las diez y diez = ten ten/10:10; note: Spanish usually says 'las diez' for 10 o'clock, and 'diez de' can appear in contexts like 'diez de cada cien' = ten out of every hundred). Use 'de' to link to a determiner or a group.
target_language_example: Encontré diez de las cartas en la mesa.
native_language_example: I found ten of the letters on the table.

meaning: 'ten of the' or 'ten (o'clock) of the'
additional_notes: This phrase fragment appears in time expressions or dates combined with a feminine noun (e.g., 'diez de la mañana' = 10 in the morning). Alone it's incomplete — usually followed by a noun (la mañana, la noche, la tarde) or part of a date expression (diez de la casa, though less common). In spoken Spanish for telling time, use 'las diez' or 'las diez de la mañana' rather than 'diez de la' by itself.
target_language_example: Llegamos a las diez de la mañana.
native_language_example: We arrive at ten in the morning.

meaning: ten thousand.
additional_notes: A cardinal number used to count or quantify (10,000). Used same way as in English: before nouns (e.g., diez mil estudiantes) or alone as an amount. Note spacing: 'diez mil' is two words. In Spanish numbers larger than 999 are grouped by thousands (mil).
target_language_example: Hay diez mil libros en la biblioteca.
native_language_example: There are ten thousand books in the library.

meaning: Used when giving a time approximately at ten minutes past the hour (colloquial), or as the start of a list/itemization like 'ten and...' in counting contexts.
additional_notes: Alone 'diez y' is incomplete; in time expressions you normally say 'las diez y diez' (10:10) or 'las diez y cuarto' (10:15). In casual speech, people may shorten time to 'diez y diez' → 'diez y' only when the rest is implied by context, but this is uncommon. It can also appear as the beginning of a phrase listing things (e.g., 'diez y más' = 'ten and more'), but you will usually hear the full expression.
target_language_example: Son las diez y diez; llegamos tarde.
native_language_example: It's ten ten; we're late.

meaning: difference of / difference in (used to talk about how two things differ by X or in X).
additional_notes: Used to indicate the type or measure of a difference (opinion, age, price, etc.). Often followed by a noun (diferencia de opinión, diferencia de edad, diferencia de precio) or by a quantity (diferencia de cuatro años). Can be used for abstract differences (opinions, tastes) and measurable differences (age, price).
target_language_example: La diferencia de temperatura entre hoy y ayer es de diez grados.
native_language_example: The difference in temperature between today and yesterday is ten degrees.

meaning: different from; unlike
additional_notes: Used to compare two things, people, or ideas. Commonly followed by a noun or a clause introduced by 'lo que'/'la tuya' etc. In many regions you may also hear 'diferente de'—both are correct, though usage can vary by country.
target_language_example: Su opinión es diferente a la mía.
native_language_example: His/Her opinion is different from mine.

meaning: 'different from what...' or 'different from the fact that...'
additional_notes: Used to compare something to an idea, situation, or something previously mentioned. Often followed by a clause (lo + verb/adjective) or a noun phrase: e.g. 'diferente de lo que pensaba' = different from what I thought. Common variants: 'diferente a' (regional) or 'diferente de' + noun.
target_language_example: Su reacción fue diferente de lo que esperábamos.
native_language_example: His reaction was different from what we expected.

meaning: different in / different from (used to compare qualities or aspects)
additional_notes: Used to describe how something or someone differs regarding a specific characteristic, context, place, time, etc. Spanish often uses 'diferente en' + noun or clause (e.g., 'diferente en tamaño', 'diferente en personalidad'). For comparisons you may also see 'diferente de' or 'diferente a' depending on region; all can be used to express difference but the preposition choice may vary by country.
target_language_example: Este modelo es diferente en tamaño y precio.
native_language_example: This model is different in size and price.

meaning: different from
additional_notes: Used to compare one group or thing to another. In Spanish, más commonly encontrarás 'diferente de' or 'diferente a' depending on region; both mean 'different from'. Follow with the person/thing being compared (e.g., 'diferentes a nosotros', 'diferentes a ti'). You can also use 'diferentes entre sí' to say 'different from each other.'
target_language_example: Los estudiantes de primero son diferentes a los de último año.
native_language_example: First-year students are different from the seniors.

meaning: different from
additional_notes: Used to compare two or more things, people, ideas, customs, etc. Common pattern: 'X es/son diferentes de Y' or 'maneras diferentes de + infinitive' (different ways of...). In many Spanish dialects you may also hear 'diferente a' or 'diferente que' — all are widely used, though some style guides prefer 'de' or 'a' depending on construction.
target_language_example: Mis opiniones son diferentes de las tuyas.
native_language_example: My opinions are different from yours.

meaning: different in / different at (used to say things or people are different in a place, aspect, or situation).
additional_notes: Often used with a location, time period, or aspect after 'en' (e.g., en cada rincón, en Europa, en los últimos años). Can describe differences between people (different in everything) or different instances/places. Word order: 'diferentes en + [noun/phrase]'.
target_language_example: He conocido culturas diferentes en varios países.
native_language_example: I have encountered different cultures in several countries.

meaning: difficult for (someone) / hard on (someone) or something
additional_notes: 'Difícil a' is less common than 'difícil para' or 'difícil de' in modern standard Spanish. It may appear in some regional expressions, literary/older usage, or before a noun phrase to mean 'hard on' or 'difficult for' (e.g., 'difícil a la vista'). For learners, prefer 'difícil para' (followed by a person) or 'difícil de' (followed by an infinitive or clause), but 'difícil a' can be used in fixed phrases or stylistic contexts.
target_language_example: La luz intensa resulta difícil a la vista.
native_language_example: The intense light is hard on the eyes.

meaning: difficult to (do) — a sequence of 'difícil' followed by the preposition 'a' (often contracted with 'el' as 'al') appearing before an action; indicates difficulty in relation to performing that action
additional_notes: This sequence is not the most common or neutral way to introduce an infinitive in modern standard Spanish. More frequent options are 'difícil de' + infinitive (difícil de hacer), 'es difícil' + infinitive (es difícil entender), or simply 'difícil' + infinitive in some contexts. 'Difícil al' typically appears in constructions where 'a' is required for a following noun or gerund (e.g., 'al + verbo en gerundio' or 'al + infinitivo' in some regional or literary uses), often meaning 'when' or 'upon' doing something (equivalent to 'al' = 'cuando'/'al momento de'). Because of this, 'difícil al' can have the nuance 'difficult when/for [doing]' rather than the neutral 'difficult to [do]'. For learners: prefer 'es difícil (+ infinitive)' or 'difícil de + infinitive' unless you encounter 'difícil al' in context and want to match regional or stylistic usage.
target_language_example: Es difícil al intentar explicar esto a alguien que no conoce el tema.
native_language_example: It is difficult when trying to explain this to someone who doesn't know the subject.

meaning: part of a comparative/exclamative phrase meaning 'too/so ... that' (used with adjectives to express degree).
additional_notes: This fragment normally appears in longer constructions like "difícil de + infinitive" or in exclamations such as "Difícil de creer" (hard to believe) or "difícil de lo que..." Compare with complete phrases: "difícil de + infinitive" = 'difficult to [do]'; "más difícil de lo que" = 'more difficult than (what)'. On its own ('difícil de lo') is incomplete and needs more words (an infinitive, clause, or comparison) to make sense.
target_language_example: Es más difícil de lo que pensaba.
native_language_example: It's more difficult than I thought.

meaning: hard to find / difficult to find
additional_notes: Common phrase used with a noun or clause after it (e.g., difícil encontrar trabajo / difícil encontrar la verdad). Often appears with impersonal 'es' (Es difícil encontrar...) or with verbs like 'me fue/ me resultó' + adjective + infinitive to express personal difficulty (Me resultó difícil encontrar...).
target_language_example: Es difícil encontrar buenos amigos cuando te mudas mucho.
native_language_example: It's hard to find good friends when you move a lot.

meaning: ‘is difficult’ — the adjective difícil ('difficult') followed by the verb es ('is'); used to state that something is difficult, often within a larger sentence or for emphasis when placing adjective before the verb.
additional_notes: Not a standalone fixed phrase; more common order is 'Es difícil...'. 'Difícil es' appears in inverted or emphatic constructions (literary, poetic, or for contrast). Example uses include beginning a clause for emphasis: 'Difícil es...' or within a clause after a conjunction. Agreement: difícil is an adjective and may agree in number/gender when positioned differently (e.g., 'Difíciles son').
target_language_example: Difícil es aprender un idioma sin practicar.
native_language_example: Difficult is to learn a language without practicing. (Natural: It's difficult to learn a language without practicing.)

meaning: it's difficult to speak / it's hard to talk
additional_notes: A common construction using the adjective difícil + infinitive hablar to express that speaking (in general, about a topic, or in a situation) is hard. Often followed by a complement introduced with en, sobre, de, or by specifying what (e.g., en público, tres idiomas, de ello). English equivalents: "it's hard to speak," "it's difficult to talk (about it)."
target_language_example: Me resulta difícil hablar en público sin ponerme nervioso.
native_language_example: I find it difficult to speak in public without getting nervous.

meaning: hard to solve / difficult to resolve
additional_notes: Used to describe that something (a problem, task, situation) is challenging to solve. Often appears with impersonal or dative constructions: "Es difícil resolver...", "Me fue difícil resolver...", or with adverbs: "demasiado difícil". Can be followed by a noun or a clause (e.g., "resolver el problema", "resolver cómo..." ).
target_language_example: Es difícil resolver este problema sin ayuda.
native_language_example: It's hard to solve this problem without help.

meaning: literally 'difficult and' — used when describing something difficult plus another quality; often part of a larger phrase (e.g., 'difícil y caro').
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom by itself. 'Difícil y' commonly appears before another adjective or adjective phrase to link 'difficult' with that quality (for example: difícil y costoso, difícil y peligroso). Make sure a second adjective follows; otherwise the phrase is incomplete. Word order: 'difícil' comes first, then 'y' + the next adjective.
target_language_example: Este trabajo es difícil y agotador.
native_language_example: This job is difficult and exhausting.

meaning: 'say your' or 'tell your' (formal imperative + possessive).
additional_notes: Combines the formal (usted) imperative of decir—diga—with the possessive su. Often appears in questions or instructions when asking someone formally what they say or to tell something belonging to them (e.g., diga su nombre = 'state your name'). Context determines exact translation. Use 'dime/di tu' for informal (tú).
target_language_example: Diga su nombre, por favor.
native_language_example: State your name, please.

meaning: "you say to your" (subjunctive or imperative form used when telling someone to tell another person something)
additional_notes: This is not a complete fixed phrase by itself. 'Digas' is the present subjunctive (or negative imperative) of 'decir' for tú, and 'a' introduces the indirect object (the person you tell). Commonly appears in constructions like 'que le digas a tu madre' (that you tell your mother) or 'no digas a tu amigo' (don't tell your friend). Word order and use depend on the clause: e.g. 'Que le digas a tu hermano que venga' (Make sure you tell your brother to come).
target_language_example: Que le digas a tu madre que llego tarde.
native_language_example: That you tell your mother that I'm arriving late.

meaning: say that
additional_notes: A combination of digas (the tú subjunctive / negative-command form of decir) and que. It often appears after triggers like cuando for future situations, or in negative commands: No digas que... = “Don’t say/tell ... that ...”.
target_language_example: No digas que no tienes tiempo.
native_language_example: Don't say that you don't have time.

meaning: don't say a (single) — used to tell someone not to say even one word or thing
additional_notes: Commonly appears in negative commands with 'no' + subjunctive (No digas una...) to forbid saying even one word/item. Often completed with 'palabra' (word) or another noun (mentira). Tone can be strict or emphatic; add 'más' for 'not one more'.
target_language_example: No digas una palabra más sobre eso.
native_language_example: Don't say one more word about that.

meaning: I say what
additional_notes: Used to introduce what the speaker says/expresses. Common in statements like "Digo lo que pienso/veo" = "I say what I think/see." "Digo lo que" is simply the first-person singular present form (digo) + the relative phrase "lo que" (what/that which). Can be followed by a clause (e.g. pienso, veo).
target_language_example: Digo lo que necesito decir en esta reunión.
native_language_example: I say what I need to say in this meeting.

meaning: 'I say that I (verb) you' — part of phrases used to report or emphasize something you tell someone (often followed by querer/amar/imperative).
additional_notes: This sequence combines the first-person singular of decir (digo) plus que and the clitic te (you). It appears in sentences like 'Cuando digo que te amo' (When I say that I love you) or in commands/requests with te before a verb: 'Si te digo que te quedes...' (If I tell you to stay...). Word order can change: 'te digo que...' or 'digo que te...' depending on emphasis. Commonly followed by verbs like amo, quiero, quedes, vayas.
target_language_example: Si digo que te quiero, es verdad.
native_language_example: If I say that I love you, it's true.

meaning: 'I say' or 'I think' (used to give your opinion or emphasize agreement).
additional_notes: Common colloquial tag attached to a statement or used alone to assert one's opinion or agreement. Can stand alone as a short response meaning 'that's what I say' or 'I told you so' depending on context. Often used for emphasis or to reinforce what someone else said (e.g., "Eso digo yo" = "That's what I say"). Not formal but widely used in spoken Spanish.
target_language_example: Si hace calor, mejor quedarnos en casa, digo yo.
native_language_example: If it's hot, it's better to stay home, I think/I say.

meaning: ‘I said no’ or ‘as I said, no’ (used to repeat or emphasize a previous refusal or statement).
additional_notes: Combines the past-tense verb dije (I said) with no to reiterate a negative response or remind someone of something already stated. Often appears as part of a larger clause: 'Como dije, no...' = 'As I said, no...'. Common in everyday speech for emphasis or clarification.
target_language_example: Como dije, no puedo ir mañana.
native_language_example: As I said, I can't go tomorrow.

meaning: I told her.
additional_notes: Past simple first-person of decir (decir → dije). 'Le dije a ella' emphasizes the indirect object 'her' (le = to her); adding 'a ella' clarifies or contrasts (for example, to distinguish from 'le dije a él'). In speech, 'le dije' alone is often enough; 'a ella' is used for emphasis or clarity. Word order: 'le dije a ella' is more common than 'dije a ella'.
target_language_example: Le dije a ella la verdad ayer.
native_language_example: I told her the truth yesterday.

meaning: 'I told (to) the…' — first-person past of 'decir' followed by the indirect object introduced by 'al' (a + el).
additional_notes: Structure: 'dije' = I said/told (preterite). 'al' is the contraction of 'a + el' and introduces the person or role who received the information (e.g., al policía = to the policeman). Often followed by a noun or title (al reverendo, al Tom, al Mando). In English this is translated as 'I told the…' or 'I told (to) the…' depending on style; you can omit 'to' in natural English: 'I told the policeman.'
target_language_example: Le dije al profesor la verdad después de clase.
native_language_example: I told the teacher the truth after class.

meaning: "I told you this" (used to introduce something the speaker previously warned or predicted).
additional_notes: Common in spoken and written Spanish to remind someone that the speaker already warned about or predicted a situation. Often followed by a clause describing the outcome (acabó en lágrimas, no iba a funcionar, etc.). 'Te dije que esto...' literally = 'I told you that this...', where 'te' = 'to you'.
target_language_example: Te dije que esto iba a pasar, ¿por qué no me escuchaste?
native_language_example: I told you this was going to happen—why didn't you listen to me?

meaning: 'I said that you should stay in' (past reporting of a command/suggestion to stay inside or at a place).
additional_notes: Used to report what someone told another person to do: 'dije que' (I said that) + subjunctive or past subjunctive form depending on context; here 'te quedaras' is the past subjunctive of quedarse (used after a past-tense reporting verb). Often followed by a location (en casa, en la cama, en el trabajo). Can express annoyance or reminder: "I told you to stay in."
target_language_example: Te dije que te quedaras en casa cuando lloviera.
native_language_example: I told you to stay in the house when it rained.

meaning: I said everything / I said it all (usually followed by something like 'que' + clause).
additional_notes: This is a fragment of a sentence: 'dije todo lo...' often continues with 'que' + a clause (e.g., 'dije todo lo que pensaba' = I said everything I thought). Alone it sounds incomplete. Use to emphasize that you said everything on a topic.
target_language_example: Dije todo lo que necesitaba decir en la reunión.
native_language_example: I said everything I needed to say in the meeting.

meaning: I said everything that / I told (you) all that
additional_notes: Common phrase used to say you have already told all relevant information. Often followed by a clause (e.g., tenía que decir, sé). Can be used with different subjects (te, le) to indicate to whom it was said. Past tense (dije) indicates the action already happened.
target_language_example: Dije todo lo que sabía sobre el accidente.
native_language_example: I said everything I knew about the accident.

meaning: said to the (feminine singular) — part of a reported-speech phrase
additional_notes: ‘Dijo’ is the preterite of decir (to say). When reporting what someone said to a female person or to a feminine noun, Spanish uses ‘a la’ before the person/noun: e.g. ‘dijo a la profesora’. Often followed by the person or noun or by a clause introduced with que (dijo a la abuela que...). If the object is masculine use ‘a el’ → contracted to ‘al’. If the indirect object is a pronoun, you would use ‘le’ or ‘les’ instead (Le dijo a ella...).
target_language_example: Él dijo a la paciente que tomara el medicamento.
native_language_example: He said to the (female) patient that she should take the medicine.

meaning: 'said to his/her/their' (third-person past of decir + indirect object 'a' + possessive 'su').
additional_notes: This is a sequence of three words: 'dijo' (he/she/it said or you formal said), 'a' (to), and 'su' (his, her, its, your formal, or their). It introduces what was said to someone (whose relationship or role is marked by 'su'). The actual listener is usually clarified by a noun after 'su' (e.g., 'dijo a su madre' = 'he said to his mother'). Context determines whether 'su' means his/her/your/their. For clarity, Spanish often repeats the indirect object as a pronoun (e.g., 'le dijo a su madre').
target_language_example: Él dijo a su amigo que llegaría tarde.
native_language_example: He said to his friend that he would arrive late.

meaning: he/she said things; (someone) said things (about...)
additional_notes: Common, neutral phrase used to report what someone said. Often followed by details introduced with sobre (about), que (that), or an adjective (e.g., raras, sin sentido). Can be vague—context tells whether the things were positive, negative, sensible, etc.
target_language_example: Ella dijo cosas bonitas sobre mi trabajo.
native_language_example: She said nice things about my work.

meaning: 'she said' (used to report speech; puts slight emphasis on who spoke).
additional_notes: Literal word order is subject after verb (verb + subject) — common in reported speech or narrative to emphasize the speaker or as a stylistic choice. It is equivalent to 'ella dijo' but 'dijo ella' can sound more emphatic or literary. Use when reporting what a woman said.
target_language_example: —No puedo ir, dijo ella.
native_language_example: "I can't go," she said.

meaning: said (that) was / what someone said was (used to report truth or correctness).
additional_notes: Combination appears in relative clauses: 'todo lo que dijo era ...' = 'everything (that) he/she said was ...'. Used to report or evaluate what someone said (true, correct, etc.). In English you'd often add 'that' or use 'what' depending on structure: 'what he said was true' or 'everything he said was true.'
target_language_example: Lo que ella dijo era importante para la reunión.
native_language_example: What she said was important for the meeting.

meaning: he/she said that it/is (introduces reported statement about identity, quality or state).
additional_notes: Combines the past-tense verb 'dijo' (he/she said) with the connector 'que' and the present verb 'es' (is). Used to report what someone said about a person or thing (identity, trait, status). In English you usually translate it as 'said that he/she/it is...' or 'told me that...'. Subject of 'es' can be a person or an abstract idea; the original speaker is quoted indirectly. Tense in the reported clause can stay present when reporting a general truth or unchanging fact.
target_language_example: Mi hermano me dijo que es responsable del proyecto.
native_language_example: My brother told me that he is responsible for the project.

meaning: he said (emphatic: 'he said' rather than someone else)
additional_notes: Dijo is the preterite of decir (to say). Adding él after dijo is emphatic or clarifying — it stresses that 'he' (not she/they/you) said it. In natural speech the pronoun usually is omitted (Dijo), so 'dijo él' is used for contrast or emphasis: e.g., to correct someone or to point out the speaker. Word order can vary: 'él dijo' (he said) is more neutral; 'dijo él' places emphasis on 'él'.
target_language_example: — ¿Quién dijo eso? — Lo dijo él.
native_language_example: — Who said that? — He said it.

meaning: Tell me why... (ask someone to explain a reason).
additional_notes: Common spoken prompt used to request the reason for something. It combines the imperative 'dime' (tell me) + 'por' as the start of 'por qué' (why). In natural speech you should say the full question 'dime por qué...' followed by the reason or action. Use 'por favor' to be more polite.
target_language_example: Dime por qué llegaste tarde esta mañana.
native_language_example: Tell me why you arrived late this morning.

meaning: Not a fixed phrase by itself; likely part of a larger expression meaning 'money to/for' (dinero + al = 'money to the/for the').
additional_notes: This is not a standalone multiword phrase in Spanish. It appears when the noun dinero (money) is followed by the preposition a + definite article (al = a + el) to indicate direction or recipient: e.g., 'dinero al banco' (money to the bank), 'dinero al vendedor' (money to the seller). For beginners, learn: dinero = money; al = a + el = to the/at the. Combine them when saying where money goes or who receives it.
target_language_example: Le di dinero al cajero para pagar el billete.
native_language_example: I gave money to the cashier to pay for the ticket.

meaning: money (amount) every/each (period).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself; it's the noun 'dinero' (money) followed by a frequency expression 'cada' + time period (cada mes, cada semana). Used to say how much money is given, saved or sent on a regular basis. In English you usually say 'money every month/week' or 'money each month/week.' Remember to include the time unit after 'cada'.
target_language_example: Guardo un poco de dinero cada mes.
native_language_example: I save a little money every month.

meaning: 'money' + 'as' — used when comparing or describing money in a specific role ("money as ...", "money like ...").
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom; it's simply the word dinero followed by como to introduce a comparison, role, or example. Como can mean 'as', 'like', or 'such as' depending on context. Watch word order and articles: e.g. "el dinero como medio" (money as a means) or "adoraban al dinero como a un dios" (they worshipped money as a god).
target_language_example: Muchas personas ven el dinero como seguridad.
native_language_example: Many people see money as security.

meaning: money with (someone) / money that includes or comes with (something)
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase in Spanish by itself. 'Dinero con' appears as part of larger expressions, e.g. 'dinero con interés' (money with interest), 'dinero con el que pagar' (money with which to pay), or 'dinero con Juan' (money with Juan). You will usually need more words after 'con' to complete the idea: who has the money, what the money includes, or what accompanies the money. Use verb context or a noun phrase after 'con'.
target_language_example: Tengo el dinero con el que podemos pagar el alquiler.
native_language_example: I have the money with which we can pay the rent.

meaning: 'money of' or 'money for' — used to indicate whose money it is or what the money is for (often followed by a noun).
additional_notes: Common construction in Spanish where dinero (money) is followed by the preposition de to show possession or purpose: dinero de + noun (e.g., dinero de Juan = Juan's money) or dinero para + noun is more common for 'money for' but dinero de can also appear in contexts like 'dinero de la venta' (money from the sale). Use context to decide between possession ('of') and source ('from').
target_language_example: Es el dinero de la fiesta.
native_language_example: It's the party's money (the money for the party).

meaning: cash in the register / money in the till.
additional_notes: Refers to the physical cash kept in a cash register, cash drawer, or till at a store or business. Used when counting, auditing, or referring to the day's takings (e.g., "cantidad de dinero de la caja"). Not formal slang; commonly used in retail and accounting contexts.
target_language_example: Al final del turno, contamos el dinero de la caja.
native_language_example: At the end of the shift, we count the cash in the register.

meaning: not a standalone phrase; appears as part of longer expressions like 'dinero de lo que' or 'dinero de lo' (followed by a noun) meaning 'money from/of the...'.
additional_notes: By itself 'dinero de lo' is incomplete in Spanish. 'Dinero' means 'money' and 'de' means 'of/from'; 'lo' is a neuter article used in fixed structures (e.g., 'lo que' = 'what/that which') or appears before adjectives/nouns in informal phrases. You will typically see complete forms such as 'dinero de lo que esperaba' ('money from/than I expected' — though more natural is 'más dinero de lo que esperaba') or 'dinero de los padres' ('money from the parents'). Do not use 'dinero de lo' alone.
target_language_example: Gané más dinero de lo que esperaba.
native_language_example: I earned more money than I expected.

meaning: money than (used in comparisons: 'more/less money than...').
additional_notes: This phrase appears in comparative constructions after expressions like 'más' or 'menos' (e.g., 'más dinero de lo que pensaba' = 'more money than I thought'). It is followed by a clause or phrase giving the thing being compared. Common structure: 'más/menos + dinero + de lo que + [clause]'.
target_language_example: Tiene más dinero de lo que crees.
native_language_example: He has more money than you think.

meaning: literally 'money of the' — used to show possession or association (e.g., money belonging to someone or to something).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but a combination: dinero (money) + del (contraction of de + el = 'of the' or 'from the'). It commonly appears before a noun or name (dinero del banco, dinero del gobierno, dinero del cliente). Make sure the gender/number after 'del' matches the noun. If the possessed noun is feminine, use 'de la' (dinero de la empresa).
target_language_example: Encontré el dinero del cliente en la recepción.
native_language_example: I found the client's money at the reception.

meaning: 'money is' (literal — start of a statement about money)
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase on its own; it's simply the noun dinero ('money') followed by the verb es ('is'). You'll commonly see it at the beginning of a sentence that describes a quality, fact or opinion about money (e.g., "El dinero es importante"). Remember to include the subject/article if needed (el dinero, mi dinero).
target_language_example: El dinero es necesario para pagar el alquiler.
native_language_example: Money is necessary to pay the rent.

meaning: ‘the money is’ — a simple phrase combining dinero (money) with está (is, temporary state/location).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed expression; it's just the noun dinero (money) followed by the verb estar in third person singular (está). Use when describing the current state or location of money (e.g., 'El dinero está en la caja' = 'The money is in the box') or to say how money currently is (e.g., 'El dinero está disponible'). For general facts or permanent characteristics you would use 'es' instead of 'está' (e.g., 'El dinero es importante').
target_language_example: El dinero está en mi cartera.
native_language_example: The money is in my wallet.

meaning: easy money (money obtained with little effort, often implying risk or moral issue).
additional_notes: Used to refer to money gained quickly or with little work; can imply illegality, corruption, or hidden costs. Common in everyday speech and media. Context determines whether literal (small effort) or figurative (ill-gotten gains).
target_language_example: No aceptes ese trato: parece dinero fácil pero es una estafa.
native_language_example: Don't take that deal: it looks like easy money but it's a scam.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase in Spanish; a sequence 'dinero le' can appear in marked word orders or colloquial inversions meaning 'money to him/her/you (formal)' or as part of a larger clause where the indirect object pronoun follows a noun for emphasis ('dinero le ...').
additional_notes: Standard Spanish places the indirect object pronoun before the finite verb (e.g., 'le doy dinero') or attached to an infinitive/gerund/imperative ('voy a darle dinero', 'dándole dinero'). The sequence 'dinero le' by itself is ungrammatical in neutral prose but may occur in poetic, emphatic, or colloquial inversion: for example, 'Dinero le di, pero no la confianza' (colloquial/emphatic inversion for 'Le di dinero...'). If you encounter 'dinero le' in text, look for an immediately following verb or clause that completes the idea. For learners, follow the normal word order: indirect object pronoun + verb + direct object, or attach pronouns to non-finite verbs.
target_language_example: Dinero le di, pero no cambió su actitud.
native_language_example: I gave him/her money, but it didn't change his/her attitude.

meaning: 'the money it' (literal) — not a standard fixed phrase; typically a fragment where "dinero" is the noun and "lo" is a clitic pronoun referring to that money or to an idea previously mentioned.
additional_notes: Not a common multiword expression by itself. Usually appears as part of a clause where lo is the direct object pronoun: e.g. in speech fragments or topicalization. Beginners should treat 'dinero' (money) and 'lo' (it/him/neutral 'that') separately. Examples of related full sentences: "El dinero, lo guardé en el banco." or "¿Dónde está el dinero? — Dinero lo tengo en la cartera." (colloquial/topicalized).
target_language_example: Dinero lo tengo en la cartera.
native_language_example: I have the money in my wallet.

meaning: literally 'money no' — not a standard fixed phrase in Spanish; typically a fragment meaning 'no money' or used for contrast/emphasis in poetic or rhetorical contexts.
additional_notes: Not a common standalone phrase. Natural alternatives: 'no tengo dinero' (I have no money), 'sin dinero' (without money). 'Dinero no' can appear in elliptical or emphatic constructions (e.g., 'Dinero, no; amistad, sí') or in slogans/poetry where word order is inverted for effect. Alone it may sound incomplete to many speakers.
target_language_example: Dinero, no; prefiero felicidad.
native_language_example: Money, no; I prefer happiness.

meaning: literally 'money is not'; used as part of a sentence to say that money is not something (e.g., not important, not everything).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase on its own; it's the start or middle of a sentence (subject 'dinero' + negation 'no es'). You'll usually see it followed by a noun, adjective, or clause: e.g., 'El dinero no es todo' (Money isn't everything) or 'El dinero no es la felicidad' (Money isn't happiness). Pay attention to article use ('el dinero') and word order.
target_language_example: El dinero no es lo más importante en la vida.
native_language_example: Money is not the most important thing in life.

meaning: 'money for' or 'money per' (depends on context).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself — it's the noun dinero (money) followed by the preposition por. It can mean 'money for' (payment given for something) or 'money per' (rate: money for each unit). Exact translation depends on the verb or noun that follows and the context. Common uses: dinero por el trabajo (money for the work), diez euros por hora (ten euros per hour), dinero por adelantado (money in advance).
target_language_example: Me pagaron dinero por ayudar con la mudanza.
native_language_example: They paid me money for helping with the move.

meaning: the money that (to) him/her/you (formal) — used to refer to money related to someone (given, owed, lent, etc.).
additional_notes: This is a fragment combining dinero (money) with a relative clause using que and the indirect object pronoun le. It appears in contexts like 'the money that I gave him/her', 'the money that he/she owed', or 'the money that was lent to you'. le is an indirect object pronoun (to/for him, her, or you formal). The exact English translation depends on the verb in the sentence (gave, owed, lent, asked for, etc.).
target_language_example: Voy a buscar el dinero que le presté a Ana.
native_language_example: I'm going to get the money that I lent to Ana.

meaning: the money (that) (he/she/I) had
additional_notes: A relative clause describing money someone possessed. "Tenía" is the imperfect of tener, often used to describe possession in the past or an ongoing past state. The subject (he/she/I/you) is understood from context. The phrase often appears with qualifiers like "poco" (little) or "todo" (all).
target_language_example: Gastó todo el dinero que tenía en comida.
native_language_example: He spent all the money he had on food.

meaning: 'money that' — a phrase used to introduce a clause describing or specifying money.
additional_notes: Often appears as part of a larger sentence (e.g., "el dinero que recibí", "el dinero que falta"). 'Dinero' means 'money' and 'que' here functions as a relative pronoun ('that' / 'which') connecting to a clause. This is a literal, compositional construction.
target_language_example: El dinero que recibiste llegó hoy.
native_language_example: The money that you received arrived today.

meaning: 'money' followed by the clitic 'se' — not a standalone fixed phrase; 'se' will belong to a verb or construction and the sequence 'dinero se' appears when word order places the noun before the verb + clitic (e.g., in topicalization or stylistic inversion).
additional_notes: 'dinero se' by itself is not a fixed expression. In natural sentences the 'se' attaches to a verb (e.g., 'dinero se perdió', 'dinero se necesita'). The sequence can appear when the noun is fronted for emphasis or in reporting: 'Dinero se necesita para vivir' (colloquial/emphatic). Always read the full sentence to determine whether 'se' is an impersonal/passive marker, a reflexive pronoun, or part of a pronominal verb.
target_language_example: Dinero se necesita para vivir, pero no alcanza para todo.
native_language_example: Money is needed to live, but it isn't enough for everything.

meaning: Not a fixed Spanish phrase; the noun 'dinero' (money) followed by the clitic pronoun 'te' (to you / you). This sequence appears only inside larger sentences or clauses where word order is unusual for emphasis or in certain topicalizations (e.g., "dinero, te lo doy"), but 'dinero te' alone is not a standalone expression.
additional_notes: You'll more commonly see 'te' before the verb (te doy dinero) or attached to an infinitive (darte dinero). When 'dinero te' appears, it's typically because of inversion or topicalization for emphasis (e.g., 'Dinero, te lo doy' = 'As for money, I give it to you') or within coordinated or clitic constructions ('dinero te lo...' in some colloquial emphases). Grammar: 'te' is an indirect object clitic for 'you' (singular, informal).
target_language_example: Dinero te lo doy, pero no tengo tiempo.
native_language_example: Money, I give it to you, but I don't have time.

meaning: gave (someone) some / gave a little of (something).
additional_notes: Used to say someone gave a small or some amount of something (food, drink, money, etc.). Structure: [person] dio algo de [sustantivo] (or dio algo de [noun] a [persona]). Emphasizes an unspecified, modest amount. 'Algo de' can be used with uncountable nouns (pan, leche, comida, dinero) or to mean 'some' rather than a specific quantity.
target_language_example: El vecino me dio algo de fruta.
native_language_example: The neighbor gave me some fruit.

meaning: 'found' or 'came across' (he/she/it found)
additional_notes: Past tense of 'dar con' (to find, come across). Used when someone unexpectedly finds something or someone. Typically follows the subject (él/ella) as in 'él dio con...' or appears in third-person singular. Common in neutral registers.
target_language_example: Ella dio con la casa correcta después de preguntar a los vecinos.
native_language_example: She found the right house after asking the neighbors.

meaning: gave the
additional_notes: A common sequence of dio (the preterite form of dar, 'to give') + el ('the'). It is used when talking about something someone gave in the past: dio el libro, dio el cheque, dio el poder. English may sometimes use a different verb in fixed expressions, such as dio el primer paso = 'took the first step.'
target_language_example: Juan me dio el libro ayer.
native_language_example: Juan gave me the book yesterday.

meaning: gave (him/her/them) the money.
additional_notes: Past simple (pretérito) of dar + direct object 'el dinero'. Use when saying someone gave money to someone else. Often followed by an indirect object (le, me, nos) or a prepositional phrase with 'a' + person to clarify who received it.
target_language_example: Juan le dio el dinero a su hermana ayer.
native_language_example: Juan gave the money to his sister yesterday.

meaning: 'hit' or 'struck' (physically) OR 'ended up' / 'came to' (figurative, e.g. ended up doing/being)
additional_notes: This is the preterite form of 'dar en' used with a noun or gerund. With a physical object it means 'hit/struck' (e.g., dio en la cabeza = hit him in the head). With actions or states it often means 'ended up' or 'came to' when followed by a gerund or phrase (e.g., dio en decir = ended up saying). Context determines whether it's literal or figurative.
target_language_example: El balón dio en la ventana.
native_language_example: The ball hit the window.

meaning: he/she/it gave this (or 'gave this one') — past tense of dar + demonstrative 'este'.
additional_notes: Dio is the third-person singular preterite of dar (to give). 'Este' is a demonstrative adjective or pronoun meaning 'this' (near speaker). Together they typically appear as part of a larger sentence: e.g., 'Él me dio este libro' (He gave me this book) or 'Me dio este' (He gave me this one). Word order may vary; context determines whether 'este' is a noun phrase or replaces a noun.
target_language_example: Ella me dio este cuando llegué.
native_language_example: She gave me this when I arrived.

meaning: gave (her/them) the — (used with feminine plural direct objects like 'gracias' or 'buenas noches').
additional_notes: Dio is the past (preterite) of dar (to give). 'Las' is a feminine plural direct-object pronoun or article used before feminine plural nouns. Common fixed phrases: 'dar las gracias' (to give thanks = to thank) and 'dar las buenas noches' (to say good night). In English you usually translate the whole phrase (e.g., 'thanked me', 'said good night to us').
target_language_example: Ella me dio las gracias por ayudarla.
native_language_example: She thanked me for helping her.

meaning: gave all the / gave all the (something) — indicates someone gave the entirety of a specific thing.
additional_notes: This is the past (preterite) form of dar (dio = he/she/you formal gave) followed by 'todo el' (all the + masculine noun). It appears before a masculine singular noun (e.g., dinero). Use 'dio todo' + feminine noun as 'dio todo el amor' is possible because 'amor' is masculine in Spanish; otherwise adjust article/gender: 'dio toda la' for feminine singular nouns, 'dieron todo el' for plural subjects, etc. Common in phrases meaning someone gave everything they had or everything requested.
target_language_example: Ella le dio todo el dinero que tenía.
native_language_example: She gave him all the money she had.

meaning: hit (someone or something) with a punch in/at (a place).
additional_notes: Past tense third person singular of 'dar un puñetazo en' — literally 'gave a punch in/at'. Used to describe someone delivering a punch to a person or object and often followed by a body part or location (e.g., 'en la cara', 'en el estómago') or a place ('en la puerta').
target_language_example: Él dio un puñetazo en la cara del ladrón.
native_language_example: He punched the thief in the face.

meaning: hit (someone) with a punch in the (body part).
additional_notes: Literal phrase meaning '[he/she] gave a punch in the…'. Use with a body part after 'la' (e.g., 'cara' = face). Conjugate 'dio' for past tense (él/ella/usted gave). For other subjects use appropriate forms: 'di' is not correct — use 'me dio', 'te dio', 'nos dio', or change the verb (pretérito) to match the subject: 'dió' is incorrect spelling—correct is 'dio'.
target_language_example: Ella dio un puñetazo en la mandíbula.
native_language_example: She punched him in the jaw.

meaning: he/she/it gave a (single) clap or slap (with the hand).
additional_notes: Literal past tense of dar una palmada. Can mean a light clap (applaud once) or a light slap on someone or something, depending on context. Subject is él/ella/usted or any noun. Common in storytelling: dio una palmada en la mesa (he/she slapped the table) or dio una palmada para llamar la atención (gave a clap to get attention).
target_language_example: Ella dio una palmada para llamar a los niños.
native_language_example: She gave a clap to call the children.

meaning: gave a clap/strike on (or 'patted'/'slapped' depending on context).
additional_notes: Literal phrase: 'dio' = he/she/it gave, 'una palmada' = a clap/pat/slap, 'en' + body part or object indicates where. Can mean a friendly pat (e.g., on the back), a clap, or a light slap depending on context and tone. Commonly used with body parts (en la espalda, en la mano, en la mejilla).
target_language_example: Él dio una palmada en la espalda para felicitarla.
native_language_example: He gave her a pat on the back to congratulate her.

meaning: gave someone a pat (on the...) — a quick, light slap, usually friendly or reassuring.
additional_notes: Commonly followed by a body part (e.g., hombro = shoulder). Used to describe a light, non-aggressive touch: a pat, clap, or smack. Context determines tone (friendly, congratulatory, comforting). The verb form 'dio' is past tense (he/she gave). To generalize use 'da una palmada en el...' (gives a pat) or 'dio una palmada en la...' depending on the gender of the noun (el hombro, la espalda, la cabeza).
target_language_example: Ella le dio una palmada en el hombro para consolarlo.
native_language_example: She gave him a pat on the shoulder to comfort him.

meaning: literally 'god of'; used to indicate a god associated with something or (informally/figuratively) to praise someone as outstanding in a field (e.g., 'god of football').
additional_notes: Often appears in phrases naming a deity (dios de la guerra = god of war) or in colloquial praise (es un dios del fútbol = he's a football god = he's amazing at football). In formal religious contexts you may see 'Dios' (capitalized) alone to mean the monotheistic God; 'dios de' with lowercase is used for gods or figurative expressions. Use 'el/la dios/a' agreement as needed: 'dios de', 'diosa de'.
target_language_example: Es considerado el dios de la música en esa mitología.
native_language_example: He is considered the god of music in that mythology.

meaning: Oh my God; an exclamation expressing surprise, shock, frustration, or admiration.
additional_notes: Commonly used as an interjection in many situations. Tone and context determine whether it's surprise, annoyance, fear, or amazement. Can be shortened to '¡Dios!' or softened to '¡Dios mío y santo!' in emphatic speech. Be aware of religious sensitivity in very formal contexts.
target_language_example: ¡Dios mío, qué sorpresa verte aquí!
native_language_example: Oh my God, what a surprise to see you here!

meaning: to/ toward (a place or person); heading to
additional_notes: Used to indicate movement, sending, or orientation toward someone or something. Common with verbs like ir (ir dirección a), enviar (enviar algo dirección a), dirigir (dirigir la mirada dirección a). More natural alternatives are hacia or rumbo a in many contexts (e.g., rumbo a Madrid). In formal written Spanish you may also see dirección de followed by recipient for addresses.
target_language_example: Vamos dirección a la estación para coger el tren.
native_language_example: We are heading toward the station to catch the train.

meaning: the correct address or correct direction
additional_notes: Can mean 'correct address' (postal or email) or 'right/correct direction' depending on context. Use with verbs like dar, tener, enviar (dar la dirección correcta, tener la dirección correcta, enviar a la dirección correcta) or ir, seguir (seguir la dirección correcta). Gender and number: dirección is feminine (la dirección correcta; las direcciones correctas).
target_language_example: Asegúrate de enviar el paquete a la dirección correcta.
native_language_example: Make sure to send the package to the correct address.

meaning: email address
additional_notes: Common phrase used to refer to someone's email. 'Dirección' = address; 'correo electrónico' = electronic mail. Can be used in singular or plural (direcciones de correo electrónico). Often shortened in speech/writing to 'correo' or 'email' in informal contexts.
target_language_example: ¿Me das tu dirección de correo electrónico?
native_language_example: Can you give me your email address?

meaning: 'directs to' or 'leads to' (he/she/it directs [someone/something] to)
additional_notes: From the verb dirigir (to direct, to lead). 'Dirige a' is used when saying that someone or something guides, sends, or points someone toward a place, person, or resource. Followed by a noun or pronoun (e.g., dirige a la oficina / dirige a los clientes / dirige a él). Can be used for physical direction (lead to a location), for routing (redirects to a webpage or department), or for leadership (he leads people toward...).
target_language_example: La señal dirige a los visitantes al parking.
native_language_example: The sign directs visitors to the parking lot.

meaning: he/she/it directed (toward) the / led to the
additional_notes: From the verb dirigir (to direct/lead) in past simple (él/ella dirigió) plus the preposition a and the feminine singular article la. Used to say someone/something directed, guided, sent, or led toward a feminine noun or place (la ciudad, la oficina, la salida). Context determines whether it means physically directed, addressed (to someone), or caused/led to a result.
target_language_example: El guardia nos dirigió a la salida.
native_language_example: The guard directed us to the exit.

meaning: addressed to; headed to; went toward (past tense, third person).
additional_notes: From the verb dirigirse (to address, to head toward). Context determines meaning: 'dirigió al público' = 'addressed the public' (speak to); 'se dirigió al baño' = 'went toward the bathroom' (moved toward). 'Al' is the contraction of 'a + el'. The phrase shown is past simple (pretérito) for él/ella/usted.
target_language_example: Se dirigió al escenario para dar su discurso.
native_language_example: He headed to the stage to give his speech.

meaning: I'll say what I'm going to (do/say).
additional_notes: This is an incomplete phrase often followed by an infinitive (e.g., 'a hacer', 'a decir') or more words that complete the idea. Literally 'I will say what I am going' — in everyday Spanish you'd typically hear 'diré lo que voy a hacer/decir' to mean 'I'll say what I'm going to do/say.'
target_language_example: Diré lo que voy a decir en la reunión.
native_language_example: I'll say what I'm going to say at the meeting.

meaning: I'll say what I'm going to (do/say).
additional_notes: Commonly the start of a sentence where the speaker announces an intention or explains future actions. Often followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., 'hacer', 'decir', 'explicar') or a clause that completes the thought: 'diré lo que voy a hacer' or 'diré lo que voy a decir'. It's a neutral, literal phrase used in spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: Diré lo que voy a hacer mañana: llamaré al médico.
native_language_example: I'll say what I'm going to do tomorrow: I'll call the doctor.

meaning: I'll say another (one); I'll tell another (one).
additional_notes: A short phrase using the future of decir (diré) plus otra (feminine 'another'). Usually refers to saying another thing, telling another story, or giving another example/opinion. Context determines what 'otra' refers to (una palabra, una cosa, una historia). If referring to a masculine noun, speakers would say 'diré otro'.
target_language_example: No me convence esa explicación; diré otra.
native_language_example: That explanation doesn't convince me; I'll say another one.

meaning: would tell (to) — conditional of decir plus the preposition 'a' indicating the person told.
additional_notes: Used to report what someone would say or tell to someone else (conditional mood). Often followed by an indirect object pronoun or noun (a + person). Can express hypothetical or polite statements (e.g., 'I wouldn't tell someone like you').
target_language_example: No sé qué le diría a mi jefe.
native_language_example: I don't know what I would tell my boss.

meaning: would say a (feminine/singular noun) — conditional 'would say' + the indefinite article 'a'.
additional_notes: Commonly appears before a feminine noun or phrase to describe what someone would say (or would not say). Equivalent to 'would say a...' in English. Context may omit the noun if understood (e.g., 'diría una' followed by an implied idea), but more often it's followed by a noun like 'persona', 'cosa', 'sirena'. Pronunciation: dir-EE-ah OO-na. Used for hypotheticals, opinions, or moral judgments.
target_language_example: Yo diría una opinión honesta.
native_language_example: I would say an honest opinion.

meaning: 'hard drive' (computer storage device).
additional_notes: Refers to the physical or logical device used to store data on a computer. Can mean internal or external hard drive (disco duro interno / externo). Often used for storage capacity (llenar el disco duro) or for formatting/erasing (borrar el disco duro). In informal or figurative contexts it can be used metaphorically (e.g., 'disco duro supremo').
target_language_example: Necesito comprar un disco duro externo para hacer copias.
native_language_example: I need to buy an external hard drive to make backups.

meaning: to apologize for (something) — literally 'to excuse myself for'.
additional_notes: A reflexive verb phrase using disculpar(se). Use 'disculparme por' when speaking in the first person (I). Replace the reflexive pronoun for other persons (disculparte, disculparse, disculparnos, disculparos, disculparse). Commonly followed by a noun or clause (lo de anoche, eso, todo lo que dije). You can add 'quiero/quería' to soften or make it polite.
target_language_example: Quería disculparme por haber llegado tarde.
native_language_example: I wanted to apologize for having arrived late.

meaning: 'sorry for the...' or 'apologies for the...'
additional_notes: A phrase starter used to apologize for something; it is normally followed by a noun, clause, or gerund (e.g., 'disculpas por lo ocurrido', 'disculpas por lo de anoche', 'disculpas por lo que dije'). Common in informal and formal contexts. You can also use 'disculpas' alone or 'disculpa(s) por...' with a specific reason.
target_language_example: Disculpas por lo de ayer, no volverá a pasar.
native_language_example: Sorry about what happened yesterday, it won't happen again.

meaning: excuse the... / sorry for the... (polite way to apologize for something specific)
additional_notes: Polite, formal expression used to apologize for a specific inconvenience or delay. Usually followed by a noun: 'demora' (delay), 'molestia' (bother), 'tardanza' (lateness). Can be used alone as a short apology (e.g., 'Disculpe la demora.'). 'Disculpe' is formal (usted); in informal contexts use 'discúlpame' or 'perdón'.
target_language_example: Disculpe la confusión; le envío la información correcta ahora.
native_language_example: Sorry for the confusion; I'll send you the correct information now.

meaning: I apologize for / I'm sorry for
additional_notes: First-person singular present of disculparse: 'me disculpo por' is a formal or neutral way to apologize for something (an action, situation, person, etc.). Use with a noun, clause, or pronoun: 'me disculpo por el ruido', 'me disculpo por lo que dije', 'me disculpo por él' (I'm apologizing on his behalf). For more casual speech you might hear 'lo siento' or 'perdón'.
target_language_example: Me disculpo por llegar tarde.
native_language_example: I apologize for arriving late.

meaning: speech/talk in (a particular language or on a topic).
additional_notes: "Discurso" means a formal speech or discourse. When followed by "en" it usually introduces the language used (e.g., "discurso en español") or the medium/context (e.g., "discurso en público", "discurso en línea"). Use "un/ el discurso en..." depending on article and context. For "in" + language, the pattern is: "discurso en + [idioma]". For "on" a topic, prefer "discurso sobre + [tema]".
target_language_example: Dio un discurso en español durante la ceremonia.
native_language_example: He gave a speech in Spanish during the ceremony.

meaning: dressed up as / disguised as (someone or something).
additional_notes: Past tense (third person singular) of 'disfrazarse de'. Used to say someone wore a costume or disguise to look like a particular person, role, or thing. To use in other persons/tenses, conjugate 'disfrazarse' (me disfrazo, te disfrazaste, se disfrazarán, etc.). Common with occupations, genders, fictional characters, or objects.
target_language_example: Ella se disfrazó de astronauta para la fiesta.
native_language_example: She dressed up as an astronaut for the party.

meaning: enjoying (something); taking pleasure in.
additional_notes: Present participle of disfrutar + preposition de. Used to describe enjoying an activity, experience, or thing: disfrutando de + noun (disfrutando de la música) or disfrutando de + gerund/phrase. Common in progressive descriptions: 'estoy disfrutando de...' or 'disfrutando de...' as part of a sentence.
target_language_example: Estoy disfrutando de las vacaciones en la playa.
native_language_example: I'm enjoying the vacation at the beach.

meaning: literally 'shot in' — used to describe a gunshot (or similar impact) that occurs in/at a specific place or to indicate a strike/hit on a body part or object.
additional_notes: Commonly appears before a location or body part (e.g., 'disparo en la espalda' = 'a shot in the back'). Can describe a literal gunshot or be used figuratively in some contexts (e.g., 'un disparo en el pie' = 'a mistake' in some idiomatic uses, though that is less common). Remember word order: 'disparo en + [place/part]'. If you want to say 'shot at' (aimed at), Spanish often uses 'disparo contra' or 'disparo a'.
target_language_example: Recibió un disparo en el hombro.
native_language_example: He received a shot in the shoulder.

meaning: a shot (fired) in the [body part / location]; used to describe a gunshot wound located in something (e.g., 'disparo en la cabeza' = 'shot in the head').
additional_notes: This is not a complete phrase by itself; it's the start of a phrase indicating where someone was shot. It is followed by a feminine noun (la + noun) naming the body part or place: e.g., 'disparo en la pierna', 'disparo en la espalda', 'disparo en la cara'. In news or reports, you may see it used to describe injuries: 'recibió un disparo en la...' In everyday speech, 'recibió un disparo' (he/she was shot) + location is common.
target_language_example: Recibió un disparo en la pierna durante el robo.
native_language_example: He received a shot in the leg during the robbery.

meaning: to distinguish/recognize what is good (morally or qualitatively)
additional_notes: Used to talk about telling right from wrong or identifying what is beneficial or morally good. Can be used in moral, ethical, philosophical, or evaluative contexts. Commonly appears with objects like 'lo bueno' (what is good) or as an infinitive phrase after verbs: 'aprender a distinguir el bien', 'es difícil distinguir el bien del mal'.
target_language_example: Es importante enseñarle a los niños a distinguir el bien del mal.
native_language_example: It's important to teach children to distinguish right from wrong.

meaning: to distinguish good from (—); to tell good from (—).
additional_notes: This phrase is followed by 'mal' to form 'distinguir el bien del mal' — 'to distinguish good from evil/ bad'. It expresses the ability to tell right from wrong. Use with subjects (pueden, es fácil, sé) and often appears in moral or evaluative contexts.
target_language_example: Es importante enseñar a los niños a distinguir el bien del mal.
native_language_example: It's important to teach children to distinguish good from evil.

meaning: 'different from' or 'distinct from'.
additional_notes: Used to compare one thing or person with another. Often follows the preposition 'a' (distinto a) or 'de' in some regions (distinto de). Common in spoken and written Spanish to indicate difference or uniqueness. Can describe characteristics, experiences, or identities.
target_language_example: Ella es distinto a los demás en su forma de pensar.
native_language_example: She is different from the others in her way of thinking.

meaning: 'fun' or 'more fun than' when comparing; used to say something is enjoyable or to compare enjoyment.
additional_notes: Divertido means 'fun' or 'entertaining'. When followed by que + clause/noun it often appears in comparisons (más divertido que = more fun than) or in exclamations/remarks about how fun something/someone is (Lo divertido que eras = How funny/entertaining you were). It can modify verbs (hacer algo divertido = to make something fun). Note: divertido is an adjective and must agree in gender/number (divertida, divertidos, divertidas).
target_language_example: Jugar con amigos es más divertido que ver la tele.
native_language_example: Playing with friends is more fun than watching TV.

meaning: twice as (much) as / double of what
additional_notes: 'Doble de lo' is used before a noun or phrase to compare quantities or intensity, equivalent to 'double' or 'twice as ... as' in English. Often appears as 'el doble de' (the double of) or in comparisons like 'doble de lo que...' (double what.../twice what...). If followed by a verb clause, use 'doble de lo que...' or 'el doble de lo que...'.
target_language_example: Tiene el doble de lo que necesitas.
native_language_example: He has double what you need.

meaning: twice as (much) as / double than
additional_notes: Used to compare quantities or amounts: it indicates that one thing is two times another. Often appears before adjectives, nouns or verbs when comparing (e.g., "es el doble que...", "tiene el doble que..."). In Spanish it's common to use "el doble de + noun" (el doble de trabajo) or "ser/estar el doble que + clause" (es el doble que yo). Both forms convey the idea of two times as much.
target_language_example: Ella gana el doble que yo.
native_language_example: She earns twice as much as I do.

meaning: the doctor said
additional_notes: A simple past (preterite) report: 'dijo' is the third-person singular preterite of 'decir' (to say). Use to report what a doctor stated. Structure: subject + dijo + (que) + clause. 'Que' is optional before the reported clause. Can also appear with a named doctor (el doctor dijo) or with a title (la doctora dijo).
target_language_example: El doctor dijo que debo descansar una semana.
native_language_example: The doctor said I should rest for a week.

meaning: holds a PhD (literally 'doctor in' a subject).
additional_notes: Used before an academic field to indicate someone has a doctorate in that area: 'doctor en física' = 'a doctor/PhD in physics'. Can refer to the title 'Dr.' plus the specialization. Often appears in formal contexts (CVs, introductions). In spoken English you'd usually say 'has a PhD in...' or 'is a doctor of...'.
target_language_example: Ella es doctor en biología y trabaja en investigación.
native_language_example: She is a doctor in biology and works in research.

meaning: to doctor (something) — to alter, tamper with, or falsify (e.g., a document, data, or evidence).
additional_notes: Borrowed from English 'doctor' used as a verb; the construction 'doctor le' is a colloquial pattern where 'le' functions as an object clitic (often approximating 'it' or 'him/her' in informal speech). More standard Spanish uses 'doctorar' rarely or 'manipular', 'falsificar' or 'alterar'. Commonly followed by the thing that is altered explicitly (e.g., 'doctor le los resultados' is nonstandard — preferred: 'doctorar los resultados' or 'doctorle' as a spoken contraction in some dialects). Often implies dishonest or deceptive modification. Avoid in formal/legal contexts.
target_language_example: No puedes doctor le los resultados del examen; eso es fraude.
native_language_example: You can't doctor the exam results; that's fraud.

meaning: Not a standard Spanish phrase. Appears to be English ('doctor me' = have a doctor examine or treat me) or a literal bilingual calque. In Spanish, use verbs like 'examíname', 'trátame' or phrases like 'que me vea el médico'.
additional_notes: This entry documents the nonstandard/bilingual fragment 'doctor me' as sometimes seen in code-switching or literal translations from English. It is not proper Spanish grammar. Use full Spanish verbs or noun phrases when speaking Spanish. Possible intended meanings: 'examine me', 'treat me', or 'get a doctor to see me'.
target_language_example: Doctor me, por favor, que me duele mucho la cabeza.
native_language_example: Doctor me, please, my head hurts a lot.

meaning: 'documents that' or 'the documents which' — introduces a relative clause describing specific documents.
additional_notes: Used to refer to particular documents already mentioned or identified; 'que' is a relative pronoun meaning 'that/which' and links to a clause giving more information about the documents. Word order: documentos que + verb/clause. Can refer to documents you gave, received, or that accompanied someone.
target_language_example: Revisé los documentos que me enviaste.
native_language_example: I checked the documents that you sent me.

meaning: pain in
additional_notes: Use before a body part or area to indicate pain located there. Commonly followed by a noun (dolor de cabeza, dolor de estómago, dolor de espalda). Can be used with ser/estar/tener and verbs of complaining: estoy con dolor de dientes / tengo dolor de cabeza / se quejaba de dolor de espalda. Not idiomatic if used without a body part.
target_language_example: Tengo dolor de garganta desde ayer.
native_language_example: I have a sore throat since yesterday.

meaning: 'headache' (pain in the head).
additional_notes: Commonly used to describe physical pain in the head. Can be used with articles and qualifiers: 'tengo dolor de cabeza', 'tengo un dolor de cabeza leve', 'un poco de dolor de cabeza'. Also used figuratively to mean a nuisance or problem (e.g., 'esto es un dolor de cabeza').
target_language_example: Tengo un dolor de cabeza después de trabajar frente al ordenador.
native_language_example: I have a headache after working in front of the computer.

meaning: pain in the (body part).
additional_notes: Used to describe physical pain followed by a body part (e.g., 'dolor en el pecho' = 'pain in the chest'). In informal insults, the phrase 'eres un dolor en el...' (often 'trasero' or 'culo') means 'you're a pain in the ...' or 'you're a nuisance.' Context determines whether it's literal (medical) or figurative (annoyance).
target_language_example: Tengo un dolor en el hombro desde ayer.
native_language_example: I have pain in my shoulder since yesterday.

meaning: 'the pain was' — simple past description of pain or discomfort.
additional_notes: This is the phrase 'el dolor era' using the imperfect tense (era) to describe an ongoing or repeated state in the past: 'the pain was' (e.g., severe, unbearable, intense). You will often see it followed by adjectives (fuerte, insoportable, terrible) or clauses describing how the person felt or reacted. Use 'el dolor fue' (pretérito) if you want to emphasize a completed event rather than an ongoing state.
target_language_example: El dolor era constante y no me dejaba pensar.
native_language_example: The pain was constant and wouldn't let me think.
