native_language_example: She holds the national swimming record.

meaning: Literal sequence 'el río a' — not a standard fixed phrase in Spanish. It would occur when the noun phrase 'el río' is immediately followed by the preposition 'a' starting the next segment of the sentence (e.g., 'el río a orillas de...'). The meaning depends on the larger sentence: 'el río' = 'the river'; 'a' = 'to/at/by' or part of a verb construction.
additional_notes: This is not an established multi-word idiom; it's simply the article+noun followed by the preposition 'a'. Ensure the accent on í in río. Use will depend on context — often appears when linking the noun to a location or motion (e.g., 'el río a la derecha'). If seen alone, it may indicate a typographical fragment.
target_language_example: Vimos el río a lo lejos mientras conducíamos.
native_language_example: We saw the river in the distance while we were driving.

meaning: the (something) river / the most (used to form superlatives for rivers) — 'the ...-est river' (e.g. the longest river).
additional_notes: Combine 'el río más' with an adjective (e.g. largo = long) and a location to make superlatives about rivers: 'el río más largo de/ en [lugar]' = 'the longest river of/in [place]'. Use 'de' for 'of' or 'in' (de los Estados Unidos, de África). 'En' is also possible: 'el río más largo en Japón.' Word order: 'el río más + adjective + de/en + lugar' or 'el + [river name] + es el río más + adjective + de/en + lugar.'
target_language_example: El Amazonas es el río más caudaloso de América del Sur.
native_language_example: The Amazon is the most voluminous (the river with the greatest flow) in South America.

meaning: 'the meaning of' / 'the sense of' (also used in senses like 'sense of' as in direction or perception).
additional_notes: Common phrase used to talk about meaning, purpose, or a particular sense/feeling (e.g., sense of reality, sense of direction). Context determines translation: often 'the meaning of' (El sentido de la vida = the meaning of life) or 'sense of' (el sentido de la orientación = sense of direction).
target_language_example: El sentido de la amistad es muy importante para ella.
native_language_example: The meaning of friendship is very important to her.

meaning: the being; existence; a (living or philosophical) entity
additional_notes: Used in philosophical, spiritual, or formal contexts to refer to existence, an entity, or a supreme being. Can mean 'the being' (general existence), 'a being' (an individual entity), or 'the supreme being' depending on context. Not used for everyday casual reference to people (use 'persona' or 'ser humano' instead).
target_language_example: El ser humano busca sentido en la vida.
native_language_example: The human being seeks meaning in life.

meaning: on the Saturday that / the Saturday when
additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific Saturday connected to a clause that follows or precedes (often introducing a relative/time clause). Equivalent to 'the Saturday that' or 'on Saturday when' in English. You will often see it followed by a verb: el sábado que llegamos, el sábado que nos vimos, etc.
target_language_example: El sábado que viniste celebramos en mi casa.
native_language_example: On the Saturday that you came we celebrated at my house.

meaning: 'the symbol of' or 'the emblem of' (shows what something represents).
additional_notes: Used to say that a person, object, or place represents or stands for a larger idea, group, country, etc. Followed by a noun or noun phrase. Can refer to cultural, political, historical, or local symbols.
target_language_example: La paloma blanca es el símbolo de la paz.
native_language_example: The white dove is the symbol of peace.

meaning: that so-called / the aforementioned (used to talk about a person whose name was just mentioned or to refer to someone with slight distance or dismissiveness).
additional_notes: Used before a name or title to refer back to someone already mentioned or to introduce a person with a hint of distance, skepticism, or mild contempt. Equivalent to English 'that so‑called' or 'the said' (informal). Often appears as 'el tal + name' or 'la tal + name'.
target_language_example: No me fío del tal Alberto; siempre llega tarde.
native_language_example: I don't trust that so‑called Alberto; he always arrives late.

meaning: 'the time of' or 'the weather of' (depends on context).
additional_notes: This is a short phrase fragment: 'el tiempo' can mean either 'time' (duration, moment) or 'weather'. When followed by 'del' (de + el) it links to a noun: e.g. 'el tiempo del concierto' = 'the time of the concert' (when it happens); 'el tiempo del año' could mean 'the weather of the season' or 'the time of year' depending on context. You will usually see a specific noun after 'del'.
target_language_example: ¿Cuál es el tiempo del partido?
native_language_example: What is the time of the match?

meaning: literally 'the world's time' — not a common set phrase; likely means 'the (weather) time of the world' or poetic reference to time/universe depending on context.
additional_notes: This exact phrase is unusual in everyday Spanish. Interpreted literally, it combines tiempo (time or weather) and mundo (world). Possible uses: poetic/metaphorical (e.g., 'the time of the world' meaning the era or human history), or a mistaken/creative way to refer to 'el clima del mundo' (the world's weather). If you encounter it, pay attention to context to decide whether it refers to time (era, season) or to global weather/climate. Not a standard idiom.
target_language_example: En sus poemas hablaba del tiempo del mundo y de cómo cambian las cosas.
native_language_example: In his poems he spoke about the time of the world and how things change.

meaning: "time will tell" (only time will show the outcome).
additional_notes: Used to express that the result of a situation is uncertain now and will become clear in the future. Often interchangeable with 'solo el tiempo dirá' or 'sólo el tiempo dirá'. Common in both spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: No sabemos si fue la decisión correcta; el tiempo dirá.
native_language_example: We don't know if it was the right decision; time will tell.

meaning: 'time flies' — time passes very quickly.
additional_notes: Common idiom used to express that moments or periods go by fast. Can be used alone as a comment (El tiempo vuela.) or with comparisons (El tiempo vuela como una flecha). Not literal: it doesn't mean time actually flies.
target_language_example: No me di cuenta de que ya es octubre; el tiempo vuela.
native_language_example: I didn't realize it's already October; time flies.

meaning: the work beforehand / the work earlier (usually in time expressions: 'finish the work before...').
additional_notes: This phrase combines 'el trabajo' (the work / assignment / job) with 'antes' (before/earlier). Beginners will most often see it in time expressions meaning to complete or submit the work before a deadline or before a certain time/event (e.g., antes de las fiestas, antes de las seis). Word order can change: 'terminar el trabajo antes de...' or 'antes de terminar el trabajo...'.
target_language_example: Necesito terminar el trabajo antes del viernes.
native_language_example: I need to finish the work before Friday.

meaning: 'the three' (the number three) — used to refer to the numeral 3 or a group/thing labeled number three.
additional_notes: Literally 'the three'. Commonly used when counting objects, giving a number in a list, or referring to an item labeled '3' (e.g., table number, apartment number, option three). Context determines whether it means the numeral itself, a third item, or 'three of something'. For ordinal 'the third' you would normally use 'el tercero' or 'el tercer' before a masculine noun.
target_language_example: Pon la maleta en el tres, por favor.
native_language_example: Put the suitcase on number three, please.

meaning: the trafficking/traffic of; the trade or movement of (people, goods, information, vehicles, etc.).
additional_notes: Used before a noun to indicate illegal trade (e.g., 'tráfico de drogas' = drug trafficking) or the movement/flow of something (e.g., 'tráfico de vehículos' = vehicle traffic). Context determines whether it means 'trafficking' (criminal trade) or simply 'traffic/flow'. Often appears in news, legal, and formal contexts.
target_language_example: La policía investigó el tráfico de armas en la región.
native_language_example: The police investigated arms trafficking in the region.

meaning: the shift; someone's turn (to do something).
additional_notes: Commonly used for work shifts (morning/afternoon/night) and for taking turns (it's someone's turn). Context tells whether it means a work shift or a turn in a sequence. Often used with time words (de la noche, de la mañana) or possessives (mi turno).
target_language_example: Mañana tengo el turno de la tarde en el hospital.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I have the afternoon shift at the hospital.

meaning: part of the reciprocal phrase meaning 'one another' or 'each other' (used in constructions like 'el uno al otro').
additional_notes: This fragment appears in the common reciprocal expression 'el uno al otro' or 'unos a otros' to indicate mutual action or relationship between people. In English: 'each other' / 'one another'. Word order can vary: 'nos tenemos el uno al otro', 'nos miramos el uno al otro', or simply 'nos tenemos' when context makes reciprocity clear. Not used alone without the rest of the phrase ('el uno al otro' or 'el uno a otro').
target_language_example: Se ayudan el uno al otro cuando hay problemas.
native_language_example: They help each other when there are problems.

meaning: literally 'the one with' — used to identify someone or something by a distinguishing feature (e.g., 'the one with the red hat').
additional_notes: This phrase is a simple way to point out or describe a person/object by mentioning a characteristic that accompanies them. In natural Spanish it's often part of a longer phrase: 'el/ la que tiene...' or 'el uno con...' is less common than alternatives like 'el que lleva...' or 'el de la/ del...' Use gender and number to match the noun (el/la/los/las).
target_language_example: Busca al chico: el uno con la sudadera azul.
native_language_example: Look for the guy — the one with the blue sweatshirt.

meaning: with each other; mutually (used to talk about actions or feelings between two or more people).
additional_notes: Commonly appears in the full phrase 'el uno con el otro' (or 'el uno con el otro' / 'el uno con el otro' — variations include 'unos con otros' for plural). Used to emphasize mutual or reciprocal relationships or actions (we talk to each other, we are honest with each other). Often interchangeable with 'el uno al otro', 'entre sí' or 'entre nosotros' depending on context.
target_language_example: Hablaron con franqueza el uno con el otro.
native_language_example: They spoke frankly with each other.

meaning: the one of the / the first of the (depends on context)
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself. It combines the masculine singular article + uno + preposition del (de + el). It can appear in expressions like 'el uno del grupo' (the one of the group) or in dates/times like 'el uno del mes' (the first day of the month) where 'el uno' means 'the first (day)'. Context determines whether 'uno' means 'one' (as a count) or 'the first'. Watch agreement and contractions: 'del' = 'de + el' and requires a following masculine singular noun.
target_language_example: Ella es el uno del equipo.
native_language_example: She is the one of the team.

meaning: the one on (the...), or the one in (the...) — used to identify a specific item by its position or location
additional_notes: This phrase combines el uno (the one) with a preposition like en to point out something by where it is (on, in, at). You'll usually see it followed by a noun or context: e.g., "el uno en la fila" (the one in the line) or "el uno en la mesa" (the one on the table). In spoken Spanish, variations like "el primero en" or simply "el de (la)" are also common depending on formality and clarity.
target_language_example: Quiero el uno en la estantería, no el de la mesa.
native_language_example: I want the one on the shelf, not the one on the table.

meaning: the one in the (masculine) — used to identify a specific person or thing among others
additional_notes: This phrase is a short fragment often used when pointing out or distinguishing an item or person: 'el uno en el...' followed by a place, group, or characteristic (e.g., 'el uno en el equipo', 'el uno en el estante'). In natural speech speakers more commonly say 'el que está en...' or 'el de en...' depending on structure. Use masculine singular 'el uno' when referring to a male or a masculine noun.
target_language_example: Me quedo con el uno en el estante.
native_language_example: I'll keep the one on the shelf.

meaning: literally 'the one for' — used to identify a specific item intended for a purpose or person (context-dependent).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom on its own; it typically appears as part of a larger phrase such as 'el uno para mí' (the one for me) or 'el uno para la fiesta' (the one for the party). Use it to point out which item is designated or chosen for someone or something. Word order and completion matter — without the rest of the phrase it feels incomplete.
target_language_example: El uno para ti es el más pequeño.
native_language_example: The one for you is the smallest.

meaning: one for the other; each for the other (mutual exchange or reciprocity)
additional_notes: Used to describe mutual actions or exchanges between two people or things (each gives or does something for the other). Contexts: favors, gifts, support, or reciprocal behavior. Not a fixed idiom everywhere — more common in conversational phrasing like «el uno para el otro» (one for the other). Watch word order: often appears as «el uno para el otro» or «uno para el otro/otra».
target_language_example: Se ayudaban el uno para el otro en el trabajo.
native_language_example: They helped one another at work.

meaning: 'the twentieth' (date) or 'twenty percent' depending on context
additional_notes: Can refer to a day of the month when followed by a month (e.g. el veinte de julio = July 20th). In other contexts, especially with 'por ciento' or when talking about percentages, it means 'twenty percent' (el veinte por ciento). Context tells you which meaning applies. Commonly used in everyday speech for dates and percentages.
target_language_example: Nos vemos el veinte de mayo.
native_language_example: We'll see each other on May twentieth.

meaning: 'on Friday by' or 'Friday at (a deadline/time)'; used to indicate something happening or due on/around Friday (often followed by a time or phrase).
additional_notes: This is a fragment rather than a complete fixed phrase. Native speakers usually complete it with a time, deadline, or phrase (e.g., 'el viernes por la tarde' = Friday afternoon, 'el viernes por la mañana' = Friday morning, or 'el viernes por ...' meaning 'by Friday' when followed by a verb or deadline context). Word order and preposition choice depends on context: 'el viernes por la tarde' (time of day) vs. 'para el viernes' or 'antes del viernes' (deadlines meaning 'by Friday').
target_language_example: Necesito el informe el viernes por la tarde.
native_language_example: I need the report on Friday afternoon.

meaning: the last moment; at the last minute.
additional_notes: Used to refer to something happening very late or just before a deadline. Common in phrases like 'a último momento' or 'en el último momento' meaning 'at the last minute' or 'just in time.' Can describe decisions, changes, cancellations, or arrivals that occur very late.
target_language_example: Cancelaron el vuelo en el último momento.
native_language_example: They canceled the flight at the last minute.

meaning: the only animal
additional_notes: Literal phrase: used to say there is just one animal (the sole animal in a group, place, or context). 'Único' emphasizes uniqueness or exclusivity. Agreement: 'único' agrees in gender/number with the noun (e.g., la única mascota, los únicos animales).
target_language_example: En la granja, ese perro es el único animal que queda.
native_language_example: On the farm, that dog is the only animal left.

meaning: 'the only one with' (someone or something).
additional_notes: Used to say someone is the sole person who has or possesses something, or the only person who can do or be involved in something. Often followed by a noun, a prepositional phrase (con + noun), or a relative clause with 'que'/'el que'/'con quien'. Common in spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: Él es el único con una llave de la oficina.
native_language_example: He is the only one with a key to the office.

meaning: the only language
additional_notes: Used to say that a single language is the one someone speaks, understands, or that someone 'knows' or 'responds to'. Often followed by a clause introduced with que + verb (e.g., 'el único idioma que puedo hablar...'). Can be used literally (a language) or figuratively (e.g., 'la violencia es el único idioma que entienden').
target_language_example: El único idioma que entiendo bien es el inglés.
native_language_example: The only language I understand well is English.

meaning: he died.
additional_notes: This is the simple past (pretérito) of morir used with the subject pronoun 'él'. The correct written form to mean 'he' is 'él murió' with an acute accent on 'él'. Without the accent, 'el' is the masculine definite article ('the'), so 'el murió' (no accent) is a common orthographic error or ambiguous sequence. Use 'él murió' when explicitly meaning 'he died'.
target_language_example: El murió en el accidente.
native_language_example: He died in the accident.

meaning: mine
additional_notes: A possessive pronoun meaning 'mine' (masculine singular). It replaces a noun previously mentioned. Use 'la mía' for feminine singular, 'los míos' for masculine plural, and 'las mías' for feminine plural. Often appears after the noun it contrasts with (e.g., 'el mío' vs 'el tuyo').
target_language_example: Ese libro es el mío.
native_language_example: That book is mine.

meaning: the one who
additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific person or thing already known from context: "the one who/that...". It often avoids repeating a noun. The form changes with gender and number: la que, los que, las que.
target_language_example: Quiero el que está en la mesa.
native_language_example: I want the one that's on the table.

meaning: the one who is / the one that is (doing something right now)
additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific person or thing among others, emphasizing an action in progress (present continuous). Often followed by a present participle (gerund) or a clause: 'el que está leyendo', 'el que está mintiendo'. Can mean 'the one who is' or 'the one that is' depending on context.
target_language_example: ¿Ves al niño? El que está jugando con la pelota es mi primo.
native_language_example: Do you see the boy? The one who is playing with the ball is my cousin.

meaning: 'the one that I ... the most' (start of a phrase expressing preference or strongest feeling)
additional_notes: This fragment is typically followed by a verb or adjective to complete a comparison or preference: e.g. 'el que más me gusta' (the one I like the most), 'el que más me sorprende' (the one that surprises me the most). It agrees in gender/number with the noun it refers to (el/los/la/las). Common in spoken and written Spanish to single out the strongest feeling or preference.
target_language_example: De todos los cuadros, el que más me gusta es ese con flores.
native_language_example: Of all the paintings, the one I like the most is the one with flowers.

meaning: who/one who is born (in...) — used to talk about someone's birthplace or origin.
additional_notes: Literal construction: 'el que' (the one who) + verb 'nacer' (to be born). Commonly followed by a place: 'el que nace en [lugar]...' Used to make general statements about people born in a specific country or place.
target_language_example: El que nace en Canadá suele hablar inglés o francés.
native_language_example: One who is born in Canada usually speaks English or French.

meaning: 'whatever' or 'whichever (one) it may be' (non-specific choice).
additional_notes: Used to refer vaguely to a person or thing without specifying which one. Often appears in contexts expressing indifference or generality (e.g., 'elige el que sea' = 'choose whichever one'). Can be shortened in speech to 'el que sea' or combined with genders/numbers: 'la que sea', 'los que sean', 'las que sean'.
target_language_example: Compra el que sea más barato.
native_language_example: Buy whichever one is cheapest.

meaning: the one (masculine) / number one.
additional_notes: Used to refer to a single masculine noun previously mentioned (the one) or to indicate the number one/ranking. Context determines whether it means 'the one' (e.g., the person/thing) or 'one' as a number. If referring to a feminine noun, use 'la una' or 'la one' is not used—use 'la una' for time (1:00) and 'la única' for 'the one (female)'.
target_language_example: De los candidatos, él es el uno que tiene más experiencia.
native_language_example: Of the candidates, he is the one who has more experience.

meaning: each other / one another (reciprocal pronoun)
additional_notes: Used to express reciprocal actions or relationships between two or more people (they do something to or for each other). Often appears with reflexive verbs (se) like «se ven el uno al otro», «se ayudan el uno al otro». Can also appear as «los unos a los otros» for plural groups. Word order may vary («el uno al otro», «el uno al otro» is standard).
target_language_example: Se apoyan el uno al otro en los momentos difíciles.
native_language_example: They support each other in difficult times.

meaning: he doesn't / he won't / he can't / he isn't (depending on what follows)
additional_notes: For this meaning, standard Spanish spelling is "él no" with an accent on "él" (= "he"). Written as "el no" without the accent, it is nonstandard but may appear in informal typing or in text that omits accents. The exact interpretation depends on the verb or predicate that follows.
target_language_example: Cariño, el no te entiende.
native_language_example: Darling, he doesn't understand you.

meaning: he (used before a reflexive or pronominal verb; standard spelling: «él se»)
additional_notes: As written, «el se» is a nonstandard spelling if it refers to the pronoun «él» + «se»; standard Spanish writes «él se». In unaccented text, it can represent “he” before a reflexive or pronominal verb. The exact English translation depends on the verb: «el se ocupa...» = “he takes care of...”, «el se pasó por...» = “he stopped by...”.
target_language_example: Todos dicen que el se ocupa de esas cosas.
native_language_example: Everyone says that he takes care of those things.

meaning: 'elephant is' — literal combination of the noun elefante (elephant) and the verb es (is).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed Spanish phrase; it's simply the noun 'elefante' followed by the verb 'es'. It could appear in a sentence like 'El elefante es grande' (The elephant is big). Pay attention to articles and adjectives: Spanish usually requires an article ('el elefante').
target_language_example: El elefante es grande y pesado.
native_language_example: The elephant is big and heavy.

meaning: to choose the (masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Elegir = to choose. 'El' is the masculine singular definite article; together they introduce choosing a specific masculine noun (e.g., elegir el libro, elegir el momento). In many sentences the article is part of the noun phrase and may contract or change if the noun is feminine ('elegir la') or plural ('elegir los/las'). Verb form (elegir/puede/puedes) must match subject and politeness level.
target_language_example: Puedes elegir el plato que prefieras.
native_language_example: You can choose the dish you prefer.

meaning: 'ella a' is not a standard grammatical phrase in Spanish; likely a misspelling or token sequence combining the pronoun 'ella' (she) and either the preposition 'a' (to) or a mistaken auxiliary 'ha' (has). Possible interpretations include: 1) a typo for 'ella ha' (she has, auxiliary), 2) the pronoun followed by the preposition 'a' as part of a larger correct construction (e.g., 'ella a la puerta' would still be ungrammatical without a verb), or 3) a fragment from informal or erroneous writing.
additional_notes: Alone, 'ella a' is unusual and generally incorrect. If intended as the auxiliary, the correct form is 'ella ha' (ha = haber, third-person singular present). If intended as pronoun + preposition, it must be part of a full sentence (e.g., 'ella va a la tienda' or 'ella está a la puerta'), not 'ella a' by itself. Watch for typographical errors where 'a' was written instead of 'ha'.
target_language_example: Si ves 'ella a' en un texto, probablemente sea un error tipográfico por 'ella ha'.
native_language_example: If you see 'ella a' in a text, it is probably a typo for 'ella ha'.

meaning: she opened the
additional_notes: A simple past (pretérito) sentence fragment: ella (she) + abrió (opened) + la (the, feminine singular). Used before a feminine noun (la carta, la puerta, la ventana, la boca). Common in narratives. You must add the noun after la (e.g., 'ella abrió la puerta').
target_language_example: Ella abrió la caja lentamente.
native_language_example: She opened the box slowly.

meaning: 'she finishes' / 'she just (did something)' depending on context.
additional_notes: Acabar combined with a verb (acabar de + infinitive) means 'to have just (done)' — e.g., ella acaba de llegar = she has just arrived. Used alone (ella acaba) often means 'she finishes' or 'she ends' (something) and usually needs an object or phrase to be complete: ella acaba la tarea = she finishes the homework. Tense and context change the precise meaning.
target_language_example: Ella acaba de comer.
native_language_example: She has just eaten.

meaning: she now / she at this moment
additional_notes: A simple combination of the pronoun ella (she) and ahora (now). Used to say what a woman or girl is doing or what her situation is at the present time. Word order is normal: subject (ella) + time adverb (ahora). Can appear anywhere in the sentence depending on emphasis (e.g., Ahora ella... or Ella ahora...).
target_language_example: Ella ahora trabaja en una cafetería.
native_language_example: She now works in a café.

meaning: 'she before' or 'her before' (literal); not a fixed idiom by itself but the pronoun + adverb combination often appearing in contexts meaning 'she before' as part of a clause like 'ella, antes,...' or in less common word orders for emphasis.
additional_notes: Not a standalone fixed phrase. In natural Spanish, 'antes' commonly precedes verbs or appears in constructions like 'antes de que ella...' or 'antes de que ella llegara'. 'Ella antes' can appear for emphasis or contrast (e.g., 'Ella, antes, era tímida') or in colloquial speech where word order is flexible ('Ella antes vivía aquí'). Use with care—placing 'antes' before the verb is more typical ('Antes ella...') but 'Ella antes...' is grammatical when used for contrast or pause.
target_language_example: Ella antes vivía en Madrid, pero ahora vive aquí.
native_language_example: She used to live in Madrid before, but now she lives here.

meaning: she helped
additional_notes: Simple past (pretérito) of ayudar: 'ella ayudó' means 'she helped' or 'she gave help'. Often followed by 'a' + infinitive (ella ayudó a cocinar = she helped to cook) or 'a' + person (ella ayudó a su hija = she helped her daughter). Can be used with direct objects (ella ayudó a sus amigos = she helped her friends).
target_language_example: Ella ayudó a preparar la cena anoche.
native_language_example: She helped prepare dinner last night.

meaning: she still / she yet
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something continues to be true about a female subject. 'Aún' is interchangeable with 'todavía' in most contexts; word order can be 'ella aún' or more commonly 'ella aún no' / 'ella aún sí' depending on negation or emphasis. In everyday speech Spanish speakers often omit the subject pronoun ('aún' + verb) unless emphasizing 'ella'.
target_language_example: Ella aún no ha llegado.
native_language_example: She still hasn't arrived.

meaning: she almost / she nearly
additional_notes: Use 'casi' before a verb to say someone came very close to something (an accident, event, or action) but it didn't happen. 'Ella' means 'she'; combine as 'Ella casi + verb' (e.g., 'Ella casi se desmaya' = 'She almost faints'). Common with reflexive verbs (se desmayó, se ahogó) and past tenses.
target_language_example: Ella casi perdió el bus esta mañana.
native_language_example: She almost missed the bus this morning.

meaning: Not a fixed idiom; simply the pronoun 'ella' (she) followed by 'como' which can be a conjunction ('as/since') or a verb form ('I eat') — combined they typically require punctuation or additional words to be grammatical (e.g., 'Ella, como ...' = 'She, since/as ...' or in comparisons 'ella como tú' = 'she, like you').
additional_notes: 'ella como' is not a set phrase. Common uses: 1) with a comma: 'Ella, como ...' introducing an explanation (como = 'since/as'); 2) in comparisons without punctuation: 'ella como tú' meaning 'she, like you' (better punctuated: 'Ella, como tú, ...'); 3) avoid interpreting 'como' as the first-person singular of 'comer' ('I eat') after 'ella' — for 'she eats' use 'ella come'. Pay attention to punctuation and verb agreement.
target_language_example: Ella como tú no suele llegar tarde.
native_language_example: She, like you, doesn't usually arrive late.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase in Spanish; likely an incomplete fragment meaning 'she of' or part of a larger construction. On its own it is ungrammatical or unlikely outside poetic/colloquial fragments.
additional_notes: 'Ella' = 'she'; 'de' = 'of/from/about'. The normal order for expressing 'of her' is 'de ella' (not 'ella de'). 'Ella de' might appear inside a larger phrase where word order is inverted for stylistic reasons (e.g., poetry) or as part of a clause broken across lines, but it is not a phrase to memorize.
target_language_example: En el verso quedaba «ella de noche», jugando con el ritmo del poema.
native_language_example: In the line it read "she by night," playing with the poem's rhythm.

meaning: she devoted (or dedicated) — used to say someone gave time/effort/life to a cause or activity.
additional_notes: Commonly followed by 'su vida a...' (she devoted her life to...) or by a noun/infinitive indicating the object of devotion (la ciencia, la educación, el estudio de...). Past tense (dedicó) refers to a completed action. Subject 'ella' can be replaced by other pronouns/names (él dedicó, María dedicó).
target_language_example: Ella dedicó muchos años a enseñar en escuelas rurales.
native_language_example: She devoted many years to teaching in rural schools.

meaning: she devoted her (used to say what someone gave their life/time to).
additional_notes: Common structure: 'ella dedicó su + [noun] + a + [activity/person/cause]'. Often used with 'vida', 'vida entera', 'tiempo', or 'carrera'. Indicates commitment or lifelong dedication. Use 'dedicó' (past) to describe a past action; present would be 'dedica su'.
target_language_example: Ella dedicó su vida a ayudar a los demás.
native_language_example: She devoted her life to helping others.

meaning: Not a fixed phrase; the words 'ella' (she) and 'desde' (from/since) appearing adjacent in text or speech, typically as part of a larger construction. Depending on context it can read as 'she from' or 'she since'.
additional_notes: This is not a standard multiword expression in Spanish; treat as two separate words used according to grammar. They may appear together for emphasis or in elliptical constructions (e.g., in informal speech: 'Ella desde que llegó...'). Word order and punctuation determine the precise meaning. 'Desde' can mean 'since' (time) or 'from' (origin).
target_language_example: Ella desde que llegó al pueblo, se convirtió en voluntaria.
native_language_example: She since she arrived in the town, became a volunteer.

meaning: she gave to / she gave (something) to (someone or something)
additional_notes: This is the third-person singular simple past (pretérito) of dar followed by the preposition a. The phrase is typically followed by a recipient (person or entity) introduced by a, or completed by mentioning what was given before the phrase (e.g., "ella dio el libro a María"). Standing alone as "ella dio a" is incomplete and requires additional context (recipient or clause).
target_language_example: Ella dio a su amiga el regalo, aunque ella no lo esperaba.
native_language_example: She gave to her friend the gift, although she didn't expect it.

meaning: "ella" = she; "en" = in / on / at / about (preposition). Together they are not a fixed expression but can appear consecutively in sentences where 'ella' is subject and 'en' introduces a prepositional phrase.
additional_notes: Not a set phrase. 'Ella' is the third-person singular feminine subject pronoun. 'En' is a versatile preposition whose meaning depends on context. When used together you'll normally need other words (location, time, topic) to complete the phrase (e.g., 'ella en la foto', 'ella en el trabajo'). Word order and agreement rules still apply.
target_language_example: Ella en la foto parece feliz.
native_language_example: She in the photo looks happy.

meaning: literally 'she in the' — not a fixed phrase; usually part of a sentence (e.g., 'ella en el coche' = 'she in the car').
additional_notes: This is not an idiom or standalone expression. It combines the pronoun 'ella' (she) + preposition 'en' (in/on/at) + definite article 'el' (the, masculine). You will normally see it followed by a masculine noun (ella en el parque, ella en el trabajo). Make sure the article matches the noun's gender (el before masculine nouns).
target_language_example: Ella en el coche está escuchando música.
native_language_example: She in the car is listening to music.

meaning: she/her + in/on the (feminine); literal sequence 'ella en la' appears when referring to a female person and a feminine place (e.g., 'she in the...').
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase — it's simply the pronoun ella ('she' or 'her' as subject/object) followed by the preposition en and the feminine definite article la. You will see it when talking about a woman being at or in a feminine noun (la calle, la piscina, la universidad). Word order and agreement depend on the sentence; sometimes ella is the object ('con ella' = with her).
target_language_example: La vi ayer: ella en la tienda parecía feliz.
native_language_example: I saw her yesterday: she in the store looked happy.

meaning: she is the (masculine noun) — used when referring to a woman who fills a role/quality expressed by a masculine noun.
additional_notes: Spanish nouns have grammatical gender. When a woman is described by a masculine noun (e.g., el orgullo, el amor, el instrumento, el vínculo, el cerebro), the article and noun remain masculine. Use ella es el + masculine noun to say 'she is the [masculine noun]'. This is natural when the noun is fixed as masculine or emphasized in a specific, idiomatic way.
target_language_example: Ella es el corazón del grupo.
native_language_example: She is the heart of the group.

meaning: 'she is your' (used before a noun to say someone is yours or related to you)
additional_notes: This phrase is the start of a simple statement: ella (she) + es (is) + tu (your/your (informal)). In Spanish, possessive 'tu' usually needs an accentless form before a noun (tu amiga = your friend). Use 'tu' for informal singular 'your'. For formal or plural, use 'su' or 'sus' respectively. Remember agreement: use the correct noun gender and number after 'tu' (tu amiga, tu hermano, tus hijos).
target_language_example: Ella es tu vecina.
native_language_example: She is your neighbor.

meaning: 'she waits' or 'she hopes' (depends on context).
additional_notes: Verbal phrase using esperar. With a direct object or 'a' + infinitive it usually means 'to wait (for)' (ella espera a que continúe = she waits for him/her to continue). With an infinitive or clauses like 'espera poder...' it means 'to hope' or 'to expect' (ella espera poder = she hopes to be able). Context determines whether it's 'waits' (physical waiting) or 'hopes/expect(s)'.
target_language_example: Ella espera a su amiga en la cafetería.
native_language_example: She is waiting for her friend in the café.

meaning: literally 'she was at' or 'she was about to' depending on context; a fragment used before a location, state, or an infinitive phrase.
additional_notes: This is a fragment rather than a complete phrase. 'Estuvo' is the preterite of 'estar' (to be). Use 'ella estuvo a' before a location ('ella estuvo a la puerta' — she was at the door) or before expressions like 'ella estuvo a punto de...' (she was about to...). For most completed expressions you will need more words after 'a'.
target_language_example: Ella estuvo a punto de llamar, pero cambió de opinión.
native_language_example: She was about to call, but she changed her mind.

meaning: 'she was (working/acting as / temporarily in the role of...)' or 'she was at (a place) doing...'
additional_notes: This phrase is used to describe a temporary role, job, or situation. It often appears before a noun (e.g., 'ella estuvo de profesora' = she worked temporarily as a teacher) or before an action with '...de + infinitive' in some dialects. It can also be followed by a location ('ella estuvo de visita') meaning she was visiting. Context determines whether it's about a role, an activity, or being at a place. Not a complete sentence by itself; needs what follows 'de'.
target_language_example: Ella estuvo de suplente durante dos meses.
native_language_example: She was a substitute for two months.

meaning: she went to the (feminine noun).
additional_notes: A simple past (pretérito) phrase: ella (she) + fue (went) + a la (to the, feminine). Use 'a la' before singular feminine nouns (la cocina, la escuela, la estación, la universidad). If the place is masculine use 'al' (a + el). If the noun is plural use 'a las' or 'a los'.
target_language_example: Ella fue a la biblioteca a devolver un libro.
native_language_example: She went to the library to return a book.

meaning: she was the (female) — used to introduce a role, description, or first/only person
additional_notes: Commonly followed by an adjective, noun, ordinal (primera), or relative clause. 'La' agrees with a feminine noun implied or stated. Often used to emphasize that a particular woman was the first, the only, or held a specific role. Context determines whether it's literal (she was the first person) or more literary/reflective (she was the one I loved).
target_language_example: Ella fue la responsable del proyecto.
native_language_example: She was the person responsible for the project.

meaning: she does / she makes
additional_notes: Ella = she (subject pronoun). Hace is the third-person singular present of hacer (to do, to make). Use for actions or making something: "ella hace la tarea" (she does the homework) or "ella hace una sopa" (she makes a soup). For questions invert subject or use ¿qué hace ella? For past actions use hizo (ella hizo).
target_language_example: Ella hace la tarea todas las tardes.
native_language_example: She does her homework every afternoon.

meaning: "she did the..." (start of a phrase meaning 'she did [something]')
additional_notes: Ella hizo lo is not a complete phrase by itself; it's the beginning of a clause where lo introduces an idea, often followed by que + verb (e.g., "ella hizo lo que pudo" = "she did what she could") or a noun/pronoun. In many contexts Spanish uses "lo" as a neutral pronoun meaning "that" or "what". For beginners, remember you will normally see this as part of a longer expression.
target_language_example: Ella hizo lo que pudo para ayudar.
native_language_example: She did what she could to help.

meaning: she had (subjunctive, used in past subjunctive or conditional contexts like 'if she had' or 'that she had').
additional_notes: Ella hubiera is the third-person singular imperfect subjunctive form of haber (used as an auxiliary) plus the subject pronoun ella. It appears in past-subjunctive clauses (e.g., si ella hubiera venido = if she had come) and in compound subjunctive tenses (e.g., esperaba que ella hubiera llegado = I hoped that she had arrived). The pronoun ella is often omitted if context makes the subject clear (hubiera llegado).
target_language_example: Si ella hubiera sabido, habría venido.
native_language_example: If she had known, she would have come.

meaning: she plays / she is playing.
additional_notes: Ella = she. Juega is the 3rd-person singular present of jugar (to play). Used for sports/games (jugar a + sport/game), playing an instrument (tocar is more common), or figurative uses (jugar un papel = to play a role). Context determines translation: current activity (she is playing) or habitual (she plays).
target_language_example: Ella juega al fútbol los sábados por la tarde.
native_language_example: She plays soccer on Saturday afternoons.

meaning: she (subject) + her/it (direct object pronoun 'la') — used when 'ella' is the subject and 'la' refers to a feminine direct object
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but two separate words appearing together in a sentence: ella (she) as the subject and la as the feminine singular direct object pronoun (her/it). In spoken and written Spanish, the object pronoun usually appears before the verb (Ella la vio = She saw her/it). Context tells whether 'la' means 'her' (a woman) or 'it' (a feminine noun). If both subject and object refer to people, word order and stress can clarify meaning; for emphasis or clarity you can add a prepositional phrase (a ella) or use a full noun.
target_language_example: Ella la llamó por teléfono.
native_language_example: She called her on the phone.

meaning: Incorrect / nonstandard word order attempting to say 'she likes the...' or 'he/she likes it'; correct Spanish is 'a ella le gusta el ...' or 'le gusta el ...'.
additional_notes: This phrase as written is ungrammatical in Spanish because the indirect-object pronoun (le) and the prepositional phrase introducing the person (a ella) are needed for clarity: 'A ella le gusta el libro' = 'She likes the book.' Native speakers often omit 'a ella' when context is clear: 'Le gusta el libro.' Use 'ella le gusta' only when saying 'she is liked by him/her' (passive/empathetic) which is rare; correct passive would be 'ella le gusta a él' ('he likes her').
target_language_example: A ella le gusta el helado.
native_language_example: She likes ice cream.

meaning: 'she likes the' (feminine singular noun) or more generally 'she likes' before a feminine noun/phrase.
additional_notes: This is a fixed structure using the verb gustar. Spanish uses an indirect object pronoun (le) and the verb agrees with the thing liked. When the liked item is a feminine singular noun, you often see 'la' before the noun (la ensalada, la música). The full neutral pattern is 'A ella le gusta + [singular noun or infinitive]'. Use 'le gustan' for plural things and 'A ella' is optional for emphasis/clarity.
target_language_example: A ella le gusta la música clásica.
native_language_example: She likes classical music.

meaning: she likes (plural things).
additional_notes: Used to say that a female subject likes multiple items. Spanish uses an indirect object pronoun (le) plus the verb gustar; the thing(s) liked is the grammatical subject and appears after the verb. Match the article/number: 'los' for masculine plural nouns (e.g., los gatos), 'las' for feminine plural, and use 'me/te/le/nos/os/les' to match the person. For singular: 'A ella le gusta...'. Common structure: 'A + (person) + (indirect object pronoun) + gusta(n) + (thing liked)'.
target_language_example: A ella le gustan los libros de aventuras.
native_language_example: She likes adventure books.

meaning: she ... to them
additional_notes: A common word combination, not a fixed expression. ella means "she," and les is the indirect object pronoun meaning "to them" (or sometimes "to you all," depending on region). In natural Spanish, ella is often included for emphasis or clarity; many sentences would also just use les + verb without ella.
target_language_example: Ella les contó la verdad.
native_language_example: She told them the truth.

meaning: she them
additional_notes: Ella = she (subject). Los = direct object pronoun for masculine plural nouns or a neutral/unspecified group in some regions; it replaces 'them' (masculine). Together 'ella los' appears when the subject (ella) and a following direct object pronoun (los) are both used in the same clause: e.g., to emphasize who does the action and what is affected. Word order: subject + object pronoun before a conjugated verb (Ella los vio = She saw them). If there is an infinitive or gerund, the pronoun can attach to it (Ella va a verlos / Ella está viéndolos).
target_language_example: Ella los encontró en el parque.
native_language_example: She found them in the park.

meaning: a colloquial/slang way to say 'not even her' or 'she wouldn't even (do something)'; used to emphasize exclusion of a person.
additional_notes: This construction combines the subject pronoun ella with the negative particle ni for emphasis. It appears in informal spoken Spanish to stress that someone is excluded from an action or situation (e.g., 'not even she would...'). Depending on region and context, speakers may say 'ni ella' more commonly; 'ella ni' can occur in casual speech for emphasis or specific word order. Tone is usually emphatic or dismissive.
target_language_example: Ella ni se molesta en contestar los mensajes.
native_language_example: She doesn't even bother to reply to the messages.

meaning: she has nothing / she is not involved (depends on context).
additional_notes: Literal meaning: 'she has nothing.' Often used as part of longer phrases: 'ella no tiene nada en común' = 'she has nothing in common'; 'ella no tiene nada que ver con...' = 'she has nothing to do with...' In many contexts it expresses lack of possession, lack of relation, or lack of involvement. Pay attention to the words that follow to get the exact meaning.
target_language_example: Ella no tiene nada que ver con ese problema.
native_language_example: She has nothing to do with that problem.

meaning: she has no reason/obligation/need to (do something)
additional_notes: This phrase is typically followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., 'hacer', 'decir') or a subordinate clause introduced by 'hacer'/'ver' etc. It expresses that she lacks any cause, reason, duty, or justification to do something. Context determines whether it means 'no reason', 'no obligation', 'no business/role', or 'nothing to...'.
target_language_example: Ella no tiene nada que ver con ese problema.
native_language_example: She has nothing to do with that problem.

meaning: she or (used to offer an alternative referring to a female person or feminine option)
additional_notes: Ella = 'she'. O = 'or'. Together used when giving two options where the first is a female person/option: e.g., '¿María, ella o Ana?' (asking which of two women). In sentences you often see 'él o ella' (he or she). In spoken Spanish, 'o' is pronounced like English 'o'.
target_language_example: ¿Quieres hablar con Marta, ella o Laura?
native_language_example: Do you want to speak with Marta, her or Laura?

meaning: 'she asked for' / 'she requested' (past tense).
additional_notes: Ella pidió is the third-person singular past (pretérito) of pedir. Use it when saying that a woman or she requested or asked for something (could be an object, help, a favor, a drink, etc.). Common constructions: pedir + noun (pedir ayuda, pedir una taza de té) or pedir que + subjunctive for requests. Context shows both simple requests and asking someone for something.
target_language_example: Ella pidió la cuenta después de la cena.
native_language_example: She asked for the bill after dinner.

meaning: Not a fixed idiom in Spanish; the sequence is simply the pronoun 'ella' (she) followed by the preposition 'por' (for/by/through). Its meaning depends on the full sentence and word order — often you will instead see 'por ella' (for her/because of her/by her) or sentences where 'ella' is subject and 'por' begins a following phrase.
additional_notes: 'ella por' by itself is uncommon as a fixed chunk; it appears when 'por' starts a phrase that comes after 'ella' (e.g., in relative or subordinate structures, or in repetitions: "ella, por..."), or in spoken hesitation. To interpret it, read the whole sentence. Examples of possible uses include: "Ella, por lo visto, no vendrá" (She, apparently, won't come) or constructions where punctuation separates them.
target_language_example: Ella, por lo que dijo, no entiende.
native_language_example: She, from what she said, doesn't understand.

meaning: she was able to / she could (past tense of 'poder').
additional_notes: Past simple (pretérito) form of 'poder' for third person singular. Use 'ella pudo' to say that she was able to do something (completed action) or managed to do it. For negative or ongoing contexts, Spanish uses other forms (no pudo = she couldn't; podía = she could/was able to – imperfect).
target_language_example: Ella pudo terminar el proyecto a tiempo.
native_language_example: She was able to finish the project on time.

meaning: literally 'she that' — not a fixed idiom; typically part of a larger clause (e.g., 'ella que...' meaning 'she, who/and as for her...'). It introduces a comment or a relative clause about a woman previously mentioned.
additional_notes: Not a standalone phrase. Commonly used to introduce a parenthetical remark or contrast: 'Ella que...' = 'She, who/... (did/said)...' or 'And as for her...'. A comma often appears before or after it ('Ella, que...' or '...ella que...') depending on sentence structure. Translation depends on context: relative clause ('she who/that') or topical contrast ('as for her').
target_language_example: No sabía la respuesta; ella que siempre estudia se quedó callada.
native_language_example: I didn't know the answer; she who always studies remained silent.

meaning: she became / she was left / she agreed (depending on context).
additional_notes: Quedar + adjective/participial often means 'to become' or 'to be left/in a state' (e.g., quedó satisfecha, quedó sorda, quedó embarazada). Quedar + infinitive or quedar en + infinitive means 'to agree to' or 'to arrange' (Ella quedó en encontrarse = she agreed to meet). Context determines whether it's a change of state, a resulting state, or an agreement/arrangement.
target_language_example: Ella quedó sorprendida cuando llegó la noticia.
native_language_example: She was left surprised when the news arrived.

meaning: she really / she truly (emphasis on truth or intensity)
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that 'she' truly feels, thinks, or does something. 'Realmente' strengthens or clarifies the verb — similar to English 'really' or 'truly'. Can appear after subject (Ella realmente ...) or with indirect object phrasing (A ella realmente le gusta...).
target_language_example: Ella realmente quiere ayudar, no es una broma.
native_language_example: She really wants to help, it's not a joke.

meaning: she will be
additional_notes: Future tense of ser with the pronoun ella. Used to talk about what a woman or girl will be, or how she will be, in the future. In Spanish, the pronoun is often dropped, so you may also simply see será.
target_language_example: Ella será una gran doctora.
native_language_example: She will be a great doctor.

meaning: Not a common fixed phrase in Spanish; a sequence of pronoun + preposition that can appear in larger sentences depending on word order and grammar. Literally reads as 'she over' or 'her about' but in natural Spanish the order is usually 'sobre ella' (about her) or 'ella está sobre...' (she is on...).
additional_notes: On its own 'ella sobre' is not a standard expression. It may appear in poetry, inverted constructions, or when a clause boundary separates words (e.g., ending one clause with 'ella' and beginning the next with 'sobre'). For learners: prefer 'sobre ella' to mean 'about her' and 'ella está sobre...' or 'ella va sobre...' to mean 'she is on...' or 'she goes over...'. The example usage below demonstrates a plausible, if marked, sentence that contains the exact sequence 'ella sobre'.
target_language_example: Dijo ella sobre la mesa que no quería mudarse.
native_language_example: She said, over the table, that she did not want to move.

meaning: she alone / only she (feminine emphasis)
additional_notes: This sequence is uncommon and can sound awkward in many contexts. Standard alternatives: 'solo ella' (to mean 'only she') or 'ella sola' (to mean 'she alone' in the sense of being physically alone). 'Ella solo' might appear in casual speech or poetic/elliptical structures, but watch agreement: when 'solo' means 'alone' as an adjective modifying a feminine subject it should usually be 'sola' ('ella sola'). When 'solo' means 'only' it commonly precedes the phrase ('solo ella').
target_language_example: Ella solo dijo la mitad de la historia.
native_language_example: She only said half the story.

meaning: she only / only she
additional_notes: ella = 'she'. sólo (with accent) means 'only' or 'just'. Word order can change nuance: 'ella sólo' usually emphasizes that she alone (and not others) did something — equivalent to 'only she' or 'she alone'. If you mean 'she only' followed by a verb (e.g., she only sleeps), Spanish more commonly places sólo before the verb or after the subject: 'ella sólo duerme' or 'ella solo duerme' (accent on 'sólo' is optional in modern orthography; to avoid ambiguity many writers use 'solo' without accent).
target_language_example: Ella sólo quería ayudar.
native_language_example: Only she wanted to help.

meaning: she has
additional_notes: Literally means "she has." In the examples, it is followed by que + infinitive (ella tiene que...), which means "she has to..." or "she must...".
target_language_example: Ella tiene dos hermanos.
native_language_example: She has two brothers.

meaning: she still / she yet (continues to).
additional_notes: Used to say that a female person continues to be in a state or continues doing something. 'Todavía' can appear before or after the verb: ella todavía trabaja / ella trabaja todavía. In questions or negatives, context changes: ¿Ella todavía viene? (Is she still coming?).
target_language_example: Ella todavía no ha llegado.
native_language_example: She still hasn't arrived.

meaning: Not a standard or grammatical Spanish multi-word expression; if interpreted literally it would mean 'she all' or 'her all' but it is malformed.
additional_notes: This phrase is not used in natural Spanish. Possible intended corrections: 'toda ella' (all of her), 'todo sobre ella' or 'todo acerca de ella' (everything about her), 'ella lo hace todo' or 'ella hace todo' (she does everything). Use depends on context. The given ordering 'ella todo' is likely a mistaken word order or a fragment and should be avoided in standard speech and writing.
target_language_example: Ella todo lo explicó mal; eso no tiene sentido.
native_language_example: She explained everything badly; that doesn't make sense.

meaning: Not a fixed standalone phrase; literal components are "ella" (she) + "todo el" (all the/the whole [masculine singular]) and together would normally precede or follow a noun or be part of a larger clause (e.g., "ella todo el día..."). Used to indicate that she is associated with or experiences/does something involving the entirety of a masculine-singular noun.
additional_notes: This sequence by itself is uncommon and incomplete in Spanish. It requires a noun or continuation: "ella todo el día" (she [for] the whole day), "ella, todo el tiempo" (she, all the time). Remember agreement: use "todo el" with masculine singular nouns (todo el día, todo el trabajo). For feminine nouns use "toda la" (toda la noche). In natural speech you will usually see a verb between pronoun and phrase ("ella pasó todo el día"), or a comma/intonation if it's a parenthetical phrase ("ella, todo el día, estaba ocupada").
target_language_example: Ella todo el día estuvo preocupada por el examen.
native_language_example: She, the whole day, was worried about the exam.

meaning: she goes / she is going
additional_notes: Present tense of the verb ir (to go) for third-person singular. Used for actions happening now (ella va al trabajo = she is going to work) or general facts (ella va siempre en coche = she always goes by car). Combine with a preposition or destination (a, en, hacia) to show where she goes. Can also be part of future periphrasis with 'a' + infinitive (ella va a salir = she is going to leave).
target_language_example: Ella va al supermercado todos los sábados.
native_language_example: She goes to the supermarket every Saturday.

meaning: she and (used to join 'ella' with another noun or pronoun).
additional_notes: 'ella' = 'she'. 'y' = 'and'. Used like 'ella y él' = 'she and he' or 'ella y su hermano' = 'she and her brother'. In Spanish the order is flexible; contractions are not needed (unlike English 'she's' etc.). If speaking about people, you can also use 'ella' + another subject pronoun or name.
target_language_example: Ella y su amiga vienen mañana.
native_language_example: She and her friend are coming tomorrow.

meaning: Not a standard Spanish phrase; appears to be two separate pronouns 'ella' (she) and 'yo' (I) placed together without a connector. It does not form a grammatical unit on its own.
additional_notes: 'Ella yo' by itself is ungrammatical in Spanish. If you intend to join the two subjects you normally use 'ella y yo' ('she and I'). You might encounter 'ella yo' in sloppy writing, poetry for stylistic effect, or when words are separated by punctuation (e.g., 'ella. Yo...' meaning 'she. I...'), but as written with a space it should not be used as a fixed phrase.
target_language_example: Ella yo, en cambio, pensamos distinto.
native_language_example: She and I, however, think differently.

meaning: they don't
additional_notes: Not a fixed expression. ellas means "they" for an all-female group, and no makes it negative. Before a verb, it usually means "they don't"; in a contrastive reply, it can mean "not them."
target_language_example: Ellas no quieren salir esta noche.
native_language_example: They don't want to go out tonight.

meaning: both of them (two males or mixed-gender pair).
additional_notes: Used to refer to two people together. 'Ellos' is masculine or mixed; if referring to two females use 'ellas dos'. Often placed before the verb, but can appear after prepositions (e.g., 'a ellos dos'). Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Ellos dos van al cine esta noche.
native_language_example: Both of them are going to the movies tonight.

meaning: them (people) — with a negative verb; literal structure: 'to them not [verb]' (used with indirect object pronoun 'les').
additional_notes: This is part of a common Spanish construction using 'a + pronoun' + indirect object pronoun (a ellos + les) to clarify or emphasize who is affected. In these examples it's used with verbs like gustar, importar, interesar — verbs that work like 'to be pleasing/important/interesting to someone' in Spanish, so the English translation often reverses the order (e.g., 'they don't like' becomes 'it is not pleasing to them'). The full phrase often appears as 'A ellos no les + [verb]'.
target_language_example: A ellos no les gustan las películas románticas.
native_language_example: They don't like romantic movies.

meaning: "they only" or "they just" (emphasizing limitation or simple action by 'they').
additional_notes: Used to say that 'they' do only one thing or have only one intention. 'Solo' (without accent) here means 'only' or 'just'. Word order can vary: 'ellos solo quieren...' or simply 'solo quieren...' since subject pronoun is often optional in Spanish. With a verb, 'solo' usually comes before the verb; with nouns it can appear before or after the noun for emphasis. Do not confuse 'solo' (only) with 'sólo' (accent, older usage) — accent is largely obsolete. For emphasis on being 'alone', use 'solos' (plural) as an adjective: 'ellos están solos' = they are alone.
target_language_example: Ellos solo vienen los fines de semana.
native_language_example: They only come on weekends.

meaning: they already / they now (depending on context)
additional_notes: Ellos = 'they' (masculine or mixed group). Ya often means 'already' (something has happened) or 'now/anymore' depending on tense and context. Together, 'ellos ya' usually begins a sentence or clause to say that they have already done something or are now in a certain state: e.g. 'Ellos ya llegaron' = 'They already arrived.' Word order can vary: ya puede aparecer before or after the verb (Ya ellos no vienen / Ellos ya no vienen).
target_language_example: Ellos ya terminaron la tarea.
native_language_example: They already finished the homework.

meaning: to make matters worse (literally: to worsen the)
additional_notes: Common phrase used to introduce an additional negative detail that makes a situation worse. Often appears as 'para empeorar las cosas' = 'to make matters worse'. The direct object (las) refers to 'things' (cosas) and is usually used in fixed expressions; you can omit 'las' and say 'empeorar' or use 'empeorar las cosas'.
target_language_example: Para empeorar las cosas, perdimos el tren.
native_language_example: To make matters worse, we missed the train.

meaning: 'I was beginning to worry' or 'I started to worry'.
additional_notes: Imperfect tense (empezaba) + reflexive verb preocuparse. Used to describe a past, ongoing or gradual feeling of worry that began at that time. Can be adjusted for person/number: empezaste a preocuparte, empezamos a preocuparnos, etc. Commonly followed by a clause explaining the reason (por + noun / porque + clause).
target_language_example: Cuando no contestaste las llamadas, empezaba a preocuparme.
native_language_example: When you didn't answer the calls, I was beginning to worry.

meaning: I was starting to worry about...
additional_notes: Used to describe that someone began to feel concern about a person, situation, or thing. It's in the imperfect tense (empezaba = was beginning) plus a reflexive verb (preocuparme = to worry me). Replace the pronoun (me) with te, se, nos, os as needed: empezaba a preocuparte por, empezaba a preocuparse por, etc. Common with phrases like 'empezaba a preocuparme por su salud' or 'empezaba a preocuparme por el retraso'.
target_language_example: Cuando no contestó, empezaba a preocuparme por su seguridad.
native_language_example: When he didn't answer, I was starting to worry about his safety.

meaning: 'to start now' or 'to begin now'.
additional_notes: A simple instruction or statement telling someone to begin something immediately. Empezar is a common verb (to start/begin). Can be used for actions, tasks, meetings, classes, etc. If telling someone politely, you might add por favor: "empezar ahora, por favor" or use the infinitive with vamos a + infinitive (Vamos a empezar ahora).
target_language_example: Si ya están listos, podemos empezar ahora.
native_language_example: If you're ready, we can start now.

meaning: 'to start from' or 'to begin again from' (used with a following noun or phrase to indicate the starting point).
additional_notes: Commonly used in expressions like empezar de cero (to start from zero) or empezar de nuevo (to start again). It needs a complement: a place, point, state, or modifier (cero, nuevo, arriba, etc.). In many contexts empezar por + infinitive (to start by doing something) or empezar a + infinitive (to begin to do something) are used instead — empezar de focuses on the starting point or baseline.
target_language_example: Vamos a empezar de cero y rehacer el proyecto.
native_language_example: Let's start from scratch and redo the project.

meaning: to start over; to begin again from scratch.
additional_notes: Used when restarting a life, project, job, or situation with no previous progress kept. Commonly implies leaving past circumstances behind to build something new. Equivalent to 'start from scratch' or 'start over' in English.
target_language_example: Después del fracaso, decidimos empezar de cero y abrir otro negocio.
native_language_example: After the failure, we decided to start over and open another business.

meaning: 'to begin/start the' (followed by a masculine noun or expression).
additional_notes: Empezar means 'to begin' or 'to start.' When followed by the masculine definite article 'el', it introduces a specific thing or period that begins (e.g., 'el día', 'el ejercicio', 'el tercer acto'). Use the infinitive 'empezar a' when starting an action (e.g., 'empezar a correr').
target_language_example: Vamos a empezar el proyecto mañana.
native_language_example: We are going to start the project tomorrow.

meaning: to start/begin a (feminine noun) — like 'start a ...' or 'begin a ...'.
additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun (una) to say someone starts or begins something (e.g., una guerra, una pelea, una vida, una revolución). Replace 'una' with 'un' for masculine nouns (empezar un). Commonly used with actions/events: empezar una discusión, empezar una nueva vida, empezar una guerra.
target_language_example: No quiero empezar una pelea por eso.
native_language_example: I don't want to start a fight over that.

meaning: '(when) ... begins' or 'when ... starts' (subjunctive form used with que/before/once etc.)
additional_notes: Empiece is the present subjunctive (yo/él/ella/usted) of empezar (to begin). 'Empiece la' is used before a feminine noun (la presentación, la música, la fiesta, la película, la conferencia, la lucha). Common in clauses introduced by que, cuando, antes de que, una vez que, etc., to talk about actions that will begin in the future or are hypothetical. For simple statements about a scheduled start, the indicative (empieza) can also be used; subjunctive appears after expressions of waiting, uncertainty, purpose, or certain conjunctions (antes de que, para que, cuando + future-like idea).
target_language_example: Apaga las luces antes de que empiece la película.
native_language_example: Turn off the lights before the movie starts.

meaning: 'employees of' or 'staff of' (followed by a company, person, or group).
additional_notes: Used to indicate the people who work for or are employed by a specific organization, company, or person. In Spanish the noun 'empleados' can be used with a definite article or without one depending on context (e.g., 'los empleados de' vs. 'empleados de'). Follow with the name of the company, organization, or person: 'empleados de Google', 'empleados de la escuela', 'empleados de Juan'.
target_language_example: Los empleados de la tienda llegan a las ocho.
native_language_example: The employees of the store arrive at eight.

meaning: company and / company + (conjunction 'y' starting the next phrase).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase; it's simply the noun 'empresa' (company) followed by the conjunction 'y' (and). In the example sentences the 'y' connects two parts: e.g. 'la empresa y nuestros beneficios' (the company and our profits) or links clauses when part of a longer sentence split across examples ('dejó la empresa y formó una propia' = he left the company and started his own). Useful to recognize both words separately: 'empresa' = company, 'y' = and.
target_language_example: Ella trabaja en la empresa y estudia por las noches.
native_language_example: She works at the company and studies at night.

meaning: 'not at all' or 'absolutely not'.
additional_notes: Used to strongly negate something or to emphasize total absence. Commonly follows 'no' (No, en absoluto) or appears after a verb (no molesta en absoluto). It's a fixed phrase and does not mean 'absolutely' in the positive sense.
target_language_example: ¿Te importa si abro la ventana? — No, en absoluto.
native_language_example: Do you mind if I open the window? — Not at all.

meaning: in abundance; plentifully; a lot of something.
additional_notes: Used to say there is plenty or an ample supply of something. Often follows the noun (comida en abundancia) or follows a verb (hay en abundancia). Formal or neutral register; common in speech and writing.
target_language_example: En el mercado hay verduras en abundancia este mes.
native_language_example: At the market there are vegetables in abundance this month.

meaning: in accidents (as a result of accidents).
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something happens inside or because of accidents. Common with verbs like morir, resultar, lesionarse, or general statements about traffic/workplace incidents. Often appears in contexts about traffic (accidentes de tráfico / accidentes de tránsito).
target_language_example: Varias personas resultaron heridas en accidentes de tráfico.
native_language_example: Several people were injured in traffic accidents.

meaning: from now on; from this point forward; henceforth.
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something applies from a given moment onward (future or continuing effect). Can follow a time expression (e.g., "a partir de ahora", "desde hoy") or stand alone at the start of a sentence to give instructions or announce a change in policy or behavior.
target_language_example: En adelante, intenta responder los mensajes el mismo día.
native_language_example: From now on, try to reply to messages the same day.

meaning: in something; about something; with something (depends on context)
additional_notes: Literal meaning is 'in something'. Used in different contexts: 1) abstract belief or trust (En algo hay que creer = You have to believe in something). 2) to indicate interest or involvement (interesado en algo = interested in something). Often followed by a noun or idea. Not an idiom—its meaning comes from the words 'en' (in/on/about) + 'algo' (something).
target_language_example: No puedo concentrarme en algo cuando hay tanto ruido.
native_language_example: I can't concentrate on anything when there's so much noise.

meaning: in/working on/think of something that... (introduces an unspecified thing followed by a relative clause).
additional_notes: Use when referring to an unspecified object, project, idea, or thing that is then described by a following clause (que + verb). Common with verbs like trabajar (work), pensar (think), quedar (stay), sentarse (sit). Can mean "working on something that..." or "think of something to..." depending on context.
target_language_example: Estoy trabajando en algo que te ayudará.
native_language_example: I'm working on something that will help you.

meaning: about/at someone; used to indicate something affecting or directed toward a person (often in contexts like 'to be on someone' or 'to rely on someone').
additional_notes: The preposition en + alguien appears in various expressions. Its exact sense depends on the verb or phrase: e.g. confiar en alguien (to trust someone), pensar en alguien (to think about someone), caer en alguien (to fall on/affect someone). It is not a fixed idiom by itself; learners should focus on common verbs that take en + alguien. 'Alguien' means 'someone' or 'somebody.'
target_language_example: Confío en alguien que me puede ayudar.
native_language_example: I trust someone who can help me.

meaning: at some
additional_notes: Used before a feminine noun to mean 'in/at/on some (unspecified) [time/place/occasion/object]'. Often appears in phrases like 'en alguna ocasión' (on some occasion), 'en alguna conversación' (in some conversation). Implies uncertainty or indefiniteness. If the following noun is masculine, use 'en algún' instead.
target_language_example: Creo que lo dijo en alguna reunión.
native_language_example: I think he said it at some meeting.

meaning: out loud; spoken so others can hear
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something is said aloud (not silently or subvocally). Common with verbs like 'leer' (leer en alta voz = read aloud) or 'decir' (decir en alta voz = say out loud).
target_language_example: Por favor, léelo en alta voz para que todos lo entiendan.
native_language_example: Please read it out loud so everyone understands it.

meaning: in a loud voice; up/high (position) — depends on context.
additional_notes: Two common uses: 1) With verbs of speaking or reading (hablar en alto, leer en alto) it means 'aloud' or 'out loud' (speaking loudly enough to be heard). 2) With body parts (manos en alto, brazos en alto, frente en alto) it describes position: 'hands up', 'arms up', or 'hold your head high'. Context determines whether it refers to volume or physical elevation/posture.
target_language_example: Lee el texto en alto para que todos lo oigan.
native_language_example: Read the text aloud so everyone can hear it.

meaning: apparently; in appearance; seemingly
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something looks a certain way on the surface but may be different in reality. Common in written and spoken Spanish to introduce contrast between appearance and truth. Can be placed at the start or within a sentence.
target_language_example: En apariencia es un buen proyecto, pero necesita más estudio.
native_language_example: It appears to be a good project, but it needs more study.

meaning: at that time; back then
additional_notes: Used to refer to a past time previously mentioned or understood in context. Formality: neutral. Often appears at the beginning of a sentence but can be placed elsewhere. Similar to 'en ese entonces' or 'por aquel entonces'.
target_language_example: En aquel entonces, no había internet en mi pueblo.
native_language_example: Back then, there was no internet in my town.

meaning: 'in arms' or 'armed' / 'fellow fighters'
additional_notes: Used to refer to people who are armed or who are comrades in a military or fighting context. Common in phrases like "hermanos en armas" (brothers in arms) meaning comrades/soldiers. Not generally used to mean 'weapons' (that would be "armas"). Can also appear in contexts meaning 'to take up arms' (e.g., "ponerse en armas").
target_language_example: Hermanos en armas lucharon juntos por la libertad.
native_language_example: Brothers in arms fought together for freedom.

meaning: blank; empty; (of the mind) drawing a blank or empty-minded.
additional_notes: Used literally for something that is blank (e.g., a page, screen) and idiomatically for the mind when you can't think of anything (to 'draw a blank'). Common in phrases like 'la mente en blanco' (my mind went blank) or 'pon la mente en blanco' (clear your mind).
target_language_example: Cuando intentaron preguntarme, me quedé en blanco.
native_language_example: When they tried to ask me, I drew a blank.

meaning: used to start expressions meaning 'blank and...' or 'with blank ...' — often part of fixed phrases (literal: 'in blank and').
additional_notes: This fragment appears at the start of longer expressions (e.g., en blanco y en botella) but by itself is incomplete. 'En blanco' commonly means 'blank/empty' (a blank sheet, empty answer); 'y' simply means 'and'. Beginners will most often encounter 'en blanco' alone (answerar en blanco = to leave blank) or complete idioms that begin with 'en blanco y...'. Don't use 'en blanco y' by itself unless completing the phrase.
target_language_example: Dejó la hoja en blanco y sin firmar.
native_language_example: He left the page blank and unsigned.

meaning: in black and white; clear, explicit, or literal (also: in grayscale).
additional_notes: Can mean literally 'in black and white' (no color, e.g., photos or film) or figuratively 'clear/undeniable' (the facts are plain). Context tells which meaning is intended. Use for literal descriptions (images, TV) and for saying something is clearly written or obvious.
target_language_example: Los documentos están en blanco y negro, así no hay dudas.
native_language_example: The documents are in black and white, so there are no doubts.

meaning: in one's arms; being carried in someone's arms.
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is being held or carried in a person's arms. Common with people (especially babies, children, or loved ones) and also with objects when carried cradled. Can imply affection or protection when used figuratively (e.g., 'to be taken in someone's arms').
target_language_example: La niña dormía tranquila en brazos de su madre.
native_language_example: The girl slept peacefully in her mother's arms.

meaning: shortly; soon; in a little while.
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something will happen in a short amount of time. Common in both spoken and written Spanish; can be used formally (announcements) or informally. Similar to 'pronto' but slightly more formal/neutral.
target_language_example: El concierto empezará en breve, por favor tomen asiento.
native_language_example: The concert will start shortly, please take your seats.

meaning: 'in good' or 'in a good' (part of a larger phrase).
additional_notes: This is not a complete phrase on its own. 'En buen' typically appears before a masculine singular noun or in set expressions, e.g. 'en buen estado' (in good condition), 'en buen humor' (in a good mood), or 'en buena' when the noun is feminine. Pay attention to gender and number: use 'en buen' + masculine singular noun, 'en buena' + feminine singular, 'en buenos/buenas' for plural. Beginners will most often encounter full expressions rather than 'en buen' alone.
target_language_example: El coche está en buen estado.
native_language_example: The car is in good condition.

meaning: in good hands; being cared for or in a safe, competent situation.
additional_notes: Used to reassure someone that a person, situation, or object is under trustworthy, capable care (medical, professional, or general help). Commonly follows estar (está/estás/estamos). Tone is neutral and widely used.
target_language_example: No te preocupes, tu coche está en buenas manos con el mecánico.
native_language_example: Don't worry, your car is in good hands with the mechanic.

meaning: in search (of); looking for
additional_notes: Used to indicate actively looking for something or someone. Often followed by 'de' or 'del' + noun (en búsqueda de algo). More formal/literary than the everyday 'buscando'.
target_language_example: Viajamos en búsqueda de nuevas oportunidades.
native_language_example: We traveled in search of new opportunities.

meaning: in the lead; ahead (of others)
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is leading a race, competition, list, or group. Common in sports, polls, rankings, or any situation with positions. Often followed by 'de' + group or simply stands alone: 'va en cabeza' = 'is in the lead.'
target_language_example: El corredor va en cabeza desde la primera vuelta.
native_language_example: The runner has been in the lead since the first lap.
