additional_notes: Used to refer to a particular period, season, or time of year or stage (e.g., esta época del año = this time of year; esta época del curso = this part of the course). Usually followed by a noun (a specific time or thing). Commonly appears as part of phrases like "esta época del año" (this time of year) or "esta época del año se siente..."
target_language_example: Esta época del año siempre hace mucho frío aquí.
native_language_example: This time of year is always very cold here.

meaning: this was
additional_notes: Used to identify or describe something in the past. "esta" is feminine singular, so it refers to a feminine noun (like "puerta," "muñeca," or "escuela"). This is from the imperfect of "ser," often used for past descriptions or background information.
target_language_example: Esta era la razón de mi viaje.
native_language_example: This was the reason for my trip.

meaning: this (one) is going to / this is about to
additional_notes: Common spoken sequence where esta (fem. demonstrative) refers to a feminine noun or something implied, followed by va a + infinitive to express a near-future action (equivalent to 'is going to' in English). If referring to a masculine noun use 'este va a'. In casual speech the 'a' may be followed directly by an infinitive (va a salir) or contractions/colloquialisms may alter pronunciation.
target_language_example: Esta va a empezar en cinco minutos.
native_language_example: This one is going to start in five minutes.

meaning: was writing (past continuous — an action in progress in the past).
additional_notes: Used to describe an action that was ongoing at a specific moment in the past. Formed with the imperfect of estar (estaba) + gerund (escribiendo). Often appears with time expressions or when another past action interrupts it (e.g., 'cuando llegó').
target_language_example: Yo estaba escribiendo una carta cuando sonó el teléfono.
native_language_example: I was writing a letter when the phone rang.

meaning: 'was hiding' or 'was concealing' (ongoing past action).
additional_notes: Imperfect progressive: estaba (imperfect of estar) + gerund ocultando. Used to describe an ongoing or repeated action in the past (someone hiding something). Common when expressing suspicion or describing background actions. Can be followed by 'algo' (something) or a direct object.
target_language_example: Creía que él estaba ocultando la verdad.
native_language_example: I thought he was hiding the truth.

meaning: was watching the (ongoing past action, imperfect tense)
additional_notes: Combines the imperfect tense of estar (estaba) + gerund (viendo) to describe an action that was in progress in the past. The phrase is completed by a feminine singular noun introduced by la (e.g., la televisión). Commonly used to set background actions or say what someone was doing when something else happened.
target_language_example: Cuando llegué, ella estaba viendo la televisión.
native_language_example: When I arrived, she was watching the television.

meaning: was on the verge of / was at the brink of (about to experience something, often negative).
additional_notes: Used with 'de' + noun or infinitive: 'al borde de la muerte', 'al borde de llorar'. Indicates an extreme proximity to a state or event (physical, emotional, or situational). Commonly used for negative or intense situations (death, starvation, tears), but can be used more broadly (e.g., 'al borde del colapso').
target_language_example: Ella estaba al borde de llorar cuando recibió la noticia.
native_language_example: She was on the verge of crying when she received the news.

meaning: I/he/she/it was convinced; believed strongly.
additional_notes: Past imperfect of estar + convencido (convinced). Used to say someone held a firm belief or was sure about something in the past. Can refer to different subjects depending on context (yo, él, ella, etc.). Often followed by 'de' or 'de que' + clause.
target_language_example: Yo estaba convencido de que podía lograrlo.
native_language_example: I was convinced that I could achieve it.

meaning: 'was right' (used as part of the phrase 'estar en lo cierto' = to be right)
additional_notes: This appears as part of the fixed expression 'estar en lo cierto' meaning 'to be correct' or 'to be right'. In examples you often see the full phrase 'estaba en lo cierto' (I/he/she/it was right). Use past imperfect 'estaba' for ongoing or repeated past states; other tenses are possible (estoy en lo cierto, estuvo en lo cierto, ha estado en lo cierto). The fragment 'estaba en lo' on its own is incomplete in English—learners should use the full phrase 'estaba en lo cierto'.
target_language_example: Ella estaba en lo cierto sobre la fecha del examen.
native_language_example: She was right about the exam date.

meaning: was very (used to describe a past state or condition).
additional_notes: Combines the imperfect form 'estaba' (from estar) with 'muy' (very). Use for ongoing or repeated past states, descriptions, or feelings (weather, taste, emotions). For a single completed past event, Spanish often uses the preterite ('estuvo muy').
target_language_example: Cuando llegué, ella estaba muy cansada.
native_language_example: When I arrived, she was very tired.

meaning: 'she/he/it was alone' or 'was alone' (past imperfect of estar + sola, feminine).
additional_notes: Estaba sola uses the imperfect tense (estar → estaba) to describe a past ongoing or background state of being alone. sola is feminine singular; use 'solo' for masculine or gender-neutral in some contexts. Can be shortened to 'estaba solo/sola' without a subject when context is clear (e.g., 'Estaba sola.').
target_language_example: Ella estaba sola en la casa toda la noche.
native_language_example: She was alone in the house all night.

meaning: they were here
additional_notes: Uses the imperfect form estaban (from estar) plus aquí. It usually refers to people or things being in this place in the past. The imperfect often gives background information or describes an ongoing past situation. Depending on context, estaban can mean either 'they were' or 'you all were' (ustedes were).
target_language_example: Pensé que estaban aquí esta mañana.
native_language_example: I thought they were here this morning.

meaning: 'they were fine' / 'they were okay'.
additional_notes: Uses the imperfect tense of estar (estaban) + bien. Commonly describes someone's past state, health, mood, or condition. Can refer to people (they) or things in general. Context determines whether it means physically well, emotionally well, or 'well-dressed' when combined with adjectives (e.g., 'bien vestidos').
target_language_example: Después del accidente, los vecinos estaban bien.
native_language_example: After the accident, the neighbors were fine.

meaning: A multi-word expression with two main uses: (1) followed by an infinitive, it expresses that someone was about to do something or intended to do it (were about to / were going to); (2) without an infinitive, it can describe distribution or location (were all over / were scattered around).
additional_notes: Commonly appears as estar (imperfect) + por + infinitive to indicate imminent action or intention (e.g., 'estaban por salir' = 'they were about to leave'). Without an infinitive, 'por' often indicates distribution/location ('estaban por toda la casa' = 'they were all over the house'). Context and verb aspect determine nuance. Not a literal cognate of English 'for' — translation depends on construction.
target_language_example: Estaban por darle de baja por motivos de salud.
native_language_example: They were about to discharge him for health reasons.

meaning: you were with (someone) / you were on (leave) — past progressive of estar + con, used to say someone was accompanying, in a relationship with, or temporarily assigned/absent with something like leave.
additional_notes: Used to describe a past state: being together with a person (romantically or in company), being with someone at a specific time, or being 'on' something (e.g., on leave: "con licencia"). Context determines meaning — with people it's usually "together/seeing someone"; with nouns like "licencia" it means "on [type of] leave." Informal register is common in conversational contexts.
target_language_example: Creía que estabas con Ana anoche.
native_language_example: I thought you were with Ana last night.

meaning: station (train/bus); also season (of the year) depending on context.
additional_notes: The noun estación is grammatically feminine (la estación). The input includes the article 'el' (masculine) often because it appears in lists or with other masculine nouns (e.g., 'La estación, el hotel...') — don't treat 'el' as the correct article for estación. Use context to choose between a transport hub (la estación de tren/autobuses) and a season (la estación de verano).
target_language_example: Cuando llegamos a la estación, el tren ya había partido.
native_language_example: When we arrived at the station, the train had already left.

meaning: to/from the station; depends on context—usually 'to the station' or 'at the station' when combined with verbs of motion or waiting.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself; 'estación' (station) combines with prepositions (a, en, de) and verbs to mean different things. With verbs of motion (ir, fuimos) + 'a' it means 'to the station' (destination). With verbs of waiting or staying (esperar, quedarse) + 'en' is more common, but some speakers use 'estar/esperar en la estación' or 'esperar en la estación a [persona]' to mean 'wait at the station for [someone]'. In examples like 'estación a que llegara' the structure is 'en la estación a que...' meaning 'at the station waiting for...'. 'Voy a la estación a por Kioko' is colloquial: 'a por' = 'to pick up'.
target_language_example: Voy a la estación a recoger a Marta.
native_language_example: I'm going to the station to pick up Marta.

meaning: at (the) station at (a specific) time (used to state scheduled times).
additional_notes: This phrase combines estación (station) with a time expression introduced by a las (for feminine nouns and plural hours). Use 'a las' + time to say when something happens (e.g., arrival/departure at the station). If the hour is 1:00, use 'a la una' instead. Can refer to bus/train/metro stations or seasons when used alone, but here it's for locations/time.
target_language_example: El tren llega a la estación a las ocho.
native_language_example: The train arrives at the station at eight o'clock.

meaning: metro station; subway station.
additional_notes: Refers to a public transit stop for an underground/urban rail system (metro/subway). Commonly used with location verbs (estar, quedar) and directions. 'Estación' alone can mean 'station' (train, bus), so 'de metro' specifies the subway. Pronunciation: [es-TA-ción de ME-tro].
target_language_example: La estación de metro está a dos calles de aquí.
native_language_example: The subway station is two blocks from here.

meaning: train station.
additional_notes: Common phrase for the place where trains arrive and depart; used for meeting points, buying tickets, or describing location. 'Estación' alone can mean station (bus, train); 'de tren' specifies train. Often preceded by articles (la estación de tren).
target_language_example: Nos vemos en la estación de tren a las siete.
native_language_example: Let's meet at the train station at seven.

meaning: the station of / the season of (followed by a masculine noun).
additional_notes: This is a combination of estación (which can mean 'station' or 'season') plus the contraction del (de + el = 'of the'). The meaning depends on the noun that follows: e.g. estación del tren = 'train station', estación del año / estación del verano = 'season of the year / summer'. Use del before a masculine singular noun. For feminine nouns you'd see estación de la (e.g. estación de la primavera is possible, but native speakers often say 'la primavera es la estación del año' to mean 'spring is the season of the year').
target_language_example: Voy a la estación del tren para tomar el autobús.
native_language_example: I'm going to the train station to catch the bus.

meaning: literally 'station in/at' — not a fixed phrase on its own. It combines estación ('station' or 'season') + en ('in/at/on'), so meaning depends on context (e.g., 'at the station' when part of 'estación en la...' or referring to a station located in some place).
additional_notes: This is not a standalone fixed expression. Spanish normally requires the article and noun order (e.g., 'en la estación', 'estación en Madrid' as part of a larger phrase). 'Estación' can mean 'station' (train/bus) or 'season' (time of year); use context and articles accordingly. Example constructions: 'estación en [place]' to indicate a station located in a place, or 'en la estación' to indicate being at the station. Grammar: match gender/number (la estación).
target_language_example: La estación en la ciudad cierra a medianoche.
native_language_example: The station in the city closes at midnight.

meaning: This looks like two words 'estación' (station/season) and 'es' (is). By itself it doesn't form a fixed phrase; likely part of a sentence meaning 'the station is...' or 'the season is...'.
additional_notes: Not a multiword fixed expression. 'Estación' can mean 'station' (train/bus station) or 'season' (primavera, verano, etc.). 'Es' is the 3rd-person singular present of 'ser' ('is'). Together they'd appear when giving a description or stating a fact: e.g. 'La estación es grande' (The station is big) or 'La estación es verano' is incorrect — for seasons you'd say 'Es verano' or 'La estación es el verano' (less common). Beginners should use 'La estación es...' to describe a station, and just 'Es...' to name the current season.
target_language_example: La estación es muy céntrica y tiene muchas tiendas.
native_language_example: The station is very central and has many shops.

meaning: This is not a standard fixed Spanish phrase; it looks like two separate words 'estación' (station/season) and 'está' (he/she/it is / you formal are).
additional_notes: Likely a mistaken combination. 'Estación' can mean 'station' (train/bus station) or 'season' (la estación). 'Está' is the 3rd-person singular present of estar (to be) or formal usted command form. In normal Spanish you'd see them in a sentence such as: 'La estación está cerca' (The station is nearby) or 'La estación está abierta' (The station is open). If you meant a fixed phrase, check the intended order and context.
target_language_example: La estación está cerrada hoy.
native_language_example: The station is closed today.

meaning: favorite season (of the year).
additional_notes: Used to say which of the four seasons (invierno, primavera, verano, otoño) someone likes best. 'Estación' can also mean 'station' (e.g., train station) in other contexts, so here it specifically refers to seasons; word order is flexible ("Mi estación favorita es el otoño" or "El otoño es mi estación favorita").
target_language_example: Mi estación favorita es la primavera porque me gustan las flores.
native_language_example: My favorite season is spring because I like the flowers.

meaning: 'station for' or 'season for' depending on context; here 'para' marks purpose ('in order to') or suitability ('best time for').
additional_notes: This phrase combines estación (which can mean train/bus station or season) with para. With places (la estación) + para + verb, para expresses purpose ('to/in order to ...'): e.g. 'a la estación para montar' = 'to the station to board'. With seasons (la estación) + para + noun/verb, para expresses suitability or the best time ('the best season for...'). Context determines whether estación means a transport station or a season.
target_language_example: Fueron a la estación para tomar el tren.
native_language_example: They went to the station to catch the train.

meaning: Nonstandard/incorrect construction attempting to express past progressive or present perfect progressive (intended meaning: 'was looking for' / 'have been looking for'). Literal: 'been looking for' using past participle 'estado' + gerund 'buscando'.
additional_notes: This phrase is not standard Spanish. Correct alternatives: 'estaba buscando' (I/he/she was looking for), 'he estado buscando' (I have been looking for). Also, 'buscar' typically does not require 'por' before the direct object (use 'buscar mi libro', not 'buscar por mi libro'). You might hear 'buscar por' in some dialects, but it's generally unnecessary and can sound awkward or ungrammatical.
target_language_example: He estado buscando por mi pasaporte desde ayer. — (uses 'estado buscando por' within the periphrasis 'He estado')
native_language_example: I have been looking for my passport since yesterday.

meaning: have been looking everywhere (for something).
additional_notes: This is a past progressive perfect-like phrase: 'estado buscando' (have been looking) + 'por todas' (everywhere). It's informal/conversational and is often followed by 'partes' or 'lados' (por todas partes / por todos lados). Native speakers commonly say 'he estado buscando por todas partes' or shorten to 'estado buscando por todas' in casual speech. Use when emphasizing you searched in many places.
target_language_example: He estado buscando por todas (partes) mi llave y no la encuentro.
native_language_example: I have been looking everywhere for my key and I can't find it.

meaning: 'I have been thinking about' (ongoing/recent thought about someone or something).
additional_notes: Derived from the present perfect progressive idea: 'he estado' (I have been) + 'pensando en' (thinking about). Used to say you have been considering or reflecting on a person, idea, or thing recently and possibly over a period of time. Can be followed by a noun, clause, or pronoun (e.g., algo, lo que dijiste, ti).
target_language_example: He estado pensando en cambiar de trabajo.
native_language_example: I have been thinking about changing jobs.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase; likely a mistaken or fragmented combination meaning 'any state' or part of expressions like 'estado alguna vez' ('ever been/been in any state').
additional_notes: This exact two-word sequence is not a common set phrase in Spanish. It may appear as part of longer phrases (for example, 'estado alguna vez' = 'been ever/ever been' or 'en estado alguna' in archaic contexts). If you mean 'any state' in the sense of 'any condition' use 'algún estado' (masculine) or 'alguna condición' (feminine). If you mean 'ever' with 'estado', use 'estado alguna vez' or 'has estado alguna vez...'.
target_language_example: ¿Has estado alguna vez en Madrid?
native_language_example: Have you ever been to Madrid?

meaning: been in a
additional_notes: Literal phrase combining the past participle estado (been) with a feminine singular noun introduced by una. Used to say someone has had the experience of being in or on something/some situation (e.g., en una posición, en una eternidad, en una cita, en una moto). The preposition en can translate as "in" or "on" depending on the noun. Follow with the noun or noun phrase that specifies the thing or situation.
target_language_example: Nunca antes había estado en una situación tan extraña.
native_language_example: I had never been in such a strange situation before.

meaning: 'estado' (been/been in a state) + 'muy' (very) — used to describe how someone or something has been (very + adjective/adv phrase).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase; it's the verb haber (he/has/ha/hemos...) + estado (past participle of estar) followed by 'muy' plus an adjective or adverbial phrase. Use it to say someone/something has been in a certain condition recently: e.g. 'ha estado muy cerca' (has been very close) or 'he estado muy ocupado' (I have been very busy). Remember agreement: adjectives that refer to a noun (callado/callada) must match gender.
target_language_example: He estado muy cansado esta semana.
native_language_example: I have been very tired this week.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase; literal reading would be 'state never' or 'been never' depending on context — the two words can appear together in a sentence but are not a standalone idiom in Spanish.
additional_notes: This combination is not a common or grammatically correct multiword expression when presented alone. 'Estado' can be a noun (state, condition) or the past participle of 'estar' (been), and 'nunca' is the adverb 'never'. When they appear adjacent as 'estado nunca' it is usually part of a larger structure (e.g., 'ha estado nunca' in questions or colloquial emphasis, though standard order is 'nunca ha estado' or 'no ha estado nunca'). Avoid using 'estado nunca' on its own; learn full sentences like 'el estado nunca...' (the state never...) or 'no ha estado nunca...' (has never been).
target_language_example: El estado nunca ha intervenido en esa decisión; no hemos visto al estado nunca actuar así.
native_language_example: The state has never intervened in that decision; we have never seen the state act like that.

meaning: been so
additional_notes: This is the phrase 'estado tan' appearing in perfect or pluperfect constructions (e.g., 'nunca había estado tan...','he estado tan...') and is followed by an adjective. It expresses that someone has 'been' in a particular (high) degree — e.g., 'been so scared', 'been so proud', 'been so happy'. Use with past participle forms of 'estar' (estado is part of the compound tense) or as part of 'he/había estado tan + adjective'.
target_language_example: Nunca había estado tan nerviosa antes de la entrevista.
native_language_example: I had never been so nervous before the interview.

meaning: shelf of / shelf for (used to indicate what a shelf holds or is for).
additional_notes: Estante means 'shelf' or 'bookcase'. When followed by de + noun, it indicates the contents or purpose (e.g., estante de libros = shelf of books). In Spanish word order, you can also say 'estantería de' for a larger bookshelf. Use 'en el estante' to say 'on the shelf.'
target_language_example: El estante de la sala está lleno de libros.
native_language_example: The living room shelf is full of books.

meaning: to be waiting (for)
additional_notes: Compound of the verb estar + gerund esperar. Used to describe an ongoing action of waiting or expecting (often followed by 'a' or 'por' + person/thing, or with a clause). Common in progressive constructions: 'voy a estar esperando' = 'I'll be waiting'.
target_language_example: Voy a estar esperando en la puerta a las seis.
native_language_example: I'll be waiting at the door at six.

meaning: to be speaking; to be talking (right now or around the present moment)
additional_notes: Present progressive formed with estar + gerund (hablando). Used to describe an action in progress. Often translated as 'to be' + verb+ing in English. Can be followed by a preposition and object (estar hablando con alguien, estar hablando de algo).
target_language_example: Es mejor esperar; ellos están hablando en la sala.
native_language_example: It's better to wait; they are talking in the room.

meaning: to be at; to be [a certain date, distance, price, or measurement]
additional_notes: Usually part of a larger pattern rather than a complete expression by itself. It is often followed by a date, distance, price, or measurement. For example, hoy estamos a 15 de marzo means "today is March 15," and está a diez minutos means "it's ten minutes away."
target_language_example: En español, se usa estar a para indicar distancia: la playa está a diez minutos de aquí.
native_language_example: In Spanish, estar a is used to indicate distance: the beach is ten minutes from here.

meaning: to be at / to be (in a certain state) when followed by a feminine noun or expression — used with time, price, availability, or state expressions (e.g., 'estar a la venta', 'estar a la espera'). The exact meaning depends on the noun or phrase that follows.
additional_notes: Structure: 'estar a' + feminine definite article 'la' + noun/phrase. Use 'estar al' (a + el) before masculine nouns. Common uses: availability (estar a la venta), timing/status (estar a la hora), waiting (estar a la espera). Context determines whether it translates as 'to be at', 'to be for', 'to be on', or 'to be in (a state)'.
target_language_example: El libro está a la venta en la librería del centro.
native_language_example: The book is for sale at the downtown bookstore.

meaning: be about to
additional_notes: Used to describe an action that is going to happen very soon. Followed by an infinitive verb: estar a punto de + infinitive. The verb estar is conjugated to match the subject and tense (estoy a punto de salir, estuvo a punto de caer). Can express imminent positive or negative actions.
target_language_example: Ella va a estar a punto de llegar cuando suene el timbre.
native_language_example: She is going to be about to arrive when the bell rings.

meaning: to be downstairs; to be down (physically) or to be feeling down/sad (figurative).
additional_notes: Primary meaning: located on a lower floor or level (e.g., alguien está abajo en la casa). Figurative/informal uses: puede expresar ánimo bajo ('estoy abajo' = 'I'm feeling down') or indicar que algo no funciona ('el servicio está abajo' = 'the service is down'). Context determines literal vs. figurative sense.
target_language_example: Creo que mi madre debe estar abajo; la escuché andar.
native_language_example: I think my mother must be downstairs; I heard her walking.

meaning: to be at
additional_notes: This is a sequence where estar (to be) is followed by the preposition al (a + el) and requires more context to complete the idea. Common uses: 'estar al + noun' meaning 'to be at (a place, level or state)' — e.g. estar al tanto (to be aware), estar al día (to be up to date), estar al pie del cañón (to be on duty/ready). It can also appear as 'estar al + infinitive' in some set expressions. You will usually need the rest of the phrase after 'al' to know the full meaning.
target_language_example: No puedo estar al tanto de todo sin tu ayuda.
native_language_example: I can't be aware of everything without your help.

meaning: 'to be tasty' or 'to be attractive / in good health' depending on context.
additional_notes: Common idiom with several meanings: 1) Food: means 'to taste good' (e.g., La sopa está buena = The soup is good). 2) People: informal — can mean 'to be attractive' (Ese chico está bueno = That guy is hot). 3) Health/state: can mean 'to be well/healthy' or 'to be recovered' (Ahora estoy bueno = I'm feeling better). Context, region, and tone determine which meaning is intended; when referring to people it's colloquial and can be flirtatious or objectifying.
target_language_example: Esta sopa está buena; está bueno de verdad.
native_language_example: This soup is tasty; it really is good.

meaning: Not a standard Spanish expression. Intended meaning: "to be looking for" (best rendered as estar buscando or simplemente buscar).
additional_notes: This combination (estar buscar) is incorrect in standard Spanish. Use "estar + gerund" (estar buscando) for progressive actions ("estoy buscando" = "I am looking for") or the infinitive "buscar" in other constructions ("voy a buscar" = "I'm going to look for"). If you encounter "estar buscar" it may be a typo, a nonstandard/regional usage, or a mistaken attempt to combine estar with an infinitive; avoid it in formal speech and writing.
target_language_example: No deberías escribir "estar buscar"; escribe "estar buscando".
native_language_example: You shouldn't write "estar buscar"; write "estar buscando".

meaning: 'to be hot' (temperature) or 'to be sexually aroused' (colloquial).
additional_notes: Primary meaning: describes something or someone having a high temperature (e.g., comida, objetos, personas después de ejercicio, clima). Colloquial/sexual meaning: used informally to indicate sexual arousal — avoid in formal contexts. Use context to determine which meaning applies. For describing a person feeling hot (not temperature of an object) you can also use 'tener calor'.
target_language_example: La sopa puede estar caliente; deja que se enfríe.
native_language_example: The soup can be hot; let it cool down.

meaning: to be near
additional_notes: Used to indicate physical proximity or emotional/relational closeness. Can be followed by de + noun/pronoun (estar cerca de algo/alguien) for physical nearness. Also used more abstractly (e.g., 'estar cerca de la muerte' = 'to be near death'). Context determines whether it's literal or figurative.
target_language_example: Ella tiene que estar cerca de su hijo durante la operación.
native_language_example: She has to be near her son during the operation.

meaning: to be clear (understood or obvious).
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something is clear, understood, or obvious. Commonly appears in forms like 'está claro' (it is clear) or questions/commands like '¿Está claro?' (Is that clear?). Can refer to facts (obvious) or to someone's understanding. Often followed by a clause or por + infinitive when stating a reason.
target_language_example: ¿Está claro que debemos salir temprano?
native_language_example: Is it clear that we should leave early?

meaning: to be with
additional_notes: Used to indicate physical or emotional presence/companionship with someone. Can refer to spending time with someone now, in the future, or habitually (e.g., "va a estar con" = "is going to be with"). Often followed by a person or group. Not to be confused with "estar" plus adjective or location constructions.
target_language_example: Voy a estar con mi hermana este fin de semana.
native_language_example: I'm going to be with my sister this weekend.

meaning: to be with you (physically or emotionally).
additional_notes: Used to express wanting or being together with someone. 'Estar' emphasizes location, presence, or temporary state; can be romantic or platonic depending on context. Commonly follows verbs like querer (Quería estar contigo) or soñar (Sueño con estar contigo).
target_language_example: Quiero estar contigo esta noche.
native_language_example: I want to be with you tonight.

meaning: to be on; to be working as; to be temporarily in a role, activity, or situation
additional_notes: Used before a noun to express a temporary state, activity, role, or situation, as in estar de vacaciones, estar de viaje, or estar de camarero. The exact English translation depends on the noun that follows, so it often cannot be translated word for word.
target_language_example: Prefiero estar de vacaciones en septiembre.
native_language_example: I prefer to be on vacation in September.

meaning: to agree; to share the same opinion or accept something
additional_notes: Used with the verb estar (estoy, estás, está, estamos, están) plus 'de acuerdo'. Can be followed by con + person/thing (estar de acuerdo con ellos) or by a clause (estar de acuerdo en que + clause). Negative: no estar de acuerdo = to disagree. Also used in expressions like 'estar de acuerdo en' (to agree on) and 'estar de acuerdo con' (to agree with).
target_language_example: Entiendo, pero no puedo estar de acuerdo.
native_language_example: I understand, but I can't agree.

meaning: to be joking; to not be serious
additional_notes: Used to indicate that someone is making a joke or not speaking seriously. Commonly used in questions (¿Estás de broma?) or negatives (No estoy de broma). Can express surprise, disbelief, or to warn that the speaker is not joking. Structure: estar + de + broma — 'de broma' functions as a predicative phrase.
target_language_example: No estoy de broma: habla en serio cuando digo que me voy.
native_language_example: I'm not joking: speak seriously when I say I'm leaving.

meaning: 'to be standing' (to be on one's feet)
additional_notes: Used to describe someone in a standing position. Literally 'to be of foot/feet.' Common for physical posture (e.g., standing in a line, standing up after sitting). Can be used in present, past, and progressive forms: estoy de pie, estaba de pie, llevaré/estaré de pie. Often contrasts with 'estar sentado' (to be seated).
target_language_example: Después del concierto, todos estaban de pie esperando el bis.
native_language_example: After the concert, everyone was standing waiting for the encore.

meaning: to be back; to return (to a place or situation).
additional_notes: Commonly used to say you have returned somewhere or will return soon. Can be used alone (Es bueno estar de vuelta) or with a specific location/time (estar de vuelta en casa; estar de vuelta el próximo lunes). Equivalent to 'to be back' or 'to come back' in English depending on context.
target_language_example: Voy a estar de vuelta mañana por la tarde.
native_language_example: I'll be back tomorrow afternoon.

meaning: to be behind (physically) or to be responsible for / pursuing something (figurative).
additional_notes: Used both literally (someone/something is physically behind another) and figuratively (to be the one responsible for, to be the cause of, or to be pursuing/working on something). Context determines whether it indicates location, responsibility, or pursuit. Common constructions: 'estar detrás de + noun' (e.g., 'Está detrás de la puerta.') and 'estar detrás de + infinitive' when meaning 'to be working on/pursuing' (e.g., 'Está detrás de arreglar el problema').
target_language_example: ¿Quién está detrás de este proyecto?
native_language_example: Who is behind this project?

meaning: to be in; to be at
additional_notes: Used to talk about location or presence in a place, and also about being in a situation or state, as in estar en bancarrota. In English, it may translate as either 'in' or 'at' depending on context.
target_language_example: Desearía poder estar en París ahora.
native_language_example: I wish I could be in Paris now.

meaning: 'to be in bed' (usually because of illness or resting).
additional_notes: Commonly used to say someone is confined to bed due to sickness or recovering (estar en cama por la gripe). Can also simply mean lying in bed resting. Use with estar (estoy, está, estábamos).
target_language_example: Después de la operación, ella tuvo que estar en cama durante una semana.
native_language_example: After the operation, she had to be in bed for a week.

meaning: to be against; to oppose something or someone.
additional_notes: Used to express opposition or disagreement. Commonly followed by 'de' + noun/pronoun (estar en contra de algo) or by a clause introduced with 'que' or an infinitive. Conjugate 'estar' according to subject: estoy en contra, estamos en contra, etc. Often used in debates, opinions, and formal or informal contexts.
target_language_example: Creo que estar en contra de esa propuesta es comprensible.
native_language_example: I think being against that proposal is understandable.

meaning: to be against; to oppose something or someone.
additional_notes: Used to express disagreement or opposition. Conjugate 'estar' to match the subject (estoy, estás, está, estamos, estáis, están). Often followed by 'algo'/'alguien' or a verb in infinitive: Estoy en contra de la idea / Estamos en contra de fumar aquí. Can be more formal than 'no estar de acuerdo'.
target_language_example: Yo estoy en contra de esa propuesta. / Es importante decir que estamos en contra de la política.
native_language_example: I am against that proposal. / It is important to say that we are against the policy.

meaning: to be working on it; to be in the middle of it; to be dealing with it
additional_notes: Used to indicate someone is currently engaged in a task or process. Equivalent to English 'I'm on it' or 'we're working on it.' Common in informal and neutral contexts. Often appears as Estoy en ello / Estamos en ello; can be followed by context or omitted when understood from situation.
target_language_example: Estoy en ello, te aviso cuando termine.
native_language_example: I'm on it, I'll let you know when I finish.

meaning: to be sick (to be unwell)
additional_notes: Common expression to indicate someone is temporarily ill. Uses the verb estar (temporary state) rather than ser. Can be used literally for physical illness or to suggest someone is pretending to be sick (e.g., fingir estar enfermo).
target_language_example: Mi hermano debe estar enfermo.
native_language_example: My brother must be sick.

meaning: to be out (not present)
additional_notes: Commonly used to indicate someone is not at home, not in the office, or otherwise absent. Can also appear in contexts meaning 'to be turned off' (less common — prefer 'apagado'/'apagada' for devices or lights) or as part of idiomatic expressions (e.g., 'estar fuera de sí' = to be beside oneself). Context determines the best English equivalent.
target_language_example: Lo siento, Juan va a estar fuera hasta las cinco.
native_language_example: Sorry, Juan is going to be out until five.

meaning: nonstandard lemma-like combination of estar + hacer; often intended to mean 'to be doing/making'
additional_notes: This is not a normal Spanish surface form. For an action in progress, Spanish usually uses estar + gerund, e.g. estar haciendo. So estar hacer is best understood as a dictionary/lemma-style pairing rather than a phrase speakers normally say.
target_language_example: La secuencia «estar hacer» no se usa así en español; normalmente se dice «estar haciendo».
native_language_example: The sequence 'estar hacer' is not used that way in Spanish; normally people say 'estar haciendo'.

meaning: to be fed up/tired (of something); to have had enough
additional_notes: Used to express annoyance, frustration, or exhaustion with a person, situation, or repeated action. Commonly followed by de + noun/infinitive or por + reason: estoy harto de esperar / estamos hartos de sus mentiras. For feminine speaker use estoy harta. Can be strong depending on context.
target_language_example: No quiero decir 'estar harto' en abstracto: estoy harto de esperar siempre a que llegues tarde.
native_language_example: I don't want to say 'estar harto' in the abstract: I'm fed up with always waiting for you to be late.

meaning: be together
additional_notes: Used to say that people (or sometimes things) should be or remain together — can mean physically together or in a relationship/partnership context. Agreement in gender/number: juntos (masculine or mixed group), juntas (feminine group). Commonly used with nosotros/estar/other conjugations.
target_language_example: Nosotros deberíamos estar juntos.
native_language_example: We should be together.

meaning: 'to be free' (available, not busy, or not occupied).
additional_notes: Used to say someone is free/available (e.g., for a meeting) or that a place/object is unoccupied (e.g., a seat, room). Context determines whether it means 'available' or 'not imprisoned'. For 'to be free' in the sense of 'not imprisoned' you can also use 'estar en libertad' or 'ser libre' (ser for more permanent or general freedom). Common constructions: '¿Estás libre?' (Are you free?), 'Voy a estar libre mañana.' (I will be free tomorrow), 'La habitación está libre.' (The room is available).
target_language_example: ¿Vas a estar libre esta tarde para tomar un café?
native_language_example: Are you going to be free this afternoon to grab a coffee?

meaning: to be ready
additional_notes: Commonly used to say someone or something is prepared (ready) or that a task is completed/finished. Context determines whether it means 'ready' (personal readiness, preparations) or 'finished' (a job or item completed). Often followed by a time or purpose (p. ej., para, cuando).
target_language_example: Tenemos que estar listos antes de salir.
native_language_example: We have to be ready before we leave.

meaning: to be full
additional_notes: Commonly used for people (after eating: 'I'm full'), containers (a cup is full), places (a room is full/crowded), or abstract quantities (schedule is full). Conjugate estar to match subject (estoy lleno, está lleno, estábamos llenos). For feminine speakers/objects use llena/llenas/lleno as appropriate. Can be followed by de + noun to indicate what it's full of (está lleno de gente).
target_language_example: Después de comer, suelo decir "estar lleno" para indicar que no puedo comer más.
native_language_example: After eating, I usually say "estar lleno" to indicate I can't eat more.

meaning: to be (or be) very well / to be fine (health, mood, situation)
additional_notes: Common phrase to reassure about someone's health, feelings, or that a situation will turn out fine. Often used with personal pronouns and future or present tense (voy a estar, vas a estar, está). Tone is neutral/positive; can express comfort or encouragement.
target_language_example: No te preocupes, vas a estar muy bien.
native_language_example: Don't worry, you are going to be fine.

meaning: to be busy
additional_notes: Used to describe someone being engaged, occupied, or tied up (with work, tasks, or activities). Can be used literally (busy with work) or more generally (occupied mentally). Often follows a subject with the verb 'estar' + adjective 'ocupado'. In past or progressive contexts, use appropriate tense of 'estar' (e.g., 'estaba ocupado', 'estoy ocupado').
target_language_example: Hoy prefiero estar ocupado en proyectos que me gustan.
native_language_example: Today I prefer to be busy with projects I like.

meaning: to be proud (of)
additional_notes: Used to say someone feels pride about someone or something. Commonly followed by de + noun/pronoun (estar orgulloso de mí/de ti/de ellos) but can be used alone when the object is clear. Agreement in gender: orgulloso (masc.), orgullosa (fem.).
target_language_example: Deberías estar orgulloso de lo que lograste.
native_language_example: You should be proud of what you accomplished.

meaning: 'to be about to' (on the verge of doing something) or 'to be ready/available for' depending on context
additional_notes: Frequently used with an infinitive: 'estar para' + infinitive = 'to be about to (do something)'. Can also indicate suitability, purpose or mood when followed by a noun or phrase (e.g., 'No estoy para bromas' = 'I'm not in the mood for jokes'; 'Esto está para reciclar' = 'This is for recycling'). Context and the words that follow (infinitive vs noun) determine the meaning.
target_language_example: Estoy para salir en cinco minutos; espera.
native_language_example: I'm about to leave in five minutes; wait.

meaning: to be waiting for / to be keeping an eye on / to be attentive to something
additional_notes: Used to express that someone is awaiting news or an action (e.g., 'estar pendiente de una respuesta') or that someone is watching/monitoring something (e.g., 'estar pendiente del bebé'). Common in many contexts: waiting for updates, paying attention, or being concerned about someone/something.
target_language_example: Voy a estar pendiente de tu respuesta.
native_language_example: I'll be waiting for your response.

meaning: to be about to; to be inclined to; to be in favor of (depending on context)
additional_notes:
A multi-use phrase. Common uses:
- 'estar por' + infinitive often means 'to be about to' or 'to be inclined to' (e.g. Estoy por salir = I'm about to leave / I'm inclined to leave). Context decides whether it's immediate (about to) or a tendency (inclined to, feeling like).
- 'estar por' + noun or clause can mean 'to be in favor of' (Estoy por la propuesta = I'm in favor of the proposal) or 'to support' (Estoy por que hagamos esto = I'm for us doing this).
- Can be followed by an infinitive, a noun, or a subordinate clause introduced by 'que'. Not reflexive.
- Register: neutral; common in spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: Estoy por salir, dame cinco minutos.
native_language_example: I'm about to leave, give me five minutes.

meaning: to be around here / to be somewhere nearby (used when guessing location)
additional_notes: A casual phrase used to say you think someone or something is nearby or around here. Often followed by words like "alguna parte", "algún lugar" or "algún lado." Common in spoken Spanish. The literal parts: "estar" (to be), "por aquí" (around here), "en" (in/at) — together they express an estimated, uncertain location.
target_language_example: Debe estar por aquí en algún lugar; sigamos buscando.
native_language_example: It must be around here somewhere; let's keep looking.

meaning: to be sure
additional_notes: Usually means being certain about something: estar seguro de algo = "to be sure/certain about something." In phrases like para estar seguro, it can also mean "to be safe" or "to make sure," depending on context.
target_language_example: Quiero estar seguro antes de decidir.
native_language_example: I want to be sure before deciding.

meaning: to be without; to lack or be missing something or someone
additional_notes: Common construction: estar + sin + noun or infinitive. Indicates absence, lack, or deprivation (e.g., estar sin dinero = to be without money). Can also appear in idiomatic or elliptical forms where the object is implied (¿cómo va a estar sin? = how could she be without [a partner, resources]?). Often used with feelings or states (estar sin fuerzas, estar sin ganas) and with infinitives (estar sin hacer nada).
target_language_example: Mahmud aborrece estar sin nada que hacer.
native_language_example: Mahmud hates being without anything to do.

meaning: Not a fixed phrase by itself; it's the verb 'estar' ('to be') immediately followed by the masculine singular article 'un' as the start of a larger phrase (e.g., 'estar un poco', 'estar un rato', 'estar un tiempo'). On its own it carries no standalone meaning — meaning depends on the words that follow.
additional_notes: 'Estar' marks temporary states, locations, or progressive aspects. 'Un' is the masculine singular indefinite article ('a' or 'an'). Do not treat 'estar un' as a single lexical unit; always read it with the next word(s). Common continuations: 'estar un poco' (to be a little), 'estar un rato' (to be for a while), 'estar un tiempo' (to be for some time).
target_language_example: Voy a estar un rato fuera; vuelvo en media hora.
native_language_example: I'm going to be out for a while; I'll be back in half an hour.

meaning: 'will be' (used with adjectives or expressions like 'a salvo' = 'safe')
additional_notes: Estará is the future tense of estar (he/she/it will be). When followed by 'a' it often appears in set expressions like 'a salvo' (safe) or 'a su lado' (by someone's side). The pattern is: [subject] estará a + [noun/adjective phrase]. Common in sentences expressing future states or assurances. 'Nunca estará a salvo' = 'will never be safe.'
target_language_example: Él estará a salvo con nosotros.
native_language_example: He will be safe with us.

meaning: will be in the (feminine noun).
additional_notes: Estará is the future (or a future-like present) of estar: 'he/she/it/you (formal) will be' or a guess about someone's current location ('must be / is probably in'). 'En la' is used before a feminine singular place noun (la maleta, la escuela, la casa, la estación, la ducha). For masculine nouns use 'estará en el'. Often used to state or guess where someone or something is.
target_language_example: El libro estará en la maleta.
native_language_example: The book will be in the suitcase.

meaning: you will be (somewhere/condition) — used with adjectives or phrases like 'a salvo' (safe).
additional_notes: Estarás is the future tense, second person singular (tú) of estar. It combines with 'a' + adjective/phrase in expressions like 'estarás a salvo' (you will be safe). Often the 'a' is part of a fixed expression (a salvo). You can also see 'estarás' without 'a' when followed directly by an adjective (estarás bien).
target_language_example: Si te quedas aquí, estarás a salvo.
native_language_example: If you stay here, you will be safe.

meaning: 'at this point' or 'by now' (referring to a situation or stage in time).
additional_notes: Used to talk about the current stage of a situation, often implying it's late, obvious, or too late to change. Common in phrases like 'a estas alturas' (at this point). Can express surprise or resignation about what's happened so far.
target_language_example: A estas alturas, ya deberías saber la verdad.
native_language_example: At this point, you should already know the truth.

meaning: 'at this time' or 'around now / these hours' (referring to the current time of day).
additional_notes: Used to refer to the present time or the current hours of the day. Often appears in contexts like talking about when something happens or expressing surprise about timing (e.g., 'a estas horas' = 'at this hour/so late/so early'). Common fixed phrase: 'a estas horas' (with preposition 'a').
target_language_example: No puedo hablar ahora, volveré a estas horas.
native_language_example: I can't talk now; I'll come back at this time / around now.

meaning: this weekend
additional_notes: Short for "este fin de semana". Common in speech and informal writing. Use with verbs to talk about plans or events happening this coming weekend. If referring to last weekend, use "el fin pasado" or "el fin de semana pasado."
target_language_example: ¿Qué haces este fin?
native_language_example: What are you doing this weekend?

meaning: this (coming) end of — used to refer to the end of a period, often 'este fin de semana' (this weekend) or 'este fin de mes' (the end of this month).
additional_notes: Este fin de is not a complete phrase by itself; it usually appears before a time-word (e.g., semana, mes) to mean 'this end of...' or more naturally in English 'this ...-end' or 'the end of this ...'. Most common: 'este fin de semana' = 'this weekend'. Use 'este fin de' + noun. Gender/number follow the noun that completes it.
target_language_example: Vamos al cine este fin de semana.
native_language_example: Let's go to the movies this weekend.

meaning: "this big" or "this great" (depending on context).
additional_notes: Este modifies a masculine singular noun (este + noun). Gran is a shortened form of grande before a noun and can mean physical size (big) or importance/quality (great). Word order: 'este gran sofá' = 'this big sofa' or 'this great sofa' depending on meaning. Use 'esta gran' for feminine nouns.
target_language_example: Este gran proyecto necesita más tiempo.
native_language_example: This great/large project needs more time.

meaning: this son; this child (male) or used to refer to a male person in a familiar way
additional_notes: Literally 'this son.' Used when pointing out or talking about a male child or son. In informal/familiar speech it can refer to a man/boy (e.g., 'este hijo no entiende' = 'this guy doesn't understand'). Gender-specific (masculine). Plural is 'estos hijos'. Context and tone determine whether it's affectionate, neutral, or critical.
target_language_example: Este hijo llegó tarde otra vez.
native_language_example: This son arrived late again.

meaning: 'this son of...' — the beginning of an expression used to refer to someone (often angrily or jokingly), usually followed by a noun like 'puta' or 'perra' (i.e. 'this son of a ...').
additional_notes: Incomplete phrase: Spaniards and other Spanish speakers typically finish it with a noun to form an insult (e.g., 'este hijo de puta' = 'this son of a bitch'). Tone can be angry, shocked, or playful depending on context and relationship. Because it is often vulgar, use cautiously. You can also see it in milder joking contexts among friends, but it's still informal and potentially offensive.
target_language_example: No te creo, este hijo de puta me engañó de nuevo.
native_language_example: I don't believe you; this son of a bitch cheated me again.

meaning: on this side of; this side from/of (a location, boundary or comparison).
additional_notes: Used to specify the side or area nearer to the speaker or a referenced point. Common with physical boundaries (este lado de la calle) and figurative comparisons (este lado de la ciudad). Often followed by a noun or a phrase introduced by de. Can indicate limitation (nothing more on this side of X).
target_language_example: No te acerques: hay peligro en este lado de la carretera.
native_language_example: Don't come closer: there's danger on this side of the road.

meaning: this side of the line; on this side (often literal or figurative boundary)
additional_notes: Used to indicate being on one side of a physical line or boundary, or figuratively to mean being on one side of an issue/situation (e.g., 'on this side of the law', 'on our side'). Context determines whether it's literal (a street line, sports) or metaphorical (opinion, legal/ethical boundary). Commonly appears with verbs like estar, quedar, permanecer, cruzar (cruzar al otro lado de la línea = cross to the other side).
target_language_example: Quédense en este lado de la línea hasta que llegue el instructor.
native_language_example: Stay on this side of the line until the instructor arrives.

meaning: 'this way' or 'in this manner'.
additional_notes: Used to describe how something is done or the manner/way of doing it. Often appears in phrases like 'de este modo' (in this way) or 'no de este modo' (not this way). Can introduce an example, explanation, or consequence.
target_language_example: Si lo haces de este modo, será más rápido.
native_language_example: If you do it this way, it will be faster.

meaning: this gentleman / this man (polite way to refer to a man).
additional_notes: Used to point out or refer to a man who is nearby or previously mentioned. More polite than just 'este hombre' in many contexts; 'señor' can imply respect or formality. Can be used to address someone directly (with more distance) or to refer to someone for others. Gender-specific (male).
target_language_example: No te preocupes, este señor trabaja aquí y te puede ayudar.
native_language_example: Don't worry, this gentleman works here and can help you.

meaning: 'this time' (referring to a specific period or occasion)
additional_notes: Used to talk about the current period, the present moment, or a particular occasion being compared with others (e.g., 'this time' vs. 'last time'). Context decides whether it means 'this period' (e.g., season, era) or 'this occasion'. Can appear before nouns (este tiempo de crisis) or on its own (esta vez is often used for 'this time' when talking about occasions; este tiempo emphasizes duration or period).
target_language_example: Este tiempo ha sido muy difícil para todos.
native_language_example: This time has been very difficult for everyone.

meaning: this piece / this chunk (of something)
additional_notes: Used to point to or refer to a specific small part or piece of something (food, material, text, etc.). 'Este' = this (near speaker). 'Trozo' = piece, bit. Common in everyday speech when offering or identifying a portion.
target_language_example: ¿Quieres este trozo de pastel?
native_language_example: Do you want this piece of cake?

meaning: this last one; the latter (referring to the most recently mentioned item/person).
additional_notes: Used to point to the last item or person mentioned in a list or comparison. Often follows a noun or clause (e.g., 'el primero... este último'). Agrees in gender/number with the noun it replaces: esta última (fem. sing.), estos últimos (masc. pl.), estas últimas (fem. pl.). Common in both spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: Hablamos de Pedro y de María; este último llegó tarde.
native_language_example: We talked about Pedro and María; the latter arrived late.

meaning: 'this of' or 'this (one) from/of' — used to point to something, often followed by a noun or phrase specifying origin, type, or possession.
additional_notes: Combination of the demonstrative 'este' (this) and the preposition 'de' (of/from). In natural Spanish, speakers usually use 'este' + noun (este libro) or 'este de' when distinguishing between similar items (¿Quieres el rojo o este de la izquierda?) or when mentioning origin/possession (este de mi hermano). The phrase is compositional and literal but must be completed by context or a noun; standing alone it sounds incomplete.
target_language_example: Prefiero este de la mesa de abajo.
native_language_example: I prefer this one from the lower table.

meaning: This one/this (thing) is more — used to compare a quality (taller, cheaper, warmer, etc.).
additional_notes: Combine with an adjective or comparative phrase to compare the current item with others. Common pattern: 'Este es más + adjective (+ que ...)' meaning 'This one is more + adjective (+ than ...).' For quantity comparisons with numbers, use 'más' similarly (e.g., 'Este tiene más').
target_language_example: Este es más rápido que el otro.
native_language_example: This one is faster than the other.

meaning: this is one
additional_notes: A fully compositional phrase: este = “this (one),” es = “is,” and uno = “one.” It usually refers back to a masculine noun already understood from context, and it is often expanded in a longer sentence, such as este es uno de mis favoritos (“this is one of my favorites”).
target_language_example: Tengo varios cuadernos; este es uno nuevo.
native_language_example: I have several notebooks; this is a new one.

meaning: 'this one is' or 'this is' (referring to a masculine or neutral item nearby).
additional_notes: Used to point out or describe a specific item/person that is close or just mentioned. 'Este' is a demonstrative for masculine/some gender-neutral uses; 'está' is the third-person singular of 'estar' (temporary states, locations, conditions). For feminine use say 'esta está'. To refer to something farther away use 'ese está' or 'aquel está'.
target_language_example: Este está caliente, ten cuidado.
native_language_example: This one is hot, be careful.

meaning: 'this has' (third-person singular present perfect auxiliary with 'este' as demonstrative)
additional_notes: Literally 'this has'. 'Este' is a demonstrative meaning 'this'. 'Ha' is the third-person singular of haber used as an auxiliary for the present perfect (e.g., 'ha dicho' = 'has said'). You will most often see 'este ha' followed by a past participle (verb ending in -ado/-ido) to say that something 'this' thing has done or experienced something: e.g., 'este ha cambiado' = 'this has changed'. In spoken Spanish, speakers might also use 'esto ha' (neutral demonstrative) before haber when the reference is general or abstract. Make sure gender/number matches the noun: 'esta ha' for feminine singular, 'estos han' for masculine plural, etc.
target_language_example: Este ha mejorado mucho desde entonces.
native_language_example: This has improved a lot since then.

meaning: this is not
additional_notes: Usually appears before a verb, especially in patterns like "este no es..." = "this is not...". "Este" is the masculine form of "this/this one," and "no" makes it negative. On its own in contrast, it can also mean "not this one."
target_language_example: Este no funciona bien.
native_language_example: This one doesn't work well.

meaning: this one has / this one carries (possession or attribute).
additional_notes: Used to point out that a specific item/person (este = this one) possesses something (tiene = has). Common when comparing items or describing features. Can refer to tangible things (motor, cámara) or figurative states (e.g., 'has one foot in the grave'). Often used in spoken and written Spanish to contrast two or more options.
target_language_example: Ese es caro, pero este tiene mejor batería.
native_language_example: That one is expensive, but this one has a better battery.

meaning: lifestyle; the way a person or group lives, including habits, routines, and standards.
additional_notes: Used to talk about someone's general habits, standard of living, routines, or cultural way of living. Can describe health habits (e.g., 'estilo de vida saludable'), economic level (e.g., 'estilo de vida acomodado'), or personality ('estilo de vida extravagante').
target_language_example: Quiero cambiar mi estilo de vida para estar más sano.
native_language_example: I want to change my lifestyle to be healthier.

meaning: to stretch one's legs; to walk for a short time to get some exercise or relieve stiffness.
additional_notes: Common idiom used when people want to move after sitting for a while (e.g., after a long drive or sitting indoors). Literally 'to stretch the legs.' Usually used with definite article and plural (las piernas). Can be used for oneself or others: 'necesito estirar las piernas' = I need to walk/stretch my legs.
target_language_example: Después de dos horas en el coche, necesitamos estirar las piernas.
native_language_example: After two hours in the car, we need to stretch our legs.

meaning: a combination showing 'this' (esto) with a negation or emphasis using 'no' — often part of phrases meaning 'about this, no...' or 'this, no...' depending on context.
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom by itself; 'esto' means 'this' (neuter pronoun) and 'no' is the negation/particle. In sentences the two words can appear together when the speaker refers to 'this' and then adds a negative or limiting comment (e.g., 'respecto a esto, no...' = 'about this, no...'; or 'esto, no lo olvides' = 'this, don't forget it'). Pay attention to punctuation and word order: meaning depends on how they're connected in the clause.
target_language_example: Esto, no lo olvides cuando firmes el documento.
native_language_example: This — don't forget it when you sign the document.

meaning: a spoken combination used to link 'this' (esto) with a following clause; equivalent to 'this, and...' or 'this — and...'.
additional_notes: In the examples the speaker uses 'esto, y' to introduce or emphasize an action, consequence, or continuation related to 'this'. It's conversational and functions like a connector: mention 'this' then add another clause (often a result, instruction, or further comment). There is a short pause (comma) after 'esto' in speech. Not a fixed idiom — simply 'esto' + conjunction 'y'.
target_language_example: Escucha esto, y haz lo que te digo.
native_language_example: Listen to this, and do what I tell you.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase — likely a fragment meaning 'this to' or 'this at' depending on context.
additional_notes: On its own, 'esto a' is not a common, complete phrase in Spanish. 'Esto' means 'this' (neutral demonstrative used for ideas, situations, or unspecified objects). 'A' is a preposition meaning 'to', 'at', or used before indirect objects or infinitives. Together they may appear as part of a larger expression (e.g., 'esto a ti' — 'this to you', or 'esto a la vista' — 'this in sight'), but you will usually see 'esto' followed by other words (esto es..., esto de..., esto para...). If you meant a different fixed phrase (like 'esto es' — 'this is'), use that instead.
target_language_example: Esto a veces pasa cuando llueve mucho.
native_language_example: This sometimes happens when it rains a lot.

meaning: this now / this (right) now
additional_notes: Combines the demonstrative 'esto' (this, referring to an idea or an unidentified thing) with 'ahora' (now). Used to point to something immediate or to emphasize the current moment or situation. Not a fixed idiom — context determines whether it refers to a thing, a situation, or a moment. In speech it can introduce or call attention to what's happening now (e.g., 'Esto ahora no puede esperar' = 'This can't wait now').
target_language_example: Esto ahora no puede esperar; lo hacemos después.
native_language_example: This can't wait now; we'll do it later.

meaning: 'this when/if' or 'this upon' (used when followed by a verb in infinitive to indicate what happens when/if something occurs)
additional_notes: Este is a neutral demonstrative 'this'. 'Esto al' commonly appears before an infinitive (e.g., 'esto al ver...','esto al llegar...') to mean 'this when/if [verb] happens' or 'this upon [verb]-ing'. It's informal/neutral and used to introduce a reaction or consequence tied to an action. Not typically used alone without a following verb.
target_language_example: Esto al verlo me dio mucha alegría.
native_language_example: This, when I saw it, gave me a lot of joy.

meaning: this (thing) right here; emphasis on something close to the speaker
additional_notes: Used to point out or emphasize an object or situation that is physically or contextually very near the speaker. More emphatic than just "esto"; often used in spoken Spanish. Can be followed by a verb or noun phrase (e.g., "esto aquí es...", "esto aquí no sirve").
target_language_example: Mira esto aquí, está roto.
native_language_example: Look at this right here, it's broken.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase in Spanish; appears as two separate words ('esto' = 'this', 'cada' = 'each/every') that can occur adjacent in specific sentence constructions but are not a set expression.
additional_notes: Unusual as a fixed combination. Native speakers normally use 'cada' with a noun or time expression (e.g., 'cada día', 'cada vez') and 'esto' separately. Strings like 'esto cada' can appear when 'esto' is followed immediately by an adverbial phrase that begins with 'cada' (e.g., '...esto cada vez...'), but the natural phrasing is typically 'cada vez que esto...' or 'esto ocurre cada vez...' Treat 'esto' and 'cada' as separate words for learners; do not memorize 'esto cada' as an idiom.
target_language_example: Esto cada vez que sucede me sorprende.
native_language_example: This, each time it happens, surprises me.

meaning: 'this like' or 'this, like' — a filler phrase used to introduce or clarify an example or explanation.
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom; 'esto' means 'this' and 'como' here functions like English 'like' or 'as' when giving examples or clarifying: e.g., 'esto, como...' or 'esto como...' can precede an explanation. More common written forms include 'esto, como...' with a pause. In casual speech speakers may use 'como' as a filler similar to English 'like'.
target_language_example: No lo entiendo, esto como que necesitamos más tiempo.
native_language_example: I don't understand it, this is like we need more time.

meaning: a short phrase meaning 'this with' (literal), often part of larger expressions; not a fixed idiom on its own.
additional_notes: Esto = 'this' (neutral demonstrative used for ideas, situations, or unspecified objects). Con = 'with'. As a two-word sequence, 'esto con' usually appears when the speaker refers to 'this' together with something else (e.g., 'esto con eso...') or in casual speech when starting a comment ('esto, con ...'). By itself it is incomplete and needs more words to form a full idea. Useful to recognize when listening, but you will rarely use it alone in a complete sentence.
target_language_example: Esto con lo que dijiste cambia todo.
native_language_example: This, with what you said, changes everything.

meaning: 'this' (thing) with you / 'this' to take or share with you.
additional_notes: Used when referring to a specific item, information, or topic ('esto') in relation to the person addressed ('contigo' = with you). Can mean 'share this with you', 'talk about this with you', or 'take this with you' depending on context and verb. Common in everyday speech. 'Contigo' is the contraction of 'con' + 'tigo' (with you).
target_language_example: Quería hablar de esto contigo más tarde.
native_language_example: I wanted to talk about this with you later.

meaning: literally 'this when' — not a fixed idiom; usually ungrammatical or a fragment on its own
additional_notes: These two words together are not a standard fixed phrase in Spanish. 'Esto' is the neuter demonstrative for ideas or unspecified things and 'cuando' means 'when'. They can appear adjacent in speech or writing as part of a larger sentence (e.g., 'esto cuando...' within a clause), but by themselves they form an incomplete fragment. Use 'esto es cuando...' for 'this is when...' or 'cuando esto...' for 'when this...'.
target_language_example: Si hablamos de eso, esto cuando pase todo será distinto.
native_language_example: If we talk about that, this when everything passes will be different.

meaning: this (thing) right away / this immediately (colloquial)
additional_notes: Informal spoken phrase used to refer to doing or addressing 'this' immediately. Often follows a noun or situation already mentioned (e.g., 'esto de una' ≈ 'let's do this now' or 'I'll deal with this right away'). Tone is casual; more standard alternatives: 'ahora mismo', 'de inmediato'.
target_language_example: ¿Te encargo esto de una?
native_language_example: Can you take care of this right away?

meaning: 'this' (esto) followed by 'from' or 'since' (desde); literal meaning depends on context: 'this from' or 'this since'.
additional_notes: Not a fixed phrase—it's simply the demonstrative esto plus the preposition desde. Translate as 'this from' when indicating origin/place (e.g. 'I brought this from my house') or as 'this since' when indicating time or duration (less common). Word order and context determine the exact English rendering. Often appears in sentences like 'te traje esto desde mi casa' = 'I brought this from my house.'
target_language_example: Lo vi así y estoy en esto desde la semana pasada.
native_language_example: I saw it like that and I've been in this since last week.

meaning: this in / this (followed by) in — a short phrase often starting a clause where 'esto' (this) is followed by a prepositional phrase with 'en'.
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom; it's simply the pronoun 'esto' (neutral 'this') used before the preposition 'en' + a place, time, situation, or mode (e.g., 'esto en la mesa', 'esto en verano') or before a clause introduced by 'en' (e.g., 'esto en realidad...'). In natural speech you'd more often see 'esto' followed directly by 'es' or a verb; 'esto en' appears when specifying location, context, or manner. Use 'esto' for unspecified or abstract things; for a specific feminine/masculine noun use 'esta'/'esto' appropriately.
target_language_example: Esto en la carta no estaba claro.
native_language_example: This on the menu wasn't clear.

meaning: 'this' (object) + 'in/on the' — used to say 'put/do/place this in/on the [feminine noun]'.
additional_notes: Esto = 'this' (neutral pronoun for a thing or action). 'En la' is the preposition 'in/on' + feminine singular definite article. Together they appear when someone refers to putting, finding, applying, or doing 'this' in/on a feminine noun (la billetera, la piel, la boca, la comisaría, la nariz). You will change 'la' to 'el' for masculine nouns (esto en el).
target_language_example: Pon esto en la caja y ciérrala.
native_language_example: Put this in the box and close it.

meaning: 'this' used with 'between/among' (literally 'this between'), indicating placing or finding something among or between things or people.
additional_notes: Combines the demonstrative 'esto' (this) with the preposition 'entre' (between/among). Use when referring to a specific item that is located or should be placed between or among people or objects. Word order in Spanish can be 'esto entre ...' or more commonly 'entre ... está/estaba esto' depending on emphasis. 'Uds.' is the abbreviation for 'ustedes' (you plural).
target_language_example: Pon esto entre los libros en la estantería.
native_language_example: Put this between the books on the shelf.

meaning: 'this is (someone's) fault' — used to assign blame.
additional_notes: Often followed by a possessive (mía, tuya, suya, nuestra) to specify whose fault it is. Variants: "Esto es culpa mía" (It's my fault), "Todo esto es culpa tuya" (All of this is your fault). Can be used literally (blame for an event) or more loosely (responsibility, consequences).
target_language_example: No te preocupes, esto es culpa mía.
native_language_example: Don't worry, this is my fault.

meaning: 'this is exactly what' (used to introduce a clause that specifies something precise).
additional_notes: Followed by a relative clause introduced by 'que' (esto es exactamente lo que...). Used to emphasize that what follows matches perfectly what someone wants, needs, was looking for, or means. Common in both formal and informal speech. The full phrase often appears as 'esto es exactamente lo que [subject] [verb]'.
target_language_example: Esto es exactamente lo que quería para mi casa.
native_language_example: This is exactly what I wanted for my house.

meaning: this is what goes / this is how it goes / this is what's coming next
additional_notes: Used to introduce or summarize what should happen next, what belongs/works in a situation, or to explain the upcoming steps. Context determines exact translation: can mean 'this is what fits/should be used', 'this is what's going to happen', or 'this is how it works.' Common in spoken and written Spanish. Followed by a clause or list describing the thing or action.
target_language_example: Mira: esto es lo que va ahora en la lista.
native_language_example: Look: this is what goes now on the list.

esto es lo que va a

target_language_multi_word_term: esto es lo que va a
meaning: 'this is what is going to (happen / occur)'.
additional_notes: Used to introduce or announce a future event or consequence. Often followed by a verb in infinitive (e.g., pasar, suceder). Common in neutral or strong tones depending on context; can be direct or confrontational.
target_language_example: Esto es lo que va a pasar si no llegas a tiempo.
native_language_example: This is what is going to happen if you don't arrive on time.

esto es lo que vamos a

target_language_multi_word_term: esto es lo que vamos a
meaning: This is what we are going to (do) — introduces the plan or next action.
additional_notes: Common phrase to introduce a plan, instruction, or the next steps. Often followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., hacer, decir, hacer ahora) or a clause describing the action. Tone is neutral and used in spoken and written Spanish to focus attention on what follows.
target_language_example: Esto es lo que vamos a hacer: primero ordenamos, luego limpiamos y después descansamos.
native_language_example: This is what we're going to do: first we tidy up, then we clean, and afterwards we rest.

meaning: 'ago' construction: used with a time expression to say that 'this/it' happened a certain time ago (lit. 'this does/makes ... ago').
additional_notes: Appears in phrases like 'esto hace X' followed by a time expression (e.g., 'hace mucho tiempo', 'hace tres semanas'). In Spanish the typical order is 'hace + time' (meaning 'ago') and the subject ('esto', 'eso', or a verb phrase) appears before or after. Examples above use 'esto' or verbs plus 'hace' to indicate when something occurred: 'I did this a long time ago.'
target_language_example: Vi esto hace dos días.
native_language_example: I saw this two days ago.

meaning: this was going to (happen / be / occur).
additional_notes: Used to talk about a past expectation or prediction about something that would happen in the future relative to that past moment. Often followed by an infinitive verb: 'esto iba a pasar/suceder/ser...'. Equivalent to 'this was going to...' in English.
target_language_example: Yo sabía que esto iba a cambiar las cosas.
native_language_example: I knew this was going to change things.

meaning: 'this (to) him/her/you (formal)' — a combination of the demonstrative esto + indirect object pronoun le
additional_notes: Not a fixed phrase; it's simply the demonstrative esto ('this' for unspecified or abstract things) followed by the indirect object pronoun le ('to him/to her/to you formal'). You will usually see them separated in a sentence, e.g. 'Esto le interesa' (This interests him/her/you). In spoken Spanish, le can refer to usted, él, or ella depending on context. Word order: demonstrative + verb + pronoun is also common ('Esto le va a gustar').
target_language_example: Esto le va a gustar.
native_language_example: He/she/you (formal) is/are going to like this.

meaning: 'this' (neutral demonstrative) + indirect object pronoun 'to them' or 'to you (plural)'; literally 'this to them/you'.
additional_notes: Esto is a neuter demonstrative used for unspecified ideas, situations, or objects. Les is the indirect object pronoun for 'to them' or formal/plural 'to you' (ustedes). Together, esto les introduces something that affects or is given to those people (e.g., 'this gives them', 'this shows them', 'this belongs to them'). Word order in Spanish often places the pronoun after the demonstrative.
target_language_example: Esto les ayudará a entender la situación.
native_language_example: This will help them understand the situation.

meaning: this (direct object) + it/that — 'this' followed by a pronoun or clitic structure; often part of a larger phrase (e.g. 'esto lo tengo' = 'I have this').
additional_notes: Esto is a neutral demonstrative meaning 'this (thing)'. Lo is a masculine/neuter direct object pronoun meaning 'it' or a neutral 'that'. Together they usually appear when the speaker points out or refers to a thing and then uses lo as the object pronoun in the clause. In natural speech you'll often see them separated by a verb (e.g. 'esto lo vi ayer') or appear as part of fixed expressions. Not commonly used alone without a verb.
target_language_example: Esto lo vi en la tienda.
native_language_example: I saw this in the store.

meaning: 'this (to) me' — used to refer to something that affects or concerns the speaker; often begins a clause like 'esto me...' (e.g. 'esto me gusta', 'esto me preocupa').
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom by itself; 'esto' = 'this' and 'me' = indirect or direct object pronoun for 'me'. It commonly appears at the start of phrases meaning 'this pleases me', 'this worries me', 'this surprises me', etc. Pay attention to the verb that follows to know whether 'me' is direct or indirect object (e.g. 'esto me sorprende' = this surprises me (direct), 'esto me interesa' = this interests me (indirect)).
target_language_example: Esto me preocupa desde ayer.
native_language_example: This has been worrying me since yesterday.

meaning: this plus / this and more (adds something to what was said)
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom; usually appears in informal speech or writing to add another item or point to what was just mentioned, similar to English 'this, plus...' or 'this and on top of that...'. Often followed by a noun, clause, or explanation. Context determines exact translation (can indicate addition or emphasis).
target_language_example: No quiero ir, y esto más que voy cansado.
native_language_example: I don't want to go, and this (on top of that) I'm tired.

meaning: 'this is not' used to introduce a contrast with what follows (e.g. 'this is not what/this is not the same').
additional_notes: Commonly followed by que + verb or mismo. Links 'esto' (this) with a negation and a neutral article/pronoun 'lo' to point out that the thing in front is not the one expected or not equal. Used to correct, refuse, or contrast. Often completes the phrase: 'esto no es lo mismo' (this is not the same) or 'esto no es lo que...' (this is not what...).
target_language_example: Esto no es lo que acordamos en la reunión.
native_language_example: This is not what we agreed on in the meeting.

meaning: this is not (here/available/doing something) — basic negation with 'esto' + verb 'estar'.
additional_notes: Literal words: 'esto' = this, 'no está' = is not/isn't.
