Use context to determine what 'no está' refers to: location (not here), availability (not available), condition (not working), or presence (not present). To specify what is not, add a complement: e.g. 'esto no está aquí' (this is not here), 'esto no está disponible' (this is not available).
target_language_example: Lo siento, esto no está disponible ahora.
native_language_example: Sorry, this is not available right now.

meaning: 'this has not' (used to negate a recent action or state related to 'this')
additional_notes: Combines the demonstrative 'esto' (this) with the present perfect auxiliary 'ha' (has) and 'no' for negation. Used to talk about something just mentioned or the current situation: 'this has not happened / been / come / arrived.' Often followed by a past participle (pasado, sido, venido, llegado).
target_language_example: Esto no ha ocurrido todavía.
native_language_example: This has not happened yet.

meaning: this isn't going to (work/happen/end well).
additional_notes: A colloquial phrase used to express doubt or a negative prediction about a situation or plan. Usually followed by an infinitive (e.g., 'a acabar', 'a funcionar', 'a suceder') or left implied. Tone can be worried, skeptical, or resigned.
target_language_example: Tengo mala sensación: esto no va a funcionar.
native_language_example: I have a bad feeling: this isn't going to work.

meaning: this (thing) to/for us; this causes/affects us
additional_notes: A combination of the demonstrative pronoun 'esto' (this, neutral) + the clitic pronoun 'nos' (to/for us or us as direct/indirect object). Use depends on the verb and context: e.g. 'esto nos ayuda' = 'this helps us', 'esto nos afecta' = 'this affects us', or in a short phrase 'esto nos' may begin a clause that completes the idea. 'Esto' is neutral and used for unspecified ideas or situations rather than a specific masculine/feminine noun.
target_language_example: Esto nos preocupa mucho.
native_language_example: This worries us a lot.

meaning: 'this never' — used to say that something like this will never happen or be accepted.
additional_notes: Combines esto (this/this thing) + nunca (never). Common in emphatic statements: 'Esto nunca va a pasar' (This will never happen). Can express refusal, impossibility, or strong denial. Word order can vary (Nunca esto is less common and sounds more formal/poetic).
target_language_example: Esto nunca volverá a ocurrir.
native_language_example: This will never happen again.

meaning: this or (used when offering alternatives or choices)
additional_notes: A short phrase used to present two options, like 'this or that'. Often appears in spoken Spanish when giving choices: '¿Quieres esto o aquello?' It can also begin a sentence when proposing an alternative: 'Esto, o...' Note: 'esto' is a neutral demonstrative (refers to ideas or unspecified things) and 'o' means 'or'.
target_language_example: ¿Quieres esto o aquello?
native_language_example: Do you want this or that?

meaning: this is for / this for (used to introduce the purpose of something or to preface a comment)
additional_notes: Commonly used in spoken Spanish to introduce the reason, purpose, or a comment about what follows. Often followed by a verb, clause, or a noun phrase (e.g., "esto para..." + explanation). In some regions it can sound informal or colloquial. If used alone it may be incomplete; native speakers usually finish the sentence ("Esto, para..." or "Esto es para...").
target_language_example: Esto para aclarar: no firmes nada sin leerlo.
native_language_example: This is to clarify: don't sign anything without reading it.

meaning: literally 'this for' — not a fixed phrase on its own; appears in sentences where 'esto' (this) is followed by 'por' (for/because of) as part of a larger expression.
additional_notes: Alone, 'esto por' is incomplete. You'll see it when a speaker points to or refers to something ('esto') and then explains a reason, purpose, exchange, or duration using 'por'. The exact meaning depends on the words that follow. Common uses of 'por' include: cause/reason (por eso = because of that), exchange (te lo doy por ello = I give it to you for that), duration (por dos horas = for two hours), and means (por teléfono = by phone).
target_language_example: Me gusta esto por su sencillez.
native_language_example: I like this because of its simplicity.

meaning: 'this that' — used to refer to something just mentioned or to introduce a comment about something (like 'this thing that...' or 'the fact that...').
additional_notes: Common in spoken Spanish to point back to a situation, idea, or object just mentioned. Often appears at the start of a clause to emphasize or clarify what you're referring to: 'Esto que dices...' ('This that you say...' = 'About what you just said...'). It is usually followed by a clause or explanation and can sound informal in conversation but is widely used in both spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: Esto que dices no tiene sentido.
native_language_example: This thing that you're saying doesn't make sense.

meaning: this really / this truly (adds emphasis to 'esto').
additional_notes: Used to emphasize or intensify the statement about 'esto' (this). Common before verbs or adjectives: 'esto realmente me conmovió' = 'this really moved me'. Can express strong emotion, surprise, or affirmation. Word order: 'esto realmente' often followed by a verb or 'es' + adjective/noun.
target_language_example: Esto realmente me sorprende.
native_language_example: This really surprises me.

meaning: this is going to (become) / this will
additional_notes: Commonly used with a verb or adjective after 'a' (esto se va a + infinitive) to say that something will happen or change soon. Can express improvement, worsening, or that something will be resolved depending on context. 'Esto se va' by itself is incomplete; it's usually followed by 'a' + verb or 'a' + adjective (ponerse, arreglar, aclarar, etc.).
target_language_example: Esto se va a solucionar pronto.
native_language_example: This is going to be solved soon.

meaning: 'this would be' (conditional of 'ser' referring to a situation or idea)
additional_notes: Use to describe a hypothetical result, consequence, or opinion about 'this' (a situation, action, or thing). Common in conditional statements and polite or tentative comments. Often followed by an adjective, noun, or clause (e.g., 'esto sería un error', 'esto sería peligroso').
target_language_example: Si nadie ayuda, esto sería un problema grave.
native_language_example: If nobody helps, this would be a serious problem.

meaning: this alone / this only; or 'this by myself' depending on context.
additional_notes: Two common uses: 1) as a phrase meaning 'this alone' or 'this only' to limit or emphasize (e.g., "esto solo es temporal" = "this alone is temporary"); 2) as 'this by myself' when 'solo' describes the subject doing something alone (e.g., "resolver esto solo" = "solve this on my own"). Context and sentence stress determine the meaning. 'Solo' can also be written 'sólo' in older orthography when used as 'only', but modern Spanish usually omits the accent.
target_language_example: Puedo arreglar esto solo, no te preocupes.
native_language_example: I can fix this by myself, don't worry.

meaning: this only / only this (emphatic: just this)
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that only the thing being pointed to or mentioned applies. Word order can vary: 'esto sólo' or more commonly 'solo esto' or 'esto solo' (without accent on solo unless meaning 'only' vs adjective 'alone'). In spoken Spanish you might hear 'esto nomás' in some regions. Use to restrict or downplay: 'It's just this, not more.'
target_language_example: No es un problema grande, esto sólo requiere tiempo.
native_language_example: It's not a big problem, this only requires time.

meaning: 'this (to) you' — used when pointing something out or offering something to someone; often followed by a verb or phrase (e.g., 'esto te sirve' = 'this is useful to you').
additional_notes: Esto is a neutral demonstrative meaning 'this' (for an idea, situation, or unspecified thing). When followed by the indirect object pronoun te, it indicates that the thing or statement concerns, affects, or is directed at the listener. You'll typically see it as the start of a sentence like 'Esto te va a gustar' (You'll like this) or 'Esto te puede ayudar' (This can help you).
target_language_example: Esto te va a encantar.
native_language_example: You're going to love this.

meaning: all this; all of this (referring to a situation or things just mentioned).
additional_notes: Informal spoken phrase used to summarize or emphasize everything just discussed or observed. Often appears in clauses like "con esto todo" or "por esto todo" depending on context; on its own it feels colloquial and a bit redundant compared with simply "esto" or "todo esto" (the latter is more common). Use to refer to a collection of things or the whole situation.
target_language_example: No entiendo esto todo que está pasando.
native_language_example: I don't understand all this that's happening.

meaning: Not a standard Spanish phrase; likely a mistaken or fragmented sequence (no fixed meaning).
additional_notes: The sequence 'esto todo el' is not grammatical or idiomatic in Spanish as a fixed unit. It combines 'esto' (this/this thing), 'todo' (all/every), and 'el' (the - masculine singular article), which normally appear in different structures (e.g., 'esto es', 'todo el día'). If you encounter 'esto todo el' in a text, it's probably a typo, an editing error, or part of a longer phrase with missing or reordered words. You can often correct it to 'esto es todo' (this is everything/that's all), 'todo el ...' + noun (todo el día), or 'esto, todo el ...' with punctuation and additional words.
target_language_example: ¿Por qué escribiste “esto todo el” en el documento?
native_language_example: Why did you write “esto todo el” in the document?

meaning: "esto" = this (neuter demonstrative pronoun); "un" = a / one (masculine singular indefinite article).
additional_notes: "Esto un" is not a fixed or grammatical phrase by itself in standard Spanish; the words belong to different syntactic roles ("esto" as pronoun, "un" as article) and are rarely adjacent. Natural sentences that include both usually insert a verb or other words between them (e.g., "esto es un..."). However, it is possible to encounter the sequence "esto un" in informal or truncated contexts (e.g., clipped speech, subtitles, or poetic ellipsis) where words are omitted: "Esto, un milagro" (colloquial/poetic ellipsis meaning "This, a miracle"). Use the full grammatical phrase (for example, "esto es un...") to state or describe something clearly.
target_language_example: Esto, un milagro, no tiene explicación.
native_language_example: This, a miracle, has no explanation.

meaning: this one time; once (referring to a specific event or occasion)
additional_notes: Used to introduce or recall a single past event or anecdote (similar to 'one time' or 'this one time' in English). It often appears at the start of a story: 'Esto, una vez,...' or 'Esto, una vez que...'. Not a fixed idiom in all contexts—might be part of a longer phrase.
target_language_example: Esto una vez me pasó cuando viajaba solo.
native_language_example: This one time it happened to me when I was traveling alone.

meaning: 'this is going to' or 'this will' (used to talk about something that will happen or how something will turn out).
additional_notes: Commonly followed by 'a' + verb infinitive (e.g., 'esto va a ser', 'esto va a estar') to form the near-future construction. Used to make predictions, assurances, or statements about future outcomes. Neutral register; can express positive, negative, or neutral expectations depending on context and tone.
target_language_example: Esto va a ser un buen día.
native_language_example: This is going to be a good day.

meaning: 'this and' — literal connector used when listing or emphasizing 'this and (that)'.
additional_notes: Rare as a fixed phrase on its own; usually appears informally when someone trails off while listing things (e.g., 'esto y...' meaning 'this and...') or to join two items in speech. Often followed by another item or ellipsis. Not a set idiom — more a colloquial fragment used in conversation to indicate an incomplete list or to emphasize the current item before mentioning more.
target_language_example: Compré pan, leche, esto y…
native_language_example: I bought bread, milk, this and…

meaning: this already / this now (used to refer to something just mentioned or about to be dealt with)
additional_notes: Often used to emphasize that something is already the case or will be handled now. Context matters: can mean 'this already' (e.g., 'esto ya lo sé' — 'I already know this') or signal immediate action/resolution (e.g., 'esto ya lo arreglo' — 'I'll fix this right now'). Common in spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: No te preocupes, esto ya está solucionado.
native_language_example: Don't worry, this has already been resolved.

meaning: I'm peeling the (e.g., potatoes).
additional_notes: Common way to tell someone to inform another person that you are busy doing a simple task (here, peeling). The verb pelar means 'to peel'. The phrase is often completed by a noun (las patatas, las papas, las manzanas). Used in informal and neutral contexts to explain you're occupied and can't talk or come right now.
target_language_example: Dile que estoy pelando las patatas.
native_language_example: Tell him/her that I'm peeling the potatoes.

meaning: 'I am staying' or 'I am becoming/getting' depending on context.
additional_notes: Quedar(se) is a versatile verb. With quedarse + location (quedando/quédo) it means 'to stay' or 'be staying' (e.g., staying at someone's place or in a pension). With quedarse + adjective or participle it often expresses a change of state: 'getting' or 'becoming' (e.g., quedándose dormido = becoming/getting sleepy/falling asleep; quedándose corto = running short). The reflexive pronoun me indicates the subject (I). In casual speech, estoy quedando is used for ongoing actions (present progressive).
target_language_example: Me estoy quedando en casa de mi amiga esta semana.
native_language_example: I am staying at my friend's house this week.

meaning: i'm there
additional_notes: Literally means "I am there." It can describe your current location, but with a time expression like "en media hora" it often means "I'll be there." In "ya casi estoy ahí," it means "I'm almost there."
target_language_example: No te preocupes, en cinco minutos estoy ahí.
native_language_example: Don't worry, I'll be there in five minutes.

meaning: 'I am almost' or 'I'm nearly'.
additional_notes: Used with adjectives, participles, or phrases to say you are close to a state or action (e.g., 'casi listo' = almost ready; 'casi allí' = almost there). Common in everyday speech. For gender agreement, the adjective after 'casi' changes (listo/lista). 'Casi' is an adverb placed before the adjective, adverb, or phrase it modifies.
target_language_example: Estoy casi terminado con la tarea.
native_language_example: I'm almost finished with the homework.

meaning: I'm completely (in agreement / on your side / convinced) — depends on the following phrase.
additional_notes: This is not a complete phrase by itself; it's a fragment that needs a complemento: e.g. 'estoy completamente de acuerdo' (I completely agree), 'estoy completamente de tu lado' (I'm completely on your side), or 'estoy completamente de acuerdo con eso' (I completely agree with that). 'De' requires the word or phrase that completes the idea. Use it to emphasize full agreement, support, or conviction.
target_language_example: Estoy completamente de acuerdo con esa decisión.
native_language_example: I completely agree with that decision.

meaning: 'I'm on your side' or 'I support you.'
additional_notes: Used to show support, agreement, or sympathy for someone. Often said to reassure the other person. Can be shortened to "estoy de tu lado" or "estoy contigo" (both common). Tone is neutral; suitable in formal and informal contexts.
target_language_example: No te preocupes, estoy de tu lado en esta decisión.
native_language_example: Don't worry, I'm on your side in this decision.

meaning: I am too (something) / I'm overly (adjective).
additional_notes: Combines the verb estar (to be) in first person singular with demasiado (too, overly). Use before an adjective to say you have too much of that quality (e.g., demasiado cansado = too tired). Can be used in negative sentences with different nuance (No estoy demasiado X = I'm not too X / I'm not very X). Context determines whether it expresses excess or simply 'very' informally.
target_language_example: Estoy demasiado nervioso para hablar en público.
native_language_example: I'm too nervous to speak in public.

meaning: I'm pregnant.
additional_notes: A straightforward, common way for a woman to say she is pregnant. Use with appropriate context — can be said to family, friends, doctors, or teachers. Note: embarazada looks like English 'embarrassed' but is a false friend; it means 'pregnant', not 'embarrassed'.
target_language_example: Mamá, tengo que contarte algo: estoy embarazada.
native_language_example: Mom, I have to tell you something: I'm pregnant.

meaning: I'm in the middle (of something) / I'm between (two things).
additional_notes: Used to say you are physically in the middle of a place or figuratively in the middle of an activity, situation, or decision. Often followed by de + noun (estoy en medio de la reunión) or between two things using 'entre' (estoy en medio de los dos). Informal level neutral; context clarifies whether physical or figurative.
target_language_example: Lo siento, no puedo hablar ahora: estoy en medio de una llamada.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can't talk now: I'm in the middle of a call.

meaning: I'm fed up (with); I've had enough (of).
additional_notes: A colloquial phrase used with body-part idioms to express annoyance or exasperation. Common full forms: 'estoy hasta las narices' (I'm fed up), 'estoy hasta las bolas' (very vulgar), 'estoy hasta los huevos' (very vulgar), 'estoy hasta las manos' (I've had my hands full/I'm fed up). Tone ranges from neutral to strong depending on the noun; some versions are coarse—avoid in formal situations.
target_language_example: Estoy hasta las narices de que siempre llegues tarde.
native_language_example: I'm fed up with you always arriving late.

meaning: I'm more / I'm feeling more (used to compare or emphasize an increase in a state or feeling).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but a combination of the verb estar (estoy = I am) plus más (more). It appears when someone wants to say they are more of something than before or than someone/something else, or to emphasize an increased degree of a feeling or condition: e.g. 'estoy más cansado' (I'm more tired), 'estoy más tranquilo ahora' (I'm calmer now). Remember to add the adjective, adverb, or clause that completes the idea. Gender and number of adjectives must agree with the speaker ('estoy más cansada' if the speaker is feminine).
target_language_example: Después de descansar, estoy más relajado.
native_language_example: After resting, I'm more relaxed.

meaning: I am (with emphasis or contrast).
additional_notes: This is the first-person singular present of estar plus the pronoun yo. Spanish normally omits the subject pronoun (Estoy) because the verb form already shows the subject, but adding 'yo' (estoy yo) adds emphasis, contrast, or reassurance: e.g. to insist that it is you who are doing/feeling something, or to respond to a question. In neutral sentences learners usually say 'estoy' without 'yo'.
target_language_example: ¿Quién va a ayudar? — Estoy yo.
native_language_example: Who will help? — I will.

meaning: 'to star in' (to be the main actor/performer in a film, show, play, etc.)
additional_notes: Used before the work in which someone is the lead performer: 'estrella en + [obra/película/serie]'. Commonly applies to actors, singers or public figures. Spanish word order: subject + 'estrella en' + title. Can also be used in passive or promotional contexts (e.g., 'La película está protagonizada por...' is a synonym).
target_language_example: Ella estrella en la nueva serie de televisión.
native_language_example: She stars in the new TV series.

meaning: shooting star; meteor (a streak of light in the sky).
additional_notes: Literally 'fugitive/going-away star.' Used to refer to the brief bright streak caused by a small space rock burning in the atmosphere. Often used in wishes: "pedir un deseo a una estrella fugaz." Not used for actual stars.
target_language_example: Vi una estrella fugaz anoche y pedí un deseo.
native_language_example: I saw a shooting star last night and made a wish.

meaning: the most (as a superlative with 'estrella') — 'the ...-est star' or 'star that is most ...'.
additional_notes: Used to form superlatives with the noun estrella (e.g. la estrella más brillante = the brightest star). The adjective follows más: 'estrella más cercana' = 'closest star'. Not a fixed phrase on its own; context determines the quality (brillante, cercana, etc.). Remember gender/number agreement with the adjective: la estrella más brillante, las estrellas más brillantes.
target_language_example: La estrella más brillante de la noche es Sirio.
native_language_example: The brightest star of the night is Sirius.

meaning: 'stars of' or '— stars' (used to say someone is a star in a field, e.g. 'estrellas de cine' = 'movie stars').
additional_notes: This is a short phrase combining the noun 'estrellas' (stars/celebrities) with the preposition 'de' to link to a field or category (cine, rock, la noche, etc.). In English it's usually translated as 'stars of' or simply 'movie/rock stars.' Depending on context, 'estrellas' can also mean astronomical stars (estrellas de la noche = stars in the night sky).
target_language_example: Ella es una de las estrellas de la película.
native_language_example: She is one of the stars of the movie.

meaning: 'stars in' — the noun 'estrellas' (stars) followed by the preposition 'en' (in/on/at), used to indicate location or figurative comparison.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase; it's the word 'estrellas' plus the preposition 'en'. Use 'en' to show where stars are (en el cielo, en la bandera, en la noche) or in similes (brillaban como estrellas en ...). For location, follow 'en' with a noun or article + noun (en el cielo, en la galaxia).
target_language_example: Veo muchas estrellas en el cielo esta noche.
native_language_example: I see many stars in the sky tonight.

meaning: 'structure of' / '... structure' (indicates what something is made of or the arrangement/organization of something).
additional_notes: Used to describe the physical makeup or organizational layout of something. Commonly followed by a noun (la estructura de la mandíbula, la estructura de madera) or by a noun phrase explaining type/material. Can also refer to abstract structures (la estructura de una frase). Word order: 'estructura de X' = 'the structure of X' or 'a X structure' in English.
target_language_example: Me preocupa la estructura de este edificio.
native_language_example: I'm concerned about the structure of this building.

meaning: he/she studies the (or studies + feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: estudia is the verb 'estudiar' conjugated for él/ella/usted (he/she/you formal). la is the feminine singular definite article 'the'. Together they appear before a feminine noun phrase (e.g., la historia, la literatura) to say that someone studies that subject. For other subjects use 'estudia el' (masculine) or 'estudian' for they/you plural. Word order: verb + article + noun.
target_language_example: Ella estudia la biología en la universidad.
native_language_example: She studies biology at university.

meaning: studying at / in (indicates where someone is studying).
additional_notes: Used to say the place or institution where someone studies. Use 'en' + location (university, city, room, country, abroad). For institutions you can say 'estudiando en la universidad de…' or for places 'estudiando en Boston' or 'estudiando en mi cuarto'. Tense can change (estudia en, estudiaba en).
target_language_example: Ahora estoy estudiando en la biblioteca.
native_language_example: I'm studying in the library right now.

meaning: studying at his/her/their (place or institution)
additional_notes: This is a fragment rather than a complete phrase. 'Estudiando' is the gerund of 'estudiar' (studying). 'En' means 'in/at', and 'su' is a possessive meaning 'his/her/your(formal)/their'. Together they usually appear before a noun (e.g., 'estudiando en su casa' = studying at his/her house) or an institution (e.g., 'estudiando en su universidad'). Choose the noun after 'su' to clarify whose place or which location is meant.
target_language_example: María está estudiando en su universidad.
native_language_example: María is studying at her university.

meaning: studying for the (masculine noun or event).
additional_notes: This is a fragment: 'estudiando' = 'studying' (gerund) and 'para el' = 'for the' (masculine). It's used before a masculine noun or event (e.g., 'examen', 'final', 'concurso'). In full sentences you might see: 'Estoy estudiando para el examen' = 'I'm studying for the exam.' Watch spelling: 'para el' is two words; don't confuse with the contraction 'para él' (with accent) meaning 'for him.'
target_language_example: Estoy estudiando para el examen de mañana.
native_language_example: I'm studying for tomorrow's exam.

meaning: student at; student in (a school, university, class).
additional_notes: Used to say where someone studies (institution, class, time period). 'Estudiante en' is followed by a place or context (la clase, la universidad, el colegio, el nombre de la universidad). In Spanish you can also say 'soy estudiante de' + subject (e.g. 'estudiante de biología').
target_language_example: Soy estudiante en la Universidad de Salamanca.
native_language_example: I am a student at the University of Salamanca.

meaning: ‘student has’ — indicates possession by a student (singular).
additional_notes: Combines estudiante (student) + tiene (he/she has / you formal have). Common in sentences describing what each student possesses or is assigned. Used with cada (each) to mean 'each student has'. Tense/person: tiene is 3rd person singular present of tener.
target_language_example: Cada estudiante tiene un libro de texto.
native_language_example: Each student has a textbook.

meaning: students in the (feminine singular noun that follows).
additional_notes: This is a fragment used before a feminine singular place or room (e.g., sala, biblioteca, clase, calle). 'Estudiantes' = students (plural). 'En la' = in the (feminine). Choose the appropriate feminine noun after 'en la' (en la sala, en la biblioteca). If the place is masculine, use 'en el' instead (estudiantes en el aula).
target_language_example: Había muchos estudiantes en la biblioteca.
native_language_example: There were many students in the library.

meaning: 'students are' (third-person plural present of estar + noun 'estudiantes')
additional_notes: This is the phrase formed by the noun estudiantes (students) plus the verb estar in the present plural (están). Use it to describe what a group of students is doing right now, their current state, or ongoing actions (progressive actions often use estar + gerund: están estudiando). Note: 'están' is used for temporary states or ongoing actions; for permanent characteristics you would use 'son' (from ser).
target_language_example: Los estudiantes están repasando para el examen.
native_language_example: The students are reviewing for the exam.

meaning: 'students who' or 'students that' — a noun phrase + relative pronoun to introduce a relative clause about students.
additional_notes: Use 'que' to introduce a clause that gives more information about 'estudiantes' (people who do something, have a quality, or are being identified). It can refer to specific or general groups, and works with verbs in the relative clause. Word order: noun + que + verb. If the noun is indefinite or plural, verb agreement stays with the clause (e.g., 'uno de los estudiantes que participan' — 'participan' agrees with the implied plural).
target_language_example: Conozco a varios estudiantes que viven cerca de la universidad.
native_language_example: I know several students who live near the university.

meaning: to study law (as a subject at university).
additional_notes: Used to say someone is enrolled in or taking law studies (Derecho = the field of law). Commonly used in contexts about university degrees and careers (e.g., voy a estudiar Derecho, estudio Derecho en la universidad). Capitalize Derecho when referring to the academic discipline is optional but common.
target_language_example: Mi hermana va a estudiar Derecho el próximo semestre.
native_language_example: My sister is going to study law next semester.

meaning: to study (someone/something) — often used when followed by a person, group, or subject as the object of study.
additional_notes: In Spanish, estudiar is usually transitive without the preposition (estudiar matemáticas). However, 'estudiar a' is used when the direct object is a person or a group (estudiar a un autor, estudiar a los pacientes) or to emphasize the target of study. The 'a' here is the personal a used before animate direct objects. Not required with inanimate subjects (estudiar la historia).
target_language_example: Vamos a estudiar a varios autores contemporáneos este trimestre.
native_language_example: We are going to study several contemporary authors this term.

meaning: to study for (an exam) or to study by (a method) — often used with 'para' or with an object that indicates the exam or subject.
additional_notes: In Spanish, 'estudiar' usually stands alone (estudiar matemáticas). 'Estudiar de' appears in some varieties to mean 'study for' an exam (estudiar de matemáticas for an exam) or 'study by/using' (estudiar de memoria = to learn by heart). More common and neutral: 'estudiar para' (study for) or 'estudiar X' (study X). Use 'estudiar de' mainly in fixed expressions like 'de memoria' or in regional speech.
target_language_example: Tengo que estudiar de memoria la lista para el examen.
native_language_example: I have to learn the list by heart for the exam.

meaning: to study the (masculine singular noun that follows)
additional_notes: A verb + definite article sequence. 'Estudiar' means 'to study'; 'el' is the masculine singular definite article 'the'. They appear together when specifying something to study (e.g., 'estudiar el libro' = 'to study the book'). Make sure the noun that follows is masculine and singular. In speech, you may see 'estudiar' followed by a subject or topic without the article (e.g., 'estudiar matemáticas') — use 'el' only when the noun requires 'the'.
target_language_example: Voy a estudiar el examen mañana.
native_language_example: I'm going to study the exam tomorrow.

meaning: to study at (a specific place/institution) — used before a masculine singular noun preceded by the definite article 'el'.
additional_notes: This is the verb 'estudiar' + preposition 'en' + masculine definite article 'el'. Use it when stating you study or studied at a particular location: estudiar en el colegio, estudiar en el instituto, estudiar en el hospital (depending on context). If the place is feminine, use 'estudiar en la'; for plural, 'estudiar en los/las'. When the place name itself begins with 'El' (e.g., El Salvador), 'en el' can be part of the proper name and is kept. Conjugate 'estudiar' as needed: 'estudio en el...', 'estudié en el...', etc.
target_language_example: Voy a estudiar en el instituto el próximo año.
native_language_example: I am going to study at the institute next year.

meaning: to study at/in (a place or time).
additional_notes: Combine estudiar (to study) with en la to indicate the location or part of the day where someone studies (e.g., estudiar en la universidad = study at university; estudiar en la biblioteca = study in the library; estudiar en la mañana = study in the morning). Use en el for masculine nouns (estudiar en el colegio).
target_language_example: Voy a estudiar en la biblioteca esta tarde.
native_language_example: I'm going to study in the library this afternoon.

meaning: to study a lot / to study hard.
additional_notes: Common phrase used to say someone needs to put in a lot of study time or effort. Often appears with verbs like tener que (have to), deber (should), or future/conditional forms to express obligation or necessity. Not slang. Can refer to quantity of time or intensity of effort depending on context.
target_language_example: Tengo que estudiar mucho para el examen del viernes.
native_language_example: I have to study a lot for Friday's exam.

meaning: I was about to
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to say you almost did something or narrowly avoided/experienced something. It's the past (pretérito) form: 'estuve a punto de + inf.' Other tenses use estar (e.g. 'estoy a punto de' = I'm about to). Can express a near miss (positive or negative).
target_language_example: Estuve a punto de perder el tren.
native_language_example: I was about to miss the train.

meaning: I was the whole/entire (time) — used to say you spent the entire time doing something or being somewhere.
additional_notes: This phrase is normally followed by a period of time or a noun (e.g., 'día', 'fin de semana', 'tiempo') or by a gerund/phrase that completes the idea (e.g., 'estuve todo el día estudiando'). It's the first-person singular past simple (pretérito) of 'estar'. Common in everyday speech to emphasize you spent the whole duration doing something.
target_language_example: Estuve todo el día en la oficina.
native_language_example: I was at the office all day.

meaning: 'is converting' or 'is turning (into)'.
additional_notes: Present progressive of convertir: describes an action happening now — something or someone is changing, transforming, or being converted into something else. Often followed by 'en' when indicating what it becomes (e.g., 'está convirtiendo en'). Can be used for physical, figurative, or functional changes.
target_language_example: La lluvia está convirtiendo el camino en barro.
native_language_example: The rain is turning the path into mud.

meaning: is complaining about
additional_notes: Present progressive form of quejar(se) used to say someone is currently complaining about something. Commonly appears with 'se' (se está quejando de) when reflexive: 'se queja de' / 'está quejando de' (less common than 'se está quejando' + de). Use 'de' before the thing complained about. Can be phrased without progressive: 'se queja de'.
target_language_example: Él está quejando de el ruido del vecino.
native_language_example: He is complaining about the neighbor's noise.

meaning: is always / is constantly (doing or being something).
additional_notes: Used to describe a continuous or habitual state or action of a singular subject (él/ella/usted/esta + está). Often appears before a gerund (está siempre sonriendo) or an adjective/noun (está siempre lleno). Word order can also be 'siempre está' with no change in meaning. Conveys frequency/intensity — 'always' rather than a one-time occurrence.
target_language_example: Ella está siempre ayudando a los demás.
native_language_example: She is always helping others.

meaning: it's just around (the) corner from / it's nearby (very close).
additional_notes: Used to say that a place or thing is very close by, often followed by a noun indicating location (e.g., 'la esquina', 'la tienda'). Common in spoken and written Spanish. You can also use variations like 'estar a la vuelta de la esquina' (more complete) or shorten to 'a la vuelta de'.
target_language_example: La cafetería está a la vuelta de la esquina.
native_language_example: The café is just around the corner.

está a la vuelta de la

target_language_multi_word_term: está a la vuelta de la
meaning: it's just around the corner from the (place).
additional_notes: Common phrase to say something is very close in distance or time. Usually followed by a noun indicating a place (e.g., esquina, tienda) or by 'esquina' omitted if context clear. Can be used literally (location) or figuratively (an event is coming soon). Often shortened in speech to 'está a la vuelta'.
target_language_example: La farmacia está a la vuelta de la esquina.
native_language_example: The pharmacy is just around the corner.

meaning: is on the other (one) / is on the other side
additional_notes: Used to point out that someone or something is located 'on the other' item, side, person, etc. Context usually makes clear what 'otro' refers to (another room, side of the street, another person, the other seat). Common in spoken Spanish as part of a longer sentence (e.g., 'está al otro lado' or 'está al otro extremo'), but 'está al otro' by itself is a shortened colloquial fragment when the noun is understood from context.
target_language_example: ¿Dónde está mi libro? — Está al otro, en la mesa junto a la ventana.
native_language_example: Where is my book? — It's on the other one, on the table by the window.

meaning: it/he/she/you (formal) is like this / in this state
additional_notes: Common phrase used to describe someone's condition, the state of something, or the way something is arranged/behaving. Context determines whether it means 'looks/feels like this', 'is in this condition', or 'is done this way.' Often used to point to or demonstrate: ¡Mira, está así! = 'Look, it's like this.'
target_language_example: La computadora está así desde la mañana.
native_language_example: The computer has been like this since the morning.

meaning: it's okay
additional_notes: Used to say that someone or something is okay, fine, or acceptable. With a different subject, it can also mean "he/she is okay" or "that is fine," depending on context.
target_language_example: No te preocupes, todo está bien.
native_language_example: Don't worry, everything is okay.

meaning: is okay with / has enough of (depends on context).
additional_notes: This phrase can be used in different ways depending on context and region. Common uses: 1) To say someone 'is okay with' something (estar bien de + noun/infinitive) — e.g. 'está bien de ayudar' (they're fine with helping). 2) To describe having enough of something when followed by a quantity or noun — e.g. 'está bien de dinero' (he/she has plenty of money). 3) In some regions, it can sound informal. Pay attention to surrounding words to choose the right translation.
target_language_example: Ella está bien de tiempo para terminar el proyecto.
native_language_example: She has enough time to finish the project.

meaning: 'is okay for' / 'is suitable for' (used to say something is appropriate or acceptable for a person, purpose, time, etc.)
additional_notes: Commonly used to judge suitability or acceptability. Often followed by a noun, verb in infinitive, or a clause: Está bien para ti, está bien para estudiar, está bien para venir mañana. Can be formal or neutral. If speaking about general fact, use 'está bien para...' (singular); for plural subjects use 'están bien para...'.
target_language_example: Esta silla está bien para estudiar en casa.
native_language_example: This chair is okay for studying at home.

meaning: 'is it okay if' / 'it's okay if' (used to ask or say that something is acceptable)
additional_notes: Common phrase for asking permission or confirming acceptability. Use with a verb in subjunctive for polite requests (e.g., 'está bien si me siento?' or more naturally '¿está bien si me siento?') or with indicative to state acceptance ('Está bien si vienes mañana.'). Often appears in questions: '¿Está bien si...?'
target_language_example: ¿Está bien si abro la ventana?
native_language_example: Is it okay if I open the window?

meaning: it's good / it's tasty / she's attractive (depends on context).
additional_notes: Literal meaning: 'is good' (feminine). Commonly used to say food tastes good: "La sopa está buena." Informally, used to call a woman attractive: "Está buena." Tone and context determine meaning; can be flirtatious or objectifying when referring to a person. If describing a masculine noun use "está bueno."
target_language_example: La paella está buena hoy.
native_language_example: The paella is good today.

meaning: literal combination of 'is' (está) + 'each/every' (cada); not a fixed phrase — usually appears when 'está' and 'cada' happen to be next to each other in a sentence (e.g., 'está cada día mejor').
additional_notes: This is not a standalone fixed expression. 'Está' is the third-person singular present of 'estar' (to be, temporary state or location). 'Cada' means 'each' or 'every' and modifies a noun. When they appear together, the structure usually describes a state that applies to each unit/time (e.g., 'está cada vez mejor' — 'it is better each time'). Be careful: don't treat 'está cada' as one chunk; learn 'está' and 'cada' separately and common phrases that combine them (está + cada vez, está + cada día, etc.).
target_language_example: Está cada día más fuerte después de entrenar.
native_language_example: He is stronger every day after training.

meaning: is increasingly / is becoming more and more
additional_notes: Used to say that something is changing progressively over time. Often followed by an adjective, adverb, or phrase (e.g., 'está cada vez mejor' = 'it's getting better'). You can also see variants like 'cada vez más' + adjective or 'cada vez menos'. 'Está' is the third-person singular of 'estar' and points to current/state change.
target_language_example: La ciudad está cada vez más limpia.
native_language_example: The city is getting cleaner and cleaner.

meaning: is closed/locked with (something).
additional_notes: Used to say that something (often a door) is closed or locked using a specific object (e.g., llave = key). Followed by the object introduced with 'con' (with). Common phrase: 'está cerrada con llave' = 'it is locked'. Context typically describes the state of a door, window, etc.
target_language_example: La caja está cerrada con candado.
native_language_example: The box is locked with a padlock.

meaning: 'is like' / 'seems like' (used to describe appearance, state, or to introduce a comparison or approximation).
additional_notes: Common in spoken Spanish. Can be used literally to compare (Ella está como su madre = She is like her mother) or to describe a temporary state or impression (Está como cansado = He seems/looks tired). In some varieties, 'está como' + adjective is informal and conversational. Be careful: meaning depends on context — it can indicate similarity, approximation, or an observed condition.
target_language_example: Él está como preocupado hoy.
native_language_example: He seems worried today.

meaning: 'is with you' — indicates someone (often God or a person) is alongside or supports you.
additional_notes: Commonly used to say someone is present, supporting, or accompanying you. Often appears in religious contexts (e.g., 'Dios está contigo' / 'The Lord is with you') but also in everyday situations to mean someone is on your side or physically together. Use tú form (estás contigo is incorrect); the correct phrase is 'está contigo' for él/ella/usted + 'contigo' (with you, informal).
target_language_example: No te preocupes, él está contigo en esto.
native_language_example: Don't worry, he is with you in this.

meaning: is in a good (mood/condition) — part of a larger phrase like 'está de buen humor' or 'está de buen ánimo'.
additional_notes: This fragment is not a complete phrase by itself; Spanish commonly uses 'estar de + adjective/noun' to describe temporary states or moods. 'Está de buen...' is followed by words like 'humor' (mood), 'ánimo' (spirits), or 'salud' (health) to mean 'is in a good mood/spirits/health.' Use 'está' for he/she/it or formal you (usted).
target_language_example: Ella está de buen humor hoy.
native_language_example: She is in a good mood today.

meaning: is in a bad (mood) / feeling bad or unwell (colloquial)
additional_notes: Usually followed by words like humor (está de mal humor) or visto/ánimo; alone 'está de mal' is incomplete but can appear in casual speech to imply 'in a bad way' or 'not doing well'. Use to describe someone's mood or condition. Not formal.
target_language_example: Hoy está de mal ánimo y no quiere hablar.
native_language_example: Today he/she is in a bad mood and doesn't want to talk.

meaning: 'is from' or 'is of the' (depends on context) — a combination of the verb estar + the preposition 'de' + the definite article 'el' contracted as 'del'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself; it's simply the verb 'estar' (third person singular) followed by 'del' (de + el). It appears when describing location, origin, time, possession or a relationship that uses estar + de + noun. The exact meaning depends on the rest of the sentence. Note: 'del' is the contraction of 'de' + 'el' (not used with feminine 'la').
target_language_example: La llave está del lado izquierdo de la mesa.
native_language_example: The key is on the left side of the table.

meaning: is in front (of); is ahead (position or location).
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is located in front of or ahead of another person/place. Often followed by 'de' + noun or a pronoun (está delante de mí, está delante de la casa). Can also mean 'is ahead' in a sequence or line (who is in front). 'Está' is third-person singular of estar (temporary location/state).
target_language_example: La moto está delante de la puerta.
native_language_example: The motorcycle is in front of the door.

meaning: it's hard / it's tough (food is no longer soft, difficult to chew).
additional_notes: Commonly used to describe food (bread, rice, meat) that has become hard, stale, or undercooked. Context usually indicates food texture rather than emotional toughness. Can be used literally (physically hard) or metaphorically (a situation is tough), but beginner learners will most often encounter it with food.
target_language_example: El pan de ayer está duro; caliéntalo un poco.
native_language_example: Yesterday's bread is hard; warm it a bit.

meaning: there is the
additional_notes: A neutral phrase combining the verb 'estar' (to be / there is) with the definite article + noun. Used to point out or indicate the location or presence of a specific thing or person: 'there is the X' or 'here is the X'. Word order can vary (e.g., 'Allí está el Sena' = 'There is the Seine / There sits the Seine'). Often used in spoken and written Spanish for locating, introducing, or calling attention to someone or something.
target_language_example: Allí está el árbol que mencionaste.
native_language_example: There is the tree you mentioned.

meaning: she is (used for emphasis or in questions).
additional_notes: Literal order is 'is she' but Spanish normally places the subject after the verb for emphasis or when asking. 'Está ella' can appear in questions (¿Está ella en casa?) or in emphatic statements (Está ella, aunque no lo parezca). In neutral statements Spanish more often uses 'ella está' but both are correct. Use intonation or question marks to show it's a question.
target_language_example: ¿Está ella en la reunión ahora?
native_language_example: Is she at the meeting now?

meaning: is in good (shape / condition).
additional_notes: Used to say someone (or something) is healthy, fit, or in good physical condition. Common collocations: "en buena forma" (fit), "en buena condición" (in good condition). Context determines whether it refers to a person's physical fitness or the condition of an object.
target_language_example: Mi abuela está en buena forma y camina todos los días.
native_language_example: My grandmother is in good shape and walks every day.

meaning: is silent; it/he/she/everything is quiet.
additional_notes: Used to say that a person, place, or situation is quiet. 'Está' is third-person singular of 'estar' (temporary state). Can describe moments (e.g., mornings) or general current condition. For plural subjects use 'están en silencio' and for adjectives you can also say 'en silencio' after verbs (e.g., 'guardó silencio' = kept silent).
target_language_example: Por la noche, la casa está en silencio.
native_language_example: At night, the house is silent.

meaning: it's up to you / it depends on you
additional_notes: Commonly appears as part of the full phrase "está en tus manos" (literally: "it's in your hands"). Used to say that the decision, responsibility or outcome depends on the person addressed. You might also hear shorter colloquial uses like "está en ti" or the complete "está en tus manos". Use with verbs or nouns: "Está en tus manos decidir."
target_language_example: El éxito del proyecto está en tus manos.
native_language_example: The success of the project is up to you.

meaning: is on top (of) / is above; can also mean 'is on' in the sense of being physically on something
additional_notes: Use to describe physical position: someone or something resting on or covering the surface of another object. If the preposition 'de' follows (está encima de), it specifies the thing beneath. In everyday speech 'encima' can also mean 'on top of that' or 'what's more' when used adverbially, but with 'está' it usually describes location.
target_language_example: El libro está encima de la mesa.
native_language_example: The book is on top of the table.

meaning: 'is in front (of)'; indicates something is located opposite or facing something.
additional_notes: Used to say that a place or thing is directly in front of or facing another place. Often appears with 'de' or contraction 'del' when specifying what it's in front of (está enfrente de / está enfrente del). Can be used with people or places. Neutral, common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: La farmacia está enfrente del banco.
native_language_example: The pharmacy is in front of the bank.

meaning: is fed up (with); tired of; has had enough.
additional_notes: Common expression meaning someone no longer tolerates something. Typically followed by 'de' + noun or verb (infinitive) to say what they're fed up with: está harto de X. Used for both temporary annoyance and long-term frustration. Tone can be neutral to strong depending on context; sometimes informal when used with strong words (e.g., gilipolleces).
target_language_example: Está harto de su trabajo y busca otro empleo.
native_language_example: He is fed up with his job and is looking for another one.

meaning: literally 'is it' or 'it is' used when pointing something out or commenting on a situation (informal/colloquial).
additional_notes: This sequence appears in spoken, colloquial Spanish when a speaker links the verb 'estar' with the neutral pronoun 'lo' to comment on a situation or refer back to something previously mentioned (e.g., 'Está lo de siempre' = 'It's the same as always'). It's not a fixed idiom on its own; meaning depends on the words that follow. More common in some regions and informal speech. Do not confuse with the standard neutral subject 'es lo' in impersonal constructions.
target_language_example: Está lo de la reunión para mañana, ¿verdad?
native_language_example: It's about the meeting for tomorrow, right?

meaning: not a fixed phrase; likely a fragment meaning 'it/this is what...' or 'is what...'.
additional_notes: This is not a standard fixed expression in Spanish. It looks like a combination of the verb estar (está) plus the relative phrase lo que ('what' / 'that which'). In full sentences it appears as part of constructions like 'Está lo que necesito' (colloquial) meaning 'It's what I need' or 'Está lo que hace falta' meaning 'It's what is needed.' More natural alternatives are 'es lo que...' (with ser) when stating facts ('Es lo que quiero' = 'That's what I want') and 'está' used alone to describe current state ('Está bien' = 'It's fine').
target_language_example: Está lo que necesito para la receta.
native_language_example: It's what I need for the recipe.

meaning: it's wrong / it's bad; can also mean 'not bad' in some contexts (colloquial praise).
additional_notes: Primary meaning: something is incorrect, morally wrong, or in poor condition ("It's wrong/it's bad"). In informal speech, when used with a positive tone (e.g., about appearance or quality), it can mean "not bad" or "pretty good". Context and intonation determine whether it's negative or mild approval.
target_language_example: El examen está mal — tienes que repasarlo.
native_language_example: The exam is wrong — you need to review it.

meaning: 'is my' or 'it's my' (third-person singular estar + possessive pronoun 'mi')
additional_notes: This combination is not a fixed phrase; it occurs when describing the state or location of something that belongs to the speaker. 'Está' is the third-person singular of estar (to be). 'Mi' is the possessive adjective 'my' and must directly precede a noun (mi casa). Alone as 'está mi' it will normally be followed by a noun or clause: e.g. 'Está mi libro en la mesa' (nonstandard word order) is possible for emphasis, but the more natural order is 'Mi libro está en la mesa.' Use standard word order (possessive + noun) in most cases.
target_language_example: Está mi mochila en la entrada, no te preocupes.
native_language_example: My backpack is in the entryway, don't worry.

meaning: is much ...
additional_notes: Usually not a complete expression by itself. 'está' is the he/she/it or formal you form of estar. Before an adjective or comparative, it means 'much/far' (e.g. está mucho mejor = it's much better). With a place or person after it, it can mean someone is there or with them a lot (e.g. está mucho en casa = he/she is at home a lot).
target_language_example: Mi abuelo está mucho mejor hoy.
native_language_example: My grandfather is much better today.

meaning: 'is not...at all' / used with 'no' to emphasize negation (not ... at all / not ... in the least).
additional_notes: This phrase appears as part of the construction 'no + estar + nada + adjective' to strengthen a negative statement: 'no está nada mal' = 'it's not bad at all.' It is idiomatic: 'nada' intensifies the negation and goes after the verb. Common with adjectives and past participles (sorprendida, mal, bien, etc.).
target_language_example: No está nada caro — la cena estuvo excelente por el precio.
native_language_example: It's not expensive at all — the dinner was great for the price.

meaning: it's another one / there's another (one) (feminine) — used to refer to a different item or person (feminine) that is present or available
additional_notes: Literally 'is another (feminine)'. 'Otra' agrees with a feminine noun that is understood from context (e.g., otra mesa, otra persona, otra opción). Common in spoken Spanish when pointing out an alternative or another example: 'Está otra' = 'There's another one (over there/available)'. If referring to a masculine noun use 'está otro' or more fully 'hay otra'/'hay otro'. 'Está' emphasizes location or state ('it is/it’s located'); 'hay otra' is more neutral for existence.
target_language_example: No quiero esa camisa; está otra en la estantería.
native_language_example: I don't want that shirt; there's another one on the shelf.

meaning: is on / is over (located on top of or above something).
additional_notes: Used with estar to indicate physical position: 'sobre' means 'on', 'over', or 'above'. Context determines whether it's literal (La radio está sobre la mesa = The radio is on the table) or more figurative/poetic (La Sombra está sobre nosotros = The Shadow is upon/over us). For location, use 'sobre' or 'encima de' interchangeably in many contexts.
target_language_example: El libro está sobre la cama.
native_language_example: The book is on the bed.

meaning: is alone
additional_notes: Uses the verb estar (temporary state) + sola (feminine singular). Use está solo for a male or mixed-gender subject (solo = masculine). Can mean physically alone or emotionally/without company depending on context. Accent on sólo is optional; in modern Spanish 'solo' without accent is standard unless needed for clarity.
target_language_example: Ella está sola en casa esta noche.
native_language_example: She is alone at home tonight.

meaning: 'is' + possessive 'his/her/its/their' (third-person singular estar + possessive adjective 'su')
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but the combination of the verb está (he/she/it is, or you formal are) and the possessive adjective su (his, her, its, your formal, or their). Su agrees in number with the thing possessed (su libro = his/her book; sus libros = his/her books). Context determines who 'su' refers to. Use subject or surrounding context to clarify (e.g., 'Él está sucio' is different: 'sucio' is an adjective, not the possessive). Be careful: 'está su' will usually be followed by a noun (la casa, el coche) or by a past participle when forming passive-like constructions (está sucio vs. está su casa).
target_language_example: La casa está sucia porque su techo tiene goteras.
native_language_example: The house is dirty because its roof has leaks.

meaning: Not a correct standard Spanish phrase on its own; likely a fragment or typo. Could be part of either (a) an intended "está tu + [noun]" where "está" is third-person singular of estar and "tu" is the possessive adjective 'your' before a noun (though standard word order usually puts the noun before está), or (b) a mistaken/inverted form of "estás tú" (you are).
additional_notes:
As written, "está tu" is ungrammatical or anomalous in most contexts. Possible interpretations:
- "está tu + [noun]": e.g. in casual speech someone might say (nonstandard/inverted) "¿Está tu mochila aquí?" meaning "Is your backpack here?" Standard order is "¿Tu mochila está aquí?" or "¿Está tu mochila aquí?" (the latter is acceptable if "tu" immediately modifies the noun). Note that "tu" must be followed by a noun to be grammatical.
- Typo for "estás tú": a speaker may have intended the verb form for "you" (estás) plus subject pronoun "tú" — "¿Estás tú bien?"
If you encounter "está tu" ask the speaker/writer to confirm whether a noun follows or whether they meant "estás tú."
target_language_example: ¿Está tu mochila en el coche?
native_language_example: Is your backpack in the car?

meaning: formal 'are you' (polite second-person singular, present of estar).
additional_notes: Used in formal or polite questions when addressing someone with usted. Word order can be '¿Está usted...?' or more commonly just '¿Está...?' since 'usted' is often optional; 'está' is the present tense of estar (to be) and indicates temporary states, location, or health. Example contexts: asking about someone's condition, location, or availability.
target_language_example: ¿Está usted bien después del viaje?
native_language_example: Are you okay after the trip?

meaning: literally 'he is' (used when stressing or confirming that he is in a certain state or place).
additional_notes: This is the combination of the verb estar (está) + the subject pronoun él. In Spanish the subject pronoun is usually omitted because the verb conjugation already indicates the subject, but speakers sometimes include él for emphasis, contrast, or clarity (e.g., to stress that 'he' — not someone else — is the one being referred to). Can appear in questions, confirmations, or contrastive statements: ¿Está él? / Sí, está él. The accent on él distinguishes the pronoun from the article el.
target_language_example: No sé si vendrá María, pero está él dispuesto a ayudar.
native_language_example: I don't know if María will come, but he is willing to help.

meaning: we were in the
additional_notes: "Estábamos" is the imperfect form of estar for nosotros/nosotras, so it often describes where someone was or a background situation in the past. "En el" is a contraction of "en + el" and must be followed by a masculine singular noun. Depending on the noun, English may use "in," "on," or sometimes "at."
target_language_example: Cuando llegaste, estábamos en el parque.
native_language_example: When you arrived, we were in the park.

meaning: they are playing in/at (a place).
additional_notes: Present progressive of jugar (estar + gerund) used to describe an action happening now. 'En' introduces the location (en el parque, en la playa, etc.). Subject can be any plural third person (ellos/ellas) or named people (Tom y María).
target_language_example: Mis sobrinos están jugando en el jardín.
native_language_example: My nephews are playing in the garden.

meaning: they are behind / they are responsible for (something hidden or causing something)
additional_notes: Used to say that people or groups are physically behind something or, more commonly, that they are responsible for or secretly causing an event or problem. Context determines whether it is literal (location) or figurative (blame/culprits). Often followed by de + noun (e.g., están detrás del robo) or by a clause.
target_language_example: Dicen que están detrás del sabotaje.
native_language_example: They say they are behind the sabotage.

meaning: they/are + the (plural feminine) — used to say where plural feminine things are or how things stand.
additional_notes: Están is the third-person plural form of estar (to be). Las is the plural feminine definite article. Together they commonly appear before feminine plural nouns (e.g., las llaves, las cosas) or in impersonal/idiomatic expressions like "así están las cosas" (that's how things are). For masculine plural use "están los"; for singular feminine use "está la".
target_language_example: Están las toallas en el armario.
native_language_example: The towels are in the closet.

meaning: 'they are' or 'are the' (plural) — used to say where plural masculine/mixed things are.
additional_notes: Combination of the verb estar (están = they are / you plural are) + the masculine plural definite article los. Used when asking or stating the location of plural nouns that take los (or mixed-gender groups). In questions word order often changes (¿Dónde están los ...?). Pronunciation: están [es-TAHN].
target_language_example: ¿Dónde están los libros que dejé aquí?
native_language_example: Where are the books I left here?

meaning: they are up for anything / they're game for anything
additional_notes: Informal expression meaning someone (ellos/ellas/ustedes) is willing to do many different things, open to trying everything, or very energetic/enthusiastic. Often used colloquially to describe people who are eager, adventurous, or not picky. Context determines nuance (can be positive: adventurous; or negative: reckless). You may also hear similar forms like 'estoy por todo' (I'm up for anything).
target_language_example: Mis amigos están por todas: proponen ir de acampada, hacer paracaidismo o salir de viaje mañana mismo.
native_language_example: My friends are up for anything: they suggest going camping, skydiving, or taking a trip tomorrow.

meaning: they are on / they are over (something).
additional_notes: Used to say that plural subjects are located on top of, above, or figuratively 'under observation' or 'available' (e.g., 'options are on the table'). Context decides literal (physical position) vs. figurative meanings (being watched, under consideration). 'Sobre' can mean 'on', 'over', 'about', or 'concerning' depending on context.
target_language_example: Los periódicos están sobre la mesa.
native_language_example: The newspapers are on the table.

meaning: A sequence of the verb 'están' (they are) followed immediately by the conjunction 'y' (and). Not a fixed idiom—used when 'están' begins a clause and is directly followed by 'y' to link to another element.
additional_notes: This is compositional: 'están' is the third-person plural present of 'estar' (temporary states, locations, progressive actions) and 'y' is the coordinating conjunction 'and'. You may see 'están y' when the clause continues with another verb, adjective, noun phrase or clause (e.g., 'están y parecen felices', though this specific ordering is less common than alternatives). Grammar note: in many cases Spanish speakers reorder phrases or omit repetition (e.g., 'están cansados y tristes' rather than 'están y cansados'), so 'están y' often appears when 'están' ends a clause and 'y' begins the next one without other intervening words.
target_language_example: Están y siguen buscando la llave en el jardín.
native_language_example: They are and keep looking for the key in the garden.

meaning: are you okay
additional_notes: Common phrase to ask about someone's well-being or to state that someone is fine. Use 'estás bien?' as a direct question (informal tú form). As a statement, 'estás bien' means 'you are okay' or 'you're fine.' For formal/respectful address replace with 'está bien' (usted).
target_language_example: ¿Estás bien después de la caída?
native_language_example: Are you okay after the fall?

meaning: you are with / you're supporting / you're in a relationship with (depends on context).
additional_notes: A flexible phrase: literal 'to be with' (physically or in a relationship), 'to be on someone's side' or 'to support' (e.g., estar con el programa = support the program), or indicate accompaniment/association. Context and following words determine meaning (support, dating, belonging to a group, or temporarily occupied with something).
target_language_example: ¿Estás con ella o con nosotros?
native_language_example: Are you with her or with us?

meaning: 'you are far' or 'you're far away'.
additional_notes: Used to tell someone that their location is distant from the speaker or from a referenced point. Can describe physical distance or, more figuratively, emotional/figurative distance (e.g., estar lejos de la verdad = 'to be far from the truth'). Informal neutral second-person singular (tú).
target_language_example: ¿Quieres venir a mi casa? Ten en cuenta que estás lejos.
native_language_example: Do you want to come to my house? Keep in mind that you are far away.

meaning: you are (stressed/emphatic form of 'tú estás').
additional_notes: Used to emphasize the subject 'tú' (you) or to contrast/point out who is doing or being something. Common in spoken and written Spanish for emphasis or contrast; tone and word order (placing 'tú' after the verb) add focus. Equivalent to 'you are' with stress in English (e.g., 'you are the one').
target_language_example: ¿Por qué estás tú aquí si no quieres venir?
native_language_example: Why are you here if you don't want to come?

meaning: 'be' + 'so' / 'that (much)'.
additional_notes: Esté is the subjunctive form of estar (used after expressions of doubt, possibility, wishes, or impersonal phrases). Tan means 'so' or 'that (much)' and is used to compare degree. Together they appear in phrases like 'es raro que esté tan...','puede que no esté tan...','quizás no esté tan...' to express uncertainty about the extent or intensity of a state (e.g., so quiet, so busy, so bad). Use tan before adjectives/adverbs (tan callado, tan ocupado, tan mal).
target_language_example: No creo que ella esté tan cansada.
native_language_example: I don't think she is that tired.

meaning: everything be
additional_notes: esté is the subjunctive form of estar (to be). Used with todo (everything/all) to express wishes, needs, feelings, or conditions about the overall state of things (e.g., "I hope everything is...", "make sure everything is..."). Common in clauses after verbs that trigger the subjunctive (esperar, necesitar, hasta que, sentir que). Word order can vary (todo esté), and literal translation is possible but must be adapted to natural English ("that everything is" or simply "everything is").
target_language_example: Quiero que esté todo listo para la reunión.
native_language_example: I want everything to be ready for the meeting.

meaning: 'stupid of' (used to say someone did something foolish)
additional_notes: Used to comment that an action or person is foolish. Often appears in comparisons (más estúpido de...) or in formulas like "es estúpido de + (pronoun/noun) + infinitive/que..." — e.g., "Es estúpido de tu parte hacer eso" = "It's stupid of you to do that." Can also appear alone as an adjective in comparisons: "el más estúpido de todos." Tone is informal and can be insulting.
target_language_example: Fue estúpido de ella aceptar ese trato sin leerlo.
native_language_example: It was stupid of her to accept that deal without reading it.

meaning: to avoid traffic (congestion; rush-hour traffic).
additional_notes: Commonly used when talking about leaving earlier or later to dodge heavy traffic, especially during 'hora punta' (rush hour). 'Tráfico' here means vehicle congestion. Can be used with verbs like salir, ir, salir temprano/pronto, or tomar rutas alternativas.
target_language_example: Salimos antes para evitar el tráfico de la mañana.
native_language_example: We left earlier to avoid the morning traffic.

meaning: to avoid thinking (about); to try not to think
additional_notes: Commonly used to say you try or fail to stop certain thoughts. Often followed by 'en' + noun/phrase (evitar pensar en algo) or a subordinate clause introduced by 'que' (evitar pensar que...). Can be literal (trying not to think) or idiomatic (can't help thinking). Verb structure: 'evitar' + infinitive ('pensar').
target_language_example: Intento evitar pensar en el examen, pero me preocupa.
native_language_example: I try to avoid thinking about the exam, but I'm worried.

meaning: exactly at / exactly to / exactly like (depending on context).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize precision. With time or place it means 'exactly at' (El avión llegó exactamente a las nueve). With verbs of referring it means 'exactly what/to which' (Sé exactamente a lo que te refieres). With similarity (parecerse) it means 'exactly like'. Choose translation based on surrounding verbs and structure.
target_language_example: Llegó exactamente a la hora acordada.
native_language_example: He arrived exactly at the agreed time.

meaning: exactly (from/of) — used to specify an exact amount, time, measurement, or origin when followed by a noun or phrase.
additional_notes: This combination appears when 'exactamente' (exactly) modifies a phrase introduced by the preposition 'de' (of/from). Common uses: exact quantity ('exactamente de 2 litros'), exact time ('exactamente de las 3'), or precise origin/point ('exactamente de la esquina'). In many cases Spanish speakers put 'exactamente' before a full clause or before a number without 'de' (e.g., 'exactamente a las 3' or 'exactamente 2 litros'), so check context. Not an idiom—literal and compositional.
target_language_example: La receta pide exactamente de 200 gramos de harina.
native_language_example: The recipe calls for exactly 200 grams of flour.

meaning: exactly what (I/you/we) am/are talking about
additional_notes: Used with clauses introduced by 'que' (often implied) to say something is precisely the thing being discussed. Commonly appears in phrases like 'es exactamente de lo que estoy hablando' or shortened to 'exactamente de lo que (estoy/estás) hablando.' 'De lo que' literally means 'of what' and introduces the object being referred to.
target_language_example: Eso es exactamente de lo que estoy hablando.
native_language_example: That is exactly what I'm talking about.

meaning: 'exactly the' (masculine singular).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize precision about a specific masculine noun that follows (el + noun). Often appears before a noun or phrase: 'exactamente el problema' = 'exactly the problem.' If referring to a feminine noun, use 'exactamente la'. Can also appear before clauses introduced by 'que' (less common).
target_language_example: Eso es exactamente el motivo por el que vine.
native_language_example: That is exactly the reason I came.

meaning: exactly it
additional_notes: Used to emphasize agreement or to confirm a specific thing just mentioned. Often appears in phrases like "exactamente lo que..." ("exactly what...") or "exactamente lo que quería" ("exactly what I wanted"). On its own "exactamente lo" is usually followed by a relative word (que, quien) or a noun. Literal translation is possible but English more naturally uses "exactly what/that."
target_language_example: Eso es exactamente lo que necesitábamos.
native_language_example: That's exactly what we needed.

meaning: 'examen es' isn't a standard fixed phrase in Spanish; likely a fragment meaning 'exam is' (e.g., 'el examen es...').
additional_notes: This looks like two-word sequence where 'examen' = 'exam' and 'es' = 'is' (third-person singular of ser). It's not a standalone phrase — it's used as part of a sentence to describe or define an exam (e.g., 'El examen es difícil' = 'The exam is difficult'). Remember agreement and articles: commonly you'll see 'el examen es...' or 'un examen es...'.
target_language_example: El examen es mañana por la mañana.
native_language_example: The exam is tomorrow morning.

meaning: A two-word sequence where the negator 'no' follows the noun 'examen' in contexts like bullet points, labels, or contrasted phrases; not a standard standalone fixed phrase in neutral Spanish syntax.
additional_notes: The sequence 'examen no' is uncommon as a simple sentence because Spanish normally places 'no' before the verb or phrase it negates (e.g., 'no hay examen'). 'Examen no' can appear in contexts such as forms, checklists, headings, or paired contrasts (e.g., 'examen: sí / examen: no' or 'examen no presencial' when part of a larger phrase). When used this way, it functions as a label meaning 'no exam' or as the beginning of a longer modifier. For learners: prefer constructions like 'no hay examen' for sentences; use 'examen no' only in labels or truncated contexts.
target_language_example: Examen no presencial: la evaluación será en línea.
native_language_example: Exam — no in-person: the assessment will be online.

meaning: except (for) someone; excluding a specific person
additional_notes: Used to exclude a person from a general statement. Followed by a person or pronoun introduced with the preposition a (e.g., 'a mí', 'a usted', 'a una'). Common in spoken and written Spanish. If excluding things rather than people, use 'excepto' without 'a' (e.g., 'excepto las sillas').
target_language_example: Todos vinieron, excepto a María.
native_language_example: Everyone came, except for María.

meaning: 'except (for) the' — used to exclude a specific feminine singular noun or idea.
additional_notes: Excepto is a preposition meaning 'except' or 'except for'. When the noun it modifies is feminine singular, you use 'la' (excepto la casa, excepto la tentación). It can exclude people, things, or abstract ideas. If the noun is masculine use 'excepto el'; for plural use 'excepto los/las' or simply 'excepto' + plural noun.
target_language_example: Me gusta todo en el menú, excepto la sopa.
native_language_example: I like everything on the menu, except the soup.

meaning: except for the (masculine plural).
additional_notes: Used to exclude specific masculine plural nouns or days (e.g., 'excepto los viernes' = 'except on Fridays'). If the noun is feminine plural use 'excepto las'; for singular use 'excepto el/excepto la'. Common alternative: 'excepto' alone can be followed directly by a noun or phrase.
target_language_example: Voy al gimnasio excepto los miércoles.
native_language_example: I go to the gym except on Wednesdays.

meaning: 'existence of' — used to talk about whether something exists or is real.
additional_notes: Common, neutral phrase used to refer to the existence or reality of people, things, ideas, species, etc. Often followed by a noun or noun phrase. Can be used in affirmative, negative, and questioning contexts (e.g., negar la existencia de = deny the existence of).
target_language_example: Dudan de la existencia de vida inteligente fuera de la Tierra.
native_language_example: They doubt the existence of intelligent life outside Earth.

meaning: 'experience is' (used to introduce a general definition or proverb about experience)
additional_notes: Often appears at the start of proverbs or aphorisms (e.g., defining what 'experience' means). In Spanish you can use 'Experiencia es...' without the article to make a general, rhetorical statement; more commonly you'll see 'La experiencia es...' for ordinary statements. Useful for making generalizations or giving maxims.
target_language_example: Experiencia es aprender de los errores y seguir adelante.
native_language_example: Experience is learning from mistakes and moving forward.

meaning: 'explained to' (past tense of explicar + indirect object marker).
additional_notes: Used to say that someone explained something to someone. Followed by an indirect object (a + person or pronoun) and often by what was explained (explicó a María el problema / le explicó el problema). In Spanish, 'a' introduces the person who receives the explanation.
target_language_example: El profesor explicó a los estudiantes la tarea.
native_language_example: The teacher explained the homework to the students.

meaning: he/she explained the (feminine plural noun).
additional_notes: Explicó is the past (pretérito) form of explicar for él/ella/usted. Las is the feminine plural definite article 'the' and matches a following feminine plural noun (e.g., las reglas, las normas, las circunstancias). Use this construction to say someone explained specific things. For masculine plural nouns use 'explicó los'.
target_language_example: Ella explicó las instrucciones con calma.
native_language_example: She explained the instructions calmly.

meaning: he/she/it explained by (giving a reason or method); 'explicó por...' usually introduces the reason, cause or way something happened.
additional_notes: explicó is the past (preterite) of explicar. por following it typically introduces the cause, reason, method or medium (e.g., explicó por la lluvia, explicó por teléfono). In many cases a clause with 'que' or a noun follows: explicó por qué (explained why) or explicó por la tarde (explained in the afternoon) depending on context. If you want 'explained to' someone, use 'explicó a' (explicó a María).
target_language_example: El profesor explicó por qué la solución era correcta.
native_language_example: The teacher explained why the solution was correct.

meaning: an explosion in/at (location).
additional_notes: Used to report or describe an explosion that happened at a specific place. 'Explosión' is feminine; use with articles or location phrases (por ejemplo: 'una explosión en la fábrica', 'la explosión en la mina'). Can be used in news, reports, or film production (e.g., filming explosion scenes).
target_language_example: Hubo una explosión en el almacén esta mañana.
native_language_example: There was an explosion in the warehouse this morning.

meaning: to take advantage of those (things/people/opportunities)
additional_notes: Commonly used when talking about using or exploiting previously mentioned items, opportunities, or people. Tone can be neutral (make the most of) or negative (exploit, take unfair advantage) depending on context. 'Esos' must match the gender/number of the noun it refers to (esos = masculine plural). You will often see similar forms: 'explotar esas' (feminine), 'explotar este/esa/estos' depending on what is referred to.
