meaning: Not a standard Spanish phrase; likely a mistaken or fragmented combination of 'gusta' (it pleases / to like) + 'es' (is).
additional_notes: This exact two-word string 'gusta es' does not form a correct expression in Spanish on its own. It may appear when someone incorrectly combines verbs or fragments of sentences, for example mixing 'me gusta' (I like) with a following clause using 'es' ('is'). Correct alternatives depend on intent: use 'me gusta' (I like), 'le gusta' (he/she/you formal like), or a full clause like 'lo que más me gusta es...' (what I like most is...).
target_language_example: Lo que más me gusta es la música.
native_language_example: What I like most is music.

meaning: 'I/he/she/they like(s) that' — expression showing liking for something or someone (with 'esa' = that [feminine]).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but the verb gustar + demonstrative adjective (esa). Gustar is used differently than 'to like' in English: the thing liked is the subject and the person who likes it is an indirect object (me, te, le, nos, os, les). 'Esa' agrees in gender with the noun it points to (esa película, esa camisa, esa idea). Use 'ese' for masculine singular and 'esas'/'esos' for plural.
target_language_example: A Juan le gusta esa canción.
native_language_example: Juan likes that song.

meaning: likes to write / enjoys writing.
additional_notes: This is a verb phrase combining 'gustar' (to like) with an infinitive. In Spanish you normally say 'le gusta escribir' (he/she/you-formal likes to write) or 'me gusta escribir' (I like to write). The indirect object (me, te, le, nos, os, les) indicates who likes the action. Use the infinitive 'escribir' after 'gustar' to express liking an activity.
target_language_example: A Marta le gusta escribir cartas los domingos.
native_language_example: Marta likes to write letters on Sundays.

meaning: 'I like this' (literal split: gusta = it pleases me; esta = this (feminine)).
additional_notes: Combination of the verb gustar (used to say you like something) plus the demonstrative esta (feminine singular 'this'). In natural Spanish you'd usually include the indirect object pronoun (me, te, le, nos, os, les) before gusta: e.g. Me gusta esta casa = I like this house. Use esta with feminine nouns (esta casa, esta foto, esta tienda). For masculine nouns use este (me gusta este libro).
target_language_example: Me gusta esta camisa, ¿dónde la compraste?
native_language_example: I like this shirt — where did you buy it?

meaning: to like to talk / to enjoy speaking
additional_notes: Combines the verb gustar (to like) with the infinitive hablar (to speak). Use with indirect object pronouns or phrases to indicate who likes speaking: Me/Te/Le/Nos/Os/Les gusta hablar + (language/topic). In negative sentences add 'no' before the indirect object: A Tom no le gusta hablar en público. When specifying a person, use 'A + name/persona' plus 'le' (or appropriate pronoun).
target_language_example: Me gusta hablar con mis amigos por las tardes.
native_language_example: I like to talk with my friends in the evenings.

meaning: 'to like going to' (someone likes to go to a place)
additional_notes: This is the verb gustar + infinitive construction used to say someone enjoys going somewhere. Structure: (A + person) + le/te/me/nos + gusta + ir + al/a la + [place]. Use 'al' for masculine singular places (el cine, el museo) and 'a la' for feminine (la playa, la escuela). To make negative, add no before the indirect object pronoun (No me gusta ir al teatro).
target_language_example: A mí me gusta ir al parque los domingos.
native_language_example: I like going to the park on Sundays.

meaning: likes to play in/at (used to say someone enjoys playing a sport or game for a team or at a place)
additional_notes: Combines the verb gustar (to like) with an infinitive. Use with an indirect object pronoun or a named person: (A él) le gusta jugar en el equipo / (A María) le gusta jugar en el parque. 'En' introduces a team, place, league, or setting. Conjugate gustar to agree with the infinitive phrase (gusta jugar...).
target_language_example: A ella le gusta jugar en el equipo de la escuela.
native_language_example: She likes to play on the school team.

meaning: likes to play in/at the (feminine place).
additional_notes: This is a fragment: gusta (he/she/you-formal/it likes) + jugar (to play) + en la (in/at the [feminine noun]). It needs a subject (e.g., A ella le gusta) and a feminine location or context after 'la' (la playa, la casa, la escuela). For example: "A él le gusta jugar en la playa." Use 'en el' for masculine places (el parque).
target_language_example: A ella le gusta jugar en la escuela con sus amigas.
native_language_example: She likes to play at school with her friends.

meaning: you/he/she/it likes the
additional_notes: Part of the verb phrase gustar (to like). Spanish uses an indirect object pronoun (me/te/le/nos/os/les) plus 'gusta' (singular) or 'gustan' (plural) to indicate who likes something. 'Gusta la' appears before a feminine singular noun (la + noun), e.g. 'gusta la fruta' = 'likes the fruit'. Word order often includes a clarifying prepositional phrase with 'a' + person: 'A Tom no le gusta la Navidad.'
target_language_example: A ella le gusta la fruta.
native_language_example: She likes fruit.

meaning: 'like the way' or 'like the shape/form/style'
additional_notes: Used to say you like the way something is done, looks, or its shape/style. Often appears as part of a larger sentence: e.g., "Me gusta la forma en que lo hiciste" (I like the way you did it) or "Me gusta la forma de esa silla" (I like the shape of that chair). The phrase typically needs a subject (me/te/le/nos/les) before 'gusta' in normal sentences.
target_language_example: Me gusta la forma en que resolviste el problema.
native_language_example: I like the way you solved the problem.

meaning: likes the way (someone) does something / likes the way (something) is done
additional_notes: This phrase is a fragment often used when commenting on how someone performs an action or how something is presented. It usually continues with an infinitive or clause (e.g., "me gusta la forma en que lo dices" or "me gusta la forma en que trabaja"). Commonly appears with an indirect object pronoun (me, te, le, nos, os, les): "(A mí) me gusta la forma en que..."
target_language_example: Me gusta la forma en que explicas las cosas.
native_language_example: I like the way you explain things.

meaning: I/you/he/she/they like(s) to read literature (books, fiction, poetry).
additional_notes: This phrase combines the verb gustar ('to like') with an infinitive ('leer') and the noun 'literatura'. Gustar agrees with the thing liked (here the action 'leer literatura' is singular), so the usual forms are 'me gusta', 'te gusta', 'le gusta', 'nos gusta', 'os gusta', 'les gusta'. Context determines the subject: e.g. 'Me gusta leer literatura' = 'I like to read literature.'
target_language_example: A Marta le gusta leer literatura contemporánea los fines de semana.
native_language_example: Marta likes to read contemporary literature on weekends.

meaning: literally 'likes it' or 'it pleases (someone)', often appears when someone says 'gusta' followed by a clause starting with 'lo' (lo + adjective/verb phrase) — common structures: 'me gusta lo ___' or 'le gusta lo ___'.
additional_notes: On its own 'gusta lo' is incomplete. In Spanish, gustar is used with an indirect object pronoun (me/te/le/nos/os/les): e.g. 'Me gusta lo que dices' = 'I like what you say.' Here 'lo' can introduce a clause (lo que...) or refer to a neutral idea ('lo de ayer'). Remember word order: indirect object pronoun + gusta + subject (the thing liked).
target_language_example: A María le gusta lo que propusiste en la reunión.
native_language_example: María likes what you proposed in the meeting.

meaning: literally 'my [thing] pleases' — not a grammatical phrase by itself; appears when saying someone likes something about you (e.g., 'me gusta mi...' = 'I like my...').
additional_notes: Spanish uses the verb gustar with an indirect object: the thing liked is the subject and the person who likes it is an indirect object (me, te, le, nos, os, les). 'gusta mi' by itself is ungrammatical because 'mi' is a subject/possessive, not an indirect object. You will commonly say: 'Me gusta mi...' (I like my...) or 'Le gusta mi...' (He/she/you-formal likes my...). Examples: 'Me gusta mi casa' = 'I like my house.' 'Le gusta mi canción' = 'He/she likes my song.'
target_language_example: Me gusta mi trabajo.
native_language_example: I like my job.

meaning: 'likes/loves the' (he/she/it likes something a lot) — used before a masculine singular noun or definite idea.
additional_notes: This is the verb gustar construction: 'gusta' agrees with the thing liked (third-person singular). 'El' is the masculine singular definite article (the). Often appears with an indirect object pronoun (me, te, le, nos, os, les) to indicate who likes it: e.g. 'A ella le gusta mucho el chocolate.' Without the pronoun, context must make clear who likes it. Can also be followed by an infinitive (me gusta mucho bailar = I really like to dance) but then 'el' would not be used.
target_language_example: A Juan le gusta mucho el perro nuevo.
native_language_example: Juan really likes the new dog.

meaning: 'I really like the' (feminine singular noun that follows).
additional_notes: Gusta is from gustar, used to say what someone likes. With 'me' it means 'I like'. 'La' is the feminine singular direct object (or article) before a noun: e.g., la cama, la vida. Word order: indirect object pronoun (me/te/le/nos/os/les) + gusta + (mucho) + la + noun. Use 'gusta' for singular nouns or infinitive verbs. 'Me gusta mucho la cama' = 'I really like the bed.'
target_language_example: Me gusta mucho la música clásica.
native_language_example: I really like classical music.

meaning: 'doesn't like any' or 'doesn't like any of them'.
additional_notes: This phrase is not a standard fixed collocation in Spanish. It seems to combine gusta (third-person singular of gustar: 'to be pleasing to') with ninguno ('none' / 'not any'). Native Spanish typically uses constructions like 'no le gusta ninguno' (he/she doesn't like any of them) or 'no me gusta ninguno' (I don't like any). Remember that gustar uses indirect object pronouns (me, te, le, nos, os, les) and the thing liked is the grammatical subject: 'No me gusta ninguno' = 'None of them pleases me.'
target_language_example: No me gusta ninguno de estos libros.
native_language_example: I don't like any of these books.

meaning: likes to go out (enjoys leaving home to socialize, go out for fun, etc.)
additional_notes: Commonly used with an indirect-object pronoun (me, te, le, nos, os, les): (A) + le/te/me + gusta salir. Often describes a person's habit or preference for going out (to parties, restaurants, walks). If talking about others, use 'les gusta salir' or 'a + name + le gusta salir'.
target_language_example: A María le gusta salir los fines de semana.
native_language_example: María likes to go out on weekends.

meaning: 'likes his/her/its' or 'you (formal) like(s) his/her/its' depending on context
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but a sequence: gusta (third-person singular of gustar) + su (possessive 'his/her/your(formal)/their'). Gustar is used with the thing that is liked as the subject: e.g. 'Le gusta su coche' means 'He/She/You(formal) likes his/her/your(formal) car.' The indirect object (me, te, le, nos, os, les) is often included or understood from context (Le gusta su...). Without an explicit indirect-object pronoun, su combined with context can be ambiguous. Pay attention to verb agreement: gusta (singular thing) vs. gustan (plural things).
target_language_example: A Marta le gusta su trabajo.
native_language_example: Marta likes her job.

meaning: I like to have / I enjoy having
additional_notes: Combination of the verb gustar (me gusta = I like) plus the infinitive tener (to have). Used to express that someone enjoys possessing or experiencing something. Structure: (me/te/le/nos/les) gusta tener + noun or clause. Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Me gusta tener tiempo libre los fines de semana.
native_language_example: I like to have free time on weekends.

meaning: likes everything / (I/you/he/she) likes everything
additional_notes: Literal combination of the verb gustar + todo. Gustar requires an indirect object (me, te, le, nos, os, les) to indicate who likes something. Without a pronoun, the phrase is incomplete. Depending on the pronoun it becomes: 'me gusta todo' (I like everything), 'te gusta todo' (you like everything), 'le gusta todo' (he/she/you formal likes everything), 'nos gusta todo', 'os gusta todo', 'les gusta todo'. Use 'gusta' because 'todo' is treated as a singular idea (everything).
target_language_example: Me gusta todo de este restaurante.
native_language_example: I like everything about this restaurant.

meaning: 'to like to drink' or 'to like to take (photos/drinks/etc.)' — combination of gustar + infinitive tomar expressing a habitual liking for doing something.
additional_notes: Used with gustar + an infinitive (tomar) to say you like doing an action. 'Tomar' can mean 'to drink' (tomar agua, tomar café), 'to take' (tomar fotografías, tomar el sol), or 'to have' (tomar sopa). The person who likes the action is marked with an indirect object pronoun (me, te, le, nos, os, les) and often with 'A' + noun/name for clarity (A mi hermano le gusta...).
target_language_example: A mí me gusta tomar té por la tarde.
native_language_example: I like to drink tea in the afternoon.

meaning: Not a grammatical Spanish phrase; appears to be an incorrect word order for 'te gusta' (you like).
additional_notes: This sequence is not a correct fixed phrase in Spanish. The standard forms are 'te gusta' (informal singular you) or 'le gusta' (formal/third person). 'gusta tu' may result from literal word-order transfer from English ('you like') or learner error; native speakers would find it ungrammatical. Use '¿Te gusta...?' to ask 'Do you like...?' and 'Me gusta...' to say 'I like...'.
target_language_example: *This is ungrammatical Spanish:* "A mí no me gusta tu, gusta tu" — incorrect usage illustrating the misplaced pronoun.
native_language_example: *This is ungrammatical Spanish translated literally:* "To me not me it pleases you, pleases you" — shows why 'gusta tu' is incorrect.

meaning: 'likes a' or 'is pleasing a' (used before a masculine singular noun or with a masculine singular indefinite article)
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but the verb gustar ('to like' / 'to be pleasing') followed by the indefinite article 'un' + a masculine singular noun (or occasionally by a singular masculine quantity). In Spanish, gustar is usually used with an indirect object pronoun to indicate who likes something: (A mí) me gusta un libro = I like a book. Word order can vary: 'me gusta un libro' is common. Remember agreement: gusta (singular) with a singular noun, gustan (plural) with plural nouns.
target_language_example: A ella le gusta un café por la mañana.
native_language_example: She likes a coffee in the morning.

meaning: 'like to watch the' (used with feminine singular nouns, e.g., la tele = the TV/television).
additional_notes: This is part of the common structure 'me/te/le/nos/os/les gusta ver la ...' meaning 'I/you/he/she/we/they like to watch the ...'. 'Gusta' agrees with the thing liked (infinitive verb or singular noun), not the person. 'La' is the feminine singular definite article (the). Common phrase: 'ver la tele' = 'to watch TV'.
target_language_example: A ella le gusta ver la tele por la noche.
native_language_example: She likes to watch TV at night.

meaning: He likes (something) — but word order is nonstandard.
additional_notes: The sequence "gusta él" as written is grammatically unusual in Spanish. Standard phrasing places the indirect object before the verb: "a él le gusta" (literally: "to him it pleases") or uses the pronoun alone "le gusta". If you see "gusta él" it may appear in poetic, emphatic, or elliptical contexts, or as part of a larger clause (e.g., "¿Qué le gusta él?" is still nonstandard; prefer "¿Qué le gusta a él?"). Avoid using "gusta él" as a standalone affirmative sentence.
target_language_example: ¿A qué le gusta él? — (nonstandard order example showing the words together)
native_language_example: What does he like?

meaning: liked the (feminine singular noun) — past/simple imperfect: 'he/she/you (formal) used to like' or 'was liking'.
additional_notes: Combines the verb gustar in the imperfect (gustaba) with the feminine singular definite article la. Gustar is structured differently than English: the thing liked is the subject and the person who likes is an indirect object (me, te, le, nos, os, les). Example sentences often include the indirect-object pronoun or a clarifying phrase (a él, a ella). Use 'gustaba la' before a feminine singular noun (la comida, la escuela, la mostaza).
target_language_example: A Marta le gustaba la música clásica.
native_language_example: Marta liked classical music.

meaning: liked (it/them) more; preferred (something) more
additional_notes: Past imperfect of gustar + 'más' to compare preferences in the past. Use with indirect object pronouns (me, te, le, nos, os, les) to show who liked it. Often followed by the thing preferred (e.g., 'me gustaba más el otro') or by a clause introduced with 'que' (e.g., 'me gustaba más X que Y').
target_language_example: Cuando era niño, me gustaba más ir a la playa que a la montaña.
native_language_example: When I was a child, I liked going to the beach more than the mountains.

meaning: liked that (someone/something did or was something) — expresses a past liking about a situation or person, often followed by the imperfect or past subjunctive.
additional_notes: Used to say you liked something in the past. When the subject of the main clause is different from the subordinate clause, Spanish often uses the imperfect subjunctive (e.g., 'tuviera', 'fuera'). If the situation is factual or habitual with the same subject, Spanish may use 'me gustaba + infinitive' instead. Common in storytelling or describing past feelings.
target_language_example: Me gustaba que vinieras a visitarme los veranos.
native_language_example: I liked that you used to come visit me in the summers.

meaning: 'he/she/they liked the' (plural objects); past imperfect of gustar with plural noun.
additional_notes: Gustar is used differently than English 'to like'. The subject in Spanish is the thing liked (plural here), and the indirect object (me/te/le/nos/os/les) indicates who likes it. 'Gustaban' is the imperfect past tense for repeated or ongoing past actions; 'los' agrees with a masculine plural noun that follows (e.g., 'los niños', 'los trenes'). In English you usually translate with 'liked' + the person who liked them: 'He liked the trains.'
target_language_example: A Marta le gustaban los gatos cuando era niña.
native_language_example: Marta liked cats when she was a child.

meaning: 'I like the ... more' (used to compare and say you prefer one plural noun over another).
additional_notes: This is part of the comparative structure Me gustan más las X que Y. Me gustan is used for plural subjects (I like [them]). 'Más' means more (prefer). Use 'que' to introduce the thing being compared. Adjust articles (las/los) to match the gender and number of the noun: Me gustan más los libros que las películas.
target_language_example: Me gustan más las playas que las montañas.
native_language_example: I like beaches more than mountains.

meaning: 'would like to eat' (polite conditional of 'gustar' + infinitive).
additional_notes: Used to express a polite desire to eat something. Structure: (Me/Te/Le/Nos/Os/Les) gustaría comer + (food or clause). The indirect object pronoun indicates who would like to eat. Common in requests or when expressing preferences politely.
target_language_example: Me gustaría comer paella mañana.
native_language_example: I would like to eat paella tomorrow.

meaning: would like to speak (would like to talk).
additional_notes: Gustaría is the conditional form of gustar meaning 'would please' — used to express wishes politely. With hablar it means 'would like to speak' (e.g., with someone or about something). Commonly followed by con + person or de/sobre + topic: Me gustaría hablar con usted / Me gustaría hablar sobre el proyecto. Use for polite requests or offers.
target_language_example: Me gustaría hablar con usted mañana.
native_language_example: I would like to speak with you tomorrow.

meaning: would really like
additional_notes: Polite conditional form of gustar used to express a strong desire or preference. Common with infinitives (me gustaría mucho ir) or with que + subjunctive (me gustaría mucho que ...). Subject pronoun (me/te/le/nos/les) indicates who wants. 'Mucho' intensifies the desire.
target_language_example: Me gustaría mucho visitar España el próximo año.
native_language_example: I would really like to visit Spain next year.

meaning: 'I would like to be able to' or 'I wish I could'.
additional_notes: Combination of the conditional verb gustar (me gustaría = I would like) + poder (to be able to). Used to express a wish or desire to do something that is not currently possible or is hypothetical. Commonly followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., poder + hablar, ir, dar). Polite and slightly tentative.
target_language_example: Me gustaría poder viajar por el mundo algún día.
native_language_example: I would like to be able to travel the world someday.

meaning: 'I would like (someone) to ... (do something for me)'.
additional_notes: Used to express a polite wish or desire that someone else do something for the speaker. Follows a verb in the past subjunctive (hablaras, hicieras, llevaras) because it's a wish about another person's action. Often shortened in conversation to 'me gustaría que...' or replaced by 'quisiera que...'.
target_language_example: Me gustaría que me ayudaras con la mudanza.
native_language_example: I would like you to help me with the move.

meaning: 'I/he/she/it would like to be a' (conditional + infinitive phrase to express desire to become or be something)
additional_notes: Gustaría is the conditional form of gustar and is often used impersonally (me gustaría = I would like). When followed by ser un + noun it expresses desire to be something (a profession, role, type of person). Remember to include the indirect object pronoun (me, te, le, nos, os, les) before gustaría to show who wants it: Me gustaría ser un profesor. Also adjust article/gender/number after ser as needed: ser una, ser unos, ser unas.
target_language_example: Me gustaría ser un médico cuando sea mayor.
native_language_example: I would like to be a doctor when I'm older.

meaning: 'would like to have' or 'would like to get'.
additional_notes: Polite conditional form used to express a wish or desire to possess or experience something. Often appears with 'me/te/le/nos/os/les' (me gustaría tener = I would like to have). Can refer to concrete things (un jardín) or abstract/state changes (el pelo así, compañía).
target_language_example: Me gustaría tener más tiempo para viajar.
native_language_example: I would like to have more time to travel.

meaning: 'I would like to see you' or 'I'd like to see you (do something)'.
additional_notes: Polite conditional form using gustar: Me gustaría = 'I would like'. Ver(te) = 'to see you'. Can express wanting to meet someone (see them in person) or wanting to see them do/feel something (e.g., verte feliz = see you happy). Use with infinitive or place/time: Me gustaría verte mañana / Me gustaría verte intentarlo. Common in polite requests or wishes.
target_language_example: Me gustaría verte mañana en la cafetería.
native_language_example: I would like to see you tomorrow at the café.

meaning: 'I would like to ... again' (polite desire to do something another time).
additional_notes: Combines conditional of gustar (me gustaría = I would like) + volver a (to do again). Use when expressing a polite wish to return somewhere or repeat an action. Followed by a verb in infinitive (volver a + infinitive) or by a noun/pronoun indicating place or person (volver a casa, volver a verla).
target_language_example: Me gustaría volver a visitar España el próximo año.
native_language_example: I would like to visit Spain again next year.

meaning: you are liked by (someone); someone likes you.
additional_notes: Used to say that a person (or animal) likes someone. Structure: 'gustas a + [person]' where 'gustas' agrees with the person being liked (tú form). Often includes an indirect object pronoun (le, me, nos) for emphasis: 'Le gustas a Tom' = 'Tom likes you.' Negative: 'No le gustas a nadie' = 'Nobody likes you.'
target_language_example: Creo que le gustas a María.
native_language_example: I think María likes you.

meaning: colloquial filler meaning 'whatever you like' or 'as you prefer' (used to indicate choice or deference).
additional_notes: This looks like a combination of the verb gustar (to like) and the pronoun 'o' (or), but in practice 'guste o' is an informal, regional filler used when offering options or deferring to someone else's preference (similar to 'como quieras' or 'tú decides'). It may appear in spoken or casual written Spanish. Not standard in formal contexts.
target_language_example: Si prefieres pizza o pasta, elige tú, guste o.
native_language_example: If you prefer pizza or pasta, you choose—whatever you like.

meaning: 'nice to' / 'pleasure to' (used to express pleasure in meeting, seeing, or hearing someone)
additional_notes: Used before verbs in infinitive to say it's a pleasure to do something (e.g., gusto de conocerte = 'nice to meet you'). This construction is slightly formal or literary in some regions; more common alternatives in everyday speech are 'me da gusto' or simply 'mucho gusto' for introductions. When addressing people, pronouns may attach (conocerte, verte, verlos).
target_language_example: Gusto de conocerte.
native_language_example: Nice to meet you.

meaning: to taste of / to have the flavor of; also to please (someone) when used as 'dar gusto a' or 'darle gusto a'.
additional_notes: Used two ways: 1) To describe flavor: 'tener gusto a' = 'to taste like' (e.g., 'tastes of lemon'). 2) As an idiom with 'dar/ darle gusto a' = 'to please someone' or 'to do something to make someone happy' (not about taste). Word order: 'gusto a + food/ingredient' for flavor; 'dar/levar gusto a + person' for pleasing someone. Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Preparó la sopa y tiene gusto a ajo, pero lo hice para darle gusto a mi padre.
native_language_example: She made the soup and it tastes of garlic, but I did it to please my father.

meaning: used to say 'nice to' as in 'nice to meet/see' someone (formal/business phrasing).
additional_notes: Often appears in set phrases like "gusto en conocerla" or "gusto en verte" meaning 'nice to meet you' or 'nice to see you.' This construction is somewhat formal or old-fashioned; more common everyday alternatives are "mucho gusto" (Nice to meet you) or "me da gusto" / "qué gusto verte" (I'm glad to see you). Pronouns or names follow the verb (conocerla, verte, verlos).
target_language_example: Gusto en conocerte.
native_language_example: Nice to meet you.

meaning: expresses liking or pleasure that something happens (used in expressions like 'dar gusto que' or in constructions referring to pleasure about a situation): roughly 'it is pleasing that...' or 'I/it gives pleasure that...'.
additional_notes: Often appears in impersonal or reflexive-like constructions such as 'me da gusto que...' meaning 'it pleases me that...'. When used alone, 'gusto que' is not a complete grammatical unit; it's usually part of a larger phrase (e.g., 'me da gusto que...'). The subordinate clause following 'que' typically uses the indicative or subjunctive depending on certainty or control over the action. For expressing general likes, use 'me gusta' + infinitive or noun.
target_language_example: Me da gusto que te acuerdes de mí.
native_language_example: It pleases me that you remember me.

meaning: I/We/You feel like coming back; (to) want to return — expresses pleasure or desire to return.
additional_notes: Contains the noun 'gusto' (pleasure/liking) + the verb 'volver' (to return). Used to say someone feels like returning somewhere or doing something again. The exact subject depends on context and verb forms around it (e.g., 'me da gusto volver', 'tengo gusto en volver' — the standalone phrase is informal and often appears inside a larger sentence). Not a fixed idiom; more natural to use with a subject pronoun and auxiliary verb.
target_language_example: Me da gusto volver a verlos después de tanto tiempo.
native_language_example: I'm glad to see you again after so long.

meaning: (colloquial) to feel pleased or inclined to do something again; expresses a desire or pleasure in returning to an action or situation.
additional_notes: This is not a standard fixed idiom in neutral Spanish; speakers more commonly use 'tener ganas de volver a...', 'me gusta volver a...' or 'me alegra volver a...'. 'Gusto volver a' may appear in informal speech or regional usages when combined with verbs (e.g., 'gusto volver a verte'), but such forms can sound nonstandard. Use 'volver a' before an infinitive to indicate repetition of the action.
target_language_example: Me dio gusto volver a verte ayer.
native_language_example: It pleased me to see you again yesterday.

meaning: pleasure to see (someone) again; it's nice to see you again.
additional_notes: Common phrase used when greeting someone you haven't seen in a while. Often appears as part of fixed expressions: 'Fue un gusto volver a verte' (It was a pleasure to see you again), 'Me da gusto volver a verte' (I'm glad to see you again), or the shorter exclamation '¡Qué gusto verte!' Verb tense can change (da/dio/fue) to match time reference. You can add 'te' or 'verte' after 'volver a' when addressing someone directly.
target_language_example: Me da mucho gusto volver a verte después de tanto tiempo.
native_language_example: I'm very glad to see you again after so long.

meaning: 'liked the' (simple past, third person).
additional_notes: Combination of the verb gustar in the preterite (gustó) + definite article + noun. Gustar is used with an indirect object (me, te, le, nos, os, les) to indicate who likes something. English uses a subject that performs the liking; Spanish uses the thing liked as the grammatical subject and the person as an indirect object: (A él) le gustó el libro = He liked the book. In your examples, 'gustó el' appears before the noun that was liked. For negative sentences use 'no' before the indirect object: No le gustó el café.
target_language_example: A Marta no le gustó el regalo.
native_language_example: Marta didn't like the gift.

meaning: 'liked what' or 'I/they liked what (someone) did/said/bought/etc.'
additional_notes: This phrase combines the verb gustar (in past simple: gustó) with a clause introduced by 'lo que' ('what/that which'). Use it to say someone liked something that someone else said, did, bought, etc. Subject (who liked) is expressed with indirect object pronouns or by context: 'Me gustó lo que...' = 'I liked what...'; 'Les gustó lo que...' = 'They/you (plural) liked what...'. The verb agrees with the thing liked (gustó for singular idea).
target_language_example: Nos gustó lo que preparaste para la cena.
native_language_example: We liked what you prepared for dinner.

meaning: has married / has gotten married (he/she/it has married).
additional_notes: From the verb casarse (to get married). 'Se ha casado' is the present perfect (he/she has gotten married). Often used with 'con' to indicate the spouse: 'se ha casado con...' For English learners, translate as 'has married' or 'has gotten married.'
target_language_example: Ella se ha casado con su novio de toda la vida.
native_language_example: She has married her longtime boyfriend.

meaning: has realized / has noticed
additional_notes: Part of the pronominal verb darse cuenta (de). Used with an indirect object pronoun (me, te, se, nos, os) + haber (ha, han, etc.) + dado cuenta (de + something optional). Commonly followed by 'de' + noun or clause: se ha dado cuenta de su error = he/she has noticed his error. In negative questions it expresses surprise that someone hasn't noticed.
target_language_example: Él no se ha dado cuenta de su error.
native_language_example: He hasn't realized his mistake.

meaning: 'a lot has happened' or 'much has happened'.
additional_notes: Common perfect tense phrase using haber + pasado. Often used to summarize events or changes that occurred over a period of time (e.g., in someone's life or since you last met). Can refer to positive or negative events depending on context. You can change the subject (e.g., 'ha pasado mucho' — impersonal/'it' or 'se ha pasado mucho tiempo' — different meaning) or adjust tense/person: 'he pasado mucho' (I have spent / I have been through a lot).
target_language_example: Desde la última vez que nos vimos, ha pasado mucho.
native_language_example: A lot has happened since the last time we saw each other.

meaning: 'so much time has passed' or 'it's been so long'.
additional_notes: Used to say that a long amount of time has gone by. Common in statements like "Ha pasado tanto tiempo" (It's been so long) or followed by a clause (e.g., "Ha pasado tanto tiempo desde..." = "It's been so long since..."). Can be used alone as an exclamation or addressed to someone ("James, ha pasado tanto").
target_language_example: Ha pasado tanto desde la última vez que nos vimos.
native_language_example: It's been so long since the last time we saw each other.

meaning: 'has behaved' (referring to someone's behavior)
additional_notes: From the verb portarse (to behave). 'Se ha portado' is the perfect tense (has behaved / has acted). Used to describe someone's conduct recently or up to now. Common in phrases like 'se ha portado muy bien' (has behaved very well) or 'se ha portado muy mal' (has behaved very badly). You can add a direct object or indirect object for whom: 'se ha portado bien con nosotros' (has behaved well toward us).
target_language_example: Se ha portado muy bien con los niños esta semana.
native_language_example: He behaved very well with the children this week.

meaning: 'has thrown' or (in slang) 'has farted'; also 'has jumped' or 'has thrown oneself' depending on context.
additional_notes: Literal meaning: compound of haber + tirar (past participle 'tirado') — 'has thrown' or 'has pulled'. In everyday Spanish, 'tirarse un pedo' = 'to fart' (colloquial). Without an object, 'se ha tirado' can mean 'he/she has jumped' or 'he/she has thrown himself/herself' (often used for jumping onto train tracks or into something). Pay attention to reflexive 'se' and context: with 'un pedo' it's farting; with 'a la vía' it's jumping onto the tracks. Informal/colloquial in many uses.
target_language_example: Se ha tirado a la piscina sin pensar.
native_language_example: He has jumped into the pool without thinking.

meaning: to exist something; to be something (impersonal construction meaning 'there is/are something')
additional_notes: This entry refers to the impersonal verb haber used with algo (something). In practice, the infinitive form 'haber algo' appears in grammatical explanations or dictionary entries to indicate existence; in everyday speech you will see conjugated forms like 'hay algo' (there is/are something) or 'hubo algo' (there was something). It is not used as a personal verb meaning 'to have' (use tener for that).
target_language_example: Es importante haber algo que explique la situación antes de decidir.
native_language_example: It is important to have something that explains the situation before deciding.

meaning: 'there must be' or 'there has to be' (followed by a feminine noun or idea).
additional_notes: Haber (in the impersonal sense) + que/verb expresses necessity or probability: 'Debe haber...' / 'Tiene que haber...' mean 'there must be' or 'there has to be'. Alguna is the feminine singular form of 'some/any' and agrees with a following feminine noun (alguna razón, alguna explicación, alguna forma, alguna ropa). Often used when guessing that something exists or must exist.
target_language_example: Tiene que haber alguna solución para este problema.
native_language_example: There has to be some solution to this problem.

meaning: to have to say; a nonstandard or dictionary-style shorthand for forms based on haber de decir, such as he de decir ('I must say')
additional_notes: By itself, haber decir is not a standard modern Spanish expression. The usual construction is haber de + infinitive, for example he de decir. It expresses obligation and can sound formal, literary, or rhetorical.
target_language_example: La secuencia «haber decir» no se usa normalmente sin la preposición «de».
native_language_example: The sequence 'haber decir' is not normally used without the preposition 'de'.

meaning: to have been waiting
additional_notes: Compound perfect progressive: haber (to have) + estado (past participle of estar) + esperando (gerund) expresses a continuous action of waiting that has occurred up to a reference point (in the past, present, or future, depending on the tense of haber). Appears with different conjugations of haber (he, había, habrá, etc.). Often used with time expressions (desde, por) or clauses indicating duration or completion.
target_language_example: Después de haber estado esperando tanto tiempo, decidimos irnos.
native_language_example: After having been waiting so long, we decided to leave.

meaning: to have been (perfect infinitive; used to talk about a past state or condition)
additional_notes: Haber estado is the compound infinitive formed with haber + past participle 'estado'. It frequently appears in perfect constructions (e.g., to express 'to have been' before another action, regret, or reported experience). In Spanish it can be used in subordinate clauses after verbs or modal expressions (deber, tener que, sentir, decir) and in reported statements. English translations vary: 'to have been', 'must have been', 'should have been', 'I'm sorry I wasn't/for not having been', depending on context.
target_language_example: Debes de haber estado muy cansado después del viaje.
native_language_example: You must have been very tired after the trip.

meaning: haber / estar
additional_notes: No es una expresión fija ni estándar en español. Normalmente aparece solo en contextos metalingüísticos o gramaticales, al mencionar juntos dos verbos. Más natural sería escribir «haber y estar» si se quiere nombrarlos como elementos de una lista. «Haber» se usa sobre todo como auxiliar y en «hay»; «estar» significa «to be» para ubicación, estado o condición.
target_language_example: La secuencia haber estar no es una expresión fija en español.
native_language_example: The sequence haber estar is not a fixed expression in Spanish.

meaning: to have done
additional_notes: This is the perfect infinitive: haber + the past participle hecho. It is used to talk about an action that was already completed before another action, feeling, or situation. It often appears after verbs like esperar, sentir, reconocer, and poder, or after prepositions such as sin.
target_language_example: Me alegro de haber hecho esa llamada.
native_language_example: I'm glad I made that call.

meaning: to have arrived
additional_notes: Perfect infinitive used to express a completed action (arrival) relative to another point in time or modal verbs (e.g., deber de, deberíamos, podría). Common after modal verbs or expressions of emotion/regret: 'por haber llegado tarde' = 'for having arrived late.'
target_language_example: Debe de haber llegado ya.
native_language_example: He/She must have arrived already.

meaning: to have reached / to have come to (a point, decision, number, place).
additional_notes: Commonly used with abstract or concrete endpoints: llegar a + noun/infinitive (e.g., llegar a un acuerdo, llegar a casa). In the perfect tense it appears as haber llegado a + [noun/infinitive] to indicate that the arrival/reaching has already occurred. Can mean 'to end up (doing something)' when followed by an infinitive.
target_language_example: Haber llegado a un acuerdo nos alivió a todos.
native_language_example: Having reached an agreement relieved all of us.

meaning: 'there must be another' / 'there may be another' (used to suggest an alternative exists)
additional_notes: Commonly appears in impersonal constructions with deber, poder, tener que + haber + otra + (forma/manera/opción) to express that an alternative, way, or option likely exists. The exact nuance depends on the modal verb: deber/hay que = should/must, poder = may/could, tener que = must/has to. Often followed by words like forma, manera, opción, solución.
target_language_example: Tiene que haber otra solución para este problema.
native_language_example: There has to be another solution to this problem.

meaning: to have heard
additional_notes: Compound form: haber + past participle (oído) is used to form the perfect infinitive meaning 'to have heard' (something). Common in reported memory or supposition (e.g., 'debes haber oído' = 'you must have heard'). Can appear after verbs like creer, recordar, lamentar, deber, fingir. Use context to choose between 'heard (a sound/story)' and 'heard about (someone/something)'.
target_language_example: Debes haber oído sobre la fiesta de anoche.
native_language_example: You must have heard about last night's party.

meaning: to have been due to / to have been caused by (used in passive or explanatory contexts).
additional_notes: This phrase combines the perfect infinitive verb form (haber sido = to have been) with por to indicate cause, agent, or reason. It's often found in longer sentences or subordinate clauses explaining why something happened: e.g. 'haber sido por' + noun or phrase. More common alternatives include 'haber sido causado por' or using passive constructions like 'fue por' for simpler statements.
target_language_example: El retraso pudo haber sido por la lluvia.
native_language_example: The delay could have been because of the rain.

meaning: there is a
additional_notes: Not usually a fixed phrase on its own. This is the infinitive haber used in the existential sense, often in larger structures like puede haber un... or va a haber un.... In this use, haber does not mean "to have"; it means "there is/are," and the exact English translation depends on the surrounding verb.
target_language_example: Puede haber un problema con el tren.
native_language_example: There may be a problem with the train.

meaning: not a fixed modern phrase; appears when haber precedes venir in perfect tenses or in periphrastic/older obligation forms (e.g., 'ha venido' = 'has come'; 'he de venir' ≈ 'I must come').
additional_notes: 'Haber venir' is not a common standalone expression. You will most often encounter 'haber' + past participle (ha venido) for perfect tenses, or older/ formal obligation constructions where haber combines with de plus an infinitive (he de venir). For expressing obligation in everyday speech, native speakers prefer 'tener que venir' or 'debo venir'. Pay attention to context to determine whether it's a perfect tense, a regional/archaic obligation, or a miswriting.
target_language_example: He venido porque debía haber venido a la reunión.
native_language_example: I came because I had to come to the meeting.

meaning: to have seen
additional_notes: Perfect infinitive of ver. It is used after another verb to talk about a seeing action that happened earlier: debes haber visto = you must have seen, recuerdo haber visto = I remember having seen. With no, it means not to have seen.
target_language_example: Creo haber visto esa película antes.
native_language_example: I think I've seen that movie before.

meaning: to have seen (her/it/the) — part of a perfect infinitive construction used to say someone should/must have seen something.
additional_notes: This phrase combines the perfect infinitive haber visto + the feminine direct object article la (the). Often used after modal verbs (deberías, deberían, debiste, tendrías que) to express that someone should/ought to have seen something in the past (regret, recommendation, or assumption). The feminine article la can refer to a feminine noun mentioned or understood (la foto, la película, la exposición). You may also see haber visto lo (masc/neutral) or haber visto las/los for plural objects.
target_language_example: Deberías haber visto la obra de teatro; fue increíble.
native_language_example: You should have seen the play; it was amazing.

meaning: to have time (to do something).
additional_notes: Commonly appears impersonally as 'hay tiempo' (there is time), 'no hay tiempo' (there is no time), or in other tenses 'habrá tiempo' (there will be time), 'no hubo tiempo' (there was no time). Often followed by an infinitive: 'haber tiempo para + infinitive' or 'haber tiempo de + infinitive'. In everyday speech, 'tener tiempo' with a personal subject is also used ('tengo tiempo').
target_language_example: No va a haber tiempo para terminar si empezamos tarde.
native_language_example: There is not going to be time to finish if we start late.

meaning: to have written to you (literally: 'to have written you') — used to refer to having sent someone a message or letter in the past
additional_notes: This is the infinitive compound form with a reflexive/indirect-object pronoun (haberte = haber + te). Often appears after verbs or expressions (e.g., 'lamento no haberte escrito antes') or in perfect constructions (e.g., 'debería haberte escrito'). It implies a completed action of writing to 'you' (informal singular). Replace 'te' with other pronouns for different persons (habernos escrito, haberle escrito).
target_language_example: Siento no haberte escrito antes; estuve muy ocupado.
native_language_example: I'm sorry I hadn't written to you before; I was very busy.

meaning: room with his/her/your (possessive) — used when someone shares or enters a room together with someone or with their own belongings.
additional_notes: This phrase combines habitación (room) + con (with) + a possessive su (his/her/your formal/their). In examples it appears in two senses: (1) entering a room carrying one's possessions (e.g., 'entró en la habitación con su sombrero' = 'entered the room wearing/with his hat'), and (2) sharing a room with someone (often expressed as 'compartía su habitación con…' = 'shared his room with…'). su is ambiguous (his/her/your/their) — context or explicit subject clarifies meaning.
target_language_example: María comparte su habitación con su hermana menor.
native_language_example: María shares her room with her younger sister.

meaning: room of / ...'s room / room for (something).
additional_notes: This phrase is the start of a noun phrase: habitación means "room" and de shows possession, purpose, or contents. It is followed by a noun or name: e.g. habitación de invitados (guest room), habitación de María (María's room), habitación de juegos (playroom). Word order: "habitación de + [noun/name]".
target_language_example: La habitación de invitados está en el primer piso.
native_language_example: The guest room is on the first floor.

meaning: Not a grammatically correct Spanish phrase. It likely results from an incorrect combination of 'de' + 'al' (where 'al' = a + el). Possible intended forms are 'habitación del' (de + el), 'habitación de la', or 'habitación en el/la'.
additional_notes: 'De' (of/from) cannot be directly followed by the contraction 'al' (a + el). 'Habitation de al' is ungrammatical; correct alternatives: 'habitación del hotel' (room of the hotel), 'habitación de la casa' (room of the house), or 'habitación en el hotel' (room in the hotel). If 'al' begins a verb phrase (e.g., 'al abrir'), that is different and not used after 'habitación'. The target_language_example below purposely includes the exact ungrammatical string to show its incorrectness in context.
target_language_example: Intentamos usar la frase 'habitación de al' en la reserva, pero el recepcionista indicó que 'habitación de al' no es correcta.
native_language_example: We tried to use the phrase 'habitación de al' on the booking, but the receptionist said that 'habitación de al' is not correct.

meaning: the room next door; the adjoining/next room
additional_notes: Used to refer to a room adjacent to the one you are in or to indicate someone/something located in the neighboring room. Common in buildings, hotels, houses. Can be shortened in speech to "la de al lado" when context is clear (e.g., "Estoy en la de al lado").
target_language_example: Puedo oír a alguien en la habitación de al lado.
native_language_example: I can hear someone in the room next door.

meaning: 'room in' or 'room at' (used to say a room is located in/at a place)
additional_notes: Habitación means 'room'. When followed by en + place, it indicates where the room is located (e.g., habitación en el hotel = room in the hotel). Commonly used in contexts like booking or describing location. For beginner English speakers, use 'habitación' alone to mean 'room' and add en + [location] to specify where the room is.
target_language_example: Reservé una habitación en el hotel junto al mar.
native_language_example: I booked a room in the hotel by the sea.

meaning: 'habitación' = room; 'es' = is (third-person singular of ser).
additional_notes: This looks like two separate words: habitación (a noun meaning 'room' — a bedroom or any room in a building) and es (the verb 'to be' for él/ella/usted or used with nouns). On its own, 'habitación es' is not a complete natural phrase in Spanish; you would normally say 'La habitación es...' (The room is...) or 'Mi habitación es...' (My room is...). Use articles or possessives before habitación and complete the sentence with an adjective or clause after es.
target_language_example: La habitación es grande y luminosa.
native_language_example: The room is large and bright.

meaning: the room was...
additional_notes: Used to describe the state or condition of a room. 'Habitación' = room; 'estaba' is the imperfect of 'estar' (was/were) used for ongoing, background, or descriptive past situations. Common follow-ups: adjectives (oscura, silenciosa), prepositional phrases (llena de humo, con llave), or past participles (cubierta).
target_language_example: La habitación estaba húmeda después de la tormenta.
native_language_example: The room was damp after the storm.

meaning: the room is... (used to describe the state or location of a room)
additional_notes: Combines habitación (room) with the verb estar (to be) to say how a room is (clean, dark, free) or where it is (upstairs, at the end). Use estar for temporary states, conditions, locations. For possession use 'mi habitación está...' and for descriptions agree adjectives as usual (e.g., 'oscura', 'limpia', 'llena').
target_language_example: La habitación está cerca de la ventana.
native_language_example: The room is near the window.

meaning: Not a fixed Spanish phrase; literally the words 'habitación' (room) followed by 'no' (no/not). It can appear in sentences where word order places 'no' after 'habitación' for emphasis or in constructions with clauses, but beginners should prefer standard phrases like 'no hay habitación' or 'sin habitación'.
additional_notes: 'habitación no' by itself is uncommon and not a set expression. Spanish typically uses 'no' before the verb or clause (e.g., 'no hay habitación'). If you see 'habitación no' in natural text, it will usually be part of a larger phrase or clause (for example in poetry, advertising, or after a pause/emphasis). Use complete phrases to avoid misunderstanding.
target_language_example: La habitación no es adecuada para tres personas.
native_language_example: The room is not suitable for three people.

meaning: room for (someone or something); a room intended/allocated for a purpose or person.
additional_notes: Used to indicate who the room is for or its purpose. Can be followed by a person (habitación para dos/habitación para ella), an activity (habitación para estudiar), or a clause (habitación para que se quede). Often appears with verbs like preparar, necesitar, tener, or with numbers (para dos).
target_language_example: Preparé una habitación para mi hermana cuando nos visite.
native_language_example: I prepared a room for my sister when she visits us.

meaning: 'room for' or 'room per' used when specifying price, rate, or allocation (e.g., price per room or room for a person).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom by itself; 'habitación' (room) often appears with the preposition 'por' to indicate rates (habitación por noche = room per night), price (habitación por persona = room per person), or exchange (habitación por otra = room in exchange for another). You will usually see the complete phrase with the unit or noun after 'por'.
target_language_example: ¿Cuál es el precio de la habitación por noche?
native_language_example: What is the price of the room per night?

meaning: 'habitación' = room; 'se' = clitic pronoun/marker that is not part of the noun and usually belongs to the verb; 'habitación se' is not a standard fixed phrase on its own.
additional_notes: The correct noun is 'habitación' (a room). 'Se' can mark reflexive, impersonal or passive constructions and normally attaches to a verb, not the noun. If you encounter 'habitación se' it means the word 'se' belongs to the verb that follows or precedes in the sentence (e.g., 'La habitación se limpia' = 'The room is cleaned'; 'Se alquila habitación' = 'Room for rent'). Treat 'habitación' and 'se' separately and read the whole sentence to determine 'se''s function.
target_language_example: La habitación se limpia cada día.
native_language_example: The room is cleaned every day.

meaning: 'room and' — the word 'y' is the conjunction 'and'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase; it's simply the noun habitación (room) followed by the conjunction y (and). In the example sentences, 'y' sometimes begins a second clause ('habitación y no quiere irse' = 'in my room and she doesn't want to leave') or connects commands ('Ve a tu habitación y cierra la puerta' = 'Go to your room and close the door'). Don't treat 'habitación y' as a single unit — learn habitación (room) and y (and) separately.
target_language_example: Pon los juguetes en la habitación y limpia el suelo.
native_language_example: Put the toys in the room and clean the floor.

meaning: he/she/you (formal) speak(s) like; 'speaks like' (comparison using 'como').
additional_notes: Used to compare the way someone speaks to a person or type (e.g., 'habla como un policía' = 'he speaks like a policeman'). Subject can be él/ella/usted or implied; you can change verb form for other subjects (hablo como, hablas como, hablan como). Often followed by a noun or descriptive phrase. Tone can be neutral, complimentary, or critical depending on context.
target_language_example: Ella habla como una profesora paciente.
native_language_example: She speaks like a patient teacher.

meaning: he/she/you(formal) talk(s) about / speak(s) of
additional_notes: Present tense of hablar + preposition 'de'. Commonly used to introduce the topic someone is discussing. Context determines whether the subject is él, ella, or usted; it can also be used in informal reported speech (e.g., 'Habla del problema' — 'He/She talks about the problem'). For first/second/third person plurals or other forms, the verb changes (hablo, hablas, hablamos, hablan).
target_language_example: Ella habla del nuevo trabajo con entusiasmo.
native_language_example: She talks about the new job with enthusiasm.

meaning: he/she/you (formal) speaks English.
additional_notes: Habla is the third-person singular form of hablar (to speak) and can also be used for usted (formal you). Use with a subject (él, ella, usted) or alone to state someone speaks English. To say 'I speak English' use 'hablo inglés'; for 'we' use 'hablamos inglés'. Can be modified by adverbs (muy bien, excelentemente, muy alto).
target_language_example: Ella habla inglés muy bien.
native_language_example: She speaks English very well.

meaning: was speaking in/at the (feminine noun).
additional_notes: A past imperfect form (hablaba) + preposition and definite article used before a feminine noun: e.g., hablaba en la reunión (she/he/you-formal was speaking at the meeting) or hablaba en la radio (was speaking on the radio). Use 'hablaba' for ongoing or repeated past actions. If the noun is masculine, use 'hablaba en el'.
target_language_example: Ella hablaba en la reunión cuando llegaste.
native_language_example: She was speaking at the meeting when you arrived.

meaning: we speak in
additional_notes: Used to state the language or mode in which 'we' communicate. Commonly followed by a language or communication method (e.g., español, inglés, lenguaje de señas). The subject is nosotros/we (hablamos). Can be used in statements and choices (e.g., "O hablamos en X o no hablamos").
target_language_example: Hablamos en español durante las reuniones.
native_language_example: We speak in Spanish during the meetings.

meaning: native speaker (a person who learned a language as their first language).
additional_notes: Used to refer to someone whose first or primary language is the one being discussed. Commonly used when looking for tutors, conversation partners, or when describing language ability. Can refer to any language (e.g., 'hablante nativo de español'). Gender-neutral in form; you can also say 'hablante nativa' to emphasize a female speaker.
target_language_example: Busco un hablante nativo de francés para practicar conversación.
native_language_example: I'm looking for a native French speaker to practice conversation.

meaning: to speak to (someone); to address (someone).
additional_notes: Used when indicating the person you are directing speech toward. Common with people or audiences: hablar a alguien / hablar a la audiencia. More frequent in everyday speech is hablar con (to talk with) when emphasizing a two-way conversation. Use hablar a when focusing on addressing or delivering a message to someone rather than conversing.
target_language_example: El profesor va a hablar a los padres sobre el rendimiento.
native_language_example: The teacher is going to speak to the parents about performance.

meaning: to speak to (someone) in a particular way or to address (someone) at/for a specific time or occasion.
additional_notes: Hablar a la is usually followed by a noun or phrase indicating manner, audience, time, or place (e.g., hablar a la gente, hablar a la hora señalada). In many contexts Spanish uses hablar con (speak with) or hablar a (speak to) depending on whether you mean 'with someone' (conversation) or 'to someone' (addressing). Make sure to include the rest of the phrase (la + noun) — 'a la' must agree with the feminine noun that follows (a el → al, a los/las).
target_language_example: El profesor va a hablar a la clase mañana.
native_language_example: The teacher is going to speak to the class tomorrow.

meaning: to speak to (someone); to address (someone) — followed by a person or audience.
additional_notes: Commonly appears as 'hablar a' + definite article or pronoun (e.g., 'hablar al' = 'hablar a el' contracted). Use 'hablar con' when emphasizing a two-way conversation, and 'hablar a'/'hablar al' when emphasizing addressing or speaking toward someone or an audience. 'Al' is the contraction of 'a' + 'el'.
target_language_example: El profesor va a hablar al grupo sobre el proyecto.
native_language_example: The teacher is going to speak to the group about the project.

meaning: talk to
additional_notes: Used when saying who you are talking to: hablar con alguien. In English this is often "talk to" or "speak with/to" depending on context.
target_language_example: Necesito hablar con mi profesora.
native_language_example: I need to talk to my teacher.

meaning: to speak with her / to talk to the (female) person or with the (female) organization.
additional_notes: This phrase is the verb hablar + preposition con + the feminine definite article la. It must be completed by a noun or pronoun (e.g., hablar con la profesora, hablar con la directora, hablar con la vecina) or replaced by a feminine pronoun (hablar con ella). Alone, 'hablar con la' is incomplete—Spanish typically includes the person/role after 'la'. Use 'hablar con el' for masculine, and 'hablar con ellos/ellas' for plural. If referring to 'her' as an object pronoun, prefer 'hablar con ella.'
target_language_example: Necesito hablar con la doctora mañana.
native_language_example: I need to speak with the (female) doctor tomorrow.

meaning: to talk to oneself (speak internally or aloud to oneself).
additional_notes: Used when someone speaks to themselves. Can mean thinking aloud or having an internal dialogue. Often appears reflexively with 'consigo' (with oneself). In many contexts 'hablar consigo mismo/a' is more common and explicitly shows gender; 'consigo' is a shorter alternative.
target_language_example: A veces me ves caminar y hablar consigo sin darme cuenta.
native_language_example: Sometimes you see me walking and talking to myself without realizing it.

meaning: to speak/talk when (used to introduce the time or circumstance in which someone speaks or stops speaking).
additional_notes: Comes from the verb hablar + the conjunction cuando ('when'). Used to say that speaking happens (or stops) at a certain moment or under certain conditions. Context determines tense and whether it means 'speak when' (habitual) or 'stop/start speaking when' (specific event). Common in phrases like 'deja de hablar cuando...' (stop talking when...) or 'apenas había terminado de hablar cuando...' (hardly had [someone] finished speaking when...).
target_language_example: Los niños dejan de hablar cuando suena la campana.
native_language_example: The children stop talking when the bell rings.

meaning: talk about
additional_notes: Used to introduce the topic of conversation. After hablar, Spanish normally uses de where English often uses about: hablar de un problema, hablar de música, hablar de alguien.
target_language_example: No me gusta hablar de política en la cena.
native_language_example: I don't like talking about politics at dinner.

meaning: to talk about the (feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun to indicate discussing a topic. 'Hablar de' means 'to talk about'; the article 'la' specifies a feminine noun (e.g., la película, la situación). If the noun is masculine use 'hablar del' (de + el). Can be followed by names, ideas, events, etc.
target_language_example: Vamos a hablar de la película esta noche.
native_language_example: We're going to talk about the movie tonight.

meaning: to talk about (something) — used before a neuter or abstract clause (lo + adjective/verb/idea).
additional_notes: Hablar de lo + [adjective/verb/clause] introduces a general idea or abstract topic: e.g. hablar de lo importante (to talk about what is important) or hablar de lo que pasó (to talk about what happened). Often appears as 'hablar de lo que...' or 'hablar de lo + adjective'. The neutral 'lo' doesn't refer to a specific noun but to a concept or clause.
target_language_example: Tenemos que hablar de lo que ocurrió ayer.
native_language_example: We need to talk about what happened yesterday.

meaning: This is not a complete standard phrase by itself; it's the verb hablar ('to speak') followed by the definite article el ('the') and needs more words to form a full expression (e.g., hablar el idioma, hablar el mismo idioma).
additional_notes: You will not usually see 'hablar el' alone in Spanish. It appears when hablar is followed directly by a noun with the article el. Common completions: 'hablar el idioma' (to speak the language), 'hablar el mismo idioma' (to speak the same language), or in colloquial speech 'hablar el uno del otro' is incorrect—use 'hablar el uno con el otro' or better 'hablar entre sí'. When saying what language someone speaks, use 'hablar' + language without article (e.g., 'habla español') or with article in some contexts ('habla el francés' is less common than 'habla francés').
target_language_example: Ella sabe hablar el idioma correctamente.
native_language_example: She knows how to speak the language correctly.

meaning: literally 'to speak is' — usually the start of a sentence meaning 'to speak is...' or 'speaking is...'; incomplete on its own and requires continuation.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase; it's the verb hablar ('to speak') followed by the verb 'es' (from ser) forming the beginning of a clause such as 'hablar es fácil' (speaking is easy) or 'hablar es gratis' (talk is cheap/literally 'speaking is free'). By itself it is unfinished — you need an adjective, noun phrase, or clause after it. Use it when making general statements about the act of speaking.
target_language_example: Hablar es fácil, pero escuchar es difícil.
native_language_example: Speaking is easy, but listening is difficult.

meaning: to speak Spanish (ability to use the Spanish language).
additional_notes: Common phrase to say you know or can use Spanish. Often appears with verbs like 'saber' (sé/sabes/sabe) or 'poder' (puedo) and with subjects (yo, tú, él). You can also swap word order to 'hablar en español' when referring to speaking in Spanish (e.g., 'Habla en español, por favor').
target_language_example: ¿Puedes hablar español conmigo?
native_language_example: Can you speak Spanish with me?

meaning: to speak French so (much/well/fluently) — used to introduce a degree or comparison about speaking French
additional_notes: This is not a complete fixed phrase by itself. 'Hablar francés tan...' is typically followed by an adjective or adverb (e.g., 'tan bien', 'tan poco', 'tan fluido') or by a clause for comparison (e.g., 'tan bien como...'). Use it to express degree: how well or how much someone speaks French. It appears in infinitive or conjugated forms (e.g., 'habla francés tan...','hablé francés tan...').
target_language_example: Quiero hablar francés tan bien como mi hermana.
native_language_example: I want to speak French as well as my sister.

meaning: to speak French so well / to speak French as well (as someone).
additional_notes: Used to compare degree of skill in speaking French. Often appears with comparisons using 'como' (como Tom, como tú) or modal verbs expressing wish/hypothesis (desearía, ojalá, supiera). 'Tan... como' means 'as... as' (equal degree). Replace 'francés' with another language to change meaning.
target_language_example: Me gustaría hablar francés tan bien como tú.
native_language_example: I would like to speak French as well as you do.

meaning: to speak English
additional_notes: A simple verb + language phrase used to say someone has the ability to speak the English language or to request/require speaking English. Can be used in statements, commands, or descriptions of ability. For beginners: conjugate the verb hablar as needed (hablo, hablas, habla, hablamos, hablan).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes hablar inglés conmigo?
native_language_example: Can you speak English with me?

meaning: to be spoken about a lot / to talk a lot
additional_notes: Context determines meaning. With verbs like 'oír' (he oído hablar mucho de...), it means 'to hear a lot about someone/something' (they are much talked about). When used reflexively or intransitively about a person (e.g. 'yo nunca pude hablar mucho de una carrera'), it can mean 'to talk much' or 'to say much'—i.e., to speak at length or have much to say. Commonly followed by prepositions like 'de' or 'sobre' when indicating the topic.
target_language_example: He oído hablar mucho de tu restaurante.
native_language_example: I've heard a lot about your restaurant.

meaning: 'to speak for' or 'to speak on behalf of'.
additional_notes: Used when someone speaks in place of another person or represents others' opinions. Common constructions: hablar por + alguien (Habla por mí) or hablar por + sí mismo/ella/ellos (No hablo por todos). Can also be followed by una cosa to mean 'to argue/express for' (hablar por la situación), but primary use is 'speak on behalf of'.
target_language_example: No puedes hablar por todo el grupo; cada uno tiene su opinión.
native_language_example: You can't speak for the whole group; everyone has their own opinion.

meaning: 'to speak for a short time' or 'to have a quick word' (used before a noun like 'momento' or 'segundo').
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself—'hablar un' appears when followed by a time expression or noun (e.g., 'hablar un momento', 'hablar un segundo') to mean 'talk for a moment' or 'have a quick word'. Common in casual and polite requests: '¿Puedo hablar un momento?' or 'Necesito hablar un segundo contigo.'
target_language_example: ¿Podemos hablar un momento?
native_language_example: Can we talk for a moment?

meaning: literally 'to speak and' — not a fixed phrase; appears when 'hablar' is followed by another verb or clause introduced by 'y' (and).
additional_notes: This is not an idiomatic multiword expression by itself. You will see 'hablar y ...' when someone lists actions or connects clauses: e.g. hablar y escuchar (to speak and listen), hablar y decir (to speak and say). Make sure the structure after 'y' fits grammatically (usually another verb in the infinitive or a new clause).
target_language_example: Nos gusta hablar y compartir ideas después de la clase.
native_language_example: We like to talk and share ideas after class.

meaning: 'you speak English' (informal, singular 'you').
additional_notes: Second-person singular (tú) present tense of hablar + 'inglés'. Used to ask or state that someone speaks English. Can appear in questions, compliments, or conditional statements (Si hablas inglés...). For formal singular use, say 'habla inglés' (usted).
target_language_example: ¿Hablas inglés con tus compañeros de clase?
native_language_example: Do you speak English with your classmates?

meaning: I speak on behalf of / I speak from (a perspective or cause) / I speak by (means, e.g., telephone).
additional_notes: Hablar por + noun can mean different things depending on context: 'hablo por experiencia' = 'I speak from experience' (giving a source or reason); 'hablo por mi pueblo' = 'I speak on behalf of my town/people' (representing others); 'hablo por teléfono' = 'I speak by phone' (indicating the means). Use context to decide whether it indicates source, representation, or manner.
target_language_example: Hablo por mi familia cuando digo que apoyamos la propuesta.
native_language_example: I speak on behalf of my family when I say we support the proposal.

meaning: 'spoke to' or 'talked to' (past tense, third person singular).
additional_notes: Used to say who someone spoke to (often with indirect object pronoun le/les or a + name). In Spanish you can use 'le habló a [persona]' or 'habló con [persona]' — both mean 'spoke to', but 'habló a' emphasizes direction toward the person. Common in past narratives. The verb hablar is regular; adjust tense/subject as needed (hablo, hablas, habló, hablamos...).
target_language_example: Ella le habló a su jefe sobre el problema.
native_language_example: She spoke to her boss about the problem.

meaning: 'I had thought about' (past perfect of 'pensar en').
additional_notes: Used to say that someone had already (or had not) considered something before a past reference point. 'Había' is the imperfect tense of 'haber' + past participle 'pensado'. Common in sentences like 'No había pensado en eso' (I hadn't thought about that) or 'Ya había pensado en eso' (I had already thought about that).
target_language_example: Antes de la reunión, ya había pensado en varias soluciones.
native_language_example: Before the meeting, I had already thought about several solutions.

meaning: had been a
additional_notes: This is the imperfect past perfect (pluperfect) passive/neutral construction: había (pluperfect auxiliary) + sido (past participle of ser) + an indefinite article + noun. Use it to say that something in the past 'had been a/an' (e.g., a dream, an accident, a success). Often used to report or reflect on a prior event that occurred before another past moment. Can appear in both neutral descriptions and passive statements (e.g., 'había sido un éxito' — 'it had been a success').
target_language_example: Al principio pensé que había sido un error, pero luego todo quedó claro.
native_language_example: At first I thought it had been a mistake, but then everything became clear.

meaning: there was no way to / it was impossible to
additional_notes: Used to say something could not be done or was impossible. Often appears as 'No había forma de...' + infinitive or 'No había forma de que...' + subjunctive when followed by a clause with change of subject. Emphasizes impossibility or lack of any method/possibility.
target_language_example: No había forma de convencerla de quedarse.
native_language_example: There was no way to convince her to stay.

meaning: there was more
additional_notes: Imperfect form of haber (había) used to state existence or quantity in the past. Often followed by 'de' + a number/amount to mean 'more than' (había más de veinte = there were more than twenty). Can be used in negative sentences with 'no' to mean 'there wasn't/weren't more than' (No había más de cinco = there were no more than five). Use 'había' for both singular and plural English 'there was/were'.
target_language_example: En la plaza había más de cien personas.
native_language_example: There were more than a hundred people in the square.

meaning: there was no one / there wasn't anyone
additional_notes: Commonly used with negation to say that nobody was present. In standard Spanish, the negative is usually formed as 'no había nadie' (with 'no' before the verb). Alone, 'había nadie' without 'no' is ungrammatical in most contexts — learners should use 'no había nadie' to mean 'there wasn't anyone.'
target_language_example: Cuando llegamos al parque, no había nadie.
native_language_example: When we arrived at the park, there wasn't anyone.

meaning: 'there was no one in/on the...' (used to say nobody was in a place)
additional_notes: This phrase combines the imperfect form 'había' (there was/there were) with 'nadie' (no one). In natural Spanish it's more common to say 'no había nadie en el...' (placing 'no' before 'había'), as shown in the examples. Use it to describe that a place was empty in the past. Follow with a noun or location (el auto, el jardín, el parque, etc.).
target_language_example: No había nadie en el pasillo cuando llegué.
native_language_example: There was no one in the hallway when I arrived.

meaning: 'there was/there were not even' — used to emphasize that something was completely lacking
additional_notes: Common structure: 'No había ni + X' or 'No había ni + X + ni + Y' to mean 'there wasn't even X' or 'there wasn't X or Y'. Often used for emphasis/contrast (e.g., 'no había ni dios' = 'there was nobody at all'). Works with singular/plural and with indefinite words (un/una/una sola).
target_language_example: En la playa no había ni un alma.
native_language_example: On the beach there wasn't a soul.

meaning: 'there was/there were none' or 'there wasn't/weren't any' (negative existence).
additional_notes: Used with 'no' before it: 'no había ninguna' to say that something did not exist or was not present. 'Ninguna' agrees in gender (ninguno/ninguna) and number is usually singular after 'ninguno/a' though context can imply plural meaning. Common with nouns: persona, nube, pista. Formal/neutral register.
target_language_example: No había ninguna tienda abierta en el barrio.
native_language_example: There were no shops open in the neighborhood.

meaning: 'there was no' or 'there were no' (negative existence)
additional_notes: This is the imperfect form of haber (había) used to say that something did not exist or was not available in the past. In standard Spanish negative constructions normally require 'no' before the verb + 'ningún' (masculine singular) before a noun: 'No había ningún...' For feminine nouns use 'ninguna' (No había ninguna...). Use 'ningunos/ningunas' rarely; usually keep singular.
target_language_example: No había ningún restaurante abierto a medianoche.
native_language_example: There was no restaurant open at midnight.

meaning: Once upon a time (storytelling opening).
additional_notes: A set phrase used to begin fairy tales or stories in the past tense. It sets a timeless, narrative scene and is followed by characters or events. Use it to start a traditional story; it's not used for ordinary past statements.
target_language_example: Había una vez un pueblo junto al mar.
native_language_example: Once upon a time there was a village by the sea.

meaning: you had gone to (or you had been going to) — past perfect tense used to say someone had already gone somewhere or had intended to go before another past action.
additional_notes: Habías ido is the second-person singular (tú) pluperfect (past perfect) of ir. Often followed by a preposition + place (a casa, a la tienda) to mean 'you had gone to [somewhere]'. It can also appear before an infinitive (habías ido a...) to express a past intention or action that was about to happen (less common than other constructions). Use when referring to one past event that happened before another past event.
target_language_example: Cuando llegué, habías ido a la oficina y ya te habías ido.
native_language_example: When I arrived, you had gone to the office and had already left.

meaning: does something
additional_notes: Literal: third-person singular of hacer + algo. Used to say someone 'does something' or to ask/deny that someone 'does anything' depending on context. In questions or negatives, 'algo' can mean 'anything' (¿Hace algo? = Is he/she/it doing anything?). Can refer to general actions, events, or tasks. Replace 'hace' for other subjects as needed (hago algo, haces algo, hacen algo).
target_language_example: Él hace algo en el taller cada mañana.
native_language_example: He does something in the workshop every morning.

meaning: years ago / for years (depending on context).
additional_notes: Used in two main ways: 1) to say something happened 'years ago' (point in the past): "Lo hice hace años" = I did it years ago. 2) with "hacer + time + que" to express a continuing situation: "Hace años que no..." = "I haven't ... for years" or "Hace años que espero" = "I've been waiting for years." Context tells which meaning applies.
target_language_example: Hace años que no voy a esa ciudad.
native_language_example: I haven't been to that city for years.

meaning: a fairly long time ago / for quite a while (ago/now).
additional_notes: Used with time expressions to say something happened a long time ago or has been happening/continuing for a long time. Often appears as 'hace bastante tiempo' + (que) + present (to mean 'has been ... for quite a while') or without 'tiempo' to mean 'quite a while ago.' Context determines whether it's past (ago) or present perfect/ongoing (for quite a while).
target_language_example: Hace bastante tiempo que no voy al cine.
native_language_example: I haven't gone to the movies in quite a while.

meaning: does things / makes things (general, vague)
