meaning: literally 'man to' — not a standard fixed phrase in Spanish; likely the start of a phrase (e.g., 'hombre a cargo') or a transcription error.
additional_notes: Alone, 'hombre a' is incomplete and not used by itself. 'Hombre' means 'man' and is common; the following preposition or adjective is needed to complete the idea (examples: 'hombre a cargo' = 'man in charge', 'hombre a bordo' = 'man on board'). If you encountered 'hombre a' in text, check the rest of the phrase. If it was spoken, it might be a pause before adding more words or part of an interjection ('¡Hombre!') followed by a clause.
target_language_example: Es un hombre a cargo del proyecto.
native_language_example: He is the man in charge of the project.

meaning: one-on-one; man-to-man (direct, face-to-face confrontation or comparison)
additional_notes: Used to describe direct competition, confrontation or comparison between two people (often in sports or debates). Can imply an honest, straightforward encounter. Gendered literal wording — context may use 'uno a uno' or 'cara a cara' for neutral alternatives.
target_language_example: En el partido fue hombre a hombre y ganó por habilidad.
native_language_example: In the match it was one-on-one and he won by skill.

meaning: Not a standard Spanish phrase — likely a fragment (e.g., 'hombre al...' as part of a longer phrase meaning 'man at/on/to...').
additional_notes: This combination by itself is not a fixed expression in Spanish. It looks like the noun 'hombre' (man) followed by the contraction 'al' (a + el = to the / at the). You will typically see it as part of a larger phrase such as 'hombre al que...' (the man to whom/that), 'hombre al mando' (man in charge — note 'al mando' attaches to a noun), or 'hombre al frente' (man at the front). If you encounter 'hombre al' alone in a sentence, read the rest of the sentence to understand the full meaning.
target_language_example: El hombre al que vi estaba leyendo un libro.
native_language_example: The man whom I saw was reading a book.

meaning: a good man; a kind, moral, or decent man.
additional_notes: Used to describe a man who is morally good, kind, honest, or decent. Context can mean morally upright, compassionate, or simply a nice person. Common in both formal and informal contexts; can be used respectfully (usted) or familiarly (tú). Word order is normal adjective after noun in Spanish.
target_language_example: Mi vecino es un hombre bueno: siempre ayuda a los demás.
native_language_example: My neighbor is a good man: he always helps others.

meaning: literally 'man like' — used to compare someone to a typical man or to introduce an example (informal; often part of a larger phrase).
additional_notes: By itself 'hombre como' is incomplete and uncommon as a fixed phrase; you usually need more context, e.g. 'un hombre como él' (a man like him) or 'hombre, como...' (colloquial interjection similar to 'man, like...'). When used as 'hombre,' alone it can be an informal exclamation (like 'come on' or 'hey'), and 'como' can introduce comparisons or examples. Pay attention to word order and context.
target_language_example: Un hombre como él no se rinde fácilmente.
native_language_example: A man like him doesn't give up easily.

meaning: man with (used to describe a man who has or is accompanied by something/someone).
additional_notes: A simple combination of noun + preposition + determiner omitted; often followed by a noun or phrase (e.g., hombre con gafas = man with glasses; hombre con experiencia = man with experience). Can describe physical possession, characteristics, or accompaniment. Use context to complete the phrase (it is not a complete sentence by itself).
target_language_example: Vi a un hombre con un perro en el parque.
native_language_example: I saw a man with a dog in the park.

meaning: literally 'man with the' — not a fixed phrase; usually part of a larger expression (e.g., 'el hombre con el sombrero' = 'the man with the hat').
additional_notes: This is not a standalone idiom. It's the combination of 'hombre' (man) + preposition 'con' (with) + definite article 'el' (the). In Spanish, 'con el' agrees with masculine singular nouns that follow. Often appears before a noun: 'hombre con el perro' (man with the dog). Note: if the noun is omitted, the phrase is incomplete and sounds odd in isolation.
target_language_example: Vi al hombre con el paraguas en la esquina.
native_language_example: I saw the man with the umbrella on the corner.

meaning: 'man of the' (incomplete phrase used as part of a larger expression)
additional_notes: This is not a complete phrase on its own. 'Hombre de la' is the beginning of many expressions that describe a man associated with something (e.g., 'hombre de la casa' — man of the house; 'hombre de la ciudad' — man of the city). You will usually need a noun after 'la' to complete the idea. Gender and article must match the following noun (use 'del' when followed by 'el': 'hombre del país').
target_language_example: Él es el hombre de la familia que arregla todo.
native_language_example: He is the man of the family who fixes everything.

meaning: businessman; a man who works in business or commerce.
additional_notes: Used to describe a man involved in business, commerce, or entrepreneurship. Can imply experience, success, or professionalism depending on context. For a gender-neutral term use "persona de negocios" or "empresario/empresaria" (empresario is common for 'business owner' or 'entrepreneur').
target_language_example: Él es un hombre de negocios muy respetado en la ciudad.
native_language_example: He is a very respected businessman in the city.

meaning: short form of 'hombre de pocas palabras' — a man of few words; someone who speaks little.
additional_notes: This is an abbreviated phrase; the full expression is 'hombre de pocas palabras'. It describes a quiet, reserved man who doesn't talk much. Use to describe personality (neutral). If you want the feminine form, say 'mujer de pocas palabras'.
target_language_example: Es un hombre de pocas palabras, pero muy eficiente.
native_language_example: He is a man of few words, but very efficient.

meaning: a man should / men should (ought to).
additional_notes: Combines 'hombre' (man) with the conditional verb 'debería' (should/ought to). Depending on context, it can refer to a specific man ('ese hombre debería...') or to people in general using 'hombre' or 'ningún hombre' (no man). For general statements about people, Spanish often uses 'todo hombre' (every man) or 'ningún hombre' (no man). The gendered noun can be replaced with neutral/plural forms (la gente, nadie, la persona) if desired.
target_language_example: Ningún hombre debería sufrir tanta injusticia.
native_language_example: No man should suffer so much injustice.

meaning: literally 'man of' — the start of a phrase meaning 'the man from/of ...' or part of a longer expression.
additional_notes: This is not a complete phrase by itself. 'Hombre' means 'man' and 'del' is the contraction of 'de + el' meaning 'of the' or 'from the'. You'll usually see 'hombre del' followed by a noun (place, group, job, etc.): e.g. 'hombre del pueblo' (man of the town) or 'hombre del equipo' (man of the team). Word order and gender/number agreement matter (use 'de la', 'de los', 'de las' when needed).
target_language_example: Es el hombre del pueblo que organiza las fiestas.
native_language_example: He is the man of the town who organizes the festivals.

meaning: literally 'man in' — not a set phrase on its own; usually part of a larger phrase (e.g., 'hombre en...') meaning 'man in/at/on' followed by a place, situation or role.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed expression by itself. 'Hombre' means 'man' and 'en' is a preposition meaning 'in', 'on', or 'at'. Together they appear when describing a man located in or involved with something: for example, 'hombre en la puerta' = 'man at the door' or 'hombre en problemas' = 'man in trouble'. Word order and articles are important in Spanish (often 'el hombre en...' or 'un hombre en...').
target_language_example: Había un hombre en la esquina que esperaba el autobús.
native_language_example: There was a man on the corner who was waiting for the bus.

meaning: literally 'man in the' — not a fixed phrase by itself; it's a fragment used as part of a larger sentence (e.g., 'hombre en el coche' = 'man in the car').
additional_notes: This is not a standalone expression. 'Hombre' means 'man', 'en' means 'in/on/at' depending on context, and 'el' is the masculine singular definite article 'the'. You normally see this sequence followed by a noun (location or object). Remember that if the following noun is feminine you must use 'la' instead of 'el' (e.g., 'mujer en la casa').
target_language_example: Hay un hombre en el parque.
native_language_example: There is a man in the park.

meaning: literally 'man in the' — used as the start of phrases like 'a man at/in the [place]' or figuratively 'our man at/in [place]'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom by itself; it's the beginning of phrases such as 'hombre en la puerta' (a man at the door) or 'nuestro hombre en la embajada' (our man at the embassy). Can be literal (a man located somewhere) or figurative (a representative, contact, or important person in an organization or situation). Pay attention to the noun and article that follow (la/ el) and agreement/context.
target_language_example: Tenemos un hombre en la oficina que puede ayudar.
native_language_example: We have a man in the office who can help.

meaning: The sequence 'hombre es el' is not a standard, grammatically correct fixed phrase in Spanish; it reflects a mistaken word order. The normal order places the article before the noun ('el hombre es ...') or requires punctuation/context for inversion.
additional_notes: Likely a word-order error. To form a correct sentence meaning 'the man is ...' use 'El hombre es ...'. 'Hombre es el' could only appear in poetic, emphatic, or artificially inverted constructions with punctuation or additional context (e.g., 'Hombre — es el...'), but this is rare and not recommended for learners. Beginners should place the article ('el') before the noun ('hombre').
target_language_example: En el texto antiguo aparece: 'Hombre es el que sabe callar.'
native_language_example: In the old text it appears: 'Man is he who knows how to be silent.'

meaning: literally: "man is the only" — fragment meaning 'the man is the only one' or 'man is the only [one]'.
additional_notes: This appears to be a fragment rather than a complete set phrase. In Spanish you'd normally say «el hombre es el único» or «el hombre es el único que…» followed by more information (e.g. «el hombre es el único que puede…» = 'man is the only one who can…'). Context is needed to complete the idea. Use the article 'el' before 'hombre' for 'the man' or 'humankind' depending on context (for 'human' you'd usually say «el ser humano» or «el hombre» in older texts).
target_language_example: El hombre es el único que puede cambiar su destino.
native_language_example: Man is the only one who can change his destiny.

meaning: ‘man is the only animal’ — a fixed phrase used to make general statements about humans vs. animals.
additional_notes: Often followed by a verb or clause describing a uniquely human trait (e.g., capaz de..., que puede..., sujeto a...). Commonly used in generalizations or philosophical statements. 'Hombre' here means 'humankind' or 'man' in a general sense. Structure: 'El hombre es el único animal + [que/ capable de + infinitive]'.
target_language_example: El hombre es el único animal que puede crear herramientas complejas.
native_language_example: Man is the only animal that can create complex tools.

meaning: a segment meaning 'man is a' used to start descriptions about a man.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase; it's simply the sequence 'hombre es un' (man is a) used to describe or classify a man (e.g., 'El hombre es un lobo...' = 'Man is a wolf...'; 'Este hombre es un huésped' = 'This man is a guest'). For beginners: remember Spanish word order uses noun + verb + article + noun here. Choose the correct article (un/una/el/la) and adjective/agreement as needed.
target_language_example: Ese hombre es un buen amigo.
native_language_example: That man is a good friend.

meaning: ‘man/ humans are animals’ — a general statement that people are (by nature) animals with certain traits (social, rational, habitual, political).
additional_notes: Used to express a general, often philosophical observation about human nature. Context determines whether 'hombre' means 'man' (male) or 'humankind/people' (more general). Common continuations add adjectives: 'social', 'racional', 'de costumbres', or 'político'. Not an idiom—literal meaning applies.
target_language_example: El hombre es un animal social por naturaleza; necesita vivir en comunidad.
native_language_example: Man is a social animal by nature; he needs to live in community.

meaning: the man is / that man is (followed by a description or state).
additional_notes: Combines the noun 'hombre' (man) with the verb 'estar' (to be) to describe a temporary state, condition, location, or emotion. Use 'el hombre está' for 'the man is' and 'ese/este hombre está' for 'that/this man is'. Not used for permanent characteristics (use 'ser' instead). Word order can change: 'ese hombre está' or 'está ese hombre' (less common).
target_language_example: Ese hombre está cansado después del viaje.
native_language_example: That man is tired after the trip.

meaning: the man was
additional_notes: A short sequence combining the noun 'hombre' (man) and the past passive/preterite auxiliary 'fue' (from ser or ir). In these examples 'fue' is passive ('was') to form passive voice (e.g., 'was accused', 'was found'). Not a fixed idiom—it's simply 'the man was...' and will be followed by a past participle or past action. Subject–verb agreement: for plural use 'hombres fueron'.
target_language_example: El hombre fue herido en el accidente.
native_language_example: The man was injured in the accident.

meaning: Not a fixed phrase; likely two separate words: 'hombre' (man) + 'ha' (has, auxiliary).
additional_notes: This is not a standard multiword expression in Spanish. It appears to be the noun hombre followed by the auxiliary verb ha (from haber), as in part of a sentence like 'El hombre ha llegado' (The man has arrived). Do not treat 'hombre ha' as a single phrase — you will normally see 'hombre' and 'ha' used separately in sentences. 'Ha' is the third-person singular present perfect auxiliary (él/ella/usted ha + past participle).
target_language_example: El hombre ha terminado su trabajo.
native_language_example: The man has finished his work.

meaning: A sequence of the noun 'hombre' (man) followed by the clitic pronoun 'le' (indirect-object pronoun). Not a fixed idiom — grammatically incomplete by itself and uncommon in neutral standard Spanish; may appear in certain dialectal or colloquial constructions where the clitic follows a noun for emphasis or after a verb phrase that ends with a noun and clitic (e.g., in informal speech: “¿Y al hombre, le dijiste?”).
additional_notes: This is not a set phrase. In standard Spanish, clitic pronouns like 'le' typically attach to verbs (Juan le dio, dárselo) or precede conjugated verbs (le dije). Placing 'le' immediately after a noun ('hombre le') can occur in colloquial/dialectal contexts for topicalization or when the noun and pronoun belong to different syntactic positions in a sentence (e.g., after a pause or in questions), but it's considered informal and can sound redundant. For a complete, standard sentence you normally need a verb: e.g., 'Le di el libro al hombre.'
target_language_example: ¿Al hombre, le preguntaste si viene?
native_language_example: Did you ask the man if he is coming?

meaning: Not a fixed idiomatic phrase by itself; literally the noun 'hombre' (man) followed by the pronoun 'lo' (it/him/you formal neutral). Often appears across clause boundary or as part of a sentence rather than a stand-alone expression.
additional_notes: 'Hombre lo' is not a single lexicalized expression in Spanish. It can occur when '¡Hombre!' (an interjection meaning 'Wow', 'Come on', 'Well') is followed immediately by a clause that begins with the object pronoun 'lo', or when 'hombre' is the subject and 'lo' resumes a neuter or masculine direct object. Example contexts: exclamation + clause ('¡Hombre, lo sabía!'), or subject + pronoun separated by punctuation or pause. Pay attention to punctuation and intonation: without punctuation it could be parsed differently.
target_language_example: ¡Hombre lo sabía, no me sorprende!
native_language_example: Man, I knew it — it doesn't surprise me!

meaning: 'hombre' (man) plus the clitic pronoun 'me'; not a fixed idiom but can appear together in speech when 'hombre' is used as an interjection and 'me' begins the following clause (e.g. '¡Hombre, me...'). The phrase often marks surprise, annoyance, or emphasis and the meaning depends on the clause that follows.
additional_notes: Do not treat 'hombre me' as a single lexical item. 'Hombre' alone is a common interjection (¡Hombre!) meaning 'Come on', 'Well', 'Oh', or addressing a man. 'Me' is a clitic pronoun (direct or indirect object). When they appear adjacent (as in '¡Hombre me...') it's typically punctuation/intonation that separates them in speech or writing; intonation and context determine whether the tone is friendly, irritated, or surprised.
target_language_example: ¡Hombre me tienes preocupado si no llamas!
native_language_example: Come on, you make me worried if you don't call!

meaning: literally 'dead man'; used figuratively to mean someone doomed, finished, or in serious trouble
additional_notes: Often used figuratively to say someone is 'a dead man' (doomed or in trouble). Context can be literal (a dead man) but in many everyday uses it means the person has no chance, will be punished, fired, defeated, etc. Common in phrases like 'eres un hombre muerto' or 'soy hombre muerto.'
target_language_example: Si lo descubren, eres hombre muerto.
native_language_example: If they find out, you're a dead man.

meaning: literally 'more man' — not a standalone phrase in Spanish; appears only as part of larger expressions (e.g., 'el hombre más ...' = 'the most ... man').
additional_notes: On its own, 'hombre más' is not a fixed phrase. You will usually see it inside comparative or superlative constructions: 'el hombre más alto' (the tallest man), 'un hombre más serio' (a more serious man). Remember to include the article and adjective (and agreement) to form a correct phrase.
target_language_example: Él es el hombre más alto de la familia.
native_language_example: He is the tallest man in the family.

meaning: An emphatic interjection used to express strong disagreement, refusal, disbelief, or surprise — similar to 'no way', 'absolutely not', or 'come on, no'.
additional_notes: Informal, colloquial expression common in spoken Spanish. Tone, punctuation, and context change nuance (playful disbelief vs. firm refusal). Often appears with an exclamation mark or comma: both "¡Hombre no!" and "Hombre, no" occur; the form without punctuation can still be understood but is less common in writing.
target_language_example: — ¿Vas a prestarme tu coche por todo el mes? — Hombre no, lo necesito todos los días.
native_language_example: — Are you going to lend me your car for the whole month? — No way, I need it every day.

meaning: literally 'man is not' — used to say what a man (or person) is not or to introduce a general statement about what a man/people are (or aren't).
additional_notes: This phrase is part of sentences that negate or define 'un hombre' (a man) and often leads into a general truth or definition (e.g., 'A man is nothing more than...'). In English you might say 'a man is not...' or 'a man is nothing but...'. The exact meaning depends on the rest of the sentence. 'No es sino' is a more formal/literary variant meaning 'is nothing but' or 'is only'.
target_language_example: Un hombre no es solo lo que posee; también son sus acciones.
native_language_example: A man is not just what he owns; he is also his actions.

meaning: literally 'man or' — used as part of a choice 'man or ...' (i.e., 'man or woman', 'man or thing').
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but the noun 'hombre' followed by the conjunction 'o' ('or'). It appears when listing alternatives (e.g., 'hombre o mujer' = 'man or woman'). Word order and agreement are normal: you can replace 'hombre' with another noun. Beginners should treat it as two separate words: 'hombre' (man) + 'o' (or).
target_language_example: ¿Es un hombre o una mujer?
native_language_example: Is it a man or a woman?

meaning: literally 'man for'; used to describe someone suitable or assigned for a task (often incomplete phrase).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself in Spanish. 'Hombre para...' usually begins a larger expression like 'hombre para el trabajo' (a man for the job) or 'hombre para todo' (a handyman / jack-of-all-trades). Alone it sounds unfinished. Depending on context it can mean someone fit, suitable, assigned, or versatile. Use with a noun or clause after 'para'.
target_language_example: Necesitamos un hombre para el trabajo.
native_language_example: We need a man for the job.

meaning: Not a standalone fixed phrase in Spanish; likely part of larger expressions (e.g., 'hombre por hombre') or a mistranscription.
additional_notes:
On its own, 'hombre por' is incomplete. You may see it inside longer phrases such as:
- 'hombre por hombre' (man for man / one man at a time) — rare and context-dependent.
- 'hombre por delante' or 'hombre por...' when followed by more words. If you encountered 'hombre por' in a text, check the surrounding words: it usually needs a verb, preposition, or another noun to form a meaningful expression. Do not treat it as a fixed phrase.
target_language_example: Necesitamos un hombre por turno para controlar la puerta.
native_language_example: We need one man per shift to watch the door.

meaning: 'a man can' or 'a man may' (used to state what a man is able to do or experience).
additional_notes: Combines the noun 'hombre' (man) with the verb 'poder' (to be able to). In sentences it's usually part of a larger phrase: 'un hombre puede...' (a man can...), 'lo que un hombre puede...' (what a man can...). Use 'un hombre' for the general idea of 'a man'; 'el hombre' can mean 'the man' or 'humankind' depending on context. Word order and articles matter: 'hombre puede' alone is uncommon without an article or pronoun.
target_language_example: Un hombre puede aprender algo nuevo cada día.
native_language_example: A man can learn something new every day.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase in Spanish; likely a fragment (hombre + reflexive pronoun) or typo.
additional_notes: This sequence is not a common multiword expression. 'Hombre' means 'man'. 'Se' is a reflexive/impersonal/object pronoun used in many constructions (e.g., 'se lava' = 'he/she/it washes himself/herself/itself', or impersonal 'se habla' = 'one speaks'/'people speak'). If you see 'hombre se' it may be part of a sentence like 'El hombre se levantó' (The man got up) or a mistaken split of words. Do not treat it as a single phrase to memorize.
target_language_example: El hombre se levantó temprano.
native_language_example: The man got up early.

meaning: literally 'man without'; used to describe a man lacking something (e.g., resources, qualities) — not a fixed phrase on its own.
additional_notes: This is not a set idiom. It appears when describing a man missing something: 'hombre sin casa' (man without a house), 'hombre sin trabajo' (man without a job). You usually need a noun after 'sin' to say what is missing. Word order: hombre + sin + [noun].
target_language_example: Es un hombre sin trabajo que busca empleo.
native_language_example: He is a man without a job who is looking for work.

meaning: literally 'man has' — shows possession or a state for 'the man' or 'a man'.
additional_notes: This is the combination of the noun 'hombre' (man) and the verb 'tiene' (he/it has). Use 'el hombre tiene' for 'the man has' and 'un hombre tiene' for 'a man has'. 'Tiene' can indicate possession (tiene una caja), physical states/needs (tiene hambre = he is hungry), characteristics (tiene mala fama), or quantities (tiene diez dedos).
target_language_example: El hombre tiene un sombrero nuevo.
native_language_example: The man has a new hat.

meaning: literally 'man and' — this is not a fixed phrase in Spanish; it's just the word hombre ('man') followed by the conjunction y ('and').
additional_notes: Not a standalone idiom. You will see 'hombre y' when listing or connecting nouns (e.g., 'hombre y mujer' = 'man and woman'). Make sure to include appropriate articles and word order as needed (el hombre y la mujer). If you see '¡Hombre!' alone, it can be an interjection meaning 'Come on!' or 'Well!'.
target_language_example: El hombre y la mujer entraron en la tienda.
native_language_example: The man and the woman entered the store.

meaning: men of the / the men from the (used before a feminine noun phrase).
additional_notes: This is a fragment meaning 'men of the...' and must be followed by a feminine noun (la + noun) like 'aldea', 'arena', 'constructora', or a proper name with feminine article. It indicates belonging, membership, origin, occupation, or association. For masculine nouns you'd say 'hombres del' (de + el = del) or 'hombres de los' for plural. Word order: 'hombres de la' + feminine noun.
target_language_example: Los hombres de la aldea ayudaron a reparar el puente.
native_language_example: The men of the village helped repair the bridge.

meaning: men in the/men on the (depending on context).
additional_notes: This phrase combines the plural noun 'hombres' (men) with the prepositional phrase 'en el' (in the/on the + masculine singular definite article). Meaning depends on the noun that follows (e.g., 'hombres en el auto' = 'men in the car'; 'hombres en el agua' = 'men in the water'; 'en el campo' = 'men in the field' or 'on the field'). Use 'en la' if the following noun is feminine, and 'en los' / 'en las' for plural definite articles.
target_language_example: Hay tres hombres en el techo.
native_language_example: There are three men on the roof.

meaning: the phrase combines 'hombres' (men) with the indirect object pronoun 'les' meaning 'to them' or 'for them'; used in Spanish impersonal/cleft-like constructions to mark who is affected (e.g., 'to men' or 'men like/are affected by...').
additional_notes: In the examples, 'A los hombres les...' or 'A estos hombres les...' is a common Spanish structure used to say what men (as a group or specific men) like, lack, or are affected by. The full pattern is 'A + (article + noun) + les + [verb/phrase]'. The 'les' is an indirect object pronoun referring back to 'hombres'. English normally translates this with 'men (like...)', 'men are ...', or 'I trust these men with my life.' Include the article (los/estos) in natural Spanish: 'A los hombres les gusta...' Note: word order in Spanish often puts 'A los hombres' at the start for emphasis.
target_language_example: A los hombres les gusta jugar al fútbol.
native_language_example: Men like to play soccer.

meaning: 'men like (it/them)' — a non-standard/incorrect ordering; intended idea: 'a los hombres les gusta' (men like...)
additional_notes: The phrase as written is incomplete/incorrect in Spanish. Standard way to say 'men like...' is 'a los hombres les gusta' (singular subject: something pleases men) or 'a los hombres les gustan' (plural). Spanish often uses an indirect object construction with 'gustar' where the thing liked is the grammatical subject and people are the indirect object. Example: 'A los hombres les gusta el fútbol' = 'Men like soccer.'
target_language_example: A los hombres les gusta el fútbol.
native_language_example: Men like soccer.

meaning: used to introduce a superlative about men (e.g., 'one of the most ___ men').
additional_notes: Appears after a modifier to form expressions like 'uno de los hombres más + adjective' (one of the most + adjective + men). 'más' means 'more' or 'most' depending on context; here it's part of a superlative (the most). Ensure agreement and correct article/number: 'uno de los hombres más poderosos', 'uno de los hombres más ricos'.
target_language_example: Él es uno de los hombres más inteligentes que conozco.
native_language_example: He is one of the most intelligent men I know.

meaning: men who
additional_notes: A simple relative phrase combining 'hombres' (men) + the relative pronoun 'que' (who/that). Used to introduce a clause describing which men are meant. 'Que' is the most common relative pronoun in Spanish and can mean 'who', 'that' or 'which' depending on context. Word order and agreement: 'hombres' is plural, so verbs and adjectives in the relative clause should be plural when required.
target_language_example: Los hombres que trabajan aquí son muy amables.
native_language_example: The men who work here are very friendly.

meaning: men are equal / all men are equal (used to say people have equal rights or worth).
additional_notes: Often appears in legal, religious, or general statements about equality. In Spanish you'd more commonly say 'todos los hombres son iguales' or 'los hombres son iguales'. Context determines whether it means 'men (male people) are equal' or the broader idea 'all people are equal' (use 'todas las personas' for gender-neutral).
target_language_example: La constitución declara que todos los hombres son iguales ante la ley.
native_language_example: The constitution states that all men are equal before the law.

meaning: men are more / men are (+ adjective or noun) — a fragment used to compare or describe men as a group.
additional_notes: This is not a complete sentence by itself; it's a common fragment that begins comparisons or generalizations about men (e.g., "los hombres son más altos" = "men are taller"). You will usually see it followed by an adjective, an adverb, or a phrase introduced with que (e.g., "los hombres son más fuertes que las mujeres"). Include the definite article "los" when making general statements: "los hombres son más..."
target_language_example: Los hombres son más altos en promedio que las mujeres en esta muestra.
native_language_example: Men are taller on average than women in this sample.

meaning: 'honesty is' — used to state a quality or describe what honesty represents or leads to.
additional_notes: Commonly followed by a noun, adjective, or phrase that defines honesty's role or value (e.g., 'la razón principal', 'una virtud', 'la base del éxito'). It's a simple way to make general statements about honesty. Use 'la honestidad' (the noun) with 'es' (it is).
target_language_example: La honestidad es esencial en cualquier relación.
native_language_example: Honesty is essential in any relationship.

meaning: 'honest that' — appears when describing honesty in comparative, explanatory, or clause-introducing constructions (e.g., 'más honesto que...', 'tan honesto que...').
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom by itself; combines adjective 'honesto/a' with conjunction 'que' to introduce comparisons or result/explanatory clauses. Remember gender/number agreement (honesto/honesta/honestos/honestas). Common in phrases like 'es más honesto que...', 'es tan honesto que...', or 'lo más honesto que...'.
target_language_example: Es más placentero ser honesto que mentir.
native_language_example: It is more pleasant to be honest than to lie.

meaning: 'the honor of' — used to express that someone is given the privilege, distinction, or reputation to do or receive something.
additional_notes: Commonly appears in set phrases like 'tener el honor de' (to have the honor of...) to politely announce a privilege (e.g., meeting, presenting). Can also refer to reputation or dignity ('el honor de la familia' = the family's honor). Tone can be formal or dramatic depending on context.
target_language_example: Tengo el honor de presentar a la ganadora del premio.
native_language_example: I have the honor of introducing the prize winner.

meaning: an honor for; used to say something/someone is a privilege or honor to someone.
additional_notes: Commonly used in phrases like "es un honor para mí/nosotros/esta institución" to express that meeting, hosting, or having someone is a privilege. Often follows "es" or "sería" and is usually followed by "mí", "nosotros", "nuestra escuela", etc. Formal and polite; appropriate in speeches, introductions, and thank-you remarks.
target_language_example: Es un honor para mí presentar a la ganadora.
native_language_example: It is an honor for me to introduce the winner.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase by itself; typically a mistaken combination or part of a larger expression. Often results from typos or misordering of words (e.g., intended 'a la hora de', 'a la hora', or 'al + infinitive').
additional_notes: On its own 'hora al' is not standard Spanish. Learners will more commonly encounter: 'a la hora de' = 'at the time of/when', 'a la hora' = 'at (the) hour' (used with a specific time, e.g., 'a la hora convenida'), and 'al' + infinitive (e.g., 'al llegar' = 'upon arriving'). If you see 'hora al' in a text, check for a typo, missing preposition, or word order problem (examples: 'a la hora de...' or 'hora de...' or 'al + infinitive').
target_language_example: Hora al entrar en la sala, me dijeron que esperara afuera.
native_language_example: Upon entering the room, they told me to wait outside.

meaning: an hour earlier / one hour before
additional_notes: Used to indicate a time exactly one hour before a referenced time or event. Can appear with definite times (e.g., 'a las 5, una hora antes') or relative contexts ('llegó una hora antes' = 'arrived an hour earlier'). If specifying quantity, Spanish also uses 'una hora antes' (one hour before) or 'dos horas antes' (two hours before).
target_language_example: Llegó una hora antes de la reunión.
native_language_example: He arrived an hour before the meeting.

meaning: the decisive moment; the moment of truth.
additional_notes: Used to say that a crucial, revealing, or decisive moment has arrived — when the real outcome will be known. Common in formal and informal contexts. Often preceded by 'es' or 'llegó' (it's/has come).
target_language_example: Ha llegado la hora de la verdad: vamos a presentar el proyecto.
native_language_example: The moment of truth has arrived: we're going to present the project.

meaning: it's time for us to (do something) / it's time that we (do something).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a suggestion or statement that now is the appropriate time for a shared action. Follows the impersonal expression 'es hora de que' + subjunctive verb (e.g., vayamos, conozcamos). The 'nos' indicates the action involves 'us' (we/us). Common in spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: Es hora de que nos vayamos a casa.
native_language_example: It's time for us to go home.

meaning: it's time that / time for (someone) to...
additional_notes: Used to say that something should happen now or soon; often followed by a subjunctive verb: 'es hora de que se vaya' = 'it's time that he/she leaves' (use of subjunctive common). Can also appear as 'ya es hora de que...' for stronger urgency. The pronoun 'se' can be reflexive or impersonal depending on context (e.g., 'es hora de que se actúe' = 'it's time to act').
target_language_example: Ya es hora de que se tomen decisiones importantes.
native_language_example: It's about time that important decisions are made.

meaning: it's time for you to / time that you (should)...
additional_notes: This phrase is part of a larger construction usually followed by a subjunctive verb: "Es hora de que te ..." Meaning: it's time that you do something (often expresses necessity or recommendation). In everyday speech speakers may also say "Ya es hora de que te vayas" or shorten to "es hora de irte" (infinitive). Use the subjunctive after "que" when a specific subject follows.
target_language_example: Es hora de que te prepares para la entrevista.
native_language_example: It's time for you to get ready for the interview.

meaning: 'time to (do something) again' or 'it's time to return to (a place/state)'.
additional_notes: Used to say it's time to resume an action, go back somewhere, or return to a previous state. Followed by an infinitive verb (volver a + infinitive) to mean 'do again' or by a noun/place to indicate returning somewhere (often with 'casa', 'tiempos', etc.). Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Creo que es hora de volver a intentar.
native_language_example: I think it's time to try again.

meaning: an hour later / one hour after
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something happens one hour after a reference time or event. Often appears as "una hora después" (feminine "una" matches "hora"). Can be used with or without a comma: "Una hora después, ..." or within a clause: "una hora después de la medianoche."
target_language_example: Salimos a las ocho y una hora después llegamos a casa.
native_language_example: We left at eight and an hour later we arrived home.

meaning: at (a certain) time (used to indicate the time when something happens).
additional_notes: Commonly used before a clock time or time expression: 'a la hora en que...' or 'hora en' appears in phrases like 'la hora en que' meaning 'the time when'. By itself 'hora' = hour/time; 'en' = in/at — together they introduce the time context. Typically followed by a clause or a specific time.
target_language_example: La hora en que llegaste fue perfecta.
native_language_example: The time when you arrived was perfect.

meaning: used to refer to a specific time of day (lit. 'hour at the') — normally followed by a clock time (e.g., hora en la mañana/tarde) or a phrase like 'hora en la que' meaning 'the time when'.
additional_notes:
This fragment usually appears inside larger phrases: 'a la hora en la que...' or 'hora en la mañana/tarde/noche'. Alone it is incomplete; expect a following noun (mañana/tarde/noche) or clause (que...) that completes the idea. Common uses:
- 'a la hora en la que' = 'at the time when...'
- 'hora en la mañana' = 'hour in the morning' (more naturally: 'por la mañana' or 'a la(s) X de la mañana'). For beginners, prefer full expressions like 'a la una', 'a las tres de la tarde', or 'a la hora en que llegaste'.
target_language_example: Llegamos a la hora en la que empezó la película.
native_language_example: We arrived at the time when the movie started.

meaning: used when asking or stating the time (literally 'hour is' as part of a question or sentence).
additional_notes: This combination appears in questions and statements about the time, often in the phrase ¿Qué hora es? (What time is it?) or Es la una / Son las dos (It is one o'clock / It is two o'clock). Alone, 'hora es' is not a complete sentence; it functions as part of a larger phrase. Use 'es' with 1:00 (Es la una) and 'son' with other hours (Son las dos).
target_language_example: ¿Qué hora es?
native_language_example: What time is it?

meaning: overtime (extra working hour); also extra time (in sports).
additional_notes: Commonly used to refer to paid extra work hours (tener/dar horas extras). In sports, plural 'tiempo extra(s)' or 'hora extra' can mean extra period but 'prórroga' is more common. Use singular when referring to one extra hour or the concept in general: 'trabajar horas extras'.
target_language_example: Hoy voy a trabajar una hora extra para terminar el proyecto.
native_language_example: Today I'm going to work one extra hour to finish the project.

meaning: one more hour; an additional hour
additional_notes: Used to indicate one extra hour of time (e.g., staying, waiting) or to form phrases like "la hora más oscura" (the darkest hour) where "más" modifies the noun to mean 'most' or 'more' depending on context. Context determines whether it means 'one more hour' (additional time) or 'the ...est hour' when part of a superlative phrase.
target_language_example: ¿Puedes esperar una hora más?
native_language_example: Can you wait one more hour?

meaning: an hour to/for (time available or allotted for something).
additional_notes: Used to indicate a period of about one hour that is available, allotted, or necessary for an action. Can mean 'an hour to do X', 'about an hour until X', or simply 'it's a good time to...' depending on context. 'Una hora' can be approximate ('around an hour'). 'Ya es buena hora' is an idiomatic use meaning 'it's a good time/right time' (not a literal hour).
target_language_example: Tengo una hora para terminar el informe.
native_language_example: I have an hour to finish the report.

meaning: rush hour; busiest time with heavy traffic or crowds.
additional_notes: Used to refer to peak travel times (morning or evening) when roads, public transport, or places are most crowded. Often appears in the phrase 'hora punta' or 'las horas punta'. Can be used for traffic (tráfico) or workplace/customer peaks.
target_language_example: Salimos antes de la hora punta para no quedarnos atascados.
native_language_example: We left before rush hour so we didn't get stuck in traffic.

meaning: when; at the time that
additional_notes: Used to introduce a time clause. Equivalent to 'cuando' in many contexts. Often followed by a verb (e.g., 'hora que llegues'). In some regions/formal registers, 'es hora que' can mean 'it's time that' and may be followed by the subjunctive.
target_language_example: Es hora que salgamos si queremos llegar a tiempo.
native_language_example: It's time that we leave if we want to arrive on time.

meaning: 'hour and' — used when telling the time to add minutes after the hour (equivalent to '...past' in English).
additional_notes: Used in time expressions: 'hora y [minutes]'. In natural speech the article and number are included (e.g., 'las tres y cinco'). Example construction: '[hora] y [minutos]'. When minutes are 30, speakers often say 'y media' (half past). For minutes approaching the next hour (e.g., 2:50), Spanish commonly uses 'menos' (e.g., 'tres menos diez' = 2:50) instead of 'hora y cincuenta'.
target_language_example: La hora y los minutos se indican diciendo 'las tres y veinte' — aquí aparece la expresión 'hora y'.
native_language_example: The hour and the minutes are indicated by saying 'las tres y veinte' — here the expression 'hora y' appears.

meaning: of the (hour) / at the (time) — part of time expressions like 'a las horas de la mañana/tarde/noche'.
additional_notes: This fragment appears in time phrases and is usually combined with a period of the day (mañana, tarde, noche) or with a specific hour (e.g., 'a las horas de la mañana'). On its own it's incomplete; learners will more often see 'a las X horas' or 'en las horas de la mañana'. Use 'a las' + number to say 'at X o'clock' (e.g., 'a las tres').
target_language_example: Trabaja durante las horas de la mañana.
native_language_example: He works during the morning hours.

meaning: 'to the hospital' (movement toward a hospital).
additional_notes: This is the preposition 'a' (to) used after 'hospital' to indicate direction — e.g., 'llevar/ir al hospital' is more common because 'al' = 'a el' (to the). In Spanish you normally say 'al hospital' (to the hospital) or 'en el hospital' (in the hospital). Use 'hospital a' only when the phrase continues (e.g., 'hospital a domicilio' or in headings), but as a standalone 'to the hospital' you should use 'al hospital'.
target_language_example: Tienen que llevarlo al hospital ahora mismo.
native_language_example: They have to take him to the hospital right now.

meaning: the hospital is / the hospital + (estar) — describes the hospital's state, condition, or location.
additional_notes: Combines the noun 'hospital' with the verb 'estar' (to be). Use 'está' for temporary states (open/closed, under construction) or to indicate location (near). For permanent characteristics use 'es' instead. Common constructions: 'está abierto/cerrado' (is open/closed), 'está cerca' (is nearby), 'está a punto de' (is about to).
target_language_example: El hospital está abierto todos los días.
native_language_example: The hospital is open every day.

meaning: 'hospital' with the conjunction 'y' ('and'); not a fixed phrase—it's just 'hospital' followed by 'and' connecting clauses or items.
additional_notes: This is not a single idiom. In the examples, 'hospital y' appears when 'hospital' is followed by 'y' to link another idea (e.g., 'está en el hospital y...'). Use 'hospital' for 'hospital' and use 'y' to join it to the next clause or phrase. Remember Spanish uses accents (está). Pronunciation: [ospiˈtal i].
target_language_example: Está en el hospital y necesita muchas visitas.
native_language_example: He is in the hospital and needs many visits.

meaning: used before a place or name to indicate a hotel 'of' or 'at' (e.g., 'hotel of/at X').
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but the preposition 'de' following 'hotel' links the hotel to a location, person, brand, or specific name: 'hotel de la ciudad' (hotel of the city), 'hotel de lujo' (luxury hotel), or 'Hotel de Madrid' (a hotel named for Madrid). In spoken Spanish you will more often hear 'hotel en' (hotel in/at) for location (e.g., 'hotel en el centro') and 'hotel de' for ownership, type, or part of a name.
target_language_example: Nos quedamos en el Hotel de la Plaza.
native_language_example: We stayed at the Hotel de la Plaza.

meaning: hotel in (used before a place: e.g., 'hotel in Madrid').
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but the preposition 'en' following 'hotel' to indicate location ('in' or 'at' when referring to countries, regions, or certain places). In Spanish you more commonly say 'hotel en + lugar' (hotel in [a city/country]). Use 'en' for: en Madrid, en España, en la playa. For specific addresses or buildings you might use 'en el hotel' (in the hotel) or 'del hotel' (of the hotel).
target_language_example: Me quedé en un hotel en Barcelona.
native_language_example: I stayed in a hotel in Barcelona.

meaning: literally 'hotel is' — not a fixed phrase; usually part of a sentence describing a hotel (e.g., 'El hotel es grande' = 'The hotel is big').
additional_notes: This is not a standalone phrase. 'Hotel' is a masculine noun (el hotel) and 'es' is the third-person singular of the verb ser ('to be'). Together they form the start of a statement about a hotel’s characteristics, identity, location in some contexts, or classification. Remember to include articles/adjectives as needed: 'El hotel es caro.' For temporary states or locations, Spanish often prefers estar (e.g., 'El hotel está lleno' = 'The hotel is full').
target_language_example: El hotel es muy cómodo para familias.
native_language_example: The hotel is very comfortable for families.

meaning: today at (followed by a time or event).
additional_notes: Used to specify something happening today at a particular time or with respect to today's occurrence. It is a combination of 'hoy' (today) + preposition 'a' (at/to). You must add a time or phrase after it (e.g., 'hoy a las 5' = 'today at 5'). In everyday speech, native speakers often say just 'hoy' or 'hoy a las...' depending on context.
target_language_example: Hoy a las ocho tengo una reunión.
native_language_example: Today at eight I have a meeting.

meaning: today, here (used to emphasize that something is happening here today)
additional_notes: Combines hoy (today) and aquí (here). Not a fixed idiom but a natural phrase Spanish speakers use to stress time and place together, e.g. announcing an event or arrival: “Hoy aquí hay una feria” or “Hoy aquí estamos”. Word order can vary (hoy aquí / aquí hoy) depending on emphasis.
target_language_example: Hoy aquí tenemos música en vivo.
native_language_example: Today here we have live music.

meaning: nowadays; today; these days.
additional_notes: Used to talk about the present time or current habits/situations. Can mean 'today' (this specific day) or more commonly 'nowadays'/'these days' when referring to general current trends. Register: neutral; common in spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: Hoy día mucha gente trabaja desde casa.
native_language_example: Nowadays many people work from home.

meaning: today the (literal two-word sequence; not a fixed phrase).
additional_notes: This is not a set expression in Spanish. 'Hoy' means 'today' and 'el' is the masculine definite article 'the'. They may appear together when 'el' begins a noun phrase immediately after 'hoy', for example in time expressions (Hoy el partido empieza a las ocho → Today the match starts at eight). In many cases a different structure is used (e.g., 'hoy es' + noun/adjective) rather than 'hoy el'.
target_language_example: Hoy el museo abre a las diez.
native_language_example: Today the museum opens at ten.

meaning: 'today in' — used to introduce something happening or being talked about today in a specific place, program, or context.
additional_notes: This is a short sequence: 'hoy' means 'today' and 'en' means 'in' or 'on'. You will often see it in headlines, TV/radio/program schedules or program segments: e.g. 'Hoy en el programa...' (Today on the show...). It needs a following noun or phrase that specifies the place, program, topic, or location.
target_language_example: Hoy en el noticiero hablarán sobre el clima.
native_language_example: Today on the newscast they will talk about the weather.

meaning: nowadays; these days; in the present time.
additional_notes: Used to talk about the current era or present situation, often to contrast with the past. Can appear at the start, middle, or end of a sentence. Formality: neutral — appropriate in both spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: Hoy en día muchas personas compran por internet.
native_language_example: Nowadays many people shop online.

meaning: today in the (time of day).
additional_notes: Used to specify a part of today (e.g., hoy en la mañana, hoy en la tarde, hoy en la noche). Followed by a time-of-day noun (mañana, tarde, noche). Common in everyday speech to indicate when something happens today.
target_language_example: Hoy en la tarde tengo una reunión a las 3.
native_language_example: This afternoon I have a meeting at 3.

meaning: today is / today it's (used to state the date, weather, mood, situation, etc. today).
additional_notes: Hoy = 'today'. Está is the third-person singular of estar (to be) used for temporary states, locations, weather expressions, or situations. Use 'hoy está' to describe how something is today (e.g., Hoy está nublado; Hoy está ocupado). For permanent characteristics use 'es' instead (e.g., 'Hoy es martes' for the day of the week).
target_language_example: Hoy está soleado, así que vamos a la playa.
native_language_example: Today it's sunny, so let's go to the beach.

meaning: today was
additional_notes: Used to state how today was (a day, an event, or an experience). 'Hoy' = today; 'fue' is past (pretérito) of 'ser' (to be) and describes a finished event or general quality of the day. Common with adjectives (peor, bueno, inolvidable) or noun phrases (un día divertido, la lectura de hoy).
target_language_example: Hoy fue un día muy productivo.
native_language_example: Today was a very productive day.

meaning: today it / today him (depends on context) — combination of 'hoy' (today) + direct object pronoun 'lo'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase; it's just 'hoy' (today) followed by the masculine direct-object pronoun 'lo'. Meaning depends on the verb and sentence: e.g. 'hoy lo veo' = 'I see him/it today'. Word order with pronouns can vary (pronoun usually attaches before a conjugated verb: 'lo veo hoy', but both orders are possible for emphasis).
target_language_example: Hoy lo veo en el cine.
native_language_example: I see him/it at the cinema today.

meaning: today (you) give/bring it to me / today I receive it (context-dependent)
additional_notes: This is a fragment, not a complete sentence. 'Hoy' = today. 'Me' = to/for me (indirect object or reflexive). 'Lo' = it (masculine direct object). Together they usually appear inside a full sentence or command: e.g. 'Tráemelo hoy' (Bring it to me today) or 'Hoy me lo das' (You give it to me today). Word order can change depending on the verb tense and whether you attach pronouns to an infinitive/imperative/gerund. Pronouns 'me' + 'lo' combine to indicate 'it to me' or 'me it'.
target_language_example: Hoy me lo traes, ¿verdad?
native_language_example: You will bring it to me today, right?

meaning: I had (a...) today; used to say how you spent the day (often followed by an adjective: bien, genial, fatal...).
additional_notes: This phrase is the start of a common Spanish structure 'Hoy me lo pasé + [adjective]' meaning 'I had a [good/bad/great] time today' or 'I spent today [feeling ...]'. Literally: 'today I passed it to myself,' but idiomatically it refers to how enjoyable (or not) the day/event was. Common completions: 'hoy me lo pasé muy bien' (I had a great time today), 'hoy me lo pasé fatal' (I had a terrible time today).
target_language_example: Hoy me lo pasé muy bien en la fiesta.
native_language_example: I had a great time at the party today.

meaning: today (emphasizing immediacy or 'right away' today).
additional_notes: Used to stress that something will happen or should happen today, often implying urgency or immediacy (equivalent to 'this very day' or 'today itself'). Common in both spoken and written Spanish. Can be used alone (¿Puedes venir hoy mismo?) or with verbs (Lo haré hoy mismo).
target_language_example: Te llamo hoy mismo para confirmar.
native_language_example: I'll call you today to confirm (I'll call you later today).

meaning: today we / today us (used to start sentences about something happening to or done by 'us' today).
additional_notes: Combines 'hoy' (today) + 'nos' (we/us). 'Nos' can be a subject in reflexive/reciprocal constructions (nos encontramos = we meet/meet each other), a direct/indirect object (nos acompaña = accompanies us), or part of a pronominal verb (nos vamos = we leave). Common in spoken and written Spanish to introduce events or actions occurring today.
target_language_example: Hoy nos vamos de excursión al parque.
native_language_example: Today we're going on an outing to the park.

meaning: 'today for' or 'today by' — used as the start of time expressions (followed by otro/último/primera vez/etc.) or in fixed phrases like 'hoy por hoy'.
additional_notes: Alone, 'hoy' means 'today'. The two-word sequence 'hoy por' usually appears in set expressions: for example, 'hoy por hoy' means 'for now' or 'as things stand today'. It can also begin constructions like 'hoy por la mañana' (today in the morning) where a preposition follows ('por la mañana'), but in that case it's really 'hoy' + 'por' + time phrase. Context determines meaning.
target_language_example: Hoy por hoy, no podemos cambiar el plan.
native_language_example: For now, we can't change the plan.

meaning: now that / since (introduces a reason or circumstance in the present).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause that gives a reason or explains a situation that holds now. Similar to 'ahora que' and often interchangeable with it. Common in spoken and written Spanish: 'Hoy que...' + clause. Not a fixed idiom—it's a combination of 'hoy' (today/now) + 'que' (that).
target_language_example: Hoy que estás aquí, podemos empezar la reunión.
native_language_example: Now that you're here, we can start the meeting.

meaning: today I want (to)... — expresses a desire or intention for today
additional_notes: Use 'hoy quiero' to state what you want or plan to do today. It's followed by an infinitive verb (hoy quiero comer), a noun (hoy quiero el dinero), or a clause (hoy quiero que hablemos). Polite/softened alternatives include 'hoy me gustaría' or 'hoy quisiera'.
target_language_example: Hoy quiero aprender unas frases nuevas en español.
native_language_example: Today I want to learn some new phrases in Spanish.

meaning: today (someone) does/is; used to introduce actions or events happening today (often followed by a verb).
additional_notes: "Hoy" means "today." When followed by the reflexive or impersonal pronoun "se" it often introduces statements about actions that happen today in a neutral or impersonal way (e.g., "Hoy se entrega el premio" = "The prize is awarded today"). It can also appear before a verb meaning "today someone/people do [something]." Word order may vary ("Hoy se..." or "Se... hoy..."), but "hoy se" emphasizes that the action occurs today.
target_language_example: Hoy se publica el informe.
native_language_example: The report is published today.

meaning: today you / today (to) you — 'hoy' = today; 'te' = you (object).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself. 'Hoy' (today) and 'te' (informal direct/indirect object pronoun) often appear together in sentences like 'Hoy te llamo' (I'll call you today) or 'Hoy te quiero ver' (I want to see you today). Word order can vary: the pronoun usually goes before a conjugated verb (te llamo), or attached to an infinitive/gerund/affirmative command (voy a llamarte, llamándote).
target_language_example: Hoy te llamo para confirmar la cita.
native_language_example: I'll call you today to confirm the appointment.

meaning: today I have (to)... — used to say you must or need to do something today.
additional_notes: Combine 'hoy' (today) + 'tengo' (I have) typically followed by 'que' + an infinitive verb: 'Hoy tengo que + [infinitive]'. Common for stating obligations, plans, or things you need to do today.
target_language_example: Hoy tengo que estudiar para el examen.
native_language_example: Today I have to study for the exam.

meaning: "hoy" = today; "un" = a/an — together they appear before a noun as 'today a...' but this exact two-word sequence is not a fixed phrase in Spanish.
additional_notes: You will commonly see 'hoy' used alone to mean 'today' (e.g., hoy voy al cine = today I'm going to the movies). 'Un' is the indefinite article 'a' or 'an'. The sequence 'hoy un' can occur when 'hoy' modifies a noun phrase that begins with 'un' (for example: 'Hoy un amigo vino' — though more natural is 'Hoy vino un amigo' or 'Hoy un amigo me llamó'). Native word order usually places the article after the verb or the noun phrase differently, so 'hoy un' is not a set phrase; treat 'hoy' and 'un' as separate words.
target_language_example: Hoy un amigo me llamó por la mañana.
native_language_example: Today a friend called me in the morning.

meaning: ‘today we go’ — used to say what we are doing today or where we are going today.
additional_notes: Hoy (today) + vamos (we go / we are going). Commonly used to introduce plans or actions for today: 'Hoy vamos a...' followed by an infinitive or destination (e.g., 'Hoy vamos a la playa' or 'Hoy vamos a estudiar'). In casual speech the 'a' + verb or destination is often included; 'Hoy vamos' alone can imply 'we're going (somewhere) today' when the place or activity is clear from context.
target_language_example: Hoy vamos a cenar con mis padres.
native_language_example: Today we're going to have dinner with my parents.

meaning: I'm going (to) today / today I will.
additional_notes: Used to say you will do something today. Usually followed by an infinitive verb (voy a + [infinitive]). Common in everyday speech to state plans or intentions for the same day. Tone can be neutral; meaning depends on the verb that follows.
target_language_example: Hoy voy a comprar pan después del trabajo.
native_language_example: Today I'm going to buy bread after work.

meaning: today and / nowadays and (used to connect 'today' with another phrase); often starts a contrast or continuation about the present
additional_notes: 'Hoy y' is not a fixed idiom by itself but is the combination of hoy (today) + y (and). You'll see it in phrases like 'hoy y siempre' (today and always) or 'hoy y en el futuro' (today and in the future). It links 'today' with another idea and can introduce contrast (today and...) or emphasize continuity. Use it the same as 'today and' in English.
target_language_example: Hoy y siempre estaré contigo.
native_language_example: Today and always I will be with you.

meaning: 'there were/was' in conditional or hypothetical clauses (imperfect-subjunctive + article 'una')
additional_notes: Hubiera is the past (imperfect) subjunctive form of haber used to talk about hypothetical or counterfactual situations (often introduced by si/antes de que/sería bueno si). Combined with an indefinite article (una) it means 'if there were/was a...' or 'that there was a...'. Common in conditional sentences and formal/written registers; can also appear in past subjunctive subordinate clauses.
target_language_example: Si hubiera una oportunidad, la aprovecharía.
native_language_example: If there were an opportunity, I would take it.

meaning: there was a big / there was a great (used to report a large event or incident)
additional_notes: Hubo is the preterite of haber used impersonally to report that something happened. Use 'hubo un gran...' to describe a single past event (earthquake, fire, celebration, problem). For ongoing or repeated events you would use other forms. 'Gran' before a noun means 'big' or 'great' and shortens from 'grande' when placed before singular nouns.
target_language_example: Hubo un gran apagón anoche en el barrio.
native_language_example: There was a big blackout last night in the neighborhood.

meaning: he/she/it smells the (something) — literal: 'smells the'.
additional_notes: Formed from the verb oler (to smell) in third person singular (huele) + definite article el. Used when the subject smells a specific masculine noun: e.g., 'huele el café' = 'he/she/it smells the coffee.' Also appears in commands or descriptions. For other subjects use huelo (I), hueles (you), olemos (we), huelen (they). If the noun is feminine use 'huele la'.
target_language_example: Ella huele el perfume antes de comprarlo.
native_language_example: She smells the perfume before buying it.

meaning: 'it/they smell(s) very' — used to describe the strength of a smell
additional_notes: Huele is the third-person singular form of oler (to smell). 'Huele muy' is followed by an adjective (e.g., 'fuerte', 'bien', 'mal') or a past participle used adjectivally (e.g., 'huele muy quemado'). Use subject pronouns or nouns before huele if needed: 'Esto huele muy mal.' For plural subjects use 'huelen muy'.
target_language_example: La cocina huele muy bien después de cocinar.
native_language_example: The kitchen smells very good after cooking.

meaning: fingerprint (the unique pattern on a fingertip).
additional_notes: Used for identification, security, or forensic contexts. Often appears in phrases like 'tomar la huella dactilar' (to take/scan a fingerprint) or 'huella dactilar digital' (digital fingerprint/scan). Formal and neutral term.
target_language_example: La policía tomó la huella dactilar del sospechoso.
native_language_example: The police took the suspect's fingerprint.

meaning: 'eggs of' or 'eggs from' — literal possessive/partitive phrase used to describe origin or type of eggs (e.g., 'huevos de gallina' = 'chicken eggs').
additional_notes: This is a compositional, literal phrase: huevos = eggs, de = of/from. Commonly used to indicate the source, species, preparation style, or ingredient (huevos de codorniz = quail eggs; huevos de la granja = farm eggs). In some contexts 'de' can introduce what the eggs are made with or used for (huevos de chocolate = chocolate eggs). Not a fixed idiom by itself — it needs a noun after 'de'.
target_language_example: Compré huevos de gallina y huevos de codorniz.
native_language_example: I bought chicken eggs and quail eggs.

meaning: eggs in the (feminine noun that follows, e.g. 'la heladera', 'la caja', 'la cesta').
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom—it's simply the plural noun 'huevos' ('eggs') followed by the preposition 'en' and the feminine definite article 'la' before another noun. The final noun (la heladera, la caja, la cesta, la arena, etc.) tells where the eggs are. Change 'la' to 'el' if the place is masculine (e.g. 'huevos en el refrigerador').
target_language_example: Hay huevos en la mesa.
native_language_example: There are eggs on the table.

meaning: 'is human' or 'human ... is' (phrase combining adjective 'humana' + verb 'es')
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but two separate words: 'humana' (feminine form of 'humano' = 'human') and 'es' (third-person singular of 'ser' = 'is'). They appear together when describing a feminine noun: e.g. 'la historia humana es...' ('the human history is...'), 'la vida humana es...'. Adjust gender (humano/humana) and number (es/son) to match the noun.
target_language_example: La experiencia humana es compleja.
native_language_example: The human experience is complex.

meaning: humans (do) not — negative statement about people.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase; it's the plural noun 'humanos' (humans) followed by the negation 'no'. It appears in sentences to say that humans do not or cannot do something. Word order is flexible in Spanish: often 'los humanos no' (the humans do not) or 'los humanos no pueden' (humans cannot). 'No' negates the verb that follows or the clause.
target_language_example: Los humanos no entienden todo lo que ocurre.
native_language_example: Humans do not understand everything that happens.

meaning: Not a fixed phrase; appears to be two separate words: humanos (humans) + se (reflexive/impersonal pronoun).
additional_notes: This is not a single multiword expression in Spanish. 'Humanos' is the plural noun/adjective meaning 'humans' or 'human'. 'Se' is a clitic with several uses (reflexive, impersonal/passive 'se', or as part of pronominal verbs). Together they might appear in a sentence like 'los humanos se adaptan' (humans adapt) where 'se' is part of the verb form. Do not treat 'humanos se' as one unit; learn each word separately and pay attention to how 'se' is used in context.
target_language_example: Los humanos se adaptan a diferentes climas.
native_language_example: Humans adapt to different climates.

meaning: in the mood for (something) / not in the mood for (something).
additional_notes: Used with estar (estoy/estaba) + de humor para + noun or verb (infinitive) to say you feel like doing something or not. Commonly negative (no estoy de humor para...) to refuse or avoid activities. Can express temporary mood; often followed by a specific activity: una pelea, una fiesta, hablar, salir.
target_language_example: No estoy de humor para cocinar hoy.
native_language_example: I'm not in the mood to cook today.

meaning: sank into / sank in (past tense of 'hundirse' with 'en' + place or state).
additional_notes: Used with 'hundirse' (to sink, to submerge, or to collapse) in the past third person singular. Followed by a place (el mar, el horizonte, Génova) to mean 'sank into' or by a state (un sueño profundo) to mean 'sank into' figuratively. Context determines whether it's physical (a ship, bridge) or figurative (sinking into sleep, thought).
target_language_example: El barco se hundió en la tormenta.
native_language_example: The ship sank in the storm.

meaning: sank/caused to sink down to (a level), pushed down as far as
additional_notes: From the verb hundir (to sink, to plunge) in past tense (hundió = he/she/it sank or caused to sink). 'Hasta' adds the idea of extent ('up to', 'as far as'). Often used literally (e.g., a ship sank up to a certain depth) or figuratively (e.g., someone was driven to/into something). You will usually see a subject before 'hundió' and a noun or phrase after 'hasta' indicating the limit.
target_language_example: La tormenta hundió hasta la mitad del muelle.
native_language_example: The storm sank (it) up to half of the pier.

meaning: 'sank until the' or 'sank as far as the' (literal); used to describe something sinking down to a specific level or point.
additional_notes: This is a literal, descriptive phrase often followed by a noun that names the level or object reached (e.g., 'hundió hasta el fondo' — sank to the bottom). Use with past tense verbs (hundir/hundirse). Not an idiom; you usually need the rest of the clause to show what was reached.
target_language_example: El bote se hundió hasta el fondo del lago.
native_language_example: The boat sank to the bottom of the lake.

meaning: 'was going to the' or 'used to go to the' (imperfect past of ir + definite article 'la').
additional_notes: Iba is the imperfect form of ir (to go). Depending on context, 'iba a la' can describe a habitual past action ('used to go to the') or an ongoing past action ('was going to the' / 'was on the way to the'). The phrase must match the feminine singular noun that follows (la). For masculine nouns you'd see 'iba al' (a + el). If followed by an infinitive, 'iba a' + verb (without 'la') means 'was going to [do something]'.
target_language_example: Iba a la biblioteca todas las tardes.
native_language_example: I used to go to the library every afternoon.

meaning: 'was going to' / 'used to go (to/for)' or part of expressions meaning 'was about/was wearing/was acting like' depending on context.
additional_notes: Iba de is the imperfect form of ir + de. It combines 'was going' with 'to/for' or is used in idiomatic phrases: "ir de compras" (to go shopping), "ir de paseo" (to go for a walk), "ir de rosa" (to be dressed in pink) or "ir de + role" (to act like / pretend). Context determines whether it's literal movement, habitual action, clothing/appearance, or figurative role.
target_language_example: Ayer iba de compras al centro comercial cuando me encontré contigo.
native_language_example: Yesterday I was going shopping at the mall when I ran into you.

meaning: one-way (as in one-way ticket or trip).
additional_notes: Commonly used in the phrase 'ida y vuelta' (round trip) or 'solo ida'/'ida' alone. 'Ida' means the outward journey; 'ida y' is usually followed by 'vuelta' to mean 'there and back'. In listings (tickets, travel forms) you may see 'ida' for one-way and 'ida y vuelta' for round-trip.
target_language_example: Quiero un billete de ida y vuelta.
native_language_example: I want a round-trip ticket.

meaning: 'round trip' (a journey that goes there and back).
additional_notes: Commonly used for travel tickets (train, bus, plane) to indicate a return ticket. Can also describe any two-way movement. Often shortened to 'ida y vta.' in tickets or writing.
target_language_example: Compré un boleto de ida y vuelta a Madrid.
native_language_example: I bought a round-trip ticket to Madrid.

meaning: an idea/understanding of something (used before a clause or noun phrase introduced by 'lo').
additional_notes: Commonly appears in expressions like 'tener idea de lo que...' or 'no tener idea de lo que...' meaning 'to have/no have any idea what...'. 'Lo' here introduces a general concept or clause (often followed by 'que' + clause). Often used to express knowledge or lack of knowledge about a situation.
target_language_example: No tengo idea de lo que pasó anoche.
native_language_example: I have no idea what happened last night.

meaning: an idea about / an idea in (a topic or context).
additional_notes: Commonly appears as part of phrases like "tener una idea en..." or "no tengo idea en..." though more natural constructions are "idea de" (idea about) or "idea en cuanto a" (regarding). "Idea en" by itself is often followed by a noun indicating the field or context (e.g., "idea en matemáticas") but beginners should be aware that Spanish speakers more often use "idea de" or other connectors. Use with care; check context.
target_language_example: No tengo idea en qué consiste ese proyecto, necesito más detalles.
native_language_example: I have no idea what that project consists of; I need more details.

meaning: 'the idea is' or 'the point is' — used to introduce the main idea or purpose of something.
additional_notes: Commonly used in spoken and written Spanish to summarize or explain the central thought that follows. Often appears at the start of a clause: 'La idea es...' or 'Mi idea es...'. Can be followed by an infinitive (La idea es organizar...) or a clause (La idea es que venga...).
target_language_example: La idea es empezar temprano para evitar el tráfico.
native_language_example: The idea is to start early to avoid traffic.

meaning: an idea/suggestion for (something or someone).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a proposal or suggestion aimed at a project, plan, thing, or person. 'Para' shows purpose or recipient: idea para el proyecto (for the project), idea para ti (for you). Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Tengo una idea para la fiesta de cumpleaños.
native_language_example: I have an idea for the birthday party.

meaning: an idea/thought that (introduces a clause explaining the content of the idea)
additional_notes: Used to refer to a notion, opinion, or impression followed by a subordinate clause introduced by que. Common in spoken and written Spanish: e.g., la idea que tengo es que... or tengo la idea de que.... Can often be replaced by 'creencia que', 'opinión que' or rephrased with 'que' after verbs like 'pensar' or 'creer'.
target_language_example: Tengo la idea que deberíamos salir temprano.
native_language_example: I have the idea that we should leave early.

meaning: ideas for
additional_notes: Commonly used to introduce the topic or purpose of the ideas. Often followed by a noun, infinitive, or clause: ideas de regalo (ideas for gifts), ideas de negocio (business ideas), ideas de qué hacer (ideas about what to do). Grammatically, 'ideas' is plural noun and 'de' is a preposition; literal translation is possible but the exact English preposition (for/about) depends on context.
target_language_example: Tengo algunas ideas de regalo para tu cumpleaños.
native_language_example: I have some ideas for gifts for your birthday.

meaning: ideas/opinions in (someone's head) or ideas about (a topic).
additional_notes: Used after 'meter(le) ideas en la cabeza' meaning 'to put ideas into (someone's) head' — often negative (influencing someone). Also used as 'ideas en [tema]' meaning 'ideas about [topic]' (e.g., 'ideas en educación'). Context determines whether it refers to someone's mind or a subject. Common collocations: 'meter ideas en la cabeza', 'tener/ponerse ideas en la cabeza'.
target_language_example: No le metas ideas en la cabeza a los niños.
native_language_example: Don't put ideas in the kids' heads.

meaning: a difficult language (to learn or understand).
additional_notes: Used to describe a language that is hard to learn, pronounce, or understand. Can refer to complexity of grammar, pronunciation, or unfamiliar writing system. Commonly used with verbs like 'ser' (es un idioma difícil) or 'parecer' (me parece un idioma difícil).
target_language_example: El japonés es un idioma difícil para muchos estudiantes.
native_language_example: Japanese is a difficult language for many students.

meaning: foreign language
additional_notes: Used to refer to any language that is not the speaker's native language. Common in contexts like school, study, travel, and language learning (e.g., aprender un idioma extranjero).
target_language_example: Estoy aprendiendo un idioma extranjero: el francés.
native_language_example: I'm learning a foreign language: French.

meaning: This combination is not a fixed phrase in Spanish; it looks like the adjective 'muy' ('very') followed by 'idioma' ('language'), but the natural order is 'idioma muy...' rarely used—correct order is 'idioma muy X' becomes 'idioma muy ...' is awkward. Likely a mistake; correct forms: 'idioma' (language) or 'idioma muy ...' should be 'idioma muy ...' only when followed by a past participle in passive structures (rare).
additional_notes: Native Spanish normally places 'muy' before an adjective or adverb (e.g., 'muy bueno') and before adjectives modifying nouns with a linking structure (e.g., 'un idioma muy difícil' = 'a very difficult language'). 'Idioma muy' by itself is incomplete: you need an adjective after 'muy' (e.g., 'idioma muy hablado' is unusual; better: 'un idioma muy hablado' -> 'a widely spoken language' would be 'un idioma muy hablado' but more natural: 'un idioma muy hablado' is uncommon—prefer 'un idioma muy hablado' only in some contexts). For beginners: learn 'idioma' = 'language' and use 'muy' before adjectives: 'un idioma muy difícil' = 'a very difficult language.'
target_language_example: Es un idioma muy difícil de aprender.
native_language_example: It's a very difficult language to learn.

meaning: languages in / languages at (depends on context).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase; it's the noun 'idiomas' (languages) followed by the preposition 'en' (in/at). Meaning depends on the words that follow: 'idiomas en la escuela' = 'languages at school', 'idiomas en el mundo' = 'languages in the world', or 'aprender idiomas en un centro' = 'learn languages at a center'. Watch word order and context: 'en' links 'idiomas' to a location or scope.
target_language_example: Estudié idiomas en la universidad.
native_language_example: I studied languages at the university.

meaning: stupid; (insult) 'idiot' used with a following noun or descriptor (e.g., 'idiota de persona').
additional_notes: Commonly used as an insult. 'Idiota' is the noun 'idiot'; 'de' can link to a description or emphasize who/what is being insulted (e.g., 'idiota de hermano', 'idiota de idea'). In everyday speech Spanish speakers more often say simply 'idiota' or use other insults; be careful as it's offensive. Word order and exact phrasing vary by region.
target_language_example: Eres un idiota de amigo si no me ayudas.
native_language_example: You're an idiot of a friend if you don't help me.

meaning: gone to the
additional_notes: A common sequence built from ido (the past participle of ir, “to go”) plus a la before a feminine singular destination: ido a la tienda, ido a la escuela. It often appears with forms of haber (he/ha/había ido) or in se ha ido a la.... In English, “the” is often omitted with places like school, bed, or war: ido a la cama = “gone to bed.”
target_language_example: Mi madre ha ido a la farmacia.
native_language_example: My mother has gone to the pharmacy.

meaning: gone too far / been excessive
additional_notes: Past participle phrase using ir (ido) meaning 'gone' combined with demasiado ('too much' / 'too far'). Often describes actions, behavior, or changes that have exceeded a limit (e.g., someone has taken something too far, or something has become too much). Context determines whether it's physical (gone too far), emotional/intensity (too intense), or quantity (too much).
target_language_example: Con las críticas ya ha ido demasiado.
native_language_example: With the criticism, he/she has gone too far.

meaning: 'never gone' or 'have/has never gone' (past participle 'ido' used with haber + 'nunca' to express that someone has never been somewhere)
additional_notes: 'Ido nunca' appears as the participle 'ido' (from the verb ir) followed by 'nunca' (never). In natural Spanish the auxiliary haber normally appears before the participle: e.g. 'no he ido nunca' or 'nunca he ido'. Word order can vary: 'no ha ido nunca', 'no hemos ido nunca', etc. Negative markers (no, nunca) and pronouns may shift depending on emphasis. Use appropriate form of haber for different subjects and tenses.
