target_language_example: Jim no ha ido nunca al extranjero.
native_language_example: Jim has never gone abroad.

meaning: 'church with' — the words iglesia (church) + con (with).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase: it's simply the noun iglesia followed by the preposition con to describe a church that has or features something (e.g., iglesia con torre = church with a tower). You will usually see it as part of a longer phrase: iglesia con + noun or iglesia con + verb phrase (e.g., iglesia con pinturas antiguas, iglesia con misa diaria). Word order follows Spanish: iglesia (what) + con (with) + feature.
target_language_example: Visitamos una iglesia con frescos del siglo XVI.
native_language_example: We visited a church with 16th-century frescoes.

meaning: ‘church in’ — used to say a church is located in or at (a place).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself; it's the preposition construction 'iglesia (church) + en (in/at)'. Use 'en' to indicate location (in, at, on) before a place or country. You will usually see it in longer phrases like 'la iglesia en la plaza' (the church in the square) or 'la iglesia en Madrid' (the church in Madrid). Remember to add the definite article when needed: 'la iglesia en el pueblo'.
target_language_example: La iglesia en el centro está cerrada los domingos.
native_language_example: The church in the center is closed on Sundays.

meaning: literally 'church is' — not a fixed phrase; appears as part of a sentence where 'iglesia' (church) is the subject and 'es' is the verb 'is'.
additional_notes: This is not a standalone idiom. It's simply the noun iglesia (feminine) followed by the verb ser in the third person singular (es). You will see this structure when describing or identifying a church: e.g. 'La iglesia es grande' (The church is big) or 'La iglesia es antigua' (The church is old). Remember agreement: adjectives describing 'iglesia' must be feminine (e.g. antigua, grande).
target_language_example: La iglesia es muy antigua y bonita.
native_language_example: The church is very old and pretty.

meaning: the church is (…)
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase—it's simply the noun 'iglesia' (church) followed by the verb 'está' (third-person singular of 'estar'). Use when describing a church's location, condition, or temporary state. For location you can follow with 'en' + place (e.g., 'la iglesia está en la plaza'). For condition or state, follow with an adjective or phrase (e.g., 'la iglesia está cerrada'). Remember subject–verb agreement: 'la iglesia está' (singular). If referring to multiple churches, use 'las iglesias están'.
target_language_example: La iglesia está cerrada los lunes.
native_language_example: The church is closed on Mondays.

meaning: A nonstandard or incorrect juxtaposition of 'iglesia' (church) and 'los' (the, masculine plural). It is not a fixed phrase in Spanish and likely results from a typo or fragment where the article does not agree with the noun.
additional_notes: 'Iglesia' is feminine and takes 'la' (singular) or 'las' (plural). 'Los' is the masculine plural definite article and cannot correctly modify 'iglesia.' Possible sources: a cut-off sentence (e.g., 'la iglesia, los vecinos...') or an incorrect attempt to say 'las iglesias' or 'la iglesia de los...'. For learners: use 'la iglesia' for 'the church' or 'las iglesias' for 'the churches'. If you mean 'the church of the...' use 'la iglesia de los...' followed by a plural noun (e.g., 'la iglesia de los santos').
target_language_example: La iglesia los XX fue un error en la transcripción; debería ser «la iglesia» o «la iglesia de los fieles».
native_language_example: 'La iglesia los XX' was an error in the transcription; it should be 'la iglesia' or 'la iglesia de los fieles'.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase in Spanish. Taken literally, it combines 'iglesia' (church) and 'todos' (everyone/all); meaning must be clarified by context (e.g., 'everyone at church').
additional_notes: 'Iglesia todos' is not idiomatic; native speakers would reorder or add prepositions: 'todos en la iglesia', 'toda la iglesia' or 'toda la gente de la iglesia'. Use 'iglesia todos' only if quoting nonstandard speech, a headline fragment, or as a search keyword.
target_language_example: Iglesia todos estaban allí para la celebración.
native_language_example: Everyone at church was there for the celebration.

meaning: This word order is not a natural Spanish phrase by itself; likely a fragment meaning "church every/the" (e.g., 'la iglesia todos los...').
additional_notes: The sequence 'iglesia todos los' looks like a fragment rather than a complete fixed phrase. In Spanish you would usually say 'la iglesia' (the church) and then 'todos los...' to mean 'all the...' or 'every...' followed by a masculine plural noun (e.g., 'todos los domingos' = every Sunday). To be grammatical, include an article and complete the phrase: 'la iglesia todos los domingos' (the church every Sunday) or 'en la iglesia todos los sábados' (at church every Saturday).
target_language_example: Voy a la iglesia todos los domingos.
native_language_example: I go to church every Sunday.

meaning: to (go to) church every Sunday / every Sunday at church.
additional_notes: This phrase describes a habitual action or routine of attending church on Sundays. In Spanish you might say 'voy a la iglesia todos los domingos' (I go to church every Sunday) or simply 'iglesia todos los domingos' as a shorthand note or schedule entry. Use 'la iglesia' if referring to the building/attending service; omit article only in some headings or notes.
target_language_example: Voy a la iglesia todos los domingos con mi familia.
native_language_example: I go to church every Sunday with my family.

meaning: just like
additional_notes: Used to compare similarity or equality between two things or actions. Can appear before nouns, adjectives, or clauses: 'igual que + noun' (igual que él), 'igual que + clause' (igual que te dije). In informal speech it often shortens to 'igual' alone with same meaning. Not to be confused with 'igual' meaning 'maybe' in some regions.
target_language_example: Ella cocina igual que su madre.
native_language_example: She cooks just like her mother.

meaning: equal to; the same as
additional_notes: Used to compare two things or people. Often follows the noun/pronoun being compared (X es/son iguales a Y). Can express equality in quantity, quality, status, or likeness. When comparing people, watch tone — it can be neutral or carry a value judgment depending on context.
target_language_example: Sus notas son iguales a las mías.
native_language_example: Their grades are the same as mine.

meaning: 'image of' or 'picture of'.
additional_notes: Used to indicate that a picture, photo, illustration, or mental image is of something or someone. Commonly appears before a noun (imagen de la ciudad, imagen de mi abuela) or before a verb clause when describing a depiction (imagen de alguien sonriendo). Can refer to physical images or figurative/mental images.
target_language_example: Tengo una imagen de la playa en mi teléfono.
native_language_example: I have a picture of the beach on my phone.

meaning: 'image/picture that' — introduces a specific image, picture, or mental image described or identified.
additional_notes: Used to refer to a concrete picture (foto, dibujo) or a mental image/idea. Often appears with past tenses (tenía, había, encontré) to describe an image someone had, saw, or created. In many cases interchangeable with 'la imagen que' when context already makes gender/number clear.
target_language_example: La imagen que guardo de aquel viaje me hace sonreír.
native_language_example: The image that I keep from that trip makes me smile.

meaning: 'impermeable por' = 'impermeable to' or 'resistant to' (something).
additional_notes: Used to say that a material, surface, or person is not affected by or does not let something pass through. Commonly followed by a noun (e.g., agua, humedad, golpes) or a verb in infinitive introduced by 'a' or 'al' depending on structure. More often you will see the adjective 'impermeable' used alone (impermeable a/ante) or with 'a' (impermeable al agua). 'Impermeable por' is less common but can appear in constructions like 'impermeable por lluvia/por el agua' meaning 'impervious because of/against rain/water.'
target_language_example: La chaqueta es impermeable por la lluvia; no se moja.
native_language_example: The jacket is impermeable to the rain; it doesn't get wet.

meaning: literally 'raincoat/ waterproof (in case)'; used to say you bring or wear a waterproof (coat) just in case (it rains) or as a precaution.
additional_notes: Commonly appears when someone mentions taking something 'por si' (in case). You will often see just 'impermeable' (raincoat) or the full phrase 'llevar un impermeable por si llueve' (to bring a raincoat in case it rains). Use to express precaution. Not an idiom — it's the noun impermeable + the phrase por si.
target_language_example: Voy a llevar un impermeable por si llueve.
native_language_example: I'm going to bring a raincoat in case it rains.

meaning: 'matters now' / 'is important now' (what is relevant or important at this moment).
additional_notes: Commonly used to say that something is (or isn't) important at the present time. Often appears in phrases like "lo que importa ahora" (what matters now) or with negation "no importa ahora" / "nada de eso importa ahora" (that doesn't matter now). Useful for shifting focus to current priorities or concerns.
target_language_example: Lo único que importa ahora es que estemos a salvo.
native_language_example: The only thing that matters now is that we're safe.

meaning: 'it matters' or 'does ... matter' when followed by a masculine singular noun or verb phrase (impersonal construction from importar).
additional_notes: Form comes from the verb importar used impersonally. Common structures: "(No) me importa el/ella..." or questions like "¿Te importa el horario?" Often appears with indirect object pronouns (me, te, le, nos, os, les): "Me importa el resultado." For asking permission or causing inconvenience, use "¿Te importa...?" + infinitive: "¿Te importa abrir la ventana?" Here, "importa el" specifically will be followed by a masculine singular noun (el + noun) or by a clause where el begins a noun phrase.
target_language_example: ¿Te importa el ruido de la calle?
native_language_example: Does the street noise bother you / does the street noise matter to you?

meaning: 'it matters in' or 'is important in' (used to say something is important within a place, situation, or context).
additional_notes: Commonly appears as part of a larger clause: importa en + lugar/ámbito/situación (e.g., 'Lo que importa en esta empresa...'). Can also be used impersonally with 'no importa en' to say something doesn't matter in a given context. More frequently, Spanish speakers use 'importa' alone (importa mucho) or the preposition 'para' (importa para) depending on meaning — 'importa en' emphasizes importance inside a specific setting.
target_language_example: Lo que realmente importa en este proyecto es la colaboración.
native_language_example: What really matters in this project is collaboration.

meaning: 'what matters is that' / 'the important thing is that'.
additional_notes: Used to introduce the main point or essential fact. Often appears as part of the fuller expression 'lo que importa es que' or 'lo que más importa es que'. Can be followed by a clause with indicative or subjunctive depending on meaning: subjunctive if expressing desire/uncertainty (e.g., 'lo que importa es que venga'), indicative for facts ('lo que importa es que está aquí').
target_language_example: Lo que importa es que llegaste sano y salvo.
native_language_example: What matters is that you arrived safe and sound.

meaning: it matters that / it's important that
additional_notes: Used to express that something is important or matters. Often followed by a subjunctive clause when introducing a hypothetical, desire, necessity, or value judgment (e.g., importa que + subjunctive). Can also appear in impersonal constructions: "Me importa que..." (It matters to me that...).
target_language_example: Me importa que llegues a tiempo.
native_language_example: It matters to me that you arrive on time.

meaning: 'it matters what' / 'what... matters' (used to emphasize that the specific thing is important)
additional_notes: Often appears in phrases like "no importa qué" (it doesn't matter what) or in questions/clauses to stress that the particular thing is important. Alone, "importa qué" is not a complete sentence; it usually connects with negation or other words (e.g., "¿Importa qué haga?" is uncommon—more natural: "¿Importa qué haga yo?" or better "¿Qué importa?" or "No importa qué..." ). Use with verbs or context to form full ideas.
target_language_example: No importa qué diga, yo seguiré con mi plan.
native_language_example: No matter what he/she says, I'll stick to my plan.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase; taken literally it would read 'it matters you' or 'you matter' depending on context, but as written it's ungrammatical or uncommon in natural Spanish.
additional_notes: This string is not a natural two-word expression in Spanish. The correct construction to express 'does it matter to you?' is '¿Te importa?' (using the clitic te before the verb) or '¿Le importa?' (formal). To say 'you care' one uses 'te importa' (with clitic) or 'te importa algo' (you care about something). 'Importa tu' can appear in nonstandard or poetic contexts where word order is altered for emphasis, but it is not recommended for everyday use. If intended as an imperative addressing 'tú', 'importa' is not used to mean 'care' — instead use 'préocupate' or the subjunctive 'que te importe'.
target_language_example: Si importa tu opinión, dímelo ahora.
native_language_example: If your opinion matters, tell me now.

meaning: 'it matters a' or 'does it matter a...?' (used to say something is important or to ask if it matters).
additional_notes: Commonly appears in expressions like 'no me importa' (I don't care) or '¿te importa...?' (do you mind?/does it matter to you?). 'Importa un' by itself is usually followed by a noun or phrase (e.g., 'importa un comino' — it doesn't matter at all). Can be used in affirmative statements ('me importa un...') or in questions ('¿te importa un... ?').
target_language_example: A ella le importa un comino lo que digan.
native_language_example: She couldn't care less about what they say.

meaning: I don't give a damn about / I don't care at all about
additional_notes: Very strong, vulgar expression used to say you totally don't care about something. It often appears as 'me importa una mierda (lo) que...' or 'le importa una mierda (lo) que...'. Use with caution (informal and rude). Can be directed at actions, opinions, facts, or situations.
target_language_example: Me importa una mierda lo que digan de mí.
native_language_example: I don't give a damn what they say about me.

meaning: 'importance of' or 'the importance of'.
additional_notes: Used to talk about how important something is. Typically followed by a noun, infinitive verb, or clause (e.g., importancia de la educación, importancia de estudiar, importancia de que vengas). Often appears in phrases like 'la importancia de...' to introduce a topic.
target_language_example: La importancia de dormir bien no se puede subestimar.
native_language_example: The importance of sleeping well cannot be underestimated.

meaning: 'the importance of the' (used to introduce what is considered important).
additional_notes: A common phrase to talk about the significance or value of something. Typically followed by a noun or noun phrase (e.g., importancia de la paz, importancia de la situación). Can be used in formal and informal contexts.
target_language_example: Entendemos la importancia de la educación.
native_language_example: We understand the importance of education.

meaning: as important as
additional_notes: Used to compare importance between two things. Usually appears in comparative structures: 'tan importante como' (as important as) or 'igual de importante que' are more common — 'importante como' on its own is incomplete and normally requires a preceding word (e.g., 'tan') or a full clause. Follow with the thing being compared (que + clause/noun).
target_language_example: Este tema es tan importante como el otro.
native_language_example: This topic is as important as the other one.

meaning: most important (of/of the).
additional_notes: Used to say something or someone is the most important within a group or context. Often appears as 'lo más importante (de/para/en...)' for abstract things ('the most important thing'), or as 'el/la miembro más importante de...' for people. 'De la' connects the superlative to a following noun or phrase (e.g. 'de la sala', 'de la familia').
target_language_example: Fue la decisión más importante de la empresa.
native_language_example: It was the company's most important decision.

meaning: important (part) of / important to the
additional_notes: This phrase combines 'importante' (important) with the preposition 'de' + definite article (el → del) to indicate that something is an important part/aspect of something else. Commonly used with 'parte' (part) or similar nouns: 'la parte más importante del trabajo' = 'the most important part of the work.'
target_language_example: La honestidad es una parte importante del éxito.
native_language_example: Honesty is an important part of success.

meaning: 'what's important is' / 'the important thing is'.
additional_notes: Usually appears as part of the fixed phrase 'Lo importante es...' or 'Lo más importante es...'. Used to introduce the main point, conclusion, or priority. Followed by an infinitive, noun phrase, clause, or question word (e.g., 'estar...', 'la capacidad...', 'en qué...').
target_language_example: Lo más importante es ayudar a los demás.
native_language_example: The most important thing is to help others.

meaning: 'the important thing is that' / 'what matters is that'.
additional_notes: Used to introduce the main point or conclusion; often appears as 'Lo importante es que...' or strengthened as 'Lo más importante es que...'. Followed by a clause (subordinate) explaining what matters. Common in both formal and informal contexts.
target_language_example: Lo importante es que llegaste a tiempo.
native_language_example: The important thing is that you arrived on time.

meaning: 'it's important not to' / 'it's important that you do not' (used to warn, advise against, or stress that something must not be done)
additional_notes: Often used to introduce a prohibition or strong caution. It can appear at the start of a sentence or clause and is typically followed by an infinitive, a clause with que, or a directive. Tone may be formal or neutral depending on context; punctuation (colon, comma) or capitalization may vary (e.g., “Importante: no…” or “importante no…”).
target_language_example: Importante no compartir tu contraseña con nadie.
native_language_example: Important: do not share your password with anyone.

meaning: the important thing is not... (used to downplay one thing and emphasize another).
additional_notes: Often appears as part of the phrase 'Lo importante no es... sino...' or 'Lo más importante no es... sino...'. Use it to contrast two ideas: the first (introduced after 'no es') is being dismissed, and the second (after 'sino' or 'sino que') is presented as what truly matters. Common in moral or evaluative statements.
target_language_example: Lo importante no es tener mucho dinero, sino ser feliz.
native_language_example: The important thing is not having a lot of money, but being happy.

meaning: more important than the
additional_notes: Used in comparisons with 'más' (más importante que el/la/los/las) to say that one thing is more important than another. 'El' agrees with a masculine singular noun; change to 'la', 'los' or 'las' as needed. Can also appear without 'más' in constructions like 'más importante que...' and in phrases emphasizing importance (e.g., 'más importante aún').
target_language_example: Para mí, la salud es más importante que el dinero.
native_language_example: For me, health is more important than money.

meaning: how important something is; the importance of something.
additional_notes: Used in clauses like 'sé/ sabes/ no sabes lo importante que es...' to emphasize the degree of importance of an event, thing, or situation for someone. Typical verbs: saber, no saber, recordar, entender. Often followed by 'para' + person/thing (para mí, para la escuela). Word order in Spanish: 'lo importante que es' corresponds to English 'how important it is'.
target_language_example: No sabes lo importante que es para la familia.
native_language_example: You don't know how important it is for the family.

meaning: to care about it; for it to matter (to someone).
additional_notes: This construction combines the verb importar ('to matter' or 'to be important') with the direct object pronoun lo ('it'). Use it when saying that something matters or someone cares about a thing. The person affected is expressed with an indirect object pronoun (me/te/le/nos/les). Verb agreement is with the thing that matters (often third person singular/plural). Common short reply: "No me importa (lo)" — "I don't care (about it)."
target_language_example: A Juan no le importa lo que pase, pero a María sí le importa lo.
native_language_example: Juan doesn't care what happens, but Maria does care about it.

meaning: to not care at all (strong, vulgar).
additional_notes: Very informal and vulgar Spanish expression used to say someone doesn't care even a little. Equivalent to 'to not give a damn' or 'to not give a shit.' Used in spoken language; avoid in formal contexts. Often appears in negative constructions (no me importa un carajo = I don't give a damn).
target_language_example: A él no le importa un carajo lo que piensen los demás.
native_language_example: He doesn't give a damn about what others think.

meaning: impossible to / unable to be (followed by an infinitive or past participle).
additional_notes: Used before an infinitive or past participle to say something cannot be done. Common structure: 'imposible de + [infinitive]' or 'imposible de + [past participle]'. Often interchangeable with simply 'imposible' + 'de' can be omitted in some varieties (e.g., 'imposible resolver' vs. 'imposible de resolver').
target_language_example: Ese objeto es imposible de mover sin ayuda.
native_language_example: That object is impossible to move without help.

meaning: 'impression of' or 'feeling that' (a sense or perception about someone or something).
additional_notes: Used to describe a subjective perception, opinion, or feeling formed about a person, situation, or action. Often followed by a noun, an infinitive, or a clause introduced by que or haber (e.g., impresión de que, impresión de haber + past participle). Common in phrases like "dar la impresión de" (to give the impression of).
target_language_example: Ella me dio la impresión de saberlo todo.
native_language_example: She gave me the impression of knowing everything.

meaning: the impression that / the feeling that
additional_notes: Used to express a subjective perception or sense about a situation. Commonly followed by a clause introduced by 'que' (impresión de que + [clause]). Can be used with verbs like 'tener' (tener la impresión de que) or on its own (dar/causar impresión de que).
target_language_example: Tengo la impresión de que va a llover.
native_language_example: I have the impression that it's going to rain.

meaning: fire in / fire at (a location).
additional_notes: Used to say that a fire is happening in or at a specific place. Followed by a noun or location (incendio en la cocina, incendio en el edificio, incendio en la fábrica). Can refer to accidental or intentional fires; for news or emergency reports you might also see 'incendio forestal' (wildfire) or 'fuego en'.
target_language_example: Hubo un incendio en el edificio anoche.
native_language_example: There was a fire in the building last night.

meaning: leaned/bent over and (then)...
additional_notes: Combines the verb inclinar(se) in the past (se inclinó = he/she leaned/bent over) with y to link a second action that happened immediately after. Commonly used to describe physically bending toward something or someone and then doing another short action (e.g., kiss, pick up). Use se inclinó (reflexive) for someone bending their body; can also appear as inclinó without se in non-reflexive contexts.
target_language_example: Ella se inclinó y recogió el libro del suelo.
native_language_example: She leaned over and picked up the book from the floor.

meaning: even to / even at (used to add a surprising or emphatic example following a verb or preposition).
additional_notes: incluso means 'even' or 'including'. When followed by the preposition a, 'incluso a' introduces a surprising person, place, moment, or institution that receives the action: e.g. 'incluso a mi abuela' (even my grandmother) or 'incluso a las cinco' (even at five). It often emphasizes contrast or an unexpected example. Word order can vary: 'incluso a' usually comes before the noun or phrase it emphasizes.
target_language_example: Trajeron regalos, incluso a los vecinos.
native_language_example: They brought gifts, even to the neighbors.

meaning: even/of (used to emphasize or add an example related to something)
additional_notes: incluso means 'even' and often precedes a noun, pronoun or clause to add emphasis or include an unexpected example. When followed by de, it links that emphasis to a noun phrase introduced by de (e.g., 'incluso de mi familia' = 'even from my family'). This combination is less common than 'incluso' alone and appears when specifying origin, source, material, or relation with 'de'.
target_language_example: No esperaba ayuda, incluso de mis vecinos.
native_language_example: I didn't expect help, even from my neighbors.

meaning: even (to) me; used to emphasize that the speaker was also affected or included.
additional_notes: Placed before a verb or clause to stress that the action or description also applied to the speaker. 'Incluso' means 'even' and 'me' is the indirect/direct object pronoun 'me'. Can appear as 'incluso me [verb]' or 'él/ella incluso me [verb]'.
target_language_example: Incluso me dijeron que no volvería a encontrar trabajo.
native_language_example: They even told me I would never find a job again.

meaning: 'even I' or 'even me' — used to add the speaker as an unexpected or notable example.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that the speaker, as well as others, did or felt something — often to express surprise, contrast, or inclusivity. Can appear alone as a short response ("Incluso yo.") or inside a sentence. Tone can be neutral or emphatic depending on context.
target_language_example: Incluso yo fui a la fiesta, aunque llegué tarde.
native_language_example: Even I went to the party, although I arrived late.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase by itself; 'increíble' = 'incredible' or 'unbelievable', and 'de' = 'of/from' or a connector. Together they are usually part of a larger expression and need context (e.g., 'increíble de ver', 'increíble de verdad').
additional_notes: Alone, 'increíble de' is incomplete in Spanish. It commonly appears as the start of a clause or a colloquial expression (e.g., 'increíble de verdad', 'increíble de ver'). More natural alternatives include using 'es increíble', 'increíble pero cierto', or adding a verb or qualifier after 'de' (e.g., 'increíble de ver', 'increíble de creer'). Beginners should treat 'increíble' as the core adjective and expect 'de' to link to further information.
target_language_example: Es increíble de ver lo rápido que creció el barrio.
native_language_example: It's incredible to see how quickly the neighborhood grew.

meaning: an exclamation meaning 'that's incredible' or 'unbelievable' (colloquial).
additional_notes: Used as a short, emphatic reaction to express surprise or amazement. Often appears spoken and informal; word order emphasizes the adjective (increíble) before the neutral pronoun lo. You can use it alone as a response or followed by a short comment. Similar to '¡increíble!' or 'no me lo puedo creer.'
target_language_example: —¿Viste el truco? —¡Increíble lo!
native_language_example: —Did you see the trick? —That's unbelievable!

meaning: expresses surprise, disbelief or admiration about something (followed by a subjunctive clause).
additional_notes: Often used with the subjunctive after "que" to comment on a situation (Es increíble que + subjunctive). Can express positive admiration or shock. Sometimes used alone as an exclamation (Increíble que...). In casual speech the indicative may appear, but subjunctive is standard when introducing a dependent clause of emotion or judgment.
target_language_example: Es increíble que hayas aprendido tanto en tan poco tiempo.
native_language_example: It's incredible that you've learned so much in such a short time.

meaning: information in / information on (used before a language, format, topic, or location).
additional_notes: Usually followed by a noun indicating language, medium, topic or place: e.g. información en español (information in Spanish), información en línea (information online), información en la página web (information on the website). Preposition 'en' often corresponds to English 'in' or 'on' depending on context.
target_language_example: Necesito información en inglés sobre el trámite.
native_language_example: I need information in English about the procedure.

meaning: 'information is' — the phrase 'información' (information) followed by the verb 'es' (is).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom; it's simply the noun 'información' plus the third-person singular present of 'ser' (es). Used to make statements about information (e.g., qualities, status, ownership). Word order follows Spanish: noun + es + complement (e.g., 'La información es confidencial').
target_language_example: Esa información es importante para el proyecto.
native_language_example: That information is important for the project.

meaning: toward English; into English (used with verbs of translation or direction).
additional_notes: This phrase combines inglés (English) with the preposition a. It's used to indicate direction or target language after verbs like traducir (to translate) or pasar/convertir (to convert). In standard Spanish, the article is often included: al inglés (a + el) when a definite article is required. Using 'inglés a' without the article is uncommon in prescriptive Spanish but may appear in elliptical or informal constructions (e.g., listing languages: "de francés a inglés a español").
target_language_example: La tarea es pasar el texto de francés a inglés a la vez.
native_language_example: The task is to move the text from French to English at once.

meaning: 'English with' — used to indicate speaking or learning English together with someone or using English plus something/someone.
additional_notes: Commonly appears before a person or method: e.g. 'inglés con María' (English with María) meaning lessons or practice sessions led by María. Can indicate language plus another element (e.g. 'inglés con subtítulos' = English with subtitles). Word order: 'inglés con X'. Context determines whether it means 'taking English lessons with' or simply 'English accompanied by'.
target_language_example: Voy a practicar inglés con Ana esta tarde.
native_language_example: I'm going to practice English with Ana this afternoon.

meaning: literally 'English with a...', used when starting a phrase like 'English with a ...' (incomplete fragment).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself — it's a fragment that would continue with a noun or adjective (e.g., inglés con un acento fuerte = 'English with a strong accent'). Use it to describe a characteristic of someone's English. Make sure to complete the phrase with the appropriate noun or adjective.
target_language_example: Habla inglés con un acento británico.
native_language_example: He/She speaks English with a British accent.

meaning: 'English is' (the phrase formed by the noun/adjective inglés + the verb es 'is').
additional_notes: This is not a fixed expression—it's simply the word inglés (meaning 'English' as a language or as an adjective) followed by the verb es (third-person singular of ser). Use it when describing something about English: e.g. "El inglés es difícil" (English is difficult) or when identifying someone's language: "Mi idioma es el inglés". Pay attention to gender/number: inglés (m.) / inglesa (f.), and when used as a noun you may add the definite article: el inglés.
target_language_example: El inglés es mi asignatura favorita.
native_language_example: English is my favorite subject.

meaning: 'English is a...' (start of a sentence saying what English is)
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but a fragment: the noun inglés (with lowercase i) means the English language or an English person depending on context. es un is the structure 'is a' used before a masculine singular noun. You'll usually see a complete sentence like 'El inglés es un idioma difícil' ('English is a difficult language') or 'El inglés es un idioma internacional.' Make sure to include the article (el/mi) when referring to the language: 'El inglés es...' For speaking about someone who is English, use 'es inglés' (without article) or 'es un inglés' (less common, 'a/the Englishman').
target_language_example: El inglés es un idioma útil hoy en día.
native_language_example: English is a useful language nowadays.

meaning: better English (usually meaning improved English skills).
additional_notes: Literally 'English better.' Not a fixed phrase — it's typically part of a larger sentence like 'hablar un inglés mejor' or 'mejorar mi inglés'. Alone it sounds informal/elliptical; native speakers would usually say 'mejor inglés' (better English) or 'inglés más avanzado' (more advanced English). Use to talk about improving quality or level of English.
target_language_example: Quiero hablar un inglés mejor para el trabajo.
native_language_example: I want to speak better English for work.

meaning: 'not English' or 'no English' — used to say someone does not speak English or that something is not in English.
additional_notes: This short phrase appears in contexts like signs, quick replies or notes to indicate absence of English language ability or that materials are not available in English. In natural sentences you would usually see it expanded (e.g., 'No hablo inglés' = I don't speak English, or 'No hay versión en inglés' = There is no English version). Alone, 'inglés no' is a terse label, not a full grammatical sentence.
target_language_example: Lo siento, inglés no; hablo solo español.
native_language_example: Sorry, no English; I only speak Spanish.

meaning: 'English by' — used when introducing the person who speaks or translates into English, or to indicate the language used (often followed by a name or agent).
additional_notes: Common in labels, book credits, subtitles, or event listings: e.g. «Versión en inglés por Juan» (English version by Juan) or «Conferencia, inglés por la Dra. Smith» (Talk — English by Dr. Smith). Not a standalone fixed phrase; it requires a following noun (person, medium) or context. Word order: 'inglés' names the language; 'por' marks the agent/means.
target_language_example: Artículo en español; inglés por Marta.
native_language_example: Article in Spanish; English by Marta.

meaning: 'English that' or the phrase '... English that ...' used when describing a type/level/feature of English or introducing a clause about English.
additional_notes: This combination is not a fixed phrase on its own; it pairs the noun inglés (English) with the relative conjunction que (that/who/which). You will see it in sentences like "un inglés que habla rápido" (an Englishman/English person who speaks fast) or "un nivel de inglés que me permite trabajar" (an English level that allows me to work). Context determines whether inglés refers to the language, a person from England, or someone's English ability.
target_language_example: Necesito un curso de inglés que sea práctico.
native_language_example: I need an English course that is practical.

meaning: 'inglés' = English (language or adjective); 'se' = a clitic pronoun used for reflexive, impersonal/passive, or accidental constructions. Together they are not a fixed phrase and typically appear as part of a larger structure where word order matters.
additional_notes: This is not a set expression. 'inglés' is a noun/adjective; 'se' is a versatile pronoun. The sequence 'inglés se' can occur inside a sentence (e.g., when a clause ends with 'inglés' and the next clause begins with 'se'), but in standard impersonal passive constructions the correct order is 'se + verb + sujeto' (e.g., 'se habla inglés'). If you see 'inglés se' written together, check surrounding words — it may be a line break, punctuation, or part of a different clause (e.g., '...inglés. Se...').
target_language_example: En la puerta está escrito "inglés se solicita" por error.
native_language_example: On the door it is written "inglés se solicita" by mistake.

meaning: Not a standard Spanish phrase; literal reading would be 'English all' but it's ungrammatical. Likely intended meanings: 'all English (people/items)' → 'todos los ingleses', or 'English for everyone' → 'inglés para todos'.
additional_notes: This combination 'inglés todos' is not natural in Spanish because adjectives/articles and pluralization are required. Possible correct alternatives: 'todos los ingleses' (all English people), 'todo el inglés' (all of the English language), 'inglés para todos' (English for everyone). Word order and articles matter: 'todos' normally precedes a masculine plural noun phrase with an article: 'todos los ...'.
target_language_example: No digas "inglés todos"; en su lugar di "inglés para todos" o "todos los ingleses" cuando sea apropiado.
native_language_example: Don't say "inglés todos"; instead say "inglés para todos" or "todos los ingleses" when appropriate.

meaning: likely a mistaken or incomplete phrase; appears to combine 'inglés' (English) with 'todos los' (all the).
additional_notes: This sequence is not a standard fixed phrase in Spanish by itself. It looks like parts of a sentence, for example: 'inglés todos los días' (English every day) or 'el inglés, todos los estudiantes...' (English, all the...). As written it is ungrammatical/incomplete and needs more words to form a clear meaning. For learners: watch word order and agreement — 'todos los' must be followed by a masculine plural noun (e.g., 'días', 'alumnos').
target_language_example: Estudio inglés todos los días.
native_language_example: I study English every day.

meaning: 'English and' — the word inglés (English) followed by the conjunction y (and).
additional_notes: This is simply the noun inglés (the English language) immediately followed by y (and). It appears when listing languages or items (e.g., "inglés y francés" = "English and French"). Make sure to match gender/number if needed for other words (e.g., el inglés, la profesora de inglés). The phrase itself is compositional and literal.
target_language_example: Hablo inglés y alemán.
native_language_example: I speak English and German.

meaning: 'beginning of' or 'start of'.
additional_notes: Used before a noun to indicate the beginning/start of something (an event, period, era, course, season, etc.). Common in formal and neutral contexts. Followed by a noun: inicio de + [noun].
target_language_example: El inicio de las clases es el lunes.
native_language_example: The start of classes is on Monday.

meaning: innocent of (not guilty of / not responsible for something).
additional_notes: Used to say someone is not guilty or not responsible for a specific act or charge. Commonly follows with the thing/person: "inocente de + noun/infinitive/charges" (e.g., inocente de homicidio, inocente de hacer trampa). Often used in legal contexts but also in everyday denial.
target_language_example: Ella declaró que era inocente de los cargos.
native_language_example: She declared she was innocent of the charges.

meaning: musical instrument.
additional_notes: Used to refer to any device or object played to produce music (e.g., piano, guitar, flute, trumpet). Can be used generally or to name a specific instrument: 'un instrumento musical' = a musical instrument; 'mi instrumento musical favorito' = my favorite musical instrument.
target_language_example: La guitarra es un instrumento musical muy popular.
native_language_example: The guitar is a very popular musical instrument.

meaning: artificial intelligence (AI).
additional_notes: Refers to computer systems or software that perform tasks requiring human-like intelligence (learning, reasoning, pattern recognition). Used in technical and everyday contexts. Can be abbreviated as 'IA' in Spanish.
target_language_example: La empresa utiliza inteligencia artificial para mejorar las recomendaciones.
native_language_example: The company uses artificial intelligence to improve recommendations.

meaning: 'intelligence is' — used to define or describe what intelligence is.
additional_notes: This is the phrase 'inteligencia' (intelligence) followed by the verb 'es' (is). It's typically used to introduce a definition or a statement about intelligence. Use it to state general truths or opinions about what intelligence consists of. Formal/informal neutral.
target_language_example: La inteligencia es saber escuchar antes de hablar.
native_language_example: Intelligence is knowing how to listen before speaking.

meaning: as intelligent as / intelligent like (used in comparisons)
additional_notes: Used to compare intelligence (or follow the pattern 'tan + adjective + como' = 'as ... as'). Can appear in positive comparisons (tan inteligente como = as intelligent as) or in structures like 'demasiado ... como para' meaning 'too ... to'. Word order: 'tan inteligente como X' or 'inteligente como X'.
target_language_example: No soy tan inteligente como tú.
native_language_example: I'm not as intelligent as you.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase in Spanish; appears to be an incomplete fragment combining the adjective 'inteligente' (intelligent) with the preposition 'de' (of/about). Its interpretation depends on the larger context or phrase it belongs to.
additional_notes: 'Inteligente' normally appears with verbs (ser inteligente), adjectives modifiers (muy inteligente), or with prepositions like 'en' (inteligente en algo) or constructions such as 'inteligente para' (smart enough to). 'Inteligente de' could appear as part of a longer expression (e.g., 'inteligente de verdad' — colloquial for 'really intelligent', though 'de verdad' commonly follows many adjectives) or in appositive structures ('inteligente de su generación' — 'the smartest of his generation'). Alone, 'inteligente de' is not a fixed phrase and may signal a missing noun or clause.
target_language_example: Ella es la más inteligente de la clase.
native_language_example: She is the most intelligent in the class.

meaning: to try (doing something) — used with a verb or action phrase.
additional_notes: Often appears as intentarlo + de + infinitive or intentarlo + a + [verb/infinitive] depending on region; more common, neutral Spanish uses 'intentarlo' alone or 'intentar + infinitive' (e.g., 'intentarlo de nuevo' = try it again). 'Intentarlo de' by itself is incomplete and needs the rest of the phrase (e.g., 'intentarlo de nuevo', 'intentarlo de otra manera').
target_language_example: Voy a intentarlo de nuevo mañana.
native_language_example: I'm going to try it again tomorrow.

meaning: he/she/you (formal) tried to open (past).
additional_notes: From the verb intentar (to try) in the preterite (intentó) + abrir (to open). Used to describe a completed attempt in the past by one person (él/ella/usted). Can be followed by objects (una puerta, la ventana) or infinitives (intentar abrir la caja).
target_language_example: Ella intentó abrir la puerta, pero estaba cerrada con llave.
native_language_example: She tried to open the door, but it was locked.

meaning: tried to open the (feminine noun).
additional_notes: From intentar + abrir + la (feminine definite article). Used to say someone attempted to open something feminine (la puerta, la caja, la ventana...). The verb intentó is past (preterite) third-person singular or formal 'usted'. For other subjects change intentó → intenté, intentaste, intentamos, intentaron. If the noun is masculine use 'el' instead of 'la' (e.g., intentó abrir el cajón).
target_language_example: Él intentó abrir la puerta, pero no pudo.
native_language_example: He tried to open the door, but he couldn't.

meaning: tried to (do something) in/at (a place or time) — 'intentó' is past of 'intentar'; 'en' introduces location, time or context.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but two words that often appear together: 'intentó' (he/she/you formal tried) + 'en' (in, at, on). Use 'intentó' before an infinitive or an action, and 'en' to specify where, when, or in what context the attempt happened. Example structures: 'intentó en + lugar' (tried in the park), 'intentó en + año' (tried in 2010) or 'intentó en + actividad' (tried in the exercise). If you mean 'tried to [verb]', use 'intentó + infinitive' (no 'en'): e.g. 'intentó abrir la puerta.'
target_language_example: Ella intentó en la escuela aprender francés, pero le costó trabajo.
native_language_example: She tried at school to learn French, but it was hard for her.

meaning: '(something) interests (someone)' — used to say someone is interested in a subject or thing.
additional_notes: This is a common construction with the verb interesar, which works like 'gustar': the thing that interests is the subject and the person is expressed with an indirect object (me, te, le, nos, os, les). Here 'la' is the feminine singular definite article before a feminine noun (la geografía, la política, la música). To say what interests someone, use: (A + person) + indirect object pronoun + interesa(n) + article + noun. Use interesa (singular) for one thing, interesan (plural) for multiple things.
target_language_example: A Juan le interesa la historia.
native_language_example: Juan is interested in history.

meaning: interesting to (someone) / interesting about (something)
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself; 'interesante' is an adjective meaning 'interesting' and is often followed by prepositions like 'para' (interesting for/to) or 'de' (interesting about/of) depending on context. 'Interesante de' commonly appears when introducing a comment about a detail: e.g. 'Lo interesante de esto es...' = 'The interesting thing about this is...'. For basic use, prefer 'interesante para' (interesting to) when indicating who finds something interesting.
target_language_example: Lo interesante de la historia es el final inesperado.
native_language_example: The interesting thing about the story is the unexpected ending.

meaning: literally 'interesting in'; not a standard fixed phrase in Spanish — could appear in constructions where 'interesante' modifies a clause introduced by 'en' (though often sounds odd). Usually replaced by 'interesado en' (interested in) or 'es interesante (que/para/porque...)'.
additional_notes: 'Interesante en' is not commonly used as a set phrase. You might encounter it in sentences like 'es interesante en...' when a speaker is influenced by literal translation from another language or in regional/colloquial uses, but prefer alternatives: 'interesado en' for someone being interested, or 'es interesante' + preposition or clause for describing something as interesting. Examples here use 'interesante en' to show possible contexts, but they can sound awkward or nonstandard.
target_language_example: Es interesante en la novela cómo el autor trata el tema de la identidad.
native_language_example: It is interesting in the novel how the author treats the theme of identity.

meaning: "interesting that" or used in superlative phrases: "the most interesting that..."
additional_notes: Commonly appears in comparative/superlative constructions (e.g., "la cosa más interesante que..."). Introduces a clause giving what is interesting; often followed by a relative clause with verbs in indicative or subjunctive depending on tense/mood. Not an idiom—literal meaning.
target_language_example: Es la experiencia más interesante que he tenido este año.
native_language_example: It's the most interesting experience I've had this year.

meaning: 'interesting and' — used to link two adjectives or qualities, both describing the same noun or situation.
additional_notes: Commonly appears before a second adjective (e.g., interesante y entretenido). Use to join characteristics; in Spanish the second adjective must agree in gender/number with the noun when applicable. This phrase is literal and neutral (not slang).
target_language_example: El libro es interesante y fácil de leer.
native_language_example: The book is interesting and easy to read.

meaning: was interested in / became interested in (someone or something).
additional_notes: Past tense of interesarse por (to be/become interested in). Used to say that a person showed interest in a topic, person, or thing. Typically appears as reflexive 'se interesó por' for third person. Commonly followed by a noun or noun phrase.
target_language_example: Se interesó por la fotografía después de un curso.
native_language_example: He/She became interested in photography after a course.

meaning: the inside of / interior of (something).
additional_notes: Used to describe the inner part or inside area of a place or object. Followed by a noun (e.g., interior de la casa, interior del carro). When the following noun is masculine and uses the article 'el', 'de el' contracts to 'del' (e.g., interior del coche).
target_language_example: El interior de la iglesia era muy tranquilo.
native_language_example: The inside of the church was very quiet.

meaning: the inside of the (feminine noun).
additional_notes: Use before a feminine singular noun to say 'the interior/inside of the ...'. 'Interior' refers to inner space or interior part. For masculine nouns you'd say 'interior del'. Can be used for houses, caves, rooms, etc.
target_language_example: El interior de la casa necesita una pintura nueva.
native_language_example: The inside of the house needs a new paint job.

meaning: Try it again (informal, spoken) — short for 'inténtalo otra vez'.
additional_notes: This is an informal, colloquial contraction of 'inténtalo otra vez' meaning 'try it again'. Used with tú (informal 'you'). Common in spoken Spanish; in writing prefer the full phrase. You can also hear 'intenta otra' or 'inténtalo de nuevo' as alternatives.
target_language_example: Si fallaste, inténtalo otra; seguro puedes hacerlo.
native_language_example: If you failed, try it again; you can do it.

meaning: investigation of / research into
additional_notes: Used to indicate the subject or focus of an investigation or research. Common with crimes (investigación de homicidio = homicide investigation) and with scientific or academic work (investigación de SIDA = AIDS research). Followed by a noun or a person's name. In English you may often translate it as "investigation into" or "research on."
target_language_example: La investigación de fraude continúa.
native_language_example: The investigation of fraud continues.

meaning: private investigator; private detective (a person hired to investigate matters privately).
additional_notes: Used to refer to someone who conducts investigations for individuals or companies outside of law enforcement. Can be used with or without the article (un/soy). Gender changes for speakers: investigador (male) / investigadora (female).
target_language_example: Contraté a un investigador privado para que encontrara información sobre el caso.
native_language_example: I hired a private investigator to find information about the case.

meaning: investigating the (masculine noun).
additional_notes: Present participle (investigando) + definite article el. Used to say someone is investigating a specific masculine noun (el accidente, el asesinato, el asunto, el suceso). The gender matters: use 'la' for feminine nouns (p. ej. 'investigando la causa'). Common in news and police contexts.
target_language_example: La policía está investigando el incendio.
native_language_example: The police are investigating the fire.

meaning: ‘winter is’ — used to describe characteristics or opinions about winter.
additional_notes: A phrase combining the noun invierno (winter) with the verb ser (es). Use to state facts (El invierno es frío), opinions (El invierno es mi estación favorita), or general qualities. Can be followed by adjectives, noun phrases (mi estación favorita), or clauses introduced by que (Lo bueno del invierno es que...).
target_language_example: El invierno es tranquilo en esta ciudad.
native_language_example: Winter is quiet in this city.

meaning: an invitation from (someone) or to (an event) — 'invitación' = invitation; 'de' links the inviter or source.
additional_notes: Use 'invitación de' to indicate who sent the invitation or who the invitation is from (e.g., 'invitación de casamiento' = wedding invitation; 'invitación de su majestad' = an invitation from His/Her Majesty). Word order and context determine whether 'de' introduces the event (type of invitation) or the person/authority sending it. For specifying the recipient (invited person) use 'invitado' or other constructions.
target_language_example: Recibí una invitación de la embajada para la inauguración.
native_language_example: I received an invitation from the embassy for the opening.

meaning: they invited (someone) to the (feminine) ... (e.g., party).
additional_notes: Form: past (preterite) third-person plural of invitar + a + feminine definite article la. Used to say 'they invited (her/me/you) to the [feminine noun]' — for example, 'la fiesta' (the party). The direct object (person) can be expressed as a clitic (me, le) or with a relative pronoun (al que/la que) to indicate who was (not) invited. For masculine nouns use 'invitaron al' (a + el).
target_language_example: Nos invitaron a la celebración del sábado.
native_language_example: They invited us to the celebration on Saturday.

meaning: go to
additional_notes: Used to talk about moving toward a place or event: ir a Madrid, ir a la boda. Before el, a contracts to al: ir al cine. It can also be followed by an infinitive to mean 'be going to' do something (for example, voy a comer), but that is a different use.
target_language_example: Queremos ir a la playa mañana.
native_language_example: We want to go to the beach tomorrow.

meaning: to go to some (place)/to go somewhere.
additional_notes: Common way to say 'go somewhere' in Spanish. 'Algún' is an adjective used before masculine singular nouns (algún lado/sitio/lugar). Use 'alguna' for feminine (alguna parte). Often appears with words like 'lado', 'sitio', 'lugar', 'sitio', 'lado' or 'parte'. In questions or offers it expresses a nonspecific destination. For a noun after it, place 'algún' before the noun: 'ir a algún lugar'.
target_language_example: ¿Quieres ir a algún sitio esta tarde?
native_language_example: Do you want to go somewhere this afternoon?

meaning: to go get
additional_notes: Common phrase meaning to go somewhere to retrieve or pick up a person or object. Often followed by the thing or person being fetched (ir a buscar + [objeto/persona]). Can be used for errands (e.g., go pick up my laptop) or for picking someone up (e.g., go get you).
target_language_example: Voy a ir a buscar las llaves al coche.
native_language_example: I'm going to go get the keys from the car.

meaning: to go to speak (to someone) / to go and talk
additional_notes: Commonly used to say you are going somewhere specifically to speak with someone or to have a conversation. Often followed by the person or place: ir a hablar con + person, ir a hablar de + topic. Uses the verb ir + a + infinitive (near future or purpose).
target_language_example: Voy a ir a hablar con mi jefe sobre el proyecto.
native_language_example: I'm going to go and talk to my boss about the project.

meaning: to go to my (followed by a noun) — indicates movement toward something or someplace that belongs to the speaker.
additional_notes: Composed of the verb ir (to go) + the preposition a (to) + the possessive mi (my). It must be completed by a noun or place (e.g., ir a mi casa, ir a mi trabajo). In natural speech speakers sometimes omit the possessive when ownership is clear (e.g., ir a casa). Use mi before a noun: mi coche, mi habitación, mi oficina.
target_language_example: Tengo que ir a mi casa ahora.
native_language_example: I have to go to my house now.

meaning: to go to (a) Mass; to attend a Catholic church service.
additional_notes: Common phrase in Spanish-speaking countries for attending the Catholic Mass. Can be used literally (physically going to church) or more loosely (attending a religious service). Often used with subjects and time expressions: voy a misa (I'm going to Mass), fue a misa ayer (he/she went to Mass yesterday). Not typically used for non-Catholic services (use 'ir a la iglesia' for general 'go to church' or specify the denomination).
target_language_example: Mañana voy a misa temprano, así que no podré ir al trabajo.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I am going to Mass early, so I won't be able to go to work.

meaning: to end up (somewhere or in a situation); to come to a stop
additional_notes: Commonly used to describe where someone or something ends up unexpectedly or as a result: physical place (end up at a café), situation (end up unemployed), or a sudden stop (vehicle comes to a halt). Often followed by 'a' + noun/place or 'en' + noun. Can be interchangeable with 'acabar' or 'terminar' in many contexts.
target_language_example: Después de la fiesta fuimos a caminar y acabamos por ir a parar a un bar abierto.
native_language_example: After the party we went for a walk and ended up at an open bar.

meaning: to go and fetch or pick up (someone or something).
additional_notes: Common Spanish construction meaning to go somewhere with the purpose of getting or collecting a person or thing. Often used with people (ir a por mi hermano) or objects (ir a por la paga). More common in Spain; in some regions speakers might simply say ir a buscar or ir por. The preposition combination 'a por' emphasizes purpose of going to obtain.
target_language_example: Voy a ir a por las llaves al coche.
native_language_example: I'm going to go and get the keys from the car.

meaning: to be going to be (used as the periphrastic future with 'ser' to indicate that something will become or will be)
additional_notes: 'Ir a' + infinitive expresses near future or planned outcome (equivalent to English 'going to'). With 'ser' it indicates what something/someone will be or become. Conjugate 'ir' as needed (voy a ser, vas a ser, va a ser, vamos a ser, van a ser). Can be used for predictions, planned states, or expectations.
target_language_example: Creo que va a ser difícil, pero puede que vaya a ser mejor de lo que pensamos — si todo sale bien, puede ir a ser algo grande.
native_language_example: I think it's going to be difficult, but it might turn out to be better than we think — if everything goes well, it could become something big.

meaning: to go to see a (feminine noun) — used to indicate going somewhere with the purpose of seeing or watching something feminine (e.g., una película, una exposición, una amiga).
additional_notes: Construction = ir (to go) + a + ver (to see) + feminine article 'una' + feminine noun. Common in spoken and written Spanish to express future plan or intention. The following noun must be feminine. No contraction of 'a' with verbs. Can be used with different subjects and tenses (e.g., Voy a ver una…, Vamos a ver una…).
target_language_example: Mañana voy a ir a ver una exposición en el museo.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I'm going to go see an exhibition at the museum.

meaning: to get to the point; to be direct.
additional_notes: Used when someone wants to skip small talk or unnecessary details and speak directly about the main issue. Common in both formal and informal contexts. Literally 'go to the grain' but idiomatic meaning is 'go straight to the point.'
target_language_example: Bueno, voy a ir al grano: necesitamos más personal para el proyecto.
native_language_example: Okay, I'm going to get to the point: we need more staff for the project.

meaning: to go there (to that place).
additional_notes: Used to refer to going to a place that has already been mentioned or is understood from context. 'Allá' implies 'over there'—some distance from the speaker (can be farther or vague). In everyday speech, speakers may also say 'ir allí' (more neutral) or 'ir ahí' (closer).
target_language_example: No quiero ir allá hoy; hace mucho viento.
native_language_example: I don't want to go there today; it's very windy.

meaning: to go up; to go upstairs (or toward a higher place).
additional_notes: A combination of the verb ir (to go) + arriba (up). Commonly used to say someone is moving to a higher level, floor, or position. More natural forms include subir, subir arriba (redundant), or ir arriba/ir para arriba in some dialects. Use context to choose: 'ir arriba' often implies motion toward an upper area (e.g., upstairs, uphill).
target_language_example: Voy a ir arriba a buscar mi abrigo.
native_language_example: I'm going upstairs to get my coat.

meaning: to go well; to be fine or successful (about events, situations, or someone's performance).
additional_notes: Commonly used to talk about how things are progressing or the outcome of plans. Can describe situations (La reunión va bien / fue bien), someone's health or mood (¿Cómo vas? — Voy bien), or performance/ability (Le va bien en matemáticas). Often conjugated as 'va bien', 'fue bien', 'está yendo bien' or used in infinitive constructions like 'ir bien en' (+ subject).
target_language_example: Espero que todo vaya bien y que la reunión vaya bien para ti.
native_language_example: I hope everything goes well and that the meeting goes well for you.

meaning: go with
additional_notes: Commonly used to say someone accompanies someone else or that you will accompany them. Meaning can be 'go with' (leave together) or 'go along with' depending on context. With first-person expressions like "Hora de ir con mamá" it means 'go with mom' (accompany). With verbs of motion, 'ir con' conveys accompaniment; when reporting someone else's invitation/permission, it can mean 'go with her/him'. Informal register is neutral.
target_language_example: ¿Quieres ir con nosotros al concierto?
native_language_example: Do you want to go with us to the concert?

meaning: to go when (introduces the time or condition for going).
additional_notes: Combines the verb ir (to go) with the conjunction/relative adverb cuando (when). Used to indicate at what time or under what condition someone goes. Often followed by a clause or used in periphrastic constructions: ir cuando + [clause] or voy/iremos cuando + [clause]. Can appear with different tenses: "iré cuando llegue" (I'll go when I arrive) or in habitual contexts: "suelo ir cuando puedo" (I usually go when I can).
target_language_example: Voy a ir cuando termine el trabajo, pero prefiero ir cuando todos estén listos.
native_language_example: I'm going to go when I finish the work, but I prefer to go when everyone is ready.

meaning: to go ...ing
additional_notes: With activity nouns, ir de + noun means "go [activity]-ing" or "go on a/an [activity] trip," as in ir de pesca or ir de acampada. With places, often in the pattern ir de X a Y, it means "go from X to Y."
target_language_example: Los domingos nos gusta ir de pesca al lago.
native_language_example: On Sundays we like to go fishing at the lake.

meaning: to go shopping.
additional_notes: Common expression used to say you're going to buy things (groceries, clothes, etc.). Uses the infinitive ir + de + compras. For specific shopping (e.g., groceries) you can say ir de compras al mercado or hacer la compra (Spain).
target_language_example: Vamos a ir de compras esta tarde.
native_language_example: We're going to go shopping this afternoon.

meaning: to go out partying; to go to a party or go clubbing/drinking with friends
additional_notes: Common informal expression used to describe going out for fun at parties, clubs, bars, or social gatherings. Conjugate the verb ir (voy, vas, va...) and optionally add destination: 'ir de fiesta' or 'ir de fiesta a casa de Ana'. Often used with 'salir' as a synonym (salir de fiesta).
target_language_example: Vamos a ir de fiesta este sábado por la noche.
native_language_example: We're going to go partying this Saturday night.

meaning: to go hand in hand; to be closely linked or happen together
additional_notes: Used figuratively to say two things are connected, accompany each other, or develop together. Can describe ideas, events, qualities or people acting in coordination. Not literal physical holding hands unless context indicates it.
target_language_example: La educación y el empleo suelen ir de la mano.
native_language_example: Education and employment often go hand in hand.

meaning: to go too far; to exceed limits (literally or figuratively).
additional_notes: Used both literally (to travel too far) and figuratively (to cross a boundary, be excessive, or behave unreasonably). Common in phrases like «no vayas demasiado lejos» (don't go too far) or «su comentario fue ir demasiado lejos» (his comment went too far).
target_language_example: No critiques así; vas a ir demasiado lejos.
native_language_example: Don't criticize like that; you're going too far.

meaning: to go toward; to head in the direction of; to move/aim toward (literal or figurative).
additional_notes: Used with physical directions (e.g., north, a person) or figurative goals (e.g., a style, an objective). Often followed by a noun, pronoun, or phrase indicating the target. In many contexts it can be replaced by ir a or dirigirse hacia; 'hacia' emphasizes direction or tendency.
target_language_example: Tenemos que ir hacia la salida antes de que empeore el clima.
native_language_example: We have to head toward the exit before the weather gets worse.

meaning: to go tomorrow.
additional_notes: A simple phrase combining the verb ir (to go) with mañana (tomorrow). Used to say you will go somewhere the next day or to suggest attending an event tomorrow. Tense/auxiliary can change (voy a ir, nos vamos a ir, puedo ir). Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Puedo ir mañana al mercado.
native_language_example: I can go to the market tomorrow.

meaning: to go to (a place) with the purpose of; in some varieties/informal contexts, to be about to or to go and (do something) when followed by an infinitive
additional_notes: Commonly used to indicate direction + purpose: ir para + lugar (e.g., voy para Madrid = I'm going to Madrid). In some regions, especially in informal speech, ir para + infinitive can mean 'to be about to' or 'to go and (do something)' (e.g., voy para decirte = I'm going to tell you / I'm about to tell you). More typical and neutral: use ir a + infinitive for 'going to (do something)'.
target_language_example: Mañana voy para la oficina temprano; voy para ver al jefe.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I'm going to the office early; I'm going to see the boss.

meaning: 'to go if' — the verb ir (to go) followed by the conjunction si (if).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase on its own; it's simply the verb ir used in a conditional structure with si. You will see it in sentences like "Voy a ir si..." (I'll go if...) or "Iremos si podemos" (We'll go if we can). Conjugate ir to match the subject and use si to introduce the condition. Common patterns: "(No) voy a ir si...", "Iremos si...", "Iba a ir si..."
target_language_example: Voy a ir si hace buen tiempo.
native_language_example: I'll go if the weather is good.

meaning: to be late / to arrive late
additional_notes: Common phrase used to say someone arrives after the expected or scheduled time. Can refer to people, events, or actions (e.g., llegar tarde). Often used with forms of ir (voy, vas, va, vamos, van) or the verb llegar: "voy a llegar tarde". Also used in impersonal constructions: "Se me hace tarde" (I'm running late).
target_language_example: Perdón, voy a ir tarde al trabajo.
native_language_example: Sorry, I'm going to be late for work.

meaning: to manage / get by (okay but not great)
additional_notes: Informal phrase used to say someone or something is coping, surviving, or functioning adequately. Often used about work, finances, health, or general situation. Common responses to '¿Cómo estás?' or '¿Qué tal?' — e.g., 'Voy tirando' = 'I'm getting by'.
target_language_example: No tengo mucho dinero, pero ir tirando es lo que hago.
native_language_example: I don't have much money, but I'm getting by.

meaning: to go and (do something); to go somewhere and then do another action immediately after
additional_notes: Common construction: ir + a/place omitted + y + verb (infinitive) or ir + y + infinitive following a verb phrase. Conveys going somewhere (explicit or understood) and then doing something there. In spoken Spanish, the structure is frequent (e.g., "voy a ir y verlo"). Not to be confused with the simple conjunction "y" between nouns. Use with infinitive after "y" (ir y + infinitive).
target_language_example: Voy a ir y ver la exposición mañana.
native_language_example: I'm going to go and see the exhibition tomorrow.

meaning: to come and go; to go back and forth freely
additional_notes: Used to describe moving between places repeatedly or having the freedom to leave and return at will. Often appears with verbs/phrases about permission or ability (puede, puedes, no puedes) and expressions like "a tu antojo" or "a voluntad" (as you wish/at will).
target_language_example: Puedes ir y venir cuando quieras durante las vacaciones.
native_language_example: You can come and go whenever you want during the vacation.

meaning: to go now / to leave immediately (emphatic; indicates urgency or impatience)
additional_notes: 'Ir ya' combines the verb ir (to go) with ya (already/now) to demand or urge immediate departure or action. In practice speakers use conjugated forms (véte ya, vete ya, ir ya in infinitive contexts) or alternative constructions (ve ya). Tone and context determine whether it's a command, request, or statement about imminent action. Common in spoken Spanish; often informal.
target_language_example: Tenemos que ir ya si queremos llegar a tiempo.
native_language_example: We have to go now if we want to arrive on time.

meaning: we will go (to do something) / we'll go for (an activity).
additional_notes: Iremos is the first-person plural future of ir (we will go). When followed by de + noun, it commonly expresses going somewhere to do an activity (iremos de fiesta = we'll go partying; iremos de picnic = we'll go for a picnic). With a place or pronoun after de, it can mean 'leave' or 'get out of' (nos iremos de aquí = we'll leave here). Context decides whether it's 'go to do X' or 'leave'.
target_language_example: Iremos de excursión el domingo si no llueve.
native_language_example: We'll go on a hike on Sunday if it doesn't rain.

meaning: 'we will go by' or 'we will go in' (indicates future travel using a mode or vehicle).
additional_notes: Iremos is the first-person plural future of ir (we will go). En indicates the mode, vehicle, time frame or location used to travel (e.g., en coche, en autobús, en una hora — note: 'en una hora' here means 'in one hour' as a time expression). Together it commonly expresses 'we will go by [transport]' or 'we will leave in [time]'. Context decides if en marks vehicle, direction, or timing.
target_language_example: Iremos en tren mañana por la mañana.
native_language_example: We will go by train tomorrow morning.

meaning: to go well for someone; to turn out well for someone
additional_notes: Used impersonally with an indirect object pronoun (me, te, le, nos, os, les) or a prepositional phrase (a mí, a ti, a él, etc.). Literally 'to go well to someone' — it describes how things are faring for a person or the outcome they experience. Common forms: "me va bien" (it's going well for me), "le fue bien" (it went well for him/her). Can refer to ongoing situations (va bien), general tendency (le suele ir bien), or past results (le fue bien).
target_language_example: A ella le va bien en el nuevo trabajo; realmente le está yendo bien — le va bien a ella.
native_language_example: The new job is going well for her; it's really working out — it's going well for her.

meaning: to leave for / to go to (somewhere); to go away to do something (often followed by a place or an infinitive).
additional_notes: Irse is a pronominal (reflexive) verb meaning 'to leave' or 'to go away'. When followed by a + place it indicates destination (irse a España = to leave for Spain). When followed by an infinitive (irse a + infinitive) it can mean 'to go and do something' or indicate a near-future action in some dialects. Conjugate irse with the appropriate reflexive pronoun (me voy, te vas, se fue, nos vamos).
target_language_example: Ella le pidió que se quedase, pero él tenía que irse a trabajar.
native_language_example: She asked him to stay, but he had to leave to go to work.

meaning: to go to bed
additional_notes: Reflexive construction (irse) conveys leaving/going away toward bed; commonly used to indicate it's time to end the day and lie down. Can imply actually sleeping or simply getting into bed to rest/read. 'Ir a la cama' (non-reflexive) is also used but 'irse a la cama' is very common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Es hora de irse a la cama.
native_language_example: It's time to go to bed.

meaning: to leave for / to go away to (a specific masculine singular place).
additional_notes: Combines the pronominal verb irse (to leave/go away) + al (a + el) to indicate leaving to or going away to a specific masculine singular place (e.g., 'irse al extranjero', 'irse al aeropuerto', 'irse al mar'). Use irse + a + lugar; if the place is feminine use 'irse a la' (irse a la playa).
target_language_example: Decidió irse al extranjero.
native_language_example: He decided to leave for (go away to) abroad.

meaning: to go to hell / to screw off; to leave angrily or tell someone off (vulgar).
additional_notes: A strong vulgar expression used to tell someone to go away or to say you're leaving in anger. Can be used reflexively (irse al carajo) to mean 'to get out' or 'to go to hell' oneself, or directed at someone with imperative forms (e.g., 'Vete al carajo'). Avoid in formal or polite contexts; consider milder alternatives like 'irse', 'largarse' or 'vete' in most situations.
target_language_example: Me cansé de sus mentiras y decidí irme al carajo.
native_language_example: I got tired of his lies and decided to go to hell / to leave angrily.

meaning: to leave (a place); to go away from
additional_notes: Reflexive verb irse + preposición de indicates leaving a location. Commonly used with places (irse de la fiesta, irse de casa, irse de aquí). Conjugate irse appropriately (me voy, te vas, se fue, nos iremos, etc.). Can be followed by a noun or pronoun naming the place being left. Often interchangeable with salir de in some contexts but irse emphasizes the subject's departure.
target_language_example: Tuvo que irse de casa.
native_language_example: He/She had to leave home.

meaning: won't go anywhere / will go nowhere (female/neutral subject implied by context)
additional_notes: A negative phrase: 'irá' is future of 'ir' (to go) and 'ninguna' is a feminine form of 'ninguno' (none/any). Usually appears as part of a longer sentence like 'no irá a ninguna parte' (won't go anywhere). By itself 'irá a ninguna' is incomplete and needs a noun or 'parte' after 'ninguna' or must agree in gender with that noun. For masculine nouns use 'ninguno' or 'ningún'.
target_language_example: Sin ayuda, esa idea no irá a ninguna parte.
native_language_example: Without help, that idea won't go anywhere.

meaning: will go (to)/will leave — future tense of 'ir' plus preposition 'de'; used to indicate that someone will go to an activity/place or will leave a place.
additional_notes: Often appears with verbs or noun phrases for activities (e.g., 'irá de compras', 'irá de picnic') or with reflexive 'irse' as 'se irá de' to mean 'will leave (a place)'. Context decides whether it expresses attending an activity or leaving. Can be used figuratively (e.g., 'se irá de las manos' = 'will get out of hand'). The phrase requires a subject and is usually followed by a noun, location, or activity.
target_language_example: Tom quiere saber cuándo Mary irá de compras.
native_language_example: Tom wants to know when Mary will go shopping.

meaning: I'll go now / I'm going now (future/near-future)
additional_notes: From the verb ir (to go) in the simple future (iré = I will go). In spoken Spanish, 'iré ahora' can express immediate intention to leave or go do something; depending on context, speakers might prefer present 'me voy ahora' or 'voy ahora' for immediate action. Formality: neutral. Tone: can be promise or decision.
target_language_example: No te preocupes, iré ahora mismo.
native_language_example: Don't worry, I'll go right now.

meaning: I will go by
additional_notes: Future first-person form of ir + en + mode of transport or time expression. Commonly used to say how you'll travel (iré en coche = I'll go by car) or, less naturally, to indicate leaving at a time (me iré en la mañana is understandable but more common is 'me iré por la mañana' or 'saldré por la mañana'). Use with vehicles (coche, autobús, tren) or other means.
target_language_example: Mañana iré en tren a la ciudad.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I'll go by train to the city.

meaning: 'island of' (used before a place or noun to indicate an island belonging to or named for something).
additional_notes: A prepositional phrase: isla (island) + de (of). Commonly used in place names (isla de Pascua = Easter Island) or to describe an island's characteristic (isla de coral = coral island). Followed by a noun; use the appropriate article if needed (la isla de Mallorca; isla de los Lobos).
target_language_example: Visitaremos la isla de la ciudad para el fin de semana.
native_language_example: We will visit the city's island for the weekend.

meaning: island in / island on (used to indicate location or topic: 'island in [sea/river/region]' or 'island in [context]').
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom—it's simply the noun isla ('island') followed by the preposition en. Use en to say where an island is located (e.g., 'isla en el Pacífico' = 'island in the Pacific'). Word order and articles matter: 'isla en la costa' vs. 'isla en el río'. If you mean 'island of' (possession or name), use de: 'isla de Mallorca'.
target_language_example: Es una isla en el océano Atlántico.
native_language_example: It's an island in the Atlantic Ocean.

meaning: 'the island is' (simple subject + verb phrase: describes the island)
