native_language_example: She is reading in the library.

meaning: "reading his/her/their/your (formal)" — progressive form indicating someone is in the process of reading something that belongs to someone.
additional_notes: Present participle (leyendo) + possessive adjective (su). 'Su' is ambiguous: it can mean his, her, their, or your (formal) depending on context. Use context or clarify (su libro → el libro de él / de ella / de ellos / suyo) if needed. The construction is used to describe an action in progress (equivalent to 'is/are reading ...').
target_language_example: Ella está leyendo su libro en el sofá.
native_language_example: She is reading her book on the sofa.

meaning: 'laws of the' (plural) — used before a feminine noun to say 'the laws of the [something]'.
additional_notes: This is not a complete phrase by itself; it's the start of a noun phrase meaning 'the laws of the ...' followed by a feminine noun (e.g., 'leyes de la ciudad' = 'laws of the city'). 'Leyes' is plural of 'ley' (law). Use 'del' (de + el) instead when the following noun is masculine (e.g., 'leyes del país').
target_language_example: Las leyes de la ciudad protegen a los peatones.
native_language_example: The laws of the city protect pedestrians.

meaning: he/she read the (feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Past simple (pretérito) of leer + the feminine definite article 'la'. Used when referring to a completed action of reading something feminine (e.g., la carta, la nota). Word order often places the article after the verb in examples but it's simply 'leyó' (he/she read) + 'la' (the).
target_language_example: Cuando leyó la carta, se tapó la cara.
native_language_example: When he/she read the letter, he/she covered his/her face.

meaning: I read a (masculine singular) — past tense (simple) of 'leer' + the indefinite article 'un'.
additional_notes: Used to say you read one (a) thing (masculine noun) in the past: 'leí' = I read (preterite). Followed by a masculine singular noun (e.g., artículo, libro, informe). If the noun is feminine use 'leí una'. If no noun follows, 'Leí un.' can sound incomplete in Spanish; usually you name what you read or finish the sentence.
target_language_example: Leí un libro sobre historia ayer.
native_language_example: I read a book about history yesterday.

meaning: I read a (feminine singular noun) — past tense, first person.
additional_notes: Leí is the preterite (simple past) of leer (to read). Una is the feminine indefinite article, so it's used before feminine singular nouns (una carta, una historia, una novela, una frase). Use 'leí un' before masculine nouns (leí un libro). Pronunciation: [le-EE OO-na].
target_language_example: Leí una novela interesante el mes pasado.
native_language_example: I read an interesting novel last month.

meaning: was reading the letter.
additional_notes: Past continuous (imperfect) third-person singular of leer + direct object 'la carta'. Used to describe an ongoing action in the past (he/she/it was reading the letter) often alongside another simultaneous action (e.g., laughing, crying). Context determines tense nuance: imperfect (leía) emphasizes the ongoing nature; can pair with preterite for a completed action happening at the same time.
target_language_example: Él sonrió mientras leía la carta.
native_language_example: He smiled while he was reading the letter.

meaning: Read and written (intended meaning: 'read and written'), but note 'escribido' is nonstandard; correct form is 'escrito'.
additional_notes: This phrase attempts to say someone can read and write or that something has been read and written. However, 'escribido' is an incorrect/colloquial form; the correct past participle of 'escribir' is 'escrito'. Use 'leído y escrito' for 'read and written' or the verb phrase 'sabe leer y escribir' for 'can read and write'. 'Leído' is the past participle of 'leer' and is correct. Avoid using 'escribido' in formal speech or writing.
target_language_example: Sé leer y escribir, no 'leído y escribido'.
native_language_example: I know how to read and write, not 'leído y escribido'.

meaning: 'read' (past participle) + feminine singular direct object article 'the' — used in perfect tenses or as past participle before a feminine noun.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but two words that often appear together: leído (past participle of leer) and la (feminine singular definite article or direct object pronoun). Common in compound tenses (he leído = I have read) or when describing a feminine noun that was read (leído la carta). Word order and meaning depend on context: with auxiliaries (he, ha, hemos) it forms the present perfect; with 'la' as object pronoun it can attach before the verb (la he leído) or after in some constructions.
target_language_example: He leído la carta que me enviaste.
native_language_example: I have read the letter you sent me.

meaning: have read a lot (about something or someone)
additional_notes: Used with the present perfect (he leído) to say you've read many things/articles/books about a topic or person. Typically followed by acerca de / sobre + object (e.g., acerca de ellos, sobre este lugar). Useful to indicate familiarity or background knowledge.
target_language_example: He leído mucho sobre la historia de esta ciudad.
native_language_example: I have read a lot about the history of this city.

meaning: parole; conditional release from prison under supervision.
additional_notes: Refers to allowing a prisoner to serve the remainder of their sentence outside prison under specific conditions (reporting to an officer, restrictions on travel, good behavior). Commonly used in legal and everyday contexts: "estar en libertad condicional" = to be on parole. Not the same as "libertad provisional" (pretrial release).
target_language_example: Después de dos años en la cárcel, salió en libertad condicional.
native_language_example: After two years in prison, he was released on parole.

meaning: freedom of expression; the right to express opinions and ideas.
additional_notes: Common legal and everyday phrase. Refers to the right to speak, publish, protest, and share opinions without undue government censorship. Can be used in discussions about rights, politics, media, and art. Often appears in phrases like "proteger la libertad de expresión" (to protect freedom of expression) or "limitar la libertad de expresión" (to limit freedom of expression).
target_language_example: La libertad de expresión está protegida por la constitución.
native_language_example: Freedom of expression is protected by the constitution.

meaning: 'freedom is' — a phrase used to define or comment on what freedom means or represents.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom; it's the noun libertad followed by the verb es (to be). Speakers use it to introduce a statement about the nature, value, or role of freedom. Common in definitions, opinions, slogans, or philosophical statements. In Spanish word order, you can also say 'la libertad es...' (with the article) — both are natural, though many examples include the article.
target_language_example: La libertad es poder elegir con responsabilidad.
native_language_example: Freedom is being able to choose responsibly.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase in Spanish; typically a fragment where the adjective 'libre' ('free' or 'available') appears immediately before the masculine singular definite article 'el'. This order is unusual because Spanish normally places the article before the noun and adjective (e.g., 'el tiempo libre').
additional_notes: You will not find 'libre el' as a standalone expression. If you encounter 'libre el' it is likely part of a clause or an inversion for emphasis or poetic/literary effect, or a typo. More common and correct forms are 'el libro está libre', 'está libre el asiento' (colloquial inversion), or 'el acceso libre'. For learners, focus on standard patterns: article + noun + adjective (el horario libre) and the verb phrase 'estar libre' (to be free/available).
target_language_example: ¿Libre el asiento? — Sí, puedes sentarte.
native_language_example: Free the seat? — Yes, you can sit down.

meaning: free (not occupied) in / available at (a place or time).
additional_notes: Libre means 'free' or 'available'. With 'en' it often indicates where or when something/someone is free or available (e.g., 'libre en la estación' = free/available at the station; 'libre en julio' = free in July). For locations it can describe an empty seat/place. Context determines if it means 'not busy' (person) or 'unoccupied/available' (seat, spot, time).
target_language_example: Estoy libre en la tarde si quieres quedar.
native_language_example: I'm free in the afternoon if you want to meet.

meaning: 'free is' (literal) — not a standard fixed phrase; likely a fragment meaning "is free" when words are inverted or in poetic/archaic order. The normal modern phrasing is 'está libre' to mean 'is free/available.'
additional_notes: 'Libre esta' is not standard word order in contemporary Spanish. You might encounter it as a typo, poetic inversion, or in archaic/poetic texts where word order is flexible. For everyday use, say 'está libre' (third person singular of estar + libre) for temporary states or availability, and 'soy libre' for a more permanent sense of being free. 'Libre' can mean free (not occupied), available, free of charge, or free (not constrained).
target_language_example: Libre esta la casa por ahora.
native_language_example: The house is free/available for now.

meaning: free of / exempt from; free to (do something).
additional_notes: Used two ways: (1) 'libres de + noun' = 'free of' or 'exempt from' (e.g., libres de impuestos = tax-free). (2) 'ser libres de + infinitive' = 'to be free to do (something)' or 'allowed/able to do'. Context tells which meaning applies.
target_language_example: Después del pago, quedamos libres de cualquier obligación.
native_language_example: After the payment, we are free of any obligation.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase in Spanish; likely a typo or two separate words: 'libro' = 'book' and 'a' = 'to/at'.
additional_notes: As written, 'libro a' has no established meaning. Most likely the learner saw 'libro' followed by the preposition 'a' in a sentence (for example: 'le di el libro a María' = 'I gave the book to María') or a typo for a phrase like 'libro de' or 'libro acerca de'. Treat 'libro' and 'a' separately: 'libro' is a common noun meaning 'book'; 'a' is a very common preposition meaning 'to', 'at', or used to introduce indirect objects, directions, and infinitives.
target_language_example: Le presté el libro a Carlos.
native_language_example: I lent the book to Carlos.

meaning: 'book to the' (part of a phrase indicating returning or placing a book somewhere).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but a sequence showing an object (libro) followed by a prepositional phrase introduced by 'a la' meaning 'to the' (feminine singular). Commonly appears in verbs of motion or return (devolver, regresar, poner) plus a destination: 'devolver el libro a la biblioteca' = 'return the book to the library.' Adjust gender/number: 'al' = a + el for masculine nouns (ej. 'al estante').
target_language_example: Voy a devolver el libro a la biblioteca mañana.
native_language_example: I'm going to return the book to the library tomorrow.

meaning: 'the book to/for me' or part of phrases meaning 'the book to/for (someone)'.
additional_notes: This fragment appears in sentences where libro (book) is the noun and a + person (a mi, a mi esposa, a mi oficina) marks the indirect object or direction (to/for someone or to a place). Beginners should recognize 'a' introduces the recipient or destination. Word order can change: you can say 'Le di el libro a mi amigo' or 'Lleva el libro a mi oficina.'
target_language_example: Le regalaron el libro a mi hermano.
native_language_example: They gave the book to my brother.

meaning: book about (used to say what a book is about).
additional_notes: This phrase combines libro (book) + acerca (short for 'acerca de') meaning 'about' or 'concerning'. In natural Spanish you would normally say "libro sobre" or "libro acerca de" rather than just "libro acerca". Use "acerca de" before the topic: "un libro acerca de la historia" = "a book about history."
target_language_example: Encontré un libro acerca de la astronomía en la biblioteca.
native_language_example: I found a book about astronomy in the library.

meaning: Not a standalone phrase; likely 'libro' (book) followed by the preposition 'al' (a + el) as part of a larger phrase (e.g., 'libro al autor' = 'I give the book to the author' or 'libro al lector' = 'book to the reader').
additional_notes: On its own, 'libro al' is incomplete. 'Libro' = book (noun). 'Al' is the contraction of 'a' + 'el' and means 'to the' or 'at the'. You'll see 'libro al...' when saying something like 'el libro al profesor' (the book to the teacher) or in verbs that take an indirect object: 'Le di el libro al niño' (I gave the book to the child). For beginners: learn 'libro' and 'al' separately, and remember 'al' = 'a' + 'el'.
target_language_example: Le di el libro al estudiante.
native_language_example: I gave the book to the student.

meaning: 'book' + 'when' — two separate words that together appear in sentences but do not form a fixed phrase. Use 'libro' (book) and 'cuando' (when) according to normal grammar.
additional_notes: This is not an idiom or fixed expression. 'Libro' is a noun meaning 'book'. 'Cuando' is a conjunction/adverb meaning 'when' (used for time) or introducing temporal clauses. They often appear near each other in sentences like 'leer un libro cuando...' (to read a book when...) or 'escribió un libro cuando...' (he wrote a book when...). Make sure to use articles and verb tenses as required: e.g., 'un libro', 'este libro', and temporal clauses with 'cuando' usually require a verb in the main clause and a verb in the 'cuando' clause.
target_language_example: Leí un libro cuando viajé a España.
native_language_example: I read a book when I traveled to Spain.

meaning: logbook; official record book (often nautical or technical).
additional_notes: Literally 'book of the rope' but used to mean a log, register, or official record kept for a ship, machine, installation, or specific activity. Not a common everyday phrase for 'book' — you’ll see it in technical, maritime, or administrative contexts referring to formal records. Usage may vary by region; in some areas 'libro de ordenes', 'bitácora' or simply 'libro' with context are more common.
target_language_example: El capitán anotó la hora en el libro de cabo.
native_language_example: The captain wrote the time in the logbook.

meaning: used with 'cabo' to form the phrase 'de cabo a rabo' meaning 'from cover to cover' or 'completely'.
additional_notes: By itself 'libro de cabo a' is incomplete — the full idiom is 'de cabo a rabo' (literally 'from end to tail') and is used to say you read or did something thoroughly, e.g. reading a book from start to finish. Use with verbs like leer (leer un libro de cabo a rabo).
target_language_example: Leí el libro de cabo a rabo durante las vacaciones.
native_language_example: I read the book from cover to cover during the vacation.

meaning: spellbook; a book that contains spells or magical formulas.
additional_notes: Used literally in fantasy/magic contexts to refer to a book with spells. Can also be used metaphorically to describe a source of secret techniques or a guide that 'holds' the solution to a problem (e.g., "the secret is in the spellbook"). 'Libro' = book, 'hechizos' = spells; phrase is compositional.
target_language_example: Encontramos el antiguo libro de hechizos en el ático.
native_language_example: We found the ancient spellbook in the attic.

meaning: literally 'book of the' — the start of a noun phrase meaning 'the book of the (feminine noun)'.
additional_notes: This is not a standalone phrase; it's the beginning of a possessive or descriptive phrase that links 'libro' (book) with a following feminine noun introduced by the definite article 'la' (for example, 'libro de la historia' = 'book of the history' or more naturally 'history book' / 'book about history'). Common structures: 'libro de la [noun]' (book about/of the [noun]) or 'el libro de la [person/title]' (the book of the [female person or feminine noun). Use 'del' (de + el) instead of 'de la' when the following noun is masculine: 'libro del profesor'.
target_language_example: Compré el libro de la profesora para preparar el examen.
native_language_example: I bought the teacher's (female teacher) book to prepare for the exam.

meaning: textbook (a book used for study or instruction).
additional_notes: Used to refer to a book designed for teaching a subject in schools, colleges, or professional training. Can be used generally (un libro de texto) or with a specific field (libro de texto de matemáticas, libro de texto para enfermeras). Pronunciation tip: 'lee-BRO de TEKS-toh.'
target_language_example: Este libro de texto es muy claro y tiene muchos ejercicios.
native_language_example: This textbook is very clear and has many exercises.

meaning: 'book of the' (literal phrase: 'libro' = book, 'del' = of the)
additional_notes: This is not a fixed expression by itself; it's the noun libro followed by the contraction del (de + el). Use when specifying possession or association with a masculine singular noun: libro del autor (the author's book), libro del mes (book of the month). If the following noun is feminine, use de la instead (libro de la autora).
target_language_example: Encontré el libro del autor en la mesa.
native_language_example: I found the author's book on the table.

meaning: 'book where' (used as part of a clause: 'the book where/that...').
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but the words 'libro' (book) + 'donde' (where) used together to introduce a relative clause that refers to a place or location mentioned in the book. In many cases Spanish uses 'en el que' or 'que' instead of 'donde' depending on style and formality: e.g., 'el libro en el que se menciona...' or 'el libro que habla de...'. Use 'donde' when the clause describes a place: 'el libro donde vivió el autor' = 'the book where the author lived' (more naturally: 'the book in which the author lived').
target_language_example: Es el libro donde encontré la carta.
native_language_example: It's the book where I found the letter.

meaning: ‘the book where you/they found it’ (fragment used to tell someone to leave/place the book where they found it).
additional_notes: This is a clipped phrase from sentences like “Deja el libro donde lo encontraste” (Leave the book where you found it). The sequence “donde lo” + past-tense verb (encontraste/encontró/encontraron) means “where you/he/they found it.” Common in commands telling someone to put or leave something in the place it was found. Verb forms change for person/formality: encontraste (tú), encontró (usted/él/ella), encontraron (ustedes/ellos/ellas).
target_language_example: Por favor, deja el libro donde lo encontraste.
native_language_example: Please leave the book where you found it.

meaning: literally 'book in' — not a standalone phrase; appears as part of longer expressions like 'libro en papel' (book in paper/print) or 'libro en español' (book in Spanish).
additional_notes: This is not an independent fixed phrase. 'Libro' means 'book' and 'en' is a preposition meaning 'in' or 'on'. Together they introduce the language, format, location, or medium of a book (for example: 'libro en inglés' = 'book in English'; 'libro en tapa dura' = 'hardcover book'). Use with a noun or adjective after 'en'.
target_language_example: Compré un libro en español para practicar.
native_language_example: I bought a book in Spanish to practice.

meaning: literally 'book in the' — not a fixed phrase by itself; the noun 'libro' followed by the preposition 'en' and the masculine singular article 'el', used when saying a book is located in or inside something (e.g., 'libro en el estante').
additional_notes: This sequence is compositional and normally completed by a location noun: 'libro en el estante' (book on the shelf), 'libro en el coche' (book in the car). If the location noun is feminine, use 'en la' instead; plurals use 'en los' / 'en las'. There is no contraction like 'nel' in Spanish. The phrase can appear within larger sentences and is not an idiom.
target_language_example: Vi un libro en el estante junto a la ventana.
native_language_example: I saw a book on the shelf next to the window.

meaning: literally 'book in the' — not a fixed phrase; a fragment used when specifying a book's location or context.
additional_notes: This is not a standalone idiom. It's the noun 'libro' (book) followed by the preposition 'en' and the feminine definite article 'la' (the), so it precedes a feminine noun (e.g., 'librería', 'estantería', 'clase', 'lección'). Common uses: to say where a book is located (physical place), to say a book is used in a class, or to refer to when/where you'll discuss it. Remember agreement: if the following noun is masculine use 'en el' instead (e.g., 'libro en el estante' or commonly 'libro en el estante' vs 'libro en la estantería').
target_language_example: Encontré el libro en la estantería de arriba.
native_language_example: I found the book on the shelf upstairs.

meaning: 'is of' / 'belongs to' / 'is (made) of' depending on context.
additional_notes: This construction combines libro (book) with the verb ser + de. With a person or pronoun (es de la niña; es de ellos) it means 'belongs to.' With nouns indicating material, topic, or characteristic (es de varios colores; es de la vida...) it means 'is made of/has' or 'is about.' With abstract nouns (es de gran valor) it means 'has' or 'is of (great) ...' and with an infinitive phrase (es de fácil lectura) it means 'is ... to read' / 'is easy to ...'. Context decides the precise translation.
target_language_example: Ese libro es de mi hermano y trata sobre viajes.
native_language_example: That book belongs to my brother and is about travel.

meaning: '(the) book is too ...' — used to say a book has an excessive quality (too expensive, too difficult, too complicated).
additional_notes: Structure: 'El/Este libro es demasiado + adjective'. 'Demasiado' means 'too' or 'too much' and must be followed by an adjective (caro, difícil, complicado) or by 'para' + infinitive/phrase to express 'too ... to ...' (e.g., 'demasiado caro para mí', 'demasiado difícil para que lo entienda'). Use 'demasiado' before the adjective. For emphasis with nouns use 'demasiado' + de + noun (not shown here).
target_language_example: Este libro es demasiado caro para que lo compre ahora.
native_language_example: This book is too expensive for me to buy now.

meaning: "the book is very..." (used to describe a book with an adjective).
additional_notes: This phrase combines 'libro' (book) + 'es' (he/she/it is) + 'muy' (very). Use it before an adjective to emphasize a quality of the book (e.g., bueno, grande, interesante). Order: 'Este libro es muy + adjective.'
target_language_example: Este libro es muy caro.
native_language_example: This book is very expensive.

meaning: literally 'book is for' — used to say who a book is intended for or to express 'this book means/serves to someone as...'.
additional_notes: Combines libro (book) with es para (is for). Use 'es para' to indicate the intended audience or recipient (e.g., 'Este libro es para estudiantes' = 'This book is for students'). It can also appear in comparisons like 'Este libro es para mí lo que la Biblia es para ti' meaning 'This book is for me what the Bible is for you' (i.e., expresses equivalence in importance or role). Adjust pronouns and articles as needed: 'para mí', 'para usted', 'para estudiantes', 'para los estudiantes'.
target_language_example: Este libro es para principiantes que aprenden español.
native_language_example: This book is for beginners who are learning Spanish.

meaning: Not a fixed Spanish phrase; likely part of a sentence meaning 'book is a...' (e.g., 'el libro es una...').
additional_notes: This sequence is not a standalone expression in Spanish. It looks like a fragment where 'libro' (book) is the subject, 'es' is the verb 'is', and 'una' is the feminine indefinite article 'a' before a feminine noun. In a complete sentence you would normally include the feminine noun after 'una' (for example: 'El libro es una novela.' = 'The book is a novel.'). Make sure to match articles: 'libro' is masculine, so the typical full sentence would use 'un' not 'una' ('El libro es un...') unless you are talking about 'la obra' or another feminine noun and phrasing differently.
target_language_example: El libro es una novela interesante.
native_language_example: The book is an interesting novel.

meaning: "the book is" (subject + present tense of 'estar')
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase — it's simply the noun 'libro' (book) followed by the verb 'estar' in third person singular. Use when describing the temporary state or location of a book (e.g., where it is, its condition). For location or more permanent characteristics, Spanish often uses 'estar' for locations and temporary states, and 'ser' for more permanent traits. You'll usually see it as part of a full sentence like 'El libro está en la mesa.'
target_language_example: El libro está en la mesa.
native_language_example: The book is on the table.

meaning: the book was
additional_notes: A combination of the noun 'libro' (book) and the past passive auxiliary 'fue' (was) used to form passive or past descriptions about a specific book. In context you will usually see it followed by a past participle (e.g., escrito, publicado, vendido) or by additional information. 'Libro' is a noun; 'fue' is the third-person singular preterite of 'ser' used for passive voice or to state past events.
target_language_example: El libro fue traducido al inglés el año pasado.
native_language_example: The book was translated into English last year.

meaning: Not a standard Spanish phrase; likely two separate words: 'libro' (book) and 'me' (me/to myself).
additional_notes: This combination by itself isn't a set phrase in Spanish. In normal sentences the words appear together in structures like: 'Me libro de...' (I free myself from...) or 'me lo libro' (I get rid of it / avoid it) — note the reflexive verb 'librar' not the noun 'libro'. If you meant the noun 'libro' with the pronoun 'me', you'd usually need a verb: e.g. 'Dame el libro' (Give me the book) or 'El libro me interesa' (The book interests me). Check whether you intended 'me libro' (from the verb 'librar') or 'libro me' as part of a larger sentence.
target_language_example: El libro me gusta mucho.
native_language_example: I really like the book.

meaning: "libro" = book; "muy" = very (adverb).
additional_notes: "libro muy" by itself is not a natural fixed phrase in Spanish. "Libro" is a noun (book). "Muy" is an adverb used to modify adjectives or adverbs (e.g., muy interesante = very interesting). To say a book is very [adjective], place muy before the adjective: libro muy interesante. To say 'a very good book' use un libro muy bueno or mejor: un libro muy bueno / un libro excelente.
target_language_example: Es un libro muy interesante sobre historia.
native_language_example: It's a very interesting book about history.

meaning: literally 'book no' — not a standard fixed phrase; typically a fragment where 'libro' is negated or contrasted (e.g., as a clipped reply or part of a longer negation).
additional_notes: This is not a common multiword expression in Spanish. You'll usually see 'libro' alone or in phrases like 'no es un libro' (it's not a book) or 'libro no leído' (unread book). If you find 'libro no' in text or speech, check context: it may be a clipped response ('Libro no, gracias') or part of a larger sentence where words are omitted.
target_language_example: — ¿Te llevo algo de la librería? — Libro no, trae solo una revista.
native_language_example: — Should I bring something from the bookstore? — Book no, just bring a magazine.

meaning: Depends on context; 'por' after 'libro' links 'book' to a reason, price, method, or location—e.g. 'by/for/through the book' or 'book for/at (price)'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase—'por' is a very common preposition with many uses. After 'libro', possible meanings include: indicating a page or location inside the book (libro por la página = by/at page), expressing price or exchange (libro por diez dólares = book for ten dollars), indicating a very low price (por prácticamente nada = for almost nothing), or specifying a method/means (por correo = by mail). Translate based on context.
target_language_example: Te envío el libro por correo.
native_language_example: I'll send you the book by mail.

meaning: 'the book that (to) me...' — part of a relative clause referring to a book connected to the speaker (e.g., a book I was given, read, or liked).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but a common construction: libro (book) + que (that/which) + me (indirect or direct object pronoun referring to 'me'). Depending on the verb that follows, 'me' can mean 'that you gave me' (me diste), 'that I read' (me leí), or 'that I liked' (me gustó). Useful in sentences like 'el libro que me diste' (the book that you gave me) or 'un libro que me gustó' (a book that I liked). Word order and tense of the verb after 'que me' change with context.
target_language_example: Ella comentó sobre el libro que me recomendaste.
native_language_example: She commented on the book that you recommended to me.

meaning: Not a standard fixed Spanish phrase; appears to be a sequence of the noun 'libro' (book) followed by the clitic 'se'. By itself it has no independent meaning; its interpretation depends on surrounding words or word order (often a typo or part of a larger construction).
additional_notes: 'Se' is a versatile clitic used for reflexive, passive/impersonal, and other constructions. If you encounter 'libro se' it may result from unusual word order (e.g., poetry, older texts) or a typo. Possible correct nearby forms: 'se libro' (rare; could appear in reflexive 'se libró'—note accent and different verb), 'se lee el libro' (passive/impersonal), or 'el libro se (verb)'. Always check context and punctuation.
target_language_example: En el manuscrito antiguo aparece la frase "libro se conserva" sin puntuación clara.
native_language_example: In the ancient manuscript the phrase "libro se conserva" appears without clear punctuation.

meaning: a book about/on the (topic) or a book on top of the (object)
additional_notes: This phrase can mean either 'a book about [something]' (libro sobre el tema/Tourette) where 'sobre' = 'about', or 'a book on top of the [thing]' (libro sobre el escritorio) where 'sobre' = 'on/above'. Context determines the meaning. 'El' is the masculine definite article for a specific noun that follows or is understood from context.
target_language_example: Encontré un libro sobre el clima en la mesa.
native_language_example: I found a book about the climate on the table.

meaning: book about the (feminine noun that follows).
additional_notes: This is the phrase 'libro sobre la ...' used to say a book about a particular topic (the topic must be feminine: la historia, la cocina, la ciudad). 'Sobre' = about/on. If the topic is masculine use 'libro sobre el'. For plural topics use 'libros sobre las/los'.
target_language_example: Compré un libro sobre la historia de España.
native_language_example: I bought a book about the history of Spain.

meaning: used to emphasize the quality or degree of a book (e.g., 'such a book' / 'a book so...').
additional_notes: Tan + adjective expresses degree (so, such, so much). When used with 'libro' it emphasizes how good/interesting/fast/etc. the book is read. Common structures: 'un libro tan + adjective + que...' (such a... that...), 'un libro tan + adjective + como...' (a book as... as...). In comparisons use 'como' (as), and to show result use 'que' (so... that).
target_language_example: Es un libro tan emocionante que no pude dejar de leerlo.
native_language_example: It's such an exciting book that I couldn't stop reading it.

meaning: literally 'book has' — not a fixed phrase; likely part of a sentence meaning 'the book has...'.
additional_notes: This is not an independent expression. 'Libro' = book (noun); 'tiene' = he/she/it has or you (formal) have. Together they appear when describing what a book contains or possesses (e.g., 'El libro tiene 300 páginas' = 'The book has 300 pages'). Use appropriate articles and agreement: 'El libro tiene...' for singular masculine book; for plural use 'Los libros tienen...'.
target_language_example: El libro tiene muchas ilustraciones.
native_language_example: The book has many illustrations.

meaning: 'book' + 'all the' used to say someone spent an entire period (night/morning/afternoon) reading a book.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase; it's the noun libro ('book') followed by the time expression 'toda la' + time period (noche, mañana, tarde). Use 'toda la' for feminine time words (la noche, la mañana, la tarde). For plural or masculine contexts you'd use other forms (e.g., 'todo el día' for 'all day'). Common structure: [leer/estar leyendo] + [un/el] libro + toda la + [noche/mañana/tarde].
target_language_example: Leí un libro toda la noche.
native_language_example: I read a book all night.

meaning: Not a standard Spanish phrase; likely a mistaken word order for 'una libro' or 'libro' plus a verb (e.g., 'libro una' could appear in contexts like 'libro una cita' meaning 'I book/make an appointment').
additional_notes:
As written, 'libro una' is not a common fixed expression. Possible interpretations:
- If intended as 'libro' (I book) + direct object 'una ...' (feminine noun), it means 'I book a ...' (e.g., 'Libro una mesa' = 'I book a table'). Note that the correct present-tense conjugation for 'yo' of 'reservar' (to reserve) is 'reservo' and for 'librar' is different; more commonly Spanish uses 'reservar', 'hacer una reserva' or 'pedir'.
- If someone meant 'un libro' (a book), the correct form is 'un libro' (masculine) or 'un libro' and 'una' would be incorrect. For a feminine noun use 'un(a) + feminine noun' like 'una revista'.
Beginners should check context; word order matters in Spanish and 'libro una' is probably an error.
target_language_example: Libro una mesa para esta noche.
native_language_example: I book a table for tonight.

meaning: "libro y" — likely the start of a phrase meaning 'book and...' (literally 'book and').
additional_notes: By itself, 'libro y' is not a complete phrase; it appears to be the beginning of a compound or list (e.g., 'libro y revista' = 'book and magazine'). 'Libro' means 'book' and 'y' means 'and'. Use 'y' to join two nouns or phrases; note pronunciation: 'y' is pronounced /i/, but before words that start with the sound 'i' it can be pronounced /e/ to avoid a vowel clash. For counting or titles, 'libro y ...' will need a second item to be a complete idea.
target_language_example: Compré un libro y una revista en la librería.
native_language_example: I bought a book and a magazine at the bookstore.

meaning: books like / books such as
additional_notes: Used to introduce examples or a category of books similar to ones mentioned. Often followed by examples or a comparison (e.g., 'libros como Harry Potter' = 'books like Harry Potter'). Can appear in lists or comparisons: 'Me gustan libros como...' or 'Busca libros como...'. Grammar: 'libros' is plural noun; 'como' functions as 'like'/'such as'.
target_language_example: Me encantan los libros como El Principito y Alice en el País de las Maravillas.
native_language_example: I love books like The Little Prince and Alice in Wonderland.

meaning: books in the (female singular noun follows); part of a longer phrase (e.g., 'libros en la biblioteca' = 'books in the library').
additional_notes: This is not a complete fixed phrase by itself; it's the noun 'libros' (books) followed by the preposition 'en' (in) and the feminine singular definite article 'la'. It must be followed by a feminine singular place or context (la casa, la mesa, la biblioteca). For masculine nouns you would use 'en el' (e.g., 'libros en el coche').
target_language_example: Hay libros en la biblioteca.
native_language_example: There are books in the library.

meaning: books (that are) in/on my ... (followed by a place or time).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself; it's the noun 'libros' (books) plus the preposition 'en' and the possessive 'mi' (my). In natural Spanish you normally add a noun after 'mi' to specify where or when (e.g., 'libros en mi cuarto', 'libros en mi juventud', 'libros en mi tiempo libre'). Use 'mi' (not 'mío') before a noun. If the place is a room, 'cuarto' or 'habitación' are common.
target_language_example: Tengo libros en mi estantería que puedes pedir prestados.
native_language_example: I have books on my bookshelf that you can borrow.

meaning: 'books' followed by the preposition 'por' — shows different uses of por with 'libros' (reason, exchange, duration, distribution, price, etc.).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase; it's the noun libros + the preposition por. 'Por' has many meanings in Spanish depending on context: cause/reason (por placer), duration or temporary substitution (dejar los libros por un tiempo), location/distribution (por toda la casa), and exchange/price (vendí mis libros por poco dinero). Translate 'por' according to context: for/because of/for the sake of/in exchange for/through/outside. Pay attention to which meaning fits each sentence.
target_language_example: Compré libros por regalo y para estudiar.
native_language_example: I bought books as a gift and to study.

meaning: books that / books which
additional_notes: A common noun + relative pronoun combination. 'Libros' = books (plural). 'Que' introduces a relative clause describing the books: e.g. 'libros que recomiendo' = 'books that I recommend'. No change for gender/number of 'que'. If the relative clause needs a preposition or refers to a person, other forms (como 'de los que', 'que me gustan', or 'los cuales') may be used.
target_language_example: Estos son los libros que compré ayer.
native_language_example: These are the books that I bought yesterday.

meaning: "books and" — the noun 'libros' (books) followed by the conjunction 'y' (and).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase; it's simply the plural noun 'libros' + the coordinating conjunction 'y'. It appears when listing items or connecting 'books' to another noun or phrase (e.g., 'libros y revistas' = 'books and magazines'). Pay attention to word order and that 'y' becomes 'e' before words beginning with the sound /i/ (e.g., 'libros e instrucciones'). Also notice punctuation and agreement: 'libros y ropa' connects two nouns of different gender without changing form.
target_language_example: Tengo libros y cuadernos en mi mochila.
native_language_example: I have books and notebooks in my backpack.

meaning: driver's license; driving license (official ID that allows you to drive).
additional_notes: Used to refer to the official document that permits someone to drive a motor vehicle. Commonly asked for by police, at car rentals, or when proving driving eligibility. In some countries also called "licencia de manejo" or simply "licencia."
target_language_example: Por favor, muéstreme su licencia de conducir.
native_language_example: Please show me your driver's license.

meaning: used to comment on or react to something nice/pleasant (literally 'nice that').
additional_notes: This sequence appears when someone says '¡Linda que...!' or 'Qué linda que...' to introduce a comment about something pleasing, often followed by a clause or exclamation (e.g., 'Qué linda que viniste' = 'How nice that you came'). It is informal and conversational. Word order and exact phrasing can vary: 'Qué linda' + clause, or '¡Linda que...' as an interjection.
target_language_example: ¡Qué linda que viniste a la fiesta!
native_language_example: How nice that you came to the party!

meaning: "pretty and" — the adjective 'linda' (pretty/nice) followed by 'y' (and) to link another quality or noun.
additional_notes: Used to combine 'linda' with another adjective, trait or noun (e.g., 'linda y amable' = 'pretty and kind'). 'Linda' is feminine; for masculine subjects use 'lindo'. Often appears in simple descriptions and comparisons. Word order follows Spanish adjective-noun/adjective linking rules: adjective + y + another adjective/phrase.
target_language_example: Ella es linda y simpática.
native_language_example: She is pretty and friendly.

meaning: 'nice' or 'pretty' when describing something belonging to or associated with someone/something (colloquial phrasing).
additional_notes: Spanish adjective lindo means 'nice' or 'cute'. The sequence 'lindo de' appears when followed by a noun or possessive phrase (e.g., 'lindo de casa', 'lindo de mamá') or in colloquial expressions like 'qué lindo de ver' (though more common is 'qué lindo' or 'lindo para'). In many Spanish varieties, speakers prefer 'lindo', 'bonito' or 'hermoso' directly before the noun: 'un vestido lindo'. Be careful: 'de' changes meaning depending on what follows (possession, origin, purpose).
target_language_example: Es un perro lindo de mi vecina.
native_language_example: It's a cute dog of my neighbor (my neighbor's cute dog).

meaning: a list of (something abstract or previously mentioned); roughly 'list of the...'.
additional_notes: This phrase is not a fixed idiom by itself; it's the beginning of a noun phrase where lo refers to an abstract idea, quality, or previously mentioned thing (lo + adjective/phrase). Often appears as part of longer expressions like "lista de lo que..." (list of what...) or "lista de lo necesario" (list of what is necessary). Beginners will more often see "lista de" followed by a concrete noun (lista de compras) or "lista de lo que..." when referring to unspecified items or concepts.
target_language_example: Haz una lista de lo que necesitas para el viaje.
native_language_example: Make a list of what you need for the trip.

meaning: Literal word order 'lista es' corresponds to 'is ready' when the subject is feminine singular, but this exact order is uncommon in neutral declarative sentences in Spanish; most natural forms are 'está lista' (temporary state) or 'es lista' (she is clever). 'Lista es' can appear in sentences with inversion, emphasis, or relative clauses.
additional_notes: 'Lista' is the feminine singular form of the adjective 'listo' (ready/clever). 'Es' is third-person singular of 'ser'. Spanish normally uses 'estar' (está) for temporary states like being ready, and 'ser' (es) for inherent qualities (e.g., 'es lista' = 'she's clever'). The sequence 'lista es' (adjective before verb) can occur in stylistic constructions, questions with inversion, or as part of a larger clause (e.g., 'Lista es la respuesta que esperábamos'). Use with care — in everyday speech you'd usually say 'está lista' or 'es lista' with normal word order.
target_language_example: Lista es la respuesta que esperábamos.
native_language_example: Ready is the answer we were expecting. (More natural in English: The answer we were expecting is ready.)

meaning: 'the list is for' (used to explain the purpose or intended recipients of a list)
additional_notes: This phrase is typically followed by a noun or clause that states the purpose or who/what the list is for. It is a literal construction: lista (list) + es para (is for). Common in sentences like 'La lista es para invitados' or 'La lista es para comprar comida.'
target_language_example: La lista es para la fiesta de mañana.
native_language_example: The list is for tomorrow's party.

meaning: blacklist; a list of people or things to avoid or exclude.
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is excluded, banned, or marked as untrusted. Common in work, social, or service contexts (e.g., being banned from a store, a booking system, or a group's favors). Can be used literally (a list called 'blacklist') or figuratively ('you're on my blacklist' = I won't give you chances).
target_language_example: Si sigues llegando tarde, te pondré en la lista negra.
native_language_example: If you keep arriving late, I'll put you on the blacklist.

meaning: "more clever/smart than" (comparison using 'lista' feminine).
additional_notes: Lista is the feminine form of 'listo' meaning 'clever, smart, ready' depending on context. When used with 'más ... que' it compares intelligence or cleverness: 'más lista que' = 'more clever than'. Pay attention to gender: use 'listo' for masculine subjects (más listo que). Can also be used sarcastically (e.g., 'te crees más lista que yo').
target_language_example: María es más lista que su compañero en matemáticas.
native_language_example: María is smarter than her classmate in math.

meaning: 'ready to' or 'about to' (followed by an infinitive) or 'ready with' (followed by a noun).
additional_notes: listo (masculine) means 'ready'. When combined with de + infinitive it can indicate someone is about to do something (estoy listo de salir is less common; más natural: 'listo para salir' or 'a punto de salir'). 'Listo de' + noun can mean 'ready with' in some regional uses, but many speakers prefer 'listo para' or 'con'. For beginners: prefer 'listo para' + infinitive/noun or 'a punto de' + infinitive for 'about to'.
target_language_example: Estoy listo para empezar, no listo de esperar.
native_language_example: I'm ready to start, not ready to wait.

meaning: 'ready' or 'finished' (masculine singular) — literally 'ready the' when the adjective 'listo' appears adjacent to the article 'el' in colloquial or elliptical phrases.
additional_notes: This sequence is not a standard fixed phrase in Spanish; 'listo' is an adjective and normally appears before or after a noun without intervening article (e.g., 'el chico listo' or 'estoy listo'). 'Listo el' can appear in informal, clipped spoken phrases or regional uses where the article precedes an understood noun or in constructions like 'Listo, el...' (meaning 'Alright, then...' before introducing a topic). Watch agreement: femenino singular is 'lista', plural 'listos/listas'.
target_language_example: — ¿Terminaste con el informe? — Sí, listo el.
native_language_example: — Did you finish the report? — Yes, the report is ready.

meaning: ready in (time); prepared within (a period).
additional_notes: Used to say something will be ready or finished after a certain amount of time. Common structure: 'listo en + [time period]'. You can also use 'estar listo' alone to mean 'to be ready'. Example: 'La comida estará lista en diez minutos.'
target_language_example: El informe estará listo en dos horas.
native_language_example: The report will be ready in two hours.

meaning: calls at (a time)
additional_notes: This phrase is the verb 'llamar' (to call) conjugated in the third person singular present (él/ella/usted llama) followed by a time expression introduced by 'a las' (used for hours). It typically means someone calls (on the phone) at a specific time: e.g. 'llama a las ocho' = 'he/she/you (formal) calls at eight' or 'call me at eight' when used in instructions. If referring to 'you' (tú), use 'llamas a las'.
target_language_example: Él llama a las siete todos los días.
native_language_example: He calls at seven every day.

meaning: calls things (by a name); refers to how someone names or labels things.
additional_notes: Literally 'calls things'. Used to talk about how someone names, labels or refers to objects, ideas, events, etc. Often appears with a direct object or clause specifying the name: e.g. 'la gente lo llama X' or 'él llama a las cosas por su nombre' (he calls things by their name / speaks plainly). Can be part of larger expressions about naming or describing.
target_language_example: Ella siempre llama a las cosas por su nombre.
native_language_example: She always calls things by their name.

meaning: to call things by (a certain name); to refer to things as
additional_notes: Used to say that someone uses a particular word or name for things or situations. Structure: 'llama a las cosas por + [name/label]'. Often followed by a noun phrase or clause that states the label. Can be literal (naming objects) or figurative (calling situations/situations by a label). Commonly used with a subject: Él/ella/usted/ellos llaman a las cosas por...
target_language_example: Ella llama a las cosas por su nombre: siempre dice 'error' cuando algo falla.
native_language_example: She calls things by their name: she always says 'error' when something goes wrong.

llama a las cosas por su

target_language_multi_word_term: llama a las cosas por su
meaning: calls things by their (right) name; speaks plainly or calls things as they are.
additional_notes: Used to say someone is direct, honest, or blunt when describing people or situations. Often completed as "llama a las cosas por su nombre" (calls things by their name). Can imply saying uncomfortable truths. Common in everyday and journalistic Spanish.
target_language_example: Ella siempre llama a las cosas por su nombre, aunque moleste.
native_language_example: She always calls things by their (right) name, even if it annoys people.

meaning: (she/it) calls all; or imperative familiar/usted forms plus 'todas'—depends on context (often needs preposition 'a').
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom. 'llama' can be third-person singular present of llamar (ella/él/usted llama) or imperative (tú) with irregular stress in speech; 'todas' is feminine plural meaning 'all' or 'everyone' (female group or feminine nouns). For calling people, standard Spanish uses the preposition 'a' (llama a todas). Without 'a' it may be a truncated phrase (e.g., 'llama todas las tardes' would mean 'calls every afternoon' where 'todas' is part of 'todas las tardes'). Word order and missing 'a' change the meaning or make the phrase ungrammatical in some contexts.
target_language_example: Ella llama todas las tardes a sus amigas.
native_language_example: She calls all (her) friends every afternoon.

meaning: calls all the (feminine plural noun) / ring all the (feminine plural things)
additional_notes: This is the verb 'llamar' (to call) in the imperative or indicative followed by a feminine plural noun phrase. Without context it could be part of a sentence like "(Él) llama todas las noches" (he calls every night) or an instruction "llama todas las mesas" (call all the tables). Pay attention to subject and tense: 'llama' can be present (él/ella/usted calls), imperative (tú call) or informal present for 'usted' depending on context. The following words determine meaning (e.g., 'llama todas las noches' = he/you call every night; 'llama todas las personas' = calls all the people).
target_language_example: Ella llama todas las noches después del trabajo.
native_language_example: She calls every night after work.

meaning: a call from (someone) / a call about (something).
additional_notes: Used with a person or subject after 'de' to indicate who made the call or what the call was about. Commonly appears as 'recibí/tuve/una llamada de…' (I received/had/a call from…). Can refer to phone calls or figurative calls (e.g., a call for help: 'llamada de auxilio').
target_language_example: Recibí una llamada de María esta mañana.
native_language_example: I received a call from María this morning.

meaning: called on / called into (used to indicate someone calling into a program, meeting, or phone call from a location or line)
additional_notes: Often appears in contexts like 'llamada en conferencia', 'llamada en espera', or as part of longer phrases such as 'una llamada en directo' or 'una llamada en conferencia desde Madrid'. 'Llamada en' by itself is incomplete; it usually needs a noun or location after 'en' (e.g., 'llamada en conferencia', 'llamada en espera', 'llamada en vivo'). Can indicate the medium, status, or origin of a call.
target_language_example: Recibimos una llamada en conferencia desde la oficina central.
native_language_example: We received a conference call from the headquarters.

meaning: they call
additional_notes: From llamar. This is the third-person plural form plus a, often used before a person or thing being called: llaman a María = they call María / they're calling María. It can also be used in expressions like llaman a la puerta = they're knocking at the door.
target_language_example: Siempre llaman a mi hermano primero.
native_language_example: They always call my brother first.

meaning: they call him/them 'the' (used to give someone a nickname or title).
additional_notes: Literally 'they call him the...'. 'Llaman' is the third-person plural of 'llamar' (to call/name) and 'el' is the masculine definite article used before a nickname or title. Common structure: 'Lo/Le llaman el + [nickname/title]'. Use 'lo' or 'le' for the object pronoun depending on region and style. For feminine nicknames use 'la' (e.g., 'la llaman la reina').
target_language_example: Lo llaman el rey de la cocina.
native_language_example: They call him the king of the kitchen.

meaning: to attract attention; to draw notice (often negative: to seek attention).
additional_notes: Used both for unintentionally attracting notice (e.g., 'Don't attract attention') and for someone who seeks attention deliberately ('he/she likes to attract attention'). Context determines whether it's neutral or implies attention-seeking. Common in phrases like 'deja de llamar la atención' (stop attracting attention) or 'no quería llamar la atención' (didn't want to draw attention).
target_language_example: No quiero llamar la atención en la reunión.
native_language_example: I don't want to attract attention at the meeting.

meaning: I'll call you when… (used to indicate you'll call at the moment another action/event happens or is completed).
additional_notes: A common future-tense phrase followed by a subordinate clause (often with the subjunctive after 'cuando' if the action is not yet completed). Use to promise or arrange a call tied to another event: e.g. when I arrive, when it's done, when I'm closer. In English the clause after 'when' can be translated as 'when I arrive / when it's finished,' etc.
target_language_example: No te preocupes; te llamaré cuando llegue al aeropuerto.
native_language_example: Don't worry; I'll call you when I arrive at the airport.

meaning: I'll call later / I'll call more (often: I'll call again or call later).
additional_notes: Commonly used to tell someone you'll call again or call at a later time. Context decides nuance: 'llamaré más tarde' is more complete for 'I'll call later', while 'llamaré más' can imply 'I'll call more (often)' or be a shortened casual form meaning 'I'll call again/later'. Pronunciation stress on llamaré (last syllable).
target_language_example: No puedo hablar ahora; llamaré más tarde.
native_language_example: I can't talk now; I'll call later.

meaning: I call in / I call at (used when saying you are calling into a place or joining by phone); or 'I call in on' (less common) depending on context.
additional_notes: This is the first-person singular present form of llamar followed by the preposition en. Alone, it needs context (a location or medium) to be clear: e.g. "llamo en la tarde" (I call in the afternoon) or "llamo en tu oficina" (I stop by/call at your office). More commonly speakers say "llamo por" (call about/by) or "llamo a" (I call someone). Use carefully and provide the place or time after "en."
target_language_example: Mañana llamo en tu oficina para confirmar la cita.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I will call/stop by your office to confirm the appointment.

meaning: I called for / I called because of / I called to ask about (depending on context).
additional_notes: Past tense first person singular of 'llamar por'. 'Llamé por' can mean 'I called for' (to request someone or something), 'I called because of' (to explain reason), or 'I called to ask about' (followed by a topic). Context and any following noun or clause determine exact translation. Commonly used in phone contexts: 'Llamé por la cita' (I called about the appointment) or 'Llamé por ti' (I called for you).
target_language_example: Llamé por la reserva pero no me contestaron.
native_language_example: I called about the reservation but they didn't answer me.

meaning: called (someone) by / called (someone) by means of (e.g., by phone) or at (a time).
additional_notes: Depending on context, 'llamó por' can mean: 1) 'called someone by [name]' when followed by 'su nombre' (llamó por su nombre = called him/her by name); 2) 'called by means of' when followed by a method, usually 'teléfono' (llamó por teléfono = called by phone); 3) 'called at' when followed by a time expression (llamó por la tarde = called in the afternoon). The verb form 'llamó' is third person singular preterite of 'llamar'. Replace 'llamó' with other conjugations as needed (te llamó, llamé, llamaremos, etc.).
target_language_example: Mi madre me llamó por teléfono ayer por la noche.
native_language_example: My mother called me on the phone last night.

meaning: called (for) a/an — used to say someone called (summoned/requested) something or called someone a (name).
additional_notes: Can mean 'called for' (requested) something (e.g., llamar un taxi = call a taxi) or 'called someone [a name]' when followed by a noun used as an insult (Me llamó un tonto = he called me a fool). Context and the noun that follows determine whether it's requesting/ordering or naming/calling someone. The subject and indirect object often appear: Ella me llamó un taxi (She called me a taxi / She called a taxi for me).
target_language_example: Mi madre me llamó un médico cuando me desmayé.
native_language_example: My mother called a doctor for me when I fainted.

meaning: called and… (past tense, 3rd person); used to link a phone call with another action or fact.
additional_notes: Combines the preterite form of llamar (él/ella/usted llamó) with the conjunction y (and). Common in reported past events: 'X llamó y [luego/entonces/...]' or 'me llamó y [hizo/volvió/dijo/etc.]'. The subject is third person singular. In English often translated as 'called and' or 'called, and'. Context determines the second action.
target_language_example: Mi jefe llamó y canceló la reunión.
native_language_example: My boss called and canceled the meeting.

meaning: turn (something) to; used with verbs of movement to indicate turning a key toward a direction or position
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but the noun 'llave' (key) followed by the preposition 'a' that often introduces the direction or target of an action (e.g., 'gira la llave a la derecha' — 'turn the key to the right'). Useful when giving or following instructions about keys, valves, or levers. Word order: 'girar/poner/mover la llave a + [direction/posición]'.
target_language_example: Gira la llave a la derecha para encender el coche.
native_language_example: Turn the key to the right to start the car.

meaning: a part of a phrase meaning 'the key of / the ... key' (used before a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Llave means 'key' (physical key or tap/faucet valve, or figurative 'key' as in solution). 'Llave de la' is the beginning of a noun phrase and must be completed with a feminine noun (e.g., 'llave de la casa' = the house key, 'llave de la cocina' = the kitchen tap). If the following noun is masculine, use 'llave del' (llave + de + el).
target_language_example: Busco la llave de la casa.
native_language_example: I'm looking for the house key.

meaning: lit. 'key in' — used when talking about inserting or turning a key in (a lock) or figuratively 'keyed into' (less common).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed set phrase by itself; it's the verb phrase formed with 'llave' (key) plus a preposition. In Spanish you would more naturally say 'poner la llave en...' (to put/insert the key in...), 'meter la llave en...' (to put the key into...), or 'girar la llave en...' (to turn the key in...). Alone, 'llave en' needs a verb and an object (e.g., 'poner la llave en la cerradura'). For figurative senses, Spanish uses verbs like 'estar' or expressions such as 'estar al tanto' rather than 'llave en'.
target_language_example: Pon la llave en la cerradura y gírala.
native_language_example: Put the key in the lock and turn it.

meaning: part of a phrase meaning 'key in the' or 'key on the' (literal); often appears in set expressions like 'llave en la mano' (key in the hand) or 'llave en la cerradura' (key in the lock).
additional_notes: By itself 'llave en la' is incomplete and needs a noun after 'la' (feminine) to form a full idea (e.g., 'llave en la mano', 'llave en la cerradura'). 'Llave' = key; 'en' = in/on; 'la' = the (feminine). Useful when describing the location of a key.
target_language_example: Encontré la llave en la cerradura de la puerta.
native_language_example: I found the key in the door's lock.

meaning: master key (a key that opens many or all locks in a system).
additional_notes: Used literally for a key that opens multiple locks (e.g., in a building) and metaphorically sometimes for a universal solution. Common in everyday and professional contexts (security, maintenance).
target_language_example: El conserje tiene la llave maestra del edificio.
native_language_example: The janitor has the master key to the building.

meaning: give/hand (the) keys to (someone).
additional_notes: This phrase combines 'llaves' (keys) with the preposition 'a' to indicate the recipient. Use with verbs of giving or handing over (dar, llevar, entregar, pasar, etc.). In Spanish the indirect object is often expressed with 'a + person' and can also appear as an indirect object pronoun (le/les).
target_language_example: Dale las llaves a Carla.
native_language_example: Give the keys to Carla.

meaning: 'keys of' or 'keys for' (possessive or descriptive phrase used before a noun).
additional_notes: This is not a complete phrase by itself; 'llaves' means 'keys' and 'de' links them to what they belong to (e.g., 'llaves de la casa' = house keys). Common uses: llaves de casa, llaves del coche, llaves de la oficina. In Spanish word order the thing possessed often follows 'de'. If the owner is a person, you can say 'las llaves de María' (María's keys).
target_language_example: ¿Dónde están las llaves de la casa?
native_language_example: Where are the house keys?

meaning: ‘the keys of his/her/your (formal)/their’ — a possessive phrase used before a noun (llaves) to show ownership.
additional_notes: This is not a complete phrase by itself; it combines llaves (keys) with the possessive su. Su can mean his, her, your (formal), or their depending on context. In natural sentences you'd usually include the owner or the noun being possessed (e.g., las llaves de su coche, las llaves suyas). Word order options: "las llaves de su + [noun]" is common. For clarity in English, specify the possessor (his/her/their/your).
target_language_example: Buscó las llaves de su coche por toda la casa.
native_language_example: He searched for his car keys all over the house.

meaning: 'the keys of' or 'the keys to' (masculine plural noun with a following masculine singular noun)
additional_notes: This is the start of a noun phrase: llaves (keys) + del (contraction of de + el, meaning 'of the' or 'to the'). It must be followed by a masculine singular noun (e.g., llaves del coche, llaves del cuarto). For feminine nouns use 'de la' (llaves de la casa) or plural nouns 'de los/las' as appropriate.
target_language_example: Busco las llaves del coche en la bolsa.
native_language_example: I'm looking for the car keys in the bag.

meaning: the car keys.
additional_notes: Used to refer to the keys that open/start a car. Commonly used in everyday situations (asking for, looking for, or saying someone has/doesn't have them). 'Coche' means 'car' (common in Spain; in some regions 'carro' or 'auto' are used).
target_language_example: ¿Me das las llaves del coche, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you give me the car keys, please?

meaning: keys + preposition 'in/on/at' — used to say where keys are placed or left.
additional_notes: Combine 'llaves' (keys) with a preposition (en, en la, en el, en mi, etc.) to indicate location: 'en un lugar seguro', 'en la cazadora', 'en el bolsillo'. In English this often becomes 'in' or 'on' depending on context (e.g., in a pocket, on a table). Use appropriate article and noun after 'en'.
target_language_example: Dejé las llaves en la mesa para que las vieras.
native_language_example: I left the keys on the table so you'd see them.

meaning: the keys are (located/placed).
additional_notes: A simple way to say where keys are. "Las llaves están + lugar" describes location (e.g., en la cocina, encima de la mesa). In sentence 3, "las llaves están puestas" means the keys are put/placed (or in some contexts 'inserted' or 'on'), so the verb estar can describe state or placement. Use plural feminine agreement (las llaves están).
target_language_example: Las llaves están debajo del cojín.
native_language_example: The keys are under the cushion.

meaning: ‘keys and’ — literal combination of the noun 'llaves' (keys) plus the conjunction 'y' (and).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase: it's simply the plural noun 'llaves' followed by the conjunction 'y' used to link actions or items (e.g., 'las llaves y...'). In spoken Spanish you may see contractions of sentences where 'llaves y' begins a clause like 'las llaves y abrir la puerta' or 'las llaves y asegurarte...'. Pay attention to verb forms that follow (infinitive, imperative, or conjugated verbs) depending on context.
target_language_example: Saca las llaves y cierra la puerta.
native_language_example: Take the keys and close the door.

meaning: 'the ... arrives' / '... arrives' (literally: 'arrives the') used to say that a time, person or thing is coming or has come.
additional_notes: Commonly appears before a noun that specifies what is arriving (e.g., 'llega la mañana' = 'morning arrives' / 'morning comes', 'llega la hora' = 'the time comes'). It's a neutral, everyday construction: subject (the noun) is often introduced after the verb 'llegar' for emphasis. Context determines tense and nuance (literal arrival, start of a moment, or figurative/eventual occurrence).
target_language_example: Cuando llega la noche, encienden las luces.
native_language_example: When night arrives, they turn on the lights.

meaning: arrives/reaches more (farther/more) — used to say something goes farther, arrives sooner/later, or reaches a greater degree
additional_notes: Depends on context: 'más' can mean 'farther' (distance), 'sooner/later' in phrases like 'más pronto o más tarde', or 'more' in general. 'Llega' is third-person singular of 'llegar'. Common constructions: 'llega más lejos' (reaches farther), 'llega más pronto' (arrives sooner), 'todo llega más pronto o más tarde' (everything happens sooner or later).
target_language_example: Este autobús ya no llega más lejos que la plaza.
native_language_example: This bus no longer goes any farther than the square.

meaning: reached the
additional_notes: This is part of a larger phrase using the past participle 'llegado' (arrived/reached) followed by a feminine singular noun introduced by 'la'. Often appears in constructions like 'llegado a la conclusión' (reached the conclusion) or 'llegado a la terminal' (arrived at the terminal). The exact meaning depends on the noun that follows. If the noun is masculine, use 'llegado al' (a + el).
target_language_example: Después de mucho debate, hemos llegado a la conclusión correcta.
native_language_example: After much debate, we have reached the correct conclusion.

meaning: ‘has/have/has/have + arrived at (one's) / reached (one's)’. Used with 'ha/habrá/han...' to say something or someone has reached a place, moment, or state belonging to someone/something.
additional_notes: This phrase combines the past participle 'llegado' (arrived/reached) with 'a su' (to his/her/its/your formal/one's). It appears in perfect tenses (ha llegado, han llegado, habrá llegado) and can refer to physical arrival (a su destino, a su casa) or to a figurative endpoint or state (llegado a su fin = reached its end). 'Su' is context-dependent: translate as his/her/their/your (formal) depending on who is referenced.
target_language_example: El tren ha llegado a su estación.
native_language_example: The train has arrived at its station.

meaning: arrived at
additional_notes: Combination of the past participle llegado (arrived/reached) plus the preposition al (a + el = to the/at the). Commonly used with haber (hemos llegado al) to mean 'we have arrived at' or with estar/has to indicate someone 'has arrived at' a place. Use with locations: llegar a/alcanzar un lugar. Word order: verb + al + place.
target_language_example: Ya hemos llegado al centro comercial.
native_language_example: We have already arrived at the mall.

meaning: when the time comes to; once it's time to
additional_notes: Used to introduce an action or decision that will happen at the appropriate future moment. Often appears at the start of a clause: "Llegado el momento de + infinitive" or "Llegado el momento, + clause." It has a formal/register-neutral tone and implies waiting until the proper time.
target_language_example: Llegado el momento de firmar el contrato, te avisaré.
native_language_example: When the time comes to sign the contract, I'll let you know.

meaning: Not a standard Spanish phrase; likely a word order or grammatical mistake. Possible intended meanings include 'has llegado' (you have arrived), 'llegaste tú' (you arrived), or a third-person construction 'llegó tu...' (your ... arrived).
additional_notes: The sequence 'llegado tu' is ungrammatical as written. 'Llegado' is the past participle of 'llegar' and normally requires an auxiliary (haber) to form compound tenses (e.g., 'has llegado') or appears in passive/nominal phrases. If addressing second person, correct forms include 'has llegado', 'llegaste' or 'llegaste tú'. If followed by a noun, the correct third-person singular is 'llegó tu...' (e.g., 'llegó tu paquete'). If you encounter 'llegado tu' in text, it's likely a typo, misordering, or nonstandard regional usage.
target_language_example: (Incorrect/unaltered example as seen) — "llegado tu"
native_language_example: (Literal reading of the incorrect phrase) — "arrived you" (not grammatically correct English)

meaning: we reached a (we came to a ...).
additional_notes: Used to say that 'we' arrived at or achieved something (often 'acuerdo' = agreement). Follows with a noun (e.g., 'acuerdo', 'compromiso'). Common in formal and everyday contexts to report negotiation outcomes or decisions.
target_language_example: Después de hablarlo mucho, llegamos a un acuerdo.
native_language_example: After talking a lot, we reached an agreement.

meaning: to get to
additional_notes: Used for arriving at a place or reaching a point, goal, result, or even a person/thing figuratively, as in llegar a nuestro corazón ('reach our heart'). In English, this is often translated as 'get to' or 'reach' rather than a literal 'arrive to'.
target_language_example: Queremos llegar a la estación antes de las ocho.
native_language_example: We want to get to the station before eight.

meaning: to make ends meet / to have enough money to last until the end of the month.
additional_notes: Common idiom about money: describes being able to cover expenses until the month's end. Used with personal subjects and often with verbs like 'poder', 'tener', 'luchar/intentó', 'quedar' (money left). Not literal — it's about finances, not physically arriving somewhere.
target_language_example: No sé si podré llegar a fin de mes si sigo pagando tanto en alquiler.
native_language_example: I don't know if I'll be able to make ends meet if I keep paying so much for rent.

meaning: 'to become' (after a process, change, or effort).
additional_notes: Used to describe a transition or change over time into a new state, role, profession, or condition. Emphasizes reaching that state (often after effort or gradual change). Similar to ponerse or volverse but usually implies a long-term change or achievement rather than a sudden or temporary one. Common with professions, social status, or major life changes: llegar a ser + noun/adjective.
target_language_example: Después de muchos años de estudio, llegó a ser médico.
native_language_example: After many years of study, he became a doctor.

meaning: to reach/come to a (decision, agreement, end) — used figuratively to indicate arriving at a conclusion or outcome.
additional_notes: Used with nouns like acuerdo (agreement), arreglo (arrangement), fin (end) or decisión. Appears as llegar a + noun (often with un/una). Context determines English verb: reach, come to, arrive at. Can be used in formal and informal contexts depending on noun and tone.
target_language_example: La dirección se negó a llegar a un acuerdo.
native_language_example: The management refused to reach an agreement.

meaning: to arrive there (on time / at a specific time).
additional_notes: Combines llegar (to arrive) + allá (over there/there). The final 'a' often introduces a time expression (e.g., 'a tiempo' = on time) or can precede an infinitive or phrase in some dialects; in the example sentences it appears before 'tiempo' as part of 'a tiempo' (on time). Useful for saying you reached a distant/place mentioned location. Word order: llegar + allá + (a + time/phrase).
target_language_example: Si salimos ya, podremos llegar allá a tiempo.
native_language_example: If we leave now, we can arrive there on time.

meaning: to arrive by (a mode of transport) or to arrive in/at (a time or state).
additional_notes: Commonly used with a mode of transportation (llegar en coche, llegar en tren) to mean 'arrive by [vehicle]'. It can also be used with time expressions (llegar en diez minutos) to indicate arrival after a period, or with abstract states (llegar en buen momento), though 'llegar a' is more frequent for some uses. Remember verb conjugation: llego en, llegaste en, llegó en, llegamos en, llegan en, etc.
target_language_example: Llegamos en tren a las ocho.
native_language_example: We arrived by train at eight o'clock.

meaning: to go far; to get far in life or a career (to achieve success or progress).
additional_notes: Used idiomatically to talk about making significant progress, achieving success, or advancing in one's career or goals. Can refer literally to travel (to arrive far away) but is most often figurative: 'If you work hard, you can llegar lejos.' Commonly used with personal subjects (él, ella, tú, nosotros).
target_language_example: Si sigues estudiando así, vas a llegar lejos.
native_language_example: If you keep studying like that, you're going to go far.

meaning: to be late
additional_notes: Common Spanish phrase meaning to arrive after the expected or scheduled time. Used with people (llegar tarde a clase, al trabajo) or events (llegar tarde a comer). Can be followed by a preposition + noun (llegar tarde a + lugar/actividad).
target_language_example: Perdón por llegar tarde al trabajo.
native_language_example: Sorry for being late to work.

meaning: they/them arrived (when)... — used to say that a group of people or things arrived.
additional_notes: Combines the past tense verb llegar (ellos llegaron) with the masculine definite article/possessive phrase 'los' followed by a noun that identifies who arrived (e.g., los bomberos, los invitados). Often appears in time clauses introduced by 'cuando' to describe an action that happened at the same time as or after the arrival. Change 'los' to 'las' for feminine plural groups, or use a specific subject (llegaron Maria y Juan / llegó él).
target_language_example: Cerramos la puerta cuando llegaron los vecinos.
native_language_example: We closed the door when the neighbors arrived.

meaning: the ... will arrive
additional_notes: Literal meaning: 'will arrive the ...'. Used to talk about a future arrival (people, things, events) or figuratively to say that a moment/time will come. Often followed by a noun (día, tren, momento, fin, jueves). Context determines whether it's physical arrival or an anticipated moment.
target_language_example: Llegará el día en que entenderás por qué lo hice.
native_language_example: The day will come when you understand why I did it.

meaning: 'would arrive' or 'would come to' / 'would end up (doing something)' depending on context.
additional_notes: This is the conditional form of llegar + the preposition a. Use 'llegaría a' for: 1) physical arrival (e.g., llegar a tiempo = would arrive on time), and 2) idiomatic sense meaning 'to come to' or 'to end up (doing something)' (e.g., llegar a confesar = would even confess; llegar a esto = to come to this point). Context decides whether it's literal (arrive) or figurative (end up/reach a state).
target_language_example: Si saliera ahora, llegaría a tiempo.
native_language_example: If I left now, I would arrive on time.

meaning: a common part of subordinate clauses meaning '(that) [someone/something] arrives' or 'until [someone/something] arrives'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but the verb 'llegue' (subjunctive of llegar) plus the definite article 'el' that begins a noun phrase (e.g., 'el mañana', 'el sábado', 'el doctor'). It appears in clauses introduced by verbs or expressions of waiting, wanting, hoping, or time (hasta que, esperar a que, que + verb). Use the subjunctive (llegue) when the arrival is wished for, awaited, or uncertain. Replace 'el' with other articles/pronouns as needed (llegue la, lleguen los, llegue mi).
target_language_example: Estoy contando los días hasta que llegue el domingo.
native_language_example: I'm counting the days until Sunday arrives.

meaning: 'when the time comes' or 'when the moment arrives'.
additional_notes: Used to refer to a future point when something will happen or be done. Often appears in the phrase 'cuando llegue el momento' to reassure or postpone action until the appropriate time. Common in spoken and written Spanish; the verb 'llegue' is subjunctive because the moment is anticipated, not certain.
target_language_example: No te preocupes ahora; cuando llegue el momento, te ayudaré.
native_language_example: Don't worry now; when the time comes, I'll help you.

meaning: a short sequence used in subordinate clauses meaning 'arrive' or 'comes' (subjunctive form) + definite article 'the' (as in 'when the ... arrives').
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom but a fragment showing the verb llegar in the present-subjunctive (llegue) followed by the definite article la. It appears in time clauses introduced by cuando, antes de que, hasta que, etc., to talk about future or anticipated events (e.g., 'cuando llegue la primavera' = 'when spring arrives'). The verb is in the subjunctive when the action is seen as uncertain or not yet happened. Replace 'la' with the appropriate article/pronoun for other nouns (e.g., 'cuando llegue el autobús').
target_language_example: Cuando llegue la noche, cerramos las ventanas.
native_language_example: When night arrives, we'll close the windows.

meaning: 'arrived from' or 'came from' (he/she/it arrived from)
