additional_notes: Llegó is the past (pretérito) third-person singular of llegar (to arrive). De introduces the origin or place someone/something came from: 'llegó de Madrid' = 'he/she arrived from Madrid'. Can also be used with people: 'llegó de la escuela' or with events: 'llegó de vacaciones'.
target_language_example: Ella llegó de Barcelona ayer por la noche.
native_language_example: She arrived from Barcelona last night.

meaning: arrived later / came afterwards
additional_notes: A simple past phrase using llegar (to arrive) + después (after/later). Use to say someone or something arrived later than others or after a certain time/event. Can refer to chronological sequence (e.g., 'He arrived later') or to doing something afterwards. Tense can change (llegó después, llegó después de X, llegó más tarde).
target_language_example: Ella llegó después de que empezó la reunión.
native_language_example: She arrived after the meeting started.

meaning: arrived this (feminine) — used when saying that something or someone (feminine) arrived or has come.
additional_notes: This is the verb 'llegó' (past tense, third person singular of llegar) followed by the demonstrative 'esta' (this, feminine). It appears in contexts like 'llegó esta mañana' (she/it arrived this morning) or 'llegó esta caja' (this box arrived). In Spanish word order, adjectives or modifiers may follow or precede; often you'd see 'esta' before the noun ('esta caja llegó') or the time expression after the verb ('llegó esta mañana'). Both parts must agree with the noun referenced (feminine).
target_language_example: La carta llegó esta tarde.
native_language_example: The letter arrived this afternoon.

meaning: arrived (something) ago — used to say how long since someone/something arrived.
additional_notes: Combine the past tense verb (llegó = he/she/it/you formal arrived) with hace + time expression to indicate how long ago the arrival happened. Commonly used with hours, minutes, days, etc. Note: avoid adding both hace and atrás together (redundant).
target_language_example: Llegó hace dos horas.
native_language_example: He arrived two hours ago.

meaning: ‘a … arrived’ or ‘there came a …’ — indicates that something or someone arrived (past tense).
additional_notes: This is the past (pretérito) third-person singular of llegar + an indefinite article (un/una). Often used to introduce an event or person: Llegó un paquete (A package arrived) or Llegó un momento (A moment came). Word order can vary: also common is 'un X llegó' but 'llegó un...' emphasizes the arrival. Change 'un' to 'una' for feminine nouns and to plural forms ('llegaron unos/unas') for plural subjects.
target_language_example: Llegó un autobús y subimos todos.
native_language_example: A bus arrived and we all got on.

meaning: gets along (well) with
additional_notes: Used with reflexive verb 'llevarse' (llevarse bien con) to say two or more people have a good relationship. Conjugate 'lleva' depending on subject (me llevo, te llevas, se lleva, nos llevamos, se llevan). Commonly followed by 'con' + person(s).
target_language_example: Ella se lleva bien con sus vecinos.
native_language_example: She gets along well with her neighbors.

meaning: he/she/it/you (formal) carries/has (something) with him/her/it; he/she wears (something) on themselves.
additional_notes: From the verb llevar (to carry, to wear, to take) + the possessive adjective su (his/her/its/your formal/their). Used before a noun: lleva su casa (he carries his house) or lleva su abrigo (he wears his coat). Context decides whether it means 'carry', 'wear', or 'have' (e.g., lleva su documento = he has his document). Subject agreement depends on the verb (llevo, llevas, lleva, llevamos, llevan).
target_language_example: Ella siempre lleva su mochila al trabajo.
native_language_example: She always takes/wears her backpack to work.

meaning: was taking to
additional_notes: Imperfect form of llevar a. It usually describes an ongoing or habitual action in the past, often with someone being taken somewhere: me llevaba a la escuela = he used to take me to school. In some contexts, llevar a + infinitive can also mean "to lead to" or "to cause."
target_language_example: De niño, mi madre me llevaba a la biblioteca todos los sábados.
native_language_example: When I was a child, my mother used to take me to the library every Saturday.

meaning: was wearing / was carrying (female/singular object).
additional_notes: Imperfect tense of llevar + the feminine definite article 'la' before a feminine singular noun (often omitted here but appears in sentences like 'llevaba la chaqueta'). Used to describe ongoing or repeated past actions (what someone was wearing or carrying). The exact English translation depends on the noun that follows: 'was wearing the...', 'was carrying the...', or in metaphorical contexts 'carried the...'.
target_language_example: Ella llevaba la bufanda roja cuando la vi.
native_language_example: She was wearing the red scarf when I saw her.

meaning: had/been living (a) — used with 'vida', 'dieta', etc., to say someone has led or experienced something.
additional_notes: This is the past participle 'llevado' (from llevar) used with 'una' plus a noun like 'vida' or 'dieta' to mean 'have led/have had a (life/diet)'. Often appears in perfect tenses with auxiliary 'haber' (e.g., 'ha llevado una vida...') meaning 'has led/has had'. 'Se lo ha llevado una ola' is a different use: 'llevar(se)' meaning 'to carry away' (here 'ha llevado' = 'has taken/has carried away'). Context determines whether it's 'lead/have' (transitive 'llevar una vida') or 'carry away' (llevar(se)).
target_language_example: Ella ha llevado una vida tranquila desde que se mudó.
native_language_example: She has led a quiet life since she moved.

meaning: to carry out; to execute; to accomplish.
additional_notes: Common phrasal verb used for completing tasks, plans, projects, experiments, or events. Often followed by a noun (llevar a cabo un plan, una investigación). Formal and neutral register — appropriate in spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: Vamos a llevar a cabo la reunión mañana por la mañana.
native_language_example: We are going to carry out the meeting tomorrow morning.

meaning: to lead/bring someone or something to (a feminine noun); can mean 'cause to' or 'take to'.
additional_notes: Llevar a + la (feminine singular article) appears when the thing/person being taken or caused ends with a feminine noun: llevar a la estación, llevar a la cama. Can be physical (take/bring) or figurative (cause someone to do something: llevar a la gente a hacer X). For masculine nouns use llevar al (a + el). When followed by a verb clause (e.g., llevar a hacer), it means 'cause to' or 'lead to' doing something.
target_language_example: La lluvia puede llevar a la cancelación del concierto.
native_language_example: The rain can lead to the cancellation of the concert.

meaning: to have been doing something for a long time; to take a long time (that something has lasted or required a long period)
additional_notes: Used with gerunds (llevar + time + gerund) to indicate an action or state has been ongoing. Can also be used impersonally to say something has taken a long time (llevar mucho tiempo + en/para + infinitive). Common in present-continuous-like expressions: "Llevo dos años estudiando español."
target_language_example: Llevar mucho tiempo viviendo en esta ciudad no significa que conozca todos sus rincones.
native_language_example: Having lived in this city for a long time doesn't mean I know all its corners.

meaning: to be wearing (clothes, accessories).
additional_notes: Commonly used to describe what someone has on at the moment. Often appears as llevar + clothing item (llevar puesto un abrigo, llevar puesto unos zapatos). Can be shortened to llevar (¿Qué llevas?) but llevar puesto emphasizes the item is currently worn.
target_language_example: Hoy llevo puesto un suéter azul.
native_language_example: Today I am wearing a blue sweater.

meaning: to have been doing something for a certain amount of time; also used impersonally to mean that something takes time
additional_notes: Commonly used with an activity or gerund: llevar + period + gerund (e.g., llevo dos años estudiando = I've been studying for two years). Can also be used impersonally to say something 'takes' time (e.g., lleva tiempo arreglarlo = it takes time to fix it). Llevar emphasizes duration already spent; llevar tiempo + gerund stresses ongoing action.
target_language_example: Llevar tiempo aprendiendo español me ha dado mucha confianza.
native_language_example: To have been learning Spanish for some time has given me a lot of confidence.

meaning: to take a few minutes (to do something); to have been taking a few minutes
additional_notes: Commonly used with verbs in the third-person singular or impersonal constructions to say that an action requires or has required a few minutes. Often appears as 'lleva unos minutos' (it has been taking a few minutes) or 'va a llevar unos minutos' (it will take a few minutes). Useful for estimating short durations, asking for patience, or describing recent ongoing actions.
target_language_example: Está empezando; esto va a llevar unos minutos.
native_language_example: It's starting; this is going to take a few minutes.

meaning: to get along (well) with someone; to have a good relationship
additional_notes: Reflexive verb phrase used with 'con' + person (llevarse bien con alguien). Conjugates like other pronominal verbs: me/te/se/nos/os/se llevo/llevas/lleva/llevamos/lleváis/llevan. Opposites/variants: llevarse mal (to get along badly), llevarse muy bien (to get along very well). Common in spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: Es difícil llevarse bien con Tom.
native_language_example: It's difficult to get along with Tom.

meaning: will take (someone/something) to the center (the city center/downtown or a central place).
additional_notes: Future tense of llevar + destination 'al centro'. 'Llevará' is third-person singular (él/ella/usted) or impersonal future (it/he/she will take). 'El centro' commonly means the city center or downtown; context determines exact meaning. Requires a direct object or implied object (e.g., a person or thing being taken).
target_language_example: Él llevará al centro a los turistas mañana.
native_language_example: He will take the tourists to downtown tomorrow.

meaning: will take (someone) to the city center / downtown.
additional_notes: Third-person future of llevar + destination. Used to say a person, vehicle, or route will transport or lead someone to a place (here: 'el centro de la ciudad'). You can change the subject (llevaré, llevarás, llevará, llevaremos, llevaréis, llevarán) and the object pronoun (me, te, lo/la, nos, os, los/las) to match who is being taken. Common with buses, streets, or people.
target_language_example: Este taxi te llevará al centro de la ciudad.
native_language_example: This taxi will take you to the city center.

meaning: I will bring/take (from) — first person future of llevar plus preposition de.
additional_notes: Use llevaré de when you want to say you'll bring or take something from a place or person (e.g., llevaré de la tienda, llevaré de tu casa). The preposition de indicates origin or source. Conjugation is future tense (yo). In natural speech, people often omit de if context already shows the source (llevaré esto contigo).
target_language_example: Llevaré de la panadería pan fresco para la reunión.
native_language_example: I will bring fresh bread from the bakery for the meeting.

meaning: you wear/carry/take the (masculine singular noun) — present tense, informal 'tú' form.
additional_notes: From the verb llevar. Meaning depends on the noun that follows: llevar + ropa = 'to wear' (e.g., llevar el uniforme), llevar + objeto = 'to carry' or 'to take' (e.g., llevar el dinero), llevar + paso/ritmo = 'to keep/maintain' (idiomatic). Context and the noun determine the translation. This is the present indicative for tú (you).
target_language_example: ¿Por qué llevas el abrigo si hace calor?
native_language_example: Why are you wearing the coat if it's hot?

meaning: I carry/have (something) in/on (somewhere) — used to say you physically carry something or figuratively keep something inside (heart, conscience, blood).
additional_notes: Common construction: llevar + en + body part / container / place. Can be literal (llevar algo en el bolsillo = to carry something in your pocket) or figurative (llevar algo en la sangre = to have something in your blood; llevarlo en la conciencia = to carry it on your conscience). The subject is usually first person (llevo) but other persons use llevar + en. Follow with the thing carried: llevo en mi corazón (lo llevo en mi corazón).
target_language_example: Llevo en el bolsillo las llaves y el teléfono.
native_language_example: I carry my keys and phone in my pocket.

meaning: took (away) my / carried my (someone or something) away.
additional_notes: From the verb llevar (to take, carry). In these examples it describes someone or something being taken away from the speaker (often a person). Context determines tense and subject: llevó = he/she/it took. Use 'se llevó a mi...' when the action is reflexive/agent implied (someone/something removed the person). Common with family members (mi hermano, mi esposa, etc.).
target_language_example: Se llevó a mi perro anoche y no lo he vuelto a ver.
native_language_example: They took my dog last night and I haven't seen him since.

meaning: took the
additional_notes: Form: past (pretérito) of llevar + definite article 'el'. Commonly means someone took or carried something away. Usage depends on context: can mean 'took (away)' (e.g., stole or removed) or simply 'brought to mouth' (as in 'took the glass to his lips'). Followed by a noun. Not idiomatic — literal action.
target_language_example: Se llevó el paquete antes de que llegáramos.
native_language_example: He took the package before we arrived.

meaning: '(he/she/it) took my' or '(you formal) took my' — third person singular preterite of llevar + possessive 'mi'.
additional_notes: Llevó is the past (preterite) form of llevar for él/ella/usted. Combined with mi (my) it introduces something someone took or carried away in the past: e.g. 'llevó mi libro' = 'he/she took my book'. Remember to add the noun after 'mi' (mi casa, mi teléfono). If the subject is plural use 'llevaron'.
target_language_example: Ella llevó mi mochila al coche.
native_language_example: She took my backpack to the car.

meaning: took/required a lot (of time, effort, etc.) — he/she/it took a long time or required much
additional_notes: Past simple (pretérito) of llevar + mucho. 'Llevar' has many uses; here it means 'to take' or 'to require' (usually time or effort). Subject is third person singular (él/ella/usted or something neuter like 'eso'). To say 'it took me a long time' you'd use 'me llevó mucho'. For ongoing past you'd use 'llevaba mucho'.
target_language_example: La reparación llevó mucho porque faltaban piezas.
native_language_example: The repair took a long time because parts were missing.

meaning: took/lasted longer (he/she/it took more or lasted longer).
additional_notes: Past tense of llevar + más. Commonly used to say something required more time or took longer than expected: 'llevar más tiempo' → 'to take more time'. Context determines subject (he/she/it/you formal) and what was 'taken'. Often appears with a noun or clause indicating what took longer: 'La obra llevó más de lo previsto.'
target_language_example: La reparación llevó más de una semana.
native_language_example: The repair took more than a week.

meaning: took more time than (it/one expected or than ...) — indicates duration exceeded something.
additional_notes: Commonly used to compare actual time spent with an expected or usual amount. Often followed by a noun, a quantity (e.g., 'una hora'), or a clause (introduced with 'que' or an infinitive). Can refer to a task, trip, event, etc. Example structure: 'Me llevó más tiempo de lo que pensé' = 'It took me more time than I thought.'
target_language_example: La reparación del coche nos llevó más tiempo de lo previsto.
native_language_example: The car repair took us more time than expected.

meaning: he/she/it brought a
additional_notes: ‘llevó’ is the preterite (past) form of llevar. Meaning depends on context: llevar can mean 'to bring' or 'to wear' (e.g., ropa), and in impersonal constructions like 'me llevó un tiempo' / 'nos llevó un año' it means 'it took (me/us) [time]'. The subject before or after the verb clarifies which sense is intended.
target_language_example: Ella llevó un paraguas porque llovía.
native_language_example: She brought/was wearing an umbrella because it was raining.

meaning: crying in/at (someone/somewhere) — present participle + preposition to indicate where or in what someone is crying.
additional_notes: Used to describe someone currently crying and the location or context (en + place). Common in continuous actions: 'estar llorando en...' or 'encontrar a alguien llorando en...'. Not a fixed idiom; combine llorando with other prepositions as needed (p. ej. 'llorando por' = crying because of/about).
target_language_example: La niña está llorando en la sala.
native_language_example: The girl is crying in the living room.

meaning: literally 'crying all (of)'; used to describe someone crying a lot or continuously (colloquial/poetic).
additional_notes: This is a fragment rather than a standalone fixed phrase; it often appears as part of a larger expression like "llorando toda la noche" (crying all night) or "llorando toda la tarde". Use it to emphasize duration or intensity of crying. Word order may vary: more natural complete forms include "llorando toda la noche" or "está llorando todo el tiempo."
target_language_example: Estuvo llorando toda la noche después de la noticia.
native_language_example: She was crying all night after the news.

meaning: crying the whole (time/day/night/etc.) — part of a phrase meaning someone was crying the entire period mentioned.
additional_notes: This is a fragment: 'llorando' = 'crying' (gerund), 'toda la' = 'the whole' (feminine singular). It must be followed by a feminine singular noun (e.g., 'noche', 'tarde', 'vida') to complete the idea: 'llorando toda la noche' = 'crying all night.' Commonly used to emphasize duration of crying.
target_language_example: Se pasó llorando toda la noche después de la noticia.
native_language_example: She spent the whole night crying after the news.

meaning: 'to cry in' (to cry while in or during something: a place, situation, or time).
additional_notes: This is the verb llorar followed by the preposition en. It is used to say someone cries in a specific place, context, or time (e.g., llorar en público = to cry in public; llorar en la película = to cry during the movie). You usually need a noun or phrase after en. If you mean 'to cry about' something, Spanish more commonly uses 'llorar por'.
target_language_example: Ella empezó a llorar en el cine durante la escena final.
native_language_example: She started to cry in the cinema during the final scene.

meaning: 'to cry and...' — used to join crying with another action or result
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom; it's the verb llorar ('to cry') followed by y ('and') to connect crying with another verb or clause. Common in spoken and written Spanish to show two actions happening together or in sequence (e.g., 'llorar y vomitar' = 'cry and vomit', 'llorar y contar' = 'cry and tell'). Word order and tense follow normal grammar: llorar y + infinitive for general statements, or lloró y + past verb for past actions.
target_language_example: Ella empezó a llorar y se fue de la casa.
native_language_example: She started to cry and left the house.

meaning: to rain heavily; to pour (rain).
additional_notes: Idiomatic expression meaning it's raining a lot. Often used in everyday speech to describe heavy, persistent rain. Typically used impersonally (with 'llover' in its impersonal forms) or in progressive forms: 'Está lloviendo a cántaros', 'Llovía a cántaros'.
target_language_example: Está lloviendo a cántaros desde la madrugada.
native_language_example: It's been pouring since dawn.

meaning: 'to rain this' (used as part of phrases like 'llover esta tarde' = 'to rain this afternoon')
additional_notes: This isn't a fixed standalone phrase: it's the verb llover (to rain) followed by a time word introduced by esta (short for 'esta' + time of day, e.g. 'esta tarde' = 'this afternoon'). Common constructions: 'va a llover esta tarde' (it's going to rain this afternoon) or 'puede llover esta noche' (it may rain tonight). Use 'esta' to specify 'this' + time period (tarde, noche, mañana).
target_language_example: Puede llover esta noche, lleva el paraguas.
native_language_example: It may rain tonight, take an umbrella.

meaning: literally 'raining when' — used to describe that it was raining at the moment something else happened.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase on its own but a sequence you often hear in sentences like «Estaba lloviendo cuando...». It pairs the gerund of llover (lloviendo) with cuando to set background weather while another event occurs. Common construction: Estaba/Estuvo lloviendo cuando + past action.
target_language_example: Estaba lloviendo cuando salimos de la casa.
native_language_example: It was raining when we left the house.

meaning: start of a phrase meaning 'it's raining' or 'it rains', often continued with intensity or manner (e.g. 'llueve a cántaros' = 'it's raining buckets').
additional_notes: Alone, 'llueve' = 'it's raining'. 'Llueve a' is typically the beginning of fixed expressions that describe how strongly or in what way it's raining (common completion: 'llueve a cántaros' = very heavy rain). You will rarely see 'llueve a' standing alone without the rest of the expression.
target_language_example: Llueve a cántaros; mejor nos quedamos en casa.
native_language_example: It's pouring; we'd better stay home.

meaning: it rains tomorrow / if it rains tomorrow (used in conditional clauses)
additional_notes: Literally 'it rains tomorrow.' Commonly appears in 'si llueve mañana' (if it rains tomorrow) to talk about plans or consequences depending on tomorrow's weather. The verb llueve is the impersonal form of llover (to rain). Use it for general weather statements (no subject).
target_language_example: Si llueve mañana, llevaremos paraguas.
native_language_example: If it rains tomorrow, we'll take umbrellas.

meaning: a shower/period of (used to describe a lot of something falling or happening, e.g., lluvia de ideas = brainstorm).
additional_notes: This literal phrase means 'rain of' and is used in Spanish to describe a large quantity or sudden occurrence of something (often metaphorically). It's followed by a noun: lluvia de estrellas (meteor shower), lluvia de ideas (brainstorm, 'rain of ideas'), lluvia de críticas (a flood of criticism). Use it to indicate many items/events coming at once.
target_language_example: Tuvimos una lluvia de ideas para el proyecto.
native_language_example: We had a brainstorming session for the project.

meaning: "rain in" — used to say where or on what surface it rains (location or context).
additional_notes: A simple prepositional phrase: lluvia (rain) + en (in/on). Commonly followed by a place (city, season, surface) or part of a sentence describing where rain falls or lands. Not an idiom; literal meaning. Word order: "la lluvia en + lugar/tiempo/superficie". You may also see "llueve en" (it rains in) when using the verb.
target_language_example: La lluvia en la costa es constante durante el otoño.
native_language_example: The rain on the coast is constant during autumn.

meaning: used to show that the rain affected or caused something to happen to the speaker (e.g., prevented, surprised, made something impossible).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself; examples show the pattern 'la lluvia + me + [verb]' where 'me' is the indirect/object pronoun meaning 'to/for me' or 'me' as the person affected. It indicates that rain was the cause or agent that impacted the speaker (prevented them, surprised them, made something impossible). Common verbs: impedir (to prevent), pillar (to catch/surprise), fue imposible (it was impossible for me).
target_language_example: La lluvia me obligó a quedarme en casa.
native_language_example: The rain forced me to stay at home.

meaning: the rain (caused) us to ... / the rain made us ...
additional_notes: This combination shows how lluvia (rain) is the subject causing an effect on 'us' (nos). In natural sentences you'd usually see a verb after it (e.g. 'nos impidió', 'nos obligó') meaning 'prevented us' or 'forced us'. Word order: 'La lluvia nos + [verb]' = 'The rain [verb] us'. Common verbs: impedir (prevent), obligar (force), hacer (make).
target_language_example: La lluvia nos obligó a quedarnos en casa.
native_language_example: The rain forced us to stay at home.

meaning: 'rain' used with 'and' to join it to another noun or phrase (literal: 'rain and ...').
additional_notes: This is the noun lluvia ('rain') followed by the conjunction y ('and'). It appears when listing or linking rain with something else (e.g., lluvia y nieve = rain and snow). The phrase itself has no special idiomatic meaning beyond the literal; watch gender/number agreement of any adjectives or articles that come before/after (la lluvia).
target_language_example: La lluvia y el viento hicieron que cerráramos las ventanas.
native_language_example: The rain and the wind made us close the windows.

meaning: acid rain (rain containing harmful acidic pollutants).
additional_notes: Refers to rain (or other precipitation) made acidic by air pollution (sulfur and nitrogen compounds). Used in environmental and scientific contexts. Not informal; literal composition matches English term.
target_language_example: La lluvia ácida dañó los bosques cercanos.
native_language_example: Acid rain damaged the nearby forests.

meaning: as soon as possible; as quickly as possible.
additional_notes: Used to express urgency or promptness. Commonly abbreviated in writing as "lo antes posible" or shortened to "lo antes" in casual speech. Can be used with verbs: "Hazlo lo antes posible." Formal alternatives: "lo más pronto posible", "cuanto antes".
target_language_example: Envíame el informe lo antes posible.
native_language_example: Send me the report as soon as possible.

meaning: 'the good (thing)' or used in set phrases to mean 'how well' / 'the goodness of something'.
additional_notes: Lo + adjective (like 'lo bien') is a neuter use of 'lo' that refers to an abstract quality or idea ("the good/what is good"). By itself 'lo bien' is uncommon without context; more frequent are phrases like 'lo bueno', 'lo malo', or constructions such as 'lo bien que...'(= 'how well...'). In casual speech you may hear 'lo bien que lo pasamos' ('how well we had a time' → 'how much fun we had').
target_language_example: No te imaginas lo bien que se siente después de dormir ocho horas.
native_language_example: You can't imagine how good it feels after sleeping eight hours.

meaning: 'the good thing is that' / 'the good part is that'.
additional_notes: Used to introduce a positive aspect or silver lining in a situation. Common in spoken and written Spanish to contrast a drawback with something favorable. Often followed by a clause (que + verb).
target_language_example: Lo bueno es que mañana tenemos tiempo para terminarlo.
native_language_example: The good thing is that we have time tomorrow to finish it.

meaning: it changes it / it changes everything (depending on context).
additional_notes: Lo is a neutral direct object pronoun meaning 'it' or a general 'that/it.' Cambia is the third-person singular of cambiar (to change). Together, 'lo cambia' literally means 'it changes it.' In sentences like 'El amor lo cambia todo' the phrase is followed by 'todo' (everything) and the full idea is 'it changes everything.' Spanish often uses 'lo' as a neutral pronoun to refer to an abstract idea or a previously mentioned situation.
target_language_example: La noticia lo cambia todo.
native_language_example: The news changes everything.

meaning: I bought it from (someone).
additional_notes: Used with a direct object pronoun (lo/la/los/las) plus a personal indirect object introduced by a (a + person) to indicate the seller or source. Common structure: (Se) + lo/la + compré + a + [person]. In spoken Spanish 'se lo' replaces 'le lo'.
target_language_example: Se lo compré a María ayer en el mercado.
native_language_example: I bought it from María yesterday at the market.

meaning: 'the usual' or 'what's common/ordinary'.
additional_notes: Often appears in the fixed phrase 'fuera de lo común' meaning 'unusual' or 'extraordinary'. Alone, 'lo común' refers to what is typical or ordinary. Common structures: 'más de lo común' (more than usual), 'nada fuera de lo común' (nothing unusual).
target_language_example: Su comportamiento fue más de lo común después del accidente.
native_language_example: His behavior was more than usual after the accident.

meaning: the right thing; what is correct
additional_notes: Used to refer to an action, decision, or idea that is morally right, appropriate, or factually correct. Can mean 'the right thing to do' or 'being correct' depending on context. Often follows verbs like hacer, estar, parecer, sentir.
target_language_example: Haz lo correcto y pide perdón.
native_language_example: Do the right thing and apologize.

meaning: 'whether you believe it or not' / 'believe it or not'.
additional_notes: Used to introduce a surprising fact or claim; often appears in the phrase 'lo creas o no' (with 'no' optional depending on structure). Common in spoken and written Spanish to emphasize that something is true despite sounding unlikely.
target_language_example: Lo creas o no, llegó en menos de una hora.
native_language_example: Believe it or not, he arrived in less than an hour.

meaning: 'believe it or not' (used to introduce a surprising fact).
additional_notes: Common phrase to signal that what follows may be surprising or hard to believe. Can start a sentence and is followed by a comma; often used in spoken and informal contexts but also fine in neutral registers.
target_language_example: Lo creas o no, terminé el proyecto en una noche.
native_language_example: Believe it or not, I finished the project in one night.

meaning: what happened with
additional_notes: refers to a situation, event, or matter understood from context. With time expressions, it often means "what happened" then: lo de anoche = "what happened last night." With a person or thing, it can mean "the thing about..." or "what happened to/with...": lo de su marido = "what happened with your husband" / "about your husband." It is very common in apologies: siento lo de... = "I'm sorry about..."
target_language_example: No quiero hablar de lo de ayer.
native_language_example: I don't want to talk about what happened yesterday.

meaning: the thing about this / this matter (referring to a situation or detail just mentioned)
additional_notes: Colloquial expression used to refer back to a situation, topic or specific detail introduced in context. Often appears in conversation when summarizing, complaining, or asking for clarification (e.g., 'lo de esta reunión', 'lo de esta semana'). It usually needs context to identify what 'esta' (this) points to. Can be followed by a noun or left standing alone.
target_language_example: No entiendo lo de esta reunión: ¿a qué hora empieza?
native_language_example: I don't understand this meeting thing: what time does it start?

meaning: the usual thing / the same as always
additional_notes: Used to refer to a habitual, expected situation or order (e.g., your regular drink, a recurring problem, or the same routine). Common in everyday speech to avoid repeating details. Tone is neutral; context clarifies what 'the usual' is.
target_language_example: En el bar pedí lo de siempre.
native_language_example: At the bar I ordered the usual.

meaning: I owe it (to someone) / I owe him/her/you it.
additional_notes: Common short phrase using direct object pronoun 'lo' (it) plus verb 'deber' (to owe). Meaning depends on context: can mean owing money, gratitude, or a favor. Often appears with indirect object pronouns (me/te/se) before 'lo' — e.g. 'te lo debo' = 'I owe it to you' or 'I owe you for that.' When used alone 'Se lo debo' can mean 'I owe it to him/her/you (formal)/them' depending on 'se'.
target_language_example: Te lo debo por ayudarme ayer.
native_language_example: I owe you for helping me yesterday.

meaning: I owe it to (someone) / I owe (something) to (someone).
additional_notes: Used to say that a person is responsible for, or deserves credit for, something (e.g., success, life, qualities). 'Lo' refers to the thing owed (it/that), 'se' is an indirect-object pronoun replacement for le/les when combined with lo, and 'a' introduces the person (a él, a ella, a ti, a mi padre). Common in expressions like 'Se lo debo a mi padre' = 'I owe it to my father.'
target_language_example: Mi éxito lo debo a mi profesora.
native_language_example: I owe my success to my teacher.

meaning: he/she/you (formal) leaves it
additional_notes: Literal translation: "he/she/you (formal) leaves it". Context determines meaning: puede indicar dejar algo en un lugar (leave it), permitir o consentir (let it), or dejar de hacer algo (stop doing it). Subject pronoun is omitted in Spanish; verb form "deja" is third person singular of dejar. "Lo" is a masculine direct object pronoun meaning "it" or a neutral direct object. Could also be used in commands with different pronouns (e.g., "déjalo" = "leave it").
target_language_example: Si no te sirve, lo deja sobre la mesa.
native_language_example: If it doesn't work for you, leave it on the table.

meaning: they say it
additional_notes: A common combination of lo + dicen (from decir). Here lo usually refers to a thing, fact, or idea already known from context, so in English it is often translated as "it" or "so." Depending on context, dicen can mean "they say" or a general "people say."
target_language_example: Todos lo dicen, pero yo no estoy seguro.
native_language_example: Everyone says so, but I'm not sure.

meaning: 'the difficult part' or 'what's difficult'.
additional_notes: Lo + adjective turns the adjective into a noun meaning 'the [adjective] thing/part' or an abstract idea. Use to refer to the difficulty itself (lo difícil de X = the difficult thing about X). Common in phrases like 'lo difícil es...' or 'lo difícil de esto es...'.
target_language_example: Lo difícil de aprender español es la pronunciación.
native_language_example: The difficult part of learning Spanish is the pronunciation.

meaning: tell it to (someone); say it to (someone).
additional_notes: This is part of a common Spanish structure: 'decir (algo) a (alguien)'. 'Lo' refers to 'it' (a thing or information). With commands or requests negative/informal forms appear as 'no se lo digas a nadie' (don't tell anyone). The indirect object (to whom) follows 'a' (e.g., 'a Lola', 'a mi esposa'). In polite requests you may hear 'se lo ruego, no se lo diga' (formal).
target_language_example: No se lo digas a tu hermano.
native_language_example: Don't tell it to your brother.

meaning: 'told it to' or 'said it to' (he/she told it to ...).
additional_notes: This is the past tense (pretérito) third-person form of decir with the direct object pronoun lo (it/him) plus the preposition a introducing the indirect object (the person who receives the information). Common in sentences like 'Se lo dijo a María' = 'He/she told it to María.' The pronoun order: indirect object (se when le/les would appear) + lo (direct object) + dijo. If the indirect object is explicit, use 'a + name'.
target_language_example: Se lo dijo a Carlos cuando llegaron.
native_language_example: She told it to Carlos when they arrived.

meaning: gave it / gave him (masculine or neutral direct object)
additional_notes: Lo dio is the past (pretérito) form of dar with the direct object pronoun lo attached to the verb (él/ella/usted form: dio + lo). It means 'he/she/you(formal) gave it' or 'gave him' when lo refers to a masculine person or a neuter idea. Often appears with an indirect object pronoun (se le / se la) replaced by se in constructions like 'se lo dio' = 'gave it to him/her/you'. Context decides whether lo refers to a thing, a masculine person, or a general idea.
target_language_example: Ella encontró el libro y se lo dio a su hermano.
native_language_example: She found the book and gave it to her brother.

meaning: gave it to (him/her/it) / handed it to
additional_notes: A short sequence combining the direct object pronoun lo (it/him) + dio (third-person singular preterite of dar) + a (introduces the indirect object). Commonly used to say someone gave or handed an object to someone. The actual recipient follows the preposition a (e.g., lo dio a María = he/she gave it to María). If the recipient is a pronoun, it is usually stressed (e.g., lo dio a él).
target_language_example: Él lo dio a María ayer.
native_language_example: He gave it to María yesterday.

meaning: I'll tell him/her/you in/at (time or place).
additional_notes: Common way to say you'll tell someone something and specify when or where with a following time expression or place (e.g., 'en cuanto', 'en un minuto', 'en el coche', 'en el porche', 'en el camino'). 'Lo' refers to the thing to be told; verb agrees with speaker (diré = I will tell).
target_language_example: Se lo diré en cuanto llegue a casa.
native_language_example: I'll tell him/her as soon as I get home.

meaning: I give it (to you/him/her/them).
additional_notes: Common short phrase: lo = direct object pronoun (it/you formal depending on context), doy = first-person singular present of dar (to give). Use when offering or handing something or figuratively (giving information, support, permission). Context determines who 'lo' refers to (it/that/you).
target_language_example: No tengo más tiempo, así que te lo doy ahora.
native_language_example: I don't have more time, so I'll give it to you now.

meaning: you are
additional_notes: Used when "lo" refers back to a previously mentioned state, quality, or description, especially after estar. In English, "lo" often isn't translated directly: "no lo estás" usually means "you aren't."
target_language_example: Dicen que estás listo, pero yo creo que no lo estás.
native_language_example: They say you're ready, but I don't think you are.

meaning: 'in general' or 'generally'.
additional_notes: Used to talk about things in a general or overall way, not specifics. Often appears in phrases like "en lo general" (in general) or "por lo general" (generally/usually). Can precede a verb or adjective phrase: e.g., "Lo general es..." (Generally, it is...).
target_language_example: Por lo general, llego a las ocho.
native_language_example: In general, I arrive at eight.

meaning: the big thing; the important thing; greatness (abstract).
additional_notes: Lo + adjective (lo + grande) turns the adjective into a neuter noun referring to the concept, quality, or the thing that is 'big' or 'important'. Often used to talk about the main point or the quality of greatness in an abstract way: 'lo importante' = the important thing. Can refer to a concrete big thing in some contexts but normally refers to the idea/quality.
target_language_example: Lo grande de la película es su mensaje.
native_language_example: The great thing about the movie is its message.

meaning: there is one
additional_notes: Used with hay to refer back to something already mentioned, especially when asking if an item exists or is available in a certain color, size, etc. Common patterns are ¿Lo hay...? ('Do you have it...?/Is there one...?') and No lo hay ('there isn't one/they don't have it'). lo normally refers to a masculine singular item; for feminine or plural nouns, the pronoun changes.
target_language_example: ¿Lo hay en negro?
native_language_example: Do you have it in black?

meaning: "I had a great time" or "I enjoyed it very much."
additional_notes: Commonly used with 'bien' (lo he pasado muy bien) to say you enjoyed an event or time. Often appears as 'me lo he pasado muy bien' (literally 'I have had it very well for myself') — a reflexive construction meaning 'I had a good time.' Can be used in present perfect (he pasado) for recent past experiences.
target_language_example: Me lo he pasado muy bien en la fiesta.
native_language_example: I had a great time at the party.

meaning: 'I did it by/of' (incomplete phrase — usually begins a longer expression that explains how or for what reason you did something).
additional_notes: This is not a complete fixed phrase on its own. In Spanish, 'lo hice' means 'I did it' and 'de' often introduces the manner, reason, material, source, or a clause (e.g., 'lo hice de buena fe', 'lo hice de casualidad', 'lo hice de madera', 'lo hice de broma'). Beginners will usually see full expressions like 'lo hice de casualidad' (I did it by accident) or 'lo hice de buena fe' (I did it in good faith). Pay attention to what follows 'de' to understand the full meaning.
target_language_example: Lo hice de casualidad cuando abrí la puerta.
native_language_example: I did it by accident when I opened the door.

meaning: 'you did it very (well/ badly/...)' — start of a compliment or comment about how someone did something
additional_notes: This phrase is incomplete on its own; it needs an adjective or adverb after 'muy' (e.g. 'muy bien', 'muy mal', 'muy rápido'). 'Lo' refers to the action or thing previously mentioned, 'hiciste' = 'you did'. Common in spoken and written Spanish when praising or judging someone's action.
target_language_example: Lo hiciste muy bien en la presentación.
native_language_example: You did it very well in the presentation.

meaning: a combination of the object pronoun 'lo' (him/it) + the imperfect of 'ir' used with 'a' to form the periphrastic past intention 'was going to (do) it/him'.
additional_notes: Used to express a past intention or plan that was going to be carried out (e.g., 'I was going to do it', 'She was going to help him'). 'Lo' is a direct object pronoun (it, him, you formal masculine). The full structure is 'lo iba a + infinitive' (or 'iba a + infinitive' with the pronoun before iba or attached to the infinitive: 'iba a hacerlo'). In spoken Spanish the pronoun can move: 'Te lo iba a decir' = 'I was going to tell you that'.
target_language_example: Lo iba a terminar ayer, pero no tuve tiempo.
native_language_example: I was going to finish it yesterday, but I didn't have time.

meaning: 'the length' or 'the extent' (used in phrases like "a lo largo de" = 'along' or 'throughout')
additional_notes: By itself, 'lo largo' is not commonly used alone; it usually appears in the fixed prepositional phrase 'a lo largo (de)' meaning 'along' or 'throughout' (e.g., 'a lo largo del río' = 'along the river', 'a lo largo de los años' = 'over the years'). 'Lo' here is a neutral article used with an abstract notion of length or extent. Don't confuse with 'largo' (adjective: long).
target_language_example: Caminamos a lo largo del río al atardecer.
native_language_example: We walked along the river at sunset.

meaning: throughout; along (the length of); during (a period).
additional_notes: Used with a noun to indicate duration or extent across something: 'a lo largo de' is the full common phrase (often contracted to 'lo largo de' in some contexts), e.g. a lo largo del día = throughout the day; a lo largo de la costa = along the coast. Precedes the noun and frequently appears with articles (del, de la).
target_language_example: A lo largo de la semana estudié para el examen.
native_language_example: Throughout the week I studied for the exam.

meaning: throughout / along the length of (feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used before a feminine noun to indicate duration or extent across space or time. Equivalent to 'a lo largo de la' or 'a lo largo de' but often appears as 'lo largo de la' in phrases like 'a lo largo de la semana' or 'a lo largo de la costa'. If the noun is masculine use 'lo largo del' (de + el).
target_language_example: Voy a estudiar a lo largo de la semana.
native_language_example: I'm going to study throughout the week.

meaning: throughout the length of; along (the) — used with masculine singular nouns.
additional_notes: Commonly appears in the phrase 'a lo largo del' meaning 'along' or 'throughout' (e.g., 'a lo largo del río' = 'along the river'). 'Lo' here is part of the fixed prepositional phrase and must agree with a following masculine singular noun introduced by 'del' (de + el). For feminine nouns use 'a lo largo de la' or simply 'a lo largo de'.
target_language_example: Caminamos a lo largo del paseo marítimo.
native_language_example: We walked along the boardwalk.

meaning: how far; the distance (in a general sense).
additional_notes: Used to ask or talk about distance or extent. Often appears in questions or expressions like '¿Qué tan lejos...?' or 'no sé lo lejos que está'. Alone 'lo' + adjective can nominalize the adjective (e.g., 'lo lejos' = 'how far'), but 'lo lejos' by itself is less common than phrases such as 'qué tan lejos' or 'lo lejos que'.
target_language_example: No sé lo lejos que está la playa desde aquí.
native_language_example: I don't know how far the beach is from here.

meaning: I/he/she/you(formal) was carrying it
additional_notes: Compound of the object pronoun 'lo' (it/him) + imperfect tense 'llevaba' of llevar (to carry, to wear, to take, to have). Meaning depends on context: physical carrying (in pocket, encima), possession (having something in one's blood = a trait), habitual past action (used to take someone to the doctor), or emotional impact (lo llevaba fatal = I handled it terribly). Subject is inferred from conjugation (llevaba = yo/él/ella/usted in imperfect).
target_language_example: Antes lo llevaba siempre en la mochila.
native_language_example: Before I always carried it in my backpack.

meaning: that (someone) take him/it (somewhere) — past subjunctive or imperfect subjunctive form used in subordinate clauses expressing requests, wishes, or suggestions.
additional_notes: Used after verbs or expressions that trigger the subjunctive (e.g., pedir, querer, sugerir, insistir). 'Lo' is a direct object pronoun meaning 'him' or 'it' (masculine). In many regions the present subjunctive (lo lleve) or the past/imperfect subjunctive (lo llevara/lllevara) appear depending on tense and politeness. Accent mark (llévara) is optional in modern orthography only for distinguishing — standard written form is 'lo llevara' or 'lo llevase' (both imperfect subjunctive forms).
target_language_example: Mi madre pidió que lo llevara al médico.
native_language_example: My mother asked that I take him to the doctor.

meaning: the wonderful thing / how wonderful (that)…
additional_notes: Used to refer to something wonderful in general or to introduce a clause describing how wonderful something is. Can function as a noun phrase ('the wonderful thing') or as a neutral connector before an adjective + clause ('how/that … is wonderful'). Common in expressions like 'lo maravilloso es que…' or 'lo maravilloso que fue...'.
target_language_example: Lo maravilloso de este viaje fue conocer a gente tan amable.
native_language_example: The wonderful thing about this trip was meeting such kind people.

meaning: the best
additional_notes: Used to talk about the best option, result, or thing in a general sense. With lo + adjective, Spanish often means 'the ... thing' or 'what is ...', so lo mejor can mean 'the best thing' or 'what's best.' Compare with el mejor / la mejor for a specific person or noun.
target_language_example: Eso es lo mejor para todos.
native_language_example: That's what's best for everyone.

meaning: 'the best I can (do)' — what someone can do or offer given their limits.
additional_notes: Used to say that you are doing or offering the best possible action or result you can at the moment. Common in everyday speech to explain a limit, refusal, or compromise. Can be followed by a verb (e.g., 'hacer', 'ofrecer', 'es') or a clause.
target_language_example: Lo mejor que puedo hacer es ayudarte con lo que sé.
native_language_example: The best I can do is help you with what I know.

meaning: It's best not to (do something) / better not.
additional_notes: Used to advise against an action or suggest avoiding something. Often followed by an infinitive or implied action. Tone can be neutral or slightly firm depending on context. Example structures: "Lo mejor no lo digas." (Better not say it.) or "Lo mejor no ir." (Less common—prefer: "Lo mejor es no ir.").
target_language_example: Lo mejor no decir nada por ahora.
native_language_example: Better not say anything for now.

meaning: at least; the least (in expressions like 'por lo menos').
additional_notes: Often appears in the phrase 'por lo menos' meaning 'at least' or 'at the very least'. Alone, 'lo menos' can mean 'the least' (as in 'it matters the least') or be part of comparisons. Common in informal and formal speech. Use 'por lo menos' to give a minimum or to soften a statement.
target_language_example: No tengo tiempo, pero por lo menos puedo llamar mañana.
native_language_example: I don't have time, but at least I can call tomorrow.

meaning: at least one
additional_notes: Used to indicate a minimum quantity or number (one or more). Often appears in contexts like 'tener lo menos una...' or 'espera lo menos una...'. More common phrasing is 'por lo menos una' or 'al menos una' — 'lo menos una' without a preceding particle is less common but understandable in spoken Spanish.
target_language_example: Necesitamos lo menos una persona que hable inglés.
native_language_example: We need at least one person who speaks English.

meaning: 'I put it' (completed action).
additional_notes: Combination of the object pronoun lo (it, him, masculine or general object) + metí (first-person preterite of meter = to put/place). Used to say you placed something somewhere in the past. The pronoun can refer to a thing or a person (colloquially). Word order: object pronoun goes before the conjugated verb in standard grammar (me lo dieron → I was given it).
target_language_example: Lo metí en la mochila y ahora no lo encuentro.
native_language_example: I put it in the backpack and now I can't find it.

meaning: the same
additional_notes: Used to refer to the same idea, statement, question, or situation. With the neuter article lo, mismo often means "the same thing" rather than matching a noun directly. In expressions like lo mismo para ti, it means "same for you" or "same to you."
target_language_example: Siempre pedimos lo mismo en ese restaurante.
native_language_example: We always order the same thing at that restaurant.

meaning: the amount/degree of something (emphatic); roughly 'how much' or 'the much (of it)'.
additional_notes: Lo + adjective/adverb/quantity is often used to talk about the extent or degree of something. 'Lo mucho' by itself is not a complete phrase in many contexts and usually needs more context (e.g., 'lo mucho que...' = 'how much that...'). It can introduce a clause: 'Lo mucho que trabajó' = 'How much he/she worked.' Also used in comparisons or as a noun phrase meaning 'the large amount' when paired with qualifying information.
target_language_example: No sabes lo mucho que te extraño.
native_language_example: You don't know how much I miss you.

meaning: not even the slightest; the least bit
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something does not happen at all or that someone is not affected/interested in even the smallest degree. Commonly appears in negative sentences (No me importa en lo más mínimo). Can be placed after verbs or adjectives (no cedió ni en lo más mínimo).
target_language_example: No me preocupa en lo más mínimo.
native_language_example: It doesn't worry me in the slightest.

meaning: as quickly as possible; as fast as possible
additional_notes: Used to express doing something in the shortest time or at maximum speed. Often follows a verb (e.g., "hazlo lo más rápido posible") or appears with "posible" omitted in casual speech. Can be used for both actions and comparisons ("lo más rápido que puedas").
target_language_example: Ven aquí lo más rápido que puedas.
native_language_example: Come here as quickly as you can.

meaning: we need it / we need him/her (object pronoun + verb: 'need it/us').
additional_notes: Lo is a direct object pronoun that can refer to a masculine singular noun, a neutral idea, or a clause. Necesitamos is the first-person plural present of necesitar: 'we need'. Together they mean 'we need it' or 'we need him' depending on context. Placement: the pronoun normally goes before the conjugated verb (lo necesitamos). In affirmative commands or with infinitives/gerunds placement varies.
target_language_example: Ahora es el momento en que más lo necesitamos.
native_language_example: Now is the time when we need it most.

meaning: the other thing(s); something else
additional_notes: Used vaguely to refer to other unspecified things, tasks, or issues. Often appears in phrases like "esto, lo otro" (this, that/other things) or "un poco de esto, un poco de lo otro" (a bit of this, a bit of other things). In "ni uno ni lo otro" it means "neither one nor the other." Can be singular or plural in sense depending on context.
target_language_example: No quiero esto; prefiero lo otro.
native_language_example: I don't want this; I prefer the other (thing).

meaning: "it seems so" or "that seems to be the case."
additional_notes: Used to agree or confirm an impression about a situation or statement. Often follows a clause or stands alone as a short reply. Equivalent to English responses like "it seems so," "apparently," or "that appears to be the case." Tone is neutral and common in spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: No hay nadie en la oficina; lo parece.
native_language_example: There is nobody in the office; it seems so.

meaning: 'I had a very (good/bad/etc.) time' — beginning of a phrase to describe how someone experienced something.
additional_notes: This is not a complete sentence by itself; it's the start of expressions like "lo pasé muy bien" (I had a very good time) or "lo pasé muy mal" (I had a very bad time). Use with an adjective (bien, mal, cómodo, divertido, etc.). "Lo" refers to the experience or situation, and "pasé" is the past (pretérito) of "pasar" meaning 'to spend/pass (time)'.
target_language_example: Lo pasé muy bien en la fiesta.
native_language_example: I had a very good time at the party.

meaning: 'I had a great time with' or 'I enjoyed myself with (someone/something)'.
additional_notes: Used to say you enjoyed an event or time spent with someone. Common after mentioning a person or activity: lo pasé muy bien con + [persona/actividad]. Tense is preterite (lo pasé) — refers to a past occasion. You can shorten to "lo pasé bien con" for the same meaning; "muy" adds emphasis.
target_language_example: Lo pasé muy bien con mis amigos en la fiesta.
native_language_example: I had a great time with my friends at the party.

meaning: he/she/they spent (time) / had (a good or bad time) — used with 'bien' or 'mal' to say someone had a good or bad time; can also appear in other contexts like 'lo pasó' = 'he/she passed it' (less common).
additional_notes: Commonly part of the pronominal expression 'se lo pasó bien/mal' meaning 'had a good/bad time'. The structure: subject + (se) + lo + pasó. 'Se lo pasó bien' = 'He/she had a good time.' Without 'se' it can mean 'he/she passed it' (e.g., passed an exam) depending on context. For beginners, learn it as the set phrase 'se lo pasó bien/mal' to talk about enjoying (or not) an event.
target_language_example: Se lo pasó muy bien en la fiesta.
native_language_example: She had a great time at the party.

meaning: the dangerous thing(s) / what is dangerous
additional_notes: Lo + adjective turns the adjective into a neuter noun phrase referring to an abstract idea or general quality. 'Lo peligroso' means 'what is dangerous' or 'the dangerous part/thing' in a general, non-gendered sense. Commonly used to comment on a situation (e.g., "Lo peligroso de esto es..." = "The dangerous thing about this is...").
target_language_example: Lo peligroso de conducir de noche es la poca visibilidad.
native_language_example: The dangerous thing about driving at night is the low visibility.

meaning: 'he/she/it lost it' or 'he/she lost (something)'.
additional_notes: Lo is a neutral/direct object pronoun meaning 'it' (or 'him' in some contexts); perdió is the past (preterite) of perder. Together they indicate someone lost something already mentioned or understood from context. In sentences like "lo perdió todo" it means "lost everything." In "lo perdió de vista" it forms a fixed phrase meaning "lost sight of him/her/it."
target_language_example: Cuando salió de la casa, lo perdió de vista en la multitud.
native_language_example: When she left the house, she lost sight of him in the crowd.

meaning: I ask/request/order it for (a reason, person, or price).
additional_notes: Lo pido por is built from lo (it) + pido (I ask/request/order) + por (for/because/of). Use to say why you request something or for whom/what price you order it. Context determines meaning: 'por' can indicate reason (por qué), recipient (por ti), duration, exchange/price (por 10 euros), or channel (por internet). You will often hear full phrases like 'Lo pido por ti' (I order it for you) or 'Lo pido por internet' (I order it online).
target_language_example: Lo pido por ti porque no puedes venir.
native_language_example: I ask for it on your behalf because you can't come.

meaning: you (plural) can put it
additional_notes: Combination of direct object pronoun lo (it/him/that) + second-person plural present form of poder (podéis). Used in Spain with vosotros/vosotras. In Latin America you would more often hear ustedes lo pueden. Word order: object pronoun goes before the conjugated verb (Lo podéis poner = You all can put it).
target_language_example: Si no cabe en la mesa, lo podéis poner en la estantería.
native_language_example: If it doesn't fit on the table, you (all) can put it on the shelf.

meaning: 'could (do) it' or 'was able to (do) it' — refers to ability or possibility about 'it' (lo).
additional_notes: Lo is the direct object pronoun meaning 'it' (or him) and precedes the conjugated verb. Podía is the imperfect of poder (to be able to / can). Together, lo podía describes a past ability or possibility regarding something: 'he/she/you/I/it could do it' depending on subject (context gives who). The imperfect (podía) often implies ongoing, repeated, or background ability rather than a single completed instance. Word order: subject + lo + podía + (verb) or subject + lo podía + (infinitive) as in the examples.
target_language_example: No lo podía decir porque era secreto.
native_language_example: I couldn't say it because it was a secret.

meaning: the first/most important thing is; first of all
additional_notes: Used to introduce the main point, priority, or first action in a sentence. Often followed by an infinitive or a clause (e.g., 'lo primero es hablar', 'lo primero es que...'). Common in both spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: Lo primero es llamar al médico.
native_language_example: First of all, call the doctor.

meaning: the most important thing is (that)... / first of all, the main thing is (that)...
additional_notes: Used to introduce the main point or priority. Often followed by a clause introduced with 'que' (e.g. 'lo primero es lo que...') or an infinitive structure. Slightly more emphatic or stylistic than 'lo primero es que...'; common in spoken and written Spanish to order priorities or give advice.
target_language_example: Lo primero es lo que debemos resolver antes de seguir con el proyecto.
native_language_example: The most important thing is what we must resolve before continuing with the project.

meaning: First things first; put the most important thing(s) before others.
additional_notes: Used to remind someone to prioritize what matters most before dealing with less important matters. Common in conversation to refocus or organize steps. Can introduce the main priority or the first action to take.
target_language_example: Tenemos muchas tareas, pero lo primero es lo primero: pagar las facturas.
native_language_example: We have many tasks, but first things first: pay the bills.

meaning: what
additional_notes: used to refer to a thing, idea, or action: “what” / “the thing that.” It often introduces a clause in statements, as in lo que dices = “what you say.” Unlike direct-question qué, lo que is commonly used inside a longer sentence.
target_language_example: No entiendo lo que dices.
native_language_example: I don't understand what you're saying.

meaning: not a fixed phrase by itself; 'lo que' = 'what' or 'that which'; 'a' is a preposition ('to', 'at')—together they appear when 'lo que' is followed by a verb or phrase starting with 'a'.
additional_notes: Alone, 'lo que' means 'what' or 'that which'. The sequence 'lo que a' is not a standalone expression; it simply occurs when 'lo que' is followed by a clause that begins with the preposition 'a' (for example: 'lo que a decir'—though that specific example is awkward). More natural examples: 'lo que a mí me gusta' (what I like), where 'a' starts a prepositional phrase ('a mí'). Do not memorize 'lo que a' as a single unit—learn 'lo que' and prepositions separately.
target_language_example: Lo que a mí me preocupa es el dinero.
native_language_example: What worries me is the money.

meaning: that which ends / what finishes (or 'what just happened' in some contexts)
additional_notes: Lo que acaba is built from lo que ('what/that which') + acaba (he/she/it ends or finishes, or 'just' in periphrastic uses). By itself it is incomplete and usually appears in longer sentences (e.g., lo que acaba de pasar = what just happened; lo que acaba mal = that which ends badly). The exact sense depends on context: with 'de' it often means 'what has just...' (lo que acaba de ocurrir).
target_language_example: No entiendo lo que acaba de pasar.
native_language_example: I don't understand what just happened.

meaning: 'what you should (do)' or 'what you must (do)'.
additional_notes: Used to refer to the action(s) someone is expected or advised to take. 'Debes' is the present tense of 'deber' (should/must/ought to) for 'tú'. Can be used in commands, advice, or statements about obligation. Context and tone determine whether it means 'should' (advice) or 'must' (stronger obligation).
target_language_example: Si quieres arreglarlo, haz lo que debes.
native_language_example: If you want to fix it, do what you should.

meaning: 'what I should' or 'what I ought to'.
additional_notes: Lo que introduces a clause meaning 'what' or 'that which.' When followed by debo (from deber), the phrase expresses obligation, advice, or expectation from the speaker's perspective: 'what I should do / what I ought to (do).' It can appear in longer sentences: e.g. 'No sé lo que debo hacer' = 'I don't know what I should do.'
target_language_example: No estoy seguro de lo que debo decir.
native_language_example: I'm not sure what I should say.

meaning: 'what (he/she/they) say(s) is' or 'what (someone) says is'.
additional_notes: Used to refer to the content of someone's speech or statements. 'Lo que' = 'what/that which'; 'dice' = 'he/she/you (formal)/they say' (third-person singular of decir); 'es' = 'is'. Often followed by an adjective or noun (cierto, mentira, verdad, peligroso, importante). Can be used with modifiers like 'todo' (todo lo que dice = everything he/she says).
target_language_example: Lo que dice es importante para el proyecto.
native_language_example: What he says is important for the project.

meaning: 'what' or 'that which' + masculine singular article (used when the following noun is masculine), often introducing a relative clause or comparison.
additional_notes: This sequence combines the pronoun 'lo que' (meaning 'what' or 'that which') with the masculine singular article 'el' when the clause refers to a specific masculine noun that follows or is understood. It's common in comparisons ('...es para la mente lo que el ejercicio es para el cuerpo') and in relative clauses ('No olvide lo que el Estado ha hecho por usted'). In many cases 'lo que' alone is enough; 'lo que el...' appears when a specific masculine noun (el + noun) is part of the clause.
target_language_example: Lo que el maestro dijo cambió mi opinión.
native_language_example: What the teacher said changed my opinion.

meaning: what that (thing) (is/means) / whatever that is
additional_notes: A combination of the neutral pronoun 'lo' + relative 'que' plus a demonstrative 'eso'. Used to refer vaguely to something previously mentioned or pointed at. Often appears in sentences like 'No sé lo que eso significa' (I don't know what that means) or in shortened spoken forms: 'Lo que eso...' It can introduce a clause ('lo que eso implica') or act as a noun phrase ('eso' being the thing referred to).
target_language_example: No entiendo lo que eso quiere decir.
native_language_example: I don't understand what that means.

meaning: 'what this' or 'that which this' (used to refer to something just mentioned or being pointed to)
additional_notes: Lo que is a neutral relative pronoun meaning 'what' or 'that which.' When followed by esto ('this'), lo que esto is uncommon by itself; more natural phrases are lo que (alone) or esto que/esto es lo que. Use lo que to introduce a clause or refer to an idea previously mentioned. 'Lo que esto' can appear in sentences like 'Lo que esto significa...' = 'What this means...'.
target_language_example: Lo que esto significa es que tenemos que cambiar de plan.
native_language_example: What this means is that we have to change plans.

meaning: what is
additional_notes: A common fragment meaning 'what is ...', usually followed by another verb form or a description: lo que está diciendo = 'what he/she is saying', lo que está sucediendo = 'what is happening', lo que está escrito = 'what is written'. Here, lo que means 'what' or 'the thing that', and está adds 'is'.
target_language_example: No entiendo lo que está pasando.
native_language_example: I don't understand what's happening.

meaning: whatever is in (a place, container, list, etc.)
additional_notes: Used to refer to any items or things located inside or included in something. Often appears in instructions, rules, or descriptions: 'lo que esté en' + noun (e.g., 'lo que esté en la caja', 'lo que esté en la lista'). The verb 'esté' is subjunctive and implies generality or uncertainty about the items.
target_language_example: Toma lo que esté en la mochila y ven.
native_language_example: Take whatever is in the backpack and come.

meaning: Just what was missing (often said sarcastically about an additional problem or annoyance).
additional_notes: Used to express frustration or irony when something unwanted happens on top of other problems. Tone is usually negative/sarcastic: like 'great, just what we needed' in English. Can be used alone or as part of a sentence.
target_language_example: Se rompió el coche otra vez, lo que faltaba.
native_language_example: The car broke down again — just what we needed.

meaning: whatever it took; by any means necessary.
additional_notes: Used to express determination to achieve something regardless of obstacles or cost. Often follows a verb or phrase indicating effort or willingness (e.g., 'haré lo que fuera por...'). It's somewhat formal-neutral and emphasizes strong commitment.
target_language_example: Haré lo que fuera por ayudar a mi familia.
native_language_example: I will do whatever it takes to help my family.

meaning: 'what I talk about' or 'what I mean/say'.
additional_notes: Lo que hablo combines 'lo que' (that which/what) with the verb 'hablo' (I speak). It can refer to the topic someone is talking about or clarify what the speaker means. Depending on context, it may function as a fragment (e.g., answering a question) or as part of a full sentence: 'Eso es lo que hablo' (That's what I'm talking about).
target_language_example: ¿Entiendes lo que hablo cuando uso términos técnicos?
native_language_example: Do you understand what I'm talking about when I use technical terms?

meaning: what to do
additional_notes: This exact phrase is unusual on its own in standard Spanish. To say 'what to do,' Spanish usually uses qué hacer (with an accent on qué), especially after verbs like saber: No sé qué hacer. To say 'what needs to be done,' lo que hay que hacer is more natural.
target_language_example: A veces la gente escribe «lo que hacer», pero en español natural se suele decir «qué hacer».
native_language_example: Sometimes people write 'lo que hacer,' but in natural Spanish people usually say 'qué hacer.'

meaning: what they have
additional_notes: Usually the beginning of a longer clause, not a complete expression by itself. Here, han is the third-person plural form of haber, usually used with a past participle: lo que han dicho = 'what they have said,' lo que han hecho = 'what they have done.' For possession, Spanish normally uses tienen, not han.
target_language_example: No entiendo lo que han dicho.
native_language_example: I don't understand what they have said.

meaning: A combination of 'lo que' (what/that which) followed by the direct object pronoun 'lo' (it/him). Used when a clause introduced by 'lo que' is followed by an explicit pronoun referring to a masculine or neutral singular object or abstract idea previously mentioned or implied.
additional_notes: This is not a single fixed idiom but two grammatical elements in sequence: 'lo que' introduces a subordinate clause and 'lo' is a neuter/masculine direct object pronoun referring back to an idea or thing. It appears in sentences where the speaker refers back to 'what/that which' and then repeats or clarifies with 'it'. Example contexts: emphasizing or clarifying an action, or when the clause's object is replaced by a pronoun. Register is neutral; common in colloquial and formal speech depending on context.
target_language_example: No entiendo lo que lo preocupa.
native_language_example: I don't understand what it/that is worrying him.

meaning: whatever I feel like / whatever I get (to do/have)
additional_notes: Informal spoken phrase. Often completes a sentence like 'haré/diré/comeré lo que me dé' meaning 'I'll do/say/eat whatever I feel like' or 'me pondré lo que me dé la gana' (stronger: 'whatever I want'). Here 'dé' is subjunctive of 'dar' used impersonally (short for 'dé la gana'). Context determines whether it means 'feel like' or 'happen to get/receive'.
target_language_example: Hoy voy a comer lo que me dé.
native_language_example: Today I'm going to eat whatever I feel like.

meaning: what I like about/of (someone or something).
additional_notes: Used to point out a specific quality or aspect that the speaker likes about a person, place, or thing. Often followed by a noun or pronoun (e.g., 'de este país', 'de ella'). Can be used with other subjects (lo que te gusta de, lo que nos gusta de).
target_language_example: Lo que me gusta de esta ciudad es la música en las calles.
native_language_example: What I like about this city is the music in the streets.

meaning: literally ‘what/that which never’; used to emphasize that something never happens or is never the case
additional_notes: Lo que nunca combines the neuter relative 'lo que' (what/that which) with 'nunca' (never). It often appears in larger sentences to highlight something that never occurs, e.g. 'es lo que nunca dije' (it's what I never said) or 'es lo que nunca pasa' (it's what never happens). 'Lo que' is neutral and refers to an idea or situation rather than a specific noun.
target_language_example: Eso es lo que nunca entenderé.
native_language_example: That is what I will never understand.

meaning: used to introduce an explanation or reason: “the thing is” / “what happens/is that”.
additional_notes: Common spoken phrase to start explaining, justifying, or giving background information. Often followed by a clause that gives the reason or clarifies a situation. Can be shortened to "lo que pasa" in casual speech. Tone is neutral/informal depending on context.
target_language_example: Lo que pasa es que no tengo suficiente dinero para ir.
native_language_example: The thing is (what happens) I don't have enough money to go.

meaning: 'the thing is' / 'the problem is' / 'what happens is that' (used to introduce an explanation or excuse).
additional_notes: Common spoken phrase to introduce a reason, explanation, or clarification. Often used to soften criticism or give context before explaining why something happened. Can be translated in many ways depending on tone (the thing is, the problem is, it's just that, what happens is that).
target_language_example: Lo que pasa es que no tuve tiempo para terminarlo.
native_language_example: The thing is, I didn't have time to finish it.

meaning: "what we can" or "what we are able to (do)".
additional_notes: Used to introduce what a group including the speaker can do, achieve, obtain, or afford. Common in suggestions, offers, or stating limitations. Often followed by verbs like hacer, permitirnos, conseguir. Neutral register.
target_language_example: Veamos lo que podemos hacer por el proyecto esta semana.
native_language_example: Let's see what we can do for the project this week.

meaning: what you can (do)
additional_notes: Commonly used to refer to someone's abilities, possibilities or actions. Often appears inside larger clauses (e.g. "lo que puedes hacer" = "what you can do"). The verb puedes is the present tense tú form of poder (to be able to). Context determines whether to translate as "can" or "are able to."
target_language_example: Muéstrales lo que puedes hacer.
native_language_example: Show them what you can do.

meaning: 'what I can say' or 'the thing(s) I can say' (often used to introduce a comment or summary about one's opinion or knowledge).
additional_notes: Commonly used to preface a statement, give a brief opinion, or summarize what one can add to a conversation. Can be translated as 'what I can say is…' or simply 'I can say that…'. Often followed by a clause (lo que puedo decir es que...) or used alone as a short comment (Lo que puedo decir: fue una buena experiencia).
target_language_example: Lo que puedo decir es que aprendí mucho en ese trabajo.
native_language_example: What I can say is that I learned a lot in that job.

meaning: 'what I want now' or 'what I want at the moment'.
additional_notes: Used to state a current desire or need. Can appear with or without 'todo' ('todo lo que quiero ahora' = 'all I want right now'). Common in everyday speech to focus on the present moment.
target_language_example: Lo que quiero ahora es descansar un rato.
native_language_example: What I want now is to rest for a while.

meaning: what I wanted
additional_notes: Compositional phrase: lo que means "what/that which," and quise is the yo preterite of querer. On its own, it often means "what I wanted," but in phrases like lo que quise decir, it is commonly understood as "what I meant" or "what I meant to say."
target_language_example: No entendiste lo que quise decir.
native_language_example: You didn't understand what I meant.

meaning: "what I remember" or "that which I remember".
additional_notes: Used to refer to memories or things you recall. Can introduce a clause describing specific details you remember. Common in both spoken and written Spanish. Frequently appears in past or present contexts (e.g., "lo que recuerdo de aquel día" = "what I remember from that day").
target_language_example: Lo que recuerdo es que llegamos tarde y empezó a llover.
native_language_example: What I remember is that we arrived late and it started to rain.

meaning: "what I/he/she/they knew" or "what (one) knew" (depends on subject and tense).
additional_notes: A relative clause using lo que + verb in imperfect (sabía). Often refers to information, facts, or knowledge someone had in the past. Subject is understood from context (yo, él, ella, etc.). Can also be used more generally as "what was known". Use different verb forms to match tense/person (p. ej. lo que sé = what I/you/he/she know(s); lo que sabía = what I/he/she/they knew or what was known).
target_language_example: No entendí lo que sabía mi abuelo hasta que me lo explicó otra vez.
native_language_example: I didn't understand what my grandfather knew until he explained it to me again.

meaning: whatever
additional_notes: Used to mean an unspecified thing, amount, or choice: "whatever" or "anything at all." In conversation, it can also sound dismissive depending on tone, as in "sí, lo que sea" = "yeah, whatever."
target_language_example: Puedes elegir lo que sea del menú.
native_language_example: You can choose anything from the menu.

meaning: 'what + his/her/your/their' (incomplete phrase); literally 'that which his/her/your/their ...'.
additional_notes: This is not a complete fixed phrase by itself. 'Lo que' means 'what' or 'that which' and introduces a clause; 'su' is a possessive adjective (his, her, your formal, their). Together they begin a clause like 'lo que su...': e.g. 'lo que su madre dijo' = 'what his/her mother said'. You will always need a noun or verb after 'su' to finish the idea. Use gender/number of the possessed noun to match context (su hermana, sus amigos).
target_language_example: Lo que su hermano escribió fue interesante.
native_language_example: What his brother wrote was interesting.

meaning: whatever you feel like / whatever you want (to do/have).
additional_notes: Informal phrase used to tell someone to do or choose anything they prefer; often completes a verb (e.g., 'haz lo que te dé la gana', 'pon lo que te dé la gana'). Shortened forms drop the rest of the clause ('haz lo que te dé'). Can be emphatic or dismissive depending on tone. Literal parts: 'lo que' = 'what/that which', 'te dé' = 'gives you' (subjunctive of dar).
target_language_example: Come lo que te dé; yo no tengo preferencia.
native_language_example: Eat whatever you feel like; I have no preference.

meaning: 'whatever you want' or 'whatever you feel like (doing/saying)'.
additional_notes: This is part of the common phrase 'haz/di/cree/pon lo que te dé la gana' meaning 'do/say/believe whatever you want.' Literally references 'what gives you the desire'—it expresses permission or indifference and can be rude depending on tone. Use with verbs like hacer, decir, creer, pensar. Informal and colloquial.
target_language_example: Di lo que te dé la gana, pero no me culpes después.
native_language_example: Say whatever you want, but don't blame me later.

meaning: what I have is / the thing I have is
additional_notes: Used to introduce or emphasize what one possesses, experiences, or feels; commonly followed by a noun, clause, or adjective. It often contrasts or clarifies (e.g., 'Lo que tengo es X, no Y'). Can be used for tangible items, states, or explanations.
target_language_example: No quiero más explicación; lo que tengo es poco tiempo.
native_language_example: I don't want more explanation; what I have is little time.

meaning: what you had to (do)
