target_language_example: Es mejor no meterse con él.
native_language_example: It's better not to mess with him.

meaning: to get into; to enter (physically) or to become involved/interfere in (a situation or someone's affairs)
additional_notes: Literal: 'to put oneself into'. Used for physical entry (meterse en la piscina = get into the pool) and figurative involvement (meterse en problemas = get into trouble; meterse en la vida de alguien = meddle). Context determines whether neutral, positive, or negative. Reflexive verb form: meterse (conjugate the reflexive pronoun).
target_language_example: No deberían meterse en mi vida.
native_language_example: You shouldn't get involved in / meddle in my life.

meaning: he/she/you (formal) put something in / put something (somewhere).
additional_notes: From the verb meter (to put). 'Metió' is the preterite (simple past) third person singular (él/ella/usted). 'Algo' means 'something' and is a vague object. Use to say someone placed or inserted something, or more generally that someone did something with an object. Context can make it mean 'put in', 'put on', 'stuck', or even 'scored' (in some sports contexts).
target_language_example: Ella metió algo en la caja.
native_language_example: She put something in the box.

meaning: put something into (somewhere/inside).
additional_notes: Past tense form of the verb 'meter' used with an indefinite object: 'metió' = he/she/you(formal) put; 'algo' = something; 'en' = in/into. Use to describe that someone placed an unspecified object into a location. To specify object or person change 'algo' or conjugate the verb (e.g., 'metí algo en', 'metieron algo en').
target_language_example: Ella metió algo en el bolso.
native_language_example: She put something in the bag.

meaning: something got into (a body part) — used to say an object accidentally entered someone's body part (commonly the eye, nose, or mouth).
additional_notes: Often appears with an indirect-object pronoun and reflexive construction (se le metió algo en el ojo) to indicate that something entered someone's body part unintentionally. Replace 'el ojo' with other masculine body parts (el ojo, el dedo — note some body parts are feminine: la nariz, la boca). The literal subject is 'algo' (something) while the affected person is expressed with pronouns (me, te, se, le, nos, os, les). Used to explain sudden discomfort or irritation.
target_language_example: A ella se le metió algo en el ojo cuando caminaba por la playa.
native_language_example: Something got into her eye when she was walking on the beach.

meaning: put the / placed the (masculine singular object) — past simple (preterite) of meter (to put) plus masculine definite article 'el'.
additional_notes: Used to say someone put or placed a specific masculine noun somewhere. If the verb is reflexive (meterse), it can mean to put something into one's own clothing or to go into/into oneself (context matters); reflexive pronoun appears before 'metió' (e.g., 'se metió el pañuelo' = put the handkerchief into his pocket). The noun must be masculine singular because of 'el' (e.g., el libro, el jamón, el bolsillo).
target_language_example: Ella metió el teléfono en la bolsa.
native_language_example: She put the phone in the bag.

meaning: entered/put (someone or something) into the...
additional_notes: From the verb 'meter(se)' meaning to put or to get into. 'Metió en el' is the past (pretérito) third-person singular of 'meter' + 'en el' (into the). Often used with a place or container: metió en el coche (he/she got into the car), nos metió en el congelador (he/she put us in the freezer). If the subject is reflexive (meterse), it means the person entered: 'se metió en el coche' = 'he got into the car.' Watch word order: 'se metió en el coche' vs 'metió en el coche a Juan' (he put Juan into the car).
target_language_example: Ella metió en el bolso las llaves.
native_language_example: She put the keys in the bag.

meaning: literally 'put/shot a (feminine noun)'; used to say someone inserted, threw, or caused something (often sudden or violent) into/into someone or something.
additional_notes: Metió is the past tense (él/ella/usted) of meter (to put/insert). With 'una' it introduces a feminine noun (una bala, una mosca). Context determines meaning: can be literal (inserted, put in) or idiomatic (sudden occurrence, e.g., 'se me metió una mosca en el ojo' = a fly got into my eye). Often used in passive-like constructions to describe an action done to someone.
target_language_example: Alguien me metió una piedra en el zapato.
native_language_example: Someone put a stone in my shoe.

meaning: likely part of a sentence meaning 'subway is' or 'meter is' (depends on context); literally 'metro is'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself — it's the noun 'metro' (meaning either 'subway' in many Spanish varieties or 'meter' as a unit) followed by the verb 'es' ('is'). You will see it inside sentences like 'El metro es rápido' (The subway is fast) or 'Un metro es cien centímetros' (A meter is one hundred centimeters). Choose meaning from context: 'metro' = subway (transport) or meter (unit).
target_language_example: El metro es muy puntual en esta ciudad.
native_language_example: The subway is very punctual in this city.

meaning: I put (something feminine) / I inserted (something feminine) — first-person singular past of meter + feminine direct object article.
additional_notes: Metí is the preterite (past) of meter (to put/insert). La is the feminine singular direct-object pronoun/article — here it likely refers to a feminine noun mentioned earlier (e.g., la carta, la llave). Together they begin a sentence like 'metí la llave en la cerradura' (I put the key in the lock). Word order and context matter: depending on surrounding words, la could be the definite article ('the') rather than a pronoun.
target_language_example: Metí la carta en el sobre.
native_language_example: I put the letter in the envelope.

meaning: The phrase combines 'my grandfather' with the indirect object pronoun 'le' used to mark who feels or experiences something (e.g., is afraid of, loves).
additional_notes: In Spanish, people who experience feelings or states are often marked with an indirect object pronoun (me/te/le/nos/os/les). 'A mi abuelo' is used for clarity or emphasis; 'le' is the pronoun that agrees with 'a mi abuelo'. This structure is common with verbs like dar miedo (to frighten), encantar (to love/like a lot), temer (to fear), interesar (to interest), etc. You can drop the full phrase 'a mi abuelo' if context is clear and just say 'le' after the verb when the person is already known, but for beginners keep both for clarity.
target_language_example: A mi abuelo le interesan las historias de guerra.
native_language_example: My grandfather is interested in war stories.

meaning: my soul / my spirit (can be literal or used affectionately/emotionally).
additional_notes: Used both literally (the soul or spirit) and figuratively as an emotional or affectionate expression. Short phrases like "Mi alma" can be used as a term of endearment (similar to "my dear" or "my love"), an emotional exclamation ("My soul"), or in religious/spiritual contexts ("save my soul"). Context and tone determine whether it's affectionate, poetic, or literal.
target_language_example: Tu voz calma mi alma cuando estoy triste.
native_language_example: Your voice calms my soul when I'm sad.

meaning: 'my song' — indicates a song that belongs to or is favored by the speaker.
additional_notes: Used to talk about a song that is owned by, associated with, or liked by the speaker. Can mean a literal composition the speaker wrote ('my song') or simply 'my favorite song' depending on context. Commonly appears with adjectives (mi canción favorita) or verbs like tocar, cantar, gustar, pedir.
target_language_example: ¿Puedes poner mi canción favorita, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you play my favorite song, please?

meaning: my brush
additional_notes: Possessive phrase: mi = my, cepillo = brush. Used to indicate ownership of any kind of brush (hair brush, toothbrush sometimes called cepillo de dientes, paintbrush, etc.). For toothbrush, Spanish often uses "cepillo de dientes" so full phrase would be "mi cepillo de dientes."
target_language_example: ¿Dónde está mi cepillo de pelo?
native_language_example: Where is my hairbrush?

meaning: 'my boy' or 'my boyfriend' (depends on context).
additional_notes: Can mean a male child (my boy/son) or an affectionate way to refer to a romantic partner (my boyfriend/my man) depending on context and tone. In some regions it sounds tender or familiar; in others it can sound slightly old-fashioned. Use with care when addressing adults—'mi novio' is more common for 'my boyfriend.'
target_language_example: Ese es mi chico, se llama Carlos.
native_language_example: That's my boy, his name is Carlos.

meaning: my appointment; my date (depending on context).
additional_notes: Used to refer to a scheduled meeting, appointment (doctor, hairdresser, etc.) or a personal date. Context determines whether it means a formal appointment or a romantic/social date. Common verbs: tener una cita (to have an appointment/date), cancelar, posponer, perder.
target_language_example: Tengo que llamar para cambiar mi cita con el dentista.
native_language_example: I have to call to change my appointment with the dentist.

meaning: literally 'my butt'; used either literally (body part) or informally/emphatically in expressions.
additional_notes: Primarily vulgar/informal. Can refer to the speaker's buttocks literally (body part) or be used figuratively for emphasis, humor, or self-deprecation (e.g., 'my luck', 'I really want/need', or to express strong feeling). Tone varies by context—avoid in formal situations. Pronunciation and register make it common in songs, jokes, and casual speech.
target_language_example: Hoy me duele mi culo después de tanto sentarme.
native_language_example: My butt hurts today after sitting so much.

meaning: 'my address' or 'my direction' (depends on context).
additional_notes: Can mean 'my postal/address' (where you live or to send something) or 'my direction' (the way toward me). Context clarifies meaning: when talking about giving location or sending mail, use 'direccion' = address; when talking about movement or pointing, it means direction. To specify, you can say 'mi dirección postal' or 'la dirección hacia mí'.
target_language_example: Te dejo mi dirección para que me escribas.
native_language_example: I'll give you my address so you can write to me.

meaning: my pain / my grief (literal: my physical pain or emotional suffering).
additional_notes: Used to refer to something that hurts you physically or emotionally. Context determines whether it's physical pain (e.g., a headache) or emotional sorrow. Not an idiom; can appear in medical or personal contexts. For sympathy, Spanish speakers more often say "me duele" + body part (e.g., "me duele la cabeza") rather than "mi dolor", which can sound more formal or literary when referring to one's suffering.
target_language_example: He hablado con el médico sobre mi dolor de espalda.
native_language_example: I spoke with the doctor about my back pain.

meaning: 'my pain of' — a phrase starter used to say where or what kind of pain you have (e.g., mi dolor de cabeza = my headache).
additional_notes: This is not a complete phrase by itself; it begins expressions that describe a specific pain or ache. Common completions: 'mi dolor de cabeza' (headache), 'mi dolor de estómago' (stomachache), 'mi dolor de garganta' (sore throat). Use with verbs like 'tengo' (tengo mi dolor de cabeza → I have a headache) or with expressions of intensity (mucho, un poco).
target_language_example: Tengo mi dolor de estómago desde anoche.
native_language_example: I've had my stomachache since last night.

meaning: literally 'my day of' — used to name a specific day dedicated to something (e.g., 'mi día de descanso' = my day of rest).
additional_notes: Not a fixed phrase by itself; usually followed by a noun (mi día de trabajo, mi día de descanso, mi día de suerte). It expresses ownership/possession (my) plus the purpose or theme of the day. Common in spoken and written Spanish. Word order: 'mi día de' + [noun or activity].
target_language_example: Hoy es mi día de descanso, no voy a trabajar.
native_language_example: Today is my day of rest; I won't work.

meaning: literally 'my wife and (to)' — part of a Spanish indirect/direct object construction meaning 'my wife and ...' (used when listing people after a/ a la/ a los).
additional_notes: This fragment appears when you list people introduced by the preposition a (used for direct objects who are people and for indirect objects). In full phrases you'll often see 'a mi esposa y a mi hijo', 'a mi esposa y a mí' (with accent on mí when it's the stressed pronoun). When used with verbs like 'encontrar' (to find) or 'buscar' (to look for), the a marks the people as direct objects. With gustar and similar verbs, use 'a mi esposa y a mí nos gusta...' or 'a mi esposa y a mí nos interesa...'.
target_language_example: Encontré a mi esposa y a mi hijo en el parque.
native_language_example: I found my wife and my son in the park.

meaning: 'my season' or 'my station' depending on context; most commonly 'my season' (e.g., time of year) or 'my station' (e.g., train/bus station) when referring to a specific place.
additional_notes: Literal translation is 'my station' or 'my season'. Spanish estación has two main meanings: 1) 'estación' = season (primavera, verano, otoño, invierno) and 2) 'estación' = station (bus/train/radio). Use context to decide which meaning fits. 'Mi estación' can refer to your favorite season (Mi estación favorita es el otoño) or to a station you use or work at (Mi estación está cerca).
target_language_example: Mi estación favorita es la primavera.
native_language_example: My favorite season is spring.

meaning: 'my experience' — what I have personally observed, learned, or lived through
additional_notes: Used to introduce a personal observation, opinion, or lesson learned. Common in sentences like 'En mi experiencia...' (In my experience...) or 'Mi experiencia me dice...' (My experience tells me...). It can refer to a specific experience (with someone/something) or general past experience.
target_language_example: En mi experiencia, practicar todos los días mejora mucho la pronunciación.
native_language_example: In my experience, practicing every day greatly improves pronunciation.

meaning: my party / my celebration
additional_notes: Used to indicate possession: the speaker's party or celebration. Can refer to a specific party (birthday, gathering) or a favorite type of celebration (e.g., 'mi fiesta favorita'). Common in everyday speech. Tone is neutral; context clarifies what kind of celebration.
target_language_example: ¿Puedes venir a mi fiesta el sábado?
native_language_example: Can you come to my party on Saturday?

meaning: Not a complete phrase by itself; likely the start of a sentence meaning 'my cat (to/for) him/her/it' — uses the indirect object pronoun "le" after a noun.
additional_notes: This string is incomplete in Spanish. Spanish normally places the indirect object pronoun (le) before a conjugated verb (e.g., "mi gato le da comida") or attached to an infinitive/gerund. If you see "mi gato le...", expect more information: who receives the action or what is given. English word order differs: Spanish uses pronouns even when the indirect object is also explicit. Example structure: "Mi gato le trae un ratón a mi hermana."
target_language_example: Mi gato le trae un ratón a mi hermana.
native_language_example: My cat brings a mouse to my sister.

meaning: my people / my folks (can mean family, close friends, community)
additional_notes: Common informal phrase used to refer to a group you belong to or feel loyalty toward: family, close friends, community, coworkers, or supporters. Tone depends on context — can be affectionate, protective, or political. Not literal only; often means 'people like me' or 'those I trust.'
target_language_example: Siempre defiendo a mi gente.
native_language_example: I always stand up for my people.

meaning: my great / my big (used before a noun to mean 'great' or 'very good' — e.g., 'mi gran amigo' = 'my great friend').
additional_notes: Gran is a shortened form of 'grande' used before singular nouns (both masculine and feminine) to mean 'great' or 'important'. After the noun you use 'grande' (mi amigo grande = my big friend, size-wise). 'Mi gran' is common in emotional or emphatic phrases: mi gran amor, mi gran amigo, mi gran logro.
target_language_example: Mi gran amigo siempre me apoya.
native_language_example: My great friend always supports me.

meaning: my brother (followed by indirect object pronoun 'le').
additional_notes: This fragment combines the possessive phrase 'mi hermano' (my brother) with the indirect object pronoun 'le' (to him/for him). By itself it's incomplete — you need a verb and an object to make a full sentence (e.g., 'Mi hermano le dio el libro' = 'My brother gave him/her the book'). 'Le' can refer to 'him', 'her' or the formal 'you' (usted) depending on context. In many Spanish-speaking regions, 'le' is also used as a polite direct-object pronoun in colloquial speech (leísmo), but standard grammar treats it as an indirect-object pronoun.
target_language_example: Mi hermano le compró un regalo a su mejor amigo.
native_language_example: My brother bought a gift for his best friend (for him).

meaning: 'mi hija' = 'my daughter'; the following 'le' is an indirect object pronoun that requires a verb or clause to be grammatical. As written, 'mi hija le' is incomplete in standard Spanish and likely an error or an unfinished phrase.
additional_notes: Use 'mi hija' to say 'my daughter'. If you need to include an indirect object pronoun, it must be attached to a verb or appear with one (for example: 'Mi hija le dio un regalo.' = 'My daughter gave him/her a gift'). To express 'to my daughter' use the prepositional phrase 'a mi hija'. Standing alone, 'mi hija le' is ungrammatical because 'le' lacks a corresponding verb or predicate.
target_language_example: Mi hija le dio una carta a su profesora.
native_language_example: My daughter gave a letter to her teacher.

meaning: The sequence 'mi hijo' ('my son') followed immediately by the preposition 'a', used to mark recipient, destination, direction, or role/relationship in constructions like 'dar algo a mi hijo' (give something to my son) or 'mandar a mi hijo a la universidad' (send my son to university). It's not a fixed idiom but a common syntactic pattern.
additional_notes: Not a single lexical item—it's the noun phrase 'mi hijo' plus the preposition 'a' that introduces an indirect object, destination, direction, purpose, or the start of a subordinate phrase. Word order and meaning depend on the verb and context. Common verbs with this pattern: dar a, dejar a, mandar a, llevar a, enviar a. 'A' can translate as 'to', 'for', 'into', or be part of a larger structure; literal translation varies by context.
target_language_example: Dejo a mi hijo a tu cuidado.
native_language_example: I leave my son in your care.

meaning: A fragment meaning 'my son (to/for) him/her/you (formal)', showing subject + indirect object pronoun — not a complete sentence by itself.
additional_notes: This is not a standalone phrase; it combines the noun phrase 'mi hijo' (my son) with the indirect object pronoun 'le'. In Spanish, 'le' can mean 'to him', 'to her', or 'to you (formal)'. You will usually see it inside a full sentence, for example: 'Mi hijo le dio un regalo' (My son gave him/her/you a gift). Be careful: Spanish often requires both a noun and a pronoun for clarity/emphasis, but the full verb and object are needed to complete the idea.
target_language_example: Mi hijo le dio un libro a su profesora.
native_language_example: My son gave a book to his (female) teacher.

meaning: my appointment / my time (scheduled time) or my hour (literal).
additional_notes: Commonly used to refer to a scheduled appointment or reserved time (e.g., medical appointment, a meeting, or a booked slot). Context determines whether it means a literal hour ('my hour') or 'my appointment/time slot.' To specify, often followed by the context: mi hora con el médico (my appointment with the doctor).
target_language_example: Tengo mi hora con el dentista a las cuatro.
native_language_example: I have my appointment with the dentist at four.

meaning: 'my young' — a possessive + adjective used to address or describe someone younger or less experienced; often followed by a noun (amigo, aprendiz, dama).
additional_notes: Used to refer affectionately or respectfully to a younger person or someone with less experience. Common in literary, formal, or affectionate contexts. In everyday speech Spanish speakers might instead say 'mi amigo joven' (my young friend) or simply use a name or 'joven' alone when addressing someone directly (e.g., 'Joven, ¿puedo ayudarle?'). 'Mi joven' usually appears before a noun (mi joven amigo) or as a vocative (Mi joven, escucha.).
target_language_example: Mi joven estudiante, practica todos los días.
native_language_example: My young student, practice every day.

meaning: my call (usually a phone call) or my visit/appeal depending on context.
additional_notes: Commonly refers to a phone call (mi llamada telefónica). Can also mean a personal visit or a request/appeal in some contexts, but for beginners treat it as 'my call' (phone). Use with verbs like esperar (to wait for) or querer (to want).
target_language_example: Te dejaré un mensaje después de mi llamada.
native_language_example: I'll leave you a message after my call.

meaning: An emphatic, colloquial exclamation expressing surprise, dismay or exasperation; similar in force to “¡madre mía!” or “oh my goodness.”
additional_notes: Not a standard grammatically complete phrase on its own; often used in conversational speech and may be followed by additional words (e.g., «mi madre a esto...»). Regional and individual usage varies; tone and context determine strength. Informal and best avoided in formal writing.
target_language_example: ¡Mi madre a, no esperaba verte tan temprano!
native_language_example: Oh my goodness, I didn't expect to see you so early!

meaning: my best (used before a noun, e.g. 'my best friend' or 'my best show').
additional_notes: mi = my (possessive). mejor = better/best. Together they appear before a noun to mean the speaker's top/closest person or favorite thing. Commonly used with amigo (friend), opción, momento, programa, etc. Gender and number agreement: mejor stays same, but possessive changes (mi, mis). Use 'mi mejor amigo' (male friend) or 'mi mejor amiga' (female friend).
target_language_example: Ella es mi mejor amiga desde la infancia.
native_language_example: She is my best friend since childhood.

meaning: my goal / my aim / my objective.
additional_notes: Used to say what you hope to achieve in the future (short- or long-term). Commonly followed by a verb infinitive or a noun phrase (e.g., "mi meta es ser...", "mi meta en la vida es..."). Polite and neutral — suitable in everyday and formal contexts.
target_language_example: Mi meta es aprender inglés fluido este año.
native_language_example: My goal is to learn fluent English this year.

meaning: my machine / my device; can be literal (a machine) or a casual way to refer to one's car, bike, computer, or tool.
additional_notes: Literally 'my machine.' In everyday Spanish, speakers often call something they use a lot 'mi máquina' to mean their car, motorcycle, bicycle, computer, or another device—often with affection or pride. Context tells whether it's literal (industrial machine) or informal (vehicle or gadget). Use with possessive 'mi' (my).
target_language_example: Voy a poner gasolina en mi máquina antes del viaje.
native_language_example: I'm going to put gas in my car before the trip.

meaning: my (machine) for... — used to refer to a device or tool you use for a specific purpose
additional_notes: Literal phrase meaning 'my machine of/for'. Commonly followed by a noun or verb (often with -ing in English) to specify the function: e.g., mi máquina de café (my coffee machine) or mi máquina de coser (my sewing machine). In casual speech it can also be used humorously to refer to any device or gadget you rely on. Agreeing articles/possessives follow Spanish grammar (mi stays the same for singular nouns).
target_language_example: Mi máquina de café se descompuso y necesito arreglarla.
native_language_example: My coffee machine broke down and I need to fix it.

meaning: my best wishes / my regards (often short for «mi más sentido pésame» — my deepest condolences)
additional_notes: Alone, 'mi más' is incomplete and usually appears as part of a longer formula like 'mi más sentido pésame' (my deepest condolences) or 'mi más sincero agradecimiento' (my sincerest thanks). It conveys an intensified, formal sentiment ('my most...'). Not common by itself in casual speech.
target_language_example: Te mando mi más sentido pésame por la pérdida de tu padre.
native_language_example: I send you my deepest condolences for the loss of your father.

meaning: my music; the music I like, play, or create.
additional_notes: Used to refer to music that belongs to or is associated with the speaker—this can mean music they like (favorite music), music they play or perform, or music they have created. Context determines whether it means 'my favorite music', 'the music I play', or 'my compositions'.
target_language_example: Ella realmente disfruta mi música en el concierto.
native_language_example: She really enjoys my music at the concert.

meaning: ‘my computer, if…’ — offers permission to use the speaker's computer, followed by a conditional 'if'.
additional_notes: This sequence combines a possessive noun phrase (mi ordenador = my computer) with the conjunction si (if). In natural speech it introduces a conditional offer or permission: 'You can use my computer if you want.' The subject and verb before or after may change depending on formality (tú/usted/ustedes) and number (singular/plural).
target_language_example: Podéis usar mi ordenador si queréis.
native_language_example: You can use my computer if you want.

meaning: my other (one); used to refer to another person or thing paired or contrasted with one already mentioned or implied
additional_notes: Usually incomplete on its own — typically followed by a noun or understood from context (e.g., mi otro hermano, mi otra mitad). Gender must agree with the implied noun (mi otro / mi otra). Can be used to refer to another item or person previously mentioned; not commonly used alone without context in formal speech.
target_language_example: No encuentro mi otro zapato.
native_language_example: I can't find my other shoe.

meaning: 'my father' plus the preposition 'de' used before a verb or noun phrase (e.g. 'mi padre de dejar...') — this is not a fixed phrase by itself; it's the possessive 'mi padre' followed by 'de' to link to another element.
additional_notes: This sequence is simply the noun phrase 'mi padre' (my father) followed by the preposition 'de'. 'De' is used in many ways in Spanish: to introduce an infinitive after verbs that take 'de' (e.g., convencer de + infinitive or convencer a alguien de + infinitive/idea), to indicate removal (sacar a alguien de), to indicate cause/purpose (librar de), or to link possession/relationship. The examples show different constructions: 'convencer a mi padre de ...' (convince my father to...), 'librar a mi padre de ...' (free my father from...), 'sacar a mi padre de aquí' (take my father out of here), and an insult 'quiero a mi padre de regreso' uses 'de' as part of 'de regreso' (back). So learners should treat 'mi padre' as the phrase for 'my father' and learn the various uses of 'de' separately.
target_language_example: Convencí a mi padre de ayudarme con la mudanza.
native_language_example: I convinced my father to help me with the move.

meaning: literally 'my father in' — not a complete phrase by itself; likely the start of a longer expression (e.g., 'mi padre en casa', 'mi padre en el trabajo').
additional_notes: As given, 'mi padre en' is incomplete. In Spanish you need a location, situation, or clause after 'en' to finish the thought (en + noun or en + clause). Common completions: 'mi padre en casa' (my father at home), 'mi padre en el trabajo' (my father at work), 'mi padre en la foto' (my father in the photo), or 'mi padre en realidad...' (my father actually...). Don't use 'mi padre en' alone in a sentence.
target_language_example: Mi padre en casa siempre lee el periódico por la mañana.
native_language_example: My father at home always reads the newspaper in the morning.

meaning: my father likes (something).
additional_notes: This is the Spanish structure used to say that someone likes something: A + person + le + gusta + [noun/infinitive]. The thing liked is expressed with a singular noun or an infinitive verb; use gustan for plural things. 'A mí también' means 'me too.'
target_language_example: A mi padre le gusta escuchar música clásica.
native_language_example: My father likes listening to classical music.

meaning: 'my father' + que (introducing a clause) — used to say 'that/to (my) father' when reporting who is affected or who receives an action or advice.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase; it's just the possessive noun phrase 'mi padre' followed by the conjunction 'que' which introduces a subordinate clause (often with verbs of telling, advising, suggesting, wanting, etc.). English equivalents: 'that my father...' or 'to my father that...' depending on the main verb. Word order: verb + (a) + mi padre + que + clause (e.g., aconsejó a mi padre que dejara...).
target_language_example: Le expliqué a mi padre que el cambio sería para mejor.
native_language_example: I explained to my father that the change would be for the better.

meaning: my umbrella in/on (used to say where you left or found your umbrella).
additional_notes: This phrase combines 'mi paraguas' (my umbrella) with a preposition like 'en' + place (el tren, el taxi, el camión) to say where you left or found it. 'En' can mean 'in' or 'on' depending on the vehicle or context (e.g., 'en el tren' = on the train, 'en el taxi' = in the taxi). Also used with verbs like dejar (to leave), olvidar (to forget), tomar (to take).
target_language_example: Dejé mi paraguas en el autobús por la mañana.
native_language_example: I left my umbrella on the bus this morning.

meaning: my movie / my film
additional_notes: A simple possessive phrase: 'mi' (my) + 'película' (movie/film). Used to talk about a movie you own, made, like, or are watching. Context determines whether it means 'the movie I made', 'my favorite movie', or 'the movie I'm watching'. For plural use, change 'película' to 'películas' (my movies).
target_language_example: ¿Quieres ver mi película favorita esta noche?
native_language_example: Do you want to watch my favorite movie tonight?

meaning: my point (what I'm trying to say)
additional_notes: Used to state or emphasize the main idea, argument, or opinion you're making. Can appear as a complete sentence ('Mi punto.') to signal you've finished your argument or to draw attention to the central idea. Common in both formal and informal contexts.
target_language_example: Mi punto es que necesitamos más tiempo para terminar.
native_language_example: My point is that we need more time to finish.

meaning: my point of (view) / my argument about…
additional_notes: Used to introduce or refer to the speaker's opinion or argument about a topic. Often followed by a noun like vista, vista de vista (incorrect), vista? Wait—correct is "mi punto de vista" for "my point of view." However, "mi punto de" by itself is incomplete and informal; listeners expect the rest (e.g., "mi punto de vista" or "mi punto de vista es que..."). Can be used in conversational shortcuts where the rest is implied: "Mi punto de es..." — but that is nonstandard. For beginner learners, prefer the complete phrase "mi punto de vista". Note: do not confuse with "punto de" constructions like "punto de encuentro" (meeting point).
target_language_example: Mi punto de vista es que deberíamos esperar.
native_language_example: My point of view is that we should wait.

meaning: 'my luck' or 'my fate/destiny' (literally 'my luck').
additional_notes: Used to refer to one's luck, fortune, or fate. Context determines nuance: can mean good/bad luck (mi suerte se acabó = my luck has run out), fate (dejarme a mi suerte = leave me to my fate/situation), or affectionally (eres mi suerte = you're my good luck/you're my destiny).
target_language_example: Después de tanto buscar, creo que por fin llegó mi suerte.
native_language_example: After searching so long, I think my luck has finally come.

meaning: 'my train' — refers to the specific train someone is using or expecting.
additional_notes: Used to indicate possession or association with a particular train (the one you intend to take or are traveling on). Can refer to departure/arrival times, being missed, or which train has priority. In spoken Spanish, context clarifies which train (schedule, platform, ticket) is meant.
target_language_example: Mi tren sale en veinte minutos; voy corriendo a la estación.
native_language_example: My train leaves in twenty minutes; I'm running to the station.

meaning: 'my tea'.
additional_notes: A possessive phrase: mi + noun. Used to indicate that the tea belongs to or is intended for the speaker (or the person being referred to). Commonly followed by details about how the tea is prepared (con/sin azúcar, con leche, caliente, frío, etc.). Pronunciation note: té (accent) distinguishes the noun 'tea' from the pronoun 'te'.
target_language_example: Voy a calentar mi té antes de salir.
native_language_example: I'm going to heat my tea before leaving.

meaning: my real / my true (used before a noun, e.g. 'my true name')
additional_notes: Uses 'verdadero' (true/real) to specify the authentic or correct identity of something you own or are called. Commonly appears as 'mi verdadero nombre' (my real name) or 'mi verdadero yo' (my true self). Place 'mi verdadero' before the noun. Tone is neutral and standard.
target_language_example: Mi verdadero nombre es Ana.
native_language_example: My real name is Ana.

meaning: 'my life with you' — used to say you want to spend your life together with someone.
additional_notes: A romantic phrase expressing the desire to share the future with another person. Often appears with verbs like querer (quiero pasar) or amar (te amo). Can be modified with 'el resto de' to mean 'the rest of my life.' Used in declarations of love or marriage proposals.
target_language_example: Te amo y quiero pasar el resto de mi vida contigo.
native_language_example: I love you and I want to spend the rest of my life with you.

meaning: a colloquial emphatic phrase meaning 'in my life' or 'I've ever' used to stress how strongly you feel about something.
additional_notes: Often appears as part of expressions like 'En mi vida me he...' or 'Nunca en mi vida me...' to emphasize that something has (or has never) happened to the speaker. It is informal and emphatic; 'mi vida' here is not literal 'my life' but a way to stress the personal experience. Common with verbs of feeling or reaction (reír, sentir, matar [figurative]).
target_language_example: Nunca en mi vida me había emocionado tanto.
native_language_example: Never in my life have I been so moved.

meaning: my old (feminine) — used for things (or sometimes people) that are old or former.
additional_notes: Literal feminine form of "mi viejo"; agrees with a feminine noun (casa, bicicleta, espada, guarida). Commonly means "my old [thing]" (the one I used to have or that's aged). In some dialects or contexts, "mi vieja" can informally refer to one's wife or girlfriend, but here examples show possessions and places. Use "mi viejo" for masculine nouns.
target_language_example: Le presté a Marta mi vieja bicicleta hasta que arregle la suya.
native_language_example: I lent Marta my old bike until she fixes hers.

meaning: 'me too' (expresses that the same applies to the speaker).
additional_notes: Commonly used to agree or indicate the same feeling/action applies to the speaker. Typically appears with the preposition 'a' for emphasis (A mí también) and the pronoun 'mí' is usually written with an accent when used after 'a'; however, in informal contexts accents are sometimes omitted in writing. Can be used standalone as a short reply ('¡Mi también!' is nonstandard — prefer 'A mí también') or within a sentence: 'A mí también me gustan...' Informal expletives may follow in casual speech.
target_language_example: A mi también me gustan los pasteles.
native_language_example: I like cakes too.

meaning: fear of (something or someone).
additional_notes: Used to say you are afraid of a person, animal, situation, etc. Often appears with verbs like tener (tener miedo a/de). In Spanish both 'miedo a' and 'miedo de' are heard, but 'miedo a' + noun or infinitive is very common. To negate, use 'no tener miedo a' or 'no tener miedo de'.
target_language_example: No tengas miedo a volar si el avión es seguro.
native_language_example: Don't be afraid of flying if the plane is safe.

meaning: fear of the (feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used to say you are afraid of something that is a feminine noun (e.g., la oscuridad = the dark). Replace 'la' with 'el' for masculine nouns (miedo al). Commonly followed by a noun or noun phrase: miedo a la oscuridad, miedo a la soledad, miedo a la lluvia. Also appears in fixed expressions like 'tener miedo a' or simply as a noun phrase 'miedo a la ...'.
target_language_example: Tengo miedo a la oscuridad por la noche.
native_language_example: I'm afraid of the dark at night.

target_language_multi_word_term: miedo de su / miedo de su propia
meaning: 'afraid of' or 'fear of (someone or something of one's own)'.
additional_notes: Used to say someone is afraid of someone/something. When followed by 'propio/a' it emphasizes that the fear is of one's own (e.g., 'su propio marido' = 'his/her own husband', 'su propia sombra' = an idiom meaning 'very easily frightened'). In Spanish the preposition can be 'de' (tiene miedo de su padre) or the direct object can use 'a' with people (tiene miedo a los perros), but 'miedo de' is common in these examples.
target_language_example: Ella tiene miedo de su propia sombra.
native_language_example: She is afraid of her own shadow.

meaning: 'fear of' (followed by a noun or verb in gerund/infinitive context).
additional_notes: Miedo means 'fear'. 'Del' is the contraction of 'de' + 'el' (of the). Together 'miedo del' appears before a specific masculine noun (e.g., 'miedo del fracaso' = 'fear of failure'). Often you will also see 'miedo a' (fear of doing something or of someone) — use 'miedo del' when referring to 'fear of the [noun]'. If the noun is feminine use 'miedo de la'. For general 'fear of [verb]' use 'miedo de' + infinitive or more commonly 'miedo a' + infinitive.
target_language_example: Tiene miedo del examen mañana.
native_language_example: He is afraid of the exam tomorrow.

meaning: 'miedo' = fear; 'es' = is — together they would start a sentence like 'fear is...'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase on its own; it's the noun miedo (fear) followed by the verb ser (es). You'll see it at the start of definitions or descriptions (e.g., 'Miedo es una emoción...'). Use 'miedo' to talk about fear: tengo miedo (I'm afraid), dar miedo (to frighten).
target_language_example: El miedo es una reacción natural.
native_language_example: Fear is a natural reaction.

meaning: 'miedo las' no es una expresión correcta o independiente en español; parece una combinación errónea de miedo (noun) + las (article/possessive) que carece de sentido sin una preposición o contexto.
additional_notes: La secuencia sólo tiene sentido dentro de una construcción mayor: normalmente se usa 'miedo a las ...' (por ejemplo, 'miedo a las alturas') o 'miedo de las ...' (por ejemplo, 'miedo de las consecuencias'). Por sí sola, 'miedo las' es incorrecta y se considera un error. Corrija añadiendo la preposición adecuada ('a' o 'de') y el sustantivo o frase que sigue, o reordene la frase (por ejemplo, 'Tengo miedo' o 'Tengo miedo de las consecuencias').
target_language_example: Miedo las alturas no tiene sentido; deberías decir "miedo a las alturas".
native_language_example: "Miedo las alturas" makes no sense; you should say "miedo a las alturas".

meaning: used to introduce a fear or worry that something might happen (similar to English 'I'm afraid that...').
additional_notes: Often appears in constructions like 'tengo miedo (de) que...' or 'me da miedo que...'. When followed by a verb, Spanish typically uses the subjunctive after 'miedo que' because it expresses fear about a possible or uncertain event (e.g., 'Tengo miedo de que no venga.'). Many speakers include the preposition 'de' ('miedo de que'), but colloquial speech sometimes drops it ('miedo que').
target_language_example: Tengo miedo que no hayan llegado aún.
native_language_example: I'm afraid that they haven't arrived yet.

meaning: miedo = 'fear'; 'miedo y' by itself isn't a complete phrase—it's likely the start of a sentence meaning 'fear and...'.
additional_notes: miedo is a common noun meaning 'fear' or 'scared'. 'miedo y' simply joins miedo with another word using 'y' ('and'). You will usually see it as part of a larger phrase: miedo y respeto (fear and respect), miedo y ansiedad (fear and anxiety), tengo miedo y... (I'm afraid and...). Don't use 'miedo y' alone as a complete sentence.
target_language_example: Tengo miedo y necesito hablar con alguien.
native_language_example: I'm afraid and I need to talk to someone.

meaning: lies to (someone)
additional_notes: Verb phrase: miente is the third-person singular present of mentir (to lie). Use 'le' before 'miente a' when indicating 'to him/her/you (formal)' (e.g., 'le miente a Mary'). For plural subjects or other persons change verb form (yo miento, tú mientes, ellos mienten). Commonly followed by the person who is being lied to.
target_language_example: Él le miente a su amigo sobre lo que pasó.
native_language_example: He lies to his friend about what happened.

meaning: while the / as long as the (followed by a masculine singular noun or clause subject).
additional_notes: Combines 'mientras' (while/as long as) with the masculine singular article 'el'. Often begins a subordinate time or condition clause: 'mientras el maestro habla' (while the teacher speaks). If the following word is a verb, Spanish may instead use 'mientras' + subjunctive/indicative without the article. Make sure 'el' agrees with a masculine singular noun (el coche, el día, el profesor).
target_language_example: Mientras el profesor explica, toma notas.
native_language_example: While the teacher explains, take notes.

meaning: 'while she' or 'as long as she'.
additional_notes: Used to introduce an action or state that happens at the same time as, or during the period when, 'she' does something. Can express simultaneous actions (while she was crying) or a condition/duration (as long as she is here). Verb mood may change: use indicative for factual statements (está, estaba) and subjunctive (esté) when expressing uncertainty, condition, or pending actions.
target_language_example: Puedes entrar mientras ella duerma.
native_language_example: You can go in while she sleeps.

meaning: while you were (doing something).
additional_notes: Used to refer to an action or state that was happening at the same time as another past action; typically followed by a present participle (estabas + gerund) or a clause explaining what the person was doing. 'Estabas' is the imperfect of 'estar' for 'tú' (you, singular informal).
target_language_example: Mientras estabas durmiendo, llamaron al timbre.
native_language_example: While you were sleeping, someone rang the doorbell.

meaning: while (he/she/you formal) was reading the (feminine noun).
additional_notes: A short phrase combining the conjunction 'mientras' (while) with the imperfect tense 'leía' (I/he/she/you formal was/were reading) and the feminine singular article 'la'. Use to describe an ongoing action in the past that was happening when something else occurred. Replace 'la' with another article or noun as needed (e.g., mientras leía el libro, mientras leía la carta). Subject is usually clear from context or conjugation.
target_language_example: Mientras leía la carta, empezó a llorar.
native_language_example: While he/she was reading the letter, he/she began to cry.

meaning: 'while it/him/her' or 'while doing it' (depends on context).
additional_notes: Combines mientras (while) with the direct object pronoun lo/la/los/las. The phrase itself is incomplete and needs more words to be a full clause (e.g., mientras lo hago = while I do it; mientras lo esperas = while you wait for him/it). 'Lo' refers to a masculine singular direct object or a neutral idea. Use gender/number agreement if the object differs (mientras la, mientras los, mientras las).
target_language_example: No hables y mientras lo lees, subraya las ideas principales.
native_language_example: Don't talk and while you read it, underline the main ideas.

meaning: while I (am) / while I (do something).
additional_notes: Combination of 'mientras' (while) + reflexive pronoun 'me' used with reflexive verbs (ducharse, bañarse, afeitarse, etc.). Indicates two actions happening at the same time: one thing occurs while the speaker is performing the reflexive action. Use the appropriate verb form after 'me' (me ducho, me bañaba, me afeito).
target_language_example: Mientras me ducho, escucho música.
native_language_example: While I shower, I listen to music.

meaning: as long as (something does not happen); provided that not
additional_notes: Used to introduce a condition that something must not happen for the main clause to hold. Similar to 'siempre y cuando no' or 'si no'. Often followed by a verb or clause expressing the undesired action. Can also contrast two simultaneous actions when combined with 'mientras' alone, but 'mientras no' specifically emphasizes 'provided that not'.
target_language_example: Puedes salir con tus amigos mientras no vuelvas muy tarde.
native_language_example: You can go out with your friends as long as you don't come back too late.

meaning: while / whereas (to contrast two things) or 'while' meaning 'during' in some contexts.
additional_notes: Most often used to contrast two people, situations, or ideas (equivalent to English 'whereas' or 'while' in contrast). It can also mean 'while/during' when introducing an action happening at the same time, but that use is less common for beginners. Use 'mientras' alone for simple 'while' (during) sentences; 'mientras que' emphasizes contrast.
target_language_example: A ella le gusta la playa, mientras que a mí me gustan las montañas.
native_language_example: She likes the beach, whereas I like the mountains.

meaning: meanwhile; in the meantime.
additional_notes: Used to introduce an action or situation that happens at the same time as another. Can appear at the start or middle of a sentence and often followed by a comma. Common in both spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: Prepara la comida; mientras tanto, yo pongo la mesa.
native_language_example: Prepare the food; meanwhile, I'll set the table.

meaning: an emphatic or coarse way to direct anger/frustration at someone or something (like 'damn to' / 'to hell with').
additional_notes: Mierda is a strong vulgar word meaning 'shit.' When followed by 'a' plus a person or thing, it expresses anger, dismissal, or contempt toward that person/thing (e.g., 'mierda a X' ≈ 'to hell with X' or 'screw X'). Very informal and offensive — avoid in polite contexts. Usage and intensity vary by region.
target_language_example: ¡Mierda a las reglas, hago lo que quiero!
native_language_example: To hell with the rules, I'll do what I want!

meaning: literally 'shit with'; used colloquially to complain about a situation or person (like 'this shit with...' or 'the crap about...').
additional_notes: Vulgar expression. 'Mierda' is a strong swear word meaning 'shit.' Paired with 'con' it introduces what you’re complaining about (e.g., 'la mierda con este servicio' = 'this crap with this service'). Not a fixed grammatical phrase — speakers may use variants like 'la mierda de...' or simply 'mierda' + clause. Avoid in formal contexts.
target_language_example: Estoy hasta la mierda con estas excusas.
native_language_example: I'm fed up with this crap/excuses.

meaning: an emphatic, vulgar way to say 'it's shit' or 'it's terrible'.
additional_notes: Mierda is a strong vulgar word meaning 'shit'. When combined with es (is), the phrase expresses disgust, disappointment, or that something is very bad. It's informal and offensive — avoid in polite conversation. You might also see variations like 'esto es una mierda' (this is shit) or simply 'es una mierda.'
target_language_example: Esta película mierda es, no la veas.
native_language_example: This movie is shit, don't watch it.

meaning: A vulgar expletive phrase used to express frustration, surprise, annoyance, or emphasis. It is rough equivalent to 'damn it' or 'shit' in English, though the word order 'mierda la' is colloquial, fragmented, or emphatic rather than standard grammar.
additional_notes: Mierda is a strong swear word meaning 'shit'. The phrase 'la mierda' (the shit) is standard, but 'mierda la' typically appears in clipped spoken exclamations or regional emphatic constructions (e.g., '¡Mierda la que...!' or as an isolated interjection following a pause). It is offensive in formal contexts and should be avoided with strangers, in professional settings, or around children. Milder alternatives: '¡Rayos!', '¡Caramba!', '¡Vaya!'
target_language_example: ¡Mierda, la que me espera! — ¡Mierda la, siempre pasa lo mismo!
native_language_example: Shit, what awaits me! — Damn it, it always happens the same way!

meaning: An emphatic colloquial exclamation expressing annoyance, frustration, or contempt (roughly 'damn it' or stronger).
additional_notes: This is informal and vulgar. 'Mierda' means 'shit' and here is combined with 'lo' for emphasis; exact nuance depends on context and intonation. Avoid in polite situations. Not standard grammar — may appear in spoken slang or emphatic phrases.
target_language_example: ¡Mierda lo que dijo, no puedo creerlo!
native_language_example: Damn what he said, I can't believe it!

additional_notes: Used in Spanish to mean 1,000,000,000 (long scale). Common in Spain and many Spanish-speaking countries. In some regions, people may also say 'un millardo' but 'mil millones' is far more common. Use with de when counting (e.g., 'mil millones de personas').
target_language_example: Hay mil millones de estrellas visibles en esa imagen.
native_language_example: There are one billion stars visible in that image.

meaning: 'miracle that' / used to express surprise or relief that something happened (often in exclamations).
additional_notes: Literally means 'miracle that'. Commonly used in exclamatory phrases to comment that something is surprising, lucky, or unexpected — similar to English 'what a miracle that...' or 'it's a miracle that...'. Often appears with verbs in indicative or subjunctive depending on nuance, but beginners can treat it as a fixed way to show surprise or relief.
target_language_example: ¡Milagro que llegaste a tiempo!
native_language_example: It's a miracle that you arrived on time!

meaning: ‘mile of’ — used to indicate distance or a stretch/area measured in miles.
additional_notes: Milla is the feminine noun for 'mile'. 'Milla de' is followed by a noun (e.g., carretera, carretera, camino) or can be used in expressions like 'a una milla de' (one mile from). In many Spanish-speaking countries metric units (kilómetro) are more common, but 'milla' appears in contexts discussing English/imperial distances or travel in countries using miles.
target_language_example: Estamos a una milla de la salida.
native_language_example: We are one mile from the exit.

meaning: an emphatic way to say 'millions and (millions)' or 'millions upon millions' — used to stress a very large, often indefinite number.
additional_notes: Often appears in repetition (e.g., "millones y millones") to emphasize enormous quantity or age. Can be used literally (many millions of units) or figuratively (a huge, almost immeasurable amount). In sentences like "vale millones y..." it implies a very high value (millions) followed by more information.
target_language_example: Hay millones y millones de insectos en ese bosque.
native_language_example: There are millions and millions of insects in that forest.

meaning: 'mine of' or 'mine for' — used to say a place where a mineral is extracted, or metaphorically 'a source of' (e.g., a mine of information).
additional_notes: Literal: 'mina' = mine (where minerals are dug). 'Mina de' is followed by the material (mina de oro = gold mine) or can be used figuratively to mean 'a rich source of' (una mina de ideas). Use gender and number normally for nouns that follow.
target_language_example: Esta biblioteca es una mina de información para estudiantes.
native_language_example: This library is a mine of information for students.

meaning: a gold mine; literally a mine where gold is extracted; figuratively something that yields great profit or value.
additional_notes: Can be used literally for an actual gold-mining site or figuratively to describe a very profitable business, resource, opportunity, or source of useful information. In plural: minas de oro. Stress on 'mi-na de o-ro'.
target_language_example: Ese cliente es una mina de oro para nuestro negocio.
native_language_example: That client is a gold mine for our business.

meaning: lied to (someone).
additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of mentir (to lie). Use 'le' (or other indirect object pronouns: me, te, nos, les) before the verb to indicate who was lied to, or add an indirect object phrase: 'mintió a María' = 'lied to María'. Can also be used without 'a' when followed by a noun phrase for the person (mintió a la policía).
target_language_example: Él le mintió a su amiga sobre dónde estaba.
native_language_example: He lied to his friend about where he was.

meaning: 'a minute of' or 'a minute to' — used to indicate a short amount of time related to something (e.g., a minute of silence, a minute to prepare).
additional_notes: Commonly used before a noun to say 'a minute of [something]' (un minuto de silencio = a minute of silence) or in time expressions (faltan un minuto para las ocho = it's one minute to eight). When used alone, 'un minuto' often just means 'one minute' or 'just a moment'.
target_language_example: Dame un minuto de silencio antes de empezar.
native_language_example: Give me a minute of silence before starting.

meaning: one more minute; a minute longer
additional_notes: Used to ask for or indicate a short extra amount of time. Often appears with words like 'un' (one) or in negative expressions 'ni un minuto más' (not one minute more). Common in requests (Dame un minuto más) and in commands or limits (Ni un minuto más tarde).
target_language_example: Espérame sólo un minuto más.
native_language_example: Wait for me just one more minute.

meaning: a (short) amount of time before doing something; 'a minute to/for' (to allow time to... / time remaining to...).
additional_notes: Used to indicate a brief pause or a small amount of time needed (Déme un minuto para pensar = Give me a minute to think) or time available/remaining for an action (tiene un minuto para formar a la unidad = you have a minute to form the unit). Can also appear in phrases like 'minuto para el impacto' (minute before impact) or 'puntos de último minuto' (last-minute points). 'Minuto' is literal; context decides whether it means an actual 60 seconds or simply 'a moment.'
target_language_example: Dame un minuto para terminar este correo.
native_language_example: Give me a minute to finish this email.

meaning: literally 'minutes to' or 'minutes until' (used when giving the time, e.g. 'X minutes to [the next hour]').
additional_notes: Common in time expressions: 'faltan X minutos al...' or 'X minutos al...' often precedes an hour to indicate how many minutes remain until that hour. More typical phrasing: 'son las (hora menos X)' or 'faltan X minutos para las (hora)'. 'Al' here is a contraction of 'a + el' and may appear in regional or colloquial speech; in many contexts 'para' or 'a' is used instead.
target_language_example: Faltan diez minutos al mediodía.
native_language_example: There are ten minutes to noon.

meaning: 'minutes in' (literal) — commonly used as part of phrases indicating duration or time spent inside/within something, or minutes remaining/elapsed in a period (e.g., 'minutos en el partido' = minutes in the match).
additional_notes: By itself 'minutos en' is not a complete phrase; it usually appears in contexts like 'X minutos en [lugar/actividad]' meaning 'X minutes in [place/activity]' (time spent inside or elapsed during an event) or in sports commentary 'minutos en el partido' (minutes played in the match). Use with a number or additional context. Word order and preposition may vary (e.g., 'en X minutos' = 'in X minutes').
target_language_example: Llevamos quince minutos en la reunión y todavía no empezamos.
native_language_example: We've been in the meeting for fifteen minutes and still haven't started.

meaning: lit. "minutes and" — used when giving a time while rounding and adding a small extra amount (colloquial), or as part of a longer phrase (depends on context).
additional_notes: Alone, 'minutos y' is incomplete; you'll usually see it in expressions like 'cinco minutos y' (about five minutes and a bit) or in sequences: 'minutos y segundos' (minutes and seconds). In spoken Spanish, speakers may say '... minutos y...' to indicate an approximate extra amount (e.g. 'cinco minutos y pico' = about five minutes). Pay attention to the rest of the phrase to know the exact meaning.
target_language_example: Espérame cinco minutos y llego.
native_language_example: Wait for me five minutes and I'll be there.

meaning: look at (someone/something) with (a certain expression or intention).
additional_notes: This is the verb mirar followed by the preposition con + a noun that describes the manner, feeling, or intention of the look (e.g., 'mira con curiosidad', 'mira con odio'). Use it to say someone looks at something with a specific emotion, attitude, or tool (e.g., 'mira con atención'). If no noun follows, use mirar solo or mirar a + person/thing.
target_language_example: Ella mira con sorpresa la carta.
native_language_example: She looks at the letter with surprise.

meaning: 'look in' or 'look at' (used with a place or source)
additional_notes: A combination of the imperative/indicative of mirar (to look) plus the preposition en. Commonly used to tell someone to check a place, source, website, book, or section (e.g., mira en la página, mira en el cajón). Context determines exact translation: 'look in/at' or 'check in/at'.
target_language_example: Mira en el cajón; ahí están las llaves.
native_language_example: Look in the drawer; the keys are there.

meaning: Watch what you do / look at what you're doing.
additional_notes: Used to tell someone to pay attention to their actions—can be a warning, instruction, or complaint. Tone depends on context and intonation: can be gentle advice or sharp reproach. Common in informal spoken Spanish. Literally: 'look at what you do.'
target_language_example: Mira lo que haces antes de tirar eso, podrías romperlo.
native_language_example: Watch what you do before you throw that, you could break it.

meaning: 'look at my' (informal imperative + possessive)
additional_notes: Mira mi is the informal imperative of mirar (tú mira) followed by the possessive mi. It is used to ask someone to look at or check something that belongs to the speaker (e.g., 'Mira mi coche', 'Mira mi idea'). Because it uses the informal tú form, use it with friends, family, or people you address as tú. For polite requests use 'mire mi...' (usted) or 'mira esto' / 'mira esto, por favor' for softer phrasing. The phrase usually needs a noun after mi (mira mi foto, mira mi tarea).
target_language_example: Mira mi teléfono: la pantalla está rota.
native_language_example: Look at my phone: the screen is cracked.

meaning: look for / aim for (depends on context)
additional_notes: As a phrasal combination, 'mira para' can appear in different constructions. With 'mira' (from mirar) + preposition 'para' it often introduces the direction or purpose: e.g. 'mira para allá' = 'look that way'. It can also be part of 'mira para' + infinitive or noun to indicate aiming toward a goal ('mira para ganar' — colloquial, meaning 'aims to win'), though standard phrasing for 'aim to' is usually 'mira a' or 'aspira a'. Because usage varies, pay attention to context; native speakers more commonly use 'mira a', 'mira hacia' or 'mira por' depending on meaning.
target_language_example: Mira para allá: el pájaro está en la rama.
native_language_example: Look over there: the bird is on the branch.

meaning: look out for; take care of; watch over (someone or something).
additional_notes: Used to say someone watches over, cares for, or takes responsibility for another person or thing. Often followed by a noun or pronoun (mira por los niños, mira por ti). Can also mean 'consider' or 'look after' in contexts like 'mira por el bien común' (look after the common good). Conjugate the verb mirar as needed (él mira por, ella miraba por, mira por favor).
target_language_example: Mi hermana siempre mira por los niños cuando estamos ocupados.
native_language_example: My sister always looks after the children when we're busy.

meaning: used to introduce a remark, warning, surprise, or emphasis (like 'look,' 'mind you,' or 'you should know that').
additional_notes: Common conversational phrase. Depending on tone and context it can: 1) draw attention before saying something important or surprising ('look,' 'mind you'); 2) warn or scold someone ('remember that,' 'don't forget'); or 3) express surprise about a fact. Not a literal instruction to look. Often followed by a clause.
target_language_example: Mira que te lo dije, no salgas sin abrigo.
native_language_example: Mind you, I told you—don't go out without a coat.

meaning: 'look at his/her/its/their' or 'watch his/her/its/their' (imperative or present tense depending on context).
additional_notes: Mira is the verb mirar (to look/watch) in the tú (imperative or present) form or él/ella/usted present subjunctive depending on sentence. Su is a possessive meaning his, her, its, your (formal), or their. Together, mira su can start a sentence like an instruction (Mira su foto = Look at his/her/their photo) or be part of a statement (Él mira su teléfono = He looks at his phone). Context decides the subject and exact tense.
target_language_example: Mira su casa; es muy bonita.
native_language_example: Look at his/her/their house; it's very pretty.

meaning: Look and... / Watch and... (used to introduce an action or reaction you want someone to do next)
additional_notes: A conversational prompt meaning 'look' (imperative of mirar) followed by 'and' (y). Often used in spoken Spanish to draw attention then ask or tell someone to do something: 'mira y haz esto' → 'look and do this.' It can also appear alone as a short phrase to get someone's attention before continuing. Tone is informal to neutral depending on context.
target_language_example: Mira y escucha lo que te voy a decir.
native_language_example: Look and listen to what I'm going to tell you.

meaning: 'was looking at' or 'used to look at' (third person singular imperfect of mirar + feminine singular direct object article).
additional_notes: Miraba is the imperfect tense of mirar (él/ella/usted miraba) and describes a past ongoing or repeated action: 'was looking at' or 'used to look at.' La is the feminine singular definite article (the) and marks a feminine direct object that follows the verb (e.g., la luna, la película, la gente (la used with gente as a whole)). For masculine objects you'd see 'miraba el' or 'miraba lo' for neuter ideas. Word order is verb + article + noun in these examples.
target_language_example: Ella miraba la ventana durante horas.
native_language_example: She was looking at the window for hours.

meaning: 'look of' or 'a look expressing (emotion/quality)'.
additional_notes: Used to describe the type or quality of someone's look or gaze. Often followed by a noun (e.g., 'mirada de sorpresa' = 'a look of surprise') or a pronoun/name ('mirada de él'). Common in descriptions and narrative. Not a fixed idiom—combine with nouns to specify the emotion or intention.
target_language_example: Le lanzó una mirada de reproche.
native_language_example: He gave her a look of reproach.

meaning: a look directed at / gaze fixed on
additional_notes: Used to say someone looks at or fixes their gaze on something or someone. Commonly appears with verbs like fijar (fijó la mirada en), poner, clavar, or tener (una mirada en). Can describe brief glances or an intense, sustained gaze depending on context.
target_language_example: Ella clavó la mirada en la puerta esperando a que entrara.
native_language_example: She fixed her gaze on the door waiting for him to enter.

meaning: looking out for / watching over (feminine noun follows)
additional_notes: This is a fragment of the verb phrase 'mirar por' meaning to look out for, to care for, to watch over. 'La' is the feminine singular direct object or feminine article replacing a feminine noun (e.g., 'la casa', 'la niña'). Context determines whether it's literal (looking through/for something) or idiomatic (taking care of someone). You will often see 'mirando por' followed by a noun or pronoun: 'mirando por la familia', 'mirando por la salud'.
target_language_example: Ella está mirando por la salud de su abuela.
native_language_example: She is looking out for her grandmother's health.

meaning: to look at
additional_notes: Used when specifying the object/person being looked at; 'a' introduces a direct object that is a person or animate being (or sometimes a specific thing). In many contexts it is interchangeable with 'mirar' + direct object without 'a' for inanimate objects, but Spanish often uses 'a' before people. Can also imply watching (e.g., watching children play).
target_language_example: Me gusta mirar a la gente en el parque.
native_language_example: I like to watch people in the park.

meaning: to look someone in the eyes; to make eye contact.
additional_notes: Used literally (to meet/look into someone's eyes) and figuratively (to face someone honestly or confidently). Common in contexts about sincerity, confrontation, or intimacy. If subject is reflexive (mirarse a los ojos) it often means two people look at each other.
target_language_example: Le dije la verdad y me obligó a mirar a los ojos.
native_language_example: I told her the truth and she forced me to look her in the eyes.

meaning: to look around; to look/survey the area or surroundings.
additional_notes: Common phrasal expression used when scanning a place or checking surroundings. Can be used literally (looking with your eyes) or more loosely (glancing around, checking options). Often appears as 'mirar alrededor de' when specifying a place (e.g., 'mirar alrededor de la casa').
target_language_example: Voy a mirar alrededor antes de entrar.
native_language_example: I'll look around before going in.

meaning: to look up (physically) — to direct one's eyes upward.
additional_notes: Commonly used to describe the physical action of turning one's gaze toward something above. 'Mirar arriba' and 'mirar hacia arriba' are both used; for searching information Spanish prefers verbs like 'buscar' or 'consultar' rather than 'mirar'. Can be used literally (e.g., 'mirar arriba al cielo') and occasionally figuratively depending on context.
target_language_example: Cuando oímos el ruido, decidimos mirar arriba para ver qué lo causaba.
native_language_example: When we heard the noise, we decided to look up to see what caused it.

meaning: look at the
additional_notes: Common collocation of the verb mirar + the definite article el; means to direct your eyes toward something (look at) or to observe/watch something (watch the). The exact translation depends on the noun that follows (e.g., mirar el mar = look at the sea; mirar el partido = watch the match). Not a fixed idiom — it's compositional.
target_language_example: Me gusta mirar el mar al atardecer.
native_language_example: I like to look at the sea at sunset.

meaning: 'to look at the' (feminine singular object).
additional_notes: Mirar = to look/watch. 'La' is the feminine singular direct object pronoun or article ('the' or 'her/it' depending on context). Together 'mirar la' commonly appears before a feminine noun (la pantalla, la cara, la televisión) or when 'la' replaces a previously mentioned feminine noun. Use 'mirar' for both looking at (brief) and watching (ongoing), though 'ver' and 'observar' have different nuances.
target_language_example: No me gusta mirar la televisión todas las noches.
native_language_example: I don't like to watch the television every night.

meaning: to look at (feminine plural things).
additional_notes: Mirar = 'to look at' or 'to watch'. 'Las' is the feminine plural definite article (the). Use 'mirar las' before feminine plural nouns (e.g., estrellas, montañas, nubes, fotos). For masculine plural nouns use 'mirar los'. You can also use 'mirar' with other determiners (mis/estas/unas) or without an article: 'mirar fotos' or 'mirar las fotos' both possible depending on meaning.
target_language_example: Me gusta mirar las estrellas por la noche.
native_language_example: I like to look at the stars at night.

meaning: to check/see what (something is or will be); to look into what
additional_notes: Used to indicate checking or finding out information about something. Often followed by a clause or question word (e.g., 'qué', 'si', 'cómo') or used colloquially to mean 'let me see' or 'I'll check.' Context determines whether it's an instruction ('look and see what...') or a speaker deciding to check now ('I'll check what...').
target_language_example: Voy a mirar qué opciones hay para el viaje.
native_language_example: I'm going to check what options there are for the trip.

meaning: 'they looked at each other' (part of the full expression 'miraron el uno al otro' or 'miraron el uno al otro/a la otra')
additional_notes: This is a fragment of the common reciprocal phrase 'mirarse el uno al otro' or 'mirarse el uno al otro/a la otra' meaning 'to look at each other.' In natural sentences you usually include the full reciprocal 'al otro' (or 'al otro/a la otra' to match gender). The verb must agree with the subject: 'se miraron' or 'miraron el uno al otro.'
target_language_example: Después de la noticia, se miraron el uno al otro en silencio.
native_language_example: After the news, they looked at each other in silence.

meaning: they looked at each other (lit. 'they looked one at the other') — start of the full phrase 'miraron el uno al otro'.
additional_notes: This fragment is incomplete on its own; the full expression is usually 'miraron el uno al otro' (or 'miraron los unos a los otros' / 'se miraron') and means 'they looked at one another' or 'they glanced at each other.' Use 'el uno al otro' for two people and 'los unos a los otros' for more than two. Commonly replaced by the reflexive verb 'se miraron.'
target_language_example: Se miraron el uno al otro y comenzaron a reír.
native_language_example: They looked at each other and started to laugh.

meaning: Look at it / look at that (polite/formal imperative plus object).
additional_notes: Mire is the usted (formal) imperative of mirar. Lo is a masculine direct object pronoun meaning 'it' or 'that'. Used to politely tell someone (formal you) to look at something: 'Mire lo que pasó' = 'Look at what happened.' In casual speech you might also hear 'mira lo' (tú form). Word order can vary: 'mírelo' (attached) is also common in writing/speech.
target_language_example: Mire lo que encontré en la calle.
native_language_example: Look at what I found on the street.

meaning: don't look (at me) like that / don't stare like that
additional_notes: Imperative or subjunctive form of mirar used in a warning or request: often used when someone is looking at the speaker in a disapproving, surprised, or challenging way. Literal: 'you look like that' — typically said as 'no me mires así' (don't look at me like that) or simply 'no mires así'. Tone can be mild (playful) or serious depending on context and intonation.
target_language_example: No me mires así, que me pones nervioso.
native_language_example: Don't look at me like that; you're making me nervous.

meaning: 'look toward' or 'look at (in the direction of)'
additional_notes: Second-person singular subjunctive of mirar + preposition hacia. Commonly used after expressions that require the subjunctive (e.g., Ojalá mires hacia el futuro) or in commands/suggestions with negative (No mires hacia atrás). Can indicate literal direction (look toward the door) or figurative focus (focus on the future).
target_language_example: Si mires hacia la salida, la verás a la derecha.
native_language_example: If you look toward the exit, you'll see it on the right.

meaning: looked at the (feminine noun) / looked toward the
additional_notes: Past tense of mirar (él/ella/usted). 'Miró a la' is followed by a feminine noun or direction (e.g., 'cara', 'izquierda'). It can mean 'looked at the [thing/person]' or 'looked to/toward the [direction]'. If referring to a person, Spanish often uses 'mirar a' + object (me miró a la cara = he/she looked me in the face). For masculine nouns use 'miró al' (a + el).
target_language_example: Ella me miró a la espalda cuando pasé.
native_language_example: She looked at my back when I walked by.

meaning: my own eyes (emphasizes that you saw something yourself).
additional_notes: Used to stress direct personal observation or eyewitness experience. Often appears in phrases like 'lo vi con mis propios ojos' ('I saw it with my own eyes'). 'Propios' agrees in number/gender with the noun: e.g., 'mis propios ojos' (my own eyes), 'mi propia casa' (my own house).
target_language_example: Lo vi con mis propios ojos.
native_language_example: I saw it with my own eyes.

meaning: 'mission of' or 'mission for' — used to describe the purpose or type of a mission/task.
additional_notes: Commonly followed by a noun that specifies the mission's purpose, type, or target (e.g., entrenamiento, reconocimiento, alto riesgo). Can refer to military, scientific, corporate, or organizational tasks. In English it usually translates as 'mission to/for/of' depending on context; choose the preposition that fits the noun (e.g., 'mission of reconnaissance' → 'reconnaissance mission', 'misión de entrenamiento' → 'training mission').
target_language_example: La tripulación salió en una misión de rescate.
native_language_example: The crew went on a rescue mission.

meaning: 'misma' emphasizes that the subject herself did the action to 'le' (to him/her/you formal).
additional_notes: This is actually two parts: 'misma' (feminine singular of 'mismo') adds emphasis — 'herself' or 'myself' — and 'le' is the indirect object pronoun meaning 'to him/to her/to you (formal)'. Together they highlight that the woman (or speaker, if feminine) personally performed the action for that person. Word order can vary: e.g. 'Ella misma le ayudó' or 'Yo misma le di'. Use 'mismo' for masculine subjects (él mismo, yo mismo).
target_language_example: Yo misma le entregué el paquete a mi vecino.
native_language_example: I myself gave him the package.

meaning: the same house/home.
additional_notes: Used to say that two or more people or things share the identical house or home. 'Misma' agrees in gender with 'casa' (feminine); if referring to a masculine noun use 'mismo'. Can be used literally (the same physical house) or more loosely (the same household, family home).
target_language_example: Vivimos en la misma casa desde hace diez años.
native_language_example: We have lived in the same house for ten years.

meaning: the same age as me
additional_notes: Used to compare ages. Can be adjusted for formality or number: 'la misma edad que yo' (with article), 'tiene la misma edad que yo' (he/she is the same age as me). If speaking about someone older/younger use 'más' or 'menos' (más/menos mayor que yo is less common; better: 'es mayor/menor que yo').
target_language_example: Mi hermana tiene la misma edad que yo.
native_language_example: My sister is the same age as me.

meaning: the same room
additional_notes: Used to indicate two or more people or events share a single room or location. 'Misma' agrees in gender with 'habitación' (feminine). Can describe living, sleeping, being present, or events that occur in the same physical room. Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Vivimos en la misma habitación desde hace tres meses.
native_language_example: We've been living in the same room for three months.

meaning: in the same way; similarly.
additional_notes: Common phrase used to compare actions or situations. Often appears as "de la misma manera" or simply "igual" in conversation. Use to show that something is done or happens in the same manner as something else.
target_language_example: Hicimos el experimento de la misma manera que la última vez.
native_language_example: We did the experiment in the same way as last time.

meaning: in the same way as; just like
additional_notes: Used to compare actions or situations. Often appears as 'de la misma manera que' but can be shortened to 'misma manera que' in context. Followed by a clause or noun phrase showing what is being compared.
target_language_example: Ella resolvió el problema de la misma manera que yo.
native_language_example: She solved the problem in the same way as I did.

meaning: the same reason
additional_notes: Used to say that the cause, motive, or explanation is identical to one already mentioned or understood. Often appears with verbs like 'tener', 'ser', or phrases such as 'por la misma razón' (for the same reason). Agreement: 'misma' matches a feminine noun (la razón); you may also see 'mismo motivo' for a masculine variant.
target_language_example: No fui a la fiesta por la misma razón que tú.
native_language_example: I didn't go to the party for the same reason as you.

meaning: the same clothes
additional_notes: Used to say that someone is wearing/repeating identical clothing items as before or as someone else. "Misma" agrees in gender with ropa (feminine). Common in comparisons (que ayer, que llevaba) and negatives (no siempre uso la misma ropa).
target_language_example: Hoy llevo la misma ropa que ayer.
native_language_example: Today I'm wearing the same clothes as yesterday.

meaning: the same in; even in (depends on context)
additional_notes: Two-word sequence where 'mismo' (same / even) combines with the preposition 'en'. Meaning depends on surrounding words: often 'mismo' emphasizes or specifies identity ('the same in ...') or adds contrast/emphasis ('even in ...' or 'right in ...').
