Common in phrases like 'mismo en casa' (the same at home) or 'mismo en invierno' (even in winter). Word order and context determine if 'mismo' refers back to a specific noun (compositional) or adds emphasis.
target_language_example: Ella estudia matemáticas mismo en vacaciones.
native_language_example: She studies math even on vacation.

meaning: An emphatic construction combining 'mismo' (self/same, used for emphasis) with the neutral direct object pronoun 'lo' ('it' / referring to an idea or statement). It emphasizes that the very person mentioned is the one related to the action or statement (e.g., 'he himself said it').
additional_notes: 'mismo' agrees in gender and number when used adjectivally with nouns (mismo/misma/mismos/mismas), but in emphatic constructions before 'lo' it commonly appears as 'mismo lo' (or with a subject pronoun: 'usted mismo lo', 'él mismo lo'). Word order can vary: subject + 'mismo' + 'lo' + verb (e.g., 'usted mismo lo dijo') or subject + verb + 'mismo' + 'lo' in some contexts. 'Lo' often refers to an idea, statement, or unspecified neuter object. Tone ranges from neutral to emphatic; common in both formal and informal speech depending on context.
target_language_example: Usted mismo lo dijo.
native_language_example: You yourself said it.

meaning: a colloquial negation meaning 'not even' or 'no way' (used to emphasize refusal or impossibility)
additional_notes: 'mismo no' is informal and often used for emphasis in speech or casual writing. It usually follows a verb or clause to strongly reject or deny something. Depending on region and context, speakers might say 'ni siquiera' or 'de ninguna manera' instead. Word-for-word, 'mismo' = 'same' and 'no' = 'no', but together they form an emphatic negative.
target_language_example: ¿Vas a ayudarme? — Mismo no, lo hago yo solo.
native_language_example: Are you going to help me? — No way, I'll do it myself.

meaning: the same as; identical to
additional_notes: Used to compare two things or to say one thing is identical to another. Often appears as 'ser lo mismo que' (to be the same as) or with nouns/pronouns: 'el mismo que', 'ella misma que' (the latter less common). Can also emphasize sameness: 'es exactamente lo mismo que...'.
target_language_example: Este libro es el mismo que compré el año pasado.
native_language_example: This book is the same as the one I bought last year.

meaning: 'mismo' = 'same' or 'self'; 'se' = reflexive/impersonal/passive pronoun. Not a fixed idiom but a sequence that occurs when 'mismo' and 'se' appear adjacent in sentences (e.g., 'él mismo se...' = 'he himself ...' or 'lo mismo se...' = 'the same is ...').
additional_notes: This pair is compositional rather than an idiom. Common uses: 1) Emphatic reflexive: subject + mismo + se + verb (Él mismo se cortó = He himself cut himself). 2) Impersonal/passive with lo mismo se + verb (Lo mismo se dijo antes = The same was said before). Word order matters: 'se mismo' is generally incorrect except in some clitic combinations (use 'sí mismo' after prepositions).
target_language_example: Él mismo se encargará del proyecto.
native_language_example: He himself will take care of the project.

meaning: 'the same without' (used to say something/person would not be the same without someone or something).
additional_notes: Combine 'mismo' (same) with 'sin' (without). Common in sentences like 'No sería lo mismo sin ti' = 'It wouldn't be the same without you.' Often appears as part of the phrase 'no (es/era/sería) lo mismo sin...'.
target_language_example: La fiesta no fue lo mismo sin ella.
native_language_example: The party wasn't the same without her.

meaning: This combination is not a standard fixed phrase in Spanish; 'mismo' means 'same' or 'self', and 'y' means 'and'.
additional_notes: You will rarely (if ever) see 'mismo y' as a standalone phrase. 'Mismo' is used in many common expressions (e.g., 'lo mismo' = 'the same', 'el mismo' = 'the same one', 'mismo' as an intensifier: 'mismo ahora' = 'right now' or 'in person' when used as 'el mismo'/'la misma'). 'Y' simply means 'and' and connects words or clauses. If you encounter 'mismo y' in a sentence, read each word literally ('same' + 'and') and check the larger context—it's likely part of a longer structure (e.g., 'el mismo y su hermano...' = 'the same (man) and his brother...').
target_language_example: El mismo y su amigo vinieron a la reunión.
native_language_example: The same man and his friend came to the meeting.

meaning: 'mismo estoy' is not a grammatical or standard multi-word phrase in Spanish; it appears to be a mistaken word order or an incorrect combination. Native speakers would rarely (if ever) use these two words together in this order. Possible intended expressions include 'yo mismo', 'estoy seguro', or 'es lo mismo'.
additional_notes: Do not use 'mismo estoy' as a fixed phrase. If you want to emphasize the subject, use 'yo mismo' (Yo mismo lo haré). To say 'it's the same', use 'es lo mismo' or 'lo mismo'. If you intended to place 'mismo' after a verb in some regional colloquial speech, this is uncommon and not standard. The two words can appear near each other in a sentence in rare constructions (e.g., 'mismo, estoy…' with a pause), but that is punctuation-dependent, not a set phrase.
target_language_example: No existe una construcción estándar 'mismo estoy', por ejemplo: *mismo estoy* no se usa en español normativo.
native_language_example: There is no standard construction 'mismo estoy', for example: *mismo estoy* is not used in normative Spanish.

meaning: the same neighborhood
additional_notes: Used to say two or more people or events are/were located in the same neighborhood. 'Mismo' agrees in sense (not in gender here because barrio is masculine); you can change to 'mismo/a/os/as' to match nouns. Common in everyday speech to talk about where people live or grew up.
target_language_example: Vivimos en el mismo barrio cuando éramos niños.
native_language_example: We lived in the same neighborhood when we were children.

meaning: the same place / the same location
additional_notes: Used to indicate that two or more things or people share the same physical location or source. Can be used alone as a short reply (e.g., "Mismo lugar.") to confirm meeting at the same place. "Mismo" agrees in meaning with "same" and does not change for gender/number when used before "lugar" (singular).
target_language_example: Quedamos en el mismo lugar de siempre.
native_language_example: We'll meet at the same place as always.

meaning: in the same way; similarly.
additional_notes: Used to compare actions or situations, equivalent to 'de la misma manera' or 'igualmente'. Can appear as 'del mismo modo' (more common) or simply 'mismo modo' in context. Often followed by a clause or sentence showing the similar action or result.
target_language_example: Ella resolvió el problema y yo actué de mismo modo.
native_language_example: She solved the problem and I acted in the same way.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase; likely a mistaken split of 'mismo' + preposition 'a' or part of a larger construction. It does not form a common, grammatically correct multiword expression by itself.
additional_notes: If you encounter 'mismo a' it is usually a typo, a word break across lines, or part of phrases like 'a mí mismo' (to myself) or 'el mismo a quien' (the same one to whom) where 'mismo' and 'a' belong to different constituents. Prefer correct constructions such as 'a mí mismo', 'lo mismo a', or rephrase (e.g., 'incluso a mí', 'igual a').
target_language_example: No debería haber escrito 'mismo a' separado; debía poner 'a mí mismo' para indicar énfasis.
native_language_example: He shouldn't have written 'mismo a' separated; he should have written 'a mí mismo' to indicate emphasis.

meaning: 'even when' or 'even if' (used to emphasize that something is true despite a condition).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that a statement holds true despite a particular situation or condition. Often placed before or after the subordinate clause: e.g. "mismo cuando + [clause]" or "[clause], mismo cuando...". It is slightly formal/neutral and common in written and spoken Spanish. Can be interchangeable with "incluso cuando" or "aunque" in some contexts.
target_language_example: Trabajo duro, mismo cuando estoy cansado.
native_language_example: I work hard, even when I'm tired.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase in Spanish; likely a mistaken or incomplete combination. 'Mismo' means 'same' and 'de' means 'of/from'.
additional_notes: Native speakers don't usually use 'mismo de' as a set expression. You will see 'mismo' used alone (el mismo, la misma) to mean 'the same' and 'de' as a preposition meaning 'of/from'. Possible intended phrases: 'lo mismo que' (the same as), 'mismo + noun' (the same [noun]), or 'el mismo de siempre' (the same as always). If you saw 'mismo de' in context, check the surrounding words—it may be a typo, regionalism, or part of a larger construction.
target_language_example: Quiero el mismo que tú compraste, no 'mismo de' por sí solo.
native_language_example: I want the same one you bought, not 'mismo de' by itself.

meaning: Not a standard or correct Spanish phrase; likely a mistaken or nonstandard attempt to say 'the same as you' (correct: 'igual que tú' or 'lo mismo que tú').
additional_notes: You will rarely—if ever—see 'mismo de ti' in correct Spanish. Native speakers use 'igual que tú', 'lo mismo que tú', or 'como tú' to express 'the same as you'. 'Mismo' appears correctly in forms such as 'lo mismo' (the same thing) or 'el mismo' (the same (one)), but it is not combined with 'de' + pronoun in standard Spanish. If you encounter 'mismo de ti' in informal writing, treat it as an error or nonstandard regional usage; the intended meaning is probably 'igual que tú' or 'lo mismo que tú'.
target_language_example: No es lo mismo de ti; creo que quisiste decir 'lo mismo que tú'.
native_language_example: It's not 'mismo de ti'; I think you meant 'lo mismo que tú'.

meaning: I mean the same (I agree or feel the same way).
additional_notes: Informal phrase used to say you feel or think the same as someone just said. Often follows another person's statement: '—…' 'Mismo digo.' Can be used alone as a short agreement (like 'same here' or 'I say the same'). Tone and exact meaning depend on context; it's more common in some Latin American Spanish varieties.
target_language_example: Si te cansas, puedes descansar; mismo digo.
native_language_example: If you get tired, you can rest; same here.

meaning: Literal word order 'mismo es' would read 'same is' — uncommon in modern Spanish; conceptually related to 'it is the same' or to emphasize identity when word order is inverted (often literary or emphatic).
additional_notes: The two-word sequence 'mismo es' is not the normal everyday ordering; speakers normally say 'es lo mismo' to mean 'it's the same.' 'Mismo' usually follows determiners or follows the noun it modifies (el mismo, la misma). 'Mismo es' can appear in inverted or poetic constructions (e.g., for emphasis or in relative clauses) but is rare in colloquial speech. Remember agreement of 'mismo' by gender/number when used adjectivally (mismo/misma/mismos/mismas).
target_language_example: Si lo que quieres es eso mismo es lo que tengo.
native_language_example: If what you want is that same thing, that's what I have.

meaning: the same for / same as for (used to say something applies equally to someone/something else)
additional_notes: Used to compare conditions, rules, feelings, etc., indicating that what was said about one person/thing is equally true for another. Often follows the thing being compared (e.g., "Es lo mismo para..." or appears in phrases like "lo mismo para ti"). Can be replaced by "igual para" in many contexts. Tone is neutral and appropriate in formal and informal speech.
target_language_example: Es lo mismo para todos, nadie queda fuera.
native_language_example: It's the same for everyone, no one is left out.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase by itself; two separate words (mismo = same/very/self, por = for/by/because of) that can appear adjacent in some constructions but usually belong to larger expressions.
additional_notes: Alone, 'mismo por' is uncommon as a standalone set phrase. It can occur when word order places 'mismo' before 'por' (e.g., in emphatic structures or clipped clauses), but learners should recognize that meaning depends on the larger context. More common related expressions: 'por el mismo motivo' (for the same reason), 'por lo mismo' (for that very reason), 'lo mismo por' can appear in comparative or parallel lists ('lo mismo por A que por B').
target_language_example: Lo mismo por trabajo que por salud, tuvo que mudarse.
native_language_example: For reasons equally related to work as to health, he had to move.

meaning: by myself / on my own; (do it) for me personally
additional_notes: This phrase is not a fixed idiom but a combination: 'mismo' (same/same one/self) used emphatically + 'por mí' (for me). It can mean that someone does something themselves (by their own choice or effort) or that something is done 'for me' personally. Context decides emphasis: e.g. 'Lo hago yo mismo por mí' = 'I'll do it myself for my own sake.' It is informal/neutral and compositional.
target_language_example: Si quieres, lo hago yo mismo por mí.
native_language_example: If you want, I'll do it myself for me.

meaning: the same as you
additional_notes: Used to compare equality of things, actions, amounts, or opinions with the person addressed. Often appears with 'lo' (lo mismo que tú) when referring to a thing/idea previously mentioned. Can be used in statements, questions, or short replies (e.g., 'Lo mismo que tú' = 'Same as you').
target_language_example: Yo quiero lo mismo que tú.
native_language_example: I want the same as you.

meaning: 'you yourself' or 'yourself' used to emphasize the person involved (often in colloquial speech); literally 'same you' but functions as an emphatic clitic + 'mismo' after a pronoun or object pronoun
additional_notes: 'Mismo te' is not a standalone fixed phrase but occurs when 'mismo' attaches after a pronoun or clitic for emphasis (e.g., 'mismo tú', 'a ti mismo', 'mismo te lo dije' in some dialects). Placement and acceptability vary by region and formality; more standard forms are 'tú mismo' or 'a ti mismo'. 'Mismo te' often appears in colloquial spoken Spanish for emphasis: 'mismo te equivocas' = 'you yourself are wrong' (or 'you're wrong, even').
target_language_example: Mismo te lo dije y no me escuchaste.
native_language_example: I told you myself and you didn't listen to me.

meaning: the same eyes (same eye color/shape/features).
additional_notes: Commonly used to say two people share identical or very similar eyes (color, shape, expression). Often appears in descriptions of family resemblance. 'Mismos' agrees in gender/number with the noun (mismos ojos = masculine plural).
target_language_example: Tu hija tiene los mismos ojos que tú.
native_language_example: Your daughter has the same eyes as you.

meaning: half of the (feminine plural noun).
additional_notes: Used before feminine plural nouns to indicate 50% of a group or amount. If the noun is masculine plural use "mitad de los"; for singular use "la mitad de". Often followed by a noun (e.g., ganancias, bananas, veces).
target_language_example: Recibí la mitad de las ganancias.
native_language_example: I received half of the profits.

meaning: half of the (something); used to refer to half of an idea, amount, or situation (often followed by a noun phrase or clause).
additional_notes: Literally 'half of the...'. Commonly appears as 'la mitad de lo que...' (half of what...), 'la mitad de los/las...' (half of the...), or without article in casual phrases. If followed by 'que' it introduces a clause (la mitad de lo que dijo = half of what he/she said).
target_language_example: La mitad de lo que prometieron no se cumplió.
native_language_example: Half of what they promised wasn't fulfilled.

meaning: half of what (something is or that someone does).
additional_notes: Used to compare amounts, actions, knowledge, or statements to indicate 'half as much' or 'only half of what...'. Often appears with quantifiers (sólo, menos, más) or verbs. Common in comparisons and cautions (e.g., 'only half of what you hear/see').
target_language_example: Ella sabe sólo la mitad de lo que cuenta.
native_language_example: She knows only half of what she tells.

meaning: 'the way' or 'how' (the manner in which).
additional_notes: Used to describe the manner or style of an action or situation. Usually appears as 'el modo en que' or 'el modo en el que' + clause, or shortened in speech as 'el modo en que le hablas' = 'the way you talk to him/her'. Can be followed by 'que' or a relative clause.
target_language_example: No me gusta el modo en que me miras.
native_language_example: I don't like the way you look at me.

meaning: so that / in such a way that (introduces purpose or result).
additional_notes: Used to link clauses. Can express purpose (equivalent to "para que" + subjunctive) or result/consequence (followed by indicative). Context and verb mood determine meaning: use subjunctive when indicating intended purpose or hypothetical outcome; use indicative when stating an actual result. In informal speech it can be shortened to "así que" for result.
target_language_example: Organiza todo con tiempo, modo que podamos salir sin prisas.
native_language_example: Organize everything in advance so that we can leave without rushing.

meaning: literally 'ways no' — not a standard fixed phrase; likely a fragment meaning 'modes/ways (that) are not' or part of a larger expression where 'no' negates 'modos'.
additional_notes: Not a common standalone phrase in Spanish. Typically appears as two separate words in a sentence (e.g., 'modos no permitidos', 'modos no compatibles') or as part of a clause where 'no' negates a verb related to 'modos' (e.g., 'modos no funcionan'). Check surrounding words to determine whether 'no' negates 'modos' directly or belongs to a nearby verb. 'Modos' = 'manners, ways, modes'.
target_language_example: Hay modos no aceptables en esta reunión; por favor, compórtense.
native_language_example: There are modes/ways that are not acceptable in this meeting; please behave.

meaning: it bothers (someone) that / it's annoying that
additional_notes: Used to express annoyance or discomfort about a situation. Commonly appears with an indirect object (me, te, le, nos, os, les) + que + subjunctive when referring to actions or states (e.g., Me molesta que llegues tarde). Can also be used impersonally as 'molesta' with a noun or infinitive (e.g., Me molesta el ruido / Me molesta esperar).
target_language_example: Me molesta que no me avisaras antes.
native_language_example: It bothers me that you didn't warn me earlier.

meaning: a discomfort, annoyance, or problem related to (used to indicate a bother or inconvenience caused by something). Often describes physical discomfort or an annoyance originating from a specific cause.
additional_notes: 'Molestia de' is less common than constructions like 'molestia en' or 'tener molestias en', but appears in phrases specifying the source (e.g., 'molestia de estómago') or when describing a cause ('molestia de tanto escribir'). Choose preposition according to context: 'de' for origin/causa, 'en' for location. 'Molestia' can be singular or plural ('molestias').
target_language_example: Sufro de molestia de estómago después de comer mariscos.
native_language_example: I suffer from a stomach discomfort after eating shellfish.

meaning: 'one moment, please' / 'please wait a moment'.
additional_notes: Polite request asking someone to wait briefly. Common in phone conversations or when you need a short pause. You can also say just 'un momento, por favor' or the shorter 'un momento' in informal contexts.
target_language_example: Un momento, por favor. Ahora vuelvo con la información.
native_language_example: One moment, please. I'll be back with the information.

meaning: for a moment; give me a moment (to) — a request or reference to a short amount of time
additional_notes: The sequence 'momento a' by itself is uncommon and may appear as part of larger constructions (e.g., 'un momento a...' or 'un momento a ver...'). More typical expressions are 'un momento', 'un momento, por favor', or 'espera un momento'. 'Momento a' can be used informally in spoken language when followed by a verb or phrase ('momento a ver', 'momento a hablar'), but standalone 'momento a' can sound clipped or unfinished.
target_language_example: Momento a ver lo que pasa.
native_language_example: Give me a moment to see what’s happening.

meaning: not a standard fixed phrase in Spanish; likely a mistaken or incomplete phrase. Separately, 'momento' = 'moment' or 'moment/second', and 'como' = 'like', 'as', or 'how'.
additional_notes: These two words do not form a common idiomatic expression together. If you see 'momento como' it is probably a typo, missing punctuation, or part of a longer clause (e.g., 'en un momento, como...' = 'in a moment, like...' or 'un momento como ese' = 'a moment like that'). Learn the words separately: 'momento' (noun) and 'como' (conjunction/adverb/preposition).
target_language_example: En un momento como ese, no supe qué decir.
native_language_example: In a moment like that, I didn't know what to say.

meaning: a moment like this / a time like this
additional_notes: Used to refer to the current moment or a situation similar to the one being experienced. Can appear with articles or demonstratives (por un momento como este, en un momento como este) and often expresses significance, difficulty, or opportunity.
target_language_example: Nunca había vivido un momento como este.
native_language_example: I had never experienced a moment like this.

meaning: for a moment with / a moment of (time) spent with someone or something
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom on its own; usually appears as part of phrases like 'un momento con...' or 'darle un momento con...' meaning to spend a short time with someone/something or to pause briefly to do something. Context determines exact translation: can mean 'wait a moment' (un momento) + 'con' linking to a person/object (e.g., 'un momento con mamá' = a moment with mom).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes darme un momento con él para hablar en privado?
native_language_example: Can you give me a moment with him to speak privately?

meaning: 'the moment of the' or 'a moment of the' (used before a feminine noun).
additional_notes: A common phrase used to introduce a point in time or an occasion related to a feminine noun (e.g., 'momento de la verdad' = 'moment of truth'). It must be followed by a feminine noun or noun phrase. Can be used literally (a specific moment) or figuratively (an important occasion).
target_language_example: Es el momento de la decisión final.
native_language_example: It is the moment of the final decision.

meaning: 'the moment when' or 'the moment that' (the exact time something happened).
additional_notes: Used to introduce the specific instant when something occurred. Often appears as 'en el momento en que' or 'desde el momento en que' and is followed by a clause (verb). Common in past and present narratives. Not informal.
target_language_example: Lo entendí en el momento en que lo explicaste.
native_language_example: I understood it the moment you explained it.

meaning: the moment when (her); at the moment that she...
additional_notes: Used to introduce the exact time something happened concerning a female person (la = her). Often appears as part of phrases like "desde el momento en que la conocí" (from the moment I met her). Can be adapted for other subjects: "el momento en que lo vi" (the moment when I saw him).
target_language_example: La reconocí en el momento en que la vi.
native_language_example: I recognized her the moment I saw her.

meaning: 'the moment when you' or 'the time when you...'
additional_notes: This phrase introduces a specific moment or point in time relating to the person 'you' (te). It is usually followed by a verb or clause describing what happens at that moment: e.g., 'momento en que te das cuenta' (the moment when you realize). Common in storytelling and descriptions of events.
target_language_example: Recuerdo el momento en que te vi por primera vez.
native_language_example: I remember the moment when I saw you for the first time.

meaning: 'the moment is' or 'it is the moment (that)...'
additional_notes: A short phrase combining momento (moment) and the verb ser (es). By itself it is incomplete and uncommon as a fixed phrase in Spanish; you will more often see "el momento es" (the moment is...) or expressions like "el momento es ahora" (the moment is now) or "el momento es cuando...". Use with a subject/article (el) or followed by more information.
target_language_example: El momento es ahora; debemos actuar.
native_language_example: The moment is now; we must act.

meaning: literally 'moment I/he/she/it was' — a sequence of words that can appear when describing what someone or something was doing at a particular moment (not a fixed idiom).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but two common words used together: 'momento' (moment) and the imperfect form 'estaba' (was/was being). You'll see constructions like 'En ese momento estaba...' or 'Un momento, estaba...' followed by an action or state. Use 'estaba' for ongoing or repeated past actions (imperfect). To say 'at that moment, he/she/was' more naturally say 'en ese momento estaba...'.
target_language_example: En ese momento estaba estudiando para el examen.
native_language_example: At that moment I/he/she was studying for the exam.

meaning: 'just a moment' / 'wait a moment' (used when the speaker asks for a brief pause, often before explaining something about themselves)
additional_notes: Not a standard fixed phrase; likely a clipped sequence where 'momento' is followed by a clause starting with 'me' (e.g., 'Momento, me están llamando' or 'Momento, me acuerdo'). In everyday use, speakers typically say 'un momento' or 'espera un momento'. Use 'momento me' only if quoting colloquial speech or transcribing rapid dialogue.
target_language_example: Momento, me están llamando — ¿puedes esperarme un segundo?
native_language_example: Wait a moment, they're calling me — can you hold on for a second?

meaning: the happiest moment of (someone's life, childhood, etc.)
additional_notes: Used to say which point in time was the happiest for someone or something. Usually followed by a noun or possessive phrase (mi vida, mi infancia). Common in past or present: 'fue el momento más feliz de mi vida' or 'este es el momento más feliz de mi vida.'
target_language_example: Ese fue el momento más feliz de mi vida.
native_language_example: That was the happiest moment of my life.

meaning: not a moment / not now; used to refuse or postpone immediately doing something
additional_notes: This phrase is uncommon as a fixed expression; speakers more often say 'ahora no', 'no ahora' or 'en este momento no'. 'Momento' alone can mean 'moment' and is used in requests like 'un momento' (one moment). 'Momento no' would be understood as rejecting or postponing at this moment — casual and slightly abrupt. Use more natural alternatives for politeness.
target_language_example: Lo siento, momento no, estoy ocupado ahora.
native_language_example: Sorry, not right now, I'm busy.

meaning: as soon as / the moment that
additional_notes: Used to introduce the moment when something happens. Often followed by a verb in the indicative or subjunctive depending on nuance (indicative for factual past/future, subjunctive for anticipated or hypothetical actions). It is similar to 'en cuanto' or 'tan pronto como'.
target_language_example: En el momento que llegues, llámame.
native_language_example: As soon as you arrive, call me.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase in Spanish; appears as two separate words where 'momento' means 'moment' and 'se' is a pronoun that attaches to a verb. As written, it's likely a clipped fragment from a longer sentence (e.g., 'Un momento, se lo digo').
additional_notes: This exact two-word sequence 'momento se' does not form a common idiom. You'll most often see 'momento' and 'se' in different positions within a sentence (for example: 'Un momento, se lo doy' or 'En ese momento se fue'). If you encounter 'momento se' it usually means the sentence has been split or punctuation/word order differs (e.g., 'Momento: se...'). Learn 'momento' (a short time; 'un momento' = 'one moment') and the uses of 'se' (reflexive, impersonal, passive, reciprocal, or part of pronominal verbs).
target_language_example: En ese momento se detuvo.
native_language_example: At that moment he/she/it stopped.

meaning: 'moment and' — literal phrase combining momento (moment) with y (and); not a fixed idiom by itself.
additional_notes: This is simply the word momento ('moment') followed by the conjunction y ('and'). It can appear when listing actions or ideas (e.g., 'un momento y luego...' = 'one moment and then...') but by itself it doesn't form a special expression. Be careful: similar short phrases include 'un momento' (wait a moment) or 'en un momento' (in a moment).
target_language_example: Espérame un momento y hablamos después.
native_language_example: Wait for me a moment and we'll talk later.

meaning: 'coin in' — used to say a coin is located in or on something (e.g., in my pocket, on the sidewalk).
additional_notes: This is the noun moneda ('coin') followed by a preposition (en = in/on/at). Use 'moneda en' when describing where a coin is found or placed: 'una moneda en mi bolsillo' (a coin in my pocket), 'una moneda en la acera' (a coin on the sidewalk). Preposition can change meaning: 'en' = in/inside or on/surface depending on context. For 'on top of' you can also use 'sobre'.
target_language_example: Encontré una moneda en el sofá.
native_language_example: I found a coin in the sofa.

meaning: 'mountain of' — used to describe a large amount or a literal mountain made of something.
additional_notes: Literally means 'mountain of'. Often used figuratively in Spanish to emphasize a large quantity (e.g., 'una montaña de ropa' = a mountain of clothes). It must agree with the noun that follows and is followed by 'de' + noun. For a literal mountain, Spanish usually uses 'la montaña' alone (e.g., 'la montaña de la derecha'), but 'montaña de' works when specifying what the mountain is made of or when using a metaphor.
target_language_example: Tiene una montaña de libros en su escritorio.
native_language_example: He has a mountain of books on his desk.

meaning: literally 'mountain in' — not a fixed standalone Spanish phrase; typically appears as part of a larger construction (e.g., 'la montaña en la que...' = 'the mountain in which...').
additional_notes: Alone, 'montaña en' is incomplete and uncommon. You'll usually see 'montaña' with a preposition/article ordering like 'en la montaña' (in/on the mountain) or as part of a relative phrase where 'en' begins the subordinate clause: 'la montaña en la que vivimos' (the mountain in which we live). For clarity, beginners should prefer 'en la montaña' when meaning 'in/on the mountain.'
target_language_example: La montaña en la que escalamos tenía sendas peligrosas.
native_language_example: The mountain in which we climbed had dangerous paths.

meaning: literally 'mountain is' — the phrase is just the noun montaña ('mountain') plus the verb es ('is').
additional_notes: This is not a fixed multiword expression; it's simply the structure 'montaña es' used when describing a mountain (quality, location, etc.). For beginners: montaña = mountain (feminine). Es is the 3rd person singular of ser used for descriptions, identity, origin, or inherent characteristics. Use 'la montaña es...' when speaking generally (la is the definite article: la montaña es...).
target_language_example: La montaña es alta y nevada.
native_language_example: The mountain is tall and snowy.

meaning: literally 'mountain is' — the verb phrase 'está' (is) used with montaña to describe the mountain's current state or condition.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase; it's just the noun montaña (mountain) plus the verb estar (to be) in the third person singular. Use está to describe temporary states, locations, or conditions of the mountain (e.g., hidden, high, covered in snow). For permanent characteristics you might use es instead of está (La montaña es alta).
target_language_example: La montaña está cubierta de nieve hoy.
native_language_example: The mountain is covered in snow today.

meaning: the mountain is covered
additional_notes: A simple descriptive phrase: 'montaña' (mountain) + 'está cubierta' (is covered). 'Cubierta' is the past participle of 'cubrir' used as an adjective after the verb 'estar' to describe a temporary state (e.g., covered with snow, clouds, vegetation, etc.). To specify what covers the mountain, add 'de' + noun (e.g., 'está cubierta de nieve').
target_language_example: La montaña está cubierta de nieve después de la tormenta.
native_language_example: The mountain is covered with snow after the storm.

meaning: the mountain is covered with/of (something).
additional_notes: Use to describe that a mountain has a covering (snow, trees, clouds, etc.). 'Cubierta de' follows the thing covering it; can be used with definite articles when needed (La montaña está cubierta de nieve / La montaña está cubierta de nubes). For other subjects replace 'montaña' with the noun and adjust agreement (La playa está cubierta de algas).
target_language_example: La montaña está cubierta de nubes esta mañana.
native_language_example: The mountain is covered with clouds this morning.

meaning: 'the most mountainous' or 'more mountain' depending on context; comparative or superlative phrase using montaña (mountain).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself. It combines montaña (mountain) with más (more/most). Depending on word order and context, it can form comparisons: "más montaña" (more mountain-like) is uncommon; "la montaña más alta" means "the tallest mountain" (superlative). Beginners will most often encounter "más" after an article and before an adjective (e.g., "la montaña más alta").
target_language_example: La montaña más alta de la región tiene 3.500 metros.
native_language_example: The tallest mountain in the region is 3,500 meters.

meaning: a lot of things that / lots of things to (do) — indicates many items or tasks related to something.
additional_notes: Common, informal phrase used to say there are many items, tasks, or matters. Often followed by a verb or clause (e.g., 'que hacer', 'que podemos encontrar'). 'Montón' emphasizes quantity; you can also say 'muchas cosas que'.
target_language_example: Tengo un montón de cosas que preparar antes del viaje.
native_language_example: I have a lot of things to prepare before the trip.

meaning: bit the (feminine singular body part).
additional_notes: From the verb morder (to bite) in past tense (él/ella mordió) plus the feminine singular definite article la. Used when specifying that someone/something bit a feminine-noun body part (la mano, la pierna, etc.). Word order in Spanish often places the indirect object pronoun or explicit person before the verb (e.g., 'me mordió la mano' = 'he/she/it bit my hand').
target_language_example: El perro me mordió la mano.
native_language_example: The dog bit my hand.

meaning: to die of
additional_notes: Used to indicate cause of death or (informally) a strong physical or emotional reaction (e.g., morir de risa = to laugh very hard). Followed by a noun or a verb in the infinitive depending on meaning: morir de cáncer / morir de hambre / morir de miedo / morir de risa / morir de frío. Not used with the preposition 'por' to express cause.
target_language_example: Mi abuelo solía decir que tenía miedo de morir de manera inesperada.
native_language_example: My grandfather used to say he was afraid of dying unexpectedly.

meaning: 'to die of hunger' — used literally or figuratively to mean 'starve' or 'be extremely hungry'.
additional_notes: Can be used literally (to starve to death) or figuratively to express extreme hunger or worry about not having enough to eat/money. Common in phrases like 'a punto de morir de hambre' (about to starve) or in rhetorical questions expressing concern ('¿me voy a morir de hambre?').
target_language_example: Si no encontramos comida pronto, vamos a morir de hambre.
native_language_example: If we don't find food soon, we're going to starve (to death).

meaning: colloquial expression meaning to be dying (eager) for something to happen or to do something; expresses strong desire or impatience.
additional_notes: Informal and less standard than related forms like 'morir por' (morir por + infinitive) or 'morir de ganas (de)'. 'Morir que' often appears in colloquial speech before a clause introduced by que (e.g., 'morir que + subjunctive/indicative') to emphasize eagerness or impatience. Use mainly in casual contexts; some speakers may prefer 'me muero porque/por' or 'me muero de ganas de'.
target_language_example: Me muero que empiece la película.
native_language_example: I'm dying for the movie to start.

meaning: 'a fly in' (literally), used to say there is a fly in/on something (e.g., in your coffee).
additional_notes: This is a literal, common phrase used to report a fly being inside or on food/drink or in a place (e.g., 'una mosca en el café', 'una mosca en la sopa'). Not an idiom here (although 'estar como mosca en leche' in one example is an idiomatic/smaller phrase meaning 'to be out of place' or 'uncomfortable'). Use 'hay una mosca en...' to say 'there is a fly in...'.
target_language_example: Cuidado: hay una mosca en la ensalada.
native_language_example: Careful: there's a fly in the salad.

meaning: literally 'fly in the...' — starts a phrase referring to a fly (the insect) being inside or on something; incomplete fragment, not a standalone expression.
additional_notes: This is not a complete fixed phrase by itself. 'Mosca' means 'fly' (the insect) and 'en el' means 'in the' (masculine singular). You will normally see it completed with a noun: e.g. 'mosca en la sopa' (a fly in the soup) or 'mosca en el cuarto' (a fly in the room). Depending on context, 'mosca' can also be used colloquially: '¡Estate mosca!' (be alert/watch out).
target_language_example: Hay una mosca en el vaso.
native_language_example: There is a fly in the glass.

meaning: I will show the (masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Future tense of mostrar (mostraré = I will show) followed by the definite article el before a masculine singular noun. Used to promise or offer to show someone something. For feminine nouns use mostraré la; for plural use mostraré los/las or te/les mostraré + noun without article in some contexts.
target_language_example: Te mostraré el museo cuando vengas.
native_language_example: I will show you the museum when you come.

meaning: showed the (feminine singular object) — past tense of 'mostrar'.
additional_notes: Use when someone showed a specific feminine noun (la escuela, la foto, la zona, la carta). 'Mostró' is the third person singular preterite (he/she/you formal showed). If the object is masculine use 'mostró el' (or 'mostró los/las' for plural). Spanish word order can also place the indirect object after with 'a + person' (e.g., 'mostró la foto a todos').
target_language_example: Ella me mostró la foto ayer.
native_language_example: She showed me the photo yesterday.

meaning: showed a (feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Compound of the verb mostró (showed; past of mostrar) plus the indefinite article una. Use before a feminine singular noun: e.g. mostró una sonrisa (she/he showed a smile). Context determines subject (él/ella/usted). Common in past narration.
target_language_example: Ella mostró una foto de su viaje.
native_language_example: She showed a photo of her trip.

meaning: for the reason of; because of; due to
additional_notes: Usually appears as part of larger phrases (e.g., 'motivo por el que', 'motivo por...'). Often followed by a clause or noun explaining the cause. Can be singular 'motivo por' or plural 'motivos por' depending on context; standalone 'motivo por' without continuation is uncommon.
target_language_example: El motivo por el que no vino fue la lluvia.
native_language_example: The reason why he didn't come was the rain.

meaning: 'for reasons of' or 'because of' (followed by a noun).
additional_notes: Used to explain the reason for an action or situation. Commonly followed by nouns like seguridad, salud, decisión. Formal/neutral register and often used in written or official contexts (por motivos de seguridad, por motivos de salud).
target_language_example: Cancelaron el concierto por motivos de seguridad.
native_language_example: They cancelled the concert for reasons of safety.

meaning: to move the (feminine) [something]; to cause a feminine noun to change position or location.
additional_notes: Mover is a regular -er verb meaning 'to move'. 'La' is the feminine direct object pronoun or the feminine definite article depending on context. In these examples 'mover la' is followed by a feminine noun (la cama, la pierna, la oficina, la escalera, la caja). When using a direct object pronoun instead of repeating the noun, 'la' can replace a previously mentioned feminine noun: e.g., 'Voy a moverla' (I'll move it). Conjugate mover to match the subject: 'muevo, mueves, mueve, movemos, movéis, mueven'.
target_language_example: Voy a mover la mesa para limpiar.
native_language_example: I'm going to move the table to clean.

meaning: 'good luck' or 'very lucky' (depending on context).
additional_notes: Used both as a noun phrase meaning 'a lot of luck' (Tengo mucha suerte = I'm very lucky) and as a short wish 'Mucha suerte' = 'Good luck!'. Common in everyday speech. 'Mucha' modifies 'suerte' (feminine).
target_language_example: Mucha suerte en tu entrevista mañana.
native_language_example: Good luck with your interview tomorrow.

meaning: A phrase combining 'muchacha' (girl) and 'muy' (very); by itself it's incomplete—would be used as 'muy muchacha' is uncommon; likely intended as 'muchacha muy + adjective' (very [adjective] girl) or 'muy muchacha' (very girl-y).
additional_notes: This ordering ('muchacha muy') is not a natural standalone phrase in Spanish. Native speakers place 'muy' before an adjective (e.g., 'muchacha muy simpática' = 'a very nice girl'). If the intended meaning is to say someone is very much like a typical girl, you'd say 'muy muchacha' or better 'muy niña' only in specific contexts. For beginners: use 'muchacha' to mean 'girl' and 'muy' before adjectives to mean 'very'.
target_language_example: Es una muchacha muy simpática.
native_language_example: She is a very nice girl.

meaning: 'boy from' or 'boy of' (literal); used to indicate origin, possession, or association (e.g., 'the boy from ___' or 'the boy of ___').
additional_notes: This is the phrase 'muchacho' (boy) followed by the preposition 'de' (of/from). Alone it is incomplete and needs a noun, place, or phrase after 'de' to specify origin, possession, or relationship: e.g. 'muchacho de la ciudad' (boy from the city), 'muchacho de mi amigo' (my friend's son / the boy of my friend). Word order and meaning depend on what follows. 'Muchacho' is a common neutral word for 'boy' in many Spanish varieties.
target_language_example: Es el muchacho de la tienda.
native_language_example: He is the boy from the shop.

meaning: 'the boy is' (third-person statement about a boy).
additional_notes: Combines the noun muchacho (boy; young male) with the verb es (he/it is). Use to describe or identify a specific boy. Muchacho = boy/lad; can be interchangeable with chico or chaval in some regions. Es is the present tense of ser for él/ella/usted. Grammar: muchacho is the subject + es as the verb.
target_language_example: El muchacho es simpático y estudia en mi clase.
native_language_example: The boy is friendly and studies in my class.

meaning: An emphatic admonition addressed to a young man or boy; used to stop, correct, or warn someone. Depending on tone and context it can mean “no, boy,” “hey, don’t,” or “stop right there.”
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom — meaning is compositional from muchacho (boy/guy) + no (no/not). Highly dependent on intonation and context; informal and often used by elders, parents, or authority figures. Can express prohibition, surprise, disbelief, or reprimand. In many regions speakers might instead say simply “¡No!” or “¡Muchacho!” with a different intonation.
target_language_example: —¡Muchacho no! ¿Qué crees que haces?
native_language_example: —No, boy! What do you think you're doing?

meaning: This sequence by itself is not a fixed phrase; it looks like the noun 'muchacho' (boy) plus the reflexive/indirect object pronoun 'se'.
additional_notes: Alone, 'muchacho se' is incomplete and uncommon; you will usually see 'muchacho' used by itself (el muchacho = the boy) or with verbs/pronouns, e.g. 'el muchacho se levantó' (the boy got up) or 'se lo dijo al muchacho' (he told it to the boy). 'Se' can be reflexive, passive, impersonal, or replace le/les (as in 'se lo di'). Pay attention to the full sentence to understand the function of 'se'.
target_language_example: El muchacho se levantó temprano.
native_language_example: The boy got up early.

meaning: thank you very much
additional_notes: A common, polite way to express strong thanks in Spanish. Used in formal and informal situations; you can add a name or title after it (e.g., "Muchas gracias, señor"). Can be shortened to "gracias" for a less emphatic thank you.
target_language_example: Muchas gracias por tu ayuda.
native_language_example: Thank you very much for your help.

meaning: 'many times' or 'often'.
additional_notes: Used to say that something happens repeatedly or frequently. Can translate as 'many times', 'often', or 'a lot of times' depending on context. Placed before or after the verb (commonly after the verb or at the start of a sentence).
target_language_example: He visitado ese pueblo muchas veces.
native_language_example: I have visited that town many times.

meaning: 'much' or 'a lot' + preposition 'to the' (not a correct fixed phrase in Spanish).
additional_notes: This combination is not a standard or grammatically correct fixed phrase in Spanish. It looks like 'mucho' (a lot/much) followed by the contraction 'al' (a + el = to the / at the). In natural Spanish you would normally place 'mucho' before a verb or noun (e.g., 'mucho trabajo', 'trabajo mucho') or use 'mucho de' for 'much of'. If you need 'a lot to the' in English, Spanish usually expresses it differently (e.g., 'mucho que', 'mucho para', or 'mucho en' depending on context).
target_language_example: No se dice 'mucho al' — di 'mucho trabajo' o 'mucho para mí' según el contexto.
native_language_example: You don't say 'mucho al' — say 'mucho trabajo' or 'mucho para mí' depending on context.

meaning: long before; well before (a time or event).
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something happened or will happen a long time before another event. Can modify past events (e.g., 'mucho antes de...') or future expectations (e.g., 'No pasará mucho antes de...': it won't be long before...). Common in both written and spoken Spanish.
target_language_example: Mucho antes de que llegaran, ya había terminado la cena.
native_language_example: Long before they arrived, I had already finished dinner.

meaning: 'a lot here' or 'much here' — used to say there is a large amount or degree of something in this place or situation.
additional_notes: This combination is literal: mucho (much/a lot) + aquí (here). It isn't a fixed idiom in Spanish; native speakers more commonly say 'mucho' with a noun ('hay mucho tráfico aquí') or use 'aquí hay mucho'/'hay mucho aquí'. Use it to emphasize quantity or degree referring to the current location or situation.
target_language_example: Hay mucho aquí que ver.
native_language_example: There is a lot here to see.

meaning: a lot that / very (happy/satisfied) that — used with verbs like alegrarse to intensify emotion about a fact or event.
additional_notes: Commonly appears after verbs of emotion (e.g., alegrarse, sorprenderse) as 'me alegro mucho de que...' meaning 'I'm very glad that...'. It is followed by a subordinate clause introduced by 'que' and then a conjugated verb (often subjunctive). 'Mucho' intensifies the feeling; 'de' links the emotion verb to the 'que' clause.
target_language_example: Me alegro mucho de que hayas aprobado el examen.
native_language_example: I'm very glad that you passed the exam.

meaning: a lot/something has changed or happened since (a specific time or event).
additional_notes: Combines 'mucho' (a lot) with 'desde' (since). Used to say that something or someone has changed, suffered, improved, etc., a great deal compared to a past point in time. Common structures: 'ha cambiado mucho desde...' (has changed a lot since...), 'sufrió mucho desde...' (suffered a lot since...). The time point after 'desde' can be a specific time, event, or phrase (e.g., 'la última vez que...', 'la muerte de...').
target_language_example: He aprendido mucho desde que empecé a trabajar aquí.
native_language_example: I've learned a lot since I started working here.

meaning: Not a common fixed phrase; likely two separate words meaning 'a lot' (mucho) followed by the definite article 'the' (el).
additional_notes: This sequence is not a standard multiword expression in Spanish. If you see 'mucho' + 'el' in a sentence, it's usually because 'mucho' is modifying a verb/adjective/adverb and 'el' begins the next noun phrase (e.g., 'me gusta mucho el chocolate' → 'I like chocolate a lot'). Don't treat 'mucho el' as a single phrase. Correct uses: 'mucho' = 'a lot/much/very' and 'el' = 'the' (masculine).
target_language_example: Me gusta mucho el chocolate.
native_language_example: I like chocolate a lot.

meaning: "much" or "a lot" + "that (feminine)" — used to say you like or use something a lot, or that something happened a lot on a particular (feminine) noun.
additional_notes: This is the combination of the adverb "mucho" (a lot, much) and the demonstrative adjective "esa" (that, feminine singular). "Esa" agrees with a feminine noun mentioned or understood (esa ventana, esa idea, esa noche, esa costumbre, esa palabra). In English you'd normally say "that ... a lot" or "... a lot that" depending on sentence; typical translations: "I like that X a lot," "That habit has spread a lot," "It rained a lot that night." Word order in Spanish is: verb + mucho + esa + feminine noun.
target_language_example: Me interesa mucho esa película.
native_language_example: I'm very interested in that movie.

meaning: 'a lot, that one' (literally), but this exact phrase is not standard Spanish.
additional_notes: This sequence combines mucho ('a lot' / 'much' / 'many') with the demonstrative ese ('that' [near the listener]). It is not a fixed phrase in Spanish and by itself sounds odd or ungrammatical in most contexts. You might see similar combinations in colloquial speech when someone hesitates or points something out (e.g., "mucho, ese..." meaning "a lot, that one..."), but normally you would use either 'mucho' alone (No como mucho = I don't eat much) or a demonstrative with a noun (ese libro = that book). For 'that one a lot' you'd say 'mucho ese' only in very informal, fragmented speech — better alternatives: 'mucho ese' is not recommended; use 'ese mucho' is also incorrect. Use: 'mucho' + verb/adjective or 'ese' + noun.
target_language_example: No, no me gusta mucho ese.
native_language_example: No, I don't like that one very much.

meaning: 'a lot' or 'very much' + 'this' (as in 'a lot this week/area/photo') — used when 'mucho' modifies time expressions, places, or demonstratives with 'esta'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom; it's the combination of 'mucho' (a lot/much) and 'esta' (feminine singular demonstrative 'this' or part of time expressions like 'esta semana'). Common uses: 'mucho esta semana' means 'a lot this week' (often after a verb: 'He trabajado mucho esta semana' = 'I've worked a lot this week'), and 'mucho esta zona' isn't standard word order — better: 'esta zona ha sido muy afectada' or 'ha afectado mucho a esta zona'. In short, learners will most often see 'mucho' + time phrase with 'esta' as in 'mucho esta semana' or 'me gusta mucho esta fotografía' where 'mucho' modifies liking and 'esta' points to the noun.
target_language_example: He estudiado mucho esta semana.
native_language_example: I have studied a lot this week.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase in Spanish; most often a sequence of two separate words: 'mucho' (a lot) followed immediately by the hesitation filler 'este' (um/uh) or the demonstrative 'este' (this). It typically indicates either hesitation after saying 'mucho' or the start of a clarifying phrase.
additional_notes: 'Mucho este' is not an idiomatic expression to memorize. In spoken Spanish, 'este' is frequently used as a filler (like 'um') so you may hear 'mucho, este...' or 'mucho este...' in rapid speech. If intended as 'mucho' + demonstrative 'este', punctuation or context will clarify meaning (e.g., 'mucho este problema' is uncommon; more likely 'este problema es muy grande'). Do not treat it as a single lexical unit.
target_language_example: Trabajo mucho este año, este... estoy agotado.
native_language_example: I work a lot this year, um... I'm exhausted.

meaning: very cold (weather or temperature).
additional_notes: Used to describe strong coldness in the environment or how someone feels because of low temperature. Common with verbs like hacer (hace mucho frío / hacía mucho frío). Not used to mean 'very cold' as personality; it's about temperature.
target_language_example: Hoy hace mucho frío; ponte un abrigo.
native_language_example: It's very cold today; put on a coat.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase in Spanish; typically a nonstandard or mistaken word order. It can appear when words from different constructions end up adjacent (e.g., emphasis or casual speech), but correct standard alternatives exist.
additional_notes: 'Mucho lo' is not a conventional multi-word expression. Common correct forms include 'lo mucho que...' (to emphasize degree), 'lo siento mucho' (I'm very sorry), or simply 'mucho' alone. In some informal or regional speech inadvertent sequences like 'mucho lo' might occur when clauses are restructured, but they are not recommended for learners. If you encounter 'mucho lo' in text or speech, check context — it's likely a typo, inversion, or part of a larger clause where words became adjacent.
target_language_example: No es mucho lo que queda en la nevera.
native_language_example: There isn't much left in the fridge.

meaning: colloquial filler meaning 'a lot about' or 'too much about' (used to comment on a topic or situation)
additional_notes: This is an informal, conversational sequence used in spoken Spanish to refer back to a topic or situation with a degree of emphasis or judgment. It often appears before or after a noun or clause to express that something is excessive, notable, or much-discussed: e.g., 'mucho lo de X' ≈ 'there's a lot about X / that's a lot regarding X.' Usage and word order can vary regionally; it's not a fixed grammatical phrase and may sound casual or fragmented in isolation.
target_language_example: No sabía nada, pero ahora es mucho lo de ese escándalo.
native_language_example: I didn't know anything, but now there's a lot about that scandal.

meaning: a lot of what / much of what
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom but a sequence where 'mucho' modifies an understood quantity and 'lo que' introduces a clause ('what' / 'that which'). More common is 'mucho de lo que' or 'mucho de lo que...' but 'mucho lo que' can appear in colloquial or emphatic structures (often followed by a verb or clause). Use context to decide whether to include 'de'.
target_language_example: Mucho lo que dijo sorprendió a todos.
native_language_example: Much of what he said surprised everyone.

meaning: much less; let alone; even less likely.
additional_notes: Used to downplay or exclude a stronger/more extreme possibility. Often follows a negative statement to introduce something even less likely or desirable. Can also be used to express wanting to do something far less (e.g., quiero gastar mucho menos). Common in spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: No sé cocinar, mucho menos preparar postres.
native_language_example: I don't know how to cook, much less make desserts.

meaning: much taller; a lot taller
additional_notes: Used to compare height (or metaphorically, any degree) with emphasis. Commonly appears in comparisons with 'que' (than) or clauses introduced by 'de' (e.g., 'de lo que'). 'Mucho' adds emphasis to 'más' — 'más alto' = 'taller', 'mucho más alto' = 'much taller' / 'a lot taller'. Word order is fixed: 'mucho' before 'más'.
target_language_example: Ella es mucho más alto que yo.
native_language_example: She is much taller than me.

meaning: much taller than
additional_notes: Used to compare heights (or sizes) emphasizing a large difference. Structure: mucho más + adjective + que. Can be used figuratively (e.g., skills, prices) to mean 'much more ... than'.
target_language_example: Mi hermano es mucho más alto que yo.
native_language_example: My brother is much taller than me.

meaning: 'a lot, but...' used to state strong degree then introduce a contrast or reservation
additional_notes: Not an idiom; it's the adverb 'mucho' followed immediately by the conjunction 'pero'. More natural in speech when attached to a verb or adjective earlier in the clause (e.g., 'Te quiero mucho pero...'). When written, a comma often precedes 'pero'. The phrase can sound abrupt or lead into an unfinished thought.
target_language_example: Te quiero mucho pero tengo que irme ahora.
native_language_example: I love you a lot but I have to leave now.

meaning: used before a clause to mean 'it's a lot that...' or 'there's much that...'; often introduces emphasis about quantity or degree related to what follows
additional_notes: This combination appears when 'mucho' modifies an implicit noun idea or when used informally before 'que' to emphasize a following clause (e.g., 'Hay mucho que hacer' = 'There is a lot to do'). It is not a fixed idiom by itself — it usually appears as part of phrases like 'mucho que hacer', 'mucho que decir', or 'mucho que contar'. Word order: 'mucho' can precede a noun + 'que' clause or be part of expressions with 'hay' or 'tener'.
target_language_example: Hay mucho que aprender en este curso.
native_language_example: There is a lot to learn in this course.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase in Spanish; most often a fragment within a larger sentence. It can appear when a clause with 'mucho' (much) and a relative or object clause beginning with 'que' precedes a pronominal 'lo' (it/that). Meaning depends on context, e.g., 'mucho que lo...' → 'much (that) it...' or as part of comparisons ('mucho más que lo...').
additional_notes: This sequence is not a common, self-contained idiom. It is compositional and context-dependent. More natural alternatives when intending 'much more than that' are 'mucho más que eso' or 'mucho más que lo anterior'. When it appears, word order and surrounding words determine meaning; sometimes it results from ellipsis or spoken hesitation.
target_language_example: Había mucho que lo preocupaba, pero no quiso decirlo.
native_language_example: There was much that worried him/her, but he/she didn't want to say it.

meaning: 'much' or 'so much' when referring to someone (you) — used in phrases like 'how much I/they...' or 'it's been a long time that... you'.
additional_notes: This sequence appears in different constructions. 1) 'Lo mucho que te...' or 'No sé lo mucho que te...' means 'how much I/they/it ... you' (expressing intensity: need, love, etc.). 2) 'Hace mucho que te...' is part of the time expression 'Hace mucho que...' meaning 'It's been a long time that...' or 'I have known you for a long time.' 'Te' is the indirect/object pronoun 'you'. Translate according to context (intensity vs. duration).
target_language_example: No sabes lo mucho que te aprecio.
native_language_example: You don't know how much I appreciate you.

meaning: Not a correct or standard Spanish phrase; likely a mistake (possibly intended: 'mucho' + 'su' separately like 'mucho' = 'a lot' and 'su' = 'his/her/your/their').
additional_notes:
Spanish does not combine 'mucho' and 'su' into a fixed phrase. If you see 'mucho su' it is probably an error or a direct word-for-word translation from another language. Common correct patterns are:
- 'mucho + noun' (e.g., 'mucho trabajo' = 'a lot of work')
- 'su + noun' (e.g., 'su casa' = 'his/her/your/their house')
- 'mucho + de + pronoun' is incorrect; use 'mucho' with a noun or verb: 'trabaja mucho' (works a lot) or 'tiene muchos amigos' (has many friends).
If the intended idea is 'his/her/your/their many ...', place 'su' before a plural noun with a plural adjective: 'sus muchos amigos' (but usually you would say 'tiene muchos amigos').
target_language_example:
No natural example because 'mucho su' is not standard Spanish. Correct alternatives:
- 'Tiene mucho trabajo.'
- 'Tiene muchos amigos.'
- 'Su casa es grande.'
native_language_example:
No natural example because 'mucho su' is not standard. Correct alternatives:
- 'He/She has a lot of work.'
- 'He/She has many friends.'
- 'His/Her house is big.'

meaning: colloquial retort meaning roughly 'as if you're so great' or 'you think you're all that' — used to call someone presumptuous, arrogant, or self-important.
additional_notes: Informal and often sarcastic. Tone can be playful or cutting depending on context and intonation. More common in some Spanish-speaking areas as a clipped, emphatic phrase; not standard formal Spanish. Can stand alone or follow a clause.
target_language_example: ¿Vas a decirnos qué hacer otra vez? ¡Mucho tu!
native_language_example: Are you going to tell us what to do again? As if you're so great!

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase in Spanish; literally 'much/many see' but normally incorrect on its own. It may appear as a fragment of longer expressions (e.g., 'mucho que ver', 'mucho para ver') or result from a typo.
additional_notes: The two-word sequence 'mucho ver' is uncommon and usually ungrammatical by itself. In natural Spanish you'd say 'mucho que ver' ('much to see' or 'a lot to do with') or 'mucho para ver' ('a lot to see'). If you encounter 'mucho ver' in text, it may be an edited fragment, poetic compression, or an error. 'Mucho' is an adjective/adverb meaning 'a lot' or 'much'; 'ver' is the infinitive 'to see'.
target_language_example: Hay mucho ver en esta ciudad, aunque la forma completa sería 'mucho que ver'.
native_language_example: There is much to see in this city, although the complete form would be 'mucho que ver'.

meaning: 'a lot' or 'much' followed by 'and' — often part of a longer phrase meaning '...a lot and...'; used to connect two ideas where the first describes quantity/intensity.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom by itself; it's simply the adverb 'mucho' (a lot/much) followed by the conjunction 'y' (and). You will see it when someone links a comment about amount/intensity to another clause: e.g. 'comes mucho y estás enfermo' ('you eat a lot and you're sick'). Watch word order and agreement: 'mucho' can become 'mucha', 'muchos', 'muchas' to agree with nouns; when modifying verbs it stays 'mucho'.
target_language_example: Trabaja mucho y llega tarde a casa.
native_language_example: He works a lot and arrives home late.

meaning: very hot in (a place or time)
additional_notes: Use to say that a specific location or time is very hot. Usually followed by a place (en la ciudad, en el coche) or a time expression (en verano). Spanish commonly uses 'hace mucho calor en...' or simply 'mucho calor en...' in informal notes, but full sentences often include 'hace'.
target_language_example: Hace mucho calor en la playa hoy.
native_language_example: It's very hot at the beach today.

meaning: Nice to meet you; pleased to meet you.
additional_notes: Common polite phrase used when meeting someone for the first time. Can stand alone or follow a greeting (e.g., "Hola, mucho gusto"). Note: in a different sense, 'tener (buen/mal) gusto' means 'to have (good/bad) taste' — e.g., "Tus amigos no tienen mucho gusto" means "Your friends don't have much taste."
target_language_example: Hola, mucho gusto. Me llamo Ana.
native_language_example: Hello, nice to meet you. My name is Ana.

meaning: a lot of time
additional_notes: Used to talk about either the amount of time spent on something or a long duration. In natural English, it often becomes 'a lot of time' or 'for a long time' depending on the sentence.
target_language_example: Paso mucho tiempo estudiando español.
native_language_example: I spend a lot of time studying Spanish.

meaning: to take a long time to get used to (something).
additional_notes: This phrase combines 'mucho tiempo' (a long time) + the infinitive reflexive 'acostumbrarse' (to get used to). Use it when saying that adapting to a new situation, habit, person, or place requires a long adjustment period. Common structures: 'Me llevó mucho tiempo acostumbrarse a...' or 'Es mucho tiempo acostumbrarse a...'. Remember to conjugate 'acostumbrarse' appropriately and include the preposition 'a' before the thing you get used to.
target_language_example: Me llevó mucho tiempo acostumbrarse al ritmo de vida de la ciudad.
native_language_example: It took me a long time to get used to the city's pace of life.

meaning: to take a long time to get used to (something)
additional_notes: Use this phrase to say that adjusting to a new situation, habit, place, or person requires a long period. Common structures: 'me/te/le/nos/os/les lleva mucho tiempo acostumbrarse a + noun/infinitive' or 'toma/ha llevado mucho tiempo acostumbrarse a...'. The reflexive 'acostumbrarse' requires the preposition 'a' before the thing or activity.
target_language_example: Me lleva mucho tiempo acostumbrarse a levantarme tan temprano.
native_language_example: It takes me a long time to get used to getting up so early.

meaning: to take a long time to get used to (the)
additional_notes: This phrase is built from 'mucho tiempo' (a long time) + 'acostumbrarse a' (to get used to). The final 'la' is a feminine singular definite article and must match the noun that follows (e.g., la ciudad, la vida). In natural Spanish you'd usually complete the phrase with the thing you're getting used to: 'mucho tiempo acostumbrarse a la ciudad.' For English, translate as 'it takes a long time to get used to the...' or 'to take a long time to get used to the...'.
target_language_example: Me tomó mucho tiempo acostumbrarse a la ciudad.
native_language_example: It took me a long time to get used to the city.

meaning: used to say that something has been a long time (since) — similar to 'it's been a long time' or 'for a long time that...'.
additional_notes: Often appears in informal spoken Spanish in phrases like 'Hace mucho tiempo que...' or '¿Cuánto tiempo que no...?' Alone 'mucho tiempo que' is not a full grammatical phrase without a verb or 'hace' before it. Common patterns: 'Hace mucho tiempo que... + present' (action that started long ago and continues), 'Hace mucho tiempo que no... + present' (haven't done something for a long time).
target_language_example: Hace mucho tiempo que no te veo.
native_language_example: I haven't seen you in a long time.

meaning: a lot of work to (be done / do something / ahead).
additional_notes: Usually appears in phrases like "mucho trabajo por hacer" (a lot of work to be done) or "mucho trabajo por delante" (a lot of work ahead). "Por" here introduces what remains to be done or the task-oriented purpose. Common with verbs like hacer or delante; can be used in present or past contexts.
target_language_example: Todavía tenemos mucho trabajo por hacer antes de la entrega.
native_language_example: We still have a lot of work to do before the deadline.

meaning: a lot to talk about / much to discuss
additional_notes: Used after verbs or with impersonal constructions to say there is plenty to discuss or many topics to talk about. Often appears in phrases like "hay mucho de qué hablar" (there's a lot to talk about) or with pronouns/subjects: "tenéis mucho de qué hablar" (you have a lot to talk about). Word order: "mucho de qué" follows forms of 'haber', 'tener', or similar verbs.
target_language_example: Después de la reunión tendremos mucho de qué hablar.
native_language_example: After the meeting we'll have a lot to talk about.

meaning: 'a lot to' / 'much to' (something) — indicates there is a large amount of something to do, say, learn, etc.
additional_notes: Used before infinitives or verbs/activities (mucho para + infinitive) or before nouns/clauses to say there is a lot of something to do, discuss, tell, learn, etc. Common in phrases like 'mucho para decir', 'mucho para aprender', 'mucho para discutir'. Context determines the exact English phrasing (a lot to..., much to...).
target_language_example: Hay mucho para aprender en este curso.
native_language_example: There is a lot to learn in this course.

meaning: many children
additional_notes: A simple quantifier + noun phrase. 'Muchos' agrees in gender/number with the noun (muchas niñas for many girls). Used to describe a large number of children; can refer to people present (Hay/Hubo) or possession/relationship (Él tiene muchos niños).
target_language_example: En la fiesta había muchos niños jugando.
native_language_example: At the party there were many children playing.

meaning: Thank you very much / Thanks a lot.
additional_notes: An emphatic way to express strong gratitude. 'Muchísimas' is the superlative form of 'muchas' (many), so this is stronger than 'muchas gracias'. Common in both formal and informal contexts; can be followed by a reason (por...) or by a short comment. Tone depends on voice and context.
target_language_example: Muchísimas gracias por ayudarme con la mudanza.
native_language_example: Thank you very much for helping me with the move.

meaning: moved to (someone moved their home to a new place).
additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of 'mudarse a' meaning to change residence and go live in a different city, neighborhood, or country. Use with a place after 'a' (se mudó a Madrid). For other persons change reflexive pronoun: me mudé a, te mudaste a, nos mudamos a. Common in everyday and neutral contexts.
target_language_example: Se mudó a Barcelona el año pasado.
native_language_example: He/She moved to Barcelona last year.

meaning: the clause 'when the ... dies' (subjunctive: 'when the [masculine noun] dies').
additional_notes: This is the present subjunctive form of morir (muera) used in temporal clauses introduced by 'cuando' to speak about a future event that is uncertain. 'El' is the masculine definite article before a noun (e.g., 'el bosque', 'el obispo'). In English we usually say 'when the X dies'. The construction requires the subjunctive because the event is hypothetical/unknown at the time of speaking.
target_language_example: Cuando muera el director, cambiarán las reglas.
native_language_example: When the director dies, they'll change the rules.

meaning: 'very' or 'extremely' used with a noun to express a strong state or feeling (literally 'dead from/of').
additional_notes: Used after a feminine subject (muerto/ muerta vary by gender) plus 'de' + noun to indicate an intense degree of that condition: e.g. muerta de hambre (extremely hungry), muerto de risa (dying of laughter). Common in everyday spoken Spanish. For masculine subjects use 'muerto de'.
target_language_example: Estoy muerta de sueño después del viaje.
native_language_example: I'm extremely sleepy after the trip.

meaning: 'death with' (literal); not a fixed common Spanish phrase — likely part of a larger expression referring to dying while having/doing something.
additional_notes: This is not a standalone idiom in Spanish. You will most often see muerte followed by con when describing circumstances of a death: e.g. muerte con síntomas, muerte con arma de fuego, or muerte con sospecha de COVID. In those cases muerte = 'death' and con = 'with' (indicating accompanying condition, cause, or object). Use it only as part of a fuller phrase. For a straightforward way to say 'died of' or 'died from,' use murió de / murió por or murió a causa de.
target_language_example: La autopsia indicó muerte con traumatismo craneoencefálico.
native_language_example: The autopsy indicated death with traumatic brain injury.

meaning: Literally 'death of me'; an informal exclamation or phrase used to emphasize that something is exhausting, overwhelming, embarrassing, or intensely affecting the speaker (similar to 'I'm dying' or 'this is killing me').
additional_notes: Colloquial and emphatic. Often appears within exclamations (e.g., '¡La muerte de mi!') or in constructions like 'es la muerte de mi' to stress difficulty, embarrassment, or strong feeling. Not a literal statement about death. Tone and context determine whether it expresses fatigue, frustration, or exaggerated admiration. Avoid in formal situations.
target_language_example: ¡La muerte de mi, con este calor no puedo concentrarme!
native_language_example: This heat is killing me; I can't concentrate!

meaning: 'the death of' (used before a masculine noun or title).
additional_notes: Combines muerte (death) + del (contraction of de + el). Use before masculine nouns/titles: 'la muerte del rey' = 'the death of the king'. For feminine nouns use 'de la' (e.g., 'la muerte de la reina'). Often used in news, stories, legal contexts, and expressions of responsibility or cause.
target_language_example: La muerte del autor cambió la publicación del libro.
native_language_example: The death of the author changed the book's publication.

meaning: death in / death at (used to state location, time, or cause of someone's death).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase on its own but a combination: muerte (death) + preposition en. It commonly appears in contexts like 'muerte en accidente' (death in an accident), 'muerte en 1999' (death in 1999), or 'muerte en el hospital' (death in the hospital). The exact nuance depends on the noun or phrase that follows 'en'. Use 'de' for 'death of (someone)' (muerte de Juan) and 'por' for cause when emphasizing cause (muerte por asfixia).
target_language_example: La muerte en el accidente fue instantánea.
native_language_example: The death in the accident was instantaneous.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase; likely two separate words 'muerte' (death) and 'no' (no/not).
additional_notes: This sequence is not a common multiword expression in Spanish. 'Muerte' means 'death' and 'no' is the negative particle. If you see 'muerte no' it may be part of a larger sentence (e.g., 'muerte no esperada' — 'unexpected death') or an emphatic fragment like '¡Muerte, no!' (rare/poetic). For beginner learners, treat 'muerte' and 'no' separately: 'la muerte' = the death; 'no' = no / not.
target_language_example: La muerte no es el final para todos.
native_language_example: Death is not the end for everyone.

meaning: used to indicate cause of death ('death by' or 'died from').
additional_notes: Followed by a noun or phrase that names the cause (e.g., 'muerte por accidente', 'muerte por infección'). Common in news, medical reports, and formal descriptions. Not a complete sentence by itself — usually part of a longer phrase like 'muerte por' in headings or 'murió por...' in sentences.
target_language_example: La investigación confirmó una muerte por intoxicación alimentaria.
native_language_example: The investigation confirmed a death by food poisoning.

meaning: 'very hungry' or 'starving'.
additional_notes: Idiomatic expression used to say someone is extremely hungry. Literally means 'dead of hunger' but is used informally to emphasize hunger. Can describe people or oneself; often used with estar (estoy muerto de hambre) or deber de (debe de estar muerto de hambre) to guess someone is very hungry.
target_language_example: Después del partido, estaba muerto de hambre y me comí dos bocadillos.
native_language_example: After the game, I was starving and ate two sandwiches.

meaning: 'dead' (physically, emotionally) or 'deserted/quiet at a time' when followed by 'por' plus a time or cause; can indicate time, cause/agent, or idiomatic 'dead inside' sense.
additional_notes: Meaning depends on context: with times ('por la noche') it usually means 'deserted/quiet during that time' (e.g., streets, places). With agents/causes it can mark cause ('muerto por la voluntad de...') or emphatic statements about who caused someone's death. In colloquial use, 'muerto por dentro' = 'dead inside' (emotionally numb). Be careful: word agreement matters (muerto/ muerta/ muertos/ muertas) and placement; 'muerto por' must appear exactly as shown when specifying cause/time.
target_language_example: Ese barrio está muerto por las noches, no hay ni un alma en la calle.
native_language_example: That neighborhood is dead at night; there isn't a soul on the street.

meaning: a fragment used in fixed expressions meaning 'dead and...' to join 'dead' with another adjective or participle (e.g., 'muerto y enterrado' = 'dead and buried'); often emphasizes finality or completeness and requires agreement in gender/number with the noun.
additional_notes: This is a multi-word fragment rather than a standalone phrase — it usually appears followed by another word (enterrado, abandonado, arruinado). Pay attention to gender/number: muerto/muerta/muertos/muertas. Can be used literally (someone is dead and buried) or figuratively (a project is dead and buried = finished). The fragment by itself is incomplete in most contexts. Note also common colloquial uses where grammar may be lax (e.g., mistaken plural agreement in some informal speech).
target_language_example: El silencio era tan profundo que el lugar parecía muerto y abandonado.
native_language_example: The silence was so deep that the place seemed dead and abandoned.

meaning: dead in
additional_notes: Literal: 'muerto' = dead; 'en' = in. Used literally to describe someone who is dead in a particular place (e.g., 'muerto en su casa' = 'dead in his house'). Colloquially, 'muerto en' can appear in figurative expressions (e.g., 'muerto en vida' — 'dead in life' / 'dead inside'), but that exact idiom is usually 'muerto en vida'. Pay attention to context: without an object or complement after 'en', the phrase is incomplete in Spanish and needs a location or expression.
target_language_example: Lo encontraron muerto en su apartamento.
native_language_example: They found him dead in his apartment.

meaning: literally 'dead and' — part of a clause where 'muerto' (dead) is linked with 'y' to continue the sentence; shows someone has died and then adds another related idea or contrast.
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom by itself; 'muerto y' appears when a clause states that someone has died (ha muerto / había muerto / pensé que habías muerto / que yo hubiera muerto) and the sentence continues with another action, reaction, contrast or consequence.
