"Nada se" alone is not a complete sentence; it will be completed by a verb (often in passive/impersonal form). English equivalents: "nothing is/was...", "nothing happens...", "nobody..." depending on context.
target_language_example: Nada se sabe sobre el paradero del gato.
native_language_example: Nothing is known about the cat's whereabouts.

meaning: literally 'nothing if'; not a fixed phrase—rarely used together; usually words appear separately (nada = nothing, si = if/yes).
additional_notes: This combination is not a common fixed expression in Spanish. Most often you'll see 'nada' (nothing) and 'si' (if or yes) used in separate parts of a sentence (for example: 'No quiero nada si...'). If you encounter 'nada si' it will depend on context and may be part of a larger clause ('nada, si...' as a spoken hesitation) or a regional/colloquial structure. Don't memorize it as a single phrase—learn 'nada' and 'si' separately.
target_language_example: No quiero nada si no estás tú.
native_language_example: I want nothing if you're not here.

meaning: nothing so / nothing as (used to compare or to downplay something)
additional_notes: Used to soften or negate a comparison: often appears before an adjective or clause to say that something is not as X as someone might think (e.g., "nada tan difícil" = "not so difficult"). Can be followed by adjectives, adverbs, or clauses. Context often determines whether it translates as "not so" or "nothing so/that". Common in spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: No era nada tan complicado como pensábamos.
native_language_example: It wasn't nearly as complicated as we thought.

meaning: 'nothing will' / 'nothing will (do something to) you' — used to say that nothing will happen to or affect someone
additional_notes: Nada (nothing) + te (you, object pronoun) is used to say that nothing will happen to, affect, hurt, or stop the person. It appears before the verb in Spanish (Nada te hará daño = Nothing will hurt you). In casual speech you may also hear Nada te va a pasar or Nada te sucederá. The exact translation depends on the following verb (hará daño = will hurt, mantendrá fuera = will keep out, sucederá = will happen).
target_language_example: No te preocupes: nada te va a pasar.
native_language_example: Don't worry: nothing will happen to you.

meaning: has nothing / there's nothing (that) [literal: 'nothing has']
additional_notes: This phrase is a short combination of 'nada' (nothing) and the verb 'tiene' (he/she/it has, or you formal have). It appears in sentences like 'No tiene nada' (He/it has nothing) or in constructions where 'nada' is the subject: 'Nada tiene valor' (Nothing has value). Word order can change: more common is 'no tiene nada' for 'he/she doesn't have anything.'
target_language_example: No te preocupes, nada tiene importancia ahora.
native_language_example: Don't worry, nothing has importance now.

meaning: nothing works / nothing is going right
additional_notes: Used to complain that things are not functioning or that situations are going badly. Context matters: could refer to machines ('nada va' = nothing works) or to events/plans ('nada va' = nothing is going well). Often said informally and can be followed by more detail (e.g., 'nada va bien', 'nada va a funcionar').
target_language_example: Intenté encender la computadora, pero nada va.
native_language_example: I tried to turn on the computer, but nothing works.

meaning: literally 'nothing and' — not a fixed standalone phrase; usually two separate words ('nada' = 'nothing' or discourse 'anyway/well', 'y' = 'and') that appear together when a speaker links thoughts or trails off (e.g., 'nada y...' = 'and then.../so...').
additional_notes: 'Nada y' is not an idiom by itself. Treat it as two words that can appear consecutively in casual speech or writing when a speaker begins with 'nada' and immediately adds 'y' to connect another clause. Example uses include conversational fillers or when listing negative items followed by another clause.
target_language_example: Nada y luego te cuento lo que pasó.
native_language_example: Anyway, and then I'll tell you what happened.

meaning: 'swimming in the' — literal phrase used when something or someone is literally swimming in (a body of water) or, figuratively, immersed in (a situation, feeling, or abundance).
additional_notes: This is the present participle phrase of nadar (to swim) combined with the feminine singular article la. It will usually be followed by a feminine noun (la piscina, la playa, la masa, la tarea figuratively). Used literally (e.g., nadando en la piscina) or figuratively to mean 'immersed in' or 'surrounded by' (e.g., nadando en la deuda = 'drowning in debt'). Ensure the following noun agrees in gender and number.
target_language_example: Después de la tormenta, los niños estaban nadando en la piscina.
native_language_example: After the storm, the children were swimming in the pool.

meaning: to swim to (a destination) or swim up to (someone/something).
additional_notes: A combination of the verb nadar (to swim) + the preposition al (a + el) meaning 'to the'. Used when indicating direction or destination reached by swimming (e.g., nadar al otro lado — to swim to the other side). Usually followed by a noun or noun phrase. If followed by a person, it can mean 'swim up to someone.' The verb must be conjugated to match the subject (nadar al → nadamos al, nadó al, etc.).
target_language_example: Tuvimos que nadar al muelle porque el bote se había ido.
native_language_example: We had to swim to the pier because the boat had left.

meaning: to swim with (someone) or to swim regularly/with something (context-dependent).
additional_notes: Most commonly means 'to swim with' (company: someone). In some contexts (example 3) 'nadar con regularidad' uses nadar + adverb/phrase to mean 'to swim regularly' — here 'con' is part of the phrase 'con regularidad' not a fixed partner of 'nadar'. Use 'nadar con' + person to say you swim together with them (e.g., nadar con mamá).
target_language_example: ¿Quieres nadar con tus amigos este fin de semana?
native_language_example: Do you want to swim with your friends this weekend?

meaning: to swim in this (one) — used to talk about swimming in a specific nearby body of water.
additional_notes: Common phrase used with a specific nearby location (este = this). Often followed by a noun (e.g., 'río', 'lago', 'mar'). Can express ability, permission, safety, habit, or intention (e.g., 'Quería nadar en este río', 'No está permitido nadar en este río'). Remember gender/number: use 'este' for masculine singular (este río); 'esta' for feminine (esta playa); 'estos/estas' for plural.
target_language_example: ¿Te gustaría nadar en este lago mañana?
native_language_example: Would you like to swim in this lake tomorrow?

meaning: 'to swim very' — used to modify how well or how much someone swims (adverb + verb).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase; it's simply the verb nadar (to swim) combined with the adverb muy (very). You will typically see it followed by an adjective or adverb (e.g., 'nadar muy bien' = 'to swim very well') or used in comparative contexts. On its own 'nadar muy' is incomplete and needs an adjective/adverb or more context.
target_language_example: Ella puede nadar muy bien.
native_language_example: She can swim very well.

meaning: literally 'to swim and' — not a standalone phrase; appears when 'nadar' (to swim) is followed by 'y' to connect actions or clauses (e.g., 'nadar y bucear' = 'to swim and dive').
additional_notes: This is not an independent expression. 'Nadar' means 'to swim.' The conjunction 'y' means 'and.' Together they simply join 'swim' with another verb or noun. In speech or writing you will see 'nadar y' before another verb or activity. Make sure the verb after 'y' has the correct form (infinitive if you're listing activities: 'nadar y bucear').
target_language_example: Me gusta nadar y correr por la playa.
native_language_example: I like to swim and run on the beach.

meaning: 'nobody' or 'no one' (followed by a preposition like 'a' before an indirect object or verb phrase).
additional_notes: Nadie means 'nobody' or 'no one'. It is usually used alone (nadie vino = no one came) or followed by a preposition when introducing an indirect object or a complement (e.g., nadie a quien preguntarle = no one to ask). The sequence 'nadie a' appears when 'a' connects nadie to a verb phrase or noun phrase (often 'a quien', 'a nadie', or 'a + infinitive' constructions). Remember Spanish uses 'a' before direct objects that are people (the 'personal a'), but with negative pronouns like 'nadie' the structure depends on the verb and meaning.
target_language_example: No hay nadie a quien llamar esta noche.
native_language_example: There is no one to call tonight.

meaning: nobody here / no one here.
additional_notes: Used to say that no person is present in the place being referred to. Common in answers or statements: Nadie aquí sabe (Nobody here knows). Can appear with verbs in singular (nadie) and usually with 'aquí' after or before for emphasis: Aquí no hay nadie / Nadie aquí puede ayudar.
target_language_example: No hay nadie aquí, podemos entrar.
native_language_example: There is nobody here; we can go in.

meaning: no one like (someone); nobody compares to (someone).
additional_notes: Used before a noun or pronoun to praise or emphasize that no person equals the named person in some quality. Common structures: 'nadie como + [persona]' or 'nadie como + mí/ti/él/ella' in informal speech. Often followed by a verb phrase describing the quality (e.g., 'nadie como tú sabe cocinar').
target_language_example: Nadie como mi abuela hace el pan casero.
native_language_example: No one like my grandmother makes homemade bread.

meaning: nobody with / no one who has (used to say that no person possesses or is accompanied by something/quality)
additional_notes: Used to negate existence of a person having something or a quality. Usually appears as part of a larger clause: 'nadie con [noun/verb phrase]' or 'nadie con [que + verb]'. Common in sentences like 'No hay nadie con experiencia' or 'Nadie con ganas de ayudar vino.'
target_language_example: No viene nadie con preguntas, así que podemos empezar.
native_language_example: No one is coming with questions, so we can start.

meaning: 'no one from' or 'nobody among/from'.
additional_notes: Nadie means 'no one' or 'nobody'. When followed by de + noun or de + pronoun, nadie de expresses 'no one from' a group or place (e.g., nadie de la clase = no one from the class). If used alone, 'nadie' does not need 'de'. Watch word order: use 'de' before a noun/pronoun that specifies the group or source.
target_language_example: Nadie de mi familia sabe hablar japonés.
native_language_example: No one from my family knows how to speak Japanese.

meaning: nobody said / no one said
additional_notes: Used to report that no person expressed something. Often followed by a clause (que ...) or a phrase (nada, eso, nada de ...). Common in negative statements. In Spanish word order, 'nadie' (nobody) comes before the verb. Can negate an idea or deny responsibility.
target_language_example: Nadie dijo que el examen sería fácil.
native_language_example: Nobody said the exam would be easy.

meaning: 'nobody in' or 'no one in' (used before a place or group).
additional_notes: Nadie means 'nobody' or 'no one'. When followed by en + place/group it indicates that there is no one in that location or among that group (e.g., nadie en la casa = no one in the house). Common in negative statements. Word order: nadie + en + location.
target_language_example: No hay nadie en la oficina hoy.
native_language_example: There is nobody in the office today.

meaning: nobody home / no one is at home.
additional_notes: Used to say that there is no one at the house or apartment. Can be used literally (no person present) or figuratively (no one available). Common in everyday speech. You can use it in short answers: "No, nadie en casa" or in full sentences: "No hay nadie en casa" (more complete).
target_language_example: Llamé al timbre y nadie en casa, así que me fui.
native_language_example: I rang the bell and nobody was home, so I left.

meaning: 'nobody in the' or 'no one in the' (used before a feminine singular place noun).
additional_notes: Commonly used to say that a place (house, room, street, etc.) is empty of people. 'Nadie' means 'nobody/no one'. 'En la' is the preposition + feminine article — it will change to 'en el' for masculine nouns (e.g., 'nadie en el coche'). In some sentences 'nadie' can appear with different word order ('no se veía a nadie en la calle').
target_language_example: No había nadie en la cocina cuando llegué.
native_language_example: There was nobody in the kitchen when I arrived.

meaning: nobody is / no one is
additional_notes: Combines nadie (nobody/no one) with the verb ser (to be). Used to say that no person has a certain quality or role: 'nadie es + adjective/noun' or in clauses like 'nadie es perfecto' (nobody is perfect). Watch word order: subject (nadie) before the verb. For negation with other verbs, Spanish places 'nadie' after the verb (e.g., 'No vino nadie'), but when 'nadie' is the subject with ser it's 'nadie es...'.
target_language_example: Nadie es perfecto, así que perdónalos.
native_language_example: Nobody is perfect, so forgive them.

meaning: nobody's perfect; no one is perfect.
additional_notes: Common conversational phrase used to excuse or accept someone's mistake or imperfection. Can be used alone as a response (like 'well, nobody's perfect') or followed by a context (e.g., 'en eso'). Tone is informal-to-neutral and widely understood.
target_language_example: Cometí un error, pero nadie es perfecto.
native_language_example: I made a mistake, but nobody's perfect.

meaning: 'nobody was' or 'no one was' (past/ongoing state).
additional_notes: Combines 'nadie' (nobody/no one) with the imperfect past of 'estar' (to be). Used to describe that no person was in a certain state, place, or agreed with something. In many contexts you could also use 'nadie estuvo' (preterite) for a completed action; 'nadie estaba' (imperfect) emphasizes ongoing or background states in the past.
target_language_example: En la fiesta, nadie estaba hablando; todos estaban sentados en silencio.
native_language_example: At the party, nobody was talking; everyone was sitting quietly.

meaning: nobody ever; no one ever.
additional_notes: A strong negative phrase combining 'nadie' (nobody) and 'jamás' (ever/never). Used to emphasize that no person has ever done or experienced something. Often appears before the verb. Equivalent to 'nobody has ever...' or 'no one will ever...'.
target_language_example: Nadie jamás podrá olvidarlo.
native_language_example: Nobody will ever be able to forget it.

meaning: 'nobody/ no one them' — used when saying that no one did something to or with 'them' (los = them).
additional_notes: Combination of the negative pronoun 'nadie' (nobody) and the direct object pronoun 'los' (them, masculine or mixed). Word order: 'nadie' before the verb and object pronoun usually before the verb or attached (e.g., 'nadie los vio'). Use when referring to people or objects previously mentioned. In negative contexts 'nadie' cancels existence or action (nobody ...).
target_language_example: Nadie los encontró en el parque.
native_language_example: Nobody found them in the park.

meaning: no one else; nobody else.
additional_notes: Used to say that no other person (besides those already mentioned) does or will do something, or that no other person is affected. Common in negative statements. Can appear at start of sentence (as subject) or after a verb/phrase.
target_language_example: Ella lo contó sólo a su hermano; nadie más lo sabe.
native_language_example: She told only her brother; no one else knows it.

meaning: nobody/stops for — used to say that no one (does something) or that something has no one to stop it (context needed).
additional_notes: This phrase isn't a fixed idiom by itself; it typically appears as part of a larger sentence (e.g., nadie para el coche — 'nobody stops the car', or nadie para a ayudar — 'no one stops to help'). Pay attention to verb forms that follow (e.g., 'nadie para' + infinitive means 'nobody stops to [do something]').
target_language_example: Nadie para a ayudar cuando alguien tiene un accidente.
native_language_example: No one stops to help when someone has an accident.

meaning: no one turned out to be / no one was found to be
additional_notes: This phrase is used when reporting results or outcomes: e.g. after checking or investigating, it turned out that no person matched a description or no one was affected. It often appears in past tenses (resultó, resultaron) and can be followed by que + verb (resultó que nadie había llegado) or used with a noun phrase (nadie resultó herido = no one was injured).
target_language_example: Tras la búsqueda, nadie resultó herido.
native_language_example: After the search, no one turned out to be injured.

meaning: nobody noticed / nobody realized (someone/something).
additional_notes: Short form of "nadie se dio cuenta (de...)". Used to say that no one perceived, noticed, or became aware of something. Commonly followed by "cuenta (de)" or "cuenta de que + clause"; can stand alone ("Nadie se dio.") to mean no one noticed what happened. "Darse cuenta" is a reflexive verb phrase meaning "to realize" or "to notice."
target_language_example: Nadie se dio cuenta de que había dejado las llaves en la mesa.
native_language_example: Nobody noticed that I had left the keys on the table.

meaning: "nadie" = nobody / no one; "y" = and. The combination "nadie y" is not an idiomatic fixed phrase but can appear when the pronoun "nadie" is immediately followed by the conjunction "y" linking to another clause or phrase.
additional_notes: Treat this as two separate words that sometimes appear adjacent in sentences. "Nadie" is a negative pronoun used with verbs or in negative constructions; "y" is the coordinating conjunction 'and'. The sequence "nadie y" can occur naturally when "nadie" closes one clause and "y" begins the next (e.g., "Nadie y..."), or within a sentence when listing actions or consequences. Pay attention to punctuation and clause boundaries: a comma or pause may appear between them depending on sentence structure.
target_language_example: Nadie y nadie más podía explicar lo que había pasado.
native_language_example: No one and no one else could explain what had happened.

meaning: 'orange (juice), please' — a polite way to request orange juice (or an orange) in Spanish.
additional_notes: Often used when ordering drinks or asking for an orange. In many Spanish-speaking countries 'jugo de naranja' or 'zumo de naranja' means 'orange juice' (jugo common in Latin America, zumo common in Spain). You can say just 'Jugo de naranja, por favor.' or shorten to 'Naranja, por favor.' in informal ordering situations. 'Por favor' makes the request polite.
target_language_example: Dos vasos de jugo de naranja, por favor.
native_language_example: Two glasses of orange juice, please.

meaning: literally 'nose in' — used with verbs to say someone is interfering, poking their nose into something (e.g., 'meter la nariz en').
additional_notes: By itself 'nariz en' is not a complete phrase; Spanish uses expressions like 'meter la nariz en' or 'poner la nariz en' to mean 'to stick one's nose into' or 'to meddle in'. Common constructions: 'meter la nariz en (algo)' = interfere in something; 'poner la nariz en (algo)' = poke around. Often followed by 'algo' or a clause. Can be literal (physically putting nose into) or figurative (being nosy).
target_language_example: No metas la nariz en mi vida privada.
native_language_example: Don't stick your nose into my private life.

meaning: the nature of / the kind/type of
additional_notes: Used to describe the essential character, type, or cause of something. Often followed by a noun or clause (e.g. la naturaleza del problema, la naturaleza de su trabajo). Formal register is common but usable in everyday speech.
target_language_example: La naturaleza de ese problema es técnica, no financiera.
native_language_example: The nature of that problem is technical, not financial.

meaning: "nature is" or "the nature is" (usually part of a sentence describing what something is like)
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase on its own but the words 'naturaleza es' commonly appear when describing the character, essence, or type of something (e.g., 'La naturaleza es salvaje' — "Nature is wild" or 'La naturaleza es humana' — "The nature is human/people's nature is..."). In Spanish, 'naturaleza' can mean the natural world (nature) or the nature/essence/character of something. The verb 'es' is the third-person singular of 'ser' (to be).
target_language_example: La naturaleza es impredecible en primavera.
native_language_example: Nature is unpredictable in spring.

meaning: spacecraft; spaceship.
additional_notes: Refers to a vehicle designed for travel in outer space. Commonly used for both real spacecraft (e.g., rockets, capsules) and fictional spaceships in stories. 'Nave' alone can mean ship; 'espacial' = 'space' or 'space-related'.
target_language_example: La nave espacial despegó al amanecer.
native_language_example: The spacecraft took off at dawn.

meaning: urgent need; pressing requirement.
additional_notes: Used to describe a situation, resource, or action that requires immediate attention. Can refer to basic needs (food, medical care) or to urgent requests (repairs, decisions). Often used in formal or neutral contexts; can modify nouns (una necesidad urgente, necesidades urgentes).
target_language_example: Tenemos una necesidad urgente de medicinas en la clínica.
native_language_example: We have an urgent need for medicines at the clinic.

meaning: an urgent need for / a pressing need to
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is required immediately or is pressing. Commonly followed by a noun or an infinitive verb (e.g., necesidad urgente de ayuda, necesidad urgente de actuar). Formal and neutral register.
target_language_example: Hay una necesidad urgente de médicos en la zona afectada.
native_language_example: There is an urgent need for doctors in the affected area.

meaning: 'needs' or 'requires' (someone/something).
additional_notes: Used to say that someone or something requires another person, thing, or condition. Often followed by a noun or pronoun (e.g., necesita de ayuda, necesita de nosotros). In many contexts Spanish speakers also say simply necesita + direct object (necesita ayuda). Using necesita de can emphasize dependency or formality and is common with abstract needs (necesita de paciencia).
target_language_example: Ella necesita de ayuda para terminar el proyecto.
native_language_example: She needs help to finish the project.

meaning: 'needs the' (3rd person singular or formal 'you' + masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Combines the verb necesitar (to need) in third person singular (él/ella/usted necesita) with the masculine singular definite article el. Use before a masculine singular noun: necesita el libro (he/she/you formal needs the book). For feminine nouns use 'necesita la'. For plural: 'necesitan los/las'.
target_language_example: Ella necesita el coche para ir al trabajo.
native_language_example: She needs the car to go to work.

meaning: not a standard fixed phrase — appears to be two separate words 'necesita' (he/she/it/you formal needs) + 'es' (is).
additional_notes: This combination is not a set expression in Spanish and is grammatically odd when adjacent. It likely results from a sentence split, typo, or misordering. 'Necesita' is 3rd-person singular of necesitar (or formal usted); 'es' is 3rd-person singular of ser. In correct sentences they appear with other words (e.g., 'Necesita ayuda' = 'He/She needs help'; 'Es necesario' = 'It is necessary'). If you encounter 'necesita es', check for a missing punctuation, omitted words, or a word order error and rewrite to match intended meaning.
target_language_example: ¿Qué necesita es lo que vamos a discutir?
native_language_example: What 'needs is' is what we are going to discuss.

meaning: needs more / needs (someone/something) more.
additional_notes: Commonly used to say someone or something requires a greater amount, degree, or presence. Context determines what 'more' refers to (attention, support, time, resources, etc.). In sentences like "necesita más un padre" the word order emphasizes who is more needed. Can be used impersonally as "se necesita más" (more is needed) or with names: "Tom necesita más" (Tom needs more).
target_language_example: El bebé necesita más atención por la noche.
native_language_example: The baby needs more attention at night.

meaning: needs (that)
additional_notes: Used to introduce a subordinate clause with a different subject — often followed by the subjunctive (needs someone to do something or needs that something happen). Can also be followed by an infinitive when the subject is the same (necesita estudiar = he/she needs to study). Context determines whether it's a request, requirement, or necessity.
target_language_example: Ella necesita que llegues temprano.
native_language_example: She needs you to arrive early.

meaning: 'needs you' (intended literal reading but ungrammatical as written)
additional_notes: This sequence appears to combine the third-person singular verb 'necesita' with 'tu'. In standard Spanish 'tu' (without accent) is a possessive adjective ('your') and must be followed by a noun (e.g., 'necesita tu ayuda' = 'needs your help'). The subject pronoun 'tú' (with accent) is not used as a direct object; the correct object pronoun is 'te' (Él te necesita). Therefore 'necesita tu' on its own is generally ungrammatical or at least ambiguous. If intended meaning is 'needs you', use 'te necesita' or 'lo/la necesita' depending on formality/region. If intended meaning is 'needs your [noun]', follow 'tu' with the noun: 'necesita tu ayuda'.
target_language_example: ¿Por qué necesita tu ayuda si puede hacerlo solo?
native_language_example: Why does he/she need your help if they can do it alone?

meaning: needed (someone).
additional_notes: Used with a direct object person (a + name/pronoun) to say you needed someone. In Spanish, the preposition a marks a human direct object. The verb form necesitaba is imperfect (past, ongoing/continuous or habitual). Example shows both specific people (Necesitaba a Rob) and indefinite people (necesitaba a alguien).
target_language_example: Cuando estaba enfermo, necesitaba a mi madre.
native_language_example: When I was sick, I needed my mother.

meaning: we need (someone) here / we need (it) here
additional_notes: A common way to say that a person or thing is needed in the current place. 'Necesitamos' = we need; 'aquí' = here. Subject can be explicit (te, lo, le) or omitted. Use 'te necesitamos aquí' for 'we need you here' and 'lo/le necesitamos aquí' for 'we need him/it here' or 'we need you (formal) here.'
target_language_example: Te necesitamos aquí para terminar el proyecto.
native_language_example: We need you here to finish the project.

meaning: they need (someone/something specific).
additional_notes: Necesitan is the third-person plural of necesitar (to need). When the object is a specific person (or a named, definite person), Spanish often uses the preposition 'a' before the direct object (the 'personal a'). Use 'necesitan a' + person/noun to mean 'they need [that person]'. If the object is not a specific person (e.g., a thing or an indefinite person), 'a' may be omitted: 'necesitan ayuda' (they need help).
target_language_example: Necesitan a un doctor urgente.
native_language_example: They need a doctor urgently.

meaning: they need help.
additional_notes: Present tense third-person plural of necesitar + noun 'ayuda' (help). Used to say that a group of people requires assistance. In Spanish word order you can omit the subject: 'Necesitan ayuda.' Context or a subject (ellos/ellas/ustedes) can be added for clarity. 'Ayuda' is uncountable here and doesn't take an article in this use.
target_language_example: Ellos necesitan ayuda para completar el proyecto.
native_language_example: They need help to finish the project.

meaning: to need a
additional_notes: A common, straightforward combination of necesitar + un, used before a singular masculine noun or noun phrase: necesitar un trago, necesitar un guardaespaldas. In context, it often appears in conjugated forms such as voy a necesitar or vas a necesitar.
target_language_example: Voy a necesitar un mapa para llegar.
native_language_example: I'm going to need a map to get there.

meaning: 'you need help' or 'do you need help?'.
additional_notes: Present indicative of necesitar (tú necesitas) + ayuda. Used to state that someone requires help or to offer help by asking. Can be a statement (You need help) or a polite offer/question (Do you need help?). Context and intonation determine whether it's a question. Common in everyday situations.
target_language_example: ¿Necesitas ayuda con tus maletas?
native_language_example: Do you need help with your suitcases?

meaning: I need this (masculine singular item or situation).
additional_notes: Used to say you need a specific thing, amount, space, job, etc. 'Necesito' = I need; 'este' points to a nearby or specific masculine noun (este trabajo, este dinero, este lápiz). For feminine nouns use 'esta' (necesito esta mesa). Can express urgency by adding adverbs (por favor, con mucha urgencia).
target_language_example: Necesito este trabajo para pagar el alquiler.
native_language_example: I need this job to pay the rent.

meaning: I need my… (followed by a noun or object you possess).
additional_notes: A common phrase to express that you require something that belongs to you. 'Necesito' is the first-person singular present of necesitar. 'Mi' is the possessive adjective 'my' and must agree with the noun that follows (mi libro, mi teléfono). In speech you may hear the object immediately after: 'Necesito mi cargador.' If the object is omitted, it's assumed from context.
target_language_example: Necesito mi bolso para salir.
native_language_example: I need my bag to go out.

meaning: I need nothing / I don't need anything (nonstandard or emphatic).
additional_notes: Literally 'I need nothing'. Standard Spanish negation uses no + verb + nada (e.g., 'no necesito nada' = 'I don't need anything'). 'Necesito nada' without 'no' is nonstandard in most dialects and can sound incorrect; however, in some informal spoken varieties it may be used for emphasis or appear in shortened answers. For clear, correct speech use 'no necesito nada' or 'no necesito nada más' ('I don't need anything else').
target_language_example: No, gracias — no necesito nada.
native_language_example: No, thanks — I don't need anything.

meaning: 'I need to' or 'I need (something) for...' — a combination of the verb necesitar (first person singular) and the preposition para used to indicate purpose, benefit, or required item.
additional_notes: This sequence pairs necesito (I need) with para (for/to) and typically appears when seguido de un sustantivo or a clause introduced by a verb in infinitive (often as 'necesito [noun] para [infinitive]'). Using 'necesito para' alone without an object is incomplete; more natural forms include 'necesito + infinitive' (Necesito estudiar) or 'Necesito [algo] para + infinitive' (Necesito tiempo para estudiar).
target_language_example: Necesito para viajar a España conseguir mi pasaporte a tiempo.
native_language_example: I need, in order to travel to Spain, to get my passport in time.

meaning: I need your / I need his/her/its (formal: your).
additional_notes: A short phrase combining the verb necesitar (to need) with the possessive su. English translation depends on context and the possessor: su can mean his, her, its, your (formal), or their. In Spanish word order, the possessed noun usually follows (e.g., necesito su ayuda = I need your/his/her help). Use su + noun; su alone without a noun is incomplete unless context makes the noun obvious.
target_language_example: Necesito su ayuda para completar el formulario.
native_language_example: I need your help to complete the form.

meaning: I need your help.
additional_notes: Polite, direct way to ask for assistance. 'Necesito' = 'I need'; 'su' is the formal or third-person possessive ('your' formal or his/her/their depending on context). Use 'tu' instead of 'su' (necesito tu ayuda) for informal situations with friends/family. To be more polite, add 'por favor' or soften with '¿Podría...?': '¿Podría ayudarme, por favor?'
target_language_example: Disculpe, necesito su ayuda con este formulario.
native_language_example: Excuse me, I need your help with this form.

meaning: I need your help.
additional_notes: A direct, common way to ask someone for assistance. 'Necesito' = 'I need'; 'tu' is informal singular 'your' (use 'su' for formal or plural usted/ustedes). Can be used in many contexts (asking for physical help, advice, a favor). Tone depends on context and intonation.
target_language_example: Disculpa, necesito tu ayuda con este informe.
native_language_example: Excuse me, I need your help with this report.

meaning: 'business is' or 'the business is' (literal); often part of a larger sentence about a business or matter.
additional_notes: By itself 'negocio es' is not a complete fixed phrase in Spanish. 'Negocio' means 'business, shop, deal, or matter' and 'es' is the third-person singular of 'ser' (is). You will usually see this combination inside sentences like 'El negocio es rentable' (The business is profitable) or 'El negocio es mío' (The business is mine). Use it when describing what a business or matter is (identity, quality, or state).
target_language_example: El negocio es nuevo y tiene mucho potencial.
native_language_example: The business is new and has a lot of potential.

meaning: 'business in' or 'doing business in' (indicates commercial activity or businesses located in a place).
additional_notes: Used to say someone is conducting business in a location (hacer negocios en) or to indicate businesses located in a place (negocios en + lugar). Context determines whether it refers to the activity (doing business) or to establishments (businesses). Common with countries, cities, online (Internet) and locations.
target_language_example: Ella hace negocios en México.
native_language_example: She does business in Mexico.

meaning: literally 'black of the' — not a fixed phrase; appears to be part of a larger expression or sentence fragment
additional_notes: This is not a standalone idiom. 'Negra' can be an adjective meaning 'black' or a feminine noun (e.g., colloquial term for a Black woman or a dark thing) depending on context. 'De la' is the feminine singular contraction of 'de' + 'la' meaning 'of the' or 'from the'. Together, 'negra de la' would typically be followed by another noun (e.g., 'la negra de la casa' — 'the black (woman) of the house' or 'la canción negra de la radio' — 'the black song on the radio') or form part of a regional/colloquial expression. Watch for register: referring to a person as 'negra' can be affectionate in some Spanish-speaking communities but offensive in others; use with caution and follow local usage.
target_language_example: La negra de la novela tiene un papel importante.
native_language_example: The black (female) character in the novel has an important role.

meaning: the (female) black sheep of the family; a woman considered the odd or shameful member of the family
additional_notes: Colloquial and potentially offensive. Literally 'black (feminine) of the family.' Used to refer to a family member (female) viewed as an embarrassment, outcast, or who doesn't fit norms. Context and tone matter — can be very hurtful. Avoid using about real people unless you understand cultural sensitivity.
target_language_example: Siempre la han tratado como la negra de la familia, aunque ella no hace daño a nadie.
native_language_example: They have always treated her like the black sheep of the family, even though she doesn't harm anyone.

meaning: 'negro' (black) followed by the preposition 'de' (of/from) — used when describing something as black in relation to or made of something, often linking the adjective to a following noun phrase introduced by 'de'.
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom by itself; it's the adjective 'negro' plus 'de'. Appears in constructions like 'sombrero negro de ala ancha' or 'negro de carbón' where 'de' introduces material, origin, or a qualifying noun. Remember Spanish adjective placement is flexible, but 'negro de' specifically requires a subsequent noun phrase. 'Negro' can denote color or refer to race/culture — use respectfully and contextually.
target_language_example: Sombrero negro de ala ancha.
native_language_example: Black wide-brimmed hat.

meaning: (he/she/you formal) denied (to) or refused (to) someone — used when the verb negar takes an indirect object ('a alguien').
additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of negar used with an indirect object: 'negar a alguien' means to deny someone something or to refuse someone. Context determines whether it's 'denied' (e.g., denied access, denied a claim) or 'refused' (e.g., refused a request). If you want to say someone refused to do something, use 'negarse a' + infinitive (e.g., 'se negó a ayudar'). Subject can be él/ella/usted (negó). Pronouns and preposition 'a' are required when specifying the person affected: e.g., 'le negó a María' or 'les negó a los trabajadores'.
target_language_example: El director le negó a Marta la oportunidad de hablar en la reunión.
native_language_example: The director denied Marta the opportunity to speak at the meeting.

meaning: 'no idea (about) what' or 'not the slightest idea of what...'
additional_notes: Used to say you don't know something at all. Often appears in longer phrases like "no tengo ni idea de lo que..." or simply "ni idea" in casual speech. Commonly followed by a clause (lo que + verb) or a noun phrase. Polite and neutral in tone.
target_language_example: No tengo ni idea de lo que pasó anoche.
native_language_example: I have no idea what happened last night.

meaning: not even
additional_notes: used to emphasize a negative idea: that something does not happen or is not true at all, even in the smallest degree. It often appears before the verb, and in English it is frequently translated as “not even” or “didn’t even.”
target_language_example: Ni siquiera tengo tiempo para desayunar.
native_language_example: I don't even have time for breakfast.

meaning: not even the
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something (usually a person or thing introduced by 'el') is not included or does not do something. Often appears in negative sentences: 'ni siquiera' = 'not even'; 'el' is the definite article for a masculine singular noun or a masculine singular role/title (can also be used before a masculine pronoun like 'él' with accent, but here it's the article). Watch word order: 'ni siquiera el + noun' or 'ni siquiera el + pronoun/name' to single out the excluded item.
target_language_example: Ni siquiera el profesor supo la respuesta.
native_language_example: Not even the teacher knew the answer.

meaning: a contraction used to join negatives or to say 'not even' before a masculine singular infinitive or noun phrase introduced by 'a' (often part of 'ni... ni...' or 'ni... al...' constructions).
additional_notes: Common in negative constructions. 'Ni' means 'nor' or 'not even'. When followed by the preposition 'a' + article 'el', you get 'al' (a + el = al). 'Ni al' often appears before a noun or infinitive introduced by 'a' (e.g., 'ni al hablar' = 'not even by speaking' or 'ni al perro le gusta' = 'not even the dog likes it'). Context determines translation: sometimes 'not even' or 'nor to'.
target_language_example: No lo escuchó ni al profesor.
native_language_example: He didn't even listen to the teacher.

meaning: 'nor' or 'not even' used in negative constructions (often before a noun or verb phrase).
additional_notes: Used to join negative elements or to emphasize exclusion. Commonly appears in pairs like 'ni... ni...' (neither... nor...). When used alone after a negative verb it can mean 'not even' (e.g., 'No me dijo ni de su viaje' = 'He didn't even tell me about his trip').
target_language_example: No vino ni de lejos a ayudar.
native_language_example: He didn't even come close to helping.

meaning: no way; don't even mention it; absolutely not
additional_notes: Used to strongly reject an idea, topic, or suggestion. Can mean 'don't even talk about it' (don't bring it up) or simply 'no way' as a firm refusal. Common in spoken Spanish and can be standalone.
target_language_example: ¿Vas a dejar todo el trabajo para mañana? — Ni hablar.
native_language_example: Are you going to leave all the work for tomorrow? — No way.

meaning: no idea; not knowing something.
additional_notes: Used to say you don't know or have no clue. Common both in full sentences and as a short exclamation ("¡Ni idea!"). Can be used with or without a subject: "No tengo ni idea" = "I have no idea." Often informal but widely used in neutral contexts.
target_language_example: ¿Sabes quién vino anoche? — Ni idea.
native_language_example: Do you know who came last night? — No idea.

meaning: 'no idea that' or 'not a clue that' — expresses complete lack of knowledge about something
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that someone does not know or was unaware of a fact or situation. Often appears in negative sentences (with no, no tengo, etc.). Can be followed by a clause introduced by que. Tone is neutral; common in spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: No tenía ni idea de que ibas a venir hoy.
native_language_example: I had no idea that you were coming today.

meaning: 'nor the' or 'not even the' (used to negate and add items in a list).
additional_notes: 'Ni' is a coordinating negative word meaning 'nor' or 'neither'. Combined with a definite article and noun (here 'los'), 'ni los' introduces another negative item in a list. Common in sentences like: 'No quiero ni los zapatos ni la chaqueta' = 'I don't want the shoes or the jacket.' Depending on context it can emphasize exclusion ('not even the...'). After a negative verb (
target_language_example: No me gustan los libros ni los periódicos.
native_language_example: I don't like books or newspapers.

meaning: 'not even me' or used to emphasize that something does not apply to the speaker (often part of a longer phrase).
additional_notes: Ni + pronoun (ni yo, ni tú) is used for emphasis or to list negatives. 'Ni me' usually appears before verbs or clauses (e.g., 'ni me acuerdo' = 'I don't even remember'). It can mean 'I don't even...' or 'don't even (ask) me' depending on context. Not a standalone sentence in most cases — it's typically followed by a verb or phrase.
target_language_example: Ni me acuerdo de cuándo fue la última vez.
native_language_example: I don't even remember when the last time was.

meaning: not even my / nor my (used to emphasize exclusion of something belonging to the speaker)
additional_notes: Ni + noun/pronoun is used to add emphasis or to list negatives (equivalent to 'not even' or 'nor'). 'Ni mi' specifically excludes something of mine. Often part of longer phrases: 'ni mi casa' (not even my house) or 'ni mi madre' (not even my mother). In speech it can be used alone for emphasis: 'Ni mi.'
target_language_example: No me dejaron entrar, ni mi carné servía.
native_language_example: They didn't let me in; not even my ID worked.

meaning: certainly not; far from it; not by any means.
additional_notes: Used to strongly deny or reject something. Often follows or precedes a statement to emphasize that the reality is the opposite or that something is much less true than suggested. Common in spoken and written Spanish. Equivalent to 'not at all' or 'far from it.'
target_language_example: ¿Es rica? Ni mucho menos; apenas tiene para pagar las cuentas.
native_language_example: Is she rich? Far from it; she barely has enough to pay the bills.

meaning: neither... nor...; not even; used to deny or exclude two or more things
additional_notes: Commonly appears as the paired construction 'ni... ni...' to connect two negatives (e.g., 'ni A ni B'). It can also be used alone for emphasis ('¡Ni!') or in colloquial refusals. Tone ranges from neutral to informal depending on context.
target_language_example: Ni ni lo vi ni lo escuché.
native_language_example: I neither saw it nor heard it.

meaning: not even for a (single) — used in negative emphatic expressions (often followed by 'segundo', 'momento', 'instante', etc.)
additional_notes: This fragment is used to emphasize that something would not happen even for the smallest amount of time or for any reason. It usually appears in negative sentences with words like 'segundo', 'momento', 'instante', 'minuto' or before phrases like 'asomo', 'razón'. Example full pattern: 'ni por un segundo / ni por un momento.'
target_language_example: No volveré allí ni por un segundo.
native_language_example: I won't go back there not even for a second.

meaning: used to disagree, downplay or reject a statement — similar to 'as if' / 'no way' / 'it's not like...'.
additional_notes: Common in informal Spanish. Often appears at the start of a reply to show disbelief, irritation, or to deny an implied comparison. Can be followed by a clause (Ni que fuera...) or used alone/shortly (Ni que...) or with expletives for emphasis. Tone and exact meaning depend on context; here it's dismissive.
target_language_example: Ni que fuera tan fácil.
native_language_example: As if it were that easy.

meaning: used to emphasize negation or impossibility; often part of fixed expressions meaning 'not even' or 'nor even'.
additional_notes: Often appears before verbs or clauses to stress that something does not happen, not even in a minimal case. Common in structures like 'ni siquiera' (not even) or in elliptical phrases: e.g., 'Ni se inmuta' (He doesn't even flinch). Alone, 'ni se' typically requires more words to complete the idea; learners will most often see it as part of longer expressions.
target_language_example: Ni se dio por aludido cuando le llamé.
native_language_example: He didn't even think I meant him when I called.

meaning: not even his/her/its/their; neither his/her/its/their
additional_notes: Combination of 'ni' (not even / neither) + possessive adjective 'su'. Used to emphasize that something does not apply to the person or thing in question (e.g., 'ni su casa' = not even his/her house). Common in negative contexts or comparisons. Requires context for gender/number of possessed noun (su stays the same).
target_language_example: No le gustó ni su propio trabajo ni su reconocimiento.
native_language_example: He didn't like even his own work or his recognition.

meaning: not even you / don't even (do something); used to emphasize negation or to warn someone not to do something.
additional_notes: Exact meaning depends on context. As part of a negative phrase, 'ni' = 'not even' and 'te' is the object pronoun 'you' or reflexive 'yourself'. Common in constructions like 'ni te imaginas' (you can't even imagine) or as a warning 'ni te acerques' (don't you even come near). Often used for strong emphasis.
target_language_example: Ni te imaginas lo que pasó anoche.
native_language_example: You can't even imagine what happened last night.

meaning: not even you; neither you (in negative or emphatic contexts).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that someone (you) is excluded, cannot do/believe something, or is not involved. Often appears in negative sentences (Eso no te lo crees ni tú = 'Not even you would believe that') and in coordination with other subjects (Ni tú ni yo = 'Neither you nor I'). Can stand alone as a short retort (Ni tú. = 'You too' or 'Neither do/did you' depending on context).
target_language_example: Ni tú ni nadie sabía la verdad.
native_language_example: Not even you nor anyone knew the truth.

meaning: not even one
additional_notes: Used to emphasize absence or exclusion. Can appear alone as a short reply ("Ni uno.") meaning "not even one". In lists or contrasts it's often part of "ni uno ni otro" or "ni uno ni lo otro" meaning "neither one nor the other." Strong negative force—often used with other negatives.
target_language_example: No hubo ni uno que ayudara.
native_language_example: There wasn't even one person who helped.

meaning: 'refuses to' (followed by an infinitive verb) — indicates someone refuses to do something or refuses someone/something.
additional_notes: Used with a reflexive pronoun (se) for people who refuse; followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., negarse a + infinitive). Can also be used transitively (negar a alguien) to mean 'deny someone' or 'refuse someone', but in the examples it means refusing to perform actions or to cooperate. Common in formal and informal contexts.
target_language_example: Se niega a ayudarme con la mudanza.
native_language_example: He refuses to help me with the move.

meaning: 'snow of' or used to indicate a flavor/type made with snow or shaved ice (literally 'snow of').
additional_notes: Literally means 'snow of' and is often used in compound phrases like 'nieve de limón' (lemon shaved-ice/ice cream) or 'nieve de coco'. In many Spanish-speaking regions 'nieve' can mean snow, but also a type of local ice cream, sorbet, or shaved ice. You will usually see 'nieve de' followed by a noun naming the flavor or origin.
target_language_example: Quiero una nieve de mango, por favor.
native_language_example: I want a mango shaved-ice/ice cream, please.

meaning: snow from the (feminine noun) — used when saying snow was removed or came off something (e.g., 'la nieve de la calle' = the snow from the street).
additional_notes: This phrase combines nieve (snow) with a following feminine noun introduced by 'la' (for example: 'nieve de la calle', 'nieve de la entrada'). Often used with verbs like quitar, limpiar, or sacar when talking about removing snow. Change the article if the noun is masculine (nieve del coche → nieve de + el = del).
target_language_example: Quitamos la nieve de la entrada esta mañana.
native_language_example: We removed the snow from the driveway this morning.

meaning: Likely a typo or incorrect word order; not a grammatical Spanish phrase. Possible intended forms: 'la nieve' (the snow) as a noun phrase, or 'nieva' (it snows) as the impersonal verb form.
additional_notes: Two common possibilities: 1) If intended as a noun phrase, the correct form is 'la nieve' because 'nieve' is feminine. 2) If intended to express snowfall, the correct impersonal verb is 'nieva' (e.g., 'Hoy nieva'). 'nieve el' as written mixes the feminine noun with the masculine article and is ungrammatical. It may appear in written text only as a typographical error or in fragmented speech, but it should be avoided in correct Spanish.
target_language_example: En el cartel alguien escribió por error: 'nieve el' en lugar de 'la nieve'.
native_language_example: On the sign someone wrote by mistake: 'nieve el' instead of 'la nieve'.

meaning: snows in / there is snow in (a place).
additional_notes: A phrase fragment used to indicate the presence of snow in a location. More common in Spanish is the conjugated verb form 'nieva en' for current weather, but 'nieve en' can appear in descriptions, headlines, signs, or as part of longer noun phrases (e.g., 'nieve en el norte', 'nieve en la montaña'). Often followed by a place name or noun. Tone neutral; suitable for news or descriptive contexts.
target_language_example: Nieve en la sierra cubre las cabañas.
native_language_example: Snow in the mountains covers the cabins.

meaning: 'no problem' or 'not a problem'.
additional_notes: Used to say something is not an issue or to reassure someone. Ningún is the negative form of 'algún' and must agree with a singular masculine noun; with plural nouns use 'ningunos' rarely — usually 'ningún/ninguna' + singular noun is used. Common in everyday speech and polite contexts.
target_language_example: No hay ningún problema con la fecha; podemos cambiarla.
native_language_example: There is no problem with the date; we can change it.

meaning: girl of / girl from (used to describe a girl belonging to or associated with something/someone).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself; it's the word niña ('girl') followed by the preposition de ('of/from'). It appears in expressions like niña de la casa (girl of the house/the daughter who lives in the house), niña de mi barrio (girl from my neighborhood), or niña de ojos (poetic). The meaning depends on the noun or pronoun that follows de. Pay attention to gender/number agreement when the noun requires adjectives.
target_language_example: Ella es la niña de la familia más simpática.
native_language_example: She is the nicest girl in the family.

meaning: literally 'girl in' — not a fixed phrase; 'niña' means 'girl' and 'en' means 'in' or 'on'.
additional_notes: This is not a single set expression. 'Niña' (feminine noun) is commonly followed by prepositions like 'en' to indicate location or state: e.g. 'la niña en la foto' (the girl in the photo) or 'la niña en el parque' (the girl in the park). Make sure articles and adjectives agree in gender and number (la niña, las niñas).
target_language_example: La niña en la escuela está leyendo un libro.
native_language_example: The girl in the school is reading a book.

meaning: 'she is a girl' or 'the girl is' (depends on context).
additional_notes: 'Niña' means 'girl' (a female child). 'Es' is the third-person singular present of 'ser' (to be). Together they appear in sentences like 'La niña es inteligente' (The girl is smart) or in answers like 'Niña es María' (She is a girl — María). Without more context, 'niña es' is an incomplete phrase and usually needs more words (a subject/article or a complement).
target_language_example: La niña es mi hermana.
native_language_example: The girl is my sister.

meaning: the girl is / the girl is (doing/feeling/etc.)
additional_notes: This is the phrase formed by the noun niña (girl) plus the verb estar (to be). Use 'niña está' as part of a sentence to describe a temporary state, location, or condition of a girl (e.g., 'La niña está cansada' — the girl is tired). Remember subject-verb order in full sentences: usually 'La niña está...'. Without the article 'la', 'niña está' can appear in clipped contexts (headlines, notes, captions) but is not a complete neutral sentence in standard speech.
target_language_example: La niña está en el parque.
native_language_example: The girl is in the park.

meaning: likely a fragment; 'niña' = 'girl'. 'le' is an indirect object pronoun (to/for her), but 'niña le' by itself is not a complete standard phrase.
additional_notes: This looks like two separate words rather than a fixed multiword expression. 'Niña' means 'girl' (young female). 'Le' is the third-person singular indirect-object pronoun used in many Spanish varieties (to/for him, her, you formal). In standard Spanish you would usually see them combined in a sentence (e.g., 'Le di un juguete a la niña' = 'I gave a toy to the girl'). You would not normally say 'niña le' alone; word order depends on the sentence and whether you use a clitic pronoun plus a noun (often used for emphasis or clarification: 'A la niña le gusta bailar').
target_language_example: A la niña le gusta el helado.
native_language_example: The girl likes ice cream. (Literally: To the girl, ice cream is pleasing.)

meaning: 'very' + 'girl' (literal: 'very girl').
additional_notes: This combination is not a fixed phrase in Spanish. 'Niña' means 'girl' and 'muy' is an adverb meaning 'very' used to modify adjectives or other adverbs, not nouns directly. To say 'very (young) girl' or emphasize a quality, you must add an adjective after 'muy' (e.g., 'niña muy pequeña' = 'a very small/young girl'). You can also use 'muy' with adjectives that describe the girl: 'niña muy lista' (a very clever girl). Saying only 'niña muy' is incomplete.
target_language_example: Es una niña muy inteligente.
native_language_example: She is a very intelligent girl.

meaning: literally 'girl, no' — a short, informal way to tell a girl 'no' or to refuse something addressed to a girl; often a clipped reproach or firm denial when speaking directly to a girl
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom; it's simply the vocative 'niña' followed by the negative 'no'. Tone and context determine whether it's scolding, playful, or emphatic. More common orders in Spanish are 'no, niña' or using 'chica' or a name; 'niña no' appears in rapid spoken dialogue or as a brusque interruption. Informal register.
target_language_example: — ¿Puedo ir al concierto? — Niña no, todavía eres muy joven.
native_language_example: — Can I go to the concert? — Girl no, you're still too young.

meaning: 'girl who' — used to introduce a relative clause describing a girl.
additional_notes: Combines niña (girl) with the relative pronoun que (who/that). Use to add information about a specific girl: niña que + verb or adjective. In Spanish the clause follows the noun (niña que canta, la niña que vive aquí). If the noun is definite/specific, include an article (la niña que...).
target_language_example: La niña que canta en el parque es mi hermana.
native_language_example: The girl who sings in the park is my sister.

meaning: This is not a fixed phrase; it's likely just the word niña ('girl') followed by the pronoun se. Meaning depends on the full sentence.
additional_notes: You won't find 'niña se' alone as a standard multiword expression. 'Niña' means 'girl'. 'Se' is a versatile pronoun used for reflexive actions, passive/impersonal constructions, or to indicate accidental actions. To understand 'niña se' you need the rest of the sentence (for example: 'La niña se cayó' = 'The girl fell' (reflexive/accidental), or 'Se vio a la niña' = 'The girl was seen' (passive/impersonal)).
target_language_example: La niña se cayó mientras corría.
native_language_example: The girl fell while she was running.

meaning: the girl has / the girl is (literally: 'girl has').
additional_notes: Combines niña (girl) + tiene (3rd person singular of tener). Used to describe possession, feelings, physical traits, or states (e.g., 'tiene miedo' = 'is afraid'). In English you often say 'the girl has' or use 'the girl is' for states (has fear = is afraid). Adjust translation to context.
target_language_example: La niña tiene una bicicleta nueva.
native_language_example: The girl has a new bicycle.

meaning: Looks like part of a phrase meaning "girl and..." — literally "girl and".
additional_notes: This appears to be the words 'niña' (girl, feminine) followed by the conjunction 'y' (and). By itself it's incomplete; you need another noun, adjective or clause after 'y' to finish the idea (e.g., 'niña y niño' = 'girl and boy', or 'niña y feliz' would be ungrammatical — adjectives usually agree: 'niña y feliz' should be 'niña feliz' or 'niña y alegre' if two qualities). Note that 'y' is pronounced [i] and becomes 'e' before words starting with 'i' or 'hi' (e.g., 'madre e hija').
target_language_example: La niña y el niño juegan en el parque.
native_language_example: The girl and the boy play in the park.

meaning: the girls (female children) + reflexive/reciprocal clitic 'se' indicating actions they do to/for themselves or to each other (they laughed, they fell asleep, they started ...).
additional_notes: Niñas = plural feminine noun 'girls'. The short word 'se' is a clitic used with verbs to form reflexive actions (they washed themselves), reciprocal actions (they fought each other), or to mark intransitive changes of state/automatic actions (they fell asleep). In many English translations 'se' is not a separate word but included in the verb (they fell asleep / they started to laugh). Word order: subject + se + verb (Las niñas se durmieron).
target_language_example: Las niñas se lavaron las manos antes de comer.
native_language_example: The girls washed their hands before eating.

meaning: literally 'child of' or 'son of' — used to indicate belonging, origin, age group, or an affectionate/identifying phrase (e.g., 'niño de la calle', 'niño de 10 años').
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself; 'niño' (boy/child) followed by 'de' connects to another noun or phrase that describes relationship, origin, age, characteristic, or possession. Common uses: 'niño de [edad]' = 'a child of [age]'; 'niño de [lugar]' = 'child from [place]'; 'niño de [persona]' = 'child of [person]'. Word order and article usage matter (e.g., 'niño de la calle' = 'street child').
target_language_example: Es un niño de 8 años que vive en el barrio.
native_language_example: He is an 8-year-old child who lives in the neighborhood.

meaning: literally 'child in' — not a fixed phrase; usually part of a larger expression (e.g., 'niño en la escuela' = 'child in school').
additional_notes: This sequence is not a standalone idiom in Spanish. 'Niño' means 'boy' or 'child' and 'en' is a preposition meaning 'in' or 'at'. You will typically see 'niño en' followed by a place, time, or situation (niño en casa, niño en la ciudad, niño en el hospital). Pay attention to context and the article/gender/number: niño (singular, male), niña (female), niños (plural).
target_language_example: Hay un niño en la plaza.
native_language_example: There is a child in the square.

meaning: 'boy/child in the' (a short phrase combining niño + en + el).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom—it's the noun 'niño' (boy/child) followed by the preposition 'en' (in/at) and the definite article 'el' (the). It appears when specifying a location: 'the child in the [place]'. Word order will change with the location that follows ('niño en el suelo', 'niño en el garaje', etc.). Note: 'niño' can also mean 'child' (male) or be used generically for a young child; use 'niña' for a girl.
target_language_example: Vi al niño en el jardín.
native_language_example: I saw the child in the garden.

meaning: 'a child in the...'.
additional_notes: This phrase is the start of a location phrase: niño (boy/child) + en la (in the + feminine noun). The full meaning depends on the noun that follows (e.g., 'niño en la casa' = 'a child in the house', 'niño en la habitación' = 'a child in the room'). Use 'en el' before masculine nouns (niño en el coche).
target_language_example: Hay un niño en la cocina.
native_language_example: There is a child in the kitchen.

meaning: 'the child was' — simple past/state description using 'estar' with 'niño'.
additional_notes: Combines the noun 'niño' (child/boy) with the past-imperfect/preterite context of 'estar' to describe a temporary state or location. In the examples, 'estaba' describes position (echado), emotion/feeling (lleno de curiosidad, paralizado de miedo), location (perdido en el bosque) or presence (estaba en mi casa). Use 'niño estaba' when referring to what the child was like or where he was at a given time. For gender/number agreement, change 'niño' to 'niña' for a girl and 'estaba' to 'estaban' for plural.
target_language_example: El niño estaba contento después de jugar.
native_language_example: The child was happy after playing.

meaning: the child has (used as part of a sentence with a compound verb or perfect tense)
additional_notes: This is not a standalone phrase; it's the noun niño (child/boy) followed by the auxiliary ha (from haber) meaning 'has' in third person singular. You'll see it in sentences like «El niño ha comido» (The child has eaten). Remember subject-verb order in Spanish can vary, but here niño is the subject and ha is the auxiliary for the present perfect (ha + past participle).
target_language_example: El niño ha terminado su tarea.
native_language_example: The child has finished his homework.

meaning: a child speaks / the child speaks
additional_notes: A simple subject + verb phrase: niño (child / boy) + habla (he/she/it speaks). Often used with clauses like 'como si...' (as if...) to describe how the child speaks (e.g., like an adult). 'Niño' can mean 'boy' or 'child' depending on context; for a girl use 'niña'. Verb 'habla' is the 3rd person singular present of hablar.
target_language_example: El niño habla con mucha confianza, como si fuera un adulto.
native_language_example: The child speaks very confidently, as if he were an adult.

meaning: 'the boy' + indirect-object pronoun 'le' used before a verb (he to/for someone or 'to him/her')
additional_notes: This shows two separate pieces: 'el niño' = the boy, and 'le' = indirect-object pronoun meaning 'to him/to her/to you (formal)'. In Spanish word order the pronoun often appears before the verb (e.g., 'le dio' = 'gave to her/him'). 'Le' can indicate the person who receives something or the person affected by the action (e.g., 'le teme' = 'he fears him/her/it'). Pay attention to context to know whether 'le' refers to 'to her', 'to him', or another person.
target_language_example: El niño le contó un secreto a su amiga.
native_language_example: The boy told a secret to his friend.

meaning: literal combination: 'child very' — not a normal fixed phrase in Spanish; appears to be two words that would need reordering or completion (e.g., 'niño muy alto' = 'a very tall boy').
additional_notes: By itself, 'niño muy' is incomplete. In Spanish the adjective or adjective phrase follows the noun: 'niño muy + adjective' (niño muy inteligente, niño muy pequeño). You can also say 'muy niño' in some contexts to mean 'very childish' but that has a different meaning. For a simple noun phrase meaning 'very [adjective] child' use 'niño muy + adjective'.
target_language_example: Es un niño muy curioso.
native_language_example: He is a very curious child.

meaning: literally 'child more' — not a standard fixed phrase; likely part of a larger expression (e.g., 'el niño más ...' = 'the most ... child' or 'another/one more child' depending on context).
additional_notes: By itself, 'niño más' is not a common standalone phrase in Spanish. It can appear in different contexts: 1) as part of a superlative: 'el niño más alto' = 'the tallest child'; 2) to mean 'one more child' when combined with an article/number: 'un niño más' = 'one more child' or 'another child'; 3) in comparisons: 'niño más ... que' appears inside comparative structures. You will rarely use 'niño más' alone without additional words (adjective, number, or clause).
target_language_example: Quiero un niño más, por favor.
native_language_example: I want one more child, please.

meaning: 'child, no' — a vocative 'niño' followed by 'no', used to directly refuse or stop a child; literally 'child, no'.
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom; reads as addressing a child ('niño') and immediately rejecting or forbidding something ('no'). Tone and context (often urgent or corrective) determine force. Can appear with comma or pause: 'Niño no...' or 'Niño, no...'; the comma reflects natural speech but the exact two-word sequence 'niño no' occurs in spoken and written Spanish when the pause is not marked. Examples often continue with a verb or clause.
target_language_example: — ¿Puedo tocar la sartén? — Niño no, está caliente.
native_language_example: — Can I touch the pan? — Child, no, it's hot.

meaning: 'when (I) was a child, (I) could...' — expresses ability or habit in childhood
additional_notes: This phrase combines a time expression (cuando/de niño = 'when I was a child' or 'as a child') with podía (imperfect of poder) to talk about abilities, habitual actions, or general states in the past. Common alternatives: «cuando era niño», «de pequeño/a». The subject (yo) is often omitted because the verb form indicates it.
target_language_example: De niño podía leer libros largos en una tarde.
native_language_example: As a child I could read long books in one afternoon.

meaning: literally 'boy/child who' — used to start a clause describing a child (e.g., 'the child who...').
additional_notes: Composed of niño (boy/child) + que (who/that). Used to introduce a relative clause about a child. Must agree in gender/number if you change 'niño' (niña, niños, niñas). In many contexts you might see just 'el niño que...' (the child who...).
target_language_example: El niño que juega en el parque es mi primo.
native_language_example: The child who plays in the park is my cousin.

meaning: This looks like two words: niño (boy/child) and the reflexive/pronoun se; by itself 'niño se' is not a fixed phrase. It likely appears as part of a sentence where 'se' is a reflexive or passive/impersonal marker (e.g. 'el niño se cayó' = 'the boy fell').
additional_notes: Treat as two separate elements: 'niño' = boy/child (masculine noun). 'se' is a pronoun used for reflexive verbs (él se lava), for accidental/passive constructions (se me rompió), or as a passive/impersonal marker (se vende). Beginners should not memorize 'niño se' as one unit; instead learn 'niño' and the uses of 'se' and see example sentences combining them.
target_language_example: El niño se cayó y se lastimó la rodilla.
native_language_example: The boy fell and hurt his knee.

meaning: the child has / the boy has
additional_notes: Combination of niño (child/boy) + tiene (he/she/it has). Used to say that a child/ boy possesses or experiences something (e.g., tiene hambre = is hungry, tiene un juguete = has a toy). Context determines whether 'niño' means 'child' (gender-neutral in some contexts) or specifically 'boy'. Pronunciation: 'NEE-nyo TYEH-neh'.
target_language_example: El niño tiene un perro.
native_language_example: The child has a dog.

meaning: the boy has a/an — indicates possession by a boy.
additional_notes: This phrase is the start of a simple sentence showing possession: niño (boy) + tiene (has) + un (a/an). Use 'el niño' or 'este niño' to specify which boy. Change 'un' to 'una' for feminine nouns (e.g., 'la niña tiene una muñeca'). For plural, use 'los niños tienen...' and 'unos/unas' for 'some'.
target_language_example: El niño tiene un juguete nuevo.
native_language_example: The boy has a new toy.

meaning: 'child and' — literal combination of niño (child/boy) + y (and).
additional_notes: This looks like two words joined but is not a fixed phrase by itself in Spanish. 'Niño' means 'child' (often 'boy') and 'y' means 'and'. You'll see 'niño y...' when listing or combining things (e.g., 'niño y niña' = 'boy and girl'). Use gender-appropriate forms: 'niño' (male child), 'niña' (female child), and plural 'niños' (children or mixed group).
target_language_example: Había un niño y una niña en el parque.
native_language_example: There was a boy and a girl in the park.

meaning: This combination is not a standalone fixed phrase in Spanish; it is simply the plural noun 'niños' ('children') followed by the preposition 'a' ('to/at/for'). It typically appears as part of a larger phrase (for example to indicate motion toward something, an indirect object, or to introduce an infinitive).
additional_notes: 'Niños a' by itself is incomplete and uncommon; you will normally see it inside longer constructions such as 'niños a bordo', 'niños a cargo', or as part of a clause like 'los niños a la salida'. The preposition 'a' can mark direction ('a la escuela'), the indirect object ('dar algo a los niños'), or link verbs with infinitives ('enseñar a los niños a leer'). If you intended a specific idiom, provide the full phrase.
target_language_example: Darles de comer a los niños a la hora del recreo.
native_language_example: To feed the children at recess time.

meaning: likely part of a larger phrase meaning 'children at the.../children to the...'; by itself it's incomplete
additional_notes: This sequence is not a standalone phrase in Spanish. It looks like the beginning of a clause such as 'niños a la escuela' (children to/at school) or 'niños a la playa' (children at the beach). Beginners should recognize 'niños' = 'children' and the preposition 'a la' = 'to the' or 'at the' (feminine singular noun follows). You will normally see it completed with a feminine noun (la + noun).
target_language_example: Llevé a los niños a la escuela esta mañana.
native_language_example: I took the children to the school this morning.

meaning: 'children to/at' (combination of 'niños' + preposition 'al')
additional_notes: This isn't a fixed phrase on its own. It looks like the noun 'niños' (children) followed by the contraction 'al' (a + el = to the / at the). You will often see similar sequences inside longer sentences, for example 'los niños al parque' (more correctly 'los niños al parque' should be 'los niños al parque' or better 'los niños van al parque') or 'Cuidan a los niños al llegar' (better: 'cuidan a los niños al llegar' = 'they take care of the children upon arriving'). Make sure the grammar around it is correct: verbs and articles often change word order and require small words like 'a' or 'los'.
target_language_example: Llevaron a los niños al médico.
native_language_example: They took the children to the doctor.

meaning: children to (the) school / kids going to school
additional_notes: Common phrase used when talking about taking or sending children to school. Often appears in contexts like 'llevar a los niños al colegio' (to take the children to school) or 'los niños van al colegio' (the children go to school). 'Colegio' usually means primary or secondary school in Spain/Latin America. Use definite article 'el colegio' or possessive 'mis/los' as needed.
target_language_example: Mañana llevo a los niños al colegio a las ocho.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I take the children to school at eight.

meaning: children should / must
additional_notes: Combines 'niños' (children) + 'deben' (third-person plural of deber). Used to state recommendations, obligations, or expectations about children. Tone can be stronger (must/obliged) or softer (should) depending on context; context and intonation determine force. Verb agrees with 'niños' and can be replaced by other subjects (e.g., 'los estudiantes deben').
target_language_example: Los niños deben cepillarse los dientes todos los días.
native_language_example: Children should brush their teeth every day.

meaning: 'children should' (suggestion or recommendation about what children ought to do).
additional_notes: Contains 'niños' (children) + conditional form 'deberían' (from deber) used to give advice, recommendations, or express expectation. Use for general statements about what children ought to do; tone is polite/soft obligation rather than strict command. To change person or number, conjugate 'deber' (e.g., 'debería' I/he/she, 'deberíamos' we).
target_language_example: Los niños deberían lavarse las manos antes de comer.
native_language_example: Children should wash their hands before eating.

meaning: children in the (masculine singular noun follows).
additional_notes: A simple phrase meaning 'children in the...' It combines niños (boys/children) + en (in) + the masculine singular definite article el. The noun that follows el is understood from context (el lugar, el cuarto, el auto, el jardín). Use 'niñas en la' for feminine or mixed contexts with a feminine noun (la). For plural masculine/feminine nouns use 'niños en los' / 'niñas en las'.
target_language_example: Vi a los niños en el parque.
native_language_example: I saw the children in the park.

meaning: This is not a correct or complete Spanish phrase; it appears to be an ungrammatical fragment mixing the plural noun 'niños' with the singular verb 'es' (should be 'son' for plural).
additional_notes: 'Niños' means 'children' (plural). Verbs must agree in number: use 'son' for 'are' (Los niños son...) or 'están' for temporary states (Los niños están...). 'Niños es' is ungrammatical in standard Spanish. In very specific contexts it might appear as part of a larger structure with punctuation (e.g., in quoted or broken speech: «Niños, ¿es...?») but this is rare and nonstandard. Use 'los niños son' or 'los niños están' instead.
target_language_example: "Niños es" no es una combinación correcta; deberías decir "Los niños son...".
native_language_example: "Niños es" is not a correct combination; you should say "Los niños son...".

meaning: 'children are in' or 'the children are in/at (a place)'.
additional_notes: This is a short phrase combining the noun 'niños' (children) with the verb 'están' (they are) and the preposition 'en' (in/at). It needs a following location (e.g., 'niños están en la escuela') or situation ('niños están en casa'). Use 'niñas' for girls or 'los niños'/'las niñas' with articles when needed. For mixed-gender groups, 'niños' is standard.
target_language_example: Los niños están en la escuela ahora.
native_language_example: The children are in school now.

meaning: part of a standard Spanish construction meaning 'to the children' (used with gustar-like verbs).
additional_notes: Used with verbs like gustar, encantar, interesar, etc. Spanish expresses likes as 'A + (indirect object) + les/te/me + verb (third person)'. 'A los niños les encanta(n)...' = 'The children love...'. The plural verb agrees with what is liked (e.g., 'les encantan los pasteles'). The pronoun 'les' refers to 'them' (to the children) and is required even when the phrase 'A los niños' is present for clarity/emphasis.
target_language_example: A los niños les interesa la historia.
native_language_example: The children are interested in history.

meaning: children love (it); kids really enjoy (something).
additional_notes: This phrase is a reduced chunk of the full Spanish construction 'a los niños les encanta + [infinitive/noun]'. 'A los niños' marks the indirect object (to the children) and 'les encanta' means 'is very pleasing to them' (they love). Use with verbs in the infinitive or nouns: 'A los niños les encanta jugar', 'A los niños les encanta el helado.' The shorter 'A los niños les encanta.' is natural when context makes the liked thing obvious.
target_language_example: A los niños les encanta jugar en el parque.
native_language_example: The children love playing in the park.

meaning: children like (used to say that children, in general, like something).
additional_notes: This construction uses an indirect object pronoun (les) with a topicalized indirect object phrase (a los niños / a la mayoría de los niños). The verb gustar agrees with the thing liked (plural gustan for plural objects). In English word order you say 'children like ice cream', but Spanish literally expresses it as 'to children (they) are pleasing ice creams'. For singular things use 'gusta' (e.g., 'a los niños les gusta el helado').
target_language_example: A los niños les gustan los juegos en el parque.
native_language_example: Children like the games in the park.

meaning: children it / the children it (literal) — not a fixed phrase; likely part of a larger sentence (e.g., 'los niños lo...').
additional_notes: This is not a standalone phrase in Spanish. 'Niños' means 'children' and 'lo' is a neutral direct object pronoun meaning 'it' or 'him' depending on context. Together they typically appear inside a sentence (for example, 'Los niños lo rompieron' = 'The children broke it'). Word order and articles matter: more natural forms are 'los niños lo...' or 'los niños la...' depending on the gender of the object. Beginners should learn 'niños/las/los' and object pronouns separately and see examples showing them used together.
target_language_example: Los niños lo vieron en el parque.
