additional_notes: This appears when the verb 'nombrar' is used in certain conjugations where the stem is 'nombre-' (subjunctive, imperative, or first-person present indicative 'nombre' in some dialects) followed by the object marker 'a la' before a feminine noun. Common in formal contexts: e.g., 'que nombre a la directora' (that he/she appoints the director). For masculine nouns use 'al' (a + el). The canonical infinitive is 'nombrar'; 'nombre' can be a conjugated form, not a separate lexical item.
target_language_example: Espero que nombre a la directora mañana.
native_language_example: I hope he/she names/appoints the director tomorrow.

meaning: the word 'nombre' (name) used with the preposition 'al' (a + el) — part of phrases meaning 'to (the) name' or 'name someone/something as' or 'give/assign a name to'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom by itself but appears when 'nombre' is used with the indirect object introduced by 'a' + 'el' (contracted to 'al'). Common uses: 'decir/poner/le nombre al (bebé/persona/lugar)' = 'tell/give someone a name' or 'conocer de nombre al ...' = 'to know someone by name'. Word order and verbs change meaning: 'conocer de nombre al presidente' = 'I know the president by name'; 'ponerle tu nombre al bebé' = 'to name the baby after you' or 'to give the baby your name'.
target_language_example: Voy a ponerle el nombre al perro.
native_language_example: I'm going to give the dog a name.

meaning: full name (first name(s) + family name(s)).
additional_notes: Used when asking for or giving someone's full legal name. In Spanish-speaking countries, people often have multiple given names and two family names (father's then mother's), so 'nombre completo' may include middle names and both surnames. Common on forms and official documents.
target_language_example: Por favor, escriba su nombre completo en el formulario.
native_language_example: Please write your full name on the form.

meaning: used to say someone is 'named' or 'has the name' followed by something (e.g., 'named with' — common in set phrases like 'poner nombre con...').
additional_notes: This is not a fixed standalone phrase in Spanish; it's a combination of the noun 'nombre' (name) plus the preposition 'con' (with). It appears in contexts such as 'su nombre con tilde' (his name with an accent) or in constructions like 'dar nombre con...' (to give a name with...). Beginners will more often see 'llamarse' (to be called) or 'se llama...' to state someone's name. Use 'nombre con' when specifying a property or feature that goes with the name (e.g., an accent, a title, or an initial).
target_language_example: Su nombre con tilde aparece en el documento.
native_language_example: His name with an accent appears on the document.

meaning: her name (the name belonging to her).
additional_notes: Used to refer to a woman's name. In everyday Spanish, speakers more often say 'su nombre' (his/her/your formal) or 'el nombre de ella' for emphasis or contrast (to distinguish from someone else's name). 'Nombre de ella' stresses that the name belongs to 'her'.
target_language_example: No recuerdo el nombre de ella, ¿me lo recuerdas?
native_language_example: I don't remember her name, can you remind me?

meaning: 'name of the' (feminine singular noun follows)
additional_notes: A common Spanish phrase used before a feminine singular noun to indicate possession or identification (e.g., nombre de la ciudad = name of the city). If the noun is masculine singular, use "nombre del" (contraction of de + el). When speaking generally (no article), you may see just "nombre de". Agreement depends on the noun that follows.
target_language_example: ¿Cuál es el nombre de la calle?
native_language_example: What is the name of the street?

meaning: given name; first name (the personal name, not the family/surname).
additional_notes: Used to refer specifically to a person's first/given name (e.g., María, Miguel) as opposed to apellido (family name). Common in everyday speech and formal contexts.
target_language_example: Su nombre de pila es Ana, pero todos la llaman Ani.
native_language_example: Her given name is Ana, but everyone calls her Ani.

meaning: the name of a (masculine) / 'the name of a' (used before a masculine noun).
additional_notes: Literally 'name of a'. Used to indicate the name belonging to or assigned to an unspecified or generic masculine noun (un tipo, un oficial, un rival, un personaje). In Spanish articles and gender matter: 'nombre de una' would be used before feminine nouns. Can appear in many contexts (person's name, reputation: 'ensuciar el nombre de…').
target_language_example: Encontré el nombre de un autor en la portada.
native_language_example: I found the name of an author on the cover.

meaning: lit. 'name on' — used to indicate someone's name appearing on or associated with something (e.g., a poster, label, list).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but the noun nombre followed by the preposition en. It commonly appears when saying that a name is written, printed, or used 'on' something (mi nombre en un póster, tu nombre en una etiqueta). Can also be used figuratively (nombre en clave = 'code name'). Word order and articles may vary: 'ver mi nombre en esto', 'poner tu nombre en la lista'.
target_language_example: Pusieron mi nombre en la lista de participantes.
native_language_example: They put my name on the participants' list.

meaning: "name on the" — used to say that a name appears on/was written on something (e.g., the list, the board, the sheet).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but a common word order: nombre (name) + en la (on the [feminine noun]). The feminine noun that follows (hoja, pizarra, lista, pared) determines what "la" refers to. For masculine nouns you'd see "nombre en el". Often used with verbs like anotar, escribir, ver, oír, poner.
target_language_example: Vi mi nombre en la lista.
native_language_example: I saw my name on the list.

meaning: 'name is' — used when giving someone's or something's name (structure: [El/Mi/ Su] nombre es ...).
additional_notes: Common phrase to state a name. Usually appears after a possessive or subject, for example 'Mi nombre es...' (My name is...), 'Su nombre es...' (His/Her/Your formal name is...), or 'El nombre es...' when describing the name of a thing. For introductions, native speakers more often say 'Me llamo...' or 'Soy...' but 'Mi nombre es...' is perfectly correct and slightly more formal.
target_language_example: Mi nombre es Ana.
native_language_example: My name is Ana.

meaning: literally 'name is' — used when stating that a person's or thing's name (or number) is X; often part of a larger sentence (e.g., 'El nombre está en la lista').
additional_notes: This is not a standalone phrase in Spanish; it's the combination of the noun 'nombre' (name) and the verb 'estar' (to be) in third person singular. You'll see it inside sentences to say where a name is, what the name is (in some contexts), or that a name exists/appears. Depending on context, Spanish speakers more commonly say 'el nombre es...' to define someone's name, and 'el nombre está...' to indicate location or presence (e.g., 'El nombre está en la lista' = 'The name is on the list').
target_language_example: El nombre está en la primera fila del formulario.
native_language_example: The name is in the first row of the form.

meaning: literally 'name very' — not a standard fixed phrase in Spanish; appears when 'nombre' (name) is followed by the adverb 'muy' to modify an adjective that follows (e.g., 'nombre muy conocido'). On its own it is ungrammatical because 'muy' modifies adjectives/adverbs, not nouns.
additional_notes: 'Nombre muy' by itself is not a common or complete expression. If you encounter it, it's almost always part of a larger phrase: 'nombre muy conocido' (a very well-known name), 'nombre muy largo' (a very long name). If you intend to emphasize a noun, Spanish uses determiners or quantifiers (e.g., 'un nombre muy conocido', 'un nombre muy importante').
target_language_example: Ese es un nombre muy conocido en nuestra comunidad.
native_language_example: That is a very well-known name in our community.

meaning: literally 'name no' — not a standard fixed phrase; likely a fragment or mistaken word order (no + nombre means 'no name' or 'unnamed').
additional_notes: This combination is not a common set phrase in Spanish. If you want to say 'no name' or 'unnamed', you would say 'sin nombre' or 'sin nombre conocido'. To say 'my name is not ...', use 'mi nombre no es...'. If you see 'nombre no' in text, it may be a typo or part of a longer phrase (e.g., 'nombre, no ...' meaning 'name, no ...').
target_language_example: Mi nombre no es importante en este proyecto.
native_language_example: My name is not important in this project.

meaning: proper name; a personal name (name of a person, place, or specific thing).
additional_notes: Used to refer to names that identify unique people, places, organizations, etc. In grammar, 'nombre propio' (also often 'nombre propio' vs 'nombre común') is capitalized in Spanish (e.g., María, Madrid, Amazon). It can mean 'first name' in some contexts but generally covers any proper noun.
target_language_example: Mi nombre propio es Ana y vivo en Barcelona.
native_language_example: My proper name is Ana and I live in Barcelona.

meaning: ‘name that’ or 'the name that' — used to introduce or specify a name (often followed by a clause).
additional_notes: Literal combination: nombre (name) + que (that/which). Commonly appears in sentences identifying or describing a name (e.g., "el nombre que busca" = "the name that you are looking for"). Can also be used in titles or fragments (e.g., "Un nombre que resulta familiar" = "A name that sounds familiar").
target_language_example: Ese es el nombre que me dio el profesor.
native_language_example: That's the name the teacher gave me.

meaning: Not a grammatical or standard multi-word expression in Spanish. Likely a typo or clipped form (e.g., intended 'no es' = 'it is not' or an incorrect combination of pronoun 'nos' with 'es').
additional_notes: As written, 'nos es' does not occur in standard Spanish grammar. Possible interpretations: 1) Typo for 'no es' (negation + 'ser'). 2) Erroneous attempt to use direct/indirect object pronoun 'nos' with 'es' — Spanish would instead use constructions like 'nos parece' (it seems to us) or 'es para nosotros' (it is for us). 3) Truncated or mistaken form of 'nosotros somos' (we are), which should be 'nosotros somos' or 'somos'. Avoid using 'nos es' in writing or speech; correct alternatives depend on intended meaning.
target_language_example: Creo que 'nos es' es un error; deberías escribir 'no es'.
native_language_example: I think 'nos es' is an error; you should write 'no es'.

meaning: 'we had' / 'it went for us' — often part of expressions meaning how something turned out for us or that something got out of our control.'
additional_notes: A short form of 'nos fue' used to report outcomes (e.g., 'nos fue bien' = 'we did well'). It also appears in constructions with 'se' like 'se nos fue (de las manos)' meaning 'it got out of our hands / out of control' or 'we lost track of it.' Context determines translation: outcome vs. loss of control. 'Nos' marks 'for us' or 'to us.'
target_language_example: En la feria nos fue muy bien con las ventas.
native_language_example: At the fair we did very well with sales.

meaning: we like (something); it's pleasing to us.
additional_notes: Used with verbs (infinitive) or nouns. Structure: nos (indirect object pronoun) + gusta/gustan (third person) + subject (what is liked). Use 'gusta' for singular or verb infinitives, 'gustan' for plural nouns. To state who likes something, use 'a + pronoun/name' for clarity (e.g., A nosotros nos gusta...).
target_language_example: Nos gusta viajar los fines de semana.
native_language_example: We like to travel on weekends.

meaning: 'he/she/it/they look(s) at us' or 'is looking at us'.
additional_notes: A simple present (or present continuous in English) form of mirar with the object pronoun nos (us). Subject is implied by verb ending: mira = él/ella/usted or ello/ella in impersonal uses. Can be used literally (someone looks at us) or figuratively (e.g., a situation 'stares us in the face'). Word order with object pronoun is subject + nos + verb in spoken/written Spanish (Nos mira = 'He/she/it looks at us').
target_language_example: ¿Por qué ese hombre nos mira desde la puerta?
native_language_example: Why is that man looking at us from the door?

meaning: we will think of (something) / something will occur to us
additional_notes: Used to say that a solution, idea, or plan will come to mind later. Common in spoken Spanish as a reassuring or casual way to suggest you'll find something (often followed by 'algo' = 'something'). Structure: 'se nos ocurrirá (algo)'. 'Se' is impersonal/accidental and 'nos' indicates 'to us'.
target_language_example: No te preocupes, ya se nos ocurrirá una solución.
native_language_example: Don't worry, we'll think of a solution soon.

meaning: 'it seems to us' / 'we think' (used to give an opinion)
additional_notes: Literally 'it appears to us.' Commonly used to express the speaker group's opinion or impression. Can introduce a suggestion or evaluation: 'Nos parece bien' = 'We think it's fine.' Often followed by adjectives, clauses, or infinitives.
target_language_example: Nos parece una buena idea visitar mañana.
native_language_example: We think it's a good idea to visit tomorrow.

meaning: 'they can (do something) to/for us' — third person plural of poder + object pronoun 'nos' (us).
additional_notes: Combines the indirect/direct object pronoun 'nos' (us) with the verb 'pueden' (they can). Word order can be 'nos pueden + verb' or the pronoun may attach to an infinitive (e.g., 'pueden seguirnos'). Means 'they are able to' or 'they may' do the action to/for us. Context determines exact translation (follow us, manipulate us, find us, etc.).
target_language_example: Los vecinos nos pueden ayudar si llamamos.
native_language_example: The neighbors can help us if we call.

meaning: he/she/it/you (formal) loves/likes us; wants us (depending on context).
additional_notes: Nos is the object pronoun 'us'. Quiere is third-person singular of querer: can mean 'to love' (affection) or 'to want' (desire). Context tells you which: with people (Ella nos quiere) it usually means 'loves us' or 'cares about us'; with situations or God it can mean 'wants us' or 'wishes for us' (Dios nos quiere aquí = God wants us here). Pronunciation: 'nos kyeh-reh'.
target_language_example: Mi familia nos quiere tal como somos.
native_language_example: My family loves us just as we are.

meaning: 'we have to (leave/...)' or 'we must (leave/...)' (used with an infinitive to express obligation for 'us').
additional_notes: Usually appears as 'nos tenemos que' + infinitive (or 'tenemos que' + irnos) to express that the speaker and others must do something (here: leave). 'Nos' is a reflexive/pronominal object meaning 'us' and can indicate 'we must leave' when combined with 'ir' (irse). Common alternatives: 'tenemos que irnos' or 'nos tenemos que ir'.
target_language_example: Nos tenemos que ir antes de que empiece la película.
native_language_example: We have to leave before the movie starts.

meaning: we're leaving
additional_notes: First-person plural reflexive form of irse (irse → to leave/go away). Used to say that we (or you and I) are about to leave a place or are leaving for somewhere. Can be present tense ('we're leaving now') or used with time expressions for future plans ('we're leaving [for]...'). Common in spoken Spanish. Contraction with subject pronoun is normal: "nos vamos" rather than "vamos" when emphasizing leaving/going away.
target_language_example: Nos vamos al aeropuerto a las ocho.
native_language_example: We're leaving for the airport at eight.

meaning: used to say 'let's meet/see each other at' or 'we'll see each other at' (followed by a time or place).
additional_notes: This is a form of the verb verse (verse = to see each other) in the subjunctive (nos veamos) combined with the preposition de to introduce a time or context (e.g., 'nos veamos de noche' or 'nos veamos de aquí a una semana'). Common in casual speech when arranging meetings. Often appears as part of phrases like 'Nos vemos de...' or 'Que nos veamos de...'.
target_language_example: Nos veamos de aquí a una semana para revisar el proyecto.
native_language_example: Let's meet in a week to review the project.

meaning: see you
additional_notes: literally means 'we see each other.' It is very commonly used as a casual way to say goodbye, often with a time or place added: nos vemos mañana, nos vemos en el puente. It can also simply mean that two or more people will meet or see each other.
target_language_example: Bueno, me tengo que ir. Nos vemos mañana.
native_language_example: Well, I have to go. See you tomorrow.

meaning: 'see you at' (used to arrange meeting time/place)
additional_notes: Common, informal way to set a meeting or say goodbye with a planned time/place. Typically followed by a time, day, or place (e.g., nos vemos a las 5, nos vemos en la plaza). If used as a simple goodbye without 'a', use just 'nos vemos' = 'see you'.
target_language_example: Nos vemos a las 6 en la cafetería.
native_language_example: See you at 6 in the café.

meaning: See you on (day/date). Used to say you'll meet/see someone on a specific day or date.
additional_notes: Combines the common farewell/arrangement phrase "nos vemos" (see you) with a time expression introduced by "el" (the) before a day/date (e.g., "el lunes", "el 12 de mayo"). In speech people may omit "el" before weekdays ("nos vemos el lunes" or "nos vemos lunes"), but include it with calendar dates. Use to confirm a planned meeting or to say when you'll see someone next.
target_language_example: Nos vemos el viernes a las ocho.
native_language_example: See you on Friday at eight.

meaning: 'we will see each other' or 'we'll meet'.
additional_notes: Future tense of 'verse' (verse = to see each other). Used to say you'll meet or see someone in the future. Common in farewells or to arrange future meetings: can be followed by place or time (e.g., allí, esta noche). Tone is neutral; can sound final (Ya nos veremos) or reassuring (nos veremos pronto).
target_language_example: Nos veremos mañana en la estación.
native_language_example: We'll see each other tomorrow at the station.

meaning: 'we see each other again' or 'we meet again' (subjunctive, first-person plural).
additional_notes: Used with 'espero', 'quizá', 'hasta que', etc., to express hope or possibility of meeting again. 'Volvamos' is the present subjunctive of 'volver' (to return/meet again) and 'nos' marks a reciprocal action (each other). Often appears as 'nos volvamos a ver' or 'nos volvamos a encontrar'.
target_language_example: Espero que nos volvamos a ver el próximo año.
native_language_example: I hope we see each other again next year.

meaning: we will see each other again / we'll meet again
additional_notes: From the reflexive verb 'volverse a ver' (verse = to see each other). 'Nos volveremos' is future tense (nosotros) and implies a future reunion. Often appears with 'a' (nos volveremos a ver) but can omit it in informal speech. Used to express hope, certainty, or question about meeting again.
target_language_example: Espero que nos volveremos a ver el próximo año.
native_language_example: I hope we'll see each other again next year.

meaning: This combination is not a fixed idiomatic phrase in Spanish; it is simply the pronoun 'nosotros' ('we') followed by the preposition 'a' ('to', 'at', etc.). It appears when 'nosotros' is immediately followed by 'a' in a sentence (often because of a verb or clause between them is omitted or in certain constructions).
additional_notes: Treat 'nosotros' and 'a' as separate words. 'Nosotros' is the subject pronoun meaning 'we'. 'A' is a versatile preposition used for direction ('to'), location/time ('at'), indirect objects, and the personal 'a' before a human direct object. Sequences 'nosotros a' are uncommon without a verb or punctuation between them; in many cases Spanish speakers reorder or contract (e.g., use clitic pronoun: 'nos' as in 'Nos llamaron' instead of 'Llamaron a nosotros'). Example contexts where 'nosotros a' can appear: quoted text, contrasts, or ellipsis (e.g., '¿Tú a María, nosotros a Pedro?').
target_language_example: Tú a María, nosotros a Pedro.
native_language_example: You (go) to María, we (go) to Pedro.

meaning: Not a fixed idiomatic phrase; the pronoun 'nosotros' ('we') directly followed by 'al' (contraction of 'a' + 'el', meaning 'to the' or 'at the'). Typically occurs when 'nosotros' is subject and a verb is followed by a prepositional phrase beginning with 'al'.
additional_notes: 'Nosotros al' should not be treated as a single lexical unit. It appears when a sentence has the subject 'nosotros' and then later, or immediately after a verb, a prepositional phrase starting with 'al'. Depending on word order and context, 'al' may be separated from 'nosotros' by a verb (e.g., 'Nosotros vamos al...') or appear adjacent in speech or abbreviated examples. Learn 'nosotros' and 'al' separately and how verbs connect them.
target_language_example: Nosotros al salir de la oficina vimos un accidente.
native_language_example: We, upon leaving the office, saw an accident.

meaning: we two / both of us (emphatic: the two of us)
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that exactly two people (including the speaker) are involved. Common in spoken and written Spanish to clarify or contrast 'the two of us' from others. Can appear as 'nosotros dos' (masculine/mixed) or 'nosotras dos' (all-female).
target_language_example: Uno de nosotros dos tiene que quedarse en casa.
native_language_example: One of the two of us has to stay home.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase; appears to be a fragment combining the subject pronoun "nosotros" (we) with the article/pronoun "el/él". As written without accent, "el" is the definite article "the"; with an accent "él" means "he". Alone this sequence is usually ungrammatical and likely a typo, missing punctuation, or missing conjunction.
additional_notes:
Possible intended forms and corrections:
- "nosotros, él..." — to list people (we, he...)
- "nosotros y él" — we and he
- "nosotros él" in dialogue could reflect informal speech or transcription errors; consider whether "él" should have an accent. If seen in text, check for missing words or punctuation.
Grammatical notes: "nosotros" is a subject pronoun; "el" (no accent) is the masculine singular definite article; "él" (with accent) is the third-person singular subject pronoun. The sequence "nosotros el" cannot be translated idiomatically as-is without context.
target_language_example: En la lista decía: "nosotros el" (falta un "y" o una coma), así que pregunté al autor qué quiso decir.
native_language_example: On the list it said "nosotros el" (missing a "y" or a comma), so I asked the author what they meant.

meaning: 'we' (first-person plural pronoun) + preposition 'in/at' — literally 'we in', used to locate or refer to a group including the speaker in a place, situation, or context.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed expression by itself; it's simply the subject pronoun nosotros followed by the preposition en. Use nosotros when the speaker is part of the group (we). En indicates location, time, mode, or context (in, on, at, by). In natural Spanish you will often see forms like 'nosotros en la foto' (we in the photo), 'nosotros en la reunión' (us at the meeting), or 'nosotros, en cambio' (we, on the other hand) where punctuation and context change the meaning.
target_language_example: Nosotros en la foto estamos sonriendo.
native_language_example: We in the photo are smiling.

meaning: Incorrect/ungrammatical combination; 'nosotros' (we) should pair with the verb form 'somos' (we are).
additional_notes: This phrase is not correct Spanish. 'Nosotros' is the first-person plural subject pronoun and requires plural verb forms. The correct present-tense form of 'ser' with 'nosotros' is 'somos' (nosotros somos). You might see 'nosotros es' only as an error by beginners, in informal nonstandard speech, or as a typo. It can also appear in quoted mistaken usage or in language-learning examples illustrating incorrect agreement. Remember subject–verb agreement: singular subjects take singular verbs, plural subjects take plural verbs.
target_language_example: *Error:* Nosotros es feliz en la fiesta.
native_language_example: *Error:* We is happy at the party.

meaning: we (to/for) him/her/you (formal) — subject + indirect object pronoun; 'le' marks an indirect object
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but the pronoun combination 'nosotros' (we) followed by the indirect object pronoun 'le'. In Spanish, 'le' can mean 'to him', 'to her', or formal 'to you' (usted). Word order is flexible: the indirect object pronoun usually appears before a conjugated verb (e.g., 'nosotros le damos' = 'we give him/her/you (formal)') or attached to an infinitive or gerund. Context or a following noun clarifies who 'le' refers to. In some regions 'le' is also used for indirect objects regardless of gender.
target_language_example: Nosotros le enviamos la carta mañana.
native_language_example: We will send him/her/you (formal) the letter tomorrow.

meaning: 'nosotros' = we; 'por' = for/by/because of. Together they are not a fixed idiom; they appear when the pronoun 'nosotros' is followed by the preposition 'por' in a sentence, and the meaning depends on context.
additional_notes: Not a set expression. Often occurs in constructions like 'nosotros por...' to introduce a clause expressing reason, contrast, or agency (e.g., 'nosotros por...' = 'we, because of...' or 'we, for...'). More natural alternatives for 'for us' are 'para nosotros' or 'por nosotros' (the preposition after the pronoun). When emphasizing contrast use a comma: 'Nosotros, por...'. Word order matters: 'nosotros por' is simply the pronoun plus preposition and must be completed by the rest of the sentence to be grammatical and clear.
target_language_example: Nosotros por nuestra cuenta nos encargaremos del proyecto.
native_language_example: We, on our own, will take care of the project.

meaning: This combination is ungrammatical in standard Spanish — the subject pronoun 'nosotros' (we) is not used together with the third-person reflexive/object pronoun 'se'.
additional_notes: Use 'nos' for first-person plural reflexive constructions (nosotros + nos + verb): e.g., 'Nosotros nos lavamos.' 'Se' is used for third-person or impersonal constructions (ellos se lavan; 'se' impersonal). The sequence 'nosotros se' does not occur in correct Spanish; if seen, it is likely a grammatical error or a transcription of two separate elements ('nosotros' and later 'se' referring to another clause).
target_language_example: *Incorrect:* Nosotros se equivocaron.
native_language_example: *Incorrect literal reading:* We they-messed-up (this is ungrammatical) — correct would be 'Nosotros nos equivocamos' or 'Ellos se equivocaron'.

meaning: 'we do' / 'we do (indeed)' — used to affirm or emphasize that we/people including me do something.
additional_notes: Used to agree, confirm, or emphasize that 'we' perform an action or hold an opinion. Often contrasts with others (e.g., "otros no, nosotros sí") or stresses affirmation after a negative statement. Note: the sí with accent is the affirmative particle; it is not the reflexive pronoun 'se'.
target_language_example: Ellos no quieren ir, pero nosotros sí.
native_language_example: They don't want to go, but we do (indeed).

meaning: we (subject) + you (direct or indirect object) — 'we you...' (depends on verb)
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase; it's the combination of the subject pronoun 'nosotros' (we) and the object pronoun 'te' (you, informal singular). It appears before a verb in Spanish if the verb is conjugated (e.g., 'nosotros te llamamos' = 'we call you') or attached to an infinitive/gerund/affirmative imperative (e.g., 'vamos a llamarte', 'estamos llamándote', 'llámanos te' is incorrect — correct: 'llámanos' means 'call us'). Remember Spanish object pronouns usually go before a conjugated verb (nosotros te vemos) or attached to non‑finite forms (queremos verte).
target_language_example: Nosotros te ayudamos con la mudanza.
native_language_example: We help you with the move.

meaning: Incorrect/ungrammatical combination: the correct form is 'nosotros tenemos' ('we have').
additional_notes: 'Nosotros' (we) requires the verb form 'tenemos' (first person plural). 'Tiene' is third person singular (él/ella) or formal usted. The sequence 'nosotros tiene' is a subject–verb disagreement and should be avoided in standard Spanish. Example conjugation for 'tener': yo tengo, tú tienes, él/ella/usted tiene, nosotros/nosotras tenemos, vosotros/vosotras tenéis, ellos/ustedes tienen.
target_language_example: *Nosotros tiene* que corregir esto — esta construcción es incorrecta.
native_language_example: *We (nosotros) tiene* must correct this — this construction is incorrect.

meaning: 'we have to' (intended meaning), but this form is grammatically incorrect in Spanish.
additional_notes: The correct form is 'nosotros tenemos que' or simply 'tenemos que'. 'Nosotros tiene que' incorrectly mixes the plural subject 'nosotros' with the singular verb form 'tiene' (from 'tener'). This construction should be avoided; if encountered, it is likely a learner error or a typographical mistake. In spoken Spanish, subject pronouns are often omitted: say 'tenemos que ir' (we have to go).
target_language_example: *Incorrect:* Nosotros tiene que estudiar para el examen.
native_language_example: *Incorrect:* We have to study for the exam.

meaning: we go / we are going (we will), usually followed by 'a' + infinitive to mean 'we are going to [do something]'.
additional_notes: Nosotros is the subject pronoun 'we' (often optional in Spanish). 'Vamos' is the present tense of 'ir' (to go). Together, 'nosotros vamos a + infinitive' expresses a near-future action (equivalent to English 'we are going to [do something]' or 'we will [do something]'). In casual speech the subject pronoun 'nosotros' is frequently dropped: 'Vamos a alquilar un coche.' Informal or strong language in the infinitive clause (see example 5) depends on the verb/words used after 'a'.
target_language_example: Nosotros vamos a cocinar esta noche.
native_language_example: We are going to cook tonight.

meaning: we and / us and
additional_notes: Combination of the subject pronoun 'nosotros' (we) plus the conjunction 'y' (and). Used to join 'we' with another noun, pronoun, or phrase: e.g. 'nosotros y ellos' = 'we and they'. In spoken Spanish you might more often hear just 'y nosotros' (and we) when adding 'we' after another subject.
target_language_example: Nosotros y los profesores iremos al museo.
native_language_example: We and the teachers will go to the museum.

meaning: 'grades in' (school subjects) OR 'notes on/at/in' depending on context.
additional_notes: Most commonly used to talk about school grades: sacar/obtener buenas/malas notas en + subject = to get good/bad grades in [subject]. Can also mean musical notes (las notas en un pasaje) or physical notes left somewhere (dejar notas en la puerta). Context (school, music, or written notes) determines meaning.
target_language_example: Siempre saco buenas notas en historia.
native_language_example: I always get good grades in history.

meaning: news of his/her/your/their (something).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a specific piece of news about someone (su = his, her, your (formal), their). Followed by a noun (embarazo, llegada, muerte, etc.). Common structure: 'la noticia de su + [noun]'. Indicates that people received or reacted to that news.
target_language_example: La noticia de su ascenso alegró a todo el equipo.
native_language_example: The news of his/her promotion made the whole team happy.

meaning: 'news is' or 'the news is' (used to introduce information or a piece of news)
additional_notes: This phrase combines noticia (news; piece of information) with the verb ser (es). It's used to introduce or report something: e.g., 'La noticia es que...' = 'The news is that...'. Often appears as part of longer sentences (La noticia es que..., Lo que importa es..., Tengo una noticia:...). In natural Spanish speakers more commonly say 'la noticia es que...' or 'tengo una noticia' rather than 'noticia es' alone.
target_language_example: La noticia es que mañana tenemos libre.
native_language_example: The news is that we have tomorrow off.

meaning: This is not a standard fixed phrase in Spanish; it appears to be an incorrect word order or a fragment. "Noticia" = "news/notice"; "le" = indirect object pronoun (to him/her/you formal). Likely intended structures put the pronoun before a conjugated verb or attached to an infinitive/gerund (e.g., "Le doy la noticia", "Voy a darle la noticia").
additional_notes: If you encounter "noticia le" in text, it may be a typo, a misordered fragment, or part of a sentence where the verb is omitted. Correct forms include placing "le" before a conjugated verb ("Le cuento la noticia") or attaching it to an infinitive/gerund ("Voy a darle la noticia"). The two words together without a verb are not grammatical as a standalone phrase.
target_language_example: No entiendo la frase: "noticia le" parece un fragmento sin verbo.
native_language_example: I don't understand the phrase: "noticia le" seems like a fragment without a verb.

meaning: news for / news to tell someone (about something).
additional_notes: Used to say you have information (often important or personal) intended for a specific person or group. Commonly appears in phrases like 'tengo noticias para ti' (I have news for you) or 'tengo malas noticias para...' (I have bad news for...). The preposition 'para' indicates the recipient. Can be followed by a person (ti, usted, vosotros) or by a clause (e.g., 'para decirte...').
target_language_example: Tengo buenas noticias para ti: aprobaste el examen.
native_language_example: I have good news for you: you passed the exam.

meaning: 'novel of' or 'novel about' (used to say what a novel is about or who wrote it).
additional_notes: novela = novel (book). When followed by de, it introduces the subject, theme, genre, or author: 'novela de misterio' (mystery novel), 'novela de amor' (love/romance novel), or 'novela de García Márquez' (a novel by García Márquez). For beginners: think of 'de' as meaning 'of', 'about', or 'by' depending on context.
target_language_example: Es una novela de misterio muy interesante.
native_language_example: It's a very interesting mystery novel.

meaning: 'novel is' — literal combination of 'novela' (novel) + 'es' (is).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase; it's simply the noun 'novela' (a novel, a work of fiction) followed by the verb 'es' (is). You will see this structure when someone defines or describes a novel: e.g. 'La novela es...' → 'The novel is...'. Use 'la novela' for 'the novel' (feminine). For other subjects change the article or verb as needed (p. ej. 'Mi novela es...' = 'My novel is...').
target_language_example: La novela es interesante y fácil de leer.
native_language_example: The novel is interesting and easy to read.

meaning: the first part of numbers 90–99 (used like 'ninety and' before units).
additional_notes: In Spanish, numbers 90–99 are formed with 'noventa y' + unit (e.g., noventa y uno = 91). Pronunciation: the 'y' (and) is pronounced like English /ee/ and links the tens with the units. Use 'noventa' alone for exactly 90.
target_language_example: noventa y cinco
native_language_example: ninety-five

meaning: ninety-six (96).
additional_notes: A cardinal number used to state the number 96. Can refer to a year (e.g., 'el noventa y seis' meaning 1996 or 1896 depending on context) or simply the quantity. In spoken Spanish, numbers are usually pronounced without 'y' for tens and units like 'treinta y dos' — here the 'y' is standard. Used in lists, counts, addresses, ages, etc.
target_language_example: En 1996, pero también puedo decir noventa y seis como número.
native_language_example: In 1996, but I can also say ninety-six as a number.

meaning: girlfriend of / the girlfriend of (someone).
additional_notes: Used to indicate possession or relationship: 'novia de X' = X's girlfriend. 'Novia' means girlfriend (or fiancée, in some contexts). Commonly followed by a person's name or pronoun (e.g., 'la novia de Juan', 'la novia de él'). If you want to say 'my girlfriend', use 'mi novia' instead of 'novia de mí'.
target_language_example: La novia de Carlos es muy simpática.
native_language_example: Carlos's girlfriend is very nice.

meaning: 'my/your/etc. girlfriend is' (the noun novia + the verb ser 'is')
additional_notes: Novia = girlfriend (or fiancée in some contexts). Here 'es' is the third-person singular of ser (to be). Useful for describing identity, origin, profession, nationality, or characteristics (e.g., 'Mi novia es actriz', 'Mi novia es canadiense', 'Mi novia es muy hermosa'). Replace the possessive (mi/tu/su) as needed: 'Tu novia es...', 'Su novia es...'.
target_language_example: Tu novia es peruana y simpática.
native_language_example: Your girlfriend is Peruvian and friendly.

meaning: ‘my/your/his/etc. boyfriend is…’ — the phrase 'novio' (boyfriend) followed by the verb 'es' (is) to describe someone’s boyfriend.
additional_notes: Used to state or describe a person's boyfriend (gender: male partner). Replace 'novio' with 'novia' for girlfriend. Subject pronoun or possessor (mi, tu, su, etc.) normally comes before 'novio' (e.g., 'mi novio es...'). 'Es' is the third-person singular of 'ser' for permanent or defining traits (profession, nationality, identity, etc.).
target_language_example: Su novio es médico.
native_language_example: Her boyfriend is a doctor.

meaning: literally 'clouds of' — used to describe types or qualities of clouds or used metaphorically (e.g., 'nubes de verano' = summer clouds).
additional_notes: This is a prepositional phrase combining 'nubes' (clouds) with 'de' (of). Commonly followed by a noun that specifies the kind, season, color, or metaphorical quality (nubes de verano, nubes de tormenta, nubes de algodón). In metaphorical uses it can describe how something passes or appears (e.g., 'pasaron como las nubes de verano' = they passed as quickly as summer clouds).
target_language_example: Las nubes de tormenta cubrieron el cielo en minutos.
native_language_example: The storm clouds covered the sky in minutes.

meaning: 'clouds in' — used to talk about clouds being in/over a place or metaphorically having one's mind elsewhere.
additional_notes: Literal use: describes physical clouds located in or over something (e.g., en el cielo, en el suelo as shadows). Figurative use: part of the expression 'tener la cabeza en las nubes' meaning to be daydreaming or distracted. 'Nubes en' itself is just the noun 'nubes' (clouds) followed by the preposition 'en' and must be completed with the location or context (e.g., 'nubes en el cielo', 'nubes en la playa').
target_language_example: Había nubes en el horizonte y parecía que llovería.
native_language_example: There were clouds on the horizon and it looked like it would rain.

meaning: our language; our tongue.
additional_notes: Used to refer to a language shared by the speaker and others (e.g., Spanish, a regional language, or the mother tongue). Can mean 'our way of speaking' or 'our native language' depending on context. 'Nuestra' is the possessive 'our'; 'lengua' = language/tongue.
target_language_example: En nuestra lengua hay muchas palabras para describir la naturaleza.
native_language_example: In our language there are many words to describe nature.

meaning: our moon (the Moon that belongs to or is associated with us)
additional_notes: Literal possessive phrase: nuestra = our (feminine singular), luna = moon. Used to refer to Earth's Moon in a familiar or poetic way, or metaphorically to a moon belonging to a group/planet. If the speaker refers to themselves with a masculine plural group, 'nuestra' still applies because 'luna' is feminine; for masculine singular 'mi luna' would be 'my moon.'
target_language_example: Desde aquí, nuestra luna se ve grande y brillante.
native_language_example: From here, our moon looks big and bright.

meaning: 'our ... moon' — start of a possessive phrase meaning 'our [type of] moon' or part of expressions like 'nuestra luna de miel' (our honeymoon).
additional_notes: This is not a complete phrase by itself; it's the beginning of a possessive expression (nuestra = our, luna = moon). Commonly appears in set phrases such as 'nuestra luna de miel' (our honeymoon). Depending on context, it could be literal (our moon) or figurative in idiomatic expressions. Remember 'nuestra' agrees in gender and number with the noun (nuestra luna = our moon; nuestros hijos = our children).
target_language_example: Nos fuimos de viaje por nuestra luna de miel.
native_language_example: We went on a trip for our honeymoon.

meaning: 'our best' (used before a noun to say something/someone is the best we have or the best option)
additional_notes: Nuestra = 'our'. Mejor = 'best' (comparative/adjective). Combined, they modify a following noun (e.g., nuestra mejor película, nuestra mejor opción). Common with abstract things (opción, defensa) and people (espía). Agreement: mejor does not change for gender/number; use 'nuestro/nuestra' to match the noun's gender.
target_language_example: Esta ruta es nuestra mejor opción ahora mismo.
native_language_example: This route is our best option right now.

meaning: 'our day' — can mean a special day for us, a lucky day, or a planned day/event belonging to us.
additional_notes: Literal phrase meaning 'our day.' Used to say today belongs to us (e.g., it's our big day), that it's our lucky day (good luck), or to refer to a scheduled day/event (nuestro día de campo = our picnic day). Context determines whether it means 'special/important day', 'lucky day', or simply 'the day we planned.'
target_language_example: Hoy es nuestro día: por fin inauguramos la tienda.
native_language_example: Today is our day: we finally open the shop.

meaning: on our side; in our favor
additional_notes: Used to say that people, circumstances, luck, the law, etc. support or favor 'us' (the speaker and their group). Often appears in the phrase 'estar de nuestro lado' or 'tener X de nuestro lado' to mean 'X is supporting us' or 'works in our favor.'
target_language_example: Con todas las pruebas, la ley está de nuestro lado.
native_language_example: With all the evidence, the law is on our side.

meaning: our best (used before a noun or noun phrase); indicates the best one(s) belonging to 'us'.
additional_notes: Combines the possessive nuestro(a/os/as) 'our' with 'mejor' meaning 'best' or 'better'. Agreement: nuestro changes gender and number to match the noun (nuestro mejor amigo, nuestra mejor amiga, nuestros mejores jugadores). Commonly appears in expressions like 'nuestro mejor amigo' (our best friend) and 'hacer nuestro mejor esfuerzo' (to do our best).
target_language_example: Creo que este será nuestro mejor episodio.
native_language_example: I think this will be our best episode.

meaning: new star (literally); can mean a newly discovered star or a rising/new celebrity.
additional_notes: Literally refers to a star that is new or newly discovered in the sky. Commonly used figuratively to describe a new or rising talent/celebrity (e.g., 'la nueva estrella del cine'). Context tells which meaning is intended (astronomy vs. fame).
target_language_example: Han encontrado una nueva estrella en la constelación.
native_language_example: They have found a new star in the constellation.

meaning: 'new to' or 'new for' (something or someone).
additional_notes: Used to say that something is new in relation to a person, purpose, or place. 'Nueva' agrees in gender with the noun it describes (feminine singular). 'Para' indicates the beneficiary, recipient, intended use, or context. For masculine nouns use 'nuevo para'; plural forms: 'nuevas para' / 'nuevos para'.
target_language_example: Es una idea nueva para mí.
native_language_example: It's a new idea to me.

meaning: nine to (used when giving a time interval: from nine until… or a start time paired with 'a' + end time)
additional_notes: Commonly used when stating hours in ranges or schedules: 'de nueve a cinco' = from nine to five. Alone, 'nueve a' is incomplete and needs the following time (e.g., 'nueve a diez'). In spoken Spanish you may also hear 'de las nueve a las cinco' with definite articles.
target_language_example: Trabajo de nueve a cinco.
native_language_example: I work from nine to five.

meaning: 'nine o'clock' (used before a time expression like 'nueve de la mañana' or 'nueve de la noche').
additional_notes: This phrase is the start of a time expression: 'nueve de la mañana' = 9:00 AM, 'nueve de la noche' = 9:00 PM. In Spanish, use 'de la mañana/tarde/noche' to specify AM/PM. When saying the hour alone you can also say 'las nueve' (common) instead of 'nueve de la'.
target_language_example: La reunión es a nueve de la mañana.
native_language_example: The meeting is at nine in the morning.

meaning: 'nine and' — used when stating times (minutes past nine) or as the start of a compound number in some contexts, but by itself it's usually part of a time expression.
additional_notes: In Spanish times, minutes after the hour can be expressed as 'nueve y cinco' = 9:05. 'Nueve y' alone is incomplete — you need the minutes or the rest of the phrase. In numbers, Spanish does not generally form compound numbers as 'nueve y ...' (except in old or poetic forms); use full numbers (p. ej., 'noventa' for 90).
target_language_example: Son las nueve y cuarto.
native_language_example: It's a quarter past nine.

meaning: New World (the Americas); also can mean a new, unknown, or different world/situation.
additional_notes: Often capitalized as Nuevo Mundo when referring historically/geographically to the Americas after European discovery (the 'New World'). Lowercase can be used figuratively to talk about a new or unfamiliar world or situation (e.g., 'entrar en un nuevo mundo'). Context determines whether it's literal (geographic/historical) or figurative.
target_language_example: Después del viaje, sintió que había entrado en un nuevo mundo.
native_language_example: After the trip, he felt like he had entered a new world.

meaning: new to (a place, activity, job, group); inexperienced with.
additional_notes: Used to say someone is unfamiliar or recently arrived to something. Often followed by a noun or gerund: 'nuevo en la ciudad', 'nuevo en el trabajo', 'nuevo en esto'. Can refer to being new as a resident, a member, or inexperienced in an activity. Gender/number agree with the person described (nueva en, nuevos en, nuevas en).
target_language_example: Soy nuevo en la oficina, ¿me puedes mostrar dónde está la impresora?
native_language_example: I'm new to the office, can you show me where the printer is?

meaning: literally 'new is' — not a fixed Spanish phrase; likely a fragment, not a standalone expression.
additional_notes: This combination of words ('nuevo' = new, 'es' = is) is grammatical only as part of a larger sentence (for example: 'Lo nuevo es interesante' = 'The new thing is interesting'). On its own it doesn't function as an idiom or common phrase. Make sure to include the noun or subject that 'nuevo' modifies and the rest of the sentence when using these words.
target_language_example: Lo nuevo es que ahora cerramos a las diez.
native_language_example: The new thing is that we now close at ten.

meaning: new pair (of two items); a newly acquired matching set
additional_notes: Used to describe two matching items bought or obtained together (e.g., a new pair of shoes, gloves, socks). In Spanish, 'par' is masculine: 'un nuevo par' or 'el nuevo par'. When specifying the item, include it: 'un nuevo par de zapatos'.
target_language_example: Compré un nuevo par de zapatos para la fiesta.
native_language_example: I bought a new pair of shoes for the party.

meaning: 'new that' (literal); not a fixed idiom in Spanish and rarely appears as a set phrase.
additional_notes: This is simply the adjective nuevo ('new') followed by the conjunction/relative que ('that/which'). It can occur when 'nuevo' modifies a noun or phrase followed by a subordinate clause, but 'nuevo que' as a bare sequence is uncommon in standard usage. More natural alternatives include 'es nuevo', 'lo nuevo es que...', or 'nuevo en'. Use caution: some sentences with 'nuevo que' may sound awkward or require rephrasing.
target_language_example: Es nuevo que vengas mañana; no lo esperaba.
native_language_example: It's new that you are coming tomorrow; I didn't expect it.

meaning: literally 'new and' — used to add another characteristic to something described as new (often followed by an adjective or noun).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom; it's simply the adjective nuevo (new) followed by the conjunction y (and). You'll see it when listing qualities: e.g. 'nuevo y brillante' (new and shiny) or 'nuevo y mejorado' (new and improved). Make sure to match nuevo with gender and number of the noun (nuevo/nueva, nuevos/nuevas).
target_language_example: Compré un coche nuevo y barato.
native_language_example: I bought a new and cheap car.

meaning: new to (something) — describes someone inexperienced with or recently introduced to an activity, place, job, etc.
additional_notes: Construcción: nuevo (masculine) / nueva (feminine) + a + [sustantivo o actividad]. Frecuente en expresiones como "soy nuevo(a) a esto" o "es nuevo(a) a la empresa" aunque en muchas regiones se prefiere "en" (p. ej., "nuevo en el trabajo"). No se usa para indicar que un objeto es recién comprado (para objetos se usa sólo "nuevo").
target_language_example: Soy nuevo a este proyecto y todavía estoy aprendiendo los procedimientos.
native_language_example: I'm new to this project and I'm still learning the procedures.

meaning: new to (something) — indicates someone has little or no experience with a thing or place.
additional_notes: Used before an activity, place or situation: 'nuevo al + [noun/infinitive/gerund]' often appears in phrases like 'soy nuevo al trabajo' or 'es nuevo al programa'. More common alternatives are 'nuevo en' (new in/at) or 'nuevo en esto/esto' and 'no estoy acostumbrado a'. 'Nuevo al' can sound slightly less common than 'nuevo en' depending on region; choose 'nuevo en' for general use. Use 'nuevo/a' agreement with the person (soy nuevo / soy nueva).
target_language_example: Soy nuevo al trabajo y todavía aprendo las tareas.
native_language_example: I'm new to the job and I'm still learning the tasks.

meaning: This sequence is not a correct or grammatical Spanish phrase; it likely reflects a word order or typing mistake.
additional_notes: In Spanish adjectives typically follow nouns, so the correct order is 'el nuevo' (the new [one]) when referring to a masculine noun (e.g., 'el coche nuevo' or short form 'el nuevo'). 'Nuevo el' is incorrect and should be avoided. Possible intended forms: 'el nuevo' (the new), 'nuevo' (new), or 'lo nuevo' (the new thing).
target_language_example: ¿Por qué escribiste "nuevo el" en vez de "el nuevo"?
native_language_example: Why did you write "nuevo el" instead of "el nuevo"?

meaning: "never to" or "never at" (depends on context) — 'nunca' means 'never'; 'a' is a preposition that can mean 'to', 'at', 'on', etc.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed multiword expression on its own. More likely you'll see 'nunca' used with different prepositions (e.g., 'nunca a', 'nunca en', 'nunca con') depending on the verb or phrase. 'Nunca' by itself means 'never' (negates actions or states). When you see 'nunca a' it combines 'never' + the preposition 'a' and the exact translation depends on the verb and context (for example: 'nunca a tiempo' → 'never on time'; 'nunca a ella' would be unusual — you'd more likely say 'nunca a ella le dije...' as part of a larger structure). For beginners: learn 'nunca' (never) first; then learn common preposition + noun/verb patterns separately.
target_language_example: Nunca a tiempo llego a clase.
native_language_example: I never arrive to class on time.

meaning: never before; not at any previous time.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something has not happened at any time up to now. Often placed before or after the verb (e.g., 'Nunca antes te había sucedido' or 'Él no ha ido nunca antes'). Common in both spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: Nunca antes había probado sushi tan bueno.
native_language_example: I had never tried such good sushi before.

meaning: he/she/you (formal) never gave in; never yielded.
additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of 'ceder' with 'nunca' (never). Used to say someone did not give in, yield, or give up to something (e.g., temptation, pressure, an argument). Subject can be él/ella/usted; context determines the target (he/she/you formal). With different subjects you must conjugate cedió accordingly (yo cedí, tú cediste, nosotros cedimos, etc.).
target_language_example: A pesar de las presiones, ella nunca cedió.
native_language_example: Despite the pressure, she never gave in.

meaning: 'never... (with a following noun or verb phrase)'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom by itself; 'nunca' means 'never' and 'de' is a preposition that often begins a phrase (e.g., 'nunca dejes', 'nunca de mi vida'). Common constructions: 'nunca dejes' (never leave/never let), 'nunca en la vida' or colloquial emphatic 'nunca de mi vida' (never in my life). Pay attention to the words that follow—'nunca de' alone is incomplete in most contexts.
target_language_example: Nunca dejes tus llaves en el coche.
native_language_example: Never leave your keys in the car.

meaning: never say (you/he/she/they should never say); a negative command or advice with 'decir'.
additional_notes: Combines 'nunca' (never) with the imperative or subjunctive form of 'decir'. Most commonly used as advice or a warning: 'Nunca digas...' + clause. Depending on context the verb that follows may be in indicative or subjunctive (often subjunctive after expressions of doubt or emotion). Can be addressed to tú (imperative: 'Nunca digas...') or used descriptively ('Nunca digas eso' = 'Never say that').
target_language_example: Nunca digas que no lo intentaste.
native_language_example: Never say that you didn't try.

meaning: 'never say never' — a warning that something thought impossible might still happen.
additional_notes: Used to tell someone not to be too sure that something will never occur. Often said after a surprising event or when advising caution. Tone can be casual or emphatic depending on context.
target_language_example: Sé que no te gusta viajar solo, pero nunca digas nunca; podrías cambiar de opinión.
native_language_example: I know you don't like traveling alone, but never say never; you might change your mind.

meaning: never in; never at (a place or time).
additional_notes: Used to say that something has not happened or will not happen within a specific place, time period, or situation. Often followed by a noun or phrase indicating location, time, or circumstance: e.g., 'nunca en mi vida' (never in my life), 'nunca en la escuela' (never at school). In many cases Spanish speakers prefer 'nunca' alone or other constructions (no ... nunca, jamás en), but 'nunca en' is common before locations/times.
target_language_example: Nunca en mi vida he visto tanta nieve.
native_language_example: Never in my life have I seen so much snow.

meaning: 'never in my' — a fragment used to start phrases like 'never in my life' or 'never in my opinion'.
additional_notes: This is not a complete fixed phrase by itself; it typically begins expressions such as 'nunca en mi vida' (never in my life) or 'nunca en mi opinión' (never in my opinion). Use it to emphasize that something has never happened to you, never will happen, or to state a strong negative opinion. Word order: 'nunca' (never) comes before the prepositional phrase 'en mi ...'.
target_language_example: Nunca en mi vida había visto algo así.
native_language_example: Never in my life had I seen something like that.

meaning: 'it is never' or 'never is' (used to say something is never the case).
additional_notes: Combines 'nunca' (never) + 'es' (3rd-person singular of ser). Used to state that something is never true or never happens. Context determines the subject (often implied or previously mentioned): e.g. 'Nunca es fácil' = 'It is never easy.' Can appear at start or middle of a sentence. Not idiomatic or slang.
target_language_example: Nunca es tarde para aprender algo nuevo.
native_language_example: It is never too late to learn something new.

meaning: 'it's never too (something)' — usually completed with 'tarde' to mean 'it's never too late'.
additional_notes: Commonly appears as the full phrase 'nunca es demasiado tarde' meaning 'it's never too late' (to do something). Used to encourage action or change; follow with an infinitive (para + infinitive) or a clause. Can be shortened in conversation to 'nunca es demasiado' when context (like 'tarde') is understood.
target_language_example: Nunca es demasiado tarde para intentarlo de nuevo.
native_language_example: It's never too late to try again.

meaning: is never (in a certain state or place).
additional_notes: Combines 'nunca' (never) with the verb 'estar' (to be). Used to say that someone or something is never in a particular condition, location, or situation. Placement: 'nunca' usually comes before the verb. Context determines what follows (e.g., 'nunca está aquí' = 'is never here'; 'nunca está lista' = 'is never ready').
target_language_example: Mi hermano nunca está en casa los fines de semana.
native_language_example: My brother is never at home on weekends.

meaning: 'never does' (he/she/it never does something).
additional_notes: Nunca = never. Hace is the 3rd person singular present of hacer (to do/make). Used to describe that someone or something does not do an action habitually or at all. Context determines what follows (e.g., nunca hace lo que se le dice = never does what they're told). Can appear with nada (never does anything) or with clauses.
target_language_example: Ella nunca hace caso cuando le hablo.
native_language_example: She never pays attention when I talk to her.

meaning: there is never
additional_notes: Used to say that something is never present, available, or happening. hay is the form of haber used for both singular and plural, so English may use either 'there is' or 'there are' depending on what follows.
target_language_example: Nunca hay suficiente tiempo.
native_language_example: There is never enough time.

meaning: never did
additional_notes: Past tense phrase: 'nunca' = never, 'hizo' = he/she/it/you(formal) did (preterite of hacer). Used to say someone did not do something at any time in the past. Watch out for double negatives: Spanish often allows double negatives (e.g., 'Ningún policía nunca hizo...') but in standard Spanish you would normally use either 'ningún... jamás' or 'ningún... nunca' depending on emphasis; literal English typically drops the extra negative.
target_language_example: Él nunca hizo la tarea.
native_language_example: He never did the homework.

meaning: never ever; emphatic never.
additional_notes: A strong, emphatic way to say 'never' in Spanish. Used to stress that something has not happened and will not happen. Often appears in negative statements and can be used alone for emphasis (e.g., '¡Nunca jamás!'). More emotional or dramatic than simple 'nunca'.
target_language_example: Nunca jamás voy a olvidarlo.
native_language_example: I will never ever forget it.

meaning: 'never it/her' or part of a larger phrase meaning 'never ... (it/her)'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself; it's the adverb 'nunca' (never) followed by the direct object pronoun 'la' (it/her). You will commonly see it inside sentences where 'la' replaces a feminine noun mentioned earlier: e.g. 'Nunca la vi' = 'I never saw her/it.' Word order: in simple tenses the pronoun usually comes before the verb (Nunca la veo), but with infinitives, gerunds, or affirmative commands it can attach after or be placed differently (Voy a verla = I'm going to see her).
target_language_example: Nunca la vi en esa tienda.
native_language_example: I never saw her/it in that store.

meaning: 'never' + indirect object pronoun 'them' / 'to them' (used to say something never happens to or for people/things)
additional_notes: Combines 'nunca' (never) with the indirect object pronoun 'les' (to them/for them). Used when the action or state does not apply to a group: e.g. 'A mis abuelos nunca les gustaba...' = 'My grandparents never liked...'. 'Les' agrees with third-person plural (ellos/ustedes). Word order can vary: 'Nunca les digas...' (Never tell them...).
target_language_example: A los niños nunca les dieron permiso para entrar.
native_language_example: The children were never given permission to go in.

meaning: never them
additional_notes: A combination of the adverb 'nunca' (never) plus the direct object pronoun 'los' (them, masculine or mixed plural). Used to say that someone never does something to, with, or regarding 'them' (people or masculine/mixed objects). Word order varies: 'nunca los' often appears before or after a verb depending on tense and emphasis (e.g., 'Nunca los vi' or 'No los vi nunca'). In compound tenses with a helping verb, the pronoun usually goes before the conjugated verb ('Nunca los he visto').
target_language_example: Nunca los invité a la fiesta.
native_language_example: I never invited them to the party.

meaning: never again; no more (from now on).
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something will not happen again or that someone will not be seen/visited again. Can refer to a single past event that won’t be repeated or to a future refusal. Placement: often follows the verb (e.g., 'la vi nunca más') or comes at the end of the sentence ('nunca más').
target_language_example: Después de esa discusión, decidí no llamarla nunca más.
native_language_example: After that argument, I decided never to call her again.

meaning: a strong negation: 'never anything' or 'never ... anything' (used to emphasize that something never happens or does not exist).
additional_notes: This is a double-negation emphasis common in Spanish: both words are negative but used together for stronger emphasis. In English you'd usually say 'never anything' or rephrase as 'never ... at all' or 'nothing ever'. Word order can change: 'nunca nada' and 'nada nunca' are both possible, but most natural is 'no ... nunca nada' or 'nunca nada' after a verb. Context determines exact translation.
target_language_example: Desde que se fue, nunca nada ha sido igual.
native_language_example: Since they left, nothing has ever been the same.

meaning: 'I can never' or 'I can’t ever'.
additional_notes: Used to say you are never able to do something. Often followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., nunca puedo llegar a tiempo = I can never arrive on time). 'Nunca' is a negative adverb meaning 'never'; Spanish uses double negation with verbs (Nunca puedo nada is unusual — typically structure is 'Nunca puedo + infinitive' or 'No puedo + nunca' with care).
target_language_example: Nunca puedo levantarme temprano los fines de semana.
native_language_example: I can never get up early on weekends.

meaning: you/one never knows; it's impossible to be certain.
additional_notes: Common phrase using 'nunca' (never) + verb 'saber' (to know). Can refer to 'you never know' (general advice) or 'he/she/one never knows' depending on context. Often used to express uncertainty about the future or outcomes (e.g., 'you never know when...'). Subject can be explicit or implied: 'uno nunca sabe', 'uno nunca sabe' → 'one never knows'; 'nunca sabe' after a named subject means 'he/she never knows.'
target_language_example: Nunca sabe si lloverá mañana.
native_language_example: You never know if it will rain tomorrow.

meaning: you never know; it's uncertain
additional_notes: Used to express uncertainty about the future or outcomes. Common in conversational Spanish to suggest that something unexpected might happen or to justify taking a chance. Can be followed by clauses introduced with cuándo, cuánto, lo que, etc.
target_language_example: Nunca se sabe si mañana lloverá y cancelarán el viaje.
native_language_example: You never know if it will rain tomorrow and they'll cancel the trip.

meaning: I never have / I never get
additional_notes: Present-tense first-person phrase: 'nunca' (never) + 'tengo' (I have). Used to say you never possess, experience, receive or feel something. Context determines whether 'have' means possession, obligation ('tener que'), age, or experiences — here it’s the simple verb 'tener' meaning 'to have'. For negative emphasis, Spanish places 'nunca' before the verb.
target_language_example: Nunca tengo suficiente tiempo para leer.
native_language_example: I never have enough time to read.

meaning: 'I never had the...' (start of a sentence about something you never possessed or experienced)
additional_notes: This is a phrase fragment: nunca = never, tuve = I had (preterite of tener), la is a feminine singular direct object or article. It introduces a statement about something feminine you never had or experienced (e.g., la oportunidad, la oportunidad, la suerte, la culpa). Complete the thought with a feminine noun or noun phrase. For masculine nouns you'd use 'nunca tuve el'.
target_language_example: Nunca tuve la oportunidad de viajar sola.
native_language_example: I never had the opportunity to travel alone.

meaning: will never (do something) / is never going to (happen).
additional_notes: Commonly used with 'a' + infinitive (va a + infinitive) to form the near future. 'Nunca' (never) usually comes before the verb: 'nunca va a + infinitive' = 'is never going to ...' or 'will never ...'. Can express certainty about the future; tone can be negative or emphatic depending on context.
target_language_example: Ella nunca va a olvidar ese día.
native_language_example: She is never going to forget that day.

meaning: I never see (or 'I don't ever see').
additional_notes: Nunca = never. Veo is the first-person singular present of ver (to see). Used to say you never see someone or something (can mean 'meet' or 'visit' depending on context). Often followed by a direct object (a mis hijos, a nadie, a mi padre).
target_language_example: Nunca veo a mis amigos los fines de semana.
native_language_example: I never see my friends on weekends.

meaning: 'I will never' (start of a sentence meaning 'I will never...')
additional_notes: Common construction: 'Nunca voy a + infinitive' = 'I will never [do something]'. 'Nunca' = never; 'voy' is first-person present of 'ir' used with 'a' to form near future (going to). Used to make strong, definite statements about not doing something in the future.
target_language_example: Nunca voy a rendirme.
native_language_example: I will never give up.

meaning: I never go / I do not ever go
additional_notes: Nunca = never. Voy is first-person singular present of ir (to go). Used to say you never do an activity or never go to a place. Often followed by a destination introduced with a, or by an infinitive with a (voy a + infinitive) to indicate future (but in these examples 'nunca voy a ese restaurante' uses a + noun, not future). 'Nunca voy a' + place = 'I never go to...'.
target_language_example: Nunca voy al cine los lunes.
native_language_example: I never go to the cinema on Mondays.

meaning: 'number of the' — used before a feminine noun to indicate a specific number belonging to or associated with that noun.
additional_notes: This is a fragment used when specifying the number of something feminine (e.g., la casa, la página, la habitación). It must be followed by a feminine noun (or implied noun) or by a noun phrase: e.g., número de la casa, número de la página. If the noun is masculine, use 'número del' (contraction of 'de el').
target_language_example: ¿Cuál es el número de la habitación?
native_language_example: What is the number of the room?

meaning: telephone number; phone number.
additional_notes: Common phrase used to ask for or refer to someone's phone number. 'Número' = number, 'teléfono' = telephone. Used in formal and informal contexts. Can be shortened in speech to 'número' or 'teléfono' when context makes meaning clear (e.g., '¿Me das tu número?').
target_language_example: ¿Me puedes dar tu número de teléfono?
native_language_example: Can you give me your phone number?

meaning: phone number of / the telephone number belonging to (someone or something).
additional_notes: Use before a person or organization to indicate whose phone number it is. In Spanish the full phrase is often followed by a name or noun: 'el número de teléfono de María' = María's phone number. You can also shorten to 'número de' in context, but include 'teléfono' for clarity. For asking someone's number, common questions are '¿Cuál es tu número de teléfono?' or '¿Me das tu número de teléfono?'.
target_language_example: Necesito el número de teléfono de la clínica.
native_language_example: I need the clinic's phone number.

meaning: the second in rank or position; 'number two' (also a nickname for a deputy or second-in-command).
additional_notes: Used to refer to the person or thing in second place, or the deputy/second-in-command. Can be used as a label ("número dos") or in sentences like "es el número dos". Context determines whether it means simple order (#2) or a deputy/vice role.
target_language_example: Ella es el número dos del equipo.
native_language_example: She is the team's number two (the deputy).

meaning: ‘number in’ or ‘number on’ — indicates a number found in/on something or a position number within a list/record.
additional_notes: Used to say where a number appears (e.g., on a piece of paper, in a call history) or to refer to someone's position by their number in a list (número en lista). Often followed by the container: 'número en un papel', 'número en la lista', 'número en el historial'.
target_language_example: Anoté el número en la libreta para no olvidarlo.
native_language_example: I wrote the number in the notebook so I wouldn't forget it.

meaning: favorite number.
additional_notes: Used to say which number you like most. Often appears with verbs 'ser' (es) or 'tener' (no tener here). Word order flexible: 'Mi número favorito es el cuatro' or 'El cuatro es mi número favorito.' 'Número' is masculine; use 'el' with specific numbers.
target_language_example: Mi número favorito es el siete.
native_language_example: My favorite number is seven.

meaning: the number that / the number which (used to refer to a phone number or numeric identifier previously mentioned)
additional_notes: Commonly used in phone and technical contexts to refer to a specific number mentioned or dialed. 'Que' introduces a relative clause describing the number. In English you often translate it as 'the number that' or simply 'the number' + clause.
target_language_example: El número que marcaste no responde.
native_language_example: The number that you dialed does not answer.

meaning: number one; the top / first; the main person or thing
additional_notes: Used both literally (the numeral 1, first in order) and figuratively to mean 'the best', 'the main suspect', or 'top priority/rule'. Common in phrases like "regla número uno" (rule number one) or "sospechoso número uno" (prime suspect). Can appear with articles or alone when addressing someone as 'Number One'.
target_language_example: Ella es la número uno del equipo.
native_language_example: She is the number one on the team.

meaning: 'or to / or at' — a combination of the conjunction o (or) followed by the preposition a (to/at), used when listing alternatives that begin with a preposition
additional_notes: This sequence appears when two alternatives both require the preposition a (or when the second alternative is introduced with a preposition): e.g., 'voy a la playa o a la montaña' (I'm going to the beach or to the mountain). The conjunction o links alternatives; a is the preposition that belongs to the second (and often both) option(s). In speech the a is pronounced normally; if the preceding word ends with an /o/ sound, spelling still uses 'o' (not 'u') unless necessary for euphony before 'o' (rare).
target_language_example: Puedes ir al cine o a casa esta tarde.
native_language_example: You can go to the cinema or home this afternoon.

meaning: or to the / or at the (contraction of 'o a' + the masculine singular article 'el' → 'o al' rarely used; more commonly 'o a' or 'o al' when followed by a place/person).
additional_notes: This is a combination of the conjunction 'o' (or) followed by the preposition 'a' plus the article 'el' contracted as 'al' (a + el = al). It appears before a masculine singular noun: e.g. 'o al cine' = 'or to the cinema' / 'o al médico' = 'or to the doctor'. In many contexts English would omit 'to' and just use 'or the...'; in Spanish the preposition is required when indicating movement, direction, or indirect objects. Not a fixed phrase—it's compositional.
target_language_example: ¿Vamos al parque o al museo?
native_language_example: Are we going to the park or to the museum?

meaning: the Argentine (one) / the Argentine (thing) — masculine singular
additional_notes: Portuguese/Spanish note: In Spanish the masculine article is 'el' not 'o'. 'O argentino' is Portuguese for 'the Argentine' (man or masculine noun). Use to refer to a man from Argentina or an Argentine (masculine) object. If referring to a woman, use 'a argentina' in Portuguese; in Spanish use 'el argentino' / 'la argentina'.
target_language_example: O argentino chegou ontem.
native_language_example: The Argentine arrived yesterday.

meaning: 'or with' (a simple connector used to present an alternative that includes 'with').
additional_notes: Combines the conjunction o (or) with the preposition con (with). Used when offering choices that include 'with' something (e.g., '¿Quieres café o con leche?' — though more natural is '¿Quieres café solo o con leche?'). Often appears inside longer phrases (e.g., 'o con... o sin...' = 'either with... or without...'). Pronunciation and word order are the same as the separate words.
target_language_example: Puedes pedir la hamburguesa o con queso, o sin queso.
native_language_example: You can order the burger either with cheese or without cheese.

meaning: or four (used to give an approximate number or offer an alternative)
additional_notes: Commonly follows a number to indicate approximation (e.g., "tres o cuatro" = "three or four"). Also used when listing options or giving a rough estimate. Pronunciation: like English 'oh' for 'o'.
target_language_example: Voy a quedarme tres o cuatro días.
native_language_example: I'm going to stay three or four days.

meaning: 'or of' — a short combination used when listing alternatives or specifying a relationship (varies by context).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase; it's simply the conjunction o ('or') followed by the preposition de ('of', 'from', 'about', etc.). You will see 'o de' in contexts like alternatives with possession/description (e.g., "una taza o de vidrio" — 'a cup or (one) made of glass') or choices introduced before a noun phrase starting with de (e.g., "¿Pizza o de pasta?" — informal "Pizza or pasta?"). Meaning depends on the words that follow; treat it as two separate words used together in a sentence.
target_language_example: ¿Quieres té o de hierbas?
native_language_example: Do you want tea or herbal (tea)?

meaning: 'or of the' (combination of 'o' = 'or' and 'del' = contraction of 'de + el' meaning 'of the')
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but two words that often appear together in sentences where a choice (o) is followed by a prepositional phrase using 'del' (de + el). Example contexts: offering alternatives, listing options, or linking clauses. 'Del' is used before masculine singular nouns. Make sure not to confuse 'del' with 'de' + 'ella' (which would be 'de ella').
target_language_example: ¿Quieres té o del café?
native_language_example: Do you want tea or the coffee?

meaning: 'or two days' — used after a number to indicate an approximate additional amount of time (e.g., 'one or two days').
additional_notes: Commonly appears after a numeral (uno, dos, etc.) to soften exactness: 'uno o dos días' = 'one or two days'. Used to give an estimate, ask for a short wait, or set a short deadline. Often appears in everyday speech and writing; keep number agreement with surrounding words (e.g., 'uno o dos días más').
target_language_example: Necesito uno o dos días para terminarlo.
native_language_example: I need one or two days to finish it.

meaning: 'or the' (combination of the conjunction 'o' = or + the masculine definite article 'el' = the).
additional_notes: This is simply two separate words used together in a sentence when offering alternatives that include a masculine singular noun: e.g., 'o el coche' = 'or the car'. Remember Spanish contracts 'o' to 'u' before words starting with 'o' or 'ho' sound (rare), but not before 'el'. Watch out for confusion with 'ó' (accent) — modern spelling no longer uses the accent on 'o'.
target_language_example: Puedes tomar el autobús o el tren.
native_language_example: You can take the bus or the train.

meaning: 'or in' — used to offer an alternative location, state, or context (A or in B).
additional_notes: Combines the coordinating conjunction o (or) with the preposition en (in). Common when giving two possible places, states, or contexts: 'o en X' often follows another 'o' earlier ('o X o en Y') or appears as 'o en Y' after an initial option. Word order in Spanish can be flexible: you may also see 'o X o en Y' or 'o en X o en Y'.
target_language_example: Él está o en Londres o en París.
native_language_example: He is either in London or in Paris.

meaning: 'or that' / 'or so' (used to offer an alternative, suggest a possibility, or sum up briefly).
additional_notes: Common short phrase used after a statement to give an alternative explanation, to soften a claim (like 'or so'), or to conclude a thought. Often follows a clause and can stand alone as a brief reply. Tone depends on context: can be tentative, dismissive, or summarizing.
target_language_example: No era muy alto, o eso recuerdo.
native_language_example: He wasn't very tall, or so I remember.

meaning: 'or (we) will [do something to] him/her' — used to introduce a threat or consequence directed at someone (formal 'usted' object).
additional_notes: Common in threats or warnings: 'o' = 'or' (introduces the alternative/consequence); 'le' is the indirect-object or direct-object pronoun used for 'him/her' (formal). Together they often imply an implied verb like 'vamos a' or a future action: 'Do X, or we'll do Y to him/her.' Tone is aggressive; these examples show violent threats. Not a fixed idiom beyond the literal combination.
target_language_example: Tráeme eso ahora o le diré a la policía.
native_language_example: Bring me that now or I'll tell the police about him/her.
