meaning: 'or I' — the conjunction 'o' (or) followed by the first-person object/pronoun fragment 'me'; often appears as part of a larger phrase or clause (e.g., 'o me ayudas, o me voy' = 'either you help me, or I leave').
additional_notes: By itself 'o me' is not a complete phrase; it usually connects two alternatives where 'me' is the object/pronoun in the second option. In spoken and written Spanish you'll frequently see it in correlative structures with 'o... o...' (either... or...) or in conditional/emphatic contrasts (e.g., 'O me das la verdad, o me largo'). Pronunciation: 'o' = /o/ (like English 'o' in 'go' but shorter).
target_language_example: O me disculpas ahora, o no vuelvas a hablarme.
native_language_example: Either you apologize to me now, or don't speak to me again.

meaning: or less than; used to indicate a maximum amount or a lower bound (≤).
additional_notes: Commonly used after a number or quantity to say 'no more than' that amount. It often appears in phrases like "10 o menos de" (10 or less) or "una hora o menos de" (an hour or less). In everyday speech you may also hear simply "o menos" after a number (without "de").
target_language_example: Quiero beber 2 litros o menos de agua al día.
native_language_example: I want to drink 2 liters or less of water a day.

meaning: a shortened, colloquial way to say "o menos" (= "or less" / "or at least") combined with the feminine article "la"; often a fragment in speech, context-dependent.
additional_notes: This phrase looks like a fragment rather than a complete expression. "O menos" can mean "or less" (comparing quantities) or in colloquial speech "o, menos" can introduce a correction like "or rather" / "or at least." The added "la" is the feminine singular definite article and will only make sense when it refers to a previously mentioned feminine noun (e.g., "la cantidad") or in clipped spoken phrases. Beginners will mostly encounter "o menos"; include "la" only when it matches a feminine noun in context.
target_language_example: Necesitamos una hora, o menos la reunión terminará tarde.
native_language_example: We need an hour, or less — otherwise the meeting will end late.

meaning: 'or death' — used after a noun or phrase to express extreme determination or a dramatic ultimatum (e.g., 'libertad o muerte' = 'freedom or death').
additional_notes: Common in slogans, mottos, or dramatic statements. It pairs with a noun (libertad, patria, honor) to mean '... or death' — i.e., willing to die for that cause. Formality: can be used in historical, political, or rhetorical contexts; not typically used in everyday polite conversation.
target_language_example: ¡Libertad o muerte!
native_language_example: Freedom or death!

meaning: 'or very' — a short connector used to offer an alternative or to add emphasis before an adjective or adverb.
additional_notes: This combination appears when linking choices or intensifying a description: 'o' = 'or'; 'muy' = 'very'. It is compositional and literal. In natural usage you often see it in phrases like 'grande, o muy grande' (big, or very big) or in informal speech to quickly add an alternative or stronger degree. Note that spacing is standard: 'o muy'.
target_language_example: ¿Quieres té o muy caliente? — Mejor té frío.
native_language_example: Do you want tea or very hot? — Better iced tea.

meaning: or more; at least (used after numbers or quantities)
additional_notes: Placed after a number or quantity to indicate that the actual amount may be equal to or greater than the stated figure. Common in prices, measurements, ages, and descriptions (e.g., "10 personas o más"). Can be used with nouns, adjectives, or numbers.
target_language_example: Llegaremos en 15 minutos o más.
native_language_example: We'll arrive in 15 minutes or more.

meaning: 'or never' — used to present an alternative that means 'not at any time' or 'not at all'.
additional_notes: Commonly appears in choices or warnings: X o nunca (do X or never). Often used in imperative or conditional contexts to stress a last chance or absolute negation. Can also appear inside longer sentences: 'hazlo o nunca' (do it or never), though native speakers might prefer other constructions (e.g., 'ahora o nunca' = 'now or never').
target_language_example: Ahora o nunca: tienes que decidirte.
native_language_example: Now or never: you have to decide.

meaning: or for / or to (depends on context)
additional_notes: This is two separate words: o = "or" (used to offer alternatives) and para = a preposition meaning "for", "to", "in order to", etc. Together they appear when a phrase needs both an alternative and a prepositional idea (e.g., "o para..." = "or for..." or "or to..."), but they are not a fixed idiom. Pay attention to context: para may introduce purpose, recipient, deadline, or comparison.
target_language_example: Puedes usar mantequilla o para freír, usa aceite.
native_language_example: You can use butter or to fry, use oil.

meaning: or for the worse / or to make things worse
additional_notes: Used to introduce a negative consequence or to indicate that something makes a situation worse. It often follows a statement and contrasts a hoped-for or neutral outcome with a worse one. Common in conversational Spanish; context determines whether it's literal ('to make something worse') or idiomatic ('to make matters worse').
target_language_example: Llegó tarde, o para mal, sin el dinero que debía traer.
native_language_example: He arrived late, and to make matters worse, without the money he was supposed to bring.

meaning: or / alternatively; used to offer another option or reason (often followed by a verb or noun).
additional_notes: Commonly used to present an alternative (similar to 'o' alone) or to introduce a reason or motive in some constructions (e.g., 'o por eso'). In speech it can connect two options ('¿Café o por té?') though that example is colloquial—more natural: '¿Café o té?' When followed by 'qué' or a clause, it can mean 'or because/for' as in 'no vino, o por estar enfermo' (he didn't come, perhaps because he was sick).
target_language_example: Podemos ir al cine o por la tarde quedarnos en casa.
native_language_example: We can go to the movies or alternatively stay home in the afternoon.

meaning: 'what' or 'that which' (used to introduce clauses or ask about something).
additional_notes: Used in questions and relative clauses. In questions it often appears as part of ¿Qué...? but 'o que' alone can mean 'or what' in lists or spoken hesitation. Note: In Portuguese 'o que' = 'what', but in Spanish the correct form for 'what' is usually 'qué' or 'lo que' for 'that which'. 'o que' (without accent) is uncommon in standard Spanish and may appear in regional speech or typos; if you mean 'what' in Spanish, use 'qué' (question) or 'lo que' (that which).
target_language_example: No entiendo lo que dices.
native_language_example: I don't understand what you are saying.

meaning: or if (used to introduce an alternative possibility or condition).
additional_notes: Commonly used in spoken and written Spanish to present an alternative clause or condition. Often appears in choices or to suggest another option: 'Haz X, o se hace Y' (Do X, or else Y will happen). Depending on context, it can mean 'or' + reflexive pronoun (part of a verb) when split across words (e.g., 'o se va' = 'or he/she/it leaves'). Pay attention to surrounding verbs to know whether 'se' is part of a reflexive verb or just the pronoun in the alternative.
target_language_example: Puedes venir ahora, o se queda para la cena.
native_language_example: You can come now, or (he/she) stays for dinner.

meaning: 'that is', 'I mean', or 'so' — used to rephrase, clarify, summarize, or draw a conclusion.
additional_notes: Very common filler/connector. Use to restate or clarify what you just said (like 'that is' or 'I mean'), to introduce a conclusion ('so'), or to soften/introduce an explanation. Tone can be neutral or informal depending on context; in casual speech it often functions like 'I mean' in English.
target_language_example: No tengo coche, o sea, voy al trabajo en autobús.
native_language_example: I don't have a car, I mean/so I take the bus to work.

meaning: 'or if' — introduces an alternative possibility or hypothesis.
additional_notes: Used to present another possibility, condition, or speculation. Often appears at the start of a clause and can follow a comma or stand alone. In conversational Spanish it can also be used to emphasize surprise or doubt about an alternative scenario.
target_language_example: No sé si vendrá, o si prefieres que cancelemos.
native_language_example: I don't know if they'll come, or if you'd prefer that we cancel.

meaning: or without
additional_notes: 'o' means 'or' and 'sin' means 'without'. Used to offer an alternative that excludes something. Common in phrases like 'con o sin' (with or without). When spoken, 'o' may contract to 'u' before words that start with 'o' or 'ho' for sound clarity (rare in modern Spanish).
target_language_example: Quiero el café o sin azúcar, por favor.
native_language_example: I want the coffee with or without sugar, please.

meaning: or his/her/its/their (depending on context).
additional_notes: Combination of the conjunction o (or) + the possessive adjective su. Used to offer an alternative possession or to contrast whose thing it is. su can mean his, her, its, your (formal), or their — context determines meaning. In spoken Spanish spacing is the same: 'o su' appears when 'or' precedes the possessive.
target_language_example: ¿Quieres usar el bolígrafo mío o su bolígrafo?
native_language_example: Do you want to use my pen or his/her/their pen?

meaning: 'or only' / 'or just' (offers an alternative or restricts meaning)
additional_notes: Used to present an alternative (o = or) or to add a restricting comment (sólo = only/just). In modern Spanish, 'sólo' (with accent) for 'only' is optional; many style guides prefer 'solo' without accent unless needed to avoid ambiguity. When used together, 'o sólo' commonly appears in contrasts like '¿Quieres té o sólo agua?' = 'Do you want tea or just water?'.
target_language_example: ¿Vienes conmigo o sólo vas a mirar?
native_language_example: Are you coming with me or just going to watch?

meaning: or something like that / or such
additional_notes: Used after a noun, phrase, or list to indicate an approximate option, vagueness, or 'or something similar'. Common in casual speech. Can appear as 'o tal vez' meaning 'or maybe', but by itself it usually softens or broadens what was said (similar to 'or whatever' or 'or the like').
target_language_example: Podemos comprar sillas, mesas o tal.
native_language_example: We can buy chairs, tables, or something like that.

meaning: either early / sooner or later (depends on context).
additional_notes: Most commonly appears as part of the phrase 'tarde o temprano' meaning 'sooner or later'. Alone, 'o temprano' literally means 'or early' and is rarely used by itself. If you see 'tarde o temprano', translate as 'sooner or later'.
target_language_example: Tarde o temprano tendrás que decidir.
native_language_example: Sooner or later you'll have to decide.

meaning: or three; used to indicate an approximate small additional number (about two or three).
additional_notes: Commonly follows a definite number (often 'dos') to soften it and express approximation or uncertainty (e.g., 'dos o tres' = 'two or three'). Can stand alone in response as a short estimate ('O tres.'). Informal/neutral everyday usage.
target_language_example: Compraré dos o tres manzanas para el postre.
native_language_example: I'll buy two or three apples for dessert.

meaning: or three days (used to give an alternative time length)
additional_notes: This phrase is the conjunction 'o' (or) followed by a specific duration 'tres días' (three days). It appears when offering an alternative duration, e.g. 'uno o tres días' = 'one or three days'. Use after a number or duration. Pronunciation: o tres días (the 's' in 'tres' links to 'días').
target_language_example: Puedes quedarte uno o tres días.
native_language_example: You can stay one or three days.

meaning: or three times
additional_notes: Used to offer an alternative number of repetitions or quantity (e.g., "one or three times"). Commonly appears after a number or verb to indicate an optional count. Literal translation matches English word order.
target_language_example: Puedes intentarlo una o tres veces.
native_language_example: You can try it once or three times.

meaning: or you (used to present an alternative involving the person addressed)
additional_notes: 'o' is the coordinating conjunction meaning 'or'. 'o tú' is used to contrast or offer an alternative referring to 'you'. It commonly appears in questions, suggestions, choices, or comparisons. Punctuation and context affect emphasis: for example, '¿O tú?' (with question intonation) asks 'Or you?', while embedded in a sentence it simply offers 'you' as the alternative.
target_language_example: ¿O tú qué piensas?
native_language_example: Or you, what do you think?

meaning: 'or a' (feminine singular) — used to offer an alternative or choice before a feminine noun.
additional_notes: Spanish conjunction 'o' = 'or'. 'Una' is the feminine singular indefinite article ('a' / 'an'). Use 'o una' when presenting an alternative that is a feminine noun (e.g., 'o una manzana', 'o una casa'). If the next word begins with 'o-' or 'ho-' sound some speakers use 'u' instead of 'o' (e.g., 'u otra'), but that's with 'u' before words starting with 'o' sound. Agreement: if the alternative is masculine, use 'o un'.
target_language_example: Quieres té o una taza de café?
native_language_example: Do you want tea or a cup of coffee?

meaning: 'or else' / 'or (you) will see' (used to warn about a negative consequence); also used simply as 'or' in choices.
additional_notes: Often used in threats or warnings: '... o ya verás' = '...or else you'll see what happens.' In casual contexts it can function as a plain 'or' when offering alternatives (e.g., asking if someone is free or already has plans). Tone can be strong when followed by a consequence; context determines whether it's a warning or a neutral alternative.
target_language_example: Haz la tarea ahora, o ya verás las consecuencias.
native_language_example: Do your homework now, or else you'll see the consequences.

meaning: ‘or me’ — used to offer oneself as the alternative in a choice or comparison.
additional_notes: Commonly follows another option (e.g., 'tú o yo', 'Tom o yo') to indicate the speaker is the other possibility. Also appears in comparisons ('más grande que tú o yo') and in statements where one of two people will act ('O lo matas o yo te mato a ti'). Word order is flexible in Spanish (can be 'o yo' or 'yo o'), but 'o yo' often follows the first option. Not idiomatic or slang.
target_language_example: Si nadie más puede, o yo me encargo.
native_language_example: If nobody else can, I'll take care of it.

meaning: or him / or he (depending on sentence role).
additional_notes: A simple coordination: o means "or" and él is the stressed pronoun "he" / "him". Use él (with accent) when pronoun is needed for emphasis or clarity. In Spanish word order and verb forms decide whether it translates as "he" (subject) or "him" (object). The accent distinguishes the pronoun él from the article el (the).
target_language_example: Puedes llamar a Juan o él puede venir mañana.
native_language_example: You can call Juan or he can come tomorrow.

meaning: target/goal in (a specific area, field, or task).
additional_notes: Used to specify the target, aim, or objective within a particular context: e.g. 'objetivo en ventas' (target in sales) or 'objetivo en esta etapa' (goal at this stage). Often followed by a noun or a phrase that names the area or scope. Can also appear as part of compound phrases like 'el objetivo en este proyecto'.
target_language_example: Nuestro objetivo en marketing es aumentar las ventas un 10%.
native_language_example: Our target in marketing is to increase sales by 10%.

meaning: "objective/goal in (the)..." — part of a phrase meaning someone's goal in life or a target in a context.
additional_notes: This fragment is usually completed by a noun (most often "vida": "objetivo en la vida" = "goal in life"). Depending on context, "objetivo" can mean a personal goal, an intended aim, or a physical target (e.g., "objetivo en la mira" = "target in the sights"). Use the full phrase (e.g., "objetivo en la vida") for clarity.
target_language_example: Mi objetivo en la vida es viajar por el mundo.
native_language_example: My goal in life is to travel the world.

meaning: 'work of art' — a piece created for artistic value (painting, sculpture, performance, etc.).
additional_notes: Used to describe any artistic creation or something considered artistically excellent. Can be literal (a painting) or figurative (praising a performance, design, or creation). Commonly preceded by adjectives like auténtica, hermosa, etc.
target_language_example: Ese edificio moderno es una verdadera obra de arte.
native_language_example: That modern building is a true work of art.

meaning: 'obra' = work (art, book, composition, piece); 'es' = is. Together used as '[the] work is...' or 'your work is...'.
additional_notes: Obra is a feminine noun meaning a piece of art, a literary or musical work, a construction project, or generally someone's output. When combined with the verb es (from ser), it states a characteristic or identity of the work: e.g., who created it, its quality, or its genre. Common structures: 'La obra es de X' (the work is by X), 'Su obra es ficción' (his/her work is fiction), 'Tu obra es excelente' (your work is excellent).
target_language_example: La obra es de un compositor famoso.
native_language_example: The work is by a famous composer.

meaning: masterpiece; an outstanding work of art or achievement.
additional_notes: Used to refer to a person's best, most important, or most admired work (art, music, writing, architecture, etc.). Can be literal (a painting, book, composition) or figurative (a project or achievement). Commonly used with possessive pronouns (mi, su) or definite article (la obra maestra).
target_language_example: Su última novela es considerada su obra maestra.
native_language_example: His latest novel is considered his masterpiece.

meaning: literally 'work and' — here part of a larger phrase where obra means 'play/work/project' and y ('and') connects it to something else; used when referring to a play, musical piece, art work, or a workplace plus something else.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom by itself; 'obra' commonly means a theatrical play, musical composition, art piece, or construction/worksite. The 'y' simply links 'obra' to another noun or clause (e.g., 'obra y la dirigí' = 'I wrote a play and directed it'). Beginners should treat 'obra' on its own and remember 'y' means 'and'. Word meaning depends on context (theater, music, construction, etc.).
target_language_example: Escribí una obra y la presenté en el teatro.
native_language_example: I wrote a play and presented it at the theater.

meaning: obsessed with; overly preoccupied or fixated on someone or something.
additional_notes: Used to describe a strong, often excessive, interest or fixation. Matches gender/number (obsesionado/obsesionada/obsesionados) to the person. Common with 'estar' (estar obsesionado/obsesionada con) to indicate current state. Can be negative (unhealthy fixation) or neutral/affectionate depending on context and tone.
target_language_example: Está obsesionada con esa sonrisa.
native_language_example: She is obsessed with that smile.

meaning: the number 'eighty' followed by 'and' used to form numbers 81–89 (e.g., ochenta y uno = 81).
additional_notes: In Spanish, compound numbers from 21–29 and 31–99 (except tens themselves) are formed with 'veinti‑', 'treinta y', 'cuarenta y', etc. Use 'ochenta' alone for 80, and 'ochenta y' + digit for 81–89. The word after 'y' agrees with number words (uno → un before masculine nouns: ochenta y un libros → ochenta y un libros is incorrect; correct: ochenta y un libros → actually 'ochenta y un libros' is uncommon—use 'ochenta y un libros' only when needed).
target_language_example: Vivo en el piso ochenta y tres.
native_language_example: I live on the eighty-third floor.

meaning: eighty-one (81).
additional_notes: A cardinal number used for age, counts, addresses, scores, etc. In Spanish numbers agree in gender only for some compound forms (not for 'ochenta y uno'); you can also hear 'ochenta y un' before masculine nouns (e.g., 'ochenta y un años'). Often used alone as an answer or call-out (e.g., giving a number).
target_language_example: Mi abuela cumplió ochenta y uno el mes pasado.
native_language_example: My grandmother turned eighty-one last month.

meaning: 'eight of' — used to indicate eight units of something or a quantity equal to eight out of a group/measurement.
additional_notes: Usually appears before a noun or measurement: e.g. ocho de las manzanas (eight of the apples), ocho de la noche (note: in time expressions Spanish uses 'las' — 'a las ocho' — but 'ocho de la noche' can be used in spoken style), or when specifying fractions/parts (ocho de diez = eight out of ten). For telling time, common patterns are 'a las ocho' (at eight) or 'las ocho' (eight o'clock) rather than 'ocho de' alone.
target_language_example: Compré ocho de las galletas para la fiesta.
native_language_example: I bought eight of the cookies for the party.

meaning: 'eight (o'clock) in the' — used when telling time with 'la' (singular feminine hour)
additional_notes: Commonly appears in the phrase 'las ocho de la mañana/tarde/noche' or in colloquial speech 'a las ocho de la mañana'. Spanish normally uses 'a las ocho' for 'at eight o'clock'; 'ocho de la' by itself is a fragment that will be completed by a period of the day (mañana/tarde/noche) or by a noun phrase. Use 'la' (singular) only with 'una' (one); otherwise use 'las' before the hour ('a las ocho').
target_language_example: Nos vemos a las ocho de la noche.
native_language_example: See you at eight at night.

meaning: 'eight in' — literal translation; used when giving a count or placing eight of something inside/at a location (rare as a fixed phrase).
additional_notes: This is not a common fixed phrase in Spanish by itself. It would most often appear as part of a longer phrase, for example to say 'eight in the box' (ocho en la caja) or 'eight in the group' (ocho en el grupo). Use it when you want to indicate the number eight located inside or within something. Be careful: word order and articles are required in natural sentences (e.g., 'Hay ocho en la caja').
target_language_example: Hay ocho en la caja.
native_language_example: There are eight in the box.

meaning: "eight hours a" — used to say something happens for eight hours per (day, week, etc.).
additional_notes: This phrase appears before a time period word (usually día: "ocho horas al día"). It expresses frequency or duration: how many hours something occurs within each unit of time. Common structure: [number] + horas + al + [period]. In English you can translate it as "eight hours a day/week/etc."
target_language_example: Trabajo ocho horas al día.
native_language_example: I work eight hours a day.

meaning: literally 'eight and' — used when starting to say a time (8:__) or to add something after 'eight'.
additional_notes: Commonly heard when giving clock times in spoken Spanish: 'ocho y cinco' = 8:05, 'ocho y cuarto' = 8:15. It can also appear before another item in a list (e.g., 'ocho y diez' for 8:10). In some regions people prefer 'y' for minutes after the hour (instead of 'sobre' or 'pasadas'). Not a complete phrase by itself; it must be followed by minutes or another element.
target_language_example: La película empieza a las ocho y cuarto.
native_language_example: The movie starts at quarter past eight (8:15).

meaning: takes up too much (space).
additional_notes: Commonly used to say that an object uses more space than desired. Literally from ocupar (to occupy/take up) + demasiado (too much). Can refer to physical space or, less commonly, time/attention when context allows.
target_language_example: Esa estantería ocupa demasiado en la sala.
native_language_example: That bookshelf takes up too much space in the living room.

meaning: 'busy doing' or 'occupied with' (used to say someone is engaged in an activity or a place is in use).
additional_notes: Common way to say someone is busy with a specific task or that a room/place is currently in use. Often followed by a noun or verb in gerund (e.g., en la cocina; en la huerta; en limpiar). In some contexts you can also say 'ocupada con' or simply 'ocupada' + preposition depending on the activity.
target_language_example: Ella está ocupada en preparar la cena ahora mismo.
native_language_example: She is busy preparing dinner right now.

meaning: busy preparing (something, e.g. a meal).
additional_notes: Combines 'ocupada' (busy) with the gerund 'preparando' (preparing). Used to say someone is currently engaged in preparing something. Commonly followed by the direct object (la cena, los preparativos) or left understood from context. Matches English progressive 'busy preparing...'.
target_language_example: Ella está ocupada preparando la cena para mañana.
native_language_example: She is busy preparing dinner for tomorrow.

meaning: 'as busy as' (used to compare how busy someone is)
additional_notes: Used in comparisons with 'tan ... como' to say two people or things have the same degree of busyness. Often appears as 'tan ocupado como' (masculine) or 'tan ocupada como' (feminine). Can be modified with verbs (e.g., 'está tan ocupado como...') or modal phrases ('no estoy tan ocupado como...').
target_language_example: No estoy tan ocupado como tú esta semana.
native_language_example: I'm not as busy as you this week.

meaning: 'is busy' (third-person singular; literally 'busy is' — nonstandard word order), used to indicate someone or something is busy
additional_notes: This phrase places the adjective before the verb (ocupado + está) and is nonstandard in neutral Spanish; the usual order is 'está ocupado'. 'Ocupado está' or 'ocupado está' can appear for emphasis, poetic effect, or in certain fixed expressions. For normal speech use 'está ocupado', 'estoy ocupado', 'están ocupados', etc.
target_language_example: Perdón, ahora no puedo hablar; ocupado está.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can't talk right now; he/she is busy.

meaning: busy for / busy until (used to indicate being busy at a certain time or for someone); often part of phrases like 'estoy ocupado para [hora]' or 'ocupado para [actividad]'.
additional_notes: Commonly used to say you are unavailable at a specific time or for a specific activity/person. More natural alternatives: 'ocupado a las [hora]' or 'no puedo, estoy ocupado' depending on region. When referring to being busy with someone (e.g., helping), use 'ocupado con'. When giving a time range, Spanish often prefers 'ocupado hasta las [hora]'.
target_language_example: Lo siento, estoy ocupado para las tres; ¿puede ser a las cuatro?
native_language_example: Sorry, I'm busy for three o'clock; could it be at four?

meaning: to take care of / to handle / to deal with (something or someone).
additional_notes: Usually appears as reflexive 'ocupar(se) de'. 'Me ocupo de...' means 'I'll take care of...' or 'I'm handling...'. Use 'de' before the object (person, thing, task). Common in everyday and formal contexts. Conjugate 'ocupar' and include the reflexive pronoun (me, te, se, nos, os, se) to indicate who is doing the taking-care.
target_language_example: Yo me ocupo de la reserva esta tarde.
native_language_example: I'll take care of the reservation this afternoon.

meaning: 'happens once' or 'occurs once' (followed by a feminine noun or idea).
additional_notes: Ocurrir = to happen/occur. When followed by 'una' it means something happens only one time (e.g., 'una vez' implied) or 'a [feminine noun] happens'. In sentences 3–4 the structure is different: 'se me ocurre una (idea/opción)' means 'I come up with one (idea/option)' or 'one idea occurs to me.' Context determines whether it's about an event happening once or an idea occurring to someone.
target_language_example: Se me ocurre una solución para el problema.
native_language_example: One solution occurs to me for the problem.

meaning: 'to occur in' or 'to happen in' (a place, time, or context).
additional_notes: Used to say that an event or situation takes place within a specific location, time period, or context. Commonly followed by a noun or noun phrase (en la ciudad, en 1999, en la reunión). 'Ocurrir' can also be used alone when context makes the location/time clear, but 'ocurrir en' explicitly indicates where or when something happens.
target_language_example: La discusión ocurrió en la reunión de martes.
native_language_example: The discussion occurred in the Tuesday meeting.

meaning: 'happened to' (used to say that something happened to someone or something).
additional_notes: Commonly used with an indirect object (a + person) or with lo/que phrases: 'lo que le ocurrió a María' = 'what happened to Maria.' Also appears in time expressions without 'a' (e.g. 'ocurrió a las once' = 'it happened at eleven'), but when followed by a person the pattern is 'ocurrió a + [person]'. Use 'le' or another indirect-object pronoun for the person: 'lo que le ocurrió a él'.
target_language_example: ¿Sabes lo que le ocurrió a Carlos?
native_language_example: Do you know what happened to Carlos?

meaning: ‘it happened’ or ‘occurred’ + the (masculine) — used to say that something (a masculine noun or an event) took place.
additional_notes: Ocurrió is the past (pretérito) of ocurrir: 'to happen/occur.' When followed by 'el' it often introduces a specific event mentioned next (el accidente, el terremoto) or a time expression (el pasado octubre). If the event noun is feminine, use 'ocurrió la'. You can also say 'ocurrió en...' for 'happened in/at.'
target_language_example: Ocurrió el incendio la noche pasada.
native_language_example: The fire happened last night.

meaning: happened (occurred) ... ago (used to state how long ago something happened).
additional_notes: Use the past tense verb (ocurrió/ocurrieron/ocuría depending on context) followed by hace + time expression to say how long ago an event happened. Common time words: minutos, horas, días, semanas, meses, años. For negative or questioning forms adjust verb: ¿Cuánto tiempo hace que ocurrió? For plural subjects use 'ocurrieron'.
target_language_example: Eso ocurrió hace cinco años.
native_language_example: That happened five years ago.

meaning: 'it happened that' / 'it turned out that' (introduces a fact or event that happened).
additional_notes: Used to introduce what happened or to explain a situation. Common in storytelling or when giving background information. Can be followed by a clause (ocurrió que + [clause]). Neutral register; slightly more formal than 'pasó que'.
target_language_example: Ocurrió que nadie tenía la llave y tuvimos que esperar.
native_language_example: It happened that no one had the key and we had to wait.

meaning: a (good) thing/event happened — used to say that something good occurred
additional_notes: This phrase is not a fixed idiom by itself; it combines the verb ocurrió (past of ocurrir: 'happened') with una buena (short for 'una buena [cosa/noticia/sorpresa]'). Speakers often complete it with a noun (e.g., 'ocurrió una buena noticia') or leave the noun implied when context is clear. Use it to report a positive event in the past.
target_language_example: Ayer ocurrió una buena: me aceptaron en la universidad.
native_language_example: Yesterday a good thing happened: I was accepted to the university.

meaning: an idea occurred (to someone); someone had an idea.
additional_notes: Commonly appears with the impersonal reflexive construction 'se + indirect object' (e.g., 'se me ocurrió') to say 'I/you/he/etc. had an idea.' The indirect object (me, te, le, nos, os, les) indicates who had the idea. Often followed by adjectives like 'brillante', 'maravillosa', or the idea itself. Can also be used with a name: 'A María se le ocurrió...' Emphasizes the moment the idea came to mind.
target_language_example: Se nos ocurrió una idea para el proyecto.
native_language_example: An idea occurred to us for the project.

meaning: he/she/it hates the
additional_notes: Odia is the third-person singular present form of odiar (to hate). With a subject pronoun omitted, the subject is inferred from context: odia = he hates / she hates / you (formal) hate. "El" here is the masculine singular definite article meaning "the". The phrase appears before a masculine noun (e.g., "odia el fútbol" = "he hates soccer"). Word order in Spanish places the verb before the article in this short phrase.
target_language_example: Odia el ruido de la ciudad.
native_language_example: He hates the noise of the city.

meaning: 'I hate the' (feminine singular) — expresses dislike or hatred toward a specific feminine noun or person.
additional_notes: This is the first-person singular present form of the verb 'odiar' (odio = I hate) followed by the preposition 'a' (used before people or specific direct objects) and the feminine definite article 'la'. Use before a feminine singular noun or a feminine person: e.g., 'Odio a la vecina' (I hate the neighbor [female]). With a masculine noun use 'odio al' (a + el → al); with plural: 'odio a las' or 'odio a los'. 'Odio' is a strong word — in everyday speech speakers often prefer 'no me cae bien' (I don't like her) for milder dislike.
target_language_example: Odio a la profesora cuando cancela la clase sin avisar.
native_language_example: I hate the (female) teacher when she cancels class without warning.

meaning: 'I hate myself' (expressing self-hatred)
additional_notes: The standard and grammatically correct Spanish phrasing is reflexive: 'me odio' or 'me detesto.' 'Odio a mí' is nonstandard and atypical because verbs of emotion directed at oneself normally take a reflexive pronoun (me). Using 'a mí' as the object can be emphatic or stylistically marked, but many native speakers will find it awkward or incorrect in neutral contexts. Use 'me odio' for general statements; 'odio a mí' might appear in poetic, emphatic, or colloquial speech to force emphasis on 'mí' or to contrast with others, but it's rare.
target_language_example: Odio a mí mismo por haber cometido ese error.
native_language_example: I hate myself for having made that mistake.

meaning: 'I hate that' or 'I hate when' (expressing dislike about a situation or action).
additional_notes: Used to introduce something you strongly dislike; followed by a subordinate clause with the subjunctive when the action/event is not a fact or is subjective (e.g., 'odio que llegues tarde'); can also be followed by indicative when stating a general disliked fact. Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Odio que la gente tire basura en la calle.
native_language_example: I hate that people throw trash in the street.

meaning: 'I hate having to' or 'I hate that I have to'.
additional_notes: Used to express dislike or annoyance about an obligation, necessity, or repeated action. Often followed by 'que' + verb (subjunctive or infinitive with 'tener que' + infinitive) or by an infinitive construction. Common in informal and neutral contexts.
target_language_example: Odio tener que esperar tanto tiempo.
native_language_example: I hate having to wait so long.

meaning: literally 'hate is'; not a standalone phrase in Spanish — likely part of a sentence (e.g., 'lo que más odio es...' = 'what I hate most is...').
additional_notes: On its own, 'odio es' does not form a common fixed expression. 'Odio' is a noun ('hate') or the first-person present of the verb 'odiar' ('I hate'); 'es' is the verb 'to be' (he/she/it is). You will most often see 'odio' used in constructions like 'lo que odio es...' or 'mi odio por...' and the verb form 'odio' as in 'Yo odio...' followed by an object. Don't use 'odio es' alone — it's incomplete.
target_language_example: Lo que más odio es la impuntualidad.
native_language_example: What I hate most is lateness.

meaning: west of (indicates a location to the west of something).
additional_notes: Used to describe geographic position relative to another place. Followed by a noun or place name: 'oeste de Madrid' = 'west of Madrid'. Can be used with distances: 'a 10 km al oeste de...' or in compound descriptions: 'la costa al oeste de la isla'.
target_language_example: La ciudad está al oeste de la capital.
native_language_example: The city is west of the capital.

meaning: official in (used to say a language, status, or position is official within a place or institution).
additional_notes: Commonly used with languages or roles: 'la lengua oficial en X' = 'the official language in X'. Follows the noun it qualifies (e.g., 'lengua oficial en'). Use with countries, regions, institutions or organizations. Preposition 'en' indicates location or context.
target_language_example: El español es idioma oficial en varios países de América Latina.
native_language_example: Spanish is an official language in several Latin American countries.

meaning: to the office (indicating direction toward an office).
additional_notes: This phrase combines 'oficina' (office) with the preposition 'a' (to). In natural Spanish the correct word order is 'a la oficina' for 'to the office' because 'oficina' is feminine and normally requires the article. 'Oficina a' is not a standard standalone phrase and may appear only in clipped or telegraphic contexts (labels, notes, forms, or headings). Learners should prefer 'a la oficina' for full sentences and 'en la oficina' for 'in the office.'
target_language_example: Salida: oficina a las 9:00 (salgo de casa con destino oficina a las 9:00).
native_language_example: Departure: office at 9:00 (I leave home bound for the office at 9:00).

meaning: office of / office for / a(n) ... office (used with a following noun or person).
additional_notes: Used to say someone works at or something comes from a specific office, or to describe the type/purpose of an office. The noun or person that follows 'de' shows ownership, affiliation, purpose, or specialization (e.g., 'oficina de correos' = post office; 'oficina de tu papá' = your dad's office). Word order: 'oficina de + [person/organization/field]'.
target_language_example: Voy a la oficina de turismo mañana.
native_language_example: I'm going to the tourist office tomorrow.

meaning: post office
additional_notes: Refers to the public building where mail is sent, received, stamped, and sometimes where packages are shipped and basic postal services are offered. Commonly used with definite/indefinite articles (la oficina de correos, una oficina de correos) and locational phrases (en, cerca de, al final de).
target_language_example: Voy a la oficina de correos a enviar un paquete.
native_language_example: I'm going to the post office to send a package.

meaning: "the post office is" (used to say location or status of the post office)
additional_notes: A common phrase to describe where the post office is or its current state (open/closed). "Oficina de correos" = post office. "Está" is the third-person singular of estar, used for location or temporary conditions. For permanent addresses use "está" for location; for official names you might see "la oficina de correos es...", but locations and temporary states use "está".
target_language_example: La oficina de correos está abierta hasta las cinco.
native_language_example: The post office is open until five.

meaning: office (with a preposition 'in/at/by' to indicate location, time or means).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but the word oficina combined with the preposition en. Use 'en' to indicate location (en la oficina = in the office), time expressions (en Nochebuena = on Christmas Eve), travel time (en treinta minutos = in thirty minutes) or means of transport (en coche, en bicicleta). Remember to include the correct article when needed (en la oficina; in contexts with possession use 'mi oficina').
target_language_example: Estaré en mi oficina en veinte minutos.
native_language_example: I'll be in my office in twenty minutes.

meaning: 'oficina' = office; 'es' = is (3rd person singular of ser).
additional_notes: This looks like two separate words: oficina (noun) means an office or a workplace; es is the verb 'to be' (ser) used for permanent or identifying characteristics. Together 'oficina es' by itself is not a complete sentence in Spanish — you'd normally say 'La oficina es...' (The office is...) followed by a description (e.g., 'La oficina es grande' = The office is big) or identify location with 'La oficina está...' (using estar for location/temporary states).
target_language_example: La oficina es grande y luminosa.
native_language_example: The office is large and bright.

meaning: This looks like the word 'oficina' (office) followed by the conjunction 'y' (and). On its own 'oficina y' is not a fixed phrase—it's typically the start of a clause listing 'office and ...' or part of a sentence like 'went into his office and...'.
additional_notes: Not a set phrase. 'Oficina' = 'office' (place of work or business). 'Y' = 'and' used to join words, phrases, or clauses. In the example sentences the second meaning shows the structure 'entró a su oficina y [vio...]' — this is the verb + object + 'y' + another verb/clause, meaning 'entered his office and [did something]'. In the third example 'número de teléfono de su oficina y su dirección' lists two items ('office phone number and his address'). Use 'oficina' with possessive: 'su oficina' = 'his/her/your/their office'.
target_language_example: María fue a su oficina y empezó a trabajar.
native_language_example: María went to her office and started working.

meaning: 'offered to' or 'offered (something) to (someone)'.
additional_notes: Used with the verb 'ofrecer' in the past (ofreció) to say someone volunteered to do something (se ofreció a + infinitive) or gave/offered something to someone (ofreció a + person + [thing]). When someone volunteers, use the reflexive form 'se ofreció a' + infinitive (e.g., se ofreció a ayudar). When offering an item or amount to a person, use 'le ofreció a [persona] [algo]'.
target_language_example: Ella se ofreció a cocinar la cena mañana.
native_language_example: She offered to cook dinner tomorrow.

meaning: I hope (that) + feminine noun or clause (with feminine subject); expresses wish or hope.
additional_notes: Ojalá is used to express strong wishes or hopes. When followed by 'la' it likely refers to a feminine direct object or a shortened clause (e.g., 'ojalá la vea' = 'I hope I/he/she sees her/it' where 'la' is feminine). Often followed by a verb in the subjunctive (ojalá la llame, ojalá la encontremos). Use 'ojalá' alone before a verb (ojalá venga) or with pronouns to refer to people or things.
target_language_example: Ojalá la encontremos pronto.
native_language_example: I hope we find her/it soon.

meaning: 'I hope (that) he/she/they...'; expresses a wish about someone else (uses subjunctive).
additional_notes: Ojalá is used to express wishes or hopes. When followed by 'se' it refers to a wish about another person's actions or situation (reflexive or reciprocal). It commonly requires the subjunctive mood: present subjunctive for present/future wishes, past (imperfect) subjunctive for unlikely or counterfactual wishes, and pluperfect subjunctive for wishes about the past. Tone can be polite, emotional, or regretful depending on tense.
target_language_example: Ojalá se recupere pronto.
native_language_example: I hope he/she gets better soon.

meaning: I wish (that) I... — expresses a wish or regret about oneself.
additional_notes: Used with the subjunctive to express hopes, wishes, or regrets about the speaker. Common verbs: fuera/tuiviera/viviera/hubiera podido. 'Ojalá' can be used alone (ojalá + subjunctive) without 'yo' because the verb ending often shows the subject; including 'yo' emphasizes that the wish refers specifically to the speaker.
target_language_example: Ojalá yo pudiera ver el mar hoy.
native_language_example: I wish I could see the sea today.

meaning: 'eye of' — used to describe the central part or focal point of something (literal or figurative).
additional_notes: Often used literally (eye of a storm, eye of a needle/lock) to mean the center/opening. Also appears in figurative expressions to indicate the focal point or calm center amid activity. Follows the noun that specifies what kind of 'eye' it is (ojo de la tormenta, ojo de la cerradura, ojo de un huracán).
target_language_example: El ojo de la tormenta es relativamente tranquilo.
native_language_example: The eye of the storm is relatively calm.

meaning: part of the idiom 'costar un ojo de la cara' — to be very expensive / to cost an arm and a leg
additional_notes: On its own 'ojo de la' literally means 'eye of the' but is not used alone; it's recognized as the start of the idiom 'costar un ojo de la cara' (literally 'to cost an eye from the face'), meaning something is extremely costly. The phrase is idiomatic and common in spoken and written Spanish. Note: 'entrar al ojo de la tormenta' is a different expression meaning to enter the center of a storm (literal or figurative).
target_language_example: Esa computadora nueva me costó un ojo de la cara.
native_language_example: That new computer cost me an arm and a leg.

meaning: 'watch out for' or 'be careful about' (used to draw attention to something).
additional_notes: Commonly used in spoken Spanish as a warning or to emphasize something important. It often appears at the start of a sentence or clause: 'Ojo en...' or 'Ojo con...' Both mean 'be careful with/ about' but 'ojo con' is more common. Use when you want someone to pay attention to a detail, a danger, or a potential problem.
target_language_example: Ojo en la fecha de caducidad antes de comprar.
native_language_example: Watch out for the expiration date before buying.

meaning: 'eye for' — part of the idiom 'ojo por ojo' meaning 'an eye for an eye' (revenge or reciprocal justice).
additional_notes: Usually appears in the fixed phrase 'ojo por ojo' (eye for an eye). It expresses retaliation or reciprocal punishment; often used critically to warn that revenge leads to mutual harm. Also 'echar un ojo por' in sentence 1 is different: there it's part of 'echar un ojo por (mi alrededor)' meaning 'to take a quick look around'. Context determines meaning.
target_language_example: No creo en ojo por ojo; mejor buscar justicia, no venganza.
native_language_example: I don't believe in an eye for an eye; better seek justice, not revenge.

meaning: 'eyes when' — literal words that usually appear together in a clause but are not a fixed idiom on their own.
additional_notes: As given, 'ojos cuando' is not a standard standalone phrase in Spanish. It typically appears with 'ojos' followed shortly by 'cuando' within a sentence (e.g., 'sus ojos, cuando...') or as part of longer constructions ('los ojos cuando...'). For learners, treat this as two separate words that can appear adjacent in some sentence structures rather than a set expression. The phrase can occur in poetic or descriptive contexts where the noun is followed by a temporal clause.
target_language_example: Recordó los ojos cuando ella sonrió por primera vez.
native_language_example: He remembered the eyes when she smiled for the first time.

meaning: 'eyes of the' or 'eyes from the' (part of a larger phrase)
additional_notes: This is not a complete phrase on its own — 'ojos' means 'eyes' and 'del' is the contraction of 'de' + 'el' meaning 'of the' or 'from the'. You'll normally see 'ojos del' followed by a noun (e.g., 'ojos del río', 'ojos del mundo') to indicate possession, source, or a descriptive relationship. Be careful: word order and gender/number agreement depend on the noun that follows.
target_language_example: Los ojos del gato brillaban en la oscuridad.
native_language_example: The cat's eyes shone in the dark.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase in Spanish; two separate words 'ojos' (eyes) and the clitic pronoun 'me' (to/for me or reflexive marker). By themselves they usually appear as part of a larger sentence where a verb connects them (e.g., 'me duelen los ojos').
additional_notes: This exact sequence 'ojos me' is uncommon at sentence start because Spanish word order typically places the pronoun before the verb (me duelen los ojos) or after the verb in certain constructions (los ojos me duelen). If you see 'ojos me' it will usually occur within a clause where word order is inverted for emphasis or in poetic/colloquial speech: e.g., 'Los ojos me miran' or 'A veces ojos me buscan' (the latter poetic/unusual). For learners: learn common patterns with 'ojos' + verb + pronoun such as 'me duelen los ojos', 'me lloran los ojos', or the inverted 'los ojos me lloran'.
target_language_example: Los ojos me lloran cuando corto cebolla.
native_language_example: My eyes water when I cut onion.

meaning: 'to have eyes for' — to be attracted to or focused on someone or something
additional_notes: Used in expressions like "tener ojos para (alguien)" or "solo tengo ojos para (ti)" meaning to be romantically attracted to or only pay attention to that person. Also appears in literal uses describing looking at someone's eyes (e.g., "miré a los ojos para..."), but the idiomatic meaning is about attraction or exclusive attention. Context determines whether it's literal (looking) or idiomatic (being attracted/focused).
target_language_example: Desde que la conocí, solo tengo ojos para ella.
native_language_example: Since I met her, I only have eyes for her.

meaning: Not a fixed phrase in Spanish; likely a fragment. 'Ojos' = 'eyes'. 'se' is a reflexive/impersonal pronoun.
additional_notes:
This combination by itself doesn't form a standard multiword expression. You may see 'ojos se' as part of larger constructions, for example: 'se le/les/te/mi/nuestros ojos' or 'los ojos se le llenaron de lágrimas' (the eyes filled with tears). Common useful patterns with 'ojos' include:
- 'los ojos' = the eyes
- 'abrir los ojos' = to open one's eyes
- 'cerrar los ojos' = to close one's eyes
- 'se le/les/te/mi + verbo + los ojos' or 'los ojos se + verbo' to describe reflexive or passive actions involving eyes (e.g., 'los ojos se llenaron').
If you meant a specific phrase (like 'ojos se cerraron' or 'ojos se llenaron'), provide the full phrase for a precise entry.
target_language_example: Los ojos se le llenaron de lágrimas.
native_language_example: His/her eyes filled with tears.

meaning: forgets (to/about).
additional_notes: Commonly used with a reflexive pronoun (se) as 'se olvida de' meaning 'he/she/they forget(s) about' or 'forget(s) to'. Followed by an infinitive when meaning 'forget to (do something)' (e.g., 'se olvida de pagar') or followed by a clause/phrase introduced by 'que' or a noun when meaning 'forget about' (e.g., 'se olvida de qué...').
target_language_example: Ella siempre se olvida de llamar a su madre.
native_language_example: She always forgets to call her mother.

meaning: Forget it / don't worry about it (informal imperative telling someone to forget something).
additional_notes: A combination of the verb 'olvidar' (to forget) in the imperative form 'olvida' plus the direct object pronoun 'lo' (it). Used in spoken Spanish to tell someone to drop the subject or stop worrying about something. Tone can be dismissive or reassuring depending on context and intonation. For formal commands or to address 'usted', use 'olvádelo' (less common) or 'olvídelo'.
target_language_example: ¿Quieres que lo arregle ahora? — No, olvida lo, ya no importa.
native_language_example: Do you want me to fix it now? — No, forget it, it doesn't matter anymore.

meaning: forgot his/her/its (something); have/has forgotten their (something).
additional_notes: Olvidado is the past participle of olvidar (to forget). Combined with su (his/her/its/your formal/their) it indicates that someone forgot a specific item belonging to someone. In present perfect contexts use "he/has/ha/hemos/han olvidado su..."; in past perfect use "había olvidado su...". 'Su' is ambiguous (his/her/your/their) — context or clarification (de + nombre) may be needed.
target_language_example: María ha olvidado su libro en la cafetería.
native_language_example: María has forgotten her book in the café.

meaning: to forget that (followed by a clause) — used to indicate failing to remember a fact, circumstance, or piece of information.
additional_notes: Followed by a subordinate clause introduced by que + verb. Common in statements, reminders, warnings, and reflections. Often appears in imperatives (No olvides que...), negatives (No debemos olvidar que...), and personal statements (No puedo olvidar que...).
target_language_example: No puedo olvidar que Clerici fue uno de mis mejores estudiantes.
native_language_example: I cannot forget that Clerici was one of my best students.

meaning: to forget (about)
additional_notes: Reflexive verb phrase often used with a noun/pronoun or an infinitive after 'de' (e.g. olvidarse de algo / olvidarse de alguien / olvidarse de + infinitive). Commonly used to mean you didn't remember something or neglected to do it. The reflexive pronoun (me/te/se/nos/os/se) is required in conjugation: me olvidé de = I forgot. When followed by an infinitive, it indicates failing to do something (Me olvidé de llamar = I forgot to call).
target_language_example: Siempre me olvido de cerrar la puerta.
native_language_example: I always forget to close the door.

meaning: forget (to/about).
additional_notes: Commonly appears as part of the reflexive verb olvidarse (e.g., 'no se olvide de...') meaning 'don't forget to/about...'. With 'de' it introduces what is forgotten (an action or thing). In commands use formal usted: 'No se olvide de...'. Informal tú form is 'no te olvides de...'.
target_language_example: No se olvide de traer su pasaporte mañana.
native_language_example: Don't forget to bring your passport tomorrow.

meaning: 'I forgot the...'.
additional_notes: Olvidé is the first-person singular preterite of olvidar (to forget). Use 'olvidé el' before a masculine singular noun or a specific masculine item (e.g., 'olvidé el libro'). For feminine nouns use 'olvidé la'. You can also follow with an infinitive to mean 'I forgot to (do something)' using 'olvidé + (infinitive)' without an article (e.g., 'olvidé llamar').
target_language_example: Olvidé el cargador en la oficina.
native_language_example: I forgot the charger in the office.

meaning: I forgot the (feminine noun).
additional_notes: Olvidé is the first-person singular preterite of olvidar (to forget). La indicates the forgotten item is a feminine noun (la contraseña, la llave, la razón, la cita, la guía). Use olvidé el for masculine nouns. Commonly followed by 'en' (forgot it in/on) or 'para'/'por' to indicate reason or purpose.
target_language_example: Olvidé la cartera en el taxi.
native_language_example: I forgot the wallet in the taxi.

meaning: 'I forgot that...'
additional_notes: Used to introduce something you forgot — a fact, agreement, plan, or obligation. Follows with a clause (que + verb). Can express forgetting a person doing something, an event/date, or an owed action. Commonly in past tense (olvidé).
target_language_example: Olvidé que tenía una reunión esta tarde.
native_language_example: I forgot that I had a meeting this afternoon.

meaning: 'forgot to' or 'forgot about' (he/she/you formal forgot).
additional_notes: Common past tense form (pretérito) of olvidar + de. Use olvidó de + infinitive to mean 'forgot to [do something]' (Se olvidó de traer ropa = He/She/They forgot to bring clothes). Use olvidó de + noun to mean 'forgot about [someone/something]'. With a formal you (usted) the verb form is the same. In everyday Spanish, some speakers omit de after olvidar when followed by a direct object (e.g., olvidó todos sus amigos), but including de is standard and common when indicating omission/neglect.
target_language_example: Ella olvidó de llamar a su madre ayer.
native_language_example: She forgot to call her mother yesterday.

meaning: 'operation of' or 'operation for' — used to show the purpose, type, or agent of an operation/action.
additional_notes: A common prepositional phrase. 'Operación' can mean a medical surgery, a mathematical operation, or a business/technical operation; 'de' connects it to what the operation is about, who performs it, or its purpose. English translations depend on context (e.g. 'operation of the machine', 'surgery on the patient', 'operation for cleaning'). Often followed by a noun or a verb infinitive.
target_language_example: La operación de la máquina requiere un técnico.
native_language_example: The operation of the machine requires a technician.

meaning: opinion; a personal belief or view.
additional_notes: Used to state what someone thinks. Commonly appears in phrases like "En mi opinión..." (In my opinion) or "Según mi opinión..." The correct article for opinión is feminine (la opinión) despite the headword shown with "el" in the prompt; the entry retains the requested form "opinión, el" exactly as given. Typically followed by a comma and a statement.
target_language_example: En mi opinión, el alcohol no es necesariamente malo para tu salud.
native_language_example: In my opinion, alcohol is not necessarily bad for your health.

meaning: opinion about / opinion on (used before a noun or a verb in infinitive with 'el' contracted: 'al' = a + el).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself; it's the word 'opinión' followed by the preposition 'a' + the definite article 'el' (= 'al'). It appears when saying 'opinion to/on the ...' or when introducing who gives the opinion (less common). More natural constructions in Spanish are 'opinión sobre', 'opinión acerca de' or 'opinión de' + noun. Use 'al' only when the structure requires 'a el', e.g. 'opinión al público' (opinion to the public) but 'opinión sobre el público' (opinion about the public) is usually preferred.
target_language_example: Le pedí su opinión al profesor sobre el proyecto.
native_language_example: I asked the professor for his opinion on the project.

meaning: opinion of; (used in expressions like 'ser de la opinión de') to mean 'to be of the opinion that' or 'have an opinion about'.
additional_notes: Often appears in two patterns: 'opinión de [algo/alguien]' meaning an opinion about something/someone (e.g., buena opinión de Tom = a high opinion of Tom), and the fixed expression 'ser de la opinión de que + clause' meaning 'to be of the opinion that...' (followed by a full clause). Use 'la' in 'ser de la opinión' when speaking generally ('soy de la opinión de que...').
target_language_example: Soy de la opinión de que debemos empezar hoy.
native_language_example: I am of the opinion that we should start today.

meaning: 'public opinion' — what most people think about an issue or person.
additional_notes: Used to refer to the general views or attitude of the population, media, or a community. Commonly used in discussions about politics, policy, reputation, or social issues. Can be counted as singular in Spanish (la opinión pública).
target_language_example: La opinión pública favorece la reforma propuesta.
native_language_example: Public opinion favors the proposed reform.

meaning: a chance/opportunity for (someone) — used before a noun or verb phrase
additional_notes: This phrase combines oportunidad (opportunity, chance) with the preposition a (to/for). It often appears as 'dar oportunidad a [persona] de [verbo]' or 'oportunidad a [persona]'. Commonly used to say someone is given a chance to do something. For beginners, remember that 'oportunidad' is feminine (la oportunidad) and 'a' marks the indirect object or introduces the person who receives the opportunity.
target_language_example: Le dieron oportunidad a Ana de presentar su proyecto.
native_language_example: They gave Ana the opportunity to present her project.

meaning: literally 'opportunity and' — not a fixed phrase by itself; 'oportunidad' means 'opportunity' and 'y' means 'and'.
additional_notes: This is not a standalone idiom. It appears when 'oportunidad' is followed by another noun or phrase connected with 'y' (and). Use when listing or connecting ideas: e.g., 'oportunidad y riesgo' (opportunity and risk). Remember to adjust articles and agreement as needed (la oportunidad, una oportunidad).
target_language_example: Fue una oportunidad y un desafío para todos.
native_language_example: It was an opportunity and a challenge for everyone.

meaning: 'this sentence is...' (used to describe a sentence)
additional_notes: Oración means 'sentence' (or 'prayer' in other contexts). When followed by 'es' it starts a statement about the sentence's quality, truth, or characteristics. Common in grammar, writing feedback, and logic. Swap 'esta' (this) with 'esa/una' as needed.
target_language_example: Esta oración es demasiado larga.
native_language_example: This sentence is too long.

meaning: order in; instruction or arrangement within/at (a place or system).
additional_notes: Depends on context. 'Orden en' often appears as part of phrases like 'poner orden en' (to put order in/bring order to) or 'dar orden en' (to give an order in/at). It can mean a command issued within a location or organization, or the idea of putting things in order inside something. Use prepositions and verbs around it to clarify meaning (e.g., 'poner orden en la casa', 'dar orden en la oficina').
target_language_example: Tenemos que poner orden en la habitación antes de que lleguen los invitados.
native_language_example: We need to put things in order in the room before the guests arrive.

meaning: the computer is / a computer is
additional_notes: Used to describe or define 'ordenador' (computer). "Ordenador es" appears when stating qualities (El ordenador es nuevo = The computer is new) or when making general definitions (Un ordenador es un dispositivo moderno = A computer is a modern device). For singular generic statements use "Un/El ordenador es...". "Ordenador" is the common word for "computer" in Spain (Latin America more often uses "computadora").
target_language_example: Un ordenador es útil para estudiar y trabajar.
native_language_example: A computer is useful for studying and working.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase; it's simply the words 'ordenador' (computer) followed by 'si' (if) and usually appears as part of a larger sentence meaning 'computer if...'.
additional_notes: This two-word string is not an idiom — it's typically two separate words in a sentence (e.g., 'ordenador, si...'). 'Ordenador' is the common word for 'computer' in Spain; in Latin America use 'computadora' or 'computador'. Note the accent: 'si' (no accent) = 'if'; 'sí' (with accent) = 'yes'. Context determines meaning.
target_language_example: Ordenador si no puedes encenderlo, tráemelo y lo revisaré.
native_language_example: Computer — if you can't turn it on, bring it to me and I'll check it.

meaning: "proud that" — used to express pride about someone or something, followed by a clause.
additional_notes: Used to express pride about a person, action, or situation; the clause after 'que' commonly uses the subjunctive when referring to wishes, feelings, non-factual situations, or uncertainty (e.g., 'estén', 'sea'). For past non-factual or reported contexts, imperfect subjunctive can appear (e.g., 'fuera'). Agreement: 'orgulloso' changes to 'orgullosa' for feminine subjects. You can add adverbs (muy, realmente) or possessives (su, mi) as needed.
target_language_example: Estoy muy orgulloso de que todos estén aquí.
native_language_example: I'm very proud that everyone is here.

meaning: 'origin of' or 'source of' (used before a masculine noun).
additional_notes: Literal phrase used to indicate where something begins, comes from, or where its cause lies. 'Del' is the contraction of 'de' + 'el', so it appears before masculine singular nouns (e.g., 'origen del problema', 'origen del universo'). For feminine nouns you'd use 'origen de la'. Common in formal and neutral registers.
target_language_example: Estamos investigando el origen del incendio.
native_language_example: We are investigating the origin of the fire.

meaning: literally 'gold in' — the noun 'oro' (gold) followed by the preposition 'en' (in/at).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase; it's just the word 'oro' (gold) used with the preposition 'en' to indicate location, possession context, material, or source (e.g., 'gold in the valley', 'a gold watch given in thanks', 'gold in my hand'). Use depends on the verb and sentence. 'Oro' is masculine singular (el oro).
target_language_example: Encontraron oro en la montaña.
native_language_example: They found gold in the mountain.

meaning: short for 'os voy a...' = 'I'm going to (do something) to/for you (plural, informal)'.
additional_notes: Uses the indirect-object pronoun 'os' (you all, informal in Spain) plus the verb 'voy' (I go / I'm going) to form the near-future 'os voy a + [infinitive]' meaning 'I'm going to [verb] you (all)'. Common in Spain; 'os' indicates the action is directed at a group of people you address informally. Tone depends on the verb: can be friendly ('os voy a extrañar' = I'll miss you all) or threatening ('os voy a machacar' = I'll crush you all). Equivalent in Latin America would be 'les voy' or 'les voy a...'.
target_language_example: Os voy a ayudar con la mudanza el sábado.
native_language_example: I'm going to help you all with the move on Saturday.

meaning: dark in / it was dark in (some place).
additional_notes: Used to describe that a place or interior is dark. Commonly appears with estar (estaba/está) + oscuro + en + location (e.g., 'estaba oscuro en la habitación'). You can also say 'está oscuro' followed directly by the location without 'en' (e.g., 'está oscuro afuera').
target_language_example: Estaba oscuro en la cocina cuando llegué.
native_language_example: It was dark in the kitchen when I arrived.

meaning: dark and (used to connect 'dark' with another adjective or quality).
additional_notes: A common adjective + conjunction pattern: oscuro (dark) + y (and). Used to link 'dark' with another descriptor (e.g., oscuro y misterioso = dark and mysterious). In Spanish word order the noun or place being described comes before the adjectives (e.g., 'cielo oscuro y silencioso'). You will often see repeated 'y' for a list (oscuro, silencioso y frío) or stacked for style ('oscuro y silencioso y completo').
target_language_example: La habitación era oscuro y fría por la noche.
native_language_example: The room was dark and cold at night.

meaning: the other half; the other part
additional_notes: Used to refer to the remaining or opposite half of something (literal or figurative). Can mean a missing partner (e.g., spouse), the rest of a quantity, or the other portion/group. Context determines whether it's physical, numerical, or metaphorical.
target_language_example: Buscó la otra mitad del beso que le faltaba.
native_language_example: He looked for the other half of the kiss he was missing.

meaning: again
additional_notes: Used to say that something happens or is done again. It often goes after the verb, and in phrases like "No empieces otra vez" it can sound annoyed: "don't start again." Literally it is "another time," but in most everyday cases the natural English translation is "again."
target_language_example: ¿Puedes decirlo otra vez?
native_language_example: Can you say it again?

meaning: again in / once more in (used to say something happens again at a place or time)
additional_notes: Combines 'otra vez' (again) with 'en' (in/at). Used before a location, time period, or context to say something occurs again there. Word order: 'otra vez en + [place/time/context]' or simply 'otra vez' without 'en' if no location/time follows. Common in spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: Llegaron otra vez en la noche.
native_language_example: They arrived again at night.

meaning: other words; in other words (used to rephrase or clarify).
additional_notes: Literally 'other words'. Commonly used to introduce a rephrasing or clarification, similar to 'in other words' or 'that is to say'. Can precede a restatement: 'en otras palabras...' is the more usual full phrase for 'in other words'. Alone, 'otras palabras' can mean 'other words' (different words) depending on context.
target_language_example: En otras palabras, necesitamos más tiempo para terminar.
native_language_example: In other words, we need more time to finish.

meaning: a fragment meaning 'another day I ...' or 'some other day I'll ...' used to refer to doing something on a different day
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase on its own but a common sequence: 'otro día' (another day) + a verb with 'me' when the speaker talks about themselves (e.g., 'otro día me invitas' = 'invite me another day' or 'otro día me cuentas' = 'tell me another day'). Often appears in casual speech to postpone an action or suggest doing something later. Word order and the verb after 'me' will change the exact meaning.
target_language_example: Otro día me cuentas cómo te fue en el viaje.
native_language_example: Tell me another day how your trip went.

meaning: the other side of / the opposite side of
additional_notes: Used to indicate the opposite side or far side of something (street, room, moon, etc.). Often appears with definite articles: 'el otro lado de la calle', 'el otro lado de la habitación'. Can also be used figuratively (e.g., 'desde el otro lado de las sombras').
target_language_example: El coche está estacionado en el otro lado de la calle.
native_language_example: The car is parked on the other side of the street.

meaning: the other side of the (feminine noun follows).
additional_notes: Use before a feminine noun or phrase (la calle, la ciudad, la moneda, la conversación). Common in spatial (the other side of the street) and figurative uses (the other side of the story). If the following noun is masculine, use 'otro lado del' (de + el = del).
target_language_example: Está al otro lado de la calle.
native_language_example: It's on the other side of the street.

meaning: another time; at a different time
additional_notes: Used to indicate doing something on a different occasion or postponing. Can mean 'at another time' (future occasion) or 'in another era' depending on context. Common in phrases like 'lo hablaremos otro tiempo' (we'll talk another time) or 'en otro tiempo' (in another time/in the past).
target_language_example: Hablemos de eso otro tiempo, ahora estoy ocupado.
native_language_example: Let's talk about that another time; I'm busy now.

meaning: another of / one more of (from a group)
additional_notes: Used to refer to an additional item or person from a set. Often followed by a noun (otro de los libros) or by a pronoun/phrase indicating the group (otro de ellos). Can also appear as 'otro' + 'de' + article + noun to mean 'another of the...'.
target_language_example: Quiero otro de esos, por favor.
native_language_example: I want another one of those, please.

meaning: another one in / another in (context-dependent)
additional_notes: Not a fixed phrase by itself; 'otro' means 'another' or 'other' and 'en' means 'in' or 'on'. 'Otro en' appears when 'otro' modifies a noun that follows a prepositional phrase starting with 'en' or when shortened speech places 'en' after 'otro' (e.g., 'otro en la lista' = 'another one on the list'). You will usually see 'otro' + (noun) + 'en' + (place) or 'otro' + 'en' + (context). Choose the meaning based on the noun/place that follows.
target_language_example: Pon otro en la caja, por favor.
native_language_example: Put another one in the box, please.

meaning: 'another is' or 'the other (one) is'—used to refer to a different person/thing and state something about them/it.
additional_notes: Literal combination of 'otro' (another/the other) + verb 'es' (is). Common in comparisons or when contrasting two items: e.g. 'Uno es X, otro es Y' = 'One is X, the other is Y.' Often appears as part of a larger sentence rather than alone.
target_language_example: A mí me gusta el rojo; a ella otro es el azul.
native_language_example: I like the red one; for her the other (one) is blue.

meaning: 'not another' or 'no more of that; not another one'.
additional_notes: Used to reject repeating something or to say you don't want another of something. Often appears in short responses or exclamations. Context and punctuation/intonation determine meaning: could be elliptical ('otro no' = 'not another one') or part of a larger sentence ('Otro no quiere venir' would be unusual). Commonly heard as standalone reply to offers or suggestions.
target_language_example: ¿Quieres otra cerveza? — Otro no.
native_language_example: Do you want another beer? — Not another one.

meaning: another (one) for / a different one for
additional_notes: Used to indicate a second or different item intended for someone or for a purpose. Often appears in short phrases like "uno para mí y otro para ti" (one for me and another for you) or in contrasts such as "un momento para X y otro para Y." 'Otro' agrees in gender/number with the noun it replaces (otro, otra, otros, otras).
target_language_example: Tengo dos boletos: uno para ella y otro para mí.
native_language_example: I have two tickets: one for her and another for me.

meaning: not a fixed phrase; literally 'other and' — appears when 'otro' is followed by 'y' in a sentence (e.g., listing another item and continuing).
additional_notes: This is not an idiom. You'll see 'otro' (other/another) followed by the conjunction 'y' (and) when adding an additional item or idea: e.g., 'otro y...'. Pay attention to context — the meaning comes from the whole sentence, not the two words as a unit. Use 'otro' alone for 'another' or 'other', and use 'y' to connect items.
target_language_example: Compré un libro, otro y una revista.
native_language_example: I bought a book, another and a magazine.

meaning: whatever others say; regardless of what others say
additional_notes: This phrase combines 'otros' (others) with the subjunctive verb 'digan' (they say). It's used to dismiss or ignore other people's opinions: e.g., 'No me importa lo que otros digan' = 'I don't care what others say.' Often appears as part of clauses introduced by 'lo que' ('what') or after verbs/phrases expressing disregard.
target_language_example: No voy a cambiar por lo que otros digan.
native_language_example: I'm not going to change because of what others say.

meaning: ‘others for’ or part of constructions meaning 'some... others...'; used to contrast reasons or to say 'blame others for'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but a combination: 'otros' (others) plus a preposition like 'por' used in contrasts (e.g., 'algunos... otros por...') or in constructions with verbs that take 'por' (e.g., 'culpar a otros por...'). In contrast sentences it often pairs with 'algunos' or 'unos/otras' to say 'some... others...'. With verbs like 'culpar' it means 'to blame others for'. Word order: 'culpar a otros por...' (note the object marker 'a' before 'otros' when the verb is transitive).
target_language_example: Algunos trabajan para aprender, otros por el dinero.
native_language_example: Some work to learn, others for the money.

meaning: black sheep; someone who is different or considered a disgrace/outcast in a family or group.
additional_notes: Used metaphorically like in English to describe a person who doesn't fit in or who brings shame to a family or group. Can be affectionate or critical depending on context. Singular feminine/masculine: la oveja negra / el oveja negra (often 'la' since 'oveja' is feminine for the animal even if referring to a male person). Plural: las/los ovejas negras.
target_language_example: En mi familia siempre me sentí como la oveja negra.
native_language_example: In my family I always felt like the black sheep.

meaning: 'black sheep of' — used to describe someone who is the odd or disapproved member of a group or family.
additional_notes: Oveja negra (without 'de') is the fixed expression meaning 'black sheep'. When followed by 'de' it specifies the group (e.g., 'la oveja negra de la familia' = 'the black sheep of the family'). It's usually used figuratively to show disapproval, difference, or nonconformity. Tone can be negative or playful depending on context.
target_language_example: Él siempre fue la oveja negra de la familia.
native_language_example: He was always the black sheep of the family.

meaning: the black sheep of the (family/group) — someone who is different or seen negatively within a group.
additional_notes: Usually completed with a noun (e.g., 'oveja negra de la familia' = 'the black sheep of the family'). Used to describe a person who doesn't fit in or who is blamed for problems. Figurative expression; not literal. Common in everyday Spanish.
target_language_example: Juan siempre hizo las cosas a su manera; es la oveja negra de la familia.
native_language_example: Juan always did things his own way; he's the black sheep of the family.

meaning: 'heard by' or 'been heard by' when using past participle oído with preposition a to indicate the person or body that heard something (though Spanish more commonly uses por for the agent).
additional_notes: 'oído' is the past participle of oír (to hear). The combination 'oído a' can occur when marking the entity that heard or received information, but standard Spanish often prefers 'oído por' to mark the agent (or uses active constructions). 'Oído a' may also appear in fixed expressions (e.g., 'a oído' meaning 'by ear'), but that is a different structure. Use context to decide whether 'a' or 'por' is appropriate; 'a' can sometimes imply direction toward or involvement rather than a passive agent in contemporary usage.
target_language_example: La protesta fue oído a los representantes del ayuntamiento durante la sesión.
native_language_example: The protest was heard by the town council representatives during the session.

meaning: 'heard of' (to have heard about someone or something).
additional_notes: Used with the verb haber + oído (past participle) to say you have heard about a person, group, or topic. Commonly appears as 'he oído de...', 'has oído de...', 'no he oído de...'. Often followed by a pronoun or noun (ella, ellos, él). Not used to mean 'heard from' (that would be 'oído de + alguien' sometimes but more commonly 'recibido noticias de' or 'oído de él' can mean heard about him).
target_language_example: No he oído de ese restaurante antes.
native_language_example: I haven't heard of that restaurant before.

meaning: to have heard (about); to hear someone say (that)...
additional_notes: Used to report information you learned by hearing it (often with impersonal constructions: 'he oído decir que...' = 'I've heard that...'). Typically appears with a clause introduced by 'que' or with an infinitive. Common in spoken and written Spanish to relay hearsay or rumors; the subject is often 'yo' (implied) or 'se'.
target_language_example: He oído decir que van a cerrar la tienda.
native_language_example: I've heard that they're going to close the store.

meaning: I've heard (someone) say that... / I've heard that...
