target_language_example: Vamos a pasar el rato en el parque esta tarde.
native_language_example: Let's hang out at the park this afternoon.

meaning: to spend the rest (of one's life/time) — e.g., 'spend the rest of your life'.
additional_notes: Commonly appears with 'de la vida' or 'de su vida' to mean spending the remaining part of one's life with someone or doing something. Often used with verbs like 'pasar' + 'el resto de (tu/mi/su) vida' or with 'con quien' to indicate the person you will spend your life with.
target_language_example: Quiero pasar el resto de mi vida contigo.
native_language_example: I want to spend the rest of my life with you.

meaning: to spend the rest of my (time/life/etc.)
additional_notes: This phrase is usually completed with a noun indicating what will be spent (e.g., 'vida', 'tiempo', 'vida aquí'). It's used to say you will spend the remainder of something—often life or time—in a place or doing something: 'pasar el resto de mi vida' = 'spend the rest of my life.' The verb 'pasar' here means 'to spend' (time), not 'to pass.'
target_language_example: Quiero pasar el resto de mi vida viajando por el mundo.
native_language_example: I want to spend the rest of my life traveling around the world.

meaning: to spend the rest of his/her (life/time).
additional_notes: Commonly followed by a noun like vida (life) or tiempo (time) and a complement (con alguien, en algún lugar). Used to express spending remaining time or life doing something or with someone. Adjust su to mi/tu/nuestra etc. for different owners.
target_language_example: Ella quiere pasar el resto de su vida viajando por el mundo.
native_language_example: She wants to spend the rest of her life traveling around the world.

meaning: to happen in / to take place in (a location or time); or to pass into/through (less common)
additional_notes: Used to say that an event or action occurs in a particular place or time: 'pasar en + lugar/tiempo'. It's less common than 'pasar' alone or 'pasar por'. Context matters: with a place it can mean 'take place in' (La reunión pasó en la sala = The meeting took place in the room), with a time 'pasar en enero' = 'happen in January' (rare). It can also appear in phrases like 'pasar en + país' meaning 'to happen in a country'. For movement meanings, Spanish more often uses 'pasar por' (to pass by/through) or 'entrar en' (to enter).
target_language_example: La conferencia va a pasar en el auditorio el lunes.
native_language_example: The conference will take place in the auditorium on Monday.

meaning: to overlook; to ignore; to miss (something important).
additional_notes: Used when someone fails to notice something, deliberately ignores it, or treats it as unimportant. Can be used for mistakes, details, facts, or problems. Often followed by what is being overlooked (pasar por alto + noun).
target_language_example: No podemos pasar por alto esos errores en el informe.
native_language_example: We can't overlook those mistakes in the report.

meaning: to spend time (with someone or doing something).
additional_notes: Common verb phrase used to express spending time with people or in places/activities. Often followed by 'con' + person (pasar tiempo con alguien) or a prepositional phrase (pasar tiempo dentro de casa, pasando el tiempo en...). Can be used in present, past, future, etc.
target_language_example: Me gusta pasar tiempo con mi familia los fines de semana.
native_language_example: I like to spend time with my family on weekends.

meaning: to have a (good) time / to spend (a good) time (incomplete phrase needing a noun to finish the idea)
additional_notes: This sequence is usually part of larger expressions like "pasar un buen rato", "pasar un buen día" or "pasar un buen momento." On its own "pasar un buen" is incomplete; it requires a noun (rato, día, momento, susto, etc.). "Pasar" here means "to spend" or "to experience." It is commonly used in neutral or informal contexts depending on the completed phrase.
target_language_example: Si quieres pasar un buen, recuerda invitar a tus amigos (esta frase está incompleta y espera un sustantivo: por ejemplo, "rato").
native_language_example: If you want to have a good (time), remember to invite your friends (this sentence is incomplete and expects a noun: e.g., "rato").

meaning: to spend/experience (something) / to pass a (specific) [feminine] thing
additional_notes: pasar is a very common verb with many uses. 'Pasar una' often begins phrases like 'pasar una noche' (to spend a night), 'pasar una prueba' (to take/undergo a test), or 'pasar una multa' (to pay a fine). The meaning depends on the noun that follows: it can mean 'to spend' (time), 'to go through/experience' (an event or feeling), 'to hand/pass' (an object), or 'to happen' (colloquially). The article 'una' signals a feminine noun after the verb.
target_language_example: Vamos a pasar una noche en la playa.
native_language_example: We're going to spend a night at the beach.

meaning: 'pass her/the/it' or 'that she/you (informal) pass the' (imperfect-subjunctive form of pasar + feminine/article 'la').
additional_notes: Pasara is the third-person singular (or first/third-person in some contexts) imperfect subjunctive of pasar. In these examples it's used in requests or suggestions after verbs like pedir, meaning 'asked that (someone) pass (something)'. 'La' is a feminine singular direct object article (the) or pronoun (her/it). Literal translation depends on context: 'pasara la sal' = 'pass the salt' (requested). Also appears with other objects (la pimienta). The form can also appear in suggestions: 'sugirió que Mary pasara la noche' = 'suggested that Mary spend/pass the night'.
target_language_example: ¿Puedes pedirle que te pasara la mantequilla?
native_language_example: Can you ask her to pass you the butter?

meaning: to have a hard time; to feel bad or suffer (experience something unpleasant).
additional_notes: Commonly used impersonally with the pronoun 'lo' (pasarlo) plus an adjective or adverb (mal, muy mal) or in past forms (Lo pasé mal). Often refers to emotional distress, discomfort, illness, or a bad experience at an event. Can be used in various tenses and persons (lo paso mal, lo pasó mal, lo hemos pasado mal).
target_language_example: Siempre la paso mal cuando tengo que hablar en público: realmente paso lo mal cada vez.
native_language_example: I always have a hard time when I have to speak in public: I really have a hard time every time.

meaning: to go too far; to cross the line (behave in an unacceptable or excessive way).
additional_notes: Used when someone's words or actions are beyond acceptable limits. Can refer to rudeness, breaking rules, or overstepping boundaries. Often used in informal spoken Spanish and typically appears with a reflexive pronoun (e.g., "se pasó de la raya", "te pasaste de la raya").
target_language_example: No te pases de la raya; pasarse de la raya con las críticas no ayuda a nadie.
native_language_example: Don't go too far; going too far with criticism doesn't help anyone.

meaning: to spend one's life (doing something); to spend time (often habitually) doing something
additional_notes: Used to describe how someone spends most of their life or a long period of time, usually followed by an activity introduced with a gerund or 'en' + noun: pasarse la vida trabajando / pasarse la vida en la playa. Often implies habit, repetition, or excessive time spent.
target_language_example: Se pasó la vida viajando por el mundo.
native_language_example: He spent his life traveling around the world.

meaning: 'let it/the X pass' or 'for the X to pass' (subjunctive of pasar + article 'el'), used to talk about something passing (an event, time, feeling) or to let someone/something go next (in phrases like 'que pase el número uno').
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but a combination: 'pase' is the present subjunctive or formal imperative of pasar (to pass) and 'el' is the masculine definite article used before a noun (e.g. 'temporal', 'número'). Common uses: • 'que pase el número uno' — asking that person/number to come forward ('let number one come in/step up'); • 'que pase el temporal' / 'hasta que pase el temporal' — waiting for a storm/bad period to pass; • 'para que se os pase el miedo' — so that fear goes away. Translation depends on the noun that follows.
target_language_example: Que pase el próximo, por favor.
native_language_example: Let the next one come forward, please.

meaning: 'whatever happens' or 'no matter what happens'.
additional_notes: Usually appears in the phrase 'pase lo que pase' (literally 'happens whatever happens') to mean 'no matter what' or 'whatever happens'. It is used to express determination or acceptance of any outcome. Alone 'pase lo que' is incomplete; expect a final 'pase' to complete the common expression.
target_language_example: Iremos de viaje, pase lo que pase.
native_language_example: We'll go on the trip, no matter what happens.

meaning: no matter what happens; whatever happens.
additional_notes: Used to show determination or unconditional commitment. Often appears at the start or end of a sentence and can be followed by a command, reassurance, promise, or prediction. Literal word-for-word: 'happen what happens,' but idiomatic meaning is 'regardless of what happens.'
target_language_example: Pase lo que pase, voy a terminar este proyecto.
native_language_example: No matter what happens, I'm going to finish this project.

meaning: stop by
additional_notes: Commonly used when telling someone to visit a place briefly or to indicate passing through a location. Often follows a subject and is used with a place or person: (Yo) pase por tu casa, (Él) pase por la oficina. Can be conjugated: paso por, pasé por, pasaré por. Also used figuratively to mean 'go through' an experience (e.g., pasar por dificultades).
target_language_example: Pase por mi casa después del trabajo.
native_language_example: Stop by my house after work.

meaning: 'to walk (someone or something)', usually used with people or animals (often pets).
additional_notes: Commonly used with animals (pasear al perro = walk the dog) or with children/people when implying taking them for a stroll. Requires an object after 'a' (pasear a + person/animal). Can also be used reflexively as 'pasearse' meaning to take a walk oneself. Use por/por la ciudad to specify where.
target_language_example: Voy a pasear a mi perro por el parque.
native_language_example: I'm going to walk my dog through the park.

meaning: for a walk to / a trip to (used before a destination or activity; literal: 'walk to').
additional_notes: Commonly used when talking about going for a walk or short outing toward a place or to do something: 'dar un paseo a' or 'ir de paseo a'. After 'paseo a' you usually mention a destination (paseo a la playa) or a purpose (paseo a ver las luces). In speech you may also hear just 'paseo' with the destination following (voy de paseo a la plaza).
target_language_example: Vamos de paseo a la playa este sábado.
native_language_example: Let's go for a walk/trip to the beach this Saturday.

meaning: a ride or outing in/on (something); 'a ride in/on' (e.g., en coche, en barco, en carruaje).
additional_notes: Used with a mode of transport or location to say you take a ride or go for an outing in or on that thing. Commonly appears in the phrase 'ir de paseo en' or 'dar un paseo en'. Can be used for casual leisure trips (walks, boat rides, carriage rides, drives).
target_language_example: Vamos a dar un paseo en bote esta tarde.
native_language_example: We're going to take a boat ride this afternoon.

meaning: 'a ride in' or 'a walk/stroll in' (depending on vehicle/place).
additional_notes: Paseo is a noun meaning 'walk', 'stroll', or 'ride'. 'Paseo en el' is followed by a place or vehicle: e.g. paseo en el parque (a walk/stroll in the park) or paseo en el coche/auto (a ride in the car). Use for leisurely, casual trips rather than formal travel.
target_language_example: Dimos un paseo en el coche por la ciudad.
native_language_example: We went for a ride in the car around the city.

meaning: a walk/ride/stroll through or around (a place); a trip along
additional_notes: Used to describe taking a leisurely walk, drive, or short outing through a location. Paseo is a noun (a stroll, ride, outing); por indicates movement through or around. Common collocations: hacer un paseo por (to take a walk through), dar un paseo por (to take a stroll around). Can refer to walking, biking, driving, or sightseeing depending on context.
target_language_example: Vamos a dar un paseo por el parque esta tarde.
native_language_example: Let's take a walk through the park this afternoon.

meaning: to the corridor/aisle (literally 'corridor to' or 'aisle to'); used to indicate movement or direction toward a hallway or an aisle when followed by additional words (e.g., a destination or descriptor).
additional_notes: Not a fixed phrase by itself; it's the noun pasillo ('hall/corridor/aisle') combined with the preposition a ('to'). Often appears within a larger phrase or clause (e.g., 'entrar pasillo a la derecha' in colloquial speech, though grammatically standard Spanish uses 'al pasillo' or 'a el pasillo' → 'al pasillo'). Remember the contraction a + el → al (so you commonly see 'al pasillo'). The form 'pasillo a' may appear in contexts like signage, lists, or poetic/special constructions where the article or other words follow.
target_language_example: Entraron por el pasillo a la salida de emergencia.
native_language_example: They entered through the corridor to the emergency exit.

meaning: I spend (the) — used with 'día' or time period: 'I spend the day...'.
additional_notes: Common structure: 'Me paso el día + gerund' (e.g. 'me paso el día hablando') means you spend most of the day doing something (often habitually or annoyingly). 'Me paso el' is reflexive (me) + 'pasar' in present + definite article. Can be used with other time expressions (la tarde, las horas).
target_language_example: Me paso el día leyendo noticias.
native_language_example: I spend the day reading news.

meaning: I (do) pass/transfer her/it/the (feminine) OR I spend (time) — depends on context.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase; 'paso' is the first-person present of 'pasar'. With a feminine direct object ('la') it can mean 'I pass her/it' or 'I hand over the (feminine) thing'. In contexts about time, 'paso' + 'el/la/mi/...' often appears in 'paso la mayor parte del tiempo' meaning 'I spend most of the time'. Context determines meaning: 1) physical action (Les paso la lengua... = I pass my tongue over them/her/it), 2) transfer of information (Paso la información = I pass along / I share the information), 3) spending time (Paso la mayor parte del tiempo en casa = I spend most of the time at home).
target_language_example: Paso la receta a mi compañera.
native_language_example: I pass the recipe to my coworker.

meaning: literally 'step to' or 'I/you/he move on to' — used to indicate moving on to the next step, action, or topic.
additional_notes: Often appears as part of phrases like 'paso a paso' (step by step) or in constructions where someone 'pasa a' (note: standard is 'paso a' for first person present or noun+ 'a' when indicating transition). In conversational Spanish, 'paso a' can introduce the next action: e.g., 'Paso a explicar...' = 'I will now explain...' Also watch for 'paso' (noun 'step') vs. verb forms of 'pasar' (to pass/move on).
target_language_example: Paso a explicar el siguiente punto.
native_language_example: I will now explain the next point.

meaning: step by step; gradually; one step at a time.
additional_notes: Used to describe doing something slowly, in stages, or following a sequence of steps. Can be literal (walking step by step) or figurative (learning or explaining a process). Common in instructions and advice.
target_language_example: Aprende a cocinar paso a paso y no te desesperes.
native_language_example: Learn to cook step by step and don't get frustrated.

meaning: 'step back' or 'a setback'.
additional_notes: Can be used literally (physically stepping back) or figuratively to mean a reversal, a retreat, or a setback in progress or plans. Common in conversations about projects, relationships, decisions, or progress. Often used with verbs like dar (dar un paso atrás) or ser (fue un paso atrás).
target_language_example: Después del problema con el proveedor dimos un paso atrás y revisamos el plan.
native_language_example: After the problem with the supplier we took a step back and reviewed the plan.

meaning: colloquial: 'I don't feel like (doing something)' or 'I couldn't care less' (used before an infinitive or alone).
additional_notes: Informal phrase often used in Spain. Common structures: 'paso de + infinitive' (e.g., 'paso de salir' = 'I don't feel like going out') or as a short response 'paso' meaning 'I don't want to / I'm not interested'. Expresses refusal, lack of interest, or unwillingness. Tone can be dismissive; avoid in formal situations.
target_language_example: Paso de ir al cine esta noche.
native_language_example: I don't feel like going to the movies tonight.

meaning: part of a phrase meaning 'I/you/he/she/they don't care about' or 'I/you/he/she/they skip/avoid (something)'.
additional_notes: Alone, 'paso de' is colloquial and often used to say you don't want to do or be involved in something: 'Paso de eso' = 'I don't want that / I'm not interested.' 'Paso de los...' would normally be followed by a noun (e.g. 'paso de los problemas') meaning 'I avoid/ignore the problems' or 'I'm over the problems.' It's informal and common in spoken Spanish. Use with the appropriate pronoun/context: 'Paso de' (I don't care/I'm skipping), 'Pasas de' (you skip/you don't care), etc.
target_language_example: Paso de los rumores; no me afectan.
native_language_example: I don't care about the rumors; they don't affect me.

meaning: 'step in' or 'a step toward/in (a specific direction or process)'.
additional_notes: Used to describe a stage, move, or progress toward something (e.g., a direction, path, process, or evolution). Often followed by a noun phrase like 'la dirección correcta', 'el camino', or 'la evolución humana'. Not a reflexive or fixed idiom—meaning comes from the literal words 'paso' (step) + preposition 'en' (in/into/toward).
target_language_example: Ese programa es un paso en la dirección correcta.
native_language_example: That program is a step in the right direction.

meaning: 'one more step' or 'a step further/closer' depending on context.
additional_notes: Literally means 'one more step.' Used both literally (another physical step) and figuratively to indicate progress, distance, or degree (closer/further). Context determines direction: e.g. 'ni un paso más' = 'not one step further/closer' (warning), 'un paso más cerca' = 'one step closer', 'un paso más lejos' = 'one step further away'.
target_language_example: Con un paso más, llegamos a la cima.
native_language_example: With one more step, we reach the summit.

meaning: step toward / step to (something); an action taken in order to achieve something)
additional_notes: Used to describe a step, stage, or action aimed at reaching a goal. Often appears in phrases like 'el primer paso para...' (the first step toward...). Note: 'paso' can also mean 'pace' or 'step' physically; context determines meaning. The example 4 ('apresuré el paso para...') uses 'el paso' in a physical sense ('pace'), so 'paso para' can combine with different verbs/contexts.
target_language_example: El primer paso para aprender español es practicar todos los días.
native_language_example: The first step toward learning Spanish is practicing every day.

meaning: I/you/he/she/it go(es) through; I/you/he/she/it stop(s) by (depending on context).
additional_notes: Paso por is the first-person singular present (yo) or third-person (él/ella/usted) of the verb phrase 'pasar por'. It can mean 'to go through' (a place, a process, a phase) or 'to stop by/visit briefly' when used with a location. Context and prepositions or objects determine the sense: e.g. 'paso por la tienda' = 'I stop by the store'; 'paso por dificultades' = 'I go through difficulties.'
target_language_example: Paso por la oficina antes de ir a casa.
native_language_example: I stop by the office before going home.

meaning: 'step by step' — slowly or in sequence, one step at a time; used to give or follow detailed, sequential instructions.
additional_notes: Common phrase for giving directions or describing gradual progress. Can be used literally (walking step by step) or figuratively (explaining a process). Often interchangeable with 'paso a paso'.
target_language_example: Explícame paso por paso cómo usar la máquina.
native_language_example: Explain to me step by step how to use the machine.

meaning: a compound noun start meaning 'paste of' or 'dough/mixture made from'.
additional_notes: Pasta de is not a standalone phrase; it's the beginning of many compound nouns like 'pasta de dientes' (toothpaste), 'pasta de tomate' (tomato paste), or 'pasta de almendras' (almond paste). It literally links a paste/dough/mixture (pasta) with its main ingredient or purpose. Use with a noun after 'de'.
target_language_example: Compré pasta de dientes nueva.
native_language_example: I bought a new toothpaste.

meaning: toothpaste.
additional_notes: Common everyday noun meaning the paste used for cleaning teeth. Used with articles or quantifiers (un tubo de pasta de dientes, la pasta de dientes). Note: 'pasta' can mean 'paste' in other contexts (e.g., modelling paste, dough), so context matters.
target_language_example: Compré un nuevo tubo de pasta de dientes.
native_language_example: I bought a new tube of toothpaste.

meaning: meatloaf (a baked dish of seasoned ground meat, often served sliced).
additional_notes: Common food term. Used to refer to a single dish or portion. 'Pastel' here means a savory baked loaf, not a sweet cake. Can appear with articles (el/un) or without in short commands/labels.
target_language_example: Anoche comimos pastel de carne con ensalada.
native_language_example: Last night we ate meatloaf with salad.

meaning: apple pie (a dessert made with apples and pastry).
additional_notes: Common dessert in Spanish-speaking countries. 'Pastel' can mean cake or pie depending on region; 'pastel de manzana' specifically refers to apple-flavored pie/cake. Used like an item on a menu or a homemade dessert. Can be singular or plural (pasteles de manzana).
target_language_example: Mi abuela hizo un pastel de manzana para el postre.
native_language_example: My grandmother made an apple pie for dessert.

target_language_multi_word_term: pasé bien / me lo pasé bien / la pasé bien
meaning: I had a good time / I enjoyed myself.
additional_notes: Common way to say you enjoyed an event or activity. Use with reflexive verb me lo pasé bien (colloquial) or la pasé bien/lo pasé bien referring to 'the time' or 'it'. Tense can change (me lo paso bien = I have a good time/have fun). Often used with locations or activities: en la fiesta, jugando, anoche.
target_language_example: Me lo pasé bien en la excursión.
native_language_example: I had a good time on the trip.

meaning: 'I spent the' (time period).
additional_notes: Used to say how someone spent a period of time (día, año, fin de semana, resto de la tarde, tiempo, etc.). Past tense (pretérito) of pasar + definite article. Often followed by a time expression and a gerund or activity: pasé el día limpiando / pasé el fin de semana leyendo. Equivalent to 'I spent the [time] ...'.
target_language_example: Pasé el sábado estudiando para el examen.
native_language_example: I spent Saturday studying for the exam.

target_language_multi_word_term: pasé muy bien / la pasé muy bien / lo pasé muy bien
meaning: I had a great time; I enjoyed myself a lot.
additional_notes: Common way to say you enjoyed an event or time with others. Use lo or la depending on grammatical gender of implied noun (lo generally neutral or masculine, la feminine — e.g., 'la noche' → 'la pasé muy bien'). Often refers to a specific occasion (esta noche, la otra noche, contigo).
target_language_example: La pasé muy bien en la fiesta de anoche.
native_language_example: I had a great time at last night's party.

meaning: I had a great time with (someone) / I enjoyed (time) with (someone).
additional_notes: Used to say you enjoyed spending time with a person or group. Often appears as part of past-tense statements (yo pasé muy bien con..., nos pasamos muy bien con..., or simply 'lo pasé muy bien con...'). Common in casual conversation to describe events, gatherings, trips, or meetings.
target_language_example: Pasé muy bien con mis primos en la playa.
native_language_example: I had a great time with my cousins at the beach.

meaning: 'I spent (the whole...)' — used to say you spent an entire period of time doing something.
additional_notes: Commonly followed by a time period (la tarde, la noche, la mañana) and a gerund (verb ending in -ando / -iendo) or an action: e.g., pasé toda la tarde + gerund. It emphasizes that the entire period was used for that activity.
target_language_example: Pasé toda la mañana leyendo un libro.
native_language_example: I spent the whole morning reading a book.

meaning: 'I spent a' or 'I had a' (used to say how time was spent or experienced).
additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of pasar + indefinite article. Commonly followed by a time period (un año, un fin de semana) to mean 'I spent a...,' or by an experience (un buen rato) to mean 'I had a.../I enjoyed a...'. Use context to choose translation: literal 'spend' for time, 'have' or 'enjoy' for experiences.
target_language_example: Pasé un fin de semana tranquilo en la montaña.
native_language_example: I spent a quiet weekend in the mountains.

meaning: began to (do) something directed at you / moved on to you
additional_notes: Combination of the past (pasó = 'it/he/she passed' or 'it/he/she happened') + the preposition 'a' + the possessive pronoun 'tu' ('your' or 'you' as object). Context determines exact sense: often means someone or something 'moved on to you' (e.g., an action, question, turn) or 'began to do something to/for you'. You will usually see it as part of a larger clause (pasó a tu lado, pasó a tu cuenta, pasó a tu turno, pasó a tu vida). Pay attention to agreement and to whether 'tu' should be accented (tú) when meaning 'you' as subject — here 'tu' is the possessive 'your'.
target_language_example: Después de hablar con María, la conversación pasó a tu turno.
native_language_example: After talking with María, the conversation moved on to your turn.

meaning: 'happened here' (past tense of 'to happen' + 'here').
additional_notes: Used to refer to an event or something that occurred at this place. Often appears with interrogative words (qué, qué fue) or relative clauses (lo que pasó aquí = what happened here). Past tense (pasó) implies a completed action in the past.
target_language_example: No sé exactamente qué pasó aquí anoche.
native_language_example: I don't know exactly what happened here last night.

meaning: 'happened in the' (past tense phrase introducing where something occurred).
additional_notes: Used to describe that an event took place in a particular place or during a specific time (feminine noun follows 'la'). It combines 'pasó' (he/she/it happened or passed) + 'en la' (in the). Common in sentences like 'Lo que pasó en la fiesta...' ('What happened at the party...'). If the noun is masculine use 'en el' instead (p. ej. 'pasó en el concierto').
target_language_example: Lo que pasó en la reunión todavía no lo sabemos.
native_language_example: What happened in the meeting we still don't know.

meaning: 'crossed (my) mind' / 'occurred to (someone)'.
additional_notes: Used with parts like 'cabeza' or 'mente' (e.g., 'pasó por la cabeza', 'pasó por la mente') to say an idea occurred to someone or did not occur. Commonly appears with indirect object pronouns: 'se me pasó por la cabeza' = 'it didn't cross my mind' (or 'it never crossed my mind' with 'nunca'). Past tense 'pasó' is typical, but other tenses follow the same pattern.
target_language_example: No se me pasó por la cabeza llamar primero.
native_language_example: It never crossed my mind to call first.

meaning: 'passed his/her/its' or 'spent his/her/its' depending on context; literally 'passed his/its'.
additional_notes: pasó is the past (pretérito) of pasar. With a direct object (e.g., 'pasó su cuchillo') it means 'passed [someone] his/her/its [thing]'. With events or time expressions (e.g., 'pasó su infancia') it means 'spent [his/her/its] [time/period]'. With exams 'pasó su examen' can mean 'passed his exam'. In colloquial reflexive use (se pasó su paradero) it can mean 'missed' (missed his stop). The pronoun su agrees with the possessor (his, her, its, your formal, their) and must be interpreted from context.
target_language_example: Ella pasó su libro a la estudiante que estaba detrás.
native_language_example: She passed her book to the student behind her.

meaning: spent three (followed by a time period: años, meses, semanas).
additional_notes: Common past-tense phrase using pasar (pasó) + a number to say someone spent a specific amount of time doing something or being somewhere. The time unit (años, meses, semanas, días) typically follows the number. Can be used with reflexive 'se pasó' to emphasize a behavior or state that lasted that time (e.g., 'se pasó tres semanas sin afeitarse').
target_language_example: Ella pasó tres meses estudiando en Madrid.
native_language_example: She spent three months studying in Madrid.

meaning: upside down; in disorder; a mess.
additional_notes: Used to describe things that are physically upside down or a place/situation that's chaotic or disordered. Common in everyday speech. Can refer to rooms, objects, plans, or situations.
target_language_example: Después de la fiesta, la casa quedó patas arriba.
native_language_example: After the party, the house was upside down / a mess.

meaning: French fries; fried potatoes (i.e., chips/fries).
additional_notes: Common phrase for deep-fried potato strips served as a side or snack. In some Spanish-speaking regions 'papas fritas' is used instead; in the UK 'patatas fritas' can be understood as 'chips'. Use with pedir (order), querer (want), or acompañar (as a side).
target_language_example: Quiero patatas fritas con mi hamburguesa.
native_language_example: I want french fries with my burger.

meaning: peacock (male peafowl); also used figuratively for someone very proud or showy.
additional_notes: Literally the bird with a large colorful tail. Commonly used both literally (the animal) and figuratively in expressions like "estar más orgulloso que un pavo real" (to be very proud/arrogant). Used in everyday speech; neutral register.
target_language_example: Ella caminaba como un pavo real después de recibir el premio.
native_language_example: She walked like a peacock after receiving the award.

meaning: "peace to" (used when wishing peace to someone or something).
additional_notes: This is not a common fixed Spanish phrase by itself; it appears as part of longer expressions like "dar paz a" (to give peace to), "que la paz sea con..." or in religious/ceremonial formulas (e.g., "paz a los hermanos"). Make sure context completes the phrase: you normally say who receives the peace (paz a + [persona/entidad]).
target_language_example: Le deseo paz a tu familia en estos tiempos difíciles.
native_language_example: I wish peace to your family in these difficult times.

meaning: peace in / peace at (a place or area).
additional_notes: Paz = 'peace'. When followed by 'en' + location, it means there is peace within or at that place (e.g., paz en el mundo = peace in the world). Common in headlines and expressions. Not an idiom—just the noun plus preposition.
target_language_example: Queremos paz en nuestra ciudad.
native_language_example: We want peace in our city.

meaning: 'peace be' — part of a set phrase used to wish or invoke peace (often in religious or formal blessings).
additional_notes: Commonly appears in expressions like 'la paz sea contigo' or 'la paz sea con él' to mean 'peace be upon you/him'. Often used in religious contexts (e.g., when mentioning prophets) or as a polite blessing. Structure: 'Que la paz sea...' or directly 'La paz sea...'. Formal and respectful; not casual everyday speech.
target_language_example: Que la paz sea con todos los presentes.
native_language_example: May peace be with everyone present.

meaning: to/into a country (used before a country name or reference)
additional_notes: This is the preposition phrase país a + [country/name] used when talking about movement or direction toward a country (equivalent to English 'to [a/the] country' or 'into [a/the] country'). In Spanish you'd more commonly say 'al país' (a + el = al) before a masculine country name, or 'a la' before a feminine country name; if the country name follows directly you usually say 'a España', 'a México', etc. 'país a' by itself is not a fixed phrase — it's the sequence 'país' followed by the preposition 'a'.
target_language_example: Viajamos a un país a orillas del mar.
native_language_example: We traveled to a country on the seashore.

meaning: 'country of' or 'country with' — used to indicate the country something or someone belongs to or is associated with.
additional_notes: Commonly appears before a noun (e.g., país de origen, país de residencia) or before a proper name (país de España). In Spanish the preposition 'de' shows possession, origin, composition or association. Word order: 'país de' + [noun or name].
target_language_example: Mi país de nacimiento es México.
native_language_example: My country of birth is Mexico.

meaning: literally 'country of the' — the start of a phrase indicating something belongs to or is characteristic of a country (e.g., 'país del Norte' = 'country of the North').
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but the combination of país (country) + the contracted preposition + article 'del' (de + el = del). It's used before a noun to indicate possession, origin, or a descriptive label tied to a country. You will usually see it followed by a proper name, direction, region, or descriptive noun (país del cacao, país del norte, país del sol). Remember that 'del' is used only before masculine singular nouns; use 'de la' for feminine (país de la ...), 'de los'/'de las' for plurals.
target_language_example: México es el país del maíz.
native_language_example: Mexico is the country of corn (Mexico is the country of corn).

meaning: in (the) country of / in (a) country
additional_notes: Used to say that something or someone is located or happens 'in' a particular country. Follow with the country name: país en + [country]. In natural Spanish you would usually omit 'país' and say 'en [país]' (e.g., 'en España'). 'País en' can appear in longer phrases like 'un país en guerra' (a country at war) or 'personas en un país en desarrollo' (people in a developing country).
target_language_example: Viven en un país en desarrollo.
native_language_example: They live in a developing country.

meaning: 'the country is' (a phrase fragment used to describe characteristics or facts about a country).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed expression on its own but a common fragment: the noun país (country) followed by the verb ser (es). Use it to state facts or descriptions about a country: geography, population, official language, political situation, etc. Remember subject–verb order in Spanish often places the noun before the verb when making a neutral statement (e.g., "El país es grande").
target_language_example: El país es pequeño pero tiene mucha historia.
native_language_example: The country is small but has a lot of history.

meaning: literally 'country is the' — a fragment used when saying something about a country (e.g., rankings, descriptions).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but a common word order fragment: país (country) + es (is) + el (the). It appears in sentences that describe or evaluate a country (e.g., 'mi país es el más grande' = 'my country is the biggest'). Pay attention to adjectives and superlatives that follow (más grande, mejor, segundo más alto). Grammar: 'es' is the 3rd-person singular of 'ser'; 'el' is the masculine definite article and often begins a superlative phrase ('el mejor', 'el segundo').
target_language_example: Mi país es el más pequeño de Europa.
native_language_example: My country is the smallest in Europe.

meaning: the country is rich (has a lot of something).
additional_notes: Used to say a country has abundant resources, money, products, etc. Often followed by 'en' + noun (e.g., 'rico en recursos naturales') or by a specific noun (e.g., 'rico en petróleo'). For beginner use, remember word order: 'El país es rico en...' or 'Este país es rico en...'.
target_language_example: Este país es rico en pesca y agricultura.
native_language_example: This country is rich in fishing and agriculture.

meaning: A sequence of the noun 'país' followed by the auxiliary verb 'ha' (from haber), typically appearing in constructions like 'país ha + past participle' as part of a larger clause (e.g., ‘el país ha sufrido’). Not a standalone fixed phrase; its meaning depends on the full sentence—usually 'the country has' when translated literally.
additional_notes: This is not an independent idiom but a common word combination in Spanish where 'país' (country) is the subject and 'ha' is the third-person singular present of 'haber' used as an auxiliary. Expect a past participle after 'ha' (e.g., 'ha sufrido', 'ha crecido'). Agreement: 'país' is singular, so 'ha' is correct. Written with an article or determiner in natural contexts (el país ha...).
target_language_example: El país ha implementado nuevas políticas económicas.
native_language_example: The country has implemented new economic policies.

meaning: a free country (a nation with freedom/rights).
additional_notes: Used to describe a country where people have political freedoms, civil liberties, or are not under oppression. Common in simple statements about living in or referring to a nation with freedom. Word-for-word compositional: país = country, libre = free.
target_language_example: Vivimos en un país libre donde podemos hablar sin miedo.
native_language_example: We live in a free country where we can speak without fear.

meaning: 'país' = 'country'; 'muy' = 'very' (together they'd appear as 'very [adjective] country' which is not a natural fixed phrase).
additional_notes: This is not a standard multiword phrase in Spanish. 'País' is a noun meaning 'country' and 'muy' is an adverb meaning 'very' used to modify adjectives or adverbs (e.g., 'muy grande' = 'very big'). You would not place 'muy' directly after 'país' unless followed by an adjective modifying 'país' (e.g., 'un país muy grande' = 'a very big country'). For beginners: learn 'país' (country) and 'muy' (very) separately and use 'muy' before adjectives.
target_language_example: Es un país muy grande.
native_language_example: It's a very big country.

meaning: 'country more' — not a fixed standalone phrase; typically appears as part of comparative constructions (e.g., 'el país más grande' = 'the largest country' or 'país más desarrollado' = 'more developed country').
additional_notes: Alone, 'país más' is incomplete. 'País' = country; 'más' = more/most. Usually 'más' modifies an adjective following a definite article and noun (el país más X) or is used in comparisons with 'que' (un país más rico que otro). Use agreement for articles/adjectives (el/la/los/las).
target_language_example: En la región, ese es el país más competitivo, pero otro país más pequeño también destaca.
native_language_example: In the region, that is the most competitive country, but another smaller country also stands out.

meaning: 'no country' or 'country not' (literal), but this exact two-word sequence is unusual in Spanish on its own.
additional_notes: Alone, 'país no' is not a common fixed phrase in Spanish. You will see 'país' (country) followed by 'no' to negate a clause (e.g., 'país no desarrollado' is incorrect — use 'país no desarrollado' only in specific structures; more natural: 'país en desarrollo' or 'país no desarrollado' as an adjective phrase after a noun). More typical patterns: 'no hay país' (there is no country), 'país no miembro' (non-member country), or 'el país no...' (the country does not...). Pay attention to word order and context — usually you need more words to make a clear meaning.
target_language_example: El país no tiene suficientes recursos.
native_language_example: The country does not have enough resources.

meaning: 'the country' (with a reflexive/impersonal 'se' attached) — not a standalone fixed phrase; likely part of constructions like 'se país' (rare) or a typographical/morphological split.
additional_notes: This is not a standard fixed multiword expression in Spanish. 'País' means 'country'. The particle 'se' can serve many functions (reflexive, impersonal/passive 'se', accidental 'se', or part of pronominal verbs). When you see 'país se' written together it is usually a result of sentence structure (for example: 'En ese país se habla español' — 'In that country, Spanish is spoken') rather than a single phrase. Learn 'país' on its own and recognize 'se' as a separate grammatical element that changes the verb voice or meaning.
target_language_example: En ese país se celebra una fiesta nacional cada año.
native_language_example: In that country, a national holiday is celebrated every year.

meaning: literally 'country has' — used to say what a country possesses, experiences, or is characterized by.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom; it's simply the noun país (country) followed by the verb tener (to have). Use to describe features, resources, institutions, size, climate, etc. Conjugate tener as needed (este país tiene, nuestro país tiene, muchos países tienen). Watch for register: the phrase itself is neutral, but surrounding words can be informal or vulgar.
target_language_example: Nuestro país tiene muchas playas bonitas.
native_language_example: Our country has many beautiful beaches.

meaning: 'fish in' (the phrase 'peces' = fish, 'en' = in) — used to say there are fish in a place.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom; it's the noun 'peces' (plural of 'pez') followed by the preposition 'en' to indicate location (e.g., 'peces en el lago' = 'fish in the lake'). Make sure to include the place after 'en' (el lago, la pecera, este/ese lago). 'Peces' refers to multiple fish. Use 'hay' (there is/there are) when stating existence: 'Hay peces en el lago.'
target_language_example: Hay peces en la pecera.
native_language_example: There are fish in the fishbowl.

meaning: a piece of bread; (idiom) something very cheap or a small amount of food/comfort.
additional_notes: Literal meaning is 'a piece of bread'. Used literally (a slice or piece of bread). Idiomatically it can mean something very inexpensive ('for a pedazo de pan' = for very little money) or basic sustenance/need (referring to food or a small amount of help). Context shows both literal and figurative uses.
target_language_example: Compré ese libro por un pedazo de pan.
native_language_example: I bought that book for next to nothing.

meaning: ask (someone to)
additional_notes: Used when you ask or request something of a specific person. The preposition a introduces the person being asked (English: 'ask someone to do something'). Often followed by an indirect object or a verb in infinitive (e.g., pedir a María que + subjunctive / pedir a Juan que + infinitive in casual speech).
target_language_example: Voy a pedir a Ana que me ayude con el proyecto.
native_language_example: I'm going to ask Ana to help me with the project.

meaning: 'to ask for help' or 'to request help'.
additional_notes: Common verb phrase: pedir (to ask/request) + ayuda (help). Used when someone requests assistance, support, or aid. Can be used in many contexts (personal, formal, emergency). Conjugate pedir as needed: pido, pides, pide, pedimos, pedís, piden. When using the infinitive form (pedir ayuda) it often follows another verb (e.g., ir a pedir ayuda) or functions as a noun-like phrase (Necesito pedir ayuda).
target_language_example: Es mejor ir a la aldea y pedir ayuda.
native_language_example: It's better to go to the village and ask for help.

meaning: 'to apologize' or 'to offer an apology'.
additional_notes: Commonly used to say you are apologizing to someone. Can be followed by a person (pedir disculpas a alguien) or by a reason/for (por + noun/infinitive). Often used in formal and informal contexts. If you want to apologize in person, say "pedir disculpas en persona."
target_language_example: Quiero pedir disculpas a ti por llegar tarde.
native_language_example: I want to apologize to you for arriving late.

meaning: to ask (that)
additional_notes: Used to introduce a request or plea followed by a subjunctive clause (often with 'que' + verb). In English it's rendered as 'ask that' or 'request that' and is followed by a clause describing what is being asked. Can also appear in casual expressions (e.g., 'Por pedir que no quede' = 'There's no harm in asking').
target_language_example: Le voy a pedir que venga mañana.
native_language_example: I'm going to ask him to come tomorrow.

meaning: 'fart in' (literally) or used in expressions about farting or as part of idioms involving 'pedo'.
additional_notes: Pedo means 'fart'. 'Pedo en' is the literal combination 'fart in' (e.g., 'un pedo en el ascensor' = 'a fart in the elevator'). Used in neutral descriptions of someone farting and in idiomatic expressions (e.g., 'tan gracioso como un pedo en un funeral' = 'as funny as a fart at a funeral' — sarcastic). Informal and somewhat crude; avoid in formal situations. Grammar: pedo is a noun, so 'un pedo en + place' describes where the fart happened.
target_language_example: Se escuchó un pedo en la sala de cine.
native_language_example: A fart was heard in the movie theater.

meaning: I asked my/for my (someone) to do something; I requested from my (someone).
additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of pedir + indirect object 'a mi' (short for 'a mi padre/madre/jefe/etc.'). Use when saying you asked/requested something from a specific person (family member, boss, assistant...). Often followed by 'que' + verb (subjunctive) when requesting an action: 'Le pedí a mi madre que me hiciera...' or by a noun/object: 'Le pedí a mi jefe un aumento.'
target_language_example: Le pedí a mi vecina que cuidara a mi perro.
native_language_example: I asked my neighbor to look after my dog.

meaning: I asked (to) the… / I requested the… (past tense, singular 'I', followed by a masculine singular person: 'al' = a + el).
additional_notes: Used to report a past request made to a specific person. 'Pedí' is the first-person preterite of pedir (to ask/request). 'Al' is the contraction of 'a + el' and introduces the person being asked (e.g., al carnicero = to the butcher). Often followed by a subordinate clause with 'que' + subjunctive/indicative (e.g., que sacara, que me ayude) or a direct object (e.g., la pelota).
target_language_example: Pedí al médico que me recetara un antihistamínico.
native_language_example: I asked the doctor to prescribe me an antihistamine.

meaning: I asked (someone) not to (do something).
additional_notes: Uses pedir (to ask/request) + que + subjunctive to report a request or plea that someone refrain from an action. The verb after 'que' appears in the past subjunctive when the main verb is in the past (pedí). Common for asking someone not to do something; subject of pedir can be singular or plural (le, les, te...).
target_language_example: Le pedí que no celebrara tan tarde.
native_language_example: I asked him not to celebrate so late.

meaning: to shoot oneself (literally); idiomatically can mean to commit suicide or, in some contexts, to seriously harm oneself or make a very bad mistake (similar to 'shoot yourself in the foot').
additional_notes: Idiomatic and informal; can be literal (physically shooting oneself) or figurative (expressing extreme despair or self-inflicted harm/mistake). Because it references self-harm, use with caution and avoid flippant use. Register: informal; regional usage common in Spain and many Latin American countries.
target_language_example: Después de perder todo, dijo que se iba a pegarse un tiro.
native_language_example: After losing everything, he said he was going to shoot himself.

meaning: 'hit' or 'struck' (third person singular preterite of pegar + the preposition 'a' for a direct object person).
additional_notes: Pegó is the preterite (past) form of pegar; when followed by a person it takes the preposition a: 'pegó a María' = 'he/she/it hit María.' Can also mean 'it stuck to' when referring to objects (no a). Context determines whether it's physical hitting, striking, or attaching. For polite/neutral phrasing, use 'golpeó a' as a direct synonym for physical hitting.
target_language_example: El hombre pegó a su hermano en la pelea.
native_language_example: The man hit his brother in the fight.

meaning: 'hit (someone) with' or 'struck (someone) using (something)'.
additional_notes: Used to describe someone hitting another person using an object or part of the body. 'Pegó' is the past (pretérito) of 'pegar' (to hit/strike). 'Con' introduces the instrument (con la puerta, con un martillo, con sus puños). Can also mean 'hit hard' when followed by adverbs (por ejemplo, 'pegó con fuerza').
target_language_example: Él me pegó con su cinturón.
native_language_example: He hit me with his belt.

meaning: hit (someone) on/in the ... (past tense, third person).
additional_notes: Combination of the verb pegar (to hit/strike) in past tense (pegó) plus a prepositional phrase 'en la' followed by a body part (feminine noun). Used to say someone/something hit a specific part of the body. Change 'la' to 'el' for masculine body parts (pegó en el) and agreement for person/number (me pegó, te pegaron, nos pegaron).
target_language_example: La pelota le pegó en la rodilla.
native_language_example: The ball hit him/her on the knee.

meaning: 'gave a' or 'landed a' (used with a violent action: shot, punch, etc.).
additional_notes: Commonly used with violent actions (tiro, puñetazo, golpe) to mean someone delivered or inflicted that action on themselves (with reflexive se) or on someone else. With 'se pegó un tiro' it means 'he shot himself' (reflexive, often suicide or accidental self‑shooting). Without reflexive pronoun (le/lo/ella + pegó un), it can mean 'he hit him with a...'. The literal words translate as 'hit/struck a', but context determines who is the agent/recipient.
target_language_example: Ella le pegó un puñetazo al ladrón.
native_language_example: She landed a punch on the thief.

meaning: to peel (something feminine plural) — e.g., to peel the potatoes, to peel the oranges.
additional_notes: Pelar is a regular -ar verb meaning 'to peel' or 'to skin'. When used with 'las' it refers to feminine plural direct objects (las papas, las naranjas, las patatas, etc.). Conjugate pelar to match the subject (yo pelo, tú pelas, él/ella pela, nosotros pelamos, ellos pelan). In some regions 'pelar' can also mean 'to rip off' or colloquially 'to tease' depending on context, but in cooking it means 'to remove the skin.'
target_language_example: ¿Puedes pelar las papas para la cena?
native_language_example: Can you peel the potatoes for dinner?

meaning: to peel the potatoes.
additional_notes: Common kitchen instruction: 'pelar' = remove the skin/peel; 'las patatas' = the potatoes. Used literally when preparing food. Can be an imperative (Pela/Peled las patatas) or infinitive in recipes (Pelar las patatas antes de cocinar).
target_language_example: Antes de freírlas, tienes que pelar las patatas.
native_language_example: Before frying them, you have to peel the potatoes.

meaning: a danger/threat to (someone or something).
additional_notes: Used to say that a person, thing, or situation poses a risk to health, safety, society, etc. Follows with the thing at risk introduced by 'para' (e.g., 'peligro para la salud', 'peligro para la sociedad'). Often used in general or formal contexts.
target_language_example: Fumar es un peligro para la salud.
native_language_example: Smoking is a danger to (one's) health.

meaning: danger to the (feminine noun that follows).
additional_notes: This phrase is a fragment used before a feminine singular noun (e.g., 'peligro para la salud' = 'danger to health'). You will usually see it followed by the noun that is at risk. For masculine nouns you'd use 'peligro para el'.
target_language_example: Ese producto representa un peligro para la salud.
native_language_example: That product represents a danger to health.

meaning: 'hair is' (literal words).
additional_notes: This pairing is not a fixed phrase in Spanish. It looks like the verb 'es' (is) following the noun 'pelo' (hair). You will normally see 'pelo' used with verbs or adjectives (e.g., 'mi pelo es largo' = 'my hair is long') or with possessive pronouns ('tu pelo', 'su pelo'). By itself 'pelo es' is incomplete; you need a subject or possessive and an adjective or clause after 'es' to form a complete sentence.
target_language_example: Mi pelo es rizado y corto.
native_language_example: My hair is curly and short.

meaning: 'hair is' — used to describe the condition, state, or appearance of someone's hair.
additional_notes: 'pelo' = hair. 'está' is the third-person singular form of the verb estar (to be), used for temporary states, conditions, locations, or how something appears right now. Use 'mi pelo está', 'tu pelo está', 'su pelo está' to describe the current state of hair (wet, short, long, clean, messy, etc.). For permanent characteristics (e.g., 'is brown' as an inherent trait) Spanish often uses ser, but many hair descriptions use estar when referring to current styling or condition.
target_language_example: Tu pelo está muy limpio hoy.
native_language_example: Your hair is very clean today.

meaning: 'very' + 'hair' (literal combination); not a fixed phrase in Spanish.
additional_notes: This is not a standard multiword expression. It looks like the adjective muy ('very') followed by the noun pelo ('hair'). In correct Spanish you would normally say 'pelo muy ...' only when completed by an adjective (e.g., 'pelo muy largo' = 'very long hair') or restructure the sentence (e.g., 'tengo mucho pelo' = 'I have a lot of hair'). Alone, 'pelo muy' is incomplete.
target_language_example: Tiene el pelo muy rizado.
native_language_example: He has very curly hair.

meaning: literally 'hairs of'; used to describe a covering of hair/fur on something or someone (e.g., 'pelos de animal' = animal hair/fur).
additional_notes: Commonly appears before a noun to indicate the hair, fur, or fuzz belonging to that noun (pelos de la cabeza, pelos de perro). Can also appear in expressions like 'a pelos' in some regions, but 'pelos de' on its own is usually descriptive. Use 'pelo' (singular) when speaking about hair as a mass (el pelo de mi cabeza).
target_language_example: Los pelos del perro están en el sofá.
native_language_example: The dog's hairs are on the sofa.

meaning: hair standing on end; (figuratively) to be very scared or thrilled
additional_notes: Literally 'hairs on end.' Used for a physical reaction (goosebumps) or to describe a feeling of fear, shock, or strong excitement. Often appears in phrases like 'me puso los pelos de punta' (it gave me goosebumps / it terrified me).
target_language_example: Esa película de terror me puso los pelos de punta.
native_language_example: That horror movie gave me goosebumps.

meaning: 'ball' followed by 'with' — used to say someone has or uses a ball together with something or someone (literally: 'ball with').
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase; it's the noun pelota ('ball') combined with the preposition con ('with'). It appears in sentences like 'pelota con una mano' (ball with one hand) or 'jugar a la pelota con su hijo' (play ball with his/her son). Use it to describe possession, the instrument used, or playing together. Word order: 'pelota con X'.
target_language_example: Jugamos a la pelota con los vecinos.
native_language_example: We played ball with the neighbors.

meaning: ‘ball of’ or ‘... ball’ — used to indicate the type or owner of a ball (e.g., 'Pedro's ball' or 'baseball').
additional_notes: Followed by a noun to show either possession (pelota de Pedro = Pedro's ball) or the kind/type of ball (pelota de béisbol = baseball). Word order: pelota + de + noun. For possession with a person, use de + person. For specific sports or materials, use de + noun (béisbol, cuero, tenis, etc.).
target_language_example: Ella encontró una pelota de tenis en el parque.
native_language_example: She found a tennis ball in the park.

meaning: golf ball.
additional_notes: Refers to the small dimpled ball used in golf. Used literally in measurements or comparisons (e.g., 'about the size of a golf ball') and in contexts describing being hit by or finding one. Always feminine singular: 'la pelota de golf', plural 'pelotas de golf'.
target_language_example: Encontré una pelota de golf en el jardín.
native_language_example: I found a golf ball in the yard.

meaning: 'movie with' (used to say a film features someone or something).
additional_notes: Used to indicate a movie that includes a particular actor, director, character, or element. Followed by a person (actor), role, or trait: "película con [actor]" = "a movie starring/featuring [actor]". Common alternatives: "película de" (a movie about/of) or "película protagonizada por" (starring).
target_language_example: Quiero ver una película con Tom Hanks.
native_language_example: I want to watch a movie with Tom Hanks.

meaning: 'movie/film of' — used to say what a movie is about, who made it, or to link a noun to 'película'.
additional_notes: película means 'movie' or 'film'. When followed by de + noun or de + person, it indicates topic, origin, creator, or starring role (e.g., película de acción = action movie; película de Spielberg = a movie by Spielberg; película de terror = horror movie). For beginners, recognize 'de' as a basic preposition often translated as 'of', 'by', or 'about' depending on context.
target_language_example: Es una película de misterio muy buena.
native_language_example: It's a very good mystery movie.

meaning: horror movie; a film meant to frighten or shock the audience.
additional_notes: Common phrase for movies in the horror genre. Can refer to supernatural, psychological, slasher, or suspense films. Use película (feminine) so adjectives or articles must agree: 'una película de terror', 'la película de terror'.
target_language_example: Anoche vimos una película de terror y no pude dormir.
native_language_example: Last night we watched a horror movie and I couldn't sleep.

meaning: 'movie in' — used to say the language, format or location a film is in (e.g., "película en español" = "movie in Spanish").
additional_notes: Commonly followed by a language (español, inglés), a format (3D) or a place (casa, cine). Often appears in phrases like "película en español/inglés/3D" or "película en casa". If specifying language, word order is "película en + [language]".
target_language_example: ¿La proyectan como película en español o en versión original?
native_language_example: Do they show it as a movie in Spanish or in the original version?

meaning: "the movie is" (used to describe a film's state, quality, or location).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but the combination of the noun película (movie/film) and the verb estar (to be). Use 'película está' when stating how a movie is (e.g., good, boring), where it is (e.g., in theaters), or its current state (e.g., subtitled). Remember to adjust adjectives for gender/number if needed (la película está buena/la película está aburrida). For location or temporary conditions, use estar; for inherent characteristics you might use ser instead.
target_language_example: La película está muy buena; te la recomiendo.
native_language_example: The movie is very good; I recommend it to you.

meaning: "the movie/film was" — used to describe how a movie turned out or to give an opinion about it.
additional_notes: Combines película (movie/film) + fue (past tense of ser). Use to state a past characteristic, result, or judgment about a film (quality, success, reaction). You can replace película with otro sustantivo and fue with other verbs/tenses to describe other things/times. Common collocations: "fue un éxito" (was a success), "fue interesante/horrorosa" (was interesting/awful), "fue mejor de lo que esperaba" (was better than I expected).
target_language_example: La película fue divertida y muy emocionante.
native_language_example: The movie was fun and very exciting.

meaning: Not a standard or grammatical Spanish phrase; appears to be a misordering or typo combining the noun 'película' (movie) and the object pronoun 'me'.
additional_notes: In Spanish, object pronouns like 'me' attach to or precede verbs, not nouns. Correct alternatives depending on intent: 'me gusta la película' (I like the movie), 'la película me encantó' (the movie enchanted me / I loved the movie), 'me dio la película' (he/she gave me the movie). The sequence 'película me' can appear inside a larger clause if followed by a verb (e.g., 'la película me pareció aburrida'), but as an isolated two-word phrase 'película me' is ungrammatical.
target_language_example: La película me pareció interesante.
native_language_example: The movie seemed interesting to me.

meaning: literal reading: 'movie not' — not an established fixed phrase in Spanish; could appear in contexts negating or contrasting a film (e.g., 'película no recomendada', 'película no estrenada'). On its own it's usually part of a larger phrase meaning 'not a movie' or 'movie that is not…'.
additional_notes: This is not a standard standalone multi-word idiom. 'Película' is a feminine noun (la película). When 'no' follows immediately it typically begins a negation or restriction and will normally be followed by further words (e.g., 'película no recomendada', 'película no apta para menores'). Translation depends on context.
target_language_example: Esta es una película no recomendada para menores de 16 años.
native_language_example: This is a movie not recommended for viewers under 16 years old.

meaning: A fragment consisting of the noun 'película' (movie/film) followed by the conjunction 'y' (and). It indicates 'movie and...' as part of a list or compound phrase; by itself it is incomplete.
additional_notes: Not a standalone fixed expression. Use as part of lists or coordinated phrases (e.g., 'película y serie', 'película y documental'). Remember 'película' is feminine: la película, una película; plural: películas. The phrase is compositional and can be translated literally.
target_language_example: Compramos palomitas para la película y la serie que veremos esta noche.
native_language_example: We bought popcorn for the movie and the series we'll watch tonight.

meaning: the movie already / the film has already (started/been seen/etc.).
additional_notes: Película = 'movie/film'. Ya means 'already' or 'by now' and is placed before or after verbs/objects depending on emphasis. In these examples 'película ya' appears in phrases like 'la película ya (había empezado)' or 'esta película ya la he visto' — ya indicates that the action regarding the movie has already happened (started, been seen, etc.). Word order can change: 'la película ya comenzó' or 'ya comenzó la película'.
target_language_example: La película ya terminó cuando llegamos al cine.
native_language_example: The movie had already ended when we arrived at the cinema.

meaning: used to talk about a punishment (pena) for a specific crime or the grief/sorrow (pena) caused by something — followed by the thing causing the penalty or sorrow.
additional_notes: Pena is a feminine noun that can mean 'punishment' or 'sorrow/grief' depending on context. 'Pena de' is followed by a noun or clause: for legal contexts 'pena de' + [delito] = 'punishment of/for'; for emotional contexts 'pena de' + [algo] = 'sorrow over'. When referring to legal penalties, it often appears in fixed phrases like 'pena de muerte' (death penalty) or 'pena de prisión' (prison sentence).
target_language_example: Fue condenado a la pena de prisión por el delito.
native_language_example: He was sentenced to the prison sentence for the crime.

meaning: death penalty; capital punishment.
additional_notes: Refers to the legal sentence of execution for certain crimes. Used in formal/legal contexts. 'pena' = penalty/sentence, 'muerte' = death, so literal translation matches the meaning.
target_language_example: En ese país, algunos delitos graves todavía se castigan con la pena de muerte.
native_language_example: In that country, some serious crimes are still punished with the death penalty.

meaning: worth trying; it's worth the effort to try
additional_notes: Used to say that attempting something is worthwhile, even if success is not guaranteed. Often appears in phrases like 'vale la pena intentarlo' (it's worth trying). Alone, 'pena intentarlo' is a shortened, informal fragment; beginners should learn the full expression 'vale la pena intentarlo'.
target_language_example: No sabes si funcionará, pero vale la pena intentarlo.
native_language_example: You don't know if it will work, but it's worth trying.

meaning: a pity/what a shame to read (that); expressing regret about reading something
additional_notes: This phrase combines pena ('pity, shame, regret') with an infinitive (leer = 'to read'). Use it to comment that it's a shame, unfortunate, or sad to read something (often about news, a message, or a story). In natural Spanish you may hear variations like 'qué pena leer eso' or 'da pena leer...' followed by the thing that causes the regret. Tone: neutral to empathetic.
target_language_example: Qué pena leer que se canceló el concierto.
native_language_example: What a shame to read that the concert was canceled.

meaning: 'pity/sadness for' or 'sorrow for'; can also appear in phrases meaning 'worth it for' (valer la pena por).
additional_notes: Used to express feeling pity or sorrow toward someone/something (sentir pena por = to feel sorry for). 'Pena' alone can mean shame, pity, or sadness depending on context. In the phrase 'valió la pena por...', it means 'was worth it because of...'. With a person as object, translate as 'feel sorry for' or 'be sorry for'.
target_language_example: Siento mucha pena por los animales que no tienen casa.
native_language_example: I feel very sorry for the animals that don't have a home.

meaning: 'it's a pity that' / 'it's a shame that' / 'worth it' (in some constructions)
additional_notes: Usually used in impersonal expressions like "es una pena que..." to express regret or sadness about something (often followed by a subjunctive). In other contexts, "que merezca la pena" or "valer la pena" means "to be worth it" (something is worth doing or hearing). Pay attention to grammar: after "es una pena que" Spanish normally uses the subjunctive.
target_language_example: Es una pena que no puedas venir a la fiesta.
native_language_example: It's a shame that you can't come to the party.

meaning: a pity to see; it's sad to see
additional_notes: Used to express that something is unfortunate, sad, or regrettable to witness. Often appears in phrases like "es una pena ver..." or "qué pena ver..." followed by what is sad. Common in both spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: Es una pena ver cómo han cambiado las calles del barrio.
native_language_example: It's a pity to see how the neighborhood's streets have changed.

meaning: worth visiting; a shame to miss (something worth seeing).
additional_notes: Commonly used after que or vale la pena: (vale) la pena visitar means 'it's worth visiting'. By itself, 'pena visitar' is not a fixed phrase — learners will most often see 'vale la pena visitar' or 'merece la pena visitar'. Use with places or events: 'vale la pena visitar ese museo'.
target_language_example: Vale la pena visitar el pueblo por sus calles antiguas.
native_language_example: It's worth visiting the village for its old streets.

meaning: to hang by a thread; to be in a very fragile or risky situation
additional_notes: Idiomatic expression used to say that something (a situation, relationship, plan, etc.) is very uncertain or could fail easily. Often used in contexts of danger, precariousness, or when the outcome depends on something small.
target_language_example: Después del accidente, la vida del paciente pende de un hilo.
native_language_example: After the accident, the patient's life hangs by a thread.

meaning: 'thoughts and' — the phrase 'pensamientos y' is the start of a paired noun phrase meaning 'thoughts and (something else)'.
additional_notes: Used to link 'pensamientos' (thoughts) with another noun (e.g., 'sentimientos', 'recuerdos', 'oraciones'). Common in expressions like 'mis pensamientos y oraciones' (my thoughts and prayers). The full meaning depends on the second noun that follows. Grammar: 'pensamientos' is plural, so adjectives and articles agree in number.
target_language_example: Mis pensamientos y sentimientos están claros ahora.
native_language_example: My thoughts and feelings are clear now.

meaning: 'thinking about what...' or 'thinking about the fact that...'.
additional_notes: Used before clauses introduced by 'que' (pensando en lo que...) to refer to something someone said, did, or a situation. It often introduces a thought or reflection about a specific matter. Native speakers may also shorten it to 'pensando en' + clause (pensando en lo que dijiste → pensando en que dijiste). Use with verbs of thinking, imagining, remembering.
target_language_example: Ayer estuve pensando en lo que me contaste sobre el trabajo.
native_language_example: Yesterday I was thinking about what you told me about work.

meaning: thinking a lot; giving something a lot of thought.
additional_notes: Used to say you have spent considerable time thinking about something or someone. Common with perfect tenses (he estado pensando mucho) or past (estuve pensando mucho). Often followed by 'en' + noun/verb (pensando mucho en + algo / en + infinitive) or by a direct object introduced with 'lo' (lo he estado pensando mucho).
target_language_example: He estado pensando mucho en cambiar de trabajo.
native_language_example: I've been thinking a lot about changing jobs.

meaning: 'pensar al' is not a standard neutral Spanish phrase. Most likely a mistaken or dialectal form. Standard alternatives: 'pensar en' (to think about) or 'pensar + infinitivo' (to intend/plan).
additional_notes: Use 'pensar en' to indicate thinking about someone/something (e.g., 'pienso en ti'). 'Pensar al' can appear in nonstandard or regional speech or as a mistaken contraction; it is not recommended for learners. In some colloquial uses, 'pensar al' may occur before a gerund or infinitive in spoken phrases, but standard grammar prefers other constructions (e.g., 'pensar en' or 'pensar hacerlo'). When you encounter 'pensar al' check context — it may be part of a larger fixed expression or an error.
target_language_example: No deberías pensar al dejar todo para el último momento; planifica con tiempo.
native_language_example: You shouldn't pensar al leave everything until the last minute; plan ahead.

meaning: to think (in a certain way) / to have an opinion about something
additional_notes: Used to describe the manner or style of thinking (pensar de manera...) or to express one's opinion/attitude about something (¿Qué piensas de...?). In many contexts pensar en (think about) or pensar que (to think/ believe that) are used instead. 'Pensar de' + noun/pronoun is common when asking or stating an opinion; 'pensar de manera/forma' describes how someone thinks.
target_language_example: No puedo pensar de otra forma cuando estoy descansado.
native_language_example: I can't think any other way when I'm rested.

meaning: think about
additional_notes: Used with en before a person, thing, or idea. It often means having someone or something in your mind, or considering a possibility or solution. Don't confuse it with pensar que, which means 'to think that'.
target_language_example: No puedo dejar de pensar en el dinero robado.
native_language_example: I can't stop thinking about the stolen money.

meaning: to think about her/it (feminine) or to think of the feminine noun; literally 'to think in/on the' with la marking a feminine direct referent
additional_notes: Pensar en = to think about/think of. The article la indicates the thing or person thought of is feminine (la casa, la solución, la profesora, etc.). 'Pensar en la' by itself is incomplete and normally is followed by a noun (pensar en la casa) or a clipped reference in conversation (pensar en la — implying a previously mentioned feminine noun). Use 'pensar en él' for masculine or 'pensar en eso' for neuter/abstract 'that.'
target_language_example: Ayer me sorprendí al pensar en la y en cómo había cambiado todo.
native_language_example: Yesterday I caught myself thinking about her and how everything had changed.

meaning: to think about it / to think about that
additional_notes: This phrase is a combination of the verb pensar (to think) + en (about) + lo (it/that). It refers to thinking about a previously mentioned idea, thing or situation. In natural Spanish you'd more often see full forms like "pensar en eso" or "pensar en ello", or a conjugated verb plus a direct object: e.g. "Estoy pensando en ello" or "Piensa en eso." "Pensar en lo" is less common on its own and usually appears as part of a longer phrase (e.g. "pensar en lo que pasó" = "to think about what happened").
target_language_example: No puedo dejar de pensar en lo que dijiste.
native_language_example: I can't stop thinking about what you said.

meaning: Incomplete phrase: 'pensar un' by itself is not a complete, standard construction in Spanish. It can appear when 'pensar' is followed by an article + noun (pensar un/una + noun) and usually requires a preposition 'en' (pensar en un/una ...) to mean 'to think about a ...', or it can occur in contexts like 'pensar un plan/idea' where 'pensar' takes a direct object meaning 'to devise/come up with'.
additional_notes:
Common patterns:
- pensar en + un/una + noun: to think about a (someone/something). Example: 'pensar en un plan' -> to think about a plan.
- pensar + un + noun (without 'en'): possible when 'pensar' means 'to devise' or 'to conceive' (more literary/formal), e.g., 'pensar un plan' = to devise a plan. This use is less common in everyday speech; more common is 'idear' or 'planear'.
- 'pensar un' alone is incomplete and needs context (article + noun or infinitive).
target_language_example: Estoy pensando un plan para la fiesta, pero también pienso en un regalo para María.
native_language_example: I'm thinking up a plan for the party, but I'm also thinking about a gift for María.

meaning: 'I thought that the (feminine noun) ...'.
additional_notes: Used to introduce a past belief or assumption about something. 'Pensé que' = 'I thought that'. The article 'la' is the feminine singular definite article and refers to a following feminine noun (la película, la policía, la política, la muerte). If the noun is masculine use 'el' (pensé que el...). Common in spoken and written Spanish to express a prior expectation or opinion.
target_language_example: Pensé que la tienda cerraba a las nueve.
native_language_example: I thought that the store closed at nine.

meaning: I thought (that) — followed by a suggestion or question about how something is or would be (colloquial).
additional_notes: This phrase combines 'pensé que' (I thought that / I assumed that) with 'tal' used informally to introduce a suggestion or vague question about how something is (like 'how about' or 'what if'). It is colloquial and more common in some Spanish varieties; you may also hear 'pensé que tal vez' (I thought maybe) or simply 'pensé que...' followed by a clause. Use to introduce an idea you had or a tentative suggestion.
target_language_example: Pensé que tal podríamos ir mañana si te viene bien.
native_language_example: I thought maybe we could go tomorrow if that works for you.

meaning: worse than (used before a noun or phrase; 'del' = de + el).
additional_notes: Peor = comparative 'worse'. 'Del' is the contraction of 'de' + 'el' and links peor to a masculine singular noun or a situation introduced by 'el' (e.g., 'peor del mundo', 'peor del año'). For feminine nouns use 'peor de la'. Can introduce a clause when followed by a noun phrase ('es el peor del grupo') or be part of expressions like 'lo peor del día'.
target_language_example: Lo peor del viaje fue la lluvia constante.
native_language_example: The worst part of the trip was the constant rain.

meaning: worst day
additional_notes: Used to describe a day that was the most unpleasant, difficult, or unlucky (often in phrases like 'el peor día de mi vida' = the worst day of my life). 'Peor' is the comparative/absolute superlative form of 'malo' (bad). Can be used with definite article and a complement (de + noun).
target_language_example: Hoy fue el peor día del año para mí.
native_language_example: Today was the worst day of the year for me.

meaning: 'worse is' or part of comparative phrases meaning 'it's worse' / 'even worse'.
additional_notes: Peor es appears in comparisons or set phrases (often followed by 'que' or a clause) to say something is worse. Common standalone use is 'peor es' as a short way to introduce a worse alternative or consequence (English: 'even worse' / 'what's worse'). Usually part of phrases like 'peor es que...' ('what's worse is that...').
target_language_example: Peor es que no tenemos tiempo para arreglarlo.
native_language_example: What's worse is that we don't have time to fix it.

meaning: 'worse than' (used to compare two things, people, or situations).
additional_notes: Peor que is the comparative form of 'malo' (bad). Use it before a noun, pronoun, or clause to say that one thing is worse than another: 'X es peor que Y' or 'Esto es peor que antes'. When comparing adjectives before a noun, use the appropriate noun/adjective agreement: 'una situación peor'.
target_language_example: Esta película es peor que la anterior.
native_language_example: This movie is worse than the previous one.

meaning: 'worse than' (used to compare how bad something appears or turned out compared to reality or expectations).
additional_notes: Used in comparisons to say that something is worse than something else (often 'peor de lo que...' = 'worse than what...'). Common in phrases like 'peor de lo que parece' (worse than it seems) or 'peor de lo esperado' (worse than expected). Usually followed by 'lo que' + clause or a noun phrase with a comparison.
target_language_example: La situación es peor de lo que pensábamos.
native_language_example: The situation is worse than we thought.

meaning: too small for (something or someone).
additional_notes: A phrase used before mentioning what or whom something is too small for. 'Pequeña' agrees in gender with the noun it describes (feminine). For masculine singular use 'pequeño para'. Often followed by a noun or verb phrase: e.g. 'pequeña para mí', 'pequeña para correr'.
target_language_example: Esta camisa es pequeña para mí.
