native_language_example: This shirt is too small for me.

meaning: literally 'small of' or 'little of' — not a fixed phrase; appears when 'pequeño' is followed by the preposition 'de' in specific contexts (e.g., part of a longer expression).
additional_notes: By itself 'pequeño de' is not a common fixed expression in Spanish. 'Pequeño' means 'small' or 'little' and 'de' means 'of' or 'from'. You will see 'pequeño de' when describing size or age in relation to something ('pequeño de estatura', 'pequeño de edad') or in set phrases like 'el pequeño de la familia' (the youngest one in the family). Often native speakers instead use forms like 'pequeño para su edad', 'más pequeño que', or the noun phrase 'el/los pequeño(s)'.
target_language_example: Él es el pequeño de la familia.
native_language_example: He is the youngest (the little one) of the family.

meaning: lit. 'small that' — not a fixed phrase; likely part of a comparative or descriptive clause (e.g., 'más pequeño que' = 'smaller than').
additional_notes: Alone, 'pequeño que' is not a standalone expression in Spanish. You will commonly see 'pequeño' (small) combined with comparatives or clauses: - 'más pequeño que' = 'smaller than' - 'tan pequeño que...' = 'so small that...' - 'pequeño para' = 'too small for' Depending on context, a following clause or preposition is required to complete the meaning.
target_language_example: Mi coche es más pequeño que el tuyo.
native_language_example: My car is smaller than yours.

meaning: literally "small and" — the adjective pequeño followed by y (and); used to link two descriptive words or to start a coordinated description.
additional_notes: Pequeño y is not a fixed phrase by itself; it's simply the adjective pequeño ('small/young') followed by the conjunction y ('and'). Meaning depends on the word that follows: e.g. 'pequeño y sucio' = 'small and dirty', 'pequeño y débil' = 'small and weak', 'pequeño y lindo' = 'small and cute', or 'cuando era pequeño y...' uses pequeño to mean 'young' followed by a verb. Pay attention to context: pequeño can mean 'small' (size) or 'young' (age), and y just connects two qualities or clauses.
target_language_example: Era pequeño y curioso, siempre hacía preguntas.
native_language_example: He was small and curious; he always asked questions.

meaning: 'to lose sight of' (literal) / 'to lose track of' or 'to stop seeing or following someone or something' (figurative).
additional_notes: Used both literally (physically no longer seeing someone/object) and figuratively (losing contact, losing track of progress, forgetting about something). Common constructions: perder a alguien de vista (lose sight of someone), perder algo de vista (stop noticing something), or perder de vista + que/cláusula. Often appears in past tenses (perdí de vista, perdió de vista) or in infinitive constructions (no quiero perder de vista).
target_language_example: No quiero perder de vista a mi hermano en la feria.
native_language_example: I don't want to lose sight of my brother at the fair.

meaning: miss the
additional_notes: Often means 'miss' with transportation, appointments, or opportunities, not literally 'lose': perder el autobús, perder el tren. Here el is the masculine singular article; with other nouns, the pattern changes to la, los, or las.
target_language_example: Voy a perder el tren si no salgo ahora.
native_language_example: I'm going to miss the train if I don't leave now.

meaning: to waste time; to do something that has no productive result.
additional_notes: Common phrase used when an activity is unproductive or pointless. Can be used reflexively (estar perdiendo el tiempo) or in commands (deja de perder el tiempo / deje de perder el tiempo). Often used with people: 'me estás haciendo perder el tiempo' = 'you're wasting my time.'
target_language_example: Deja de perder el tiempo y termina la tarea.
native_language_example: Stop wasting time and finish the homework.

meaning: to miss the last train (literal) — can also mean to miss the last opportunity or chance to do something
additional_notes: Commonly used literally about public transport. Figuratively, it warns that an opportunity has passed (similar to 'miss the boat' in English). If you say 'voy a perder el último tren', it usually means you'll have no train options left that day.
target_language_example: Si no sales ahora, vas a perder el último tren.
native_language_example: If you don't leave now, you're going to miss the last train.

meaning: to lose one's temper, to lose control, or to act irrationally (literally: to lose one's head).
additional_notes: Common idiom used when someone becomes very angry, panicked, or behaves irrationally. Can refer to losing emotional control (anger, fear, love) or making reckless decisions. Tone ranges from informal to neutral depending on context.
target_language_example: Cuando vio la deuda en el extracto, empezó a perder la cabeza y llamó a todos sus acreedores.
native_language_example: When he saw the debt on the statement, he began to lose his temper and called all his creditors.

meaning: to lose one's temper; to become very angry or lose control emotionally.
additional_notes: Idiomatic expression used when someone suddenly gets angry, upset, or behaves irrationally. Common in everyday speech. Literally refers to 'losing the stirrups' (estribos), but the meaning is figurative and not related to riding.
target_language_example: Empezó a perder los estribos cuando le dijeron que tendría que trabajar el fin de semana.
native_language_example: He began to lose his temper when they told him he would have to work on the weekend.

meaning: to lose weight.
additional_notes: Commonly used for reducing body weight through diet, exercise, or temporary measures (e.g., cutting weight for sports). Can be literal (body weight) or figurative in contexts about reducing load. Often used with verbs like 'querer', 'intentar', 'necesitar'.
target_language_example: Quiero perder peso antes del verano.
native_language_example: I want to lose weight before summer.

meaning: to lose a (masculine singular noun) — used before masculine singular nouns (e.g., perder un tren, perder un amigo).
additional_notes: Perder means 'to lose' or 'to miss'. When followed by 'un' it indicates losing or missing a specific masculine singular thing or opportunity. Change 'un' to 'una' for feminine nouns (perder una). For people/relationships you can also say 'perder a' (e.g., perder a un amigo).
target_language_example: No quiero perder un tren importante.
native_language_example: I don't want to miss an important train.

meaning: you will miss the (something) / you will lose the (something).
additional_notes: Perderás is the future tense (tú) of perder. With "el + noun" it's commonly used to say you'll miss transportation (el bus, el tren) or lose/lose control (el control). Context determines whether 'miss' (e.g., a bus/train) or 'lose' (e.g., control, opportunity) is meant. Often appears in warnings after "o" (or) as in "Date prisa, o perderás el..."
target_language_example: Date prisa o perderás el último autobús.
native_language_example: Hurry up or you'll miss the last bus.

meaning: past participle + preposition used with 'perder' to indicate having lost someone (physically separated, missing, or deceased)
additional_notes: Appears in constructions like 'he perdido a...' or 'había perdido a...'. Used specifically before people (the preposition 'a' marks a person). Context determines whether it means 'lost' as in 'can't find' or 'lost' as in 'died' (formal or emotional contexts often imply death). Conjugate 'perder' as needed; the phrase here shows the participle 'perdido' together with 'a' before the person.
target_language_example: He perdido a mis amigos.
native_language_example: I have lost my friends.

meaning: lost a / lost one (something or someone).
additional_notes: Used with a masculine singular noun or numeral to say that something/someone is lost or has been lost. Context determines exact translation: can mean 'a [thing] is lost' (He perdido un arete = I've lost an earring) or 'a [person] is missing' in announcements (se ha perdido un niño = a child is missing). In some contexts like 'has perdido un paso' it means 'you missed/skipped a step'. Verb tense and pronoun (he/has/se ha) change the subject (I have lost / you have lost / a ... has been lost).
target_language_example: He perdido un libro que tenía en la mesa.
native_language_example: I've lost a book that I had on the table.

meaning: 'lost a' or 'have lost a' (past participle + indefinite article)
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but a phrase fragment: 'perdido' is the past participle of perder (to lose) and combines with an auxiliary (haber) to form perfect tenses (e.g., 'ha perdido', 'he perdido', 'habíamos perdido'). 'Una' is the feminine indefinite article meaning 'a' or 'one'. Together they indicate that someone or something has lost one (feminine) item or occurrence. The full meaning depends on the auxiliary verb and context (e.g., 'ha perdido una oreja' = 'has lost an ear'; 'he perdido una pelea' = 'I have lost a fight').
target_language_example: He perdido una llave y no puedo entrar.
native_language_example: I have lost a key and I can't get in.

meaning: literally 'losing the' — part of a progressive phrase meaning 'losing the (something)' or 'wasting the (something)'.
additional_notes: Perdiendo is the gerund of perder (to lose). 'Perdiendo el' will normally be followed by a masculine singular noun (el + noun) or by a masculine singular article + noun phrase: e.g. 'perdiendo el tiempo' (wasting time) or 'perdiendo el partido' (losing the match). It appears in continuous (progressive) constructions to show an ongoing action: 'está perdiendo el...' or 'estoy perdiendo el...'.
target_language_example: Estamos perdiendo el partido, hay que reaccionar.
native_language_example: We are losing the match, we have to react.

meaning: 'they lost' or 'they missed the' (masculine singular object).
additional_notes: Perdieron is the past (preterite) third-person plural of perder (to lose; to miss). With 'el' it introduces a masculine singular noun (el tren, el autobús, el juego). Can mean they lost (a game) or they missed (a train/bus). Context tells whether it’s 'lost' (defeat) or 'missed' (failed to catch).
target_language_example: Perdieron el partido por un gol en el último minuto.
native_language_example: They lost the match by one goal in the last minute.

meaning: they lost the / they (fem.) lost the (depending on noun).
additional_notes: Perdieron is the past (preterite) form of perder for 'ellos/ellas/ustedes' — 'they lost'. The article la (the, feminine singular) agrees with a feminine noun that follows (la esperanza, la batalla, la vida). In examples where the lost thing is masculine, la would be replaced by 'el' (perdieron el). 'Perdieron la vida' is an idiomatic way to say 'they lost their lives' / 'they died'.
target_language_example: Después del accidente, perdieron la casa que tanto querían.
native_language_example: After the accident, they lost the house they loved so much.

meaning: 'lost by' (used to talk about losing something by a margin, or losing possession of something to someone).
additional_notes: Commonly appears in past tense descriptions with a number or amount after it (e.g., perdió de 3 puntos = 'lost by 3 points'). It can also be used when someone lost an object or opportunity to someone else if followed by a noun or phrase (context determines whether it's margin/score or losing possession). In many regions you may also see alternatives like 'perdió por' (lost by) or 'perdió frente a' (lost against).
target_language_example: El equipo perdió de tres puntos en el último minuto.
native_language_example: The team lost by three points in the last minute.

meaning: he/she/you(formal) lost the last one / missed the last (chance/item).
additional_notes: Literal meaning: someone lost or failed to get the last item, opportunity, game, etc. Context determines what 'el último' refers to (the last match, last piece, last chance). The subject is usually third person singular (perdió) or usted. To say 'I lost the last one' use 'perdí el último'.
target_language_example: En la final, Juan perdió el último punto y no ganó el torneo.
native_language_example: In the final, Juan lost the last point and didn't win the tournament.

meaning: lost in (something); was defeated in (a game, match, competition, or situation)
additional_notes: Past tense of perder (él/ella/usted). Used to say someone lost within a specific context: a sport, a competition, a round, or a situation (e.g., 'perdió en la final', 'perdió en tiempo extra'). Followed by a place, event, round, or cause introduced by 'en'.
target_language_example: El equipo perdió en la semifinal ayer.
native_language_example: The team lost in the semifinal yesterday.

meaning: lost in the (masculine singular noun that follows).
additional_notes: Perdió is the third-person singular preterite of perder (to lose). 'Perdió en el...' is used to say someone lost in a specific place, contest, game, round, or situation; the noun that follows must be masculine and singular (el partido, el torneo, el intento, el examen, etc.). To mention who lost, include the subject before 'perdió' (e.g., 'Él perdió en el...').
target_language_example: Ella perdió en el partido de ayer.
native_language_example: She lost in yesterday's match.

meaning: lost hope of / gave up hope of (doing or becoming something).
additional_notes: Used to say someone stopped hoping to achieve or become something. Commonly followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., volverse, ser) or a noun phrase describing the goal. 'Perder las esperanzas' is the general expression; here it's in the past (perdió).
target_language_example: Ella perdió las esperanzas de ganar la competencia.
native_language_example: She lost hope of winning the competition.

meaning: I lost (someone).
additional_notes: Use 'perdí a' when referring to having lost a person (through death, separation, or disappearance). The preposition 'a' marks a direct object that is a person. Context usually makes clear whether it means 'lost' as in 'died' or 'lost' as in 'lost track of' or 'lost to someone/something'. Commonly followed by a noun or possessive (mi esposa, nuestro hijo, a los míos).
target_language_example: Perdí a mi padre el año pasado.
native_language_example: I lost my father last year.

meaning: I lost track (of time, the context, reality).
additional_notes: Used to say you stopped being aware of something (often time: 'perdí la noción del tiempo') or lost sense of context/reality. Common in past tense: 'perdí la noción'. Can be followed by 'del tiempo', 'de la hora', 'de la realidad', etc.
target_language_example: Leí tanto que perdí la noción del tiempo.
native_language_example: I read so much that I lost track of time.

meaning: I lost track of (the) — commonly used with 'tiempo' to mean 'I lost track of time'.
additional_notes: Usually followed by a noun (most often 'tiempo'). Means you stopped being aware of how much time has passed or lost sense/awareness of something. Common in past tense ('perdí') but can be used with other tenses (pierdo, perdí, he perdido).
target_language_example: Perdí la noción del tiempo mientras leía.
native_language_example: I lost track of time while I was reading.

meaning: I lost the / I lost (my) — feminine plural noun(s).
additional_notes: Perdí is the first-person singular past (pretérito) of perder (to lose). Las is the feminine plural definite article, so this phrase is followed by a feminine plural noun (fuerzas, esperanzas, ganas, llaves). In English you can translate as "I lost the..." or more naturally "I lost my..." depending on context (e.g., "perdí las esperanzas" = "I never lost hope" or literally "I didn't lose the hopes").
target_language_example: Ayer perdí las llaves y no pude entrar.
native_language_example: Yesterday I lost the keys and couldn't get in.

meaning: 'perfectly it' — adverb + direct object pronoun; used to emphasize that something applies completely to 'it' (or 'him')
additional_notes: 'Perfectamente' is an adverb meaning 'perfectly' or 'completely'; 'lo' is a masculine singular direct object pronoun ('it' or 'him' formal). The sequence 'perfectamente lo' can appear in sentences for emphasis, but word order in Spanish is flexible and native speakers more often place the pronoun before a conjugated verb or attached to an infinitive. Using 'perfectamente lo' with the adverb before the pronoun is grammatical but somewhat marked; it often appears inside clauses or for rhythmic/emphatic effect (e.g., 'Sé perfectamente lo que quieres decir.'). For beginners, more common natural orders are 'Lo sé perfectamente' or 'Lo entiendo perfectamente'.
target_language_example: Sé perfectamente lo que quieres decir.
native_language_example: I know perfectly what you mean.

meaning: lay low; keep a low profile (stay unnoticed or avoid attention).
additional_notes: Used to say someone wants to avoid attention, publicity, or trouble. Common after verbs like mantener, tener, llevar, or in commands. It's an idiomatic expression but literal words help understand it.
target_language_example: Después del escándalo, decidió mantener un perfil bajo.
native_language_example: After the scandal, he decided to keep a low profile.

meaning: 'newspaper of' or 'newspaper about' (used to indicate the newspaper belonging to or covering something).
additional_notes: Periódico means 'newspaper'. When followed by de + noun, it indicates ownership (the newspaper of X) or topic (a newspaper about X). Common in phrases like periódico de la ciudad (the city's newspaper) or periódico de ciencia (science newspaper). Use de before the noun or noun phrase; contractions like del (de + el) are used when appropriate (periódico del país).
target_language_example: Leí un artículo en el periódico de la ciudad.
native_language_example: I read an article in the city's newspaper.

meaning: "periódico" = newspaper; "es" = is. Together used in sentences like 'the newspaper is...'/ 'the newspaper is [something]'.
additional_notes: This combines the noun periódico (newspaper) with the verb ser (es = is). Use periódico for a physical or online newspaper. Ser (es) describes identity, origin, material, characteristics, or general facts (e.g., 'es de ayer' = it's from yesterday; 'es gratis' = it's free). For 'what the newspaper says' use 'lo que dice el periódico'.
target_language_example: El periódico es interesante hoy.
native_language_example: The newspaper is interesting today.

meaning: driver's license; driving license.
additional_notes: Used to refer to the official document that allows someone to drive a motor vehicle. Commonly used in Spain and many Latin American countries. Often appears in contexts like showing ID (e.g., police), saying you don't have one, or talking about getting one.
target_language_example: Necesito renovar mi permiso de conducir este mes.
native_language_example: I need to renew my driver's license this month.

meaning: 'don't allow/let (someone) to...' (negative command: tell someone not to allow something)
additional_notes: Second-person singular imperative (tú) in negative commands: 'No permitas que...' means 'Don't let/allow that...'. It introduces a subordinate clause with a verb in subjunctive (e.g., esté, mueran, se vaya). Used to tell someone not to let something happen or not to allow someone to do something.
target_language_example: No permitas que te convenzan de renunciar.
native_language_example: Don't let them convince you to quit.

meaning: a contrastive phrase meaning 'but no' or 'however, no' used to introduce a correction, refusal, or to soften/redirect a previous idea.
additional_notes: Used to oppose or qualify what was just said. Often followed by a clause that corrects, denies, refuses, or changes the topic (e.g., 'but no, it's not like that', 'but no, don't say that'). The comma after 'pero' is common in spoken/written dialogue to mark a pause. Not an idiom—straightforward combination of 'pero' (but) + 'no' (no/not).
target_language_example: Quería ayudar, pero, no puedo hacerlo ahora.
native_language_example: I wanted to help, but no, I can't do it now.

meaning: 'but' + 'for' / 'but as for' — a spoken connector pairing used to introduce a contrast or qualification and then specify purpose, recipient, condition, or point of view.
additional_notes: This is not a single fixed phrase but two common words used together in speech/writing. 'Pero' = 'but' (contrast). 'Para' = 'for', 'in order to', 'to', or 'as for' depending on context. When used together (often with a pause or comma), they introduce a contrast with a following clarification, purpose, condition, or intended recipient: e.g. 'But, as for...' or 'But to (do) ...'. Pay attention to the verb after 'para' — it can mark purpose (para + infinitive) or the beneficiary (para + noun/pronoun).
target_language_example: Pero, para participar en el proyecto, tienes que inscribirte hoy.
native_language_example: But, to participate in the project, you have to sign up today.

meaning: but to / but at (used when contrast is followed by a prepositional phrase or verb phrase introduced by 'a')
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom; 'pero' is a contrasting conjunction ('but') and 'a' is a preposition or preposition introducing an infinitive. You will see 'pero a' when the sentence continues with a prepositional phrase (e.g., 'pero a partir de...') or an infinitive (e.g., 'pero a decir la verdad...'). Keep spacing: 'pero' and 'a' are separate words. Frequency depends on the words that follow; often used in spoken and written Spanish to introduce contrast with a following action, direction, or specification.
target_language_example: Quería ayudar, pero a decir la verdad no sabía cómo.
native_language_example: I wanted to help, but to tell the truth I didn't know how.

meaning: but to the / but at the (feminine singular noun follows).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but a sequence where 'pero' (but) is followed by the preposition 'a' plus a feminine singular noun or phrase starting with a feminine article (la) or a feminine demonstrative (la). It appears in sentences like 'pero a la hora...' ('but at the time...') or 'pero a la larga...' ('but in the long run...'). Choose the feminine noun that follows (la hora, la larga, la vez, etc.).
target_language_example: Quería ir, pero a la hora no pude.
native_language_example: I wanted to go, but at the time I couldn't.

meaning: 'but there' or 'but then' (used to contrast what comes next with what was said before)
additional_notes: Commonly used in spoken Spanish to introduce a contrasting point, exception, or consequence. Meaning depends on context: can point to a place (literal 'but there') or to a moment/idea ('but then' / 'however'). Often appears in longer phrases: 'pero ahí viene el problema' (but that's where the problem comes) or 'quedó bien, pero ahí...' (it turned out fine, but then...).
target_language_example: Quería ayudar, pero ahí me di cuenta de que no sabía cómo.
native_language_example: I wanted to help, but then I realized I didn't know how.

meaning: a combination of 'pero' (but) + the contracted preposition 'al' (a + el); used when 'but' is immediately followed by 'al' in a sentence (e.g., 'but when/to the').
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase—it's simply the conjunction 'pero' followed by the contraction 'al' (a + el). You will see it when a clause beginning with 'pero' is followed by 'al' + noun or infinitive construction (for example: 'pero al llegar...' = 'but upon arriving...'). Translate each part normally: 'pero' = 'but', 'al' = 'to the' or 'upon' + verb (when followed by an infinitive).
target_language_example: Quería ayudar, pero al ver la situación decidí irme.
native_language_example: I wanted to help, but upon seeing the situation I decided to leave.

meaning: but something / but somewhat / but a little (depends on context).
additional_notes: This short phrase combines 'pero' (but) with 'algo', which can mean 'something', 'somewhat', or 'a little'. In conversation it often softens a contrast: e.g. 'es caro, pero algo justo' (it's expensive, but somewhat fair) or 'quiero comer, pero algo ligero' (I want to eat, but something light). Context determines whether 'algo' refers to an unspecified thing ('something') or an adverb meaning 'somewhat'/'a bit'.
target_language_example: El café está caliente, pero algo amargo.
native_language_example: The coffee is hot, but somewhat bitter.

meaning: but someone / yet someone (used to introduce an unknown or unspecified person who did something).
additional_notes: Combines 'pero' (but/yet) with 'alguien' (someone). Used to add a contrasting or unexpected detail about an unspecified person—often to introduce that an unknown person performed an action, spoiled a surprise, left a message, etc. Tone is neutral; common in spoken and written Spanish. The phrase does not identify who the person is.
target_language_example: Quería regalarlo en secreto, pero alguien ya lo abrió.
native_language_example: I wanted to give it secretly, but someone already opened it.

meaning: but here; however, in this place or situation
additional_notes: Combines 'pero' (but) with 'aquí' (here). Used to contrast what was said before with what is true 'here' or 'in this situation'. Can introduce a differing fact, exception, or emphasis. Tone depends on context and intonation—can be neutral or emphatic. Common in spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: Quería salir temprano, pero aquí hay mucho trabajo.
native_language_example: I wanted to leave early, but here there is a lot of work.

meaning: but that's how it is / but that's the way (things) are.
additional_notes: Used to acknowledge or accept a situation while contrasting it with something else; often follows a statement and softens it. Can translate as 'but like that' or more naturally 'but that's how it is' or 'but it's always been that way.'
target_language_example: Puedes quejarte, pero así es.
native_language_example: You can complain, but that's how it is.

meaning: 'but still' / 'but even so' (used to contrast and add emphasis).
additional_notes: Often appears before a clause to introduce a contrasting idea or to emphasize that something remains true despite what was just said. Can be written with or without accent on 'aun' depending on meaning: 'aún' (with accent) often means 'still' or 'yet' and is common in this phrase; without accent ('aun') can mean 'even'. In many contexts 'pero aun' and 'pero aún' are interchangeable and equivalent to 'sin embargo' or 'pero todavía'.
target_language_example: No me gusta la peli, pero aun la veré contigo.
native_language_example: I don't like the movie, but I'll still watch it with you.

meaning: an interjection like 'well,' 'oh well,' or 'come on' used to react, express surprise, mild disbelief, or to soften a remark.
additional_notes: Very common in spoken Spanish. Tone and context determine meaning: can show surprise ("Well!"), mild annoyance or disbelief ("Come on"), resignation ("Oh well"), or be used to introduce a counterpoint. Often followed by a clause or stands alone. Not strongly formal; fits in everyday conversation.
target_language_example: Pero bueno, ¡no me digas que vas a cancelar otra vez!
native_language_example: Well, don't tell me you're going to cancel again!

meaning: but almost; however, nearly.
additional_notes: Used to contrast a preceding idea with something that nearly happened or is almost true. Common in spoken and written Spanish to soften a contrast (e.g., 'I meant X, but almost Y') or to correct/explain. Placement: 'pero casi' usually follows the clause it modifies (e.g., 'Quería salir, pero casi no llego').
target_language_example: Quise ayudar, pero casi no lo logro.
native_language_example: I tried to help, but I almost didn't make it.

meaning: but (like) / but how; used to introduce a contrast, clarification, or explanation—often spoken and followed by an example or justification.
additional_notes: Common in conversational Spanish. 'Pero' = 'but'; 'como' here can mean 'like' or 'as' and is often used to introduce an explanation, example, or emphasis after a contrast: e.g. "Quería ir, pero como estaba lloviendo..." (‘I wanted to go, but since it was raining...’). In informal speech it can also appear as filler (similar to 'but, like...' in English). Context determines whether it's causal ('since') or illustrative ('like').
target_language_example: Quería ayudarte, pero como no sabía la contraseña, no pude.
native_language_example: I wanted to help you, but since I didn't know the password, I couldn't.

meaning: but with / however with (introduces a contrast followed by an accompaniment or condition).
additional_notes: Used to contrast a previous idea and then add a qualifier, condition, accompaniment or exception. Common in spoken and written Spanish. Often equivalent to 'but' + 'with' in English, though sometimes it's closer to 'however, given' or 'except that' depending on context. Follows the clause it contrasts with and connects to the detail that modifies or limits that clause.
target_language_example: Quería ir al parque, pero con lluvia no es buena idea.
native_language_example: I wanted to go to the park, but with rain it's not a good idea.

meaning: but with the (masculine singular noun that follows)
additional_notes: A connector phrase used to contrast or add information about something, followed by a masculine singular noun or pronoun (el). Often appears before a noun phrase or before a clause introduced by 'el que' or similar. Context determines exact translation (e.g., 'but with the plan', 'but with him'). If the following word is a verb phrase, speakers may instead use 'pero con' + gerund or another structure.
target_language_example: Quería ir al concierto, pero con el trabajo no puedo.
native_language_example: I wanted to go to the concert, but with the job I can't.

meaning: 'but I think' or 'but I believe'.
additional_notes: Commonly used to soften or qualify a statement by adding the speaker's opinion. Often follows a contrasting clause: [statement], pero creo [que + clause]. 'Creo' is the first-person singular of 'creer' (to think/believe).
target_language_example: No es perfecto, pero creo que funcionará.
native_language_example: It's not perfect, but I think it will work.

meaning: but (that) / except that (used to introduce a contrasting detail or correction)
additional_notes: Commonly appears in spoken and written Spanish to add a caveat or small correction to a previous idea. Often followed by a clause introduced with que or by a verb/phrase. In many contexts it can be replaced by pero or sino que depending on contrast type; 'pero de' often softens or specifies the contrast (e.g., 'Pero de que...' ≈ 'But that...').
target_language_example: Quería ayudar, pero de que no tenía tiempo.
native_language_example: I wanted to help, but that I didn't have time.

meaning: but you should / but you ought to
additional_notes: Combines 'pero' (but) with the conditional form 'deberías' (you should). Used to give advice or make a suggestion while contrasting or qualifying something previously said. 'Deberías' is polite/soft advice; stronger: 'debes'. Can be followed by an infinitive or a clause: 'pero deberías + infinitive' or 'pero deberías + que...'.
target_language_example: Me gusta esa película, pero deberías verla con subtítulos.
native_language_example: I like that movie, but you should watch it with subtitles.

meaning: but (he/she/it) said; 'but' followed by 'said' (third person past).
additional_notes: Combines the conjunction 'pero' (but) with the preterite third-person singular of 'decir' (dijo). Common in reported speech to introduce a contrasting statement or to relay someone's words. Subject (he/she/it/you formal) is implied by context. Pronunciation and stress follow normal rules: 'pe-ro di-jo'.
target_language_example: Quería ayudar, pero dijo que no tenía tiempo.
native_language_example: He wanted to help, but he said he didn't have time.

meaning: but the
additional_notes: A common connector meaning 'but' followed by the definite article 'el' (the) or the masculine pronoun 'él' (he). In writing accents distinguish the pronoun (él) from the article (el), but spoken Spanish sounds the same. Context tells whether 'el' is the article + noun (but the X) or the pronoun referring to a previously mentioned masculine person or thing (but he/it). Very frequent in everyday speech to introduce contrast or correction.
target_language_example: Pero el coche no tiene gasolina.
native_language_example: But the car doesn't have gas.

meaning: but she (emphasizing contrast or exception)
additional_notes: Combines the conjunction 'pero' (but) with the pronoun 'ella' (she). Used to contrast a previous idea or to single out a woman as an exception, emphasise her action, opinion, or situation. In spoken Spanish, stress often falls on 'ella' (e.g., 'Pero ella sí' = 'But she does').
target_language_example: Quería ayudar, pero ella no quiso.
native_language_example: I wanted to help, but she didn't want to.

meaning: 'but they' — a contrastive phrase used to introduce or emphasize information about 'them'.
additional_notes: Combines the conjunction 'pero' (but) with the pronoun 'ellos' (they, masculine or mixed group). Used to contrast, contradict, add exception, or emphasize something about a group. Tone and emphasis can change meaning (e.g., surprise, correction, reinforcement). In spoken Spanish 'ellos' can sometimes be omitted if context is clear, but here it's included for contrast.
target_language_example: Quería ir, pero ellos no pudieron venir.
native_language_example: I wanted to go, but they couldn't come.

meaning: but in / however in (used to introduce a contrast or clarification about something in a specific context/location/time)
additional_notes: Combines the contrast conjunction pero (but) with the preposition en (in/on/at). Often appears before a noun, time expression, or clause to contrast what was just said with a more specific situation. Example contexts: "Quería ir, pero en la tarde ya no pude" (I wanted to go, but in the afternoon I couldn't), or "Me gustó la idea, pero en la práctica fue difícil" (I liked the idea, but in practice it was difficult). Not a fixed idiom—just two common words used together.
target_language_example: Quería ayudar, pero en el trabajo estaba muy ocupado.
native_language_example: I wanted to help, but at work I was very busy.

meaning: but in the (feminine singular noun that follows)
additional_notes: Combines 'pero' (but) + the preposition 'en' (in/on) + the feminine definite article 'la'. Used when contrasting or adding information about something located or happening inside/within a feminine noun (e.g., la casa, la Soyuz). The exact meaning depends on the noun that follows.
target_language_example: Pero en la Soyuz, ellos estarán cálidos.
native_language_example: But in the Soyuz, they will be warm.

meaning: a clipped phrase used to introduce or emphasize an explanation or contrast (literally: "but it is the...").
additional_notes: This fragment often appears in spoken Spanish as part of longer expressions such as "pero es lo que..." or "pero es lo que pasa" to introduce an explanation, reason, or common outcome: "but that's what (happens/it is)". On its own it is incomplete and informal — usually followed by "que" + clause or a noun phrase. It is common in casual conversation to soften or emphasize a contrast.
target_language_example: No me sorprendió, pero es lo que pasa cuando no estudias.
native_language_example: I wasn't surprised, but that's what happens when you don't study.

meaning: used to introduce an explanation, objection, or strong reason (like "but the thing is" / "it's just that").
additional_notes: Common conversational filler that softens or strengthens a contradiction or provides a justification. Often appears at the start of a sentence or clause after a contrasting statement. Tone can be defensive, explanatory, or emphatic depending on context.
target_language_example: Quería ir, pero es que tenía mucho trabajo.
native_language_example: I wanted to go, but the thing is I had a lot of work.

meaning: 'but that' (masculine singular) — used to contrast or correct information, pointing to a specific male person or masculine thing previously mentioned or implied.
additional_notes: Commonly appears in spoken Spanish when introducing a contrast or exception about a particular masculine noun or person: 'pero ese...' (but that one...). The speaker often continues the sentence to add the contrasting information. If referring to a feminine noun use 'pero esa'. If neutral/unspecified plural use 'pero esos/esas'.
target_language_example: Quería comprar el libro, pero ese es muy caro.
native_language_example: I wanted to buy the book, but that one is very expensive.

meaning: 'but I/we/they hope' or 'but I/you/he/she hope(s)'.
additional_notes: Combines the conjunction 'pero' (but) + the verb 'esperar' (to hope). Used to add a contrasting clause that expresses hope or expectation. The subject of 'espero' depends on context (often 'yo' = I). Often followed by 'que' + a clause: 'pero espero que...'.
target_language_example: Vine a estudiar aquí, pero espero volver pronto a casa.
native_language_example: I came here to study, but I hope to return home soon.

meaning: 'but this (one)'.
additional_notes: Combines 'pero' (but) + 'esta' (this, feminine). Used to contrast or introduce a specific thing/situation already in focus. 'Esta' agrees in gender with a feminine noun; 'esto'/'este'/'esta' vary by gender or neutrality. Often followed by a noun or clause: 'pero esta es...' = 'but this is...'.
target_language_example: Quieren ayudar, pero esta es mi decisión.
native_language_example: You want to help, but this is my decision.

meaning: but we are
additional_notes: Combination of the conjunction pero (but) + the verb estamos (we are). Used to contrast or add a counterpoint to the previous statement. Tone and meaning depend on the clause that follows (location, state, opinion, condition). Contraction "we're" is common in English equivalents. Not idiomatic or slang.
target_language_example: Pero estamos listos para empezar.
native_language_example: But we are ready to start.

meaning: but this / however, this one
additional_notes: 'pero' means 'but' or 'however'; 'este' is a demonstrative meaning 'this' (masculine) and can refer to a thing just mentioned or about to be specified. Together, 'pero este' is used to contrast with a previous idea and then point to a specific person/thing. Word order and gender must match the noun (use 'pero esta' for feminine, 'pero esto' for neutral/abstract).
target_language_example: Me gusta el otro coche, pero este es más barato.
native_language_example: I like the other car, but this one is cheaper.

meaning: 'but these' — a contrastive phrase used to introduce or emphasize specific people/things.
additional_notes: Combine the conjunction pero (but) with the demonstrative estos (these, masculine plural). Used to contrast or add information about particular items or people just mentioned or in view. Gender/number must agree: 'pero estas' for feminine plural, 'pero este/esta' for singular. Common in spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: Me gusta la idea, pero estos libros están muy viejos.
native_language_example: I like the idea, but these books are very old.

meaning: 'but thanks' — a polite way to refuse or decline something while thanking the other person.
additional_notes: Used to gently reject an offer, invitation, suggestion or compliment. Often appears with short refusals like 'no' or clauses explaining why (e.g., 'no puedo', 'no lo quiero'), and can be followed by 'de todos modos' / 'de todas formas' for extra politeness. Tone is polite and conversational.
target_language_example: No puedo acompañarte, pero gracias por invitarme.
native_language_example: I can't join you, but thanks for inviting me.

meaning: but (it/has) — depends on context
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself; it's simply the conjunction 'pero' (but) followed by the auxiliary verb 'ha' (has) — often the start of a compound tense (e.g., 'pero ha dicho...' = 'but he/she has said...') or part of a clause ('pero, ha...') where 'ha' agrees with a third-person subject. Context determines the full meaning. Useful when connecting contrast ('pero') to a perfect tense ('ha' + past participle).
target_language_example: Quería venir, pero ha cambiado de opinión.
native_language_example: He wanted to come, but he has changed his mind.

meaning: but (he/she) speaks — contrasts a characteristic with the fact that someone speaks a language or speaks in a certain way.
additional_notes: This is the conjunction 'pero' (but) followed by the verb 'habla' (he/she/you formal speak). Used to contrast an expected idea with the fact that the person speaks a language (or speaks in a particular manner). Context determines whether it highlights surprise, contrast, or a negative trait (e.g., 'attractive, but talks too much'). Replace 'habla' with other verb forms as needed for different subjects or tenses.
target_language_example: Es tímido, pero habla muy bien inglés con confianza.
native_language_example: He's shy, but he speaks English very well and confidently.

meaning: 'but it's been' or 'but it makes' depending on context — often part of expressions about time (e.g. 'pero hace X que...') or weather/conditions ('pero hace frío').
additional_notes:
This is not a fixed idiom by itself; 'pero' = 'but' and 'hace' = 'it makes/it has been' (from hacer). Common uses:
- 'pero hace + tiempo/veces' appears in time expressions: 'Pero hace dos años que no lo veo' (But it's been two years since I saw him).
- 'pero hace + [weather adjective]' describes weather contrast: 'Me gustaría salir, pero hace frío' (I'd like to go out, but it's cold).
Meaning depends on the verb 'hacer' construction: with a duration it means 'it's been (X)'; with weather adjectives it means 'it is (X)'.
target_language_example: Quería ir al parque, pero hace mucho frío.
native_language_example: I wanted to go to the park, but it's very cold.

meaning: but the line / however, the line
additional_notes: Literal phrase combining 'pero' (but) + 'la línea' (the line). Without context it usually introduces a contrast or exception related to a 'line' (literal line, a phone line, a deadline/queue, or a boundary). Common in spoken/written Spanish when contrasting something previously said: e.g., 'Me gusta, pero la línea...' followed by clarification. Not a fixed idiom; meaning depends on the noun 'línea' in context.
target_language_example: Quería seguir viajando, pero la línea de crédito se terminó.
native_language_example: I wanted to keep traveling, but the line of credit ran out.

meaning: but the line was (busy / engaged).
additional_notes: Common phrase used when calling someone on the phone to say the line/connection was busy. Often completed with an adjective (e.g., ocupada = busy). 'La línea' refers to the phone line or call connection. You can substitute pronouns/names before this phrase (e.g., 'La llamé, pero la línea estaba ocupada').
target_language_example: Llamé a Carlos, pero la línea estaba ocupada.
native_language_example: I called Carlos, but the line was busy.

meaning: but honestly / but the truth is
additional_notes: Used to introduce a frank opinion, contrast, or clarification. Common in spoken and written Spanish to soften a statement or emphasize honesty. Often followed by a clause (e.g., 'es que...', 'no sé...') or an opinion.
target_language_example: Quería ir a la fiesta, pero la verdad, estoy muy cansado.
native_language_example: I wanted to go to the party, but honestly, I'm very tired.

meaning: 'but to him/her/you (formal)' — the conjunction 'pero' (but) followed by the indirect object pronoun 'le'.
additional_notes: Used to add a contrast or objection while referring to an indirect object (le = to him, to her, or to you formal). 'Le' can refer to a person previously mentioned; context determines whether it means 'to him', 'to her', or 'to you (formal)'. In spoken Spanish, 'le' often appears before verbs (e.g., 'le prometí', 'le dije', 'le falta'), and combined with 'pero' it simply links a contrasting remark to that indirect-object action. Not idiomatic — literal composition of 'but' + indirect object pronoun.
target_language_example: Quería venir, pero le llamé y no contestó.
native_language_example: He wanted to come, but I called him/her and he/she didn't answer.

meaning: but tomorrow / however, tomorrow
additional_notes: Combines the conjunction 'pero' (but) with the time expression 'mañana' (tomorrow). Used to contrast or qualify a previous statement by introducing something that will happen or be different tomorrow. Tone and punctuation can change meaning: '...pero mañana' often links two clauses (e.g., 'Hoy no, pero mañana sí').
target_language_example: No puedo ir hoy, pero mañana puedo acompañarte.
native_language_example: I can't go today, but tomorrow I can go with you.

meaning: a combination of 'pero' (but) plus object pronouns 'me' (to me) and 'lo' (it/him) used when contrasting or adding information and referring to something affecting the speaker ('but they told it to me', 'but I smelled it', 'but I had it').
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom but a sequence that appears when 'pero' introduces a contrast and the following clause contains the clitic pronouns 'me' + 'lo' (or part of a verbal construction like 'me lo contaron', 'me lo olía', 'me lo pasé', 'me lo han mandado', 'me lo robaron'). Translate 'me lo' depending on the verb: 'they told it to me', 'I suspected it', 'I enjoyed it', 'they sent it to me', 'they stole it from me'. Word order: in compound tenses and after infinitives/gerunds pronouns attach to the verb (me lo han mandado, me lo robó).
target_language_example: No fui al concierto, pero me lo contaron todo y suena increíble.
native_language_example: I didn't go to the concert, but they told me all about it and it sounds amazing.

meaning: 'but I'm afraid' / 'but I fear' (used to introduce bad news, a problem, or a negative opinion politely).
additional_notes: A polite, slightly formal way to soften bad news or disagree. Often followed by a clause describing the problem or negative information (e.g., 'pero me temo que...'). Can be used in spoken and written Spanish. Tone: apologetic/hesitant.
target_language_example: Quisiera ayudar, pero me temo que no tengo tiempo.
native_language_example: I'd like to help, but I'm afraid I don't have time.

meaning: but my / but I (with emphasis) — depends on context
additional_notes: Not a fixed phrase on its own. 'Pero mi' appears when 'pero' (but) is followed by a possessive 'mi' (my) or the pronoun 'mí' (me) after a preposition. Watch the accent: 'mi' (no accent) = my; 'mí' (with accent) = me (used after prepositions). Example uses: 'pero mi casa...' = 'but my house...'; 'pero a mí no me importa' (note: here you'd use 'a mí' rather than 'pero mí'). For emphasis with the pronoun 'me' you usually say 'pero a mí'.
target_language_example: Quería salir, pero mi casa estaba muy lejos.
native_language_example: I wanted to go out, but my house was very far.

meaning: but look / well, look (used to draw attention or emphasize a point).
additional_notes: Common conversational phrase used to get someone's attention, point something out, or soften what you're about to say. 'Pero' adds contrast ('but' / 'well'), so it often introduces a clarification, objection, or new viewpoint. Can be followed by a demonstrative (esto/eso), a direction (a tu alrededor, dentro), or stand alone as an interjection. Tone and context determine politeness or urgency.
target_language_example: No te enojes, pero mira lo que pasó aquí.
native_language_example: Don't be mad, but look at what happened here.

meaning: but very / however very (used to add a strong contrast or emphasis).
additional_notes: Combines the conjunction 'pero' (but/however) with the intensifier 'muy' (very). Commonly appears before adjectives or adverbs to contrast a previous idea while strongly emphasizing the following quality: e.g. 'Quería ir, pero muy cansado.' (though note word order in natural Spanish usually places 'muy' before the adjective: 'pero estaba muy cansado'). In natural speech you’ll more often see 'pero muy' linking short phrases (e.g. 'Es caro, pero muy bueno') or in constructions like 'pero muy' + adjective/adverb. Not a fixed idiom—just the two words together.
target_language_example: La película es corta, pero muy entretenida.
native_language_example: The movie is short, but very entertaining.

meaning: but more / but rather more (used to add a stronger contrast or to modify a previous statement)
additional_notes: Combines 'pero' (but) with 'más' (more). Often used to soften a correction or to emphasize an exception or stronger degree: e.g. 'Quería ir, pero más tarde' → 'I wanted to go, but later on.' Can appear before adjectives, adverbs, verbs or clauses to shift or intensify meaning. Context determines whether it means 'but rather' (contrast) or 'but more' (greater degree).
target_language_example: Me gusta la idea, pero más si es gratis.
native_language_example: I like the idea, but even more if it's free.

meaning: but nothing / but no (nothing changed or nothing at all).
additional_notes: Commonly used to downplay, dismiss, or negate what was just said. Can mean 'but nothing (happened)' or 'but no — (don't worry)'. Often appears at the end of a sentence to soften or reject a previous idea. Tone and context determine whether it's factual (nothing occurred) or conversational (stop, never mind).
target_language_example: Le expliqué el problema, pero nada.
native_language_example: I explained the problem, but nothing (happened).

meaning: 'but you need' or 'but one needs' (contrast followed by a necessity)
additional_notes: Combines the conjunction 'pero' (but) with the verb 'necesitas' (you need — second person singular, informal). Used to introduce a contrast or exception and then state something necessary. Adjust the verb form for different subjects (necesito, necesitamos, necesita, necesitan). Often followed by an infinitive verb or a noun phrase.
target_language_example: Quiero viajar, pero necesitas ahorrar primero.
native_language_example: I want to travel, but you need to save first.

meaning: but not in/from (that way/context); introduces a limitation or exception.
additional_notes: Used to contrast what is true with what is not true, often followed by a noun or phrase indicating the specific aspect being excluded (e.g., 'nombre', 'vista', 'esta manera', 'archivos físicos', 'conciencia'). Common in expressions like 'conozco de nombre, pero no de vista' (I know by name but not by sight). English equivalents: 'but not by/with/in...', 'but not in that sense'.
target_language_example: Lo recuerdo por la historia, pero no de los detalles pequeños.
native_language_example: I remember it for the story, but not for the small details.

meaning: 'but (for) us' or 'but we/they... (with object pronoun nos)',
additional_notes: 'pero' means 'but'. 'nos' is the first-person plural direct or indirect object pronoun ('us') or a reflexive pronoun ('ourselves'). Together they appear when a contrast introduced by 'pero' refers to something affecting 'us' (e.g., 'pero nos dijeron' = 'but they told us'). Word order is normally 'pero' + clause where 'nos' appears before the verb (nos as object): 'Pero nos falta tiempo.' = 'But we are missing time / But we don't have enough time.' Not a fixed phrase—just two common words that occur together in sentences.
target_language_example: Queríamos ir, pero nos cancelaron el vuelo.
native_language_example: We wanted to go, but they canceled our flight.

meaning: 'but to' or 'but for' — used to contrast and introduce purpose, cause, or exception (depends on context).
additional_notes: This is a combination of the conjunction pero (but) + the preposition para (for/to). It can appear when contrasting a statement and then introducing a purpose, destination, recipient, deadline, or condition. Depending on the sentence, English may translate it as 'but to', 'but for', 'but in order to', or simply 'but'. Pay attention to the verb or noun that follows para to choose the right translation. Not a fixed idiom — meaning comes from the two words.
target_language_example: Quería ir al concierto, pero para comprar las entradas ya era tarde.
native_language_example: I wanted to go to the concert, but to buy the tickets it was already too late.

meaning: 'but it seems' / 'but it appears'.
additional_notes: Used to add contrast or objection and then present an observation or impression. Often followed by que + clause (pero parece que...) or by a noun/phrase (pero parece X). Softens a statement — it's less direct than saying something as fact.
target_language_example: Quería ayudar, pero parece que ya resolvieron el problema.
native_language_example: I wanted to help, but it seems they already solved the problem.

meaning: but I thought / but I believed
additional_notes: A short phrase used to introduce a contrast between what the speaker believed or expected and what actually happened or what someone else said. Common in past-tense narratives or when correcting a misunderstanding. It often appears at the start of a clause: 'pero pensé que...' (but I thought that...).
target_language_example: Quería ir al cine, pero pensé que ya estaba cerrado.
native_language_example: I wanted to go to the cinema, but I thought it was already closed.

meaning: 'but I lost' / 'but I missed' (depending on context).
additional_notes: Combination of the conjunction pero (but) + the past tense yo form of perder (perdí). Used to introduce a negative outcome or contrast: e.g. missing transportation (missed the bus/train), losing interest, or losing someone's trail. Context determines whether 'perdí' means 'missed' (a vehicle/opportunity) or 'lost' (an object, track, or feeling).
target_language_example: Quería verlo llegar, pero perdí la oportunidad.
native_language_example: I wanted to see him arrive, but I missed the opportunity.

meaning: 'but because' or 'but for' — used to link a contrasting clause that gives a reason or condition.
additional_notes: This combination appears when a contrast (pero = but) is followed by a phrase that introduces a cause, reason, or condition using por (por + noun, por + eso, por + infinitive, etc.). It's not a fixed idiom; it's just two common words used together. Examples: 'Quería ir, pero por el trabajo no pude.' ('I wanted to go, but because of work I couldn't.'). Watch word order: por typically introduces the reason or motive after pero.
target_language_example: Quería ayudar, pero por la distancia no fue posible.
native_language_example: I wanted to help, but because of the distance it wasn't possible.

meaning: a combination of 'but' + 'because of' or 'for the' depending on context; literally 'but for the'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase; it's the sequence of words 'pero' (but) followed by a prepositional phrase starting with 'por el' (because of the / for the). Meaning depends on the sentence: often introduces a contrast (pero) and then gives a reason or cause (por el...). Example: 'Quería venir, pero por el tráfico no pude' = 'I wanted to come, but because of the traffic I couldn't.' Word order and punctuation may vary.
target_language_example: Quería ayudar, pero por el trabajo no tengo tiempo.
native_language_example: I wanted to help, but because of work I don't have time.

meaning: 'but probably' — introduces a contrast and expresses likelihood (softens a statement).
additional_notes: Combines pero (but) + probablemente (probably). Used to contrast a previous idea while indicating that the following clause is likely true. Common in speech and writing; tone ranges from neutral to tentative depending on context. Can appear with affirmative or negative clauses (e.g., "pero probablemente sí" / "pero probablemente no").
target_language_example: Quisiera ir, pero probablemente no podré.
native_language_example: I'd like to go, but I'll probably not be able to.

meaning: but soon; however, shortly after (something happens).
additional_notes: Combines 'pero' (but) with 'pronto' (soon). Used to contrast a current/problematic situation with a quick or imminent positive change or resolution. Common in spoken and written Spanish to indicate that whatever follows will happen shortly.
target_language_example: No veo la solución ahora, pero pronto la encontraré.
native_language_example: I don't see the solution now, but I'll find it soon.

meaning: 'but it/you/he/she/they can' — 'pero' = 'but', 'puede' = 'can/may' (third-person or formal you)
additional_notes: Common combination where 'pero' introduces a contrast and 'puede' expresses possibility or ability. 'Puede' is the third-person singular of poder (él/ella/usted) and is also used for polite/formal 'you' (usted). English translations depend on context: 'but it can...', 'but he/she may...', or 'but you can...' (formal). Pay attention to subject in the sentence or implied subject from context.
target_language_example: Quiero ayudar, pero puede que no funcione.
native_language_example: I want to help, but it may not work.

meaning: but that / however (introduces a contrasting clause or adds emphasis)
additional_notes: Used to link two clauses, similar to 'pero' + subordinate clause. Often appears before subordinate clauses introduced by que: e.g., 'Quería ir, pero que estaba enfermo' (colloquial) or more naturally 'Quería ir, pero que estaba enfermo' can be heard in some dialects—standard Spanish prefers 'pero' + independent clause or 'pero' + no que. Can also introduce an objection or added emphasis: '¡Pero que cómo lo hiciste!' (expressing surprise).
target_language_example: Quería ayudar, pero que no tuve tiempo.
native_language_example: I wanted to help, but I didn't have time.

meaning: but (I/he/she/you formal) wanted / but I/he/she/you wanted to
additional_notes: Combination of 'pero' (but) + the imperfect form 'quería' (from querer). 'Quería' expresses past desire or polite wish; often used to soften requests (e.g., 'Quería pedir información' = 'I wanted to ask for information'). Context determines subject (yo, él/ella, usted). When used after a clause beginning with 'pero', it introduces a contrast or qualification about what someone wanted.
target_language_example: Llegó tarde, pero quería ayudar.
native_language_example: He arrived late, but he wanted to help.

meaning: an exclamation meaning 'what!' or 'how (could you)!' used to express surprise, disbelief, annoyance, or emphasis
additional_notes: Often appears at the start of a sentence or clause and is followed by an exclamation or question. Tone and context determine meaning: can be surprised (¡Pero qué sorpresa!), disbelieving (¿Pero qué dices?), or annoyed (¡Pero qué vergüenza!). Common in spoken Spanish. It is not a fixed literal translation; the exact English equivalent varies.
target_language_example: ¡Pero qué dices! Eso no puede ser.
native_language_example: What are you saying! That can't be true.

meaning: but it/he/she/they/you know(s) / but it tastes
additional_notes: This phrase combines the conjunction 'pero' (but) with the verb 'saber'. 'Saber' has two common meanings relevant here: 'to taste' (when referring to food: 'sabe delicioso' = 'tastes delicious') and 'to know' (for facts or information: 'sabe mucho' = 'knows a lot'). Use context to decide which meaning applies. Word order: 'pero' usually comes before the verb or clause it contrasts.
target_language_example: El plato huele raro, pero sabe muy bien.
native_language_example: The dish smells strange, but it tastes very good.

meaning: 'but you know' / 'but (you) know' — a conversational phrase used to introduce or remind someone of a fact or to soften a statement.
additional_notes: Common in spoken Spanish. Often begins a clause to contrast or add information (like 'but you know...'). Can be followed by a full sentence or a short tag question. Subject 'tú' is usually implied. Tone can be neutral, corrective, or persuasive depending on context.
target_language_example: Pero sabes que no puedo ir mañana.
native_language_example: But you know that I can't go tomorrow.

meaning: but I am
additional_notes: A straightforward combination of pero + soy. It introduces a contrast: something like “however, I am...”. Soy is the first-person singular of ser, used for identity, profession, origin, and more permanent characteristics. For temporary states, Spanish usually uses estoy instead.
target_language_example: Quiero ayudarte, pero soy muy malo cocinando.
native_language_example: I want to help you, but I'm very bad at cooking.

meaning: 'but his/her/its' — the conjunction 'pero' (but) followed by the possessive adjective 'su' (his/her/its/your formal/their).
additional_notes: Used to contrast two clauses or ideas, where the second part specifies possession. English equivalents: 'but his...', 'but her...', 'but its...', 'but their...' depending on context. 'Su' is ambiguous (can mean his, her, your (formal), or their) — use context to decide. Example: 'Quería ayudar, pero su madre dijo que no.' = 'He/she wanted to help, but his/her mother said no.'
target_language_example: Quise comprar el libro, pero su precio era demasiado alto.
native_language_example: I wanted to buy the book, but its price was too high.

meaning: but such; but like that / but that kind of (used to contrast or qualify something mentioned)
additional_notes: Commonly used to introduce a contrast or soften a statement by referring to a previously mentioned situation or quality (tal = 'such' / 'that kind of'). Often appears in phrases like 'pero tal cosa' or 'pero tal que...' and may sound informal in some contexts. Context determines whether it means 'but like that' (manner) or 'but such' (type).
target_language_example: No me gustó la película, pero tal escena estuvo bien.
native_language_example: I didn't like the movie, but that scene was good.

meaning: 'but they have' — a contrastive phrase used to introduce something that the subject possesses or experiences despite a previous statement.
additional_notes: Combines the conjunction pero (but) + the verb tener in third person plural (they have). Use when contrasting a prior idea with something the same people/things possess, experience, or show. Can begin a sentence or follow a clause. Tener must agree with the subject (pero tengo, pero tienes, pero tiene, etc.).
target_language_example: No son perfectos, pero tienen corazón.
native_language_example: They aren't perfect, but they have heart.

meaning: but you have (to)
additional_notes: Combines the conjunction 'pero' (but) with the second-person singular present of 'tener' (tienes). Often used to add a requirement or obligation introduced by 'que' + infinitive (pero tienes que + verb) meaning 'but you have to... / but you must...'. Context determines whether it's a soft obligation ('you have to') or stronger ('you must').
target_language_example: Pero tienes que llamar antes de venir.
native_language_example: But you have to call before coming.

meaning: 'but you have' or 'however you have' (contrasts two ideas).
additional_notes: Combines the conjunction 'pero' (but/however) with the verb 'tienes' (you have). Used to contrast a previous statement and then mention something the listener/subject possesses, feels, or thinks. Common in spoken and written Spanish. Pronoun 'tú' is implied in 'tienes'.
target_language_example: Quieres cambiar de trabajo, pero tienes miedo del cambio.
native_language_example: You want to change jobs, but you are afraid of the change.

meaning: but all that / but everything that
additional_notes: This phrase combines 'pero' (but) with 'todo lo' (everything that / all that). It's not a fixed idiom by itself; you'll usually see it as part of a larger clause, e.g. 'pero todo lo que...' (but everything that...). On its own 'todo lo' needs a following relative word (often 'que') or an adjective (e.g. 'todo lo necesario').
target_language_example: Quería ayudar, pero todo lo que sabía era insuficiente.
native_language_example: I wanted to help, but everything that I knew was insufficient.

meaning: but everyone / but all (of them).
additional_notes: 'pero' means 'but' and 'todos' means 'all' or 'everyone'. Together they connect a contrasting idea: 'but everyone...' or 'but all...'. Context decides whether 'todos' refers to people (everyone) or things (all of them). Word order can change (e.g., 'todos, pero...') and you may see gender/number agreement: 'todas' for feminine groups, 'todo' for singular.
target_language_example: Quería ayuda, pero todos estaban ocupados.
native_language_example: I wanted help, but everyone was busy.

meaning: but you — used to contrast or object regarding the person addressed
additional_notes: Used to introduce a contrast, objection, or emphasis about the person addressed. Tone depends on context: neutral (simple contrast), surprised, reproachful, or insistent. Frequently appears within a sentence or as a short retort: 'Pero tú...' or exclamatory '¡Pero tú!'. Note the accented í in tú (subject pronoun) distinguishes it from the possessive tu.
target_language_example: No quiero discutir, pero tú siempre cambias de tema.
native_language_example: I don't want to argue, but you always change the subject.

meaning: but a / however a (used to add contrast before a singular masculine noun or number)
additional_notes: Composed of the conjunction 'pero' (but) + the indefinite article 'un'. Commonly appears when correcting, limiting, or adding contrast to a statement: e.g., 'Sí, pero un problema...' or 'Quería ir, pero un imprevisto...'. Followed by a masculine noun or number. In spoken Spanish it may introduce an objection or limitation. If the noun is feminine use 'pero una'.
target_language_example: Quería ayudar, pero un compromiso me lo impidió.
native_language_example: I wanted to help, but a prior commitment prevented me.

meaning: 'but you' (plural) — used to contrast or introduce a point addressed to a group of people.
additional_notes: Combines the conjunction 'pero' (but) with the plural pronoun 'ustedes' (you all). Commonly used to disagree, contrast, or point out something to a group. Tone depends on context and intonation: can be neutral, corrective, surprised, or emphatic. In Spain, 'vosotros' is often used instead of 'ustedes' in informal contexts; in Latin America 'ustedes' is standard for both formal and informal plural you.
target_language_example: Quieren ayudar, pero ustedes no dijeron nada antes.
native_language_example: You want to help, but you didn't say anything before.

meaning: but come on / well, actually (adds contradiction, surprise, or emphasis)
additional_notes: Informal spoken phrase used to introduce a counterpoint, express mild disbelief, or soften a correction. Tone and exact sense depend on context and intonation: can mean 'but come on' (encouraging disagreement), 'well, actually' (correction), or 'still/anyway' (adding emphasis). Common in conversation; often followed by a clause or interjection.
target_language_example: No estaba tan mal, pero va, podríamos mejorar la presentación.
native_language_example: It wasn't that bad, but come on, we could improve the presentation.

meaning: 'but it's going to' / 'but he/she/it is going to' (contrasting clause introducing a future action or result).
additional_notes: Combines 'pero' (but) with the periphrastic future 'va a' + infinitive to introduce a contrasting future event or outcome. Use when you want to add a contrasting point about something that will happen. Subject (él/ella/usted/eso) is understood from context or stated earlier. Common in spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: No tengo mucho dinero, pero va a funcionar.
native_language_example: I don't have much money, but it's going to work.

meaning: okay, fine; used to accept or agree (often conversational filler).
additional_notes: Common spoken phrase in Spain. 'Pero' literally means 'but' and 'vale' means 'okay' or 'alright'. Together they soften agreement, show reluctant acceptance, or transition the conversation (like 'but okay' / 'alright then'). Tone and context determine if it's enthusiastic, resigned, or just moving on.
target_language_example: No quiero salir ahora, pero vale, vamos si insistes.
native_language_example: I don't want to go out now, but fine, let's go if you insist.

meaning: colloquial filler meaning 'but okay, (let it be)' or 'but fine, (then)'.
additional_notes: This is an informal spoken fragment used to concede a point or accept something reluctantly. Often part of longer phrases like 'pero, vale, la verdad...' or 'pero vale, la dejamos así'. It functions like English 'but okay' or 'alright then' and may be followed by an explanation or the end of the discussion. Not a complete sentence on its own.
target_language_example: No estoy muy de acuerdo, pero vale la dejamos así.
native_language_example: I'm not very happy with it, but okay, let's leave it like that.

meaning: 'but (he/she/it) comes' or the colloquial connector 'but still — it/that/this comes/arrives/occurs'.
additional_notes: Literally 'pero' (but) + 'viene' (comes). Used both literally ('but he/she/it is coming') and colloquially to soften or add a contrasting remark like 'but still' or 'that still applies/holds'. Context determines whether it's about a person arriving, something happening, or introducing an aside. Subject (he/she/it/that) is implied from context.
target_language_example: Llegará tarde, pero viene igual.
native_language_example: He'll arrive late, but he's coming anyway.

meaning: but (he/she/it) lives; however, (it) survives
additional_notes: Combines the conjunction 'pero' (but) with the verb 'vive' (he/she/it lives, or you formal live). Context determines subject: common uses include contrasting statements (e.g., 'No tiene dinero, pero vive feliz' — 'He doesn't have money, but he lives happily') or commenting that something still exists/continues despite difficulties ('Perdió su casa, pero vive' — 'He lost his house, but he is still alive' or 'but he still lives'). Verb tense is present indicative. For different subjects or tenses change 'vive' (vivo, vives, vivimos, vivieron, etc.).
target_language_example: No tiene trabajo, pero vive tranquilo.
native_language_example: He doesn't have a job, but he lives peacefully.

meaning: a clause starter meaning 'but he [himself]...'; introduces a contrast involving a male subject and a reflexive/action verb.
additional_notes: Combines 'pero' (but) + 'él' (he) + reflexive pronoun 'se' or start of a verb phrase (e.g., se negó, se quedó, se volvió). Used to contrast what someone else did with what he did (or didn't do). The 'se' is part of a reflexive or pronominal verb and should remain attached to the verb (se negó = he refused). In some examples the 'se' may be omitted if the verb is not reflexive (pero él negó — less common).
target_language_example: Todos salieron a la fiesta, pero él se quedó en casa.
native_language_example: Everyone went to the party, but he stayed at home.

meaning: Not a standard Spanish phrase; likely a fragment or typo. Literally reads 'dog to/at' but lacks the required object or complement.
additional_notes: This sequence is not a conventional multi-word expression in Spanish. 'Perro' means 'dog' and 'a' is a preposition meaning 'to/at/for' that requires an object or phrase after it (e.g., 'perro a la vista' would be ungrammatical; correct: 'perro a la orden' is rare). If you see 'perro a' in text, it's likely missing words, part of a larger phrase, or a transcription error. Possible intended constructions include 'perro a punto de...' (dog about to...), 'perro atado a...' (dog tied to...), or 'perro a sueldo' (dog on the payroll — figurative).
target_language_example: Vi un perro a la orilla del río.
native_language_example: I saw a dog at the riverbank.

meaning: Not a complete phrase by itself; likely part of a larger phrase meaning 'dog to/at' (perro + preposition 'al' = 'to the/at the').
additional_notes: Al is the contraction of 'a + el' meaning 'to the' or 'at the'. 'Perro al' alone is incomplete — you need a verb or more context (e.g., 'el perro alzó la cabeza' or 'el perro al lado'). Watch for correct article use: 'al' must be followed by masculine singular noun; with 'la' you'd use 'a la'.
target_language_example: El perro alzó la cabeza cuando oyó la puerta.
native_language_example: The dog raised its head when he heard the door.

meaning: a dog like (that one) / someone who is (just) like any other (informal, comparative)
additional_notes: Literally 'dog like'. Used to compare a specific dog to another (e.g., 'a dog like that'). In some contexts, calling a person 'un perro como cualquiera' is colloquial and can mean 'an ordinary person' or carry a mild negative connotation (e.g., 'a worthless/typical guy') depending on tone and region. The phrase is compositional (meaning follows from the words) but can be idiomatic when applied to people.
target_language_example: No necesito un perro como ese; prefiero uno más tranquilo.
native_language_example: I don't need a dog like that; I prefer a calmer one.

meaning: literally 'dog of' — a prepositional phrase used to show possession or association (e.g., 'perro de María' = 'María's dog').
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself; it's the noun perro followed by the preposition de to link the dog to a person, place, or characteristic. In Spanish, possession is often expressed with 'de' (owner after the noun) instead of an apostrophe + s. It can also form descriptions (e.g., 'perro de caza' = 'hunting dog'). Word order and articles matter: 'el perro de Juan' = 'John's dog', while 'un perro de la calle' = 'a street dog'.
target_language_example: El perro de Ana es muy juguetón.
native_language_example: Ana's dog is very playful.

meaning: literally 'dog two' — not a standard Spanish phrase; likely a label or name (e.g., 'Dog #2').
additional_notes: This is not a common idiom in Spanish. If you see 'perro dos' it is probably being used as a simple identifier (like naming animals in a list, kennel labels, or captions: 'perro 2' / 'perro dos' = 'Dog 2'). In normal speech you would more often hear 'el segundo perro' (the second dog) or 'perro número dos' (dog number two).
target_language_example: En la lista de adopción, el perro dos tiene tres años.
native_language_example: On the adoption list, dog two is three years old.

meaning: Not a fixed phrase; literal reading 'dog in' — usually part of a larger phrase (e.g., 'perro en casa').
additional_notes: This is not a standalone expression in Spanish. 'Perro' means 'dog' and 'en' means 'in' or 'on'. Together they must be followed by a place or context (e.g., 'perro en la calle' = 'dog in the street'). Beginners should treat 'perro' and 'en' separately and build full phrases: subject + 'en' + location.
target_language_example: El perro en el jardín está durmiendo.
native_language_example: The dog in the garden is sleeping.

meaning: 'the dog was' (past progressive: describes what the dog was doing)
additional_notes: Combines the noun perro (dog) with the imperfect progressive estaba + gerund (e.g., cavando, ladrando) to describe ongoing or repeated actions in the past. Use estaba + gerund to say 'was ...-ing'. Subject can change (yo estaba, ella estaba, etc.).
target_language_example: El perro estaba durmiendo en el sofá.
native_language_example: The dog was sleeping on the couch.

meaning: ‘the dog is in/on’ — states where a dog is located (use with a place).
additional_notes: This phrase combines perro (dog) + está (third-person singular of estar, used for location/temporary states) + en (in/on/at). Replace perro with another noun to say where someone or something is. Use estar (not ser) for locations. Commonly followed by a place: la casa, la silla, el garaje, algún lugar, la perrera.
target_language_example: El perro está en el jardín.
native_language_example: The dog is in the garden.

meaning: 'the dog was' (past passive construction: 'was' + past participle follows).
additional_notes: This sequence shows a subject (perro) + the past form of ser/ir (fue) used to form the passive voice with a past participle (e.g., 'fue atropellado' = 'was run over'). In Spanish the full passive usually includes the agent introduced by 'por' (por un auto), but the agent can be omitted. 'Fue' is the third-person singular preterite of ser/ir and here functions as an auxiliary for the passive.
target_language_example: El perro fue rescatado por los vecinos.
native_language_example: The dog was rescued by the neighbors.

meaning: This looks like a mistaken or nonstandard sequence (likely an error). 'Perro' means 'dog'; 'le' is an indirect object pronoun ('to/for him, her, you formal, it').
additional_notes: As written, 'perro le' is not a grammatical phrase in Spanish. Possible intended forms: - 'El perro le...' starts a sentence meaning 'The dog (to/for) him/her/...': e.g. 'El perro le mordió' (The dog bit him/her). - 'Perro leal' (loyal dog) is a correct adjective + noun. - 'Perro, le...' could appear in colloquial speech if someone addresses a person as 'perro' (insult/slang) and then continues with 'le...,' but that's informal and uncommon. If you see 'perro le' in text, check for missing words or a typo.
target_language_example: El perro le dio la pelota al niño.
native_language_example: The dog gave the boy the ball.

meaning: This is not a standard Spanish phrase; likely an error or two separate words ('perro' = dog, 'lo' = it/him/neutral object pronoun).
additional_notes: In Spanish, 'perro' means 'dog'. 'Lo' is a direct object pronoun used for masculine or neutral objects (it/him). They are not normally combined as 'perro lo'—word order would be either 'lo perro' (incorrect) or more commonly 'lo' placed before a conjugated verb or attached to an infinitive/gerund/imperative (e.g., 'lo vi', 'quiero verlo', 'estoy viéndolo'). If you meant a phrase like 'el perro lo...' this would introduce a clause where 'lo' refers back to something else: e.g., 'El perro lo mordió' = 'The dog bit him/it.'
target_language_example: El perro lo mordió cuando tocó la cerca.
native_language_example: The dog bit him/it when he touched the fence.

meaning: Not a standard Spanish phrase; likely two separate words ('perro' = dog, 'me' = me/myself).
additional_notes: This combination does not form a fixed expression in Spanish. 'Perro' is a noun meaning 'dog'. 'Me' is a clitic pronoun used for first person singular (me/myself, to me). They only appear together in sentences when the dog is the subject and 'me' functions as an object or reflexive pronoun in the same clause (e.g., 'El perro me mira' = 'The dog looks at me'). If you saw 'perro me' alone, it's incomplete — you need a full sentence.
target_language_example: El perro me sigue por toda la casa.
native_language_example: The dog follows me all around the house.

meaning: literally 'dog no' — not a standard fixed phrase in Spanish; usually a fragment or mistaken word order rather than an idiom
additional_notes: This sequence by itself isn't a conventional expression.
