meaning: that's why it is / that's why (something) is (so).
additional_notes: Used to explain a reason or cause for a state or fact. Often appears as part of a larger sentence (e.g., 'Por eso es importante...' — 'That's why it's important...'). Can be followed by an adjective, noun phrase, or clause. Tone is neutral and suitable for everyday and formal contexts.
target_language_example: Por eso es tan difícil terminar a tiempo.
native_language_example: That's why it's so hard to finish on time.

meaning: for that reason / because of that (used before a feminine noun or pronoun reference)
additional_notes: Por eso means "therefore" or "because of that." When followed by a feminine noun or a reference to a feminine idea, a speaker may say "por eso la..." (e.g., "por eso la fiesta fue cancelada" = "that's why the party was canceled"). Depending on context, the feminine word after la can be an explicit noun (la fiesta) or a shortened reference to something feminine mentioned earlier (la razón, la situación). This is not an idiom — it's just por eso + the feminine definite article/la + noun or clause.
target_language_example: No había electricidad, por eso la reunión se pospuso.
native_language_example: There was no electricity, so the meeting was postponed.

meaning: around these
additional_notes: Commonly used as part of phrases like 'por estos días' (around these days), 'por estos lados' (around here/these parts) or 'por estos caminos' (along/through these paths). Meaning depends on context and the noun that follows: with time words (días, tiempos) it means 'around/these days'; with places (lados, sitios) it means 'around/these parts'; with paths or routes it can mean 'along/through these'.
target_language_example: Por estos días hace mucho calor.
native_language_example: It's very hot around these days.

meaning: because of an excess; due to too much (of something).
additional_notes: Used to indicate a harmful or excessive amount of something (e.g., speed, work). Commonly appears in phrases like 'por exceso de velocidad' (for speeding) or 'por exceso de trabajo' (from overwork). Often followed by 'de' + noun.
target_language_example: Se enfermó por exceso de trabajo.
native_language_example: He got sick from overwork.

meaning: please
additional_notes: Used to make requests more polite. It can also express pleading or urgency, as in por favor no hagas eso ('please don't do that'). It can appear at the beginning, middle, or end of a sentence.
target_language_example: Pásame la sal, por favor.
native_language_example: Pass me the salt, please.

meaning: 'please leave' or 'please stop' depending on context.
additional_notes: Por favor = please. Deja is the informal (tú) imperative or present of dejar (to leave, to let, to stop). Combined, it can mean 'please leave (something/someone)' (e.g., 'please leave a message', 'please let my daughter go') or 'please stop' when followed by a gerund/infinitive (e.g., 'por favor deja de reír' = 'please stop laughing'). Use deja when addressing one person informally. For formal/plural commands use 'por favor deje' (usted) or 'por favor dejen' (ustedes).
target_language_example: Por favor deja la puerta abierta.
native_language_example: Please leave the door open.

meaning: 'please don't' (a polite request asking someone not to do something).
additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone to stop or to not do a specific action. Can be followed by an infinitive, a clause, or stand alone as a short plea. Tone depends on context and intonation — can be soft request or stronger plea. Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Por favor no toques eso, está muy frágil.
native_language_example: Please don't touch that, it's very fragile.

meaning: finally
additional_notes: Used to express relief or satisfaction that something desired or expected has happened after a delay. Can appear at the start, middle, or end of a sentence (e.g., "Por fin terminé" or "Terminé por fin").
target_language_example: Por fin llegó el autobús.
native_language_example: The bus finally arrived.

meaning: 'finally we' or 'at last we' (followed by a verb referring to 'us' or 'we').
additional_notes: Por fin = 'finally/at last'. When followed by nos (the object/pronoun 'us' or reflexive 'ourselves'), it introduces actions or states that happen to or are done by/for 'us' (e.g., conocemos = we meet/know each other; dejará en paz = will leave us alone; mudamos = we move). The exact English structure depends on the verb: 'we finally meet', 'they finally leave us alone', 'we finally moved'.
target_language_example: Por fin nos reunimos para celebrar.
native_language_example: We finally got together to celebrate.

meaning: 'for no good reason' or 'just because / for fun' (doing something without practical purpose or benefit).
additional_notes: Used to say someone does something without necessary reason, benefit, or intent—often 'just for fun', 'just because', or 'needlessly'. Can be neutral (doing something for pleasure) or negative (needlessly, pointlessly). Common with actions like criticizing, calling, or helping when there's no gain.
target_language_example: No trabajó en el proyecto por gusto; quería aprender.
native_language_example: He didn't work on the project just for fun; he wanted to learn.

meaning: for speaking; because of speaking; to speak (as a reason or purpose).
additional_notes: Depends on context. 'Por hablar' can indicate a reason ('because of speaking') or a motive/purpose ('to speak'/'for speaking'). It often appears in longer sentences (e.g., 'Lo hizo por hablar' = 'He did it just to talk/speak' or 'Se quedó afónico por hablar tanto' = 'He lost his voice because of speaking so much'). Pay attention to surrounding verbs and tense to determine if it's causal (por + gerund/infinitive) or purposive.
target_language_example: Se quedó ronco por hablar toda la noche.
native_language_example: He became hoarse from speaking all night.

meaning: 'because of doing it' / 'to do it' (depends on context).
additional_notes: This phrase can mean different things depending on context. Often, por + infinitive expresses reason ('because of doing something') as in 'Me preocupé por hacerlo' = 'I worried because of doing it.' It can also appear in idiomatic expressions: 'estar por hacerlo' = 'to be about to do it'; 'morirse por hacerlo' = 'to be dying to do it' (very eager); and 'hacer esperar por hacerlo' indicates being delayed because of someone. Word order and surrounding words change the nuance, so translate based on the whole sentence.
target_language_example: Estoy por hacerlo ahora mismo.
native_language_example: I'm about to do it right now.

meaning: per hour; by the hour.
additional_notes: Used to talk about rates or frequency measured each hour (e.g., pay rate: 'se le paga por hora' = 'he/she is paid per hour'). Can also appear alone as a short response meaning 'for now' in some contexts, but primary meaning is 'per hour'.
target_language_example: Trabajo por hora en la cafetería.
native_language_example: I work for an hourly wage at the café.

meaning: for today; (I'm) done for today.
additional_notes: Used to say that an activity is finished or will stop for the rest of the day. Often follows a verb (e.g., 'Terminé por hoy' = I'm finished for today). Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Ya he hecho todo el trabajo por hoy.
native_language_example: I've already done all the work for today.

meaning: 'by instinct' or 'instinctively' — because of natural, automatic impulses rather than conscious thought.
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something acts without deliberate reasoning, guided by innate tendencies or gut feeling. Common with animals and humans. Can describe a general tendency (Los animales actúan por instinto) or a specific immediate reaction (Por instinto, me aparté).
target_language_example: Por instinto, tomé el paraguas antes de salir.
native_language_example: Instinctively, I took the umbrella before leaving.

meaning: thank you for inviting me to (something / somewhere).
additional_notes: Used to express gratitude for being invited. The structure is: gracias por invitarme a + (place, event, or action). 'Invitarme' is the verb 'invitar' (to invite) with the pronoun 'me' (me). You can change the object after 'a' to a noun (la fiesta), a place (tu casa) or an infinitive/phrase (sentarme a la mesa).
target_language_example: Gracias por invitarme a la cena mañana.
native_language_example: Thank you for inviting me to dinner tomorrow.

meaning: for going; because of going; about to go (depends on context)
additional_notes: ‘Por ir’ is not a fixed idiom by itself; its meaning depends on context. It often appears as part of a larger phrase: e.g. expressing reason ('por ir a la tienda' = 'because of going to the store'), indicating purpose or intent can sometimes use 'para ir' instead, and in some constructions it can mean 'about to go' or 'on the verge of leaving' when combined with verbs (regional/use-specific). Use context to determine whether it expresses reason, purpose (prefer 'para' for clear purpose), or an action in progress.
target_language_example: No pude venir por ir a una reunión.
native_language_example: I couldn't come because I had to go to a meeting.

meaning: through/by the (door) of; used to indicate movement through or via a specific door or entrance.
additional_notes: Followed by a noun (often a place or person-related noun) to specify which door or entrance is used. Common in physical contexts (entering/exiting a building or room). Can be used literally (walking through a door) or figuratively in some expressions (e.g., 'entrar por la puerta de atrás' = enter by the back door, implying secrecy or indirectness). Match gender/number of 'la' if the noun requires a different article (e.g., 'por el portal de', 'por las puertas de').
target_language_example: Entramos por la puerta de atrás para no molestar.
native_language_example: We went in through the back door so as not to disturb anyone.

meaning: through/out the back door; by a back/side exit. (literally and figuratively)
additional_notes: Used literally to mean entering or leaving via a back door. Also used figuratively to mean doing something secretly, quietly, unofficially, or by an indirect/underhanded way (e.g., avoiding formal process). Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Sal de la casa por la puerta de atrás para no despertar a nadie.
native_language_example: Leave the house through the back door so you don't wake anyone.

meaning: a clause meaning 'because of which I am' or 'for which I am' (used to link a cause/reason or a situation to the speaker).
additional_notes: This phrase is part of a larger sentence and needs context to be complete. It often follows a noun or idea introduced earlier: e.g. 'la razón por la que estoy...' = 'the reason for which I am...' or 'la situación por la que estoy pasando...' = 'the situation I am going through...' The exact translation depends on the preceding noun and the verb that follows ('estoy' = 'I am').
target_language_example: Esa es la razón por la que estoy preocupado.
native_language_example: That is the reason why I am worried.

meaning: 'for the', 'by the', or 'through the' (depends on context) — a common preposition + article combination.
additional_notes: Por is a versatile preposition with many meanings: cause/reason (por la lluvia = because of the rain), movement through/along (caminar por la calle = walk along the street), duration/time (por la mañana = in the morning), exchange (pagar por la entrada = pay for the ticket), and agent in passive voice (fue escrita por la autora = was written by the author). La is the feminine singular definite article 'the'. Together they must agree with a feminine singular noun that follows (por la casa, por la tarde). The exact English translation depends on the verb and noun in the sentence.
target_language_example: Caminamos por la playa al atardecer.
native_language_example: We walked along the beach at sunset.

meaning: for which / because of which (feminine plural relative or prepositional phrase).
additional_notes: Used to refer back to a plural feminine noun or idea. Can function as a relative clause connector (e.g., 'las razones por las que...') meaning 'the reasons for which/why', or as part of a prepositional phrase meaning 'because of which' when explaining cause. If referring to masculine plural, use 'por los que'.
target_language_example: Estas son las preguntas por las que vine hoy.
native_language_example: These are the questions for which I came today.

meaning: to be read; because of reading; for reading (depending on context).
additional_notes: Por leer is a short phrase usually used as part of a larger sentence. It can describe something that remains 'to be read' (e.g., 'queda por leer') or indicate a reason/cause 'because of reading' (less common). Context determines meaning—common constructions: 'queda por leer' (still to be read), 'por leer' after a noun can mean 'for reading' (e.g., 'libro por leer' = book to read).
target_language_example: Tengo varios artículos por leer este fin de semana.
native_language_example: I have several articles to read this weekend.

meaning: for that
additional_notes: Usually not a complete expression on its own. lo is a neuter word that refers to an idea, fact, or situation rather than a specific noun, so por lo can have a broad sense like 'for that' depending on context. Beginners will often see it as part of longer expressions such as por lo menos ('at least'), por lo general ('generally'), or por lo tanto ('therefore').
target_language_example: Gracias por lo de ayer.
native_language_example: Thanks for what happened yesterday.

meaning: generally; usually; in general.
additional_notes: Used to describe what typically happens or is true. Often placed at the start of a sentence or before the verb. Comma after the phrase is optional. Synonyms: 'generalmente', 'normalmente'.
target_language_example: Por lo general desayuno a las siete.
native_language_example: I usually have breakfast at seven.

meaning: at least; at the very least
additional_notes: Used to indicate a minimum amount, number, degree, or to soften/limit a statement (e.g., 'at least' in English). Can appear mid-sentence for emphasis ('eso, por lo menos') or at the start ('por lo menos...'). Common in everyday and formal speech.
target_language_example: Por lo menos tráete una chaqueta.
native_language_example: At least bring a jacket.

meaning: 'at least one'.
additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun (una) to say that the minimum quantity required or expected is one. Common in everyday speech and writing. It is interchangeable with 'por lo menos' + number/quantity (e.g., 'por lo menos una persona', 'por lo menos una vez').
target_language_example: Necesitamos por lo menos una silla más.
native_language_example: We need at least one more chair.

meaning: because of which
additional_notes: Commonly used to link a cause or reason to a result ("because of which" / "so"), or to refer back to 'that which' (similar to 'what' in English). Context determines exact translation: in causal sentences it means 'because of which' (e.g., 'offended because of what he said'); in expressions of apology or gratitude it can mean 'for what' / 'for that which' (e.g., 'sorry for what I am' or 'thanks for what you have made possible').
target_language_example: Lo agradezco por lo que has hecho por mí.
native_language_example: I thank you for what you have done for me.

meaning: because of what had (happened/done); for what had…
additional_notes: Used to refer back to an action or event in the past (pluperfect: 'había' + past participle). Commonly translated as 'because of what had...' or 'for what had...'. The rest of the clause usually completes the idea (e.g., hecho, pasado, ocurrido). Tone is neutral and suitable for formal and informal contexts.
target_language_example: Me disculpé por lo que había dicho.
native_language_example: I apologized because of what I had said.

meaning: because of what (someone) did/said to him/her; for what (someone) did to him/her.
additional_notes: Used to refer back to an action or words that affected a third person (le = to him/her). Often follows a noun or clause that names the person affected: 'Es por Lola, por lo que le hiciste a su padre' = 'It's because of Lola, for what you did to her father.' Can introduce a reason ('por lo que' = 'because of what') or refer to the specific thing someone said/did ('por lo que le dijo/hiciste').
target_language_example: Por lo que le contaste, ahora está molesta con él.
native_language_example: Because of what you told her, she's upset with him now.

meaning: As far as I know; based on what I know.
additional_notes: Used to introduce information the speaker believes is true but not certain. Common in spoken and written Spanish to hedge a statement. Often followed by a clause (por lo que sé, + clause). Can be replaced by 'que yo sepa'.
target_language_example: Por lo que sé, la reunión empieza a las nueve.
native_language_example: As far as I know, the meeting starts at nine.

meaning: as far as I (am concerned) / from my point of view
additional_notes: Used to introduce the speaker's opinion or perspective; often followed by a verb or clause (e.g., 'por lo que yo veo', 'por lo que yo sé', 'por lo que yo diría'). Common in spoken and written Spanish. Can be shortened in casual speech (e.g., 'yo creo' or 'por lo que veo').
target_language_example: Por lo que yo sé, la reunión empieza a las nueve.
native_language_example: As far as I know, the meeting starts at nine.

meaning: therefore; so; consequently.
additional_notes: Used to express a logical conclusion or result from what was said before. Common in both spoken and written Spanish; can appear at the start of a sentence or between clauses, often set off by commas.
target_language_example: No tenía dinero, por lo tanto no pudo comprar el billete.
native_language_example: He had no money, so he couldn't buy the ticket.

meaning: 'apparently' or 'it seems' (based on what is known or reported).
additional_notes: Used to introduce information that the speaker believes to be true based on evidence, reports, or appearance. Common in conversational and written Spanish to soften a statement or report hearsay. Can be followed by a clause or a short response (e.g., "Por lo visto, sí.").
target_language_example: Por lo visto, van a cerrar la tienda mañana.
native_language_example: Apparently, they're going to close the store tomorrow.

meaning: around the years of; roughly in the time period of
additional_notes: Used to give an approximate date or time period (often followed by a decade or specific year). Similar to 'around' or 'in the years of' in English. Common in spoken and written Spanish to indicate approximation (e.g., 'por los años de 1990' = 'around 1990').
target_language_example: Empezaron a construir el edificio por los años de 2005.
native_language_example: They started building the building around the year 2005.

meaning: by the skin of one's teeth; narrowly; just barely.
additional_notes: Informal idiom used to say something happened with very little margin — barely succeeding, escaping, or avoiding something. Often used with verbs like aprobar (pass), librarse (escape), salvarse (be saved).
target_language_example: Aprobé el examen por los pelos.
native_language_example: I passed the exam by the skin of my teeth.

meaning: 'by means of' / 'through' / 'via' (shows the instrument, method, or means used)
additional_notes: Used to indicate the method, instrument, channel, or intermediary by which something is done. More formal than 'con' or 'a través de' in some contexts but largely interchangeable with 'mediante' and 'a través de'. Often followed by a noun (por medio de + noun).
target_language_example: Enviaron la información por medio de correo electrónico.
native_language_example: They sent the information by means of email.

meaning: as for me / on my part / from my side (expressing personal stance or responsibility).
additional_notes: Used to introduce the speaker's opinion, attitude, or responsibility. Can indicate personal responsibility (e.g., admitting fault) or simply state that the following comment applies to the speaker alone. Often appears with commas: "Yo, por mi parte,..." or at the start: "Por mi parte,..."
target_language_example: Por mi parte, estoy de acuerdo con la propuesta.
native_language_example: As for me, I agree with the proposal.

meaning: 'for my life' — used to say someone is in danger, fleeing, or very strongly swearing (depending on context).
additional_notes:
Common uses:
- Literal/urgent: expresses fear for one's life or running/fighting to save oneself (e.g., estoy luchando/temo/huí por mi vida = I'm fighting/fear/ran for my life).
- Figurative/colloquial: can be used hyperbolically in song or expression to mean 'with all my energy' (bailo por mi vida) or as a strong oath (te lo juro por mi vida = I swear to you on my life). Context determines whether it's literal danger or emphasis.
Often appears in past participle/verbs of motion (corrí/huí) or verbs of emotion (temo, temo por mi vida).
target_language_example: Corrí por mi vida cuando escuché las explosiones.
native_language_example: I ran for my life when I heard the explosions.

meaning: for moments; occasionally; at times
additional_notes: Used to describe something that happens occasionally or in short bursts. Common in phrases like 'por momentos pensé...' (for a moment I thought...) or 'por momentos estuvo nublado' (at times it was cloudy). Tone is neutral and it's frequent in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Por momentos pensé que había perdido mi billetera.
native_language_example: For a moment I thought I had lost my wallet.

meaning: 'for many' / 'because of many' (used before a noun to indicate 'by/through/for many [things/people/reasons]').
additional_notes: Used with a following plural noun (e.g., 'por muchas razones', 'por muchas dificultades', 'por muchas criaturas'). Can mean 'because of many' (giving a cause/reason) or 'by/through many' (indicating being known/experienced by many). The exact translation depends on the verb and context.
target_language_example: He cambiado por muchas experiencias a lo largo de los años.
native_language_example: I've changed because of many experiences over the years.

meaning: even if (used with quantities or intensity) / no matter how much
additional_notes: Often appears in phrases like "por mucho que..." meaning "no matter how much/however much..." It introduces a concession: something happens or is true despite a large amount or effort. Alone, "por mucho" can precede a noun (e.g., "por mucho dinero") to mean "for a lot of.../despite a lot of..." Common structures: "por mucho que + subjunctive" (contrasting hypothetical or general statements) and "por mucho + noun".
target_language_example: Por mucho que estudies, a veces los exámenes son difíciles.
native_language_example: No matter how much you study, sometimes exams are difficult.

meaning: no matter how / however much (introduces a contrast: despite trying or despite something happening)
additional_notes: Used to introduce a concession: it emphasizes that even with effort or to whatever extent, the result is (usually) negative or unchanged. Followed by a verb in indicative or subjunctive depending on nuance; in many beginner contexts present indicative or past tense appears. Common in spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: Por mucho que lo intente, no puedo resolver este problema.
native_language_example: No matter how much I try, I can't solve this problem.

meaning: by/for a long time; 'no matter how' when followed by que + clause; or 'not by much' in short phrases (context-dependent).
additional_notes:
Two common uses:
- As part of 'por mucho que + [subjunctive clause]' it means 'no matter how' or 'however much' (e.g., Por mucho que lo intentó... = However much he tried...).
- In other contexts it can mean 'for/by a long time' (less common) or appear in short responses like 'Ni por mucho' / 'No por mucho' to mean 'not by much' or 'not much (at all)' depending on tone. Context determines meaning; when followed by que it needs the subjunctive in the clause that follows.
target_language_example: Por mucho que practiques, mejorarás si sigues intentándolo.
native_language_example: No matter how much you practice, you'll improve if you keep trying.

meaning: used to introduce a contrast meaning 'no matter how' or 'however much'.
additional_notes: Often appears in fixed phrases like 'por más que' + subjunctive/indicative (e.g., 'Por más que lo intento...') to say that despite trying or no matter how much something happens, the result doesn't change. Can be followed by a verb, noun, or clause. Use 'por mucho que' as a close alternative.
target_language_example: Por más que estudio, no entiendo este tema.
native_language_example: No matter how much I study, I don't understand this topic.

meaning: for more than; indicating a duration or amount that exceeds a number or period.
additional_notes: Commonly used before time expressions or quantities (un mes, una hora, treinta años). Equivalent to 'for over' or 'for more than' in English. Use 'por más de' with durations or numeric amounts. Can be followed by a number + noun or a clause.
target_language_example: Vivió en esa ciudad por más de diez años.
native_language_example: He lived in that city for more than ten years.

meaning: for me
additional_notes: Used to ask someone to do something as a favor or to indicate doing something on one's behalf or for one's benefit. Can also express indifference in contexts like “por mí, como quieras” (for all I care / suit yourself).
target_language_example: Haz esto por mí, por favor.
native_language_example: Do this for me, please.

meaning: for nothing / over nothing / about nothing (depends on context)
additional_notes: Common phrase with different meanings depending on context: 1) 'for nothing' meaning with little or no cost (e.g., vender/comprar por nada). 2) 'for no reason' or 'over nothing' to say someone gets upset easily. 3) in negative constructions it can mean 'about nothing' or 'not need to worry about anything' (e.g., no necesitas preocuparte por nada). Choose sense from surrounding words.
target_language_example: Se enfadó por nada y luego pidió perdón.
native_language_example: He got upset over nothing and then apologized.

meaning: part of the phrase 'por nada del mundo' meaning 'for nothing in the world' (i.e. 'under no circumstances').
additional_notes: Alone 'por nada del' is incomplete — it's normally followed by 'mundo' to form 'por nada del mundo'. Used to emphasize a strong negative: 'I would never...' or 'under no circumstances'. Can be used in spoken and written Spanish. Example variants: 'por nada del mundo', 'por nada del planeta' (less common).
target_language_example: Por nada del mundo iría sola a esa zona de noche.
native_language_example: I would never go alone to that area at night.

meaning: "not for anything in the world" — used to say you would never do something or must not do something under any circumstances.
additional_notes: Strong, emphatic negative expression. Often used with verbs in negative commands or statements (No lo haría por nada del mundo / No lo hagas por nada del mundo). Can stand alone as a short reply meaning 'no way' or 'absolutely not.'
target_language_example: No viajaría sola por nada del mundo.
native_language_example: I wouldn't travel alone for anything in the world.

meaning: by nobody / for nobody / because of nobody (depends on context).
additional_notes: Por nadie is a short phrase combining the preposition por with nadie (nobody). It often appears in negative constructions: e.g., 'no... por nadie' or 'por nadie + verb' to emphasize that no one does or causes something. Exact translation depends on context: 'by nobody' (agent), 'for nobody' (benefit), or 'because of nobody' (cause).
target_language_example: No cambiaría mi opinión por nadie.
native_language_example: I wouldn't change my opinion for anyone.

meaning: nowhere; not anywhere.
additional_notes: Used to say that someone or something is not to be found in any place or that something doesn't appear anywhere. Common in negative sentences. Equivalent to 'en ningún lado' / 'en ningún lugar'.
target_language_example: Busqué por toda la casa, pero no lo encontré por ningún lado.
native_language_example: I searched the whole house, but I couldn't find it anywhere.

meaning: 'for not' / introduces a reason tied to something not happening (often part of a longer phrase).
additional_notes: Por no is not a standalone fixed idiom in Spanish; it often appears as part of expressions explaining why something didn't happen or to mean 'because of not' before an action or state (e.g., por no + infinitive / por no haber + past participle). In many cases Spanish speakers prefer other constructions (porque no, por no haber, por no decir). Pay attention to context—sometimes you'd use porque/no because to answer 'why'.
target_language_example: Por no avisarme, llegué tarde a la reunión.
native_language_example: Because they didn't warn me, I arrived late to the meeting.

meaning: by the work of; through the action of (used to indicate who/what caused something)
additional_notes: Formal or literary phrase used to state the agent or cause of an event or result. Often followed by a person, group, or force (e.g., 'por obra de Juan', 'por obra de la casualidad'). Can be replaced in everyday speech by 'por' or 'gracias a' depending on context. Common in written, historical, or formal contexts.
target_language_example: La ciudad fue restaurada por obra de un comité local.
native_language_example: The city was restored by the work of a local committee.

meaning: per eye; for each eye (used when counting or pricing by eye)
additional_notes: Literally means 'per eye.' Used in contexts like medical billing, pricing for items sold/treated per eye, or describing measurements/amounts applied to each eye. Not a common idiom outside these literal uses. If used figuratively, clarify context.
target_language_example: El tratamiento cuesta 50 euros por ojo.
native_language_example: The treatment costs 50 euros per eye.

meaning: on the other hand / furthermore
additional_notes: Used to introduce a contrasting point or an additional remark. Commonly placed at the start or middle of a sentence and often followed by a comma. Similar to 'por otro lado' and 'en cambio'.
target_language_example: Me gusta el trabajo; por otra parte, necesito más tiempo libre.
native_language_example: I like the job; on the other hand, I need more free time.

meaning: 'because of' / 'for another' / 'by another' depending on context; often part of phrases meaning 'for another [thing/person/way]'.
additional_notes: This phrase is not a fixed expression by itself; its meaning depends on the words that follow. Common uses: "por otro camino" = 'by/through another path' or 'via a different route'; "por otro hombre" = 'for/by another man' (e.g., left someone for another man); "por otro nombre" = 'by another name' (known by a different name). "Por" can indicate cause, reason, means, or agent. Use the following noun to determine the exact translation.
target_language_example: Se mudaron por otro trabajo.
native_language_example: They moved for another job.

meaning: on the other hand; alternatively; in another place (literal).
additional_notes: Commonly used to introduce a contrasting idea (like 'on the other hand'). Can also be literal when talking about a different location ('pasea por otro lado' = 'walk somewhere else'). Often paired with 'por un lado' to present two sides.
target_language_example: Por otro lado, creo que deberíamos esperar.
native_language_example: On the other hand, I think we should wait.

meaning: by word; verbally; by spoken agreement
additional_notes: Used to indicate something done or agreed upon by spoken words rather than in writing. Common in contexts like 'dar por palabra' (to take someone's word) or 'quedaron por palabra' (they agreed verbally). Not very formal — for legal or official matters, written confirmation is preferred.
target_language_example: No hay contrato escrito; lo acepté por palabra.
native_language_example: There is no written contract; I accepted it verbally (on the word).

meaning: by (someone); on the part of; from the side of.
additional_notes: Used to indicate who performed an action, who holds an attitude, or the source/side responsible. Common in formal and neutral contexts: 'por parte de + pronoun/noun'. Can also mean 'from the family of' in kinship phrases (e.g., 'por parte de padre').
target_language_example: Fue un error por parte de la empresa.
native_language_example: It was a mistake on the part of the company.

meaning: in parts; piece by piece; step by step.
additional_notes: Used to say something is done or explained in separate pieces or stages. Common in instructions or when describing something broken into sections. Can be used like 'hacer algo por partes' (to do something in parts) or 'explicar por partes' (explain in parts).
target_language_example: Vamos a resolver el problema por partes.
native_language_example: Let's solve the problem in parts / step by step.

meaning: by step; per step (literal) — not a common fixed phrase in Spanish
additional_notes: This combination is unusual in Spanish as a standalone phrase. If intended literally, it would mean 'for each step' or 'by step' (e.g., describing movement or a process step by step) but native speakers usually say paso a paso, por cada paso, por paso/a paso, or por etapas. Check context: it may be a typo or mistranslation. Use 'paso a paso' for 'step by step' and 'por cada paso' for 'for each step.'
target_language_example: Avanzamos paso a paso, no por paso.
native_language_example: We move forward step by step, not 'por paso.'

meaning: for losing; because of losing; to lose (depending on context)
additional_notes: Por perder is a phrase built from the preposition por + the infinitive perder. It can indicate a reason ('because of losing'), an aim or consequence ('to lose' — often after verbs like 'arriesgarse por perder' is uncommon), or appear in fixed expressions like 'no hay por perder' (nothing to lose). Context matters: more natural constructions for 'in order to lose' use 'para perder'.
target_language_example: No tenemos nada por perder si lo intentamos.
native_language_example: We have nothing to lose if we try.

meaning: almost; nearly (used to say something almost happened, often with a negative result)
additional_notes: Common adverbial phrase. Often followed by verbs in simple past or preterite (cometí, no lo logramos) or used before clauses like "por poco + verb". Can appear as "por poco + no + verb" to emphasize that something almost didn't happen (e.g., "Por poco no lo logramos" = We almost didn't make it). Tone can be dramatic; used in both spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: Por poco pierdo el tren esta mañana.
native_language_example: I almost missed the train this morning.

meaning: for the first (time) — used before words like vez, vez en la vida, ocasión.
additional_notes: Usually appears as part of the phrase 'por primera vez' (for the first time). It precedes a noun or phrase indicating an initial occurrence. Can be followed by 'vez', 'ocasión' or a verb phrase (often with 'que' + clause).
target_language_example: Por primera vez, viajé solo al extranjero.
native_language_example: For the first time, I traveled abroad alone.

meaning: for the first time
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something happened at the initial occurrence. Common with verbs of action (fui, montó, conocí). Can appear anywhere in the sentence but often follows the verb or phrase it modifies. Not formal/slang.
target_language_example: Hoy voy a probar sushi por primera vez.
native_language_example: Today I'm going to try sushi for the first time.

meaning: for the first time in my (life / experience); used to introduce something happening to the speaker for the first time
additional_notes: This is a partial phrase that normally continues with a noun like "vida", "memoria" or "recuerdo" (e.g. "por primera vez en mi vida"). It emphasizes that the event or feeling is novel for the speaker. Can be followed by a verb phrase describing what happened.
target_language_example: Por primera vez en mi vida, viajé solo a otro país.
native_language_example: For the first time in my life, I traveled alone to another country.

meaning: through/by (the) doors; via doorways
additional_notes: A literal prepositional phrase used to indicate movement or passage through doors or entrances. In natural Spanish it's more common to include an article or determiner (por la puerta, por las puertas, por una puerta), but por puertas can appear in contexts emphasizing 'through doors' in general rather than specific ones (e.g., describing multiple exits or a pattern). Word order and articles may vary.
target_language_example: Pasaron por puertas para evitar el pasillo principal.
native_language_example: They went through doors to avoid the main hallway.

meaning: 'why' (por qué) or 'for which/that' (por que).
additional_notes: Written as two words with an accent (por qué) it is the question word 'why' used in direct and indirect questions: ¿Por qué...? Without an accent (por que) it appears when 'por' and the relative pronoun 'que' appear together (por que = 'for which', 'because of which', 'so that' depending on context) or in some fixed constructions. Do not confuse with 'porque' (one word, no accent), which means 'because'.
target_language_example: La razón por que no viniste todavía no está clara.
native_language_example: The reason for which you didn't come yet is not clear.

meaning: why
additional_notes: Used in direct and indirect questions to ask for the reason. It is written as two words with an accent on qué when it means "why" (compare porque = "because"). It can also appear inside expressions like no tener por qué, meaning there is no reason to or no need to.
target_language_example: No entiendo por qué estás enojado.
native_language_example: I don't understand why you're angry.

meaning: 'to know' in the sense of wanting or being eager to know; part of the phrase 'tener curiosidad por saber' meaning 'to be curious to know'.
additional_notes: Not a fixed standalone verb; usually appears after expressions of interest/curiosity/need (e.g., 'tener curiosidad por saber', 'estaban impacientes por saber'). It introduces the information someone wants to know (what, who, why, etc.). In some contexts 'por saber' can be part of shorter phrases (e.g., 'por saber persuadir' = 'to be good at persuading' or 'for knowing how to persuade'), but for beginners focus on its common use with curiosity/impatience.
target_language_example: Tengo ganas de saberlo; estoy curioso por saber la verdad.
native_language_example: I really want to know it; I'm curious to know the truth.

meaning: separately; apart; individually.
additional_notes: Used to say that people or things are not together or are handled individually. Common with actions (arrive, pay) and with items sold individually. Can appear before or after verbs depending on sentence. Informal/neutral everyday phrase.
target_language_example: Prefiero que las cuentas se paguen por separado.
native_language_example: I prefer the bills to be paid separately.

meaning: 'in case' (to express a precaution or possibility).
additional_notes: Use 'por si' before a clause or phrase that states a possible situation you want to prepare for. Often followed by a verb in indicative or subjunctive depending on speaker's view of likelihood (both are common in speech). Common in everyday Spanish to express precaution: 'por si hace frío, trae una chaqueta.'
target_language_example: Voy a dejar las luces encendidas por si vuelves tarde.
native_language_example: I'll leave the lights on in case you come back late.

meaning: just in case; in case something happens
additional_notes: Used to express precaution or preparation for a possible (but not certain) event. Can appear at start, middle, or end of a sentence. Often followed by a clause or an action (e.g., llevar, poner, llamar). Common in everyday speech and polite instructions.
target_language_example: Voy a llevar un paraguas por si acaso.
native_language_example: I'll take an umbrella just in case.

meaning: just in case it rains / in case it rains
additional_notes: Used to express doing something as a precaution against the possibility of rain. Often follows verbs like 'llevar', 'poner', 'traer', 'cerrar', or stands alone after a noun phrase (e.g., 'lleva un paraguas por si llueve'). Can be shortened to 'por si' when context makes 'llueve' clear (e.g., 'Lleva un paraguas, por si').
target_language_example: Voy a llevar un impermeable por si llueve.
native_language_example: I'm going to bring a raincoat just in case it rains.

meaning: forever; for all time.
additional_notes: Used to say something lasts indefinitely or eternally. Common in both serious (emotions, memories) and playful contexts (songs, slogans). Can be replaced by 'para siempre' — both are correct and largely interchangeable, though 'para siempre' is slightly more common in some regions.
target_language_example: Te querré por siempre.
native_language_example: I will love you forever.

meaning: 'on one's own', 'by oneself', or 'independently'.
additional_notes: Used to say someone does something alone, independently, or without help. Can refer to living alone, working independently (self-employed), or acting on one's own initiative. Context determines nuance: 'por su cuenta' = alone/independently; 'por su cuenta y riesgo' adds 'at one's own risk'.
target_language_example: Ahora vive por su cuenta y paga sus propias facturas.
native_language_example: Now he lives on his own and pays his own bills.

meaning: luckily; fortunately.
additional_notes: Used to say that something good happened or that luck was on someone's side. Often placed at the start of the sentence but can appear elsewhere. Tone is neutral and common in spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: Por suerte encontré mi teléfono perdido.
native_language_example: Luckily I found my lost phone.

meaning: of course
additional_notes: A very common fixed phrase used to show clear agreement, certainty, or that something is obvious or expected. It can be used on its own as a reply or inserted into a sentence.
target_language_example: —¿Puedo ayudarte? —Por supuesto.
native_language_example: —Can I help you? —Of course.

meaning: by oneself; on its own; alone (without help or intervention).
additional_notes: Used to indicate that a person or thing acts without assistance or that something happens naturally/automatically. Gender and number can vary in related phrases (e.g., "por sí mismo/a", "por sí solos/as"). Modern Spanish typically writes "solo" without an accent. Context determines whether it emphasizes lack of help, spontaneity, or occurrence without external causes.
target_language_example: El gato se subió al techo de mi casa por sí solo.
native_language_example: The cat climbed onto my house roof by itself.

meaning: by oneself; on one's own; by itself (referring to a thing or person acting without help).
additional_notes: Used to indicate that someone or something does something without help from others. Agrees in gender/number when used as a pronoun phrase (por sí mismo, por sí misma, por sí mismos, por sí mismas). Can refer to a person deciding/learning alone or to a thing that reveals something 'by itself'.
target_language_example: Aprendió a cocinar por sí mismo.
native_language_example: He learned to cook by himself.

meaning: therefore / consequently
additional_notes: A linking phrase used to draw a conclusion or indicate a result from what was just said. It is slightly formal but common in both spoken and written Spanish. Can appear at the start or middle of a sentence and is interchangeable with 'por lo tanto' or 'por consiguiente'.
target_language_example: No había pruebas; por tanto, decidieron cerrar el caso.
native_language_example: There was no evidence; therefore, they decided to close the case.

meaning: everywhere; all over the place.
additional_notes: Used to say something is present or happening in many places or throughout an area. Common in spoken and written Spanish. Can describe people, objects, noises, smells, rumors, etc. Synonyms: 'por todas partes' ≈ 'en todas partes' or 'por doquier'.
target_language_example: Había basura por todas partes después de la fiesta.
native_language_example: There was trash everywhere after the party.

meaning: for everything
additional_notes: Commonly used to thank someone (gracias por todo = thanks for everything) or to apologize/express responsibility (perdóname por todo = forgive me for everything). Can also mean 'about everything' or 'over every little thing' in contexts like "te preocupas por todo" (you worry about everything). In contexts like "él pagará por todo" it means 'pay for everything' (cover the costs).
target_language_example: Gracias por todo lo que has hecho.
native_language_example: Thanks for everything you've done.

meaning: for all that; because of everything (used before a masculine abstract noun or clause)
additional_notes: Used in phrases like 'por todo lo anterior' (because of all the above) or 'por todo lo dicho' (for all that has been said). Typically followed by an abstract noun or a past participle (lo dicho, lo anterior) or a clause introduced by que. Common in formal/written Spanish to summarize reasons or consequences.
target_language_example: Por todo lo dicho, tomaremos una decisión mañana.
native_language_example: For all that has been said, we will make a decision tomorrow.

meaning: for everything you have (done).
additional_notes: Common part of the phrase 'por todo lo que has hecho' used to thank someone for actions or help. Often followed by a past participle (hecho). Can be used with 'por mí', 'por nosotros' to specify the beneficiary. Formality: neutral; polite and common in spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: Gracias por todo lo que has hecho por mí.
native_language_example: Thank you for everything you have done for me.

meaning: everywhere; all over; everywhere around.
additional_notes: Used to say something or someone is in many places or all around a place. Common in everyday speech. Can be followed by a person or thing (Busqué a Tom por todos lados) or a noun (Hay agua por todos lados).
target_language_example: Encontré mis llaves por todos lados, hasta debajo del sofá.
native_language_example: I looked for my keys everywhere, even under the sofa.

meaning: by all means; using every possible way or effort
additional_notes: Used to say someone will do something using every available method or that something should be done at all costs. Can also be a short exclamation meaning "absolutely" or "certainly" (e.g., agreeing with a suggestion). Context usually indicates whether it's about effort or strong agreement.
target_language_example: Debes conseguir el billete por todos los medios.
native_language_example: You must get the ticket by all means / at any cost.

meaning: by everyone in / for all in (depending on context) — indicates something done or felt by all people within a group or place.
additional_notes: This phrase is not a fixed idiom; it combines the preposition por (by/for) + todos (everyone/all) + en (in/at). Meaning depends on context and word order. Common patterns: 'por todos' = by everyone or throughout; 'por todos en + lugar' can mean 'by everyone in [place]'. Be careful: native speakers often use 'entre todos' (among everyone) or 'por todos lados' (everywhere) instead. Use when you want to say an action or feeling involves all people in a specific location or group.
target_language_example: La decisión fue tomada por todos en la oficina.
native_language_example: The decision was made by everyone in the office.

meaning: because of work; for work reasons; due to work
additional_notes: Used to explain a motive or cause related to work. Often appears in phrases like 'por trabajo tuve que...' (because of work I had to...) or 'estoy aquí por trabajo' (I'm here for work). Can be followed by verbs, clauses, or nouns describing the work-related reason or purpose.
target_language_example: Vine a la ciudad por trabajo y volveré el lunes.
native_language_example: I came to the city for work and I'll return on Monday.

meaning: for your own (use) / by yourself (feminine/neuter agreement depends on noun that follows)
additional_notes: Por tu propio is not a complete phrase by itself; it's part of longer expressions like 'por tu propio bien' (for your own good) or 'por tu propio riesgo' (at your own risk). 'Propio' must agree in gender and number with the noun that follows: tu propio libro (m. sing.), tu propia decisión (f. sing.), tus propios errores (pl.). When referring to the person doing something alone, Spanish more commonly uses 'por ti mismo/a' (masc./fem.) rather than 'por tu propio'.
target_language_example: Lo hago por tu propio bien.
native_language_example: I do it for your own good.

meaning: on one hand; from one point of view
additional_notes: Used to introduce one side of a contrast or argument, often paired with 'por otro lado' or 'por el otro' to present the opposite side. Common in spoken and written Spanish to compare two perspectives or reasons.
target_language_example: Por un lado quiero viajar, pero por otro lado necesito ahorrar dinero.
native_language_example: On one hand I want to travel, but on the other hand I need to save money.

meaning: for a short time; for a little (while) / by a small amount (context-dependent).
additional_notes: Most commonly used to mean 'for a short time' or 'for a little while' (por un rato is more common). Can also mean 'by a little' when describing small differences (similar to 'by a bit'). Usage depends on context — native speakers often prefer alternatives like 'por un rato', 'por poco' (which has different meanings), or 'un poco'.
target_language_example: Me quedé en la cafetería por un poco antes de ir a clase.
native_language_example: I stayed in the café for a little while before going to class.

meaning: for a cup (of)... — used to express wanting, exchanging, or going to get a cup (usually of a beverage).
additional_notes: Commonly appears with drinks (e.g., café). Can mean: 1) desire/regret ('I'd give my left arm for a cup of decent coffee' = I'd really want one), 2) to go get something ('Voy por una taza de café' = I'm going to get one), or 3) in exchange ('te lo doy por una taza de arroz' = I give it to you in exchange for a cup of rice). Context determines whether it's desire, movement to fetch, or an exchange.
target_language_example: Voy por una taza de té, ¿quieres una?
native_language_example: I'm going to get a cup of tea, do you want one?

meaning: for once; at least this one time
additional_notes: Used to express that something happens (or should happen) at least this one time, often with impatience, surprise, or criticism. Common in commands or comments to urge someone to do something differently than usual.
target_language_example: Por una vez, haz caso a mi consejo.
native_language_example: For once, listen to my advice.

meaning: for one
additional_notes: A context-dependent phrase meaning literally 'for one' or 'per one.' It often appears after another number in offers or prices, especially in expressions like dos por uno ('two for one'). On its own, it can sound incomplete without more context.
target_language_example: Hoy hay una oferta de dos por uno en el cine.
native_language_example: Today there's a two-for-one deal at the movie theater.

meaning: 'to be yet to be seen' / 'to be eager to see' (depends on context).
additional_notes: Two main uses: 1) impersonal expression meaning 'it remains to be seen' or 'that's yet to be seen' (e.g., Eso está por ver; Queda por ver quién gana). 2) with a person, 'morir/estar por ver' or 'tener curiosidad por ver' expresses desire or eagerness to see something (e.g., me muero por ver, tenía curiosidad por ver). Context determines whether it's about uncertainty (future outcome) or wanting to see something now/soon.
target_language_example: Queda por ver si el proyecto funcionará.
native_language_example: It remains to be seen whether the project will work.

meaning: per time; at a time (used in expressions like 'a veces' or 'una por vez').
additional_notes: Alone 'por vez' is seldom used by itself; it appears in phrases such as 'una por vez' (one at a time), 'cada vez' (each time), or 'por vez primera' (for the first time). It indicates repetition or counting of occurrences — how many or how often something happens or is done at once.
target_language_example: Toma los platos una por vez para no romper ninguno.
native_language_example: Take the plates one at a time so you don't break any.

meaning: for life; for a lifetime
additional_notes: Used to indicate something lasts the whole life of a person or thing (e.g., a sentence, a membership, a commitment). Often appears in phrases like 'condenado por vida' (sentenced for life) or 'miembro por vida' (lifetime member).
target_language_example: Le ofrecieron una beca por vida.
native_language_example: They offered him a scholarship for life.

meaning: for living; to live (used after verbs or expressions to indicate reason, purpose, or something remaining to be lived)
additional_notes: Used after verbs or expressions to indicate purpose, cause, desire, or remaining time to be lived. Context determines nuance: can mean 'because of living' (e.g., 'pagar por vivir' = pay to live), 'yearning to live' (e.g., 'deseo por vivir' = desire to live), or 'a day/month/year to live' (e.g., 'otro día por vivir' = another day to live). Common with verbs like pagar por, impaciente por, deseo por, and expressions about time left.
target_language_example: Estoy impaciente por vivir esta nueva experiencia.
native_language_example: I'm eager to live this new experience.

meaning: for coming back; because of returning; in order to return (depends on context).
additional_notes: This short phrase combines the preposition por with the infinitive volver. Its exact meaning depends on context: it can indicate a reason ('because of returning' or 'for returning'), a purpose with a sense of intent ('in order to return'), or appear in fixed expressions (e.g., 'por volver a empezar' — 'to start again'). Pay attention to surrounding verbs and tense to determine whether it's causal, purposive, or part of a larger phrase.
target_language_example: Viajó por volver con su familia después de la mudanza.
native_language_example: He traveled to come back with his family after the move.

meaning: for the last time; one final time.
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something is being done or said for the final time (often as a warning or to close a topic). Common with verbs like pedir, preguntar, decir, intentar, hablar. Tone can be firm or final.
target_language_example: Te lo explico por última vez: sigue las instrucciones.
native_language_example: I'm explaining it to you for the last time: follow the instructions.

meaning: finally; lastly; in the end.
additional_notes: Used to introduce the final item in a list or the concluding point. Can mean 'finally' (after other things) or 'lastly' when giving examples or steps. Often appears at the start of a sentence or clause and is followed by a comma.
target_language_example: Por último, quiero agradecer a todos los que ayudaron.
native_language_example: Lastly, I want to thank everyone who helped.

meaning: because (conjunction) — used to give a reason; 'porque a' by itself is not a standard fixed phrase in Spanish
additional_notes: Standard Spanish uses 'porque' alone to mean 'because' (e.g., 'Lo hice porque quería'). 'Porque a' can appear when 'a' begins the following clause or phrase (e.g., 'porque a veces...' = 'because sometimes...') or in regional/colloquial speech as part of a longer expression. Do not treat 'porque a' as a single inseparable unit; learn 'porque' first and pay attention to the word that follows it.
target_language_example: No salí porque a esas horas ya llovía.
native_language_example: I didn't go out because it was already raining at that time.

meaning: 'because now' — gives a reason that starts with a change or new situation now
additional_notes: Combines 'porque' (because) + 'ahora' (now). Used to explain a reason that is tied to the present moment or a recent change (e.g., a new situation, new responsibility, or current feeling). It often appears at the start or middle of a sentence and is followed by the result or consequence.
target_language_example: Porque ahora trabajo más, puedo ahorrar dinero.
native_language_example: Because now I work more, I can save money.

meaning: because here / because it's here (gives a reason related to the current place or situation).
additional_notes: Combines 'porque' (because) with 'aquí' (here) to give a reason tied to the location or immediate context. Often part of a larger sentence (e.g., 'no podemos entrar porque aquí hace frío' — 'we can't go in because it's cold in here'). Usage is natural in spoken and written Spanish. Word order can vary depending on emphasis: 'porque aquí...' or 'aquí, porque...'.
target_language_example: No nos sentamos allí porque aquí hace demasiado calor.
native_language_example: We didn't sit there because it's too hot in here.

meaning: because I believe / because I think
additional_notes: Used to give a reason based on the speaker's belief or opinion. Often follows a clause: 'Lo digo porque creo que...' or stands alone after a statement: 'Es importante, porque creo…'. Can be followed by 'que' + clause when specifying the belief.
target_language_example: No deberíamos ir, porque creo que va a llover.
native_language_example: We shouldn't go, because I think it's going to rain.

meaning: because when; used to give a reason and introduce a circumstance or time.
additional_notes: Combines porque (because) + cuando (when). Often appears in spoken and written Spanish to explain why something happens and then describe the situation or timing. Can introduce a clause that explains cause and then a temporal or conditional detail: "porque cuando + [clause]...". Not idiomatic on its own — it depends on the following clause to complete the idea.
target_language_example: No voy a salir porque cuando llueve me enfermo.
native_language_example: I'm not going out because when it rains I get sick.

meaning: 'because the' (masculine singular).
additional_notes: Combines the conjunction porque (because) + the masculine singular definite article el. Used to give a reason and introduce a masculine singular noun or clause with a masculine subject: e.g., Porque el médico dijo que… In spoken Spanish you may also hear porque followed directly by a verb or clause (Porque llegó tarde). Ensure el is appropriate (masculine singular); for feminine use porque la, for plural porque los/las.
target_language_example: No fui a la fiesta porque el coche se averió.
native_language_example: I didn't go to the party because the car broke down.

meaning: 'because in' (used to introduce a reason followed by a place, time, situation, or context).
additional_notes: This is a combination of the conjunction 'porque' (because) + the preposition 'en' (in/on/at). It appears when the reason includes a location, time, context, or abstract situation: e.g. 'porque en la oficina...' = 'because in the office...'. Often followed by a clause or phrase that explains the context. Not a fixed idiom — just two words that occur together when 'because' needs 'in'.
target_language_example: No pude ir porque en la oficina había una reunión importante.
native_language_example: I couldn't go because there was an important meeting in the office.

meaning: because that / because of that (used colloquially to give a short justification or point to something/someone previously mentioned)
additional_notes: A colloquial combination: porque (because) + ese (that/he/that guy). Usage depends on context — it can mean 'because of that' or 'because that (person/thing)'. Often used in spoken Spanish to justify or explain briefly; tone can be emphatic. Not a fixed idiom in standard grammar but common in casual speech. Pay attention to what 'ese' refers to (a thing, person, or idea in prior sentence).
target_language_example: No voy a ayudarlo, porque ese nunca cumple su palabra.
native_language_example: I'm not going to help him, because that guy never keeps his word.

meaning: because that / because of that (gives a reason referring to something just mentioned)
additional_notes: Used to introduce a cause or explanation that refers back to a previous idea or statement. Often follows a clause and links the previous information to the reason. In spoken Spanish it can sound slightly redundant depending on context, but it's common and natural. Placement: can come after a clause (… , porque eso …) or start a sentence to continue an explanation.
target_language_example: No quiero ir, porque eso me haría sentir incómodo.
native_language_example: I don't want to go, because that would make me feel uncomfortable.

meaning: because that's what (someone/something) does/is/would do.
additional_notes: Used to introduce an explanation or justification followed by a clause with 'que' + verb or adjective (e.g., 'que hacen', 'que soy', 'que tiene que pasar'). It often appears in spoken and written Spanish to state a general truth, characteristic, or expected action. The phrase is incomplete on its own and is normally followed by 'que' + clause.
target_language_example: Me voy a ofrecer ayuda, porque eso es lo que hacen los buenos vecinos.
native_language_example: I'll offer to help, because that's what good neighbors do.

meaning: 'because this' — used to give a reason, often pointing to something just mentioned or about to be explained.
additional_notes: Literal combination of 'porque' (because) + 'esto' (this). Common in spoken and written Spanish when introducing a cause tied to a specific situation, statement, or fact. Often followed by a clause or explanation: 'porque esto...' + [explanation]. Can sound slightly informal or conversational depending on context; in more formal writing you might see 'porque' followed directly by a full clause without 'esto' or phrases like 'debido a esto'.
target_language_example: No salió al parque porque esto le causa alergia.
native_language_example: He didn't go to the park because this causes him allergies.

meaning: 'because I am' — gives a reason followed by a present‑progressive or state about the speaker.
additional_notes: Used to introduce the speaker's reason or explanation. Often followed by a verb in the present progressive (estoy + gerund) or an adjective/noun describing the speaker's state (estoy + adjective/noun). Common in everyday speech to explain actions, feelings, or situations.
target_language_example: No puedo salir esta noche porque estoy trabajando.
native_language_example: I can't go out tonight because I am working.

meaning: because you are / because you're (doing/feeling something).
additional_notes: Combines 'porque' (because) + 'estás' (you are, tú form of estar). Used to give a reason linked to the listener's current state, condition, or feeling. Context determines the rest of the clause (e.g., 'porque estás inquieto' = 'because you're restless'). Common in spoken and written Spanish. 'Estás' is informal singular (tú); use 'porque está' for formal/singular (usted) or 'porque están' for plural (ustedes).
target_language_example: No digas eso porque estás cansado.
native_language_example: Don't say that because you're tired.

meaning: because it/there is (used to give a reason about weather or someone's actions)
additional_notes: Porque introduces a reason ('because'). Hace + time/weather expression is a common impersonal construction meaning 'it is' or 'there is' (e.g., hace frío = it's cold; hace calor = it's hot; hace un rato = a little while ago). In some examples 'hace' refers to someone's action (he/she does). Context determines whether 'hace' is impersonal (weather/time) or from the verb hacer (to do).
target_language_example: No salimos porque hace mucho viento.
native_language_example: We didn't go out because it's very windy.

meaning: because it was (weather-related); introduces a reason using past weather conditions.
additional_notes: Combines 'porque' (because) with the imperfect of 'hacer' to describe ongoing or repeated past weather (e.g., hacía frío = it was cold). Used to give a reason in the past. Imperfect tense conveys background condition, not a single completed event.
target_language_example: No salimos porque hacía mucha lluvia toda la tarde.
native_language_example: We didn't go out because it was raining a lot all afternoon.

meaning: because there is / because there are
additional_notes: Common causal phrase: 'porque' gives the reason and 'hay' indicates existence (there is/are). Used to explain why something happens or a condition (e.g., porque hay mucho tráfico = because there is a lot of traffic). Can be followed by nouns with gender/number (mucho/mucha/muchos/muchas) or clauses.
target_language_example: Llegamos tarde porque hay mucho tráfico.
native_language_example: We arrived late because there is a lot of traffic.

meaning: because my
additional_notes: A combination of the conjunction 'porque' (because) followed by a possessive 'mi' (my). Used to give a reason that relates to something belonging to the speaker. It is not a fixed phrase on its own; you will usually see it as the start of a clause, e.g. 'porque mi casa está lejos' (because my house is far). Remember word order: 'porque' + subject/possessor + noun/verb phrase. If you need 'because I...' use 'porque yo...' or simply 'porque...' before a verb.
target_language_example: No puedo ir porque mi perro está enfermo.
native_language_example: I can't go because my dog is sick.

meaning: 'because I need' — gives a reason and refers to a present personal need
additional_notes: Used to introduce a reason for an action or feeling. Followed by an infinitive, noun, clause, or object. In spoken Spanish it can start a sentence (as in examples) to explain motivation; when used mid-sentence it connects cause and result. The subject 'yo' is implied in 'necesito'.
target_language_example: Te llamo ahora porque necesito confirmar la hora.
native_language_example: I'm calling you now because I need to confirm the time.

meaning: 'because we' or 'because us' (introduction to a reason involving 'nos' = 'we'/'us')
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase; it's the conjunction porque ('because') followed by the pronoun nos (direct/indirect object or reflexive for 'we/us' depending on verb). In most cases here it starts a clause meaning 'because we...' (porque + nos + verb) or 'because (it) affects us' (porque nos + [verb like quedamos, van a ...]). Use nos when the action involves 'us' as subject or object (e.g. nos sentábamos = we used to sit; nos quedamos = we ran out).
target_language_example: No fuimos al cine porque nos cansamos.
native_language_example: We didn't go to the movies because we got tired.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase in Spanish; usually a sequence where 'porque' ('because') is followed by 'por' ('for/by') due to hesitation, emphasis, or clause continuation rather than forming a single grammatical unit.
additional_notes: 'Porque por' is not a conventional expression. It can appear in spoken or informal written Spanish when a speaker starts to give a reason with 'porque' and then restarts or adds another prepositional phrase with 'por' (e.g., 'porque por...' or 'porque... por...'). Often one of the words is redundant or they belong to different clauses. Interpret context carefully: either the speaker is hesitating/clarifying, or there is an omitted or elliptical construction. Equivalent: check whether it should be 'porque' + clause or 'por' + noun phrase.
target_language_example: No salgas, porque por la lluvia no se puede ir en coche.
native_language_example: Don't go out, because due to the rain you can't drive by car.

meaning: 'because his/her/its' — the conjunction 'porque' (because) followed by the possessive adjective 'su' (his/her/its/their).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but two common words that often appear together: 'porque' introduces a reason, and 'su' marks possession. Together they start clauses like 'porque su casa...' (because his/her/your formal/their house...). Pay attention to context to determine who 'su' refers to (él, ella, usted, ellos).
target_language_example: No salió a la calle porque su perro estaba enfermo.
native_language_example: He didn't go out because his dog was sick.

meaning: just because; for no particular reason (often emphatic).
additional_notes: Used to say that there is no specific reason or to dismiss the need for an explanation. Can be neutral ('just because') or emphatic/defensive ('because I said so' / 'just because!'). Often appears alone as a short answer.
target_language_example: No quiero ir, simplemente porque sí.
native_language_example: I don't want to go, simply just because.

meaning: because I have (to)... / because I must...
additional_notes: Common phrase used to give a reason for an action or decision. Followed by an infinitive verb (tengo que + infinitive) to express obligation or necessity: 'because I have to ...'. Can also appear in explanations: 'porque tengo...' + noun/phrase. 'Porque' introduces the reason; 'tengo' is first-person singular of 'tener'.
target_language_example: No puedo salir porque tengo que estudiar para el examen.
native_language_example: I can't go out because I have to study for the exam.

meaning: because you
additional_notes: A causal phrase combining 'porque' (because) with the subject pronoun 'tú' (you). In Spanish, subject pronouns are often omitted because the verb form indicates the person; including 'tú' adds emphasis or clarity. When followed by a verb, the verb must be conjugated for 'tú' (e.g., 'porque tú quieres'). The written pronoun 'tú' carries an accent to distinguish it from the possessive 'tu'.
target_language_example: No vine porque tú no me invitaste.
native_language_example: I didn't come because you didn't invite me.

meaning: 'because a' (literal), used when explaining a reason that begins with 'a' + noun (e.g., 'porque un amigo...')
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but the combination of the conjunction 'porque' (because) followed by the indefinite article 'un' (a). It appears when giving a reason that starts with 'a' + masculine singular noun. In natural sentences you will usually see the full clause (e.g., 'Porque un amigo me ayudó' = 'Because a friend helped me'). Pay attention to gender/number: use 'una' for feminine nouns and 'unos/unas' for plurals.
target_language_example: No fui a la reunión porque un amigo necesitaba ayuda.
native_language_example: I didn't go to the meeting because a friend needed help.

meaning: 'because you' (formal).
additional_notes: Combines the causal conjunction 'porque' (because) with the formal second-person pronoun 'usted'. Used to give a reason that involves or attributes something to the person you're addressing respectfully. Word order is the same as in English: 'porque usted + verb/phrase'. Note that in many contexts Spanish speakers might omit 'usted' if it's clear from context or use 'tú' in informal situations.
target_language_example: Lo hice porque usted me lo pidió.
native_language_example: I did it because you (formal) asked me to.

meaning: because you go / because you're going
additional_notes: Combines the conjunction 'porque' (because) with the verb 'vas' (you go / you are going). Used to give a reason tied to the fact that someone goes or will go somewhere or does something. Context determines tense/aspect: 'vas' is present indicative of 'ir' for tú. Often appears in explanations like 'porque vas a...' (because you're going to...).
target_language_example: No vengas en coche porque vas a encontrar mucho tráfico.
native_language_example: Don't come by car because you're going to find a lot of traffic.

meaning: because he / because of him
additional_notes: Combines the conjunction 'porque' (because) with the subject pronoun 'él' (he). Used to give a reason that involves a male person. In Spanish, the subject pronoun is often omitted when the verb follows (e.g., 'porque llegó' = 'because he arrived'), so 'porque él' typically appears when followed by additional information, contrast, or emphasis (e.g., 'porque él dijo que...'). It can also appear at the end of a sentence as a clipped reason: 'No vino porque él.' (less common; sounds incomplete without context).
target_language_example: No fui a la reunión porque él no me avisó.
native_language_example: I didn't go to the meeting because he didn't tell me.

meaning: 'behaves well' (he/she/they behave(s) well).
additional_notes: From the reflexive verb portarse. Used to describe someone's behavior or manners (especially children). Commonly appears as 'se porta bien' (he/she behaves well). To say 'behave badly' use 'portarse mal'.
target_language_example: Mi sobrino se porta bien cuando hay visitas.
native_language_example: My nephew behaves well when there are visitors.

meaning: literally 'carried/behaved very' — used as part of constructions describing someone as having behaved very well; by itself it's not a standalone phrase.
additional_notes: 'Portado' is the past participle of the verb portarse (to behave). Native Spanish normally uses constructions like 'se portó muy bien' or 'ha estado portado muy bien' (the latter is uncommon). 'Portado muy' without the reflexive pronoun or auxiliary is incomplete; include 'se' and the correct tense: 'se portó muy bien' (he/she behaved very well) or 'se ha portado muy bien' (has behaved very well).
target_language_example: Se ha portado muy bien durante la visita; ha estado portado muy respetuoso.
native_language_example: He has behaved very well during the visit; he has been very respectful.

meaning: 'to behave well' or 'to behave oneself (well)'.
additional_notes: Used to describe someone acting politely, responsibly, or following rules (often said to children or about pets). Commonly reflexive: portarse (bien/mal). Opposite: portarse mal = 'to behave badly'. Can be used in present (se porta bien), past (se portó bien), or as an instruction (¡Pórtate bien!).
target_language_example: Tienes que portarse bien cuando estés en la escuela.
native_language_example: You have to behave yourself when you're at school.

meaning: possible with (something); indicates that something can be done thanks to or using a tool, resource, or condition.
additional_notes: Used after an adjective (posible) plus 'con' + a noun to say that an action or result is achievable because of that thing. Common in statements like 'Todo es posible con...' ('Everything is possible with...'). Can also appear in comparisons of degree (e.g., 'la máxima fuerza posible con...').
target_language_example: Todo es posible con una buena conexión a internet.
native_language_example: Everything is possible with a good internet connection.

meaning: 'possible to' or 'able to' (used to introduce an action or result that can happen), though this exact construction is nonstandard in neutral Spanish
additional_notes: This construction is not standard in neutral Spanish. More common equivalents are 'es posible + infinitive' (es posible llegar) or 'es posible que + subjunctive' (es posible que lleguemos). 'Posible de' can appear in some regional varieties or in colloquial/faulty calques (e.g., 'si es posible de conseguir'), but learners should generally avoid it. If you encounter it, consider rephrasing to the standard forms above.
target_language_example: Si es posible de conseguir entradas, avísame.
native_language_example: If it's possible to get tickets, let me know.

meaning: possible to; able to (do something).
additional_notes: Used before an infinitive or noun to say that something can be done or is feasible for someone/something. Often appears as '¿Es posible para mí...?' or 'posible para + noun' but more common constructions in Spanish use 'es posible (que)' or 'posible de' depending on region. For beginners, you can use 'posible para' to express 'possible for' someone or something, e.g. 'posible para ti' = 'possible for you'.
target_language_example: ¿Es posible para nosotros terminar hoy?
native_language_example: Is it possible for us to finish today?

meaning: might not / it's possible that ... not
additional_notes: Used to express doubt or possibility that something is not the case. Often appears with a verb in subjunctive (e.g., 'sea', 'quiera') or indicative depending on certainty; common in spoken and written Spanish. Can be part of fuller phrases like 'es posible que no...' or '¿cómo es posible que no...?'.
target_language_example: Es posible que no podamos ir mañana.
native_language_example: It's possible that we can't go tomorrow.

meaning: 'position on' or 'position in' — someone's stance, role, or physical placement related to something.
additional_notes: Used for both abstract meanings (a person's stance or opinion about a topic: 'posición en la cuestión') and concrete/physical meanings (a location or placement within/in relation to something: 'posición en la rampa'). Commonly followed by a noun (posición en X).
target_language_example: Mi posición en este proyecto es la de coordinador.
native_language_example: My position in/on this project is that of coordinator.

meaning: to postpone/delay (something feminine: la + noun).
additional_notes: Posponer means 'to postpone' or 'to put off.' 'La' is the feminine direct object/article (e.g., la reunión, la cita). You will often see the verb with an explicit object: posponer la reunión (to postpone the meeting). Conjugate posponer as needed (yo pospongo, él pospone).
target_language_example: Vamos a posponer la reunión hasta mañana.
native_language_example: We are going to postpone the meeting until tomorrow.

meaning: 'the price of' (followed by a masculine noun).
additional_notes: Used to talk about the cost or price of something. 'Del' is the contraction of 'de + el', so it appears before masculine singular nouns (el aceite, el arroz, el auto). For feminine nouns use 'de la' (el precio de la gasolina). Can refer to literal prices (goods, services) or figurative costs (e.g., 'el precio del pecado').
target_language_example: El precio del pan subió esta semana.
native_language_example: The price of bread went up this week.

meaning: literally 'price is' — the beginning of a sentence stating the price of something.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom; it's simply the phrase used when giving the cost of an item or service. In natural Spanish you'd usually include an article or subject (El precio es..., El precio de esto es..., El precio por persona es...) or say 'cuesta' (Cuesta 10€). Use 'precio es' to form statements like 'El precio es 20 euros.'
target_language_example: El precio es veinte euros.
native_language_example: The price is twenty euros.

meaning: 'precisely that' or 'exactly that' (used to emphasize or confirm a specific idea or object previously mentioned).
additional_notes: Formed from 'precisamente' (precisely/exactly) + 'lo' (neutral/masculine direct object pronoun meaning 'it' or 'that').
