additional_notes: Used after a noun or expression to introduce a clause describing something that will go, happen, or fit. In sentences it can mean 'that is going to happen' (que vaya a pasar), 'who will say' (que vaya a decirme) — though sentence 2 is ungrammatical and likely intended as 'Nadie que me vaya a decir esto' — or 'that goes to/with' when describing suitability (que vaya al aeropuerto / que vaya con este traje). Verb form may be 'vaya' (subjunctive) or part of 'ir a + infinitive' (vaya a + infinitive).
target_language_example: Busco una camisa que vaya con estos pantalones.
native_language_example: I'm looking for a shirt that goes with these pants.

meaning: to see
additional_notes: Often appears after a noun, as in "lugares/cosas que ver" = "places/things to see." In the common expression "tener algo/nada que ver (con)," it means "to have something/nothing to do (with)."
target_language_example: Hay mucho que ver en esta ciudad.
native_language_example: There's a lot to see in this city.

meaning: 'to do with' / 'to have to do with' — expresses relation or connection between things or people.
additional_notes: Used in negative or positive contexts to say something is related (tiene que ver con) or unrelated (no tiene nada que ver con). Common construction: (no) tener (nada) que ver con + noun/pronoun. In English: 'have something to do with' or simply 'be related to'.
target_language_example: Esto no tiene nada que ver con mi trabajo.
native_language_example: This has nothing to do with my job.

meaning: to do with him/it; related to him/it
additional_notes: Used after a noun, verb phrase, or clause to indicate a connection or relevance to a masculine singular person or masculine/neutral noun. Common in constructions like "no tiene que ver con él" (it has nothing to do with him/it). Note: the pronoun él has an accent; without the accent (el) it would be the article. Gender/number change the pronoun/article (p. ej. "que ver con ella", "que ver con ellos").
target_language_example: Eso no tiene nada que ver con el problema; tiene que ver con el sistema.
native_language_example: That has nothing to do with the problem; it has to do with the system.

meaning: that has to do with that / related to that
additional_notes: This phrase is a fragment used to say something is connected or relevant to a previously mentioned thing (ese = that). Often appears inside larger sentences, e.g. 'no tiene que ver con ese problema' (it has nothing to do with that problem). 'Ese' can be replaced by other demonstratives (esto, eso, aquella cosa) or a noun (esa decisión).
target_language_example: No creo que tenga que ver con ese accidente.
native_language_example: I don't think it has anything to do with that accident.

meaning: to do with this / to be related to this (often in negative: 'have nothing to do with this').
additional_notes: Commonly appears in the phrase 'nada que ver con este' or 'no tener nada que ver con este...', meaning 'to have no connection/relation to this'. Use with subjects: 'Yo no tengo...', 'Él no tiene...', or past forms 'no tuvo', 'no tenía'.
target_language_example: Yo no tengo nada que ver con este problema.
native_language_example: I have nothing to do with this problem.

meaning: to do with this / to have to do with this (often used in negative: 'nothing to do with this').
additional_notes: Used to say whether someone or something is related or involved in the matter. Commonly appears in phrases like 'no tiene nada que ver con esto' (has nothing to do with this). Can be used in questions or speculative sentences (e.g., 'tiene algo que ver con esto' = 'does it have something to do with this?').
target_language_example: No creo que eso tenga que ver con esto.
native_language_example: I don't think that has anything to do with this.

meaning: to do with me / to be related to me
additional_notes: Used to say that something is connected or relevant (or not) to the speaker. Often appears in negative constructions: 'no tiene nada que ver conmigo' = 'it has nothing to do with me.' Can be used literally (relation) or figuratively (responsibility, involvement).
target_language_example: Ese problema no tiene nada que ver conmigo.
native_language_example: That problem has nothing to do with me.

meaning: who came
additional_notes: Used in a relative clause after a noun to identify the person or thing that came. Here, que means "who/that," and vino is the preterite form of venir ("to come").
target_language_example: La mujer que vino esta mañana dejó un mensaje.
native_language_example: The woman who came this morning left a message.

meaning: 'that/who saw' or 'which/that he/she/it saw' (past tense of ver).
additional_notes: Combines the relative pronoun que ('that/who/which') with vio (preterite of ver: he/she/it saw). Used to link a noun to something it or someone saw. English equivalents depend on context: 'who saw,' 'that saw,' or 'that/which (he/she/it) saw.' Subject of vio is usually third person singular (él/ella/usted) or a named person (e.g., Tom).
target_language_example: Ella mostró las fotos que vio en el museo.
native_language_example: She showed the photos that she saw at the museum.

meaning: who lives at (a place) — used before a specific location
additional_notes: This is a fragment combining the relative pronoun 'que' (who/that) + the verb 'vive' (lives) + the preposition 'a' or contraction 'al' (at the/to the). It's used to describe a person who lives at a particular address or place: e.g. 'la mujer que vive al lado' (the woman who lives next door). Ensure the correct article: 'a' + 'el' = 'al'. Often followed by a location (calle, lado, número).
target_language_example: Conozco al vecino que vive al lado de mi casa.
native_language_example: I know the neighbor who lives next to my house.

meaning: that to live
additional_notes: The sequence 'que vivir' by itself is uncommon; it typically appears inside a larger clause (e.g., 'algo que vivir' or 'un lugar que vivir') where 'que' is a relative pronoun meaning 'that/which' and 'vivir' is the infinitive 'to live'. It often introduces a clause describing purpose or necessity ('para que vivir' = 'why live' or 'what's the point of living') or forms part of infinitive constructions after expressions like 'tener que vivir' (rare). Context is needed to choose the correct English rendering.
target_language_example: No hay nada que vivir si pierdes la esperanza.
native_language_example: There is nothing to live for if you lose hope.

meaning: that already
additional_notes: Que ya is a short linking phrase often used in spoken Spanish to add emphasis, explain, or introduce information that the speaker considers obvious or already known. It commonly appears in sentences like 'Es tarde, que ya nos vamos' (It's late, we're leaving now) or 'No te preocupes, que ya lo hice' (Don't worry, I already did it). Depending on context it can function similarly to 'that', 'since', or 'because' and is informal/spoken-register. Word order and punctuation vary; it frequently begins a clause after a comma.
target_language_example: No te preocupes, que ya lo terminé.
native_language_example: Don't worry, I already finished it.

meaning: "that I said" (emphatic way to refer to something you previously stated).
additional_notes: Used to point back to something the speaker said earlier. Adding yo emphasizes the speaker (contrast with others) or stresses that it was the speaker who said it. Common in statements like Eso es/ Eso fue lo que yo dije. Can be used with different tenses (fue, dije, dije antes) depending on context.
target_language_example: Eso es exactamente lo que yo dije ayer.
native_language_example: That's exactly what I said yesterday.

meaning: 'that I to him/her/it' — part of a clause; not a complete phrase on its own
additional_notes: This sequence combines the conjunction/relative pronoun 'que' + subject 'yo' + indirect object pronoun 'le'. It typically appears inside a larger sentence (e.g., 'dijo que yo le ayudara' or 'espero que yo le explique'). Alone it is incomplete and needs a verb or rest of clause. 'Le' can mean 'to him', 'to her', or the formal 'you' (usted), depending on context. Word order may change in spoken Spanish (e.g., 'que yo le' vs. 'que le yo' — the latter is uncommon).
target_language_example: Espero que yo le pueda ayudar mañana.
native_language_example: I hope that I can help him/her/you (formal) tomorrow.

meaning: that I (do) not / which I don't
additional_notes: A short phrase often used inside larger clauses to add a negative statement about the speaker (e.g., 'que yo no...'). It depends on context and usually follows another clause or verb: e.g., 'dijo que yo no sabía' = 'he said that I didn't know'. Alone it's incomplete — you need the rest of the sentence. In casual speech, 'que' can introduce reported speech, explanations, or relative clauses.
target_language_example: Ella piensa que yo no puedo ir, pero sí puedo.
native_language_example: She thinks that I can't go, but I can.

meaning: a short phrase often used to introduce a clause about what I (subject) do/feel for you or what I tell you (object).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom on its own but a common word sequence: que (that/which) + yo (I) + te (you, indirect or direct object). It appears in longer sentences like «que yo te diga…», «que yo te ayude…», «que yo te quiera…». Meaning depends on the verb that follows. Useful for forming clauses meaning 'that I (will) [verb] you' or 'that I [verb] to you'.
target_language_example: Que yo te ayude, no hay problema.
native_language_example: That I help you is not a problem.

meaning: that he
additional_notes: A compositional phrase made of que + él. Most often it means "that he" in a clause, as in reported speech or opinions. Because Spanish often drops subject pronouns, él is usually included for emphasis, contrast, or clarity. In comparisons, que él can also mean "than him/he." The accent in él is important: él = "he," while el = "the."
target_language_example: Creo que él no entiende la pregunta.
native_language_example: I think that he doesn't understand the question.

meaning: "what he says" (referring to the things he says).
additional_notes: Used to refer to the content of a man's speech or opinions. Commonly appears after words like 'lo', 'todo', 'en', or 'a' (e.g., 'lo que él dice', 'todo lo que él dice', 'en lo que él dice'). Can be used to agree, disagree, or comment on his statements.
target_language_example: No estoy de acuerdo con lo que él dice.
native_language_example: I don't agree with what he says.

meaning: 'what he says is' (used to introduce or report a statement about someone's words).
additional_notes: This phrase combines a relative clause (lo que = what/that which) + subject (él) + verb (dice) and a linking verb (es). It's used to report or evaluate what someone has said (e.g., true, false, correct). Often appears as 'lo que él dice es...' or shortened to 'lo que dice es...'.
target_language_example: Lo que él dice es importante para la decisión.
native_language_example: What he says is important for the decision.

meaning: that he was (doing/being)...
additional_notes: A short clause used to report or describe what a male person was doing, feeling, or where he was. Commonly appears after verbs or expressions that introduce reported information (e.g., dijo que él estaba..., pensé que él estaba...). In spoken Spanish the subject pronoun él is often omitted (dijo que estaba). Use context or an infinitive/gerund/adjective to complete the idea: 'que él estaba cansado', 'que él estaba trabajando', 'que él estaba en casa'.
target_language_example: Ella dijo que él estaba cansado después del viaje.
native_language_example: She said that he was tired after the trip.

meaning: 'that he did' or 'which he did'.
additional_notes: A relative clause or complement phrase used to refer back to an action performed by a male subject (él). Commonly follows a noun or idea: 'la tarea que él hizo' = 'the homework that he did.' In spoken Spanish the subject pronoun él is often omitted if context is clear: 'la tarea que hizo.'
target_language_example: La película que él hizo fue un éxito.
native_language_example: The movie that he made was a success.

meaning: that he wanted / which he wanted.
additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause referring to something desired by a male person (él). Common after verbs or nouns: e.g., 'la casa que él quería' = 'the house that he wanted' or 'dijo que él quería' = 'he said that he wanted'. If subject is feminine or plural, change pronoun accordingly (que ella quería, que ellos querían).
target_language_example: Compró el libro que él quería.
native_language_example: He bought the book that he wanted.

meaning: 'so, where' — a conversational phrase combining 'así que' (so/therefore) and '¿dónde?' (where?).
additional_notes: Used to start or continue a question or conversation: 'Así que, ¿dónde...?' can introduce a question about location, situation, or the next step. 'Así que' softens or links the question to previous context (means 'so'/'therefore'/'well then'). Common in spoken Spanish.
target_language_example: Así que, ¿dónde vamos ahora?
native_language_example: So, where are we going now?

meaning: 'that' (que) / 'what' (qué) — common connector and question word.
additional_notes: que (without an accent) is a very common conjunction meaning 'that', used to link clauses. qué (with an accent) is an interrogative pronoun/adverb meaning 'what' and appears in questions. In many spoken questions Spanish uses structures like '¿Qué es lo que...?' or '¿Qué haces?' Note word order and accent: que vs. qué changes the meaning.
target_language_example: Así que, ¿qué piensas hacer ahora?
native_language_example: So, what do you plan to do now?

meaning: May God bless you.
additional_notes: A common blessing or good wish used in Spanish-speaking cultures. Can be used formally or informally and added after expressions of good wishes (e.g., 'Buena suerte, que Dios te bendiga'). Often followed by a term of endearment (cariño, hermano, hijo). Tone can be sincere, affectionate, or traditional; not specifically religious in casual use.
target_language_example: Que Dios te bendiga, mamá.
native_language_example: May God bless you, Mom.

meaning: 'that to her' or 'than her' depending on context
additional_notes: This short sequence appears in different structures. As part of a clause with a verb (e.g., "dijo que a ella le importaba"), it functions like 'that to her' and often introduces what concerns or affects 'her' — frequently combined with verbs like 'importar', 'gustar', 'parecer'. In comparisons using 'más/menos ... que a ella' it means 'than her'. In everyday speech the preposition 'a' marks the indirect object (clarifier or emphasis) and is required with pronouns: 'le' + clarifier 'a ella'. The sequence can occur inside subordinate clauses or after comparative expressions; word order and presence of other pronouns determine exact meaning.
target_language_example: Dijo que a ella le molestaba ese ruido.
native_language_example: He said that that noise bothered her.

meaning: 'than the' (used in comparisons) or 'that to the' depending on context; commonly appears in comparative structures like 'más ... que a los ...' or after verbs expressing preference/fear (e.g. 'preferir ... a los ...').
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but a sequence of words that often appears in comparisons or with verbs that take an indirect object introduced by 'a' plus a plural masculine article 'los'. Depending on the sentence, 'que' can be the conjunction 'than' (in comparisons) or a relative/conjunction meaning 'that', while 'a los' marks 'to the' or 'toward the' (or simply the object of verbs like 'preferir', 'temer', etc.). Translate by considering the whole clause: e.g. 'prefiero a los hombres españoles que a los ingleses' = 'I prefer Spanish men to English men.'
target_language_example: Temo más a los perros que a los gatos.
native_language_example: I fear dogs more than cats.

meaning: as for me / regarding me / in my case
additional_notes: Used to introduce a personal perspective or to specify how something relates to the speaker. Often appears in colloquial speech as part of phrases like 'que a mí me parece...' or 'que a mí no me gusta'. The pronoun 'a mí' emphasizes that the statement applies to the speaker. Word order can vary (e.g. 'a mí me parece que...'). Informal register is common in spoken Spanish.
target_language_example: Que a mi no me convence esa idea.
native_language_example: As for me, that idea doesn't convince me.

meaning: A fragment used in negative contexts to reinforce negation; roughly 'that (to) nothing' or part of phrases meaning 'that ... not at all'. It is not a standalone idiom and usually appears with surrounding negatives.
additional_notes: This sequence is uncommon by itself and often results from combining 'que' with negative phrases containing 'a nada' (e.g., 'para nada' or 'sirva a nada' in some regional uses). More natural and frequent forms are 'que no', 'para nada', or 'no ... para nada'. Use caution: native speakers rarely say 'que a nada' in isolation; check surrounding grammar. The entry's translation can sometimes be rendered literally, but idiomatic equivalents are usually clearer.
target_language_example: No digo que a nada de lo que hice valga la pena.
native_language_example: I'm not saying that anything I did is worth it.

meaning: This sequence is not a fixed phrase in Spanish; taken literally it would be 'that to/than nothing in' and typically does not stand alone.
additional_notes: The words 'que', 'a', 'nada' and 'en' are common Spanish words but together 'que a nada en' is not a standard multiword expression. Possible sources of confusion: it could appear as part of a longer clause (e.g., 'que a nada en la vida...' — though that exact order is unlikely) or as a result of a typo or incorrect word order. Learn each component separately: 'que' (that/which/what), 'a' (to/at), 'nada' (nothing/not anything), 'en' (in/on). If you think you saw this phrase in a sentence, check surrounding words for correct order or intended meaning.
target_language_example: No uses 'que a nada en' como una frase fija; revisa el contexto.
native_language_example: Don't use 'que a nada en' as a fixed phrase; check the context.

meaning: that (to) nobody / than anyone (depending on context).
additional_notes: A short phrase used as part of larger clauses. Common uses: negative comparisons or restrictions (e.g., 'más que a nadie' = 'more than anyone'), or to emphasize exclusion (e.g., 'no le importa que a nadie...' though that specific ordering is uncommon). It normally appears inside a sentence; you won't use it alone. Pay attention to surrounding words and negatives: Spanish word order can differ from English.
target_language_example: Le quiero más que a nadie.
native_language_example: I love him/her more than anyone.

meaning: likely the sequence 'que a su' appears as part of a larger phrase (e.g. 'que a su vez') and by itself doesn't have a standalone meaning
additional_notes: This exact three-word string is incomplete in Spanish and usually appears as part of longer expressions. The closest common sequence is 'que a su vez' meaning 'which/that in turn'. If you see 'que a su' in writing, check the surrounding words — it's not a fixed phrase on its own.
target_language_example: La propuesta, que a su vez mejora el sistema, fue aprobada.
native_language_example: The proposal, which in turn improves the system, was approved.

meaning: that to everyone / which applies to everyone
additional_notes: Literal phrase made of que (that/which) + a todos (to everyone). Used to introduce a clause or comment referring to all people concerned. Common in constructions like «es algo que a todos nos importa» (it's something that matters to all of us) or «dijo algo que a todos sorprendió» (he said something that surprised everyone). Word order and pronouns may be added (e.g., «que a todos nos...», «que a todos les...») depending on the verb and emphasis.
target_language_example: Es una regla que a todos nos afecta por igual.
native_language_example: It's a rule that affects all of us equally.

meaning: that to him / which is for him (used to refer to something concerning or directed at a male person)
additional_notes: Combines the relative/conjunction 'que' (that/which) with the prepositional phrase 'a él' (to him / for him / about him). Used to link a clause or phrase to a specific male person. In spoken Spanish 'él' is often omitted when context makes the person clear: 'que a él' emphasizes or clarifies that it refers specifically to him.
target_language_example: Dijeron que a él le gustaba la música clásica.
native_language_example: They said that he liked classical music.

meaning: that (he/she/you formal) open(s) — present subjunctive used in subordinate clauses expressing requests, wishes, commands, or recommendations.
additional_notes: Used after verbs or expressions that request, ask, want, or order someone to do something (e.g., quiero que..., le pidió que...). 'Abra' is the present subjunctive form of abrir for él/ella/usted. In English it's often rendered 'that he/she/you open' or simply as an imperative depending on context.
target_language_example: Quiero que abra esta puerta ahora mismo.
native_language_example: I want him/her to open this door right now.

meaning: that (someone) open(ed) / that (someone) would open (imperfect-subjunctive clause).
additional_notes: Used after verbs of asking, telling, requesting, or similar to introduce a subordinate clause in the past or conditional context. 'Abriera' is the imperfect subjunctive of abrir. English often translates as 'that (someone) open' or 'that (someone) would open' / 'to open' depending on context: e.g. 'She asked (me/him) to open the window.'
target_language_example: Me pidió que abriera la ventana porque hacía calor.
native_language_example: She asked me to open the window because it was hot.

meaning: that (someone) open(ed) the… (subjunctive past/imperfect; used after verbs of request or asking).
additional_notes: Commonly appears after pedir (to ask/request) or pedir que. Uses the imperfect subjunctive (abrir → abriera) to report a request about a past or hypothetical action. The phrase is incomplete by itself — 'la' is a feminine singular noun (e.g., la ventana, la puerta). In English you'd say 'that (someone) open the…' or 'to open the…' depending on context.
target_language_example: Le pedí que abriera la puerta antes de salir.
native_language_example: I asked him/her to open the door before leaving.

meaning: likely part of a clause meaning 'that (to) open' or 'which to open' — not a standalone fixed phrase
additional_notes: ‘que abrir’ is not an independent phrase in Spanish. It appears when the conjunction/relative pronoun que is followed by an infinitive (abrir). Common contexts: after verbs or expressions that require a subordinate clause (e.g., 'tengo que abrir' = 'I have to open') or in relative constructions ('la puerta que abrirás' = 'the door that you will open'). For beginners: learn 'tengo que + infinitive' for obligations and relative clauses using que + verb for 'that/which'.
target_language_example: Tengo que abrir la ventana porque hace calor.
native_language_example: I have to open the window because it's hot.

meaning: that (you/we/they) must/will have to accept it.
additional_notes: This phrase combines the conjunction/relative 'que' with the verb phrase 'aceptarlo' (accept it). In the example sentences 'tener que aceptarlo' appears frequently and expresses obligation or necessity: 'have to accept it' or 'must accept it.' The subject and tense are shown by the conjugated 'tener' (tenemos que, tendrás que, tienes que, tuve que, teníamos que). 'Aceptarlo' = aceptar + lo (it).
target_language_example: Sé que no te gusta, pero tienes que aceptarlo.
native_language_example: I know you don't like it, but you have to accept it.

meaning: and also / which besides (adds information).
additional_notes: Used to add extra information or another point. Often appears in the middle of a sentence connecting clauses: '... que además ...' = '... and (it) also ...' or '... which, moreover, ...'. Tone is neutral and common in both spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: Es un buen restaurante, que además tiene precios razonables.
native_language_example: It's a good restaurant, and it also has reasonable prices.

meaning: to have to put up with; to tolerate (something or someone).
additional_notes: Commonly used to complain about an annoying or unpleasant situation or person. Often appears as part of a sentence like "¡Que (no) aguanto + noun/verb!" or with verbs: "Tengo que aguantar..." (I have to put up with...). In informal speech you may also hear just "aguantar" without "que."
target_language_example: Tengo que aguantar tanto ruido en mi edificio.
native_language_example: I have to put up with so much noise in my building.

meaning: 'which/that now is' or 'that is now' — indicates a present state or condition.
additional_notes: Used to point out a current situation or status that has changed or is relevant now. Often follows a clause introduced by 'que' (that/which) and is followed by a noun, adjective, or phrase describing the new state. Common in spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: Me contaron la historia, que ahora es parte de la tradición familiar.
native_language_example: They told me the story, which is now part of the family tradition.

meaning: there that / that over there (used in spoken Spanish to refer to something just mentioned or pointed out)
additional_notes: Informal, colloquial connector used in many Spanish varieties. Often appears in spoken phrases like 'es que ahí...' or 'digo que ahí...' to introduce or emphasize a point about a place, situation, or reason. Usage and exact sense depend on context — it can mean 'that is where,' 'because,' or simply add emphasis. Not standard in formal writing.
target_language_example: No vayas por esa calle; que ahí hay mucho tráfico.
native_language_example: Don't go down that street; because there is a lot of traffic there.

meaning: 'that' or 'which' + 'when' or 'to the' (depends on context); it's the sequence of 'que' followed by the contraction 'al' (a + el).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but the combination of the relative/conjunction 'que' and the contraction 'al' (a + el). Meaning depends on the sentence: often introduces a clause where 'que' links and 'al' starts a verb phrase (e.g. 'que al entrar...' = 'that when entering...') or a prepositional phrase (e.g. 'que al lado...' = 'that to the side...'). Pay attention to grammar: 'al' = 'a' + 'el' (to the) and is used before masculine singular nouns or infinitives to mean 'upon/when'.
target_language_example: Dijo que al llegar todos se sorprendieron.
native_language_example: He said that when everyone arrived, they were surprised.

meaning: 'that something' or 'that anything' (used after expressions to refer vaguely to an unspecified thing).
additional_notes: Que + algo is not a fixed idiom but a combination: que (that/which) + algo (something/anything). It often appears in clauses like 'es que algo...' or after verbs/adjectives to refer vaguely to an unspecified object or event. Context determines whether it means 'something' (positive) or 'anything' (in questions/negatives).
target_language_example: Dijo que algo cambió en el plan.
native_language_example: He said that something changed in the plan.

meaning: that something is (going) — used to introduce a thought or feeling that something is wrong or happening
additional_notes: Commonly appears after verbs like parecer, temer, presenciar/ presentir, sentir, creer, etc. In these examples it signals an intuition or observation that 'something is wrong' (algo va mal). The construction 'que + clause' introduces the content of the thought/feeling. You can swap 'va' for other verbs (pasa, funciona) to change meaning: e.g. 'que algo pasa' = that something is happening.
target_language_example: Creo que algo va a cambiar pronto.
native_language_example: I think that something is going to change soon.

meaning: that/such that some (used before a masculine singular noun or to introduce a clause with 'algún' meaning 'some' or 'any').
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but a sequence of words that can appear together in sentences (e.g., 'que algún problema...' or 'que algún día...'). 'Algún' is the shortened form of 'alguno' used before a masculine singular noun. Context determines exact translation: sometimes 'que' is a relative conjunction ('that') and 'algún' modifies a following noun ('some/any').
target_language_example: Espero que algún día vengas a visitarme.
native_language_example: I hope that some day you will come visit me.

meaning: that (some) day; expressing hope or expectation that something will happen in the future
additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause expressing a wish, hope or expectation about a future time. Often appears after verbs or expressions like 'espero', 'deseo', 'pienso', or in relative clauses: 'algo que algún día...' It is general and neutral in register.
target_language_example: Espero que algún día viajemos juntos.
native_language_example: I hope that someday we'll travel together.

meaning: "that/which there" or "that/which over there" (refers to something located in or mentioned as 'there')
additional_notes: Used to link a noun or idea to a location previously mentioned or implied. Often appears inside longer clauses (e.g., 'la casa que allí está' = 'the house that is there'). In everyday speech Spaniards might more commonly say 'que está allí' or simply 'allí' depending on context. The phrase alone is incomplete; it functions as a connector within a sentence.
target_language_example: La tienda que allí ves cierra a las ocho.
native_language_example: The shop that you see over there closes at eight.

meaning: 'that both' or 'that both of (them)'.
additional_notes: Used to introduce or refer to two people/things previously mentioned. Often appears in clauses like 'dije que ambos...' or 'es importante que ambos...'. In English it functions like 'that both' or 'both of them', and is followed by a verb or noun phrase. Not a fixed idiom—compositional from its parts.
target_language_example: Es importante que ambos estén de acuerdo.
native_language_example: It's important that both are in agreement.

meaning: that last night / which happened last night (depends on context).
additional_notes: 'que' can introduce a clause or add emphasis; combined with 'anoche' (last night) it refers to something that occurred the previous night. Often appears inside longer sentences, e.g. 'La noticia que anoche salió...' or in spoken corrections like 'Que anoche no dormí' (informal emphasis). Word order and punctuation determine exact meaning—it's not a fixed idiom but a sequence used to link 'that' + 'last night.'
target_language_example: La película que anoche vimos fue muy buena.
native_language_example: The movie that we watched last night was very good.

meaning: that/which barely, hardly, or just (scarcely).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause that emphasizes something happened only a little, just now, or almost not at all. Context determines whether it means 'barely/hardly' (e.g., negative or limited degree) or 'just' (recently). Common in spoken and written Spanish: e.g., 'que apenas' + verb. Not idiomatic; meaning is compositional from 'apenas' ('barely/just').
target_language_example: Llegó tarde, que apenas vimos la película.
native_language_example: He arrived late, so we barely saw the movie.

meaning: have to learn / must learn.
additional_notes: This is the combination of the modal expression 'tener que' (to have to) plus the infinitive 'aprender' (to learn). In a full sentence you'll usually see the conjugated form 'tienen que aprender', 'tengo que aprender', etc. It expresses obligation or necessity to learn something.
target_language_example: Tengo que aprender nuevas palabras todos los días.
native_language_example: I have to learn new words every day.

meaning: 'have to learn to be' or 'must learn to be'.
additional_notes: This phrase combines 'tener que' (to have to) + 'aprender a' (to learn to) + an adjective or noun that describes the desired state or behavior. It expresses obligation or necessity to acquire a quality, habit, or role (e.g., 'tener que aprender a ser más cuidadoso' = 'must learn to be more careful'). In natural Spanish you'd usually see the full verb 'tener' conjugated (tengo, tienes, tiene) before 'que aprender a ser'.
target_language_example: Ella tiene que aprender a ser más paciente con los niños.
native_language_example: She has to learn to be more patient with the children.

meaning: that here / which here (depends on context)
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase on its own; it's the conjunction/relative pronoun 'que' followed by the adverb 'aquí'. It can introduce a clause referring to something 'here' (e.g., 'la casa que aquí ves' = 'the house that you see here') or be used in colloquial expressions emphasizing location ('¿Qué, aquí?'' = 'What, here?'). Meaning and translation depend on the sentence.
target_language_example: La tienda que aquí vemos cierra a las ocho.
native_language_example: The shop that we see here closes at eight.

meaning: that here is / which here is (used to point out or identify something in this place)
additional_notes: A short phrase used in Spanish when introducing or identifying something immediately present or about to be shown. Often appears inside a larger sentence, e.g. to explain or emphasize what something here is or does. Context and intonation determine if it’s restrictive (that here is) or explanatory (which here is). Not a fixed idiom — its meaning comes from the separate words.
target_language_example: Mira la caja, que aquí es donde guardamos las facturas.
native_language_example: Look at the box, because here is where we keep the bills.

meaning: that (he/she/it) is here / which is here
additional_notes: Commonly used to point out someone or something that is present or nearby. Can introduce a clause (que + subject + aquí está) or act as a relative phrase meaning “which is here.” Tone is neutral and fits spoken and written Spanish. Word order may vary: e.g., «Mira, que aquí está» (Look, there he is).
target_language_example: No te preocupes, que aquí está tu libro.
native_language_example: Don't worry, your book is here.

meaning: Not a fixed idiom; this sequence typically appears when the conjunction/relative pronoun 'que' is followed by the verb 'asistir' in a larger clause. 'Asistir' usually means 'to attend' (requires 'a' for events) or less commonly 'to help'.
additional_notes: 'Que asistir' is not a standalone phrase. In correct Spanish, when referring to attending an event, use 'asistir a' (e.g., 'asistir a la reunión') or verb constructions like 'voy a asistir'. If 'que' introduces a relative clause with 'asistir', word order and prepositions matter: for example, 'la conferencia a la que asistiré' or informally 'la conferencia que voy a asistir' (the latter is considered less formal and regionally variable). When using 'que asistir' directly, ensure the surrounding words make a grammatical subordinate or relative clause.
target_language_example: La lista de invitados que asistir confirmará su asistencia mañana.
native_language_example: The list of guests who will attend will confirm their attendance tomorrow.

meaning: that/so that; used to introduce a result, explanation, or to quote a manner (often colloquial).
additional_notes: Que así appears in spoken and informal written Spanish in several ways: to introduce an explanation or reason (similar to 'because' or 'so'), to report or quote how something happened ('that like this'), or to add emphasis after a statement (e.g., 'y que así fue'). Exact meaning depends on context; it's not a single fixed idiom. Often contracted and more common in Latin American colloquial speech.
target_language_example: Me dijo que así era mejor para todos.
native_language_example: He told me that that way was better for everyone.

meaning: that (must) be attended to / that needs attention
additional_notes: Often appears after nouns or clauses to indicate something requiring attention, care, or consideration. Can be part of expressions like "tengo cosas que atender" (I have things to take care of). The verb atender here means 'to attend to', 'to take care of', or 'to deal with'. Context determines if it's obligation, necessity, or simply noting something that requires action.
target_language_example: Tengo varios asuntos que atender esta semana.
native_language_example: I have several matters to attend to this week.

meaning: that (which) to find out / that I/we/you must find out
additional_notes: Used with hay, tener, or other verbs to introduce something that needs to be discovered or figured out. Often appears as 'hay que averiguar' (one must find out) or 'tengo que averiguar' (I have to find out). 'Averiguar' = to find out, to investigate. Use 'qué' with an accent for 'what' when asking or specifying: 'qué le pasó'.
target_language_example: Tengo que averiguar dónde están las llaves.
native_language_example: I have to find out where the keys are.

meaning: that/which helps; (used to introduce something that will help or be helpful)
additional_notes: Literal combination of que (that/which) + ayudar (to help). Not a fixed idiom by itself — often appears inside longer clauses like 'algo que ayudaría' (something that would help) or 'cosas que ayudan' (things that help). Use depending on context; word order and verb forms may change (que + verb infinitive or que + conjugated verb).
target_language_example: Necesito algo que ayudar a mi concentración.
native_language_example: I need something that helps my concentration.

meaning: to have to dance / that (one) dance (depends on context) — not a fixed phrase; likely part of a larger construction.
additional_notes: On its own 'que bailar' is incomplete in Spanish. It can appear in constructions like 'tener que bailar' (to have to dance) or after expressions using 'que' + infinitive to express obligation, purpose, or a clause ('es que bailar...' is informal/explanatory). For beginner learners, recognize that verbs often follow 'que' but the meaning depends on surrounding words and grammar.
target_language_example: Tengo que bailar esta canción.
native_language_example: I have to dance this song.

meaning: 'to drink' when used as an obligation or part of a clause (literally 'that/to drink').
additional_notes: The phrase 'que beber' often appears inside larger structures: as part of an obligation with 'tener que' (tener que beber = to have to drink), or after verbs/expressions introducing a subordinate clause (parece que sabe que beber — here 'que' introduces the clause 'beber'). Word order and auxiliary verbs matter: 'tienes que beber' = 'you must/you have to drink'; 'se la tiene que beber' = 'he/she has to drink it' (reflexive/object pronouns attach before the conjugated verb in many constructions). 'Que' can be a subordinating conjunction ('that') or part of the fixed obligation 'tener que'.
target_language_example: Tienes que beber agua antes de salir.
native_language_example: You have to drink water before leaving.

meaning: How nice / That's great / How good (depending on tone).
additional_notes: An exclamation or comment used to express pleasure, approval, or relief. Correct spelling for the exclamation uses the accent: '¡qué bien!'. In casual writing people sometimes omit the accent. Tone, punctuation, and context change nuance (e.g., sincere vs. ironic). Can appear alone or followed by a clause: '¡Qué bien!' or 'Qué bien que...'.
target_language_example: Que bien, entonces nos vemos a las seis.
native_language_example: Great, then we'll see each other at six.

meaning: that each / so that each (depends on context)
additional_notes: Que cada appears when 'que' links clauses and 'cada' means 'each' or 'every'. Common patterns: 'para que cada...' (so that each...), 'espero que cada...' (I hope that each...). Meaning depends on the surrounding verb and prepositions. 'Cada' is followed by a singular noun (cada día, cada persona).
target_language_example: Espero que cada estudiante entienda la lección.
native_language_example: I hope that each student understands the lesson.

meaning: 'to have to change the' or 'one must change the' (followed by a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: This sequence combines the impersonal expression 'hay que' (one must/it's necessary to) or the modal verb 'tener que' (to have to) plus the infinitive 'cambiar' and the masculine singular article 'el' before a noun (e.g., 'el estilo', 'el parabrisas', 'el título'). It indicates necessity to replace or alter something specific. In natural speech you'll more often see the full phrases 'hay que cambiar el...' or 'tenemos que cambiar el...'.
target_language_example: Hay que cambiar el filtro del agua.
native_language_example: We need to change the water filter.

meaning: 'to need/should change the' (used with a noun); expresses that something must be changed.
additional_notes: This phrase appears as part of constructions like 'hay que cambiar las...' or 'tenemos que cambiar las...', where 'que' combines with a verb phrase to indicate necessity/obligation. The noun that follows (e.g., cosas, normas, fechas, llantas, reglas) is feminine plural, so 'las' agrees with it. Common patterns: 'hay que cambiar las...' (one must change the...), 'tener que cambiar las...' (to have to change the...).
target_language_example: Hay que cambiar las ventanas de la casa.
native_language_example: We need to change the house windows.

meaning: 'that/so that (someone or something) changes (from)'.
additional_notes: This phrase is a clause introducer using the subjunctive after 'que' or part of a larger sentence: 'que cambie de' often appears before a noun or gerund indicating what is being changed (e.g., que cambie de opinión, que cambie de trabajo). It can express a desire, request, or condition that someone or something make a change. The verb 'cambie' is the present subjunctive of 'cambiar'.
target_language_example: Espero que cambie de opinión antes de decidir.
native_language_example: I hope he/she changes his/her mind before deciding.

meaning: that almost / which almost
additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause that says something nearly happened or is nearly true. Often appears in spoken and written Spanish after verbs or expressions (e.g., 'dijo que casi...' or 'es que casi...'). Depending on context, it can connect clauses ('que' = that/which) plus 'casi' = almost. Word order and punctuation depend on the sentence.
target_language_example: Dijo que casi llega a tiempo.
native_language_example: He said that he almost arrived on time.

meaning: This sequence by itself is not a fixed phrase; it's part of a sentence meaning 'that (to) close the...'.
additional_notes: This is not a standalone expression. It's a fragment: 'que' (that/which/that to) + infinitive 'cerrar' (to close) + feminine singular definite article 'la' (the). You'll typically see it when the noun being referred to follows (e.g., 'que cerrar la puerta' = 'that (to) close the door') or when word order changes in speech/writing. Be careful: word order and punctuation determine the exact meaning (subordinate clauses, commands with 'que', or relative clauses).
target_language_example: Es importante que cerrar la puerta después de usarla.
native_language_example: It's important that (to) close the door after using it.

meaning: 'that/so that it closes' or 'to close (subjunctive clause)'.
additional_notes: Que cierre is the present subjunctive form used after expressions that require the subjunctive (e.g., quiero que cierre, espero que cierre) or in relative clauses meaning 'that closes' (la puerta que cierre). Context determines if it means 'so that it closes' (purpose) or simply 'that it closes' as a wish/request. For beginners: pair with verbs like querer, esperar, pedir (quiero que cierre = I want it to close).
target_language_example: Quiero que cierre la puerta cuando salgamos.
native_language_example: I want the door to close when we leave.

meaning: 'what to cook' — used to ask or talk about which food or recipe to prepare
additional_notes: Often appears in questions or in subordinate clauses. Remember that interrogative/exclamatory qué carries an accent: ¿Qué cocinar? In statements after verbs like saber, preguntar, decidir, use qué with an accent even without question marks: No sé qué cocinar. The phrase is compositional (qué + infinitive cocinar) and can be translated literally.
target_language_example: No sé que cocinar esta noche.
native_language_example: I don't know what to cook tonight.

meaning: 'have to take' (need to take — e.g., transport).
additional_notes: Combines the verb 'tener' (conjugated) + 'que' + infinitive 'coger' to express obligation or necessity: 'tener que coger' = 'to have to take'. Commonly used with modes of transport (tren, avión, autobús). In many Spanish varieties, 'coger' simply means 'to take' (but note: in some Latin American countries, 'coger' is vulgar — there 'tomar' is safer). Conjugate 'tener' for the subject (tengo que coger, tienes que coger, tenemos que coger...).
target_language_example: Mañana tengo que coger el tren a las ocho.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I have to take the train at eight.

meaning: that (to) hang / which to hang
additional_notes: This combination is not a fixed phrase on its own. It likely appears in sentences where 'que' introduces a clause or relative phrase and 'colgar' is the verb 'to hang' (also 'to post' as in 'to upload' or 'to hang up' the phone). Context determines meaning: e.g. 'que colgar' can be part of a relative clause ('la foto que colgarás' — the photo that you will post/hang) or a subordinate clause after verbs or expressions ('tengo algo que colgar' — I have something to hang/post).
target_language_example: Tengo una foto que colgar en la pared.
native_language_example: I have a photo to hang on the wall.

meaning: 'that to begin' or 'to start (something)'.
additional_notes: This looks like a sequence of the relative/complementizer 'que' plus the infinitive 'comenzar'. In Spanish, 'que' before an infinitive often appears in colloquial phrases or after expressions (e.g., "tengo que comenzar" = "I have to start"). Alone, 'que comenzar' is incomplete; you usually need a verb or expression before it (tener que comenzar, hay que comenzar, para que comenzar). Pay attention to context to know if 'que' is part of a larger construction (obligation, impersonal expression, purpose, etc.).
target_language_example: Tengo que comenzar mi tarea ahora.
native_language_example: I have to start my homework now.

meaning: to have to eat something / must eat something
additional_notes: This construction combines the impersonal/obligational 'tener que' (to have to) with 'comer algo' (eat something). In full sentences you'll usually see the conjugated verb: 'tengo que comer algo', 'tienes que comer algo'. Use to express necessity or advice about eating (often when someone hasn't eaten).
target_language_example: Tengo que comer algo antes de salir.
native_language_example: I have to eat something before leaving.

meaning: that/which like/as I (eat) / that, as I... (depends on context)
additional_notes:
This is not a fixed phrase by itself; it's two words that commonly appear together in different grammatical contexts. Possible uses:
- As a relative clause + comparison: '... que, como ...' meaning 'that, as/like ...' (e.g., 'Dijo que, como no vino, empezamos' = 'He said that, since he didn't come, we started').
- As 'que' (that/which) followed by 'como' (how/like/as) when introducing an example or manner: 'el problema que como lo ves...' (less common, often informal or dialectal).
- As 'que' + verb 'comer' in the first person singular subjunctive/indicative appears identical only when clipped: 'que como' can mean 'that I eat' (e.g., 'algo que como todos los días' = 'something that I eat every day').
Because meaning depends on surrounding words, pay attention to punctuation and context.
target_language_example: Busco recetas que como a menudo.
native_language_example: I'm looking for recipes that I eat often.

meaning: Literally 'that to buy one' — not a standard fixed Spanish phrase. It reads as a fragment combining que + comprar + uno and usually needs rephrasing to be grammatical.
additional_notes: This sequence is not a standalone, idiomatic expression. Possible situations where the words appear together: 1) As part of a longer clause with omitted words (e.g., 'dijo que comprar uno...' is incomplete and should be 'dijo que comprara uno' or 'dijo que comprar uno era necesario'). 2) A learner's direct attempt to translate 'that to buy one' — Spanish typically uses infinitive phrases ('comprar uno'), interrogatives ('qué comprar') or subjunctive constructions ('que compre uno'). Use full, grammatical alternatives depending on meaning: - 'comprar uno' = 'to buy one (of them)'. - 'qué comprar' = 'what to buy'. - 'que compre uno' = 'that he/she/one buys one' (subjunctive).
target_language_example: Me dijeron que comprar uno era suficiente, pero no estoy seguro.
native_language_example: They told me that buying one was enough, but I'm not sure.

meaning: 'to have to buy (for myself)'.
additional_notes: Combines the obligation phrase tener que (to have to) with a reflexive pronoun -me, indicating the action is for the speaker (buy for myself). In natural speech the order can be 'tengo que comprarme' or 'tendré que comprarme'; the reflexive can also attach to the infinitive (comprarme) or appear before the conjugated verb (me tengo que comprar). Common when talking about buying something you need or replacing a lost item.
target_language_example: Tengo que comprarme unas zapatillas nuevas para el gimnasio.
native_language_example: I have to buy myself new sneakers for the gym.

meaning: depends on / that depends on (followed by a noun or clause).
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something varies depending on or is influenced by something else. Commonly appears as part of a larger phrase (e.g., "va a ser que con...", "eso depende que con..."), but on its own it links a comment to the condition or factor introduced after "con". In many contexts speakers prefer "depende de" for "depends on."
target_language_example: Todo cambia que con la temporada, hay menos turistas en invierno.
native_language_example: Everything changes depending on the season; there are fewer tourists in winter.

meaning: 'to drive' (infinitive) — but this exact two-word phrase is not a standard standalone expression in Spanish.
additional_notes: The verb conducir means 'to drive' or 'to lead'. In Spanish the infinitive is just conducir. 'Que conducir' could appear inside a larger construction (e.g., 'tener que conducir' = 'to have to drive' or 'que' as a relative/conjunction followed by 'conducir'), but by itself it's incomplete and uncommon. Be careful: Spanish often combines que with verbs in phrases (tener que + infinitive, hay que + infinitive, etc.).
target_language_example: Tengo que conducir hasta el aeropuerto mañana.
native_language_example: I have to drive to the airport tomorrow.

meaning: the clause form used with the verb 'confiar' to introduce what is trusted/expected (literally: 'that to trust' as part of constructions like 'confiar que...')
additional_notes: 'Que confiar' itself is not a standalone fixed phrase; it appears when 'que' follows or precedes 'confiar' in certain syntactic contexts (e.g., 'no hay que confiar' or 'que confiar en alguien es difícil' in subordinate clauses). More common constructions are 'confiar en' + noun/pronoun or 'confiar en que'/'confiar que' + clause to mean 'to trust/hope that...'.
target_language_example: No hay que confiar en desconocidos; que confiar ciegamente suele traer problemas.
native_language_example: You shouldn't trust strangers; that trusting blindly usually brings problems.

meaning: to have to trust/rely on (someone or something)
additional_notes: This phrase combines the obligation phrase 'tener que' (to have to) with the verb 'confiar en' (to trust/rely on). In the examples the structure is often shortened in speech: 'Tenemos que confiar en él' = 'We have to trust him.' Use 'confiar en + person/thing' to indicate trust or reliance. For a noun: confiar en algo; for a person: confiar en él/ella/ti/usted.
target_language_example: Tengo que confiar en mis compañeros para terminar el proyecto.
native_language_example: I have to trust my teammates to finish the project.

meaning: that (he/she/you) knew
additional_notes: Common sequence: 'que' (that) + verb in imperfect 'conocía' (knew/was familiar with). Used to report what someone thought, said, or realized in the past. Subject is determined by surrounding clause (e.g., 'Ella me dijo que conocía a mi hermano' = 'she said that she knew my brother'). English often uses 'knew' or 'was familiar with' depending on context.
target_language_example: Creí que conocía la ciudad, pero me perdí.
native_language_example: I thought I knew the city, but I got lost.

meaning: that you meet/know my… (incomplete phrase — needs a noun/pronoun after 'mi')
additional_notes: This string is not a complete phrase by itself. In Spanish, 'que' can introduce a clause ('that' or a wish/command), 'conozcas' is the present subjunctive of 'conocer' (to meet/know) used after expressions of desire, suggestion, or emotion, and 'a mi' means 'to my' (usually followed by a noun like 'amigo', or it may be a mistaken/informal shortening of 'a mí' meaning 'me'). Common complete forms: 'Quiero que conozcas a mi amigo' (I want you to meet my friend) or 'Ojalá que conozcas a mí' is incorrect — use 'a mí' only when the verb takes an object 'a' + person. Watch the difference between 'mi' (my) and 'mí' (me).
target_language_example: Quiero que conozcas a mi hermana este fin de semana.
native_language_example: I want you to meet my sister this weekend.

meaning: Used when the conjunction 'que' and the verb 'conseguir' appear together in a clause; conveys obtaining or managing to get something (or that someone managed to get something) depending on context, tense and punctuation.
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom by itself; appears in different grammatical contexts: with an accent on qué it can form indirect questions (e.g., 'qué conseguir' = 'what to get'); without accent 'que conseguir' can appear in reported speech or subordinate clauses (e.g., 'dijo que conseguiría...'). Pay attention to accents, tense and subjunctive vs. indicative. Spelling matters: 'qué' (with accent) for questions/indirect questions; 'que' (no accent) as conjunction.
target_language_example: Me pregunto que conseguir antes de salir de casa.
native_language_example: I wonder what to get before leaving the house.

meaning: let it be noted / let it be on record; used to state something formally or to make clear you're recording a fact or opinion.
additional_notes: Commonly used to emphasize that what you're saying should be officially or clearly recorded (verbally or in minutes). Can be used in informal contexts to stress a disclaimer ("just so you know"). Often followed by a clause or used alone as a parenthetical remark.
target_language_example: Que conste que ya te lo dije antes.
native_language_example: Let it be on record that I already told you.

meaning: 'to have (something) to tell' / 'to count (as) / to matter' depending on context
additional_notes: This phrase appears in different structures. 1) After verbs like tener (tengo que contar) it means 'to have something to tell' (I have a lot to tell). 2) In impersonal constructions with hay/ahora había que contar historias means 'one had to' or 'it was necessary to' (had to tell). 3) With tener que contar hasta... it means 'to have to count' (as in counting money). 4) In expressions like 'tener que contar para' it means 'to count for / to matter'. Pay attention to surrounding verbs (tener que + infinitive = obligation; que contar as noun phrase = 'something to tell').
target_language_example: Tengo mucho que contar sobre mi viaje.
native_language_example: I have a lot to tell about my trip.

meaning: that I have to tell you / to tell you (something).
additional_notes: Commonly appears after verbs like 'tener' (tengo que contarte) or phrases like 'hay algo que tengo que contarte'. It introduces that the speaker must tell the listener something—often news, a secret, or important information. Word order: Spanish places 'que' before the infinitive + indirect object pronoun (contarte = contar + te). 'Contarte' literally means 'to tell you.'
target_language_example: Mamá, hay algo que tengo que contarte.
native_language_example: Mom, there's something I have to tell you.

meaning: depends on context; can be part of constructions meaning 'what to believe' (qué creer) or 'that [one] believe' (que creer) — often it is not used alone but within a clause
additional_notes: Forms and meaning depend on accent and context: 'qué creer' (with accent on qué) = 'what to believe' (interrogative/indirect question). 'que creer' (no accent) can appear after verbs or conjunctions to introduce a subordinate clause meaning 'that [one] believe' or as part of phrases like 'no sé que creer' (colloquially written without accent but more correctly 'qué'). Alone 'que creer' is uncommon; pay attention to punctuation and accents.
target_language_example: No sé que creer ahora que han salido nuevas pruebas.
native_language_example: I don't know what to believe now that new evidence has come out.

meaning: that (he/she) believed that... — introduces someone's belief or opinion about something.
additional_notes: Used to report what someone thought or believed. Often appears in reported speech after verbs like decir, mencionar, pensar, creer. The subject of creía can be the same as the reporting subject (Tom dijo que creía que...) or another person; context determines who believed it. Tense agreement: creía is imperfect (past, ongoing or tentative belief).
target_language_example: Ella dijo que creía que él ya se había ido.
native_language_example: She said that she believed he had already left.

meaning: 'to have to cross' (need/obligation to cross) or part of constructions with the infinitive 'cruzar' following a conjugated verb.
additional_notes: This appears when a conjugated verb (e.g., creer, tener) is followed by the infinitive 'cruzar'. With 'tener que cruzar' it means 'must/need to cross'. With verbs like 'cree que cruzar...' it can introduce a clause: 'he/she thinks that crossing...'. Use 'cruzar' to mean to go across (a street, river, room, legs, vehicles).
target_language_example: Tengo que cruzar la calle antes de que se haga tarde.
native_language_example: I have to cross the street before it gets late.

meaning: that when / which when (linking phrase used to introduce a time clause or a clause explaining circumstances)
additional_notes: Commonly appears as part of a larger sentence to connect a main clause with a time or circumstance introduced by 'cuando'. 'Que' can be a relative pronoun ('that/which') or a conjunction ('that'), so 'que cuando' often means 'that when' or 'which when'. Usage depends on context; not a fixed idiom. In speech it may be contracted or elided.
target_language_example: Dijo que cuando llegáramos empezaríamos la reunión.
native_language_example: He said that when we arrived we would start the meeting.

meaning: 'to have to take care of' (someone).
additional_notes: This is the structure with the modal verb 'tener' in a conjugated form + 'que' + 'cuidar a' + person: e.g. 'tengo que cuidar a...' = 'I have to take care of...'. 'Cuidar a' is used when the direct object is a person or pet; include 'a' before people. It expresses obligation or necessity to look after someone.
target_language_example: Tengo que cuidar a mi hermano esta noche.
native_language_example: I have to take care of my brother tonight.

meaning: to have to take care of / to need to look after (someone).
additional_notes: This appears with a conjugated form of 'tener' + 'que' + 'cuidar de' (e.g., 'tienes que cuidar de...') to express obligation: 'you have to take care of...'. 'Cuidar de' means 'to care for' or 'look after' someone or something. Use 'cuidar a' also in many regions (both 'cuidar de María' and 'cuidar a María' are common).
target_language_example: Mañana tengo que cuidar de mi hermano pequeño.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I have to take care of my little brother.

meaning: 'to have to serve/fulfill' — used with obligations, duties, promises, or prison sentences (tener que cumplir ... / cumplir con ...).
additional_notes: Commonly appears after a conjugated form of 'tener' (tener que cumplir) meaning 'must/has to fulfill' or with 'cumplir con' meaning 'to carry out/meet' an obligation, duty, promise, or to 'serve' a sentence (cumplir una condena). Use with direct objects (cumplir una promesa, cumplir mi parte) or with 'con' (cumplir con el deber).
target_language_example: Tengo que cumplir con mi promesa.
native_language_example: I have to keep/fulfill my promise.

meaning: a structure meaning 'to have to give/do a (something)'; used with verbs like dar + noun after que/tener que/ir a to express obligation or necessity to perform an action (e.g., give an injection, take a shower, give a lesson).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom but shows common patterns: 'tener que dar una ...' or 'me tengo que dar una ...' where dar + noun indicates performing an action (dar una inyección = give an injection; darse una ducha = take a shower). Subjects and reflexive forms change meaning: 'dar una ducha' (to give someone a shower) vs 'darse una ducha' (to take a shower). Often appears with obligation expressions (tener que, va a tener que, tendré que).
target_language_example: Mañana tendré que dar una presentación en clase.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I'll have to give a presentation in class.

meaning: 'that must (be)' or 'which is probably/likely'
additional_notes: Used to express probability or a logical conclusion about something mentioned earlier. 'De' after 'deber' softens certainty in many regions: 'debe' = stronger obligation/likelihood, 'debe de' = likely/probable. Often appears in relative clauses: 'la casa que debe de ser antigua' = 'the house that is probably old.' Context and regional usage vary; some speakers omit 'de'.
target_language_example: Es la tienda que debe de cerrar a las ocho.
native_language_example: It's the shop that probably closes at eight.

meaning: that we should
additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause expressing what is advisable, recommended, or expected. "Que" means "that," and "deberíamos" is "we should / we ought to," often sounding softer or more tentative than a direct command.
target_language_example: Creo que deberíamos salir temprano.
native_language_example: I think that we should leave early.

meaning: that you should talk (or speak) — used to recommend or suggest someone talk about something
additional_notes: This phrase combines 'que' (that/which) with 'deberías' (you should, conditional of deber) and the infinitive 'hablar' (to speak/talk). It's often part of a larger sentence: e.g., 'Es algo que deberías hablar con él' (It's something you should talk to him about). Use 'hablar de' or 'hablar con' to specify the topic or person: 'hablar de tu idea' (talk about your idea), 'hablar con María' (talk to María).
target_language_example: Es un problema que deberías hablar con tu jefe.
native_language_example: It's a problem that you should talk to your boss about.

meaning: that you should go
additional_notes: This is a clause often used after verbs or expressions (e.g., 'dijo que deberías ir' = 'he said that you should go') or to report advice. 'Deberías' is the conditional form of 'deber' (should/ought to). In spoken Spanish the subject pronoun is usually omitted: 'que deberías ir' implies 'que tú deberías ir'.
target_language_example: Ella dijo que deberías ir al médico.
native_language_example: She said that you should go to the doctor.

meaning: 'that I decided' / 'which I decided'.
additional_notes: Combines the relative pronoun/connector 'que' with the first-person past tense verb 'decidí' (from decidir). Used to introduce a clause describing what the speaker decided. Common in sentences like 'la opción que decidí' or 'que decidí hacer'. Can link to an action, choice, or opinion made by the speaker. Tone is neutral and appropriate in formal and informal contexts.
target_language_example: Compré la casa que decidí porque tenía jardín.
native_language_example: I bought the house that I decided on because it had a garden.

meaning: 'to tell me' (something you must or need to say to me)
additional_notes: This phrase combines the relative/connector 'que' with the infinitive 'decir' plus the indirect object pronoun 'me'. It's commonly used after verbs like 'tener' (tener que decirme = to have to tell me) or in questions (¿Qué tienes que decirme?). It can introduce what someone must tell the speaker (facts, location, names, truth, etc.). Word order can change: "tienes que decirme" (you have to tell me) or in questions "¿qué tienes que decirme?" (what do you have to tell me?).
target_language_example: Tienes que decirme la verdad ahora.
native_language_example: You have to tell me the truth now.

meaning: to tell you
additional_notes: Usually part of a larger pattern, not a fixed expression by itself. Very commonly it appears in 'tener que decirte' = 'have to tell you'. It can also follow words like algo, nada, or mucho: 'algo que decirte' = 'something to tell you'.
target_language_example: Tengo algo importante que decirte.
native_language_example: I have something important to tell you.

meaning: that I have something to tell you / that I need to tell you something.
additional_notes: Commonly appears in phrases like 'tengo que decirte algo' (I have to tell you something) or 'hay que decirte algo' (there is something I need to tell you). It's used to introduce important, surprising, or private information. Word order: 'decirte' is the infinitive 'decir' + indirect object pronoun 'te' (to you).
target_language_example: Tengo que decirte algo importante.
native_language_example: I have to tell you something important.

meaning: that (to) defend / which to defend (literal phrase); often incomplete—requires context or rephrasing.
additional_notes: As written, 'que defender' is not a complete or standard Spanish phrase. It looks like a literal combination of 'que' (that/which) + the infinitive 'defender' (to defend). It could appear inside a larger sentence (e.g., 'algo que defender' = 'something to defend' or 'que defender' as part of a question or relative clause), but by itself it is unusual. Common complete forms: 'algo que defender' (something to defend), 'nada que defender' (nothing to defend), 'que defender' inside questions commonly becomes '¿qué defender?' (what to defend) — note the accent on 'qué' when it's interrogative.
target_language_example: No tengo nada que defender en esta discusión.
native_language_example: I have nothing to defend in this discussion.

meaning: 'to stop (doing something)'; used after expressions that require 'que' + verb phrase (e.g., decir que dejar de...)
additional_notes: This sequence combines the conjunction/relative 'que' with the verb phrase 'dejar de' (to stop doing something). It appears in reported speech or structures where 'que' introduces a subordinate clause: e.g., 'Me dijo que dejar de fumar' (He told me to stop smoking) — note that more natural Spanish uses an infinitive after verbs of telling/ordering (e.g., 'me dijo que dejara/dejase de fumar' or 'me dijo que dejara de fumar' or 'me dijo: "deja de fumar"'). Learners will more often see 'dejar de' alone to mean 'stop (doing)'.
target_language_example: El doctor dijo que dejar de fumar sería lo mejor para tu salud.
native_language_example: The doctor said that stopping smoking would be best for your health.

meaning: A sequence where 'que' introduces a clause followed by the verb 'dejar' and the feminine singular definite article 'la'. Meaning depends on context: could be obligation/necessity ('tener que dejar la...'), a subjunctive/reported structure ('es necesario que deje la...'), or other constructions where 'dejar la' means 'to leave the (feminine noun)', 'to stop the (feminine noun)', or 'to allow the (feminine noun)'.
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom by itself; it's a compositional fragment that appears when the clause requires the feminine singular direct object or noun phrase introduced by 'la'. The meaning depends on the verb form and surrounding words. Examples: 'Tengo que dejar la casa' (I have to leave the house); 'Es mejor que deje la reunión' (It's better that [he/she] leave the meeting). Watch for verb conjugation: 'dejar' vs 'deje'.
target_language_example: Tengo que dejar la casa a las seis.
native_language_example: I have to leave the house at six.

meaning: that (he/she/it) leave(s)
additional_notes: Que deje is a short phrase that appears in different structures. It can be part of a subordinate clause after verbs of saying or thinking: "dice que deje" = "he says that (someone) leaves/should leave." It can also appear with dejar + de + infinitive to mean "stop (doing something)" (e.g. "deje de ser tonto" = "stops being stupid"). In contexts like "para que deje de..." it means "so that (someone) stops..." or "to make/let someone stop..." Subject and tense depend on surrounding verbs; "deje" here is present or present-subjunctive form of dejar. Watch the difference between "dejar" (to leave, to let) and the phrase "dejar de" (to stop doing).
target_language_example: Voy a hablar con él para que deje de fumar.
native_language_example: I'm going to talk to him so that he stops smoking.

meaning: 'to have to demonstrate' or 'to need to show/prove'.
additional_notes: Often appears after a conjugated verb + 'tener' (tener que demostrar = to have to show/prove). Used to talk about needing to prove something, show ability, value, solidarity, etc. When followed by a clause, it introduces what must be proven (e.g., 'tienes que demostrar que...').
target_language_example: Tengo que demostrar que puedo hacerlo.
native_language_example: I have to prove that I can do it.

meaning: 'to have to rest' (expression showing obligation to rest)
additional_notes: This appears as part of constructions with tener + que + infinitive (tener que descansar) to express necessity or obligation: 'you have to rest / I have to rest / he has to rest.' In spoken Spanish the subject pronoun is often dropped and conjugation changes by person (tengo, tienes, tiene, tenés). 'Que descansar' alone usually follows a conjugated form of 'tener' (or is a clipped written form), so include the full pattern 'tener que descansar' when using it.
target_language_example: Ahora tienes que descansar un rato.
native_language_example: Now you have to rest for a while.

meaning: that (we/you/I) must discover / to find out
additional_notes: "que" here introduces a clause meaning "that" or "what"; combined with "tener que" or "tener que descubrir" it expresses obligation (have to discover). In sentence 3, the structure is "descubrir qué..." meaning "find out what..." Word order varies: "que tienes que descubrir" = "that you have to discover"; "tenemos que descubrir" = "we have to find out."
target_language_example: Es algo que tenemos que descubrir juntos.
native_language_example: It's something that we have to find out together.

meaning: 'that I get rid of' or 'what to get rid of' (used with verbs expressing uncertainty, necessity, or desire).
additional_notes: Typically follows verbs or expressions like 'no sé', 'tengo', 'no sé bien' and refers to items one wants to discard, sell, donate, or stop keeping. Grammatically it's the relative/indefinite pronoun 'que' plus the reflexive infinitive 'deshacerme' (deshacer + me). Common in colloquial and neutral registers.
target_language_example: No sé qué deshacerme de, así que lo pondré en una caja por ahora.
native_language_example: I don't know what to get rid of, so I'll put it in a box for now.

meaning: 'to have to return' or 'must return' (used after verbs like tener, tenerse que or in constructions expressing obligation to give back something).
additional_notes: This phrase appears as part of obligation constructions in Spanish (e.g., 'tengo que devolver' = 'I have to return'). 'Devolver' means 'to return' or 'to give back' (an object, a person, etc.). Use it with direct objects: devolver algo / devolver a alguien. When conjugated, the structure is typically [tener]+que+devolver or another modal verb (e.g., 'tener que devolver', 'tenemos que devolver', 'tuvieron que devolver').
target_language_example: Tengo que devolver la chaqueta mañana.
native_language_example: I have to return the jacket tomorrow.

meaning: that (he/she/it) say(s) / that (someone) say(s) — used in subordinate clauses to introduce what is said or should be said.
additional_notes: Commonly appears after verbs or expressions that require the subjunctive (e.g., esperar, alegrarse, impedir) or after verbs of telling/wanting. Can express reported content ('that he says...'), a wish ('that he say...'), or allow/indifference ('let him say...'). Context and main verb determine whether it's indicative or subjunctive in meaning; here it's often subjunctive.
target_language_example: Quiero que diga la verdad en la reunión.
native_language_example: I want him/her to tell the truth at the meeting.

meaning: that you should apologize / for you to apologize
additional_notes: "que disculparte" is not a fixed standalone phrase in Spanish. It looks like part of a larger sentence (subordinate clause) and would normally follow verbs or expressions that require a subordinate clause with 'que' + infinitive. For example: 'Es importante que disculparte' is incorrect — correct is 'Es importante que te disculpes' (subjunctive) or 'Tengo que disculparte' would be unusual; more natural would be 'tengo que disculparme' (I have to apologize) or 'tengo que disculparte a ti' (I have to excuse you). In short, avoid using 'que' directly before an infinitive with a reflexive pronoun attached this way; use correct verb forms (infinitive without extra 'que' after certain verbs, or use 'que' + subjunctive when introducing a clause).
target_language_example: Necesito disculparme; no es correcto decir "que disculparte" aquí.
native_language_example: I need to apologize; it's not correct to say "que disculparte" here.

meaning: 'to discuss' or 'to have something to discuss' (often used after verbs or expressions indicating there is a topic to talk about).
additional_notes: que + infinitive (e.g., que discutir) often appears in constructions like 'tener algo que discutir' (to have something to discuss) or 'hay que discutir' (it must be discussed). By itself 'que discutir' is not a complete sentence; it functions as a subordinate phrase meaning 'to discuss (something)'.
target_language_example: Tenemos mucho que discutir esta tarde.
native_language_example: We have a lot to discuss this afternoon.

meaning: 'to sleep' (infinitive phrase; looks like 'to sleep' with que before it — used after certain expressions)
additional_notes: This is the infinitive verb 'dormir' ('to sleep') with the conjunction/relative word 'que' before it. On its own 'que dormir' is not a fixed phrase in Spanish; it appears in sentences like 'antes de que dormir' (incorrect) — correct uses are 'tener que dormir' (to have to sleep) or constructions such as 'que dormir...' inside a larger clause (e.g., 'es importante que dormir lo suficiente' — note: subjunctive usually required: 'es importante que duermas'). Beginners should know 'dormir' = to sleep and that 'que' can introduce subordinate clauses or follow verbs ('tener que + infinitive' = to have to + verb).
target_language_example: Tengo que dormir ocho horas cada noche.
native_language_example: I have to sleep eight hours every night.

meaning: 'what two' or 'that two' — often not a fixed phrase; usually part of a larger sentence (e.g., que dos [cosas] = 'that two [things]').
additional_notes: On its own, 'que dos' is not a common fixed expression in Spanish. It can appear when 'que' introduces a clause or phrase and is followed by the number 'dos' (two). Meaning depends entirely on context: for example, 'que dos opciones' = 'that two options' (usually you'd say 'que son dos opciones' or 'que las dos opciones'). Beginners will more often see 'que' used as 'that' or 'which' and 'dos' as the number 'two.'
target_language_example: Dijo que dos personas vendrán mañana.
native_language_example: He said that two people will come tomorrow.

meaning: depends on context — often part of expressions meaning 'to throw away', 'to spill', 'to put in', or 'to need to (have) something to add'; not a fixed phrase by itself.
additional_notes: This is not a standalone fixed phrase. 'Echar' is a very common Spanish verb with many meanings (to throw, to pour, to put, to send away, to add, to start, etc.). When you see 'que echar' it usually appears inside a larger clause: e.g. after verbs like 'tener' ('tener que echar' — rarely used) or in relative clauses ('algo que echar' — 'something to add/put in/throw'). Meaning changes with context and the object that follows. For beginners, focus on learning common uses of 'echar' (echar de menos = to miss; echar la basura = to throw out the trash; echar sal = to add salt; echar a correr = to start running).
target_language_example: No tengo nada que echar en la olla.
native_language_example: I don't have anything to put in the pot.

meaning: the other one / than the other (depends on context).
additional_notes: This phrase appears when comparing or distinguishing between two people or things: 'que el otro' often completes a clause (e.g., 'más caro que el otro' = 'more expensive than the other'). Alone it is incomplete; you usually need a verb or adjective before it. It can refer to a person or an object already mentioned. Word order and surrounding words determine exact translation.
target_language_example: Este libro es mejor que el otro.
native_language_example: This book is better than the other one.

meaning: 'that Mr. (someone)'.
additional_notes: Used when reporting information about a man (formal 'señor') introduced by a clause with 'que' (that). Common in sentences like 'I think that Mr. X...' or 'It is said that Mr. X...'. 'Señor' is a polite title; use with a surname. Word order: verb + que + el señor + Name.
target_language_example: Creo que el señor García llegará mañana.
native_language_example: I believe that Mr. García will arrive tomorrow.

meaning: 'which to choose' or 'what to choose' (often used in indirect questions or after verbs expressing doubt).
additional_notes: Standard Spanish normally writes the interrogative pronoun with an accent: 'qué elegir' when used in direct or indirect questions. Without the accent, 'que' can be a conjunction with a different function. The two-word sequence 'que elegir' may appear in informal writing missing the accent or in contexts where 'que' is a relative conjunction plus an infinitive, but most commonly you should use 'qué elegir' for 'what to choose.'
target_language_example: Me pregunto que elegir en la tienda.
