You will see it inside longer clauses, e.g. 'dijo que llegarían tarde' (he said that they would arrive late) or in periphrastic constructions like 'tengo que llegar' (I have to arrive/get there). Pay attention to verb conjugation and context to determine tense and subject.
target_language_example: Ella dijo que llegarían a las ocho.
native_language_example: She said that they would arrive at eight.

meaning: 'that to reach' / literal sequence 'que llegar a'—not a standalone idiom; 'llegar a' means 'to reach', 'to come to', or 'to end up (doing)' and the preceding 'que' arises when the phrase appears inside a subordinate clause (often requiring conjugation agreement).
additional_notes: 'Que llegar a' is simply the word 'que' followed by the infinitive construction 'llegar a'. It is not a fixed phrase by itself; in correct Spanish you normally find a conjugated verb in the subordinate clause (e.g., '...que llegue a...') rather than the infinitive after 'que'. However, 'que llegar a + infinitive' can appear in contexts like reported or reduced clauses after certain verbs or in colloquial speech. Pay attention to verb agreement and register. Examples show how the sequence appears inside a clause; to be grammatically standard, adjust conjugation when needed.
target_language_example: Dijeron que llegar a ser profesional no sería fácil.
native_language_example: They said that becoming a professional would not be easy.

meaning: 'that (something/someone) reach/attain a (something)'; part of a larger clause meaning 'that (someone) manage to/come to a (point/place/condition)'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed standalone phrase but a sequence often found inside sentences: 'que llegar a un...' introduces the idea that someone/something reaches, attains, or comes to a particular noun (un + noun). Depending on context, it can mean 'to arrive at a (place)' or 'to reach/achieve a (state, conclusion, number)'. You will normally see it inside longer clauses, e.g. 'para que llegar a un acuerdo' (actually correct form: 'para llegar a un acuerdo' or 'que se llegue a un acuerdo'). Watch word order and verb forms: often the verb appears as 'llegar' (infinitive) after prepositions like 'para' or with subjunctive constructions ('que llegue').
target_language_example: Esperamos que llegar a un acuerdo sea posible pronto.
native_language_example: We hope that reaching an agreement will be possible soon.

meaning: that (they) arrive / until the (they) arrive (used in time clauses: before/until the [group] arrives).
additional_notes: Common in subordinate clauses introduced by verbs of time or commands with 'antes de que' (before) or 'hasta que' (until). 'Lleguen' is subjunctive (used because arrival is anticipated or not yet happened). 'Los' is a masculine plural definite article referring to a group (soldiers, refuerzos, etc.). Replace 'los' with other articles/pronouns as needed (las, los, them, etc.).
target_language_example: Salgan ahora, antes de que lleguen los policías.
native_language_example: Leave now, before the police arrive.

meaning: 'that/which arrived the' — a fragment used to introduce something that has just arrived (often followed by a noun)
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase on its own but a common sequence in sentences: 'que llegó el/ la/ los/ las ...' Introduces or specifies the thing or person that has arrived. Gender and number of the article (el/la/los/las) must match the noun that follows. In English you would usually translate it as 'that arrived' or 'which has arrived' plus the noun.
target_language_example: Te doy la chaqueta que llegó el paquete de la tienda.
native_language_example: I'll give you the jacket that arrived in the package from the store.

meaning: A fragment rather than a complete fixed phrase; likely part of a question or clause meaning 'what to bring/wear (the...)' or 'that to take/wear the...'. It is incomplete and needs more words (e.g., a noun after 'el') and normally 'qué' (with accent) is used in questions.
additional_notes: This is not a standard multi-word expression in Spanish. It looks like an unfinished chunk: 'que' could be relative 'that' or interrogative 'qué' (what). For questions use the accented 'qué' and idiomatic constructions such as '¿Qué llevar el día de la excursión?' or better '¿Qué llevar para el picnic?'. Word order often requires a preposition before a noun (e.g., 'al' = a + el). Keep in mind accent: interrogative 'qué' needs an accent. Example with the exact fragment is possible in casual or clipped speech but remains nonstandard.
target_language_example: ¿Qué llevar el día de la excursión?
native_language_example: What should (we) bring on the day of the excursion?

meaning: to have to take it
additional_notes: This phrase combines obligation (hay que / tengo que / tendremos que / hubo que, etc.) with the verb llevar (to take) and the direct object lo (it/him). The exact subject and tense change the meaning: 'hay que llevarlo' = 'one must take it' or 'it must be taken'; 'tengo que llevarlo' = 'I have to take it'; 'tendré que llevarlo' = 'I'll have to take it'. Use with locations (a casa, al veterinario) or people (con mi padre).
target_language_example: Tengo que llevarlo al veterinario mañana.
native_language_example: I have to take it to the vet tomorrow.

meaning: 'to have to take you' (obligation + 'take/bring you')
additional_notes: Que + infinitive here expresses obligation ('tener que' → 'have to'). In the examples the full form is often 'tengo que llevarte' or 'tenemos que llevarte' meaning 'I/We have to take you (somewhere)'. 'Llevarte' = llevar + te (to take/bring you). Use when saying you must give someone a ride or escort them somewhere.
target_language_example: Tengo que llevarte al trabajo esta mañana.
native_language_example: I have to take you to work this morning.

meaning: to make (someone) cry / to be worth crying about
additional_notes: Phrase appears as part of larger expressions. On its own, 'que' can introduce a subordinate clause (that/which) and 'llorar' means 'to cry'. Common uses: 'hacer que llorar' (to make someone cry), 'no vale la pena que llorar' (not worth crying about), or colloquially 'hay que llorar' (one must cry). Word order and surrounding verbs determine the exact meaning.
target_language_example: No hay razón para que llorar por eso.
native_language_example: There is no reason to cry about that.

meaning: that/which it/he/she is (used to emphasize that something is indeed the case).
additional_notes: Common in responses for emphasis after an affirmation: 'Claro que lo está' = 'Of course it is.' 'Que' introduces the clause and 'lo' refers to the thing being discussed; 'está' is the verb 'to be' (temporary/state). Used to insist or confirm strongly.
target_language_example: ¿No estás seguro? ¡Claro que lo está!
native_language_example: Not sure? Of course it is!

meaning: that you had (done it/seen it/etc.).
additional_notes: Combination of the conjunction 'que' + object pronoun 'lo' + past perfect (pretérito pluscuamperfecto) of 'haber' + past participle implied after. Used to express a past assumption or expectation about an action someone else had completed before another past moment. The specific action is given by the past participle that follows (e.g., dejado, visto).
target_language_example: Creí que lo habías entendido.
native_language_example: I thought that you had understood it.

meaning: 'that you have (it/it done)'.
additional_notes: This sequence appears when using the conjunction que + direct object lo + the auxiliary has (from haber) in the present perfect (tú). It combines with a past participle (has hecho) to mean 'that you have done (something)' or with a clause like lo has dicho 'that you have said it'. It can also appear for emphasis (Sí que lo has hecho = You really have done it). The subject is usually tú (informal you).
target_language_example: Parece que lo has entendido.
native_language_example: It seems that you have understood it.

meaning: that the best (thing) / may it be best
additional_notes: This fragment is not a complete fixed phrase by itself. It typically appears as part of longer sentences or expressions, e.g. after verbs or conjunctions: 'Espero que lo mejor esté por venir' (I hope the best is yet to come) or 'Dijo que lo mejor era esperar' (He said the best thing was to wait). 'Lo mejor' means 'the best' or 'the best thing,' and 'que' can introduce a clause (that/that…) or be used after verbs of saying/thinking/feeling. Beginners should look for full sentences to understand the function.
target_language_example: Creo que lo mejor es descansar un día antes del examen.
native_language_example: I think the best thing is to rest one day before the exam.

meaning: used in the phrase 'Ahora que lo pienso' = 'now that I think about it' or 'come to think of it'.
additional_notes: Commonly appears as the fixed phrase 'Ahora que lo pienso' to introduce a thought or realization that just occurred. Used to add a new idea, correct oneself, or draw a conclusion after reconsidering. Followed by a clause with what you now realize or decide.
target_language_example: Ahora que lo pienso, debería llamar a mamá.
native_language_example: Now that I think about it, I should call Mom.

meaning: that I can (do) it / which I can (do) it
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but a sequence: que (that/which) + lo (it) + puedo (I can). It appears in sentences like «Dijo que lo puedo arreglar» (He said that I can fix it) or «Es algo que lo puedo hacer» (less natural — better: «Es algo que puedo hacer»). In Spanish, the object pronoun lo usually appears before the conjugated verb (lo puedo), but when there's an infinitive it can attach to the infinitive (poder hacerlo). Native speakers often prefer "que puedo" + verb without repeating lo, or "que lo puedo + [infinitive]" if emphasizing the object.
target_language_example: Ella dijo que lo puedo reparar mañana.
native_language_example: She said that I can repair it tomorrow.

meaning: used to emphasize contrast or correction; similar to 'no — but rather' or 'it's not —, it's that —'.
additional_notes: Common in colloquial Spanish to correct or contrast a previous idea. Often appears in constructions like «no es que X, es que Y» or in reduced emphatic phrases like «más que lo que…» depending on region. Not a fixed idiom with a single translation; translate according to context as a corrective or contrasting connector.
target_language_example: No es que no quiera, que lo que pasa es que estoy muy ocupado.
native_language_example: It's not that I don't want to, it's that I'm very busy.

meaning: 'that the only (thing)'.
additional_notes: Used within the phrase 'lo único que...' to introduce the single thing, person, option, or circumstance relevant or true in a situation. Common in restricting or emphasizing statements (e.g., 'lo único que puedes hacer...'). Typically appears as part of a larger clause rather than standing alone.
target_language_example: Así que lo único que puedes hacer es fingir que haces algo.
native_language_example: So the only thing you can do is pretend you're doing something.

meaning: 'have to fight' or 'must fight' (expressing obligation or necessity to fight).
additional_notes: This is the infinitive phrase 'que luchar' used after 'tienes/vas a/tuviste' constructions to indicate obligation or necessity (tener que + infinitive). In full sentences you'll usually see the conjugated form 'tener que luchar' (e.g., 'tendrás que luchar' = 'you will have to fight'). It can be literal (physically fight) or figurative (compete, struggle for something).
target_language_example: Tendrás que luchar si quieres ese puesto.
native_language_example: You will have to fight if you want that position.

meaning: 'that later' / 'which later' — used to refer to something that happens afterward or to add a comment about what comes next.
additional_notes: Common in spoken Spanish to link ideas: can introduce a consequence, an afterthought, or a clarification. Often followed by a verb or phrase describing what happens afterward (e.g., 'que luego pasó...' or 'que luego, no sé...'). In many contexts it functions like 'and then' or 'which later on...'. Tone is neutral and fits informal and neutral speech.
target_language_example: Me llamó temprano, que luego vino a casa más tarde.
native_language_example: He called me early, and then he came home later.

meaning: "that/which mom" or part of a clause referring to 'mom' (literally 'that mom' or 'which mom')
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself; it's typically part of a larger sentence (e.g., 'que mamá dijo' = 'that mom said' or 'que mamá compra' = 'which mom buys'). 'Que' here can be a relative pronoun ('that/which/who') or a conjunction ('that') depending on the sentence. Pay attention to context and verb form after it.
target_language_example: El libro que mamá compró está en la mesa.
native_language_example: The book that mom bought is on the table.

meaning: 'que mandar' is not a fixed idiom; it can appear as part of constructions meaning 'that to send', 'what to send', or as part of obligation phrases ('tener que mandar' = 'to have to send'). Exact meaning depends on context and accent: 'qué mandar' (with accent) = 'what to send' (question); 'que mandar' (without accent) often links clauses (e.g., 'lo que mandar') or appears after verbs.
additional_notes: Not a standalone phrase. Watch the accent: 'qué' (with accent) is interrogative/exclamative; 'que' (without accent) is a relative conjunction or complementizer. Common real uses include 'lo que mandar' ('that which to send' / 'what to send') and 'tener que mandar' ('to have to send'). Translation depends on surrounding words.
target_language_example: No sé lo que mandar, pero creo que debo preguntar antes de que mandar sin permiso.
native_language_example: I don't know what to send, but I think I should ask before sending without permission.

meaning: 'to have to keep' / 'you have to keep' (necessity + maintain/keep)
additional_notes: Combines the impersonal/needing construction (tener que) with the verb mantener (to keep, maintain). In context it expresses obligation: 'you must keep/maintain' something (distance, order, cleanliness, a promise, etc.). Conjugate 'tener' for the subject (tengo que mantener, tienes que mantener, etc.) and then add the thing to keep + adjective or phrase.
target_language_example: Tienes que mantener la puerta cerrada.
native_language_example: You have to keep the door closed.

meaning: phrase fragment meaning 'that/which to maintain the' (used before a feminine noun)
additional_notes: This is not a standalone fixed phrase but a fragment: que (that/which) + mantener (to maintain) + la (feminine definite article). You'll see it inside longer sentences, e.g. 'la política que mantener la paz' (the policy to maintain peace). It introduces a clause or purpose referring to keeping or preserving something feminine (la casa, la calma, la paz). Word order and context determine exact translation; often rendered as 'to maintain the...' or 'that maintains the...'.
target_language_example: Tenemos una estrategia que mantener la paz en la región.
native_language_example: We have a strategy to maintain the peace in the region.

meaning: 'that/to (have) keep ourselves' — part of the structure 'tener que mantenernos' meaning 'we have to keep/maintain ourselves (in some state)'.
additional_notes: This phrase appears as part of the construction 'tener que mantenernos' or 'tenemos que mantenernos', meaning 'we have to stay/keep ourselves' + adjective or prepositional phrase (e.g., unidos, al margen, saludables, calientes). Use it to say you must remain or keep yourselves in a certain condition. The literal components are compositional, but the phrase alone is incomplete without context (who 'we' are and what to keep).
target_language_example: Tenemos que mantenernos atentos durante la reunión.
native_language_example: We have to keep ourselves attentive during the meeting.

meaning: an emphatic colloquial phrase used to express extreme annoyance or that someone/something makes you feel like doing something violent (hyperbolic); similar to 'makes me want to kill' or 'it’s infuriating' in English
additional_notes: Informal and hyperbolic — can sound violent; use with caution. More commonly heard as part of larger constructions (e.g., "me dan ganas que matar" in some regional speech), though the most standard colloquial form is "dan ganas de matar". Regional usage and exact grammar vary; not appropriate for formal contexts.
target_language_example: Con ese vecino que matar, no dejo de perder el sueño.
native_language_example: With that neighbor — makes me want to kill — I can't stop losing sleep.

meaning: that tomorrow / which tomorrow (depends on context).
additional_notes: This short sequence can appear in different constructions. Often used after verbs or expressions to introduce a clause referring to tomorrow: e.g. 'Dijo que mañana viene' = 'He said that tomorrow he'll come.' Alone, '¿Que mañana?' can be a clipped question meaning 'You mean tomorrow?' or 'That (happening) tomorrow?'. Word order and punctuation determine whether it's a conjunction ('que' = that) or an informal echo question.
target_language_example: Ella dijo que mañana nos veremos.
native_language_example: She said that we'll see each other tomorrow.

meaning: that I gave myself / that I realized (context-dependent).
additional_notes: This fragment can appear in different contexts. Most commonly it's part of a larger clause: as 'que me di cuenta' meaning 'that I realized' (literal: 'that I gave myself account') or 'que me di X' meaning 'that I gave myself X' (e.g., 'que me di un regalo' = 'that I gave myself a gift'). By itself it's incomplete—listen for the surrounding words to know whether it's about realizing something (me di cuenta) or giving/doing something for oneself (me di + noun/verb).
target_language_example: Fue algo que me di cuenta después.
native_language_example: It was something that I realized afterward.

meaning: that I left (to) / so I left to (somewhere or to do something).
additional_notes: Common in narratives to explain a reason + result: '... así que me fui a...' = '... so I left to go to...'. Followed by a place (casa, bar) or an infinitive/activity with 'a' + verb (acostar, acostarme). 'Me fui' = 'I left' or 'I went away' (reflexive form of ir). The 'que' often connects to a previous clause (e.g., 'Estaba cansado, así que...').
target_language_example: Estaba aburrido, así que me fui a caminar por el parque.
native_language_example: I was bored, so I left to walk in the park.

meaning: "that/which has (to me)" — part of a subordinate clause with the present perfect (ha + past participle) referring to something affecting the speaker.
additional_notes: Commonly appears in sentences where 'que' introduces a clause explaining, reporting, or describing something that has happened to the speaker. 'Me' is the indirect/object pronoun (to me / me), and 'ha' is the third-person singular of 'haber' used to form the present perfect (ha + past participle). Translate according to context: e.g. 'that has (made) me...', 'that has (told) me...', 'that has (seen) me...'.
target_language_example: Es algo que me ha alegrado mucho.
native_language_example: It's something that has made me very happy.

meaning: that you do (for me) / that you make (for me) — used to request or ask someone to do something for the speaker.
additional_notes: This is the subjunctive construction 'que' + pronoun + verb (hacer, subjunctive 'hagas'). Common in requests, desires, or commands: 'Quiero que me hagas X' = 'I want you to do X for me.' The exact English verb depends on the object (favor = do a favor, promesa = make a promise, caso = pay attention). Context determines formality.
target_language_example: ¿Puedes que me hagas un favor esta tarde?
native_language_example: Can you do me a favor this afternoon?

meaning: that I was going to / that I was about to (do something).
additional_notes: Commonly appears as part of a larger clause with a verb in the infinitive (e.g., 'que me iba a...') to report a past intention, expectation, or fear. Can express planned actions ('mudar', 'casar'), expected events, or imagined outcomes ('morir', 'volver loco'). In English often translated as 'that I was going to' or 'that I was about to.'
target_language_example: Le dije a mi hermano que me iba a mudar la semana que viene.
native_language_example: I told my brother that I was going to move next week.

meaning: that you were going to (do something) for me / to me.
additional_notes: This is part of a longer clause: 'que me ibas a + infinitive' (or sometimes 'que me ibas' with context). It reports what someone said or what the speaker expected — past intention or plan of 'you' toward the speaker. Translate as 'that you were going to...' or 'that you would...'. Common in reported speech and in expressions of expectation, surprise, or reproach.
target_language_example: Creí que me ibas a llamar ayer.
native_language_example: I thought you were going to call me yesterday.

meaning: 'that they kill me' (used figuratively to express strong emotion, disbelief or dramatic resignation)
additional_notes: Literally means 'that they kill me' and is grammatically a subordinate clause often used after verbs or exclamations (e.g., '¡Que me maten si...'). In everyday speech it's usually hyperbolic, similar to English 'I swear' or 'you can kill me' or 'I'd die' in informal, dramatic contexts. Can be strong language — avoid in very formal or sensitive situations.
target_language_example: ¡Que me maten si no recuerdo su nombre!
native_language_example: I'd swear I don't remember his name! (literally: 'May they kill me if I don't remember his name!')

meaning: that I will stay / that I will remain
additional_notes: This is a clause fragment combining the relative/conjunction 'que' ('that') with the reflexive verb 'quedarse' in future tense ('me quedaré' = I will stay). You usually see it as part of a larger sentence (e.g., 'Dije que me quedaré en casa' — 'I said that I will stay at home'). Use 'quedaré' to express a future action of staying or remaining; 'me' indicates the action applies to the speaker (I).
target_language_example: Ella dijo que me quedaré aquí hasta mañana.
native_language_example: She said that I will stay here until tomorrow.

meaning: 'that (needs) improving' or 'to be improved'.
additional_notes: Often appears after nouns or clauses to indicate something requires improvement. In many cases it's part of a larger phrase (e.g., 'hay que mejorar' = 'one must improve/there is room for improvement'). Alone, 'que mejorar' usually implies 'something to improve' or 'needs improving'.
target_language_example: Hay muchas cosas que mejorar en este proyecto.
native_language_example: There are many things that need improving in this project.

meaning: 'that (he/she/it) look' or 'that (someone) look/watch' — present subjunctive of mirar used in subordinate clauses
additional_notes: Used after verbs or expressions that trigger the subjunctive (e.g., querer, pedir, decir + que). Refers to someone else looking, watching, or checking something. The subject of 'mire' is different from the main clause subject. Can translate as 'that he/she/you (formal)/they look' or simply 'to look' depending on context.
target_language_example: Quiero que mire las fotos y me diga cuál le gusta.
native_language_example: I want him/her to look at the photos and tell me which one they like.

meaning: that his/her/its ... died (literally) — part of a clause describing the death of something or someone belonging to someone.
additional_notes: This sequence combines the relative/conjunction 'que' ('that') + the past tense 'murió' (he/she/it died) + the possessive adjective 'su' (his/her/its). By itself it's incomplete: 'su' must be followed by a noun (e.g., su hermano, su perro). It appears in sentences like 'Me contó que murió su padre' (He told me that his father died). Word order and agreement: 'murió' is third-person singular; the possessor is indicated by 'su'.
target_language_example: Ella dijo que murió su abuelo la semana pasada.
native_language_example: She said that her grandfather died last week.

meaning: 'que' + 'muy' used together for emphasis (often colloquial) — roughly 'that very' or 'so very', depending on context.
additional_notes: This combination appears when 'que' introduces a clause or exclamation and 'muy' intensifies an adjective or adverb that follows. It is not a fixed idiom by itself; its meaning depends on the surrounding sentence. In spoken Spanish you might see constructions like '¡Que muy bien!' (emphatic praise) or 'Es que muy caro' (colloquial/emphatic, sometimes ungrammatical in formal speech). Use carefully: some combinations are natural (e.g., 'que muy buena idea'), others sound informal or ungrammatical.
target_language_example: ¡Que muy buenas noticias nos trajiste!
native_language_example: What very good news you brought us!

meaning: what else / anything else
additional_notes: Common in questions to ask about additional items, information, or actions. Often appears in phrases like "¿Qué más?" or in longer questions such as "¿Qué más necesitas?" Note that interrogative qué carries an accent when written: qué más. Can be used on its own as a short question.
target_language_example: ¿Qué más?
native_language_example: What else?

meaning: that was born / who was born
additional_notes: Commonly used as a relative clause introducing someone's or something's birth (past). 'Nació' is the preterite of 'nacer' (to be born). Use 'que' = 'that' or 'who' to connect to a noun: e.g. 'la niña que nació' = 'the girl who was born'. Can refer to people, animals, or things (for events/dates).
target_language_example: Mi amigo, que nació en Argentina, habla español y portugués.
native_language_example: My friend, who was born in Argentina, speaks Spanish and Portuguese.

meaning: 'no way' / 'not at all' (used to reject or deny something emphatically)
additional_notes: Informal, used to strongly deny, refuse, or correct someone. Tone can be dismissive or emphatic depending on context. Often appears alone as an interjection (¡Que nada!) or within a sentence (—¿Te importa? —¡Que nada!). Similar to 'para nada' or 'de ninguna manera' but more colloquial.
target_language_example: —¿Te molesta si lo hago yo? —¡Que nada, hazlo tú!
native_language_example: —Does it bother you if I do it? —No way, go ahead!

meaning: that/which swims in (literal) — used to describe something that floats or exists in a liquid or figurative environment
additional_notes: A literal phrase: que = that/which, nada = swims, en = in. Often appears in descriptions (poetic or literal) like 'el pez que nada en el río' (the fish that swims in the river). Can also be used figuratively (e.g., ideas that 'swim in' or circulate in a context), but this uses 'nadar' metaphorically and is less common. Make sure agreement and tense of the verb match the subject when using different forms (nada/nadan).
target_language_example: Vimos al delfín que nada en la bahía.
native_language_example: We saw the dolphin that swims in the bay.

meaning: 'that/which no' or 'that no (one/thing) ...'
additional_notes: This combination appears in negative constructions and is typically followed by a noun (e.g., que ningún hombre) or pronoun to mean 'that no one/thing...' or to emphasize absence. It often appears after verbs or clauses: e.g., 'dijo que ningún...' or 'pensó que ningún...'. In many cases Spanish uses 'que' as a relative/conjunction and 'ningún' (short form of 'ninguno') as the negative determiner before a singular masculine noun. If the noun is feminine use 'ninguna' (e.g., que ninguna). For general negatives without a following noun you might see 'que ninguno' (masculine pronoun) or 'que ninguna'.
target_language_example: Me contó que ningún vecino supo lo que pasó.
native_language_example: He told me that no neighbor knew what happened.

meaning: 'that you shouldn't' or 'which you shouldn't'.
additional_notes: Used to introduce advice, a warning, or a statement about something someone ought not to do. It often follows verbs or clauses (e.g., 'es algo que no deberías hacer' = 'it's something you shouldn't do'). Tone can be neutral or firm depending on context.
target_language_example: Es una decisión que no deberías tomar a la ligera.
native_language_example: It's a decision that you shouldn't make lightly.

meaning: that it/he/she/wasn't
additional_notes: Used after verbs like 'creer', 'parecer', 'saber', 'decir' to introduce a subordinate clause meaning 'that it/he/she/wasn't' or 'that it didn't happen / wasn't the cause'. The exact English pronoun/context (it/he/she) is determined by the previous noun. Often used to deny responsibility, explain causes, or reject an interpretation.
target_language_example: Sé que no fue su culpa.
native_language_example: I know that it wasn't his/her fault.

meaning: 'that/which/when there had not been' or 'that [someone] had not (done something)' (past perfect negation).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a subordinate clause in the past perfect (pluscuamperfecto) or past context to say something did not happen or someone had not done/seen/heard something. Common after verbs of saying, believing, explaining (dijo/aseguró/tuvo) or to give reasons (debido a que no había...). The subject and verb that follow determine the exact English translation: 'that he/she/they had not...' or 'that there hadn't been...'.
target_language_example: Ella dijo que no había entendido la pregunta.
native_language_example: She said that she had not understood the question.

meaning: that you haven't
additional_notes: Commonly used after verbs or phrases (e.g., me temo que, veo que, parece que) to report or comment that someone has not done or experienced something. Followed by a past participle (perfect tense) or other verb forms: "que no has entendido" = "that you haven't understood." Used in spoken and written Spanish; tone depends on context (neutral, disappointed, critical, etc.).
target_language_example: Me preocupa que no has comido hoy.
native_language_example: I'm worried that you haven't eaten today.

meaning: 'that you weren't going to' (you were not going to do something).
additional_notes: Common part of a subordinate clause introduced by verbs of thinking, saying or believing (creer, pensar, decir). Follows expressions like 'creí', 'pensé', 'dijiste' and is usually followed by an infinitive (e.g., 'a venir', 'a participar'). Used to report an expectation or a statement about a future action that did not occur or was unexpected.
target_language_example: Creí que no ibas a entenderme.
native_language_example: I thought that you weren't going to understand me.

meaning: that you can't
additional_notes: Commonly follows impersonal expressions (e.g., 'es una lástima/pena') to express regret that someone cannot do something. 'Puedas' is the present subjunctive of 'poder' and is used after expressions of emotion, doubt, desire, or possibility. The subject is 'tú' (you, informal). For formal 'you' use 'que no pueda'.
target_language_example: Me preocupa que no puedas terminar a tiempo.
native_language_example: I'm worried that you can't finish on time.

meaning: 'that it/he/she/you/etc. not be too' or 'that it not be too (much/late/etc.)'
additional_notes: Common clause used after verbs of hoping/wishing (espero, esperamos, ojalá) to express a desire that something not be excessive or not happen too late. The verb following 'demasiado' is often an adjective (e.g., tarde) or adverb. Structure: [verb of hope] + que + no + subjunctive (sea) + demasiado + [adjective/adverb].
target_language_example: Espero que no sea demasiado difícil para ti.
native_language_example: I hope it's not too difficult for you.

meaning: I hope you don't mind / that you won't be bothered by it.
additional_notes: Used to politely introduce or apologize for something you did or will do. Common in phrases like 'Espero que no te importe...' (I hope you don't mind...). It's polite and neutral — suitable in formal and informal contexts depending on tone. Literally: 'that it doesn't matter to you.'
target_language_example: Espero que no te importe que traje a mi perro.
native_language_example: I hope you don't mind that I brought my dog.

meaning: 'that you don't have' or 'that you have not'.
additional_notes: Common structure combining the relative/complementizer 'que' with a negated possession/experience verb phrase (no tienes = you don't have). Used to report opinions, explanations or reported speech: 'He said that you don't have...', 'I think that you don't have...'. Often followed by nouns (nada, para qué, que + infinitive) or clauses explaining what's lacking.
target_language_example: Creo que no tienes tiempo para venir mañana.
native_language_example: I think that you don't have time to come tomorrow.

meaning: that (it) will not happen again / that (someone) will not return
additional_notes: Commonly used after verbs like prometer (to promise) or saber (to know). In contexts with events (ocurrir/pasar/suceder) it means 'that it will not happen again'. With people or things, it can mean 'that (he/she/it) will not come back' (no volverá). Often followed by 'a + infinitive' (no volverá a ocurrir = will not happen again). Tone can be reassuring or final.
target_language_example: Te prometo que no volverá a ocurrir.
native_language_example: I promise you it won't happen again.

meaning: that will not (do something) again / that will no longer
additional_notes: Used to introduce an action or situation that will not be repeated in the future. Often follows a noun or clause (e.g., 'una decisión que no volverá a tomar' = 'a decision that you won't make again') or appears after verbs like 'prometer' or 'decir'. The exact verb that will not be repeated is usually given after 'a' (infinitive).
target_language_example: Tomó una decisión que no volverá a tomar.
native_language_example: He made a decision that he will not make again.

meaning: 'that I am not going to' or 'that I won't' (followed by an infinitive).
additional_notes: This phrase combines the connector que ('that') with the first-person present of ir + a (voy a) used to form the near future. It introduces a subordinate clause stating what the speaker will not do. It must be followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., voy a salir, voy a participar, voy a quedarme). Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Te prometo que no voy a rendirme.
native_language_example: I promise you that I am not going to give up.

meaning: 'that we are' or 'that we are (doing...)' — part of a clause used to describe an ongoing action or state for 'we'.
additional_notes: This is not a standalone phrase but a sequence often found inside longer sentences (e.g., 'es que nos estamos equivocando' = 'it's that we are making a mistake'). It combines the conjunction/relative word 'que' + the pronoun 'nos' (we/us, reflexive or object) + the present progressive auxiliary 'estamos' (we are). Used to introduce what 'we' are doing or experiencing now. The exact meaning depends on the verb or clause that follows (often a gerund: 'estamos haciendo', 'estamos equivocando', or a past participle in passive-like constructions).
target_language_example: Es que nos estamos acostumbrando a la nueva rutina.
native_language_example: It's that we are getting used to the new routine.

meaning: that we become / that we turn (into) / that we return (to each other) — depends on context.
additional_notes: Phrase uses the subjunctive verb 'volvamos' (from volver). Meaning depends on context: 'volver' can mean 'to return' (physically or emotionally), 'to turn' (change into), or 'to do again'. With 'que' it often introduces a wish, hope, cause, or subordinate clause (e.g., 'Espero que nos volvamos a ver' = I hope we see each other again). 'Nos' indicates reflexive/plural 'we/each other.'
target_language_example: Espero que nos volvamos a ver pronto.
native_language_example: I hope that we see each other again soon.

meaning: a sequence of the relative pronoun que (that/who/which) followed by the possessive nuestro/a(s) (our); used in clauses referring to something belonging to us or associated with us.
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiomatic phrase. 'Que nuestro' often appears within larger constructions (e.g., 'la casa que nuestro abuelo compró' is grammatical because 'nuestro' modifies 'abuelo'). When 'que' introduces a clause about possession, Spanish more commonly uses 'que es nuestro' or 'que pertenece a nosotros'. Word order matters: 'que nuestro' is grammatical when 'nuestro' is an adjective modifying a noun that follows (i.e., 'que nuestro + noun'), or when 'nuestro' attaches to a noun earlier in the sentence ('nuestro + noun que ...').
target_language_example: La casa que nuestro padre compró está en la colina.
native_language_example: The house that our father bought is on the hill.

meaning: 'to have to obey' or 'must obey' (expresses obligation to follow orders, rules, laws).
additional_notes: Commonly appears with 'tener que' + infinitive (tener que obedecer) or with modal expressions indicating obligation. Used to talk about needing to follow rules, orders, laws, or someone's instructions. In the example sentences the construction implies necessity: 'tengo que obedecer' = 'I have to obey.'
target_language_example: En esta empresa, tenemos que obedecer las instrucciones de seguridad.
native_language_example: In this company, we have to obey the safety instructions.

meaning: that I take care of / to take care of for me
additional_notes: This is a short chunk combining the conjunction 'que' with the reflexive infinitive 'ocuparme' (ocupar + me). It often appears in larger sentences: e.g. 'Es algo que ocuparme' (something for me to take care of) or 'Quiero que ocuparme de eso' (nonstandard; standard: 'Quiero ocuparme de eso' or 'Quiero que alguien se ocupe de eso'). Beginners should note the usual correct patterns: 'ocuparme de' = 'to take care of (something) myself' and 'que' may introduce relative clauses ('algo que ocuparme') or subordinate clauses but word order matters.
target_language_example: Tengo muchos asuntos que ocuparme este mes.
native_language_example: I have many matters to take care of this month.

meaning: that I take care of / that I deal with
additional_notes: This structure appears after verbs or expressions that introduce a subordinate clause (e.g., 'dijo que ocuparme de...') and uses the infinitive 'ocuparme' with the reflexive pronoun 'me' (to indicate 'for me' or 'I will'). It implies responsibility or action someone will perform. Commonly seen as 'que me ocupe de' (subjunctive) or 'que ocuparme de' in informal spoken reductions, but the fully correct forms are 'que me ocupe de' (subjunctive) or 'que me ocupe de'/'para ocuparme de' depending on context.
target_language_example: Dijo que ocuparme de la reserva del hotel.
native_language_example: He said that I should take care of the hotel reservation.

meaning: 'how I hate' / 'that I hate' (expresses strong dislike)
additional_notes: Used to emphasize strong dislike for something. Often appears in exclamatory phrases like "¡Qué odio cuando...!" or in colloquial complaints: "Que odio que...". Written accent on "Qué" is required in exclamations (¡Qué!) but is sometimes omitted in casual writing. When used as a clause introducer ("Que odio que..."), the accent is often still written on "qué" when it means "what/that" in some contexts; usage varies informally. Followed by a noun or clause describing what is hated.
target_language_example: Que odio que se acabe la batería del móvil.
native_language_example: How I hate that the phone battery runs out.

meaning: 'that I hear' / 'that I listen to' (used after expressions like 'es la primera vez' or 'cada vez' to introduce what is heard).
additional_notes: Commonly follows verbs or phrases like 'es la primera vez', 'cada vez' or 'siempre que' to introduce the thing heard. In these examples, 'oigo' is first-person singular present of 'oír' (to hear). Use it to talk about hearing sounds, songs, news, or mentions of someone. Not formal or slang—just standard Spanish grammar.
target_language_example: No puedo creer que oigo esto ahora mismo.
native_language_example: I can't believe that I hear this right now.

meaning: 'to have to tidy/organize' or 'to have to order (something)'.
additional_notes: Depending on context, 'ordenar' has two common meanings: 1) to tidy/organize (rooms, ideas, shoes) and 2) to order (from a menu) or to give an order (command). When used with 'tener que' or 'voy a tener que', it expresses obligation: 'have to' do something. Pay attention to context to choose the correct English translation.
target_language_example: Tengo que ordenar mi escritorio antes de estudiar.
native_language_example: I have to tidy/organize my desk before studying.

meaning: 'may it go (well) for you' — a wish of good luck or well-being addressed to 'vosotros' or a plural 'you'.
additional_notes: Common in Spain (vosotros form) or when addressing more than one person informally. Often followed by 'bien' (well) or a noun (la vida). Equivalent to 'que les vaya' in Latin America (usted/ustedes forms). Used to express hope or a blessing: 'I hope things go well for you.'
target_language_example: Que os vaya bien en el examen.
native_language_example: May things go well for you on the exam.

meaning: that (something) became dark / that (someone) darkened; past-subjunctive phrase used to express purpose, cause, desire, or hypotheticals about darkening.
additional_notes: Que + past subjunctive (oscurecer → oscureciera) appears in subordinate clauses after verbs or expressions requiring the subjunctive. Common uses: wishes (quería que oscureciera), purpose or result (para que no oscureciera), reported desires, or after impersonal/causal constructions. Context decides translation: it can mean 'so that it would get dark', 'that it darkened', or 'that he/she/it darkened.' The form is somewhat formal/literary; colloquially you might hear 'que oscureciera' or use other tenses like 'que oscurezca' (present subjunctive) or 'que se oscurezca'.
target_language_example: Esperaba que oscureciera antes de salir para no llevar paraguas.
native_language_example: I hoped that it would get dark before leaving so I wouldn't need an umbrella.

meaning: 'than another' or 'than others' (used in comparisons).
additional_notes: Commonly appears in comparative phrases, often after a comparative adjective or expression: e.g. 'me gusta más este que otro' (I like this one more than another). It can also appear in contexts meaning 'than any other' when paired with words like 'ningún' or superlatives. Word order and articles/pronouns around it matter: Spaniards often say 'que ningún otro' (than no other).
target_language_example: Este libro es mejor que otro que leí el año pasado.
native_language_example: This book is better than another I read last year.

meaning: literally 'that to hear' — not a standard fixed phrase; may appear when a clause uses que + oír in noncanonical word order or in exclamatory fragments meaning surprise about what was heard
additional_notes: This sequence is uncommon as an isolated phrase. More natural are 'oír que...' (to hear that...) or exclamations like '¡Qué fuerte!' to react. 'Que oír' can appear in literary or colloquial inversions (e.g., after conjunctions or in poetry) but is not a set idiom. Use 'oír que + clause' to report news: 'Oí que...'
target_language_example: ¡Que oír eso me dejó sin palabras!
native_language_example: To hear that left me speechless!

meaning: 'to have to pay the' (introduces an obligation to pay something specific).
additional_notes: This sequence appears when you need to say someone must pay a specific item: 'tener que pagar + el/la + [noun]'. In English: 'we have to pay the rent', 'I have to pay the meter'. The subject and correct article/gender follow in normal sentence order (e.g., 'tenemos que pagar el alquiler', 'tengo que pagar la multa').
target_language_example: Tengo que pagar el recibo antes del viernes.
native_language_example: I have to pay the bill before Friday.

meaning: that (one) must pay for / that costs (to be paid by someone).
additional_notes: Used to introduce the thing or reason someone has to pay. Often appears after verbs or nouns: e.g., 'es algo que pagar por' or 'tengo algo que pagar por' (I have something I must pay for). In many contexts Spanish prefers 'que' + infinitive or relative constructions; word order and exact phrasing may vary (e.g., 'algo que pagar' or 'que tengo que pagar').
target_language_example: Es un servicio que pagar por mes.
native_language_example: It's a service that you pay for monthly.

meaning: "that/which dad" or part of a clause referring to 'dad' (literal), often appears in longer sentences (e.g., 'que papá dijo' = 'that dad said').
additional_notes: Alone, 'que papá' is not a complete phrase in Spanish; it's typically part of a relative or reporting clause (introduced by 'que') referring to 'papá' (dad). Depending on context, 'que' can mean 'that', 'which', or introduce reported speech. You will normally see it inside sentences like 'La carta que papá escribió' (the letter that dad wrote) or 'Dijo que papá vendrá' (He said that dad will come).
target_language_example: La foto que papá tomó está en la mesa.
native_language_example: The photo that dad took is on the table.

meaning: so much that; to the point that; such that (used to introduce a result or extreme degree).
additional_notes: Commonly used in informal spoken Spanish to emphasize a consequence or extreme degree: 'era tan... que para...' or simply 'que para...' before stating the surprising result. Often appears in constructions like 'era tan caro, que para comprarlo...'. Can also appear in comparisons or to introduce a purpose in some regional uses, but primary use is to mark a result or emphasis.
target_language_example: Llegó tarde, que para colmo se había olvidado las llaves.
native_language_example: He arrived late, and to make matters worse he had forgotten his keys.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase in Spanish; likely a fragment of a larger clause. 'Que' can be a conjunction or interrogative, 'pasar' means 'to pass/happen/spend', and 'la' is the feminine definite article or object pronoun. Together they usually appear as part of expressions like 'que pasar la noche' or in clauses where additional words complete the meaning.
additional_notes: This sequence of words is not a common standalone expression. Interpret it by examining surrounding context. Possible continuations include 'que pasar la noche' (to spend the night) or constructions where 'la' refers back to a feminine noun (e.g., 'que pasar la responsabilidad'). Beginners should learn components separately and common collocations such as 'pasar la noche', 'que pasa?', and pronominal uses like 'pasarla bien'.
target_language_example: No entiendo lo que quieres decir con 'que pasar la' en esa oración; por favor, escribe la frase completa.
native_language_example: I don't understand what you mean by 'que pasar la' in that sentence; please write the complete phrase.

meaning: when I pass by
additional_notes: In these examples, que is usually part of the larger pattern cada vez que, meaning 'every time' or 'whenever'. paso is the yo form of pasar and here usually means 'I pass by' or 'I go past' a place. Don't confuse que paso with qué pasó, which means 'what happened?'
target_language_example: Cada vez que paso por aquí, pienso en mi abuelo.
native_language_example: Every time I pass by here, I think about my grandfather.

meaning: 'that (to) think about me' — a clause introducer 'que' followed by the infinitive phrase 'pensar en mi' (note: standard orthography in Spanish requires an accent on 'mí' when it's a pronoun, but user requested 'mi' so entry reflects that exact sequence)
additional_notes: This sequence appears when a clause (introduced by que) contains the infinitive phrase 'pensar en mi' ('to think about me'). In standard written Spanish the pronoun should be 'mí' (accented) after prepositions: 'pensar en mí'. The unaccented 'mi' is normally the possessive 'my' and is not standard here, but the exact sequence 'que pensar en mi' may appear in informal writing or as a transcription. It commonly follows verbs, impersonal expressions, or is embedded in larger clauses: e.g., 'Dijo que pensar en mi le daba miedo.' The phrase is compositional: meaning derives from its parts ('que' + 'pensar en mi').
target_language_example: Ella dijo que pensar en mi le impedía dormir.
native_language_example: She said that thinking about me kept her from sleeping.

meaning: that I thought
additional_notes: Usually not a fixed expression on its own, but part of a longer sentence. Without an accent on que, it normally introduces a clause meaning 'that/which I thought.' Pensé is the simple past form of pensar, meaning 'I thought.' If written as ¿qué pensé?, with an accent and question marks, it would mean 'what did I think?'
target_language_example: Hice lo que pensé que era mejor.
native_language_example: I did what I thought was best.

meaning: 'that (he/she/they) thought that' — introduces a reported past thought or belief.
additional_notes: Used in reported speech to convey what someone thought in the past. The subject (he/she/they) is usually mentioned earlier (e.g., Mary dice que pensó que...). In English this often becomes "said/thought that (he/she) thought that..." It can introduce a clause with a past-tense idea (could do, knew, seemed, etc.).
target_language_example: Ella dijo que pensó que iba a llover.
native_language_example: She said that she thought that it was going to rain.

meaning: nothing to lose / nothing to be lost (often in expressions like 'no hay que perder' or 'no tienes que perder'),
additional_notes: Alone 'que perder' is not a complete phrase; it appears in constructions expressing that there is 'nothing to lose' (no hay que perder / no tienes que perder) or in comparisons (algo que perder = something to lose). Often used after negation (no hay/ no tienes) or with tener. Pay attention to context and articles/verbs surrounding it.
target_language_example: No tienes que perder nada si lo intentas.
native_language_example: You have nothing to lose if you try it.

meaning: 'that/which to forgive me' — part of constructions meaning someone must forgive me or I have to forgive myself (depending on context).
additional_notes: This string combines the conjunction/relative word 'que' with the infinitive 'perdonarme' (to forgive me). In everyday Spanish you will more often see 'tener que' + infinitive to say 'to have to' (e.g., 'tendré que perdonarme' = 'I'll have to forgive myself') or the subject + 'tiene que perdonarme' = 'he/she/you (formal) has to forgive me'. Context determines whether the action is forgiving the speaker (perdonarme) or the speaker forgiving themselves (me perdonar). 'Perdonarme' is the infinitive + object pronoun 'me'.
target_language_example: Tienes que perdonarme por llegar tarde.
native_language_example: You have to forgive me for arriving late.

meaning: that I lost / that I have lost
additional_notes: Que introduces a subordinate clause here meaning "that". Perdí is the first-person preterite of perder (to lose). Together, que perdí is used to report something you or someone else lost (physical items like "mis llaves" or abstract things like "la cabeza" = "lost my head/mind"). In English it often becomes "that I lost" or simply "I lost..." depending on context.
target_language_example: Creo que perdí mi boleto.
native_language_example: I think that I lost my ticket.

meaning: that (to) remain / that stay
additional_notes: This looks like a combination of the relative/complementizer 'que' + the infinitive 'permanecer' (to remain/stay). Alone it's not a fixed phrase in Spanish; it appears in clauses like 'es posible que permanecer...' or 'decidimos que permanecer...' but standard Spanish usually uses a conjugated verb after 'que' (e.g., 'que permanezca', 'que permanezcan') or an infinitive without 'que' after certain verbs (e.g., 'decidimos permanecer'). Using 'que permanecer' directly is uncommon in natural speech; learners will more often see 'que' + conjugated verb or just the infinitive by itself.
target_language_example: Decidieron que permanecer en casa era lo mejor.
native_language_example: They decided that staying at home was best.

meaning: 'that you think' (introduces what someone believes or assumes).
additional_notes: Used to report or refer to another person's thought or belief. Often follows verbs like sé (I know), supongo (I suppose), creo (I believe). In English it's usually translated as 'that you think' or 'you think that'. Word order in Spanish: 'que' + verb (piensas) + 'que' + clause; here the first 'que' can be part of the main clause (e.g., 'Sé que...') and 'piensas que' introduces the subordinate clause.
target_language_example: Sé que piensas que no debo ir, pero quiero intentarlo.
native_language_example: I know that you think I shouldn't go, but I want to try.

meaning: that we could
additional_notes: Usually appears after verbs like pensar or creer to introduce an idea, possibility, or suggestion. podríamos is the conditional form of poder, so it often sounds softer and less direct than podemos.
target_language_example: Creo que podríamos hablar mañana.
native_language_example: I think we could talk tomorrow.

meaning: what to put on it / what to add (to something).
additional_notes: Commonly used when deciding what to add, put on, or give to an object, dish, outfit, etc. Often appears in questions or informal decisions: ¿Qué ponerle? = "What should I put on it?" Typically includes the clitic -le referring to the item receiving the addition; context (the item) may be explicit or implied.
target_language_example: ¿Qué ponerle al sándwich?
native_language_example: What should I put on the sandwich?

meaning: which to put on for (an event or situation); what to wear to
additional_notes: This is a fragment often used when asking or talking about what clothing to wear for a specific occasion. It usually appears inside questions or clauses, e.g. «¿Qué ponernos al...?» or «No sé qué ponernos al...». In full sentences you will more commonly hear «qué ponernos para» or the interrogative «qué me pongo para...». The construction uses the infinitive ponerse (to put on oneself) with the reflexive pronoun and can be adjusted for person: «qué me pongo» (what should I wear), «qué ponernos» (what should we wear).
target_language_example: No sé qué ponernos al concierto de esta noche, ¿tienes alguna idea?
native_language_example: I don't know what to wear to tonight's concert, do you have any idea?

meaning: 'we need to catch up' or 'we need to get up to date'.
additional_notes: Common phrase used to say someone needs to update themselves or catch up on tasks, news, or progress. Often appears after 'tenemos' (we have) or 'hay que' (one must). Can refer to work (finish pending tasks), information (share news), or a meeting to update each other. Literal image: 'ponerse al día' = 'to put oneself up to the day'.
target_language_example: Tenemos que ponernos al día esta semana con los correos pendientes.
native_language_example: We need to catch up this week on the pending emails.

meaning: 'that' or 'which' + 'for' (literal combination); often appears in clauses like 'que por...' introducing a reason or cause (equivalent to 'because' or 'since' in some contexts).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom by itself; it's simply the relative/connector que followed by the preposition por. It commonly appears when giving reasons or explanations (e.g., '...que, por ser...' = '...which, because it is...') or in causal phrases ('que por eso...' = 'which is why...'). Pay attention to punctuation: a comma often precedes 'que por' when it introduces an explanatory clause.
target_language_example: No vino, que por la lluvia no quería salir.
native_language_example: He didn't come, because he didn't want to go out due to the rain.

meaning: used to add emphasis or polite insistence, similar to 'please' or 'I ask you, please'.
additional_notes: 'que por favor' is a colloquial emphatic phrase used to plead, insist politely, or express frustration when asking someone for something. It often appears in spoken Spanish and can follow a request or interjection: e.g. '¡Hazlo, que por favor!' It adds urgency or frustration but remains polite. Not all Spanish speakers use it; context and intonation matter.
target_language_example: Dime la verdad, que por favor necesito saberlo.
native_language_example: Tell me the truth, please — I really need to know.

meaning: that/which to practice; (used to introduce something one should practice)
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase on its own; it's the relative pronoun 'que' followed by the infinitive 'practicar'. It appears in sentences like 'tengo que practicar' (I have to practice) or in relative clauses 'cosas que practicar' (things to practice). Pay attention to context: 'tengo que practicar' means obligation, while 'que practicar' after a noun usually describes purpose or selection.
target_language_example: Tengo cosas que practicar antes del examen.
native_language_example: I have things to practice before the exam.

meaning: that I prefer / which I prefer
additional_notes: Used to introduce something you prefer, often following a clause or noun. Common in sentences like 'Es algo que prefiero evitar' (It's something I prefer to avoid) or 'El libro que prefiero es...' (The book that I prefer is...). 'Que' can mean 'that' or 'which' and links to the thing being preferred; 'prefiero' is first person singular present of 'preferir'.
target_language_example: La opción que prefiero es la segunda.
native_language_example: The option that I prefer is the second one.

meaning: to have to ask; must ask / just ask (imperative sense in some contexts).
additional_notes: Often appears after verbs like 'tener' (tener que preguntar = to have to ask) or in phrases like 'solo tienes que preguntar' (you only need to ask). Depending on word order and context, it can mean an obligation ('I had to ask') or a simple instruction/encouragement ('just ask'). In Spanish sentences the full structure usually includes a conjugated verb (e.g., 'tienes que preguntar', 'tenía que preguntar').
target_language_example: Si tienes dudas, solo tienes que preguntar.
native_language_example: If you have doubts, you just have to ask.

meaning: to have to prepare / must prepare
additional_notes: This phrase combines the modal 'tener que' (to have to) with the verb 'preparar' (to prepare). In natural Spanish you usually see the full form 'tener que preparar' or a conjugated form like 'tengo que preparar', 'tienes que preparar', 'me tengo que preparar' (reflexive when preparing oneself). It expresses obligation or necessity to get something ready (food, exam, body/mind, etc.).
target_language_example: Tengo que preparar la presentación para mañana.
native_language_example: I have to prepare the presentation for tomorrow.

meaning: Not a standard, standalone Spanish phrase. Appears as a fragment where que introduces a clause with the verb prestar; meaning depends on the full clause (e.g., 'that [someone] lend', 'that [someone] pay').
additional_notes:
As written, «que prestar» is usually an incomplete fragment. It can occur when words are omitted (ellipses) or in written fragments. Possible contexts:
- part of a subordinate clause: «que prestar atención» (that [one] pay attention)
- subjunctive structures: «que prestar» followed by a subjunctive conjugation (e.g., «que prestarías»/«que me prestes») when words are missing
- may be a transcription or typing error for phrases like «qué prestar» (what to lend)
For clarity, ask for the full sentence. Beginners should look for the object and verb conjugation following prestar to determine meaning.
target_language_example: Dices que prestar atención es importante, y tienes razón.
native_language_example: You say that paying attention is important, and you're right.

meaning: 'to have to pay attention' or 'must pay attention'.
additional_notes: This phrase combines the verb phrase 'prestar atención' (to pay attention) with 'que' to express obligation—equivalent to 'tener que' + infinitive in many contexts (e.g., 'tenéis que prestar atención' = 'you (pl.) have to pay attention'). Common in instructions and reminders. Use 'prestar atención a' when specifying what to pay attention to.
target_language_example: Tienes que prestar atención a los detalles en la clase.
native_language_example: You have to pay attention to the details in class.

meaning: 'that/probably' used to introduce a clause expressing probability (that ... probably ...).
additional_notes: Combines the conjunction 'que' (that) with 'probablemente' (probably). Used to report or comment on something likely to happen or be true. Common in spoken and written Spanish; word order is flexible (e.g., 'probablemente que...' is less common than 'que probablemente...').
target_language_example: Me dijo que probablemente vendrá mañana.
native_language_example: He told me that he'll probably come tomorrow.

meaning: 'to try' or 'to taste' (infinitive probar preceded by que); often appears after verbs/expressions like 'tener', 'hay', or 'algo que' meaning 'something to try' or 'that to try'.
additional_notes: Alone 'que probar' is not a fixed phrase; it combines the relative/connector 'que' with the verb 'probar' (to try, to taste, to test). Common uses: 'algo que probar' = something to try/taste; 'no hay que probar' (rare) would be part of a larger clause. Word order and meaning depend on the surrounding sentence. 'Probar' can mean to try out (an experience), to taste food, or to test something.
target_language_example: Tengo algo que probar en el restaurante nuevo.
native_language_example: I have something to try at the new restaurant.

meaning: that (you) promise me / (you) must promise me.
additional_notes: This phrase appears in commands or requests: 'tienes que prometerme' or 'tiene que prometerme' means 'you have to promise me' / 'you must promise me'. 'Que' here often follows verbs like 'tienes' or 'tiene' forming an obligation ('tienes que' = 'you have to'). 'Prometerme' is the infinitive 'prometer' + object pronoun 'me' (to promise me). Use the correct conjugation for the subject: 'tienes que prometerme' (informal you), 'tiene que prometerme' (formal he/she/you formal).
target_language_example: Tienes que prometerme que vendrás mañana.
native_language_example: You have to promise me that you will come tomorrow.

meaning: how soon; so soon
additional_notes: Used to comment on the shortness of time until something happened or will happen. Often appears in exclamations (¡Que pronto pasó el tiempo!) or in relative/clauses to emphasize quickness. Not a fixed idiom—combines 'que' (what/how) + 'pronto' (soon). Tone can be surprised or impressed.
target_language_example: ¡Que pronto llegó el verano este año!
native_language_example: How quickly summer arrived this year!

meaning: that (to) protect / which to protect
additional_notes: This is a short phrase made of the relative pronoun or conjunction 'que' plus the infinitive 'proteger' (proteger → to protect). Alone it is incomplete and typically appears inside a larger sentence, e.g. after words like 'algo', 'nada', or in relative clauses: 'algo que proteger' (something to protect) or 'que proteger' as part of a clause: 'Tengo que proteger...' (I have to protect...). Context determines whether 'que' is a relative pronoun ('which/that') or part of a periphrasis ('tener que' = have to). Note spelling: in Spanish 'proteger' has an accent on the second 'e' only in some conjugations (no accent in infinitive).
target_language_example: Tengo algo que proteger.
native_language_example: I have something to protect.

meaning: that I can trust (you); that I can rely on (you).
additional_notes: Commonly appears after verbs expressing knowledge, feeling, or supposition (e.g., sé, siento, supongo, ahora sé). Often followed by 'en' + person: 'que puedo confiar en ti' = 'that I can trust you.' In everyday English this is usually rendered as 'that I can trust you' or 'that I can rely on you.'
target_language_example: Ahora sé que puedo confiar en ti.
native_language_example: Now I know that I can trust you.

meaning: Depends on context — 'que' introduces a subordinate clause and 'quedar' is the verb meaning to remain/be left, to meet/arrange, to fit, or to end up. Together they appear when a clause uses quedar (e.g., 'que quedar' = 'that (to) remain' or 'that (to) meet/arrange'), but they are not a fixed idiom.
additional_notes: This is not a set phrase; 'que' is a relative/conjunction ('that/which' or introducing reported speech) and 'quedar' is the main verb. Examples: 'algo que quedar' appears in relative clauses ('algo que queda' = 'something that remains'); in reported speech/commands you may see subjunctive forms after 'que' (e.g., 'dijo que quedáramos' = 'he said that we should meet'). Pay attention to tense, mood, and subject agreement. For learners: study common uses of 'quedar' (remain, arrange to meet, fit, result) and remember 'que' often just means 'that'/'which' before the verb.
target_language_example: Dijo que quedaramos en la plaza, pero al final no vinieron.
native_language_example: He said that (we should) meet in the square, but in the end they didn't come.

meaning: 'to have to stay' (literally: 'that I stay' — used after expressions of obligation like 'tener que').
additional_notes: This phrase combines the obligation construction 'tener que' (to have to) with the reflexive verb 'quedarse' (to stay). In Spanish the infinitive can follow 'tener que': 'tengo que quedarme' = 'I have to stay'. Often shortened in speech to 'tengo que quedarme' or simply 'tengo que' + verb. Use 'quedarme' when the subject is 'I' (me). Change the pronoun for other subjects (quedarte, quedarse, quedarnos, quedaros, quedarse).
target_language_example: Tengo que quedarme en casa esta noche.
native_language_example: I have to stay at home tonight.

meaning: that I stay in / for me to stay in
additional_notes: This is a short sequence that can appear inside larger clauses after verbs or expressions that require a subordinate clause (e.g., 'decidí que quedarme en casa era mejor'). It uses 'que' as a subordinating conjunction + infinitive with reflexive pronoun 'me' attached to the infinitive 'quedar' (quedarme). It often expresses a decision, reason or preference about someone staying somewhere. Word order can vary: 'decidí que quedarme en casa era mejor' or 'decidí quedarme en casa' (the second is more natural; the form with 'que' appears when embedding the idea in a larger clause).
target_language_example: Decidieron que quedarme en casa sería lo mejor.
native_language_example: They decided that me staying at home would be best.

meaning: that (there is) something to complain about / what to complain about
additional_notes: Used to express that there is a reason or cause for complaining. Often appears in phrases like 'no hay que quejarse' (there's nothing to complain about) or 'hay que quejarse' (one should complain). 'Que' here introduces the idea/reason; the phrase is somewhat idiomatic and depends on context.
target_language_example: No hay que quejarse: el servicio fue rápido y amable.
native_language_example: There's nothing to complain about: the service was fast and friendly.

meaning: that they want
additional_notes: Usually appears inside a longer sentence after verbs like decir, creer, or suponer. Here que means "that" (not a question word). Note the contrast with ¿qué quieren?, with an accent and question marks, which means "what do they want?" or "what do you all want?".
target_language_example: Pienso que quieren venir mañana.
native_language_example: I think they want to come tomorrow.

meaning: that they want to talk (or who want to talk)
additional_notes: A relative clause using que + verb phrase. Can introduce a noun phrase meaning "people/things that want to talk" or follow a noun: e.g., "las personas que quieren hablar" = "the people who want to talk." Context determines whether it's part of a larger sentence. "Quieren" is present tense (they want).
target_language_example: Hay varios estudiantes que quieren hablar después de clase.
native_language_example: There are several students who want to talk after class.

meaning: 'that/which really' or 'that truly' — used to emphasize truth or reality of a statement.
additional_notes: Que realmente combines the relative word 'que' (that/which) with 'realmente' (really/truly). It's used to add emphasis or confirm that what follows or is described is true. It appears in sentences like 'Es algo que realmente me importa' (It's something that really matters to me) or 'Lo dijo alguien que realmente sabe' (He said it someone who truly knows). Word order: 'que' + 'realmente' + verb/adjective/phrase.
target_language_example: Es una decisión que realmente cambia todo.
native_language_example: It's a decision that really changes everything.

meaning: 'to have to pick up (someone)'.
additional_notes: Used after verbs like 'tener' (tener que) to say you must go pick someone up (from a place). 'Recoger a' takes a person as direct object (recoger a mi hermano, recoger a los niños). Common for picking up from home, school, a friend's house, etc.
target_language_example: Tengo que recoger a mi hermana del colegio a las cuatro.
native_language_example: I have to pick up my sister from school at four.

meaning: 'to have to admit' or 'must admit / acknowledge'.
additional_notes: Used with different subjects and tenses. Often appears as 'tener que reconocer' (to have to admit) or 'hay que reconocer' (one must admit / it must be acknowledged). Commonly followed by a clause or a noun phrase (e.g., 'que...','sus derechos','la fuente'). Useful for conceding a point or acknowledging facts or rights.
target_language_example: Tengo que reconocer que fue una buena idea.
native_language_example: I have to admit that it was a good idea.

meaning: to remember; that to remember (depends on context).
additional_notes: Alone, 'recordar' means 'to remember'. 'Que recordar' can appear in phrases like 'hay que recordar' (one must remember / it's important to remember) or 'no hay que recordar' depending on structure. In Spanish you usually need surrounding words to make the phrase grammatical (e.g., 'que' can introduce a clause or be part of 'hay que').
target_language_example: Hay que recordar traer los pasaportes.
native_language_example: One must remember to bring the passports.

meaning: that (to) recover / which to recover (depends on context)
additional_notes: This sequence appears when 'que' introduces a subordinate clause or relative phrase with the verb 'recuperar' (to recover, to get back). Exact translation varies by context: it can be part of 'algo que recuperar' (something to recover), 'tengo que recuperar' (I have to recover / I have to make up), or 'que recuperar' inside longer clauses. Pay attention to verb forms and surrounding words to decide if 'recuperar' is infinitive (to recover / to make up) or part of a relative clause.
target_language_example: Tengo que recuperar el tiempo perdido.
native_language_example: I have to make up for lost time.

meaning: that (one) should/recommends reduce; 'to reduce' introduced by que (often after verbs or impersonal expressions).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but the conjunction que plus the infinitive reducir. It often appears after expressions like 'es importante que reducir' in colloquial speech, but more correct Spanish uses a subjunctive clause (e.g., 'es importante reducir' or 'es importante que se reduzca'). In everyday usage you will see 'que reducir' in shortened headlines, notes, or informal spoken lists: 'Hay que reducir gastos' means 'We must reduce expenses.' Here 'hay que' is the impersonal construction meaning 'one must' or 'it's necessary to'.
target_language_example: Hay que reducir el consumo de plástico.
native_language_example: We must reduce plastic consumption.

meaning: 'must respect' or 'have to respect' (obligation to respect someone or something).
additional_notes: In Spanish, 'hay que respetar' or constructions with 'tener que' + infinitive express obligation. Examples: 'Hay que respetar a...' (one must respect...), 'teníamos que respetar...' (we had to respect...), 'tiene que respetar...' (he/she/you formal has to respect...). The phrase pairs the obligation marker (hay que / tener que) with the verb 'respetar' (to respect).
target_language_example: Tenemos que respetar las opiniones de los demás.
native_language_example: We have to respect other people's opinions.

meaning: 'to have to reply/respond to' (used with obligations: someone must respond to something).
additional_notes: This is the structure with the modal verb 'tener (que) + infinitive' meaning 'to have to'. Here 'responder a' means 'to reply to' or 'to answer' something (a question, letter, etc.). In sentences the indirect object or thing replied to follows 'a' (e.g. responder a la carta / a la pregunta). Conjugate 'tener' and keep 'responder a' in the infinitive.
target_language_example: Tengo que responder a ese correo hoy.
native_language_example: I have to reply to that email today.

meaning: that you knew / (I thought) you knew
additional_notes: This is the conjunction 'que' + the verb 'saber' in the imperfect (tú sabías) used to report or comment on someone's knowledge. Often appears in sentences like 'Creí que sabías' (I thought you knew) or with more information after it: 'que sabías + infinitive' (that you knew how to...). Can be used to express surprise, misunderstanding or assumption about what someone knew. Word order and tense can change (p. ej. 'que supieras', 'que sabías') depending on nuance.
target_language_example: Pensé que sabías arreglar esto.
native_language_example: I thought you knew how to fix this.

meaning: 'que' (that/who/which) + infinitive 'salir de' (to leave/from). Used in clauses where 'que' introduces an action of leaving or coming out of a place; literal, compositional structure rather than a fixed idiom.
additional_notes: Not an idiomatic fixed phrase: it's the relative or subordinating 'que' followed by the infinitive or a conjugated form of 'salir de' in a clause. In natural usage you'll often see a conjugated verb (salió, sale, salga) rather than the infinitive together with 'que', e.g. 'la persona que salió de la casa' or 'es importante que salga de la habitación'. Word order and agreement follow normal Spanish grammar. 'Salir de' means to leave/from (a place).
target_language_example: La persona que salir de la habitación no ha vuelto todavía.
native_language_example: The person that leave from the room has not returned yet.

meaning: that I left
additional_notes: Used to report that the speaker left or went out at a specific time or before/after another event. In sentences like 'desde que salí' it means 'since I left.' Can also appear in reporting clauses ('dile que salí...') or resultive contexts ('salí en los diarios' — I appeared in the newspapers). The tense of salir is determined by context (here it's past: salí = I left).
target_language_example: Si te llaman, diles que salí hace una hora.
native_language_example: If they call you, tell them that I left an hour ago.

meaning: that (he/she/it) was going to
additional_notes: This phrase is a combination of the relative/conjunction que + the pronominal verb form se iba (imperfect/near-future sense of irse or ir). In the examples it expresses an expectation or prediction about a future or imminent action (was going to do / would do). The subject (he/she/it/they) is understood from context. It can be followed by an infinitive (e.g., que se iba a morir, que se iba a sentar) or used with other verbs (e.g., que se iba a hundir).
target_language_example: Pensé que se iba a quedar en casa.
native_language_example: I thought that she was going to stay home.

meaning: 'that (he/she/I) felt' or 'that (he/she/I) was feeling'.
additional_notes: Used to report someone's feelings or states in the past (reported speech). The verb sentirse (me siento, te sientes) means 'to feel' (emotion or physical state). The subject is implied by the reflexive pronoun (se = he/she/you formal/they). In English this is usually translated as 'that he/she felt' or 'that he/she was feeling.'
target_language_example: Ella dijo que se sentía nerviosa antes del examen.
native_language_example: She said that she felt nervous before the exam.

meaning: 'that it is about' / 'that it concerns' (used to say what something is about or what it involves).
additional_notes: Used after verbs like creer, pensar, confirmar to introduce what something concerns or what something is (often followed by de + noun/phrase). It can be translated as 'that it's about', 'that it's a', or 'that it concerns'. Common in statements and questions. If followed by 'de' plus noun, English often uses 'that it's a...' or 'that it concerns...'.
target_language_example: Creo que se trata de un malentendido.
native_language_example: I believe that it's a misunderstanding.

meaning: 'that it is too' / 'that it's too [adjective]'.
additional_notes: Used as part of a clause expressing that something is excessive or more than desired. Often follows verbs or expressions like 'temo que sea demasiado' (I fear that it may be too much) or 'no quiero que sea demasiado caro' (I don't want it to be too expensive). 'Sea' is the present-subjunctive of 'ser' and is used when the speaker expresses doubt, desire, emotion, or hypothetical situations.
target_language_example: Me preocupa que sea demasiado para ella.
native_language_example: I'm worried that it may be too much for her.

meaning: that it might be too late / before it's too late.
additional_notes: Commonly used in clauses with 'antes de' (before) or 'es posible que' to warn that action should be taken now to avoid a missed opportunity or negative consequence. It uses the subjunctive 'sea' because it expresses possibility or uncertainty. Often appears in set phrase 'antes de que sea demasiado tarde' (before it's too late).
target_language_example: Llama al médico antes de que sea demasiado tarde.
native_language_example: Call the doctor before it's too late.

meaning: that it/he/this be the
additional_notes: A combination of the subjunctive verb phrase «que sea» plus the article «el». Used to express hope, desire, uncertainty, or to single out something as 'the' thing (may it be the...). Context determines translation: can mean 'that it is the' (expressing possibility) or an exclamation/wish 'let it be the'/'may it be the'. Often followed by a noun (e.g., caso, mejor desayuno, café, postre, fin de semana).
target_language_example: Que sea el mejor día de todos.
native_language_example: May it be the best day of all.

meaning: may it be the last time / let this be the last time.
additional_notes: Used to express a wish or demand that something not happen again (often after a complaint or warning). Commonly appears as 'Que sea la última vez' = 'Let this be the last time.' It can be followed by a clause introduced with 'que' (e.g. 'Que sea la última vez que...'). Tone ranges from frustrated to emphatic; often used in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Que sea la última vez que me interrumpes durante las reuniones.
