meaning: stayed/was left in the (masculine singular place) — 'stayed in the...'
additional_notes: Used with third-person singular past (quedó) to say someone stayed or remained at a specific masculine singular location introduced by 'el' (el coche, el hotel, el tren, el cine). Use 'quedó en la' for feminine nouns (la casa), 'quedaron en el' for plural subjects, or change article as needed.
target_language_example: Se quedó en el aeropuerto hasta la noche.
native_language_example: He/she stayed in the airport until night.

meaning: 'ended up / stayed in the (feminine noun)'.
additional_notes: Used with third-person singular (quedó) to say someone stayed in or ended up at a place expressed with a feminine noun (la casa, la calle, la posición). Depending on context, quedar can mean 'to stay' (remain somewhere) or 'to end up/finish in' a state or place. The definite article 'la' agrees with the following feminine noun.
target_language_example: Después del accidente, se quedó en la cama varios días.
native_language_example: After the accident, he/she stayed in bed for several days.

meaning: I burned the (feminine noun).
additional_notes: Informal past (preterite) first-person singular of quemar (quemé = I burned). Followed by a feminine noun: e.g. 'quemé la cena' (I burned the dinner) or 'quemé la carta' (I burned the letter). In speech, context makes clear what was burned. Accent on 'é' marks preterite stress. Use 'quemé el' for masculine nouns.
target_language_example: Ayer quemé la cena y nadie quiso comerla.
native_language_example: Yesterday I burned the dinner and no one wanted to eat it.

meaning: to love (someone)
additional_notes: Used with people (or sometimes pets) to express love or affection. 'Querer' alone can mean 'to want' or 'to love' depending on context; when followed by 'a' + person it specifically means to love/care for that person. Commonly conjugated (te quiero, la quiero, queremos a nuestros hijos).
target_language_example: Yo quiero a mi familia. -> ejemplo que contiene 'querer a' en su forma conjugada.
native_language_example: I love my family.

meaning: to love someone (express affection or love directed at a person).
additional_notes: Used to express affection or love toward a person (family, friends, or a romantic partner). Spanish typically uses querer + a + person to indicate loving someone; without the preposition 'a' it can mean to want something (querer algo). Often less intense than 'amar' for some speakers, but commonly used for deep affection as well.
target_language_example: Cuando eres joven, puedes aprender a querer a alguien de maneras que no esperabas.
native_language_example: When you are young, you can learn to love someone in ways you didn't expect.

meaning: to mean
additional_notes: Literally "to want to say," but the established meaning is "to mean." It is commonly used to ask about the meaning of a word, phrase, or statement, and also to explain what someone is trying to express.
target_language_example: Eso puede querer decir muchas cosas.
native_language_example: That can mean many things.

meaning: to want to talk; to want to speak
additional_notes: A very common pattern in Spanish is querer + infinitive to express wanting to do something. In this phrase, hablar can mean either "talk" or "speak," depending on context.
target_language_example: Es normal querer hablar con alguien de confianza.
native_language_example: It's normal to want to talk with someone you trust.

meaning: I/he/she wanted something / wanted something (general).
additional_notes: Querían/quería is the imperfect of querer (to want) used for past habitual actions, background descriptions, or polite/softened requests. 'Algo' means 'something' or 'anything' depending on context. Together, 'quería algo' often describes a past desire or a polite way to ask for something (e.g., in a store or restaurant: 'Quería algo para beber' = 'I'd like something to drink'). Context (who is speaking and tense) determines whether it's first person (quisiera is more formal/polite) or reported speech (he said he wanted something).
target_language_example: Quería algo para llevar, por favor.
native_language_example: I wanted something to take away, please.

meaning: 'wanted the' (past, polite/neutral) — quería = I/he/she/you (formal) wanted; el = the (masculine singular)
additional_notes: This is the combination of the imperfect/past-tense verb querer (quería) plus the masculine singular definite article el. Context determines the subject (yo, él/ella, usted) and the object that follows (a noun). Common in sentences like "Querían el coche" (They wanted the car) or "Yo quería el libro" (I wanted the book). If addressing someone formally, quería can be a polite request when used with infinitive (e.g., "Quería el menú" sounds like a polite way to ask for the menu). Watch pronunciation: 'el' can contract in meaning but not change form; don't confuse with 'él' (with accent) meaning 'he'.
target_language_example: Yo quería el último ejemplar, pero ya se había vendido.
native_language_example: I wanted the last copy, but it had already been sold.

meaning: 'cheese made from' or 'cheese of' (used to indicate the type or source of cheese, e.g., queso de cabra = goat cheese).
additional_notes: Commonly followed by the animal or ingredient that indicates the cheese's origin or flavor (cabra = goat, vaca = cow, oveja = sheep). Can also appear in fixed phrases (queso de mesa, queso de bola). Use 'el/los' or 'un/unos' as needed: 'el queso de cabra' = the goat cheese.
target_language_example: Quiero probar el queso de oveja.
native_language_example: I want to try sheep cheese.

meaning: fresh (unaged) cheese; a soft, mild Mexican/Latin American cheese often used in cooking.
additional_notes: Refers to a soft, crumbly, mild cheese that is eaten fresh (not aged). Common in Mexican and Latin American cuisine — used in tacos, salads, enchiladas, and desserts. In some regions it may simply mean 'fresh cheese' and can refer to different local varieties (panela, queso blanco, etc.).
target_language_example: Añade queso fresco encima de la ensalada.
native_language_example: Add queso fresco on top of the salad.

meaning: 'who is' or 'who's'.
additional_notes: Used to ask or identify a person. As an interrogative it should be written with an accent on 'quién' and with inverted question marks: ¿Quién es...? The unaccented form 'quien' appears in certain subordinate clauses (e.g., 'la persona quien es...') but for direct questions use 'quién'. When followed by a name or role, it asks for identity (¿Quién es ese hombre? — Who is that man?).
target_language_example: ¿quien es ella?
native_language_example: Who is she?

meaning: Not a correct standard phrase in Spanish; likely an incorrect word order intended to mean 'who speaks' or 'who will speak'.
additional_notes: The sequence 'quien hablar' is ungrammatical. Correct forms: '¿Quién habla?' (Who is speaking?) or '¿Quién va a hablar?' (Who is going to speak?). In relative clauses use 'quien' without an accent (e.g., 'la persona quien habla' is possible but more common is 'la persona que habla'). Accent rules: 'quién' with an accent for direct/indirect questions and exclamations; 'quien' without an accent in relative clauses. If you must include both words exactly in a sentence, they can appear separated by other words but the pair 'quien hablar' as adjacent words is not standard.
target_language_example: No sé quién hablar en la reunión; necesito una lista.
native_language_example: I don't know who will speak at the meeting; I need a list.

meaning: 'who (to) him/her' — part of relative clauses that combine quien (who) with an indirect-object pronoun (le).
additional_notes: Used when referring to a person (quien) who receives or is affected by something expressed with the indirect-object pronoun le. Often appears in relative clauses: alguien a quien le importa (someone who cares), para alguien a quien le gusta (for someone who likes). Word order can vary (quien le + verb or verb + quien le). 'Le' can be singular formal or neutral (him/her/you formal).
target_language_example: Busca a la persona a quien le interesa el proyecto.
native_language_example: Look for the person who is interested in the project.

meaning: 'who (to) me' — used to say which person performed an action affecting the speaker (object = me).
additional_notes: Combines the relative pronoun 'quien' (who) with the indirect/direct object pronoun 'me' (me). Used to identify the person who did something to or for the speaker: e.g. 'fue quien me invitó' = 'was the one who invited me.' Often appears with verbs in past or present. Word order is flexible: 'tú eres quien me envía...' or 'fuiste tú quien me pidió...'.
target_language_example: Ella es quien me llamó anoche.
native_language_example: She is the one who called me last night.

meaning: 'who/whom ... not' — used to form relative clauses or general statements meaning 'who does not' or 'someone whom... not'.
additional_notes: Often appears in two uses: 1) as part of relative clauses after a noun or pronoun (quien/ con quien/ a quien) meaning 'who' or 'whom' — e.g., 'alguien a quien no debía olvidar' = 'someone I shouldn't forget'; 2) at the start of general or proverbial sentences to mean 'whoever does not...' (quien no estudie = whoever doesn't study). 'Quien no' itself isn't a fixed phrase; meaning depends on context and any following verb or preposition.
target_language_example: Quien no ayuda, no tiene derecho a quejarse.
native_language_example: Whoever doesn't help has no right to complain.

meaning: Likely a mistaken or incomplete phrase — 'quien puedo' (missing accent and/or words) is not a correct standalone Spanish expression. Literally reads as 'who I can' or 'who can I' depending on intended order, but it's ungrammatical without context or proper question structure.
additional_notes: Not a proper phrase by itself. Possible intended corrections: "¿quién puede...?" (Who can...?) or "¿con quién puedo...?" (With whom can I...?) or "¿a quién puedo...?" (To whom can I...?). Remember question words require an accent: 'quién'. If written without an accent in informal text, it may be a typo. The example below uses the exact sequence 'quien puedo' to reflect how it might appear in user input (unaccented and ungrammatical).
target_language_example: Perdón, escribí 'quien puedo' por error; quería preguntar: ¿con quién puedo hablar sobre esto?
native_language_example: Sorry, I wrote 'quien puedo' by mistake; I meant to ask: Who can I speak with about this?

meaning: 'whom I love' / 'whom I want' (object after a preposition — 'whom I...').
additional_notes: Quien quiero is used in relative or cleft sentences to refer to a person who is the object of querer (to love/want). In Spanish, cuando the person is introduced with a preposition or in a cleft structure (Es a X a quien...), 'quien' functions like 'whom' in English. The phrase often appears as 'a quien quiero' because querer takes a direct object but Spanish frequently uses the preposition 'a' before people. Use 'quien' (singular) for 'who/whom' and 'quienes' for plural.
target_language_example: Es a María a quien quiero.
native_language_example: María is the one I love.

meaning: 'who I' — a fragment used when referring to oneself as the subject in a relative or emphatic clause.
additional_notes: This is not a complete phrase by itself in Spanish; it typically appears inside longer sentences (e.g., «quien yo soy», «quien yo era») where it introduces information about the speaker. In everyday speech speakers more often use 'yo' alone or constructions like 'que yo' or 'como yo'. Use 'quien' (who) with related verbs: 'quien soy' = 'who I am'.
target_language_example: Quien yo soy no importa para esta decisión.
native_language_example: Who I am doesn't matter for this decision.

meaning: may God (grant it); God willing; I hope God allows it.
additional_notes: An expression used to express hope or wish that something will happen, often equivalent to 'God willing' or 'hopefully'. It can appear on its own or within longer phrases (e.g., 'quiera Dios que...' = 'may God grant that...'). Formality: neutral to slightly formal/religious; common in spoken and written Spanish in religious or emphatic contexts.
target_language_example: Quiera Dios que mañana haga buen tiempo para la celebración.
native_language_example: God willing, tomorrow the weather will be good for the celebration.

meaning: a (subjunctive) expression used to introduce a wish, hope, or condition meaning 'whether or not' or 'even if' depending on context
additional_notes: Often appears after verbs or phrases that express wanting, fearing, or hypothetical situations and is followed by a verb in subjunctive (e.g., quiera que no + subj.). It can mean 'whether or not' (introducing contrast) or 'even if' (concessive). It is somewhat formal/literary and less common in everyday speech; speakers may use constructions like 'aunque no' or 'aunque' instead.
target_language_example: Quiera que no, habrá consecuencias si seguimos así.
native_language_example: Whether we like it or not, there will be consequences if we continue like this.

meaning: 'needs' or 'requires' (formal/neutral)
additional_notes: Uses the verb querer + preposition de to indicate that someone or something requires or depends on something. More common with impersonal/abstract subjects (e.g., 'Esto quiere de paciencia' → 'This requires patience'). In everyday speech Spaniards often say 'necesita' instead, but 'querer de' appears in written or formal contexts and in some regional uses. Not to be confused with 'quiere' alone ('wants').
target_language_example: Este trabajo quiere de mucha paciencia.
native_language_example: This work requires a lot of patience.

meaning: what ... wants is
additional_notes: Not usually treated as a standalone expression. It is most commonly seen inside a larger pattern such as "lo que quiere es...", meaning "what he/she wants is...". Here, "quiere" means "he/she/you (formal) wants" and "es" means "is". In some Latin American varieties, "quiere es + infinitive" can also be used for emphasis.
target_language_example: Lo que quiere es descansar un rato.
native_language_example: What he wants is to rest for a while.

meaning: wants it — 'quiere' (he/she/you formal want(s)) + direct object pronoun 'lo' (it, masculine or neutral)
additional_notes: Combines the verb querer with the direct object pronoun lo. Standard Spanish places the pronoun before a conjugated verb (lo quiere), but in spoken or emphatic contexts speakers sometimes say quiere lo. Use quiere lo mainly in colloquial speech or for emphasis; in formal writing prefer lo quiere. 'Lo' can refer to a masculine noun or an abstract idea/statement.
target_language_example: ¿Quiere lo o no?
native_language_example: Does he/she/you (formal) want it or not?

meaning: 'wants more' (he/she/you formal wants more)
additional_notes: From the verb querer (to want) + más (more). Commonly used to say someone wants a larger amount, another helping, or more of something (food, information, time, etc.). Context and subject determine meaning: quiere can be él/ella/usted. For 'you want more' informal (tú) use quieres más. To form questions or negatives, add punctuation or no: ¿Quiere más? / No quiere más.
target_language_example: Él quiere más pan, por favor.
native_language_example: He wants more bread, please.

meaning: 'wants that his/her/your/their ...' — expresses desire about someone’s possession or relation (su + noun) with a subordinate clause.
additional_notes: Combines the verb querer (to want) + subordinate connector que + the possessive su + a noun. Used to say someone wants something to happen concerning another person's possession/relationship (e.g., su hija, su jefe). The person referred by su depends on context (his, her, your formal, their). After quiere que, use the subjunctive for the verb in the subordinate clause (e.g., tenga, sea).
target_language_example: Ella quiere que su hermano venga mañana.
native_language_example: She wants her brother to come tomorrow.

meaning: he/she/you(formal) wants his/her/your (own) — literal combination of the verb querer and the possessive su.
additional_notes: Use quiere su when someone wants something that belongs to someone (su + noun follows) or when expressing desire for a noun: quiere su libro (he/she wants his/her/your book). Context determines possession (su can mean his, her, your formal, their). For 'you' informal (tú) use quieres su (rare) or quieres tu for 'your' informal. To say 'wants to' + verb, use quiere + infinitive (quiere comer).
target_language_example: Ella quiere su chaqueta.
native_language_example: She wants her jacket.

meaning: Literal components look like 'quiere' (he/she wants; from querer) + 'tú' (subject pronoun). As written, it is ungrammatical in standard Spanish; the correct forms depend on intended meaning (e.g., 'te quiere' = he/she wants/loves you; '¿Tú quieres...?' = Do you want...?).
additional_notes: 'Quiere tu' with an unaccented tú and this word order is not correct for normal sentences. If the intended sense is 'he/she wants you' use 'te quiere'. If the intended sense is a question addressing 'tú', use '¿Tú quieres...?' or '¿Quieres tú...?'. 'Quiere tú' might appear in nonstandard speech, poetic inversion, or as a transcription error. Note that 'tú' must carry an accent when used as subject pronoun.
target_language_example: Él quiere tu apoyo, pero lo dijo mal: "quiere tu" en vez de "te quiere".
native_language_example: He wants your support, but he said it wrong: "quiere tu" instead of "te quiere".

meaning: 'do you want to have' (informal second-person singular)
additional_notes: Combination of the verb querer (to want) in the tú form (quieres) + tener (to have). Used to ask someone informally whether they want to possess, experience, or do something that involves 'having' something. Context often determines whether 'tener' means to own, to hold, to be allowed, or to experience (e.g., tener hambre = to be hungry). For polite or plural forms use ¿quiere tener? (usted) or ¿quieren tener? (ustedes).
target_language_example: ¿Quieres tener un perro este año?
native_language_example: Do you want to have a dog this year?

meaning: 'I love you' or 'I care for you' with emphasis on 'you' (informal/formal depending on context).
additional_notes: Standard Spanish uses 'te quiero' for 'I love you' (affectionate) or 'te amo' for stronger love. 'Quiero a ti' is a marked word order used to emphasize 'ti/you'—more common: 'te quiero a ti' or simply 'solo te quiero'/'solo te quiero a ti' to say 'I only want/love you.' The phrase is informal in tone and addresses someone directly. Use 'te' before the verb in normal word order: 'te quiero'.
target_language_example: Solo te quiero a ti; no quiero a nadie más.
native_language_example: I only love you; I don't love anyone else.

meaning: I want (it) now / I want to (do it) now.
additional_notes: Combines the verb querer (to want) in first person singular with ahora (now). Context determines what 'quiero' refers to: a thing, an action, or a request. You can add an object or infinitive after quiero: quiero ahora agua (nonstandard order) or quiero ahora salir (less common than 'quiero salir ahora'), though usual placement is 'quiero ... ahora' — using 'quiero ahora' at the start emphasizes immediacy. Tone can be urgent or demanding depending on context and intonation; add por favor to soften requests: "quiero ahora, por favor."
target_language_example: Quiero ahora el informe.
native_language_example: I want the report now.

meaning: 'I want something' or 'I want something (unspecified)'.
additional_notes: Used to express desire for an unspecified thing or a general wish. Can refer to a specific type (e.g., 'algo dulce' = something sweet) or to a stronger goal (e.g., 'quiero algo de veras' = I really want something). 'Quiero' is the first-person singular of 'querer'.
target_language_example: Quiero algo para leer antes de dormir.
native_language_example: I want something to read before sleeping.

meaning: Literally 'I want with' — not a fixed set phrase. Appears when 'quiero' (I want) is followed by the preposition 'con' (with) to introduce with whom or with what you want something or with whom you want to do something.
additional_notes: Not an independent idiom; it's compositional grammar: 'quiero' + object/infinitive + 'con' + person/thing. Context determines structure and meaning (e.g., 'quiero un sandwich con jamón' or 'quiero salir con ella'). The two words may be separated by other words (object or verb phrase) in natural sentences, but the sequence 'quiero con' can occur when the verb is followed immediately by 'con' (e.g., when an omitted object or clause follows). Pay attention to agreement and register; construction is neutral (not inherently informal).
target_language_example: ¿Te quiero con o sin maquillaje?
native_language_example: Do I want you with or without makeup?

meaning: I mean
additional_notes: Common filler phrase used to clarify, rephrase, or emphasize what you just said (like English “I mean” or “I mean, ...”). Often appears at the start of a sentence or clause. Can introduce an explanation, correction, or stronger opinion.
target_language_example: Quiero decir, fue la mejor decisión que pudimos tomar.
native_language_example: I mean, it was the best decision we could make.

meaning: I want to throw/put/take (depending on context).
additional_notes: Echar is a very common, flexible verb in Spanish with many meanings (to throw, to put, to pour, to send, to take [a nap], etc.). 'Quiero echar' combines the verb querer (to want) with echar and needs a complement to know the exact meaning: e.g. 'quiero echar la carta' (I want to send/throw the letter), 'quiero echar gasolina' (I want to put/give gasoline), 'quiero echar una siesta' (I want to take a nap). Pay attention to the object or phrase that follows.
target_language_example: Quiero echar una siesta después de comer.
native_language_example: I want to take a nap after lunch.

meaning: 'I want in' — a literal combination of quiero (I want) + en (in); used when asking to join or participate.
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom in Spanish by itself. Native speakers more often say quiero entrar, quiero participar, quiero apuntarme, o 'yo también' depending on context. 'Quiero en' can appear in informal spoken language or casual writing (e.g., chats) to mean 'I want to be included' or 'count me in.' Use cautiously; it's informal and context-dependent.
target_language_example: Si vais a cenar fuera, quiero en.
native_language_example: If you're going out to dinner, I want in.

meaning: Literally: "I want in me" or "I want inside me." Not a common standalone phrase; usually incomplete and requires additional words to be natural.
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom. 'Quiero en mi' combines 'quiero' (I want) with 'en mí' (in me/inside me) but typically a noun or clause follows ('quiero paz en mí', 'quiero amor en mí'). Using it alone sounds unfinished; for clarity use 'quiero (tener) ... dentro de mí' or include the desired noun after 'en mí'. Note the written accent: 'mí' (with accent) when meaning 'me/inside me'.
target_language_example: Quiero en mí la fuerza para seguir adelante.
native_language_example: I want in me the strength to keep going.

meaning: I want (the thing) is that... / What I want is that...
additional_notes: Used to introduce what someone wants or wishes to happen. Often appears in the structure 'Lo que quiero es que + [subjunctive clause]' when expressing desires about someone else's actions or future situations. In everyday speech speakers may shorten to 'quiero que' without the 'es'. Use subjunctive after 'que' when the clause expresses desire, doubt, or influence.
target_language_example: Lo que quiero es que vengas mañana.
native_language_example: What I want is for you to come tomorrow.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase; a sequence of words that is ungrammatical as written. Literally reads 'I want is a...' but lacks linking structure.
additional_notes: This exact sequence does not form a grammatical expression in Spanish. It may result from joining two clauses incorrectly (e.g., 'Lo que quiero es una...' or 'Quiero una...'). For correct alternatives: use 'Quiero una...' (I want a...) or 'Lo que quiero es una...' (What I want is a...). The sequence 'quiero es una' could appear in speech only if words are misordered or part of a longer sentence with omitted words; avoid using it as written.
target_language_example: Lo que quiero es una bicicleta; "quiero es una" no es correcto por sí solo.
native_language_example: What I want is a bicycle; "quiero es una" is not correct by itself.

meaning: 'I want that (one)'.
additional_notes: A simple, colloquial way to say you want a specific item that is visible or has just been mentioned. 'Ese' agrees in gender with a masculine noun; for a feminine noun use 'esa' (quiero esa). Often used when pointing at something: quiero ese, por favor. For a more complete sentence you can add the noun (quiero ese libro) or politeness markers (quiero ese, por favor).
target_language_example: ¿Cuál prefieres? — Quiero ese, por favor.
native_language_example: Which one do you prefer? — I want that one, please.

meaning: 'I want this.'
additional_notes: A simple phrase used to indicate you want a specific item that is nearby or being shown. 'Quiero' = I want; 'este' = this (masculine, near speaker). If the item is feminine use 'esta' (quiero esta) or for plural use 'estos/estas' (quiero estos/estas). To be more polite, use 'quiero este, por favor' or 'quisiera este' / 'me gustaría este'.
target_language_example: Quiero este, por favor.
native_language_example: I want this, please.

meaning: Literally 'I want out' or 'I want (someone/something) out.' Not a standalone fixed phrase in standard Spanish; meaning depends on context and usually requires additional words to be grammatical.
additional_notes: Formed from the verb 'querer' + 'fuera' (adverb/adjectival form meaning 'out' or 'outside'). By itself 'quiero fuera' sounds incomplete in most contexts. Possible uses: • As a clipped or emphatic phrase in informal speech to demand removal: '¡Lo quiero fuera!' ('I want him/her/it out!'). • Rarely used to mean 'I want to be out' — better expressed as 'quiero salir' or 'quiero estar fuera'. More natural alternatives when asking someone to leave: 'quiero que se vaya', 'quiero que salga', or '¡fuera!'.
target_language_example: ¡Lo quiero fuera ahora mismo!
native_language_example: I want him/her/it out right now!

meaning: I want to go to the (e.g., bed/place) — used to say you want to leave for somewhere (often 'la cama').
additional_notes: Commonly followed by a feminine noun (la cama, la casa, la habitación). 'Irme' is the reflexive infinitive of 'ir' with 'me' (to leave/go away). The full phrase often appears as 'quiero irme a la cama' meaning 'I want to go to bed' or simply 'quiero irme' to mean 'I want to leave.'
target_language_example: Estoy cansado, quiero irme a la cama.
native_language_example: I'm tired, I want to go to bed.

meaning: I want to call (to make a phone call) or I want to call (someone or something).
additional_notes: Commonly used to express the desire or intention to phone someone or to call out to someone. Often followed by a direct object introduced with "a" for a person (quiero llamar a María) or by "por"/"para" in other contexts. Can also be used with reflexive or pronominal forms (quiero llamarme no — I want to call myself — is uncommon). In casual speech, the subject Yo is usually omitted: "Quiero llamar ahora."
target_language_example: Quiero llamar a mi mamá ahora.
native_language_example: I want to call my mom now.

meaning: 'I want to kill' — expresses a desire to kill someone or something.
additional_notes: A direct, strong phrase. Use very carefully: it literally states an intention or desire to kill and can be used figuratively in angry speech but may be interpreted as a real threat. Often followed by a direct object (e.g., a person). In polite or neutral conversation, use milder alternatives (e.g., "no quiero seguir" — "I don't want to continue" or "me dan ganas de..." for figurative feelings).
target_language_example: No quiero matar a nadie; solo quiero salir de aquí.
native_language_example: I don't want to kill anyone; I just want to get out of here.

meaning: 'I want my...' (beginning of a sentence where the speaker asks for something that belongs to them).
additional_notes: Quiero = 'I want'. Mi = possessive 'my' used before a noun (mi teléfono, mi dinero). This fragment is not a complete sentence by itself — you normally add a noun or clause after mi (e.g., 'quiero mi libro' or 'quiero mi dinero de vuelta'). In spoken Spanish the phrase can express demand or complaint when asking for possession back.
target_language_example: Quiero mi mochila, por favor.
native_language_example: I want my backpack, please.

meaning: "I love/want ... more than" or "I want ... more than anything/anyone" (expresses greater degree or preference).
additional_notes: Used to compare how much you love, want, or prefer someone/something relative to others or to everything else. Often followed by a person (a nadie, a nadie en este mundo), a thing (nada), or a clause (que + verb). In contexts with querer meaning 'love,' it expresses deep affection. Word order: 'Te/Le quiero más que a nadie' = 'I love you more than anyone.'
target_language_example: Te quiero más que a nada en este mundo.
native_language_example: I love you more than anything in this world.

meaning: I want nothing / I don't want anything (colloquial/incorrect word order).
additional_notes: This phrase is nonstandard in Spanish. The correct negative form is 'no quiero nada' or 'no quiero nada de eso'. Native speakers sometimes drop the initial 'no' in casual speech or in certain dialects for emphasis or irony, but it can sound ungrammatical. Use 'no quiero nada' to say you don't want anything.
target_language_example: No quiero nada; gracias.
native_language_example: I don't want anything; thanks.

meaning: I want another (one).
additional_notes: Used to ask for or say you want an additional item, chance, or instance. 'Otra' agrees in gender with a feminine noun (otra cerveza, otra oportunidad). Use 'otro' for masculine nouns (quiero otro bocadillo). Can stand alone when the noun is clear from context: 'Quiero otra.' = 'I want another one.'
target_language_example: ¿Te queda una galleta? Sí, quiero otra, por favor.
native_language_example: Do you have another cookie? Yes, I want another one, please.

meaning: literally 'I want for' — not a standalone fixed phrase; typically appears as part of a larger sentence meaning 'I want [something] for [purpose/person]'.
additional_notes: This combination is not a complete phrase by itself. Quiero = 'I want'. Para = 'for', 'to', 'in order to', or 'by (a deadline)'. Together they appear when expressing wanting something intended for a purpose or person: e.g. 'Quiero algo para ti' (I want something for you) or 'Quiero tiempo para estudiar' (I want time to study). Word order and context matter; Spanish often uses 'quiero + noun + para + purpose' or 'quiero + infinitive' instead of 'quiero para + infinitive'.
target_language_example: Quiero para ti lo mejor.
native_language_example: I want the best for you.

meaning: 'I want to go through/attend the.../I want to pass the...'
additional_notes: This fragment appears before a masculine noun (el ...) and can mean different things depending on context: to pass by or through a place (pasar por), to attend or spend time (pasar el rato), or to pass an exam or checkpoint (pasar el examen / pasar el control). Alone it is incomplete; you must add the noun or phrase that follows 'el' to know the exact meaning. Common continuations: 'quiero pasar el rato' (I want to spend time), 'quiero pasar el examen' (I want to pass the exam), 'quiero pasar el control' (I want to get past security/checkpoint).
target_language_example: Quiero pasar el rato contigo esta tarde.
native_language_example: I want to spend time with you this afternoon.

meaning: I want to spend the rest (of my life/time/day/etc.)
additional_notes: This phrase is followed by a period of time or situation understood from context (e.g., 'la vida', 'el día', 'mis días'). It expresses a desire to spend the remaining portion of something in a certain way or with someone. You can complete it: 'quiero pasar el resto de mi vida contigo' — 'I want to spend the rest of my life with you.'
target_language_example: Quiero pasar el resto de mi vida contigo.
native_language_example: I want to spend the rest of my life with you.

meaning: 'I want to spend the rest of (my life / the day / my time)'.
additional_notes: Used to say you want to spend the remainder of a period (life, day, week, time) doing something or with someone. Usually followed by a noun or a verb phrase like 'mi vida', 'el día', 'mi tiempo', or 'contigo' (with you). Common in romantic or long-term intentions: 'quiero pasar el resto de mi vida contigo.'
target_language_example: Quiero pasar el resto de mi vida contigo.
native_language_example: I want to spend the rest of my life with you.

meaning: I want to think; I would like to consider or believe (that...).
additional_notes: A combination of the verb querer + infinitive pensar. Used to express desire to think, to take time to consider something, or tentatively state an opinion (I want to think that... / I would like to believe that...). Context determines whether it means 'I want to take time to think' or 'I want to believe.' Common in spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: Quiero pensar antes de tomar una decisión.
native_language_example: I want to think before making a decision.

meaning: I want (that) her/it + (feminine) — start of a clause expressing a desire about a feminine noun or object.
additional_notes: This is not a complete sentence by itself; it's the beginning of a subordinate clause using querer + que + subjunctive when referring to a feminine direct object or person (la). Often followed by a verb in the subjunctive: quiero que la veas, quiero que la cuides. If referring to a feminine noun as a direct object without a following verb, context is needed (e.g., quiero la guitarra → I want the guitar).
target_language_example: Quiero que la llames cuando llegues.
native_language_example: I want you to call her when you arrive.

meaning: I want to stay / I want to remain (somewhere or with someone).
additional_notes: Commonly used to express a desire to stay in a place or to remain with someone. In Spanish it's often said as "(me) quiero quedar" or the more colloquial ordering "quiero quedarme". With "me" it emphasizes staying oneself ("I want to stay"). Can be followed by a time expression (un poco más, un par de días), a location (aquí, en la casa) or a person (contigo).
target_language_example: No tengo prisa; me quiero quedar hasta la tarde.
native_language_example: I'm not in a hurry; I want to stay until the afternoon.

meaning: I want everything / I want it all.
additional_notes: Common phrase to express wanting all of something (literal) or wanting everything in general. Context determines whether it refers to a specific set (e.g., items on a menu, parts of a project) or to life/possessions in general. Can sound emphatic or greedy depending on tone. To soften, you can add 'por favor' or be specific: 'quiero todo esto' (I want all of this).
target_language_example: En la fiesta, Marta dijo: «Quiero todo, gracias».
native_language_example: At the party, Marta said, 'I want everything, thanks.'

meaning: 'I want to see (what...)' — used to introduce curiosity about something that follows (usually with 'que' + clause).
additional_notes: Common pattern: 'Quiero ver lo que...' + [clause]. Literally 'I want to see the thing that...,' but in English it's usually 'I want to see what...'. Used to express desire to find out or look at something. Often followed by verbs like 'encontró', 'hay', 'me ofrecen', 'hará'.
target_language_example: Quiero ver lo que pasa en esa reunión.
native_language_example: I want to see what happens in that meeting.

meaning: literally 'I want and' — not a fixed phrase on its own; a fragment where 'quiero' (I want) begins a clause and 'y' (and) connects to another action or idea.
additional_notes: Not a common standalone phrase. 'Quiero y' appears when a speaker starts with 'Quiero' and immediately adds another element with 'y' (e.g., combining two desires or actions). Context completes the meaning: 'Quiero y...' is typically followed by verbs, nouns, or clauses (e.g., 'Quiero y necesito tiempo', 'Quiero y debo hacerlo'). It can occur in spoken Spanish when someone lists or contrasts wants.
target_language_example: Quiero y debo decir la verdad.
native_language_example: I want and I must tell the truth.

meaning: fifteen syllables
additional_notes: Literal phrase used to state the number of syllables in a word, line, verse, or phrase. Common in discussions of poetry, meter, spelling/pronunciation, or language study. Sílabas = syllables; quince = fifteen.
target_language_example: Esa palabra tiene quince sílabas.
native_language_example: That word has fifteen syllables.

meaning: I wanted ... to
additional_notes: Used to express a desire or wish in the past. Quise is the preterite form of querer ('I wanted'). After quise que, Spanish normally uses the subjunctive because it introduces what someone wanted to happen, often with a different subject: quise que fueras feliz = 'I wanted you to be happy.' If the subject stays the same, Spanish usually uses an infinitive instead: quise ir = 'I wanted to go.'
target_language_example: Quise que me dijeras la verdad.
native_language_example: I wanted you to tell me the truth.

meaning: i would like a
additional_notes: A polite way to ask for or order one masculine thing, common in shops and restaurants. Use quisiera una with a feminine singular noun.
target_language_example: Quisiera un café, por favor.
native_language_example: I'd like a coffee, please.

meaning: remove (something) from (a place); get (something) out of the way
additional_notes: Imperative form of quitar + preposition; used to tell someone to take something away or move it out of a spot. Common in commands like 'Quita de aquí' (Take it away from here) or 'Quita de en medio' (Move it out of the middle). Object may be explicit ('quita de aquí esta basura') or implied ('quita de en medio'). Tone can be firm or commanding.
target_language_example: Quita de aquí la caja, por favor.
native_language_example: Remove the box from here, please.

meaning: to take off one's hat; used literally or figuratively to express admiration, respect, or praise (equivalent to 'to take/raise one's hat to' or 'I take my hat off').
additional_notes: Can be used literally (physically removing a hat) or figuratively to show respect or admiration for someone's actions or achievements. Common constructions include reflexive forms like 'me quito el sombrero' or impersonal/infinitive uses like 'quitarse el sombrero ante...'. Neutral formality — appropriate in spoken and written contexts.
target_language_example: Me gusta verlo trabajar; realmente hay que quitarse el sombrero ante su esfuerzo.
native_language_example: I like watching him work; you really have to take your hat off to his effort.

meaning: to kill oneself; to commit suicide.
additional_notes: A sensitive, formal expression used to refer to suicide. It is impersonal and commonly used in news, reports, or polite conversation instead of blunt verbs like "suicidarse". Use with care and avoid casual or joking contexts. When talking about someone who attempted or died by suicide, you can say "se quitó la vida" (he/she took his/her own life).
target_language_example: Después de años de depresión, intentó quitarse la vida y fue hospitalizado a tiempo.
native_language_example: After years of depression, he attempted to take his own life and was hospitalized in time.

meaning: to feel relieved (after a worry or burden is removed).
additional_notes: Literally 'to remove a weight from oneself.' Used when someone no longer has a worry, responsibility, or fear and feels lighter or relieved. Common in everyday speech; can refer to emotional relief (worry, guilt) or practical relief (a difficult task finished).
target_language_example: Se quitó un peso de encima cuando terminó el proyecto a tiempo.
native_language_example: She felt a weight lifted off her shoulders when she finished the project on time.

meaning: to take off your (plural clothing/item) — e.g., 'take off your shoes'. It’s the reflexive verb quitarse with the informal singular pronoun te plus the definite plural article los.
additional_notes: This form addresses tú (informal singular) and is used when instructing someone to remove plural items (zapatos, calcetines, guantes, etc.). Change pronoun for other persons: quitarme los (yo), quitarse los (él/ella/usted/ellos/ellas), quitaros los (vosotros). Word order can vary in sentences (e.g., 'tienes que quitarte los zapatos' or with an imperative 'quítate los zapatos').
target_language_example: No tienes que quitarte los zapatos.
native_language_example: You don't have to take off your shoes.

meaning: took off (his/her) coat.
additional_notes: Common past-tense phrase using quitarse (reflexive) + definite article. Means someone removed their coat and can be used with other garments (me/quité el abrigo, se quitó la chaqueta). Context shows simple, physical action; subject gender/number changes pronoun (me/te/se/nos).
target_language_example: Cuando entró en la casa, se quitó el abrigo.
native_language_example: When he/she entered the house, he/she took off his/her coat.

meaning: took off (his/her/the) hat.
additional_notes: Literal phrase describing the physical action of removing a hat. Often used in simple past (se quitó el sombrero). In Spanish reflexive verb 'quitarse' + article + item. Use when speaking about someone removing their hat; can also imply a polite gesture (e.g., greeting, respect).
target_language_example: Cuando entró en la iglesia, se quitó el sombrero.
native_language_example: When he entered the church, he took off his hat.

meaning: took off the
additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of quitar + feminine plural direct object (las). Used when someone removed or caused removal of plural feminine items (e.g., botas, gafas, medias, ganas). Context decides translation: physical removal (took off/removed) or figurative (took away, as in 'quitó las ganas' = 'took away the desire'). Subject can be reflexive (se quitó las ...) meaning 'he/she took off his/her ...'.
target_language_example: Ella se quitó las botas antes de entrar.
native_language_example: She took off her boots before going in.

meaning: removed/ took off his/her/its (something).
additional_notes: Quitó is the preterite (past) form of quitar (to remove, take off, or take away). Su is a possessive adjective meaning his, her, its, your (formal), or their depending on context. Together they say that someone removed or took off a specific possession in the past. Use based on gender/number of the object after su (e.g., quitó su abrigo, quitó sus zapatos).
target_language_example: Ella quitó su sombrero cuando entró.
native_language_example: She took off her hat when she came in.

meaning: perhaps the / maybe the
additional_notes: Quizá (or quizás) means 'perhaps' or 'maybe' and is used before a noun or phrase. 'El' is the masculine definite article 'the'. Together they introduce a tentative statement about a specific masculine noun (e.g., 'quizá el problema' = 'perhaps the problem'). Word order is flexible: you can also say 'el quizá' in rare, poetic uses, but the common form is 'quizá el ...'. Use 'quizás' interchangeably with 'quizá'.
target_language_example: Quizá el tren llegue tarde.
native_language_example: Perhaps the train will arrive late.

meaning: maybe she / perhaps she
additional_notes: Quizá (or quizá(s)/quizas) expresses possibility or uncertainty and is followed by a verb in indicative or subjunctive depending on speaker's perception: indicative for likely actions/states, subjunctive for doubt/future/hypothetical. 'Ella' simply specifies 'she'. Common in spoken and written Spanish; placement of quizá can be before the pronoun (quizá ella) or before the verb (ella quizá).
target_language_example: Quizá ella no quiera venir esta noche.
native_language_example: Maybe she doesn't want to come tonight.

meaning: maybe in / perhaps in (followed by a time, place, or situation)
additional_notes: Quizá (or quizás) means 'maybe' or 'perhaps'. When followed by 'en' it introduces a time, place, or context: e.g. 'quizá en agosto' (maybe in August), 'quizá en la oficina' (perhaps in the office), or 'quizá en ese caso' (maybe in that case). Use quizá or quizás interchangeably; word order can vary (e.g. 'en agosto quizá' is also possible but less common).
target_language_example: Quizá en verano vayamos a la playa.
native_language_example: Maybe in summer we'll go to the beach.

meaning: maybe it is / perhaps it is
additional_notes: Quizá (or quizás) means 'maybe' or 'perhaps' and is used before a verb or clause to express possibility. When followed by 'es' it suggests the speaker thinks something might be true now (e.g., 'quizá es verdad' = 'maybe it's true'). Tone can be formal or neutral; you can also use 'quizás'. Word order can be 'quizá es' or 'es quizá' depending on emphasis, but 'quizá es' is more common.
target_language_example: Quizá es la mejor opción para nosotros.
native_language_example: Maybe it is the best option for us.

meaning: 'maybe I' or 'perhaps I' (expressing possibility about oneself).
additional_notes: Quizá (or quizás) means 'maybe' or 'perhaps'. When followed by a reflexive or direct-object pronoun like me, it modifies the speaker: 'quizá me...' introduces a tentative statement about the speaker's feelings, abilities, deservingness, etc. Use indicative or subjunctive after depending on nuance (both are common).
target_language_example: Quizá me equivoqué en la respuesta.
native_language_example: Maybe I was wrong about the answer.

meaning: maybe / perhaps + more (adds uncertainty before 'more')
additional_notes: Quizá (or quizás) means 'maybe' or 'perhaps'. When combined with más, it expresses uncertainty about an increase, extension, addition, or later time: 'maybe more', 'maybe later', 'perhaps happier', or 'maybe longer'. It is adaptable: position can vary (quizá más tarde, quizá más feliz, Por un año, quizá más). Use quizá/quizás interchangeably.
target_language_example: Llegaremos quizá más tarde de lo previsto.
native_language_example: We might arrive later than planned.

meaning: 'maybe your' or 'perhaps your' (expresses possibility about something belonging to 'you')
additional_notes: Quizá (also spelled quizás) means 'maybe' or 'perhaps' and is used before a noun or clause to indicate uncertainty. When followed by tu (your), it modifies the noun that follows: 'quizá tu amigo' = 'maybe your friend'. In spoken Spanish the accent on quizá is optional in writing (quizás is an alternative). The phrase does not imply certainty and is commonly used for polite speculation.
target_language_example: Quizá tu coche necesite una revisión.
native_language_example: Maybe your car needs a check-up.

meaning: 'maybe I' or 'perhaps I' (expresses uncertainty about something the speaker might do or be).
additional_notes: Quizá (also spelled quizás) means 'maybe' or 'perhaps'. When followed by yo it emphasizes that the speaker is the one who might do or be something. It can be used with verbs in different tenses and is often followed by the subjunctive (e.g., 'sea', 'encuentre') for wishes or possibilities, but can also appear with the indicative for likelihood. Tone is neutral and suitable for everyday speech.
target_language_example: Quizá yo pueda ayudar mañana.
native_language_example: Maybe I can help tomorrow.

meaning: maybe she / perhaps she
additional_notes: Used to express possibility or uncertainty about a female person. 'Quizás' (or 'quizá') can be followed by different verb moods: indicative for likely possibilities (e.g., 'viene'), subjunctive for more hypothetical or polite possibilities (e.g., 'pueda', 'supiera'). Word order can vary: 'quizás ella' or 'ella quizás'.
target_language_example: Quizás ella llegue más tarde.
native_language_example: Maybe she will arrive later.

meaning: perhaps it is / maybe it is
additional_notes: Quizás (or quizá) means 'perhaps' or 'maybe'. When followed by 'es' (the 3rd-person singular of 'ser'), it expresses uncertainty about a statement (e.g., 'quizás es verdad' = 'maybe it is true'). In everyday speech you might also hear 'quizá sea' using the subjunctive ('sea') instead of the indicative ('es'); both are common, though the subjunctive is often used when expressing doubt.
target_language_example: Quizás es mejor esperar hasta mañana.
native_language_example: Maybe it is better to wait until tomorrow.

meaning: perhaps the / maybe the (feminine noun following)
additional_notes: Quizás means 'perhaps' or 'maybe'. When followed by the feminine definite article la, it introduces uncertainty about a specific feminine noun (e.g., 'quizás la respuesta' = 'maybe the answer'). In everyday speech 'quizá' (without s) is also common and interchangeable. Placement: it usually comes before the article/noun or before a verb clause.
target_language_example: Quizás la película empiece más tarde.
native_language_example: Maybe the movie starts later.

meaning: 'maybe' or 'perhaps' + reflexive/impersonal pronoun (used before verbs like se casó, se perdió).
additional_notes: Quizás = maybe/perhaps. When followed by se, it precedes verbs that are reflexive (se casó), passive/impersonal (se perdieron), or pronominal constructions. Use with different tenses: Quizás se casó (maybe he/she got married) or Quizás se haya perdido (maybe he/she has gotten lost). Tone is tentative/unconfirmed.
target_language_example: Quizás se olvidó el libro en la escuela.
native_language_example: Maybe he/she forgot the book at school.

meaning: maybe a / perhaps a (used before a singular noun or expression).
additional_notes: Quizás (or quizás) means 'maybe' or 'perhaps' and is often followed by an article + noun or a verb phrase. 'Quizás un' is used when suggesting one example or possibility (e.g., 'quizás un taxi', 'quizás un problema'). Use 'quizás' interchangeably with 'tal vez'. Note that 'quizá' (without 's') is also correct and slightly more formal/poetic; both are common.
target_language_example: Quizás un café te ayude a despertarte.
native_language_example: Maybe a coffee will help you wake up.

meaning: 'who is' (used to ask or refer to which person is doing something or in a certain state).
additional_notes: Combines the question word quién (who) with the verb estar (to be). Used in questions or indirect questions: literal questions (¿Quién está aquí?), embedded clauses (No sé quién está), and expressions like 'veamos quién está...' It often appears with a gerund (quién está haciendo) or with adjectives/locations (quién está aquí). Accent on quién is required in direct/indirect questions.
target_language_example: Vamos a ver quién está diciendo la verdad.
native_language_example: Let's see who is telling the truth.

meaning: who I'm talking about / whom I mean.
additional_notes: Used when referring to a person already known from context. Often follows verbs like saber (to know) or preguntar (to ask): 'Sabes de quién hablo' = 'You know who I'm talking about.' Note word order: Spanish uses 'de quién' (of whom/about whom) before the verb. Can be shortened in speech to 'sabes quién' but 'de quién hablo' emphasizes 'about whom (I'm speaking)'.
target_language_example: No digas su nombre; ya sabes de quién hablo.
native_language_example: Don't say their name; you already know who I'm talking about.

meaning: Who would have thought? / You'd never guess.
additional_notes: An expression used to show surprise or irony about an unexpected fact or outcome. Often said alone or after a sentence. Tone can be positive, amused, or ironic depending on context. Contraction of 'quién lo habría dicho' but commonly used in present form.
target_language_example: Ganaste la lotería, ¿quién lo diría?
native_language_example: You won the lottery — who would have thought?

meaning: 'who' (with 'me') — used when asking about a person doing something to/for me or asking who I should/shouldn't do something to/for.
additional_notes: Quién is the question word 'who'. When combined with 'me' it appears in questions like '¿Quién me llamó?' (Who called me?) or indirect questions/clauses like 'No sé quién me ayudó' (I don't know who helped me). Word order and punctuation change depending on whether it's a direct question (inverted order, question marks) or a clause.
target_language_example: ¿Quién me dejó este paquete?
native_language_example: Who left me this package?

meaning: who doesn't / who wouldn't (used rhetorically or in questions to express that most people do something)
additional_notes: Commonly used in exclamations or rhetorical questions to express agreement or that something is obvious. Often follows a verb or statement: '¿Quién no ...?' = 'Who wouldn't ...?' or 'Who doesn't ...?'. Can imply that almost everyone does or feels that way. Not a fixed idiom—it's the word 'quién' (who) plus 'no' (not).
target_language_example: ¿Quién no quiere ser feliz?
native_language_example: Who doesn't want to be happy?

meaning: 'who knows' — used to say something is uncertain or possible.
additional_notes: Common expression to express uncertainty, speculation, or shrugging off a question. Can stand alone (like 'who knows') or start a sentence. Pronunciation note: 'quién' is stressed; when used alone it often conveys a casual, resigned, or teasing tone depending on context.
target_language_example: ¿Vendrás a la fiesta? Quién sabe, tal vez sí.
native_language_example: Will you come to the party? Who knows, maybe yes.

meaning: 'who goes' or 'who is going'.
additional_notes: Used to ask which person or people will go/do something. Common in questions: '¿Quién va?' = 'Who is going?' Can be followed by a verb or location: '¿Quién va a la fiesta?' (Who is going to the party?). Accent: 'quién' has an accent when used in questions or exclamations.
target_language_example: ¿Quién va a venir mañana al trabajo?
native_language_example: Who is going to come to work tomorrow?

meaning: How good / That's great / What a good thing (expresses approval or pleasant surprise).
additional_notes: Used to praise something (ability, appearance, smell) or to show relief/pleasure that something happened. Tone can be enthusiastic or simply approving depending on context and intonation. Often followed by a clause with que (qué bien que...) to mean "I'm glad that..." Can also stand alone as an exclamation: "Qué bien."
target_language_example: Qué bien que viniste a la fiesta.
native_language_example: How great that you came to the party.

meaning: 'why are you' (used to ask reason or cause for someone's state or location).
additional_notes: A common informal way to start questions asking why someone is in a place or in a certain state. Usually followed by a location (aquí, al lado de...) or an adjective (tan tenso). Often appears as part of ¿por qué estás...? In spoken Spanish the full form 'por qué' is typical; 'qué estás' alone is incomplete without context or 'por'.
target_language_example: ¿Por qué estás tan callado hoy?
native_language_example: Why are you so quiet today?

meaning: How easy (it is). / That's easy.
additional_notes: Used to comment on the ease of doing or saying something. Can be exclaimed alone (Qué fácil.) to express surprise, irony, or sometimes frustration (e.g., implying something is easier said than done). Often followed by a verb clause: Qué fácil es + infinitive/verb phrase.
target_language_example: Qué fácil es decirlo, pero hacerlo es otra historia.
native_language_example: How easy it is to say, but doing it is another story.

meaning: what are you doing
additional_notes: Common spoken question. Depending on context and intonation, 'qué haces' usually asks what someone is doing right now (literal) but in many situations—especially with 'por' preceding it as in the examples ('¿por qué haces...?)—it combines with 'por qué' to ask why someone is doing something. You can use it to express surprise, confusion, or to request an explanation. Informal: common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: ¿Qué haces con ese libro?
native_language_example: What are you doing with that book?

meaning: 'qué lo' by itself is not a fixed phrase; it's typically part of a larger expression (e.g., 'qué lo sepas', 'qué lo diga', 'qué lo haya hecho') and usually means 'that' or 'what' followed by a verb or clause referring to 'it' or 'that fact'.
additional_notes: You won't often see 'qué lo' alone. 'Qué' can introduce exclamations or indirect questions ('qué...') and 'lo' is a neuter object pronoun meaning 'it' or 'that (fact)'. Together they appear when 'qué' introduces a clause that contains 'lo'. Examples: '¡Qué lo sepas!' (a warning/emphasis: 'Just so you know!'), 'No sé qué lo causó' (I don't know what caused it). Pay attention to word order and the verb that follows.
target_language_example: ¡Qué lo sepas: no pienso cambiar de opinión!
native_language_example: Just so you know: I don't intend to change my mind!

meaning: how (to what degree or extent).
additional_notes: Used to ask about the degree, intensity, or extent of something. Commonly appears before adjectives or adverbs (e.g., qué tan difícil, qué tan rápido). Often interchangeable with 'qué tan' ≈ 'qué tan + adjective/adverb' and in some regions 'qué tan' can be replaced by 'qué tan' synonyms like 'cuán' or phrases with 'qué tan' meaning 'how'. More formal/written Spanish may use 'cuán' or 'qué tan' is more colloquial but widely used.
target_language_example: ¿Qué tan difícil es el examen?
native_language_example: How difficult is the exam?

meaning: How good / That's great / I'm glad (used to express happiness or relief about something).
additional_notes: Common expression to react positively to news or a situation. Can mean 'what a good thing' or simply 'great'/'that's good.' Tone and exact meaning depend on context: supportive (Qué bueno que hayas venido temprano = I'm glad you came early), pleased to see someone (Qué bueno verte), or brief agreement/satisfaction (Sí, qué bueno).
target_language_example: Qué bueno que aprobaste el examen.
native_language_example: I'm so glad you passed the exam.

meaning: what the hell / what the f*** (strong, vulgar surprise or anger)
additional_notes: Very informal and vulgar. Used to express shock, confusion, disbelief or anger about something or someone. Can be directed at a person (¿Qué carajo haces?) or at a situation (¿Qué carajo pasó?). Avoid in polite or formal settings; use with friends or in strong-emotion contexts.
target_language_example: ¿Qué carajo estás haciendo aquí a estas horas?
native_language_example: What the hell are you doing here at this hour?

meaning: what (thing); an informal/emphatic way to ask or react — 'what?' or 'what a thing'.
additional_notes: Used to ask 'what?' or to express surprise, emphasis, or commentary about something. Can appear alone (Qué cosa?) as a surprised 'What?'. With context it can mean 'what (kind of) thing' or 'how/what a ...' (e.g., Qué cosa más rica = What a delicious thing). Informal and more common in spoken, emphatic Argentine/Colombian usages but understood broadly. Tone and intonation change the nuance.
target_language_example: ¿Qué cosa dijiste que pasó ayer?
native_language_example: What did you say happened yesterday?

meaning: what the hell / what on earth (expresses surprise, annoyance, or disbelief).
additional_notes: Informal and mildly strong; used to show surprise, anger, confusion or disbelief. Can be directed at a situation or a person (¿Qué demonios pasa? = What's going on?). Often interchangeable with qué diablos or qué carajo in some regions. Avoid in very formal contexts.
target_language_example: ¿Qué demonios estás haciendo con mi teléfono?
native_language_example: What the hell are you doing with my phone?

meaning: 'what the heck' / 'what the hell' (expresses surprise, anger, or confusion).
additional_notes: Informal and emphatic phrase used to show strong surprise, annoyance, or confusion. Can be more or less rude depending on tone and context; 'diablos' literally means 'devils'. Often used in questions: '¿Qué diablos...?'. Avoid in very formal situations.
target_language_example: ¿Qué diablos estás diciendo?
native_language_example: What the heck are you saying?

meaning: How nice / What a pleasure (to...)
additional_notes: Used to express pleasure or happiness about seeing someone, someone's arrival, or an event. Often followed by an infinitive, a clause with que + subjunctive, or an object (e.g., verte, que hayas venido, verla). Common in spoken and polite social contexts.
target_language_example: ¡Qué gusto verte de nuevo!
native_language_example: How nice to see you again!

meaning: What time is it?
additional_notes: Common, polite way to ask for the current time. Used in questions; you can add 'por favor' or 'disculpa' for politeness. In casual speech intonation alone marks it as a question; written Spanish uses the opening and closing question marks: ¿qué hora es?.
target_language_example: Disculpa, ¿qué hora es?
native_language_example: Excuse me, what time is it?

meaning: what a pity / that's too bad
additional_notes: Used to express regret, disappointment, or sympathy about something. Can stand alone (Qué lástima) or introduce a clause (Qué lástima que...). Tone can be mild or sincere depending on context and intonation.
target_language_example: Qué lástima que no puedas venir al concierto.
native_language_example: What a pity that you can't come to the concert.

meaning: what a shame / that's too bad / what a pity
additional_notes: Used to express sympathy, disappointment, regret, or mild pity. Can be said alone as a short reaction ("Qué pena.") or followed by a clause ("Qué pena que..." + subjunctive when referring to unreal or wished-for situations). Tone can be sincere or ironic depending on context.
target_language_example: Qué pena que no puedas venir a la fiesta.
native_language_example: What a shame you can't come to the party.

meaning: 'what kind' or 'what type (of)'.
additional_notes: Used to ask or exclaim about the kind, type, or quality of someone or something. Can introduce a noun with de (qué tipo de libro) or be used alone before an adjective for emphasis (Qué tipo extraño = What a strange guy). Tone can be neutral (questions) or expressive (surprise, judgment, praise).
target_language_example: ¿Qué tipo de película te gusta?
native_language_example: What kind of movie do you like?

meaning: 'what is that' or 'what is that (thing/idea)?'
additional_notes: Used to ask what something is (an object, idea, situation, or behaviour). Can be direct (pointing to an object) or used more abstractly to question someone's action or a situation (e.g., "¿qué es eso de...?" = "what's this about...? / how can you...?"). Common in spoken Spanish; informal tone depends on context.
target_language_example: Eh, ¿qué es eso en tu mano?
native_language_example: Hey, what is that in your hand?

meaning: 'what (we) are' — used to ask what is happening, what is being talked about, or what people are doing
additional_notes: Common in questions. Often part of phrases like ¿qué estamos esperando? (what are we waiting for?) or ¿de qué estamos hablando? (what are we talking about?). The pronoun 'we' is implied by 'estamos' (first-person plural). Context determines tense/meaning (present progressive/ongoing situation).
target_language_example: ¿Qué estamos haciendo ahora?
native_language_example: What are we doing now?

meaning: what is
additional_notes: Used to ask or refer to what someone/something is doing or what is happening. Often appears in questions (¿qué está haciendo?, ¿qué está pasando?) or in subordinate clauses (se olvida de qué está hablando = he/she forgets what he/she is talking about). Followed by a gerund (haciendo, pasando), a past participle in passive constructions (siendo...), or a present participle/verb phrase. In casual speech, English contractions like "what's" match the register.
target_language_example: ¿Qué está ocurriendo en la cocina?
native_language_example: What's happening in the kitchen?

meaning: 'what are you' (used to ask about someone's state, condition, or what they are doing/what they're made of in expressions)
additional_notes: Combined from the question word 'qué' (what) + the verb 'estar' (to be). Common in questions like '¿Con qué estás ocupado?' (What are you busy with?) or in idiomatic expressions 'A ver de qué estás hecho' / 'Vamos a ver de qué estás hecho' meaning 'Let's see what you're made of' (test someone's character or abilities). Word order and context determine exact translation: sometimes asks about current activity, condition, or material/character.
target_language_example: ¿Con qué estás ocupado ahora?
native_language_example: What are you busy with right now?

meaning: what was it
additional_notes: Used to ask or refer to the identity or cause of something that occurred or was seen. Can mean either ‘what was it?’ (identifying an object or thing) or ‘what happened?’ (asking about an event), depending on context. Often appears in questions and indirect questions (e.g. no sé qué fue = I don't know what it was / what happened). In informal speech you may also hear Qué fue? as a brief 'what's up?' or 'what happened?'.
target_language_example: No sé qué fue el ruido en la noche.
native_language_example: I don't know what the noise was at night.

meaning: 'what was the' (start of a question or clause asking about something that happened or the identity/meaning of something).
additional_notes: This sequence appears when forming questions or relative clauses about a past event or the nature/identity of something: e.g., 'qué fue lo que pasó' = 'what was it that happened' or 'qué fue lo que dijo' = 'what was it that he/she said'. Native speakers usually include 'que' after 'lo' ('lo que') or use the full phrase 'qué fue lo que...'. It's formal/neutral and often used to emphasize or clarify the thing being asked about.
target_language_example: ¿Qué fue lo que ocurrió anoche?
native_language_example: What was it that happened last night?

meaning: 'what has' (used to ask or refer to something that has happened; part of present perfect questions/statements).
additional_notes: Commonly appears in questions or embedded clauses with the present perfect (haber + past participle). Often followed by a past participle (pasado, ocurrido, hecho). In spoken Spanish the accent on 'qué' signals a question or emphasis. Use to ask 'what has happened/been done' or to say 'what has ...'.
target_language_example: No sé qué ha pasado en la reunión.
native_language_example: I don't know what has happened at the meeting.

meaning: 'what you're talking about' or 'what you mean'.
additional_notes: Usually appears in phrases like 'no sé de qué hablas' (I don't know what you're talking about) or 'sé de qué hablas' (I know what you're talking about). Often used to express (lack of) understanding or to question someone's meaning. Grammatically, 'de qué' introduces the content/topic and 'hablas' is the verb 'you speak/talk'.
target_language_example: No entiendo de qué hablas en esa reunión.
native_language_example: I don't understand what you're talking about in that meeting.

meaning: 'what I'm talking about' or 'what I mean'.
additional_notes: Usually appears in the phrase 'saber (de) qué hablo' or 'sabes de qué hablo' to say the listener knows (or should know) the topic or meaning the speaker refers to. It often follows verbs like 'saber' and is used to point to something already understood from context. English equivalents: 'what I'm talking about', 'what I mean', 'what I'm referring to.'
target_language_example: Créeme, sé de qué hablo cuando digo que es peligroso.
native_language_example: Believe me, I know what I'm talking about when I say it's dangerous.

meaning: 'what is there' / 'what's up' / 'what is it about' (depends on context).
additional_notes: Used to ask about existence, location or state of something (What's there? / What's in...). Can also be part of phrases meaning 'what needs to be done' (qué hay que + infinitive = what must be done) or colloquially as 'what's up?'. Context determines exact translation.
target_language_example: No sé qué hay en la caja.
native_language_example: I don't know what's in the box.

meaning: 'what (to) me' — part of questions or exclamations meaning 'what ... to me' or 'what (does) ... to me' (often expresses surprise, doubt, or asks what someone should do/feel).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but a sequence that appears in questions and exclamations: e.g. ¿Qué me dices? (What are you telling me?/You don't say), ¿Qué me importa? (What do I care?/How does it matter to me?), ¿Qué me pasa? (What's wrong with me?/What's happening to me?). The verb that follows (dices, importa, pasa) completes the meaning. Use in everyday Spanish; tone depends on verb and intonation.
target_language_example: ¿Qué me importa a mí lo que digan?
native_language_example: What do I care about what they say?

meaning: what's up
additional_notes: Informal greeting or question used to ask how someone is or to inquire about a situation. Tone and meaning depend on context: as a greeting it equals "what's up?"; when concerned it means "what's wrong?" or "what's happening?" Common in spoken Spanish.
target_language_example: Hola, ¿qué pasa?
native_language_example: Hey, what's up?

meaning: 'what happened' or 'what's wrong' (asking about an event or problem).
additional_notes: Common informal question used to ask about a past event or to check if someone has a problem. Can be used neutrally (What happened?) or more urgently (What's wrong?). Often pronounced with rising intonation when asking directly.
target_language_example: ¿Qué pasó anoche en la fiesta?
native_language_example: What happened at the party last night?

meaning: 'what you can (do)'; asks about someone's ability or options.
additional_notes: Commonly used after verbs like 'ver', 'mira' or in questions to invite someone to try, explore options, or state possible actions. Can be a direct question (¿qué puedes hacer?) or part of a suggestion (A ver qué puedes hacer). Often followed by an infinitive (hacer, construir, encontrar).
target_language_example: A ver qué puedes arreglar en una hora.
native_language_example: Let's see what you can fix in an hour.

meaning: 'what can be done' or 'what is possible'.
additional_notes: Used to ask or state what actions are possible in a situation. Common in questions (¿qué se puede hacer?) to express resignation or to explore options. Often followed by an infinitive (hacer, cambiar, mejorar). Neutral register.
target_language_example: Veamos qué se puede hacer para arreglar esto.
native_language_example: Let's see what can be done to fix this.

meaning: 'what are' (asking to identify or define people, things, or categories).
additional_notes: Used to ask what something or someone is (identity, nature, category). Appears in questions and embedded clauses after verbs like saber, preguntar, decir. In informal spoken Spanish you might hear Qué son? alone to ask 'What are they?' or combined with subject pronouns (¿Qué son ustedes?).
target_language_example: ¿Qué son esos objetos en la mesa?
native_language_example: What are those objects on the table?

meaning: literally 'what I know' or used colloquially to mean 'who knows' / 'I don't know' depending on context.
additional_notes: Alone 'qué sé' is incomplete in standard Spanish; it often appears in informal speech as part of phrases like 'qué sé yo' (meaning 'who knows' or 'I don't know') or as a clipped form in casual fragments. Use in neutral contexts: 'qué sé yo' expresses uncertainty, indifference, or a vague suggestion. Not typically used in formal writing.
target_language_example: Podríamos ir al cine, o qué sé yo, quedarnos en casa.
native_language_example: We could go to the movies, or, I don't know, stay home.

meaning: I don't know / who knows / whatever — a vague expression to show uncertainty or indifference.
additional_notes: Used informally to indicate that the speaker doesn't know, is unsure, or doesn't care to specify details. Can stand alone (Qué sé yo.) or appear inside a sentence. Tone ranges from shrugging indifference to genuine uncertainty. Similar to English 'I don't know' / 'who knows' / 'whatever'.
target_language_example: ¿Vendrán mañana? Qué sé yo, tal vez sí.
native_language_example: Will they come tomorrow? Who knows, maybe yes.

meaning: How are you? / How's it going? / How about...?
additional_notes: A common informal greeting used to ask how someone is or to suggest/ask about an idea (e.g., "¿Qué tal una taza de café?" = "How about a cup of coffee?"). Often interchangeable with "¿Cómo estás?" in casual contexts. Can be followed by a name or used alone. Tone and context determine whether it's a greeting or a suggestion.
target_language_example: Hola, ¿qué tal?
native_language_example: Hi, how's it going?

meaning: 'what can I tell you' / 'what to tell you' (used to express resignation, explanation, or to introduce a comment).
additional_notes: A conversational phrase used to introduce an explanation, express resignation or acceptance, or soften a remark. Tone depends on context and intonation: can mean 'what can I say' (resignation), 'let me tell you' (introducing info), or 'you know' (seeking empathy). Common in spoken Spanish.
target_language_example: Llegó tarde otra vez, qué te digo.
native_language_example: He was late again, what can I tell you.

meaning: 'what (it/he/she) has' or 'what is wrong/about it' depending on context
additional_notes: This phrase can appear in different structures. When followed by an infinitive and 'que' (e.g., 'qué tiene que decir'), it means 'what (someone) has to (do/say)' = 'what ... has to + verb'. In questions like '¿qué tiene de malo?', it asks 'what's wrong with it?' or 'what bad thing does it have?'. Word order and context determine if it's literal possession ('what it has') or an idiomatic 'what's wrong/about it'.
target_language_example: ¿Qué tiene este libro que a todos les gusta tanto?
native_language_example: What does this book have that everyone likes so much?

meaning: 'what do you have' or 'what's on your mind/what do you mean' depending on context.
additional_notes: Literally 'what do you have'. Used to ask about physical objects (¿Qué tienes en la mano?), thoughts or intentions (¿Qué tienes en mente?), obligations or things someone must do/say (¿Qué tienes que decir?) and to challenge someone to provide evidence (¿Qué tienes para demostrarlo?). Tone depends on context and intonation—can be neutral, curious, or confrontational.
target_language_example: ¿Qué tienes en la mochila?
native_language_example: What do you have in the backpack?

meaning: No way / of course not / expresses strong disagreement or dismissal (or asks/points to what something is about in another use).
additional_notes: Common informal phrase. Most often used alone or at start of a sentence to disagree, dismiss an idea, or say something won't happen (similar to “no way” or “come on”). In sentence 4 it appears inside 'saber de qué va' meaning 'to know what it's about' — there it's literal: 'what it's about.' Tone depends on context and intonation.
target_language_example: ¿Vendrás mañana? — ¡Qué va, tengo que trabajar!
native_language_example: Are you coming tomorrow? — No way, I have to work!

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase; an uncommon adjacent pairing of the question word 'qué' (what/which) and the article 'el' (the, masc. sing.). It usually appears as part of a larger sentence or through informal/sloppy speech, typographical errors, or elision.
additional_notes: This is not a conventional standalone phrase in Spanish. Correct standard alternatives depend on context (e.g., '¿Cuál es el...?', '¿Qué...?'). In casual writing or speech you might encounter 'qué el' when words are omitted, when someone types quickly, or in certain regional colloquialisms, but it should generally be avoided in careful speech. Learn 'qué' and 'el' separately: 'qué' = what/which; 'el' = the (masculine singular).
target_language_example: ¿Qué el problema que mencionas?
native_language_example: What (is) the problem you mention?

meaning: 'what she' or 'that she' (combination of qué + ella; not a fixed idiom)
additional_notes: Qué ella by itself is not a standard fixed phrase. It arises when qué (what/that) appears next to the subject pronoun ella, but in natural Spanish the combination usually occurs with additional words or altered forms (e.g., ¿Qué dijo ella? or lo que ella...). A standalone sequence 'qué ella' can appear in colloquial or emphatic constructions (e.g., «¡Qué, ella...?», though punctuation and intonation matter) or in clipped speech, but it's uncommon to see 'qué' directly followed by 'ella' without a verb or connector.
target_language_example: ¿Qué ella piensa hacer?
native_language_example: What does she plan to do?

meaning: 'why (he/she/it) was' or 'what (he/she/it) was' in certain contexts; most commonly part of 'por qué estaba' meaning 'why (someone) was (feeling/located/etc.)'.
additional_notes: Qué = 'what' or 'why' depending on context; with 'por' ('por qué') it means 'why'. Estaba is the imperfect of estar (to be) used for ongoing or past states, locations, or feelings. 'Por qué estaba' is used to ask or report reasons for a past state or situation (e.g. why someone was sad, why someone was there). Without 'por', 'qué estaba' can appear in reported clauses meaning 'what (someone) was (doing/feeling)' but is less common.
target_language_example: No entiendo por qué estaba sola en casa.
native_language_example: I don't understand why she was home alone.

meaning: 'why we are' or 'what we are' depending on context; most often 'why we are' when followed by an adjective or location (e.g., por qué estamos aquí = why we are here).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but a combination of the question word 'qué/por qué' and the verb 'estar' (we form = estamos). 'Por qué estamos...' = 'why we are...'; 'qué estamos...' could mean 'what we are...' when used without 'por'. In the example sentences, 'por qué estamos aquí' means 'why we are here.' Use 'por qué' for reasons and 'qué' to ask for identification or definition.
target_language_example: No entiendo por qué estamos en esta situación.
native_language_example: I don't understand why we are in this situation.

meaning: "why you did that" (asking/referencing the reason someone did something).
additional_notes: Used to ask or state the reason someone performed an action. 'Por qué' = 'why'; 'hiciste' = second-person singular preterite of 'hacer' (you did). Can appear in questions (¿Por qué hiciste eso?) or statements reporting that someone knows the reason (Sé por qué hiciste eso). Formality: neutral, common in spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: ¿Por qué hiciste eso sin avisarme?
native_language_example: Why did you do that without telling me?

meaning: 'what' or 'which' + indirect object pronoun 'to him/her/you(formal)/it' (depends on context).
