Used to talk about hypothetical or real situations when someone or something lacks something. Context determines subject: puede referirse a él, ella, usted, or a noun (it). Often followed by a result clause: 'si no tiene X, [entonces]...'.
target_language_example: Si no tiene coche, puede tomar el autobús.
native_language_example: If he/she/you (formal) doesn't have a car, you can take the bus.

meaning: if (you) ever / if (one) ever (does something)
additional_notes: Commonly used to introduce a conditional idea about something that might happen at any time. Often appears in phrases like "si nunca ...", "si nunca lo hiciste," or "si nunca has..." Depending on context, it can be followed by past, present perfect, or subjunctive forms. English equivalents: "if you ever...", "if (someone) ever..."
target_language_example: Si nunca visitas Madrid, deberías ver el Museo del Prado.
native_language_example: If you ever visit Madrid, you should see the Prado Museum.

meaning: if I/you/he/etc. had never (done something) — conditional clause referring to a past hypothetical
additional_notes: This is the start of a past unreal conditional in Spanish (third or mixed conditional). It introduces a hypothetical or counterfactual situation in the past: something that did not happen. It normally requires a past participle after 'hubiera' (e.g., 'si nunca hubiera visto', 'si nunca hubiera dicho'). The subject can be implied or explicit (si nunca hubiera ido / si nunca hubieras ido). Commonly appears with a main clause using a conditional perfect (habría) or a present conditional result.
target_language_example: Si nunca hubiera conocido a María, mi vida sería muy diferente.
native_language_example: If I had never met María, my life would be very different.

meaning: if you (plural) can / whether you (plural) can
additional_notes: Common conditional phrase using the conjunction 'si' (if) + the verb 'poder' in the present indicative for ustedes/ellos/ellas. Used to ask or talk about ability or possibility directed at a group (you all). In informal contexts with friends in Spain you might hear 'si podéis' (vosotros). Pronunciation note: 'pueden' = ['pweðen'] (Spain) or ['pweden'] (Latin America).
target_language_example: Díganme si pueden ayudar esta tarde.
native_language_example: Tell me if you (all) can help this afternoon.

meaning: if I can
additional_notes: Used to introduce a condition or uncertainty about the speaker's ability or permission to do something. Can function as 'if I can' (conditional) or 'whether I can' (indirect question). Often followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., 'si puedo hacerlo').
target_language_example: Me pregunto si puedo ayudártelo mañana.
native_language_example: I wonder if I can help you with it tomorrow.

meaning: if he/she wanted
additional_notes: Often used in indirect questions after verbs like preguntar, saber, or ver. Here si means "if/whether" (not sí = "yes"). Quería is the imperfect of querer and can also refer to usted, so it may mean "if you wanted" in a formal context.
target_language_example: No sabía si quería venir con nosotros.
native_language_example: I didn't know if she wanted to come with us.

meaning: if he/she/it knows; whether (someone) knows
additional_notes: Conditional/subordinate phrase: 'si' = 'if' and 'sabe' is the third-person singular (usted/él/ella) or formal command root of 'saber' (to know). Used to introduce a condition or indirect question about someone's knowledge. Context and subject may vary (e.g., 'si sabe' can refer to usted/él/ella). For first/second person you'd use 'si sé', 'si sabes', etc. In polite questions you may see 'si sabe usted...' (Do you know... / If you know...).
target_language_example: No sé si sabe la respuesta.
native_language_example: I don't know if he/she knows the answer.

meaning: if his/her/its/their (formal: your) — conditional + possessive: 'if his/her/its/your (formal) ...'
additional_notes: Si = 'if'. Su is a third-person (and formal second-person) possessive adjective: su libro = his/her/your (formal)/their book. Together 'si su...' begins a conditional clause referring to something belonging to that person or thing: e.g. 'Si su coche llega' = 'If his/her/your car arrives.' Context determines whether su = his, her, its, their, or your (usted/ustedes).
target_language_example: Si su vuelo llega tarde, llamémosle.
native_language_example: If his/her/their flight arrives late, let's call them.

meaning: 'if only' or 'I wish that' (expresses regret or a strong wish).
additional_notes: Used to express a wish or regret about something that is not true or unlikely. Can be followed by a verb in the imperfect or past subjunctive (e.g., 'si sólo supiera', 'si sólo hubiera sabido'). Note: In modern Spanish the accent on sólo is optional and often omitted; to avoid ambiguity many writers now use 'solo' without an accent. When you mean 'only' (solamente), use 'si solo' would be unusual—'si sólo' here specifically functions as 'if only'/'I wish'.
target_language_example: Si sólo supiera la verdad, sería diferente.
native_language_example: If only I knew the truth, it would be different.

meaning: 'if it/that makes you' (followed by an emotion or state).
additional_notes: Commonly used to introduce a reason based on how something affects the listener. Usually followed by a verb like sentir (sentir) + adjective (mal, mejor, feliz) or a noun. The implied subject can be 'it', 'that', or a previously mentioned thing or action (e.g., 'si te hace sentir mejor' = 'if that makes you feel better').
target_language_example: Si te hace feliz, dilo.
native_language_example: If it makes you happy, say it.

meaning: if he/she/it has
additional_notes: Conditional phrase: 'si' = if. 'tiene' is third-person singular (él/ella/usted) of tener (to have). In context it can mean 'if he/she/it has' or polite 'if you have' (usted). Used to introduce a condition. In informal tú speech you'd hear 'si tienes'. Can be followed by nouns (si tiene fiebre), infinitives with subject (si tiene que...) or used impersonally (ver si tiene arreglo = see if it can be fixed).
target_language_example: Llámame si tiene alguna pregunta.
native_language_example: Call me if you have any questions.

meaning: if everyone / if all (of them)
additional_notes: Si todos is the conditional 'if' + 'everyone' and is used to introduce a hypothetical condition about a group. It often appears at the start of a clause: 'Si todos...' and is followed by a verb (e.g., 'si todos vienen...'). Depending on context, it can mean 'if everyone' or 'if all of us/you/them' — speaker should clarify the subject if needed (todos, nos, ustedes, etc.).
target_language_example: Si todos ayudan, terminamos antes.
native_language_example: If everyone helps, we finish sooner.

meaning: if you (do something); introduces a conditional clause referring to 'you'.
additional_notes: Conditional phrase using 'si' (if) followed by the stressed subject pronoun 'tú' (you). Subject pronouns are often omitted in Spanish, so including 'tú' adds emphasis or contrast (e.g., to stress who would act). Commonly followed by a verb in present, future, or subjunctive/conditional depending on the intended meaning (e.g., 'si tú vienes', 'si tú quieres', 'si tú fueras').
target_language_example: Si tú quieres, vamos al cine.
native_language_example: If you want, we'll go to the movies.

meaning: if a (singular, masculine) — introduces a conditional clause about one thing or one person.
additional_notes: Si = 'if'. Un = masculine singular indefinite article 'a' or 'one'. Together they start conditional sentences like 'if a/one ...' or 'if someone/one thing ...'. Often followed by a noun and then a verb. Gender/number of the noun may change the article (si una, si unos, si unas). Common in everyday and formal Spanish.
target_language_example: Si un amigo necesita ayuda, llámame.
native_language_example: If a friend needs help, call me.

meaning: if (he/she/it) goes; if (you) go (depending on context).
additional_notes: Common conditional phrase: 'si' = if + conjugated verb 'va' (from ir). Subject is understood from context (él/ella/usted). Used to introduce a condition about someone/something going or traveling. In English the subject may change: 'if he/she/it goes', 'if you go' (formal usted), or 'if it goes' depending on context.
target_language_example: Si va en tren, llegaremos más tarde.
native_language_example: If he/she goes by train, we'll arrive later.

meaning: whether already / if... yet
additional_notes: Used to introduce a yes/no subordinate clause asking whether something has already happened. Common with verbs in past or perfect contexts. Equivalent to English 'if... already' or 'whether... yet'. Often appears with verbs like enviar, recordar, añadir, llegar, etc.
target_language_example: Dime si ya compraste los billetes.
native_language_example: Tell me if you've already bought the tickets.

meaning: been / been like that (used to say something has been that way).
additional_notes: Commonly appears after a form of 'haber' or 'ser/estar' (e.g., 'ha sido así', 'siempre he sido así'). Used to state that a situation, quality, or condition has been that way (and often continues). Can express surprise, resignation, or acceptance (e.g., 'no ha sido así' = 'it hasn't been like that').
target_language_example: No ha sido así desde que cambiaron las reglas.
native_language_example: It hasn't been like that since they changed the rules.

meaning: '(have) been yesterday' used in the expression 'como si hubiera sido ayer' meaning 'as if it were yesterday' (to say something feels very recent).
additional_notes: Usually appears in the full phrase 'como si hubiera sido ayer' or 'como si todo hubiera sido ayer'. It's a way to express that a memory or event feels very recent or vivid. Uses the past subjunctive ('hubiera sido') after 'como si'. In English: 'as if it were yesterday' or 'like it was yesterday.'
target_language_example: Lo recuerdo como si hubiera sido ayer.
native_language_example: I remember it as if it were yesterday.

meaning: been difficult
additional_notes: This phrase combines the past participle 'sido' (from 'ser') with the adjective 'difícil'. It appears in perfect constructions (e.g., 'ha sido difícil' = 'has been difficult'). English translation depends on the auxiliary: 'ha sido difícil' = 'has been difficult'; 'ha sido difícil para ti' = 'has been difficult for you'.
target_language_example: Ha sido difícil adaptarme a la nueva ciudad.
native_language_example: It has been difficult for me to adapt to the new city.

meaning: been more (used to say someone/thing would have had a greater degree of some quality)
additional_notes: Appears after auxiliary verbs (haber, debería, podría, habría, habría sido, etc.) in perfect or conditional perfect constructions. 'Más' modifies an adjective or adverb that usually follows 'sido' (e.g., 'sido más cuidadoso' = 'been more careful'). Common in hypothetical or regretful statements about how things could have been different.
target_language_example: Habría sido más honesto si me lo hubieras pedido.
native_language_example: It would have been more honest if you had asked me.

meaning: has/have always been (or 'been always'); indicates something has been true for all time up to now.
additional_notes: Used after a past participle (sido) to stress that a state or situation has existed continuously up to the present. Common in perfect constructions with 'ha(n) sido' (he/she/it has been, han sido = they have been). Can follow different subjects: 'ha sido siempre' (it/he/she has always been), 'han sido siempre' (they have always been).
target_language_example: Tu amabilidad ha sido siempre un consuelo para mí.
native_language_example: Your kindness has always been a comfort to me.

meaning: it's been a (kind of) day / it has been a (type of) day.
additional_notes: Used to summarize how the day was, often followed by an adjective (largo, duro, agotador, de mierda). Common in spoken Spanish to express tiredness, frustration, or that something is enough for the day (e.g., implying you don't want more problems). Literal components: 'ha sido' = 'has been', 'un día' = 'a day'.
target_language_example: Hoy ha sido un día imposible, necesito descansar.
native_language_example: Today has been an impossible day; I need to rest.

meaning: "as always" or "as usual" (with a feminine noun or phrase following)
additional_notes: Common phrase: "Como siempre, ..." = "As always, ..." The example "siempre, la" appears when emphasizing a recurring quality linked to a feminine noun or idea (la diplomacia, la verdad, la eterna carcajada). For learners, the usual fixed expression is "como siempre"; here "la" simply begins the following noun phrase. Use it to introduce something that regularly happens or is typical.
target_language_example: Como siempre, la paciencia del profesor se agotó.
native_language_example: As always, the teacher's patience ran out.

meaning: 'always at' or 'always to' (depends on context) — used when 'siempre' (always) is followed by the preposition 'a'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase; it's simply the adverb siempre ('always') followed by the preposition a ('to/at/for'). Meaning depends on the verb or expression that follows. Common uses: • siempre a + infinitive (colloquial) can emphasize habitual action (e.g., 'siempre a llegar tarde' = 'always arriving late'). • siempre a + noun/place = 'always at' a place/time (e.g., 'siempre a las ocho' = 'always at eight'). Watch word order and register: in standard Spanish you'd normally say 'siempre llega tarde' or 'siempre llega a las ocho', not 'siempre a llegar tarde'.
target_language_example: Ella está siempre a las ocho en la oficina.
native_language_example: She is always at eight at the office. (Meaning: She is always at the office by eight.)

meaning: always like this; always that way.
additional_notes: Used to say that something (a situation, behavior, or condition) is consistently the same. Can describe a habitual state (Siempre es así: It's always like that) or express resignation about a continuing situation (No será siempre así: It won't always be like this). Tone can be neutral or slightly emotional depending on context.
target_language_example: No podemos seguir siempre así; necesitamos un cambio.
native_language_example: We can't keep being like this forever; we need a change.

meaning: 'always with' or 'always (doing/having)'; indicates something that is constantly accompanied by or repeatedly in a certain state or behavior.
additional_notes: Commonly used to say someone or something is continuously accompanied by another person, thing, emotion, or habit. Can mean 'always with' literally (always accompanied by X) or idiomatically to describe a recurring attitude or behavior (e.g., 'always with long faces' = always looking unhappy). Word order: 'siempre con + noun' or 'siempre con + verb (gerund/condition)' in context.
target_language_example: Ella va siempre con una sonrisa.
native_language_example: She always goes around with a smile.

meaning: literally 'always of/from'; used rarely as part of fixed expressions or regional usages — not a common standalone phrase
additional_notes: Most often Spanish speakers do not use 'siempre de' by itself. You may see it in longer expressions (e.g., 'siempre de parte de' meaning 'always on behalf of') or in poetic/colloquial contexts where 'de' links to a noun or pronoun. Check the full sentence to understand the meaning; otherwise use 'siempre' (always) alone or 'siempre que' (whenever/whenever that) for common uses.
target_language_example: Siempre de parte de los trabajadores, la organización defendió sus derechos.
native_language_example: Always on behalf of the workers, the organization defended their rights.

meaning: 'must always' or 'should always' (expresses that something ought to happen consistently)
additional_notes: Combines 'siempre' (always) + 'debe' (he/she/it must or should). Used to give general advice, rules, or expectations. Tone can be prescriptive; context determines whether it's stronger ('must') or softer ('should'). Subject may be explicit (yo/él) or implicit (uno/uno siempre debe...).
target_language_example: Siempre debe revisarse la lista antes de salir.
native_language_example: You should always check the list before leaving.

meaning: 'always the' (literal — used before a masculine singular noun)
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase; it's simply the adverb siempre ('always') followed by the masculine definite article el. You will see it when 'always' modifies a masculine singular noun or a habitual/characteristic mention (e.g., 'siempre el mismo' = 'always the same'). Word order is the same as in English: siempre + el + noun. Be careful not to confuse with 'siempre que' (whenever) or the set phrase 'siempre lo mismo'.
target_language_example: Siempre el mismo problema me detiene.
native_language_example: Always the same problem stops me.

meaning: 'always in' or 'always at' (used before a place, situation, or state)
additional_notes: Siempre means 'always'. When followed by a preposition like en, it indicates a consistent presence or condition in a place, time, or situation (e.g., siempre en casa = always at home; siempre en problemas = always in trouble). Commonly used in everyday speech. Word order: siempre + preposition + noun/phrase.
target_language_example: Él está siempre en casa los fines de semana.
native_language_example: He is always at home on weekends.

meaning: it is always
additional_notes: A common combination of the adverb 'siempre' (always) and the verb 'ser' in the third-person singular present ('es'). Used to state that something is always the case. English order is usually 'it is always' or 'always is' depending on emphasis. Can appear with other subjects (e.g., 'ella siempre es puntual' = 'she is always punctual').
target_language_example: En esta ciudad, siempre es difícil encontrar estacionamiento.
native_language_example: In this city, it is always difficult to find parking.

meaning: you are always
additional_notes: A present-tense phrase combining 'siempre' (always) + second-person singular 'estás' (you are). Used to state a habitual condition or repeated action about 'you'. Context may be neutral, affectionate ("siempre estás en mi corazón"), descriptive ("siempre estás ocupado"), or critical ("siempre estás listo para hablar mal de los demás"). For formal address to one person use "siempre está"; for plural "siempre están".
target_language_example: Siempre estás ahí cuando te necesito.
native_language_example: You're always there when I need you.

meaning: 'there's always a first time' (used to say everyone tries or experiences something for the first time).
additional_notes: A common phrase used to comfort or encourage someone facing something new or trying something for the first time. Often completed as "siempre hay una primera vez" or "siempre hay una primera vez para todo." Can be said jokingly or sympathetically.
target_language_example: No te preocupes si te equivocas; siempre hay una primera.
native_language_example: Don't worry if you make a mistake; there's always a first time.

meaning: always it/her (depends on context); 'siempre' = always, 'la' = feminine direct object or feminine pronoun.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase—it's the adverb 'siempre' (always) followed by the feminine direct-object pronoun 'la' or a feminine noun. The meaning depends on the verb and context: 'la' can mean 'her' (person), 'it' (feminine noun), or refer to an abstract feminine concept. Word order (verb + la) is common in spoken Spanish: e.g. 'siempre la caga' = 'he/she always messes it/her up'; 'siempre la cuidaría' = 'I would always take care of her/it'; 'siempre la guardo' = 'I always keep it/her.'
target_language_example: Siempre la llamo cuando tengo noticias.
native_language_example: I always call her when I have news.

meaning: always cries / she/he always cries.
additional_notes: Combines 'siempre' (always) + the verb 'llorar' (to cry). Use to say someone cries habitually or always in a given situation. Subject can be implied (e.g., 'Siempre llora' = 'He/She always cries'). Followed by a clause introduced with 'cuando' (when) to describe the trigger.
target_language_example: Siempre llora cuando escucha una canción triste.
native_language_example: She always cries when she hears a sad song.

meaning: always the same; same old thing
additional_notes: Used to complain about repetition or predictability. Can be a full sentence ("Siempre lo mismo.") to express frustration—equivalent to "same old thing" or "here we go again." Also appears in neutral statements about consistency (e.g., comparisons).
target_language_example: Otra vez llegaste tarde—siempre lo mismo.
native_language_example: You arrived late again—same old thing.

meaning: always them / always [object masculine plural] (used before a masculine plural direct object pronoun or noun phrase).
additional_notes: Siempre = always. Los is the masculine plural direct object pronoun ('them') or the masculine plural definite article when followed by a noun. In these examples, 'los' mostly functions as 'them' (referring to previously mentioned masculine plural things or people). Word order: 'siempre los' = 'I always them...' in Spanish; in English you'd usually say 'I always [verb] them.' Context determines the exact translation.
target_language_example: Siempre los llevo en la mochila.
native_language_example: I always carry them in my backpack.

meaning: ever more; increasingly; more and more
additional_notes: Used to say that something continues to increase or intensify over time. Often placed before an adjective, adverb, or verb phrase (e.g., 'siempre más difícil', 'siempre más caro'). Can be interchangeable with 'cada vez más'. Formality: neutral; commonly used in spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: La tarea se vuelve siempre más difícil cada semana.
native_language_example: The homework becomes increasingly more difficult each week.

meaning: whenever; as long as (depending on context).
additional_notes: Used to mean 'whenever' (every time that) when talking about repeated events (e.g., "Siempre que oigo..." = "Whenever I hear..."). It can also mean 'provided that' or 'as long as' to introduce a condition (similar to 'provided that' or 'if'). Context determines whether it's temporal (whenever) or conditional (as long as/provided that).
target_language_example: Siempre que estudies todos los días, mejorarás rápidamente.
native_language_example: Whenever/As long as you study every day, you'll improve quickly.

meaning: always wants; is always wanting to
additional_notes: Combines 'siempre' (always) with the verb 'quiere' (he/she/you formal wants) or used with a name/pronoun (e.g., 'Tom siempre quiere...') to say someone repeatedly wants or insists on something. Common for complaining about repeated behavior. Can be followed by an infinitive (siempre quiere discutir) or a noun (siempre quiere todo).
target_language_example: Ella siempre quiere ayudar, aunque esté cansada.
native_language_example: She always wants to help, even when she's tired.

meaning: 'always had' or 'was always (having)'.
additional_notes: Past imperfect of tener (tener = to have). Used to describe repeated or continuous states or habits in the past (something someone regularly had or experienced). Can be followed by nouns (dolores, un nudo) or by clauses with 'que' or relative phrases. Context determines exact translation: 'always had' (possession or condition) or 'was always' + gerund/doing (when describing repeated actions or problems).
target_language_example: Cuando era joven, siempre tenía sueño después de la escuela.
native_language_example: When I was young, I was always tired after school.

meaning: 'they always have' or 'always have (something)'.
additional_notes: Combines siempre (always) + tienen (they have). Used to state that people or things habitually possess something (a quality, object, feeling, etc.). Followed by a noun, adjective (with tener + noun phrase, e.g., hambre), or a clause. Common in general statements about others.
target_language_example: Mis amigos siempre tienen ideas nuevas.
native_language_example: My friends always have new ideas.

meaning: always a / always one (used before a noun to emphasize that something is consistently the same type or amount)
additional_notes: siempre means "always." When followed by an indefinite article (un/una) plus a noun, "siempre un" emphasizes that there is consistently one of something or that a thing is always of a certain kind. Common in phrases like "siempre un problema" (always a problem) or "siempre un placer" (always a pleasure). Word order and gender/number must agree: use "siempre una," "siempre unos," or "siempre unas" as needed.
target_language_example: Con esta familia, siempre un motivo para reír.
native_language_example: With this family, always a reason to laugh.

meaning: 'always' used before another word or phrase (common fixed combination: siempre y cuando = 'as long as' / 'provided that').
additional_notes: Alone, siempre means 'always.' The fragment siempre y appears mainly in set expressions (most common: siempre y cuando → 'as long as' / 'provided that'; siempre y cuando que is less common). It can also start emphatic phrases like siempre y cuando lo hagas (provided that you do it). Not used by itself as a complete phrase — expect a following word or clause.
target_language_example: Te ayudaré, siempre y cuando me digas la verdad.
native_language_example: I'll help you, as long as you tell me the truth.

meaning: provided that; as long as; on the condition that.
additional_notes: Used to introduce a condition. Equivalent to 'if' or 'as long as' in English; commonly follows or precedes the main clause. Can be used in formal and informal contexts. Often interchangeable with 'si' in simple conditions, but 'siempre y cuando' emphasizes the requirement or restriction.
target_language_example: Puedes venir, siempre y cuando traigas tu identificación.
native_language_example: You can come, provided that you bring your ID.

meaning: being the / remaining the (masculine singular).
additional_notes: Combines the gerund 'siendo' (being / remaining) with the masculine singular article 'el'. Used to say someone or something continues to be a certain person, role or thing. Forms change with gender/number (siendo la, siendo los, siendo las) and with different subjects (sigo siendo = I remain; sigues siendo = you remain; sigue siendo = he/she/it remains; seguimos siendo = we remain; siguen siendo = they remain). Often followed by a noun or adjective.
target_language_example: Aunque haya cambiado de trabajo, sigo siendo el mismo.
native_language_example: Even though I've changed jobs, I'm still the same (person).

meaning: it/you/he/she 'feels like' or 'feels as if'.
additional_notes: Used to describe a sensation, impression, or state by comparing it to something else. Commonly appears as 'se siente como' (it/one feels like) or with a person: 'él/ella se siente como...' For physical sensations, emotions, or situations (positive or negative). In casual speech you may also hear 'se siente' followed directly by an adjective (e.g., 'se siente mal').
target_language_example: Se siente como estar de vacaciones.
native_language_example: It feels like being on vacation.

meaning: 'feels as if' or 'it feels like (someone/something) is/was...'
additional_notes: Used to describe a sensation or impression, often followed by a verb in the subjunctive (si + [verbo] in imperfect subjunctive) when expressing hypothetical or unreal situations. Common in phrases like 'se siente como si fuera...' ('it feels as if it were...').
target_language_example: Se siente como si nunca hubiera pasado nada.
native_language_example: It feels as if nothing had ever happened.

meaning: feels better (is improving in health or mood).
additional_notes: Third-person singular of 'sentirse' (to feel oneself). Used to say someone is recovering or feeling less unwell/upset. Often appears with a reflexive pronoun (se siente mejor). Can be used formally/politely (¿Se siente mejor?) or as a simple statement (Se siente mejor).
target_language_example: Después de descansar, ella se siente mejor.
native_language_example: After resting, she feels better.

meaning: is/feels very
additional_notes: Literal components: siente = he/she/it feels or you (formal) feel (from sentir), mucho = very/a lot. Without context this phrase is ambiguous — it can describe strong feelings (e.g., "siente mucho cariño" = "feels a lot of affection") or be part of an expression about regret when used reflexively as "siento mucho" (I am very sorry). Note the difference: "siente mucho" (third person singular) vs "siento mucho" (first person singular, commonly used to apologize).
target_language_example: Ella siente mucho respeto por su profesor.
native_language_example: She feels a lot of respect for her teacher.

meaning: 'feels very' — used with emotions or physical states (se siente muy + adjective).
additional_notes: Commonly appears as 'se siente muy ...' (reflexive 'sentirse') to describe how someone feels physically or emotionally: e.g. se siente muy mal (feels very ill/bad), se siente muy solo (feels very lonely). The subject is usually él/ella/usted or a name; adjective must agree in gender/number (solo/sola, feliz/felices).
target_language_example: Ella se siente muy cansada después del viaje.
native_language_example: She feels very tired after the trip.

meaning: I'm sorry, I can't / I’m sorry, I cannot.
additional_notes: Common, polite way to refuse or explain inability to do something. Often begins with "Lo siento" (I'm sorry) followed by "no puedo" and a verb or clause. Can be used for physical inability, refusal, or lack of permission/information. Tone and context determine softness of refusal.
target_language_example: Lo siento, no puedo asistir a la reunión mañana.
native_language_example: I'm sorry, I can't attend the meeting tomorrow.

meaning: I'm sorry, but no / I'm sorry, but I can't (or won't).
additional_notes: A polite way to refuse, disagree, or say you cannot do something. Often used with a verb or clause after 'no' (e.g., 'no puedo', 'no es', 'no tengo'), but can stand alone as a brief refusal. Tone and context determine softness—adding reasons makes it less abrupt.
target_language_example: Lo siento, pero no puedo ir al concierto contigo.
native_language_example: I'm sorry, but I can't go to the concert with you.

meaning: 'I feel like I'm in' or 'I feel as if (I'm) in...'
additional_notes: Used to express a feeling of being in a situation, place, or emotional state. Often followed by a noun or clause introduced by 'que' (e.g., siento como en casa; siento como en un sueño; siento como en que todo va mal). In casual speech speakers may drop 'como' and say 'siento que estoy en...' or simply 'siento en...' depending on region. Tone: neutral.
target_language_example: Siento como en casa cuando estoy con ustedes.
native_language_example: I feel like I'm at home when I'm with you.

meaning: Literally 'I feel of' — not a standard or common fixed phrase in Spanish. If encountered, it's usually nonstandard, a regionalism, or the result of a calque; standard alternatives are 'siento' + noun, 'lo siento', or 'siento que' + clause. Rarely used in correct Spanish except in mistaken or dialectal contexts.
additional_notes: 'Siento de' is generally incorrect in standard Spanish when used to mean 'I'm sorry about' or 'I feel for'. Use 'lo siento', 'siento (algo)', or 'siento que...' instead. In some informal or regional speech you may see 'me siento de...' intended to indicate origin or group (e.g., 'me siento de aquí'), but standard Spanish uses 'soy de' or 'vengo de' for origin and 'me siento identificado con' for identification. Treat 'siento de' as a nonstandard construction.
target_language_example: A: ¿Por qué estás triste? B: Siento de la situación, pero no sé cómo ayudar.
native_language_example: A: Why are you sad? B: I feel (sorry) about the situation, but I don't know how to help.

meaning: I feel in / I feel (something) in (a part of the body) or I sense in (a place).
additional_notes: Siento is the first-person singular present of sentir (to feel). When followed by en + noun it expresses where you feel a sensation or emotion (e.g., 'siento en el pecho' = 'I feel it in my chest'). It can also be used with locations to say you sense something somewhere (e.g., 'siento en la cocina que alguien cocina' — less common). For physical sensations use body parts; for emotions you can say 'siento (algo) en + body part'.
target_language_example: Siento en el estómago que algo va mal.
native_language_example: I feel in my stomach that something is wrong.

meaning: I feel bad / I'm feeling unwell; can mean emotionally guilty or physically unwell depending on context.
additional_notes: Used with 'me' (me siento mal) to say you feel bad. Context decides meaning: often emotional (I'm sorry/guilty) when followed by 'por...' (for...), or physical (I'm sick/unwell) when talking about health. More natural Spanish often uses 'me siento mal' for both; for stronger apology you can say 'me siento muy mal' or 'lo siento' for 'I'm sorry.'
target_language_example: Me siento mal por no haber contestado antes.
native_language_example: I feel bad for not replying earlier.

meaning: I feel very... (used to intensify an emotion or physical state)
additional_notes: This is the verb sentir(se) in the first person singular (me siento) plus 'muy' to strengthen the adjective that follows: e.g. me siento muy feliz, me siento muy mal. Often appears as 'me siento muy + adjective'. Use 'me siento' for feelings/states and 'me siento muy' to emphasize.
target_language_example: Me siento muy agradecido por tu ayuda.
native_language_example: I feel very grateful for your help.

meaning: I feel more / I'm sorry more (depends on context).
additional_notes: This phrase is ambiguous. As a form of the verb sentir (yo siento), it most often means 'I feel more' when followed by an emotion, sensation, or clause (e.g., 'siento más cariño por él' = 'I feel more affection for him'). It can also appear in apologetic contexts where 'siento' = 'I'm sorry' and 'más' adds emphasis (colloquially) meaning 'I'm even more sorry' or 'I'm very sorry,' but that use is less common; Spanish speakers usually say 'lo siento mucho' for 'I'm very sorry.' Pay attention to what comes after: if followed by que + clause, it means 'I'm sorry that...'; if followed by a noun or adverb, it usually means 'I feel more [noun/adverb].'
target_language_example: Después de hablar con ella, siento más respeto por su trabajo.
native_language_example: After talking with her, I feel more respect for her work.

meaning: I don't feel anything / I feel nothing.
additional_notes: Commonly used in negative sentences to say you have no physical sensation or no emotion/feeling. In Spanish, the more standard negative form is "no siento nada" (with 'no' before the verb). Depending on context it can mean physical numbness (e.g., "no siento nada entre mi cuello y mis pies") or emotional indifference (e.g., "no siento nada por él").
target_language_example: No siento nada cuando toco esa zona.
native_language_example: I don't feel anything when I touch that area.

meaning: I feel/I'm sorry for (someone or something).
additional_notes: From the verb sentir (to feel). 'Siento por' is used to express sympathy or regret about someone or something. More common is 'siento' alone before a clause (e.g. 'Lo siento') or 'siento que...' For sympathy, Spanish speakers often say 'siento por + noun' (e.g. 'Siento por él') or use 'siento mucho'/'siento mucho lo de...'. Pay attention to context: to feel sorry (sympathy) vs. to feel (emotion) about something.
target_language_example: Siento por tu pérdida; lo siento mucho.
native_language_example: I'm sorry for your loss; I'm very sorry.

meaning: 'I feel so' (used before an adjective)
additional_notes: This is the first-person singular form of 'sentir(se)' + 'tan' (so). It introduces a speaker's emotional or physical state and is followed by an adjective or an adjective phrase: me siento tan feliz / tan solo / tan inútil. In sentences 1–3 the reflexive pronoun 'me' is required in full phrase 'me siento tan ...' — without 'me' 'siento tan' could be used in some non-reflexive senses but for feelings use 'me siento tan'.
target_language_example: Me siento tan cansado después del viaje.
native_language_example: I feel so tired after the trip.

meaning: 'nap in' (used to say someone takes a nap in/at a place).
additional_notes: Combines siesta (nap) with a preposition indicating location (en = in/at). Common verbs with this phrase: tomar una siesta, echar una siesta, echarse una siesta. Use en + place: en la oficina, en el sofá, en la escuela. 'Echar(se) una siesta' is a set phrase meaning 'to take a nap.'
target_language_example: Voy a echar una siesta en el sofá.
native_language_example: I'm going to take a nap on the sofa.

meaning: 'seven of' — used to indicate quantity (seven) of something, often followed by a noun or a time (e.g., seven of a month, seven o'clock in some contexts).
additional_notes: Literal phrase combining the number siete (seven) with the preposition de ('of'/'from'). Commonly appears in phrases like 'siete de la mañana' (seven in the morning) or 'siete de cada diez' (seven out of ten). Use depends on what follows: with times use 'siete de la mañana/tarde/noche', with quantities use 'siete de' + noun or partitive context (e.g., 'siete de ellas').
target_language_example: Llegaré a las siete de la noche.
native_language_example: I will arrive at seven in the evening.

meaning: a time expression meaning 'seven o'clock' when followed by a period (e.g., mañana/tarde/noche) or part of a longer time phrase like 'siete de la mañana' (7:00 AM).
additional_notes: This is not a complete phrase by itself — it's typically followed by a time-of-day word: mañana, tarde or noche. Spanish often uses 'las' for plural hours (e.g., 'las siete'), but colloquially people say 'a las siete' or simply 'siete de la mañana' to specify 7:00 AM. Use 'de la mañana/tarde/noche' to distinguish AM/PM.
target_language_example: Nos vemos a las siete de la noche.
native_language_example: See you at seven at night (7:00 PM).

meaning: "seven is" (literal — the number seven followed by the verb 'to be').
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase in Spanish; it's simply the number 'siete' (7) + the verb 'es' (third person singular of ser). You might see it in sentences that state a fact about the number seven (e.g., "Siete es un número primo" — "Seven is a prime number") or as part of a larger clause. For most learners, treat 'siete' as the number word and 'es' as the verb 'is'. Word order follows normal Spanish sentence structure: Subject (siete) + verb (es) + complement.
target_language_example: Siete es un número primo.
native_language_example: Seven is a prime number.

meaning: 'seven and' — used to say times like 'seven and a quarter' or to list numbers (seven and ...).
additional_notes: Commonly appears in telling time: 'siete y cuarto' = 7:15, 'siete y media' = 7:30. Also used when listing numbers (e.g., 'tres, siete y diez' = 'three, seven and ten'). In time expressions the part after 'y' specifies minutes past the hour. Pronunciation: 'siete y' = /ˈsjete i/.
target_language_example: La fiesta empieza a las siete y cuarto.
native_language_example: The party starts at 7:15.

meaning: 'follow' (formal imperative or subjunctive form of seguir + preposition a, meaning to follow someone/something)
additional_notes: Used with a direct object introduced by a (person, vehicle, river, etc.). 'Siga' is the usted (formal) imperative or present subjunctive form of seguir. In commands (imperative) it means 'follow (that person/thing)' when addressing usted or giving formal orders (e.g., Taxi, siga a ese coche = Sir/driver, follow that car). In other contexts (subjunctive) it can express desire, doubt, or purpose (e.g., El que nos siga... = Whoever follows us...). Verb 'seguir' requires a preposition a before a person or thing being followed.
target_language_example: Siga a la persona con la chaqueta roja.
native_language_example: Follow the person with the red jacket.

meaning: means 'means nothing to' or 'is/means nothing to (someone)'.
additional_notes: Used to say that something or someone has no importance, value, or emotional significance to the speaker (or to someone). Common structure: [Subject] + no + significa nada + para + [person]. Often contracted in speech to 'no me significa nada' (to me). Can be used for both people and things/events.
target_language_example: Ese regalo no significa nada para mí.
native_language_example: That gift means nothing to me.

meaning: vital signs (measurements that show a person's basic body functions, e.g., heart rate, blood pressure, temperature, respiration).
additional_notes: Commonly used in medical contexts. Refers to objective measurements that help assess a patient's immediate health. In Spanish, always plural. You can hear it when doctors or nurses report a patient's condition.
target_language_example: La enfermera tomó sus signos vitales antes de la operación.
native_language_example: The nurse took his vital signs before the operation.

meaning: 'the next (one) is' or 'what follows is'.
additional_notes: Used to introduce the next item, step, sentence, or idea. Often appears in lists, instructions, or explanations. In Spanish you can say 'el siguiente es...' (masculine) or 'la siguiente es...' (feminine) to agree with the noun being referred to. Can also appear without the article in contexts like 'lo siguiente es...' meaning 'what follows/is next is...'.
target_language_example: Lo siguiente es preparar los ingredientes.
native_language_example: The next step is to prepare the ingredients.

meaning: 'next station' (the next stop on a train/bus/metro).
additional_notes: Used to tell someone where to get off public transport or to indicate the upcoming stop. Common in announcements and everyday speech. Can be combined with verbs like bajar(se) (to get off) — e.g., 'Me bajo en la siguiente estación.'
target_language_example: Disculpe, necesito bajar en la siguiente estación.
native_language_example: Excuse me, I need to get off at the next station.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase in Spanish; literally 'silence is'.
additional_notes: This pair of words by itself does not form a common expression. You might see 'silencio' (silence) used alone as a command ('Silencio, por favor' = 'Silence, please') or as a noun ('Hay mucho silencio' = 'There is a lot of silence'). 'Es' is the third-person singular of 'ser' (to be): 'es' = 'is'. If you encounter 'silencio es' in a sentence, it's likely part of a larger clause (e.g., 'El silencio es necesario' = 'Silence is necessary').
target_language_example: El silencio es importante durante el examen.
native_language_example: Silence is important during the exam.

meaning: literally 'silence for' — used to indicate silence during or out of respect for something or someone (e.g., 'silence for a moment', 'silence for the victims').
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom by itself; it's the noun 'silencio' followed by the preposition 'por' to explain the reason, duration, or occasion for the silence. Common uses: 'silencio por un minuto' (silence for a minute), 'silencio por respeto' (silence out of respect), 'silencio por los caídos' (silence for the fallen). Word order: 'silencio por + [reason/duration/person]'.
target_language_example: Guardaron un silencio por respeto a las víctimas.
native_language_example: They kept silence out of respect for the victims.

meaning: 'chair of' or 'chair for' — the start of a noun phrase that describes the purpose, material, owner, or type of a chair (e.g., silla de madera = wooden chair; silla de oficina = office chair).
additional_notes: This is not a complete phrase by itself; it's a prepositional phrase beginning with the noun silla (chair) followed by de + noun or adjective to specify type, material, use, or possession. Common patterns: 'silla de + material' (madera, plástico), 'silla de + lugar/uso' (oficina, comedor), 'silla de + persona' (niño, barbero), or 'silla de + nombre' to indicate ownership (la silla de María). Use the appropriate article and agreement as needed: 'una silla de madera', 'la silla del comedor' (de + el = del).
target_language_example: Compré una silla de oficina cómoda.
native_language_example: I bought a comfortable office chair.

meaning: wheelchair.
additional_notes: A common term for a mobility device with wheels used by people who cannot walk or have difficulty walking. Often used with articles or possessives (una silla de ruedas, su silla de ruedas) and can be singular or plural (sillas de ruedas).
target_language_example: Mi abuelo usa una silla de ruedas para salir al parque.
native_language_example: My grandfather uses a wheelchair to go to the park.

meaning: "the chair is" — used to describe the chair's characteristics or compare it.
additional_notes: Literal combination of noun + verb (silla = chair, es = is). Used to state facts or opinions about a specific chair (material, comfort, weight, comparison, size, etc.). Change adjective/gender/number as needed (e.g., "la silla es cómoda"). For plural: "las sillas son". Verb "es" is the third-person singular of "ser" (permanent/essential traits or comparisons).
target_language_example: Esa silla es demasiado baja para mi espalda.
native_language_example: That chair is too low for my back.

meaning: "the chair is" (subject + verb) — a simple statement about the chair's state or location.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but the combination of the noun 'silla' (chair) and the verb 'estar' in the third person singular ('está'). Use it to describe how or where a chair is: e.g., 'La silla está rota' (the chair is broken) or 'La silla está en la cocina' (the chair is in the kitchen). Remember agreement: 'la silla' is feminine singular, so use 'está'.
target_language_example: La silla está al lado de la mesa.
native_language_example: The chair is next to the table.

meaning: chair for / chair to (used to indicate purpose or recipient)
additional_notes: Used with a person to mean 'a chair for [someone]' (recipient). Also appears before an infinitive to show purpose ('a chair to [do something]') or with reflexive verbs (sentarse) in contexts like 'una silla para que [alguien] se siente'. Word order and context determine whether it means 'for [person]' (recipient) or 'in order to' (purpose).
target_language_example: Pon una silla para la abuela junto a la ventana.
native_language_example: Put a chair for grandma by the window.

meaning: at first sight; at first glance
additional_notes: Used to say how something appears initially or superficially. Often appears in the phrase "a simple vista" (or more commonly "a primera vista") but "simple vista" by itself is understood as 'at first glance' in many contexts. Can describe impressions that might change on closer inspection.
target_language_example: A simple vista, el edificio parece abandonado.
native_language_example: At first glance, the building looks abandoned.

meaning: 'just it' / 'simply it' — used to emphasize an action done to 'it' or 'him' (lo = him/it, direct object).
additional_notes: simplemente = 'simply' or 'just' (used for emphasis or to downplay reasons). lo is the masculine direct-object pronoun (him/it). Together they appear before the verb in most Spanish sentences when used as object pronoun + verb (e.g., 'Lo dejó' = 'he left it'). In the examples here the order is stylistic: 'Simplemente lo dejó' = 'He just left it there.' Remember to match lo with masculine singular objects/people; use la for feminine.
target_language_example: No hubo discusión; simplemente lo compré.
native_language_example: There was no discussion; I just bought it.

meaning: 'just a' or 'simply a' — downplays or minimizes what follows.
additional_notes: Used to reduce emphasis or present something as ordinary or not important. Often interchangeable with 'solo un' or 'simplemente' + noun phrase. Tone can be neutral or dismissive depending on context (e.g., 'just a soldier' vs. 'just a know-it-all'). Agreement: if noun is plural, use 'simplemente unos/unas' (e.g., 'simplemente unos modelos').
target_language_example: No es un genio, es simplemente un profesor dedicado.
native_language_example: He's not a genius; he's simply a dedicated teacher.

meaning: without sugar; sugar-free.
additional_notes: Used to request or describe a drink/food that has no sugar added. Common in cafés and menus. Can be used alone as a short reply (e.g., ordering). 'Azúcar' is uncountable here. For packaged products, 'sin azúcar' often means sugar-free or no added sugar.
target_language_example: Quiero mi café sin azúcar, por favor.
native_language_example: I want my coffee without sugar, please.

meaning: without stopping; continuously; nonstop.
additional_notes: Used to describe an action that keeps happening without interruption. Common with verbs of action or weather (e.g., 'llover', 'reír', 'sufrir'). Formal or neutral register; can be used in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Llovió sin cesar durante toda la noche.
native_language_example: It rained nonstop all night.

meaning: without saying a (single) word; silently.
additional_notes: Commonly completed as 'sin decir una palabra' (without saying a word). Used to describe actions done in silence—no words spoken. Can be followed by 'palabra' but sometimes 'una' stands alone in casual speech or lists. Tone is neutral; used in narration and everyday speech.
target_language_example: Se fue sin decir una palabra.
native_language_example: He left without saying a word.

meaning: 'without a doubt' / 'undoubtedly' / 'certainly'.
additional_notes: Used to express strong agreement, certainty, or to emphasize that something is true. Can appear at the start, middle (set off by commas), or end of a sentence. Polite and neutral — appropriate in formal and informal contexts.
target_language_example: Sin duda será una gran oportunidad para ella.
native_language_example: It will undoubtedly be a great opportunity for her.

meaning: without the (masculine singular).
additional_notes: A combination of the preposition sin (without) + the masculine singular definite article el. Used before masculine singular nouns (e.g., sin el libro = without the book). Note that Spanish often contracts de + el → del, but sin + el does not contract. If the next word is feminine, use sin la; for plural use sin los/sin las.
target_language_example: No puedo salir sin el abrigo.
native_language_example: I can't go out without the coat.

meaning: however
additional_notes: A common conjunctive adverb used to introduce a contrast or contradiction with what was said before. Can appear at the start of a sentence (often followed by a comma), mid-sentence, or alone for emphasis. Synonyms: pero, no obstante (very similar).
target_language_example: Quería ir al parque; sin embargo, empezó a llover.
native_language_example: I wanted to go to the park; however, it started to rain.

meaning: without me
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something happens or is done in someone's absence or excluding that person. The pronoun 'mí' carries an accent to distinguish it from the possessive 'mi'. Often appears after verbs or prepositions (e.g., 'salir sin mí', 'ir sin mí').
target_language_example: No hagan planes sin mí.
native_language_example: Don't make plans without me.

meaning: simply; without further explanation or reason; just like that
additional_notes: Used to describe an action or situation done abruptly or without further detail, justification, or ceremony. Often appears alone ("sin más") or with verbs ("se fue sin más"). Tone can be neutral or slightly critical depending on context.
target_language_example: Se fue sin más, sin decir adiós.
native_language_example: He left just like that, without saying goodbye.

meaning: 'without us'.
additional_notes: Used to say that something happens, continues, or exists in the absence of the speaker and others (we/us). Common in statements about surviving, continuing, or excluding the group. Can be emphatic (e.g., political slogan: 'Nothing about us without us').
target_language_example: No pueden tomar decisiones importantes sin nosotros.
native_language_example: They can't make important decisions without us.

meaning: 'speechless' or 'lost for words.'
additional_notes: Used to say you have no words to express surprise, emotion, or disbelief. Common in both present (estoy sin palabras) and past (me quedé sin palabras). Can be literal (no words left) or figurative (overwhelmed).
target_language_example: Cuando vi la sorpresa, me quedé sin palabras.
native_language_example: When I saw the surprise, I was speechless.

meaning: without thinking; thoughtlessly or automatically.
additional_notes: Used to say someone does something without thinking first, either impulsively (Ella actuó sin pensar) or habitually/automatically (I can't think of X without thinking of Y). Context determines whether it means 'without reflection' or 'whenever X happens, Y also comes to mind' (as in 'no puedo X sin pensar en Y').
target_language_example: Contestó sin pensar y luego se arrepintió.
native_language_example: He answered without thinking and then regretted it.

meaning: without prior (warning/notice); unexpectedly
additional_notes: Used with nouns like aviso (warning/notice) to say something happened unexpectedly or without prior notice. Often appears as 'sin previo aviso'. Common in formal and everyday contexts (e.g., meetings, job dismissals, visits).
target_language_example: Llegó sin previo aviso y nos sorprendió a todos.
native_language_example: He arrived without prior notice and surprised all of us.

meaning: without a problem; no problem / no worries.
additional_notes: Used to say something can be done easily or that there is no objection. Common in casual and neutral contexts. Can stand alone as a short reply (like 'no problem').
target_language_example: Puedo ayudarte sin problema.
native_language_example: I can help you, no problem.

meaning: by accident; unintentionally.
additional_notes: Used to say that an action was not done on purpose. Common in everyday speech. Can modify verbs to indicate lack of intent (e.g., 'lo dije sin querer' = 'I said it by accident').
target_language_example: Lo rompí sin querer.
native_language_example: I broke it by accident.

meaning: without his/her/its/their (possessive) — used before a noun to indicate absence of possession or accompaniment
additional_notes: sin = without. su is a formal/neutral third-person (or usted) possessive adjective that can mean his, her, its, your (formal), or their depending on context. Use sin su + noun (sin su ayuda, sin su coche). If number/clarity is needed, Spanish often uses 'sin sus' for plural nouns (sin sus amigos). Context determines whose possession is meant.
target_language_example: Salió de la casa sin su abrigo.
native_language_example: He left the house without his coat.

meaning: homeless; without a roof (used to describe people without shelter).
additional_notes: Common phrase to describe a person or group without a home/shelter. Can be used as a noun phrase (los sin techo, un sin techo) or adjectivally (personas sin techo). Neutral to slightly formal; avoid as the only descriptor—use respectfully (persona sin hogar) when appropriate.
target_language_example: Hay varias personas sin techo cerca del parque.
native_language_example: There are several homeless people near the park.

meaning: without time / out of time (not having enough time)
additional_notes: Used to say someone has no time left (to do something) or didn't have enough time. Often appears with quedarse (quedarse sin tiempo) meaning 'run out of time'. Can describe a current lack of time or that time ran out in the past.
target_language_example: Nos estamos quedando sin tiempo para terminar el proyecto.
native_language_example: We're running out of time to finish the project.

meaning: without a (masculine singular noun)
additional_notes: sin means "without." When followed by the article un it indicates absence of a singular, masculine, countable thing or person. It contracts with other articles (e.g., sin + la stays sin la), and gender/number change the article: sin una, sin unos, sin unas. Often used before nouns: sin un problema, sin un amigo.
target_language_example: Salió de la casa sin un paraguas.
native_language_example: He left the house without an umbrella.

meaning: 'without you' (formal or polite).
additional_notes: Used to indicate the absence of the person addressed (usted = formal 'you'). Common in formal or polite contexts; in casual speech you'd often hear 'sin ti'. Can appear in statements about actions taken, consequences, or hypothetical situations.
target_language_example: No podemos empezar sin usted.
native_language_example: We can't start without you.

meaning: without seeing; not having seen; (in some contexts) still not understanding or noticing
additional_notes: Commonly used with an object after it (sin ver + a/que + noun/verb) to mean 'without seeing' or 'without having seen'. Can also be used idiomatically to express 'still not understanding' (sigo sin ver el problema = I still don't see the problem). Use with verbs in infinitive (sin ver que...) or with people/things (sin ver a su marido).
target_language_example: Llevo dos semanas sin ver a María.
native_language_example: I haven't seen María for two weeks.

meaning: but rather to / instead (to) — used to correct or contrast a preceding idea when the object is introduced with 'a'.
additional_notes: Used after a negation (no ...) to replace or correct the previously mentioned object or person; combines 'sino' (but rather) with the preposition 'a' when the contrasting element requires 'a' in Spanish (e.g., for indirect objects or after verbs that take 'a'). Common in sentences like 'No X, sino a Y' meaning 'Not X, but rather Y.'
target_language_example: No invité a Juan, sino a María.
native_language_example: I didn't invite Juan, but rather María.

meaning: but rather the (feminine direct object) — used to correct or contrast a previous negative statement.
additional_notes: Sino is used after a negative clause to introduce an alternative or correction. When the noun that follows is feminine singular, the article/la (or other feminine determiner) appears: e.g., 'no X, sino la Y' = 'not X, but rather the Y.' Often appears as 'no ... sino' + noun, pronoun, or clause. Do not use 'sino' after affirmative sentences; in affirmative contexts use 'pero'.
target_language_example: No es mi culpa, sino la responsabilidad del gerente.
native_language_example: It's not my fault, but rather the manager's responsibility.

meaning: 'felt that' or 'felt (that)...' — introduces a feeling or inner perception followed by a clause.
additional_notes: Used to report someone's subjective feeling or sense about a situation. The verb sentir here is in the past (sentir → sintió). After 'que' follows a clause (often imperfect or past) describing what was felt. Common in storytelling and everyday speech.
target_language_example: Ella sintió que había tomado la decisión correcta.
native_language_example: She felt that she had made the right decision.

meaning: used to introduce the minimum or least expected action or thing (equivalent to 'even to' or 'at least to').
additional_notes: Siquiera is often used to mean 'at least' or 'even' and appears before verbs, nouns, or pronouns. In the form 'siquiera a + [infinitive/person]', it emphasizes the smallest action or concession toward someone or something (e.g., 'siquiera a él' = 'at least to him'). It's more common to see 'siquiera' alone ('ni siquiera' = 'not even'). 'Siquiera a' is somewhat formal/literary and may be replaced by 'al menos a' in everyday speech.
target_language_example: No le habló siquiera a su vecino.
native_language_example: He didn't even speak to his neighbor.

meaning: at least the (masculine singular) — used to emphasize a minimum or to introduce the smallest expected thing
additional_notes: Siquiera is often used to mean 'at least' or 'even' and can appear before nouns, verbs, or clauses. When followed by a masculine singular noun, it becomes 'siquiera el'. Common in negative or concessive contexts: to say someone didn't do even the smallest thing. Word order: 'no hizo siquiera el trabajo' = 'he didn't even do the work' or 'no tengo siquiera el dinero' = 'I don't even have the money.'
target_language_example: No tengo siquiera el dinero para el boleto.
native_language_example: I don't even have the money for the ticket.

meaning: at least is / even is (used to emphasize a minimum fact)
additional_notes: siquiera often appears alone (e.g., 'ni siquiera' = 'not even') or before verbs to mean 'at least' or 'even'. When followed by 'es', 'siquiera es' emphasizes that something at minimum 'is' a certain way. It's somewhat formal/literary and not as common in everyday speech; in many contexts English speakers would say 'at least' or 'even'. Word order: 'siquiera' can be placed before the verb for emphasis.
target_language_example: Siquiera es una solución, aunque imperfecta.
native_language_example: At least it is a solution, even if imperfect.

meaning: 'not even to him/her/it' or 'not even [verb] him/her/it' (used to emphasize negation).
additional_notes: Siquiera is used to add emphasis to negative statements and often pairs with no (no siquiera = not even). When combined with an indirect object pronoun like le, it highlights that the action or thing didn't happen/wasn't given to that person/thing. Word order can vary (e.g., 'ni siquiera le...','no le dio siquiera'). Common in formal and everyday speech.
target_language_example: No siquiera le avisaron antes de irse.
native_language_example: They didn't even tell him before leaving.

meaning: 'even it' or part of phrases meaning 'not even it/that' (used to emphasize minimal extent or absence).
additional_notes: Siquiera is an adverb meaning 'even' or 'at least'. Paired with a direct object pronoun like lo, it emphasizes that not even that thing/action happens or is true. Often appears in negative contexts: 'no siquiera lo hizo' = 'he didn't even do it.' In many cases you will see 'siquiera' alone or with other pronouns (me, nos, etc.). Word order can vary: 'no lo hizo siquiera' is also possible but less common.
target_language_example: No siquiera lo miró cuando entré.
native_language_example: He didn't even look at it when I entered.

meaning: 'at least' (used before a verb to say even the smallest amount or action applies to me)
additional_notes: Siquiera is often used to mean 'at least' or 'even' and is placed before a verb or pronoun+verb. When combined with a pronoun (siquiera me, siquiera nos, etc.) it emphasizes that even I (or we) did or experienced something — usually in negative or regretful contexts: e.g., 'No siquiera me llamó' = 'He didn't even call me.' In positive sentences it can express the minimal expectation ('Si siquiera me ayudas, sería mejor'). Note word order: 'siquiera' commonly appears before the pronoun/verb.
target_language_example: No siquiera me avisaron de la reunión.
native_language_example: They didn't even warn me about the meeting.

meaning: 'I can even' or 'I can at least' (used to emphasize ability or minimal possibility).
additional_notes: This combines 'siquiera' (used to mean 'even' or 'at least' in negative or minimal contexts) with a verb. In Spanish, 'siquiera' often appears after a negation (no siquiera puedo = I can't even) or to stress the smallest possibility (al menos puedo/siquiera puedo...). Alone 'siquiera' is somewhat formal; word order can vary (no siquiera puedo, siquiera puedo).
target_language_example: No siquiera puedo ayudar hoy, lo siento.
native_language_example: I can't even help today, sorry.

meaning: used to emphasize that something doesn't even happen or isn't even done (roughly 'not even' or 'don't even').
additional_notes: siquiera is often used with negatives to mean 'even' (no ... siquiera = not even). When followed by a reflexive verb form like 'se', it appears in constructions highlighting that an action doesn't even occur to someone or isn't even done for someone: e.g. 'no se siquiera...' or 'ni siquiera se...'. Common in spoken and written Spanish for emphasis. Word order can vary: 'ni siquiera se dio cuenta' = 'he didn't even notice.'
target_language_example: Ni siquiera se despidió antes de irse.
native_language_example: He didn't even say goodbye before leaving.

meaning: at least I know / even I know
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that the speaker (at minimum) knows or is aware of something, often in contrast to others or to express resignation. It commonly appears after a verb in negative or comparative contexts (e.g., 'no siquiera sé' = 'I don't even know'). Tone can be defensive or exasperated.
target_language_example: No me importa lo que digan; siquiera sé quién soy.
native_language_example: I don't care what they say; at least I know who I am.

meaning: at least you / even you (used to emphasize a minimum or surprising inclusion)
additional_notes: siquiera is an adverb used to indicate a minimum, a bare degree, or surprise/contrast (similar to 'at least' or 'even'). When placed before a pronoun and verb (siquiera te + [verb]), it emphasizes that the action applies to you at least or even you. Common in negative or contrastive contexts: e.g. 'No viniste siquiera' = 'You didn't even come.' Word order can vary: 'ni siquiera' is a very common fixed form meaning 'not even.'
target_language_example: Ojalá siquiera te llamara para avisarme.
native_language_example: I wish you would at least call me to let me know.

meaning: at least I have / I even have (used to emphasize possession or existence, often in negative or contrastive contexts)
additional_notes: Siquiera is an adverb meaning 'at least' or 'even'. When combined with a verb like 'tengo' it emphasizes that, despite expectations or negatives, the speaker has something. Common in sentences expressing scarcity, contrast, or minimum consolation: e.g. 'No tengo dinero; siquiera tengo comida' (I have no money; at least I have food). Word order can vary: 'ni siquiera tengo' (not even I have) is a frequent stronger negative form.
target_language_example: No tengo dinero, pero siquiera tengo trabajo.
native_language_example: I don't have money, but at least I have a job.

meaning: 'at least you' or 'even you' (used to single someone out as the minimum or surprising example)
additional_notes: Siquiera is used to indicate the minimum expectation or to emphasize that someone is included when others are not. Placing tú after siquiera emphasizes that the speaker expects at least that person should do or have something, or is surprised that even that person did/said something. Common in negative or disappointing contexts: 'No vino ninguno; siquiera tú' = 'No one came; at least you (should have).' Tone can be reproachful, disappointed, or surprised depending on context.
target_language_example: Siquiera tú podrías haberme avisado.
native_language_example: You could have at least told me.

meaning: at least one; even one (used to emphasize a minimum amount or number).
additional_notes: Often appears in negative or conditional contexts to stress that not even a single item/person/instance exists or is available. Common structures: 'ni siquiera un...' (not even one) and 'al menos siquiera un...' (less common). Often used with verbs in negative sentences: 'No hay siquiera un...' or 'No vino siquiera un amigo.'
target_language_example: No había siquiera un bolígrafo en la mesa.
native_language_example: There wasn't even a single pen on the table.

meaning: at least I / even I
additional_notes: Combination of 'siquiera' (meaning 'at least' or 'even') with a subject pronoun for emphasis. Used to say that, among people or possibilities, 'I' would do or feel something — often to emphasize contrast or surprise. Can appear in contexts like 'ni siquiera yo' (not even I) or simply 'siquiera yo' to stress that at least I can/should/...
target_language_example: Siquiera yo puedo ayudar en ese proyecto.
native_language_example: At least I can help on that project.

meaning: 'system is' — literal combination of noun + verb (used to state what a system is or does).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase; it's simply the noun sistema (system) followed by the verb es (he/she/it/you-formal of ser). Use it to give descriptions or definitions about a system: e.g., 'El sistema es seguro' (The system is secure). Note that grammar requires agreement with articles/adjectives and context may call for other verbs (está, funciona, tiene).
target_language_example: El sistema es complicado para los usuarios nuevos.
native_language_example: The system is complicated for new users.

meaning: "the system is" (third-person singular present of estar)
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but the verb 'estar' (to be) conjugated for third-person singular after the noun 'sistema'. Use to describe current states or conditions of a system (e.g., location, status, temporary condition). For permanent characteristics use 'el sistema es' (from 'ser') instead. Remember agreement: 'el sistema está' (masculine singular).
target_language_example: El sistema está funcionando correctamente.
native_language_example: The system is working correctly.

meaning: the solar system (the Sun and the planets that orbit it).
additional_notes: Refers to our Sun's system of planets, moons, asteroids, etc.; often used for other star systems by context (e.g., 'fuera del sistema solar' = beyond the solar system). 'Sistema' = system, 'solar' = solar (from the Sun).
target_language_example: Vivimos en un sistema solar con ocho planetas.
native_language_example: We live in a solar system with eight planets.

meaning: site/place of; used to indicate the location or source of something.
additional_notes: Common phrase: sitio (place, site) + de (of/from). Used before a noun to say 'place of' or 'site of' (e.g., sitio de trabajo = workplace; sitio de reunión = meeting place). Can also mean 'website of' when referring to a web page (sitio web de). Requires a noun after 'de'.
target_language_example: El sitio de la fiesta está cerca del parque.
native_language_example: The site of the party is near the park.

meaning: "sitio" = place, site; the two-word string "sitio es" would typically be part of a sentence meaning "the place is..."
additional_notes: Alone, "sitio" means place, spot, site (physical location or figurative). "es" is the verb "ser" (to be) for él/ella/usted or used after a noun phrase: e.g., "El sitio es bonito" = "The place is beautiful." You will not normally say "sitio es" by itself; it appears inside a sentence: article or determiner usually precedes "sitio" (el, un, este).
target_language_example: El sitio es perfecto para una foto.
native_language_example: The place is perfect for a photo.

meaning: Literally 'site/place no' — not a natural standalone phrase in Spanish. Often appears as part of a larger phrase meaning 'site/place not...' or a truncated label (e.g., 'sitio no disponible' = 'site not available'). In context it conveys negation related to a place or site (no place, not available, no room) but you should use full expressions like 'no hay sitio' or 'sitio no disponible'.
additional_notes: This exact two-word sequence ('sitio no') is uncommon by itself and usually incomplete. Common alternatives: 'no hay sitio' ('there is no room'), 'ningún sitio' ('no place/nowhere'), or adjectival phrases such as 'sitio no disponible' ('site not available'). 'Sitio' means 'place, site, room, space'. If you encounter 'sitio no' in UI text or labels, it likely prefixes a following adjective or past participle (e.g., 'sitio no autorizado').
target_language_example: Sitio no disponible: vuelva a intentarlo más tarde.
native_language_example: Site not available: please try again later.

meaning: website; a collection of web pages accessible online.
additional_notes: Common Spanish term for an internet site. Often shortened to 'sitio' in context, or 'web' in informal speech. Used for business, personal, or institutional websites. Plural: 'sitios web' (web stays invariable).
target_language_example: He creado un sitio web para mi negocio.
native_language_example: I created a website for my business.

meaning: 'situation of' / 'the situation regarding' (used to introduce what something concerns).
additional_notes: A common phrase used to say what something is about or to describe the state/condition of someone or something. Often followed by a noun: situación de la empresa (the company's situation), situación de emergencia (emergency situation), situación de María (María's situation). Can be used in formal and neutral contexts.
target_language_example: Queremos hablar de la situación de la economía local.
native_language_example: We want to talk about the situation of the local economy.

meaning: situation in / state of affairs in (a place or context).
additional_notes: Used to talk about the condition, circumstances, or status of something within a specific location or context. Often followed by a place, time, or area (e.g., 'situación en el país', 'situación en la empresa'). Can introduce descriptions, updates, or comparisons.
target_language_example: La situación en la ciudad ha mejorado este mes.
native_language_example: The situation in the city has improved this month.

meaning: 'the situation is' — used to describe or explain a current state of affairs
additional_notes: This is the phrase 'la situación es' often shortened in speech to 'situación es' when introducing an explanation or description. It precedes a statement about circumstances, problems, or facts. In full form you'd usually say 'la situación es...' or 'la situación es que...' to add more detail.
target_language_example: La situación es que necesitamos más tiempo.
native_language_example: The situation is that we need more time.

meaning: 'the situation is' — a short phrase used to describe the current state or condition of something.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom but the combination of the noun 'situación' (situation) and the verb 'estar' (to be). It's typically followed by an adjective, noun phrase, or subordinate clause: e.g. 'La situación está difícil' or 'La situación está bajo control.' Use 'está' for singular situations (ella/él/usted form). For plural, use 'las situaciones están'.
target_language_example: La situación está bajo control por ahora.
native_language_example: The situation is under control for now.

meaning: imperative 'sit' + preposition 'to' used before a verb or noun phrase: 'sit down to (do/experience/ eat, etc.)'.
additional_notes: Siéntate is the tú (informal) singular imperative of sentarse (to sit down). The preposition 'a' often introduces an action (siéntate a comer = sit down to eat), an activity, or a position relative to someone (siéntate a mi lado = sit down beside me). Use 'siéntese' (usted) or 'siéntense' (ustedes) for formal or plural commands. In casual speech the accent on 'siéntate' is important for stress but often omitted in informal writing.
target_language_example: Siéntate a leer un rato conmigo.
native_language_example: Sit down to read for a while with me.

meaning: feel like (as if) — used to invite someone to relax or act at ease (often in 'siéntete como en casa').
additional_notes: Commonly followed by 'en casa' or 'en tu casa' to mean 'make yourself at home.' 'Siéntete' is the informal imperative (tú) of 'sentirse' (to feel). Use with friends/family; for formal/polite use to one person say 'siéntase como en casa.'
target_language_example: Siéntete como en casa y ponte cómodo.
native_language_example: Make yourself at home and get comfortable.

meaning: Not a recognized Spanish multiword phrase. Likely a typo, mis-segmentation, or fragment (e.g., intended 'su color de', 'so' as misspelling of 'so' in English, or 'sólo color de'). No fixed meaning without context.
additional_notes: This exact string 'so color de' does not occur as a standard expression in Spanish. Possible explanations: typo ('su color de' = 'its/your color of…'), missing accent or word break ('sólo color de' = 'only color of…' though uncommon), or fragment of a larger phrase. Provide the original sentence for an accurate interpretation. Treat any translation cautiously and ask for context.
target_language_example: No entiendo 'so color de' en ese texto; ¿puedes escribir la frase completa que contiene 'so color de' para aclararlo?
native_language_example: I don't understand 'so color de' in that text; can you provide the full sentence containing 'so color de' to clarify?

meaning: about something; concerning something.
additional_notes: Used to introduce a topic or refer to an unspecified thing/event. Common in phrases like "hablar sobre algo" (to talk about something) or to indicate location on top of something when context implies 'on/over something' (e.g., caer sobre algo = fall onto something). Neutral register.
target_language_example: Necesito decirte algo sobre algo que pasó ayer.
native_language_example: I need to tell you about something that happened yesterday.

meaning: about that / on that (referring to something near in context).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a topic or refer to a specific thing previously mentioned or visible. 'Sobre' here means 'about' (topic) in most examples. When combined with 'ese' it points to a masculine singular item (that one). In some contexts 'por sobre ese' can mean 'over that' physically (see example 5), but the common use is 'about that.'
target_language_example: No tengo mucha información sobre ese libro.
native_language_example: I don't have much information about that book.

meaning: 'about the' or 'on the' (used before a masculine singular idea or clause)
additional_notes: Sobre lo is a combination of the preposition sobre ('about', 'on', 'over') + the neutral/demonstrative lo. It often appears before a clause or abstract idea (e.g., 'sobre lo que...') or before a noun phrase when referring to a general idea. Common structures: 'sobre lo que...' = 'about what/which...', 'sobre lo ocurrido' = 'about what happened'. If followed directly by a verb clause, use 'sobre lo que' + verb.
target_language_example: Hablamos sobre lo que pasó ayer.
native_language_example: We talked about what happened yesterday.

meaning: literally 'about my' or 'on my' — used before a plural noun to mean either 'about my (something)' or 'on my (something)' depending on context.
additional_notes: Esta frase combina la preposición 'sobre' (which can mean 'about' or 'on/over') with the possessive 'mis' (my, plural). Use 'sobre mis' before a plural noun: e.g. 'sobre mis viajes' (about my trips) or 'sobre mis hombros' (on my shoulders). The exact meaning depends on the noun and context.
target_language_example: Quiero escribir un artículo sobre mis experiencias en la universidad.
native_language_example: I want to write an article about my experiences at university.

meaning: about nothing / on nothing (used to mean 'about anything' in negative contexts).
additional_notes: Literal meaning is 'about nothing.'
