additional_notes: This is simply two separate words that can appear consecutively when 'suelo' (used before an infinitive) begins a clause and is followed by a verb or phrase joined with another action by 'y'. Example pattern: 'Suelo [infinitive] y [infinitive]...'. There is no special contraction or idiomatic meaning when the two words appear together — they remain compositional and literal.
target_language_example: Suelo y prefiero descansar los domingos.
native_language_example: I usually and prefer to rest on Sundays.

meaning: '(something) rings' or 'a (sound) is heard' — used to say a sound (often a bell, alarm, or phone) starts or can be heard.
additional_notes: Suena is the third-person singular of sonar (to sound, to ring). When followed by an indefinite article + noun (un/una), it describes that a single, non-specific sound occurs: suena un timbre, suena una alarma, suena un teléfono. Use suena + el/la + noun to refer to a specific known sound. Common in phrases like 'suena un teléfono' (a phone is ringing) or 'suena una alarma' (an alarm is going off).
target_language_example: De repente suena un teléfono en la otra habitación.
native_language_example: Suddenly a phone rings in the other room.

meaning: 'luck to' or 'luck with' — a non-standard/rare construction that may appear in regional or informal uses when wishing or referring to luck directed toward someone or something.
additional_notes: This is not a common fixed multiword expression in standard Spanish. Preferred standard phrases are 'tener suerte', 'buena suerte', 'mucha suerte' or constructions with 'suerte con + noun/infinitive'. 'suerte a' might appear in some dialectal or poetic uses (e.g., 'que le dé suerte a...') but learners should avoid relying on it in formal speech.
target_language_example: Que la suerte a ti te acompañe en el viaje.
native_language_example: May luck accompany you on the trip.

meaning: 'luck with' or 'luck in/with (someone or something)'.
additional_notes: Used to say someone has had good or bad luck regarding a person, situation, or thing. Often appears in past tense (tuvimos suerte con) or as a standalone wish (¡Suerte con eso! = Good luck with that). Can be followed by a noun or pronoun (suerte con él, suerte con los hombres).
target_language_example: Tuve suerte con mi primer trabajo.
native_language_example: I was lucky with my first job.

meaning: 'luck of the' or 'fortune of the'
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself; it's the noun 'suerte' (luck/fortune) followed by the preposition 'de' contracted with the definite article 'el' (del = of the). It begins a phrase that describes whose or what kind of luck/fortune is being talked about (e.g., la suerte del principiante = the beginner's luck). Use with a noun after 'del'.
target_language_example: La suerte del principiante a veces ayuda en los juegos.
native_language_example: The beginner's luck sometimes helps in games.

meaning: 'luck in' or 'good/bad luck with' (used to talk about having luck regarding something).
additional_notes: Used with a noun or verb (infinitive) to say someone has (or doesn't have) luck in a particular area: suerte en + noun (suerte en el amor) or suerte en + infinitive (suerte en ganar). Often appears in phrases like 'tener suerte en...' (to be lucky in...), 'mucha suerte en...' (good luck in...). For negative use, 'mala suerte en...' or 'no tener suerte en...'.
target_language_example: Te deseo mucha suerte en tu examen.
native_language_example: I wish you lots of luck in your exam.

meaning: luck in the (context/thing that follows); used to say someone has luck with something.
additional_notes: This phrase is not a complete fixed expression by itself—it needs a noun or situation after it (e.g., 'suerte en la vida', 'suerte en la prueba'). It literally means 'luck in the...' and is used to comment on someone's fortune regarding a specific area. Word order: 'suerte en + la/el + [noun]'.
target_language_example: Te deseo suerte en la entrevista de trabajo.
native_language_example: I wish you luck in the job interview.

meaning: literally 'luck and' — not a fixed phrase; appears as part of expressions combining 'suerte' (luck) with another noun or clause (e.g., 'suerte y salud').
additional_notes: By itself 'suerte y' is incomplete. 'Suerte' means 'luck' and is often joined with other words using 'y' (and) to form wishes or set phrases (e.g., 'suerte y salud' = 'luck and health', 'suerte y éxito' = 'luck and success'). Use only as part of a larger phrase; the meaning depends on the word that follows.
target_language_example: Te deseo mucha suerte y éxito en tu nuevo trabajo.
native_language_example: I wish you lots of luck and success in your new job.

meaning: used to say someone dreams about or of something (dreams involving a person, place, or thing).
additional_notes: Combines sueño (dream) with the preposition en to indicate the content or setting of a dream: 'sueño en' + noun or pronoun. More common alternatives are 'soñar con' (to dream about/of) or 'soñar que' (to dream that). 'Sueño en' is less common as a verb phrase by itself and may appear in expressions like 'tengo un sueño en el que...' ('I have a dream in which...') or poetic uses.
target_language_example: Anoche tuve un sueño en el que volaba sobre la ciudad.
native_language_example: Last night I had a dream in which I was flying over the city.

meaning: My dream is to become... (used to introduce a future profession/role you aspire to).
additional_notes: This phrase is built from sueño (dream) + es (is) + convertirme (to become me / to become [for me]). It normally continues with a noun or phrase: "Mi sueño es convertirme en médico." In Spanish, convertirme en + profession/role expresses what you want to become. If the speaker is female, the verb form remains convertir + -me (no gender change); the profession noun may change gender (médico → médica).
target_language_example: Mi sueño es convertirme en profesora y enseñar en una escuela rural.
native_language_example: My dream is to become a teacher and teach in a rural school.

meaning: 'my dream is to become' (used to say what you want to be in the future).
additional_notes: Commonly used with a first-person subject: Mi sueño es convertirme en + profession/role. If speaker is female, convertirme can be changed to convertirme (same spelling) — gender is expressed in the noun that follows (un/una, doctor/doctora). You can also use 'mi sueño es ser' as a shorter alternative.
target_language_example: Mi sueño es convertirme en ingeniera aeronáutica.
native_language_example: My dream is to become an aerospace engineer.

meaning: a strange/odd dream.
additional_notes: Used to describe a dream that felt unusual, weird, or unexpected. Commonly appears with verbs like tener (tuve) or soñar (soñó). 'Sueño' = dream; 'extraño' = strange. Neutral register.
target_language_example: Anoche tuve un sueño extraño sobre volar en la ciudad.
native_language_example: Last night I had a strange dream about flying over the city.

meaning: dream come true (something that has been achieved or realized).
additional_notes: Often appears in the phrase 'un sueño hecho realidad' (a dream come true). Alone, 'sueño hecho' is a shortened way to refer to a dream that has been made/fulfilled. Use to describe goals, wishes or ideal outcomes that have been realized.
target_language_example: Mudarnos al campo fue un sueño hecho realidad.
native_language_example: Moving to the countryside was a dream come true.

meaning: Not a correct or standard Spanish multi-word expression; likely a mistaken word order, typo, or fragment. It does not function as a fixed phrase in Spanish.
additional_notes:
Spanish does not use 'sueño se' as a conventional phrase. Possible intended forms include:
- 'se sueña' (impersonal/passive: 'one dreams' or 'is dreamed')
- 'se me hace sueño' / 'me da sueño' (I feel sleepy)
- 'tengo sueño' (I'm sleepy)
- 'sueño' alone means 'sleep' (noun: tiredness) or 'dream' (noun: dream content)
If you tried to combine 'sueño' with the reflexive pronoun 'se', the typical constructions are different (e.g., 'se sueña' or verbs like 'soñarse' are rare and dialectal). Treat 'sueño se' as an incorrect fragment and revise to one of the correct forms above.
target_language_example: No uses 'sueño se' en Español; 'sueño se' no es una frase correcta.
native_language_example: Don't use 'sueño se' in Spanish; 'sueño se' is not a correct phrase.

meaning: '(the) dream has' — used to start a passive/perfect phrase meaning a dream has come true or become reality.
additional_notes: This fragment combines sueño (dream) with the present perfect auxiliary se ha + past participle (e.g., hecho, realizado, convertido) to say that someone's dream has been fulfilled. In full sentences you usually see: 'Mi/su/tu sueño se ha hecho realidad' or 'El sueño se ha realizado.' The reflexive 'se' here makes the action happen to the subject (the dream).
target_language_example: Nuestro sueño se ha hecho realidad después de tanto esfuerzo.
native_language_example: Our dream has come true after so much effort.

meaning: '(the) dream will come true' or 'dream will be realized'.
additional_notes: This phrase uses the noun sueño (dream) plus the future passive construction se hará (from hacer) to say that a dream will become real. Common in hopeful or reassuring statements: Algún día mi/su/tu sueño se hará realidad = Someday my/your/their dream will come true. You can replace sueño with other nouns (e.g., plan se hará realidad).
target_language_example: Un día mi sueño se hará realidad.
native_language_example: One day my dream will come true.

meaning: 'dreams of' or 'dreams about' (possession or topic of dreams).
additional_notes: Used to indicate what someone dreams about or aspires to. Often followed by a noun or verb infinitive (e.g., sueños de viajar, sueños de éxito). Can refer to literal dreams during sleep or figurative aspirations/ambitions.
target_language_example: Tiene sueños de viajar por el mundo.
native_language_example: He has dreams of traveling around the world.

meaning: A fragment consisting of the plural noun 'sueños' (dreams) followed by the singular verb 'es' (is). Not a grammatically correct standalone phrase in standard Spanish; likely part of a larger sentence or a mistaken pairing. If intended meaning is 'dreams are,' the correct form is 'los sueños son...'; if 'a dream is,' use 'un sueño es...'.
additional_notes: As written, 'sueños es' mixes plural noun and singular verb and is ungrammatical in most contexts. It can appear in poetic, colloquial, or erroneous writing where grammar is deliberately altered or mistakenly used. To fix: match number (sueños son) or change noun to singular (un sueño es).
target_language_example: En ese verso, 'sueños es' suena intencionalmente fragmentario para enfatizar la idea.
native_language_example: In that verse, 'sueños es' sounds intentionally fragmentary to emphasize the idea.

meaning: 'dreams' (with the reflexive construction 'se hacen realidad' = 'become/are made real')
additional_notes: This appears as part of the common phrase 'los sueños se hacen realidad' meaning 'dreams come true' or 'dreams are made real.' The verb 'se hacen' is a passive/reflexive construction used to say something happens (literally 'are made'). Use different tenses: 'se hacen realidad' (present), 'se hicieron realidad' (past), 'se harán realidad' (future). You don't say 'sueños se' alone in normal Spanish; it appears with the verb phrase (e.g., 'se hacen realidad').
target_language_example: Algún día mis sueños se harán realidad.
native_language_example: Someday my dreams will come true.

meaning: enough with / it's enough to (expressing that something is sufficient or should stop).
additional_notes: Used to say that something is sufficient, should stop, or that merely doing X is/was enough. Often appears as an imperative to tell someone to stop ("¡Suficiente con eso!") or in statements meaning "it's not enough with..." when saying an action alone doesn't suffice. Commonly followed by a noun, clause, or verb phrase introduced by que/infinitive.
target_language_example: Suficiente con las excusas; ahora haz tu parte.
native_language_example: Enough with the excuses; now do your part.

meaning: literally 'enough for' or 'sufficient for' (used to indicate adequacy or sufficient amount for something).
additional_notes: Used before a noun, infinitive, or clause to say that something is enough for a purpose or person. More common is 'suficiente para' in many contexts; 'suficiente por' can appear in regional varieties or fixed expressions (e.g., 'suficiente por hoy' meaning 'enough for today'). Check context—'por' often emphasizes time, reason, or a limit.
target_language_example: Ya es suficiente por hoy; terminamos temprano.
native_language_example: That's enough for today; we're finished early.

meaning: big/large enough to (do something) or to hold/fit something.
additional_notes: Used to say that size or capacity is adequate for a purpose. Often appears with a verb or noun after 'para' (e.g., para cuidarte, para cubrir). Can be shortened in speech to 'lo suficientemente grande para...' or simply 'suficiente para' in some contexts.
target_language_example: ¿La mesa es lo suficientemente grande para seis personas?
native_language_example: Is the table big enough for six people?

meaning: rich enough; wealthy enough (or sufficiently rich in flavor/textures, depending on context).
additional_notes: Literal composition: 'suficientemente' = sufficiently/enough, 'rico' = rich/tasty/wealthy. Commonly used to say someone has enough money (es suficientemente rico) or that a food/dish is rich enough in flavor or texture. Tone is neutral; meaning depends on context (financial vs. sensory).
target_language_example: ¿Eres suficientemente rico para comprarte esa casa?
native_language_example: Are you rich enough to buy that house?

meaning: 'sum of' or 'amount of' (refers to a total quantity or amount, often money or a mathematical total).
additional_notes: Can be used literally in math (la suma de 2 y 3) or figuratively to talk about an amount of money (una suma de dinero) or a total/result (la suma de las partes). Common collocations: 'una suma de dinero', 'la suma de X y Y'.
target_language_example: Ella recibió una suma de dinero por su trabajo.
native_language_example: She received a sum of money for her work.

meaning: I knew from (a certain moment).
additional_notes: Used to say you realized or became certain of something starting at a specific time or moment. 'Supe' is the past (pretérito) of 'saber' meaning 'I knew' or 'I found out'; 'desde' means 'from' or 'since'. Common constructions: 'supe desde el momento en que...', 'supe desde el principio', 'supe desde la primera vez que...'.
target_language_example: Supe desde la primera vez que hablamos que eras honesto.
native_language_example: I knew from the first time we spoke that you were honest.

meaning: 'surface of' or 'area of' (depending on context).
additional_notes: Can mean the physical surface (outer layer) of something or the measured area/size of a region (e.g., country, planet). Use context to choose translation: for geography/measurements translate as 'area of' or 'surface area of'; for tactile/visual contexts translate as 'surface of' or 'the surface'.
target_language_example: La superficie de la mesa está limpia.
native_language_example: The surface of the table is clean.

meaning: 'the survival of' (continuing to live or exist).
additional_notes: Used to talk about the continued existence or survival of a person, group, place, species, or abstract thing (e.g., planet, community). 'Supervivencia' is a noun; 'de' introduces who or what survives. Common in formal and neutral contexts.
target_language_example: La supervivencia de la comunidad depende del agua.
native_language_example: The survival of the community depends on water.

meaning: 'I wanted you to know that' / 'that you knew' (subjunctive form used to express informing or assuming someone knows).
additional_notes: From the verb saber (to know) in the imperfect subjunctive (tú supieras). Common in phrases like "Quería que supieras que..." meaning "I wanted you to know that..." Used to gently inform someone or to state something you assume/expect they know (e.g. "como si no supieras..."). Often appears in polite or explanatory statements.
target_language_example: Quería que supieras que puedes llamarme a cualquier hora.
native_language_example: I wanted you to know that you can call me any time.

meaning: assuming that
additional_notes: A fairly formal way to introduce an assumption or premise. It can be similar to si or suponiendo que, and it is often followed by the subjunctive when the situation is hypothetical. Don't confuse it with por supuesto que, which means 'of course'.
target_language_example: Supuesto que no haya tráfico, llegaremos a las ocho.
native_language_example: Assuming that there isn't traffic, we'll arrive at eight.

meaning: 'given that', 'assuming that', or 'supposing that'.
additional_notes: Used to introduce a hypothesis, condition, or assumption. Can be followed by an indicative or subjunctive depending on how certain or hypothetical the speaker considers the situation. Often interchangeable with 'si' (if) in some contexts but 'supuesto que' feels slightly more formal or explicit about assuming something.
target_language_example: Supuesto que llegues temprano, podemos ir al cine antes de la cena.
native_language_example: Given that you arrive early, we can go to the cinema before dinner.

meaning: literally 'supposed that it is' — used to refer to an assumption or alleged fact; typically part of a larger clause (e.g., 'el supuesto que es...') and often needs context to be complete.
additional_notes: Not a fixed standalone idiom. More commonly you will see 'supuesto que' meaning 'assuming that' or 'given that'. 'Supuesto que es' functions as a noun phrase meaning 'the assumption that it is...' and usually continues with further information (e.g., 'el supuesto que es necesario' or 'el supuesto que es falso'). Use with context to avoid ambiguity.
target_language_example: El problema parte del supuesto que es falso: creyendo eso, tomaron la decisión equivocada.
native_language_example: The problem stems from the supposed fact that it is false: believing that, they made the wrong decision.

meaning: literally 'supposed that I am'; used when presenting a hypothetical or assuming something about oneself ("assuming that I am...").
additional_notes: This phrase often appears as part of a larger conditional or hypothetical clause (e.g., "suponiendo/supuesto que estoy..." or "en el supuesto de que estoy..."). It sounds somewhat formal; in everyday speech Spaniards usually say "supongamos que estoy" or "si supongo que estoy" or simply "si estoy...". Use it to introduce an assumption about your own state or action.
target_language_example: Supuesto que estoy equivocado, ¿qué haríamos diferente?
native_language_example: Assuming that I am wrong, what would we do differently?

meaning: 'supposed that' or 'assuming that' (used to introduce a hypothesis); not a fixed standalone phrase but a sequence that can appear inside longer constructions.
additional_notes: This sequence combines 'supuesto' (assumption), 'que' (that) and the pronoun 'lo' (it). It's more common to see established alternatives like 'suponiendo que', 'en el supuesto de que', or 'dado que'. Word order and the referent of 'lo' depend on context; by itself 'supuesto que lo' is incomplete and typically continues with a verb or clause.
target_language_example: Si estamos en el supuesto que lo pidan, tendremos que preparar más material.
native_language_example: If we are in the situation assuming that they request it, we'll have to prepare more material.

meaning: 'supposed that I' / 'assuming that I' (used to introduce a hypothesis about oneself)
additional_notes: This phrase combines supuesto (assumption/supposed) with que (that) and me (reflexive or indirect object for 'me'). In natural Spanish you'd more often find forms like "se supone que me...", "supongo que me..." or "supuesto que..." followed by a clause. "Supuesto que me" by itself is typically part of a longer sentence: e.g. "Supuesto que me invites, iré" (Assuming you invite me, I'll go) or "Supuesto que me lo digan" (Provided that they tell me). Use to introduce a condition or hypothesis about the speaker.
target_language_example: Supuesto que me invites, aceptaré la oferta.
native_language_example: Assuming that you invite me, I'll accept the offer.

meaning: assuming that not / provided that not (i.e., unless or on the condition that something is not true)
additional_notes: Often used to introduce a condition that negates something, similar to 'unless' or 'provided that not'. It is somewhat formal; more common alternatives in speech are 'a menos que' or 'si no'. Context determines whether it means 'assuming that it's not the case' or 'provided that it isn't.'
target_language_example: Iré al parque, supuesto que no llueva.
native_language_example: I'll go to the park, provided that it doesn't rain.

meaning: assuming that (he/it/you) doesn't (do/do it).
additional_notes: A clipped phrase used to introduce a hypothesis or condition; often appears as part of a larger clause (e.g., "suponiendo/supuesto que no lo haga", "supuesto que no lo dijo"). 'Lo' refers to a previously mentioned action or thing. Informal register possible in spoken Spanish. More common full forms: "supuesto que no lo sea", "supuesto que no lo haga", or simply "si no lo..."
target_language_example: Supuesto que no lo acepte, ¿qué haremos?
native_language_example: Assuming that he doesn't accept it, what will we do?

meaning: used to confirm or assume that something is true; 'I suppose so' / 'assumed yes'.
additional_notes: Common in spoken Spanish to express agreement by assuming the answer is yes. It can be a response to a question or a comment when you accept a premise or make a tentative confirmation. Tone/context determines strength: can be casual (agreeing) or cautious (not fully certain).
target_language_example: ¿Vendrás a la reunión? — Supuesto que sí, solo tengo que terminar un informe.
native_language_example: Will you come to the meeting? — I suppose so, I just need to finish a report.

meaning: 'his/her/their days' (literal) or 'his/her/their time is limited' (idiomatic)
additional_notes: Can be literal (e.g., 'sus días de estudiante' = 'his/her student days') or idiomatic: 'sus días están contados' means someone's remaining time, influence, or chances are limited (often used about careers, life, power). 'Sus' agrees with the possessor (his/her/their) based on context.
target_language_example: Sus días como director están contados; van a reemplazarlo este año.
native_language_example: His days as director are numbered; they're going to replace him this year.

meaning: 'his/her/their children to' or 'their children to (somewhere or someone)'.
additional_notes: A combination of the possessive pronoun 'sus' (his, her, your(formal), their) + 'hijos' (children/sons) + the preposition 'a' (to). It appears before a verb or place: e.g. 'condujo a sus hijos a la piscina' = 'he drove his children to the pool'. 'A' can also introduce a person or direction ('reunió a sus hijos a su alrededor' = 'gathered his children around him'). The exact English possessive depends on context (sus can mean his, her, your, or their).
target_language_example: Llevó a sus hijos a la escuela esta mañana.
native_language_example: She took her children to school this morning.

meaning: 'his/her/their three' — refers to three people or things that belong to someone (plural possessive).
additional_notes: Sus is the plural possessive adjective (his, her, its, your formal, their) used before a plural noun. 'Sus tres' is followed by a noun (e.g., hijos, autos) and means 'the three [of theirs]'. Gender of the noun determines agreement of any adjectives that follow (e.g., 'sus tres hijos' vs. 'sus tres hijas'). Context decides whether sus means his, her, your, or their.
target_language_example: María llamó a sus tres amigos para invitarles.
native_language_example: María called her three friends to invite them.

meaning: a sigh of (something); used to describe a brief, audible exhalation expressing an emotion (relief, sadness, wind, etc.).
additional_notes: Commonly followed by a noun that names the emotion or cause (e.g., alivio = relief). Can describe both people sighing and non-human brief sensations (e.g., 'suspiro de viento' = a slight gust). Used to convey a small, fleeting expression.
target_language_example: Todos respiraron y soltaron un suspiro de alivio.
native_language_example: Everyone breathed and let out a sigh of relief.

meaning: suéter + es = 'the sweater is' (used to describe a sweater).
additional_notes: This combines the noun suéter (sweater) with the verb es (third-person singular of ser: 'is'). Use to describe qualities or colors of a sweater: temperature, color, comfort, etc. In Spanish you can also say 'mi suéter es...' or 'este suéter es...' depending on the subject (mi = my, este = this, su = his/her/your).
target_language_example: Este suéter es muy cómodo y cálido.
native_language_example: This sweater is very comfortable and warm.

meaning: 'Saturday is' — the noun 'sábado' (Saturday) followed by the verb 'es' (is). This two-word sequence appears when 'sábado' is the subject and is followed by 'es' for predication, though it's not the usual word order for stating the day.
additional_notes: Not a fixed phrase; in natural speech Spanish typically uses 'es sábado' (it's Saturday). 'sábado es' can appear in contexts like lists, contrasts, or poetic inversion, or when 'sábado' is topicalized. Example: in a sentence enumerating days with descriptions, or in emphatic constructions: 'Sábado es el mejor día.'
target_language_example: Sábado es el día que más me gusta.
native_language_example: Saturday is the day I like the most.

meaning: 'on Saturday' (used before a time expression or part of day)
additional_notes: This is a partial phrase: sábado por ... is typically followed by a time (e.g., la mañana, la tarde, la noche) or an expression (por la mañana, por la tarde). More common full forms are 'el sábado por la mañana/tarde/noche' or simply 'el sábado'. Without the article 'el' it can appear in casual speech ('el sábado por la noche'). Use 'por' to indicate a nonspecific time during that day (during the morning/afternoon/night).
target_language_example: El sábado por la mañana voy al mercado.
native_language_example: On Saturday morning I'm going to the market.

meaning: 'on Saturday' (used with a time expression that follows) — literally 'Saturday by the ...'.
additional_notes: This fragment appears before a time expression (e.g., sábado por la mañana/tarde/noche) to mean 'on Saturday in the morning/afternoon/night'. It is incomplete by itself and needs a noun indicating the part of the day: mañana, tarde, noche. Use 'el sábado' when not specifying part of day (el sábado = on Saturday).
target_language_example: Vamos a la playa sábado por la tarde.
native_language_example: We're going to the beach on Saturday afternoon.

meaning: literally 'Saturday that' — used when referring to a specific Saturday in a sentence (usually followed by a clause).
additional_notes: Not a fixed phrase on its own; it's simply the noun 'sábado' (Saturday) followed by the conjunction 'que' used to introduce more information about that Saturday (e.g., to specify which Saturday, what happened that Saturday, or why it's important). English equivalents: 'the Saturday that...' or 'Saturday when...'. You will usually see it as part of a longer sentence: 'el sábado que...' or 'el sábado que viene...'.
target_language_example: El sábado que vinimos, no paró de llover.
native_language_example: The Saturday that we came, it didn't stop raining.

meaning: I know, but (I don't)... / I do know, but (I don't)... — used to acknowledge something and then contradict or limit it.
additional_notes: Common conversational pattern combining 'sé' (I know) or 'no sé' (I don't know) with 'pero no' to introduce a contrast, limitation, denial, or uncertainty. Follows with a verb or clause (e.g., 'recuerdo', 'soy', 'creo que...'). Tone can be defensive, corrective, or simply clarifying. Replace 'sé' with 'no sé' when you want to say 'I don't know, but...' in the same structure.
target_language_example: Lo sé, pero no recuerdo dónde dejé las llaves.
native_language_example: I know, but I don't remember where I left the keys.

meaning: 'I know, and...' — the phrase 'lo sé' (I know) followed by 'y' (and) to add more information, contrast, or reaction.
additional_notes: This isn't a fixed idiom; it's simply the combination of 'lo sé' (or 'sé' in responses) plus the conjunction 'y' to continue the sentence. Common uses: to add an explanation, express regret, contrast, or thank someone. 'Lo sé' can be shortened in speech to 'sé' or appear with 'sí, lo sé'. The following clause can be personal (e.g. 'y lo siento'), factual ('y todo porque...'), or appreciative ('y se lo agradezco').
target_language_example: Lo sé, y no volveré a hacerlo.
native_language_example: I know, and I won't do it again.

target_language_multi_word_term: hasta donde sé / por lo que yo sé
meaning: as far as I know; to my knowledge.
additional_notes: Used to introduce information the speaker believes to be true but not certain about. Both forms are common: 'hasta donde sé' is slightly more formal; 'por lo que yo sé' emphasizes the speaker's personal knowledge. Often followed by a comma and a clause about someone or something.
target_language_example: Hasta donde sé, él vive cerca de aquí.
native_language_example: As far as I know, he lives near here.

meaning: 'I know what you...' (start of a sentence: 'I know what you [are/mean/want]')
additional_notes: This is the beginning of a clause: sé (I know) + a qué (what / to what) + te (you, object). It needs a verb or continuation to complete the thought, for example 'sé a qué te refieres' (I know what you mean) or 'sé a qué te dedicas' (I know what you do for a living). 'A qué' often introduces what someone is doing, referring to, or intending.
target_language_example: Sé a qué te refieres.
native_language_example: I know what you mean.

meaning: “be absolutely” — imperative (tú) of ser + adverb; tells someone to be absolutely (something).
additional_notes: Sé is the informal singular imperative (command) of ser (to be). When followed by absolutamente it strengthens the command: 'be absolutely [something]'. Because it's a fragment, it usually needs an adjective or participle after it (e.g., sé absolutamente honesto). Not common by itself; more natural phrasing often puts the adverb before an adjective (sé absolutamente honesto) or uses other verbs (estate absolutamente seguro is incorrect—use 'está absolutamente seguro').
target_language_example: Sé absolutamente honesto conmigo.
native_language_example: Be absolutely honest with me.

meaning: I know absolutely nothing (about it).
additional_notes: Used to strongly deny any knowledge of something. Typically appears in the phrase "No sé absolutamente nada" or followed by a preposition + topic (acerca de / sobre / al respecto). Tone is emphatic; interchangeable with "no sé nada" but stronger.
target_language_example: No sé absolutamente nada sobre ese tema.
native_language_example: I know absolutely nothing about that topic.

meaning: 'I know how' (to do something).
additional_notes: Combines the verb saber (first-person singular present: sé) + como (how). Used to say you know the method or way to do something. In standard written Spanish, when followed by an infinitive it's usually written with an accent on 'cómo' only in direct questions or exclamations — here 'como' is correct (no accent). In spoken Spanish contraction and word order may vary: "sé cómo hacerlo" is also common and equally correct if you include the question/exclamative accent when appropriate.
target_language_example: Sé como arreglar la bicicleta.
native_language_example: I know how to fix the bicycle.

meaning: 'I don't know how, but...' — introduces a statement whose cause or explanation is unknown to the speaker.
additional_notes: Use this phrase to admit you don't understand the reason or method for something, then state the surprising fact. It often appears as "No sé cómo, pero..." (with 'No') to mean "I don't know how, but..." In the provided form 'sé cómo, pero' without 'No' is uncommon; learners should remember the common full phrase is "No sé cómo, pero..." The structure is followed by a clause describing the surprising outcome.
target_language_example: No sé cómo, pero encontré las llaves justo antes de salir.
native_language_example: I don't know how, but I found the keys right before leaving.

meaning: I know about the / I know of the (followed by a noun or clause).
additional_notes: Sé is the first-person singular present of 'saber' (to know). 'Sé de lo...' is used to say you have knowledge or experience of something; often continues with 'que' + clause or a noun phrase introduced by 'lo' (e.g., 'sé de lo que hablas' or 'sé de lo difícil que es'). In many contexts speakers say 'sé de lo que hablas' or simply 'sé de eso'.
target_language_example: Sé de lo difícil que puede ser mudarse a otro país.
native_language_example: I know how difficult it can be to move to another country.

meaning: Not a standard Spanish phrase; likely a typo or mistaken combination of 'sé' (I know or imperative 'be') and 'es' (he/she/it is). Appears rarely and is not grammatically correct as a fixed multi-word expression.
additional_notes:
This exact combination 'sé es' does not occur in correct Spanish. Possible intended interpretations:
- A typographical error for two separate clauses, e.g. 'sé, es...' (I know, it is...) where a comma separates them.
- Confusion between 'sé' (with accent) and 'se' (pronoun). 'Se es' is also generally incorrect; impersonal or passive constructions use 'se' differently (e.g., 'se es conocido' is not standard).
- Could be a mistaken attempt at 'si es' (if it is) or 'sé si es...' (I know if it is...).
Common confusions:
- 'sé' (accent) vs 'se' (pronoun).
- 'sé' as 'yo sé' (I know) vs imperative 'sé' (informal command of 'ser' = be).
target_language_example: Sé es un error; quería decir 'sé, es...'
native_language_example: 'Sé es' is an error; I meant to say 'sé, es...'

meaning: 'what I/you/he/etc. know is that...' — introduces the information someone knows (often limited).
additional_notes: This construction appears in phrases like "lo que sé es que...", "todo lo que sé es que..." or "lo único que sé es que...". Use it to present a fact or limited knowledge. The literal components are understandable (sé = I know), but the full phrase is formulaic. Change "sé" to other persons if needed (e.g., "lo que sabe es que...").
target_language_example: Lo que sé es que llegará mañana.
native_language_example: What I know is that he will arrive tomorrow.

meaning: I know how much (someone/something means to you) / I know how much (you want it).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause that expresses the extent or importance of something to someone: 'Sé lo mucho que...' + verb or clause. Common in empathetic statements (I understand how much...). 'Sé' is from 'saber' (I know). The phrase often ends with 'que' + a verb phrase (e.g., 'que significa para ti', 'que quieres esto').
target_language_example: Sé lo mucho que te importa este trabajo.
native_language_example: I know how much this job matters to you.

meaning: 'I know what I should (do)' or 'I know what I owe' depending on context.
additional_notes: This phrase uses the verb saber (sé = I know) + lo que (what/that which) + debo (I should / I must / I owe). Debo can mean 'should' (obligation) or 'owe' (debt) depending on context. Commonly used to indicate you understand your duty, responsibility, or the correct action. Tone is neutral; choose context to make meaning clear (e.g., deber + infinitive = 'should do something' vs. deber + dinero = 'owe money').
target_language_example: Sé lo que debo hacer para mejorar.
native_language_example: I know what I should do to improve.

meaning: I know what I have.
additional_notes: A simple declarative phrase using the verb saber (sé = I know) + lo que (what/that which) + tengo (I have). Used to say you understand or are aware of what you possess, what situation you are in, or what options you have. Context determines whether it refers to possessions, skills, feelings, or circumstances.
target_language_example: No te preocupes por explicarlo otra vez; sé lo que tengo.
native_language_example: Don't worry about explaining it again; I know what I have.

meaning: 'I know what (is going to) ...' — start of a sentence meaning 'I know what is going to [happen/say/etc.]'.
additional_notes: This is the beginning of the phrase 'sé lo que va a ...' used to say you already know what will happen or what someone will say. 'Sé' = I know (from 'saber'). The full construction usually continues with 'a' + infinitive (e.g., 'va a pasar', 'va a decir'). Common in spoken Spanish; 'ya sé' adds 'already'.
target_language_example: Sé lo que va a pasar mañana en la reunión.
native_language_example: I know what is going to happen tomorrow at the meeting.

meaning: I know what you are (going to) ... / I know what you mean (in context).
additional_notes: This is not a complete, standard fixed phrase on its own. It appears as the start of a sentence meaning 'I know what you are going to [do/say]' or 'I know what you mean.' It requires continuation (e.g., 'a hacer' or 'a decir') or context to clarify the action. 'Sé' is the first-person singular of 'saber' (to know); 'lo que' = 'what/that which'; 'vas' is from 'ir' (you go/you are going) and often forms periphrasis 'vas a + infinitive' = 'you are going to...'.
target_language_example: Sé lo que vas a decir, y no tienes que explicarlo.
native_language_example: I know what you are going to say, and you don't have to explain it.

meaning: be more; know more (depends on context).
additional_notes: Sé is the first-person singular imperative or present indicative of 'ser' (to be) or the imperative/subjunctive form of 'saber' (to know) can also be 'sé' for 'know!'. In 'sé más' most commonly it's an imperative: a command meaning 'be more…' (e.g., 'sé más paciente' = 'be more patient') or less often 'know more' in contexts like 'sé más sobre esto' (though standard would be 'sabe más' or 'sapé' isn't used—so prefer 'aprende más' or 'entérate más' for 'learn/know more'). Use 'sé más' + adjective to tell someone to become more of that quality. Pronunciation: accent on sé.
target_language_example: Sé más paciente con los niños.
native_language_example: Be more patient with the children.

meaning: I know nothing about (something).
additional_notes: This exact string is not standard Spanish: native speakers would usually say "no sé nada sobre..." or "no sé nada de..." The pattern places the negation before the verb: "no sé" = "I don't know." Use "no sé nada sobre eso" to say "I know nothing about that."
target_language_example: No sé nada sobre esa película.
native_language_example: I know nothing about that movie.

meaning: I don't know why, but... (introduces a surprising opinion or observation despite not knowing the reason).
additional_notes: Common phrase to express that you don't know the reason for something, followed by a statement or feeling. Structure: 'No sé por qué, pero + [clause]'. Used to introduce a contrast, surprise, or unexpected reaction. Tone is neutral and suitable for everyday speech.
target_language_example: No sé por qué, pero me pone nervioso hablar en público.
native_language_example: I don't know why, but public speaking makes me nervous.

meaning: 'I know because' (first person singular present: 'I know' + 'because')
additional_notes: Combines the verb saber in the first-person singular (sé = I know) with porque (because). Used to give a reason or explanation for what the speaker knows. In writing, note the accent on sé distinguishes it from the reflexive 'se'. Common in spoken and written Spanish. Example sentences may drop punctuation: some contexts use 'Lo sé porque...' (I know it because...).
target_language_example: Lo sé porque te dije la verdad ayer.
native_language_example: I know because I told you the truth yesterday.

meaning: I know that the (feminine noun follows).
additional_notes: Sé que = 'I know that'. When followed by la, it introduces a clause about a specific feminine noun (la familia, la policía, la tarjeta, la torre). Use for statements about things you know. If the noun is masculine use 'sé que el'.
target_language_example: Sé que la reunión empieza a las nueve.
native_language_example: I know that the meeting starts at nine.

meaning: 'I know that (he/she/they/it) ...' — the start of a clause reporting what the speaker knows about someone or something.
additional_notes: Sé = first-person singular of saber ('I know'). Que introduces a subordinate clause. Se is the impersonal/reflexive/auxiliary pronoun used with verbs like irse, acabarse, ponerse, or with passive/impersonal constructions (se fue = 'he/she left'; se acabó = 'it's over'; se han estado preguntando = 'they/people have been wondering'). Together 'sé que se ...' = 'I know that (someone or people) ...'. Context determines who 'se' refers to.
target_language_example: Sé que se fue sin avisar.
native_language_example: I know that he/she left without warning.

meaning: I know what
additional_notes: Usually followed by more information: sé qué pasó, sé qué quieres, etc. Here qué has an accent because it introduces an indirect question (“what”). Compare it with sé que (without the accent), which means “I know that.”
target_language_example: Sé qué necesitas.
native_language_example: I know what you need.

meaning: This exact sequence is not a correct or standard Spanish phrase; it likely reflects a misspelling or misplacement of an accent and/or a pronoun. The user probably intended forms like "sé que..." (I know that...) or "sé que le..." followed by a verb (e.g., "Sé que le duele").
additional_notes: - "sé" (with accent) is the first-person singular of "saber" (I know). - "que" (no accent) is a conjunction meaning "that." - "qué" (with accent) is an interrogative/exclamative pronoun meaning "what." The sequence "sé qué le" mixes the accented interrogative "qué" with "sé," which is not grammatical in typical declarative sentences. Possible corrections: "Sé que le..." + verb ("Sé que le duele") or "Sé lo que le..." ("I know what to him/her..." often completed as "Sé lo que le pasa").
target_language_example: Sé qué le dije ayer en el mensaje (incorrect: mixes interrogative accent; should be "Sé que le..." or reformulated).
native_language_example: I know what I told him/her yesterday in the message (example shows the incorrect mixed-accent form).

meaning: I know what happened.
additional_notes: Contraction of saber in the first person singular present (sé) + qué pasó ('what happened'). Used to say you already know the cause or details of an event or situation. Common in everyday speech. Accent on sé is required to distinguish it from 'se' (reflexive pronoun).
target_language_example: No te preocupes, sé qué pasó y puedo ayudar.
native_language_example: Don't worry, I know what happened and I can help.

meaning: I know if it/is (I know whether it is...).
additional_notes: Combines the verb saber (sé = I know) + si (if/whether) + es (he/she/it is or formal you are). Used to say you know whether something is the case. Context determines what 'es' refers to (e.g., una situación, correcto, posible). For questions or uncertainty use 'no sé si es...' (I don't know if it is...).
target_language_example: Sé si es verdad, así que puedo decírtelo.
native_language_example: I know if it's true, so I can tell you.

meaning: 'I know if it' or 'I know whether it' (start of a clause) — short for 'sé si lo...' followed by a verb or clause.
additional_notes: This phrase is a combination of 'sé' (I know) + 'si' (if/whether) + the direct object pronoun 'lo' (it). In natural Spanish you will usually hear 'sé si' + clause (e.g., 'sé si viene') or 'lo sé' (I know it). 'Sé si lo...' is used when the speaker begins a sentence meaning 'I know whether it...' and then adds more information (e.g., 'sé si lo hizo' = 'I know whether he/she did it'). Word order matters: 'lo sé' = 'I know it' (different meaning).
target_language_example: Sé si lo hizo, pero no quiero contarlo.
native_language_example: I know whether he/she did it, but I don't want to tell.

meaning: 'I don't know if (someone) ... me' or 'I know if ... me' depending on context; here often used as 'I don't know if someone does something to/for me' (with sé negated in examples: No sé si me ... = I don't know if someone ... me).
additional_notes: This sequence combines the verb saber (sé = I know) + si (if/whether) + a reflexive or object pronoun me (me). In many examples it's used with no to form No sé si me + verb/phrase = "I don't know if ... me / whether ... me." The verb that follows (dás, dijeron, lleve, lo preguntará, amas) completes the idea. Literal structure: "(I) know if/whether me ..." — in natural English reorder to "I don't know if ... me" or "I don't know whether someone ... me."
target_language_example: No sé si me llamará mañana.
native_language_example: I don't know if he/she will call me tomorrow.

meaning: 'I know about' or 'I know (things) about'.
additional_notes: Sé is the first-person singular of saber (to know). When followed by sobre (about), it expresses knowledge concerning a person, topic, document, etc. Often used with a noun or pronoun (sé sobre él, sé sobre las fotos) or with a clause after qué (sé sobre qué...). In everyday speech, Spanish speakers might also say 'sé de' instead of 'sé sobre'.
target_language_example: Sé sobre la historia de la ciudad.
native_language_example: I know about the history of the city.

meaning: short for 'sé' (from saber) followed by 'y' meaning 'and' — often appears in writing when listing verbs or commands like 'sé y...' but it is not a fixed phrase
additional_notes: This is not a common fixed expression. 'Sé' can be the imperative (tú) of 'ser' (be) or the first-person singular present of 'saber' (I know) with an accent: 'sé' (I know) or 'sé' (be!). 'y' means 'and'. When seen together ('sé y'), it's simply the word 'sé' followed by the conjunction 'y' and should be read normally in context. Pay attention to accent: 'se' (without accent) is a reflexive pronoun; 'sé' with accent is either 'I know' (saber) or the affirmative command 'be' (from ser).
target_language_example: Sé y actúa con calma en esa situación.
native_language_example: Be and act calmly in that situation.

meaning: 'it's me' or 'I know' depending on context (colloquial).
additional_notes: This is a short, colloquial Spanish phrase. Most commonly, 'sé yo' is used parenthetically to mean 'that's me' / 'that's how I am' or to indicate personal opinion or uncertainty like 'I guess' / 'I suppose' (similar to English 'I dunno' or 'as for me'). It can also appear in emphatic replies where 'sé' is the verb 'saber' ('I know') plus 'yo' for emphasis: '¡Sé yo!' = 'I know!' (emphatic). Usage and exact meaning depend on intonation and context. Not formal.
target_language_example: Si quieres llegar temprano, sé yo, toma el tren en vez del autobús.
native_language_example: If you want to arrive early, I guess I would take the train instead of the bus.

meaning: 'be a' (imperative: telling someone to be something)
additional_notes: Sé is the informal (tú) imperative of ser (to be). 'Sé un ...' is used to tell or urge someone to behave like, act as, or become a certain kind of person (e.g., 'sé un buen chico' = 'be a good boy'). Tone can be instructive, encouraging, or commanding depending on context; sometimes used bluntly (e.g., 'sé un hombre' = 'be a man'). Use with tú (informal).
target_language_example: Sé un buen amigo y escucha cuando te hablen.
native_language_example: Be a good friend and listen when someone talks to you.

meaning: 'yes it is' — used to affirm that something is true or exists.
additional_notes: Often used to confirm or agree with a preceding statement. In many contexts speakers prefer shorter forms like 'sí' or 'sí, lo es', or fuller phrases such as 'sí es verdad' or 'sí es así'. 'Sí es' can sound slightly formal or emphatic depending on intonation; it normally requires an understood subject (por ejemplo, 'es' refers back to something just mentioned).
target_language_example: ¿La película es buena? — Sí es.
native_language_example: Is the movie good? — Yes, it is.

meaning: 'yes' or 'indeed' + direct object pronoun 'her/it' (feminine).
additional_notes: This is a combination of the adverb 'sí' (affirmation: yes/indeed) and the feminine singular direct-object pronoun 'la' (her/it). Depending on context, 'la' can refer to a person (her) or a feminine noun (it). Word order: 'sí la' is used when stressing affirmation before the pronoun (e.g., correcting, confirming, or emphasizing). The comma is often used: 'Sí, la conozco' or 'Sí la conozco' both occur in speech.
target_language_example: Sí la invité a la fiesta.
native_language_example: Yes, I invited her to the party.

meaning: adds emphasis about something you (te) did or are; roughly 'you really/definitely...'.
additional_notes: Sí que + pronoun/verb is used to strongly emphasize or confirm an action, state, or quality related to the person (te = to you / you). Tone can be approving, surprised, ironic, or critical depending on context and intonation. Common in spoken Spanish.
target_language_example: Sí que te preocupaste por los detalles.
native_language_example: You really took care of the details.

meaning: an emphatic combination used to confirm, contrast, or reinforce a statement (like 'yes, indeed' or 'actually/it is that...').
additional_notes: Sí is 'yes' and se is a reflexive/impersonal pronoun; together they often add emphasis or contrast to a clause. Common patterns: 'Sí se puede' (Yes, it can be done / Yes we/you can), 'Sí se nota' (You can really tell / It is noticeable), or in corrective responses 'Sí se...' to stress that something does happen. Meaning depends on context and the verb that follows.
target_language_example: Sí se puede lograr con esfuerzo.
native_language_example: Yes, it can be achieved with effort.

meaning: by himself/alone (male) — emphasizes doing something alone or without help
additional_notes: Used to stress that a male person acted alone or can do something without assistance. Feminine form is 'sí sola'. Often follows the noun or pronoun it refers to (e.g., 'él sí solo', 'Juan sí solo'). Can also appear without the accent as 'si solo' in contexts meaning 'if only' but that is different; here 'sí' with an accent means 'yes' or emphatic 'himself'.
target_language_example: Juan lo arregló sí solo.
native_language_example: Juan fixed it by himself.

meaning: indeed; used to confirm or emphasize agreement and immediately add another point (like 'and what's more' / 'indeed, and').
additional_notes: Commonly used in spoken Spanish as the adverb 'sí' (yes/indeed) followed directly by the conjunction 'y' (and). Often introduces an additional or contrasting clause and carries an emphatic tone. Not a fixed idiom—it's compositional and usually followed by further information.
target_language_example: Sí y además no tenemos tiempo para eso.
native_language_example: Indeed, and besides we don't have time for that.

meaning: 'yes, maybe' or 'yeah, maybe' (agreement + tentative suggestion)
additional_notes: This combination pairs an affirmation (sí) with tal (short for tal vez) to soften or hedge the agreement — similar to saying 'yes, maybe' or 'yeah, could be' in English. Common in spoken Spanish; tal here is colloquial and often followed by quizá/vez understood. You can also hear 'sí, tal vez' in full.
target_language_example: — ¿Vendrás a la fiesta? — Sí, tal.
native_language_example: — Will you come to the party? — Yes, maybe.

meaning: A short affirmative reply meaning 'yes, it will' or 'yes, he/she/it will'.
additional_notes: Used to agree and confirm that something will happen or that someone/it will do something. 'Va' is the 3rd-person singular of 'ir' or used in the periphrastic future 'va a + infinitive' = 'is going to + verb'. Depending on context it can mean 'it will', 'he/she will', or 'they (formal) will'. The comma and pause mimic spoken reassurance: 'Sí, va a...' = 'Yes, it’s going to...'.
target_language_example: —¿Lloverá mañana? —Sí, va a llover.
native_language_example: —Will it rain tomorrow? —Yes, it will.

meaning: yes, sir; an emphatic 'yes' used to agree, obey, or show respect.
additional_notes: Commonly used to confirm agreement, to obey an instruction, or to express respectful affirmation. Tone can be formal or playful/ironic depending on context and intonation. Can be repeated for emphasis ("sí señor, sí señor").
target_language_example: Sí señor, ahora mismo.
native_language_example: Yes sir, right now.

meaning: himself / herself / themselves (emphatic reflexive pronoun referring back to the subject)
additional_notes: Reflexive emphatic pronoun used to refer back to the subject for emphasis or clarity. Gender and number agree with the subject (sí mismo / sí misma / sí mismos / sí mismas). Common after verbs or prepositions (e.g., para sí mismo, confiar en sí mismo). Not used for 'myself' (use mí mismo in some contexts) and not combined as a separate subject pronoun (e.g., Él se mira a sí mismo).
target_language_example: Eso indica su integridad y confianza en sí mismo.
native_language_example: That indicates his integrity and self-confidence.

meaning: only to / just to (indicates limitation toward a person, place, time, or purpose)
additional_notes: Combination of 'sólo' (only/just) + preposition 'a'. Use when you want to limit or specify the target, recipient, time, direction, or purpose of an action: e.g. 'only to him', 'only at 5', 'only for this'. Note: In modern Spanish, 'sólo' (with accent) is often written without the accent as 'solo' unless needed to avoid ambiguity; both forms are common. Context determines the exact translation into English.
target_language_example: Se lo di sólo a María.
native_language_example: I gave it only to María.

meaning: only in that way; only like that; only then
additional_notes: Used to say that a result or condition happens only if something is done in a specific way. Can mean 'only then' (temporal) or 'only by doing that' (conditional). Often follows or begins a clause that describes the necessary action or condition. 'Sólo' can be written with or without an accent (solo), but the accent is still commonly seen to avoid ambiguity.
target_language_example: Sólo así podremos terminar a tiempo.
native_language_example: Only in that way can we finish on time.

meaning: only with; just with.
additional_notes: Used to limit something to a single condition, person, thing, or method. 'Sólo' (or 'solo') means 'only' and 'con' means 'with'. In modern Spanish 'solo' without accent is common; context decides stress. Be careful: 'sólo con' differs from 'solo con' in accent usage but meaning is the same. Often followed by a noun, pronoun, or verb phrase (with infinitive when expressing means).
target_language_example: Puedo ir sólo con una mochila.
native_language_example: I can go only with one backpack.

meaning: only when; at the time that and not otherwise.
additional_notes: Used to limit a condition or action to a specific time or circumstance. Often introduces a clause that specifies the single situation in which something happens. Can be followed by a subjunctive or indicative depending on whether the action is hypothetical/anticipated or factual/habitual.
target_language_example: Te ayudaré sólo cuando me lo pidas.
native_language_example: I will help you only when you ask me.

meaning: only; merely (followed by a noun or phrase introduced by 'de').
additional_notes: sólo (accent optional: sólo/solo) means 'only' or 'just'. When used as 'sólo de' it typically appears before a noun phrase introduced by 'de' to limit or specify (e.g., 'sólo de estudiantes', 'sólo de broma'). Be careful: in modern Spanish the accent on 'sólo' is often omitted (solo) except to avoid ambiguity. 'Sólo de' is not a fixed phrase—it's just 'sólo' + preposition 'de'.
target_language_example: Era sólo de estudiantes, no de profesores.
native_language_example: It was only of students, not of teachers.

meaning: 'only the' (masculine singular) — used to limit or single out a specific noun.
additional_notes: Sólo (or sólo with an accent historically; modern RAE allows 'solo' without accent except to avoid ambiguity) means 'only' or 'just'. When followed by a masculine singular noun, you often see 'sólo el' before that noun or phrase: e.g. 'sólo el coche' = 'only the car'. Make sure gender and number agree: 'sólo la' (feminine), 'sólo los' (masculine plural), 'sólo las' (feminine plural). In many contexts you can drop 'sólo' and use 'solo' (no accent).
target_language_example: Sólo el profesor puede entrar en la sala.
native_language_example: Only the teacher can enter the room.

meaning: only in; only at (used to limit time, place, situation)
additional_notes: Used to restrict something to a specific place, time, situation, or context. Commonly followed by a noun or phrase (e.g., 'sólo en verano', 'sólo en casa', 'sólo en casos especiales'). Note: In modern Spanish, the accent on sólo is optional; to avoid ambiguity many writers omit it. If ambiguity arises, context determines whether sólo means 'only' or the adjective 'solo' (alone).
target_language_example: Entramos sólo en la sala principal.
native_language_example: We enter only in the main room.

meaning: it was only / it was just (used to downplay what something was)
additional_notes: Used to minimize or explain that something was nothing more than what follows (a joke, a game, a suggestion, etc.). Often precedes a noun or clause. Note: modern Spanish often writes 'solo' without the accent unless ambiguity would occur; both 'sólo era' and 'solo era' are seen.
target_language_example: Sólo era una broma; no te enojes.
native_language_example: It was just a joke; don't be mad.

meaning: it's only the / this is only the (masculine noun).
additional_notes: Used to downplay or limit importance — 'sólo' (only) + 'es' (is) + masculine definite article 'el' before a masculine noun. Can mean 'it's just the...' or 'this is only the...'. Context determines whether referring to something present ('this/that is') or a general statement. Note: Spanish now often writes 'solo' without an accent, but accent still appears in some texts.
target_language_example: Eso sólo es el comienzo de la historia.
native_language_example: That is only the beginning of the story.

meaning: just/is only (doing something) — emphasizes that someone is merely doing or in a temporary state.
additional_notes: Used to downplay or limit an action/state (equivalent to 'is just' or 'is only' + present participle/gerund in English). Often appears before a verb or gerund (e.g., 'sólo está haciendo...') or before an adjective/noun to indicate a temporary condition. In informal writing, 'sólo' (with accent) can also be written 'solo' — both are common; the accent distinguishes 'only' from 'alone' but is optional in modern orthography.
target_language_example: No te preocupes, sólo está dormido.
native_language_example: Don't worry, he's just asleep.

meaning: it was only
additional_notes: Used to downplay or minimize something that happened; emphasises that whatever occurred was minor, single, or not serious. Common before nouns, adjectives or short clauses. 'Sólo' (accented) here means 'only/just' — note that modern Spanish often omits the accent ('solo fue') except to avoid ambiguity. Verb 'fue' is the past (preterite) of 'ser' (to be).
target_language_example: Sólo fue una broma; no te lo tomes a pecho.
native_language_example: It was only a joke; don't take it personally.

meaning: has only / has just (done) — indicates that something has happened recently or that the amount is limited
additional_notes: sólo = only / just; ha is the third-person singular present of haber used in the present perfect (ha + past participle). Together, sólo ha + past participle means 'has only/just done' something (e.g., sólo ha llegado = has just arrived / has only arrived). In modern Spanish the acute accent on sólo is optional; many style guides omit it except to avoid ambiguity. Be careful: without a past participle after ha, sólo ha by itself is incomplete.
target_language_example: Sólo ha terminado el informe.
native_language_example: He has only/just finished the report.

meaning: Just do (it); simply do (what's said).
additional_notes: A command form using 'sólo' (only/just) + imperative 'haz' (from hacer, tú). Commonly used to tell someone to follow instructions or do exactly as told. Tone can be firm; context and intonation determine politeness. 'Sólo' can also be written 'solo' (both accepted), though RAE recommends no accent unless ambiguity. Use 'haz' for tú; other persons require different forms (haga, hagan, hazte, etc.).
target_language_example: Sólo haz lo que te dije y no habrá problemas.
native_language_example: Just do what I told you and there won't be any problems.

meaning: only her / only it (feminine) — emphasizes exclusivity or limitation.
additional_notes: Sólo (or sólo) means "only"; la is the feminine direct object pronoun (her/it) or a feminine definite article depending on context. In these examples it usually functions as the pronoun meaning "her" or "it (feminine)". Placement: sólo typically comes before the pronoun or verb (e.g., "sólo la saludé" = "I only greeted her"). Be aware: in modern Spanish the accent on sólo is often omitted (solo), but both forms are commonly seen.
target_language_example: No la llamé; sólo la miré.
native_language_example: I didn't call her; I only looked at her.

meaning: 'only to them' or 'I/you/he/she only (do something) to/for them'.
additional_notes: Sólo means 'only' or 'just'. Les is the indirect-object pronoun for 'them' or 'to them' (also 'you' formal plural in some regions). Together they indicate that the action is limited to those people: e.g. 'I only told them' or 'I only ask them'. Word order can vary (e.g. 'les sólo dije' is less common), and in modern Spanish the accent on sólo is optional; context usually makes meaning clear.
target_language_example: Sólo les expliqué la situación a ellos.
native_language_example: I only explained the situation to them.

meaning: only the / only those (masculine plural) — restricts which people or things are meant.
additional_notes: Used to limit or specify a group (masculine plural nouns or mixed-gender groups). 'Sólo' (or 'solo') means 'only'; 'los' is the definite article/pronoun 'the' or 'them'. Common in phrases like 'sólo los que...' (only those who...) or 'sólo los dos' (only the two of them). If referring to feminine plural use 'sólo las'. In modern Spanish the accent on 'sólo' is often omitted unless needed for clarity.
target_language_example: Sólo los invitados pueden entrar a la sala.
native_language_example: Only the guests can enter the room.

meaning: 'only my' or 'just my' (modifies a noun to indicate exclusivity belonging to the speaker)
additional_notes: Sólo (or sólo with accent in older orthography; modern RAE allows 'solo' without accent except for ambiguity) means 'only' or 'just'. When followed by a possessive like mi, it restricts the noun to something that belongs to or concerns the speaker alone: e.g., sólo mi problema = only my problem. In natural speech, speakers often use 'solo' or drop it depending on emphasis. Make sure the phrase is followed by a noun (sólo mi libro, sólo mi opinión).
target_language_example: Eso fue sólo mi culpa.
native_language_example: That was only my fault.

meaning: just/only not; used to negate or limit a statement (often casual).
additional_notes: sólo (or sólo with accent, though accent is optional per current orthography) means 'only' or 'just'. When combined with no, 'sólo no' is used in spoken Spanish to soften a negation or to say 'it's just that... not...' — often introducing an objection or limitation. Placement and punctuation matter: 'Sólo no puedo' = 'I just can't.' It is informal/casual and not a fixed idiom but a simple combination of words.
target_language_example: Quería ir, sólo no tengo tiempo.
native_language_example: I wanted to go; I just don't have time.

meaning: only us / just us
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that the group in question is limited to 'us' (exclusive). Can appear alone as a short reply (e.g., "Sólo nosotros.") or with numbers ("Sólo nosotros tres"). In contexts like sentence 4, 'no éramos sólo nosotros' means 'it wasn't just us', so watch word order and negation.
target_language_example: Sólo nosotros fuimos al concierto.
native_language_example: Only we went to the concert.

meaning: just/only because of (him/it/the ...).
additional_notes: Used to indicate the sole reason or motive for something. Depending on context, 'el' can refer to a masculine noun previously mentioned (el trabajo, el dinero, el oso) or mean 'him' (él) in colloquial speech — though grammatically 'por él' with accent is used for 'him'. Often appears as 'sólo por + [noun]'. 'Sólo' (or 'solo') here means 'only/just'.
target_language_example: No lo hice sólo por el dinero.
native_language_example: I didn't do it just for the money.

meaning: 'only/just be' — used to suggest a minimal possibility or hypothetical state.
additional_notes: Often appears in phrases like "aunque sólo sea...", "quizás sólo sea..." or "puede que sólo sea..." to downplay or limit what is being stated (e.g., "maybe it's only...", "even if it's only..."). Use to express doubt, a hypothetical, or to indicate that something is no more than a small/limited thing.
target_language_example: Quizás sólo sea un malentendido.
native_language_example: Maybe it's only a misunderstanding.

meaning: we only have to / we just need to
additional_notes: Used to say that only one (usually simple) action or requirement remains. 'Sólo' (or 'solo') means 'only' or 'just' here; 'tenemos' is the present tense 'we have' from tener. Common in instructions or reassurances: 'we just need to...'.
target_language_example: Sólo tenemos que esperar un poco más.
native_language_example: We just need to wait a little longer.

meaning: 'he/she/it only has' or 'you (formal) only have' — indicates possession limited to one thing or that something/someone has only a certain quality/time.
additional_notes: Sólo (or sólo with accent; modern Spanish often omits the accent) means 'only' or 'just'. Tiene is the third-person singular present of tener ('to have'). Together they limit what is possessed, available, or true about someone/something (e.g., only one bed, only five minutes, only good news). Context tells whether 'tiene' refers to possession, age, time, or characteristics.
target_language_example: Él sólo tiene tres libros en la estantería.
native_language_example: He only has three books on the shelf.

meaning: you only have to
additional_notes: Commonly followed by 'que' + an infinitive to indicate a simple obligation or the only necessary action (Sólo tienes que + infinitive = you just have to...). 'Sólo' can also be written without the accent as 'solo' in modern orthography unless needed for disambiguation; meaning is 'only/just'. Used in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Sólo tienes que practicar todos los días.
native_language_example: You just have to practice every day.

meaning: I'm just going to / I'll only (do something).
additional_notes: Used to soften an intention or reassure someone — indicates a single, brief, or limited action. Usually followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., 'a dar', 'a mirar', 'a hablar'). In many dialects, writing 'solo' without the accent is common; both forms are understood. Tone is often calming or minimizing.
target_language_example: Sólo voy a mirar, no te preocupes.
native_language_example: I'm just going to look, don't worry.

meaning: only me / just me
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that the action or situation applies to the speaker alone. 'Sólo' (with an accent) traditionally marks 'only' — note that modern Spanish orthography allows 'solo' without accent unless needed for ambiguity. Can appear in different positions: 'sólo yo' (only me), 'solo yo pude hacerlo' (only I could do it).
target_language_example: En la fiesta, sólo yo conocía a todos.
native_language_example: At the party, only I knew everyone.

meaning: only him / only he (emphatic) — emphasizes that it is him and no one else.
additional_notes: Used to stress that a specific person (male) is the one and no other person is meant. In modern Spanish, the accent on 'sólo' is optional; many style guides recommend no accent unless needed to avoid ambiguity with 'solo' (alone). Word order can change for emphasis (e.g., 'él sólo' or 'sólo él'); context decides whether it translates better as 'only him', 'only he', or 'he alone'.
target_language_example: En la fiesta, sólo él sabía la verdad.
native_language_example: At the party, only he knew the truth.

meaning: as / just as / in the way that; used to compare or indicate exact sameness or manner.
additional_notes: Commonly used to introduce a comparison or to say that something is exactly like something else (tal como + clause or tal como + noun). Can mean 'just as', 'as', 'in the way that', or 'exactly as'. Useful with verbs (tal como dije), with time references (tal como antes), or to refer to how someone/something is (tal como era).
target_language_example: Hazlo tal como te expliqué.
native_language_example: Do it just as I explained.

meaning: maybe
additional_notes: Used to express possibility or uncertainty. It can come before a time expression, number, or noun phrase, as in the examples, or before a full clause. Before a verb, Spanish often uses the subjunctive, though the indicative is also common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Tal vez podamos ir mañana.
native_language_example: Maybe we can go tomorrow.

meaning: such and / so and (used to link a noun or idea with an example, explanation, or consequence)
additional_notes: Tal y is often followed by que, como, o otro elemento to introduce a result, example, comparison, or emphasis: e.g. 'tal y como' = 'just as/like', 'tal y que' = 'so much that'. It is somewhat formal and appears in set phrases. Alone it usually combines with another word (tal y como, tal y como tal).
target_language_example: Tal y como dijiste, la reunión fue breve.
native_language_example: Just as you said, the meeting was brief.

meaning: 'just as' / 'exactly as' / 'the way that'.
additional_notes: Used to compare or describe something being the same as another thing or situation. Commonly followed by a clause or an adjective (e.g., 'tal y como dijo', 'tal y como eres'). In everyday English it often corresponds to 'just as', 'exactly as', or 'the way that'.
target_language_example: Te acepto tal y como eres.
native_language_example: I accept you just as you are.

meaning: such friends; friends like those.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize the type or quality of friends (often positive: 'friends like those'). Can be used with different pronouns/genders (tales amigos, tales amigas). 'Tales' = 'such' or 'those kind of'. Common in expressions like 'tener tales amigos' = 'to have friends like that'.
target_language_example: Eres muy afortunado de tener tales amigos.
native_language_example: You are very lucky to have friends like that.

meaning: 'size of' or 'the size of'.
additional_notes: Used to indicate the size or dimensions of something in relation to another object or measurement. Common in comparisons: 'del tamaño de...' = 'about the size of...'. Followed by a noun or noun phrase. Can be used literally (physical size) or figuratively/colloquially.
target_language_example: Tenía aproximadamente el tamaño de una pelota de tenis.
native_language_example: It was about the size of a tennis ball.

meaning: also to / as well to (adds someone or something to what was just mentioned).
additional_notes: ‘también’ means 'also' or 'too'. When followed by the preposition 'a' it often introduces the indirect object or recipient being added (e.g., 'también a María' = 'also to María'). Word order can vary: 'a María también' is also common. Use it to indicate inclusion or addition. Note: 'también a' is simply 'también' + the preposition 'a' and isn't a fixed idiom.
target_language_example: Enviaré el paquete también a Juan.
native_language_example: I will send the package also to Juan.

meaning: I also bought / I bought ... too.
additional_notes: Combines 'también' (also/too) + the preterite first-person singular of 'comprar' (compré). Used to add an item to a list of things you purchased or to say you, too, bought something someone mentioned. Word order can vary: 'también compré X' or 'compré X también'.
target_language_example: Fuimos al mercado y también compré pan.
native_language_example: We went to the market and I also bought bread.

meaning: 'also the' or 'the... too' (used to add one more item or person, with the definite article 'el')
additional_notes: This is simply the adverb 'también' (also) followed by the masculine singular definite article 'el'. It appears when you want to add or include another masculine noun or person already introduced: e.g. 'También el profesor vino' = 'The teacher came too.' Make sure word order fits Spanish: 'también' can go before the verb or before the noun/article for emphasis. If referring to a feminine noun use 'también la'.
target_language_example: También el niño participó en la presentación.
native_language_example: The boy also took part in the presentation.

meaning: 'also in' or 'too in' (adds that something applies in a specific place, situation, time, or category)
additional_notes: también means 'also' or 'too'. When followed by en + noun or en + clause, también en emphasizes that whatever is stated applies 'in' that place, context, time, or category as well. Word order is flexible: también can come before or after en, but 'también en' puts the focus on the added location/context.
target_language_example: También en España se celebra esta tradición.
native_language_example: This tradition is celebrated in Spain as well.

meaning: 'you are also' or 'you're also' (second-person singular, informal).
additional_notes: Combines 'también' (also/too) + 'estás' (second-person singular present of 'estar'). Used to indicate the person addressed shares the same state, location, or condition as someone/something else. Word order can vary: 'tú también estás' or just 'también estás' depending on emphasis and context. For formal address use 'también está'.
target_language_example: Si tú también estás cansado, deberíamos descansar.
native_language_example: If you are also tired, we should rest.

meaning: 'also has' (present perfect auxiliary: indicates that someone/something has also done or experienced something).
additional_notes: Combines 'también' (also) with the auxiliary 'ha' (from haber) used to form the present perfect (ha + past participle). Use when adding 'also' to statements like 'has done', 'has been', 'has come', 'has returned', etc. Word order: 'también' usually appears before the verb ('también ha venido'). Can refer to people or things.
target_language_example: Ella también ha visitado ese museo.
native_language_example: She has also visited that museum.

meaning: 'also her' or 'her too' (often 'also it' depending on gender/reference).
additional_notes: Tambien = 'also/too'. La is the feminine direct object pronoun ('her' or 'it' for a feminine noun). Together 'también la' usually means 'her too' or 'also it' when referring to a feminine person or noun mentioned earlier. Word order in Spanish places 'también' before the pronoun. Context determines whether 'la' refers to a person (her) or a feminine thing (it).
target_language_example: Yo la conozco, y también la quiero.
native_language_example: I know her, and I love her too.

meaning: also the/also those (masculine plural).
additional_notes: Combines 'también' (also) with the masculine plural direct object/article/possessive 'los' or part of a noun phrase. Used to add that something applies to additional masculine plural people or things already mentioned or understood from context. Word order can vary (e.g., 'los también' is uncommon); 'también' typically comes before the pronoun/article.
target_language_example: En la reunión hablaron los jefes y también los empleados.
native_language_example: At the meeting the bosses spoke and also the employees.

meaning: 'me too' or 'also me' (colloquial), used to say you feel the same or have the same opinion/experience.
additional_notes: This is an informal, colloquial combination of 'también' (also/too) + the subject pronoun or possessive-like 'mi' used for emphasis in casual speech or memes (similar to English 'also me'). It often appears in texts, social media, or spoken language to express personal identification with a statement. Grammatically, standard Spanish uses 'yo también' or 'también yo' for 'me too'. Use 'también mi' only in informal contexts or when imitating casual internet speech.
target_language_example: —Me encanta esa serie. —¡También mi!
native_language_example: —I love that show. —Also me!

meaning: I also need / I need ... too.
additional_notes: Combination of 'también' (also/too) + 'necesito' (I need). Use 'también necesito' to add another thing you require. Can appear at start, middle, or end of a sentence depending on emphasis: e.g., 'También necesito leche.' (I also need milk.) or 'Necesito leche también.' (I need milk too.). For polite requests, you can add 'por favor'.
target_language_example: Además de pan, también necesito huevos.
native_language_example: Besides bread, I also need eggs.

meaning: you can also / you may also
additional_notes: Used to suggest an additional option or to encourage someone that they are able to do something. 'También' = 'also'; 'puedes' is the tú form of 'poder' (to be able to). Tone is neutral; common in spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: Si quieres, también puedes llamar más tarde.
native_language_example: If you want, you can also call later.

meaning: 'I also want' or 'I want too'.
additional_notes: Used to add the speaker's desire in addition to something already mentioned. 'También' means 'also/too' and is placed before the verb or phrase it modifies. Can express wanting the same thing as someone else or an additional wish.
target_language_example: Yo quiero un helado. También quiero uno de chocolate.
native_language_example: I want an ice cream. I also want a chocolate one.

meaning: I am also
additional_notes: Combines 'también' (also) with the first-person singular of 'ser' (to be). Used to add that the speaker shares a quality, role, or state mentioned or implied. Common in statements like 'también soy X' or 'yo también soy X'. Can be followed by a noun, adjective, or phrase (e.g., profesión, característica, opinión).
target_language_example: No tienes que hacerlo sola; también soy padre.
native_language_example: You don't have to do it alone; I'm also a father.

meaning: I also know / I know too
