additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is early for a specific time or event. Often followed by a noun or time expression (e.g., temprano a la reunión, temprano a las ocho). In many cases Spanish speakers simply say 'temprano' (no preposition) or 'llegar temprano a' for 'arrive early to'. The structure 'temprano a' is less common on its own than full verbs like 'llegar temprano a'.
target_language_example: Llegó temprano a la cita.
native_language_example: He arrived early to the appointment.

meaning: early to (followed by a time or place noun phrase, e.g. 'la cama' = to bed).
additional_notes: Used to say someone does something early with a following feminine noun introduced by 'la' (e.g. 'temprano a la mañana' or more naturally 'temprano por la mañana'; 'temprano a la cama' = 'early to bed'). In many cases Spanish speakers prefer 'temprano por la mañana' or simply 'temprano' + verb; but 'temprano a la cama' is common for 'to bed'.
target_language_example: Me voy temprano a la cama esta noche.
native_language_example: I'm going to bed early tonight.

meaning: 'early each' — used to say something happens early on each occasion or every (time/unit) early
additional_notes: This is not a fixed set phrase in Spanish by itself. Temprano means 'early' and cada means 'each' or 'every'. They can appear together in sentences like 'temprano cada día' (early every day) or 'temprano cada mañana' (early every morning). On its own, 'temprano cada' needs a time word after it (día, mañana, semana, vez) to be natural.
target_language_example: Llegamos temprano cada mañana para preparar la tienda.
native_language_example: We arrive early every morning to prepare the shop.

meaning: early in / early at (used to say something happens early during a period or at a time).
additional_notes: Commonly used with time expressions (la mañana, el verano, la Navidad), places (el colegio, el parque) or events to indicate 'early during' or 'early at' that time/place. In English you might say 'early in the morning', 'early in summer' or 'early at school'. Word order: 'temprano en + [time/place/period]'.
target_language_example: Llegaron temprano en la mañana para preparar todo.
native_language_example: They arrived early in the morning to prepare everything.

meaning: early in the (time period/place).
additional_notes: Used to indicate 'early' within a specific time frame or part of a day/week/etc. It needs a noun after 'la' (e.g., 'temprano en la mañana', 'temprano en la semana' — though 'temprano en la semana' is less common than 'a principios de la semana'). If referring to a masculine noun use 'temprano en el' (e.g., 'temprano en el día'). Common alternatives: 'temprano por la mañana' or 'a primeras horas de la mañana.'
target_language_example: Llegamos temprano en la mañana para evitar la fila.
native_language_example: We arrived early in the morning to avoid the line.

meaning: literally 'early this' — not a standalone fixed phrase; it appears when 'temprano' and 'esta' occur together in a time expression (e.g., part of 'temprano esta mañana' or in less natural word orders).
additional_notes: Not idiomatic as written; natural Spanish typically orders as 'esta mañana temprano' or uses 'temprano' with a following time noun ('temprano esta mañana' can occur but is less common). The entry reflects the co-occurrence of 'temprano' (early) and 'esta' (this).
target_language_example: Temprano esta mañana llegué tarde al trabajo.
native_language_example: Early this morning I arrived late to work.

meaning: early for (a time or event)
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is early with respect to a specific time, appointment or event. It usually appears before a time expression or noun (e.g., 'temprano por la mañana', 'temprano por la cita') or followed by a clause introduced with 'ser' or 'estar' when context provides the reference. More common phrasing is 'temprano para' (early for a scheduled event) or simply 'temprano' plus the time ('temprano en la mañana'). Use 'por' when indicating a part of the day ('por la mañana/tarde/noche').
target_language_example: Llegó temprano por la mañana para preparar todo.
native_language_example: He arrived early in the morning to prepare everything.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase; likely a mistaken combination. 'Temprano' = 'early'.
additional_notes: As written, 'temprano que' is not a common Spanish phrase. Beginners likely encounter 'temprano' alone to mean 'early' (e.g., 'llegué temprano' = 'I arrived early'). 'Que' following 'temprano' may appear in mistakes or in regional speech, but standard structures use: 'es temprano para...' (it's early to...) or 'más temprano que...' (earlier than...). If you meant a comparison, use 'más temprano que' = 'earlier than'.
target_language_example: Llegamos más temprano que ellos.
native_language_example: We arrived earlier than them.

meaning: imperative 'have' or 'take' (informal singular): used to offer or tell someone to take/receive something or to wish them to have something
additional_notes: Ten is the tú command (imperative) of tener. 'Ten un ...' can be used to offer something (Ten un caramelo = here, have a candy), to tell someone to keep something handy (Ten un buen diccionario a mano), to wish someone well (Ten un buen día), or to urge someone to adopt a feeling or attitude (Ten un poco de paciencia/fe). Use with tú (informal). For polite/formal use, use 'tenga' (tenga un...).
target_language_example: Ten un poco de cuidado cuando cruces la calle.
native_language_example: Take a little care when you cross the street.

meaning: 'we will have in' or as part of phrases meaning 'we will take into account' / 'we will have (someone/something) in [time]'.
additional_notes:
This is the future-first-person-plural form of 'tener' (to have) followed by 'en'. Its meaning depends on the rest of the phrase: 
- With 'cuenta' (lo tendremos en cuenta) it means 'we will take (it) into account' or 'we will consider (it)'.
- With a time expression (lo tendremos en un par de horas / te tendremos en cinco minutos) it means 'we will have it/you in [time]'—i.e., 'we will have it ready in.../we will have you (ready) in...'. In English this is often rendered as 'we'll have it in X' or 'we'll see you in X.'
Use context to decide whether it means 'take into account' (with 'cuenta') or a time-related 'have in'.
target_language_example: No te preocupes; te tendremos en diez minutos.
native_language_example: Don't worry; we'll have you in ten minutes.

meaning: will have the (feminine noun) — future tense of 'tener' + definite article 'la'.
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something will possess or hold a specific feminine noun (la oportunidad, la póliza, la mente, la piedra, etc.). Context determines the noun that follows; the phrase is simply the verb 'tendrá' (he/she/it/you-formal will have) plus 'la' (the). Note: Spanish word order may place the noun after 'la' (e.g., 'tendrá la póliza') or include additional words ('tendrá la mente ocupada').
target_language_example: Mañana ella tendrá la llave del cajón.
native_language_example: Tomorrow she will have the key to the drawer.

meaning: 'I'll keep (it) in mind' or 'I'll take (it) into account.'
additional_notes: Common phrase used to say you will remember, consider, or take someone's information or advice into account. It's normally completed as 'tendré en cuenta' or 'tendré en mente'. Used in polite responses or to acknowledge advice. Literal components: 'tendré' = I will have, 'en' = in; phrase is semi-compositional when completed.
target_language_example: Gracias por el consejo; lo tendré en cuenta.
native_language_example: Thanks for the advice; I'll keep it in mind.

meaning: 'we have' + definite direct object (we have the... / we've got the...).
additional_notes: Tenemo s al is the combination of the verb tener (present tense, nosotros) + the masculine singular definite article 'el' contracted after a preposition? Note: In Spanish, 'a' before a person marks the personal direct object (the 'personal a'). 'Tenemos al' = 'tenemos a el' → contracted to 'al'. Use when the direct object is a specific person or personified animal (or sometimes a specific animal). Not used with non-personal objects (no 'a'). Example contexts: possession, capture, identification (e.g., 'we have the pilot', 'we've got the judge').
target_language_example: Tenemos al médico que buscábamos.
native_language_example: We have the doctor we were looking for.

meaning: we have something in common
additional_notes: Often used as "tenemos algo en común." Means two or more people share a trait, interest, or experience. Common in casual and neutral contexts. You can drop "común" in very informal speech if context makes it clear, but standard phrase includes "común."
target_language_example: Aunque seamos diferentes, tenemos algo en común.
native_language_example: Even though we're different, we have something in common.

meaning: we have things that / we have stuff to (do/say) — introduces something we possess or need to do/say
additional_notes: Commonly used to introduce a list, explanation, obligation, or unfinished idea (e.g., 'tenemos cosas que hacer' = we have things to do). Often followed by an infinitive, a relative clause (que + verb), or a noun phrase. Context determines whether it means obligations ('things to do'), possessions ('things that...'), or topics to discuss ('things to say/about').
target_language_example: Tenemos cosas que discutir antes de salir.
native_language_example: We have things to discuss before leaving.

meaning: 'we have nothing' or 'we don't have anything/anything in common' (depends on context).
additional_notes: Literally 'we have nothing.' Often appears in negative sentences with no (nada) to mean 'we don't have anything' or in set phrases like 'no tenemos nada en común' ('we have nothing in common'). Note that Spanish negatives usually require the negation word (no) before the verb: 'no tenemos nada.' Alone, 'tenemos nada' without 'no' is ungrammatical or used in colloquial/emphatic contexts only with inversion or questions. Use 'no tenemos nada' to say you lack something.
target_language_example: No tenemos nada en común, así que hablamos de temas diferentes.
native_language_example: We have nothing in common, so we talk about different topics.

meaning: we have nothing to
additional_notes: Commonly used in negative sentences with 'no' (No tenemos nada que ...) to say there is nothing for us to do/lose/discuss/etc. Followed by an infinitive (e.g., discutir, ocultar, perder) or a verb phrase. The literal word order is 'no tenemos nada que + [verb]'.
target_language_example: No tenemos nada que esconder, dime la verdad.
native_language_example: We have nothing to hide, tell me the truth.

meaning: we have all / we have the whole (feminine singular noun follows).
additional_notes: A common phrase meaning 'we possess all of' or 'we have the entire/whole' when followed by a feminine singular noun (e.g., la evidencia, la casa, la noche, la ventaja). If the noun is masculine singular use 'tenemos todo' (e.g., todo el día). For plural nouns use 'tenemos todas' (feminine) or 'tenemos todos' (masculine). Context determines whether it means 'all of' (quantity) or 'the whole' (entire time/space/advantage).
target_language_example: Tenemos toda la información sobre el proyecto.
native_language_example: We have all the information about the project.

meaning: to have (something) nearby or within reach; to keep on hand
additional_notes: Used when you or someone keeps an object or information available and easy to reach. Often followed by a direct object (e.g., "tener un bolígrafo a mano"). Can be used literally (physical object) or figuratively (information, resources).
target_language_example: Siempre procuro tener a mano un cargador cuando viajo.
native_language_example: I always try to keep a charger on hand when I travel.

meaning: to have (someone) (in a certain state) / to keep or cause someone to be (doing something or feeling something); appears when tener is followed by the preposition 'a' + the article 'el' (al) before a masculine singular person or noun.
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom on its own but a common construction: 'tener a' + person + adjective/gerund/participial phrase (written as 'tener al' when the person is masculine singular and the article 'el' contracts with 'a'). Can indicate possession, responsibility, or that someone is being kept in or caused into a state (e.g., entertained, asleep, worried). Context and the complement (adjective/gerund) determine the nuance. Remember 'al' = 'a' + 'el'.
target_language_example: No quiero tener al niño preocupado por esto.
native_language_example: I don't want to have the boy worried about this.

meaning: to have something to do with; to be related to or connected with
additional_notes: Used to say that one thing is connected, relevant, or involved with another. Commonly followed by a noun or clause (tener algo que ver con + noun / que + clause). Neutral register, very frequent in spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: Creo que esto puede tener algo que ver con el retraso en el envío.
native_language_example: I think this might have something to do with the delay in shipping.

meaning: to be (a certain age)
additional_notes: Used with a number to indicate someone's age: tener + número + años (e.g., tengo 20 años = I am 20 years old). Common in questions and statements about age (¿Cuántos años tienes? / Tiene veinte años). Spanish uses tener for age where English uses 'to be'.
target_language_example: Mi hermana dice que va a tener años cuando celebre su cumpleaños.
native_language_example: My sister says she is going to be years old when she celebrates her birthday.

meaning: to have enough; to be fed up with / to have had enough (depends on context)
additional_notes: Primary, compositional use: 'tener bastante' + noun/amount = to have enough of something (e.g., tener bastante comida = to have enough food). Idiomatic/frustration use: with 'de' or followed by a clause/object it can mean to be fed up or to have had enough (e.g., 'tener bastante de algo' or 'tener bastante con + infinitive'). Context and sentence structure determine whether it refers to quantity or to annoyance. Not a cognate; can be translated literally when used for quantity.
target_language_example: No quiero discutir más, ya tengo bastante.
native_language_example: I don't want to argue anymore, I already have had enough.

meaning: to be kind, generous, or good-hearted.
additional_notes: Used to describe a person with a compassionate, generous nature. Often applied to behavior and character rather than the physical heart. Can describe someone's usual disposition (e.g., 'she has a good heart') or explain why they acted kindly.
target_language_example: Tiene buen corazón y siempre comparte lo que tiene con los demás.
native_language_example: She has a good heart and always shares what she has with others.

meaning: to have a good eye; to be good at noticing or judging things (e.g., spotting quality, talent, details).
additional_notes: Used to say someone is skilled at perceiving, selecting, or evaluating — for example, a talent scout who notices potential, a buyer who recognizes quality, or someone with a good sense of style. Often appears as 'tener buen ojo para' + noun (tener buen ojo para los detalles / para los colores / para fichar jugadores).
target_language_example: María siempre tiene buen ojo para fichar jugadores talentosos.
native_language_example: María always has a good eye for scouting talented players.

meaning: to be clear about; to know something for sure
additional_notes: Used when someone understands or is certain about a fact, idea, plan, or opinion. Often followed by a noun, clause (que + clause), or an infinitive: tener claro + (qué/que + clause) / tenerlo claro. Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Es importante tener claro el presupuesto antes de reservar el viaje.
native_language_example: It's important to be clear about the budget before booking the trip.

meaning: to have class / to have a lesson (to attend a scheduled class)
additional_notes: Commonly used to indicate someone has a scheduled lesson (school, university, language class, etc.). Conjugate tener as needed: Tengo clase, Tienes clase, Tenemos clase. Often followed by the subject: Tengo clase de matemáticas. Also used for saying when a class takes place: La clase tiene lugar a las nueve / Tengo clase a las nueve. Neutral register; common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: ¿Vas a tener clase esta tarde?
native_language_example: Are you going to have class this afternoon?

meaning: to have company; to be with someone or to have someone visit/stay with you.
additional_notes: Used when you are not alone — either when someone is visiting, staying over, or simply present with you. Can refer to companionship (emotional) or physical presence. Commonly used in everyday conversation: Tengo compañía = I have company / someone is here. Can be used in different tenses (tenía compañía, voy a tener compañía).
target_language_example: Esta noche no quiero estar solo; voy a tener compañía.
native_language_example: Tonight I don't want to be alone; I'm going to have company.

meaning: to be careful
additional_notes: Common fixed expression used to warn or advise caution. Often followed by de + infinitive/phrase (e.g., tener cuidado al cruzar / tener cuidado con). Can be used impersonally (Uno debe tener cuidado) or with pronouns (ten cuidado — informal tú command).
target_language_example: Tendrás que tener cuidado al manejar con lluvia.
native_language_example: You'll have to be careful when driving in the rain.

meaning: to be careful about/with something (that)...
additional_notes: Used to warn someone to pay attention or be cautious regarding a specific thing or situation. Often followed by a clause introduced with que (tener cuidado con que...) or lo que + verb to refer to 'what' to be careful about. In everyday speech you may also hear tener cuidado con + noun (tener cuidado con el perro).
target_language_example: Tienes que tener cuidado con lo que dices delante del jefe.
native_language_example: You need to be careful about what you say in front of the boss.

meaning: to have pain; to be in pain (in a part of the body).
additional_notes: Used to say that someone feels pain in a specific body part. Common pattern: tener dolor de + [body part] (e.g., tener dolor de cabeza = to have a headache). Can also use with plural parts: tener dolores de [parte]. For general 'to hurt' you can also use the verb doler (me duele la cabeza).
target_language_example: Tengo dolor de estómago desde anoche; he tenido tener dolor en el abdomen todo el día.
native_language_example: I've had a stomachache since last night; I've had pain in the abdomen all day.

meaning: to have the
additional_notes: Not usually a fixed expression on its own. It is simply tener ('to have') + el ('the'), and it normally needs a masculine singular noun after it, such as tener el libro ('to have the book'). The article changes with the noun: tener la, tener los, tener las.
target_language_example: Necesito tener el boleto antes de entrar.
native_language_example: I need to have the ticket before entering.

meaning: to have in; to hold/keep (in) — a light verb construction where 'tener' combines with the preposition 'en' and requires an object or fixed expression; meaning depends on context (literal placement or part of idioms like 'tener en cuenta').
additional_notes: By itself 'tener en' is incomplete and must be followed by a noun, phrase, or fixed expression (e.g., 'tener en la caja', 'tener en cuenta'). Often used in idiomatic constructions; translation depends on the full phrase. It is compositional when used literally and idiomatic when part of set expressions.
target_language_example: Ten el documento y mantenlo, no lo tengas en la mesa todo el día.
native_language_example: Hold the document and keep it; don't have it on the table all day.

meaning: 'to take into account', 'to keep in mind', or 'to consider'.
additional_notes: Used when advising someone to consider a fact, circumstance, or person before deciding or acting. Often followed by a direct object (tener en cuenta algo) or a clause (tener en cuenta que...). Common in both formal and informal speech.
target_language_example: Debes tener en cuenta el tiempo antes de salir.
native_language_example: You should take the weather into account before leaving.

meaning: to keep in mind; to remember or consider something when deciding or planning.
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something should be remembered, considered, or taken into account. Common in advice, planning, or reminders. Can be followed by a noun or a subordinate clause (tener en mente que...).
target_language_example: Debes tener en mente las fechas límite antes de enviar la solicitud.
native_language_example: You should keep in mind the deadlines before submitting the application.

meaning: to have/hold that (conversation, attitude, adventure, etc.).
additional_notes: Tener esa is the combination of the verb tener (to have) + the demonstrative esa (that, feminine). It’s used before a feminine noun mentioned or implied (e.g., aventura, actitud, conversación, charla). In English you often translate it as “have that” or more naturally “have that conversation/attitude/etc.” Context determines the noun; sometimes the noun is omitted because it’s understood from context.
target_language_example: Tenemos que tener esa conversación pronto.
native_language_example: We need to have that conversation soon.

meaning: to be cold (to feel cold).
additional_notes: Common Spanish expression using the verb tener (to have) + noun frío. Used to talk about a person's physical sensation of cold. You can modify intensity: 'tener mucho frío' (to be very cold). To ask someone: '¿Tienes frío?' or '¿Tiene frío?'
target_language_example: ¿Tienes frío? Puedo cerrar la ventana si quieres porque no me gusta tener frío.
native_language_example: Are you cold? I can close the window if you want because I don't like being cold.

meaning: to feel like (doing something); to want/feel a desire to do something.
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive: tener ganas de + [infinitive]. Literally 'to have desires' but idiomatically means 'to feel like' or 'to want to.' Can express mild or strong desire depending on context and intonation. Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Siempre tengo ganas de viajar cuando veo fotos de otros países.
native_language_example: I always feel like traveling when I see pictures of other countries.

meaning: to feel like; to want to (do something)
additional_notes: Use with an infinitive to say you want or feel like doing that action: tener ganas de + verb. Can also be used with a noun to express desire for something: tener ganas de + noun. Common, neutral-register expression for desire or inclination.
target_language_example: Siempre tengo ganas de viajar cuando veo fotos de otras ciudades.
native_language_example: I always feel like traveling when I see photos of other cities.

meaning: to be lucky; to have good luck or fortune.
additional_notes: Informal idiom used to say someone has luck or things go their way (e.g., winning, succeeding easily). Not about literally having milk. Common in Spain and some Latin American countries; tone is casual. Use context to indicate luck (tener suerte is more neutral).
target_language_example: Siempre parece tener leche cuando juega a la lotería; nunca pierde.
native_language_example: He always seems to have luck when he plays the lottery; he never loses.

meaning: to have it / to have that (object or idea) — literal combination of the verb 'tener' and the neutral direct object pronoun 'lo'; used when referring back to something previously mentioned
additional_notes: In normal Spanish sentence order, the pronoun 'lo' usually appears before a conjugated verb (lo tengo) or attached to an infinitive (tenerlo). Writing 'tener lo' as two separate words can occur in contexts like quoted fragments, emphatic structures, or when showing the infinitive and pronoun separately for explanation, but it's not the most common standalone surface form. Use 'lo' for masculine or abstract/neutral objects; use 'la' for feminine objects. Remember that in actual speech/writing you'll most often see 'lo tengo', 'tengo lo' (rare/emphatic), or 'tenerlo'.
target_language_example: Voy a decir que quiero tener lo que prometiste.
native_language_example: I'm going to say that I want to have what you promised.

meaning: to take place; to happen (an event occurs).
additional_notes: Used to describe when or where events occur. Often appears in passive or impersonal constructions (e.g., 'La reunión tendrá lugar mañana' = 'The meeting will take place tomorrow'). Can be used in various tenses: tuvo lugar, tiene lugar, tendrá lugar. Common in formal and neutral contexts.
target_language_example: La conferencia va a tener lugar en el auditorio a las diez.
native_language_example: The conference will take place in the auditorium at ten.

meaning: to have my
additional_notes: A combination of the verb tener (to have) plus the possessive adjective mi (my). Used before a noun to express possession or desire to possess something (e.g., tener mi casa = to have my house). Common in phrases expressing wishes or goals (Espero tener mi...). Word order and agreement follow normal Spanish rules: mi is invariable (does not change for gender or number), while the noun that follows does.
target_language_example: Espero tener mi propio coche el próximo año.
native_language_example: I hope to have my own car next year.

meaning: to be afraid
additional_notes: Used to express fear or lack of fear. Commonly follows the verb tener + miedo (literally 'to have fear') in Spanish but translates as 'to be afraid' in English. Can be followed by de + noun or de + infinitive to indicate the object of fear (tener miedo de algo / de hacer algo).
target_language_example: No debes tener miedo del futuro.
native_language_example: You shouldn't be afraid of the future.

meaning: to have a lot of (used before a feminine noun or abstract noun).
additional_notes: Commonly used with qualities or needs (paciencia, hambre, suerte, confianza). Because mucha is feminine, the noun that follows is feminine (mucha paciencia, mucha hambre). For masculine nouns use 'mucho' (tener mucho frío). Often used with 'tener que' + infinitive for obligation (tienes que tener mucha paciencia = you have to be very patient).
target_language_example: Tienes que tener mucha paciencia con los niños.
native_language_example: You have to have a lot of patience with children.

meaning: to be over
additional_notes: Meaning depends on context. With ages (tener + number) it means "to be over" a certain age (e.g., tener más de cincuenta años = to be over fifty). In other contexts it can mean "to have more" of something (quantity, information, time). Can also appear in future/idiomatic constructions (tener más sobre esto = to have more on this / to cover more about this).
target_language_example: Debe de tener más de cuarenta años.
native_language_example: He must be over forty years old.

meaning: to have nothing / to have anything (in negative or interrogative contexts)
additional_notes: The phrase 'tener nada' is not typically used in affirmative declarative sentences by itself. It appears when combined with negation ('no tener nada' = to have nothing) or in certain dialectal/emphatic contexts. For questions Spanish more commonly uses 'tener algo' (anything) rather than 'tener nada' unless preceded by negation or specific constructions. Literal translation is possible but context-dependent.
target_language_example: No quiero tener nada que ver con eso.
native_language_example: I don't want to have anything to do with that.

meaning: to have nothing against (someone or something); to not oppose or dislike
additional_notes: In natural Spanish the phrase typically appears with negation as 'no tener nada en contra' (e.g., 'no tengo nada en contra de...'). Used to express lack of objection or ill will. It is followed by 'de' or 'a' depending on the noun/pronoun (e.g., 'no tengo nada en contra de ella' or 'no tengo nada en contra de esa idea'). Without the 'no' it is awkward or ungrammatical in isolation.
target_language_example: No quiero que pienses que quiero tener nada en contra de nadie; realmente me importa.
native_language_example: I don't want you to think that I want to have anything against anyone; I really care.

meaning: to have a flair for writing; to be a good or stylish writer (idiomatic); can also be literal: to have a pen.
additional_notes: Literally 'to have a pen' but commonly used idiomatically to praise someone's writing talent or elegant style. Usage varies by region and is not equally common everywhere; context determines whether it's literal or figurative.
target_language_example: Ella tiene pluma; escribe cuentos con mucho estilo.
native_language_example: She has a flair for writing; she writes stories with a lot of style.

meaning: to consider; to regard (someone or something as); to hold the opinion that
additional_notes: Used to indicate that someone regards or considers a person or thing in a certain way. Often followed by a noun or adjective (tener a alguien por + sustantivo/adjetivo) or by que + clause (tener por + que + cláusula). More formal or literary than pensar/creer in some contexts. Examples: Lo tengo por experto; Lo tengo por cierto que vendrá.
target_language_example: La mayoría tiende a tener por líder competente a quien toma decisiones con calma.
native_language_example: Most people tend to consider as a competent leader someone who makes calm decisions.

meaning: to keep in mind; to be aware of; to consider.
additional_notes: Used to remind someone to remember or consider something when making decisions or speaking. Common in advice, instructions, and formal or neutral contexts. Often followed by a noun, clause (que + subj/indic), or infinitive: tener presente X / tener presente que + clause / tener presente + infinitive.
target_language_example: Debes tener presente que el tráfico es peor los lunes por la mañana.
native_language_example: You should keep in mind that traffic is worse on Monday mornings.

meaning: to be wearing (something); to have on (clothing or accessories).
additional_notes: Used to indicate that someone currently has an item of clothing or accessory on. Common construction: tener puesto + [ropa/objeto]. Often interchangeable with llevar or llevar puesto in everyday Spanish; tener puesto can emphasize the item is placed on the person at the moment. Typically used in present tense for current state (e.g., Él tiene puesto un sombrero).
target_language_example: Ella tiene puesto un abrigo rojo.
native_language_example: She is wearing a red coat.

meaning: to have to
additional_notes: Used before an infinitive to express obligation or necessity: tengo que estudiar = "I have to study." The form of tener changes with the subject and tense (tengo que, tienes que, van a tener que, etc.).
target_language_example: Odio tener que depender de usted.
native_language_example: I hate having to depend on you.

meaning: to have to go
additional_notes: Part of the very common pattern tener que + infinitive, which expresses obligation or necessity. Here the infinitive is ir ('to go'). Conjugate tener for the subject when used in a normal sentence: tengo que ir, tienes que ir, etc. In the infinitive, as listed here, it can appear after another verb, as in no quiero tener que ir. Without a destination, it can also mean 'to have to leave.'
target_language_example: No quiero tener que ir mañana.
native_language_example: I don't want to have to go tomorrow.

meaning: to have to come; to need to come (somewhere).
additional_notes: Uses the periphrasis tener que + infinitive to express obligation or necessity. Context determines whether 'venir' means physically coming, attending, or appearing. Commonly used to indicate that someone is required or expected to arrive/attend. Conjugate 'tener' appropriately for person and tense (e.g., "tengo que venir", "tenías que venir").
target_language_example: Voy a decirle que tiene que venir mañana.
native_language_example: I'm going to tell him/her that he/she has to come tomorrow.

meaning: to be right
additional_notes: Used to say that someone is correct about something. Literally it means "to have reason," but the usual English equivalent is "to be right." You can also use it with "en" to specify the topic: "tener razón en algo" = "to be right about something."
target_language_example: Creo que puedes tener razón.
native_language_example: I think you may be right.

meaning: to make sense; to be logical or meaningful
additional_notes: Used to state that something is logical, understandable, or has meaning. Commonly appears in inflected forms (empieza a tener sentido, empezó a tener sentido, no tiene sentido). Can express both understanding ('now it makes sense') and lack of meaning ('it doesn't make sense' / 'it has no meaning').
target_language_example: Entonces todo empezará a tener sentido.
native_language_example: Then everything will start to make sense.

meaning: to have sex; to engage in sexual intercourse.
additional_notes: A neutral, straightforward way to say 'to have sex' in Spanish. Common in both spoken and written language. Can be used with pronouns or reflexive constructions (e.g., 'tener sexo con alguien'). Be aware of context—it's explicit and may be considered private or intimate language.
target_language_example: No quiero tener sexo si no hay confianza.
native_language_example: I don't want to have sex if there's no trust.

meaning: to be lucky
additional_notes: Used to say someone experiences good luck or favorable circumstances. Commonly appears with verbs like poder, deber, or esperar (e.g., 'podrías tener suerte' = 'you might be lucky'). Not idiomatic; literal composition (tener = to have, suerte = luck) matches English.
target_language_example: Si te presentas temprano, podrías tener suerte y conseguir una plaza.
native_language_example: If you arrive early, you might be lucky and get a spot.

meaning: to be sleepy; to feel drowsy or ready to sleep.
additional_notes: Used with the verb tener + the noun sueño to express that someone feels sleepy (e.g., Tengo sueño). Common in everyday speech for physical tiredness or need for sleep; not used to mean 'to be bored'. To say 'to make someone sleepy' use other constructions (e.g., dar sueño).
target_language_example: Después de correr cinco kilómetros, suelo tener sueño.
native_language_example: After running five kilometers, I tend to be sleepy.

meaning: to have such (things/characteristics); to possess those kinds of (qualities/items).
additional_notes: Tener tales is not a fixed idiom by itself; it's the verb tener + demonstrative adjective tales (such, those). It usually appears with a noun or clause following (e.g., tener tales problemas, tener tales habilidades) or in contexts where the noun is understood from context. It can mean 'to have such' or 'to be the kind of person who has those characteristics.' Formality: neutral; common in both spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: No quiero tener tales preocupaciones ahora.
native_language_example: I don't want to have such worries right now.

meaning: to have a job; to be employed; to have work
additional_notes: Used to state that someone is employed or has work to do. Can refer to holding paid employment or having tasks to complete (e.g., "tener trabajo por hacer"). Common in everyday conversation about employment status.
target_language_example: Ella dice que va a tener trabajo a partir del lunes.
native_language_example: She says she will have a job starting Monday.

meaning: 'to have your' (used before a noun to indicate possession/experience belonging to 'you')
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase—it's the verb tener (to have) followed by the possessive adjective tu (your). It appears before a noun (tener tu apoyo = to have your support) or before edad to say you had the same age (Yo solía tener tu edad = I used to be your age). Use tu (informal you) for friends/family; for formal or plural you, use su / su(s).
target_language_example: Quiero tener tu confianza antes de empezar.
native_language_example: I want to have your trust before starting.

meaning: to succeed; to be successful.
additional_notes: Commonly used to talk about achieving goals, doing well in life, work, projects, etc. Conjugate 'tener' to match the subject (e.g., 'tengo éxito', 'tienes éxito', 'tuvo éxito', 'va a tener éxito'). Often followed by infinitives or context explaining the area of success (tener éxito en algo / tener éxito + gerund/infinitive).
target_language_example: Si trabajas duro, puedes tener éxito.
native_language_example: If you work hard, you can succeed.

meaning: to have you (here/with me); to have someone on/at (a particular side or in a role).
additional_notes: Tenerte de combines the verb tener (to have) plus the object pronoun te. Meaning depends on the rest of the sentence: often used in phrases like 'tenerte de regreso' (to have you back) or 'tenerte de mi lado' (to have you on my side). It's colloquial but neutral; the structure is 'tener + te + de + [noun/phrase]'.
target_language_example: Me alegra tenerte de nuevo en el equipo.
native_language_example: I'm glad to have you back on the team.

meaning: 'have a' used in polite wishes or commands (subjunctive usted/ustedes form).
additional_notes: Common in set phrases to wish someone well: 'Que tengan un buen día' = 'Have a good day' (polite/plural or formal). 'Que' + subjunctive expresses a wish; 'tengan' is the ustedes/ustedes-form subjunctive of 'tener'. Can be used with singular formal usted as 'tenga un'.
target_language_example: Que tengan un feliz cumpleaños.
native_language_example: Have a happy birthday.

meaning: you have to / that you have to (subjunctive form used after expressions requiring subjunctive).
additional_notes: Tengas que is the present subjunctive of 'tener que' (to have to) and appears in subordinate clauses after verbs or expressions that trigger the subjunctive (e.g., emotion, doubt, commands, negation). It often translates as 'you have to' or 'that you have to' in contexts like 'anything you have to say' or 'whoever you have to tell'. Use when the main clause requires the subjunctive (e.g., 'no quiero oír nada de lo que tengas que decir').
target_language_example: Dime si tienes algo que tengas que decir antes de irte.
native_language_example: Tell me if you have something that you have to say before you leave.

meaning: 'when you have time' (used to ask someone to do something at a convenient moment).
additional_notes: Common phrase using the subjunctive (tener → tengas) after 'cuando' to refer to a future or non-specific time. Polite and flexible—can be used to request calls, visits, signing papers, or reading something. Tone depends on context: can be casual or polite. You can shorten it to 'cuando puedas' for 'when you can.'
target_language_example: Llama mañana cuando tengas tiempo.
native_language_example: Call tomorrow when you have time.

meaning: you have a
additional_notes: Contains tengas, the tú present subjunctive of tener, plus un. It is commonly used after que in expressions of hope, wishes, advice, or possibility: espero que tengas un buen viaje = 'i hope you have a good trip.' In wishes, que tengas... can also work like 'have a...' in English.
target_language_example: Ojalá tengas un buen día.
native_language_example: I hope you have a good day.

meaning: have a good (one)
additional_notes: This is a fragment from the subjunctive phrase 'que tengas un buen...' used to wish someone well (e.g., 'que tengas un buen día' = 'have a good day'). 'Tengas' is the tú form of the present subjunctive of 'tener'. Often appears after 'que' or in longer polite/wishing expressions. Fill in a noun after 'buen' (día, viaje, fin de semana, etc.).
target_language_example: Que tengas un buen día.
native_language_example: Have a good day.

meaning: 'have a good day' (wishing someone a good day).
additional_notes: Common polite/imperfect-subjunctive phrase used to wish someone well. Often said after 'que' as a short formula: 'Que tengas un buen día.' Can be used with names or contexts (e.g. 'en la oficina'). Tone is friendly or neutral; works with family, friends, colleagues, strangers. If speaking formally to one person, use same phrase; for plural (you all) use 'tengan un buen día.'
target_language_example: Que tengas un buen día en tu nuevo trabajo.
native_language_example: Have a good day at your new job.

meaning: have a good day in (some place or context) — a friendly wish that someone enjoys their time somewhere.
additional_notes: This is the present-subjunctive form of 'tener' (tengas) used in a polite wish or hope. It is usually followed by a place, event, or activity (e.g., 'tengas un buen día en el trabajo', 'tengas un buen día en la escuela'). Commonly used in spoken and written farewells or messages. Formality: neutral/informal depending on context.
target_language_example: Espero que tengas un buen día en la oficina.
native_language_example: I hope you have a good day at the office.

meaning: 'you have a' (subjunctive) — used when speaking about someone having something, often in wishes, requests, or after certain conjunctions
additional_notes: Tengas is the second-person singular (tú) present subjunctive form of tener. Used after verbs or expressions that trigger the subjunctive (e.g., querer que, alegrarse de que) and after certain conjunctions (e.g., cuando, una vez que) to refer to a non-realized or anticipated situation. Una simply means "a" (feminine) and agrees with a feminine noun that follows (una duda, una copia, una vida, una paz, una conexión).
target_language_example: Espero que tengas una buena semana.
native_language_example: I hope you have a good week.

meaning: I have (someone/something) as
additional_notes: Tengo a + noun/pronoun + adjective/role is used to say you have someone in a particular role or consider someone a certain way (e.g., "tengo a Juan como amigo" → I have Juan as a friend / I consider Juan a friend). In everyday speech the verb often appears without 'como' ("tengo a Juan preocupado" = "I have Juan worried" or "Juan is worrying me"). Context determines whether it means possession, responsibility, or emotional/attitudinal stance toward the person. Common with direct objects (me tienes a alguien) and with feelings: "la tengo preocupada" = "I have her worried."
target_language_example: Tengo a Marta como mi mejor amiga.
native_language_example: I have Marta as my best friend.

meaning: I don't have anyone with (me/it).
additional_notes: This exact sequence is ungrammatical in standard Spanish. It likely mixes two correct patterns: 'no tengo a nadie' (I don't have anyone) or 'no tengo a nadie con [mí/usted/nosotros]' (I don't have anyone with me/you/us). For beginners, use 'no tengo a nadie' to say 'I don't have anyone' or 'no tengo a nadie conmigo' / 'no tengo a nadie conmigo' to say 'I don't have anyone with me.'
target_language_example: No tengo a nadie conmigo en la fiesta.
native_language_example: I don't have anyone with me at the party.

meaning: I have (it) here / I have here (something).
additional_notes: Used to say that you possess or are holding something and that it is physically nearby or present. 'Tengo' = I have; 'aquí' = here. Often followed by a direct object or by 'por algún lado' (somewhere around). Tone is neutral and common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Lo tengo aquí, en mi bolso.
native_language_example: I have it here, in my bag.

meaning: I have good
additional_notes: A short phrase combining the verb tener (to have) in first person present and the adjective buena (feminine form of "good"). It must be completed by a feminine noun (ropa, memoria, puntería, vista) or a feminine adjective-noun phrase. Use "tengo buen" (masculine) before masculine singular nouns (e.g., "tengo buen amigo"). For beginners: translate as "I have good..." and add the specific noun in English (e.g., "I have good memory" → natural English: "I have a good memory").
target_language_example: Tengo buena memoria.
native_language_example: I have a good memory.

meaning: I'm hot (I feel warm).
additional_notes: Common way to say you feel hot/uncomfortably warm. Literally 'I have heat.' Used for physical temperature (not usually for 'hot' as attractive). Can be used with other feelings: tengo frío (I'm cold), tengo hambre (I'm hungry).
target_language_example: Hace mucho sol y tengo calor.
native_language_example: It's very sunny and I'm hot.

meaning: 'I have with' (literal) — not a fixed idiom; it is the verb 'tener' in first person singular ('tengo') followed by the preposition 'con', used when indicating that what you have involves or is with someone/something (e.g., appointments, agreements, problems).
additional_notes: Not a standalone expression — normally part of a larger phrase where the object or person follows. Use when saying you 'have' something that is with/related to someone or something: 'tengo una cita con...', 'tengo un problema con...'. Ensure the noun or pronoun that completes the idea appears after 'con'.
target_language_example: Tengo con el gerente una reunión programada.
native_language_example: I have a scheduled meeting with the manager.

meaning: I have things (to do / to say).
additional_notes: A common informal phrase meaning you have unspecified tasks, matters, or things to say. Often followed by 'que...' + verb (e.g., 'tengo cosas que hacer' = I have things to do) or used alone to imply being busy or having other priorities. Tone ranges from neutral to casual; context clarifies whether it means obligations, plans, or topics to mention.
target_language_example: Lo siento, ahora no puedo hablar: tengo cosas que terminar.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can't talk now: I have things to finish.

meaning: 'I have (no) place' — used with a negative to mean 'I don't have anywhere (to ...)', e.g. to sleep or stay.
additional_notes: This phrase appears in constructions like "no tengo dónde + infinitive" or "no tengo dónde + verb", and is followed by an action (dormir, quedarme, pasar la noche) or implied context. It literally means "I have where", but Spanish requires the structure to express lack of a place when combined with "no" (No tengo dónde dormir = I don't have anywhere to sleep).
target_language_example: Esta semana no tengo dónde quedarme durante la conferencia.
native_language_example: This week I don't have anywhere to stay during the conference.

meaning: I have a feeling/intuition that...
additional_notes: Used to express a vague sense, intuition, or premonition about something that will or might happen. Often followed by 'que' + clause. Slightly formal/neutral; common in spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: Tengo el presentimiento de que todo saldrá bien.
native_language_example: I have a feeling that everything will turn out fine.

meaning: Not a correct Spanish phrase; likely a mistaken combination of 'tengo' (I have) and 'es' (is).
additional_notes:
In Spanish you would not normally say 'tengo es'. 'Tengo' is first-person singular of 'tener' (to have). 'Es' is third-person singular of 'ser' (to be). They cannot be combined directly. If you see 'tengo es' it is almost certainly a typo, transcription error, or nonstandard fragment. Possible correct alternatives depending on intended meaning:
- 'Tengo' + noun: 'Tengo un perro.' (I have a dog.)
- 'Es' + adjective/noun: 'Es importante.' (It is important.)
- 'Lo tengo.' / 'La tengo.' to say 'I have it.'
- 'Tengo que' + infinitive to express obligation: 'Tengo que irme.' (I have to leave.)
- To introduce a clause about what exists use 'tengo' with 'que' plus a clause: 'Tengo que decir que es...' (I have to say that it is...).
If you need to keep both words, they could appear consecutively in a sentence across a clause boundary (e.g., 'Tengo — es decir, tengo…'), but that is not standard as a single phrase.
target_language_example: Si en el texto aparece 'tengo es', probablemente es un error tipográfico: 'tengo es' no es correcto en español.
native_language_example: If the text shows 'tengo es', it's probably a typo: 'tengo es' is not correct in Spanish.

meaning: I'm hungry
additional_notes: A common way to say you are hungry in Spanish. Uses the verb tener (to have) + hambre (hunger); literally 'I have hunger'. Used for current physical appetite. To say 'not hungry', add no: 'no tengo hambre'.
target_language_example: Ahora sí, tengo hambre — ¿vamos a comer?
native_language_example: Now I am hungry — shall we eat?

meaning: 'I intend' or 'I have the intention (to...)'.
additional_notes: Used to express a plan, purpose, or lack of willingness to do something. Often followed by 'de' + infinitive (e.g., tengo intención de ir). Can be used in negative form 'no tengo intención de...' to say you do not plan or do not want to do something.
target_language_example: No tengo intención de mudarme este año.
native_language_example: I don't intend to move this year.

meaning: 'I have the feeling' / 'I have a sense (that...)'.
additional_notes: Used to express a personal impression, intuition, or suspicion about something. Often followed by que + clause (Tengo la sensación de que va a llover) or de + noun/infinitive (Tengo la sensación de déjà vu). Polite/neutral phrasing common in spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: Tengo la sensación de que ya nos hemos visto antes.
native_language_example: I have the feeling that we've met before.

meaning: 'I have bad (news)'; short for 'tengo malas noticias'.
additional_notes: Used to introduce bad news. Native speakers often shorten 'tengo malas noticias' to 'tengo malas' in casual speech; context implies 'noticias'. Often followed by the bad information. Formal: use full phrase 'tengo malas noticias'.
target_language_example: Tengo malas: el vuelo se canceló.
native_language_example: I have bad news: the flight was canceled.

meaning: I have a wife / I am married (I have a wife).
additional_notes: Literally 'I have wife.' Common way in Spanish to say you are married or that you have a wife. Used in everyday speech; context clarifies whether emphasizing marriage or simply stating family composition (e.g., when listing family members). Note: Spanish often omits the article before kinship terms (no 'una').
target_language_example: Tengo mujer y trabajo los fines de semana.
native_language_example: I have a wife and I work on weekends.

meaning: 'I have nothing' (colloquial negative construction used after 'no')
additional_notes: This phrase appears in negative sentences with 'no' before the verb: 'No tengo nada' = 'I don't have anything / I have nothing.' Native speakers often drop the pronoun 'yo'. In positive word order 'tengo nada' without 'no' is ungrammatical in standard Spanish — use 'no tengo nada' or the alternative 'no tengo nada que...'. Can be used for possessions, documents, proofs, etc.
target_language_example: No tengo nada que mostrar.
native_language_example: I don't have anything to show.

meaning: I have nothing in / I don't have anything in (something).
additional_notes: This is an ungrammatical or nonstandard Spanish word order for negation. Standard Spanish uses 'no tengo nada en...' or 'no tengo nada' to say 'I don't have anything in...'. Some speakers might drop the initial 'no' in casual speech or dialects, but for beginners learn the standard 'no tengo nada en...'. 'En' introduces a location or container (e.g., 'en la nevera', 'en el bolso').
target_language_example: No tengo nada en la mochila.
native_language_example: I don't have anything in the backpack.

meaning: I have no idea (about/of).
additional_notes: Used to say you don't know anything about a topic or question. Often followed by a clause introduced by de, a question word (qué, a qué, cuántos, etc.), or an infinitive. Colloquial and very common in spoken and written Spanish.
target_language_example: No tengo ni idea de cuándo llegará el tren.
native_language_example: I have no idea when the train will arrive.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase; likely part of constructions like 'no tengo ni...' meaning 'I don't even have...' or 'I don't have any...'.
additional_notes: Alone 'tengo ni' is incomplete. In Spanish, 'no tengo ni...' is common to emphasize lack (e.g. 'No tengo ni idea' = 'I have no idea' or 'No tengo ni un peso' = 'I don't have a single peso'). It pairs 'no' + 'tengo' + 'ni' before a noun or phrase. Avoid using 'tengo ni' without 'no'.
target_language_example: No tengo ni idea de dónde está.
native_language_example: I have no idea where it is.

meaning: I don't have any / I have no ... (used to negate existence of something I possess or experience)
additional_notes: This combination is actually ungrammatical in standard Spanish as written: the correct negative forms are either "no tengo ningún/ninguna..." (with "no" before the verb) or "no tengo ningún...". In the example sentences the intended pattern is "no tengo ningún/ninguna + noun" (e.g., "No tengo ningún plan"). Use "ningún" before a masculine singular noun and "ninguna" before a feminine singular noun. For plural or when not using "ningún/ninguna", Spanish often uses "ninguno/ninguna" or other constructions (e.g., "No tengo tiempo" or "No tengo ningún lugar donde quedarme").
target_language_example: No tengo ningún amigo en esta ciudad.
native_language_example: I don't have any friends in this city.

meaning: I have other (ones); I have other things/options.
additional_notes: Used to say you possess other items, options, tasks, ideas, etc. Often followed by a noun (tengo otras cosas) or a clause (tengo otras formas de...). The gender/number of 'otras' must agree with the noun it refers to: otras (f. pl.), otros (m. pl.). If the noun is omitted, context tells what 'other ones' refers to.
target_language_example: No te preocupes, tengo otras soluciones.
native_language_example: Don't worry, I have other solutions.

meaning: I have (enough) for / I can afford to / I have time/money to (do something).
additional_notes: Depends on context and what follows. Often used with an infinitive or a noun to say you have enough of something (time, money, resources) or to express ability/availability: "Tengo para + infinitive" = I can/I'm able to (do something) or "Tengo para + noun" = I have enough for (that). Tone is neutral and common in spoken Spanish; exact meaning comes from what is being referred to.
target_language_example: No te preocupes, tengo para pagar la cuenta.
native_language_example: Don't worry, I have enough to pay the bill.

meaning: 'I have full...' or 'I fully have...'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase on its own; 'tengo plena' is the start of a sentence meaning 'I have complete/total [something]' or 'I fully [feel/know/have]' and needs a noun or participle to finish the idea (e.g., 'tengo plena confianza', 'tengo plena seguridad', 'tengo plena conciencia'). 'Plena' agrees in gender with a following feminine noun; use 'pleno' for masculine nouns (e.g., 'tengo pleno control').
target_language_example: Tengo plena confianza en tu trabajo.
native_language_example: I have full confidence in your work.

meaning: I have no reason to / I don't need to (do something).
additional_notes: Used in negative constructions as 'no tengo por qué + infinitive' to say you have no reason, obligation, or need to do something. Literal parts ('tengo' = I have, 'por qué' = why/reason) help understand it, but the phrase functions as a fixed expression in this structure.
target_language_example: No tengo por qué mentir sobre eso.
native_language_example: I have no reason to lie about that.

meaning: 'I have all' / 'I have the whole' (feminine noun follows)
additional_notes: This is the verb tener (to have) in first person plus the feminine adjective 'toda' that agrees with a following feminine noun. It can mean 'I have all/the whole' (e.g., toda la información, toda la casa) or be part of expressions like 'No tengo toda la...' (I don't have all/the whole...). Context determines whether it refers to quantity ('all of') or entirety ('the whole of'). Use 'todo' before masculine nouns (tengo todo) and 'todas' for plural feminine (tengo todas).
target_language_example: Tengo toda la tarde libre.
native_language_example: I have the whole afternoon free.

meaning: I have everything
additional_notes: Literal meaning is 'I have everything' or 'I have all'. Context can narrow it: before a noun or phrase it often means 'I have all the [something]' (e.g., 'tengo todo mi dinero' = 'I have all my money'). In sentences like 'Tengo todo el derecho a/ de...' it’s a fixed expression meaning 'I have every/ full right to...' ('todo el derecho' = 'every/full right'). When followed by an indefinite noun with emphasis ('tengo todo un tren'), it adds intensity: 'I have a whole train (to unload)' = 'I have an entire train'.
target_language_example: Tengo todo mi pasaporte y billetes.
native_language_example: I have all my passport and tickets.

meaning: I have all the / I have everything (followed by a noun or clause).
additional_notes: Incomplete phrase: usually part of a longer sentence such as "tengo todo lo necesario" (I have everything necessary) or "tengo todo lo que necesito" (I have everything I need). "Lo" is a neutral direct object pronoun used before adjectives, past participles, or clauses. After "todo lo" you often see an adjective, past participle, or "que" + clause.
target_language_example: Tengo todo lo que necesito para el viaje.
native_language_example: I have everything I need for the trip.

meaning: 'I have a friend whose...'.
additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause that describes or gives possession/relationship for 'un amigo' (a friend). 'Cuyo' agrees in gender and number with the thing possessed (not with the possessor). Common structure: 'Tengo un amigo cuyo/ cuya/ cuyos/ cuyas + [noun] + [verb/clause]'. Example: 'tengo un amigo cuyo perro es grande.'
target_language_example: Tengo un amigo cuyo perro vive en la playa.
native_language_example: I have a friend whose dog lives on the beach.

meaning: 'I have a question.'
additional_notes: Common phrase to indicate you want to ask something or request clarification. Used in formal and informal contexts. Can be followed by the question itself or by a polite pause (e.g., 'tengo una pregunta: ...').
target_language_example: Disculpe, tengo una pregunta sobre el horario.
native_language_example: Excuse me, I have a question about the schedule.

meaning: I have (with emphasis or contrast).
additional_notes: Literally 'I have', but placing 'yo' after the verb adds emphasis or contrast (e.g., 'I do have' or 'I have, unlike others'). Common in spoken Spanish to stress that the speaker possesses something or feels differently. Not a fixed idiom; it's the regular first-person present of 'tener' plus the pronoun 'yo' for emphasis.
target_language_example: No quiero ir, pero tengo yo la llave del coche.
native_language_example: I don't want to go, but I do have the car key.

meaning: had time
additional_notes: Commonly appears as part of perfect tenses with haber (e.g., 'he tenido tiempo' = 'I have had time', 'no he tenido tiempo' = 'I haven't had time'). Used to say someone was/has been able to spare time for something. Can appear in conditional or pluperfect contexts (e.g., 'hubiera tenido tiempo' = 'had had time').
target_language_example: No he tenido tiempo para leer el correo.
native_language_example: I haven't had time to read the mail.

meaning: a phrase used to indicate 'tennis of' or 'sneakers of' depending on context; often starts a noun phrase like 'tenis de correr' (running shoes) or 'tenis de mesa' (table tennis).
additional_notes: Tenis can mean the sport 'tennis' or 'sneakers' (shoes) depending on region. When followed by 'de' + noun, it usually shows purpose or type: 'tenis de mesa' = the sport table tennis; 'tenis de correr' = shoes for running. Word order matters: to talk about the sport, Spanish more commonly uses 'tenis' alone or 'tenis de mesa' for table tennis; for shoes, many speakers say 'tenis' or 'zapatillas'.
target_language_example: Compré unos tenis de correr nuevos.
native_language_example: I bought new running shoes.

meaning: table tennis (ping-pong).
additional_notes: Refers to the sport played on a table with small paddles and a lightweight ball. 'Ping pong' is an informal/synonymous term often used interchangeably. Used as both a noun for the sport and in contexts like 'jugar al tenis de mesa' (to play table tennis).
target_language_example: Vamos a jugar al tenis de mesa esta tarde.
native_language_example: Let's play table tennis this afternoon.

meaning: tennis (played) in / at (a place) — 'tenis' = tennis; 'en' = in/at.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but the combination of the noun tenis (often used with the preposition 'en' to indicate location: 'en el parque', 'en el club') or with the verb jugar (jugar al tenis en ...). In Spanish many speakers say 'jugar al tenis' (using the article + preposition 'a' → 'al'), but you can also see 'juego tenis' followed by 'en' to indicate where. Use 'en' to say where the activity happens (en Francia, en el parque, en el club).
target_language_example: Juego al tenis en el parque los domingos.
native_language_example: I play tennis in the park on Sundays.

meaning: Likely a fragment; not a standard fixed phrase in Spanish. 'Tenis' = tennis (the sport) or tennis shoes; 'es' = is.
additional_notes: This looks like two separate words rather than an established phrase. In context you might see 'El tenis es...' ('Tennis is...') to begin a sentence (e.g., El tenis es un deporte popular). Or 'Los tenis' (plural) can mean 'sneakers' in some Spanish varieties, so 'Los tenis son...' = 'The sneakers are...'. Alone, 'tenis es' is ungrammatical without surrounding words.
target_language_example: El tenis es divertido para muchas personas.
native_language_example: Tennis is fun for many people.

meaning: 'the tennis (shoes) — plural with article' or 'tennis shoes' (with the definite article 'los')
additional_notes: The correct Spanish order is 'los tenis' (article before noun). 'Tenis los' is the article+noun reversed and is ungrammatical in standard Spanish unless used in a specific poetic, emphatic, or colloquial inversion (e.g., in a fragment or after a pause). 'Tenis' (pronounced like English 'tennis') commonly means 'sneakers' or 'tennis shoes' in many Latin American varieties. Use 'los tenis' to say 'the sneakers'.
target_language_example: ¿Por qué tenis los en la puerta?
native_language_example: Why are the sneakers (tenis) at the door?

meaning: sports shoes / sneakers (colloquial phrase meaning 'all-purpose sneakers')
additional_notes: This phrase combines tenis (sneakers) with todo ('all' or 'everything') to imply casual, all-purpose trainers. It's informal and regional — not a fixed dictionary phrase — but understandable: e.g., someone might say 'me pongo unos tenis todo' to mean plain, everyday sneakers. Use in casual speech when referring to comfortable, everyday shoes.
target_language_example: Voy a ponerme unos tenis todo para salir a caminar.
native_language_example: I'm going to put on some everyday sneakers to go for a walk.

meaning: Not a complete standard phrase by itself; literally 'tenis all the...' — could be part of expressions referring to 'tennis' or 'sneakers' followed by a masculine singular noun. Needs an additional noun to be meaningful (e.g., 'tenis todo el día', 'tenis todo el equipo').
additional_notes: 'Tenis' can mean the sport 'tennis' or, in many Latin American varieties, 'sneakers' (shoes). 'Todo el' is the masculine singular form of 'all the' and must be followed by a masculine singular noun. As written, 'tenis todo el' is incomplete and ambiguous; provide the noun that follows to clarify meaning.
target_language_example: Los tenis todo el día no me dejaron descansar.
native_language_example: The sneakers all day didn't let me rest.

meaning: had good (followed by a noun) — e.g., had good reasons/intentions.
additional_notes: Commonly used with nouns like razones (reasons) or intenciones (intentions). Tenía is the imperfect past of tener (he/she/it/you formal had). Use to describe ongoing or repeated past states or explanations. Word order: tenía + buenas + [noun].
target_language_example: Ella tenía buenas razones para decir la verdad.
native_language_example: She had good reasons to tell the truth.

meaning: I/he/she/it/you (formal) had five / was five (years old) — depends on context.
additional_notes: Tenía is the imperfect past tense of tener (to have). With a number alone (e.g., "tenía cinco") it often means 'was five' when referring to age (short for "tenía cinco años"). With a noun after the number it means 'had five [things]' (e.g., "tenía cinco libros"). The subject is understood from context or previous sentence.
target_language_example: Cuando era niño, tenía cinco años y me encantaban los dinosaurios.
native_language_example: When I was a child, I was five years old and I loved dinosaurs.

meaning: had four (used to say someone possessed four of something).
additional_notes: Imperfect past tense of tener (tenía) + the number cuatro. Commonly used to describe past possession or a repeated/state situation in the past (e.g., games, cards, objects). Subject can be explicit or implied (yo, él, ella, etc.).
target_language_example: Ella tenía cuatro libros en su mochila.
native_language_example: She had four books in her backpack.

meaning: had in the (something) — indicates possession or that something was located inside/on a masculine singular container, place, or body part in the past (imperfect).
additional_notes: 'Tenía' is the imperfect of 'tener' and describes an ongoing or repeated past state. The phrase is compositional and can change to tenía en la / tenía en los / tenía en las depending on the gender/number of the following noun. Commonly used with words like bolsillo, maletín, pelo, bus (el bus), coche, etc. Can be translated literally in most contexts.
target_language_example: No puedo haber perdido las llaves otra vez; las tenía en el bolsillo hace un momento.
native_language_example: I can't have lost the keys again; I had them in the pocket a moment ago.

meaning: had (something) in the + noun (e.g., head, mind, face); indicates possession/mental or physical placement inside or on a body part or location.
additional_notes: This is the imperfect past of 'tener' plus the preposition 'en' and the definite article 'la' before a feminine noun (e.g., la cabeza, la mente, la cara). It often appears in phrases meaning 'to have (something) in one's head/mind/face' — i.e., to hold an idea, remember something, or display a facial expression. Context determines whether the object is literal (physical placement) or figurative (thoughts, feelings). If the noun is masculine, you'd see 'tenía en el'.
target_language_example: Siempre tenía en la cabeza la canción del verano.
native_language_example: She always had the summer song in her head.

meaning: I/he/she/it had an idea / I thought (that) / I had the impression (that).
additional_notes: Past imperfect of tener + idea. Often used to express a past belief, impression, or plan that existed over some time (e.g., 'tenía idea de...' = 'I had the idea/plan to...') or to say you thought something ('tenía idea de que...' = 'I thought that...'). Context decides whether it's about a plan or a belief. Pronoun depends on context (tenía = yo, él, ella, usted).
target_language_example: Tenía idea de llamarte ayer, pero se me olvidó.
native_language_example: I had planned/thought about calling you yesterday, but I forgot.

meaning: 'to have an idea/knowledge of' — used in the negative to mean 'to have no idea (that/of)'.
additional_notes: Commonly appears in negative sentences (No tenía idea de...) to say you didn't know something. Followed by a clause introduced with que, de + infinitive, de + qué, de a qué, de por qué, or de qué + subjunctive/conditional depending on sentence. Tense of tenía is imperfect; other tenses possible (no tengo idea de, no tuve idea de).
target_language_example: No tenía idea de que ibas a venir hoy.
native_language_example: I had no idea you were going to come today.

meaning: 'had the' (past tense, third-person or yo formal) — used to say someone possessed or experienced something specific.
additional_notes: Combination of the imperfect past tense of tener (tenía = 'he/she/you(formal)/I used to have' or 'was having') plus the feminine singular article la. Commonly followed by a feminine noun (la opción, la aprobación, la sensación, la mirada). Used to describe possession, feelings, states, or tendencies in the past. Subject is determined by context or prior clause.
target_language_example: Ella tenía la llave del armario.
native_language_example: She had the key to the closet.

meaning: 'was afraid of' (past tense: used to say someone felt fear of something or someone).
additional_notes: Imperfect past tense of tener miedo a + noun or pronoun. Commonly followed by a thing or person introduced with 'a' (tenía miedo a los perros, tenía miedo a la oscuridad, le tenía miedo a su padre). Use 'tener miedo de' with verbs (tener miedo de hablar) or 'tener miedo a' with nouns/people. The construction 'le tenía miedo a...' emphasizes fear directed at a specific person/being.
target_language_example: Antes tenía miedo a volar, pero ahora ya no.
native_language_example: I used to be afraid of flying, but now I'm not.

meaning: had nothing / didn't have anything
additional_notes: A combination of the imperfect tense of tener (tenía) plus nada (nothing). Commonly appears in negative statements to say someone didn't have something (often preceded by no: no tenía nada). In affirmative contexts without 'no' the phrase is uncommon; learners should use 'no tenía nada' to express 'I/he/she/they didn't have anything.'
target_language_example: No tenía nada que decir.
native_language_example: I didn't have anything to say.

meaning: had no idea / I had no idea.
additional_notes: Used to say you were completely unaware or didn't know something. Common in past narration (tenía) but can appear as short reply "No tenía ni idea." Equivalent present: "no tengo ni idea." "Ni" here reinforces "idea" (means 'not even an idea').
target_language_example: Cuando me lo explicó, yo no tenía ni idea de qué hablaba.
native_language_example: When he explained it to me, I had no idea what he was talking about.

meaning: had no idea (about/of).
additional_notes: Used to say someone was completely unaware of something. Often followed by 'que' + clause or 'de' + noun/infinitive. Common in past tense (tenía) but can appear with other tenses (no tengo ni idea, no tenía ni idea). 'Ni' emphasizes total lack of idea.
target_language_example: No tenía ni idea de que ibas a venir hoy.
native_language_example: I had no idea you were coming today.

meaning: 'didn't have any' (negative: had no ...)
additional_notes: This phrase combines the imperfect of tener (tenía) with the negative word ninguna to say someone 'had no' something in the past or 'didn't have any'. In standard Spanish you normally need the negative particle no before the verb: no tenía ninguna. Without the initial no (as in the input), it would be ungrammatical or mean something different in context. Ninguna agrees in gender/number with the noun it modifies (ningún before a masculine singular noun: no tenía ningún problema). Common in statements about doubts, reasons, relations, illnesses, etc.
target_language_example: No tenía ninguna duda sobre la decisión.
native_language_example: He had no doubt about the decision.

meaning: didn't have any / had no (something).
additional_notes: This occurs when describing the lack of something in the past using tener (imperfect). In correct Spanish, a negative construction normally uses 'no tenía ningún/ninguna' (note the 'no' before the verb). 'Ningún' agrees in gender and is used before singular masculine nouns; use 'ninguna' for feminine nouns. Common English equivalents: 'didn't have any', 'had no', or 'there was no'.
target_language_example: No tenía ningún libro que leer.
native_language_example: He didn't have any book to read.

meaning: had no other (choice/option)
additional_notes: Context determines meaning. Commonly appears in negative phrases like "no tenía otra (opción/alternativa/elección/salida)" meaning "had no other (choice/option/alternative/way out)." Without "no," as in "tenía otra pregunta," it means "had another (one)" or "I had one more." "Tenía otra" is past imperfect (tener) and often refers to possession or availability in the past.
target_language_example: No tenía otra opción, así que acepté.
native_language_example: I had no other option, so I accepted.

meaning: had/was completely (followed by a noun or abstract noun) — emphasizes totality or completeness.
additional_notes: Used with feminine singular nouns after tenía (imperfect of tener) to say someone possessed or experienced the whole/entire of something. Can modify concrete things (toda la casa), categories (toda clase de herramientas) or abstract ideas (toda la razón = completely right). Word agreement: 'toda' agrees with the noun in gender and number (toda, todo, todas, todos).
target_language_example: Ella tenía toda la información sobre el proyecto.
native_language_example: She had all the information about the project.

meaning: theory of / the theory that (used to name or refer to a particular theory about something).
additional_notes: Common phrase used to name a theory followed by a noun or concept (e.g., 'teoría de la evolución' = 'theory of evolution'). Can introduce formal scientific theories or informal/metaphorical theories (e.g., 'teoría de la bala mágica'). Often followed by 'la', 'el', or a noun phrase.
target_language_example: La teoría de la relatividad cambió la física moderna.
native_language_example: The theory of relativity changed modern physics.

meaning: 'third grade' (school level) OR 'third-degree' (mathematical) OR 'intense interrogation/torture' (idiomatic)
additional_notes:
Has multiple meanings depending on context:
- Education: 'tercer grado' = the third year of primary/elementary school. Example: 'estuvo en tercer grado' (he/she was in third grade).
- Mathematics: describes degree of a polynomial or equation (e.g., 'ecuación de tercer grado' = cubic equation).
- Idiomatic (colloquial, somewhat dated): 'poner a alguien al tercer grado' or 'someter al tercer grado' means to give someone harsh questioning or intense interrogation; comparable to 'the third degree' in English.
Choose the meaning from context. The phrase can be translated literally as 'third grade' when referring to school; for the idiom, English often uses 'the third degree.'
target_language_example: Cuando estaba en tercer grado, aprendí a multiplicar.
native_language_example: When I was in third grade, I learned to multiply.

meaning: 'finish (doing something)'.
additional_notes: Used with a verb in infinitive to say someone finishes or should finish an action (termina de + infinitive). Can be a simple statement (Él termina de hablar) or a command/urging (Termina de comer = finish eating / hurry up and finish).
target_language_example: Termina de leer el libro antes de devolverlo.
native_language_example: Finish reading the book before returning it.

meaning: 'finish the' or 'finish it/the (masculine noun)'.
additional_notes: A command or statement using the verb terminar (to finish) followed by the masculine singular definite article el + noun or implied masculine object. In commands it can be an informal (tú) imperative: "¡Termina el juicio!" = "Finish the trial!" When the noun is omitted, context supplies the masculine thing to finish (e.g., el trabajo, el libro, el filete). Use termina (he/she/it finishes or tú imperative informal) depending on context; for formal commands use termine.
target_language_example: Termina el informe antes de salir.
native_language_example: Finish the report before leaving.

meaning: having finished the + (masculine singular noun) — indicates something is completed
additional_notes: Commonly appears after auxiliary verbs (haber, haber de, tener que) or in participial phrases. 'Terminado' is the past participle of 'terminar' and agrees in gender/number with the noun it modifies (terminado el informe, terminada la tarea, terminados los proyectos). Often used in perfect constructions (ha terminado el informe) or in reduced clauses (Habiendo terminado el trabajo...).
target_language_example: He terminado el informe esta mañana.
native_language_example: I have finished the report this morning.

meaning: 'finished' or 'completed' + feminine singular noun (past participle used with a feminine noun)
additional_notes: This is the past participle 'terminado' used with the feminine definite article 'la' before a feminine noun that follows (e.g., 'la tarea', 'la carrera', 'la tarta'). In Spanish the past participle must agree in gender and number when used in compound verbs with 'haber' it does not change (e.g., 'he terminado la tarea'), but when used with 'ser' or as an adjective it does (e.g., 'la tarea está terminada'). The examples show various compound tenses (pretérito perfecto, pluscuamperfecto, futuro perfecto, conditional forms).
target_language_example: He terminado la tarea, ¿puedo salir ahora?
native_language_example: I have finished the homework, can I go out now?

meaning: 'his/her/its/your (formal)/their ... finished' — the past participle terminado (finished) followed by the possessive su, used to indicate that something belonging to someone has been completed.
additional_notes: Not a fixed set phrase by itself; typically part of a larger phrase and must be followed by a noun or appear within a clause (e.g., El proyecto terminado su fecha de entrega → note: this particular word order is uncommon; more natural: su proyecto terminado). Agreement: terminado must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies (terminada/terminados/terminadas). Context determines the meaning of su (his, her, its, your formal, their). Often used with verbs like estar or haber to form complete sentences (e.g., está terminado su trabajo; ha terminado su turno).
target_language_example: El informe quedó terminado su revisión.
native_language_example: The report ended up finished its review. (Note: this sentence reproduces the exact sequence 'terminado su' but is somewhat marked — more natural would be 'su revisión quedó terminada' or 'la revisión del informe quedó terminada'.)

meaning: to end in / to finish with (a result, ending, or final part)
additional_notes: Used to describe how something finishes or what the final result is. Common with events, stories, situations, or numbers/details (e.g., 'terminar en empate' — end in a tie; 'la película termina en tragedia' — the movie ends in tragedy). Can also be used for endings like phone numbers or license plates: 'termina en 5'.
target_language_example: La reunión suele terminar en terminar en acuerdo entre todos.
native_language_example: The meeting usually ends in an agreement among everyone.

meaning: 'finish this' or 'complete this' (feminine singular object).
additional_notes: Termin ar = to finish/complete.
