target_language_example: Ellos tomaron un autobús hacia la ciudad.
native_language_example: They took a bus to the city.

target_language_multi_word_term: tomaré como / me lo tomaré como
meaning: I'll take it as / I'll consider it as (used to accept an action/comment as having a particular meaning).
additional_notes: Used to express that you will interpret someone's words, actions, or events in a certain way (often positively). 'Me lo tomaré como' adds a reflexive/object pronoun meaning 'I'll take it (for myself) as...'. Commonly followed by 'un cumplido' (a compliment), 'un sí' (a yes), 'una señal' (a sign), etc.
target_language_example: Si vas a ayudarme, me lo tomaré como una señal de buena voluntad.
native_language_example: If you're going to help me, I'll take it as a sign of goodwill.

meaning: I'll take it as a (something); I will interpret it as a (something).
additional_notes: Used when saying how you will interpret a comment, action, or situation. Usually followed by a noun or phrase that completes the interpretation (e.g., 'insulto', 'aviso', 'favor'). Common in conversational Spanish: 'Tomaré eso como un cumplido' = 'I'll take that as a compliment.'
target_language_example: Si no respondes, lo tomaré como un no.
native_language_example: If you don't reply, I'll take it as a no.

meaning: 'take the' (formal command/subjunctive) or 'he/she takes the' depending on context.
additional_notes: Tome is either the formal (usted) imperative of tomar (take) or the present subjunctive/third-person present (tome). 'Tome la' is followed by a feminine noun (la + noun) as in 'tome la decisión' or by a feminine object like 'la botella'. Context decides if it's a command (¡Tome la siguiente salida!) or part of a clause (que tome la decisión = that he/she make/take the decision).
target_language_example: Por favor, tome la carretera que va al centro.
native_language_example: Please take the road that goes to downtown.

meaning: 'take a' or 'have a' (plural imperative: you all take/have a ...).
additional_notes: Plural formal/informal command (ustedes) telling a group to take, have, or grab something. Common with nouns like 'descanso' (break), 'trago' (drink), 'trozo' (piece), or food items. Use to give instructions or offers to multiple people. If addressing one person use 'toma un' (informal) or 'tome un' (formal).
target_language_example: Tomen un descanso y vuelvan dentro de diez minutos.
native_language_example: Take a break and come back in ten minutes.

meaning: imperative/subjunctive form telling someone to 'take the ...' (e.g., take the bus/metro/plane); often appears in commands or wishes (tú tomes + definite article).
additional_notes: ‘Tomes’ is the present subjunctive (used for commands, wishes, recommendations) or negative imperative for tú (with no pronoun). Here it combines with a masculine noun introduced by the definite article 'el' (e.g., el autobús, el metro, el avión, el mando). Context determines tone: can be a suggestion ('Que tomes el autobús') or a prohibition when negated ('No tomes el avión'). Also appears in idiomatic phrases (No me tomes el pelo = Don't pull my leg / Don't make fun of me).
target_language_example: Por favor, toma el tren, pero no tomes el último vagón; mejor que tú tomes el primero.
native_language_example: Please take the train, but don't take the last car; better that you take the first one.

meaning: 'I take the... (transportation)' or 'I drink the... (beverage)' depending on context.
additional_notes: Tomo is the first-person singular present of tomar. With transport (metro, autobús, tren, tranvía, vuelo) it means 'I take' (I ride or I catch). With beverages (té, café) it means 'I drink' or 'I'll have'. The article (el) agrees with the following noun (el metro, el autobús, el tren). Common in everyday speech to describe daily routines (Tomo el metro todos los días).
target_language_example: Tomo el autobús para ir al trabajo.
native_language_example: I take the bus to go to work.

meaning: I took (from) / I drank (of) — past first person of tomar + preposition 'de'.
additional_notes: Tomé is the preterite (simple past) of tomar (to take, to drink, to photograph, etc.). Adding de indicates the source or what it was taken from (e.g., 'tomé de la nevera' = I took [it] from the fridge) or partitive/measure contexts (e.g., 'tomé de su mano' = I took [it] from his/her hand). Without context it could also mean 'I drank of' (tomé de la botella = I drank from the bottle). English object is often omitted in Spanish when clear from context.
target_language_example: Tomé de la botella porque tenía sed.
native_language_example: I drank from the bottle because I was thirsty.

meaning: took from the (feminine noun) / he/she/it took from the (feminine noun)
additional_notes: Compound of tomó (past tense of tomar: 'to take') + de la (preposition 'from the' for feminine singular nouns). Use before a feminine noun: e.g., tomó de la mesa (took from the table), tomó de la caja (took from the box). If the following noun is masculine, use 'del' (de + el) instead: tomó del libro. Context determines who 'took'—subject can be él/ella/usted or it.
target_language_example: Ella tomó de la nevera una botella de agua.
native_language_example: She took a bottle of water from the fridge.

meaning: took the trouble (to do something); made an effort to do something for someone.
additional_notes: Used to describe someone who went out of their way or made a special effort—often politely—to do a helpful or considerate action. Typically followed by 'de' + verb infinitive (se tomó la molestia de + infinitive). Can be used sincerely or with mild irony depending on tone.
target_language_example: Se tomó la molestia de dejarme un mensaje cuando llegué tarde.
native_language_example: He took the trouble to leave me a message when I arrived late.

meaning: drank a cup (of something) / took a cup
additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of tomar + una taza. Commonly used to say someone drank a cup of coffee, tea, or another beverage (tomó una taza de café). Can also mean physically picked up a cup (took a cup). Context tells whether it refers to drinking or taking. For a more explicit beverage mention, add 'de' + beverage (e.g., tomó una taza de té).
target_language_example: Esta mañana tomó una taza de café antes de salir.
native_language_example: This morning he/she drank a cup of coffee before leaving.

meaning: he/she/it/you (formal) took several / took various (feminine plural noun implied).
additional_notes: Tomó is the past (pretérito) of tomar (to take). Varias is a feminine plural adjective meaning 'several' or 'various' and must agree with a following feminine plural noun that is often omitted when clear from context (e.g., tomó varias fotos → took several photos). The subject can be él, ella, usted, or una thing (e.g., la película tomó varias semanas: the film took several weeks).
target_language_example: Ella tomó varias fotos durante la fiesta.
native_language_example: She took several photos during the party.

meaning: 'so foolish/so stupid as' (used in comparisons, often with 'tan' to mean 'so ... as to ...')
additional_notes: Usually appears as 'tan tonto como' or 'ser tan tonto como para + (infinitive)' to say someone was foolish enough to do something. It compares degree (tan ... como) or expresses 'foolish enough to' when followed by 'para' + infinitive. Tone is neutral to slightly critical; 'tonto' is an everyday word meaning 'stupid' or 'silly'.
target_language_example: No seas tan tonto como para firmar sin leer.
native_language_example: Don't be so foolish as to sign without reading.

meaning: to run into; to come across (someone or something) unexpectedly.
additional_notes: Used when you meet someone or find something by chance. Often used with people or unexpected situations. Commonly conjugated reflexively (me topo, te topas, se topa, nos topamos, etc.). Synonyms: encontrarse con, encontrarse con. Can be used in both literal (meet) and figurative (encounter a problem) senses.
target_language_example: Ayer me topé con mi vecino cuando iba al trabajo; fue sorprendente toparse con él tan temprano.
native_language_example: Yesterday I ran into my neighbor on my way to work; it was surprising to come across him so early.

meaning: 'I ran into' or 'I bumped into' (met someone unexpectedly).
additional_notes: Used to say you met someone by chance. Commonly conjugated from the verb 'topar (con)' (me topé con, te topaste con, se topó con...). Informal-to-neutral; frequently used in everyday speech. Can be followed by a person or a thing encountered.
target_language_example: Me topé con Ana en la cafetería ayer.
native_language_example: I ran into Ana at the café yesterday.

meaning: I ran into / I came across (someone or something).
additional_notes: Common past tense phrase from 'toparse con' meaning to meet someone unexpectedly or to come across something by chance. Used for people or things (e.g., a person on the street, an object, or a book). In English it corresponds to 'run into', 'come across', or 'bump into'.
target_language_example: Ayer me topé con una antigua profesora en el supermercado.
native_language_example: Yesterday I ran into an old teacher at the supermarket.

meaning: curfew (an order requiring people to stay indoors at certain hours).
additional_notes: Used to describe an official or imposed restriction that people must be home or off the streets during set hours (often for safety, emergencies, or public order). Commonly used with verbs like declarar, imponer, aplicar, cumplir. Not a casual phrase — usually refers to a legal or official rule.
target_language_example: Anunciaron un toque de queda desde las 22:00 hasta las 06:00.
native_language_example: They announced a curfew from 10:00 PM to 6:00 AM.

meaning: 'I twisted the' or 'I sprained the' (first-person past of torcer + definite article)
additional_notes: Torcí is the preterite (simple past) of torcer (to twist, to sprain). It must be followed by a noun (el/la/los/las + body part or object): e.g. torcí el tobillo (I sprained my ankle) or torcí el cuello (I twisted my neck). Use context to know whether it means 'twist' (an object) or 'sprain' (a body part).
target_language_example: Ayer torcí el tobillo jugando al fútbol.
native_language_example: Yesterday I sprained my ankle playing soccer.

meaning: 'storm of' or 'storm (with)'.
additional_notes: Used to describe a specific type of storm by adding a noun after 'de' (e.g., 'tormenta de nieve' = snowstorm, 'tormenta de verano' = summer storm, 'tormenta de hielo' = ice storm). Can also be used alone with context as 'the storm' plus a specification. Common in weather reports and everyday speech.
target_language_example: Viene una tormenta de viento esta noche.
native_language_example: A wind storm is coming tonight.

meaning: uses of 'tormenta' with a reflexive/impersonal 'se' to say a storm is doing something (approaching, worsening, turning into...); often expresses that the storm acts or changes on its own (e.g., 'the storm is approaching').
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but examples of 'tormenta' followed by the pronoun 'se' plus a verb (se acerca, se empeora, se hizo, se volvió, se dirige). Spanish uses 'se' here to form reflexive/impersonal/medio constructions that indicate the storm undergoes or produces a change or simply 'does' the action. Common verbs: acercarse (to approach), empeorar(se) (to get worse), hacerse/volverse (to become), dirigirse (to head toward). Translate contextually: 'la tormenta se acerca' = 'the storm is approaching.'
target_language_example: La tormenta se dirige hacia la costa esta noche.
native_language_example: The storm is heading toward the coast tonight.

meaning: 'around' or 'about' (used to indicate approximation in time or quantity) and also 'around/near' when referring to location; can mean 'about' as in approximately.
additional_notes: Commonly used before numbers, times, or quantities to mean 'around/approximately' (e.g., 'torno a las ocho' = 'around eight o'clock'). It can also appear in phrases for location (less common) or be part of fixed expressions. Not formal or slang—neutral everyday Spanish.
target_language_example: Llegaré torno a las siete y media.
native_language_example: I'll arrive around seven thirty.

meaning: the phrase combination of 'torta' (cake) plus the preposition 'en' used to say 'cake' and to indicate division or location ('into' / 'in').
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom; it's the noun torta (cake) followed by the preposition en. Use 'torta en' when specifying where the cake is (e.g., en la panadería = in the bakery) or how it is divided (e.g., en seis pedazos = into six pieces). For division, English uses 'into' — in Spanish use 'dividir/partir + torta + en + (número)'.
target_language_example: Cortó la torta en cuatro trozos.
native_language_example: He cut the cake into four pieces.

meaning: completely (about/of). Used before a noun or phrase introduced by 'de' to emphasize degree or to mean 'completely in/with' something.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase on its own; 'totalmente' means 'completely' and is often followed by 'de' when linking to a noun, adjective, or clause introduced by 'de' (e.g., 'totalmente de acuerdo' = completely in agreement). Depending on context, it can mean 'completely of' (possession/characteristic) or 'completely in/with' (agreement, belief, convinced). Ensure the following word or phrase after 'de' completes the idea.
target_language_example: Estoy totalmente de acuerdo con esa idea.
native_language_example: I totally agree with that idea.

meaning: totally in; fully (located) in / completely into (something)
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something or someone is completely inside, involved in, or focused on a place, situation, or activity. Often followed by a noun or clause (e.g., 'totalmente en casa', 'totalmente en el proyecto'). In everyday speech speakers might prefer 'completamente en' or simply 'totalmente' depending on context.
target_language_example: Estoy totalmente en el proyecto y trabajaré todos los días.
native_language_example: I'm totally in the project and I'll work every day.

meaning: completely out / totally not (present, involved, or aware).
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is completely outside a situation, not participating, or not aware/with it. Context decides nuance: can mean 'outside the place' (physically out), 'out of touch' or 'not focused/aware' (colloquial). Often follows a noun or pronoun: 'está totalmente fuera' = 'he/she/it is totally out/checked out.'
target_language_example: Después de trabajar tanto, estoy totalmente fuera esta noche.
native_language_example: After working so much, I'm totally out tonight.

meaning: completely out of (place, fashion, context); totally inappropriate or not fitting.
additional_notes: Used to say something is inappropriate, awkward, not suitable, or not in style/context. Often followed by nouns like lugar (place), moda (fashion), lugar/contexto, or phrases indicating what it's out of. 'Totalmente' intensifies 'fuera de'.
target_language_example: Ese comentario fue totalmente fuera de lugar en la reunión.
native_language_example: That comment was totally out of place at the meeting.

meaning: works for / works because of / works during (depends on context).
additional_notes: The preposition por changes the meaning: 1) 'trabaja por la oferta más alta' = 'works for' (in exchange for; for the highest offer). 2) 'trabaja por el bienestar social' = 'works for' (in favor of / on behalf of). 3–4) 'trabaja por la mañana/por la noche' = 'works during' (in the morning/at night). Context tells whether por indicates purpose/reason, beneficiary, exchange, or time period.
target_language_example: Ella trabaja por la comunidad los fines de semana.
native_language_example: She works for the community on weekends.

meaning: working hard on (something).
additional_notes: Present participle phrase from trabajar: 'trabajando' (working) + 'duro' (hard) + preposition 'en' (on). Used to say someone is putting a lot of effort into a task, project, job, or skill. Follows a subject (estoy, estamos, está) or can appear in progressive tenses: 'Estoy trabajando duro en mi proyecto.'
target_language_example: Estamos trabajando duro en el proyecto final.
native_language_example: We are working hard on the final project.

meaning: working hard on the (masculine singular noun that follows)
additional_notes: This is the gerund phrase 'trabajando duro' (working hard) followed by the masculine singular definite article 'el'. It must be completed with a masculine noun or noun phrase (e.g., 'trabajando duro en el proyecto'). Use 'en la' for feminine nouns. Commonly used to describe effort on a task, project, job, problem, etc.
target_language_example: Estoy trabajando duro en el proyecto de la escuela.
native_language_example: I'm working hard on the school project.

meaning: to work (in/at) — used before a place, age, or with a person/thing being observed doing work
additional_notes: This is the verb trabajar followed by the preposition a. Common uses: 'trabajar a [lugar]' = to go/work in a place (often with motion: ir a trabajar a París), 'trabajar a [edad]' = start working at a certain age, and 'ver/tratar/oir + trabajar a [persona]' = to see someone (person or group) working. Context determines translation; sometimes English omits 'to' or uses 'in/at'.
target_language_example: Ella fue a trabajar a Londres el invierno pasado.
native_language_example: She went to work in London last winter.

meaning: work at / to (the verb 'trabajar' followed by the contraction 'al' = a + el; used before masculine singular nouns or certain time expressions).
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom on its own but a common sequence: 'trabajar' + 'al' (a + el). Appears in phrases like 'trabajar al lado (de)' = work next to, 'trabajar al mediodía' = work at noon, 'trabajar al aire libre' = work outdoors. 'Al' is used only when the following noun is masculine singular and requires the definite article 'el'. If the noun takes 'la', 'las', 'los', or an indefinite article, there is no contraction (e.g. 'trabajar a la hora', 'trabajar a una hora').
target_language_example: Tienen que trabajar al lado de la carretera durante la obra.
native_language_example: They have to work next to the road during the construction.

meaning: 'to work as' (to perform duties or hold a position in the role of...)
additional_notes: Used with a noun or role (trabajar como + [sustantivo/rol]). Can describe formal paid employment or informal/figurative roles; context determines meaning and register. Can emphasize hardship when used with words like 'esclavos' or 'criada'.
target_language_example: Es terrible verlos trabajar como esclavos en este calor.
native_language_example: It's terrible to see them working as slaves in this heat.

meaning: to work as (to have a job/role as).
additional_notes: Used to indicate someone’s job or role. Followed by a noun: job title, profession, or role (trabajar de camarero, trabajar de profesora). In many contexts trabajar de and trabajar como are interchangeable. Articles are usually omitted after trabajar de when stating a profession (trabaja de enfermero, not 'del enfermero'), though regional variation exists.
target_language_example: Ella va a trabajar de arquitecta a la empresa nueva.
native_language_example: She is going to work as an architect at the new company.

meaning: to work hard; to put in a lot of effort.
additional_notes: Common phrase used to describe making a strong effort at work, study, or any task. Can be used in commands, promises, descriptions of effort and fatigue. Literally composed of trabajar (to work) + duro (hard).
target_language_example: Si quieres mejorar, tendrás que trabajar duro todos los días.
native_language_example: If you want to improve, you'll have to work hard every day.

meaning: to work on (something); to practice or train a specific skill or aspect
additional_notes: This is the verb trabajar followed by a direct object introduced without a preposition (e.g., trabajar el inglés, trabajar el problema). Common when talking about working on a task, improving a skill, or addressing a specific issue. Context determines the object (what is being worked on). For many English equivalents you will use 'work on' or 'practice'.
target_language_example: Tengo que trabajar el vocabulario antes del examen.
native_language_example: I have to work on the vocabulary before the exam.

meaning: to work together; to collaborate.
additional_notes: Used to say that two or more people cooperate on the same task or project. 'Trabajar' is the verb 'to work'; 'juntos' means 'together'. Agreement: when the group is all female, you can say 'trabajar juntas'. In formal contexts you might use 'trabajar en conjunto' or 'colaborar'.
target_language_example: Podemos trabajar juntos en la presentación.
native_language_example: We can work together on the presentation.

meaning: 'to work a lot' / 'to work hard' (do a large amount of work or put in a lot of effort).
additional_notes: Used to say someone must put in a lot of time or effort. Can mean long hours (work a lot) or high effort (work hard) depending on context. Common with verbs like tener que, acostumbrarse a, and modal constructions.
target_language_example: Ella tiene que trabajar mucho para terminar el proyecto a tiempo.
native_language_example: She has to work a lot to finish the project on time.

meaning: to work for / to work during (a time) — depends on context.
additional_notes: Can mean 'to work for' someone, something, or a cause (e.g., work in exchange for pay or to support a goal) or 'to work during' a time period when followed by a time expression. Context decides meaning. Common structures: 'trabajar por [persona/causa]' (work for someone/for a cause) and 'trabajar por la mañana/tarde/noche' (work in the morning/afternoon/night).
target_language_example: Algunos no quieren trabajar por ese privilegio; otros sí.
native_language_example: Some do not want to work for that privilege; others do.

meaning: to work all (of something) / to work the whole time (informal phrase fragment)
additional_notes: This is not a fixed set phrase by itself in Spanish. 'Trabajar todo' often appears before a noun or phrase to mean 'to work all [day/night/week/etc.]' (e.g., 'trabajar todo el día') or with 'el tiempo' to mean 'to work the whole time'. On its own it's incomplete; you usually need an object or time expression. Use with articles or time words: trabajar todo el día / trabajar todo el tiempo / trabajar todo el año.
target_language_example: Este mes voy a trabajar todo el día para terminar el proyecto.
native_language_example: This month I'm going to work all day to finish the project.

meaning: to work the whole (day/time/etc.) — used to say someone works all of a specified period
additional_notes: This phrase is not a complete fixed expression by itself; it needs a noun after 'el' (e.g., 'trabajar todo el día', 'trabajar todo el fin de semana'). Commonly used to emphasize working for the entire duration of that period. 'Todo el' agrees with a masculine singular noun; use 'toda la' for feminine nouns (e.g., 'toda la noche').
target_language_example: Voy a trabajar todo el día mañana.
native_language_example: I'm going to work the whole day tomorrow.

meaning: 'work at' or 'work on' (part of a verb phrase indicating the place, rate, or manner of work).
additional_notes: This is not a complete fixed phrase by itself; 'trabajo a' typically appears before a noun, number, or infinitive to show how/where/at what rate someone works: e.g. trabajo a tiempo completo (I work full-time), trabajo a distancia (I work remotely), trabajo a $10 la hora (I work at $10 an hour), trabajo a reparar el coche (I work on repairing the car). Match preposition use to context; often followed by 'tiempo', 'distancia', a rate, a place, or an infinitive.
target_language_example: Trabajo a tiempo parcial los sábados.
native_language_example: I work part-time on Saturdays.

meaning: before work / earlier at work
additional_notes: A simple phrase combining trabajo (work, job) and antes (before). Depending on context it can mean 'before work' (e.g., something you do before going to your job) or 'earlier at work' (referring to an earlier time during the workday). Use articles or verbs to make full sentences: e.g., 'antes del trabajo' (before work/the workday) or 'trabajé antes' (I worked earlier).
target_language_example: Salgo a correr trabajo antes de ir a la oficina.
native_language_example: I go for a run before work before going to the office.

meaning: work (job) here; can mean 'a job located here' or 'my/your work here' depending on context.
additional_notes: Used to refer to a job or to the work/task someone does at the current place. Context decides whether it means 'a job here' (employment) or 'the work I'm doing here' (task completed). Common with verbs like tener, conseguir, hacer, estar (estar hecho = finished).
target_language_example: Tengo un trabajo aquí desde hace dos meses.
native_language_example: I have a job here since two months ago.

meaning: I/you/he/she/we/they work well; (something) works well.
additional_notes: Combination of the noun/verb 'trabajo' (work/job) and the adverb 'bien' (well). Depending on context, it can mean 'I/you/etc. do a good job' or 'it functions properly'. For correct grammar, remember to conjugate the verb 'trabajar' when used as a verb: e.g., 'Trabajo bien' (I work well) or use 'funciona bien' for 'it works well.' As a short phrase, 'trabajo bien' is most often 'I work well' (with 'trabajo' = I work) or could be part of a larger sentence like 'Hace un buen trabajo' / 'Trabaja bien.'
target_language_example: Trabajo bien cuando tengo un horario claro.
native_language_example: I work well when I have a clear schedule.

meaning: 'job as' / 'work as' — used to indicate someone's job, role, or the act of working in a specific capacity.
additional_notes: Can function as a noun phrase ('un trabajo como...') or appear in descriptions of someone's employment. Often followed by a profession or role (e.g., 'trabajo como ingeniera'). Context determines whether it's describing a position or the act of working in that capacity.
target_language_example: Ella consiguió un trabajo como ingeniera de grabación.
native_language_example: She got a job as a recording engineer.

meaning: I/you/he/she/they work with (depending on subject) — 'trabajo' is first-person singular present of 'trabajar' + 'con' meaning 'with'.
additional_notes: Used to say who or what someone works with (people, companies, tools, materials). Change the verb form to match the subject: trabajo con (I work with), trabajas con (you), trabaja con (he/she/you formal), trabajamos con (we), trabajan con (they). Can also be used for collaborations or use of tools (e.g., 'trabajo con madera' = I work with wood).
target_language_example: Trabajo con un equipo internacional en proyectos de diseño.
native_language_example: I work with an international team on design projects.

meaning: part-time job (literal: 'job of half' or 'half job')
additional_notes: Used to refer to a part-time position. The more common full phrase is trabajo a tiempo parcial or trabajo de medio tiempo; trabajo de medio is a shortened, colloquial form in some regions. Use trabajo a tiempo parcial for formal contexts.
target_language_example: Busco un trabajo de medio mientras estudio.
native_language_example: I'm looking for a part-time job while I study.

meaning: the work of / the job of (masculine noun follows)
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but a combination: trabajo (work, job) + del (contraction of de + el, 'of the' or 'from the'). It's used before a masculine singular noun: trabajo del doctor, trabajo del grupo, trabajo del mes. Context determines whether it means 'the work of' (possession) or 'work from' (origin/source). If the noun is feminine, use trabajo de la.
target_language_example: Este es el trabajo del equipo.
native_language_example: This is the work of the team.

meaning: literally 'I work the' or 'work the...' — not a standalone phrase; likely a fragment where 'trabajo' (I work/job) is followed by the article 'el'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed multiword expression. It looks like part of a sentence such as 'trabajo el lunes' (I work on Monday) or 'trabajo el turno de noche' (I work the night shift). 'Trabajo' can be a noun (work/job) or the first-person present of 'trabajar' (I work). When followed by 'el' it usually introduces a specific noun (the + noun). Beginners should treat this as a fragment and look for the noun that follows 'el' to understand the full meaning.
target_language_example: Trabajo el turno de mañana.
native_language_example: I work the morning shift.

meaning: 'I work on' / 'I work at' (depending on context); describes working on a task or working at a place.
additional_notes: Used with first-person (trabajo en...) or other persons (trabaja en..., trabajamos en...) followed by a noun or clause. Use 'trabajo en' + project/task (trabajo en un informe, trabajo en mejorar mi español) to mean 'I am working on'. Use 'trabajo en' + place (trabajo en una tienda, trabajo en la oficina) to mean 'I work at/for'. If you want 'I work for (a company)', you can also say 'trabajo para [empresa]'.
target_language_example: Trabajo en un proyecto importante esta semana.
native_language_example: I'm working on an important project this week.

meaning: literally 'work in the' or 'work on the' — used at start of a phrase to say someone works at or on a specific place or project (followed by a noun).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but a common chunk: trabajo (I work / work) + en (in/at/on) + el (the, masculine). It must be followed by a masculine singular noun or a masculine singular place (e.g., trabajo en el hospital, trabajo en el proyecto). For other nouns/genders/use 'trabajo en la', 'trabajo en los', 'trabajo en las' or change verb/person (trabajas, trabaja, trabajamos...).
target_language_example: Trabajo en el hospital desde hace dos años.
native_language_example: I work at the hospital for two years.

meaning: teamwork; working together as a group.
additional_notes: Refers to coordinated effort by a group toward a common goal. Used in workplaces, sports, military, school projects, etc. Can describe the concept (el trabajo en equipo) or a specific collaborative task (un trabajo en equipo).
target_language_example: Para terminar el proyecto a tiempo necesitamos trabajo en equipo.
native_language_example: To finish the project on time we need teamwork.

meaning: a phrase meaning 'work/job at/in the' (used before a feminine noun or place).
additional_notes: Commonly used to say where someone works or where a task takes place. 'Trabajo' can mean a job (employment) or a piece of work/task; 'en la' is the preposition + feminine definite article that must agree with the following noun (e.g., 'la oficina', 'la planta', 'la capital'). If the following noun is masculine use 'trabajo en el'.
target_language_example: Ella tiene trabajo en la oficina del centro.
native_language_example: She has a job at the downtown office.

meaning: work/job in a (used in time or place expressions).
additional_notes: This chunk appears in two common uses: 1) trabajo en + time expression (e.g., 'trabajo en un día' = 'work in one day' meaning to finish something within that time), and 2) trabajo en un + place (e.g., 'trabajo en un restaurante' = 'I work in a restaurant'). The exact translation depends on context: for time it means 'in/within one...', for place it means 'at/in a...'.
target_language_example: No puedo terminar todo el trabajo en un día.
native_language_example: I can't finish all the work in one day.

meaning: this phrase by itself is not a fixed expression; it likely combines trabajo (work/job) with era (was) — 'work was' or 'the job was'.
additional_notes: Not a standalone set phrase in Spanish. You will most often see 'trabajo' (work/job) and 'era' (the imperfect of 'ser' — 'was') used together in a sentence, e.g. to describe past qualities of a job: 'Mi trabajo era aburrido' = 'My job was boring.' Treat this as two separate words rather than a fixed multiword term.
target_language_example: Mi trabajo era muy exigente el año pasado.
native_language_example: My job was very demanding last year.

meaning: ‘work is’ or ‘the job is’ — the noun trabajo (work/job) followed by the verb estar in third person singular, used to describe location, temporary states, or conditions of the work or workplace.
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom; a compositional phrase. Ensure the accent in está is present when writing the verb in standard Spanish (está). Use appropriate subject context if needed (e.g., El trabajo está...). Estar is used for locations, temporary conditions, or states. Verb must agree with the subject.
target_language_example: El trabajo está terminando esta semana y trabajo está más tranquilo ahora.
native_language_example: The job is finishing this week and work is calmer now.

meaning: the work/job is (in a certain state); 'the work is...'.
additional_notes: A simple subject–verb phrase: 'trabajo' (work/job) + 'está' (third-person singular of estar). Use with adjectives or past participles to describe the state or completion of a task (e.g., casi terminado = almost finished; hecho = done). 'Estar' emphasizes current state or condition. For completed actions you can also say 'el trabajo está hecho' or use 'el trabajo está terminado'.
target_language_example: El trabajo está casi terminado.
native_language_example: The work is almost finished.

meaning: Not a fixed Spanish phrase. It is simply the noun "trabajo" (work, job) followed by the auxiliary "ha" (has). This sequence is not grammatical on its own; "ha" typically precedes a past participle (e.g., "ha trabajado").
additional_notes: Treat as two separate words, not a set phrase. "Trabajo" can be a noun (el trabajo = the work/job) or the verb form "yo trabajo" (I work). "Ha" is the third-person singular present of haber used as an auxiliary to form compound tenses (e.g., "ha comido"). The string "trabajo ha" could appear across a sentence boundary or in fragments, but by itself it's ungrammatical. To express "has worked" use "ha trabajado"; to say "work has" (as in "work has changed") reorder and add a participle or clause (e.g., "el trabajo ha cambiado").
target_language_example: El trabajo ha cambiado mucho en los últimos años.
native_language_example: Work has changed a lot in recent years.

meaning: Not a fixed phrase by itself. Literally the words 'trabajo' (I work / work [noun]) and 'hace' (he/she/it does, or 'ago' as a time marker). Meaning depends on sentence order and grammar—possible interpretations include part of a clause where 'trabajo' is a noun followed by 'hace' as verb ('work does/makes' — rare), or more commonly appearances where the two words appear near each other across phrase boundaries (e.g., '... trabajo, hace ...' or in questions).
additional_notes: This word pair is not an idiom; its interpretation depends entirely on syntax and context. In standard Spanish, the sequence 'trabajo hace' is uncommon as a contiguous fixed phrase; when it appears it may be: 1) part of a larger clause with inversion or emphasis (e.g., 'Trabajo, hace mucho, en la tienda' — colloquial/informal punctuation needed), 2) across clause boundaries ('El trabajo hace que cambies' where 'trabajo' + 'hace' are separated by a relative structure), or 3) in reported speech or questions where word order changes ('¿Trabajo hace él?' — nonstandard). To understand it, identify whether 'hace' is the verb 'hacer' (does/makes) or the temporal 'hace' meaning 'ago'.
target_language_example: El trabajo hace que me canse más de lo normal.
native_language_example: Work makes me more tired than usual.

meaning: Not a standard standalone Spanish phrase; appears to be the noun trabajo ('work') followed by the clitic me ('me'/'to me'), which is ungrammatical without a verb or reordering.
additional_notes: This exact sequence 'trabajo me' does not form a correct phrase in standard Spanish. Clitic pronouns like 'me' attach to verbs (e.g., 'me trabaja', 'me da trabajo') or appear before conjugated verbs ('me trabaja'). If you encounter 'trabajo me' it may be a fragment produced when words are omitted or in colloquial/poetic inversion, but it's not a grammatical unit to learn. For learners: study 'trabajo' (work/job) and 'me' (first-person object/indirect pronoun) separately and learn common constructions such as 'me da trabajo' (it’s hard for me) or 'me trabaja' (it works for me / it bothers me).
target_language_example: Trabajó tanto que, cuando le pregunté si quería salir, solo respondió: "Trabajo, me..."
native_language_example: He worked so much that when I asked him if he wanted to go out, he just replied: "Work, me..."

meaning: literally 'I/you/he etc. work very' — it's not a fixed phrase on its own; 'trabajo' (I work / work (noun)) + 'muy' (very).
additional_notes: This is not a standalone expression in Spanish. It's simply the combination of the word trabajo (which can be the first-person singular of the verb trabajar: 'I work', or the noun 'work' / 'job') and the adverb muy ('very'). You will normally see them inside a larger sentence, for example: 'Trabajo muy tarde' (I work very late) or 'Tengo un trabajo muy interesante' (I have a very interesting job). Pay attention to word order: muy modifies adjectives or adverbs, not verbs directly (so use 'trabajo mucho' to say 'I work a lot').
target_language_example: Trabajo muy tarde entre semana.
native_language_example: I work very late during the week.

meaning: 'work' or 'job' + 'very' (used when describing a job or the quality of work).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase; it's the noun trabajo ('work, job, task') followed by the adverb muy ('very'). Use to intensify an adjective that describes work (e.g., trabajo muy bueno, trabajo muy aburrido). Make sure the adjective agrees where necessary (trabajo is masculine singular).
target_language_example: Ella hace un trabajo muy cuidadoso.
native_language_example: She does very careful work.

meaning: "no work" or the noun trabajo modified by negation no; not a fixed standalone phrase — usually appears within a larger sentence to negate or contrast 'trabajo'.
additional_notes: As written ('trabajo no') combines the noun trabajo ('work, job') with the negation/no particle no. It is not a complete common phrase by itself; native speakers typically use structures like 'no hay trabajo', 'sin trabajo', or 'trabajo no remunerado'. 'Trabajo no' can appear in clauses for emphasis or contrast (e.g., 'Trabajo no, descanso sí'). Word order and context determine the exact sense.
target_language_example: Trabajo no remunerado afecta a muchas mujeres.
native_language_example: Unpaid work affects many women.

meaning: "job" or "work" when followed by 'o' meaning 'or' (used in lists/choices).
additional_notes: This shows the noun trabajo used with the conjunction o (or). In Spanish you often see "trabajo o algo" (a job or something) or contrasting alternatives: "trabajo o hijos" (work or children). Also note 'trabajo' can mean 'a job' or 'work' (uncountable). The example "hacer el trabajo o no" uses the full phrase 'o no' (or not) to form a yes/no alternative.
target_language_example: ¿Buscas trabajo o prefieres estudiar?
native_language_example: Are you looking for a job or do you prefer to study?

meaning: 1) 'work due by' or 'work for (a deadline)'; 2) 'a job/task for (someone/organization)'; 3) 'a job for someone' (assigning work).
additional_notes: Depends on context: 'trabajo para + deadline' means a piece of work that must be finished by that time (due by). 'Trabajo para + alguien/entidad' can mean that the work is intended for or performed for someone (e.g., 'para la policía' = for the police) or that someone works for an employer (with 'trabaja para'). With a person as indirect object ('un trabajo para ti') it means a task assigned to that person.
target_language_example: Tengo un trabajo para mañana que debes terminar.
native_language_example: I have a job for tomorrow that you must finish.

meaning: 'work' + 'because' — literally 'work because'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase; it's the noun trabajo ('work' / 'job') followed by the conjunction porque ('because'). Use it when 'work' is the word in the sentence and 'because' introduces the reason. Word order in Spanish is the same as in English: trabajo porque + clause. Examples show meanings like 'at work', 'a job', or 'to be fired from work' depending on context.
target_language_example: Cambié de trabajo porque quería un horario mejor.
native_language_example: I changed jobs because I wanted a better schedule.

meaning: 'work that' or 'job that' (literal); often part of a larger phrase connecting 'trabajo' with a clause.
additional_notes: Alone, 'trabajo que' is not a complete phrase — it's usually followed by a verb or clause (e.g., 'trabajo que hace', 'trabajo que necesito'). It can introduce a relative clause describing the work: 'el trabajo que' = 'the work that / the job that'. In spoken Spanish you may also hear it in expressions like 'tengo trabajo que hacer' ('I have work to do').
target_language_example: Tengo trabajo que terminar antes del lunes.
native_language_example: I have work that I need to finish before Monday.

meaning: I work alone / I work by myself (or 'he/she/it works alone' depending on context).
additional_notes: Literal phrase from trabajar (to work) + solo (alone). Can be used as a short reply to say you work alone or that a task is done by one person. Depending on context, subject can be yo (trabajo solo/a), él/ella/esto (trabaja solo), or used as a descriptive phrase (trabajo solo significa que no hay equipo). Remember to match solo's gender: solo (masc) / sola (fem) when describing the speaker.
target_language_example: Normalmente trabajo solo en proyectos pequeños.
native_language_example: I usually work alone on small projects.

meaning: "work" (trabajo) followed by "and" (y) — simply the word 'trabajo' used in phrases joined with 'y'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed multiword idiom; it's the noun trabajo ('work, job, labor') appearing before the conjunction y ('and'). Learn 'trabajo' as a basic noun: meanings include job (employment), work (activity/tasks), and sometimes construction/site. 'Y' just connects items. Pay attention to context to know whether it means 'job', 'work' (uncountable), or 'piece of work.' Examples above show different uses: possession (mi trabajo), activity (salir del trabajo = leave work), and lists (trabajo y dinero).
target_language_example: Salió del trabajo y fue al supermercado.
native_language_example: He left work and went to the supermarket.

meaning: ‘translated the’ (past tense, 3rd person singular).
additional_notes: Tradujo is the preterite (simple past) of traducir for él/ella/usted. La is the feminine singular direct object pronoun or a feminine definite article depending on context; here it's most likely the pronoun 'her/it' (feminine). Together, 'tradujo la' commonly means 'he/she/you(formal) translated it/her' when referring to a feminine noun. If la is an article, you'd expect a noun after (e.g., 'tradujo la carta' = 'he translated the letter').
target_language_example: Ella tradujo la novela al español.
native_language_example: She translated the novel into Spanish.

meaning: bring (someone) a / bring a (something).
additional_notes: From the verb traer (to bring) in the imperative or present tense (él/ella/usted trae). In commands with tú, use trae (informal) or trae una + noun to ask someone to bring one of something. Can be used to request or say someone brings an item. Context determines whether it's a request (Bring a...) or a statement (he/she brings a...).
target_language_example: Trae una toalla para la playa.
native_language_example: Bring a towel for the beach.

meaning: to bring a (feminine singular object)
additional_notes: Composed of the verb traer (to bring) + the feminine singular indefinite article una. Use when referring to bringing one feminine noun (ej.: una silla, una taza, una linterna, una cosita, una paz). Verb form will change with subject and tense (e.g., 'voy a traer una', 'tráeme una'). Replace una with un for masculine nouns. Common in requests, statements, and descriptions.
target_language_example: No te voy a traer una taza de café; mejor tráeme una botella.
native_language_example: I'm not going to bring you a cup of coffee; better bring me a bottle.

meaning: 'suit of' / 'dress of' (used to describe what something is made of or what type it is)
additional_notes: Commonly used before a noun to describe a type, style, or material (e.g., traje de baño = swimsuit, traje de noche = evening gown, traje de neopreno = wetsuit). Literally 'suit of' or 'outfit of'. Often part of fixed compounds (traje de baño, traje de novia).
target_language_example: Compré un traje de baño nuevo para el verano.
native_language_example: I bought a new swimsuit for the summer.

meaning: I brought a / (he/she/you) brought a — past tense of traer + the indefinite article 'un'.
additional_notes: Traté 'traje' is the first person singular (yo traje) or third person preterite (él/ella/usted trajo is irregular but 'traje' is only yo) — actually 'traje' is the preterite form for 'yo' (I brought). In casual speech you may see word order: 'Te traje un regalo' = 'I brought you a gift' or 'Traje un libro' = 'I brought a book.' The phrase 'traje un' must be completed by a noun (masculine singular) like 'regalo', 'libro', or 'ayudante'. Use 'traje una' for feminine nouns.
target_language_example: Te traje un sándwich para el almuerzo.
native_language_example: I brought you a sandwich for lunch.

meaning: 'I brought a' (past tense, first person singular) or 'I brought one/a'.
additional_notes: Traté 'traje' is the preterite of 'traer' (to bring) for 'yo' (I). 'Una' is the feminine indefinite article meaning 'a' or 'one'. Use before feminine nouns (una visita, una muñeca, una cerveza, una cosita). If the noun is masculine, use 'traje un' (e.g., 'traje un regalo'). The phrase indicates you brought something to someone (often as a gift or offering).
target_language_example: Ayer traje una sorpresa para mi hermana.
native_language_example: Yesterday I brought a surprise for my sister.

meaning: 'suit/costume of' or 'the ... suit/costume of' — used to describe the type or owner of a suit/costume/clothing item.
additional_notes: Commonly used to say what kind of suit or costume someone is wearing (traje de pirata = pirate costume) or to indicate possession (el traje de tu padre = your father's suit). 'Traje' can mean formal suit, costume, or outfit depending on context. Use 'de' + noun (role, person, thing) to specify type or owner.
target_language_example: Ella tiene un traje de astronauta para la fiesta.
native_language_example: She has an astronaut costume for the party.

meaning: 'swimsuit' or 'bathing suit' (clothing worn for swimming).
additional_notes: Used for both men's and women's swimwear in Spanish. Context or adjectives clarify type (e.g., traje de baño de una pieza, bikini, bañador). Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Ella compró un nuevo traje de baño para las vacaciones.
native_language_example: She bought a new swimsuit for the vacation.

meaning: 'traje' = suit (clothing) or I/he/she brought/shot (depending on context); here 'traje es' by itself is incomplete — likely part of a sentence (e.g. 'el traje es...').
additional_notes:
This entry shows two separate items: 'traje' as a noun (a suit, conjunto formal de ropa) and 'traje' as the first- or third-person preterite form of the verb 'traer' (I/he/she brought). 'Es' is the present tense of 'ser' (is). Together, 'traje es' is not a complete standard phrase in Spanish; you will usually see 'el traje es...' (the suit is...) or 'traje' used in a clause like 'yo traje...' (I brought...). Make sure the article or subject is included. Example uses:
- El traje es caro. (The suit is expensive.) — noun + ser
- Yo traje el regalo. (I brought the gift.) — verb (pretérito) + object
target_language_example: El traje es elegante.
native_language_example: The suit is elegant.

meaning: 'brought to' or 'brought (someone/something) to (a place/state)'.
additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of traer + the preposition 'a' contracted with the article (al = a + el) or used before a place/phrase. Used for physical bringing (e.g., brought to a place) and figurative expressions (e.g., 'brought into the world' = born). Subject and object determine exact translation.
target_language_example: Él me trajo al restaurante anoche.
native_language_example: He brought me to the restaurant last night.

meaning: 'brought the' (past tense, third person singular of traer + definite article 'el')
additional_notes: Trajo is the preterite (simple past) form of traer (to bring) for él/ella/usted. 'Trajo el' begins a clause meaning someone brought a specific masculine noun (el + noun). You'll often see it followed by a noun: e.g., 'trajo el libro' = 'he/she brought the book.' Context determines the subject (he/she/you formal).
target_language_example: Ella trajo el postre a la fiesta.
native_language_example: She brought the dessert to the party.

meaning: to cheat on (someone) or to set a trap in/at (a place) — depends on context.
additional_notes: This phrase combines trampa (trap, cheating) with the preposition en. Alone, 'trampa' is a noun: 'hacer trampa' = to cheat. 'Trampa en' often appears before a location or situation (e.g., 'trampa en el examen' = cheating on the exam) or before a person/context when describing deception (less common: 'trampa en la relación' = cheating in the relationship). For beginner learners, it's safer to learn set expressions: 'hacer trampa en' (to cheat in/on) and 'poner una trampa en' (to set a trap in/at).
target_language_example: No debes hacer trampa en el examen.
native_language_example: You must not cheat on the exam.

meaning: a trap in the (something) / 'trap in the' (used as part of a phrase referring to a trap located in a specific place)
additional_notes: This is not a fixed standalone phrase but the beginning of a phrase: trampa en el + [lugar] (e.g., trampa en el jardín, trampa en el camino). Use it to say there is a trap located in a particular place. 'Trampa' means 'trap' or 'cheat', and 'en el' means 'in the/the (masculine singular)'. Adjust the article if the following noun is feminine (en la) or plural (en los/las).
target_language_example: Hay una trampa en el jardín junto a la puerta.
native_language_example: There is a trap in the garden next to the door.

meaning: calm/peaceful (while) in; describing someone or something being calm or living peacefully in a place or situation.
additional_notes: Tranquila is the feminine form of tranquilo. Used before or after a place or situation introduced by en (in). Commonly describes a person's state (e.g., 'está tranquila en los terremotos' = she stays calm during earthquakes) or a lifestyle ('vida tranquila en el campo' = peaceful life in the countryside). Adjust gender (tranquilo/a) and number (tranquilos/as) to match the noun.
target_language_example: Quiero estar tranquila en la playa durante las vacaciones.
native_language_example: I want to be calm on the beach during the vacation.

meaning: calm, comfortable, or fine with (being) in/at (a place or situation).
additional_notes: Used to say someone is relaxed, comfortable, or not worried about being in a particular situation or place. Often appears with a pronoun or name (e.g., 'estoy tranquilo en casa' — I'm relaxed at home) or with verbs that express feeling/sensing. Can also mean 'safe' or 'ok' in some contexts. 'Tranquilo' must agree in meaning, not form, so the phrase remains 'tranquilo en' regardless of gender when used in many colloquial statements; for feminine speaker use 'tranquila en'.
target_language_example: Estoy tranquilo en casa después del trabajo.
native_language_example: I'm relaxed at home after work.

meaning: to turn into; to become; to transform into.
additional_notes: Used with reflexive verb construction (se transforma en) or active (transforma en) to indicate that one thing changes into another (physical change, metaphorical change, or becoming). Common with natural processes (agua se transforma en gas) and figurative uses (la cara se transforma en la de Dios). Followed by the new state or thing introduced by 'en'.
target_language_example: La oruga se transforma en mariposa.
native_language_example: The caterpillar turns into a butterfly.

meaning: public transportation; buses, trains, metros, etc. used by the general public.
additional_notes: Refers to government-run or shared transport services (bus, metro, tram, train) used by many people. Commonly used when talking about commuting, city planning, accessibility, or convenience. Can be singular when speaking generally (el transporte público) or plural with specific modes (los transportes públicos) but the singular is far more common.
target_language_example: Vivo cerca del transporte público, así que no necesito coche.
native_language_example: I live near public transportation, so I don't need a car.

meaning: after a year; one year later (nonstandard/elliptical form)
additional_notes: This sequence is uncommon and sounds elliptical in Spanish; standard forms are 'tras un año', 'al cabo de un año' or 'un año después'. 'Tras' means 'after' and usually takes an explicit time expression (often with an article). In context, 'tras año' can be understood as 'after a year' but is more likely in poetry, headlines, or colloquial speech where words are omitted.
target_language_example: Tras año de esfuerzos, lograron abrir la empresa.
native_language_example: After a year of effort, they managed to open the company.

meaning: after a day; one day later
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something happens following a day (often in the sense of 'the next day' or 'after one day has passed'). Slightly formal or literary—more common spoken alternatives are 'al día siguiente' or 'al día siguiente' / 'un día después'. Often appears in narratives or written descriptions.
target_language_example: Tras día de espera, por fin llegó la carta.
native_language_example: After a day of waiting, the letter finally arrived.

meaning: after another; one after the other
additional_notes: Used to indicate sequence or succession: something happening following something else. Commonly appears as part of phrases like 'uno tras otro' (one after another) or 'vino tras otro' (one came after another). It's neutral register and literal in meaning.
target_language_example: Llegaron uno tras otro y ocupamos todas las mesas.
native_language_example: They arrived one after another and we took all the tables.

meaning: the back of / the rear of (something).
additional_notes: Used to refer to the rear side or back portion of an object, vehicle, animal, building, etc. 'Trasera' often appears with 'parte' as 'parte trasera' (the back part). Common preposition: 'de' to indicate what it belongs to (e.g., 'la parte trasera de la casa').
target_language_example: Pusieron la caja en la parte trasera del camión.
native_language_example: They put the box in the back of the truck.

meaning: the back/rear of (something).
additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun (del = de + el). 'Trasera' means the rear or back side of an object or vehicle. Common in descriptions (e.g., la parte trasera del coche = the back of the car).
target_language_example: La trasera del edificio tiene un jardín.
native_language_example: The back of the building has a garden.

meaning: 'treats (someone/something) as' or 'treat (someone/something) like'.
additional_notes: Second-person singular or third-person singular form of the verb phrase tratar + como. Use with a subject: (él/ella/usted) trata como or (yo/ellos) trato/ tratan como. Followed by a noun, pronoun, or clause that describes how someone/something is being treated (e.g., 'trata como un niño', 'me trata como si fuera tonto'). Common in both literal and figurative contexts.
target_language_example: Ella me trata como a un amigo.
native_language_example: She treats me like a friend.

meaning: 'treats (someone) like (someone/something)'.
additional_notes: Used with a person or group as direct object: trata a alguien como a + [noun/pronoun]. Often shortened in speech to 'trata como' when the personal 'a' is clear. Followed by a noun, pronoun, or clause that describes how the person is treated (e.g., 'trata como a un niño', 'trata como a si fuera un extraño'). The first 'a' is the Spanish personal 'a' marking a direct object when it's a person.
target_language_example: Ella trata como a un miembro de la familia a todos los voluntarios.
native_language_example: She treats all the volunteers like members of the family.

meaning: treats (someone) like a (something/someone).
additional_notes: Used to say someone treats another person as if they were a certain kind of person or thing. The phrase requires an object before it (e.g., 'me trata...') and a noun after 'un/una' (e.g., 'niño', 'idiota'). Often expresses criticism or complaint. Word order: [person] + trata + como + a + [article] + [noun].
target_language_example: Mi jefe me trata como a un aprendiz, aunque tengo experiencia.
native_language_example: My boss treats me like an apprentice, even though I have experience.

meaning: treats (someone/something) as if (they/it were ...).
additional_notes: Used to say that someone behaves toward a person or thing as though a hypothetical situation were true. Often followed by a clause introduced with 'fuera' or a past subjunctive (e.g., 'fuera', 'hubiera'). Can be used with different subjects: 'me trata como si fuera tonto' = 'he treats me as if I were stupid.'
target_language_example: Me trata como si no supiera nada.
native_language_example: He treats me as if I knew nothing.

meaning: 'tries/attempts to (deal with) me' or 'is about me' depending on context.
additional_notes: This phrase uses the verb 'tratar' plus the preposition 'de' or the indirect object pronoun 'me'—be careful: 'trata de mí' (with the preposition 'de' + mí) means 'is about me' (e.g., 'Ese libro trata de mí' = 'That book is about me'). Without 'de' and as 'me trata' it means 'treats me' (e.g., 'Me trata bien' = 'He/she treats me well'). The sequence 'trata de mi' (without written accent) is often seen in casual writing, but grammatically the prepositional pronoun should be 'mí' (accented) when used after 'de'. Context decides meaning; punctuation and accent matter.
target_language_example: Ese artículo trata de mí y de mi familia.
native_language_example: That article is about me and my family.

meaning: tries/attempts to ensure that; aims to make (something happen).
additional_notes: Commonly used with verbs in the subjunctive after 'que' (e.g., 'trata de que + subjunctive') to indicate effort or intention to achieve a result. Can also appear as 'trata de' + infinitive when meaning 'tries to (do something)'. Context determines whether it's about trying to do an action or trying to get someone/something to do/be something.
target_language_example: Trata de que lleguen a tiempo para la reunión.
native_language_example: He tries to make sure they arrive on time for the meeting.

meaning: Addresses someone using the informal 'tú' (treats you as 'tú').
additional_notes: Used when asking someone to use the informal second person (tú) instead of the formal usted, or to describe that one person addresses another informally. Often appears in commands or descriptions: 'Trátame de tú' (address me as tú) or 'Ella trata de tú a todos' (she addresses everyone with tú). Note spelling: written with accents when required (trátame, but the fixed phrase here shown without accent in 'trata de tu' per user request).
target_language_example: Si quieres que nos llevemos bien, trata de tu a los compañeros nuevos.
native_language_example: If you want us to get along, address the new colleagues with tú.

meaning: it's about / it's a matter of (referring to the topic or issue).
additional_notes: Used impersonally with 'se' (se trata de/ del) to introduce the topic or to say what something concerns. 'Se trata del' = 'it's about the' or 'it's a question of the'. Often contrasts what something is or isn't about. Followed by a noun or clause. 'Tratar de' without 'se' can mean 'to try to' or 'to deal with' in other contexts.
target_language_example: No se trata del precio, sino de la calidad.
native_language_example: It's not about the price, but about the quality.

meaning: he/she/it treats (it) / deals with (it) — third person singular of 'tratar' + direct object 'el'.
additional_notes: Trata is the third-person singular (or formal usted) present indicative of 'tratar'. When followed by 'el' it means 'treats the' or 'deals with the' (masculine singular noun which follows). Context decides whether 'tratar' means 'treat', 'deal with', 'try', 'talk about', or 'attempt'. Word order can change (e.g., 'lo trata' is more common than 'trata el' when the object is a pronoun).
target_language_example: El doctor trata el problema con mucho cuidado.
native_language_example: The doctor treats the problem very carefully.

meaning: try this; deal with/handle this (imperative, informal)
additional_notes: Commonly used as an informal command. 'Trata' is the tú imperative (from 'tratar') meaning 'try' or 'attempt' and can also mean 'deal with' depending on context. 'Trata esto' = 'try this' (e.g., a suggestion to taste, test, or attempt something) or 'handle this' (ask someone to take care of a task). For formal/respectful speech use 'trate esto' (usted) or 'pruebe esto' for 'try this' when offering something to taste.
target_language_example: Trata esto, creo que te va a gustar.
native_language_example: Try this, I think you'll like it.

meaning: (he/she/it) treats/deals with everything or 'treats all' (third-person singular of tratar + todo).
additional_notes: Literally combines the verb tratar (to treat, to try, to deal with) with todo (everything/all). Without context it can mean 'he/she treats everything', 'it deals with everything' or 'try everything' if used as imperative 'trata todo' (informal tú command). Note verb form and meaning change with context: as a statement 'trata todo' = 'he/she treats everything' (present tense, third person). As an informal command to tú it would be 'trata todo' = 'try everything' or 'deal with everything'. To say 'I treat everything' you'd use 'trato todo'.
target_language_example: Ella trata todo con paciencia.
native_language_example: She treats everything with patience.

meaning: 'tried to' (past participle + 'to' — indicates an attempt to do something).
additional_notes: From the verb tratar (to try/attempt). Commonly appears as 'he tratado de...', 'has tratado de...', 'traté de...' to say 'I have tried to...' or 'I tried to...'. Use 'de' + infinitive verb. Often followed by actions (hablar, venir, sacar, traducir, ascender).
target_language_example: He tratado de aprender español todos los días.
native_language_example: I have tried to learn Spanish every day.

meaning: to deal with, to handle (someone or something).
additional_notes: Used when talking about handling a person, problem, situation, or task. Can mean 'to cope with' or 'to deal with' depending on context. Commonly followed by a noun or pronoun (tratar con alguien / tratar con esto).
target_language_example: Tengo que tratar con ese problema mañana.
native_language_example: I have to deal with that problem tomorrow.

meaning: to try to
additional_notes: Used before an infinitive to say someone makes an effort to do something: tratar de + infinitive. Don't confuse it with other uses of tratar, which can mean things like 'to deal with' or 'to be about.'
target_language_example: Voy a tratar de llegar temprano.
native_language_example: I'm going to try to arrive early.

meaning: 'deal done' or 'it's a deal' — used to confirm an agreement.
additional_notes: Common phrase to accept or confirm a proposal; equivalent to 'agreed' or 'deal' in English. Used in spoken and informal/formal contexts. Can stand alone as a reply.
target_language_example: Si me ayudas con la mudanza, yo pago la cena. — Trato hecho.
native_language_example: If you help me with the move, I'll pay for dinner. — It's a deal.

meaning: 'he/she/it tried (to)'; or 'he/she/it dealt with' depending on context.
additional_notes: Trató is the past (pretérito) form of tratar (to try, to treat, to deal with). 'Trató en' often appears before an infinitive (trató de + infinitive is more common for 'tried to') or before a noun/phrase introduced by 'en' meaning 'dealt with' or 'addressed in'. Without more context, 'trató en' could be part of: 'trató de' (tried to do), 'trató en su libro' (he dealt with in his book), or 'se trató en la reunión' (was discussed in the meeting). Subject is third person singular (él/ella/usted).
target_language_example: En su libro trató en detalle el problema de la contaminación.
native_language_example: In his book he dealt with the pollution problem in detail.

meaning: 'through', 'by means of', or 'via'.
additional_notes: Used to indicate movement through a physical space or the means/medium by which something is done (e.g., communication, method, channel). Often appears before nouns. Can be written 'a través de' (with spaces); sometimes informally seen as 'a través' but standard is 'a través de'.
target_language_example: Envié el documento a través de correo electrónico.
native_language_example: I sent the document via email.

meaning: through the / by means of the (feminine plural).
additional_notes: A prepositional phrase used before a feminine plural noun to indicate movement, passage, means, or method. Equivalent to 'through the' or 'by means of the'. It often appears in contexts like 'through the streets' (a través de las calles) or 'by means of the tests' (a través de las pruebas). Note the full phrase commonly includes the preposition 'a' as 'a través de las'.
target_language_example: Caminamos a través de las calles antiguas.
native_language_example: We walked through the old streets.

meaning: through a / by means of a
additional_notes: Used to indicate movement, action or means via something/someone. Commonly appears as 'a través de' (through/by means of) followed by a noun; the article 'un' makes it 'through a' or 'by a'. Can describe physical passage (through a tunnel), communication (through a message), or method (via a tool).
target_language_example: Recibí la información a través de un amigo.
native_language_example: I received the information through a friend.

meaning: 'brought something' (I/you/he has brought something to someone).
additional_notes: Past participle form of traer (traído) used with a personal pronoun and auxiliary verb (usually 'he', 'has', 'hemos', 'os he', etc.). Commonly appears in sentences like 'Te he traído algo' = 'I brought you something' or 'I've brought something for you.' The phrase is usually followed by what was brought (e.g., comida, hielo, para leer) or left vague as 'algo' (something).
target_language_example: Te he traído algo de comer porque sé que tienes hambre.
native_language_example: I've brought you something to eat because I know you're hungry.

meaning: brought/dragged (someone or something) up to/until a point or place
additional_notes: Compound of traer (to bring) in participle form (traído) + hasta (up to/until). Used to indicate that someone or something has been brought to a specific location, situation, time, or limit. Context determines whether literal (physically brought) or figurative (brought to a state/point). Often appears in passive or perfect constructions: 'ha sido traído hasta...' or 'lo trajeron hasta...'.
target_language_example: Lo trajeron y lo dejaron traído hasta la puerta.
native_language_example: They brought him and left him at the door.

meaning: I/you/he/she have/has brought a (feminine singular item).
additional_notes: Combination of the past participle 'traído' (brought) with the indefinite article 'una'. Common in sentences like 'Te he traído una X' meaning 'I've brought you a X'. Subject is expressed by the verb conjugation (he, has, ha, hemos, han). The noun following 'una' must be feminine (una foto, una taza, una sorpresa).
target_language_example: Te he traído una chaqueta nueva.
native_language_example: I've brought you a new jacket.

meaning: 'thirty and' — used to form numbers from 31 to 39 (e.g., treinta y uno = 31).
additional_notes: In Spanish number formation, 'treinta y' combines with units (uno, dos, tres, etc.) to make numbers 31–39. When speaking, 'y' (and) is pronounced; in writing there is a space before and after 'y'. For 30 alone, say 'treinta' (no 'y').
target_language_example: treinta y cinco
native_language_example: thirty-five

meaning: thirty-five (35).
additional_notes: A cardinal number used for counting, ages, quantities, etc. Spanish numbers from 31 to 99 are often formed with 'treinta y [número]' (thirty and [number]). Pronunciation: 'TREIN-ta ee SIN-ko'.
target_language_example: Tengo treinta y cinco libros en la estantería.
native_language_example: I have thirty-five books on the shelf.

meaning: 'thirty-two' (the number 32).
additional_notes: Used to state the number 32 in age, quantity, distance, etc. Spanish numbers are formed by joining tens and units with 'y' (e.g., treinta y dos). Pronunciation: ['trein-ta ee dos']. Can appear alone as an answer or as part of a sentence.
target_language_example: Tengo treinta y dos años.
native_language_example: I am thirty-two years old.

meaning: thirty-six (36).
additional_notes: A cardinal number used for counting, ages, distances, years, multiplication results, etc. Spanish numbers use 'y' between tens and units for 21–99 (except round tens). Pronunciation: treinta (TREIN-ta) y seis (SEIS).
target_language_example: Tengo treinta y seis libros en la estantería.
native_language_example: I have thirty-six books on the shelf.

meaning: 'train to' — used to indicate a train going to a specific destination (e.g., tren a Madrid = train to Madrid).
additional_notes: Followed by a place name. Commonly appears on timetables, tickets, announcements and when asking for directions or schedules. In speech you might also hear 'el tren a...' or 'un tren a...'.
target_language_example: Voy a tomar el tren a Barcelona.
native_language_example: I'm going to take the train to Barcelona.

meaning: literally 'train of' — used to describe a type or purpose of train, or as the start of expressions like 'tren de alta velocidad' (high-speed train) or 'tren de carga' (freight train).
additional_notes: This is a compositional phrase: tren = train, de = of/from. It usually appears before a noun or adjective that specifies the train's function, type, route, or characteristic. Not a fixed idiom by itself — you need the following noun (e.g., tren de pasajeros, tren de cercanías).
target_language_example: Vamos a tomar el tren de cercanías esta mañana.
native_language_example: We're going to take the commuter train this morning.

meaning: the train of the (e.g., 'the morning train', 'the afternoon train').
additional_notes: Used to specify a particular train by time or part of day (e.g., 'tren de la mañana' = morning train, 'tren de la tarde' = afternoon train). You must add the time-of-day noun after 'la' (mañana, tarde, noche). If the noun is masculine (e.g., 'tren de la noche' is less common), adjust article if needed: 'tren de la mañana' is standard. Commonly followed by 'primero' (first) or 'segundo' (second) to indicate sequence: 'el primer tren de la mañana'.
target_language_example: Tomaré el tren de la tarde para llegar después del trabajo.
native_language_example: I'll take the afternoon train to arrive after work.

meaning: 'train on' or 'train in' (depends on context) — a sequence of the noun 'tren' and the preposition 'en' used in Spanish phrases to indicate being on/by a train or as part of other constructions.
additional_notes: By itself 'tren en' is not a complete phrase and will usually be followed by a location, destination, or complement (e.g., 'tren en marcha', 'tren en servicio', or 'ir en tren' where the natural word order is 'en tren'). In many cases Spanish uses 'en tren' (preposition then noun) rather than 'tren en', so occurrences of 'tren en' are often part of larger constructs or inverted in fixed expressions. Do not confuse with the verb 'entrenar' (to train).
target_language_example: El tren en servicio llegará a las 10:00.
native_language_example: The train in service will arrive at 10:00.

meaning: the train is (somewhere or in some state).
additional_notes: Combination of the noun tren (train) and the verb estar (to be). Used to describe location, condition, or status of a train: donde está el tren? / el tren está retrasado. Subject–verb order is typical: el tren está + adjective or prepositional phrase.
target_language_example: El tren está en la estación.
native_language_example: The train is at the station.

meaning: 'train no' taken literally as the noun tren followed by negation no; can occur in fragments to negate that something is a train
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom. Appears as a fragment or elliptical response (noun + no) in spoken or colloquial contexts, though full negative sentences usually place no before the verb (e.g., 'No es un tren.'). Using 'tren no' as a standalone fragment is informal and context-dependent — often part of a longer utterance or reply ('Tren, no, es otra cosa').
target_language_example: — ¿Qué es eso en la vía? — Tren, no, es un tranvía.
native_language_example: — What is that on the track? — Train, no, it's a tram.

meaning: A sequence of the noun 'tren' followed by the preposition 'por' used when indicating means, route, agency, or passage relating to a train. It is not a fixed idiom by itself; its meaning depends on the larger phrase (e.g., 'mandado por tren' = sent by train; 'el tren por la costa' = the train along/through the coast).
additional_notes: Not a standard standalone phrase. Spanish speakers more commonly say 'en tren' for 'by train' when indicating means of travel. Use 'por' after 'tren' when the sentence structure requires the preposition (agency, route, cause, or movement through a place). Pay attention to articles and word order: often you'll see 'por tren' rather than 'tren por' unless the phrase is part of a clause ('el tren por la costa'). For clarity, beginners should prefer 'en tren' for 'by train.'
target_language_example: Vieron el tren por la costa mientras conducían.
native_language_example: They saw the train along the coast while they were driving.

meaning: the train (as subject) + pronominal marker 'se' used with verbs (e.g., se retrasó = the train was delayed / delayed itself).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but the noun 'tren' followed by the reflexive/pronominal clitic 'se' attached to a verb (tren se retrasó, tren se fue, tren se descarriló). In Spanish many verbs use 'se' to form intransitive or passive-like constructions: it often indicates that the action happens to or by the subject (the train) rather than being done by someone. Translate depending on the verb: se retrasó = was delayed, se fue = left, se descarriló = derailed.
target_language_example: El tren se detuvo en la estación durante veinte minutos.
native_language_example: The train stopped at the station for twenty minutes.

meaning: "train and" (literal conjunction: 'train' + 'and').
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase—it's simply the noun tren (train) followed by the conjunction y (and). You will see this when listing items or combining 'train' with something else (e.g., 'tren y autobús' = 'train and bus'). Use y before words that do not start with the sound 'i'; before words that start with 'i' or 'hi' (sounding like 'i') Spanish often uses e (tren e internet).
target_language_example: Tomamos el tren y el autobús para llegar a la montaña.
native_language_example: We took the train and the bus to get to the mountain.

meaning: 'the train already (left) / already gone' — used to say the train has already departed.
additional_notes: Ya is an adverb meaning 'already' (or 'yet' in negatives/questions). With 'tren' it indicates the train has departed. Use with compound past (haber + salido/ido) or simple past: 'el tren ya se ha ido', 'el tren ya salió'. In affirmative commands or suggestions, 'ya' can mean 'now' or 'right away' (e.g., 'subir al tren ya' = 'get on the train now').
target_language_example: Cuando llegamos, el tren ya se había ido.
native_language_example: When we arrived, the train had already gone.

meaning: Not a fixed phrase; likely a fragment meaning 'the train already' or 'train already (does/has)...'.
additional_notes: This looks like a sequence of three words rather than an established idiom. 'tren' = train; 'ya' = already/now; 'se' = reflexive pronoun or passive/impersonal marker. Depending on context it could start sentences like 'El tren ya se fue' (The train already left) or appear in impersonal/passive constructions 'El tren ya se vende' (The train is already sold) — though that exact wording would be uncommon. Beginners should treat 'ya' as 'already/now' and 'se' as a grammatical particle whose meaning depends on the verb that follows.
target_language_example: El tren ya se fue hace cinco minutos.
native_language_example: The train already left five minutes ago.

meaning: the numbers three, four, five (used when counting).
additional_notes: These are ordinal elements of the basic Spanish number sequence. Used in counting, giving combinations, phone numbers, steps, etc. Pronunciation: tres (tres), cuatro (KWA-tro), cinco (SEEN-ko). They are literal numerals and are used just like 'three, four, five' in English.
target_language_example: Cuenta conmigo: uno, dos, tres, cuatro, cinco.
native_language_example: Count with me: one, two, three, four, five.

meaning: three friends (masculine or mixed group).
additional_notes: Literal phrase: 'tres' = three, 'amigos' = friends. Use for three male friends or a mixed-gender group. For three female friends, use 'tres amigas'. In Spanish, adjectives and nouns must agree in gender and number.
target_language_example: Fuimos al cine los tres amigos.
native_language_example: The three friends went to the movies.

meaning: three years older (than someone).
additional_notes: Used after a noun or pronoun with 'que' to compare ages: X es tres años mayor que Y = X is three years older than Y. You can change the number (dos, cuatro, etc.). For feminine subjects use same form 'mayor' (unchanged). If comparing yourself, common pattern: 'Él/ella es tres años mayor que yo.'
target_language_example: Mi hermana es tres años mayor que yo.
native_language_example: My sister is three years older than me.

meaning: three years older/older by three years than
additional_notes: Used to compare ages or ages of things (e.g., cars). Place after the number and unit (años) and before the person or thing being compared. Often implies 'is older by three years' when referring to people or objects.
target_language_example: Mi hermano tiene tres años más que yo.
native_language_example: My brother is three years older than me.

meaning: literally 'three things' — used to refer to three specific items, points, or matters.
